Recording technology bifurcates the era: 1920-1925 used acoustic-horn pre-electrical recording (singer projecting into a horn directly coupled to the cutting stylus, no microphone, modest dynamic range, treble-loss bias), 1925-1929 used Western-Electric microphone-and-amplifier electrical recording (full bandwidth, fuller bass, dynamic range). Session pianists span Fletcher Henderson, Clarence Williams, James P. Johnson, Porter Grainger, Fats Waller, and Perry Bradford; session horn players include Louis Armstrong, Joe Smith, Buster Bailey, Coleman Hawkins, Don Redman, and Charlie Green. Label distribution: Columbia (Bessie Smith, Clara Smith, Ethel Waters), OKeh (Mamie Smith, Sippie Wallace), Paramount (Ma Rainey, Ida Cox, Alberta Hunter, Trixie Smith), Black Swan (Ethel Waters early sides, the early Black-owned label). Distinguished from contemporaneous hokum blues by the despairing-and-melismatic emotional register over hokum's comedy-and-double-entendre register and by piano-led-jazz-combo instrumentation over hokum's jug-band-and-country instrumentation; distinguished from Delta blues by urban-and-theatrical-performance-context over rural-solo-acoustic-guitar context; distinguished from later swing-era female jazz vocal (Holiday, Fitzgerald, Vaughan) by deeper-blues-tonal-language and pre-microphone or early-microphone-era apparatus that shaped the projecting vocal practice. Lineage forward feeds Billie Holiday's acknowledged debt to Bessie Smith, Mahalia Jackson's gospel adaptation of the vocal style, and the eventual passage into mid-century jazz vocal, R&B, and soul.

items.name: Talking blues
items.lineage: Spoken-rhythmic-narrative blues form codified by Chris Bouchillon in 1926 (his Talking Blues 78 being the founding commercial recording) and extended through the Dust Bowl Ballads era by Woody Guthrie (his 1940 RCA Victor Dust Bowl Ballads sessions the founding documents), then carried forward through the post-WWII folk revival via Pete Seeger, Phil Ochs, and the early Bob Dylan (Talkin New York 1962, Talkin John Birch Paranoid Blues 1962 — the Dylan talking-blues period)
items.description: Talking blues / Dust Bowl talking-tradition (codified 1920s-1930s through Robert Lunn and Chris Bouchillon's pioneering talking-blues recordings, with Woody Guthrie's 1930s-1940s Dust Bowl talking-narrative tradition extending the form into political-protest songwriting), the spoken-rhythmic-narrative form descended from country-blues talking. Defined by spoken-rhythmic-narrative vocal delivery over basic acoustic-guitar accompaniment (rather than sung-melodic delivery), conversational rhythm-and-rhyme verse structure with tag-lines closing each verse, repertoire of social-commentary, political-protest, and humorous-narrative subjects (Guthrie's Dust Bowl Ballads as the example of the political-protest extension), AAB or AABA rhyme-and-cadence structures, and folk-revival and country-music both adopting the form as compositional template. Distinguished from straight blues by spoken-not-sung delivery; distinguished from later country talking-songs (Hank Williams's I Saw the Light tradition) by political-and-Dust-Bowl-specific extension; distinguished from rap by acoustic-folk-and-country lineage rather than hip-hop-tradition.

items.name: Chanson classique
items.lineage: Mid-twentieth-century French chanson canon centered on the Left Bank Paris cabaret scene — codified through Édith Piaf, Charles Trenet, Yves Montand, Jacques Brel (Belgian-Flemish but Paris-resident), Georges Brassens, and Léo Ferré; characterized by literary-poetic lyrical register, music-hall accompaniment, and the chanteuse / chansonnier solo performer tradition
items.description: Chanson classique / mid-century French chanson (codified 1930s-1960s Paris cabaret and music-hall, with the Rive Gauche cabaret circuit of the postwar through 1960s as crystallizing era), the literary-text-foreground French chanson canon. Defined by literary-text-as-foundation aesthetic where lyric and melodic phrasing follow French-language prosody (no syllabic compromises for rhythmic regularization), accompaniment built on accordion, piano, or small string-and-clarinet ensemble providing harmonic support without taking foreground, vocal delivery prioritizing intelligibility and emotional inflection over operatic projection or pop-melisma, repertoire spanning composer-and-lyricist team songs and singer-songwriter material, and performance context of intimate cabaret theatre seating 100-300 attentive listeners. Distinguished from later chanson pop modern by acoustic-instrumentation and pre-electric-pop era; distinguished from operetta and musical-theatre by literary-not-theatrical-narrative orientation; distinguished from American singer-songwriter by chanson's stronger commitment to literary text-as-primary.

items.name: Fado de Coimbra
items.lineage: Academic male-student fado tradition centered on the University of Coimbra (Portugals oldest university, founded in the 13th century) — distinct from fado de Lisboa in vocal register (male tenor/baritone), repertoire (poetry-set songs, student songs, serenata), and performance context (outdoor stone-paved quadrangle and Sé Velha cathedral steps rather than intimate tavern); performers wear the traditional black student capa-e-batina cape
items.description: Fado de Coimbra (codified 19th century onward in Coimbra Portugal university-student community, with the Coimbra Academic Tradition's continuous transmission through to present), the Coimbra-university male-student fado tradition. Defined by Portuguese-guitar-and-classical-guitar duo accompaniment (the same instrumental palette as Lisbon fado but with Coimbra-specific tuning and stylistic conventions), male-student vocal performance (the Coimbra fado tradition is exclusively male-vocal, distinguishing from Lisbon's predominantly-female lead), university-student lyric content addressing academic life, Coimbra-city geographic-and-architectural features, romantic-melancholy, and Coimbra-specific cultural references, performance contexts of student-serenade in university courtyards and Coimbra night-time-streets and academic-festival celebrations, and traditional black-academic-cape costume during performance. Distinguished from Lisbon fado by male-student vocal exclusivity and university-student context; distinguished from broader Portuguese folk by university-academic specificity; distinguished from Brazilian or Cape Verdean fado-derivative genres by Portuguese-mainland and Coimbra-academic centrality.

items.name: Greek éntechno
items.lineage: Greek literary art-song composer tradition emerging in the late 1950s, codified by Mikis Theodorakis (Epitaphios song-cycle setting Yannis Ritsos poetry 1960, Zorba the Greek 1964 Oscar-winning film score), Manos Hadjidakis (Never on Sunday 1960 Oscar-winning score, Reflections song-cycle), Stavros Xarchakos, Nikos Mamangakis — setting modern Greek poetry (Ritsos, Elytis, Seferis, Kavafis) to compositions that fuse Greek traditional modal vocabulary with Western classical orchestration
items.description: Greek éntechno (codified 1960 onward through Mikis Theodorakis and Manos Hadjidakis establishing the éntechno ("art") song tradition during late-Junta-era cultural ferment), the Greek art-song composer tradition. Defined by composer-driven settings of modern-Greek-poetry by Greek poets (Yannis Ritsos, Giorgos Seferis, Odysseas Elytis, Nikos Gatsos) to original melodic material, Greek-folk-derived modal-and-melodic vocabulary drawing on rebetiko and Eastern-Mediterranean modal traditions, instrumentation centered on bouzouki and laouto with guitar-and-piano-and-orchestra arrangement options, vocal delivery prioritizing literary-text-clarity over operatic projection, and performance contexts spanning concert hall, recording studio, and laiko (popular) theatrical venues. Distinguished from rebetiko by composer-not-folk-anonymous origin and literary-poetry-not-marginal-urban-text content; distinguished from later laiko by intellectual-and-literary register; distinguished from Greek folk by composed-not-traditional repertoire.

items.name: NWOBHM (New Wave of British Heavy Metal)
items.lineage: Late-1970s through mid-1980s UK metal revival movement that emerged in response to the punk-and-disco displacement of mid-1970s hard rock — codified through Iron Maiden (the NWOBHM founding band, Iron Maiden 1980, The Number of the Beast 1982, Powerslave 1984), Judas Priest (the older band that became NWOBHM-adjacent through British Steel 1980 and Screaming for Vengeance 1982), Saxon, Diamond Head (whose Lightning to the Nations 1980 directly influenced Metallica), Def Leppard (early album On Through the Night 1980 before their pop-metal commercial turn), Motörhead
items.description: New Wave of British Heavy Metal (codified 1979-1983 across UK metal-revival scene through Iron Maiden, Saxon, Diamond Head, Def Leppard, Angel Witch, and dozens of regional bands releasing on independent labels), the late-1970s into early-80s UK metal revival. Defined by twin-guitar harmony lead-lines (two electric guitars playing harmonized melodic lines in parallel-thirds or sixths — the NWOBHM-signature lead-guitar configuration), galloping-rhythm rhythm-guitar foundation (the syncopated triplet eighth-note rhythmic pattern that became NWOBHM's identifying riff feel), high-tenor lead vocal often with operatic-projection ambition, fantasy-and-historical-and-occult lyric content (dragon, knight, witch, war themes), DIY-fanzine-and-independent-label distribution, and strong influence on later thrash metal and power metal subgenres. Distinguished from earlier hard rock by twin-guitar-harmony-foreground and post-1979 timestamp; distinguished from later thrash metal by retention of melodic-lead-guitar over palm-muted-aggression; distinguished from American metal counterparts by UK-specific late-70s economic-and-cultural context.

items.name: Progressive metal
items.lineage: Metal-prog-rock hybrid subgenre codified through Queensrÿche (Operation: Mindcrime 1988), Fates Warning (Awaken the Guardian 1986), Dream Theater (Images and Words 1992), Symphony X, and Watchtower; characterized by operatic-clean-vocal performances, virtuosic-twin-guitar lead lines, complex multi-meter compositions, and the conceptual-album / fantasy-narrative lyrical subject-matter tradition
items.description: Progressive metal (codified 1986 onward through Queensrÿche's Operation: Mindcrime and Dream Theater's Images and Words establishing the sound, with continuous tradition through to present), the metal sub-style importing prog-rock compositional ambition. Defined by odd-meter passages (5/8, 7/8, 11/8, 13/8, and other unusual time signatures with frequent metric-modulation), virtuoso instrumental performance from each ensemble member with extended solo passages and arranged unison-passages requiring high-skill execution, long-form song structures (regularly extending past 8-15 minutes with multiple distinct sections), concept-album structural ambition with album-length narrative or thematic threads, and full retention of metal-genre instrumentation (downtuned guitars, double-kick drumming, distorted guitar-tone, but often clean-singing rather than growled vocal). Distinguished from straight metal by prog-rock structural ambition and odd-meter foreground; distinguished from straight prog-rock by metal-derived guitar-tone and rhythm-section weight; distinguished from later djent by classic-prog-rock heritage rather than 8-string-and-polymetric-djent specialty.

items.name: Power metal (European)
items.lineage: European-rooted melodic metal subgenre codified through Helloween (Keeper of the Seven Keys 1987-88), Blind Guardian, Stratovarius, Sonata Arctica, Rhapsody (Italian symphonic-power) — characterized by major-key triumphant choruses, twin-guitar harmony lead lines, high-register clean vocals, and fantasy/Tolkien-derived lyrical subject matter
items.description: Power metal European (codified 1985 onward through Helloween's Walls of Jericho and Keeper of the Seven Keys establishing the Eurometal sound, with second-wave Italian and Finnish bands extending the tradition), the European-rooted metal sub-style emphasizing major-key melodic-anthem songwriting. Defined by major-key melodic-anthem songwriting (a deliberate departure from death-and-black-metal's minor-key gloom, embracing uplift-and-triumph melodic vocabulary), high-tenor lead vocal performance often with operatic-projection ambition, twin-guitar harmonized lead-lines drawing on NWOBHM melodic-harmony tradition, dual-bass-drum rapid-pedaling, lyric content addressing fantasy-medieval-and-mythological subjects (dragons, knights, magic, battle), and tempos around 140-180 BPM with characteristic gallop-and-march rhythmic foundation. Distinguished from American-style power metal (a slower-and-bluesier parallel) by European-Eurometal lineage and faster-anthem aesthetic; distinguished from speed metal by retention of song-form melody-foreground over tempo-foreground; distinguished from symphonic metal by guitar-not-orchestral primary foundation.

items.name: Symphonic metal
items.lineage: Metal-orchestral-choral hybrid subgenre codified through Nightwish (Oceanborn 1998), Within Temptation (Mother Earth 2000), Epica (The Phantom Agony 2003), Therion, and Edenbridge; characterized by operatic-soprano-led-vocal performances, full-orchestral arrangements (often with film-score session ensembles), choral-backing-vocal stacks, and fantasy-and-mythology lyrical subject-matter tradition
items.description: Symphonic metal (codified 1996 onward through Therion's Theli, Nightwish's Angels Fall First, and the broader European symphonic-metal scene establishing the sound), the metal sub-style integrating orchestral and choral arrangements with metal back-line. Defined by full-orchestral arrangements (string section, brass section, woodwind section, timpani, optional choir) layered with metal-band core (electric guitars, bass, drum-kit), female-soprano lead vocal performance often with operatic-projection ambition (the symphonic-metal-operatic-vocal aesthetic), occasionally male-growl supplementary vocal as contrast, lyric content addressing fantasy-medieval-and-mythological subjects, and tempos around 120-180 BPM with metal-genre rhythmic foundation. Production aesthetic combines orchestral-recording (often pre-recorded orchestral-stems integrated with live-band tracking) with metal-band live performance. Distinguished from power metal by orchestral-foreground over twin-guitar-harmony foreground; distinguished from gothic metal by retention of operatic-vocal aesthetic; distinguished from straight orchestral metal by retention of song-form structure.

items.name: Folk metal (European)
items.lineage: European metal-folk-instrument hybrid subgenre codified through Skyclad (UK 1990, the first folk-metal album The Wayward Sons of Mother Earth), Korpiklaani (Finnish), Eluveitie (Swiss-Celtic), Ensiferum (Finnish-Viking) — characterized by fiddle, accordion, hurdy-gurdy, and bagpipe alongside metal instrumentation, with regional-folk melodic vocabularies
items.description: Folk metal European (1990s onward, codified through Skyclad's debut, then second-wave Finnish, Scandinavian, Celtic, and Eastern-European bands), the metal subgenre integrating regional folk-instrument and folk-melodic-modal vocabulary into a metal back-line. Defined by traditional folk instruments (fiddle, hurdy-gurdy, accordion, bagpipes, tin whistle, jaw harp, recorder, bouzouki, nyckelharpa) playing alongside or in dialogue with electric guitar-bass-drums metal core, folk-modal melodic vocabulary (Aeolian, Dorian, Phrygian, regional pentatonic) replacing standard heavy-metal blues-pentatonic, lyric and visual themes drawing on Norse mythology, Celtic legend, regional folk-tale traditions, and historical-medieval imagery, and tempos varying from mid-tempo battle-metal to up-tempo folk-dance pace. Distinguished from regional folk by metal instrumentation and aggression; distinguished from symphonic metal by folk-instrument-foreground rather than orchestral foreground; distinguished from black metal by clean-singing prominence and absence of corpse-paint blast-beat orthodoxy.

items.name: Avant-garde metal
items.lineage: Experimental-leaning metal subgenre codified through Voivod (Canadian dissonant prog-metal), Sigh (Japanese avant-black-metal), Mr. Bungle, Diabolic Masquerade, and the broader Tzadik / Hydra Head label ecosystem — characterized by atonal harmony, irregular meter, genre-collage composition, and prog-metal sectional architecture
items.description: Avant-garde metal (1991 onward, with seeds in late-80s prog and 90s industrial-metal experimentation), the experimental-leaning metal sub-style that imports avant-garde art-music vocabulary, free-improvisation, and progressive-rock structural complexity into a metal sonic frame. Defined by non-standard song structures (suite-form, through-composed pieces, sectional juxtaposition), unusual time signatures and metric modulation, extended guitar techniques (prepared guitar, microtonal bending, drone tunings), incorporation of acoustic and chamber-music instruments alongside the metal core, and a willingness to abandon metal genre signifiers mid-piece. Distinguished from progressive metal by greater willingness to break out of metal genre entirely; distinguished from mathcore by less hardcore-punk lineage and more art-music orientation; distinguished from post-metal by greater riff-foreground retention.

items.name: Deep house (soulful)
items.lineage: Soulful-jazz house sub-style codified through 1990s New York and New Jersey production — Kerri Chandler, Masters at Work, Blaze, and Kenny Bobien (vocalist), extending the 1980s Chicago deep-house template of Larry Heard / Mr. Fingers — characterized by jazz-chord harmonic vocabulary, gospel-soul vocal performances, and warm analog-instrument production aesthetic
items.description: Soulful deep house (1992 onward, originating in New York and New Jersey through Larry Levan's Paradise Garage lineage and codified through Kerri Chandler, Masters at Work, and the Naked Music label), the soulful-jazz-derived house subgenre. Defined by lush extended-chord harmonic vocabulary (major-7th, minor-9th, and altered-dominant chord changes drawn from soul-jazz and Rhodes-electric-piano traditions), Rhodes-electric-piano and warm synth-pad textures providing harmonic foundation, smooth soulful-vocal performances foregrounded in the mix, deep round subbass under house four-on-floor kick, tempos around 118-126 BPM, and song-form built on extended grooves with vocal verses surfacing over instrumental beds. Distinguished from Chicago house by post-1992 timestamp and lusher harmonic vocabulary; distinguished from US garage by mid-tempo deep-track focus rather than gospel-soul vocal foregrounding; distinguished from Detroit techno by soul-vocal centrality and warm rather than mechanical aesthetic.

items.name: Garage house
items.lineage: NYC Paradise-Garage house lineage named for the Larry Levan-resident Paradise Garage nightclub (1977-1987) — codified through Larry Levan, Frankie Knuckles (before his Chicago move), and the Salsoul / West End / Prelude labels; characterized by gospel-vocal-led songs, four-on-the-floor 120 BPM tempo, and live-instrument production retaining disco-era warmth
items.description: Garage house / Paradise Garage style (1977-1987 New York City, codified through Larry Levan's residency at the Paradise Garage club at 84 King Street establishing the gospel-and-soul-vocal-foreground house lineage), the Paradise-Garage-derived house subgenre. Defined by gospel-and-soul vocal performances foregrounded in the mix (often female lead vocals delivering anthemic-chorus material over dance-floor builds), more-syncopated four-on-floor than Chicago house (with kicks displaced and shuffled rather than locked to grid), Larry-Levan-style percussion-and-effects mixing-board work (heavy use of reverb-aux sends, EQ-sweep manipulation, intro-and-break-and-build construction), tempos around 116-122 BPM, and song-form built on extended remixes of soul and disco source material. Distinguished from Chicago house by older origin (Paradise Garage 1977 predates Frankie Knuckles's Warehouse 1981) and gospel-soul-vocal-foreground; distinguished from later UK garage by US-not-UK lineage and four-on-floor not 2-step rhythm; distinguished from disco by mid-tempo deeper-track aesthetic.

items.name: Lo-fi house
items.lineage: 2010s deliberately-degraded-aesthetic house revival codified through Mall Grab, Ross from Friends, DJ Boring, and the broader Soundcloud-and-Bandcamp ecosystem — characterized by tape-saturation simulation, sample-noise foregrounded, vintage-drum-machine reverence, and post-vaporwave nostalgic-aesthetic posture
items.description: Lo-fi house (codified 2014 onward through Bandcamp and SoundCloud bedroom-DAW production scenes, with DJ Boring's Winona breakthrough exemplifying genre crystallization), the 2010s-onward house subgenre with deliberately-degraded production aesthetic. Defined by tape-saturation-and-cassette-warble processing applied to standard house elements (the deliberate fidelity-imperfection that gives the genre its name), reverb-and-vinyl-crackle textures layered over the standard four-on-floor and synth-bass-and-pad foundation, often-distorted house piano-and-Rhodes samples, vocal samples often pitched-and-stretched into ghostly textural elements rather than foreground vocal performance, and home-DAW production with deliberately-amateur mixing aesthetic. Distinguished from straight deep house by deliberate-fidelity-imperfection production aesthetic; distinguished from chillwave by retention of dance-floor-functional structure; distinguished from vaporwave by song-form-rather-than-loop construction and house-not-corporate-Muzak source palette.

items.name: Italo house
items.lineage: Late-1980s and early-1990s Italian house tradition codified through Black Box "Ride on Time" (1989), Cappella, FPI Project, Quartz — characterized by major-key euphoric piano-stab figures, female diva-vocal samples (often uncleared at the time), and the Italo-disco euphoric production aesthetic
items.description: Italo house piano (codified 1988-1992 Italian production scene, with Black Box Ride on Time and Starlight Numero Uno as crystallizing records), the late-80s and early-90s Italian-developed house subgenre. Defined by piano-stab hook foundation (a single chord-progression repeated as the song's melodic-and-harmonic primary, often in major-key uplift register), italo-disco-derived rhythm-section heritage with extra-syncopated four-on-floor and offbeat-emphasis hi-hats, female-soprano vocal performance often as long-pitched anthemic phrases over the piano vamp, repurposed earlier-Italo-disco synth-and-bass elements layered with new-house production, and tempos around 122-128 BPM. Distinguished from Chicago house by piano-stab-foreground and Italian-production-lineage; distinguished from garage-house by Italian-not-NYC-Paradise-Garage origin; distinguished from later italo-dance by piano-foreground over saw-lead-foreground.

items.name: Latin house
items.lineage: Latin-percussion-driven house subgenre codified through New York 1990s production — Louie Vega, Kenny "Dope" Gonzalez (Masters at Work duo), Frankie Feliciano — characterized by congas, timbales, and bongo accents layered over four-on-the-floor house foundation, Spanish-language vocal hooks, and son-and-salsa percussion vocabularies
items.description: Latin house percussion-foreground (codified 1990s onward, descending from Chicago and New York house lineages with parallel and successor work in Latin-American DJ and production communities), the house sub-style integrating Latin-percussion programming and Latin-music-derived vocal-and-melodic conventions. Defined by Latin-percussion programming layered over four-on-floor house kick (congas, timbales, claves, and cowbell programmed in tumbao-and-clave patterns rather than straight house-percussion), Spanish-and-Portuguese-language vocal performance often referencing salsa, merengue, samba, or other Latin-vocal traditions, melodic-and-harmonic vocabulary drawing on Latin-music chord progressions and instrumental colorings (montuno piano vamps, brass-section stabs), tempos around 122-128 BPM, and dance-floor association with Latin-American and US-Latino club scenes. Distinguished from straight house by Latin-percussion-foreground and Latin-vocal-and-melodic vocabulary; distinguished from salsa by four-on-floor kick foundation; distinguished from reggaeton by absence of dembow-rhythm signature and retention of house tempo.

items.name: Black gospel (choir tradition)
items.lineage: African-American Pentecostal and Baptist sacred-music choir tradition codified by Thomas A. Dorsey (the father of gospel music, who pivoted from his blues piano career to founded the gospel song-form in 1932 with Take My Hand Precious Lord) and developed through the 20th-century lineage: Mahalia Jackson (the solo gospel voice, How I Got Over 1947, Move on Up a Little Higher 1948), the Reverend James Cleveland (the post-WWII choir tradition figure, his Southern California Community Choir and broader Gospel Music Workshop of America), Edwin Hawkins (Oh Happy Day 1969), Walter Hawkins, the Mississippi Mass Choir, Bishop Paul S. Morton, and the modern Kirk Franklin and Mary Mary contemporary-gospel extension
items.description: Black gospel choir (codified 1930s onward through Chicago's Pilgrim Baptist gospel-blues lineage and the National Baptist Convention's Sunday-morning church-music apparatus, with golden-age 1945-1965 and contemporary-gospel revival 1980-present), the African-American Pentecostal-and-Baptist sacred song tradition organized around the choir-and-soloist-and-organ ensemble. Defined by the 12-50-voice SATB+ choir performing call-and-response with a virtuosic lead soloist (often improvising melismatically over choir's sustained chords), Hammond B-3 tonewheel organ providing both rhythmic comping and atmospheric pads, electric bass and drum kit on rhythm, blues-inflected harmony moving through extended dominants and minor-flat-third tonality, and active congregational participation (clapping, vocal interjections, dance) during performance. Distinguished from Southern Gospel by African-American-not-white-Protestant tradition and blues-derived harmonic language; distinguished from Southern soul by sacred-text and church-not-club-context.

items.name: Sacred Harp singing
items.lineage: Southern-US shape-note congregational hymn-singing tradition preserved through the Sacred Harp tunebook (compiled by B.F. White and E.J. King 1844, revised through successive editions, the 1991 revision still in current use) — the tradition uses 4-shape and 7-shape notation (shapes assigned to scale degrees as a pedagogical mnemonic, facilitating singing without keyboard training), with the singing-square arrangement of four sections (treble / alto / tenor / bass) seated facing inward and led by a rotating song-leader who beats time with the hand
items.description: Southern-US shape-note congregational hymn-singing tradition; four-part open-fifth-and-octave-emphasis harmony, hollow-fifth modal voice-leading, all-voices-at-full-volume aesthetic, square-formation seating.

items.name: Russian Orthodox liturgical chant
items.lineage: Russian Orthodox liturgical chant tradition codified across the medieval-Kievan and Muscovite periods, drawing on the Byzantine octoechos modal system through the znamenny notation tradition — characterized by unaccompanied male-choir performance, the four-part choral harmonization style developed from the seventeenth century onward, deep-bass octavist register, and the obikhod and obihod-derived modern liturgical settings used across the Russian Orthodox parish-and-monastic-foundation network
items.description: Russian Orthodox chant (codified 11th century onward through Byzantine-Greek liturgical chant adapted into Slavonic-language Eastern Orthodox practice, with continuous tradition through to present and major reform periods including 17th-century Nikon reforms and post-Stalin 1950s-onward revival), the Russian Orthodox liturgical chant tradition. Defined by unaccompanied (a-cappella — Orthodox liturgical practice excludes instrumental accompaniment) SATB-and-bass-octavist choral singing with characteristic Russian deep-bass register (the bass-octavist Russian-vocal-tradition specialty of singing an octave below standard bass), occasional priest-and-deacon solo chant on liturgical-prayer-recitation texts, eight-mode (osmoglasie) tone system inherited from Byzantine practice with Russian-specific melodic-and-harmonic modifications, and repertoire spanning znamenny-chant (the older monodic Russian chant), kievan-and-kievopechersky chants (regional polyphonic-derivative styles), and modern-composed liturgical works (Tchaikovsky-and-Rachmaninoff Liturgy and Vespers settings). Distinguished from Greek Byzantine chant by Slavonic-language and Russian polyphonic adaptations; distinguished from Roman Catholic Gregorian by Eastern-Orthodox lineage and absence of monodic uniformity; distinguished from secular Russian choral music by liturgical function.

items.name: Bro-country
items.lineage: 2010s mainstream country-pop-rap hybrid codified through Florida Georgia Line "Cruise" (2012), Luke Bryan, Jason Aldean, and the Nashville radio-format that adopted hip-hop-derived production cues — characterized by 808-bass-and-drum-machine programming, party-celebrating lyrical subject matter, and pop-rock guitar work over country-vocal lead
items.description: 2010s mainstream Nashville country production fusing country-songwriting templates with hip-hop-and-pop-rock production sensibilities; truck-and-party-girl lyric subjects, beat-driven back-line, hooky chorus-emphasis arrangement.

items.name: Hot country
items.lineage: 2010s mainstream country radio format dominated by Nashville Music Row major-label production — Carrie Underwood, Miranda Lambert, Eric Church, Jason Aldean, and the radio-format Top 40 country chart; characterized by stadium-pop production scale, modern country-vocal performance, and the moving boundary between country and rock-pop crossover
items.description: 2010s mainstream Nashville country radio sound; pedal-steel-and-fiddle preserved as country-signifier alongside arena-rock-derived production, romantic-lifestyle lyric subjects, polished-and-radio-optimized arrangement.

items.name: Country rap (hick-hop)
items.lineage: Country-hip-hop hybrid subgenre codified through Cowboy Troy, Big Smo, Colt Ford (Ride Through the Country 2008), and the broader Average Joes Entertainment label catalog — characterized by trap-derived 808 production with country-rapped vocals, banjo and steel-guitar accents, and rural-Americana lyrical subject matter
items.description: Country rap / hick-hop (2004 onward, with Cowboy Troy and Big Smo as early codifiers and a 2010-onward streaming-platform niche following), the country-hip-hop hybrid genre fusing rap-derived MC vocal delivery with country-signifier instrumentation. Defined by banjo-and-pedal-steel acoustic-instrumentation laid over trap-derived programmed kick-and-808 percussion, MC vocal verses alternating with sung country-style choruses, lyric content combining hip-hop boast-and-narrative tropes with country-signifier subjects (pickup trucks, rural pride, cold beer, hunting, small-town nostalgia), and a Southern-rural fan demographic distinct from both mainstream country and mainstream hip-hop audiences. Distinguished from country pop with rap features (occasional crossovers like Nelly-Tim McGraw) by full-time genre commitment; distinguished from rap-rock and trap-metal by country-not-rock instrumentation; distinguished from Southern hip-hop by deliberate country-signifier framing and rural-not-urban subject focus.

items.name: Yambú
items.lineage: Slow-tempo Cuban rumba subform 1850s-onward, the oldest of the three rumba subforms and the precursor parent-form to guaguanco and rumba-columbia. Traditionally played on cajones wooden-shipping-crate-percussion (originating in dockworker-and-warehouse-improvised-drumming) rather than congas, alongside palitos stick-rhythm-and-clave 3-2 wood-block. Performed at funerals, wakes, and elder-honoring contexts, the yambú is the only rumba subform that prohibits the vacunao symbolic-pursuit choreographic-element — the dance is restrained, near-stationary, with subtle-hip-rotational gesture and exaggerated-elderly-mock-tremulous movement. The repertoire preserves the oldest pre-conga rumba percussion vocabulary.
items.description: Rumba yambú (codified 19th century Cuba as the oldest of the three Cuban rumba sub-styles, with continuous tradition through to present in Cuban folkloric-revival contexts), the slow-tempo Cuban couple-dance rumba sub-style. Defined by slow tempo (the yambú is markedly slower than guaguancó or columbia), couple-dance choreography of elderly-courtship pantomime (the yambú is sometimes called the rumba of the old folks — danced as a slow stylized courtship without the vacunao sexual-pursuit gesture of guaguancó), original cajón wooden-box-drum percussion (the yambú originally used cajones rather than the tumbadora-conga set adopted later for guaguancó), call-and-response between lead-vocalist and chorus, and claves and palitos sticks providing rhythmic foundation. Performance contexts: Afro-Cuban folkloric-tradition settings, family-and-community gatherings, professional folkloric-revival performances. Distinguished from guaguancó by slower tempo and absence of vacunao gesture; distinguished from columbia by couple-dance format and 2/4-not-6/8 metric framework; distinguished from later salsa by acoustic-percussion-only ensemble.

items.name: Columbia
items.lineage: Fast-tempo Cuban rumba subform 1880s-onward, the male-virtuoso-solo-dance variant of the three rumba subforms (alongside slower yambú and middle-tempo guaguancó). Built on accelerated-version-of-guaguancó conga-pattern with three-conga (tumbador, tres-dos, quinto) plus palitos stick-pattern, claves 3-2 wood-block, and one-or-two-male-vocalists. The dance features acrobatic-male-solo (often climbing-on-objects, knife-and-bottle-skill-play, machismo-display) rather than couple-pursuit; columbia originated in rural Matanzas dock-worker-and-railroad-worker communities (etymology from the Colón rail-line) and remains the most rural and afro-derived of the rumba subforms. The vocal-style features Yoruba-Bantu invocations (Lucumí ritual fragments embedded in the lalaleo non-lexical opening) mixed with Spanish-language verse.
items.description: Rumba columbia (codified 19th century Cuba alongside yambú and guaguancó as the third Cuban rumba sub-style, with continuous tradition through to present in Cuban Afro-Cuban-tradition contexts), the fast-tempo Cuban solo-male rumba sub-style. Defined by 6/8-clave metric framework (the columbia uses a 6/8-feel rather than the 2/4 of yambú and guaguancó), virtuosic solo-male-dancer interaction with the lead-quinto-drummer (the dancer-and-drummer duel where each tries to anticipate and respond to the other's improvisations, the columbia-specific aesthetic challenge), repertoire of inspired-improvised vocal verses on melody frameworks, claves and palitos sticks providing rhythmic foundation alongside tumbadora-and-quinto-and-conga drums, and call-and-response between lead-vocalist and chorus. Performance contexts: Afro-Cuban folkloric-tradition settings, ceremonial cabildo-association events, professional folkloric-revival performances. Distinguished from yambú by faster tempo and 6/8-rather-than-2/4 metric framework; distinguished from guaguancó by solo-male-dancer-foreground over couple-dance choreography; distinguished from later salsa by acoustic-percussion-only ensemble and absence of melodic-instrument-foreground.

items.name: Traditional doom
items.lineage: Traditional doom metal lineage descending directly from the Black Sabbath template (Black Sabbath 1970, Master of Reality 1971) — codified through Pentagram (Bobby Liebling, founded 1971, the underground US doom band whose first commercial album waited until 1985), Saint Vitus (Los Angeles SST Records canon, Saint Vitus 1984, Born Too Late 1986), Candlemass (the Swedish epic-doom canon, Epicus Doomicus Metallicus 1986), Trouble (Chicago, Psalm 9 1984)
items.description: Early-1970s English heavy-blues-rock-derived classic doom-metal sub-style; slow-tempo down-tuned riffing, melodic-vocal delivery, dirge-like song structures, gothic-pessimist lyric subjects, occult-and-fantastic imagery.

items.name: Funeral doom
items.lineage: Extreme-slow doom-metal sub-style codified through Thergothon (Finnish, Stream from the Heavens 1994), Skepticism, Mournful Congregation, and Esoteric — characterized by sub-30 BPM tempo, sustained heavy-distortion guitar drones, glacial drumming, and bell-like cathedral-organ accents; ritual-funereal lyrical and visual identity
items.description: Funeral doom (1991 onward, codified through Thergothon's Stream from the Heavens and Skepticism's Stormcrowfleet establishing the genre's extreme-slowness and funeral-mood foundations), the extreme-slow doom-metal sub-style. Defined by sub-30 BPM tempos that push the listener past metric-perception threshold (where individual snare-hits read as separate sonic events rather than rhythmic pulse), growled-vocal delivery far below conversational pitch, massive sustained-chord-as-event composition where each chord-change is a structural marker rather than a phrase-element, downtuned guitars (often 7-string or further detuned) processed through heavy reverb to produce long sustaining drones, and song-lengths regularly exceeding 15 minutes with single-piece-per-side album organization. Distinguished from straight doom by tempo extremity; distinguished from drone metal by retention of metal song-form and percussion-foreground; distinguished from death-doom by slower tempo and greater commitment to funeral mood over death-metal aggression.

items.name: Technical death metal
items.lineage: Virtuosic death-metal sub-style codified through Atheist (Piece of Time 1990, Unquestionable Presence 1991), Cynic (Focus 1993), Death’s later records (Human 1991, Individual Thought Patterns 1993), and the Suffocation 1990s lineage — characterized by complex multi-meter compositions, fretboard-acrobatic guitar work, and jazz-fusion influences
items.description: Virtuosic death-metal sub-style emphasizing technical-instrumental displays; extended-chord harmonic vocabulary, odd-meter passages, dense polyrhythmic back-line, jazz-fusion-derived improvisational elements.

items.name: Brutal death metal
items.lineage: Extreme-aggressive death-metal sub-style codified through Suffocation (Effigy of the Forgotten 1991), Cannibal Corpse (Tomb of the Mutilated 1992), Cryptopsy (None So Vile 1996), Disgorge — characterized by guttural-pig-squeal vocals, sub-200-BPM blast-beat drums, and downtuned-baritone-guitar low-end
items.description: Extreme-aggressive death-metal sub-style emphasizing maximum-intensity speed and brutality; pig-squeal-and-gutturalized vocal delivery, blast-beat-saturated back-line, body-horror-and-violence lyric subjects.

items.name: Gospel quartet (male)
items.lineage: Black-American male-quartet gospel tradition that emerged from late-19th-century Fisk Jubilee Singers university choirs and the parallel post-WWI Black Church male-quartet tradition — codified through the Golden Gate Quartet (the pre-WWII quartet, founded 1934), the Soul Stirrers (where Sam Cooke fronted before his secular pop crossover), the Dixie Hummingbirds, the Mighty Clouds of Joy, the Swan Silvertones, the Five Blind Boys of Alabama, the Pilgrim Travelers — most active 1930s-60s, with the modern continuation through the Williams Brothers and the broader gospel-quartet circuit
items.description: Black-American male-quartet gospel tradition; four-voice tight-harmony lead-and-background vocal arrangement, ecstatic-falsetto soloist, hand-clapping tambourine accompaniment, hard-gospel touring scene.

items.name: Contemporary urban gospel
items.lineage: Late-twentieth-century-onward African-American gospel music tradition modernizing the traditional church-choir-and-piano repertoire through R-and-B, funk, hip-hop, and quiet-storm production techniques — codified through Kirk Franklin (Why We Sing 1993), Mary Mary, Yolanda Adams, Donnie McClurkin, Israel and New Breed, with the genre serving as the contemporary mainstream of African-American sacred music
items.description: Modern Black-American gospel tradition fusing R&B-and-hip-hop production with gospel-tradition vocal performance; contemporary-songwriter format, polished studio production, congregation-and-personal-testimony lyric subjects.

items.name: Southern gospel quartet
items.lineage: White-Southern shape-note male-quartet gospel tradition codified through the Stamps-Baxter (founded 1924 Dallas) and James D. Vaughan (founded 1912 Lawrenceburg TN) shape-note songbook publishing infrastructure — performed by quartets including the Stamps Quartet (founded 1924), the Blackwood Brothers, the Statesmen Quartet, the Jordanaires (who backed Elvis Presley on his RCA gospel albums), Cathedral Quartet, the Gaither Vocal Band; characterized by male vocal quartet (first tenor, second tenor, baritone, bass) with piano or tonewheel organ accompaniment
items.description: Southern gospel quartet (codified 1910s onward through Stamps-Baxter Music Company shape-note songbook publication and singing-school traveling-circuit establishing the repertoire, with golden era 1945-1965 of professional-quartet recording-and-touring industry), the white-Southern-US shape-note quartet gospel tradition. Defined by four-part SATB-style harmony (with characteristic bass-emphasis bottom-voice carrying both rhythmic-and-melodic interest beyond mere harmonic foundation), shape-note pedagogical tradition (the seven-shape solfege system that simplified hymn-learning for amateur singers), professional-touring-quartet performance format (groups like the Blackwood Brothers, Statesmen Quartet, Cathedral Quartet establishing the four-male-voice configuration), gospel hymn repertoire combining 19th-century revivalist-tradition hymns with newer composed works, and Southern-Protestant-revival-meeting performance contexts. Distinguished from Black gospel by white-Southern-Protestant tradition and shape-note-pedagogy heritage; distinguished from straight choral hymnody by professional-quartet specialization; distinguished from later contemporary Christian by Southern-gospel-specific musical conventions.

items.name: Bluegrass gospel
items.lineage: Bluegrass-derived sacred-song tradition that emerged alongside secular bluegrass through Bill Monroe (his early Blue Grass Boys gospel-quartet sections), the Stanley Brothers (whose sacred-song catalog includes O Death and Angel Band), Lester Flatt and Earl Scruggs (their gospel-song interludes within concert programs), Doyle Lawson and Quicksilver (the modern bluegrass-gospel quartet), Ricky Skaggs (his Bluegrass Rules and Soldier of the Cross gospel-bluegrass crossover work); preserves the high-lonesome harmony vocal aesthetic of bluegrass applied to Protestant Christian sacred-song repertoire
items.description: Bluegrass-derived sacred song tradition; tight high-tenor-lead-and-baritone-bass vocal harmony arrangement, full bluegrass back-line, gospel-themed song repertoire from shape-note and sacred-song traditions.

items.name: Modern vocal jazz (crooner revival)
items.lineage: Late-1990s onward mainstream jazz-vocal revival — Diana Krall, Norah Jones, Michael Bublé, Cassandra Wilson, Madeleine Peyroux — revisiting the Great American Songbook canon with modern recording-aesthetic polish
items.description: Late-90s onward jazz-vocal mainstream tradition reviving Great-American-Songbook performance practice with contemporary recording aesthetics; jazz-quartet accompaniment, mid-tempo swing-and-ballad emphasis, melismatic-and-conversational vocal interpretation.

items.name: Cool jazz vocal
items.lineage: Late-1950s/60s cool-school West-Coast-jazz vocal aesthetic — Chet Baker (Sings, 1954), June Christy, Anita ODay, Julie London — restrained delivery, intimate microphone presence, small-group accompaniment, contrasted against the muscular East Coast hard bop of the same period
items.description: Late-50s and 60s cool-school jazz-vocal sub-tradition emphasizing understated-conversational delivery; West-Coast cool harmonic vocabulary, bossa-and-samba-inflected back-line, intimate-club-recording aesthetic.

items.name: Tech-house
items.lineage: House-and-techno hybrid subgenre codified through Mr. C’s End-Recordings, Terry Francis, Eddie Richards, Layo and Bushwacka — characterized by minimal-techno-derived rhythmic foundation with house-tempo (124-128 BPM), jazz-funk influence, and the European-clubland 2000s production aesthetic
items.description: Classic tech house (codified 1995 onward through UK and US producers fusing house and techno aesthetics, with golden era 2002-2010 establishing the sound through Mark Knight, Carl Cox, Loco Dice, and the broader tech-house circuit), the house-and-techno hybrid sub-style. Defined by minimal-techno percussion programming (the tech-house-specific use of restrained-and-precise percussion programming with sparse hi-hats and clipped-snare-and-clap sounds), house-music groove-and-tempo foundation (four-on-floor kick around 122-128 BPM, mid-tempo groove rather than techno's harder peak-time aesthetic), house-derived bass-and-pad textures with techno-derived percussion-and-effects palette, song-form built on extended sectional vamps with build-and-drop construction, and DJ-set-functional production aesthetic. Distinguished from straight house by techno-derived percussion programming; distinguished from straight techno by house-tempo and groove-foreground over kick-foreground; distinguished from minimal house (microhouse) by retention of warm-house harmonic-and-melodic vocabulary.

items.name: Minimal tech-house
items.lineage: Minimalist tech-house subgenre codified through Romanian producers (Rhadoo, Petre Inspirescu, Raresh) and the !K7 / Sunday Music label ecosystem — characterized by restrained production palette, long-form 8-12-minute tracks, glitchy-percussion accents, and deep-listening dancefloor aesthetic
items.description: Minimalist sub-variant of tech-house emphasizing sparse arrangement and hypnotic-loop architecture; minimal-techno-derived percussion economy, very-long-form track structures, subterranean-club-DJ oriented.

items.name: Drone metal
items.lineage: extreme-minimalist sustained-tone metal — guitar-as-feedback-and-pure-overtone genre established by Earth (Earth 2 1993, Pentastar 1996) and Sunn O))) (the Earth-tribute project become canon through ØØ Void 2000, Black One 2005, Monoliths and Dimensions 2009), with Boris (drone-era), Khanate, and Nadja in the broader continuum — distinct from doom metal by abandonment of riff-progression-as-song-form in favor of sustained-distorted-chord-as-event compositional approach
items.description: Drone metal (codified 1993 onward through Earth's Earth 2 — the foundational guitar-as-pure-sustained-tone record — and Sunn O)))'s Earth-tribute project through ØØ Void 2000, Black One 2005, and Monoliths and Dimensions 2009 establishing the genre as a coherent practice, with Boris drone-era, Khanate, Nadja, and Bell Witch in the broader continuum), the extreme-minimalist sustained-tone metal genre. Defined by sustained-distorted-chord-as-event compositional approach (single chord held for minutes at a time as the entire compositional gesture, with timbral evolution and feedback-and-overtone development substituting for harmonic motion), near-tempo-less timing (drums absent or reduced to ritualistic impact-events rather than time-keeping function), hour-long track-scale (forty-minute single tracks not unusual, full albums conceived as continuous sustained pieces), ritualistic-volume-as-physical-experience performance aesthetic (the Sunn O))) live-performance template of robed-figures-in-smoke at concert volumes physically felt rather than only heard), and cathedral-or-large-room recording capturing sustained-tone tail. Distinguished from doom metal by abandonment of riff-progression-as-song-form in favor of pure-sustained-event compositional approach; distinguished from drone-music in the experimental-electronic tradition by amplified-guitar foreground and metal sonic-vocabulary; distinguished from noise music by retention of tonal-pitch-foreground rather than texture-as-foreground.

items.name: DSBM (depressive-suicidal black metal)
items.lineage: Depressive suicidal black-metal sub-style — codified through Bethlehem (Dictius Te Necare 1996), Forgotten Tomb, Shining (Swedish, V: Halmstad 2007), Silencer (Death - Pierce Me 2001), and Xasthur — characterized by slow-to-mid-tempo dirges, atmospheric-and-melancholic guitar work, false-fold ventricular shrieked vocals, and depressive-themed lyrical content centered on isolation and self-destruction
items.description: Depressive-suicidal sub-style of black metal; slower tempo, dirge-melodic riffing, anguished-screamed vocal delivery often pushed to edge-of-articulation, despair-and-mortality lyric subjects, lo-fi cassette-recording aesthetic.

items.name: Jam band
items.lineage: Late-1960s onward improvisational rock tradition with extended-form live solos and audience-tape-trading culture — Grateful Dead, Allman Brothers, Phish, Widespread Panic, Dave Matthews Band, String Cheese Incident
items.description: Long-form improvisational rock tradition centered on extended live exploration of song frames. Audience-recording and tape-trading culture; setlists and song-versions valued for their per-night uniqueness. Multi-instrumentalist ensembles often featuring two guitars, bass, drums, organ-or-electric-piano, and dedicated percussion.
exemplars: Allman Brothers Band — At Fillmore East

items.name: Free improvisation (non-idiomatic)
items.lineage: Post-1960s European and American non-idiomatic improvisation tradition — codified through Derek Bailey’s Improvisation: Its Nature and Practice in Music (1980) as theoretical foundation, the Spontaneous Music Ensemble (London 1966 onward), AMM, Music Improvisation Company, the Globe Unity Orchestra, and the Bay Area / Knitting Factory NYC American scenes — characterized by genre-disavowal posture, no-pre-arranged-material premise, and timbre-and-extended-technique-foreground performance
items.description: Non-idiomatic free improvisation tradition emerging in 1960s European and American avant-garde scenes. Performance proceeds without pre-composed material, fixed pitch systems, or metric pulse; extended techniques and instrumental preparations central. Process-and-listening orientation, often documented on small independent labels.

items.name: Electroacoustic improvisation
items.lineage: 1990s-onward electronics-foregrounded improvisation tradition — codified through the Erstwhile Records catalog (Jon Abbey-curated), the Tokyo Off-Site scene (Otomo Yoshihide, Sachiko M, Toshimaru Nakamura), Berlin Echtzeitmusik scene, and Vienna sin: ned label; characterized by no-input-mixer feedback, contact-mic preparations, and sustained low-amplitude texture exploration
items.description: Improvised performance tradition emerging in the 1990s with laptops, prepared electric instruments, and modular electronics as primary sound sources. Often quiet and spectral; emphasis on texture, microsound, and granular processing. Lowercase, onkyo, and reductionist sub-scenes; documentation on Erstwhile, For 4 Ears, and similar small-run labels.

items.name: J-rock
items.lineage: Japanese-language alternative-rock and visual-kei tradition codified through X Japan (1980s-90s), Luna Sea, B’z, Mr. Children, L’Arc-en-Ciel, and the Buck-Tick visual-kei progenitor lineage — characterized by Western-rock instrumentation with Japanese-language vocals, dramatic stage personas, and extensive crossover with anime soundtrack production
items.description: Japanese rock tradition encompassing visual-kei, J-rock proper, and Japanese alt-rock. Importing Anglosphere distorted-rock vocabulary into Japanese-language vocal-melodic context with high-production-value studio aesthetic and theatrical performance presentation; anime tie-in opening-and-closing-theme commission a parallel context.

items.name: Anadolu rock
items.lineage: Late-1960s-onward Turkish psychedelic-folk rock genre codified through Cem Karaca, Erkin Koray (whose 1974 Elektronik Türküler is the album), Barış Manço, the Moğollar band, the Mavi Çocuklar — fusing Turkish folk-saz repertoire and Anatolian regional song-traditions with electric instrumentation, rock rhythm-section foundation, and characteristic distorted-electric-saz lead-voice
items.description: Turkish psychedelic and folk-rock tradition fusing Anatolian-folk melodic-modal materials with late-1960s rock-band instrumentation. Electric saz-baglama as signature lead instrument carrying microtonal makam inflections through fuzz amplifiers; Turkish-language vocals with traditional ornament; aksak rhythmic patterns alongside standard rock 4/4.

items.name: Russian rock
items.lineage: Late-Soviet (1980-1991) and post-Soviet (1991-onward) Russian-language rock tradition centered in Leningrad/Saint Petersburg (Boris Grebenshchikov / Aquarium, Viktor Tsoi / Kino, Yuri Shevchuk / DDT, Auktyon) and Moscow (Andrei Makarevich / Mashina Vremeni); the Leningrad Rok-klub legitimized the underground in 1981 under tight KGB oversight, with the perestroika era 1986-1991 enabling above-ground commercial release through Melodiya
items.description: Russian-language rock tradition emerging in the late-Soviet underground and continuing through the post-Soviet era. Strong literary-and-poetic lyric tradition descending from bardic song; magnitizdat tape-circulation under Soviet bloc as foundational mode of distribution; standard rock-band instrumentation with frequent acoustic-guitar foregrounding for ballad-oriented material.

items.name: Latin alternative
items.lineage: Spanish-language alternative-rock tradition codified through Mexican Café Tacuba, Argentine Soda Stereo and Café Tacvba, Chilean Los Prisioneros, and the broader Hispanic-American post-1990s indie-rock ecosystem; characterized by rock instrumentation with regional-Latin folk and electronic crossovers, and Spanish-language alternative-poetic lyrical register
items.description: Spanish-language alternative rock tradition centered on Mexican, Argentine, and Spanish scenes. Importing distorted-rock vocabulary while incorporating Latin-percussion textures, regional melodic-modal materials, and Spanish-language vocal cadences. Rock en Español umbrella with strong cross-pollination from cumbia, bolero, and ska.
exemplars: Heroes del Silencio — Senderos de Traición

items.name: Musique concrète
items.lineage: Post-WWII Paris-school tape-collage composition tradition founded by Pierre Schaeffer at RTF in 1948 — Schaeffer’s Études aux chemins de fer (1948) the genre-founding work, joined by Pierre Henry (Symphonie pour un homme seul 1950), Luc Ferrari, and the GRM (Groupe de Recherches Musicales) studio that institutionalized the practice through the 1950s-1970s
items.description: Post-WWII Paris-school tradition composing from manipulated recorded sound. Tape splicing, slowing, reversal, and looping as primary techniques; recorded-sound-as-instrument philosophy with focus on the "sound object" abstracted from its source; institutional context of the Groupe de Recherche de Musique Concrète and successor studios.
exemplars: Pierre Schaeffer — Étude aux chemins de fer
Pierre Henry — Variations pour une porte et un soupir

items.name: Electroacoustic composition
items.lineage: Post-1960s academic electroacoustic concert music tradition descended from musique concrète and Cologne elektronische Musik — codified through Karlheinz Stockhausen’s tape works, Iannis Xenakis’s UPIC synthesizer compositions, the Bourges IMEB festival circuit, and CCRMA/IRCAM institutional research centers
items.description: Academic-conservatory concert music tradition extending musique concrète practice into 1960s-onward electroacoustic composition. Studio-composed pieces presented in concert with multichannel diffusion; spectral-and-textural focus; institutional development through GRM, IRCAM, the Columbia-Princeton Electronic Music Center, and successor university electronic-music studios.

items.name: Plunderphonics
items.lineage: 1980-present sample-collage composition tradition coined by John Oswald (Plunderphonics 1989) — characterized by appropriated-pop-recording manipulation as compositional material; the Negativland (Christianity Is Stupid 1987), the Tape-beatles, People Like Us / Vicki Bennett lineage, and the broader fair-use-and-copyright contested terrain
items.description: Sample-collage composition tradition emerging in the 1980s, treating recorded music as raw source material to be re-composed. Layering, chopping, and re-contextualizing recorded sources into new works; copyright-confrontational by design; spans avant-garde art-music, hauntology, and noise-pop scenes.
exemplars: The Avalanches — Since I Left You

items.name: Early rock-and-roll (1954–1958)
items.lineage: Mid-1950s rhythm-and-blues into rock-and-roll transitional zone — codified through Bill Haley and His Comets ("Rock Around the Clock" 1954), Chuck Berry ("Maybellene" 1955), Elvis Presley’s Sun Records sessions (1954-55) and RCA crossover (1956), Little Richard ("Tutti Frutti" 1955), Fats Domino, and Jerry Lee Lewis — characterized by 12-bar-blues form adapted to teen-pop subject matter, electric-guitar-led instrumentation, and the Sun / Chess / Specialty / Atlantic indie-label distribution ecosystem
items.description: Late-1950s rhythm-and-blues-into-rock-and-roll transitional zone. Live-band tracking with single-take performance, jump-blues backbeat shifted to 2-and-4 emphasis, boogie-woogie piano patterns, electrified blues guitar, blues-shouter vocal delivery. The hinge between Black rhythm-and-blues and what becomes mass-market rock — recordings from 1954 through 1958 inhabit this transitional position.

items.name: Rockabilly
items.lineage: Mid-1950s American Mid-South rockabilly genre codified at Sun Studios Memphis under Sam Phillips production — Elvis Presley Thats All Right Mama 1954 (the founding rockabilly recording), Carl Perkins Blue Suede Shoes 1955, Jerry Lee Lewis Whole Lotta Shakin Goin On 1957, Johnny Cash I Walk the Line 1956, Roy Orbison Ooby Dooby 1956; characterized by slap-bass upright bass, Gretsch hollowbody or Fender Telecaster electric guitar with travis-picking right-hand technique, the Sun Studios slapback short-tape-delay processing, and the country I-IV-V harmonic foundation fused with blues pentatonic vocabulary
items.description: American rock-and-roll subgenre emerging in mid-1950s Memphis and the Mid-South, fusing country-and-western harmonic conventions with R&B rhythmic drive. Trademark instrumental palette: semi-hollow electric guitar (Gretsch hollowbody and similar) with twang-heavy single-note riffing, upright bass slap-and-thump rhythmic foundation, snare-driven kit, single-mic vocal with characteristic slapback tape echo. Sun Studios (Memphis, Sam Phillips engineering, 1950-1968) as infrastructure: single-mic-per-source live-tracking, monaural mastering, tape slap-echo as identity signature. Earliest commercial intersection of country-and-western and African-American R&B audiences via crossover radio formats.

items.name: Pre-sampling hip-hop (1979-1985)
items.lineage: Founding commercial-recording era of hip-hop — pre-sampling-technology, when hip-hop tracks were built with live session-band recreations of the breakbeats that DJs had isolated and looped from existing records during the Bronx block-party era. Recordings include the Sugar Hill Gang Rappers Delight 1979 (the commercial breakthrough, built on a session-band recreation of Chics Good Times bassline), Grandmaster Flash and the Furious Five The Message 1982 (the socially-conscious hip-hop breakthrough), Afrika Bambaataa Planet Rock 1982 (the Kraftwerk-Trans-Europe-Express-derived electro-funk hip-hop fusion), Run-DMC self-titled debut 1984
items.description: Founding-decade hip-hop (1979–1985), pre-sample-based-production. Live-band-backing recreates disco breaks while MCs rap over the rhythm. Party-record formats (12-inch single dominant), call-and-response between MCs, foundational lyric vocabulary (boasts, party-rocking, social commentary, neighborhood pride). The pre-recorded canon of the genre — recordings before this period don’t exist commercially.
exemplars: Grandmaster Flash & The Furious Five — The Message (1982)
Afrika Bambaataa & Soul Sonic Force — Planet Rock (1982)

items.name: Golden-age sample-collage hip-hop (1986-1991)
items.lineage: The golden-age sampler-defined era of hip-hop, codified by the E-mu SP-1200 (released 1987) and Akai S950 (released 1988) drum-and-sampler workstations that enabled the boom-bap breakbeat-and-sample-collage production aesthetic — Public Enemy It Takes a Nation of Millions to Hold Us Back 1988 produced by the Bomb Squad (Hank Shocklee), Boogie Down Productions Criminal Minded 1987 produced by KRS-One and Scott La Rock, Eric B and Rakim Paid in Full 1987, EPMD Strictly Business 1988, A Tribe Called Quest The Low End Theory 1991, De La Soul 3 Feet High and Rising 1989, the broader Native Tongues collective
items.description: 1986–1991 sample-based hip-hop era between live-band founding decade and 1990s boom-bap proper. SP-1200 / S900 / S950 sampler-defined production with eclectic sample-source approach (jazz, soul, funk, rock, library music). Native Tongues / D.A.I.S.Y. Age aesthetic centered on positive-Afrocentric expression. Four-bar-loop construction, lyric-forward MC craft, pre-Pro-Tools tracking workflow.
exemplars: De La Soul — 3 Feet High and Rising (1989)
A Tribe Called Quest — The Low End Theory (1991)
Eric B & Rakim — Paid in Full (1987)
Public Enemy — It Takes a Nation of Millions to Hold Us Back (1988)

items.name: Contemporary R&B (late-90s–2000s)
items.lineage: Late-1990s-and-2000s producer-team-era contemporary R&B aesthetic codified by the Darkchild, Jam-and-Lewis (later Flyte Tyme), Timbaland, She'kspere, and Rodney Jerkins production-lineage. Built on the breath-admixed close-miked intimate-vocal-aesthetic with stacked harmony backgrounds (typically 4-to-8 voice layered), neo-soul jazz-extended chord-vocabulary (minor-9, major-7-sharp-11, sus-2, sus-4 voicings), and programmed drum-machine kit (typically Roland TR-909, Akai MPC60-3000, or Korg M1) playing swung-and-shuffled hi-hat-and-snare-with-808-kick. The genre layered Atlanta-Memphis-NYC studio-clusters and bridged classic-Motown-and-Philly-soul lineage to 2010s-modern-R&B and trap-soul.
items.description: Late-1990s into early-2000s contemporary R&B production tradition. Darkchild / Jam-Lewis / Timbaland producer-team era. Programmed beats with syncopated kick patterns, multitracked vocal stacks (lead + harmonies + ad-libs + doublings), melismatic R&B vocal phrasing, sub-bass synthesis, sampled drum hits. Hip-hop-adjacent production aesthetic crossed with traditional R&B vocal performance.
exemplars: Brandy & Monica — The Boy is Mine (1998)

items.name: Garage-rock revival (2001–2010)
items.lineage: 2000s deliberate-vintage garage-rock movement reviving 1960s garage-rock sonic and stylistic vocabulary through fuzz-and-reverb single-coil-guitar production, raw vocal delivery, and short-song-form construction — codified through The White Stripes (White Blood Cells 2001, Elephant 2003), The Strokes (Is This It 2001), The Hives (Veni Vidi Vicious 2000), Yeah Yeah Yeahs, The Vines, with revival-aesthetic continuing through Black Lips and the Burger Records scene
items.description: 2001–2010 international garage-rock revival movement. Deliberate vintage-aesthetic production — tube tape, mono mixing, fewer overdubs, raw simple arrangements, period-correct equipment as artistic choice. Back-to-basics rock-and-roll songwriting with simplified instrumentation, fashion-cohesive scene aesthetic across international cities (NYC, Detroit, London, Stockholm, Sydney).
exemplars: The White Stripes — Seven Nation Army (2003)
The Hives — Hate to Say I Told You So (2002)

items.name: Minneapolis synth-funk-pop
items.lineage: 1980s Minneapolis funk-pop hybrid centered on the Paisley Park studio aesthetic — codified through Prince (1999 1982, Purple Rain 1984, Sign O the Times 1987), the Time (the Morris Day vehicle, What Time Is It 1982), Sheila E (The Glamorous Life 1984), Jesse Johnson, the Family — characterized by drum-machine-led groove construction, dirty-funk synth-bass, falsetto vocal lead, and explicit sexual-and-spiritual thematic mixing
items.description: Early-to-mid-1980s Minneapolis-centered synth-funk-pop hybrid tradition. LinnDrum + Oberheim/Yamaha analog-poly-synth + tight rhythm guitar + electric bass interlock + funk-derived vocal arrangements + dance-pop song structure. Auteur-multitrack production (single creator playing all parts), professional-grade home studio defining the workflow.

items.name: TikTok-era streaming pop
items.lineage: 2020s short-form-platform-native pop crafted for algorithmic discovery on TikTok and Instagram Reels — characterized by hook-foregrounded sub-thirty-second song structures, mid-song genre-and-tempo pivots, viral-dance-and-challenge-targeted composition, and rapid-iteration release cycles — exemplars include Olivia Rodrigo (SOUR 2021), Lil Nas X (Old Town Road 2019), Doja Cat, PinkPantheress, Ice Spice, with the form representing a structural shift from album-era pop construction
items.description: 2020s streaming-platform-native pop tradition. Short-form-video-platform-optimized song construction (sub-2-minute tracks, hooks front-loaded, repetition-friendly choruses). Bedroom-DAW production with sample-flipped breakbeats, pitched-up bedroom-vocal, intimate-but-streaming-loud mastering. Distribution and discovery primarily through algorithmic streaming-platform recommendation rather than radio or critical reception.

items.name: Globalized African-pop crossover
items.lineage: 2020s Africa-meets-Western-pop streaming-era hybrid tradition — codified through Wizkid ("Essence" featuring Tems 2020), Burna Boy (African Giant 2019, Twice as Tall 2020), Tems, Rema, Tiwa Savage, and the broader Afrobeats-to-international-mainstream wave; characterized by Afrobeats / amapiano rhythmic foundations under English-and-Pidgin vocals, major-label distribution, and feature collaborations with North American and European pop artists
items.description: 2020s globalized African-pop crossover tradition. Amapiano log-drum back-line and afrobeats syncopation crossed with Western pop melodic structure, English-language hooks, multi-producer cross-continental workflow. Streaming-era global distribution. Bridges African source-traditions with Western pop architecture — distinct from any single regional source-tradition by virtue of its hybridized production approach.

items.name: British R&B and British Invasion (1962–1968)
items.lineage: Mid-1960s British R&B and blues-rock interpretation of American sources — codified through The Rolling Stones (The Rolling Stones 1964, their early Chess-blues covers), The Animals ("The House of the Rising Sun" 1964, "I’m Crying" 1964), The Yardbirds (Five Live Yardbirds 1964), and Them (Van Morrison’s early band) — characterized by white English musicians performing African-American blues and R&B repertoire with electric-rock-band instrumentation through Marshall amplifiers and the British studio sound
items.description: Mid-60s British R&B and blues-rock tradition (1962–1968): the Soho-club-circuit cohort interpreting American R&B and Chicago-blues source material through a tight-band British engineering aesthetic. Defined by the combo-organ-and-clean-edge-guitar instrumental signature, blues-shouter vocal delivery, single-take small-room tracking, and a specifically British producer-led discipline targeting AM-radio singles rather than album-side construction. The transitional zone between American rhythm-and-blues source material and what became British hard rock — distinct from later British classic-rock by both era (predates 1968 multitrack adoption) and by R&B-cover-orientation rather than blues-rock-original-orientation.
exemplars: The Animals — House of the Rising Sun (1964)
The Yardbirds — Heart Full of Soul (1965)
The Rolling Stones — (I Can't Get No) Satisfaction (1965)
Manfred Mann — Do Wah Diddy Diddy (1964)
The Pretty Things — Don't Bring Me Down (1964)
Spencer Davis Group — Gimme Some Lovin' (1966)
The Kinks — You Really Got Me (1964)

items.name: Khayal (Hindustani classical vocal)
items.lineage: The most common North Indian Hindustani classical vocal genre, replacing dhrupad as the dominant vocal form from the 18th century onward — codified through the Gwalior, Agra, Kirana, Patiala, Atrauli-Jaipur gharana lineages; characterized by the bilampat-laya-vilambit-laya (slow tempo) opening composition (cheez or bandish) followed by improvisation through alap, bol-banav (word-elaboration), tan (rapid melodic runs), and laykari (rhythmic variation)
items.description: Slow-tempo improvisatory vocal genre that became the dominant Hindustani classical form from roughly the 18th century onward, displacing dhrupad as the primary court-art tradition. Two-part structure (badā khyāl / chōṭā khyāl), elaborate raga-exposition (āḷāp) followed by tāl-locked composition. Voice as primary improvisation vehicle with tabla and sarangi as co-improvisers within tabla-bound rhythmic-cycle constraints.

items.name: Tappa (Punjabi-origin Hindustani semi-classical)
items.lineage: Hindustani semi-classical vocal genre originating in late-18th-century Punjab through Mian Ghulam Nabi Shori (Shori Mian), who adapted Punjabi camel-driver folk songs into a fast-melisma classical-vocal genre — characterized by its rapid-fire intricate ornamental melisma patterns (different from khayal sustained-then-fast structure) and continued through the Banaras gharana lineage (Girija Devi, Naina Devi, Shobha Gurtu)
items.description: Fast-melismatic semi-classical North Indian vocal genre derived from Punjabi camel-drivers’ songs, codified for art-music context in the late 18th century by Mian Shori Mian. Defined by extremely rapid taan (melodic-figure) sequences within compact compositions. Hybrid position between khayal and thumri — more rhythmically driven than the former, more melodically agile than the latter.
exemplars: Girija Devi — Tappa in Raga Khamaj
Malini Rajurkar — Tappa in Raga Kafi
Shobha Gurtu — Tappa in Raga Bhairavi

items.name: Dadra (Hindustani semi-classical light-vocal)
items.lineage: Hindustani semi-classical light-vocal genre cast in the dadra tala (six-beat rhythmic cycle, 3+3 grouping) — typically performed at the end of a thumri concert as a lighter-mood companion piece, with romantic-and-devotional Brij Bhasha and Awadhi lyrical content
items.description: Light-classical North Indian vocal genre in dadra-tāl (six-beat cycle), shorter and more song-like than thumri but sharing thumri’s romantic / devotional poetic register. Boundary genre between mehfil-court-music and the regional folk traditions of Uttar Pradesh and Punjab. Often performed as concert closer following a thumri set.
exemplars: Girija Devi — Dadra in Raga Khamaj

items.name: Tarana (Hindustani vocalized-syllable composition)
items.lineage: Hindustani vocal genre using non-lexical vocalized syllables (tom, na, dir, dani, todani, yala, nadiri, drim) attributed by tradition to Amir Khusraus 13th-century court innovation — typically performed at the end of a khayal concert as a fast-tempo rhythmically dazzling concert-closer, with the syllables functioning as vocal-equivalent to tabla bols
items.description: Hindustani vocal genre using meaningless rhythmic syllables (tom, dir, ta, na, ra) as compositional material. Attributed to Amir Khusrau (13th–14th century) but most famously developed in Mughal-court khayal lineage. Typically performed as a fast closer to a khayal set, the syllables enabling extreme rhythmic dexterity that meaningful text would constrain.
exemplars: Pandit Jasraj — Tarana in Raga Bhairav
Rashid Khan — Tarana in Raga Hamsadhwani
Bhimsen Joshi — Tarana in Raga Yaman

items.name: Kriti (Carnatic devotional composition)
items.lineage: The central composition-form of Carnatic classical music, codified by the early-19th-century Trinity (Tyagaraja set Telugu and Sanskrit devotional poetry to ~600 kritis predominantly to Rama; Muthuswami Dikshitar composed in Sanskrit predominantly to various deities; Syama Sastri composed predominantly to the Goddess) — every kriti has the standard pallavi (refrain) / anupallavi (upward-developing second section) / charanam (longer extending section) structure
items.description: Foundational compositional form of Carnatic (South Indian) classical music. Three-section structure (pallavi / anupallavi / charanam) on devotional Hindu poetry, primarily in Sanskrit, Telugu, or Tamil. Attributed compositions of the Trinity (Tyāgarāja, Muthuswāmy Dīkshitar, Śyāma Śāstri, all early 19th century) form the repertoire. Differs from Hindustani forms by being substantially text-bound rather than rāga-improvisation-bound.

items.name: Padam (Carnatic slow-tempo lyrical genre)
items.lineage: Carnatic slow-tempo lyrical genre setting Tamil and Telugu nayika-bhava (heroine-emotion) poetry to elaborated single-line-per-section vocal exposition — typically performed in the second half of a Carnatic kutcheri after the main kriti, with the 17th-century padam composer Kshetrayya (Telugu) and the Tamil padam tradition continued through Subbarama Iyer
items.description: Slow-tempo Carnatic vocal genre, typically setting love-poetry (often shringara-rasa Sanskrit or Telugu verse) addressed to the divine beloved. Performed primarily in concert and bharatanatyam-dance contexts. Extreme tempo dilation enables word-painting and microtonal raga-elaboration on individual syllables that faster forms cannot accommodate.

items.name: Javali (Carnatic light-classical love-song)
items.lineage: Carnatic light-classical romantic-love song genre at faster tempo than padam, setting Telugu and Tamil and Kannada erotic-and-romantic poetry to elaborated vocal performance — emerged in the 19th century at the Mysore and Tanjore courts, codified through Patnam Subramania Iyer and Veene Sheshanna
items.description: Light-classical Carnatic vocal genre treating overtly erotic and worldly themes — distinct from padam by being faster, simpler in structure, and explicit rather than sublimated in religious framing. Late-19th-century courtly origin, sometimes performed by devadasis. Rapid tempo and direct text foregrounded.

items.name: Tillana (Carnatic concert-closer rhythmic showpiece)
items.lineage: Carnatic rhythmic showpiece genre using non-lexical jathi syllables (dhim, tarana, dhirana) alongside short Sanskrit or Telugu praise-text — the Carnatic counterpart of the Hindustani tarana, typically performed as the concert-closer of a kutcheri; composers Swati Tirunal Rama Varma (Maharaja of Travancore, 1813-1846), Pallavi Seshayyar, the modern composer Lalgudi Jayaraman
items.description: Carnatic counterpart to the Hindustani tarana — concert-closer using rhythmic syllables (tana, nom, tom) interspersed with brief text. Faster tempo than typical Carnatic forms, virtuosic display piece. Often choreographed for bharatanatyam dance. Composers Lalgudi Jayaraman and Patnam Subramania Iyer contributed repertoire.
exemplars: Lalgudi Jayaraman — Tillana in Raga Behag
M. Balamuralikrishna — Tillana in Raga Bhairavi
Sudha Ragunathan — Tillana in Raga Kuntalavarali

items.name: Sufi sama (Indian-subcontinental Sufi devotional ceremony)
items.lineage: Chishti-order Sufi devotional ceremony tradition centered on sama (Arabic for listening), the practice of group listening to qawwali-style devotional poetry-singing as a path toward divine union; performed at dargah (Sufi shrine) settings across the Indian subcontinent, with the Nizamuddin Auliya shrine in Delhi and the Khwaja Moinuddin Chishti shrine in Ajmer as the principal pilgrimage sites
items.description: South Asian Sufi mystical-listening ceremony, distinct from but related to qawwali. Performed at Chishti-order Sufi shrines (dargahs), focused on poetic-mystical-text rendering rather than the stadium-format projection of qawwali. Smaller ensemble, more variable tempo, longer ecstatic-state-cultivation sections. Cultural-context layer beneath the qawwali genre.

items.name: Tropicália
items.lineage: Brazilian late-1960s art-pop counter-cultural movement (1967-1969 peak) emerging in Salvador-Bahia-and-São-Paulo as fusion of bossa-nova harmonic-sophistication, Northeast forró-and-baião rhythmic-vocabulary, Anglo-American psychedelic-rock instrumentation (electric-guitar, fuzz, distortion), Stockhausen-and-Cage avant-garde electroacoustic-experimentation, and Brazilian-modernist-poetry pau-brasil concrete-and-anthropophagic literary-aesthetic. Built politically in opposition to the 1964-1985 Brazilian military dictatorship through ironic-pop subversion. The canonical recordings of the late-1960s tropicália phase shaped Brazilian-mainstream MPB 1970s-onward and influenced global art-rock through the 1990s-onward Western re-discovery wave.
items.description: Late-1960s Brazilian art-music movement (1967–69) collaging bossa nova, MPB, psychedelic rock, electronic experimentation, concrete poetry, and political critique under military dictatorship. Defined by a deliberate juxtaposition aesthetic — kitsch and high-art, indigenous and imported elements, traditional Brazilian and Anglo-American rock all coexisting in the same arrangement.

items.name: MPB (Música Popular Brasileira)
items.lineage: Brazilian MPB (Música Popular Brasileira) post-bossa-nova-and-tropicália sophisticated-popular-music umbrella-tradition emerging 1965-onward from the bossa-nova-tropicália-festival circuit. Built on harmonically-extended chord-vocabulary (minor-7-and-maj-7-and-9-and-11 jazz-extensions), Brazilian-rhythmic foundation (samba, baião, choro, bossa derivatives), and singer-songwriter literary-poetic-lyrical-sophistication. The 1970s mpb-jovem-guarda commercial-pop wave, the 1980s mpb-de-câmara chamber-mpb, and 1990s-onward mpb-as-heritage-institution comprise the genre's historical arc. Canonical instrumentation: violão acoustic-guitar nylon-string fingerstyle-led, with optional flute, piano, cavaquinho, and contemporary-rhythm-section. The MPB-canon overlaps significantly with samba-canção and bossa-nova but retains a distinct singer-songwriter-as-poet aesthetic identity.
items.description: Catchall term for sophisticated post-bossa Brazilian popular music — the artists who emerged from the bossa nova / tropicália generation and became the long-form mainstream of Brazilian song. Acoustic-guitar-and-voice texture preserved from bossa, harmonic vocabulary inherited from jazz, lyric craft inherited from samba lineage, all integrated as the ongoing Brazilian pop format.
exemplars: Djavan — Não É Azul, Mas É Mar (1989)

items.name: Maracatu
