items.lineage: Vedic chant — the canonical three-thousand-year-continuous Sanskrit recitation tradition for the four Vedas (Rgveda, Yajurveda, Sāmaveda, Atharvaveda) preserved through the gurukula master-disciple oral-transmission lineage; defined by the three-tone udatta-anudatta-svarita pitch-accent system (udatta the raised pitch, anudatta the lower pitch, svarita the falling-pitch tone) inherited from Proto-Indo-European prosody, with the additional Sāmaveda musical-melodic elaboration (the Sāman chant tradition that uses seven svaras and is considered the source of later Indian classical raga); transmission preserved through the canonical paṭha (recitation-style) variants — Saṃhitā (continuous), Padapāṭha (word-by-word), Krama-pāṭha (interlocking pairs), Jaṭā-pāṭha (woven pattern), and Ghana-pāṭha (dense pattern) — each designed to lock the text against transmission error; the Nambudiri Brahmin community of Kerala preserves the most archaic Sāmavedic chanting layer, with parallel Tamil-Brahmin, Maharashtrian, and Kashi (Banaras) regional preservation lineages
items.description: Vedic chant, the canonical three-thousand-year-continuous Sanskrit recitation tradition for the four Vedas — Rgveda, Yajurveda, Sāmaveda, and Atharvaveda — preserved through the gurukula master-disciple oral-transmission lineage. Defined by the three-tone udatta-anudatta-svarita pitch-accent system (udatta the raised pitch, anudatta the lower pitch, svarita the falling-pitch tone) inherited from Proto-Indo-European prosody, with the additional Sāmaveda musical-melodic elaboration (the Sāman chant tradition uses seven svaras and is considered the source of later Indian classical raga). Transmission preserved through the canonical paṭha (recitation-style) variants — Saṃhitā (continuous), Padapāṭha (word-by-word), Krama-pāṭha (interlocking pairs), Jaṭā-pāṭha (woven pattern), and Ghana-pāṭha (dense pattern) — each designed to lock the text against transmission error through redundant ordering systems. The Nambudiri Brahmin community of Kerala preserves the most archaic Sāmavedic chanting layer with documented continuous transmission, with parallel Tamil-Brahmin, Maharashtrian, and Kashi (Banaras) regional preservation lineages. Distinguished from later Hindu devotional bhajan-and-kirtan traditions by ametrical recitation form and absence of musical-instrumental accompaniment; distinguished from Buddhist Pali chant by Sanskrit-specific Vedic-pitch-accent system; distinguished from broader Hindu temple music by ritual-prescribed paṭha-system transmission discipline.

items.name: Silbo Gomero whistled language
items.lineage: Silbo Gomero whistled-language tradition of La Gomera island, Canary Islands — a fully grammatical whistled register of the Spanish language using turbulent lip-and-tongue-formed source (no vocal-fold vibration, distinct from the M3 whistle vocal register) to encode vowels and consonants across the mountain-canyon distances of the island terrain (sound carries 2-5 km across canyon walls); whistled vowels mapped onto two pitches (high and low) and whistled consonants mapped onto two-and-more types of pitch-transition (interrupted vs continuous, with rising vs falling), giving sufficient phonemic-distinction-capacity to transmit any Spanish-language utterance; preserved through the La Gomera school curriculum (1999-onward compulsory instruction) and the ethnographic lineage of Ramón Trujillo who established the linguistic-phonological description in the 1970s-80s; parallel related whistled-language traditions include Sfyria (Antia village Greek), Mazatec (Oaxaca Mexico), Kuşköy (Turkish Black Sea), and the Hmong courtship-whistle traditions
items.description: Silbo Gomero whistled-language tradition of La Gomera island in the Canary Islands, a fully grammatical whistled register of the Spanish language using turbulent lip-and-tongue-formed source (no vocal-fold vibration, mechanistically distinct from the M3 whistle vocal register). Vowel-and-consonant phonemic distinctions encoded through pitch contours and articulation-transition types — whistled vowels mapped onto two pitches (high and low) and whistled consonants mapped onto two-and-more types of pitch-transition (interrupted vs continuous, with rising vs falling contours) — gives sufficient phonemic-distinction-capacity to transmit any Spanish-language utterance across the mountain-canyon distances of the island terrain (sound carries 2-to-5 km across canyon walls). Preserved through the La Gomera school curriculum (compulsory instruction since 1999) and the linguistic-phonological description lineage of Ramón Trujillo (1970s-80s University of La Laguna research program). Parallel related whistled-language traditions include Sfyria (Antia village Greek), Mazatec (Oaxaca Mexico), Kuşköy (Turkish Black Sea), and the Hmong courtship-whistle traditions. Distinguished from vocal-fold-based singing by turbulent-lip-source phonation mechanism; distinguished from musical whistling by full-grammatical-linguistic encoding capacity; distinguished from broader whistled-call signaling by sufficient-phonemic-distinction for unrestricted Spanish-language utterance.

items.name: Sfyria whistled language (Antia, Greece)
items.lineage: Sfyria whistled-language tradition of Antia village on Mount Ochi in Evia island, Greece — a fully grammatical whistled register of the Greek language using turbulent lip-and-tongue-formed source to encode Greek phonemes across the mountain-and-canyon terrain of Mount Ochi; documented by the contemporary linguistic-anthropology lineage including Sotiris Apostolopoulos and the Onassis Foundation cultural-preservation initiatives; the smaller and more endangered sibling of Silbo Gomero, with only a handful of remaining fluent speakers in the Antia village; the whistled-language family includes the Kuşköy Turkish Black Sea whistled-Turkish tradition, the Hmong courtship-whistle, Mazatec, and other documented whistled-languages globally
items.description: Sfyria whistled-language tradition of Antia village on Mount Ochi in Evia island, Greece — a fully grammatical whistled register of the Greek language using turbulent lip-and-tongue-formed source to encode Greek phonemes across the mountain-and-canyon terrain of Mount Ochi. The smaller and more endangered sibling of Silbo Gomero, with only a handful of remaining fluent speakers in the Antia village. Documented by contemporary linguistic-anthropology lineage including the Onassis Foundation cultural-preservation initiatives and field-research from European linguistic institutions. The whistled-language global family includes Silbo Gomero, the Kuşköy Turkish Black Sea whistled-Turkish tradition, the Hmong courtship-whistle, Mazatec (Oaxaca Mexico), and other documented whistled-languages. Distinguished from vocal-fold-based singing by turbulent-lip-source phonation mechanism; distinguished from Silbo Gomero by Greek-language phonemic-encoding system and Mount Ochi geographic-specific preservation lineage; distinguished from broader whistled-signaling by full-grammatical-encoding capacity sufficient for unrestricted Greek-language utterance.

items.name: Albanian iso-polyphony
items.lineage: Albanian iso-polyphony of the Toskëria and Labëria regions of southern Albania. Drone-based polyphony with named voice-parts marrës (the lead-taker who initiates each verse), kthyes (the turner who answers and counters), and in the four-voice Lab variant the hedhës (the thrower who launches contrapuntal interjections), all sustained over an iso choral drone group. Tosk iso is continuous and sung on the syllable "e" with staggered breathing; Lab iso is sometimes rhythmically articulated to text and supports a four-voice complement against the three-voice Tosk standard. The 1920s-1930s Neço Muko field recordings in Vlorë and Tirana established the four-voice canon. Heartland villages of Gjirokastër, Përmet, Tepelenë, Vlorë, and Korçë sustain transmission lineages. Distinguished from Sardinian cantu a tenore by absence of guttural-ventricular bass and continuous "e" syllable iso; distinguished from Corsican paghjella by iso-drone foundation; distinguished from Bulgarian diaphonic women's choir by male-voice configuration and southern-Albanian regional dialect-specific cadential conventions

items.name: Azerbaijani mugham
items.lineage: Azerbaijani classical modal art-music tradition of the modal-improvisatory dastgah suite system. The seven-dastgah canonical sequence — Rast, Shur, Segah, Chargah, Bayati-Shiraz, Shushtar, Humayun — each suite built from a tonal-center microtonal modal vocabulary with characteristic shifted-third intervals, extended through gushe sub-section sequences. Khananda singer-led trio with tar long-necked plucked lute (eleven-or-twelve-string mulberry-wood double-bowl body, redesigned by Sadigjan in the 1870s into its modern form) and kamancha four-string spike fiddle, with the khananda holding a gaval frame-drum. The Shusha "conservatory of the East" lineage established the Garabagh school as the canonical performance dialect. Twentieth-century founding figures include Jabbar Garyaghdioglu (1861-1944), Khan Shushinski (1901-1979), Seyid Shushinski, with Uzeyir Hajibeyov (1885-1948) founding the symphonic mugham and the 1908 opera Leyli and Majnun. Distinguished from Iraqi maqam by Garabagh-Shusha dialect-specific gushe-sequence conventions; distinguished from Persian radif by Azerbaijani-Turkic vocal-ornamentation grammar; distinguished from Turkish makam by the dastgah modal-cycle structural framework

items.name: Shashmaqam (Tajik-Uzbek classical)
items.lineage: Bukharan Central Asian classical six-modal-cycle tradition shared between Tajikistan and Uzbekistan. The six modal cycles — Buzruk, Rost, Navo, Dugoh, Segoh, Iroq — each a multi-movement suite structure. Origin in Bukhara city under the Bukharan emirate, present form crystallized in the eighteenth century. Canonical instrumentation: tanbur long-necked plucked lute as the primary maqom voice carrier, dutar two-string fretted lute, sato bowed tanbur, ghijak spike fiddle (analogue to Azerbaijani kamancha), doira frame-drum with internal jingles, nay end-blown reed flute. The Bukharan Jewish community preserved the most archaic transmission layer through Soviet-era suppression and subsequent diaspora-recovery in the United States and Israel. Twentieth-century master Turgun Alimatov (tanbur, dutar, sato virtuoso) anchored the post-Soviet revival. Distinguished from Azerbaijani mugham by six-maqom-cycle structure (vs Azerbaijani seven-dastgah); distinguished from Persian dastgah-i radif by Bukharan ensemble configuration and Tajik-Persian-language sufyiana-poetry textual base; distinguished from Uyghur muqam by Bukharan-Tajik dialect-specific cadential and modal vocabulary

items.name: Kyrgyz Manas epic-recital
items.lineage: Kyrgyz Manas heroic-epic recital tradition. The Manas trilogy — Manas, Semetey, Seytek — reaches up to 553,000 verse-lines in the canonical recension. Classical manaschi epic-reciter performs voice-only with hand-gesture and cadence patterning, often in near-trance state; the akyn improvising sung-poet variant accompanies with the komuz three-string fretless lute. Sometimes shamanic in framing — the manaschi receives the epic in dream-summons from the spirit of Manas. Twentieth-century canonical figures include Sagymbay Orozbakov (1867-1930), Sayakbay Karalaev (1911-1971, whose recension is the largest documented corpus and whose portrait appears on the 500-som banknote), and contemporary Talantaaly Bakchiev (born 1971). Bishkek State Manas Theater established as state-level performance venue. Distinguished from Turkic dastan traditions by the Kyrgyz-language-specific narrative-cadence grammar and the trance-summons performance framing; distinguished from Kazakh kuy by voice-led (vs instrumental-led) tradition structure

items.name: Khmer pinpeat royal-court ensemble
items.lineage: Khmer pinpeat ceremonial ensemble — the largest classical Cambodian instrumental tradition, accompanying the Royal Ballet of Cambodia and Sbek Thom shadow-puppet. Pre-Angkor Khmer roots; royal court and wat temple ceremonial repertoire. Canonical instrumentation of nine-to-ten instruments dominated by wind and percussion: roneat ek high bamboo xylophone (twenty-one bars, boat-shaped resonator, melodic lead), roneat thung low bamboo xylophone (second voice, counterpoint to ek), sralai quadruple-reed conical-bore oboe (palm-leaf reed, sustained melodic lead), sampho double-headed barrel timekeeper drum (sets tempo and cadence — ensemble leader), skor thom large barrel drum pair (stick-struck bass), kong vong thom large gong circle (sixteen tuned bronze bossed gongs in rattan frame — melodic skeleton sustaining the harmonic foundation), ching small finger cymbals (time-keeping). Seven-equal-tempered tuning shared with Thai piphat. The Khmer Rouge era 1975-1979 nearly destroyed the tradition; post-1980 reconstruction led by surviving masters including Chum Ngek, with the Royal University of Fine Arts Phnom Penh restoring transmission infrastructure. Distinguished from Thai piphat by Khmer-language repertoire and dialect-specific cadential conventions; distinguished from Lao seb-noi by the larger pinpeat ensemble configuration and royal-court ceremonial repertoire base

items.name: Māori waiata + taonga pūoro
items.lineage: Aotearoa New Zealand Māori vocal tradition. Pre-European foundation built on narrow-range melody (frequently around a minor third), microtonal glissandi and pitch-bends, and antiphonal-or-unison choral response to the kaiwaiata lead. Nineteenth-century Christian-mission introduction of four-part hymnody overlaid onto the pre-contact base, producing the kapa haka collective-performance form combining waiata sung-song, haka chanted-dance, and poi rhythmic implement. Performance contexts include the pōwhiri formal welcome, tangihanga funeral, whakatau informal welcome, and hui collective-assembly. Taonga pūoro ("singing treasures") secondary to voice: kōauau small notched flute (albatross-wing-bone or carved hardwood, three holes, sung-into for accompaniment of lament/lullaby/charm), pūtōrino unique-to-Aotearoa wooden bugle-flute (split-hollowed hardwood torpedo-or-case-moth profile, plays as flute OR trumpet, dual voicing represents the female and male voices of Hine Raukatauri), pūkāea long wooden trumpet (signaling), pūtātara pūmoana conch shell, pūrerehua bullroarer, porotiti spinning disc, pakuru teeth-held resonant rods, poi rhythmic ball. The twentieth-century revivalist lineage of Hirini Melbourne, Richard Nunns, and Horomona Horo restored taonga pūoro from near-extinction. Distinguished from Tahitian himene tarava by Aotearoa-specific microtonal narrow-range melodic vocabulary and pūtōrino-dual-voicing instrumental signature; distinguished from Hawaiian mele oli by waiata-haka-poi compound performance form

items.name: Hawaiian mele oli sacred-chant
items.lineage: Hawaiian mele (chant/song/poetry, broad category) and oli (chant without dance or instrument, solo, prayer/genealogy/name function). Pre-contact sacred-chant tradition. Two register-styles: kepakepa rapid rhythmic recitation (used for prayer mele pule); ho'āeae soft drawn-out vowels (used for love mele ho'oipoipo and lamentation). Functional inventory: mele pule prayer, kō'ihonua cosmogeny, kū'auhau genealogy, hānau birth, inoa name-giving, ma'i procreation, kanikau lamentation, ho'oipoipo love. Performance with terminal pitch-drop closing each line, the characteristic 'i'i quavering vibrato sustained on long vowels, and characteristic vocal-strain register in genealogy and prayer mele. Hula kahiko (ancient hula) uses sacred instruments — pahu coconut-log sharkskin drum (originally heiau temple instrument), ipu and ipu heke single and double gourds, pū'ili bamboo split-rattle, 'ulī'ulī feathered gourd rattle, 'ili'ili water-worn lava stones, pū conch — while hula 'auana (post-1832 modern hula) uses Western-instrument accompaniment. Distinguished from Māori karanga + pōwhiri by Hawaiian 'i'i quavering-vibrato terminal-drop ornament; distinguished from Tahitian himene by absence of polyphonic congregational-hymn structure and presence of unaccompanied sacred-chant convention

items.name: Mbaqanga (South African township jive, 1960s-1980s)
items.lineage: South African mbaqanga township-jive tradition emerging in early 1960s Johannesburg township studios (Soweto and Alexandra). Roots in 1920s-1930s marabi shebeen piano-and-banjo and 1950s kwela pennywhistle jive. Studios: Mavuthela (the Black-music division of Gallo Record Company, established 1964) under producer Rupert Bopape. Sound: electric instrumentation over township 8/8 beat, with Zulu vocal harmonies in five-part configuration (not Western four-part). "Groaning" basso-profundo male vocal — canonical bass-register growl with hyper-low fundamental — paired against female-trio harmonies (Mahotella Queens, Dark City Sisters). Backing-band canonical lineup of Makgona Tsohle Band: Marks Mankwane lead electric guitar, Joseph Makwela electric bass, West Nkosi tenor saxophone (later producer in his own right), Vivian Ngubane rhythm guitar, Lucky Monama drums. Mgqashiyo dance variant emerged late 1960s. The word "mbaqanga" is Zulu for cornmeal porridge / steamed bread. The 1986 Graceland sessions brought international revival. Distinguished from kwela by electric-instrumentation and 8/8 township-beat configuration; distinguished from isicathamiya by groaning-bass + female-trio configuration vs male-only close-harmony; distinguished from marabi by electric vs acoustic shebeen-piano-banjo instrumentation

items.name: Ethiopian azmari minstrel-poet (centuries-old)
items.lineage: Ethiopian azmari itinerant minstrel-poet tradition, etymologically from Amharic mazammar (to sing), with centuries-old documentation. Compared in performance-economic role to medieval European troubadours and West African griots — improvisational extemporaneous-poetry minstrel performing for patrons in tej bet (honey-wine houses) and after the 1970s in dedicated azmari bet performance venues. Canonical instruments: masenqo one-string bowed lute (held vertically on the knee, virtuosic) and krar five-or-six-string bowl-lyre (held against the chest), with kebero conical drum and washint end-blown notched flute in larger ensembles. Modal vocabulary built on the Ethiopian qenet pentatonic mode-system: tizita (the nostalgic mode), bati (the praise-mode), ambassel (the festive-mode), anchihoye (the mournful-mode), all in pure-temperament (not equal-tempered). Eskista shoulder-dance characteristic accompaniment-form. Famous twentieth-century azmari include Asnaketch Worku (krar player and Ethiopia's first theatre actress), Bahru Qäññé, and Yerga Dubalä. Kazanchis district of Addis Ababa peaked at approximately seventeen azmari venues in the 1970s, with Fendika (founded 1990s, under Melaku Belay since 2008) now the last-bastion of the district's azmari-bet performers' styles and teacher's teacher transmission lineage. Distinguished from West African griot by Ethiopian qenet pentatonic-mode vocabulary and masenqo-and-krar instrumental signature; distinguished from Sudanese azmari-cognate traditions by Amhara-language repertoire and Addis-Ababa-Kazanchis venue-context

items.name: Medieval Latin chant and Notre Dame organum
items.lineage: Medieval Western European liturgical music tradition spanning monophonic Gregorian chant (canonized late ninth century, eight church modes, Latin liturgical text) and the early-polyphonic organum that emerged from it. Ninth-century parallel organum (the chant doubled at the fifth or fourth, with optional octave doubling); twelfth-century melismatic organum (the chant slowed to drone-tone in the lower voice while the upper voice elaborates ornamentally over each chant pitch). The Notre Dame school, Paris, c.1160-1250, codified the rhythmic-modes system and expanded to three-and-four-voice organum: Léonin (c.1135-1201), credited with the Magnus Liber Organi (the great book of organum), set the two-voice canonical repertoire; Pérotin (fl. c.1200), expanded to three and four voices and composed canonical large-scale organum-quadruplum settings of Viderunt omnes (1198) and Sederunt principes. Cantus firmus practice: the chant melody remains in one voice (typically the tenor) while the other voices counterpoint above. Anonymous IV (English theorist, c.1270s, his treatise survives in a thirteenth-century Bury St Edmunds manuscript) preserves the attribution of these works to Léonin and Pérotin. Distinguished from Renaissance sacred polyphony by limited-voice-count and modal-not-tonal harmonic vocabulary; distinguished from Byzantine chant by Latin-language and Roman-rite cantus-firmus framing; distinguished from Old Roman chant by Frankish-redacted melodic-formulae lineage

items.name: Renaissance sacred polyphony (1450-1600)
items.lineage: Renaissance European sacred-music tradition c.1450-1600, the mass-cycle and motet repertoire of the Franco-Flemish and Italian schools. Canonical compositional features: imitative counterpoint with successive voice-entries on the same melodic subject; smooth melodic voice-leading with stepwise motion and small leaps; controlled dissonance through suspension-and-resolution; modal scales transitioning gradually into tonal practice; a cappella ideal with optional organ accompaniment for liturgical performance. Canonical composers: Josquin des Prez (Franco-Flemish, c.1450-1521, founding figure of the imitative-mass tradition); Giovanni Pierluigi da Palestrina (Roman, 1525-1594, Missa Papae Marcelli 1567 the Counter-Reformation touchstone for the smoothness-and-clarity ideal); Thomas Tallis (English, c.1505-1585, the forty-voice motet Spem in alium c.1570); William Byrd (English, c.1543-1623, Mass for Four Voices); Orlande de Lassus (Flemish, 1532-1594); Tomás Luis de Victoria (Spanish, 1548-1611). Geographical centers: Cambrai, Antwerp, Rome (Cappella Sistina), Venice (San Marco), London (Chapel Royal). Distinguished from medieval organum by full imitative counterpoint and tempered-meantone tuning vocabulary; distinguished from Baroque sacred polyphony by absence of basso continuo and absence of operatic-aria stylistic vocabulary; distinguished from Orthodox liturgical chant by Latin-text Roman-rite (vs Slavonic / Greek Orthodox-rite) liturgical framework

items.name: Wagogo nindo and cipande polyphony (Tanzania)
items.lineage: Wagogo polyphonic singing tradition of central Tanzania (Dodoma region), one of sub-Saharan Africa's most structurally distinctive choral traditions. Multi-part harmony built on overlapping ostinato pattern-cycles with characteristic diaphonic-and-triadic intervals — nindo work-songs and msunyunho ritual songs sit alongside the cipande circumcision-initiation repertoire. Polo Vallejo's 1995-2002 fieldwork in Nzali village (published as Mbudi Mbudi na Mhanga, Madrid 2004) and David Fanshawe's 1969-1975 East African field recordings (Saydisc CMIL 98 Fabulous Gogo Music) constitute the canonical documentation. Performance involves women's choral antiphonal patterns over zeze board-zither and kebero drum accompaniment, with characteristic call-and-response between soloist and group across staggered melodic entries. Modal vocabulary draws on pentatonic-and-hexatonic frameworks with characteristic equiheptatonic-leaning inflections distinct from neighboring Bantu traditions. Distinguished from Burundi inanga-chuchotée by Wagogo's open-voiced choral-with-instruments configuration; distinguished from Aka and Baka pygmy polyphony by Wagogo's ostinato-cycle (vs hocketed yodel) architecture; distinguished from Maasai and Sukuma neighbors by Wagogo-Dodoma dialect-specific cadential conventions.

items.name: Ju|'hoansi healing songs (Kalahari)
items.lineage: Ju|'hoansi (formerly !Kung) trance-healing song tradition of the Nyae Nyae region of Namibia and adjacent Botswana Kalahari, central to the n|om trance-dance ceremony. Nocturnal gatherings around a fire-circle: women sit in concentric ring clapping and singing named medicine-songs (giraffe medicine, sun medicine, gemsbok medicine, honey medicine), while men dance in the outer ring until they enter !kia trance-state and lay hands on participants for healing. Vocal architecture features yodel-edge falsetto-and-chest-register alternation, hocketed interlocking pattern-cycles, and characteristic descending-melodic contours over staggered group ostinato. Gilbert Rouget's 1957 Smithsonian Folkways FE 4487 recordings (Bushmen Music and Pygmy Music), Lorna Marshall's 1950s-1980s Harvard Peabody documentation (published as Nyae Nyae !Kung Beliefs and Rites, 1999), and Emmanuelle Olivier's 1993-1995 doctoral fieldwork at the British Library Sound Archive constitute the documentary canon. The tradition predates by millennia the more recent Kalahari population entries, with linguistic and genetic evidence supporting deep continuity. Distinguished from Xhosa umngqokolo by Ju|'hoansi's polyphonic-ensemble-over-solo-overtone configuration; distinguished from Aka and Baka rainforest polyphony by Kalahari open-desert acoustic context and trance-healing functional framing.

items.name: Xhosa umngqokolo overtone singing
items.lineage: Xhosa overtone-singing tradition of the Lumko / Ngqoko region of the Eastern Cape, South Africa — one of only a handful of split-tone overtone vocal practices documented globally and the only sub-Saharan African instance. Women produce a sustained chest-register fundamental while shaping mouth-resonance to amplify upper partials of the harmonic series into a clearly audible whistle-tone melody floating above the fundamental. The uhadi gourd-resonator mouth-bow accompanies, with the player's mouth serving as a second resonance chamber that the bow's single struck string excites — producing a parallel split-tone effect in the instrumental voice. Dave Dargie's 1985-1988 Lumko fieldwork (Xhosa Music: Its Techniques and Instruments, David Philip 1988) and his AIMP / VDE-Gallo CD-879 South Africa: Xhosa Women's Songs (1996) constitute the documentary canon, with NoFinishi Dywili as the principal informant. The Ngqoko Women's Ensemble (founded 1983) has carried the tradition into the international circuit, with NoWayilethi Mbizweni among the second-generation performers. Distinguished from Tuvan and Mongolian khoomei by Xhosa's women-only practice and chest-register (rather than throat-tension) fundamental production; distinguished from Sardinian cantu a tenore guttural overtone by Xhosa's single-voice split-tone vs Sardinian four-voice ensemble configuration.

items.name: Tuareg tendé pestle-rhythm song
items.lineage: Tuareg desert song tradition of the southern Sahara — Niger's Azawagh basin, the Aïr Mountains, southern Algerian Hoggar, northern Mali Adagh-n-Ifoghas, and the Tassili-n-Ajjer plateau. The tendé pestle-drum (wooden mortar with stretched goatskin head, struck in alternation by two women using wooden pestles) anchors the rhythm while two further women hold the mortar steady — the four-woman configuration is canonical. Women sing antiphonal call-and-response over the tendé pulse, with men sometimes responding from a separate position; men of high social rank participate in the parallel takamba ceremonial repertoire on tehardent three-string lute. The repertoire spans courtship songs, camel-praise songs (the canonical Saharan poetic-praise form), and ceremonial cycles tied to the Festival in the Desert traditions that pre-date the modern eponymous festival. Caroline Card-Wendt's 1976-1978 doctoral fieldwork in the Azawagh (Tuareg Music and Social Identity, Indiana 1982), the AIMP/VDE-Gallo Niger series, Smithsonian Folkways FE 4470 (1960), and the Ocora Nomades du Niger catalog constitute the documentary anchors. Distinguished from sub-Saharan West African griot traditions by Tuareg's pestle-drum-with-women-singers (vs kora-or-balafon-with-griot-singer) instrumental configuration; distinguished from Wolof and Mandé Sahel by the Tamasheq Berber language and Saharan-pastoral repertoire base.

items.name: Maasai adumu warrior jumping-song
items.lineage: Maasai East African pastoral vocal tradition of southern Kenya and northern Tanzania (Kajiado, Narok, Ngorongoro, Serengeti boundary regions). Performance centers on the eunoto warrior-graduation ceremony and adumu jumping-dance: young moran (warriors) in a competitive circle, each leaping vertically to maximum height while the surrounding warriors sing a polyrhythmic guttural-vocal pattern of pitched grunt-and-throat-call accompanied by hyper-rapid breath-and-tongue-clicking and the rhythmic call-and-response of the olaranyani song-leader. No melodic instrument tradition — vocal-only, with the song-leader's melodic line answered by the warrior chorus in unison-or-octave-leap configuration with characteristic vocal-rasp and chest-voice projection. Naomi Kipury's 1983 ethnographic collection (Oral Literature of the Maasai, East African Educational Publishers, Nairobi) and the 2001-2003 Smithsonian Maasai Field Recordings (Daniel Johnson / Simon Saitoti) provide the principal documentation. Repertoire functions span warrior-formation cycles, cattle-praise, ilkipoot-elder oratorical-rhetorical cycles, women's parallel choral repertoire (lipsmacking eunoto-women's songs), and warrior-mourning. Distinguished from neighboring Sukuma and Kikuyu vocal traditions by Maasai's exclusive vocal-only (no instrument) configuration and characteristic guttural-rasp male-warrior projection; distinguished from Samburu (a closely-related Nilotic group) by Maasai's adumu-jumping-as-primary-performance-architecture.

items.name: Ethiopian Tewahedo zema chant
items.lineage: Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo liturgical chant tradition, attributed by tradition to Saint Yared (sixth century), the system's tradition-attribution-founder. The threefold ge'ez modal system — ge'ez (the foundational mode, associated with weekdays and the Lent fasts), ezel (the sober mode, associated with Saturday and funerals), and araray (the festive mode, associated with Sunday celebration and major feasts) — structures the entire liturgical year. Cantor (debteras) train at monastic schools for years to memorize the corpus, with the melekket notation system (handed-down annotated marks in liturgical books indicating melodic formulae) serving as memory-aid rather than full prescription. Performance includes characteristic instruments: tsenatsil sistrum, kebero drum (single conical drumhead with leather lacing), begena ten-string box-lyre (Old-Testament-king-David-iconography, devotional only), and meleket end-blown trumpet (reserved for high feasts). Rock-hewn churches of Lalibela (twelfth century) and Aksumite stone basilicas provide canonical performance contexts. Modal vocabulary draws on the broader Ethiopian qenet pentatonic mode-system with mode-specific cadential formulae. The Kay Kaufman Shelemay and Peter Jeffery three-volume Ethiopian Christian Liturgical Chant: An Anthology (A-R Editions 1993-1997) constitutes the definitive Western scholarly documentation. Distinguished from Coptic Orthodox chant by Tewahedo's ge'ez-ezel-araray three-mode system (vs Coptic's eight-mode oktoechos lineage); distinguished from Syriac Orthodox chant by Ge'ez liturgical-language and Aksumite-Ethiopian regional rite; distinguished from Byzantine chant by absence of ison-drone and presence of instrumental accompaniment in feast contexts.

items.name: Berber ahidus and ahwash (Atlas Mountains)
items.lineage: Berber (Imazighen / Amazigh) collective song-and-dance tradition of the Atlas Mountain ranges across Morocco, with ahidus the central-and-northern Middle-Atlas form (Tamazight-speaking populations) and ahwash the Souss-region southern-Atlas form (Tashelhiyt-speaking populations). Performance involves two facing rows of dancers (mixed men and women in ahidus, often single-sex in ahwash) executing synchronized arm-and-shoulder choreography while singing antiphonal call-and-response over bendir frame-drum accompaniment, with the amdyaz (poet-leader) improvising the opening verse-line that the chorus answers in unison. Modal vocabulary draws on regional pentatonic frameworks with characteristic Atlas-region melodic-contour conventions. The amzwaj poetic-form (couplet-and-response architecture) governs verse structure, with seasonal-and-occasional repertoires for harvest, wedding, and tribal-assembly contexts. Miriam Rovsing Olsen's 1990s Atlas fieldwork (published as Chants et danses de l'Atlas, Actes Sud / Cité de la musique 1997, with Ocora-Radio France C 559035 companion recordings) is the principal scholarly documentation. Distinguished from Berber Rif and Kabyle vocal traditions by Atlas-region poly-strophic verse structure and bendir-frame-drum-dominant percussion; distinguished from Andalusi-Maghrebi nuba by Tamazight-language and outdoor-village (not court-and-chamber) performance context; distinguished from Tuareg by sedentary-village (not nomadic-pastoral) base and bendir (vs tendé pestle-drum) percussion.

items.name: Mongolian khoomei overtone singing
items.lineage: Mongolian khoomei overtone-singing tradition. The technique produces a sustained chest-register fundamental while shaping the vocal tract to amplify upper partials of the harmonic series, generating a clearly audible whistle-tone melody floating above the fundamental. Khalkh-Mongol vocabulary distinguishes several techniques: kharkhiraa (low-register subharmonic kargyraa-equivalent), iisgerekh (mid-register sygyt-equivalent whistle-tone), shakhaa (constricted-throat variant), bagalzuuriin (deep throat-tension), and uyangiin (a singing-leaning lyrical variant). Performance contexts span solo concert, pastoral solo (a shepherd alone on the steppe), morin-khuur-accompanied ensemble, and the contemporary international touring circuit. Sundui, Tserendavaa, and Ganbold are the canonical twentieth-century khoomei masters; the post-1990 Mongolian state cultural-revival has produced a major export of khoomei performers internationally. The Smithsonian Folkways field recordings provide the principal Western-distributed documentation. Distinguished from Tuvan khoomei by Mongolian-Khalkh dialect-specific technique nomenclature and Mongolian-state-cultural-context performance framework (vs Tuvan-state-cultural-context); distinguished from Xhosa umngqokolo by Mongolian khoomei's throat-tension fundamental production (vs Xhosa's chest-register relaxed-fundamental); distinguished from Tibetan multiphonic yang chant by Mongolian khoomei's solo (vs ensemble-monastic) and secular (vs liturgical) configurations.

items.name: Tuvan kargyraa subharmonic throat-singing
items.lineage: Tuvan kargyraa subharmonic throat-singing tradition of the Republic of Tuva (southern Siberia, Russian Federation, bordering northwestern Mongolia). Kargyraa technique produces a fundamental pitched a full octave below the singer's normal speaking range through false-vocal-fold (ventricular) co-oscillation: the true vocal folds vibrate at one frequency while the ventricular folds vibrate at half that frequency, producing a rumbling subharmonic. Over this fundamental the singer shapes upper-partial overtone melodies. Two named regional variants: dag kargyraa ("mountain kargyraa," more open and resonant, associated with the Yenisei river valley) and khovu kargyraa ("steppe kargyraa," more compressed and growling, associated with the dry-steppe lowlands). Performance contexts span solo pastoral, hunters' contexts (the throat-singing reproducing animal-call and natural-sound mimesis), and contemporary international concert circuit. Often accompanied by igil (the two-string upright fiddle that is the Tuvan parallel to Mongolian morin khuur). Ted Levin's Where Rivers and Mountains Sing (Indiana UP 2006) is the principal English-language scholarly documentation; Zoya Kyrgys's The Mystery of Tuvan Khoomei (2002) the principal Tuvan-language reference; Smithsonian Folkways SFW40017 Tuva: Voices from the Center of Asia (1990, Levin/Hunt) the canonical Western-distributed recording. Distinguished from Mongolian kharkhiraa by Tuvan-Tyva dialect-specific technique nomenclature and characteristic dag-vs-khovu regional variants; distinguished from Tibetan yang chant by Tuvan kargyraa's solo-secular (vs ensemble-monastic-liturgical) framework; distinguished from sygyt by kargyraa's low-subharmonic (vs sygyt's high-overtone) register.

items.name: Tuvan sygyt high-whistle overtone
items.lineage: Tuvan sygyt high-whistle overtone-singing tradition of the Republic of Tuva. The sygyt technique produces a clear, piercing whistle-tone in the upper harmonic-series range (typically the eighth through twelfth partials above the fundamental) by tightly constricting the lips and tongue to filter a single overtone out of the harmonic spectrum of a sustained low-register fundamental. The result is a whistle-melody floating two-to-three octaves above the singer's chest-register fundamental drone. Sygyt is the most virtuosic and technically demanding of the Tuvan overtone techniques — masters can sustain a continuous fundamental while producing rapid melodic figures in the whistle-overtone, sometimes with secondary mid-register overtones flickering simultaneously. Performance contexts span solo pastoral, contest contexts at the annual Khoomei-in-the-Center-of-Asia festival in Kyzyl, and international touring. Igil (two-string upright fiddle) or doshpuluur (long-necked plucked lute) sometimes accompany. Anatoli Kuular is among the canonical twentieth-century sygyt masters. Ted Levin's Where Rivers and Mountains Sing (Indiana UP 2006) and Smithsonian Folkways SFW40017 are the principal documentary anchors. Distinguished from Mongolian iisgerekh by Tuvan-Tyva dialect-specific technique nomenclature; distinguished from kargyraa by sygyt's high-overtone (vs kargyraa's subharmonic) register; distinguished from Mongolian khoomei "narrow" technique by Tuvan sygyt's more piercing and precisely-pitched whistle-tone configuration.

items.name: Sakha olonkho heroic epic
items.lineage: Sakha (Yakut) olonkho heroic-epic recital tradition of the Republic of Sakha (Yakutia, far-eastern Siberia, Russian Federation). Olonkhosut epic-reciters perform multi-day continuous recitations of heroic-epic cycles — Nyurgun Bootur the Swift, the canonical olonkho narrative codified in the twentieth-century thirty-six-thousand-verse recension by Platon Oiunsky (1893-1939, founding Sakha writer), provides the type-specimen. Performance alternates between sung-melodic passages for character-voices (each major character has an assigned melodic-mode signature) and rhythmic-recitation narrative passages for the omniscient narrator. Sung passages employ the kylyhakh ornamental vibrato — a characteristic Sakha throat-ornament with a tight, fluttering quality — and the Sakha pentatonic modal vocabulary. The olonkho cycles preserve pre-Christian Sakha cosmology (the three-world division: upper-world abaahy spirits, middle-world humans, lower-world demons), with the Tengrist sky-religion still legible in the cosmographic framing. Performance traditionally in winter, in the balagan log-and-earth dwelling, lasting multiple nights. V.L. Seroshevsky's 1896 ethnography Yakuts is the foundational Russian scholarly documentation; the Soviet-era Sakha Republic cultural-revival institutions provide ongoing transmission infrastructure. Distinguished from Mongolian and Kyrgyz heroic-epic traditions by Sakha-language-specific narrative-cadence grammar and kylyhakh-vibrato vocal-ornament signature; distinguished from Buryat-Mongol epic by Sakha-Yakutia far-eastern Siberian regional dialect.

items.name: Ainu yukar epic recitation
items.lineage: Ainu yukar heroic-epic recitation tradition of Hokkaido (northern Japan) and historically of Sakhalin and the Kuril Islands. Yukar are sung-narrated mytho-heroic cycles featuring the culture-hero Aynurakkur (the Ainu-version of the central-protagonist figure) and adjacent cosmological narratives. Performance involves the chanter (yukar-uta-kur) sitting with a rhythm-stick (rep-ni) struck against the edge of the cise (traditional dwelling) hearth-box, marking a continuous rhythmic pulse beneath the recitation. The narrative voice alternates between named characters; the chanter does not move position but conveys character distinction through subtle vocal-register and melodic-cadence shifts. The yukar parent-form spans related narrative genres: kamuy yukar (god-yukar, cosmological-creation cycles), mat-yukar (women-yukar, female-protagonist cycles), tuita (folk-tales), and uwepeker (didactic-tales). The Bronisław Piłsudski cylinder recordings (1902-1905, preserved at the Phonogrammarchiv in Vienna and reissued by Adam Mickiewicz University in Poznań) are the earliest sound documentation of the tradition; the linguistic-and-cultural scholarship of Kyōsuke Kindaichi and his Ainu informant-collaborators (1910s-1950s) and the subsequent work of Mashiho Chiri (1909-1961, the first major Ainu-descended Ainu-language scholar) constitute the canonical documentary corpus. The closely-related rekuhkara throat-game tradition went extinct in the early twentieth century. Distinguished from Japanese gidayū-bushi by Ainu-language-specific narrative-cadence and rep-ni rhythm-stick (vs shamisen accompaniment) configuration; distinguished from Sakha olonkho by Ainu yukar's sung-and-spoken alternation register and the rep-ni accompaniment.

items.name: Vietnamese ca trù
items.lineage: Vietnamese ca trù chamber-vocal tradition of northern Vietnam. The form crystallized in the fifteenth century in Hanoi guild-house culture and developed through the late-imperial Lê and Nguyễn dynasties as the canonical literary-chamber form for the male literati class. Performance configuration: a female singer (ả đào) accompanies herself on the phách bamboo clapper (struck with a hardwood stick to mark cadence), with a male instrumentalist on đàn đáy (three-string long-necked fretted lute with unusually high frets enabling string-bending ornament) and a male patron-listener on the trống chầu praise-drum (struck to signal critical acclaim during performance — the patron is structurally part of the ensemble through this critical-response convention). The repertoire comprises forty-six canonical "thể-types" (poetic-meter categories) including hát nói (sung-recitation), múa bài bông (flower-offering dance accompaniment), hát giai (banquet song), and others — each thể with characteristic rhythmic-and-melodic conventions. Lyric base draws on classical Sino-Vietnamese poetic-meter forms. The mid-twentieth-century revolutionary-period cultural-policy suppressed ca trù as feudal, leading to near-extinction; the post-1990 revival under the guild-house Câu Lạc Bộ Ca Trù Hà Nội (Hanoi Ca Trù Club) and master-singer Quách Thị Hồ (1909-2001) restored continuity. Distinguished from southern Vietnamese hát ả đào by northern-dialect-specific cadential conventions; distinguished from chèo folk-opera by ca trù's solo-singer-with-chamber-trio (vs ensemble-theatrical) configuration; distinguished from quan họ by literary-chamber (vs village-festival-call-and-response) functional context.

The form crystallized in the fifteenth century in Hanoi guild-house culture and developed through the late-imperial Lê and Nguyễn dynasties as the canonical literary-chamber form for the male literati class. The repertoire comprises forty-six canonical "thể-types" (poetic-meter categories).
exemplars: Barley Norton — Songs for the Spirits (U. Illinois 2009)

items.name: Vietnamese quan họ Bắc Ninh
items.lineage: Vietnamese quan họ Bắc Ninh antiphonal courtship-song tradition of the Bắc Ninh province, the Red River Delta region north of Hanoi. Performance involves paired female-and-male choral groups (liền chị women, liền anh men) from neighboring villages who exchange improvised verse-and-response over the course of a year of festival visits, with the courtship-exchange the formal narrative-arc of the repertoire. Vocal style features unaccompanied (originally — modern stage performance often adds chamber-ensemble accompaniment) two-or-three-voice female and male chorus in heterophonic-melodic-elaboration register, with characteristic Vietnamese pentatonic-modal vocabulary and the distinctive vibrato-ornament called nẩy hột ("rice-grain vibrato," a precisely-articulated rapid pitch-and-amplitude wobble unique to quan họ vocal-aesthetic). Verse-forms draw on canonical four-line, six-eight-line, and seven-seven-six-eight Vietnamese poetic-meter structures. The forty-nine documented "kết-chạ" (sworn-sister-village) pair-relationships constitute the social-structural infrastructure of the tradition. Documentation records two hundred and forty-nine quan họ villages across the region. Distinguished from ca trù by quan họ's village-festival-collective (vs chamber-literary) functional context; distinguished from xoan (the adjacent ritual-village tradition) by quan họ's courtship-exchange (vs ancestor-veneration) functional framing; distinguished from southern Vietnamese đờn ca tài tử by northern Red-River-Delta dialect-specific cadential conventions.

items.name: Vietnamese hát xoan
items.lineage: Vietnamese hát xoan ancestral-spring-ritual song tradition of Phú Thọ province, the heartland of the Hùng-Kings legendary first-Vietnamese-dynasty mythos. Performance occurs at the Hùng-Kings temple (Đền Hùng) and adjacent communal-house đình precincts during the lunar new-year and Hùng-Kings death-anniversary festivals (lunar tenth day of third month). Three movement types: thờ (worship, slow ceremonial-cadence verse for ancestor-veneration), quả cách (formal-narrative cyclical sections, fourteen canonical pieces), and hội (festival, faster celebratory cadence with audience-participation call-and-response). Performance configuration: a male choir of phường xoan villagers from one of four canonical guild-villages (An Thái, Phù Đức, Kim Đới, Thét), accompanied by phách bamboo clapper and trống cơm small barrel-drum. Modal vocabulary draws on Vietnamese pentatonic with mode-specific cadential conventions. The tradition was nearly extinct by the 1990s, but systematic transmission-revival has since spread across the four guild-villages. Distinguished from quan họ by xoan's ritual-ancestor-veneration (vs courtship-festival) functional framing; distinguished from ca trù by xoan's village-collective-male-choir (vs chamber-female-soloist) ensemble configuration.

items.name: Cambodian chapei dang veng
items.lineage: Cambodian chapei dang veng narrative-and-improvisatory song tradition. The chapei (two-string long-neck fretted plucked lute) accompanies a single male singer-performer who alternates between strophic-narrative verse passages (drawing on Khmer historical-epic, Reamker / Ramayana, and contemporary-social-commentary repertoires) and improvised satirical-and-praise-poetry verses that respond to the present audience and occasion. The form is genealogically connected to broader Southeast-Asian narrative-poet traditions (the Lao mor lam genealogically adjacent, the Thai mor lam-thai also related) and to the Indic-derived bardic-poet lineages that traveled along the Theravada Buddhist transmission routes. Performance contexts span village wedding feasts, temple-festival night entertainments, and the post-1980 revival concert circuit. The Khmer Rouge era 1975-1979 nearly extinguished the tradition (only a handful of master practitioners survived); the post-1980 revival has been driven by master Kong Nay (born 1944, blind from childhood, the canonical twentieth-century chapei singer) and his students under the Cambodian Living Arts foundation. Modal vocabulary draws on the seven-equal-tempered tuning shared with broader Khmer classical traditions. Distinguished from pinpeat by chapei's solo-narrative-with-lute (vs court-ensemble) configuration; distinguished from Lao mor lam by Khmer-language repertoire and chapei (vs khaen mouth-organ) instrumental accompaniment; distinguished from Cambodian smot Buddhist-chant by chapei's secular-narrative (vs liturgical) functional context.

items.name: Hudhud chants of the Ifugao
items.lineage: Ifugao hudhud chant tradition of the Cordillera mountain region of northern Luzon, Philippines. The hudhud is a sung narrative-recital cycle performed by an elder female cantor (mumbaki) with chorus response, during agricultural work in the rice terraces (rice-transplanting and rice-harvesting), at wakes for the dead, and during the bogwa exhumation-and-reburial ceremony. Individual hudhud recitations can extend to days, and the canonical hudhud cycles narrate the deeds of culture-heroes Aliguyon, Bugan, and other Ifugao mytho-historical figures across hundreds of episodes. Performance involves the cantor's solo recitative-melodic line answered by the choral group in unison-or-octave response, with characteristic terminal pitch-drop closing each verse and a narrow-range melodic vocabulary built around three-to-five pitches. The Ifugao language is a Northern Philippine Cordilleran language; the hudhud repertoire preserves archaic Ifugao narrative-poetic conventions. Father Francis Lambrecht (Belgian CICM missionary, 1950s-1960s Kiangan-region fieldwork) produced the foundational documentation; the Kiangan municipality cantor lineage continues active transmission. Distinguished from neighboring Cordilleran traditions (Kalinga, Bontoc, Kankanaey, Tinguian) by Ifugao's narrow-range narrative-recital cycle and rice-terrace-work functional context; distinguished from lowland Philippine vocal traditions by Cordilleran-mountain-region pre-colonial continuity.

items.name: Korean gagok lyric-song
items.lineage: Korean gagok lyric-song tradition. Gagok is the formal courtly literary-chamber lyric-song genre of the Joseon-dynasty literati class (yangban), with origins traced to the late Goryeo through middle-Joseon periods (fifteenth-seventeenth centuries) and the canonical repertoire codified through the Cheong-gu-yeong-eon and Hae-dong-ga-yo song-book anthologies. Performance configuration: solo singer (male or female, with distinct namchang men's-repertoire and yeochang women's-repertoire repertoires) accompanied by the canonical jeongak ensemble — geomungo (six-string fretted board-zither, struck with bamboo plectrum), gayageum (twelve-string moveable-bridge plucked board-zither), daegeum (large bamboo end-blown flute), piri (cylindrical-bore double-reed pipe), haegeum (two-string upright fiddle), and janggu (hourglass barrel-drum). Twenty-six canonical men's songs and fifteen canonical women's songs constitute the core repertoire. Sijo poetic-form (three-line structure: initial verse, parallel verse, conclusion-with-twist) provides the lyric base. Slow tempo (a single song can take ten to fifteen minutes), wide melisma, and characteristic pitch-and-amplitude vibrato (nonghyeon) define the vocal aesthetic. Cho Soon-ja and Lee Dong-gyu among the twentieth-century canonical performers; the National Gugak Center maintains the institutional transmission. Distinguished from sijo (the closely-related but more austere sung-poetry form) by gagok's full ensemble accompaniment and longer melodic-elaboration register; distinguished from gasa (the longer narrative-lyric form) by gagok's strict sijo-poetic-meter base; distinguished from minyo folk-song by gagok's literary-chamber-with-jeongak-ensemble functional context.

items.name: Jeju haenyeo songs
items.lineage: Jeju Island haenyeo women's sea-diving culture and accompanying song repertoire. The haenyeo ("sea women") of Jeju are women who free-dive (without breathing apparatus, in pre-modern leather-suit and modern wetsuit) to harvest shellfish, sea-urchin, sea-cucumber, and seaweed from the seabed around the island. The accompanying song repertoire includes ieo-do-sa-na (the rowing song sung while paddling out to the diving grounds, with distinctive sumbisori-breath-whistle as the haenyeo surface for air), nodeu-jak (the work-song sung between dives on the boat or rocky shore), and minyo (general folk-song repertoire). Vocal style features unaccompanied female-group antiphonal call-and-response with characteristic Jeju-dialect-specific melodic-contour conventions and a chest-register projection developed through the sea-diving-breath-control discipline. The tradition is matrilineal (mother-to-daughter transmission) and tied to the haenyeo cooperative-economic-collective structure (the village haenyeo guild divides diving territories and harvest income collectively). The 2016 ICH inscription explicitly frames the entire haenyeo culture as the heritage element, with the song repertoire as one component alongside diving practice, ecological knowledge, and the collective social structure. Field-recording archive at the Jeju Haenyeo Museum constitutes the institutional documentary base. Distinguished from mainland Korean minyo by Jeju-dialect-specific vocabulary and sea-diving-work functional context; distinguished from Japanese ama-diver tradition by Jeju's antiphonal-group-song and matrilineal cooperative-economic structure.

items.name: Chinese kunqu opera
items.lineage: Chinese kunqu opera. Kunqu crystallized in the Kunshan region (south of Suzhou, Jiangsu province) during the late Ming dynasty (1550-1560, sixteenth century) under the founding theorist-composer Wei Liangfu (c.1489-1566), who codified the kunqu-tunes system based on the older Kunshan-region folk-tune vocabulary. The genre flourished through the Ming-Qing transition as the dominant elite-class theatrical-and-musical form, with the canonical play-cycles of the Mudan Ting (Peony Pavilion, 1598, Tang Xianzu) and Changsheng Dian (Palace of Eternal Life, 1688, Hong Sheng) constituting the core repertoire. Performance integrates singing, stylized dance-movement, recited dialogue, and instrumental accompaniment in a fully-integrated theatrical form. Vocal style features wide melisma, characteristic dyhayou portamento sliding-pitch ornament, and an elaborate ornament-vocabulary tied to specific text-tones and emotion-categories. The accompanying ensemble centers on the qudi flute (the principal melodic carrier, a transverse bamboo flute), sanxian (three-string plucked lute), pipa (four-string pear-shaped plucked lute), and a percussion battery for theatrical-cue work. The mid-twentieth-century cultural-revolutionary period nearly extinguished the form; the post-1980 revival under conservatory programs and the touring company circuit has restored continuity. Yu Zhenfei (1902-1993) is among the twentieth-century canonical performers. Distinguished from later Beijing opera (jingju) by kunqu's elite-literary-elegant register and slower tempo; distinguished from Cantonese opera (yueju) by Wu-Mandarin lyric-language and Jiangnan-region cadential conventions.

items.name: Tibetan ache lhamo opera
items.lineage: Tibetan ache lhamo ("sister-goddess") folk-opera tradition. Origin traced by tradition to the fourteenth-century yogi-engineer-saint Thangtong Gyalpo, who is said to have founded the form and organized the first performance-troupe to raise funds for his iron-chain suspension-bridge construction projects across Tibet. The canonical repertoire comprises eight classical plays drawn from Indo-Tibetan Buddhist narrative cycles, including Sukyi Nyima (the deer-girl), Drowa Sangmo (the celestial-bride), Chöyi Nyima, Pema Wöbar, Drimé Künden, Nangsa Wöbum, Gyasa Belsa, and Donyö Dondrup. Performance integrates singing (with distinctive named melodic-modes), stylized dance-and-mime movement, recited dialogue, and percussion accompaniment (rolmo large paired cymbals and damaru double-headed hand-drum the principal instruments — no melodic instruments, the form is essentially voice-and-percussion). The Lhasa-region Kyumolung style and the Shang and Gyenpa regional styles constitute the three main lineages. Performance traditionally outdoors during summer festivals, particularly the Shotön (yogurt-festival) at Norbulingka in Lhasa. The Tibetan Institute of Performing Arts (TIPA, Dharamshala, India) maintains the principal exile-community transmission lineage post-1959. Distinguished from the parallel monastic-liturgical yang chant by ache lhamo's secular-narrative (vs liturgical) functional framework and absence of long-trumpets and double-reed monastic-ensemble instrumentation; distinguished from Chinese jingju by Tibetan-language repertoire and characteristic voice-and-percussion-only ensemble configuration.

items.name: Tibetan multiphonic yang chant
items.lineage: Tibetan Buddhist monastic multiphonic yang chant tradition of the Gelug-school tantric colleges Gyuto and Gyume (founded 1474 and 1485, respectively, by Sherab Sengge, a direct disciple of Tsongkhapa). The yang chant technique produces a chest-register-pitched fundamental enriched with audible upper-partial overtones such that a single voice produces what sounds like a chord — the third, fifth, and sometimes higher partials being amplified into clearly audible voice-leading register. Multiple monks chanting in unison produce a thick texture of fundamental-plus-overtones across the assembly. Repertoire centers on the Lama Chöpa (Guru Puja), the Yamantaka tantric cycles, the Guhyasamaja tantric cycles, and the Chakrasamvara tantric cycles. Accompaniment by the canonical monastic-ensemble percussion: rolmo large paired cymbals, dril-bu small hand-bell, damaru double-headed hand-drum, dung-chen long telescoping copper-or-brass trumpet (the four-meter-long ceremonial instrument, played in pairs, capable of producing the very-low subharmonic that anchors the ensemble), rgya-gling double-reed oboe (the melodic-leading instrument when wind voices are present), and kangling thigh-bone trumpet (for specific wrathful-deity cycles). Huston Smith's 1967 Music of Tibet recordings (GemsTone GT1003-CD reissue 2005) and David Lewiston's 1971 Nonesuch Explorer H-72071 Tibetan Ritual Music constitute the principal Western-distributed documentation. Distinguished from Mongolian khoomei by Tibetan yang chant's ensemble (vs solo) and liturgical (vs secular) framework; distinguished from Sakya-school chant by Gelug-specific tantric-cycle repertoire; distinguished from Bön pre-Buddhist Tibetan chant by Buddhist tantric-text base.

items.name: Japanese gidayū-bushi (Bunraku narration)
items.lineage: Japanese gidayū-bushi sung-and-spoken narration tradition, the canonical narrative-vocal style of ningyō jōruri Bunraku puppet-theater. Named after the founding seventeenth-century narrator Takemoto Gidayū (1651-1714), who codified the style at the Takemoto-za puppet-theater in Osaka beginning in 1684 and whose canonical works (such as the Sonezaki Shinjū love-suicide play, 1703, written by his collaborator Chikamatsu Monzaemon) established the genre's core repertoire. Bunraku-as-form. Performance configuration: a single tayū (narrator) sits on a raised platform stage-right, holding the maruhon scroll-text and shifting between speaking voices for multiple characters and the omniscient narrator, while a shamisen player (three-string plucked lute, specifically the heavy-bodied futozao shamisen reserved for jōruri) sits beside providing accompaniment that is structurally inseparable from the vocal narration — a single composition of tayū-and-shamisen voice. The narrative style spans a vast emotional and acoustic range: from quiet bedchamber confidence to climactic suicide-scene wails, from comedic banter to mortal-injury death-rattle, with the tayū employing a striking range of voice-types and registers. Repertoire genealogically connected to the older Heike-monogatari biwa-narrative and to the medieval Buddhist sermon-chant traditions. Twentieth-century canonical tayū include Toyotake Yamashiro-no-Shōjō, Takemoto Tsudayū, and contemporary masters of the National Bunraku Theatre lineage. Distinguished from gagaku court music by gidayū's narrative-theatrical (vs ceremonial-orchestral) functional framework; distinguished from kabuki nagauta by jōruri's puppet-theater accompaniment context.

items.name: Rajasthani Manganiyar tradition
items.lineage: Rajasthani Manganiyar hereditary musician tradition of the Thar Desert region of western Rajasthan, India (Jaisalmer, Barmer, and Jodhpur districts), with the parallel Langa community sharing many features. The Manganiyar are Muslim-by-religion-but-Hindu-by-patron-relation hereditary musicians whose performance-economic configuration centers on the jajmani patron-relationship: each Manganiyar family is bound to specific Rajput patron-families across generations, performing at patron weddings, births, and funerals as the ritual-and-aesthetic specialist providers. Canonical instrumentation: kamaicha (gourd-bowled bowed lute with sympathetic strings) as the primary melodic carrier in deeper-register sustained-tone repertoire, plus khartal wooden-castanet-pair, dholak two-headed barrel drum, and sometimes algoza double-flute or sarangi. Repertoire spans devotional Sufi qawwali-adjacent material, Rajput court-praise repertoire, panihari water-bearer women's-song accompaniment, and the canonical drone-and-narrative-improvisation pieces such as Niambat Khan and Padharo Mhare Des. Modal vocabulary draws on regional raga-frameworks distinct from Hindustani classical but related — the Manganiyar mode-system uses approximately just-intonation tonal hierarchies. Komal Kothari's Rupayan Sansthan in Borunda (founded 1960s) and the Archives & Research Center for Ethnomusicology (AIIS Gurugram, Shubha Chaudhuri) provide the principal scholarly documentation; Daniel Neuman & Shubha Chaudhuri's Bards, Ballads and Boundaries (Seagull 2006) anchors the contemporary scholarship. Sakar Khan and Anwar Khan among the canonical twentieth-century kamaicha and singing masters. Distinguished from Hindustani classical by Manganiyar's jajmani-patron-relationship economic structure and folk-classical hybrid modal system; distinguished from Langa (the parallel Sindhi-influenced hereditary community) by Manganiyar-Marwari dialect and Rajput-patron-relationship base.

items.name: Croatian klapa Dalmatian close-harmony
items.lineage: Croatian klapa Dalmatian close-harmony multipart-singing tradition of the Adriatic coastal region (Split, Šibenik, Zadar, Dubrovnik and the Adriatic islands). The classical klapa configuration is a male a-cappella quartet or quintet: lead tenor (prvi tenor), second tenor (drugi tenor), baritone (bariton), and bass (bas), with the optional addition of a second bass voice for fuller texture. Vocal architecture features close-harmony chordal-block writing (almost always homophonic, with all voices moving together rhythmically), characteristic Mediterranean modal-tonal ambiguity (major-mode tonic with frequent flattened-seventh and minor-mode plagal cadences), and the canonical klapa "Dalmatian" intonation with slightly stretched intervals producing a bright, resonant ensemble sound when sung in stone-walled outdoor narrow-street alleys (the canonical performance acoustic). Repertoire spans the dramatic Mediterranean-coastal love-and-loss ballad cycles, the religious-procession-and-feast-day repertoire, sea-and-fishing lament cycles, and the contemporary klapa-festival-composed repertoire of newer pieces in the traditional style. Klapa Cambi, Klapa Šufit, and Klapa Sebenico among the canonical twentieth-century ensembles. The annual Omiš Festival of Dalmatian Klapa (founded 1967) constitutes the principal performance-and-competition venue. Distinguished from Sardinian cantu a tenore by Croatian klapa's close-harmony tonal-chord-block (vs Sardinian drone-and-overtone) architecture; distinguished from Corsican paghjella by Croatian's four-or-five-voice quartet-with-bass (vs Corsican's three-voice male-trio) configuration; distinguished from Albanian iso-polyphony by Croatian's tonal-chord-block (vs Albanian iso-drone) foundation.

items.name: Croatian Istrian two-part-in-Istrian-scale
items.lineage: Croatian Istrian two-part-in-Istrian-scale (dvoglasno pjevanje na tijesno) tradition of the Istrian peninsula (northwestern Croatian Adriatic coast, with related material in adjacent Slovenian Istria). The form is a two-voice male diaphonic vocal practice in which the two voices move in characteristic parallel-second-and-minor-third intervals, ending each phrase strictly in unison-or-octave cadence, all within the non-tempered six-tone Istrian scale codified in the 1920s by composer-theorist Ivan Matetić Ronjgov (1880-1960). The Istrian scale is a regional folk-tonal system with paired-second intervallic structure and characteristic non-tempered intonation that no Western equal-tempered transcription captures faithfully. Performance involves the lead voice (kantadur) and the answering voice (kontradur), with the two singers standing close together and projecting outward in unison facing the audience or open landscape. Parallel instrumental form exists in the sopele (paired large-and-small conical-bore double-reed shawms playing the same intervallic vocabulary as the two voices) and the šurla (similar paired shawms in the southern Istrian dialect). Performance contexts include outdoor village squares, processions, and the contemporary folk-festival circuit. Distinguished from broader Croatian klapa by Istrian's two-voice diaphonic (vs four-voice close-harmony) architecture and non-tempered Istrian-scale (vs twelve-tet tonal-chordal) vocabulary; distinguished from Slovenian-folk-singing by Istrian-specific Croatian regional dialect.
items.description: Croatian Istrian two-part-in-Istrian-scale (dvoglasno pjevanje na tijesno) tradition of the Istrian peninsula (northwestern Croatian Adriatic coast, with related material in adjacent Slovenian Istria). The form is a two-voice male diaphonic vocal practice in which the two voices move in characteristic parallel-second-and-minor-third intervals, ending each phrase strictly in unison-or-octave cadence, all within the non-tempered six-tone Istrian scale codified in the 1920s by composer-theorist Ivan Matetić Ronjgov. Performance involves the lead voice (kantadur) and the answering voice (kontradur). Parallel instrumental form exists in the sopele paired large-and-small conical-bore double-reed shawms.

items.name: Macedonian Glasoechko male diaphonic
items.lineage: Macedonian Glasoechko male two-voice diaphonic singing tradition of the Dolni Polog and Drimkol-Golo Brdo regions of western North Macedonia. The form features two-voice male singing in characteristic parallel-second and minor-third intervals over a sustained drone-tone (often an organ-point sustained by the second voice while the lead voice elaborates the melodic content), with most phrases cadencing on a unison-or-octave close. Distinguished from neighboring Balkan two-voice traditions by Glasoechko's Mijak-and-Šop dialect-specific cadential vocabulary and the characteristic Macedonian-pastoral functional context. The melodic vocabulary draws on regional pastoral-and-shepherd-call modal frameworks with characteristic narrow-range melodic-contour conventions. Accompanying instrumental contexts sometimes include the kaval end-blown shepherd-flute and the gajda Balkan bagpipe with double-reed chanter and drone-pipe. Performance traditionally outdoors in mountain-pasture contexts during summer transhumance, with the long-distance acoustic projection of the two-voice configuration suited to mountain-valley environments. The mid-twentieth-century rural depopulation of the Polog and Drimkol regions reduced active practitioners. Distinguished from Croatian Istrian diaphonic by Macedonian Glasoechko's drone-and-melody (vs Istrian's strict-two-voice-parallel) configuration and Macedonian-pastoral functional context; distinguished from Albanian iso-polyphony by Glasoechko's two-voice (vs Albanian three-or-four-voice) configuration; distinguished from neighboring Bulgarian male diaphonic by Macedonian-Mijak-dialect-specific cadential conventions.

items.name: Lithuanian sutartinės multipart
items.lineage: Lithuanian sutartinės multipart-singing tradition of northeastern Lithuania (Aukštaitija region). Sutartinės are female-group (occasionally mixed-or-male) polyphonic songs in characteristic parallel-second intervals — two-or-three voices moving in tight major-second-and-minor-second clusters, with strict canonical-imitative entry-patterns at the second or fourth. The genre includes vocal-only (sutartinės-as-song) and instrumental variants performed on kanklės (board zither, finger-plucked) and skudučiai (multiple-tube pan-pipes played by multiple players in hocketed pattern, with each player blowing only one tube and the melodic line resulting from the rapid alternation across players). Sutartinė structure typically alternates between an opening-formula sung by one voice, an answering response from the second voice, and the eventual building-up of the canonical two-or-three-voice texture. Repertoire spans work-song accompaniment, calendar-rite celebrations, wedding-cycle songs, and the broader Baltic narrow-range narrative-poetic tradition. Modal vocabulary draws on the Lithuanian sutartinės parallel-seconds vocabulary, considered one of the most archaic tonal systems in Europe with possible deep Indo-European ritual-music continuity. Zenonas Slaviūnas's three-volume 1820-sutartinė edition (1958-1959) is the foundational corpus-documentation; Stasys Paliulis's instrumental-sutartinė collection complements the vocal corpus; Distinguished from Latvian dainas by Lithuanian sutartinės parallel-seconds polyphonic configuration (vs Latvian-dainas-as-mostly-monophonic-or-heterophonic); distinguished from Estonian Setu leelo by Lithuanian's strict-canonical-imitation (vs Setu's call-and-response-with-drone-bourdon) architecture.

items.name: Estonian Setu leelo polyphonic song
items.lineage: Estonian Setu leelo polyphonic women's-song tradition of the Setu region (southeast Estonia and adjacent Pechory district of Russia). The Setu are a distinct Estonian-and-Russian-borderland Finno-Ugric ethnic group whose linguistic-cultural identity preserves archaic Finno-Ugric features lost in mainstream Estonian. Leelo is performed by a women's group with the lead singer (sõnoline, "the word-singer") improvising the verse text and melodic line, answered by the choral group (torrõ, "the resonators") in unison or in a sustained drone-bourdon below the melodic line. The drone configuration distinguishes leelo from neighboring Baltic polyphonic traditions: the torrõ chorus holds a sustained pedal-tone while the sõnoline elaborates above, producing a drone-and-melodic-elaboration register more akin to certain Slavic and Central-Asian traditions than to the parallel-second sutartinė style. Vocabulary draws on a regional Estonian-Setu pentatonic-leaning modal system. Verse-form is Kalevala-meter (the canonical Finno-Ugric four-stress eight-syllable line shared with the Finnish-Karelian Kalevala epic). Repertoire spans calendar-rite celebrations, wedding-cycle songs (Setu weddings featured the most elaborated leelo repertoire, with sung-confrontation-and-praise sequences between bride-and-groom parties), funeral-lament cycles, and the contemporary Värska-Obinitsa Setu cultural-festival circuit. Mipu Music MIPUCD 104 — Setusongs (1991, recorded May 1990) provides the canonical Western-distributed documentation. Distinguished from Lithuanian sutartinės by Setu leelo's drone-and-melody (vs Lithuanian parallel-seconds) configuration; distinguished from Karelian rune-singing by Setu's antiphonal-with-drone (vs Karelian's strict-alternation) architecture; distinguished from mainland Estonian regilaul by Setu-dialect-specific vocabulary and Estonian-Russian-borderland regional context.

items.name: Swedish kulning herding-call
items.lineage: Swedish kulning (and the cognate Norwegian kuløkk and laling) high-volume female herding-call tradition of the mountain-pasture fäbod summer-grazing settlements of central and northern Sweden (Dalarna, Hälsingland, Härjedalen, and Jämtland provinces) and adjacent western Norway. Performed by women (the milkmaids who managed cattle and goats at the summer pastures) as a long-distance projecting call to bring grazing animals home at evening milking-time, kulning developed as a specialized vocal-projection technique using a tightly-focused upper-chest-and-head register that can carry several kilometers across mountain valleys. The technique employs characteristic ornamentation: a rapid initial pitch-glide upward to the calling-pitch, characteristic falling-fourth and falling-fifth interval ornaments, and a distinctive crystalline high-register timbre produced by tight glottal-and-supralaryngeal compression. Repertoire spans the practical herding-calls (lockrop) used to summon specific animals, calling-songs (lockläte) sung to entertain or comfort the cattle, and the broader corpus of fäbod-related work-song. The Svenskt visarkiv (Swedish Folk Music Archive) field-recordings beginning in the 1940s, and Susanne Rosenberg's twenty-first-century scholarship and performance, anchor the documentation. The mid-twentieth-century industrialization of Swedish dairy-farming eliminated the fäbod system as functional infrastructure; kulning persists as a heritage-art practice with active transmission through folk-music schools and concert-revival performers including Jonna Jinton in the post-2010 social-media revival. Distinguished from Norwegian kuløkk by Swedish-dialect-specific vocabulary and Dalarna-Härjedalen regional fäbod context; distinguished from Sámi yoik by kulning's pastoral-call functional context (vs yoik's personal-and-ancestor-evocation function) and tight-focused projection technique (vs yoik's nasal-resonance and narrow-range vocabulary).

items.name: Northern Sámi luohti yoik
items.lineage: Northern Sámi luohti yoik tradition of the Sápmi region of northern Norway, Sweden, Finland, and the Russian Kola Peninsula. Luohti is the principal yoik subgenre of the Northern Sámi (Davvisámegiella-speaking) population — a sung-vocal form whose conceptual orientation is fundamentally different from Western lyric song: a yoik does not sing "about" its subject but rather is the subject — to yoik a person, a place, or an animal is to evoke and bring-present that subject through the act of yoiking. Vocal style features narrow-range melody (two-to-five pitches typically), characteristic nasal-resonant timbre, characteristic descending-melodic-contour shapes, repeated melodic-formula cycling, and a strikingly non-strophic open-ended performance temporality (a yoik does not have a definite beginning or ending — the singer enters and exits a yoik mid-phrase). Pre-tempered tonal system with characteristic fourth, fifth, and octave intervals as the structural skeleton. Repertoire is personal: each Sámi person traditionally has an assigned-or-received luohti that names them, and natural-feature luohti exist for specific mountains, lakes, and reindeer-herd boundaries. The Sámi Christian-mission suppression-era 1850s-1950s pushed the tradition underground; the post-1970s Sámi cultural revival (anchored in the founding of the Sámi Parliament and the Sami University College) has restored public-performance space, with figures such as Nils-Aslak Valkeapää, Mari Boine, and Wimme Saari among the canonical twentieth-century revival figures. Arnt Bakke's 1949-1972 field-recording collection at UiT The Norwegian Arctic University Museum (Tromsø) and Ola Graff's continued 1982-2019 collection constitute the principal documentary anchor. Distinguished from Skolt and Southern Sámi yoik by Northern-Sámi-Davvisámegiella dialect; distinguished from Finnish joiku by language-specific cadential and intonation vocabulary.

items.name: Skolt Sámi leuʹdd
items.lineage: Skolt Sámi leuʹdd vocal tradition of the Skolt Sámi (Nuõrttsää'mǩiõll-speaking) population of the easternmost Sámi homeland — historically the Pechenga (Petsamo) region of the Russian Kola Peninsula, displaced post-1944 to the Sevettijärvi-Nellim region of northeastern Finland. Leuʹdd differs from the Northern Sámi luohti in functional orientation: rather than the open-ended personal-or-natural-feature evocation of luohti, leuʹdd are narrative-personal-history songs telling the life-stories of specific individuals (the singer's own life, or the life of a deceased relative). The leuʹdd repertoire thus constitutes an oral-historical archive of the Skolt Sámi community, particularly significant given the community's displacement-trauma history. Vocal style features narrow-range melody (often even narrower than Northern Sámi luohti, sometimes restricted to three pitches), with characteristic micro-pitch-inflection on syllables, narrative-strophic structure (longer narratives extending across many strophes with melodic-formula return), and a more text-bearing register than luohti's pure-sound-evocation. The Skolt Sámi were converted to Russian Orthodoxy (not Lutheran like the Northern Sámi), so leuʹdd survived alongside Orthodox liturgical chant rather than under the suppression-pressure of the Lutheran Sámi-mission. The Marko Jouste-led Saami Culture Archive at the University of Oulu maintains the primary documentation; the Sevettijärvi leuʹdd ensemble continues active transmission. Distinguished from Northern Sámi luohti by Skolt-dialect-specific narrative-personal-history (vs luohti-evocation) functional framework; distinguished from Southern Sámi vuelie by Skolt-Sámi Kola Peninsula regional origin and post-1944 Finnish-displacement context.

items.name: Southern Sámi vuelie
items.lineage: Southern Sámi vuelie yoik tradition of the Southern Sámi (Åarjelsaemien gïele-speaking) population of central Norway and adjacent Swedish Härjedalen and Jämtland. Vuelie ("yoik" in the Southern Sámi language) features differ from the Northern Sámi luohti and Skolt leuʹdd: typically a slightly wider melodic range, a more strophic-and-cyclical formal structure, and characteristic ornamental conventions distinct from the Northern Sámi vocabulary. The Southern Sámi homeland is the most geographically southern and linguistically distinct of the Sámi communities, with the language considered the most endangered of the Sámi languages. Repertoire spans the personal-evocation yoik (parallel to Northern Sámi luohti), the place-and-reindeer-herd vuelie, and the narrative-historical sequences. The Southern Sámi mid-twentieth-century cultural-revival lineage — including Frode Fjellheim, whose contemporary vuelie composition "Eatnemen Vuelie" featured in the 2013 Disney film Frozen, bringing international visibility — has restored public-performance space for the tradition. Heikki Laitinen's scholarship in Folkmusik i Sverige (Lundberg & Ternhag 2005) provides Swedish-side documentation; the Norwegian Sami Center maintains parallel institutional infrastructure. Distinguished from Northern Sámi luohti by Southern-Sámi dialect and characteristic wider-range cyclical-strophic structure; distinguished from Skolt leuʹdd by Southern Sámi's evocation-and-place (vs Skolt narrative-personal-history) functional framework; distinguished from Lule and Pite Sámi (the intermediate dialect-regions) by southern-most-geographic origin and the distinct Åarjelsaemien linguistic-cultural identity.
