Goliardic Carmina Burana Italian-university lineage canonical

items.name: Scottish bothy ballad (Northeast farm-laborer drinking-song)
items.lineage: Scottish bothy-ballad tradition continuous from 19th-century Northeast-Scotland Aberdeenshire-and-Moray farm-laborer (bothy = "farm-laborer's outbuilding") drinking-and-grievance-song tradition through 20th-century revival into modern Scottish-folk-revival continuous practice; the bothy-ballads document farm-laborer drinking-and-courting-and-employer-grievance life in agricultural-Scotland 1840s-1900s
items.description: The Scottish bothy-ballad tradition continuous from 19th-century Northeast-Scotland Aberdeenshire-and-Moray farm-laborer (bothy = "farm-laborer's outbuilding," the seasonal-housing for unmarried farm-laborers) drinking-and-grievance-song tradition through 20th-century revival (the canonical Greig-Duncan Folk Song Collection 1900-1914 documents the bothy-ballad corpus) into modern Scottish-folk-revival continuous practice. The bothy-ballads document farm-laborer drinking-and-courting-and-employer-grievance life in agricultural-Scotland 1840s-1900s with characteristic Scots-language text register, narrative-verse-and-chorus structure, Scottish-modal melodic vocabulary, characteristic strophic-narrative arrangement. Distinguished from the broader Scottish-and-Irish pub-drinking-song tradition by the specific agricultural-laborer occupational context.
exemplars: Greig-Duncan Folk Song Collection 1900-1914 (canonical scholarly documentation)

items.name: Czech pijácká píseň (drinking song)
items.lineage: Czech drinking-song (pijácká píseň) tradition continuous from medieval Bohemian-tavern-song origins through 19th-century Czech-Republican-era Smetana-and-Dvořák-folk-collection era continuous through 20th-century Czechoslovak-and-Czech continuous pub-practice; foundational repertoire includes "Pivo, pivo, pivo" (Beer, beer, beer)
items.description: The Czech drinking-song (pijácká píseň) tradition continuous from medieval Bohemian-tavern-song origins through 19th-century Czech-Republican-era Smetana-and-Dvořák-folk-collection era (the Czech-folk-collection movement documented the broader pijácká corpus integrated into the Czech national-music project) continuous through 20th-century Czechoslovak-and-Czech continuous pub-practice (the Czech pivnice and hospoda beer-pub culture is the documented context). Foundational repertoire includes "Pivo, pivo, pivo" (Beer, beer, beer — canonical), "Šel rytíř na koni" (the knight rode on horseback — drinking-narrative), "U panského dvora" (canonical Bohemian-folk-drinking), "Trio, kde jsi kde" canonical Czech-Republican-era. Defined by accordion-and-voice arrangement, Czech-language text register, festive uptempo crowd-singing arrangement, characteristic Czech-beer-pub context.
exemplars: Karel Hašler — Czech early-20th-century drinking-song canonical

items.name: Hungarian bordal (wine song)
items.lineage: Hungarian bordal (wine-song) tradition continuous from medieval-Hungarian wine-and-tavern-song origins through 19th-century Hungarian-national-Romantic-era Liszt-and-Bartók-folk-collection continuous through 20th-century Hungarian continuous wine-cellar (pince) and tavern (csárda) practice; the Hungarian wine-region tradition (Tokaj, Eger, Villány) integrates extensive wine-celebration song-repertoire
items.description: The Hungarian bordal (wine-song) tradition continuous from medieval-Hungarian wine-and-tavern-song origins through 19th-century Hungarian-national-Romantic-era Liszt-and-Bartók-folk-collection (Bartók's extensive Hungarian-folk-collection 1905-1918 documents the bordal corpus) continuous through 20th-century Hungarian continuous wine-cellar (pince) and tavern (csárda) practice; the Hungarian wine-region tradition (Tokaj, Eger, Villány, Badacsony) integrates extensive wine-celebration song-repertoire. Foundational repertoire includes "Akácos út" (Acacia road — canonical Hungarian csárda-drinking song), "Kék virág, kék virág" (Blue flower — canonical Hungarian bordal), "Nincsen apám, nincsen anyám" (I have no father, no mother — canonical orphan-drinking lament). Defined by fiddle-and-cimbalom-and-voice arrangement (the canonical Hungarian-Roma cigányzene tavern-ensemble), Hungarian-language text register, characteristic Hungarian-Gypsy-Roma cigányzene stylistic-inheritance.
exemplars: "Nincsen apám, nincsen anyám" canonical Hungarian bordal

items.name: Polish biesiadne (feast and drinking songs)
items.lineage: Polish biesiadne (feast-and-drinking-song) tradition continuous from medieval-Polish tavern-and-noble-feast song-tradition through 19th-20th-century Polish-Romantic-era and Communist-era continuous performance into modern Polish wedding-and-pub continuous practice; foundational repertoire includes "Sto lat" (the canonical Polish birthday-and-toast song), "Hej, sokoły" (canonical Polish-Ukrainian dance-and-drinking)
items.description: The Polish biesiadne (feast-and-drinking-song) tradition continuous from medieval-Polish tavern-and-noble-feast song-tradition through 19th-20th-century Polish-Romantic-era and Communist-era continuous performance into modern Polish wedding-and-pub continuous practice; foundational repertoire includes "Sto lat" (the canonical Polish birthday-and-toast song, sung at every Polish celebration), "Hej, sokoły" (canonical Polish-Ukrainian dance-and-drinking), "Czerwone jagody" (Red berries — canonical), "Wańka i kucharka" canonical Polish-Russian-borderlands drinking. Defined by accordion-and-voice arrangement, Polish-language text register with characteristic biesiada (feast-gathering) vocabulary, festive uptempo crowd-singing arrangement, characteristic Polish-Slavic-folk melodic-and-harmonic vocabulary, integration into Polish wedding-and-celebration ritual.
exemplars: "Pije Kuba do Jakuba" canonical Polish drinking-toast

items.name: Russian zastol'naya pesnya (table song / drinking song)
items.lineage: Russian zastol'naya pesnya (table-song / drinking-song) tradition continuous from medieval-Russian feast-and-tavern song-tradition through 19th-century Russian-Romantic-era Glinka-and-Mussorgsky-folk-collection through Soviet-era continuous performance into modern Russian-and-Russian-diaspora continuous feast-and-pub practice; foundational repertoire includes "Калинка" (Kalinka) and "Подмосковные вечера" (Moscow Nights — though both are more broadly folk-popular than strictly drinking-songs)
items.description: The Russian zastol'naya pesnya (за́стольная пе́сня "table-song / drinking-song") tradition continuous from medieval-Russian feast-and-tavern song-tradition through 19th-century Russian-Romantic-era Glinka-and-Mussorgsky-folk-collection (the Russian national-music project documented and elevated the zastol'naya corpus) through Soviet-era continuous performance into modern Russian-and-Russian-diaspora continuous feast-and-pub practice. The Russian zastol'naya tradition is integrated into the canonical Russian feast-ritual where each toast (тост, tost) is accompanied by extended-song-performance; foundational repertoire includes "Из-за острова на стрежень" (Out from the island to the deep — Stenka Razin canonical), "Степь да степь кругом" (Steppes around — drinking-elegy), "Ой, мороз, мороз" (Oh frost, frost — canonical Russian-folk-drinking), "Шумел камыш" (The reed rustled — canonical).
exemplars: "Из-за острова на стрежень" Stenka Razin canonical
"Степь да степь кругом" canonical Russian drinking-elegy

items.description: The Macedonian-Serbian-and-broader-Balkan kafana (tavern) drinking-song tradition continuous from Ottoman-era kafana-cafe-tavern song-tradition through 20th-century Balkan-Yugoslav continuous performance into modern Serbian-Macedonian-and-Balkan-diaspora kafana-practice; the kafana is the documented Balkan-Slavic tavern-context where extended drinking-songs span multi-hour evening performance integrating Eastern-Balkan-modal melodic vocabulary, melismatic vocal-foreground, and characteristic rakija-drinking accompaniment. Defined by accordion-and-violin-and-darbuka and characteristic kafana-tavern ensemble, Balkan-Eastern-modal vocabulary, Serbian-Macedonian-Bulgarian-and-Albanian text register, melismatic vocal practice, characteristic sevdah (Bosnian) and starogradska (Serbian "old-town") drinking-song sub-traditions.
exemplars: Šaban Šaulić — Serbian kafana-pop modern canonical
"Idem kući, a već je svanulo" canonical Serbian kafana

items.name: Georgian supra feast-singing
items.lineage: Georgian supra-feast drinking-and-singing tradition continuous from medieval-Georgian feast-and-toast tradition through 19th-20th century continuous performance into modern Georgian-and-Georgian-diaspora continuous practice; the Georgian supra is the documented multi-hour ritual-feast-and-toast-ceremony where the tamada (toast-master) directs the extended-toast-and-song sequence
items.description: The Georgian supra-feast drinking-and-singing tradition continuous from medieval-Georgian feast-and-toast tradition through 19th-20th century continuous performance into modern Georgian-and-Georgian-diaspora continuous practice; the Georgian supra is the documented multi-hour ritual-feast-and-toast-ceremony where the tamada (toast-master) directs the extended-toast-and-song sequence integrating chacha-vodka and Georgian-wine-drinking, polyphonic-three-voice singing (the unique Georgian-polyphonic three-voice harmony with no European equivalent), and characteristic toast-ritual progression (toasts to family, ancestors, peace, friendship, fertility, country). Defined by polyphonic-three-voice unaccompanied-or-panduri-accompanied vocal arrangement, Georgian-modal melodic vocabulary, Georgian-language text register, characteristic supra ceremonial-context.

items.name: Korean jubu-ga (drinking-and-celebration songs)
items.lineage: Korean drinking-and-celebration song tradition continuous from premodern Korean banquet-and-tavern song-tradition through Japanese-colonial-era and post-1945 continuous performance into modern Korean-and-Korean-diaspora continuous noraebang (가요방, song-room) and drinking-establishment practice; the broader Korean drinking-culture integrates extensive trot (트로트) and folk-drinking-song repertoire
items.description: The Korean drinking-and-celebration song tradition continuous from premodern Korean banquet-and-tavern song-tradition (the Joseon-era hwagangbap court-banquet-music had extensive ceremonial-drinking repertoire) through Japanese-colonial-era and post-1945 continuous performance into modern Korean-and-Korean-diaspora continuous noraebang (가요방, song-room, the karaoke-room culture endemic to East-Asian drinking-establishment context) and drinking-establishment practice. The broader Korean drinking-culture integrates extensive trot (트로트, the canonical Korean-popular drinking-and-soju-bar genre) and folk-drinking-song repertoire alongside contemporary Korean-pop selections. Defined by acoustic-guitar-and-voice arrangement in traditional context (and ensemble-pop in modern noraebang context), Korean-Hangul text register, characteristic Korean-soju-bar (소주집) and pojangmacha (포장마차 street-tent-bar) drinking-context.
exemplars: "홍도야 우지 마라" (Hongdoya Uji Marra) canonical trot-drinking

items.name: Japanese izakaya enka (居酒屋演歌, tavern enka)
items.lineage: Japanese izakaya (居酒屋, tavern) enka drinking-song tradition continuous from postwar-Japanese enka-popularization era (1950s-1960s Misora Hibari era) through 20th-century continuous performance into modern Japanese-and-Japanese-diaspora continuous izakaya-and-snack-bar (スナック) practice; the izakaya-enka repertoire emphasizes melancholic-drinking-song aesthetic distinct from the more-celebratory Korean-jubu-ga or German-trinklied
items.description: The Japanese izakaya (居酒屋, tavern) enka drinking-song tradition continuous from postwar-Japanese enka-popularization era (1950s-1960s Misora Hibari era when enka emerged as the canonical Japanese-popular-emotional-vocal-genre) through 20th-century continuous performance into modern Japanese-and-Japanese-diaspora continuous izakaya-and-snack-bar (スナック) and karaoke-box (カラオケボックス) practice; the izakaya-enka repertoire emphasizes melancholic-drinking-song aesthetic with characteristic enka-vocal-ornamentation (kobushi, the canonical enka vocal-trill), Japanese-in-scale modal vocabulary, sake-and-drinking-ritual lyric content, urban-loneliness-and-romantic-loss thematics. Defined by acoustic-guitar-and-shamisen-and-voice arrangement (with occasional koto and accordion), Japanese-language text register, characteristic enka-vocal-ornament practice.
exemplars: "夜霧の慕情" (Yogiri no Bojō) canonical enka-drinking

items.name: Mexican cantina drinking song (mariachi-and-ranchera lineage)
items.lineage: Mexican cantina-drinking song tradition continuous from 19th-century post-Independence Mexican ranchera-and-corrido tradition through 20th-century mariachi-and-banda canonical performance into modern Mexican-and-Mexican-American continuous cantina-practice; foundational repertoire includes "El Rey," "Volver, volver," "La Llorona" (canonical cantina-drinking-grief)
items.description: The Mexican cantina-drinking song tradition continuous from 19th-century post-Independence Mexican ranchera-and-corrido tradition through 20th-century mariachi-and-banda canonical performance into modern Mexican-and-Mexican-American continuous cantina-practice; foundational repertoire includes "El Rey" (the canonical Mexican drinking-and-defiance anthem by José Alfredo Jiménez), "Volver, volver" (canonical cantina-drinking-longing), "La Llorona" (canonical cantina-drinking-grief — the wailing-woman folkloric song), "El Mariachi Loco," "Cielito Lindo." The José Alfredo Jiménez songbook (1950s-1970s) constitutes the canonical Mexican-cantina-drinking-and-grief lyric tradition. Defined by mariachi-ensemble (nylon-guitar-and-guitarrón-and-trumpet-and-violin) arrangement, Mexican-Spanish text register, characteristic cantina-tequila-drinking ritual-context.
exemplars: José Alfredo Jiménez — "El Rey" / "Camino de Guanajuato" / "Ella" canonical cantina-corpus
Mariachi Vargas de Tecalitlán — canonical mariachi-cantina ensemble

items.name: American drinking song (frat, sea-shanty-derived, country)
items.lineage: American drinking-song tradition continuous from 18th-19th century English-Irish-and-Scottish-imported drinking-song-and-sea-shanty repertoire through 19th-century American-frontier and Civil-War-era expansion through 20th-century college-fraternity drinking-song-and-country-music drinking-song lineage into modern American continuous bar-and-roadhouse practice; foundational repertoire includes "99 Bottles of Beer," "Show Me the Way to Go Home," "Beer Barrel Polka," "Drink to Me Only with Thine Eyes"
items.description: The American drinking-song tradition continuous from 18th-19th century English-Irish-and-Scottish-imported drinking-song-and-sea-shanty repertoire through 19th-century American-frontier and Civil-War-era expansion through 20th-century college-fraternity drinking-song-and-country-music drinking-song lineage into modern American continuous bar-and-roadhouse practice; foundational repertoire includes "99 Bottles of Beer" (the canonical counting-down-drinking song), "Show Me the Way to Go Home" (the canonical American-British pub-singalong), "Beer Barrel Polka" (Czech-American polka-drinking crossover), "Drink to Me Only with Thine Eyes" (English-American genteel-drinking), "John Barleycorn" (English-American agricultural-and-distillation allegorical-drinking). Defined by acoustic-guitar-and-banjo-and-harmonica-and-voice arrangement, English-American text register, festive-or-melancholy crowd-singing arrangement spanning honky-tonk to college-fraternity-house contexts.
exemplars: "99 Bottles of Beer" canonical American counting-drinking
"Show Me the Way to Go Home" canonical Anglo-American pub-singalong
George Thorogood — "I Drink Alone" canonical modern American drinking
Toby Keith — "I Love This Bar" canonical modern country-drinking

items.name: Norwegian skipperslåttar (sailor work-songs)
items.lineage: Norwegian-Scandinavian sailor work-song tradition (skipperslåttar = "ship-sailor tunes," skanssanger = "quarterdeck songs") continuous from 18th-19th-century Norwegian-and-broader-Scandinavian maritime-trade work-song practice through 20th-century Norwegian-folk-revival into modern Norwegian-coastal-cultural-practice; foundational repertoire includes "Pål sine høner" (sailor work-coordination song), Norwegian sea-shanty translations
items.description: The Norwegian-Scandinavian sailor work-song tradition (skipperslåttar = "ship-sailor tunes," skanssanger = "quarterdeck songs") continuous from 18th-19th-century Norwegian-and-broader-Scandinavian maritime-trade work-song practice (Norwegian shipping was historically among the largest in Europe and the Norwegian merchant-marine workforce constituted a substantial percentage of Norwegian male labor through the 19th-century) through 20th-century Norwegian-folk-revival into modern Norwegian-coastal-cultural-practice. Defined by accordion-and-voice arrangement, Norwegian-language text register, Nordic-modal melodic vocabulary with drone-and-double-stop traditional Norwegian-folk inheritance, call-and-response work-coordination structure shared with the broader Atlantic sea-shanty tradition.
exemplars: Norwegian-coast sailor work-song traditional documentation (Norsk Folkemusikksamling)
Norsk Folkemusikksamling (Norwegian Folk Music Collection) maritime-rep

items.name: Russian Volga boat-haulers' work song (бурлацкая песня)
items.lineage: Russian Volga boat-haulers (бурлаки burlaki) work-song tradition documented from 17th-19th century Russian river-haulage-laborer practice (the burlaki towed cargo-barges upstream against the Volga current by rope-and-shoulder before steam-tug-substitution in the 1860s-1880s) through 19th-century Russian-Romantic-era documentation into 20th-century revival; the canonical "Эй, ухнем!" (Ey, ukhnem!, "Hey, heave-ho!") is the foundational repertoire
items.description: The Russian Volga boat-haulers (бурлаки burlaki) work-song tradition documented from 17th-19th century Russian river-haulage-laborer practice (the burlaki towed cargo-barges upstream against the Volga river-current by rope-and-shoulder before steam-tug-substitution in the 1860s-1880s — Ilya Repin's canonical painting "Burlaki na Volge" 1870-1873 depicts the labor) through 19th-century Russian-Romantic-era documentation (Fyodor Chaliapin's 1900s-1910s opera-stage performance of "Ey, Ukhnem!" canonicalized the burlaki song for international audiences) into 20th-century revival. The canonical "Эй, ухнем!" (Ey, ukhnem!, "Hey, heave-ho!") is the foundational repertoire. Defined by unaccompanied call-and-response group-vocal work-coordination arrangement, Russian-language work-song text register, Russian-minor-modal melodic vocabulary, characteristic burlaki occupational-context.
exemplars: "Эй, ухнем!" (Ey Ukhnem) canonical Russian burlaki work-song
Fyodor Chaliapin — 1900s-1910s burlaki opera-stage performance canonical
Ilya Repin — "Burlaki na Volge" 1870-1873 painting (canonical art-historical documentation)
Russian Volga-river boat-haulage work-song traditional rep

items.name: Greek Cretan tabachaniotika (Cretan urban sea-faring song)
items.lineage: Greek-Cretan tabachaniotika (urban-Cretan sea-faring-and-port-side song) tradition continuous from late-19th-and-early-20th century Cretan-urban-port (Heraklion, Chania, Rethymno) song-and-tavern tradition through Cretan-Greek-Turkish population-exchange 1923-aftermath integration with Asia-Minor refugees into modern Cretan-folk-revival continuous practice; the tabachaniotika is the canonical Cretan-port-side-and-sea-faring repertoire
items.description: The Greek-Cretan tabachaniotika (urban-Cretan sea-faring-and-port-side song) tradition continuous from late-19th-and-early-20th century Cretan-urban-port (Heraklion, Chania, Rethymno) song-and-tavern tradition through Cretan-Greek-Turkish population-exchange 1923-aftermath integration with Asia-Minor refugees (the tabachaniotika absorbed Asia-Minor-Greek-Turkish-musical influences via the refugee-arrival into Crete) into modern Cretan-folk-revival continuous practice. The tabachaniotika is the canonical Cretan-port-side-and-sea-faring repertoire, distinguished from the broader rebetiko of Athens-and-Piraeus by its specific Cretan-urban-and-rural integration. Defined by cretan-lyra-and-oud-and-voice arrangement, Greek-Cretan dialect text register, Eastern-modal melodic vocabulary, melismatic vocal practice, sea-faring-port-life lyric content.

items.name: Scottish Hebridean iorram (rowing song)
items.lineage: Scottish-Hebridean Gaelic rowing-song (iorram, pronounced "ear-ram") tradition continuous from medieval-Hebridean-Gaelic maritime practice through 18th-19th-century continuous performance on Scottish-Western-Isles fishing-boats and ferries into 20th-century Scottish-Gaelic revival; the iorram coordinates the synchronized-oar-stroke timing of multi-oar Hebridean fishing-boats
items.description: The Scottish-Hebridean Gaelic rowing-song (iorram, pronounced "ear-ram") tradition continuous from medieval-Hebridean-Gaelic maritime practice through 18th-19th-century continuous performance on Scottish-Western-Isles fishing-boats and ferries into 20th-century Scottish-Gaelic revival (the canonical Marjorie Kennedy-Fraser Songs of the Hebrides 1909-1921 collection documented the iorram corpus alongside other Hebridean-Gaelic vocal-music). The iorram coordinates the synchronized-oar-stroke timing of multi-oar Hebridean fishing-boats with characteristic short-cycle rhythmic-structure matching the oar-pull pace. Defined by unaccompanied solo-precentor-and-group-vocal call-and-response arrangement, Scottish-Gaelic text register, Hebridean-modal melodic vocabulary, characteristic narrow-range short-cell oar-stroke-coordinated structure.
exemplars: "Fear a' Bhàta" canonical Hebridean Gaelic boat-song
Marjorie Kennedy-Fraser — Songs of the Hebrides 1909-1921 canonical
Julie Fowlis — modern Hebridean Gaelic canonical vocalist

items.name: Cape Verdean funaná (maritime-and-island work-song)
items.lineage: Cape Verdean Atlantic-island music tradition with maritime-and-emigration thematic integration; the broader Cape Verdean musical tradition (morna, coladeira, funaná, batuque) developed across 16th-onward Portuguese-colonial-era through post-1975 independent-Cape-Verdean continuous practice; the Cape Verdean maritime-emigration culture integrates extensive maritime-and-port-departure-lament repertoire
items.description: The Cape Verdean Atlantic-island music tradition with maritime-and-emigration thematic integration; the broader Cape Verdean musical tradition (morna, coladeira, funaná, batuque) developed across 16th-onward Portuguese-colonial-era through post-1975 independent-Cape-Verdean continuous practice. The Cape Verdean maritime-emigration culture integrates extensive maritime-and-port-departure-lament repertoire — Cape Verdean men historically emigrated en masse for maritime work across Atlantic-shipping-routes, leaving women-and-elders on the islands; morna in particular addresses the sodade (longing) of separation by sea. Defined by classical-guitar-and-cavaquinho-and-accordion-and-voice arrangement, Cape Verdean Crioulo text register, Portuguese-Atlantic stylistic-inheritance crossed with Cape-Verdean-distinct melodic vocabulary.

items.name: Newfoundland outport sea-shanty and work-song
items.lineage: Newfoundland-Labrador outport (Atlantic-fishing-village) sea-shanty and work-song tradition continuous from 17th-onward English-and-Irish-immigrant Newfoundland-cod-fishery work-song practice through 20th-century Newfoundland-folk-revival into modern Atlantic-Canadian-folk continuous practice; foundational repertoire includes "I'se the B'y" (canonical), "The Squid-Jiggin' Ground," "Lukey's Boat"
items.description: The Newfoundland-Labrador outport (Atlantic-fishing-village) sea-shanty and work-song tradition continuous from 17th-onward English-and-Irish-immigrant Newfoundland-cod-fishery work-song practice through 20th-century Newfoundland-folk-revival (the canonical Kenneth Peacock Songs of the Newfoundland Outports 1965 canonical scholarly documentation, Gerald S. Doyle Songs of Newfoundland 1927 canonical popular publication) into modern Atlantic-Canadian-folk continuous practice. Foundational repertoire includes "I'se the B'y" (the canonical Newfoundland anthem), "The Squid-Jiggin' Ground" (canonical outport work-song), "Lukey's Boat" (canonical Newfoundland-folk), "Petty Harbour Bait Skiff" (canonical outport tragic-narrative). Defined by acoustic-guitar-and-fiddle-and-concertina-and-voice arrangement, Newfoundland-English dialect text register with characteristic Newfoundland-vocabulary, festive pub-singing arrangement.
exemplars: Great Big Sea — modern Newfoundland-folk-revival canonical 1990s-2000s
Kenneth Peacock — Songs of the Newfoundland Outports 1965 canonical

items.name: Trinidad calypso-soca road march
items.lineage: Trinidadian Carnival road-march tradition continuous from 19th-century post-emancipation Carnival celebrations through 20th-century calypso (1930s-1960s Lord Kitchener and Mighty Sparrow era) and soca (1970s-onward Lord Shorty era) into modern Trinidad-and-Tobago Carnival continuous practice; the "Road March" is the canonical Carnival competition for the song most-played during Carnival processional
items.description: The Trinidadian Carnival road-march tradition continuous from 19th-century post-emancipation Carnival celebrations through 20th-century calypso (1930s-1960s Lord Kitchener, Mighty Sparrow, Atilla the Hun era) and soca (1970s-onward Lord Shorty Endless Vibrations era) into modern Trinidad-and-Tobago Carnival continuous practice; the "Road March" is the canonical Carnival competition for the song most-played during Carnival processional (announced annually based on Ash-Wednesday tallies of plays during Carnival Monday-and-Tuesday parade routes). Defined by steel-pan-and-brass-and-drum-kit ensemble, English-Trinidadian-and-French-Creole text register, soca-dembow rhythmic vocabulary at high-tempo road-march pace, characteristic mass-participation jump-and-wave processional context, double-fast Power Soca and slower Groovy Soca sub-categories competing annually.
exemplars: Lord Kitchener — Road March winner multiple decades canonical
Machel Montano — modern soca Road March canonical
Bunji Garlin — modern soca Road March

items.name: Brazilian samba-school enredo (samba-enredo, Carnaval processional)
items.lineage: Brazilian Rio Carnaval samba-school enredo (samba-enredo, "theme-samba") tradition continuous from 1928 first samba-school Deixa Falar foundation through the 1930s-1980s Estação Primeira de Mangueira and Portela canonical-school era into modern Sambódromo-procession continuous practice; the enredo is the canonical annual samba composition that narrates the parade-school's theme
items.description: The Brazilian Rio Carnaval samba-school enredo (samba-enredo, "theme-samba") tradition continuous from 1928 first samba-school Deixa Falar foundation through the 1930s-1980s Estação Primeira de Mangueira and Portela canonical-school era into modern Sambódromo-procession continuous practice; the enredo is the canonical annual samba composition that narrates the parade-school's annual theme (each samba-school competing in the Sambódromo selects a yearly enredo theme — historical, cultural, mythological — and the entire parade is built around it). Defined by call-and-response puxador-and-bateria-and-crowd vocal arrangement, cavaquinho-and-tamborim-and-pandeiro-and-surdo bateria-ensemble (300-400 percussionists in major schools), Brazilian-Portuguese text register, samba 2-4 telecoteco rhythmic vocabulary, characteristic Sambódromo-procession context with parade-school competing for the championship.
exemplars: Estação Primeira de Mangueira samba-school enredos canonical
Beija-Flor de Nilópolis samba-school enredos canonical

items.name: New Orleans Mardi Gras Indians
items.lineage: New Orleans Mardi Gras Indian tradition continuous from mid-19th-century Afro-American-and-Native-American cultural exchange in New Orleans through 20th-century continuous tribal-performance into modern New Orleans continuous Mardi Gras practice; the Mardi Gras Indian "tribes" (Wild Magnolias, Wild Tchoupitoulas, Golden Eagles, Black Eagles) perform handmade-feathered-suit processional with characteristic call-and-response chants
items.description: The New Orleans Mardi Gras Indian tradition continuous from mid-19th-century Afro-American-and-Native-American cultural exchange in New Orleans (the documented tradition of African-American working-class New Orleans residents "masking Indian" emerged from cultural exchange with Indigenous nations historically present in Louisiana, including Choctaw and Atakapa) through 20th-century continuous tribal-performance into modern New Orleans continuous Mardi Gras practice; the Mardi Gras Indian "tribes" (the Wild Magnolias, Wild Tchoupitoulas, Golden Eagles, Black Eagles, and many others, organized into hierarchical roles — Big Chief, Spy Boy, Flag Boy, Wildman) perform handmade-feathered-suit processional with characteristic call-and-response chants ("Iko Iko," "Indian Red," "Two Way Pock-A-Way," "Shallow Water Oh Mama"). Defined by tambourine-and-shaker-and-cowbell-and-voice arrangement, English-and-Creole text register with characteristic Mardi-Gras-Indian-secret-language vocabulary, call-and-response Big-Chief-and-tribe-membership vocal arrangement.
exemplars: Wild Magnolias — canonical Mardi Gras Indian recordings
Big Chief Bo Dollis — Wild Magnolias Big Chief canonical
"Iko Iko" canonical Mardi Gras Indian song
Donald Harrison Sr. — Big Chief canonical-tradition-bearer

items.name: New Orleans brass band second-line
items.lineage: New Orleans brass-band second-line tradition continuous from late-19th-century African-American funeral-and-celebration brass-band practice through early-20th-century jazz-foundation era through late-20th-century brass-band-revival (Dirty Dozen Brass Band, Rebirth Brass Band 1980s-onward) into modern New Orleans continuous brass-parade practice; the second-line is the documented processional form where mourners-and-celebrants-and-onlookers parade behind the band
items.description: The New Orleans brass-band second-line tradition continuous from late-19th-century African-American funeral-and-celebration brass-band practice (the canonical "jazz funeral" with slow-dirge processional outbound to cemetery and uptempo joyful-celebration processional return) through early-20th-century jazz-foundation era (Buddy Bolden and the brass-band era directly preceding the foundation of jazz) through late-20th-century brass-band-revival (Dirty Dozen Brass Band 1977-onward, Rebirth Brass Band 1983-onward, Stooges Brass Band) into modern New Orleans continuous brass-parade practice. The second-line is the documented processional form where mourners-and-celebrants-and-onlookers parade behind the band. Defined by brass-ensemble (trumpet, trombone, sousaphone-tuba) plus snare-and-bass-drum arrangement, English-American text register when sung (the second-line is predominantly instrumental with occasional vocal-interjection), characteristic brass-and-percussion arrangement.
exemplars: Stooges Brass Band — canonical modern brass-revival

items.name: Cologne Karneval (Kölner Karneval)
items.lineage: Cologne (Köln) Karneval tradition documented from medieval Catholic-Rhineland Carnival-celebration practice (the documented Cologne-Karneval lineage extends to medieval-era Karnevalsumzug processionals) through 19th-century 1823-founded modern-Karneval-Festkomitee codification into modern Cologne Karneval Rosenmontagszug processional and Stunksitzung-and-Kostümsitzung continuous practice
items.description: The Cologne (Köln) Karneval tradition documented from medieval Catholic-Rhineland Carnival-celebration practice (the documented Cologne-Karneval lineage extends to medieval-era Karnevalsumzug processionals across the Catholic-Rhineland) through 19th-century 1823-founded modern-Karneval-Festkomitee codification (the modern Cologne Karneval was institutionally reorganized in 1823 with the founding of the Festkomitee Kölner Karneval) into modern Cologne Karneval Rosenmontagszug processional (the canonical Rose-Monday parade through downtown Cologne with Triumphwagen floats) and Stunksitzung-and-Kostümsitzung continuous practice. Defined by brass-band-and-accordion-and-vocal ensemble, Kölsch-German-dialect text register with characteristic Karneval-vocabulary, call-and-response Karnevalsruf "Alaaf!" interjection structure, festive-uptempo crowd-singing arrangement.
exemplars: "Mer losse d'r Dom in Kölle" canonical Bläck Fööss Cologne anthem
Cologne Karneval Rosenmontagszug Sängers and Veedel-Floats canonical

items.name: Bahamian Junkanoo
items.lineage: Bahamian Junkanoo tradition continuous from late-18th-and-19th-century Bahamian-African Christmas-and-Boxing-Day celebration practice through 20th-century continuous performance into modern Bahamas Boxing-Day-and-New-Year's-Day Junkanoo continuous practice; Junkanoo is documented as having African origins (possibly West-African origin via the slave trade) integrated with Caribbean-British Boxing-Day timing
items.description: The Bahamian Junkanoo tradition continuous from late-18th-and-19th-century Bahamian-African Christmas-and-Boxing-Day celebration practice (Boxing-Day December-26 and New-Year's-Day January-1 were the documented two days of the year when enslaved-Africans on Bahamian plantations were granted relative freedom to perform their own cultural practice) through 20th-century continuous performance into modern Bahamas Boxing-Day-and-New-Year's-Day Junkanoo continuous practice. Junkanoo is documented as having African origins (the name likely from West-African Akan-Akye "John Canoe" or Yoruba-related figure) integrated with Caribbean-British Boxing-Day timing. Defined by cowbell-and-goombay-drum-and-vocal percussion-foreground arrangement (the cowbell-and-goombay-drum is the canonical Junkanoo sonic-signature), English-Bahamian text register, call-and-response group-vocal participation, characteristic massed-cowbell-and-drum walking-parade processional.
exemplars: Ronnie Butler — canonical Bahamian Junkanoo and rake-and-scrape
Modern Nassau Bay-Street Junkanoo parade continuous-tradition

items.name: Bolivian diablada de Oruro (Carnaval de Oruro)
items.lineage: Bolivian Carnaval de Oruro diablada (devil-dance) processional tradition continuous from pre-Hispanic Andean ritual-dance practice through Spanish-colonial-era integration with Christian-Catholic devil-dance imagery (the post-1606 syncretism of Andean-Tio-deity worship with Catholic-devil-iconography) into modern Carnaval de Oruro continuous practice
items.description: The Bolivian Carnaval de Oruro diablada (devil-dance) processional tradition continuous from pre-Hispanic Andean ritual-dance practice (the Andean Tio-deity-worship of Bolivian-tin-mining culture) through Spanish-colonial-era integration with Christian-Catholic devil-dance imagery (the post-1606 syncretism of Andean-Tio-deity worship with Catholic-devil-iconography produced the canonical diablada masked-procession where the diablos perform a quasi-Christian-morality narrative of triumph-over-evil) into modern Carnaval de Oruro continuous practice. Defined by quena-and-siku-and-brass-and-snare-drum ensemble, Spanish-Quechua-Aymara text register, Andean-huayno rhythmic vocabulary, characteristic masked-diablo-and-china-supay (devil-and-devil-mistress) costumed-processional context.
exemplars: Diablada Ferroviaria canonical Oruro Carnaval dance-group
Sociedad Folklórica Diablada Oruro canonical group
Llamerada and Morenada complementary Andean processional traditions

items.name: Japanese matsuri festival drumming (祭, matsuri-bayashi)
items.lineage: Japanese matsuri (祭, festival) drumming tradition continuous from premodern Shinto-Buddhist festival-procession practice through Edo-period (1603-1868) codification of canonical city-festival drumming (the Tokyo-Asakusa Sanja Matsuri, Kyoto Gion Matsuri, Osaka Tenjin Matsuri, Aomori Nebuta Matsuri) into modern Japanese-and-Japanese-diaspora continuous festival-practice
items.description: The Japanese matsuri (祭, festival) drumming tradition continuous from premodern Shinto-Buddhist festival-procession practice through Edo-period (1603-1868) codification of canonical city-festival drumming (the Tokyo-Asakusa Sanja Matsuri, Kyoto Gion Matsuri, Osaka Tenjin Matsuri, Aomori Nebuta Matsuri are the canonical four large-city matsuri across Japan, with each integrating distinct local matsuri-bayashi musical-and-drumming repertoire) into modern Japanese-and-Japanese-diaspora continuous festival-practice. Defined by taiko-and-shamisen-and-fue-and-vocal ensemble (the matsuri-bayashi instrumental-ensemble), shouted-vocal "wasshoi" or "soiya" matsuri-call interjections, Japanese-language text register, characteristic Edo-period codified festival-music vocabulary, mikoshi-shrine-portable-shrine processional context.
exemplars: Modern Japanese taiko-ensemble Kodō and Ondekoza canonical-revival

items.name: Venetian Carnevale (masquerade-ball processional)
items.lineage: Venetian Carnevale tradition documented from medieval-Venetian Carnival celebration (the documented Venetian-Carnevale lineage extends to 11th-12th-century with the canonical post-1268 Doge-mandated Giovedi Grasso celebration) through 18th-century peak-Carnevale era through 1797-Napoleonic suppression through 1979 modern-revival into modern Venice Carnevale continuous practice
items.description: The Venetian Carnevale tradition documented from medieval-Venetian Carnival celebration (the documented Venetian-Carnevale lineage extends to 11th-12th-century with the canonical post-1268 Doge-mandated Giovedi Grasso celebration where Venetian populace celebrated freedom from Aquileia rule) through 18th-century peak-Carnevale era (when Venetian Carnevale extended over six weeks of masquerade-and-public-celebration with documented canonical masks the bauta, moretta, volto, pantalone, and arlecchino) through 1797-Napoleonic suppression through 1979 modern-revival into modern Venice Carnevale continuous practice. Defined by acoustic-guitar-and-fiddle-and-recorder-and-vocal small-ensemble arrangement, Italian-and-Venetian-dialect text register, characteristic Renaissance-and-Baroque period-instrument timbre (in revival-context), masquerade-ball-and-procession ceremonial-context.
exemplars: "La Biondina in Gondoleta" canonical Venetian-Carnevale boat-song
Modern Venetian Carnevale processional canonical-mask-and-ball ceremonial

items.name: Indian Holi-and-Diwali festival processional
items.lineage: Indian Holi (festival of colors) and Diwali (festival of lights) processional tradition continuous from premodern Indian festival celebration practice through 19th-20th century continuous performance into modern Indian-and-Indian-diaspora continuous festival-practice; Holi processional integrates extensive dholak-and-shehnai-and-vocal participation alongside color-throwing, Diwali integrates devotional kirtan-and-bhajan with lamp-procession
items.description: The Indian Holi (festival of colors, late-February/March) and Diwali (festival of lights, October/November) processional tradition continuous from premodern Indian festival celebration practice through 19th-20th century continuous performance into modern Indian-and-Indian-diaspora continuous festival-practice. Holi processional integrates extensive dholak-and-shehnai-and-vocal participation alongside color-throwing (gulal powder-tossing) and bhang-and-thandai drinking, with foundational Holi repertoire including "Rang Barse" (Amitabh Bachchan film canonical) and traditional Hindustani-Holi rep. Diwali integrates devotional kirtan-and-bhajan with lamp-procession (diya lamps lit across homes), with foundational Diwali repertoire including Lakshmi-stuti praise-songs and Ram-Rajya celebration kirtan. Defined by dholak-and-shehnai-and-tabla-and-vocal ensemble, Hindi-Urdu-and-Sanskrit text register, festive uptempo crowd-singing arrangement.
exemplars: "Rang Barse Bheege Chunarwali" canonical Holi from Silsila 1981
Mathura-Vrindavan Lath Mar Holi canonical-regional Holi-festival

items.name: Trinidadian Panorama steelpan competition
items.lineage: Trinidadian Carnival Panorama steelpan-orchestra competition tradition continuous from 1963 first Panorama-competition founding through 20th-21st century continuous competitive performance into modern Trinidad-and-Tobago Carnival annual Panorama; the steelpan-orchestra (40-100 panmen-and-panwomen) performs a single arranged calypso/soca tune in 8-12 minute concert-piece arrangement competing for the National Panorama Champion title
items.description: The Trinidadian Carnival Panorama steelpan-orchestra competition tradition continuous from 1963 first Panorama-competition founding through 20th-21st century continuous competitive performance into modern Trinidad-and-Tobago Carnival annual Panorama; the steelpan-orchestra (40-100 panmen-and-panwomen organized into tenor-pan, double-second, guitar-pan, cello-pan, six-bass sections) performs a single arranged calypso/soca tune in 8-12 minute concert-piece arrangement competing for the National Panorama Champion title (the canonical victors include Renegades, Desperadoes, Phase II Pan Groove, Despers, Trinidad All Stars). Defined by all-steel-pan-ensemble arrangement (the steel pan tuned-chromatic 12-TET pitched-percussion-vocabulary), instrumental-only no-vocal-content, complex multi-section arrangement-and-counterpoint-and-improvised-soloing.
exemplars: Renegades Steel Orchestra — canonical Panorama winner multiple decades
Phase II Pan Groove — canonical Len "Boogsie" Sharpe arranger-led
Trinidad All Stars — canonical Panorama winner
Modern Panorama Savannah-Stage annual competition continuous-tradition

items.name: Bulgarian zhetvarski pesni (harvest songs)
items.lineage: Bulgarian harvest-song (zhetvarski pesni, женски pesni women's-songs) tradition continuous from premodern Bulgarian-agricultural village-labor practice through 19th-century Bulgarian-folklorist documentation through 20th-century Le Mystère des Voix Bulgares-era canonization into modern Bulgarian-folk-revival continuous practice; foundational harvest-song repertoire integrates women's-group-vocal close-harmony arrangement with characteristic Bulgarian-folk modal vocabulary
items.description: The Bulgarian harvest-song (zhetvarski pesni, "harvest-songs") tradition continuous from premodern Bulgarian-agricultural village-labor practice (the Bulgarian-village women-laborers performed harvest-songs throughout the summer harvest-season — grain-cutting, wheat-binding, threshing — with songs scheduled to specific labor-tasks) through 19th-century Bulgarian-folklorist documentation through 20th-century Le Mystère des Voix Bulgares-era canonization (the 1975 onwards Marcel Cellier-produced canonical recordings) into modern Bulgarian-folk-revival continuous practice. Defined by unaccompanied women's-group-vocal close-harmony arrangement, Bulgarian-language text register with characteristic harvest-folk vocabulary, characteristic close-second-interval Bulgarian-folk harmonic vocabulary, characteristic narrow-range terraced-melismatic-vocal practice.
exemplars: Le Mystère des Voix Bulgares — 1975-onward canonical
Trio Bulgarka — Yanka Rupkina, Stoyanka Boneva, Eva Georgieva canonical

items.name: Romanian colinde de seceriş (harvest carols)
items.lineage: Romanian harvest-carol (colinde de seceriş, "harvest-colinde") tradition continuous from premodern Romanian-agricultural village-labor practice through 19th-century Romanian-folklorist documentation (Vasile Alecsandri and Constantin Brăiloiu documented the Romanian harvest-carol corpus) through 20th-century Béla Bartók-and-Constantin-Brăiloiu canonical-ethnomusicology into modern Romanian-folk-revival continuous practice
items.description: The Romanian harvest-carol (colinde de seceriş, "harvest-colinde" — though the broader colinde-tradition is canonically associated with Christmas-and-New-Year, the harvest-context colinde-rep is documented as a distinct seasonal sub-tradition) tradition continuous from premodern Romanian-agricultural village-labor practice through 19th-century Romanian-folklorist documentation (Vasile Alecsandri Poezii populare ale românilor 1852-1853 and Constantin Brăiloiu mid-20th-century ethnomusicological-documentation) through 20th-century Béla Bartók-and-Constantin-Brăiloiu canonical-ethnomusicology (Bartók's 1909-1917 Romanian-folk-collection documented the Romanian harvest-and-ritual-song corpus extensively) into modern Romanian-folk-revival continuous practice. Defined by unaccompanied group-vocal arrangement, Romanian-language text register, characteristic Romanian-folk modal vocabulary, characteristic women's-group seasonal-labor performance-context.
exemplars: Vasile Alecsandri — Poezii populare ale românilor 1852-1853 (canonical foundational)
Constantin Brăiloiu — Romanian Folklore Institute mid-20th-century canonical

items.name: Hungarian aratónóta (harvest songs)
items.lineage: Hungarian aratónóta ("harvest-song") tradition continuous from premodern Hungarian-agricultural village-labor practice through 19th-century Hungarian-folklorist documentation through Béla Bartók and Zoltán Kodály 1905-1918 Hungarian-folk-collection canonical-ethnomusicology into modern Hungarian-folk-revival continuous practice; foundational repertoire includes harvest-binding songs accompanying grain-bundle-stacking and threshing-floor labor
items.description: The Hungarian aratónóta ("harvest-song") tradition continuous from premodern Hungarian-agricultural village-labor practice through 19th-century Hungarian-folklorist documentation through Béla Bartók and Zoltán Kodály 1905-1918 Hungarian-folk-collection canonical-ethnomusicology (Bartók and Kodály's extensive Hungarian-folk-collection across Transylvanian-Hungarian and Slovak-Hungarian and Romanian-Hungarian regions documented the aratónóta corpus) into modern Hungarian-folk-revival continuous practice. Foundational repertoire includes harvest-binding songs accompanying grain-bundle-stacking and threshing-floor labor, with characteristic strophic verse-and-refrain structure permitting infinite work-task accompaniment. Defined by unaccompanied group-vocal arrangement, Hungarian-language text register, characteristic Hungarian-folk modal vocabulary (the Hungarian-pentatonic-and-modal lineage documented by Bartók-Kodály), women-laborers-and-men-laborers separate-and-mixed group-vocal arrangements.
exemplars: "Akkor szép az erdő" canonical Hungarian-folk-aratónóta type

items.name: Russian zhnitvenye pesni (Russian harvest songs)
items.lineage: Russian harvest-song (жнитвенные песни zhnitvenye pesni) tradition continuous from medieval-Russian-agricultural village-labor practice through 19th-century Russian-folklorist documentation through Soviet-era Pyatnitsky and Voronezh-Russian-Folk-Choir canonical performance into modern Russian-folk-revival continuous practice; foundational repertoire integrates rye-and-wheat-harvest songs accompanying scything-and-binding labor
items.description: The Russian harvest-song (жнитвенные песни zhnitvenye pesni) tradition continuous from medieval-Russian-agricultural village-labor practice through 19th-century Russian-folklorist documentation through Soviet-era Pyatnitsky and Voronezh-Russian-Folk-Choir canonical performance (the Soviet-era Russian-folk-choir movement institutionalized and partly-staged the Russian-harvest-song corpus) into modern Russian-folk-revival continuous practice. Foundational repertoire integrates rye-and-wheat-harvest songs accompanying scything-and-binding labor (the Russian three-field-rotation agricultural-system meant harvest-songs were performed across distinct seasonal-task contexts). Defined by unaccompanied women's-group-vocal arrangement, Russian-language text register, characteristic Russian-folk modal vocabulary, characteristic group-women-labor seasonal-context.
exemplars: Pyatnitsky Russian Folk Choir — canonical Soviet-era Russian-folk

items.name: Mande-Wolof West-African harvest-and-field song
items.lineage: Mande-and-Wolof West-African harvest-and-field song tradition continuous from premodern Mande-and-Wolof agricultural village-labor practice through colonial-period continuous performance into modern West-African-and-West-African-diaspora practice across Mali, Senegal, Guinea, Gambia, Burkina Faso; foundational repertoire integrates rice-planting and millet-harvesting and rice-pounding songs accompanying specific agricultural-tasks
items.description: The Mande-and-Wolof West-African harvest-and-field song tradition continuous from premodern Mande-and-Wolof agricultural village-labor practice through colonial-period continuous performance into modern West-African-and-West-African-diaspora practice across Mali, Senegal, Guinea, Gambia, Burkina Faso, and the broader Sahel; foundational repertoire integrates rice-planting and millet-harvesting and rice-pounding songs accompanying specific agricultural-tasks. The Mande-Wolof harvest-song tradition is distinct from the broader Mande-Wolof praise-song-jeli tradition by labor-coordination-task primary-function rather than praise-of-named-individuals. Defined by call-and-response group-vocal foreground with kora-and-balafon optional-accompaniment, Manding-Maninka-Wolof text register, Mande-pentatonic modal vocabulary, characteristic agricultural-labor task-coordination structure.
exemplars: Mande-Wolof village rice-planting and millet-harvest continuous-living tradition
Toumani Diabaté — Mali field-song integrated kora canonical
Salif Keita — Mali field-and-labor song lineage canonical
Hugh Tracey — early-20th-century West-African field-recordings canonical

items.name: Chinese chayang-diao (插秧调, rice-planting tunes)
items.lineage: Chinese rice-planting song (chayang-diao, 插秧调) tradition continuous from premodern Chinese-agricultural village-labor practice across rice-growing Southern China (Hunan, Jiangsu, Fujian, Jiangxi, Sichuan, Yunnan) through 20th-century Chinese-folklorist documentation into modern Chinese-rural-and-folk-revival practice; foundational repertoire integrates rice-paddy planting and weeding and harvest-song coordination
items.description: The Chinese rice-planting song (chayang-diao, 插秧调 — also chayanggewu 插秧歌舞 in some regional traditions) tradition continuous from premodern Chinese-agricultural village-labor practice across rice-growing Southern China (Hunan, Jiangsu, Fujian, Jiangxi, Sichuan, Yunnan all have distinct regional chayang-diao traditions) through 20th-century Chinese-folklorist documentation (the 1950s-1960s Chinese-Communist-Party folk-collection-and-codification movement documented chayang-diao corpus as canonical "people's-art") into modern Chinese-rural-and-folk-revival practice. Defined by call-and-response group-vocal foreground with dizi-and-sheng optional-accompaniment, Mandarin-and-regional-Chinese-language text register, Chinese-pentatonic modal vocabulary, characteristic rice-paddy task-coordination structure.
exemplars: Fujian regional rice-planting song traditional canonical
Yang Liping — modern Chinese-folk-dance with chayang-diao-derived rep
Chinese rural village rice-planting continuous-living tradition

items.name: Korean nongak (농악, farmer's percussion-and-dance)
items.lineage: Korean nongak (농악, "farmer's music") tradition continuous from premodern Korean-agricultural-village labor-and-festival practice through Japanese-colonial-era and post-1945 continuous performance into modern-recognized Korean-folk continuous practice; the nongak is the canonical Korean village-festival-and-labor music integrating samul (four-instrument) percussion with vocal-and-dance accompaniment
items.description: The Korean nongak (농악, "farmer's music") tradition continuous from premodern Korean-agricultural-village labor-and-festival practice through Japanese-colonial-era and post-1945 continuous performance into modern-recognized Korean-folk continuous practice; the nongak is the canonical Korean village-festival-and-labor music integrating samul (the four-instrument percussion-set of janggu hourglass-drum, kkwaenggwari small-gong, jing large-gong, buk barrel-drum) percussion with vocal-and-dance accompaniment. Defined by samul-percussion-ensemble foreground, Korean-Hangul text register when sung (the nongak is predominantly instrumental-and-dance with vocal-interjection), characteristic Korean-folk modal vocabulary, characteristic rice-paddy-planting and harvest-celebration ritual-context.
exemplars: Imsil Pilbong Nongak — Korean continuous-tradition canonical
SamulNori — modern Korean concert-staging of nongak-derived rep (1978-onward)

items.name: Vietnamese hò (work-coordination song)
items.lineage: Vietnamese hò (work-coordination call-and-response song) tradition continuous from premodern Vietnamese-agricultural-and-maritime labor practice through 19th-20th century continuous performance into modern Vietnamese-folk-revival practice across Northern, Central, and Southern Vietnam; the hò is the canonical Vietnamese work-coordination song-form integrating leader-and-group call-and-response across rice-paddy-planting, fishing, boat-rowing, and other labor-contexts
items.description: The Vietnamese hò (work-coordination call-and-response song) tradition continuous from premodern Vietnamese-agricultural-and-maritime labor practice through 19th-20th century continuous performance into modern Vietnamese-folk-revival practice across Northern, Central, and Southern Vietnam; the hò is the canonical Vietnamese work-coordination song-form integrating leader-and-group call-and-response across rice-paddy-planting, fishing, boat-rowing, and other labor-contexts. Regional variants include the Northern Hò Sông Mã (Ma River boat-song), the Central Hò Đối-Đáp (call-and-response question-and-answer hò of central Vietnam), the Southern Hò Cấy (rice-planting hò of the Mekong Delta). Defined by unaccompanied call-and-response leader-and-group vocal arrangement, Vietnamese-language tonal-language-constrained vocal-melody, characteristic Vietnamese-folk pentatonic vocabulary, task-coordination labor-context.
exemplars: Hò Sông Mã (Ma River boat-song) canonical Northern-Vietnamese hò
Hò Cấy (rice-planting hò) canonical Southern-Vietnamese Mekong-Delta
Hò Mái Nhì canonical Hue-region rowing-hò

items.name: Bengali bhatiali (boatmen's song)
items.lineage: Bengali bhatiali (boatmen's song) tradition continuous from premodern Bengali-riverine-and-Sundarbans-delta boatmen labor practice through 19th-20th century Tagore-era literary-elevation (Tagore composed extensively in the bhatiali idiom) into modern Bengali-and-Bangladeshi continuous practice; the bhatiali is the canonical Bengali downstream-rowing-song integrating long-held-vocal phrases matched to slow downstream-rowing strokes
items.description: The Bengali bhatiali (boatmen's song) tradition continuous from premodern Bengali-riverine-and-Sundarbans-delta boatmen labor practice (the Padma-Ganges-Brahmaputra-Meghna river-delta of Bengal supported extensive boat-trade and fisher-population) through 19th-20th century Tagore-era literary-elevation (Tagore composed extensively in the bhatiali idiom under his Rabindra-Sangeet broader-song project) into modern Bengali-and-Bangladeshi continuous practice. The bhatiali is the canonical Bengali downstream-rowing-song integrating long-held-vocal phrases matched to slow downstream-rowing strokes (distinct from the uptempo upstream-rowing-song traditions). Defined by dotara-and-ektara-and-voice arrangement, Bengali-language text register, Hindustani-folk modal vocabulary, characteristic long-melismatic-phrase boat-context.
exemplars: Abbasuddin Ahmed — canonical 20th-century Bengali bhatiali vocalist
"Allah meghde paani de" canonical Bengali bhatiali

items.name: Japanese taue-uta (田植唄, rice-planting songs)
items.lineage: Japanese taue-uta (田植唄, "rice-planting songs") tradition continuous from premodern Japanese-agricultural village-labor practice through Edo-period continuous performance into modern Japanese-and-Japanese-diaspora continuous rural practice (where it survives) and into intangible-heritage status for certain regional variants; foundational repertoire integrates rice-paddy planting and weeding-songs with characteristic Japanese-folk pentatonic vocabulary
items.description: The Japanese taue-uta (田植唄, "rice-planting songs") tradition continuous from premodern Japanese-agricultural village-labor practice through Edo-period continuous performance into modern Japanese-and-Japanese-diaspora continuous rural practice (where it survives — the documented decline of taue-uta practice is well-attested as Japanese-agricultural mechanization removed the labor-coordination need) and into intangible-heritage status for certain regional variants (the Mibu-no-Hana-Taue rice-planting-ritual of Hiroshima Prefecture). Defined by shamisen-and-voice arrangement (and occasionally fue-flute and small-drum accompaniment in some regional variants), Japanese-language text register, Japanese-in-scale or yo-scale pentatonic vocabulary, characteristic women-singers (sa-otome rice-planting-women in some regional variants) labor-context.

items.name: Indonesian rice-planting song traditions
items.lineage: Indonesian rice-planting song tradition across Javanese, Sundanese, Balinese, Sumatran-Minangkabau, and Sulawesi regional-cultures continuous from premodern Indonesian-agricultural village-labor practice through colonial-period continuous performance into modern Indonesian-rural continuous practice; the Indonesian rice-paddy planting and harvest-songs integrate gamelan-and-vocal arrangements distinct to each regional culture
items.description: The Indonesian rice-planting song tradition across Javanese, Sundanese, Balinese, Sumatran-Minangkabau, and Sulawesi regional-cultures continuous from premodern Indonesian-agricultural village-labor practice through colonial-period continuous performance into modern Indonesian-rural continuous practice; the Indonesian rice-paddy planting and harvest-songs integrate gamelan-and-vocal arrangements distinct to each regional culture, with Javanese rice-planting song notably integrating slendro-and-pelog tunings, Sundanese rice-songs using kacapi-and-suling accompaniment, Balinese rice-songs integrating with broader Balinese-temple-ritual context. Defined by slendro-pelog tuning vocabulary, regional-Indonesian language text register, characteristic call-and-response group-vocal arrangement, characteristic rice-paddy task-coordination structure.
exemplars: Javanese village rice-planting song traditional canonical
Balinese rice-planting song integrated with Subak irrigation-ritual
Sundanese rice-planting song traditional with kacapi-suling

items.name: West-African rice-planting song (Senegambian-Mande)
items.lineage: West-African Senegambian-Mande rice-planting song tradition continuous from premodern Senegambian-and-Guinean rice-agriculture village-labor practice through colonial-period continuous performance into modern West-African-rural continuous practice; the West-African Senegambian rice-planting song tradition was demonstrably the documented lineage origin point for the South-Carolina Lowcountry rice-cultivation work-songs continuous into the broader American-South work-song tradition
items.description: The West-African Senegambian-Mande rice-planting song tradition continuous from premodern Senegambian-and-Guinean rice-agriculture village-labor practice (the Sahelian-rice-belt of modern Senegal, Gambia, Guinea-Bissau, Sierra Leone and the rice-growing-knowledge that traveled with enslaved-Africans transported to the South-Carolina-Georgia Lowcountry) through colonial-period continuous performance into modern West-African-rural continuous practice. The West-African Senegambian rice-planting song tradition was demonstrably the documented lineage origin point for the South-Carolina Lowcountry rice-cultivation work-songs continuous into the broader American-South work-song tradition (per Judith Carney Black Rice 2001 canonical-scholarly-documentation). Defined by kora-and-voice arrangement (in modern documented context), Manding-Maninka-Wolof text register, Mande-pentatonic modal vocabulary, characteristic rice-paddy task-coordination structure.
exemplars: Judith Carney — Black Rice 2001 (canonical scholarly documentation)
Sierra Leone Mende rice-cultivation song traditional

items.name: San (Khoisan) hunting and trance song
items.lineage: San (Khoisan) hunting-and-trance song tradition continuous from premodern Kalahari-Desert hunter-gatherer practice through 20th-21st century continuous performance into modern San practice across Botswana, Namibia, and South Africa
items.description: The San (Khoisan) hunting-and-trance song tradition continuous from premodern Kalahari-Desert hunter-gatherer practice through 20th-21st century continuous performance (where it survives — the San cultural-practice is increasingly endangered with documented language-and-cultural-erosion) into modern San practice across Botswana, Namibia, and South Africa; the San hunting-song tradition integrates trance-dance with hunting-magic and game-divination ritual (the canonical San trance-dance documented by Lorna Marshall and Megan Biesele). Defined by unaccompanied women's-group-vocal clapping-percussion arrangement with men entering the trance-dance circle, characteristic Khoisan-click-language text register with extensive click-consonants and ideophones, characteristic narrow-range polyphonic vocal arrangement.
exemplars: Lorna Marshall — The !Kung of Nyae Nyae 1976 canonical
Megan Biesele — Women Like Meat 1993 canonical-ethnography
Eland Bull Song canonical San hunting-magic

items.name: Sami yoik — animal-tracking and hunting song
items.lineage: Sami yoik (joik) tradition continuous from premodern Sami reindeer-herding-and-hunting-and-fishing practice across the Sápmi-region of northern Norway, Sweden, Finland, and Russia through colonial-era Christianization-suppression continuous through 20th-century revival
items.description: The Sami yoik (joik) tradition continuous from premodern Sami reindeer-herding-and-hunting-and-fishing practice across the Sápmi-region of northern Norway, Sweden, Finland, and Russia through colonial-era Christianization-suppression (the Sami yoik was actively suppressed by Lutheran-Norwegian-and-Swedish missionary-and-state-policy from 17th-19th centuries with documented yoiking-prohibition laws) continuous through 20th-century revival. The yoik is the canonical Sami-vocal-genre integrating animal-tracking (the yoiker performs a yoik OF the animal — not ABOUT it — that captures the essence of the reindeer, bear, wolf, or other game-animal), person-naming, and place-naming functions. Defined by unaccompanied solo-vocal recitative arrangement, Sami-language text register, narrow-range pentatonic-leaning melodic vocabulary, characteristic free-meter recitative-style.
exemplars: Mari Boine — canonical modern Sami yoik-vocalist
Inga Juuso — canonical traditional Sami-Norwegian yoik

items.name: Aboriginal Australian hunting songlines
items.lineage: Aboriginal Australian hunting-and-songlines tradition continuous from at-least-65,000-year-continuous Indigenous-Australian cultural-practice through colonial-era continuous performance into modern Aboriginal-and-Torres-Strait-Islander continuous practice
items.description: The Aboriginal Australian hunting-and-songlines tradition continuous from at-least-65,000-year-continuous Indigenous-Australian cultural-practice through colonial-era continuous performance into modern Aboriginal-and-Torres-Strait-Islander continuous practice; the songlines (Tjukurpa "Dreaming" tracks in Pitjantjatjara-Yankunytjatjara terminology, or Wongar in Yolngu terminology) integrate hunting-game knowledge with cosmological-ancestral narrative across documented multi-thousand-kilometer song-cycles (the songlines are an Indigenous-Australian cartographic-and-knowledge-encoding system where specific land-features, water-sources, game-trails, and ritual-sites are encoded in song-sequence). Defined by didgeridoo-and-clapstick-and-voice arrangement, Aboriginal-language text register with regional-language variation, characteristic narrow-range narrative-recitative style.
exemplars: Wagilag Sisters Project canonical Yolngu Sister-songlines
Songlines as documented by Bruce Chatwin Songlines 1987
Geoffrey Gurrumul Yunupingu canonical modern Yolngu vocalist

items.name: Apache hunting-medicine song (Native American)
items.lineage: Apache-and-broader-Native-American hunting-medicine song tradition continuous from premodern Indigenous-North-American hunting-and-ritual practice through colonial-era continuous performance into modern Native-American continuous practice
items.description: The Apache-and-broader-Native-American hunting-medicine song tradition continuous from premodern Indigenous-North-American hunting-and-ritual practice through colonial-era continuous performance into modern Native-American continuous practice across Apache (Western Apache, Mescalero, Jicarilla, Chiricahua), Navajo (Diné), Lakota-Dakota-Nakota, and broader Indigenous-North-American cultures; the hunting-medicine songs invoke spiritual-power for successful game-pursuit (the canonical Apache "deer-medicine song" was historically performed before deer-hunting expeditions). Defined by powwow-drum-circle (or hand-drum in solo-ritual context) and voice arrangement, characteristic vocables-and-Indigenous-language text register, characteristic pentatonic-or-narrow-mode melodic vocabulary.
exemplars: Northern Cree — canonical powwow-drum-circle modern recordings
Frances Densmore early-20th-century Native-American song-documentation canonical scholarly

items.name: Hebridean waulking song (òrain luaidh)
items.lineage: Scottish-Hebridean Gaelic waulking-song (òrain luaidh) tradition continuous from medieval-and-early-modern Hebridean Gaelic wool-fulling labor practice through 19th-20th century continuous performance into modern Scottish-Gaelic revival
items.description: The Scottish-Hebridean Gaelic waulking-song (òrain luaidh) tradition continuous from medieval-and-early-modern Hebridean Gaelic wool-fulling labor practice (the waulking, Gaelic luadh, was the process by which freshly-woven wool-tweed cloth was shrunk and softened by being soaked in stale-urine and beaten rhythmically on a long table by groups of 8-12 women) through 19th-20th century continuous performance into modern Scottish-Gaelic revival (the canonical Marjorie Kennedy-Fraser Songs of the Hebrides 1909-1921 documented waulking-songs, and the Tobar an Dualchais / Kist o Riches archive preserves extensive field-recordings). Defined by unaccompanied women's-group-vocal call-and-response arrangement with fist-on-table rhythmic-percussion, Scottish-Gaelic text register, characteristic Hebridean-modal melodic vocabulary, characteristic narrow-range short-cycle waulking-stroke-coordination structure.
exemplars: Capercaillie — modern Scottish-Gaelic waulking-song revival canonical
Mary Smith — canonical Hebridean waulking-song traditional 20th-century
Catherine-Ann MacPhee — canonical Lewis Gaelic singer
Marjorie Kennedy-Fraser Songs of the Hebrides 1909-1921 canonical

items.name: Irish spinning song (amhrán snímh)
items.lineage: Irish-Gaelic spinning-and-domestic-labor song tradition continuous from medieval-and-early-modern Irish-rural domestic-textile-labor practice through 19th-20th century continuous performance into modern Irish-Gaelic-and-Scottish-Gaelic revival
items.description: The Irish-Gaelic spinning-and-domestic-labor song tradition continuous from medieval-and-early-modern Irish-rural domestic-textile-labor practice (the spinning-wheel-and-distaff context where women performed wool-and-flax spinning while singing) through 19th-20th century continuous performance into modern Irish-Gaelic-and-Scottish-Gaelic revival; foundational Irish spinning-song repertoire includes "Bean Phaidin" (Paddy's wife, Connemara canonical), "Eileanóir a Rún" (Eleanor my treasure), "An Mhaighdean Mhara" (The Mermaid, canonical Donegal-Gaelic), "Dónall Óg" (Young Donal). Defined by unaccompanied women's-solo or small-group vocal arrangement, Irish-Gaelic-language text register, characteristic Connacht-and-Donegal modal vocabulary, characteristic sean-nós-style melismatic-ornament practice.
exemplars: Mairéad Ní Mhaonaigh — modern Donegal-Gaelic canonical (Altan)
Iarla Ó Lionáird — modern sean-nós canonical
Connacht and Donegal sean-nós continuous-living tradition

items.name: Sami vuolle and domestic-labor song
items.lineage: Sami vuolle (Lule-Sami "yoik" variant) and broader Sami domestic-labor song tradition continuous from premodern Sami reindeer-herding-and-domestic-textile practice across the Sápmi-region through colonial-era continuous performance into modern Sami-cultural-revival
items.description: The Sami vuolle (Lule-Sami "yoik" variant) and broader Sami domestic-labor song tradition continuous from premodern Sami reindeer-herding-and-domestic-textile practice across the Sápmi-region through colonial-era continuous performance into modern Sami-cultural-revival; the vuolle is the Lule-Sami yoik-variant distinct from the Northern-Sami juoiggus, with the broader Sami domestic-song repertoire covering child-rearing, sewing, and domestic-textile-labor coordination. Defined by unaccompanied solo-vocal narrative-and-recitative arrangement, Lule-Sami-language text register, narrow-range pentatonic-leaning melodic vocabulary.
exemplars: Mari Boine — Northern-Sami juoiggus canonical (broader Sami-vocal lineage)
Inga Juuso — canonical traditional Sami-Norwegian yoik

items.name: Romanian cântece de tors (spinning songs)
items.lineage: Romanian spinning-song (cântece de tors) tradition continuous from premodern Romanian-rural domestic-textile-labor practice through 19th-century Romanian-folklorist documentation through 20th-century Béla Bartók Romanian-folk-collection canonical into modern Romanian-folk-revival continuous practice
items.description: The Romanian spinning-song (cântece de tors) tradition continuous from premodern Romanian-rural domestic-textile-labor practice (the wool-and-flax-spinning context where Romanian women performed evening spinning-bee gatherings called șezătoare in the documented social-context of multi-generational-household evening gatherings) through 19th-century Romanian-folklorist documentation through 20th-century Béla Bartók Romanian-folk-collection canonical into modern Romanian-folk-revival continuous practice. The Romanian șezătoare context integrated spinning-labor with extended narrative-song-and-doina performance. Defined by unaccompanied women's-solo-or-small-group vocal arrangement, Romanian-language text register, characteristic Romanian-folk modal vocabulary, characteristic narrow-range narrative-style.
exemplars: Romanian doina tradition integrated with spinning-context

items.name: Andean Quechua-Aymara spinning song
items.lineage: Andean Quechua-and-Aymara spinning-and-weaving song tradition continuous from pre-Hispanic Andean-textile labor practice through Spanish-colonial-era continuous performance into modern Quechua-and-Aymara-speaking Andean-rural continuous practice across Bolivia, Peru, and Ecuador
items.description: The Andean Quechua-and-Aymara spinning-and-weaving song tradition continuous from pre-Hispanic Andean-textile labor practice (the Andean textile-tradition is documented as among the most-elaborate in pre-Columbian Americas with extensive women's-textile-labor song-coordination; the canonical pre-Hispanic Inca-era cumbi-and-ahuasca textile-tradition involved hereditary aclla-cuna textile-women performing labor-coordination song) through Spanish-colonial-era continuous performance into modern Quechua-and-Aymara-speaking Andean-rural continuous practice. The Andean spinning-song integrates extended drop-spindle and back-strap-loom weaving with multi-hour song-performance, with characteristic intimate-melancholic style distinct from the festive huayno-de-trabajo work-song tradition. Defined by unaccompanied women's-solo vocal arrangement, Quechua-Aymara-and-Spanish text register, Andean-pentatonic modal vocabulary.

items.name: Bengali jata gita / Indian grinding-mill song
items.lineage: Bengali jata gita (grinding-mill song) and broader Indian-subcontinent grinding-and-millstone song tradition continuous from premodern South-Asian domestic-grain-processing labor practice through 19th-20th century continuous performance into modern Bengali-Bangladeshi-and-broader-Indian continuous practice
items.description: The Bengali jata gita (grinding-mill song) and broader Indian-subcontinent grinding-and-millstone song tradition continuous from premodern South-Asian domestic-grain-processing labor practice (women-laborers performed evening-and-pre-dawn grain-grinding at the stone-grinding-mill jata with extensive song-coordination; the jata gita is documented across Bengali, Maharashtrian, Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, and broader Indian-rural domestic-labor contexts) through 19th-20th century continuous performance into modern Bengali-Bangladeshi-and-broader-Indian continuous practice. The Maharashtrian Marathi ovi (grinding-song verse) tradition is among the most-documented variants; the Pune-based GRINDmill Songs Project has documented over 100,000 women's grinding-mill song verses since 1990s. Defined by unaccompanied women's-solo vocal arrangement, regional-Indian-language text register, characteristic Hindustani-folk modal vocabulary.
exemplars: GRINDmill Songs Project Pune 1990s-onward canonical documentation
Karnataka and Tamil Nadu women's grinding-song traditional
Bahinabai Chaudhari — canonical Marathi peasant-poet (broader ovi tradition)

items.name: Wolof-Senegambian grain-grinding women's song
items.lineage: Wolof-Senegambian women's grain-grinding song tradition continuous from premodern Senegambian domestic-grain-processing labor practice through colonial-era continuous performance into modern Senegambian continuous practice
items.description: The Wolof-Senegambian women's grain-grinding song tradition continuous from premodern Senegambian domestic-grain-processing labor practice (the millet-and-sorghum and rice grain-grinding context where women performed extended labor with mortar-and-pestle pounding; the canonical Senegambian women's pestle-pounding rhythm with two-or-three women alternating-strokes on a single mortar is documented as foundational to broader West-African polyrhythm) through colonial-era continuous performance into modern Senegambian continuous practice. The grain-grinding-song tradition integrates pestle-pounding rhythmic-coordination with extensive group-vocal song (the Senegambian women's mortar-and-pestle two-or-three-woman alternating-stroke pattern is also the documented origin point for some Afro-diasporic Caribbean percussion-traditions). Defined by call-and-response group-vocal arrangement with pestle-pounding rhythmic-foundation, Wolof-Mandinka-and-broader-Senegambian text register, characteristic Mande-pentatonic modal vocabulary.
exemplars: Hugh Tracey early-20th-century West-African field-recordings canonical scholarly

items.name: Korean baennoraega and domestic-women's song
items.lineage: Korean baennoraega (뱃노래, "boatmen's song") and broader Korean women's-domestic-labor song tradition continuous from premodern Korean-rural domestic-labor practice through Joseon-dynasty continuous performance into modern Korean-folk-revival
items.description: The Korean baennoraega (뱃노래, "boatmen's song") and broader Korean women's-domestic-labor song tradition continuous from premodern Korean-rural domestic-labor practice through Joseon-dynasty continuous performance into modern Korean-folk-revival; the baennoraega coordinates fishing-boat-rowing while parallel women's-domestic-labor songs accompanied weaving, grain-grinding, and household-textile labor. The canonical Korean min'yo (folk-song) tradition integrates both maritime and domestic-textile sub-genres with characteristic Korean-minsogak-mode melodic vocabulary. Defined by unaccompanied women's-or-men's solo-or-small-group vocal arrangement, Korean-Hangul text register, characteristic Korean-folk modal vocabulary (yukjabaegi-tori, gyeongtori, mereumdori), characteristic regional-Korean dialect variation.
exemplars: Kim So-hee — canonical 20th-century Korean min'yo vocalist
Korean-rural women's domestic-labor song continuous-living tradition

items.name: Yiddish spinning-and-domestic song (Oyfn Pripetshik lineage)
items.lineage: Yiddish spinning-and-domestic-lullaby tradition continuous from medieval-Ashkenazi-Jewish domestic-and-textile labor practice through 19th-century Yiddish folksongbook canonization into modern Yiddish-revival continuous practice
items.description: The Yiddish spinning-and-domestic-lullaby tradition continuous from medieval-Ashkenazi-Jewish domestic-and-textile labor practice through 19th-century Yiddish folksongbook canonization (the canonical "Oyfn Pripetshik" 1880s by Mark Warshawsky is the foundational Yiddish learning-spinning-domestic song where the rabbi-teacher teaches the alef-beys alphabet to small-children with the women-mothers spinning by the hearth-fire — the song integrates Yiddish-domestic-textile-and-childcare context with Jewish-religious-learning) into modern Yiddish-revival continuous practice. Other foundational repertoire includes "Tumbalalaika" (riddle-song) and "Rozhinkes mit Mandlen" (Raisins and Almonds, the canonical Yiddish lullaby). Defined by unaccompanied women's-solo vocal arrangement, Yiddish-language text register, characteristic Ashkenazi-freygish modal vocabulary, characteristic hearth-and-spinning-wheel domestic-context.
exemplars: "Oyfn Pripetshik" 1880s Mark Warshawsky canonical Yiddish spinning-song
"Rozhinkes mit Mandlen" canonical Yiddish lullaby-spinning crossover

items.name: Sardinian boci de tela (weaving songs)
items.lineage: Sardinian boci de tela ("weaving songs") and broader Sardinian women's-domestic-textile-labor song tradition continuous from medieval-Sardinian-rural domestic-textile labor practice through 19th-20th century continuous performance into modern Sardinian-folk-revival
items.description: The Sardinian boci de tela ("weaving songs") and broader Sardinian women's-domestic-textile-labor song tradition continuous from medieval-Sardinian-rural domestic-textile labor practice through 19th-20th century continuous performance into modern Sardinian-folk-revival; the Sardinian weaving-song integrates the back-strap-loom-and-vertical-loom textile-labor (Sardinian-traditional carpets and tapestries are documented as among the most-elaborate Mediterranean-textile traditions) with extensive narrative-and-improvised-song. The Sardinian women's domestic-textile-song tradition is distinct from the Sardinian a tenore men's-polyphony tradition but shares the broader Sardinian-traditional vocal-aesthetic and modal-vocabulary. Defined by unaccompanied women's-solo-or-small-group vocal arrangement, Sardinian-language text register, Mediterranean-polyphonic-modal vocabulary, characteristic narrow-range narrative-style.
exemplars: Modern Sardinian-village women's weaving-song continuous-living tradition
Maria Giovanna Cherchi — modern Sardinian-folk canonical
