Defined by a four-on-the-floor house frame at roughly 118-130 BPM carrying a two-to-eight-bar disco, funk or soul loop sampled off vinyl rather than replayed, with the loop's extended seventh-and-ninth harmony inherited from 1970s Philadelphia and New York disco left intact as the entire chord progression; by resonant band-pass and low-pass filter sweeps opened and closed by hand across that loop so the filter, not new material, produces the build and the drop; by aggressive bus compression keyed to the kick, giving the audible ducking pump that is the style's fingerprint; by phaser, flanger and retained vinyl saturation and hiss as timbre; and by vocoder and talkbox toplines in the later Daft Punk and Modjo phase. Landmark records are Motorbass's Pansoul (1996), de Crécy's Super Discount (1996), Daft Punk's Homework (1997), Alan Braxe's Vertigo (1997), Stardust's Music Sounds Better With You (1998) and Modjo's Lady (Hear Me Tonight) (2000). Distinguished from Chicago house by its sampled-loop rather than drum-machine-programmed foundation and its French disco-crate source material; distinguished from contemporaneous American filtered disco house (Masters at Work, Armand Van Helden) by the tight Paris label network and by the extremity of the filter-and-pump gesture; distinguished from later nu-disco and future funk by predating them and by its analog apartment-studio chain rather than in-the-box revivalism.
exemplars: Stardust — Music Sounds Better With You (1998)

items.name: Urbano latino
items.lineage: Pan-Hispanic commercial umbrella consolidated around 2015-2020 across the Miami-San Juan-Medellín label axis (Rimas, Sony Latin, Universal Music Latino) as reggaetón, Latin trap and dancehall-pop merged into one radio-and-streaming format — 88-96 BPM dembow or halftime trap grids, TR-808 sub-glides, Auto-Tuned Spanish hooks doubled in stacked thirds, minor-key four-chord synth loops, and sung-rapped verses over near-identical percussion programming regardless of subgenre origin
items.description: Urbano latino is the industry-level category that absorbed reggaetón, Latin trap, dembow and Spanish-language dancehall into a single commercial format after 2015, driven by streaming playlisting rather than a single scene. Its sonic signature is a fully in-the-box build: a programmed dembow or trap kit, a sub-heavy 808 line carrying the harmony, four-bar minor loops, and heavily tuned lead vocals stacked into wide hook choruses. It differs from reggaetón proper by not committing to the dembow pattern, and from Latin trap by keeping the melodic pop chorus as the structural centre.

items.name: Música mexicana (modern regional umbrella)
items.lineage: Streaming-era umbrella term adopted around 2020-2023 for the whole modern regional-Mexican field — banda sinaloense, norteño-sax, sierreño, mariachi-pop and corridos tumbados marketed together out of Culiacán, Guadalajara and Los Angeles by labels such as Rancho Humilde, Street Mob and Fonovisa — unified by 2/4 polka and 3/4 vals frames, tuba or tololoche bass on the downbeat with bajo sexto offbeats, twin-trumpet or requinto lead lines, and plain-toned chest-voice duet singing in close thirds
items.description: Música mexicana is the 2020s marketing-and-scene label under which banda, norteño, sierreño and tumbado acts are grouped, after regional Mexican music became one of the fastest-growing streaming categories in the US. Sonically it retains the polka and vals metric backbone, the tuba-or-tololoche downbeat, bajo sexto or requinto chording, and unadorned paired vocals, but is now tracked to a modern loudness-normalized digital chain rather than the mid-century Mexico City orchestral chain. It is broader than banda sinaloense or norteño alone, and distinct from Tejano in retaining the Mexican rather than Texan instrumentation and diction.

items.name: Permanent wave
items.lineage: Retroactive streaming-derived category for the durable Anglo-American alternative-rock mainstream of roughly 1991-2010 — the post-Nevermind radio format built by Nirvana, Radiohead, Foo Fighters, Muse and Coldplay — characterized by mid-tempo 90-140 BPM 4/4 backbeats, quiet-verse/loud-chorus dynamics driven by pedal switching between clean single-coil arpeggios and saturated humbucker power chords, close-miked dry drums, and unornamented mid-range male lead vocals doubled at the chorus
items.description: Permanent wave names the alternative-rock lineage that stayed on mainstream rock radio continuously from the early 1990s onward, absorbing grunge, Britpop and post-Britpop stadium rock into one long-lived format. The sound is a four-piece band tracked in a large commercial room to a late-analog or hybrid digital chain: dry backbeat kit, clean-to-distorted guitar dynamic contrast, root-motion bass, and a plainly recorded lead voice carrying an anthemic chorus. It is broader and more radio-oriented than grunge, and less abrasive than noise rock or 1980s American indie, from which it inherits its verse-chorus dynamic device.
exemplars: Coldplay — A Rush of Blood to the Head

items.name: Sierreño
items.lineage: Acoustic trio format from the Sierra Madre Occidental (Sinaloa, Durango, Chihuahua) that spread through Southern California Mexican-American communities in the 1990s-2000s — requinto or twelve-string lead guitar picking the melody, second guitar strumming the 2/4 polka or 3/4 vals rhythm, and tuba or tololoche walking the bass, under two unornamented chest voices in parallel thirds narrating corridos at 90-130 BPM with no drum kit at all
items.description: Sierreño is the stripped acoustic corrido format of the western Sierra Madre, built on a requinto or twelve-string lead line, a strummed rhythm guitar, and a tuba or tololoche bass, with no percussion. Two voices sing in close parallel thirds with flat, conversational delivery, letting the narrative text dominate. It differs from norteño by dropping the accordion and drum kit, and from banda by replacing the whole brass ensemble with a single bass horn and guitars — a sparseness that made it the direct acoustic template for corridos tumbados.
exemplars: Los Plebes del Rancho de Ariel Camacho

items.name: Corridos tumbados
items.lineage: Fusion codified in 2019-2020 by Natanael Cano and the Rancho Humilde label in Los Angeles and Hermosillo, grafting trap-rap phrasing, cadence and lyric attitude onto the sierreño acoustic trio — requinto lead over strummed rhythm guitar and tuba or tololoche bass at 70-100 BPM, sometimes with added 808 sub and trap hi-hat rolls, and rapped-sung nasal lead vocals with light Auto-Tune narrating contemporary narco and flex themes
items.description: Corridos tumbados emerged around 2019 when young Sonoran and Los Angeles artists kept the sierreño acoustic instrumentation but adopted trap vocal cadence, slang and occasionally 808 sub-bass and hi-hat rolls. The result is a hybrid where a requinto still carries the melodic hook and a tuba still marks the bass, but the vocal is delivered in loose rapped-sung phrases with mild pitch correction rather than the squared-off ballad diction of the traditional corrido. It is distinguished from plain sierreño by that vocal rhythm and production, and from Latin trap by keeping acoustic strings and horn bass as the primary instrumentation.

items.name: Reggaetón colombiano
items.lineage: Medellín-centred variant that took over the reggaetón mainstream between 2010 and 2020 through producers Sky Rompiendo, Ovy on the Drums and Mosty working with J Balvin, Maluma and Karol G — softening the Puerto Rican dembow into a lighter 90-96 BPM pattern with brushed shaker and rim-click layers, foregrounding major-key or bright-minor synth and plucked-guitar loops, and replacing hard rapped delivery with melodic paisa-accented crooning and airy stacked hooks
items.description: Reggaetón colombiano is the Medellín strain of reggaetón that displaced San Juan as the genre's commercial centre in the 2010s. Its producers thinned the dembow — quieter snare, more shaker and rim layers, more space — and built tracks around bright melodic loops and sung rather than rapped hooks, aiming at global pop radio. Against Puerto Rican reggaetón it is lighter, more major-key and more overtly pop; against urbano latino generally it stays committed to the dembow pulse rather than drifting toward trap.

items.name: Alt-Z
items.lineage: Streaming-era alternative pop category consolidated around 2018-2022 out of American and Anglo bedroom-production scenes (Billie Eilish and Finneas in Highland Park, Clairo, girl in red) — 80-110 BPM halftime or trap-derived programmed beats, sub-heavy 808 or synth bass, deliberately dry close-miked whisper-register lead vocals with audible breath and lip noise, sparse harmonic beds of detuned pads or muted guitar, and confessional first-person lyrics
items.description: Alt-Z is the Gen-Z alternative-pop format that grew out of home-studio production around 2018, defined more by vocal proximity and restraint than by any single rhythm. Tracks are typically built in a bedroom DAW: a sparse programmed beat, a dominant sub-bass, minimal harmonic filler, and a very close, very dry lead vocal sung near a whisper with breath deliberately left in the mix. It differs from mainstream pop in its low dynamic level and unpolished vocal texture, and from hyperpop in avoiding extreme processing and maximalist density.
exemplars: Billie Eilish — When We All Fall Asleep, Where Do We Go?

items.name: Indietronica
items.lineage: Indie-electronic hybrid formed circa 1999-2008 around Morr Music (Berlin), Ghostly International (Ann Arbor) and the early Postal Service axis — laptop-sequenced glitch and click percussion under live guitar, bass and analog synth, 100-130 BPM 4/4 grids with deliberately quantized micro-edits, soft untrained indie lead vocals mixed level with the beat, and sample-and-hold or granular textures used as counter-melody rather than effect
items.description: Indietronica names the turn-of-the-2000s meeting of indie-pop songwriting with laptop electronic production, associated with Morr Music, Ghostly and a cluster of American and German artists. Tracks keep verse-chorus song structure and a soft, untrained indie vocal, but the rhythm section is programmed — clicks, glitched fragments, drum machines — and synth textures replace much of the traditional band arrangement. It is more song-shaped than IDM and more electronically constructed than indie pop, sitting between the two rather than in either.
exemplars: Caribou — The Milk of Human Kindness

items.name: Rock en español
items.lineage: Spanish-language rock movement that matured across Mexico City, Buenos Aires, Santiago and Madrid in the 1980s and peaked commercially 1988-1998 through the Mexico City rock urbano scene and BMG/Sony Latin signings — post-punk and new-wave guitar textures and synth pads over 4/4 rock backbeats, frequent grafting of ska, cumbia, bolero and Andean rhythms onto rock instrumentation, and declamatory Spanish lead vocals carrying overtly political or urban-social lyrics
items.description: Rock en español is the Spanish-language rock mainstream that consolidated in Mexico, Argentina, Chile and Spain during the 1980s and became a continental commercial force in the 1990s. It combines post-punk and new-wave guitar and synth vocabulary with Latin American rhythmic borrowings — ska upstrokes, cumbia bass figures, bolero ballad forms — and a strongly declaimed Spanish vocal usually carrying social or political content. It differs from Anglo alternative rock in that rhythmic hybridity and lyrical register, and from Latin alternative in being more straightforwardly rock-band-shaped.

items.name: K-pop boy group
items.lineage: Seoul idol-agency format codified from the mid-1990s (SM Entertainment's H.O.T., 1996) and industrialized through SM, YG, JYP, Big Hit and HYBE — multi-member male ensembles performing 100-130 BPM hybrid tracks that cut between rap verses, sung pre-choruses and a hook-dense chorus, over EDM, trap or new-jack-swing programming, with dense multitracked unison-and-harmony vocal stacks, sharp English-Korean code-switching, and arrangements written to synchronized choreography
items.description: The K-pop boy group is a production format as much as a genre: a trained multi-member male ensemble recording songs assembled by international writing camps and finished in Seoul agency studios. Tracks are structurally restless, switching between rap, sung melody, chant-like hooks and a post-chorus dance break, and are mixed with very dense stacked vocals against club-derived programming. Compared with K-pop girl-group production it leans harder on rap sections and low-end weight, and compared with Western boy bands it uses far more abrupt sectional contrast and hip-hop vocabulary.

items.name: Agronejo
items.lineage: Brazilian sertanejo substrain named in the late 2010s around Goiás and Mato Grosso agribusiness culture and its rodeo-festival circuit — mid-tempo 90-120 BPM sertanejo universitário arrangements of viola caipira, acoustic guitar, accordion and full drum kit, with major-key parallel-third duet singing, big live-DVD stadium mixes, and lyrics explicitly celebrating farm, cattle, pickup-truck and rural-proprietor identity
items.description: Agronejo is the agribusiness-identified branch of Brazilian sertanejo that took shape in the late 2010s on the Centre-West rodeo and agro-festival circuit. Musically it is sertanejo universitário — viola caipira and acoustic guitar over a full pop-country rhythm section, sung in the traditional two-voice parallel-third duet — but its repertoire is thematically dedicated to farming, cattle, machinery and rural wealth, and much of its canon is released as arena live recordings rather than studio albums. It differs from sertanejo raiz by its electrified pop-country arrangement and from sertanejo universitário generally only in lyrical program and festival context.

items.name: Trap argentino
items.lineage: Buenos Aires trap scene that grew directly out of the El Quinto Escalón freestyle battle plaza (Parque Rivadavia, 2012-2017) and turned professional 1017-1019 through Duki, Bizarrap and Neo Pistea — 130-150 BPM halftime trap grids with rolled hi-hats and long 808 glides, dark minor-key synth loops, heavy Auto-Tune on rioplatense-accented Spanish, and lunfardo battle-rap diction carried over from freestyle into melodic song forms
items.description: Trap argentino is the Buenos Aires branch of Spanish-language trap, unusual in having grown out of a live freestyle-battle culture — El Quinto Escalón — rather than a studio scene, which left its lyricism sharper and more competitive than most urbano. Productions are bedroom-DAW trap: halftime kick placement, triplet hi-hat rolls, long detuned 808 glides, spare minor synth motifs, and saturated Auto-Tune on a distinctly rioplatense accent. It is distinguished from Puerto Rican Latin trap by that accent and lunfardo vocabulary, and from reggaetón by rejecting the dembow pattern outright.

items.name: UK Dance
items.lineage: British commercial dance-pop consolidated in London and Manchester from the late 2000s as garage, house and drum-and-bass producers crossed into the singles chart — Duke Dumont, Disclosure, Rudimental, Gorgon City, Sigala and Chase & Status codifying a 120-128 BPM four-on-the-floor (or 174 BPM liquid D&B) template built on filtered piano-and-organ house stabs, sidechained sub-bass, chopped garage-swing hi-hats and a full-throated guest topline sung rather than rapped.
items.description: UK dance is the British radio-facing wing of club music, formed in the late 2000s when the country's garage and house undergrounds were absorbed into the pop singles market. It is defined by a swung or shuffled hi-hat grid inherited from 2-step, hard sidechain pumping under piano and organ stabs, and a soul-trained guest vocalist carrying a full verse-chorus song form rather than a looped sample. Against American EDM it is warmer and more song-shaped, with less white-noise buildup and drop architecture; against deep house it is faster, brighter and structurally conventional.

items.name: Post-Teen Pop
items.lineage: North American and British mainstream pop of the 2010s made by artists who graduated out of teen-idol machinery into adult authorship — Ariana Grande, Selena Gomez, Demi Lovato, Halsey and Shawn Mendes working with Max Martin, Ilya Salmanzadeh and Ryan Tedder — built at 90-110 BPM on trap-derived hi-hat rolls and 808 sub-bass under sparse keyboard-and-plucked-synth beds, with stacked, heavily comped, lightly retuned vocal arrangements and whisper-to-whistle-register dynamic staging replacing the four-on-the-floor of prior teen pop.
items.description: Post-teen pop names the 2010s style of former teen-market singers whose records absorbed hip-hop and R&B rhythm while keeping pop song architecture. Sonically it is spare and vocal-forward: 808 sub-bass and rolled trap hi-hats under thin synth pads, with the majority of the frequency spectrum given over to a dense, multitracked lead vocal carrying melisma and register shifts. Compared with the boy-band and bubblegum pop it descends from, it is slower, harmonically flatter, less chorus-band-driven and far more dependent on vocal production as the arrangement itself.

items.name: Grupera
items.lineage: Mexican regional-popular style formed in Michoacán, Sinaloa and Nuevo León across the late 1970s and 1980s and codified by Los Bukis, Bronco, Los Temerarios and Los Yonic's — small self-contained 'grupos' replacing the mariachi and banda ensembles with electric bass, drum kit, electric guitar and layered polyphonic synthesizer, playing rancheras, cumbias and romantic baladas at 90-130 BPM under a plaintive lead tenor with close-harmony backing and openly sentimental lyric content.
items.description: Grupera emerged in provincial Mexico in the late 1970s as touring dance groups downsized from horn-and-string ensembles to a synthesizer-led combo that one van could carry. The defining sound is a bright polyphonic-synth pad and lead line doubling the melody over a simple kit-and-electric-bass ranchera or cumbia pulse, with a high, emotionally unguarded male lead and thirds-harmony backing vocals mixed close. It is distinguished from banda sinaloense by the absence of a brass section, from norteño by the demotion of the accordion to a colour rather than the lead, and from bolero by its dance-floor tempo.
exemplars: Los Bukis — Me Volví a Acordar de Ti
Los Temerarios — Mi Vida Eres Tú

items.name: OPM (Original Pilipino Music)
items.lineage: Filipino popular song codified in Manila from the mid-1970s through the Metro Manila Popular Music Festival and the work of Ryan Cayabyab, Freddie Aguilar, APO Hiking Society and later Eraserheads and Rivermaya — Tagalog-language verse-chorus writing over a Western pop-rock and soft-rock instrumentation of piano, clean electric guitar, electric bass and kit at 70-120 BPM, with wide-interval, high-tessitura melodies engineered for full-throated belting and dense stacked backing harmony inherited from the country's choral and vocal-group culture.
items.description: OPM is the umbrella term for Tagalog-language popular songwriting that emerged in Manila during the 1970s as a deliberate nationalist alternative to imported Anglo-American pop. Its recordings favour piano or acoustic guitar foundations, restrained kit, sweetened string-machine or synth pads, and above all a soaring belted lead vocal with wide leaps and sustained high climaxes, supported by tight multi-part backing harmony. It differs from Cantopop and J-pop in its rock-band rather than orchestral-arranger foundation, and from Anglo soft rock in its melodic reach and its lyric register of direct sentiment.

items.name: Boy Band
items.lineage: Manager-assembled male vocal-group pop running from Motown-era harmony acts through New Kids on the Block, and codified between 1993 and 2001 by Backstreet Boys and NSYNC recording with Denniz PoP and Max Martin at Cheiron Studios Stockholm — four or five non-instrumentalist singers trading lead lines over a 90-110 BPM programmed R&B-swing or four-on-the-floor track of sampled kit, slap-and-sub bass, sawtooth pad stacks and orchestral-hit punctuation, with block-harmony choruses and a mandatory unaccompanied a-cappella breakdown.
items.description: The boy band is a production format rather than a scene: a vocal-only male group whose records are assembled by a writer-producer team around traded solo lines and massed block harmony. The Cheiron-era template that fixed the sound uses gated programmed drums, a compressed synth bass on the octave, layered saw pads, and an unusually loud, dry, heavily doubled vocal stack sitting well above the track. It separates from 1960s girl groups by its programmed rather than live rhythm section, and from post-teen pop by its density, faster tempos, and reliance on group harmony over a single star vocalist.

items.name: Stomp and Holler
items.lineage: Anglo-American indie-folk revival style of roughly 2008-2015 — Mumford & Sons, The Lumineers, Of Monsters and Men, Edward Sharpe and The Head and the Heart — built on strummed dreadnought guitar and clawhammer or rolled banjo at 100-140 BPM, a kick-drum-and-tambourine floor pulse played by the singers themselves, communal 'hey!' shouts and massed unison choruses, and a soft-verse-to-full-band-crescendo dynamic arc borrowed from post-rock and applied to acoustic instrumentation.
items.description: Stomp and holler is the arena-scaled acoustic revival that dominated Anglo-American festival billing around 2010, taking string-band instrumentation and playing it with rock dynamics. Its markers are a driving eighth-note strum, banjo used as a rhythmic texture rather than a soloing voice, a bass drum stomped on every beat, handclaps and gang shouts, and an arrangement that withholds the full band until an explosive final chorus. It is distinguished from bluegrass by the absence of instrumental soloing and high-lonesome modality, and from earlier indie folk by its sheer volume and communal chorus writing.
exemplars: Of Monsters and Men — My Head Is an Animal
Edward Sharpe and the Magnetic Zeros — Up from Below

items.name: Contemporary Christian Music
items.lineage: American evangelical pop-rock formed out of the late-1960s California Jesus Movement and Maranatha! Music, professionalized in Nashville through the 1980s by Amy Grant, Michael W. Smith and Steven Curtis Chapman, and re-founded in the 2000s as congregational 'modern worship' by Hillsong, Chris Tomlin and Bethel — 68-80 or 130-140 BPM, delay-drenched arpeggiated electric guitar over piano pads and four-on-the-floor kit, diatonic I-V-vi-IV loops in singable narrow-range keys, and a build-to-anthemic-bridge form designed for a congregation to join.
items.description: CCM is evangelical Protestant devotional music written and recorded to mainstream pop-rock production standards, centred on Nashville and, since the 2000s, on the megachurch worship-album pipeline. The characteristic sound is a washed, dotted-eighth-delay guitar figure over sustained piano and pad, an unhurried kit, and a lead vocal in a comfortable middle register singing four-chord diatonic loops with lyrics addressed in the second person to God. It parts from Black gospel in its avoidance of blue notes, melisma and call-and-response, and from Southern gospel in dropping quartet harmony for solo-plus-congregation texture.

items.name: Hip Pop
items.lineage: American crossover style of roughly 1998-2010 in which pop and R&B singers built records on hip-hop production and rap features — Nelly, Ne-Yo, Fergie, Gwen Stefani and Chris Brown working with The Neptunes, Timbaland, Jermaine Dupri and will.i.am — using 88-105 BPM programmed breakbeats, syncopated 808 and Moog sub-bass, staccato synth-and-keyboard riffs and chopped vocal samples under a sung hook, with a guest rapper occupying the middle-eight in place of an instrumental solo.
items.description: Hip pop describes the turn-of-the-millennium fusion in which chart pop adopted rap production wholesale while retaining a sung hook and verse-chorus structure. Its production hallmarks are dry, tightly quantized programmed drums with prominent handclap or snare on the backbeat, a melodic sub-bass line doubling the riff, spare percussive keyboard motifs, and an obligatory rapped guest verse. It differs from contemporary R&B in its harder, sparser rhythm-first arrangements and from hip-hop proper in that the rapper is a featured guest rather than the record's author and voice.
exemplars: Gwen Stefani — Love. Angel. Music. Baby.

items.name: Piano Rock
items.lineage: Anglo-American rock strain in which an acoustic or upright piano rather than electric guitar carries the riff and harmony, running from Little Richard and Jerry Lee Lewis through its 1970s codification by Elton John with Gus Dudgeon and Paul Buckmaster, Billy Joel and Randy Newman, and its 1990s-2000s revival by Ben Folds Five, Keane and The Fray — mid-tempo 90-130 BPM rock-band backing under octave-doubled left-hand bass patterns, gospel-derived suspended and inverted triads, hammered eighth-note chordal comping and an unguarded belted lead vocal.
items.description: Piano rock inverts the standard rock hierarchy by putting a struck-string keyboard at the front of the arrangement, with guitar reduced to colour or removed entirely. The recorded sound depends on a stereo-miked grand tracked live with the rhythm section in a large room, its low octaves reinforcing the bass and its right hand supplying both riff and pad, frequently with an added string arrangement. Compared with singer-songwriter piano ballads it keeps a full backbeat kit and rock dynamics; compared with boogie-woogie or barrelhouse it works from major-key pop and gospel voicings rather than twelve-bar blues.
exemplars: Elton John — Goodbye Yellow Brick Road
Ben Folds Five — Whatever and Ever Amen
The Fray — How to Save a Life

items.name: Metropopolis
items.lineage: Algorithmically named 2010s internet-era style of sleek electro-funk pop, made largely in home studios across Los Angeles, Auckland and Tokyo-facing online scenes and shaped by Tuxedo, Yumi Zouma, Anderson .Paak's polished side and the Japanese city-pop and French-touch revivalists — 100-118 BPM programmed or tightly played funk kit with a clean sixteenth-note hi-hat, slap or synth-octave bass, glassy FM electric-piano and chorused clean guitar chords, and a light, close, often processed or vocoded lead vocal singing over lush major-seventh and ninth harmony.
items.description: Metropopolis is a 2010s streaming-era category for glossy, urban-evoking synth pop that reworks late-1970s and 1980s boogie, city pop and French touch through modern in-the-box production. Its signature is warm FM electric-piano and chorused clean guitar over a soft-clipped funk drum programme and a melodic bass line, with reverb kept short and the mix polished, never lo-fi. It is more harmonically rich and slower than nu-disco, more song-based than future funk's sample-chop approach, and cooler and more restrained in vocal delivery than mainstream synth pop.
exemplars: Toro y Moi — Anything in Return

items.name: Europop
items.lineage: Continental European chart pop consolidated between the mid-1970s and the late 1990s through the Eurovision circuit, ABBA's Polar Studios records with Michael B. Tretow, Italo-disco, Stock Aitken Waterman's London hit factory and the Scandinavian and Benelux dance-pop of Ace of Base, Aqua and Dr. Alban — 118-140 BPM four-on-the-floor kick with offbeat eighth-note keyboard or hi-hat, unambiguous major-key diatonic progressions, English-as-second-language lyrics chosen for phonetic clarity, and glossy multi-tracked unison-and-thirds choruses.
items.description: Europop is the pan-continental commercial pop idiom that grew out of Eurovision, Schlager and Italo-disco and reached its peak in Scandinavian and Benelux studios between the 1980s and late 1990s. The sound is deliberately bright and frictionless: a hard four-on-the-floor kick with an offbeat keyboard stab, saturated polysynth and string-machine pads, a prominent melodic bass, and stacked, precisely tuned choral hooks sung in accented English. It differs from Anglo-American pop of the same period in its avoidance of blues inflection and its preference for major-key stepwise melody built for cross-language singability.

items.name: Urbano Español
items.lineage: Spanish-state urban music consolidated in Madrid, Barcelona and Sevilla from roughly 2015, when the trap generation around PXXR GVNG, Yung Beef and Bad Gyal and the flamenco-schooled work of Rosalía with El Guincho and C. Tangana with Alizzz fused Puerto Rican reggaetón and Atlanta trap with palmas, cante jondo melisma and copla lyric idiom — 90-100 BPM dembow or halftime trap grids, 808 sub-bass and rolled hi-hats layered against handclap compás, Andalusian-cadence guitar, and Auto-Tuned melismatic vocals in caló-inflected Castilian.
items.description: Urbano español is the Spanish-state branch of Latin urban music that emerged after 2015 by grafting Andalusian flamenco practice onto reggaetón and trap production. Its distinguishing feature is rhythmic bilingualism: an 808-driven dembow or halftime trap pattern running against, or dropping out entirely for, hand-clapped twelve-beat compás, with the vocal carrying flamenco melisma and quejío under Auto-Tune. It is separated from Puerto Rican reggaetón and Latin trap by that flamenco harmonic and rhythmic vocabulary, the Phrygian Andalusian cadence, and a Castilian rather than Caribbean lyric register.

items.name: Soundtrack (hybrid screen scoring)
items.lineage: Contemporary film, television and game underscore as codified in Los Angeles and London from the mid-1990s by Hans Zimmer's Media Ventures and its descendants — sample-library and live-orchestra hybrids built to picture in a DAW, ostinato-driven minor-modal cells at 100-140 BPM, sub-bass braams and processed percussion loops layered under divisi strings, cues locked to timecode with click and stem-delivered for the dub stage
items.description: Hybrid screen scoring is the dominant post-1995 practice of writing to picture in a sequencer with sampled orchestra, then overdubbing live players and processing the result as a production rather than a performance. Its markers are static harmony over pedal points, short repeating rhythmic cells that can be stretched to any cue length, heavily compressed low percussion, and synthetic sub-bass and reverse swells welded to string writing. It differs from traditional orchestral soundtrack in that the sound design and the notes are authored together and mixed in stems for the film dub, and it differs from concert art music in being subordinate to edit points and dialogue frequency space.

items.name: Orchestral Soundtrack (symphonic film score)
items.lineage: Symphonic screen music codified at the Hollywood studio orchestras between 1933 and 1960 by Max Steiner, Erich Korngold and Alfred Newman out of late-Romantic Viennese practice, revived in 1977 by John Williams — full 70-100 piece orchestra recorded live to picture on a scoring stage, leitmotivic theme-and-transformation writing, rubato cues conducted to streamers and punches, and brass-and-string tutti climaxes with harp and celesta coloration
items.description: The orchestral soundtrack is the symphonic underscore tradition established on the Hollywood scoring stages in the 1930s and renewed from Star Wars onward, written in full score and performed live by a conducted orchestra to projected picture. It is marked by leitmotif — named themes transformed in mode, orchestration and tempo across a film — chromatic late-Romantic harmony, and a tutti sound built around horns, divisi strings and a wide natural hall image captured with a Decca tree. Against hybrid scoring it uses no synthetic layer and derives its motion from harmonic development rather than looped cells; against concert symphonic writing it is cut into two- to four-minute cues shaped by dramatic timing rather than sonata argument.

items.name: R&B français
items.lineage: French-language contemporary R&B formed in Paris around 1996-2002 through Wallen, Matt Houston and the Secteur Ä and Alliance Ethnik orbits, revived after 2015 by Aya Nakamura and Dadju — mid-tempo 85-100 BPM programmed swing with Antillean zouk and coupé-décalé rhythmic inflection, layered close-harmony backing stacks, sung-rapped melisma over minor-seventh keyboard pads, and hooks alternating French, Nouchi and Lingala
items.description: R&B français is the francophone branch of contemporary R&B that took shape in Paris in the late 1990s alongside the rap scene it shares studios and features with, and that returned to dominance after 2015 with Aya Nakamura and Dadju. The sound keeps American R&B's stacked vocal harmony and extended minor-seventh harmony but sits it on Afro-Caribbean rhythm — zouk guitar figures, coupé-décalé hi-hat patterns, and a lighter kick than US productions — with lyrics moving fluidly between French, Lingala, Arabic and Antillean Creole. It is distinguished from US contemporary R&B by that rhythmic base and multilingual delivery, and from Afrobeats by its ballad-weighted song forms and heavier vocal layering.

items.name: Trap Triste (Latin melancholic trap)
items.lineage: Spanish-language melancholic trap crystallized in San Juan, Medellín and Madrid around 2016-2019 through Bad Bunny's early SoundCloud sides, Duki and Cazzu — 130-145 BPM half-time trap with rolled hi-hats and long 808 glides, minor-key detuned piano or guitar loops soaked in reverb, and heavily Auto-Tuned confessional vocals about heartbreak and dissociation delivered in a slurred, near-spoken register
items.description: Trap triste is the melancholic wing of Latin trap that surfaced on SoundCloud and YouTube between 2016 and 2019 across Puerto Rico, Argentina, Colombia and Spain. It keeps the trap skeleton — half-time 130-145 BPM kicks, triplet hi-hat rolls, sliding 808 bass — but strips the arrangement to a single reverb-drowned minor loop and foregrounds saturated Auto-Tune as an expressive rather than corrective device, with lyrics of romantic ruin, insomnia and drug fog. It differs from mainstream reggaetón in abandoning the dembow pattern and dance function, and from US emo rap in its Spanish-language bolero-inherited romantic vocabulary and its debt to reggaetón's vocal cadence.

items.name: Dirty South Rap
items.lineage: Southern US rap consolidated in Atlanta, New Orleans, Memphis and Houston between 1993 and 2001 through Organized Noize and Goodie Mob, No Limit and Cash Money, and the Three 6 Mafia circle — 70-95 BPM half-time grooves with TR-808 kick-and-sub, live bass and Rhodes from the Dungeon Family sessions, Miami-bass-descended double-time hi-hats, chanted call-and-response hooks and drawled regional vernacular
items.description: Dirty South rap is the mid-1990s consolidation of Southern regional hip-hop styles into a commercial force, anchored by OutKast and Goodie Mob in Atlanta, Master P and the Hot Boys in New Orleans, and Three 6 Mafia in Memphis. Its sonic signature is a slow half-time pocket built on booming 808 sub-kick, live Rhodes, funk bass and gospel-tinged backing vocals in the Atlanta studios, or crude synth-and-drum-machine bounce in New Orleans, always with a shouted chantable hook. It differs from East and West Coast rap of the same years by its lower tempo, church-and-blues harmonic color and party-chant hook design, and from later trap by its live instrumentation and absence of triplet hi-hat rolls.

items.name: Melancholia (contemporary melancholic neoclassical-ambient)
items.lineage: Post-2005 European neoclassical-ambient current shaped in Reykjavík, Berlin and Leipzig by Jóhann Jóhannsson, Nils Frahm, Ólafur Arnalds and the Erased Tapes and Type catalogues — slow felted piano and close-miked string quartet writing over tape-saturated drones, 50-70 BPM or unpulsed, diatonic minor loops with suspended fourths, and mechanical noise (hammer felt, pedal, room hum) retained as a deliberate timbral layer
items.description: Melancholia names the melancholic neoclassical-ambient repertoire that consolidated across Northern Europe after 2005 and became the default sound of introspective playlists and screen underscore. It is built from close-miked upright or felt piano, small string ensemble, tape and granular drone, and an aesthetic of audible mechanism — pedal creak, hammer noise, tape hiss — deployed as texture; harmony stays diatonic and slow-moving, often a four-chord loop with added seconds and fourths. It differs from ambient proper in retaining recognisable acoustic performance and melodic phrase, and from minimalism in the concert tradition by its short loop-based forms and studio-mediated intimacy rather than process-driven structure.

items.name: Lounge (exotica-era easy listening)
items.lineage: American easy-listening instrumental style codified in Los Angeles and New York 1954-1965 by Martin Denny, Les Baxter, Esquivel and Henry Mancini for the new stereo hi-fi market — 80-120 BPM cocktail-tempo arrangements of standards and originals for vibraphone, muted brass, bongos and wordless choir, lush non-functional added-note harmony, exaggerated stereo ping-pong panning and bird calls or novelty percussion as ornament
items.description: Lounge is the arranger-led instrumental easy-listening music made for American home stereo systems and hotel bars between roughly 1954 and 1965, with Martin Denny's Hawaiian exotica, Les Baxter's pseudo-ethnographic tone poems and Esquivel's space-age stereo experiments as its poles. The style is defined by soft cocktail tempos, vibraphone and muted brass over bongos and Latin percussion, wordless choir, added-sixth and ninth harmony that avoids tension, and demonstrative stereo effects made to show off two-channel playback. It differs from jazz in that improvisation is minimal and the arrangement is the work, and from later mood music in its self-conscious exoticism and novelty sound effects.

items.name: Contemporary Worship
items.lineage: Congregational rock-band worship codified in Southern California through Calvary Chapel's Maranatha! Music in the 1970s, then internationally by Hillsong Sydney and Passion/Bethel from the 1990s — 68-80 BPM anthemic 4/4 with delay-drenched arpeggiated guitars, pad-and-piano beds, verse-chorus-bridge forms built for congregational singability in a narrow tenor range, and long unmetered spontaneous-worship sections recorded live in the auditorium
items.description: Contemporary worship is the congregational song repertoire of evangelical and charismatic churches, running from the Jesus Movement choruses of 1970s Calvary Chapel to the globally exported Hillsong, Bethel and Elevation catalogues. Its defining traits are a four-chord diatonic loop with the melody kept inside an octave so an untrained congregation can sing it, arpeggiated dotted-eighth delay guitar and swelling pads, a slow build to a repeated bridge tag, and live capture of a large room with audible congregation. It differs from Black gospel by its rock-band rather than choir-and-organ instrumentation and its avoidance of melisma, and from CCM radio pop by being written for group singing rather than performance.

items.name: Trap Italiana
items.lineage: Italian-language trap formed in Milan and Rome 2015-2017 around the Dark Polo Gang, Sfera Ebbasta and producer Charlie Charles — 130-145 BPM half-time beats with rolled hi-hats, glassy detuned bell and plucked-synth loops over long 808 slides, heavily Auto-Tuned melodic delivery exploiting Italian open vowels, and ad-lib-saturated hooks mixing Milanese slang with English tags
items.description: Trap italiana broke out of Milan's periphery between 2015 and 2017 with Sfera Ebbasta, Dark Polo Gang and Ghali, produced largely by Charlie Charles, and displaced the older conscious Italian rap tradition on the charts within two years. The sound follows the Atlanta template closely — half-time 808 patterns, triplet hi-hat rolls, sparse bell and pluck loops — but the vocal is distinct: Italian's open vowels and syllable-timed rhythm give the Auto-Tuned melodies a sustained, almost canzone-like line rather than the clipped English cadence. It differs from earlier Italian rap by abandoning boom-bap and political content for melodic brand-conscious hedonism, and from French trap by its lighter percussion and stronger pop-melodic hooks.

items.name: Quiet Storm
items.lineage: Late-night radio-format soul named for Smokey Robinson's 1975 album and codified as programming by Melvin Lindsey at WHUR Washington DC in 1976 — 60-85 BPM ballad tempos, brushed or lightly gated drums low in the mix, Rhodes and fretless bass, breathy close-miked lead vocal with soft head-voice falsetto, sustained string and horn pads, and extended fade-out vamps designed for uninterrupted overnight sequencing
items.description: Quiet storm began as a radio format at Howard University's WHUR in 1976 and became a recognised production style through the late 1970s and 1980s, defined as much by what it removes as what it adds. Tempos sit under 85 BPM, drums are soft and mixed back, harmony is jazz-inflected with major sevenths and ninths on Rhodes, bass is often fretless, and lead vocals are recorded very close with breath and falsetto intact over sustained strings and a saxophone obbligato. It differs from Philadelphia soul by its smaller, more intimate arrangements and slower pulse, and from smooth jazz by keeping the sung romantic lyric as the centre rather than an instrumental lead.

items.name: Rap conscient (French conscious rap)
items.lineage: Francophone conscious rap consolidated in Paris and the Île-de-France banlieues circa 1990-1998 through IAM, Assassin, La Rumeur and Kery James, setting dense literary alexandrine-leaning French flows and anti-colonial, anti-police lyric argument at 88-96 BPM over boom-bap breaks, jazz and North African string samples, filtered contrabass loops and heavily scratched hooks.
items.description: Rap conscient formed in Paris and Marseille in the early 1990s as the politically argumentative wing of French hip-hop, built on sample-based boom-bap and dense, rhyme-saturated written French. Beats favour minor-key jazz, soul and Maghrebi string loops with filtered upright bass and turntable hooks; the voice sits forward, dry and declamatory rather than melodic. It is distinguished from later French trap and from US conscious rap by its formal literary register and its explicit engagement with colonial history and the banlieue.
exemplars: La Rumeur — L'Ombre sur la mesure
Kery James — Á l'ombre du show business

items.name: Barbadian pop
items.lineage: Barbadian pop crystallised in Bridgetown and the transatlantic studio circuit from the mid-2000s, when Rihanna, Shontelle and Livvi Franc carried the island's bashment-soca and spouge rhythmic accents into mainstream radio production — mid-tempo 95-105 BPM dembow-and-soca hybrid drum programming, glossy synth pads, Bajan-inflected melisma and clipped consonant phrasing over four-bar loop forms.
items.description: Barbadian pop is the export-facing strand of Bajan popular music that emerged after 2005, fusing the island's soca, bashment and spouge rhythmic feel with international top-line pop and R&B production. Its markers are half-time-leaning dembow or soca kick patterns, wide stacked vocal harmony, bright digital synth pads and an accented Bajan diction preserved in the lead vocal. It differs from Trinidadian soca in its slower tempo and song-form (rather than fete) construction, and from generic US pop in the persistence of Caribbean rhythmic phrasing under the chorus.
exemplars: Livvi Franc — Now I'm That Bitch

items.name: Funk paulista (São Paulo funk)
items.lineage: São Paulo's branch of Brazilian funk emerged in the city's periferia from roughly 2008, running from funk ostentação (Mc Guimê, Mc Boy do Charmes) into the mandelão and bruxaria styles of DJ Kevin, DJ Arana and Mc GW — 128-135 BPM, a single distorted tamborzão or beat-mandela kick-and-atabaque pattern, extreme sub-bass, pitched siren stabs, chopped and reversed vocal snippets and shouted MC ad-libs produced entirely on cracked DAWs.
items.description: Funk paulista is the São Paulo variant of Brazilian funk, distinct from Rio's carioca lineage in tempo, timbre and lyric subject. Ostentação used bright synth stabs and consumerist boasting at a steady 130 BPM; the later mandelão and bruxaria strains strip that away for grotesquely distorted sub-bass, pitch-bent metallic percussion, sirens and heavily processed vocal fragments. Where Rio funk leans on the sampled tamborzão break, paulista producers build the beat from scratch in the DAW and push it into deliberate clipping, releasing straight to YouTube and streaming as lossy files.

items.name: Bedroom R&B
items.lineage: Bedroom R&B took shape on SoundCloud and Bandcamp from roughly 2013 through Steve Lacy, Sza's early tapes, Yellow Days, Mahalia demos and the Internet's side projects — slow 65-85 BPM swung drum programming, detuned Rhodes and nylon-guitar loops, close-miked untreated-room lead vocals with audible sibilance and noise floor, tape-saturated stacked harmony and short through-written forms tracked entirely on laptop interfaces.
items.description: Bedroom R&B is the DIY, self-produced strand of 2010s alternative R&B, made by singer-producers working alone on laptops rather than in commissioned sessions. Its sound is defined by soft-clipped low-fidelity drums, detuned electric piano and single-coil guitar, extended jazz-adjacent voicings and a lead vocal recorded close in an untreated room so that room tone and breath stay in the mix. It differs from mainstream alternative R&B in its deliberately unpolished noise floor and from bedroom pop in its harmonic vocabulary and groove-first construction.
exemplars: Yellow Days — Is Everything Okay in Your World?

items.name: Trap queen (woman-led Southern trap)
items.lineage: Woman-led Southern trap consolidated in Atlanta, Houston and Miami between 2016 and 2020 through Cardi B, Megan Thee Stallion, City Girls, Latto and producers Metro Boomin, Juicy J and LilJuMadeDaBeat — 130-145 BPM half-time grids, long-decay 808 slides, 32nd-note hi-hat rolls and a hard-consonant, largely unsung declamatory flow foregrounding sexual authorship and money, cut in commercial Atlanta rooms with heavy vocal doubling.
items.description: The woman-led wing of Southern trap that broke commercially in the late 2010s, built on the same Atlanta production template — 808 glides, triplet hi-hat rolls, sparse minor plucks — but organised around aggressive, rhythmically percussive rapping and call-and-response ad-libs rather than melodic Auto-Tuned hooks. Vocals are tracked in commercial Atlanta rooms and layered in dense doubles and octave stacks, sitting louder and drier than in melodic trap. It is distinguished from mumble and melodic trap by its consonant-forward diction and near-total absence of sung passages.

items.name: Urbano chileno (Chilean urbano)
items.lineage: Chilean urbano emerged from Santiago's Puente Alto and La Florida comunas around 2016-2019 via Pablo Chill-E, Polimá Westcoast, Paloma Mami, Young Cister and Cris Mj — home-produced trap and reggaeton hybrids at 90-100 BPM with dembow and half-time trap grids, glassy detuned plucks, heavy Auto-Tune and unmistakably Chilean slang and elided-consonant diction, released first on YouTube and later through the 2022 'tumbao chileno' club sound.
items.description: Urbano chileno is the Santiago-centred scene that turned Chile into a net exporter of Spanish-language urban music after 2019, moving between trap, reggaeton and the buoyant 'tumbao chileno' club rhythm. Productions are largely self-made in home rooms: thin bright plucks, deep 808s, saturated Auto-Tune and often a swung dembow rather than the flat Puerto Rican grid. Its clearest marker against trap boricua is diction — dropped final consonants and dense Chilean slang — plus a lighter, more melodic and less menacing production palette.
exemplars: Cris Mj — Una Noche en Medellín

items.name: World worship (global contemporary worship)
items.lineage: Global contemporary worship spread from Sydney and Brisbane megachurches (Hillsong, Planetshakers) and Charlotte's Elevation from the mid-1990s onward, translated into Portuguese, Spanish, Korean, Mandarin and dozens of African languages — 68-78 BPM anthemic 4/4 builds, pad-and-delay guitar swells, four-chord diatonic loops, congregational unison melody in a narrow octave range and long repeated tag sections captured live before a crowd.
items.description: World worship is the globally franchised form of contemporary congregational song, exported from Australian and American megachurches since the 1990s and localised into scores of languages with the arrangements, keys and chord charts largely intact. Its sound is a slow-building 4/4 anthem over a diatonic I-V-vi-IV loop, ambient delay-washed electric guitar, sustained synth pads and a lead voice doubled by a live congregation, almost always recorded in front of an audience. It differs from Black gospel in its narrow melodic range, absence of melisma and improvisation, and from Southern gospel in its rock-band rather than quartet instrumentation.
exemplars: Bethel Music — We Will Not Be Shaken

items.name: Anime rock (anison rock)
items.lineage: Japanese anime theme rock formalised in Tokyo from the late 1970s (Ichirou Mizuki, MIO) and hardened in the 1990s-2000s through JAM Project, Flow, Asian Kung-Fu Generation and Granrodeo — 160-200 BPM driving eighth-note guitar, modulating key-change bridges, wide diatonic-to-chromatic pre-chorus harmony compressed into 90-second TV-edit forms, and a high, forward, vibrato-heavy lead vocal doubled in octaves.
items.description: Anime rock is the opening- and ending-theme repertoire written for Japanese television animation, a commissioned form that compresses a full pop-rock song into a 90-second broadcast edit. Its markers are fast eighth-note distorted guitar, a densely harmonised pre-chorus, at least one late modulation, and a high bright lead vocal sung with tight vibrato and doubled at the octave. It differs from ordinary J-rock in its formal constraint and hook-front loading, and from Western TV themes in its full band arrangement and sung-through structure.

items.name: R&B en español
items.lineage: Spanish-language alternative R&B took form between Mexico City, Bogotá, Santiago and Los Angeles from around 2015 with Girl Ultra, Kali Uchis, Sabino, Paloma Mami and Elsa y Elmar — 70-95 BPM swung or half-time programmed drums, extended seventh and ninth voicings on Rhodes and nylon guitar, bolero-derived melodic contour, breathy close-miked Spanish vocals and stacked harmony over short loop-based forms.
items.description: R&B en español is the Spanish-language branch of 2010s alternative R&B, developed largely by Latin American and US-Latina singer-producers working outside the reggaeton industry. It keeps neo-soul's extended harmony, laid-back swung programming and warm Rhodes-and-nylon-guitar palette while drawing melodic shape from bolero and Latin ballad phrasing, with an intimate breathy lead vocal. Unlike urbano it avoids dembow and trap grids almost entirely, and unlike Anglo alt-R&B it foregrounds Latin romantic-song contour and often code-switches within a single verse.
exemplars: Kali Uchis — Sin Miedo (del Amor y Otros Demonios)
Elsa y Elmar — Ya No Tengo Miedo

items.name: Downtempo
items.lineage: Downtempo formed in the chill-out rooms of London, Bristol, Vienna and Washington DC between 1990 and 1997 through Kruder & Dorfmeister, Thievery Corporation, Nightmares on Wax and Zero 7 — 80-105 BPM sampled or programmed breakbeats with heavy swing, dub-derived delay and spring reverb, filtered upright-bass and Rhodes loops, jazz and bossa samples, and either wordless textures or a single languid guest vocal.
items.description: Downtempo is the slow, groove-based electronic music that grew out of the chill-out rooms attached to early-1990s rave and club culture, then became a stand-alone album format. It is built on swung breakbeats at roughly 90 BPM, dub-scale delay and reverb sends, sampled jazz, bossa and soundtrack material, filtered bass and long unhurried arrangements with little dynamic escalation. It differs from trip-hop in its lighter, less claustrophobic affect and from ambient in retaining a continuous drum pulse throughout.
exemplars: Thievery Corporation — Sounds from the Thievery Hi-Fi

items.name: Compositional ambient (notated post-minimal ambient)
items.lineage: Compositional ambient emerged where post-minimalist concert writing met ambient production, from Harold Budd and Gavin Bryars in the late 1970s through Max Richter, Ólafur Arnalds, Nils Frahm and Hania Rani after 2000 — slow through-written string and piano writing in diatonic or Aeolian modes, notated parts rather than loops, close-miked felted piano with audible mechanism, long convolution and plate reverb tails, and pieces of 4-12 minutes built on gradual additive layering.
items.description: Compositional ambient is ambient music written out rather than generated or looped, sitting between post-minimalist concert composition and studio ambient production. Scored piano and string ensemble parts move slowly through modal diatonic harmony, captured with close small-diaphragm miking that keeps felt, hammer and bow noise audible, then placed in long artificial reverb. It is distinguished from generative and drone ambient by having discrete notated events, phrase structure and through-composed form, and from concert minimalism by its studio-built spatial signature and record-length pieces.
exemplars: Harold Budd & Brian Eno — The Pearl
Gavin Bryars — The Sinking of the Titanic

items.name: Afropop
items.lineage: International-facing African popular song codified in Lagos, Abidjan, Nairobi and the Paris/London diaspora studios between roughly 1978 and 1995, built on clean interlocking single-coil guitar lines derived from highlife and soukous, a mid-tempo 110-125 BPM kit-and-conga groove with hi-hat on the offbeat, sung-chorus call-and-response in Yoruba, Lingala, Swahili or English, and horn or polysynth pads replacing the older brass sections.
items.description: Afropop is the export-oriented consolidation of West and East African guitar-band music that took shape in the late 1970s and peaked commercially in the 1980s, when Lagos, Abidjan and Paris studios pushed highlife, juju and soukous idioms into four-minute radio songs. Its signature is the bright, chorused electric guitar weaving two-part lines over a conga-reinforced kit groove, with polysynth pads and horn stabs marking sections. It differs from Congolese rumba in its shortened seben-free song form and from later Afrobeats in being played by a live band rather than programmed.

items.name: Kindermusik
items.lineage: Early-childhood music-and-movement pedagogy derived from West German Musikalische Früherziehung of the 1960s, brought to the United States in 1974 and formalized as a licensed curriculum from Greensboro, North Carolina in 1993, using short diatonic call-and-response songs at walking tempo (roughly 90-120 BPM), steady duple meter for locomotor play, adult-led unison singing in a comfortable child register, and unpitched hand percussion, resonator bells and glockenspiel handed to the children themselves.
items.description: Kindermusik is a codified early-childhood music curriculum, descended from German Musikalische Früherziehung and licensed in North America since the 1990s, whose recorded repertoire exists to be sung along with in a classroom of caregivers and toddlers. Sonically it is deliberately narrow: clean diatonic melodies in a small range, unwavering duple pulse, transparent acoustic scoring around guitar, bells and hand percussion, and a warm unprocessed adult lead voice with plenty of space for a child to answer. It differs from commercial children's pop in avoiding drum programming and dense production, and from traditional nursery rhyme repertoire in being purpose-composed and sequenced by developmental stage.
exemplars: Kindermusik Our Time: Away We Go
Kindermusik Imagine That: Cities Busy Places

items.name: Rock nacional brasileiro (BRock)
items.lineage: Brazilian-language rock consolidated in Rio de Janeiro, Brasília and São Paulo between 1982 and 1989 — codified by Blitz, Barão Vermelho, Legião Urbana, Titãs and Os Paralamas do Sucesso and broadcast nationally after Rock in Rio 1985 — built on chorused clean-to-overdriven guitar, driving eighth-note bass, straight 4/4 kit at 130-160 BPM with occasional reggae or ska upstrokes, DX-era synth pads, and declamatory Portuguese vocals delivering long narrative and political lyrics.
items.description: Rock nacional brasileiro, usually shortened to BRock, is the 1980s Brazilian rock wave that followed political opening and the first Rock in Rio, centred on Brasília's post-punk bands and Rio's pop-rock groups. The sound is mid-80s major-label analog rock — chorus-drenched guitars, prominent melodic bass, gated snare, tasteful polysynth — but with dense, literate Portuguese lyrics carried by an unornamented declaimed vocal. It is distinguished from MPB by its band format and rock harmony, and from Anglo new wave by its narrative lyric weight and its absorption of ska and reggae rhythms from Paralamas onward.

items.name: Afrofuturism (musical practice)
items.lineage: Black speculative-music practice running from Sun Ra's Chicago Arkestra of the mid-1950s through Parliament-Funkadelic's 1975-79 mythology, Detroit techno and Drexciya in the 1990s, and 2000s-2010s artists such as Janelle Monáe and Flying Lotus — marked by cosmological concept narratives, analog and FM synth timbres treated as alien voices, vocoded or heavily processed vocals, modal or static harmony over funk and electro rhythm cells, and extended suite-like sequencing rather than verse-chorus song form.
items.description: Afrofuturism as a musical practice is less a single genre than a recurring compositional stance in Black music since the 1950s: the studio and the synthesizer used to build a speculative elsewhere, with space-and-diaspora mythology carried across a full album rather than a single. Sonically it is defined by electronically estranged timbre — modular and FM synthesis, vocoders and pitch-shifted voices, treated horns — set over funk, electro and techno rhythm cells and static modal harmony. It differs from ordinary electronic dance music in its narrative and conceptual architecture, and from mainstream funk or jazz in privileging synthetic timbre and studio construction over live ensemble balance.

items.name: Cumbia pop
items.lineage: Radio-facing cumbia hybrid consolidated in Argentina, Uruguay and Mexico from the late 1990s and dominant across the Southern Cone from about 2010, codified by Los Ángeles Azules' orchestral cumbia sonidera and by Uruguayan groups such as Rombai and Márama — a bright 95-105 BPM 4/4 with güiro on every eighth, scraped-and-clicked timbal fills, a two-note synth bass or electric bass on the downbeat, sustained keyboard or accordion melody, and clean romantic tenor lead vocals with sung group choruses.
items.description: Cumbia pop is the mainstream-pop refinement of cumbia that took hold across Argentina, Uruguay and Mexico from the late 1990s onward, replacing the raw sound-system aesthetic of cumbia villera and sonidera with polished production, romantic lyrics and hooks built for radio and streaming. The groove keeps the güiro-and-timbal cumbia skeleton but sits in a clean digital mix with synth pads, tight electric bass and lightly tuned lead vocals. It is distinguished from cumbia villera by its lyrical register and production gloss, and from cumbia electrónica by keeping a real percussion section and song-form choruses rather than club edits.

items.name: Funk consciente
items.lineage: Socially engaged strain of Rio de Janeiro funk carioca that emerged in the favelas around 1994-2000, codified by MC Leonardo e MC Junior's 'Rap da Felicidade' and by MV Bill's Cidade de Deus recordings, using the Miami-bass-derived Volt Mix and later the tamborzão pattern at 125-135 BPM with sampled atabaque and timbal hits, a booming 808 kick, minimal synth bass, and rapid declaimed Portuguese verses that report police violence, poverty and favela life over sung refrains.
items.description: Funk consciente is the protest wing of Rio's funk carioca, formed in favela home studios in the mid-1990s when MCs turned the baile's Miami-bass template toward reportage about policing, inequality and life in the communities. Musically it is stripped almost to rhythm: a Volt Mix or tamborzão loop of sampled atabaque, timbal and 808 kick, a sparse bass figure, and a dry, forward, hard-consonant vocal with almost no harmonic movement. It differs from funk proibidão in rejecting gang affiliation and from funk melody in replacing romantic refrains with documentary verse.
exemplars: MC Leonardo e MC Junior — Rap da Felicidade

items.name: Música chihuahuense
items.lineage: Norteño repertoire and performance style of the Mexican state of Chihuahua and its Ojinaga-Presidio border corridor, running from the polka, redova and chotis dance forms brought by 19th-century German and Czech settlers through the 1990s romantic-norteño boom codified by Conjunto Primavera and Los Rieleros del Norte — diatonic button accordion carrying the melody in thirds over bajo sexto bass-and-chord strumming, 2/4 polka or 3/4 vals at 110-150 BPM, tololoche or electric bass on the downbeat, and paired baritone-tenor vocal harmony on corridos and romantic canciones.
items.description: Música chihuahuense is the norteño tradition as practised in Chihuahua, where the European dance forms carried up the Camino Real — polka, redova, vals, chotis — were absorbed into the accordion-and-bajo-sexto conjunto and, from the 1990s, into a saxophone-tinged romantic style built for radio and dance halls on both sides of the Ojinaga border. Its markers are the diatonic accordion doubling the vocal in parallel thirds, an insistent oom-pah bass and bajo sexto, and two-part vocal harmony on corrido narratives and love songs. It is distinguished from Tejano by its acoustic conjunto core and absence of orquesta horns and synth pop, and from banda sinaloense by having no wind band at all.

items.name: Tejano (Tejano pop and orquesta)
items.lineage: Mexican-American popular music of South and Central Texas, running from the 1940s orquesta tejana of Beto Villa through the 1960s Sunny Ozuna era to the Tejano pop boom of 1985-1995 codified by La Mafia, Mazz, Emilio Navaira and Selena — polka-derived 2/4 and cumbia 4/4 at 100-140 BPM, accordion and bajo sexto set against horn-section or DX7-and-polysynth arrangements, a full drum kit and electric bass, and Spanish-language lead vocals with pop phrasing and close backing harmony.
items.description: Tejano is the Texas-Mexican popular tradition that layered orquesta horn arranging and, later, 1980s pop-synth production onto the conjunto core of accordion and bajo sexto, reaching national scale in the decade before Selena's death in 1995. A typical track alternates polka-ranchera and cumbia grooves under a polished Spanish lead vocal, with synth pads, brass punches and a rock-solid kit-and-bass rhythm section. It differs from Chihuahuan and Monterrey norteño in its studio-pop instrumentation and English-language pop harmonic vocabulary, and from Mexican grupero in being written and recorded on the US side of the border for Texas dance halls.

items.name: Nova MPB
items.lineage: Brazilian singer-songwriter revival that formed in São Paulo, Rio and Brasília from roughly 2008 onward on independent labels and streaming platforms, codified by Tiago Iorc, Silva, Tulipa Ruiz, Marcelo Jeneci and Anavitória — nylon-string guitar and Rhodes-or-piano harmony carrying bossa and samba-derived voicings at relaxed 75-105 BPM, light pandeiro and brushed kit, discreet synth pads and programmed textures, and close-miked breathy Portuguese vocals with conversational phrasing.
items.description: Nova MPB is the post-2008 wave of Brazilian songwriters who took up the MPB lineage on independent labels and streaming rather than through the old major-label and festival system. It keeps the extended bossa and samba harmony and Portuguese lyricism of classic MPB but places it in a quiet, close-miked, digitally assembled setting: nylon guitar or electric piano, soft pandeiro or brushed kit, ambient synth beds, and an intimate near-whispered vocal. It differs from 1970s MPB in its reduced dynamic range and absence of large arrangements, and from Brazilian indie rock in retaining the tradition's harmonic language.

items.name: Sigilkore
items.lineage: Internet-native microgenre that emerged on SoundCloud and Discord around 2020 out of the digicore and hyperpop scenes, associated with Ravenna Golden, Kurtains and the occult-imagery corner of underground rap — typically 140-165 BPM half-time trap skeletons with distorted and clipped 808 glides, detuned wavetable or bell leads, granular and reversed vocal fragments, and heavily pitch-shifted, formant-warped vocals delivered in short whispered or screamed phrases over sigil-and-occult lyric imagery.
items.description: Sigilkore is a small, largely online microgenre that surfaced around 2020 where digicore, underground trap and occult internet aesthetics overlap, produced entirely in DAWs by teenage and early-twenties artists and distributed through SoundCloud, Discord and short-form video. The sound is deliberately damaged: overdriven and clipped 808 glides, detuned bell or wavetable leads, granular and reversed vocal shards, and vocals so pitch-shifted and formant-warped that words blur. It differs from hyperpop in its darker, sparser, rap-derived rhythmic frame, and from witch house in being contemporary-trap rather than 2010s-synth in construction.

items.name: Rap de conciencia
items.lineage: Spanish-language conscious hip hop consolidated in Madrid, Zaragoza, Santiago de Chile and Mexico City from the mid-1990s onward, codified by El Chojin and Nach in Spain and by Portavoz and Ana Tijoux in the Southern Cone — boom-bap and jazz-sample production at 85-95 BPM with filtered upright bass loops, dusty drum breaks and piano or horn samples, and dense multisyllabic Castilian or Latin American Spanish verses on colonialism, class, migration and political memory, delivered in a measured, articulated flow over sung or scratched hooks.
items.description: Rap de conciencia is the politically engaged wing of Spanish-language hip hop, running in parallel in Spain and across Latin America since the mid-1990s and continuous with the region's protest-song lineage. Production stays close to sample-based boom bap — jazz and soul loops, filtered upright bass, dusty breaks, turntable hooks — because the emphasis is on lyric legibility: long, tightly rhymed verses about inequality, state violence and historical memory, rapped with clear diction and little vocal processing. It differs from Latin trap in its sample sourcing and unmodified voice, and from US conscious rap in drawing its references from Latin American and Iberian political history.

items.name: Adoração (Brazilian evangelical worship)
items.lineage: Brazilian Portuguese-language evangelical congregational worship music that consolidated in the 1990s-2000s out of Pentecostal and neo-Pentecostal churches in São Paulo, Rio and Belo Horizonte — codified by Diante do Trono (Ana Paula Valadão, from 1998) and later Fernandinho, Gabriela Rocha and Morada, built on slow-to-mid 4/4 and 6/8 anthem tempos (60-84 BPM), suspended-chord acoustic and delay-washed electric guitar, pad-and-piano beds, congregational unison singing rising to belted soprano ad-libs, and long modulating vamps recorded live before a stadium-scale congregation.
items.description: Adoração is the Brazilian evangelical worship-song repertoire that grew out of Pentecostal and neo-Pentecostal congregations in the 1990s and became a mass recording industry through live-album culture. Its sound is congregational unison over sustained pads, arpeggiated clean electric guitar with long delay, piano voice-leading and a build-and-release dynamic arc that peaks in extended repeated refrains and spontaneous sung prayer. It differs from Anglo-American contemporary worship mainly in language, in a heavier reliance on live congregational recording, and in a more openly Pentecostal ecstatic register than the tighter studio pop of its US counterparts.

items.name: Ska argentino
items.lineage: Buenos Aires ska-punk scene that formed at the end of the 1980s and peaked in the 1990s — codified by Los Fabulosos Cadillacs, Los Auténticos Decadentes, Karamelo Santo and above all Los Cafres and Los Calzones/Todos Tus Muertos adjacents, fusing Jamaican upstroke guitar on the offbeat at 150-190 BPM with a loud four-piece brass section, walking or root-fifth electric bass, punk-tempo drum kit, murga and candombe percussion imported from the Río de la Plata carnival, and shouted chorus-driven Spanish lyrics of urban and political satire.
items.description: Ska argentino is the Argentine branch of the third-wave ska revival, formed in Buenos Aires in the late 1980s and dominant in the 1990s festival and club circuit. It takes the Jamaican offbeat guitar and horn-riff vocabulary at punk tempo and layers in local carnival percussion — murga bombo and candombe patterns — plus a shouted, comic-satirical Spanish vocal delivery. Compared with British 2 Tone or the Californian ska-punk of the same years it is brassier, more percussion-heavy and more explicitly rooted in Río de la Plata carnival rhythm than in rocksteady.

items.name: Pixie (quirky indie pop)
items.lineage: Anglo-American female-fronted twee-adjacent indie pop cluster of roughly 2004-2012, centred on London, New York and Los Angeles and defined by Regina Spektor, Kate Nash, Lily Allen and Ingrid Michaelson — mid-tempo 90-120 BPM piano or ukulele-led songs, brushed or programmed light kit, glockenspiel and handclap sweeteners, close-miked conversational girlish soprano with spoken asides, hiccup phrasing and diaristic first-person lyrics, arranged in tight verse-chorus pop forms with chamber-pop string or brass cameos.
items.description: Pixie names the mid-2000s wave of quirky, female-fronted piano-and-ukulele indie pop that crossed from blog culture into the mainstream charts. Its markers are a very close, dry, personality-forward vocal with audible breath and speech inflection, light acoustic keyboard-led arrangements, toy-percussion and glockenspiel color, and lyrics that read as spoken diary rather than sung poetry. It is brighter and more chart-facing than twee indie pop proper, and less austere and confessional than the singer-songwriter tradition it borrows from.

items.name: Cumbia villera
items.lineage: Greater Buenos Aires villa-miseria cumbia that emerged in 1999-2000 with Flor de Piedra, Yerba Brava, Damas Gratis (Pablo Lescano) and Pibes Chorros — 95-105 BPM cumbia paseo carried by cheap Korg/Roland preset organ and whistle patches, a driving synth-and-electric bass line, güiro and timbal on a stiff programmed grid, nasal shouted male lead with gang-chorus responses, and lurid first-person lyrics about drugs, theft, police and slum life.
items.description: Cumbia villera appeared in the shantytowns ringing Buenos Aires at the turn of the millennium, during Argentina's economic collapse, and became the country's dominant working-class dance music within two years. Musically it strips cumbia to a cheap preset-keyboard riff, a hard synth bass, a metronomic güiro-and-timbal grid and a shouted lead answered by a crowd chorus, recorded fast on minimal budgets so the preset timbres remain audibly stock. What separates it from earlier Argentine tropical cumbia is the deliberately cheap synth palette and the explicit criminal-realist lyric stance drawn from gangsta rap.

items.name: Video game music
items.lineage: Interactive score composed for game hardware, from the 1980 arcade and 1983-1994 console chip era — Koichi Sugiyama, Nobuo Uematsu, Koji Kondo and Yuzo Koshiro writing three-to-eight-voice PSG and FM parts under strict polyphony and memory limits — through the CD and streamed-audio era after 1995; the persistent markers are short seamlessly loopable cues, fast arpeggiated pseudo-chords standing in for missing voices, wide leaps and rapid modal modulation to stay memorable at 120-160 BPM, and layered or branching arrangements that respond to player state.
items.description: Video game music is score written under interactive and hardware constraints, first for the programmable sound generators and FM chips of 1980s arcade cabinets and consoles, later for streamed and orchestral delivery. The chip-era idiom — arpeggio chords, duty-cycle pulse leads, noise-channel percussion, tight seamless loops — remains its recognizable core even as budgets moved to live orchestra. What distinguishes it from film scoring is the requirement that a cue loop indefinitely and adapt to unpredictable player action rather than track a fixed timeline.

items.name: Rap canario
items.lineage: Canary Islands Spanish-language hip-hop, active in Las Palmas and Santa Cruz de Tenerife from the mid-1990s and prominent nationally from the 2010s through Cruz Cafuné, Bejo, La Pantera and the Elton Mackay circle — 80-140 BPM beats built in the DAW over trap hi-hat rolls or dembow-leaning bounce, melodic autotuned hooks, and rapping in the Canarian accent with island slang, guagua-and-barrio imagery and frequent code-switching into Latin American Spanish and English.
items.description: Rap canario is the hip-hop scene of the Canary Islands, distinct within Spanish rap for its accent, vocabulary and Atlantic-Caribbean orientation. Its 2010s wave leans on sung-rapped melodic hooks, heavily processed vocals, trap and dembow rhythmic frames, and lyrics saturated with island geography and slang, produced almost entirely in home DAW setups. Against Madrid or Barcelona rap it is less boom-bap-oriented and more openly melodic and Latin-facing, a consequence of the islands' migration ties to the Caribbean and Venezuela.

items.name: Mollywood (Malayalam film song)
items.lineage: Malayalam-language film song of Kerala's cinema industry, recorded in Madras and Trivandrum from the 1950s and codified by composers G. Devarajan, M. S. Baburaj, Salil Chowdhury, Raveendran and later Johnson and Ouseppachan with lyricist Vayalar Ramavarma and singers K. J. Yesudas and P. Susheela — Carnatic raga-derived melodies with sparing gamaka, light 6/8 and kaiyaal-derived 4/4 rhythms carried by tabla and mridangam alongside a Western string section, harmonium and flute, and a clear un-nasal legato vocal delivery closer to concert Carnatic tone than to Bombay filmi.
items.description: Mollywood song is the playback repertoire of Malayalam cinema, produced largely on Madras scoring stages and shaped by a Kerala literary tradition that gave its lyrics unusual prominence. Melodies sit close to Carnatic raga contours and are sung with an open, minimally ornamented legato — Yesudas being the defining voice — over arrangements that pair mridangam and tabla with a modest Western string section and flute. Compared with Hindi filmi of the same decades it is less orchestrally maximal, slower in tempo, and markedly more melody- and text-centred than dance-centred.

items.name: Electro latino
items.lineage: Spanish-language electro-house-and-reggaeton hybrid of roughly 2008-2014, made across Miami, San Juan, Madrid and Medellín by Dyland & Lenny, Sensato, Fito Blanko and the Pitbull-adjacent club circuit — 125-130 BPM four-on-the-floor kicks with sidechained saw-lead hooks and filter risers borrowed from Dutch big-room house, dembow accents dropped in on breakdowns, heavily autotuned melodic hooks over shouted club chants, produced entirely in the box for radio and festival PA.
items.description: Electro latino is the late-2000s crossover in which reggaeton and Latin club pop absorbed the sound design of European big-room electro house: sidechain-pumped four-on-the-floor kicks, distorted saw leads, long filter builds and drops. Vocals are Spanish-language, hook-driven and pitch-corrected hard enough that the tuning artifact is part of the timbre, with dembow patterns surfacing mainly in breakdowns rather than running throughout. It differs from contemporaneous reggaeton in its straight house pulse and from mainstream EDM in retaining Latin percussion and Spanish chant hooks.

items.name: Skate Punk
items.lineage: Southern-Californian punk offshoot codified 1985-1998 around Epitaph and Fat Wreck Chords (Bad Religion, NOFX, Pennywise, Lagwagon), built on 180-230 BPM d-beat-derived skank and blast-adjacent single-stroke snare, downpicked palm-muted power chords over major-key diatonic riffs, octave-doubled bass following root motion, and stacked 'oozin' aah' three-part gang harmonies replacing the shouted unison of hardcore.
items.description: Skate punk consolidated in Southern California between the mid-1980s and late 1990s as hardcore's tempo and aggression were fused to melodic, major-key songwriting and choral backing vocals. The defining sound is a very fast skank beat with a bright, tightly gated snare, brittle downpicked distorted guitars recorded with little low-mid, and multi-tracked harmony refrains. It differs from its hardcore parent by its consonant harmony and studio polish, and from pop-punk proper by keeping tempos and rhythmic density far higher.

items.name: Noise Pop
items.lineage: Anglo-American indie style formed 1985-1992 (The Jesus and Mary Chain's Psychocandy, My Bloody Valentine, Yo La Tengo, Black Tambourine), setting 60s girl-group and Velvets-derived three-chord pop melodies at moderate 110-150 BPM under continuous fuzz, feedback and tremolo-arm detuning, with dry deadpan or breathy vocals mixed level with or beneath the guitar noise floor.
items.description: Noise pop emerged in Britain and the United States in the second half of the 1980s, applying saturated fuzz, feedback and hiss to songs whose underlying harmony and melody remain plainly pop. The signature is the ratio: an unambiguous verse-chorus tune buried under a constant abrasive guitar texture, with drums often kept simple and mid-forward and vocals recorded dry and close. Unlike shoegaze it keeps song structures short and the beat crisp rather than dissolving into reverb wash, and unlike noise rock it never abandons consonant melody.
exemplars: The Jesus and Mary Chain — Psychocandy

items.name: Rap Marseillais
items.lineage: French hip-hop regional school formed in Marseille's northern quartiers from 1989 onward — IAM and the Chourmo/Fonky Family circle, later Psy 4 de la Rime, SCH and Jul — pairing Egyptological and Mediterranean sample sources (Arabic strings, Italo-film soundtracks, raï) with heavy 88-96 BPM boom-bap breaks, Provençal-accented rolled-r delivery, and dense internal-rhyme wordplay sung over sung-hook choruses.
items.description: Marseille rap took shape at the end of the 1980s as the southern counterweight to Parisian hip-hop, drawing on the port city's Maghrebi, Comorian and Italian populations. Its beats favour minor-key Mediterranean and Arabic sample material over the funk and jazz loops of the Paris school, with a fatter, slower boom-bap pocket and prominent sung or chanted refrains.
