items.lineage: Soul and R&B made in Britain from the mid-1960s onward — Dusty Springfield's Atlantic-styled orchestral soul, the Northern Soul club circuit's uptempo four-on-the-floor imports, and the decisive 1980s London wave of Soul II Soul, Loose Ends and Mica Paris working out of Black community studios in Brent and Brixton, using swung 90-110 BPM breakbeat programming, dubwise bass weight, lush string and Rhodes pads, and a restrained, melisma-light lead vocal over stacked group harmony.
items.description: British soul runs from the mid-1960s Anglo readings of American R&B through to the 1980s London sound that fused soul singing with reggae bass, jazz-funk chords and hip-hop-derived breakbeat programming. Its defining qualities are a cooler, less gospel-declamatory lead vocal, heavy sub-weighted low end inherited from Jamaican sound-system practice, and arrangements that let a single sampled drum loop carry the whole track under strings and Rhodes. Against American soul it is more understated in vocal delivery and more sound-system-shaped in its bass, and against UK lovers rock it is less strictly reggae in rhythm.

items.name: Japanese idol pop (aidoru kayō)
items.lineage: Japanese teen-idol pop formalised by talent agencies and TV variety programming in Tokyo from the early 1970s — Momoe Yamaguchi and then Seiko Matsuda in the 1980s establishing the template, extended by Onyanko Club and later Morning Musume and AKB48 — bright 120-145 BPM major-key songs with Brill-Building-style key-change choruses, session-band backing with syncopated slap bass and gated snare, sweetened brass and synth-string beds, and a deliberately thin, high, unrehearsed-sounding solo or unison-group vocal recorded very close.
items.description: Aidoru kayō is the agency-managed Japanese teen-idol pop that dominated television-driven Japanese charts from the 1970s and reorganised itself around large group formats after 2000. Musically it is written and played by elite session professionals — the arrangements carry city-pop-grade chord substitutions and horn writing — while the vocal is intentionally kept youthful, light and imperfect, mixed loud and dry at the front. That contrast between polished backing and untrained-sounding lead is precisely what separates it from J-pop's adult vocal tradition and from the harder-produced dance vocabulary of K-pop.

items.name: Japanese technopop (electropop)
items.lineage: Tokyo synthesizer pop launched by Yellow Magic Orchestra in 1978 with Haruomi Hosono, Ryuichi Sakamoto and Yukihiro Takahashi sequencing a Roland MC-8 microcomposer against live drums, joined by Hikashu and P-Model, and revived from the mid-2000s by Yasutaka Nakata's work with capsule and Perfume — 110-135 BPM four-on-the-floor or stiff sixteenth-note sequences, pentatonic and exotica-derived melodic hooks, vocoder and heavy formant-shifted or pitch-corrected vocals, and analogue polysynth stabs later replaced by sidechained in-the-box production.
items.description: Japanese technopop began with Yellow Magic Orchestra's late-1970s use of microprocessor sequencing as a compositional method rather than a studio convenience, and became a continuous national lineage through 1980s new-wave bands and the 2000s Nakata-produced idol-electro of Perfume. The sound is deliberately mechanical: quantised sequencer lines, clipped synthetic percussion, vocoded or aggressively processed voices, and bright pentatonic hooks that read as playful rather than austere. It differs from European synthpop in its lighter, exotica-tinged melodic vocabulary and from Detroit or Berlin electronic music in remaining firmly a vocal pop form.

items.name: Japanese soundtrack scoring
items.lineage: Japanese screen and game scoring consolidated from the 1950s onward — Toru Takemitsu's sparse modernist film scores for Kobayashi and Teshigahara, Joe Hisaishi's minimalist ostinato-and-melody writing for Miyazaki from 1984, Ryuichi Sakamoto's synth-and-orchestra hybrids, and the game lineage of Koichi Sugiyama and Nobuo Uematsu whose chiptune themes were later rescored for full orchestra — built on long-breathed diatonic or yo-scale themes, ostinato piano or harp figuration, restrained rubato, and orchestral colour weighted toward strings, woodwind solos and celesta.
items.description: Japanese soundtrack scoring is the composed screen music of Japanese cinema, anime and video games, running from Takemitsu's postwar modernism through Hisaishi's Ghibli scores to the orchestral game repertoire now performed in concert halls. Its recurring traits are a strong, singable principal theme stated and restated over a repeating accompaniment figure, transparent orchestration that leaves individual instrumental colours audible, and pentatonic or modal inflections folded into otherwise Western tonal harmony. Compared with Hollywood scoring it is thinner in texture, less driven by brass, and far more willing to leave silence and single-line writing exposed.

items.name: T-pop (Thai idol and mainstream Thai pop)
items.lineage: Bangkok mainstream pop consolidated in the mid-1980s around the Grammy Entertainment and RS Promotion label system — Thongchai 'Bird' McIntyre and Asanee-Wasan set the template of string (สตริง) band-pop sung in central Thai over 100-125 BPM programmed backbeats — and re-formed after 2015 as idol-group T-pop (BNK48, 4EVE, PROXIE) built on K-pop-style synth-and-808 arrangements, tight unison choreography vocals, and occasional luk thung phrasing or khaen and ranat timbres dropped into otherwise Western-harmonised choruses.
items.description: Thai-language mainstream pop from Bangkok, industrialised by Grammy and RS from the mid-1980s and relaunched as idol-driven T-pop after 2015. The sound is heavily programmed — sub-weighted 808 kicks, bright supersaw and plucked-synth hooks, hard-tuned lead vocals with stacked group harmony — with Thai tonal-language phrasing shaping melodic contour and occasional khaen, ranat or phin colour marking it as Thai rather than imported. It differs from luk thung and luk krung, its parents, by abandoning their live-band and orchestral arrangements and their rural or crooner vocal delivery for grid-locked electronic production.

items.name: Mainland Chinese pop (neidi liuxing yinyue)
items.lineage: Mainland Chinese popular song revived after 1978 as gangtai imports met domestic tongsu singing, hardened into the 1994 Beijing 'new music' generation (Na Ying, Sun Nan, Gao Feng) and then into the post-2005 televised-talent and streaming era dominated by Hunan TV, Modern Sky and Tencent Music — the mainstream form is a 70-100 BPM 4/4 ballad with piano, string pad and programmed kit, declamatory wide-vibrato tongsu vocal projection over Western functional harmony, often with erhu, dizi or guzheng overdubs signalling 'guofeng' national style.
items.description: Mandarin-language popular music produced inside the PRC, distinct from the Taipei and Hong Kong industries that seeded it. The dominant register is a big-voiced ballad — full-throated tongsu projection with pronounced vibrato, dense string-and-piano beds, heavy bus compression and mastering loudness — shaped by television singing competitions that reward sustained high notes. Its guofeng subcurrent layers erhu, dizi, guzheng and pentatonic hooks over the same Western harmony, a nationalist colouring largely absent from Taiwanese Mandopop's more understated songwriter aesthetic.

items.name: Malaysian pop (pop Melayu / muzik pop Malaysia)
items.lineage: Kuala Lumpur's Malay-language pop industry grew out of 1950s-60s P. Ramlee film song and 1970s pop yeh yeh guitar bands, then codified in the 1980s-90s through EMI Malaysia, BMG and the Anugerah Juara Lagu competition — Sheila Majid's jazz-inflected balada, Search and Wings' rock kapak power ballads, and Siti Nurhaliza's irama Malaysia recordings that set florid melismatic cengkok ornament over 60-100 BPM 4/4 or 6/8 with gendang, kompang, accordion and string pads.
items.description: Malay-language mainstream pop centred on Kuala Lumpur, running from 1980s balada and rock kapak through the irama Malaysia revival of the late 1990s. Its most distinctive feature is vocal: dense cengkok ornamentation and long melismatic tails inherited from asli and ghazal singing, laid over Western-harmonised ballad arrangements with string pads, and in irama Malaysia over gendang, kompang and rebana patterns in zapin, joget or inang rhythms. Compared to Indonesian dangdut it is slower, less percussion-forward and far more ballad-weighted; compared to Mandopop it carries much heavier melodic ornament.

items.name: Pinoy R&B
items.lineage: Manila-based Filipino R&B emerged in the early 1990s as OPM absorbed American new jack swing and quiet-storm soul — Jaya, Kyla and later Nyoy Volante and Jay-R built it on 65-95 BPM swung sixteenth programmed kits, electric-piano and pad-heavy chord beds, and a heavily melismatic belt-and-riff vocal culture nurtured by nationwide karaoke and church choirs — with a 2010s neo-soul and alt-R&B turn through Careless Music and the Manila indie scene.
items.description: Filipino R&B made in Metro Manila, sung in English, Tagalog or a code-switching mix. It is defined by vocal maximalism — runs, melisma, full-belt climaxes and gospel-derived ad-libs over the last chorus — sat on soft-attack electric piano, warm sub bass and swung programmed drums, with the 2010s wave trading gloss for hazier neo-soul chords and looser rhythmic placement. Where mainstream OPM ballads foreground the songwriter and a straight-eighth piano arrangement, Pinoy R&B foregrounds groove and improvised vocal embellishment.

items.name: Pinoy trap
items.lineage: Filipino trap formed after 2015 in Metro Manila and the provincial bedroom-producer scene — Ex Battalion, Shanti Dope, Al James and the Ownmuzik and Uprising collectives built it on 130-150 BPM half-time 808 patterns with long pitched sub-glides, triplet hi-hat rolls, dark minor-key plucked or bell loops, and Taglish rap alternating rapid triplet flows with sung Auto-Tuned hooks, circulated first through YouTube and SoundCloud rather than radio.
items.description: Trap-derived Filipino rap made largely in bedrooms around Metro Manila from the mid-2010s. The beats follow the Atlanta template — sustained 808 sub with glide, snare or clap on the third beat of a half-time bar, stuttering hi-hat triplets, sparse minor loops — but the rapping is Taglish, and the hooks lean on heavily Auto-Tuned melodic singing shaped by Filipino balladry. It is distinguished from earlier Pinoy rap, which used boom-bap breaks and Francis Magalona's declamatory social-commentary delivery, by its cyclic loop structure and vocal processing.

items.name: Punjabi pop
items.lineage: Punjabi-language pop crystallised in the early 1990s across Jalandhar, Delhi and the UK diaspora as folk boliyan and tappe were set to programmed beats — Malkit Singh, Gurdas Maan and Daler Mehndi's cassette-era hits established the form of a driving 100-140 BPM dhol chaal with tumbi or algoza riff, harmonium or synth chord stabs, and an open-throated declamatory tenor with sharp gamak-like grace notes — remade after 2010 by Diljit Dosanjh and the Punjabi-Canadian axis into a slick DAW production still anchored to the dhol pattern.
items.description: Non-film Punjabi popular song from Indian Punjab and the diaspora, commercially formalised in the cassette boom of the early 1990s. Its constant is the dhol: a loud, sharply accented chaal or bhangra pattern, doubled by programmed kick and clap, under a tumbi or algoza ostinato and a loud unornamented-but-gamak-inflected male lead with call-and-response chorus shouts. It differs from UK bhangra, which foregrounds reggae and house production, and from Punjabi filmi playback, which subordinates the dhol to an orchestral arrangement.

items.name: Punjabi hip hop
items.lineage: Punjabi rap grew from mid-2000s UK and Canadian diaspora records (Bohemia's Delhi-Punjabi Urdu rap, RDB's bhangra-rap fusions) into a mass Indian form after 2017 through Sidhu Moose Wala, Karan Aujla and the Brampton-Ludhiana production axis — 90-160 BPM tracks that graft trap 808s and half-time snares onto dhol chaal accents and tumbi riffs, with rapped or half-sung Punjabi verses in a hard, chest-forward register and lyric matter running from village pride to gangster narrative.
items.description: Punjabi-language rap made across Indian Punjab and the Canadian and British diaspora, mass-market since the late 2010s. Production hybridises trap — sustained 808 sub, triplet hats, sparse minor loops — with live or sampled dhol accents and tumbi or algoza motifs, and the vocal sits between rapping and the declamatory bhangra tenor rather than committing to either. Against mainstream Punjabi pop it is slower, darker and lyric-forward; against US trap it retains folk instrumentation and a folk-derived melodic phrasing.

items.name: Bhojpuri pop
items.lineage: Bhojpuri-language commercial song exploded in the 1980s-90s cassette economy of eastern Uttar Pradesh and Bihar — T-Series and small Varanasi and Patna labels mass-pressed devotional, wedding and double-entendre albums by Bharat Sharma Vyas, Manoj Tiwari and later Pawan Singh — built on 110-150 BPM dholak and nagara patterns in kaharwa and dadra tal, harmonium and reedy synth doubling the tune, and a nasal high-register folk vocal carried straight over from birha, kajri and chaita repertoire.
items.description: Commercial popular song in Bhojpuri from Bihar and eastern Uttar Pradesh, built on the cheap cassette-duplication economy of the 1980s onward and later on video and YouTube. Musically it stays close to its folk sources: dholak-led kaharwa grooves, harmonium and a thin synth reed doubling a repetitive pentatonic-leaning tune, minimal harmonic movement, and a piercing nasal vocal that projects like open-air folk singing. Unlike Hindi filmi pop it is regionally self-contained, arranged for speed and low cost rather than orchestral scale, and its lyric registers — Chhath devotional, wedding, and frank double-entendre — have no filmi equivalent.

items.name: Gujarati pop
items.lineage: Gujarati commercial pop grew out of the Navratri garba and raas industry of Ahmedabad, Vadodara and Surat, professionalised from the late 1980s by cassette labels and by the arena-scale garba productions of Falguni Pathak and Atul Purohit — the core form is a hemiola-free but relentlessly cyclic garba pattern at 90-160 BPM on dhol and dholak with clap accents, tabla or programmed kit doubling, harmonium or synth chords, and a bright female-led vocal in call-and-response with a mass chorus, accelerating across a long single cycle.
items.description: Gujarati-language popular song from Gujarat, dominated by the garba and dandiya-raas repertoire recorded for the nine nights of Navratri and for dance-floor use year-round. It is the most cyclic of the Indian regional pops: a fixed dhol-and-clap pattern repeats across ten-minute tracks with gradual tempo acceleration, a lead singer trading short phrases with a mass unison chorus, and harmony limited to two or three chords on harmonium or synth. Compared with Bhojpuri or Haryanvi pop, it is dance-functional rather than narrative, female-vocal-dominant, and organised around one long accelerating cycle rather than verse-chorus form.

items.name: Haryanvi pop
items.lineage: Haryanvi commercial song emerged from ragini and saang folk theatre of Haryana and western UP, went cassette-commercial in the 1990s, and became a national YouTube phenomenon after 2015 through Sapna Choudhary's stage-dance videos and the songwriting of Raju Punjabi, Vicky Kajla and MD-KD — the sound is a 120-150 BPM dholak-and-nagara pattern reinforced by programmed kick and clap, a blunt harmonium or square-synth riff, tumbi or shehnai colour, and a loud declamatory chest-voice delivery in Haryanvi over almost static harmony.
items.description: Haryanvi-language popular song from Haryana and adjoining western Uttar Pradesh, distributed chiefly as low-budget video singles since the mid-2010s. Its grammar is percussive and harmonically flat — a hard dholak-nagara groove doubled by programmed kick and handclap, a two-chord harmonium or saw-synth riff, no modulation — with the interest carried by a shouted, tightly syllabic vocal derived from ragini stage declamation. It is drier and more rhythmically rigid than Punjabi pop, lacking the dhol chaal's swing and the tumbi's melodic hook role.

items.name: Haryanvi hip hop
items.lineage: Haryanvi rap appeared around 2017-2019 in Rohtak, Hisar and the Gurugram-Delhi belt as Haryanvi pop producers absorbed trap — Gulzaar Chhaniwala, KD Desi Rock and Khasa Aala Chahar built 70-150 BPM half-time 808 beats with triplet hats over dholak or nagara samples and desi harmonium or shehnai loops, rapped in a low blunt Haryanvi chest register with rustic-pride, caste-village and gym-and-tractor imagery, released almost entirely as YouTube singles.
items.description: Haryanvi-language rap from the Rohtak-Hisar-Gurugram belt, essentially a trap-production overlay on Haryanvi pop's rhythmic and lyrical world. Beats are sparse and sub-heavy, with 808 glides and hi-hat rolls placed against sampled dholak or nagara hits and a single looped harmonium or shehnai figure; the vocal is low, blunt and heavily syllabic rather than melodic. It is harmonically flatter and less melody-driven than Punjabi hip hop, and its subject matter stays village-local rather than diasporic.

items.name: Tamil pop (independent non-film)
items.lineage: Non-film Tamil popular music took shape in the 1990s when the Chennai studio culture around Ilaiyaraaja and A. R. Rahman spilled into standalone albums — Unnikrishnan and Bombay Jayashri's light-music records, then the 2000s Tamil rock and indie wave (Kadal Pura, Anthony Daasan) and after 2015 an internet-native scene of Hiphop Tamizha, Sean Roldan and Santhosh Narayanan side projects — typically 80-130 BPM 4/4 productions blending programmed kits and synth pads with mridangam, thavil, nadaswaram or urumi accents and Carnatic-trained vocal gamaka over Western chord progressions.
items.description: Tamil-language popular music produced outside the film-playback system, based in Chennai and its diaspora. It carries the arranging vocabulary of Kollywood scoring — layered synth pads, folk percussion overdubs, sudden metric shifts — into standalone album and single formats, and its vocals keep Carnatic gamaka ornament even over Western functional harmony. It differs from Tamil filmi playback in having no picturisation to serve, so song forms are shorter, arrangements sparser, and lyric subject matter more personal or political.

items.name: Desi Pop (Indipop)
items.lineage: Non-film Indian popular song that broke out of Bombay's playback monopoly in the late 1980s and peaked 1993-2002 through Biddu's productions for Alisha Chinai, Daler Mehndi's dhol-driven bhangra-pop and Lucky Ali's acoustic ballads, distributed on T-Series and Magnasound cassettes: 90-130 BPM four-on-the-floor or dhol-derived chaal patterns, DX7 and Korg M1 pads, tumbi and dholak layered over programmed kits, and film-trained melismatic vocals sung in Hindi-Punjabi code-mixing.
items.description: Desi pop, or Indipop, formed in India in the late 1980s as the first commercially viable non-filmi popular song market, driven by cassette economics and the arrival of MTV India and Channel V in 1993. Its sound couples film-playback vocal technique — heavy meend, nasal placement, Hindi-Punjabi lyric — with imported synth-pop and bhangra rhythm programming, usually a dhol or dholak pattern doubled by a drum machine. Unlike filmi song it answers to no picturization or narrative cue, and unlike UK bhangra it is produced for Indian domestic radio rather than diaspora dancefloors.
exemplars: Daler Mehndi — Bolo Ta Ra Ra

items.name: Desi Trap
items.lineage: South Asian adaptation of Atlanta trap that consolidated in Mumbai, Delhi and the Punjabi diaspora circa 2015-2020 through DIVINE, Raftaar, Sidhu Moose Wala and producers Karan Aujla and Sez on the Beat: 130-150 BPM half-time grids, long-decay 808 glides, triplet hats and rolls, tumbi or sarangi and harmonium samples pitched into minor-key loops, and Hindi-Punjabi-English rapping tracked into a laptop rig.
items.description: Desi trap emerged around 2015 as Indian and Punjabi-diaspora rappers moved off boom-bap toward Atlanta's half-time 808 template, accelerating after Gully Boy (2019) mainstreamed Mumbai street rap. The defining sound is a sub-808 with portamento glides under triplet hi-hat rolls, with a single melancholic loop sourced from tumbi, sarangi, harmonium or filmi strings rather than a soul sample. It differs from UK bhangra and from Punjabi pop in retaining rap cadence and a trap drum grid, and from US trap in its modal, ornament-inflected loop material and multilingual delivery.

items.name: Indian Instrumental (raga instrumental recital)
items.lineage: The instrument-led branch of Hindustani and Carnatic performance codified on record from the 1950s through HMV Dum Dum and All India Radio, shaped by Ravi Shankar, Ali Akbar Khan, Vilayat Khan and Hariprasad Chaurasia: unmetered alap over a tanpura drone, then jod and jhala, then gat cycles in tintal or jhaptal with tabla, built on meend, gamak and sympathetic-string resonance rather than sung text.
items.description: Indian instrumental recital is the purely instrumental realization of raga, established as a recorded genre in the LP era when the long-playing side finally accommodated an unmetered alap followed by composed gat and improvised tans. Its sonic signature is a continuous tanpura drone, microtonal meend between fixed swaras, sympathetic strings ringing under the melody line, and a tabla partner trading tihais against a fixed tala cycle. It is distinguished from khyal and Carnatic kriti by the absence of text — melodic ornament carries what a singer's syllables would — and from fusion or new-age sitar records by strict adherence to raga grammar and cyclic tala.

items.name: Pakistani Pop
items.lineage: Urdu-language guitar-and-synth pop that began with Nazia and Zoheb Hassan's Biddu-produced Disco Deewane (1980) and was codified by Vital Signs' Dil Dil Pakistan (1987) and Junoon's Sufi rock of the 1990s, recorded at EMI Pakistan Karachi and Lahore: 100-130 BPM backbeat kits, chorused clean guitar and Juno-class pads, tabla or dholak doubling the snare, and Urdu vocals that sit between ghazal phrasing and Western pop melody.
items.description: Pakistani pop formed in the early 1980s under Zia-ul-Haq-era broadcast restriction, where PTV's limited music programming and EMI Pakistan's studios made a small number of bands nationally definitive. The sound is Western pop-rock instrumentation — clean chorused guitar, polysynth pad, backbeat kit — carrying Urdu lyric sung with ghazal-derived ornament, and from Junoon onward a qawwali-inflected vocal and dholak layer over distorted guitar. It differs from Indipop in its rock-band basis and lyrical formality, and from qawwali proper in being strophic, secular and studio-composed.

items.name: Vietnamese Melodic Rap
items.lineage: Hanoi and Ho Chi Minh City rap-sung hybrid that consolidated after 2017 and exploded with the Rap Viet and King of Rap television formats in 2020, led by Den Vau, Binz, Karik and producers Touliver and Masew: 80-140 BPM trap and lo-fi grids, Auto-Tuned sung hooks, guitar or dan bau and dan tranh loops, and conversational Vietnamese verses whose six-tone prosody forces melodic rather than flat rap delivery.
items.description: Vietnamese melodic rap became the country's dominant popular form between 2017 and 2021, when underground Hanoi and Saigon crews moved onto national television and streaming. Its defining trait is the blurring of rap and song: Vietnamese is a tonal language, so rapped lines already carry contour, and artists lean into that with sung-through Auto-Tuned hooks over warm, mid-tempo trap or lo-fi beats often built on an acoustic guitar or dan bau sample. It is gentler and more diaristic than US trap, and distinguished from V-pop ballad by its beat-first construction and first-person verse structure.
exemplars: Den Vau — Bai Nay Chill Phet

items.name: Panamanian Pop
items.lineage: Panama City popular song shaped by the isthmus's West Indian labor migration, running from the 1980s Spanish-language dancehall of El General and Nando Boom through Ruben Blades' salsa-song crossover to the 2015-onward melodic urbano of Sech and Boza: 90-100 BPM dembow and reggae-derived one-drop patterns under sung hooks, tipico accordion and conga colorings, and Spanish lyrics delivered half-sung, half-toasted.
items.description: Panamanian pop is the mainstream popular song of a country whose Canal-Zone Anglophone Caribbean population made it the first place reggae and dancehall were sung in Spanish, in the mid-1980s. Its through-line is a sung-toasted vocal over a dembow or reggae-derived groove, sweetened by tipico accordion, conga and horn colorings drawn from the local cumbia panamena and salsa lineages. It differs from Puerto Rican reggaeton in prioritizing melody and Caribbean-English phrasing over rap cadence, and from Colombian tropical pop in its dancehall rather than vallenato rhythmic base.

items.name: Colombian Hip Hop
items.lineage: Rap in Spanish rooted in Bogota's Ciudad Bolivar and Medellin's Comuna 13 from the early 1990s, codified by La Etnnia's El Ataque (1995), then extended by Alcolirykoz, Crack Family and the Pacific-coast fusion of ChocQuibTown: 85-95 BPM boom-bap breaks and later trap grids, samples drawn from salsa, currulao marimba and vallenato records, and dense, socially documentary Spanish verse in Bogota and paisa accents.
items.description: Colombian hip hop took shape in Bogota's southern comunas in the late 1980s and early 1990s and in Medellin during the years of cartel violence, with La Etnnia's home-built studio serving as the scene's first infrastructure. The music runs on sampled breaks and, in the Medellin school, jazz- and salsa-derived loops under long declamatory verses that function as neighborhood reportage; the Pacific branch instead builds beats on currulao marimba and cununo patterns. It differs from Mexican rap in its lower-slung, sample-first production and from reggaeton in rejecting the dembow grid entirely.

items.name: Venezuelan Hip Hop
items.lineage: Caracas barrio rap that emerged in the 1990s in Petare and 23 de Enero and was defined by Vagos y Maleantes, Guerrilla Seca and above all Canserbero between 2005 and 2013: 85-95 BPM boom-bap and later dark orchestral trap beats, samples of salsa, tambor and Venezuelan gaita records, and a heavily rhymed, existential Spanish verse style in Caraqueno slang delivered over sparse minor loops.
items.description: Venezuelan hip hop consolidated in Caracas in the mid-1990s and reached its widest reach through Canserbero, whose Vida and Muerte albums made a sparse, piano-and-strings minor-key production style the national default. Verses are unusually literary and mortality-obsessed, packed with internal rhyme and delivered in a flat, insistent Caraqueno cadence over beats that avoid hooks. Compared to Colombian rap it is bleaker and less sample-collage-driven, and compared to the country's own gaita and salsa traditions it strips percussion back to a single break rather than a full tropical battery.

items.name: Argentine Hip Hop
items.lineage: Buenos Aires rap running from Sindicato Argentino del Hip Hop and Mustafa Yoda in the 1990s to the plaza freestyle-battle circuit of El Quinto Escalon (2012-2017) that produced Duki, Wos and Trueno: 85-95 BPM boom-bap in the older wave, 130-145 BPM half-time trap in the newer, with tango, rock nacional and cumbia villera samples and a distinctive rioplatense voseo cadence honed in acapella competition.
items.description: Argentine hip hop has two distinct eras: a 1990s boom-bap underground centered on Sindicato Argentino del Hip Hop, and a far larger 2015-onward wave that grew directly out of the free-entry freestyle battles of El Quinto Escalon in Parque Rivadavia. That battle origin is audible — flows are built for improvised competition, with dense multisyllabic rhyme and voseo phrasing — and it fed straight into an Argentine trap sound of Auto-Tuned melodic hooks over 808 glides. Its improvisational weighting sets it apart from Spanish and Mexican rap, and its rock-nacional and cumbia sample palette from Caribbean urbano.

items.name: Mexican Hip Hop
items.lineage: Rap in Mexican Spanish rooted in Mexico City's Neza and Monterrey's colonias, codified by Control Machete's Mucho Barato (1996) produced by Jason Roberts and Toy Selectah, then extended by Cartel de Santa, Akwid and Aleman: 88-98 BPM heavy boom-bap with banda, norteno accordion and mariachi horn samples, plus later trap grids, over a low, drawled chilango or regio delivery.
items.description: Mexican hip hop broke nationally in 1996 with Control Machete, a Monterrey group whose producers layered banda brass and norteno accordion over hard boom-bap drums and made regional Mexican sound sources a permanent part of the genre's palette. The vocal approach is low, deliberate and slang-dense, with Mexico City and Monterrey accents functioning as scene markers, and later Cartel de Santa and Aleman moved the same materials onto trap and 808-driven grids. It is heavier and more brass-inflected than Colombian or Argentine rap, and unlike corridos tumbados it keeps rap cadence rather than adopting sung norteno phrasing.

items.name: Turkish Hip Hop
items.lineage: Rap in Turkish begun by Gastarbeiter youth in Germany — Islamic Force in Berlin and Cartel's 1995 debut — then repatriated to Istanbul through Ceza and Sagopa Kajmer in the early 2000s: 90-100 BPM boom-bap and later trap, saz, zurna and arabesk-string samples over minor and hicaz-flavored loops, and an exceptionally fast, agglutination-driven Turkish flow with heavy end-syllable rhyme.
items.description: Turkish hip hop originated in the German diaspora in the early 1990s, where Berlin and Frankfurt crews rapped in Turkish about migrant life, and became a domestic Istanbul genre after 2000 with Ceza and Sagopa Kajmer. Its signature is the collision of a very rapid, syllable-dense Turkish flow with sample beds drawn from arabesk, Anadolu psych and saz recordings, which pull hicaz and other makam colorings into otherwise Western minor-key loops. That microtonal-leaning source material and the language's rhyme-friendly suffixes distinguish it from European and US rap, while its rap cadence separates it from arabesk pop.

items.name: Greek Trap
items.lineage: Athens trap scene that formed around 2015-2017 in Sepolia and the western suburbs through Light, Snik, Mad Clip and Sin Boy, with beats by Simon Rex and Pin Up Beats: 130-150 BPM half-time 808 grids with triplet hat rolls, Auto-Tuned melodic hooks, and loops sampling laiko and rebetiko bouzouki records over minor and hicaz-tinged progressions sung in Greek street argot.
items.description: Greek trap emerged in Athens around 2015, initially as YouTube-native releases from the working-class western suburbs, and by 2019 was the dominant sound in Greek youth music. It uses the standard Atlanta template — long 808s, triplet hats, sparse minor loops, heavy Auto-Tune — but repeatedly draws its melodic material from laiko and rebetiko, sampling or replaying bouzouki and baglamas lines whose Eastern modal contour gives the beats their local accent. That laiko lineage, plus its argot and its debt to the earlier Greek boom-bap of Active Member and Goin Through, separates it from ordinary imported trap.

items.name: Detroit rock
items.lineage: Consolidated in Detroit and Ann Arbor between 1966 and 1972 through the MC5, the Stooges, the Amboy Dukes, SRC and Grand Funk Railroad, working the Grande Ballroom circuit — high-volume twin-humbucker guitars run into overdriven amplifiers, mid-tempo 4/4 backbeats around 120-150 BPM played hard on the snare, one- and two-chord blues-pentatonic riff vamps, and a shouted, hectoring lead vocal derived from Detroit R&B revue delivery.
items.description: The high-energy amplified rock that came out of Detroit and Ann Arbor venues in the late 1960s, most of it cut fast and near-live to eight or sixteen tracks. Defining traits are saturated guitar tone taken from the amplifier rather than the console, a heavy unswung backbeat, riff-based one-chord vamps, and confrontational vocals delivered at the top of the range. It is louder and more repetitive than contemporary West Coast psychedelia and precedes punk by nearly a decade while sharing its brevity and aggression.

items.name: Houston rap
items.lineage: Codified in Houston's Fifth Ward and South Park between 1986 and 2000 by James Prince's Rap-A-Lot Records, the Geto Boys, Scarface, UGK and the Screwed Up Click — mid-tempo 80-95 BPM tracks built on live-feel funk and soul interpolations, heavy TR-808 sub kicks, thick Rhodes and organ pads, and a slow, low-register conversational flow that leaves space for the beat.
items.description: Houston's label-driven rap tradition, running from Rap-A-Lot's late-1980s roster through the Screwed Up Click of the 1990s. The sound is slow and bass-forward: 808 sub kicks, warm Rhodes and blues-guitar interpolations, sparse arrangements, and unhurried baritone delivery emphasizing narrative detail. It is heavier and more soul-sample oriented than Atlanta trap, and it supplies the source material that chopped-and-screwed tape culture then slowed further.
exemplars: Geto Boys — We Can't Be Stopped

items.name: Bronx drill (sample drill)
items.lineage: Formed in the Bronx around 2020-2022 through Kay Flock, B-Lovee, Dougie B and producers such as Great John and Yammy Beatz — 140-150 BPM drill grids in which the minimal synth motif is replaced by a chopped, pitched-up sample of 1990s R&B, salsa or Latin pop, sitting over sliding 808s, offbeat kicks and rapid triplet hi-hat rolls, with aggressive, register-jumping vocal delivery.
items.description: A Bronx-centered variant of New York drill that took hold around 2021, distinguished by melodic sample flips in place of programmed synth riffs. Producers loop recognizable R&B, bachata or salsa hooks pitched up over the standard sliding-808 drill drum grid, giving the style a brighter, more nostalgic surface than Brooklyn drill's cold minimalism. Vocals are denser and more shouted, often traded rapidly between multiple crew members.

items.name: Florida drill
items.lineage: Coalesced in Broward County, Miami-Dade and Jacksonville from roughly 2020 onward, adapting New York drill's sliding-808 template to South Florida's existing SoundCloud and Jacksonville street-rap scenes via artists such as Wizz Havinn, Loe Shimmy and Hotboii — 140-150 BPM beats with distorted 808 glides, bell and plucked-synth motifs, doubled ad-lib layers and a melodic, half-sung delivery rather than New York's flat bark.
items.description: A South and North Florida strain of drill that appeared in the early 2020s, produced almost entirely in bedroom DAW setups. It keeps the sliding 808 and offbeat kick of New York drill but pushes the bass into audible distortion and favors bright bell and pluck leads, with vocals sung as much as rapped and stacked in thick ad-lib layers. This melodic, clipped-low-end profile separates it from both Brooklyn drill and the earlier Florida SoundCloud rap it grew out of.

items.name: New York City rap (five-borough mainstream)
items.lineage: The commercial mainstream of New York rap from roughly 1993 to 2005, centered on Bad Boy, Def Jam, Roc-A-Fella and Loud, with production by DJ Premier, RZA, Just Blaze and the Trackmasters — 88-100 BPM boom-bap grids of hard filtered kick and snare, chopped soul and jazz loops, prominent live or sampled bass, and dense multisyllabic rhyming delivered with pronounced borough accent.
items.description: The major-label New York sound of the mid-1990s through mid-2000s, cut in Manhattan commercial rooms like the Hit Factory and Battery. It pairs sampler-built boom-bap drums and soul-loop harmony with high-budget vocal chains and heavily doubled hooks, and it prizes lyrical density and cadence variation over melodic hooks. It is more polished and more song-structured than the golden-age sample collage that preceded it, and lyrically busier than the Southern rap that displaced it commercially.
exemplars: The Notorious B.I.G. — Ready to Die

items.name: Philadelphia rap
items.lineage: Built in North and West Philadelphia from the late 1980s through the 2010s by Schoolly D, DJ Jazzy Jeff & the Fresh Prince, the Roots, Beanie Sigel's State Property and later Meek Mill — 90-100 BPM tracks that alternate between live-band drum-and-Rhodes backing and hard sampled loops, with an aggressive, front-of-the-beat, breath-driven vocal attack and gospel-inflected sung hooks.
items.description: Philadelphia's rap tradition, shaped by the city's soul-session infrastructure and its long-standing live-band culture. Two strands run through it: the Roots' instrumental hip-hop, tracked with a real kit and keys at Philly studios, and the harder sample-and-808 street rap of Beanie Sigel and Meek Mill. Both share a loud, breath-forward vocal delivery pushed slightly ahead of the beat, more percussive and confrontational than New York's laid-back pocket.
exemplars: Beanie Sigel — The Broad Street Bully

items.name: Pittsburgh rap
items.lineage: Emerged from Pittsburgh's East End and Point Breeze in the late 2000s through the free-mixtape careers of Wiz Khalifa and Mac Miller with producers ID Labs and Big Jerm — 75-90 BPM half-time beats over warm, dusty jazz and soul loops, soft filtered drums, prominent Rhodes and vinyl noise, and relaxed, half-sung conversational flows aimed at internet blog distribution rather than radio.
items.description: A late-2000s and 2010s scene centered on the ID Labs studio in Pittsburgh and distributed almost entirely through free mixtapes and music blogs. The sound is warm and unhurried: dusty jazz-soul loops, soft-attack drums, audible vinyl crackle, and easy half-sung delivery. It is more melodic and lower-intensity than East Coast boom-bap and predates the trap-hat vocabulary that later Pittsburgh artists absorbed.

items.name: Baton Rouge rap
items.lineage: Codified in Baton Rouge, Louisiana between 1998 and the mid-2010s through Trill Entertainment's Lil Boosie and Webbie, then NBA YoungBoy — 70-85 BPM half-time beats with hard 808 kicks, sharp snares and rolling hats, thin minor-key synth strings and bells, and an anguished, near-shouted melodic delivery that slides between rapping and singing over narratively autobiographical lyrics.
items.description: Louisiana's capital-city rap scene, distinct from New Orleans bounce and driven by the Trill Entertainment roster in the 2000s and NBA YoungBoy after 2015. Beats are sparse and 808-heavy with thin, mournful synth string and bell lines, leaving the voice fully exposed. The defining trait is emotional delivery: cracked, high-register melodic shouting over first-person hardship narrative, more raw and less codified than Atlanta trap's cadence conventions.

items.name: Seattle hip-hop
items.lineage: Grew in Seattle's Central District from Sir Mix-A-Lot's Nastymix electro-funk records of 1985-1992 through the 2000s Massline and Sub Pop generation of Blue Scholars, Shabazz Palaces and Macklemore — 85-100 BPM beats moving from 808 electro programming to jazz-and-Pacific-Rim sample collage, with clean live bass, ambient pads, and clear, enunciated, often politically explicit vocal delivery.
items.description: Rap made in Seattle from the mid-1980s onward, sustained by local indie labels rather than major-label offices. The earlier phase is 808 electro-funk; the later, larger phase is textural and sample-collage based, with ambient pads, jazz sources and unusually clean mixes drawn from the city's indie-rock studio infrastructure. Compared with California rap it is quieter, more overtly political and more experimental in texture.

items.name: Nashville hip-hop
items.lineage: Developed in North Nashville from the late 1990s onward through Young Buck's move into G-Unit and the independent Cashville circuit of Starlito, Don Trip and All Star — 70-90 BPM half-time Southern beats with 808 sub kicks, rolling triplet hats, sparse guitar and organ interpolations drawn from the city's session infrastructure, and dry, plainspoken conversational delivery.
items.description: Nashville's rap scene, largely independent and mixtape-driven, running alongside the city's country-music industry since the late 1990s. It uses standard Southern trap architecture — 808 sub kicks, triplet hats, thin minor loops — but often folds in guitar and keyboard parts played by local session musicians. Its distinguishing feature is delivery: flat, unhurried, detail-heavy storytelling with little melodic singing, closer to Memphis narrative rap than to Atlanta's cadence-first style.

items.name: Hamburg Hip Hop
items.lineage: Hamburg's German-language rap scene formed in the early 1990s around the St. Pauli and Eimsbüttel districts and the Yo Mama and Buback labels, codified by Absolute Beginner, Fettes Brot, Fünf Sterne deluxe and Samy Deluxe — 88–96 BPM sample-based boom-bap built on filtered jazz and soul loops, live-played bass and Rhodes overdubs, scratched hooks, and a witty, wordplay-heavy High-German flow with Plattdeutsch and English code-switching that set it against Stuttgart's soul-conscious and Berlin's harder street schools.
items.description: Hamburg hip hop is the northern German rap school that broke Deutschrap into the mainstream in the mid-1990s, built on warm sampled jazz-funk loops, live bass and keys overdubs, and heavy turntable cutting. Its signature is verbal humour and internal-rhyme density delivered in a relaxed, slightly behind-the-beat German flow. It is brighter and more playful than the Frankfurt/Berlin battle lineage and less soul-earnest than Stuttgart's Kolchose scene, and it kept live instrumentation in the loop longer than most European rap of the period.
exemplars: Fettes Brot — Auf einem Auge blöd

items.name: Rap Napoletano
items.lineage: Neapolitan-dialect rap emerged from the early-1990s centri sociali of Naples, codified by 99 Posse, Almamegretta and La Famiglia and carried forward by Co'Sang, Clementino and Rocco Hunt — 88–100 BPM boom-bap and dub-reggae hybrids with tammorra and reggae-offbeat guitar layered under sampled loops, ragga-toasting and posse-cut delivery, melodic hooks quoting canzone napoletana melody, and militant anti-camorra and anti-fascist lyrics sung entirely in napulitano.
items.description: Rap napoletano is Italian hip hop's most linguistically separatist branch, rapped in Neapolitan rather than standard Italian and grown out of the squatted social centres of early-1990s Naples. Its defining sound folds dub bass, ragga toasting and tammurriata frame-drum patterns into sample-based beats, with sung refrains that carry the melismatic contour of classic canzone napoletana. Compared with Milanese rap it is more overtly political and more Mediterranean-melodic; compared with the Roman school it leans harder on reggae and dub rather than pure boom-bap.

items.name: Rap Genovese
items.lineage: Genoa's rap scene formed in the mid-2010s in the Certosa and Sampierdarena quarters around the Sacre Scuole collective (Izi, Tedua, Vaz Tè) with Bresh, Disme and Nader following — 130–150 BPM trap grids heard in half-time, rolling 808 glides, reverb-washed minor-key piano and pad loops, and a distinctively melodic sung-rapped delivery with heavy Auto-Tune, Ligurian dialect inserts and cinematic Genoa-port imagery.
items.description: Rap genovese is the Ligurian wave of Italian trap that broke nationally after 2016, built in bedroom studios on cheap interfaces and DAW trap templates. Its markers are melodic, heavily pitch-corrected hooks, reverb-drenched piano loops, sliding 808 basses, and lyrics threaded with Genoese place-names and dialect. It is more melancholic and melody-forward than the Milan trap school and less politically declamatory than the Neapolitan tradition, closer in temperament to cloud rap than to boom-bap.

items.name: Old School Atlanta Hip Hop
items.lineage: Atlanta's first rap generation ran from roughly 1986 to 1995, moving from Miami-bass-derived 808 booty music (Kilo Ali, MC Shy D, Raheem the Dream, Success-N-Effect on Ichiban and DJ Toomp's boards) into the LaFace/Organized Noize live-band Southern soul of OutKast and Goodie Mob — 95–108 BPM with long-decay TR-808 kicks and open hats, live Fender Rhodes, wah guitar and P-funk bass overdubs, gospel-choir backing pads, and a drawled, laid-back Southern flow that Northern critics initially dismissed.
items.description: Old school Atlanta hip hop covers the city's pre-crunk decade, when local labels like Ichiban and Wrap fed a bass-music club circuit and LaFace then built a Southern rap canon around live musicianship. The sound is defined by booming 808 sub-kicks inherited from Miami bass, replayed rather than sampled funk and gospel parts, and a slow, syllable-stretching drawl. It differs from Miami bass in tempo and lyrical scope, and from the crunk and trap that followed in its warm analog live-band texture and comparative rhythmic patience.
exemplars: Kilo Ali — America Has a Problem (Cocaine)
MC Shy D — Comin' Correct in 88
Arrested Development — 3 Years, 5 Months and 2 Days in the Life Of...

items.name: Classic Texas Country
items.lineage: Texas country took shape in the beer-hall circuit between Fort Worth and San Antonio from the late 1930s through the 1960s, codified by Ernest Tubb, Lefty Frizzell, Ray Price and Willie Nelson — 110–140 BPM shuffles and 2/4 dance beats with a walking upright or electric bass, twin-fiddle harmony, pedal steel and single-coil electric lead over acoustic rhythm guitar, brushed or lightly-swung snare, and a plainspoken slurred baritone vocal built to carry across a wooden dance floor.
items.description: Classic Texas country is the dance-hall-first branch of honky-tonk, shaped by a live circuit where the shuffle and the two-step mattered more than the record. Its markers are the 4/4 Ray Price shuffle, twin fiddles, crying pedal steel, an unhurried behind-the-beat baritone, and songwriting that stays conversational and unadorned. It kept the fiddle and steel front and centre exactly when the Nashville Sound was replacing them with strings and vocal choirs, which is what made Texas the base for later outlaw and neotraditional revivals.
exemplars: Ernest Tubb — Walking the Floor Over You
Lefty Frizzell — If You've Got the Money I've Got the Time

items.name: Classic Oklahoma Country
items.lineage: Oklahoma country grew out of the Tulsa and Oklahoma City ballroom and radio circuit of the 1930s–60s, codified by Bob Wills' Texas Playboys at Cain's Ballroom, Hank Thompson's Brazos Valley Boys and Wanda Jackson — 130–180 BPM western-swing two-beats and polkas with amplified steel guitar, fiddle section, jazz-derived horn or piano comping and Charlie Christian-lineage electric lead, plus the laid-back Tulsa Sound shuffle of Leon Russell and J.J. Cale that later loosened the tempo and softened the vocal to a mumble.
items.description: Oklahoma country is a swing-inflected, dance-oriented country tradition centred on Tulsa's Cain's Ballroom and the state's strong radio-barn-dance culture. It is more harmonically adventurous than most honky-tonk, absorbing jazz chord changes, take-a-solo band arrangements and amplified steel decades before Nashville allowed them. Its later Tulsa Sound offshoot swapped the big band for a small greasy shuffle combo, giving Oklahoma a second identity distinct from both Texas dance-hall country and the Nashville studio system.
exemplars: Bob Wills and His Texas Playboys — Live at Cain's Ballroom
Hank Thompson — The Wild Side of Life
Vince Gill — When I Call Your Name

items.name: Arkansas Country
items.lineage: Arkansas country formed along the Delta cotton belt and the Ozark foothills and reached record in the 1950s through the Memphis studios two hours east, codified by Johnny Cash, Sonny Burgess, Charlie Rich and Conway Twitty — 120–180 BPM slapped-upright-bass boom-chicka rhythm, single-coil tremolo-and-slapback electric lead, no drums or minimal brushed snare, and a low, flat, hymn-inflected vocal delivering Delta hardship and Pentecostal imagery in plain first-person narrative.
items.description: Arkansas country is the Delta-edge strain of American country that fed directly into Sun Records rockabilly, drawing on sharecropper hymnody, Ozark ballad singing and the blues heard across the river. Its trademarks are the boom-chicka-boom of slapped bass and muted guitar, slapback tape echo, near-absent drums, and a stark declarative vocal. It is sparser and bluesier than Texas dance-hall country and rougher than Kentucky's bluegrass lineage, defined more by narrative gravity than by instrumental display.
exemplars: Johnny Cash — With His Hot and Blue Guitar
Glen Campbell — Gentle on My Mind

items.name: Kentucky Roots
items.lineage: Kentucky's string-band and mountain-song tradition runs from Appalachian and western-Kentucky coalfield ballad singing through the 1927 Bristol-era commercial recordings to the codification of bluegrass by Bill Monroe of Rosine in 1945 — 100–160 BPM two-beat with driving mandolin chop on the backbeat, three-finger five-string banjo roll, fiddle double-stops, guitar bass runs and slapped upright, and the tenor-above-lead 'high lonesome' vocal harmony, alongside Merle Travis's thumb-picked guitar syncopation from Muhlenberg County.
items.description: Kentucky roots covers the Bluegrass State's own line of mountain ballad, coalfield song, thumb-picked guitar and the bluegrass ensemble that Bill Monroe assembled from those parts. Its defining features are the drumless but hard-driving two-beat carried by mandolin chop and banjo roll, modal and pentatonic melody, and pinched high-tenor harmony sung above the lead. It is faster and more soloistically competitive than Appalachian old-time, and unlike honky-tonk it takes no electric instruments and no drum kit at all.
exemplars: Bill Monroe and His Blue Grass Boys — Blue Moon of Kentucky
J.D. Crowe and the New South — 0044

items.name: Melbourne Bounce
items.lineage: Melbourne bounce emerged in Melbourne's inner-north club and Melbourne-shuffle scene around 2012–2014 out of Dutch house and Melbourne's earlier 'Melbourne shuffle' hard-dance culture, codified by Joel Fletcher, Will Sparks, Timmy Trumpet and the Orkestrated crew — 128–132 BPM four-on-the-floor with a heavily sidechained detuned offbeat saw bass on the upbeat eighths, aggressive open-hat rides, long white-noise risers into silent-drop breakdowns, and chopped pitched-up vocal or trumpet hooks in place of sung toplines.
items.description: Melbourne bounce is an Australian club style of the early-to-mid 2010s that stripped Dutch house down to a single hard-sidechained offbeat bass stab and an open hat. The genre's whole identity sits in that rubbery detuned upbeat bassline, the pumping compressor breathing against the kick, and blunt drop-focused arrangements with almost no harmonic movement. Compared with big-room EDM it is drier, lower-fidelity and less anthemic, and unlike tech-house it has no groove subtlety at all — it is built for the shuffle-dance floor.
exemplars: Will Sparks — Ah Yeah So What

items.name: Art Punk
items.lineage: Formed 1976-79 in the UK and US art schools (Leeds, Cleveland, New York) as punk's conceptual wing — Wire, Gang of Four, Pere Ubu and The Pop Group replaced three-chord acceleration with angular non-blues guitar intervals, treble-forward scratch rhythm playing, high-register melodic basslines carrying the hook, clipped 140-170 BPM disco-derived and stop-start drum figures, and declamatory half-spoken vocals delivering Marxist or absurdist texts over deliberately dry, unreverbed studio space.
items.description: Art punk emerged in 1976-79 among art-school-trained musicians who took punk's rejection of virtuosity as license for formal experiment rather than speed. The sound is defined by dry, effect-light production, scratchy single-coil guitar playing unresolved intervals rather than power chords, a melodically dominant bass, and hard-edged funk or disco rhythmic borrowings under spoken-shouted vocals. Unlike straight punk it avoids blues pentatonics and anthemic choruses, and unlike post-punk proper it retains punk's brevity and aggression rather than dissolving into atmosphere.
exemplars: Devo - Q: Are We Not Men?

items.name: Britpunk
items.lineage: Codified in London and Manchester 1976-1978 by the Sex Pistols, The Clash, The Damned and Buzzcocks, working from pub-rock and Stooges/New York Dolls models — barre-chord downstroke guitar through overdriven Marshall stacks, 160-200 BPM straight-eighth drumming with snare on 2 and 4 and minimal fills, root-note eighth-note bass, and sneered, glottal-accented English vocals cut fast and cheap in small commercial studios like Wessex and Pathway.
items.description: Britpunk is the original 1976-78 British punk wave, formed around London's Roxy and 100 Club and Manchester's Lesser Free Trade Hall. Its markers are massed downstroke rhythm guitar with almost no lead playing, a rigid straight-eighth backbeat, two-to-three-minute song lengths, and vocals delivered in undisguised regional English accents with class-political or nihilist lyrics. It differs from US punk of the same years in its overt political framing and thicker, more distorted guitar tone, and from later UK82 hardcore in retaining pop songcraft and singalong choruses.
exemplars: Sex Pistols - Never Mind the Bollocks
Buzzcocks - Another Music in a Different Kitchen

items.name: College Rock
items.lineage: Named for the US campus radio format that broke it circa 1981-1989, centered on Athens GA, Minneapolis, Hoboken and Austin — R.E.M., the dB's, Hüsker Dü and The Replacements built jangling Rickenbacker-style arpeggios, mid-tempo 110-140 BPM backbeats, melodic countrapuntal bass, close two-part harmony, and mixed-low, often unintelligible vocals, tracked on modest budgets at regional studios such as Reflection and Nickel with tape and 80s inline desks.
items.description: College rock is the American guitar-band idiom of roughly 1981-1990 defined by its distribution channel — non-commercial campus radio and independent labels like I.R.S., Twin/Tone and Homestead — rather than a single sound. Its common thread is jangling clean-to-lightly-overdriven guitar, unpolished mid-fidelity production, melodic bass, and vocals buried in the mix rather than spotlit. It is less abrasive than the hardcore scene it grew alongside and less studio-processed than mainstream 80s rock, and it became the direct commercial precursor to 1990s alternative.
exemplars: Camper Van Beethoven - Telephone Free Landslide Victory

items.name: Crossover Thrash
items.lineage: Formed 1984-1987 where American hardcore punk scenes met Bay Area and New York thrash metal — D.R.I., Suicidal Tendencies, Corrosion of Conformity and S.O.D. fused hardcore's 200-250 BPM d-beat and blast-adjacent skank beats with palm-muted metal downpicking, chromatic riffing and short shredded solos, topped by barked gang-chorus shouts, in songs typically under two minutes tracked loud and dry at metal studios.
items.description: Crossover thrash names the mid-1980s convergence of hardcore punk and thrash metal, most visibly in Venice CA, Raleigh NC and the New York hardcore scene. It keeps hardcore's brevity, skank-beat drumming and shouted gang vocals while adopting metal's palm-muted downpicked riff construction, tighter double-tracked guitars and occasional lead breaks. It is faster and less riff-elaborate than pure Bay Area thrash and more technically played than straight hardcore, and it fed directly into the emergence of grindcore and death metal.

items.name: Emotional Hardcore
items.lineage: Codified in Washington DC during the 1985 Revolution Summer by Rites of Spring, Embrace, Beefeater and Moss Icon on Dischord Records, tracked by Don Zientara at Inner Ear — hardcore's fast 8th-note drive is broken by ringing open-chord passages and dynamic drops, guitars use suspended and octave voicings rather than power chords alone, and vocals shift between melodic singing and cracked, throat-shredding screams over confessional first-person lyrics.
items.description: Emotional hardcore is the original DC variant of 1985, when members of the city's hardcore bands deliberately slowed and opened out the form to admit melody, dynamic contrast and personal rather than political lyrics. Recordings are dry, thin-toned and near-live, with guitars ringing rather than saturated, and the vocal is the focal instrument, alternating sung lines with unfeigned screaming. Compared to the hardcore that preceded it, tempos vary within songs and structures abandon verse-chorus regularity; compared to later 90s emo it is rawer, faster and far less produced.
exemplars: Rites of Spring - Rites of Spring
Moss Icon - Lyburnum Wits End Liberation Fly

items.name: Emocore
items.lineage: The mid-1990s Midwest and Pacific Northwest development of DC emotional hardcore, carried by Cap'n Jazz, Braid, Sunny Day Real Estate, Jawbreaker and Texas Is the Reason circa 1992-1998 — twin-guitar interlocking arpeggios in odd or shifting meters, loud-quiet dynamic architecture, busy tom-heavy drumming, and strained tenor vocals that break into shouts, tracked to analog tape at mid-budget indie studios.
items.description: Emocore is the 1990s Midwest reading of emotional hardcore, in which the DC template gained interlocking clean-guitar arpeggios, unconventional time signatures and full loud-quiet-loud song architecture. Recordings are warmer and more layered than the 1985 originals, with real low end, double-tracked guitars and audible reverb, while vocals remain untrained and often deliberately off-pitch at emotional peaks. It sits between hardcore and indie rock, distinguished from college rock by its scream-capable vocal and from later mainstream emo pop-punk by the absence of polished hooks.
exemplars: Texas Is the Reason - Do You Know Who You Are?

items.name: Experimental Rock
items.lineage: Emerged internationally 1967-1980 through Captain Beefheart, Faust, This Heat, Frank Zappa and later Sonic Youth and Swans, using the rock band as raw material rather than form — polymetric interlocking parts, altered and prepared guitars, tape splicing and musique concrete inserts, non-functional harmony, extended or absent song structure, and vocals treated as timbre, usually self-produced in converted non-studio spaces on multitrack tape.
items.description: Experimental rock is the practice, running from the late 1960s onward, of retaining rock instrumentation while discarding its formal conventions — steady meter, functional harmony, verse-chorus structure and clean recording norms. Typical procedures include prepared or detuned guitars, collaged tape material, extreme durations, unrepeated sections and studio noise treated as content. It is distinguished from progressive rock by its rejection of virtuosic composition in favor of process and texture, and from noise rock by its wider palette of non-rock materials and its frequent use of the studio itself as the compositional instrument.

items.name: Steampunk
items.lineage: A retrofuturist neo-Victorian music scene formed in the US Pacific Northwest and California circa 2005-2012 around Abney Park, Vernian Process and Steam Powered Giraffe, growing out of convention culture rather than a geographic club scene — cabaret and sea-shanty song forms in 6/8 or brisk 2/4, accordion, fiddle and pump organ layered over rock rhythm section and industrial or orchestral samples, theatrical narrative vocals in character, produced entirely in the box in home project studios.
items.description: Steampunk music is a costume-and-narrative-driven scene that emerged in the mid-2000s from the literary and convention subculture of the same name, without a single home city or fixed instrumentation. Its recurring sonic markers are minor-key cabaret and shanty song forms, acoustic folk instruments such as accordion, fiddle and harmonium set against a rock rhythm section, mechanical or clockwork sound effects, and vocals performed in persona with heavy narrative diction. It is defined by aesthetic program more than technique, which separates it from goth's fixed guitar sound and from folk rock's traditional repertoire.
exemplars: The Cog is Dead - Steam Powered Stories

items.name: African Blues
items.lineage: Consolidated in Mali, Niger and the wider Sahel from the 1970s onward — Ali Farka Toure, Boubacar Traore, Tinariwen and Tamikrest recast Songhai, Mande and Tuareg modal repertoire for electric guitar, keeping the ngoni and tehardent's cyclic pentatonic ostinato, one-chord drone-based harmony, calabash and hand-clap 6/8 and 4/4 patterns around 90-120 BPM, and call-and-response singing in Songhai, Bambara or Tamasheq over guitar lines that ornament rather than resolve.
items.description: African blues names the Sahelian electric guitar idiom that developed in Mali and the Tuareg diaspora from the 1970s, in which existing Songhai, Mande and Tamasheq modal repertoire was transferred from ngoni and tehardent to guitar. It is built on a single unchanging harmonic center, endlessly cycling pentatonic ostinati with a raised fourth in Tuareg practice, interlocking calabash and handclap patterns, and antiphonal group vocals rather than a soloist over changes. Its resemblance to Mississippi blues is structural rather than derivative — it lacks the twelve-bar cycle and dominant-tonic motion entirely, staying modal and cyclic throughout.

items.name: Blues Shouter
items.lineage: A Kansas City and territory-band vocal role codified 1936-1950 by Jimmy Rushing with Count Basie, Big Joe Turner, Wynonie Harris and Big Maybelle — unamplified or barely amplified singers projecting over a full riffing big band, delivering twelve-bar blues in shouted chest voice at the top of the range, with 12/8 shuffle or medium 4/4 swing behind them, sectional horn riffs answering each vocal line, and boogie-woogie piano and walking bass underneath.
items.description: The blues shouter tradition arose in Kansas City's territory-band circuit of the 1930s and 40s, where singers had to carry over a loud riffing orchestra without reliable amplification. The result is a full-throated, largely vibrato-free chest voice delivering twelve-bar blues at forte across the whole phrase, answered by call-and-response horn section riffs over a 12/8 shuffle or medium swing. It differs from the acoustic country blues in its ensemble setting and fixed bar count, and from later soul singing in its lack of melisma and its relentless dynamic level, and it fed directly into jump blues and early rock and roll.
exemplars: Jimmy Rushing with Count Basie - Sent for You Yesterday
Walter Brown with Jay McShann - Confessin' the Blues

items.name: Country Blues
items.lineage: Rural Southern US solo guitar-and-voice blues consolidated on race records between 1926 and 1935 through Blind Lemon Jefferson, Charley Patton, Blind Blake and Mississippi John Hurt — free-floating 8-to-13-bar stanzas at 70-110 BPM, thumb-driven alternating or monotonic bass under treble string answers, bottleneck slide and heavy string bending, and a declamatory field-holler vocal that the guitar answers phrase for phrase.
items.description: Country blues is the solo, self-accompanied rural blues captured by talent scouts across the South from the mid-1920s, before amplification standardized the form. Its signature is elasticity: bar counts stretch to fit the sung line, the guitar carries bass, chords and answering treble figures simultaneously, and slide or bent strings imitate vocal inflection. Unlike the vaudeville-orchestra classic blues of the same decade or the later electric city styles, there is no band to keep time and no fixed twelve-bar grid.

items.name: Detroit Blues
items.lineage: Postwar Michigan electric blues built by Delta migrants working the auto plants, codified 1948-1962 by John Lee Hooker, Eddie Burns, Baby Boy Warren and Bobo Jenkins on Sensation, Fortune and JVB — one-chord droning boogie at 90-130 BPM over amplified guitar with heavy tremolo, stomping foot as the only percussion on early sides, later a small combo with amplified harp and a shuffling drum kit.
items.description: Detroit blues is the electric style that grew in the Black Bottom and Hastings Street bars after wartime migration from Mississippi carried country blues north to the auto plants. It is markedly more modal and hypnotic than Chicago's twelve-bar band blues: John Lee Hooker's one-chord boogies keep an irregular vocal-led bar count and drive on stomped foot and tremolo guitar rather than an ensemble shuffle. Small local labels recorded it raw, with little of the Chess house arranging that defined Chicago.

items.name: Doom Blues
items.lineage: Slow, minor-key blues rendered through doom metal weight, formed in Birmingham 1969-1972 when Black Sabbath recast Delta twelve-bars in tritone-heavy riffs, and revived from the 1990s by Down and Orange Goblin — 55-85 BPM, downtuned humbucker guitar through cranked valve heads, blues pentatonic bends stretched over sustained power chords, and a keening or bellowed vocal riding a lurching half-time drum feel.
items.description: Doom blues is the branch of doom metal that keeps the blues form audible rather than dissolving it into riff cycles: twelve-bar and eight-bar shapes survive, but at funeral tempo with tritone emphasis and saturated downtuned guitar. It descends directly from Sabbath's earliest sides, where Tony Iommi's slow bends and Ozzy Osbourne's wailing lines sit over a stalled shuffle. Against stoner rock it is darker and slower, and against traditional slow blues it substitutes amplifier mass and sustain for the small-combo dynamics of a Chicago band.

items.name: Folk Blues
items.lineage: Concert-and-coffeehouse acoustic blues consolidated in the US and British revival circuits 1948-1965 by Lead Belly, Josh White, Big Bill Broonzy, Brownie McGhee and Sonny Terry — moderate 80-120 BPM twelve-bar and ballad forms on fingerpicked acoustic or twelve-string guitar with harmonica, delivered in clear enunciated diction for a listening audience rather than a dance floor, often with topical or narrative lyrics.
items.description: Folk blues is the acoustic blues repertoire as reframed for the mid-century folk revival: staged in clubs and concert halls, presented as heritage, and sung with clear diction to audiences who had come to listen. Musically it regularizes country blues — steady bar counts, tidier tempi, twelve-string strum and harmonica obbligato — and often carries topical or narrative texts absorbed from the labor-song movement. It differs from country blues in intent and setting rather than repertoire, and from the electric styles in rejecting amplification outright.

items.name: Gospel Blues
items.lineage: Sacred blues sung to blues guitar accompaniment, crystallized on race records 1927-1935 by Blind Willie Johnson, Rev. Gary Davis and Washington Phillips and carried into the 1940s by Sister Rosetta Tharpe — 70-110 BPM twelve-bar and hymn-derived forms, bottleneck slide answering the voice, hand claps and congregational responses, and a rasped or shouted delivery preaching rather than lamenting.
items.description: Gospel blues applies the blues guitar vocabulary — slide, bent thirds, call-and-response between voice and instrument — to sacred texts, a fusion that flourished on prewar race records and in Holiness storefront churches. The vocal delivery is preacherly: rasp, shout, and sermonic aside rather than the confessional first person of secular blues. It differs from jubilee quartet singing in being guitar-led and largely solo, and from later black gospel in its unadorned blues harmony and absence of piano-and-organ arrangement.

items.name: Harmonica Blues
items.lineage: Amplified diatonic harp blues codified in Chicago 1948-1960 by Little Walter, Sonny Boy Williamson II, Big Walter Horton and Junior Wells — cross-harp second position at 90-140 BPM, hand-cupped harp driven through a bullet mic and small valve amp into saturation, tongue-blocked chording and bent draw notes carrying the melodic lead over a shuffle band.
items.description: Harmonica blues is the postwar style in which the amplified diatonic harp, not the guitar, takes the melodic lead. Little Walter's practice of cupping a bullet microphone against the harp and overdriving a small tube amp turned the instrument into a horn-like voice with its own distortion and feedback vocabulary, and cross-harp position made bent draw notes the core expressive device. Distinct from harmonica's supporting role in country blues, it is a lead-instrument tradition with instrumental features and a full shuffle band behind it.

items.name: Hill Country Blues
items.lineage: North Mississippi hill-country style of Marshall, Tate and Panola counties documented by David Evans and Alan Lomax from the 1960s and carried onto record by Mississippi Fred McDowell, R.L. Burnside, Junior Kimbrough and the Turner family fife-and-drum bands — one-chord modal vamps at 85-125 BPM with no chord change, droning guitar riffs over a steady dance groove, and West African-derived polyrhythmic snare-and-bass-drum patterns behind cane fife.
items.description: Hill country blues comes from the north Mississippi uplands east of the Delta, where a picnic-and-dance function kept the music on a single droning chord instead of the twelve-bar changes that defined Delta and Chicago blues. Guitar parts are hypnotic riff cycles with heavy string drone, and the associated cane fife-and-drum bands preserve a polyrhythmic bass-and-snare pattern with clear West African antecedents. Its refusal of chord movement and its trance-length grooves are what separate it most sharply from its Delta neighbour.

items.name: Kansas City Blues
items.lineage: Big-band blues shouting developed in Pendergast-era Kansas City 1928-1945 around Bennie Moten and Count Basie and codified by Big Joe Turner, Jimmy Rushing and Walter Brown — riff-based twelve-bars at 120-180 BPM over a smooth four-to-the-bar walking bass, head arrangements of stacked brass and reed riffs, tenor saxophone solos, and an unamplified voice built to cut through a full orchestra.
items.description: Kansas City blues is the blues as swung by a jazz orchestra, the product of a wide-open nightclub economy that let bands play all night on riff-based head arrangements. Blues shouters like Big Joe Turner and Jimmy Rushing sang without amplification over stacked brass and reed riffs and a light, even four-beat rhythm section, with tenor saxophone taking the solo role the guitar holds elsewhere. It is the direct ancestor of jump blues and early rhythm and blues, and it stands apart from Chicago and Delta blues in its orchestral scale, harmonic literacy and dance-band swing.

items.name: Memphis Blues
items.lineage: Beale Street blues of Memphis and the Tennessee-Mississippi corridor, named by W.C. Handy in 1912 and shaped 1927-1935 by the Memphis Jug Band, Cannon's Jug Stompers, Memphis Minnie and Furry Lewis before its 1950s electric revival at Sun — 90-140 BPM ragtime-tinged good-time repertoire on guitar, kazoo, harmonica and blown jug, with duet guitar interplay and a hokum-leaning lyric wit.
items.description: Memphis blues is the urban, entertainment-facing blues of Beale Street: lighter, faster and more ragtime-influenced than the Delta styles feeding into the city, and organized around jug bands and guitar duets rather than lone singers. Kazoo, blown jug, washboard and mandolin give it a timbral variety unusual in prewar blues, and the lyrics run to hokum double entendre and party material. The postwar Sun sessions carried the same brisk, good-humoured feel into electric form and on toward rockabilly.

items.name: New Orleans Blues
items.lineage: Crescent City blues shaped at Cosimo Matassa's J&M studio 1947-1962 by Professor Longhair, Roy Brown, Guitar Slim, Smiley Lewis and Dave Bartholomew's band — 100-150 BPM blues carried on rolling rhumba-boogie piano and a second-line street-parade drum pattern, with a full horn section, tenor sax solos, and shouted or crooned vocals over Afro-Caribbean tresillo bass figures.
items.description: New Orleans blues is the local dialect in which the blues absorbed the city's Caribbean and parade traditions: Professor Longhair's rhumba-boogie left hand, Earl Palmer's second-line drum patterns, and Dave Bartholomew's horn arrangements. Rhythm is the distinguishing feature — a tresillo-derived bass and syncopated street-beat drumming where Chicago blues would play a straight shuffle. It is also more heavily horn-led than guitar-led, which places it on the direct path from blues into rhythm and blues and early rock and roll.

items.name: Piano Blues
items.lineage: Solo blues piano of the barrelhouse, rent party and lumber camp circuit, recorded from 1923 and codified by Leroy Carr, Roosevelt Sykes, Little Brother Montgomery, Memphis Slim and Otis Spann — twelve-bar forms from 60 to 200 BPM, a walking or rolling ostinato left hand against right-hand blue-note tremolos and crushed grace notes, on hard-struck upright pianos left deliberately unrepaired.
items.description: Piano blues is the keyboard branch of the tradition, developed where a guitar was too quiet: barrelhouses, turpentine and lumber camps, and urban rent parties. The left hand supplies bass, chords and time in a self-sufficient ostinato while the right hand imitates vocal blue notes through crushed seconds and rapid tremolo, a division of labour that makes the pianist a one-person band. It encompasses everything from Leroy Carr's soft urbane accompaniment to the hammering boogie-woogie of the rent-party players, and differs from jazz stride in staying inside blues harmony and repetition.

items.name: Punk Blues
items.lineage: Blues form played with punk attack, emerging from US and Australian garage scenes 1985-2001 through the Gun Club, the Cramps, the Jon Spencer Blues Explosion, Beasts of Bourbon and the White Stripes — 120-180 BPM one- and twelve-bar structures, blown-out fuzz guitar and slide, minimal or drummer-only rhythm sections, and a howled, unpitched vocal recorded fast and deliberately distorted.
items.description: Punk blues takes the repetition and slide vocabulary of prewar and hill country blues and plays it with hardcore tempo, volume and distortion, usually in stripped two- or three-piece lineups. Recording practice is part of the style: cheap microphones, overloaded tape and analogue-only studios like Toe Rag are chosen so the record sounds damaged. Unlike blues rock, it does not aim at instrumental virtuosity or extended soloing — the appeal is the collision of a primitive one-chord riff with punk's attack.

items.name: Ragtime Blues
items.lineage: Southeastern US fingerpicked blues idiom crystallized in the 1920s-30s Piedmont corridor from Georgia to Virginia and codified on record by Blind Blake, Blind Boy Fuller and Rev. Gary Davis, marrying ragtime's syncopated right-hand melody and I-VI-II-V parlor-piano harmony to a steady alternating-bass thumb on guitar at a brisk 100-140 BPM, with light-toned conversational vocals, frequent kazoo/jug/harmonica breaks and instrumental rags played without any vocal at all.
items.description: Ragtime blues formed in the 1920s among Southeastern songsters who absorbed published piano rags and adapted their syncopation to the six-string guitar, reaching commercial record via Paramount and ARC sessions cut direct to shellac. Its signature is a metronomic alternating thumb bass under a treble line that lands off the beat, richer in secondary dominants and diminished passing chords than Delta blues, and often abandoning the twelve-bar frame for sixteen-bar rag strains. Against Piedmont blues generally it is faster, brighter and more instrumental; against Delta blues it is harmonically ornate and free of slide or drone.

items.name: Soul Blues
items.lineage: African-American blues idiom re-voiced through 1960s-70s Southern soul arrangement practice — Memphis, Muscle Shoals and later Jackson's Malaco label — codified by Bobby Bland, Little Milton, Z.Z. Hill and Johnnie Taylor: 12/8 or slow 6/8 ballad grooves and mid-tempo shuffles at 60-100 BPM, horn-section punches, Hammond pads, clean-toned single-note guitar fills, and gospel-schooled melismatic lead vocals with rasp and preached asides over 12-bar or soul-ballad AABA frames.
items.description: Soul blues emerged as postwar blues singers adopted the horn charts, organ beds and rhythm-section discipline of Southern soul, and it consolidated commercially at Malaco in Jackson, Mississippi from the late 1970s onward, where it remains a living chitlin-circuit format. The sound is arranged rather than jammed: written brass figures, a pocket drummer, sparse clean guitar answers, and a vocal that carries almost all the expressive weight in gospel melisma and spoken interjection. It differs from Chicago electric blues by subordinating instrumental solos to song form, and from soul proper by keeping blues harmony, adult narrative lyrics and the twelve-bar as recurring reference.

items.name: St. Louis Blues (piano-led Mississippi River blues)
items.lineage: Piano-centred blues that formed in St. Louis and East St. Louis during the 1920s-30s Great Migration and was codified on Decca and Bluebird sides by Roosevelt Sykes, Peetie Wheatstraw, Walter Davis and Henry Townsend — a rolling barrelhouse left hand of walking octaves and light boogie eights at 80-120 BPM, guitar doubling in single-string counterpoint rather than slide, dry declamatory vocals with a taunting spoken edge, and 12-bar frames padded with piano turnarounds; a second postwar generation around Ike Turner and Albert King electrified the same repertoire.
items.description: St. Louis blues names the piano-and-guitar duo style that dominated the river city's tenement and tavern scene between the wars, when the town's recording agents funnelled dozens of players to Chicago and Grafton studios. Its markers are a barrelhouse left hand rather than a guitar bassline, terse unornamented singing, and a rhythmic feel that sits between Delta rubato and Chicago's fixed backbeat. It is drier and more urbane than Delta blues and less band-driven than postwar Chicago blues, and its piano-first texture distinguishes it from the guitar-led Memphis idiom downriver.

items.name: Swamp Blues
items.lineage: South Louisiana blues style cut almost entirely at J.D. Miller's Crowley studio for Nashville's Excello label between 1955 and 1965 and defined by Slim Harpo, Lightnin' Slim, Lazy Lester and Silas Hogan — languid mid-tempo shuffles and slow 12/8 at 70-100 BPM, a single tremolo-tinged guitar, amplified cupped harmonica, brushed or cardboard-box percussion, prominent tape slapback and echo, and a laconic half-spoken nasal vocal delivery.
items.description: Swamp blues is the Baton Rouge-area sound built in J.D. Miller's small Crowley studio, where limited tracks and heavy tape echo produced a spacious, unhurried variant of postwar electric blues. It runs slower and sparser than Chicago blues, keeps the harmonica soft and breathy instead of overblown, and lets Louisiana dance-hall rhythm colour the shuffle with a light Cajun-adjacent lilt.
