items.lineage: Swedish and British offshoot of power electronics codified around 1987-1995 by Brighter Death Now, Cold Meat Industry and Megaptera, defined by slow or beatless heaving low-frequency drones, tape-loop churn, metallic scrape and clang, and buried distorted or whispered vocals — texturally dense, funereal in pace, and constructed on four-track cassette rather than mixed for clarity.
items.description: Death industrial split from power electronics in the late 1980s, largely through the Swedish Cold Meat Industry roster, by trading shrieked confrontation for slow, oppressive low-end drone and decayed tape texture. Recordings are deliberately murky: layered subsonic hum, metallic percussion striking at long intervals, and vocals submerged under distortion rather than declaimed. Where power electronics is high-frequency and aggressive in real time, death industrial is subsonic, static, and atmospheric, closer to dark ambient with an industrial residue.

items.name: Electro-Industrial
items.lineage: Formed in Canada and Belgium circa 1987-1992 by Skinny Puppy, Front Line Assembly and the Antler-Subway roster, layering EBM's 120-135 BPM sequenced bass over multi-tracked sampler collage, dense atmospheric pads, snarled and heavily-effected vocals, and dialogue samples, tracked to DAT and Akai/Emulator sampler racks in mid-sized 1980s studios.
items.description: Electro-industrial developed at the end of the 1980s as EBM absorbed the sampler, chiefly through Vancouver's Skinny Puppy and Front Line Assembly and Belgium's Antler-Subway scene. The result is dark, thickly layered dance music: a hard sequenced bass and machine kick underneath stacked sample collage, cinematic pads and distorted, snarled vocals. It is denser and more atmospheric than the spare stomp of classic EBM, and more song-structured than the beatless textures of death industrial.

items.name: Futurepop
items.lineage: Named by VNV Nation's Ronan Harris and Apoptygma Berzerk's Stephan Groth around 1999-2000, this melodic descendant of EBM runs at 130-140 BPM with trance-derived supersaw arpeggios and gated pads, four-on-the-floor kicks with offbeat basslines, uplifting minor-key chord cycles, and clean, sung, lightly-processed baritone vocals — produced entirely in-the-box for club and festival playback.
items.description: Futurepop appeared at the turn of the 2000s when EBM acts began borrowing trance production wholesale — long arpeggiated builds, supersaw stacks, sidechained pads — while keeping industrial-scene lyrical themes. Its defining feature against the rest of that scene is the clean, melodic, intelligible lead vocal and the anthemic major-lift chorus. It is the melodic opposite of aggrotech, which occupies the same clubs and tempo range with distorted screamed vocals.

items.name: Neue Deutsche Härte
items.lineage: German fusion of industrial dance and metal codified by Rammstein's Herzeleid (1995) after Oomph!'s early-1990s template, built on mid-tempo 90-120 BPM four-on-the-floor kick patterns, downtuned palm-muted single-note guitar riffs doubled by synth stabs, orchestral or choir samples, and declaimed rolled-R German vocals in a low baritone, produced with heavy compression and grid-tight editing.
items.description: Neue Deutsche Härte took shape in Germany in the mid-1990s, joining the danceable four-on-the-floor pulse of EBM to metal guitar and sung-declaimed German lyrics. Its sonic markers are the rigid marching kick, a simple riff played in unison by guitar and synth, layered choir or string samples, and a theatrically enunciated low male voice. It is far more rhythmically regular and vocally intelligible than industrial metal from the American scene, and unlike coldwave or EBM the guitar is the primary harmonic instrument.

items.name: Japanoise
items.lineage: Japanese noise scene of Osaka, Tokyo and Kyoto from the late 1970s onward — Hijokaidan, Incapacitants, Merzbow, Hanatarash — built on maximal-density junk-electronics improvisation, overloaded mixer feedback and homemade pedal chains, mixed at total saturation with no dynamic reserve and released in obsessive editions on Alchemy, PSF and self-run cassette labels.
items.description: Japanoise names the distinctly Japanese branch of noise that grew out of the late-1970s Kansai underground and dominated the international noise economy through the 1990s. Its signature is total-spectrum saturation without pause or dynamic relief — cascading feedback from self-patched mixers and effects, played as continuous physical improvisation. Compared with Anglo-European power electronics it is largely instrumental and non-declamatory, driven by sheer density rather than by transgressive vocal texts.

items.name: Power Electronics
items.lineage: British subgenre named by William Bennett of Whitehouse circa 1981 around the Come Organisation label, consisting of shrieked or bellowed vocals over static high-frequency synthesizer feedback and cracked oscillator tones with no beat and no bass, recorded direct to cassette or two-track at clipping levels, with deliberately confrontational spoken texts and minimal, sleeve-only presentation.
items.description: Power electronics was defined in early-1980s Britain by Whitehouse and the Come Organisation as the most stripped and confrontational form of industrial sound: screamed vocals foregrounded over piercing synthesizer squeal and feedback, with the low end almost entirely absent. There is no rhythm section, no melody and minimal editing; the recording is a single sustained assault at fixed level. It is the vocal-led counterpart to instrumental noise, and the high-frequency inverse of death industrial's subsonic drone.

items.name: Power Noise
items.lineage: Rhythmic-noise style codified in Germany from 1994 onward by Ant-Zen, Hymen and acts such as Converter and Winterkälte, applying distorted 4/4 kick-drum sequencing and clipped percussive loops at 130-160 BPM to noise source material, with layered granular texture, no vocals, and hardware-plus-DAW production aimed at industrial dancefloors.
items.description: Power noise, also called rhythmic noise or distorted beat, emerged in mid-1990s Germany when noise producers imposed a strict techno pulse on saturated source material. Tracks are almost entirely instrumental: an overdriven kick loop, clipped metallic percussion layers, and evolving noise textures cycling over long durations with minimal harmonic content. It differs from industrial techno in the deliberate clipping and absence of melody, and from noise proper in its rigid quantized meter.

items.name: Praise and Worship
items.lineage: Contemporary congregational church music formed in the 1970s Jesus-Movement and Vineyard/Maranatha! circles of Southern California and codified globally from the 1990s by Hillsong (Sydney), Integrity/Hosanna!, and later Bethel and Elevation — mid-tempo 4/4 or 6/8 at 70-90 BPM, diatonic I-V-vi-IV loops in guitar-friendly keys, layered acoustic and delay-drenched electric guitar with pad synth beds, worship-leader voice doubled by a congregation-scale choir, and open-ended repeated 'bridge' vamps designed for extended live singing.
items.description: Praise and Worship is the contemporary congregational repertoire that grew out of 1970s California Jesus-Movement coffeehouse choruses and was industrialized from the 1990s by Hillsong, Integrity Music, and Bethel. Its sound is a soft-rock band — strummed acoustic, ambient delay-and-reverb electric guitar, sustained synth pads, restrained kit — under a lead vocal that a large live congregation answers, with arrangements built to swell from whispered verse to a repeated anthemic bridge. Unlike Black gospel it avoids melisma-heavy soloing and complex reharmonization in favour of singable diatonic loops; unlike traditional hymnody it is band-led, amplified, and written for anonymous congregational participation rather than four-part hymnal reading.

items.name: March (concert and military band)
items.lineage: The European and American wind-band march, standardized in 19th-century military service bands and codified for the concert stage by John Philip Sousa's US Marine Band from 1880 and by Kenneth Alford in Britain — duple time at 112-120 BPM, an unvarying alternating-bass snare-and-bass-drum tread, multi-strain AABBCC form with a modulating trio and a piccolo or cornet obbligato descant, scored for cornets, clarinets, low brass, and sousaphone with no strings.
items.description: The concert and military march is the core repertoire of the wind band, fixed in its modern form by Sousa's Marine Band arrangements of the 1880s-1900s and by British bandmasters such as Kenneth Alford. It is fully notated, strictly duple, and built on a rigid multi-strain plan — introduction, two repeated strains, then a softer trio in the subdominant that returns fortissimo with piccolo descant and a break-strain — over a metronomic bass-drum-and-snare tread. It differs from the brass-band contest repertoire of northern England in its inclusion of clarinets and saxophones, and from processional street music such as second line or banda in its complete absence of improvisation and its fixed European harmonic vocabulary.
exemplars: John Philip Sousa - 'The Stars and Stripes Forever'

items.name: Blue Note (hard bop house style)
items.lineage: The house style of Alfred Lion and Francis Wolff's Blue Note Records, formed in New York 1955-1967 and given its sonic signature by engineer Rudy Van Gelder at Hackensack and Englewood Cliffs — medium-up 4/4 swing at 160-240 BPM with 12/8 gospel shuffles, trumpet-and-tenor front lines over piano, walking bass and ride-cymbal-led kit, blues-and-gospel-inflected original heads in place of standards, and rehearsal-paid sessions producing tight arranged ensembles.
items.description: Blue Note names both a label and the hard-bop studio aesthetic it standardized between 1955 and 1967, with Alfred Lion paying for rehearsals and Rudy Van Gelder supplying a close-miked, tube-warm, piano-forward sound that other labels imitated for decades. Musically it is arranged hard bop: catchy blues- and gospel-derived original heads, sharply voiced two- or three-horn front lines, hard-swinging ride cymbal, and soloists working advanced changes with a deliberately vocal, blues-rooted attack. It differs from West Coast cool in its heat and its Black church vocabulary, and from Prestige's contemporaneous catalogue in being composed and rehearsed rather than assembled from blowing sessions on standards.
exemplars: Art Blakey and the Jazz Messengers - 'Moanin''

items.name: British Dance Band
items.lineage: The hotel and broadcast dance orchestra of interwar Britain, centred on London's Savoy, Ciro's and Mayfair hotels and BBC late-night relays 1925-1940, led by Jack Hylton, Ray Noble, Ambrose and Lew Stone — smooth foxtrot and quickstep tempos around 100-200 BPM, arranged saxophone-and-brass sections with muted-trumpet obbligati, banjo or rhythm guitar and slap bass, and a light-vibrato megaphone-derived 'refrain vocalist' entering for a single chorus.
items.description: The British dance band was the interwar equivalent of the American sweet orchestra, sustained by London hotel residencies, BBC broadcasts, and prolific 78rpm sessions between roughly 1925 and 1940. Its sound is fully arranged and lightly swung: reed choir in close harmony, muted brass answering figures, banjo-then-guitar chugging the rhythm, brushed or side-stick drums kept low for the disc cutter, and a discreet vocal refrain sung once in the middle of the record. It is more restrained than contemporaneous Harlem big bands — less blue, less soloistic, tempo strictly suited to ballroom steps — and unlike later British swing it is oriented toward dancers and radio listeners rather than jazz audiences.
exemplars: Ray Noble and the New Mayfair Orchestra

items.name: Cape Jazz
items.lineage: South African jazz idiom formed in District Six and the Cape Flats from the late 1950s, codified by Abdullah Ibrahim, the Blue Notes, Robbie Jansen and Basil Coetzee — mid-tempo 4/4 with a lilting ghoema carnival rhythm and marabi-derived cyclic I-IV-V vamps, hymn-like piano voicings from Cape Malay and mission-church singing, penny-whistle and alto-sax lead lines, and an anthemic, deliberately communal ensemble sound.
items.description: Cape jazz emerged in Cape Town's District Six from the late 1950s, fusing American bebop with marabi's three-chord cycle, the ghoema drum rhythm of the Cape Malay carnival, and mission-church hymnody; Abdullah Ibrahim's 'Mannenberg' (1974) is its founding statement. It is built on short, repeating diatonic vamps rather than changing standards, with hymnlike block-chord piano, swaying two-beat ghoema propulsion, and long modal saxophone solos over a groove that never resolves away. It is more cyclic and less harmonically restless than American hard bop, and distinct from mbaqanga and township jive in tempo, in its jazz solo language, and in its Cape rather than Witwatersrand rhythmic roots.

items.name: Chamber Jazz
items.lineage: Small-group jazz played with classical restraint, formed in the early 1950s with John Lewis's Modern Jazz Quartet and Jimmy Giuffre's drummerless trios and extended from 1969 by Manfred Eicher's ECM productions in Oslo — soft dynamics, brushes or no drums at all, contrapuntal written passages framing improvisation, vibraphone, clarinet, piano and arco bass timbres, and rubato or slow-modal tempos captured in long natural reverb.
items.description: Chamber jazz is small-ensemble jazz that borrows the textures, dynamics, and written counterpoint of the classical chamber tradition, initiated by the Modern Jazz Quartet and Jimmy Giuffre in the 1950s and given a lasting recorded identity by ECM from 1969. Its signature is quietness and space: brushed or absent drums, arco and pizzicato bass treated as an equal melodic voice, transparent contrapuntal heads, and engineering by Jan Erik Kongshaug that places instruments in a large, cool, decaying hall. It is distinguished from cool jazz by its formal written architecture rather than merely relaxed phrasing, and from free jazz by strict dynamic control and pre-composed frames even when harmony is left open.

items.name: Continental Jazz
items.lineage: Continental European jazz of 1930-1960, centred on the Hot Club de France in Paris with Django Reinhardt and Stephane Grappelli and extending to Scandinavian and Italian radio orchestras — swing at 140-260 BPM carried by la pompe rhythm guitar rather than drums, Selmer-guitar and violin leads, minor-key Romani and musette melodic inflection, and accordion-and-clarinet colours absent from American swing.
items.description: Continental jazz is the European reworking of American swing between the wars and just after, its canonical form being the Quintette du Hot Club de France, where two rhythm guitars and a bass replaced the drum kit with the chugging 'la pompe' pulse and Django Reinhardt's Selmer guitar and Grappelli's violin carried the front line. Its harmonic language absorbs Parisian musette, Romani minor modes, and Italian song alongside American standards, and its recordings, cut direct to 78 in small European studios, are drier and more soloist-forward than their American counterparts. It differs from American swing by the absent drums and string-led front line, and from later gypsy-jazz revivalism by being a working commercial dance idiom rather than a repertoire style.
exemplars: Quintette du Hot Club de France

items.name: Dark Jazz
items.lineage: Slow noir-jazz idiom formed in Germany and the Netherlands from the mid-1990s, codified by Bohren & der Club of Gore's 'Sunset Mission' (2000) and The Kilimanjaro Darkjazz Ensemble — funereal 40-70 BPM tempos, sustained Rhodes and vibraphone chords, breathy near-static tenor saxophone lines, bowed bass and brushed kit under heavy reverb, film-noir minor modality, and long through-composed pieces with no soloing in the bebop sense.
items.description: Dark jazz, or doom jazz, appeared in the late 1990s when the German band Bohren & der Club of Gore slowed hardcore's weight into a jazz instrumentation, and was extended in the Netherlands by The Kilimanjaro Darkjazz Ensemble and its Mount Fuji offshoot. It is extremely slow and quiet, with sustained Rhodes and vibraphone chords, a saxophone playing long single tones rather than lines, bowed bass drones, sparse brushed cymbals, and post-production reverb and tape haze that treat the ensemble as one blurred texture. Unlike cool jazz it has almost no improvisation and no swing pulse; unlike ambient it retains a real jazz rhythm section and a noir harmonic vocabulary drawn from Angelo Badalamenti and 1950s crime scores.
exemplars: Bohren & der Club of Gore - 'Sunset Mission'

items.name: Dixieland
items.lineage: New Orleans-derived collective-improvisation jazz recorded from 1917 by the Original Dixieland Jass Band and revived nationally from the late 1930s by Lu Watters, Turk Murphy and Eddie Condon — brisk 2/4 and 4/4 at 180-240 BPM, a cornet lead ornamented simultaneously by clarinet obbligato above and trombone tailgate below, banjo and tuba or string bass rhythm, and multi-strain march-and-rag forms ending in stop-time breaks.
items.description: Dixieland is the name attached to New Orleans-style polyphonic jazz as it spread through white bands from 1917 and returned in the trad-jazz revival of the 1940s-1950s. Its defining texture is simultaneous collective improvisation: cornet states the melody, clarinet weaves a decorated countermelody above it, trombone slides supporting glissandi beneath, all over banjo and brass or string bass keeping a two-beat pulse, with a final chorus of breaks and a rideout. It is distinguished from swing by the absence of written section arranging and the survival of the front-line polyphony, and from the Black New Orleans lineage of King Oliver and Bunk Johnson largely by repertoire, tempo, and revivalist performance context.
exemplars: Lu Watters' Yerba Buena Jazz Band

items.name: Free Funk
items.lineage: New York idiom of 1975-1990 joining free-jazz pitch freedom to electric funk rhythm, codified by Ornette Coleman's Prime Time and his harmolodic theory and extended by Ronald Shannon Jackson's Decoding Society and James Blood Ulmer — dense 4/4 backbeats at 100-140 BPM played by doubled electric guitars and basses, atonal or key-ambiguous unison heads, simultaneous multi-line soloing, and no fixed harmonic centre beneath the groove.
items.description: Free funk is the harmolodic electric music Ornette Coleman built with Prime Time from 1975 onward, in which two guitars, two basses and two drummers lay a hard funk backbeat while every voice improvises melodically without a governing key. Its allied bands — Ronald Shannon Jackson's Decoding Society and James Blood Ulmer's trios — kept the same equation of danceable groove plus unresolved collective polyphony, recorded loud and close on early-1980s New York analogue desks. It differs from jazz-fusion by discarding modal or chord-scale improvisation entirely, and from acoustic free jazz by insisting on a fixed backbeat and amplified rock instrumentation.
exemplars: Ornette Coleman and Prime Time - 'Dancing in Your Head'
Ronald Shannon Jackson and the Decoding Society
James Blood Ulmer - 'Are You Glad to Be in America?'

items.name: Indo Jazz
items.lineage: Fusion of Hindustani and Carnatic classical practice with modern jazz, formalized in London 1965-1968 by composer John Mayer and Jamaican altoist Joe Harriott on the Indo-Jazz Suite recordings and extended by John McLaughlin's Shakti from 1975 — raga-derived modal frames and tala cycles of 7, 10 and 16 beats, sitar, tabla and Carnatic violin scored against jazz reeds and rhythm section, alap-style rubato openings, and alternating written Indian-idiom passages with jazz solo choruses.
items.description: Indo jazz names the deliberate scoring of Indian classical materials for jazz ensembles, first realized systematically by John Mayer and Joe Harriott's double quintet in London from 1965, where a jazz rhythm section and a raga ensemble of sitar, tabla, flute and violin played written and improvised music side by side. The idiom keeps genuine raga melodic grammar and long tala cycles rather than merely borrowing scales, and alternates unmetered alap textures with swung or straight solo choruses. It differs from the psychedelic 'raga rock' of the same years by being composed by trained Indian classical musicians, and from later world-fusion by its jazz-first improvisational form and its 1960s British studio sound.

items.name: Neo-Bop
items.lineage: 1980s American acoustic-jazz revival centered on New York's Village Vanguard and Blue Note/Columbia rosters, codified by Wynton and Branford Marsalis, Kenny Garrett and the Jazz Messengers alumni network, restoring the bebop/hard-bop language of fast 4/4 swung eighths at 200-300 BPM, ii-V-heavy chord cycles, unison horn heads over walking bass and ride-cymbal timekeeping, and virtuosic linear improvisation, but recorded with clean 1980s digital-era fidelity rather than 1950s tape grit.
items.description: Neo-bop is the 1980s reassertion of acoustic bebop vocabulary against fusion and free jazz, driven by young conservatory-trained players signed to major labels. It keeps the small-combo format, head-solos-head form and rapid harmonic motion of 1950s bop, but with wider dynamic range, tighter ensemble execution and clean digital recording. Where hard bop was blues-saturated and loose, neo-bop is deliberately polished and canon-conscious.

items.name: Orchestral Jazz
items.lineage: Formed in 1920s-30s New York and Chicago as written large-ensemble jazz, codified by Duke Ellington, Fletcher Henderson, Ferde Grofé's charts for Paul Whiteman and later extended by Gil Evans and Stan Kenton, using sectional reed/brass/rhythm scoring, through-composed extended forms and concert-hall dynamics over a 4/4 swing pulse, with individual soloists framed by notated orchestration rather than head-and-changes routine.
items.description: Orchestral jazz treats the jazz ensemble as a composer's instrument, with extended multi-section works, unusual doublings and voicings drawn from concert-hall practice. Timbral variety is its hallmark: muted brass choirs, low reeds, French horns and tuba coloring writing far beyond dance-band function. Unlike big-band swing, it prioritizes notated form and orchestration over riff-driven dance repetition, and unlike straight-ahead jazz it subordinates solo blowing to the score.

items.name: Ska Jazz
items.lineage: Kingston-rooted, New-York-codified hybrid: the Skatalites' late-1960s bebop-schooled horn section reinterpreted through the 1990s Ska Jazz Messengers and New York Ska-Jazz Ensemble, laying jazz standards and modal originals over the offbeat 'skank' guitar/piano upstroke at 130-160 BPM, walking or bubbling electric bass, one-drop-adjacent kit and extended trombone and tenor sax solos in a bop idiom.
items.description: Ska jazz is instrumental ska played by musicians fluent in bebop harmony, descending directly from the Skatalites' habit of recasting jazz repertoire over Jamaican rhythm. The rhythm section holds a rigid offbeat skank while horns take long modal or changes-based solos, giving it far more improvisational room than vocal ska or two-tone. It is distinguished from straight-ahead jazz by its unswung, upstroke-locked groove and from rocksteady by its horn-led, solo-driven form.

items.name: Straight-Ahead Jazz
items.lineage: Post-1960 mainstream American acoustic jazz practice consolidated in New York clubs and on Blue Note, Riverside and Prestige, codified by Cannonball Adderley, Hank Mobley, Dexter Gordon and later Ron Carter's and Cedar Walton's rhythm sections, defined by swung 4/4 ride-cymbal timekeeping, walking bass, comping piano, standards and blues/rhythm-changes forms, and successive full-chorus solos at medium to bright tempos.
items.description: Straight-ahead is the default idiom of mainstream jazz after hard bop: acoustic quartet or quintet, swing feel, standard song forms, and improvisation running the changes. It is defined as much by what it excludes — electric fusion textures, free abandonment of meter, backbeat rock rhythm — as by any single stylistic marker. Against neo-bop it carries no revivalist agenda, being simply the continuous working-musician lingua franca of clubs and jam sessions.

items.name: Baithak Gana
items.lineage: Indo-Caribbean 'sitting song' tradition carried by Bhojpuri-speaking indentured laborers to Suriname, Guyana and Trinidad from the 1870s and codified as a recorded genre in 1960s-80s Paramaribo and Nickerie by singers such as Ramdew Chaitoe and Droopatie Ramgoolam, built on harmonium drone-and-melody, hard-driving dholak in fast 8-beat kaharwa/dadra cycles, ringing dhantal steel rod on every beat, and high nasal declamatory male vocals in Sarnami Hindustani.
items.description: Baithak gana descends from north Indian folk and light-classical singing preserved in the Dutch and British Caribbean, performed seated in a circle rather than on a stage. The sound is austere and relentless: harmonium drone, a single voice at the top of its range, dholak filling every subdivision and dhantal marking a bright metallic pulse. It differs from Indian chutney, its dancefloor descendant, by keeping slower, more devotional and text-centered forms without brass, drum machines or soca beats.
exemplars: Ramdew Chaitoe's 'King of Suriname Baithak Gana'

items.name: Lambada
items.lineage: Formed in Belém do Pará and Porto Seguro, Brazil, in the mid-1980s from carimbó, Caribbean merengue and Dominican-influenced guitar, then codified globally by Kaoma's 1989 'Chorando Se Foi' and the Bahian beach-resort dance circuit — fast 2/4 at roughly 120-140 BPM with a lilting merengue-derived bass, saw-toned accordion or synth lead, clean chorused electric guitar riffs, congas and kit, and bright unison Portuguese vocal refrains.
items.description: Lambada is an Amazonian-Bahian dance-pop style that fused local carimbó with imported merengue and Antillean guitar phrasing before becoming a worldwide 1989 craze. Its signature is a quick, buoyant duple pulse with a bouncing bass line, chorused guitar figures and prominent accordion or keyboard lead over polished late-80s digital production. Compared with forró it is faster and more Caribbean in bass articulation, and unlike zouk it is guitar- rather than drum-machine-centered.

items.name: Samba Rock
items.lineage: Emerged in São Paulo's Black dance clubs and Rio studios in the mid-1960s, codified by Jorge Ben, Trio Mocotó and Bebeto, grafting American soul and rock backbeat guitar onto samba's 2/4 telecoteco: strummed nylon or semi-hollow guitar playing percussive rhythm-chords, electric bass on the samba surdo accent, pandeiro and cuíca alongside a drum kit, tamborim breaks, and shouted call-and-response Portuguese vocals at 100-120 BPM.
items.description: Samba rock is the São Paulo Black-club dance music that put soul and rock instrumentation on a samba rhythmic base in the late 1960s and 1970s. Its identity sits in the guitar hand: a percussive, chord-chopping strum that functions as another drum, over electric bass and a hybrid kit-and-hand-percussion section. Where bossa nova is quiet and harmonically intricate, samba rock is loud, riff-driven and built for partner dancing, and unlike samba-enredo it is small-band rather than bateria-scale.

items.name: Zouk-Lambada
items.lineage: Late-1990s Brazilian hybrid formed in Porto Seguro and Rio dance schools when lambada dancers adopted the slower French Antillean zouk-love groove of Kassav' and Ophélia, codified through Brazilian 'lambazouk' bands and Cape Verdean-Antillean crossovers — programmed 4/4 at 90-110 BPM with a syncopated gwo-ka-derived kick pattern, glossy DX-style electric piano and synth pads, chorused guitar arpeggios, and soft breathy Creole or Portuguese vocals.
items.description: Zouk-lambada, or lambazouk, is what happened when Brazilian lambada dancers slowed to Antillean zouk-love tempos and the music followed. Production is fully sequenced and glossy: sampled or drum-machine kit, sustained synth pads, chorused clean guitar and intimate close-miked vocals with heavy reverb. It is markedly slower and softer than lambada proper and less percussion-dense than Caribbean zouk béton, built around sensual partner dancing rather than carnival propulsion.

items.name: Criolla
items.lineage: Cuban art-song genre created in Havana in 1909 by Luis Casas Romero with 'Mujer Bayamesa' and developed by Jorge Anckermann and Eliseo Grenet through the 1920s-40s teatro vernáculo, a slow lyrical 6/8 derived from the clave cubana and criolla-bolero: nylon guitar and tres accompaniment with a gently rocking hemiola, subtle claves and maracas, and refined duo or solo voices singing pastoral, patriotic and nostalgic texts.
items.description: The criolla is a composed Cuban song genre of the early twentieth century, slower and more literary than the guajira or clave from which it derives, and closely tied to Havana's vernacular theater. Its texture is deliberately sparse: guitar or tres arpeggios in a swaying 6/8, light hand percussion, and a lyrical vocal line with sentimental portamento. Unlike the bolero it stays in compound meter and avoids the cinquillo, and unlike son it is not dance music at all.

items.name: Nuevo Flamenco
items.lineage: Madrid and Andalusian scene of the late 1970s-1980s, codified by Paco de Lucía's sextet, Camarón's 'La Leyenda del Tiempo' (1979), Ketama, Pata Negra and Lole y Manuel, keeping flamenco's 12-beat compás and Phrygian cadence while adding Peruvian cajón, electric bass, Latin percussion, jazz and Brazilian harmony, saxophone or flute lines, and studio-produced song forms alongside traditional palmas and cante jondo delivery.
items.description: Nuevo flamenco is the fusion current that opened traditional flamenco to jazz harmony, Latin American percussion and pop production from the late 1970s onward. The cajón — imported by Paco de Lucía from Peru in 1977 — became near-universal, and bass, keyboards and horns filled space that was formerly guitar and palmas alone. It retains the compás cycles and Andalusian cadence that define flamenco, but replaces the tablao's raw acoustic immediacy with arranged, multitracked studio texture.

items.name: Raíces
items.lineage: Pan-Latin-American folkloric roots revival crystallizing in the Andes and Southern Cone from the late 1960s through groups such as Inti-Illimani, Quilapayún, Los Jaivas and Bolivia's Los Kjarkas, who took village huayno, carnavalito and bailecito repertoire onto the concert stage — charango and ronroco strumming in fast 2/4 or lilting 6/8, quena and siku panpipe pairs trading interlocking halves of the melody, bombo leguero on a heavy dotted pulse, and unforced chest-voice unison or parallel-third choruses in Spanish and Quechua.
items.description: Raíces is the roots-recovery current in Latin American popular music, formed when urban ensembles of the late 1960s and 1970s went to the countryside for repertoire and instruments and brought altiplano panpipes, charangos and bombos into arranged concert and record form. The sound is acoustic and mid-forward: breathy quena, tightly doubled siku halves, dense strummed charango tremolo, and unison choral singing with little vibrato. It differs from nueva canción, with which it overlaps politically, by centering instrumental folkloric idiom over the solo singer-songwriter, and from unmediated village practice by its fixed arrangements and studio balance.

items.name: Pagan Metal
items.lineage: European metal branch formed in the mid-1990s across Finland, the Baltic and Central Europe — Moonsorrow, Skyforger, Kroda and early Ensiferum — that carried black and death metal's tremolo riffing and blast-capable drumming into long, mid-tempo, folk-modal arrangements built on pre-Christian myth, adding kantele, jouhikko, bagpipe and frame-drum lines, hymn-like clean male chorus against a harsh rasped lead, and often eight- to twelve-minute through-built structures rather than verse-chorus form.
items.description: Pagan metal took shape in the mid-1990s as bands in Finland, Latvia and Ukraine turned black metal's tremolo textures toward pre-Christian folklore and native modal melody. Tracks are long and terraced: distorted guitar layers doubled by kantele, bowed lyre or pipes, mid-tempo hypnotic riff cycles, massed clean unison choruses answering a rasped lead, and keyboard pads filling the low mids. It is slower, more solemn and more compositionally sprawling than folk metal's tavern strain, and unlike black metal proper it prioritizes melodic and choral clarity over lo-fi abrasion.

items.name: Viking Metal
items.lineage: Swedish-Norwegian offshoot of black metal defined by Bathory's Hammerheart and Twilight of the Gods (1990-91) and extended by Enslaved, Einherjer and Amon Amarth — slow-to-mid tempo tremolo and power-chord riffs in minor modes, martial toms and mid-paced double-kick rather than constant blasting, wide reverberant multitracked male chant choruses over Norse-mythological lyrics, keyboard horn and choir pads, and epic six-to-ten minute forms with long instrumental build sections.
items.description: Viking metal was effectively invented on two Bathory albums at the turn of the 1990s, when Quorthon slowed black metal down, drenched it in reverb and stacked his own voice into a mead-hall chorus. The style keeps distorted tremolo and power-chord riffing but moves at marching tempo with tom-heavy drumming, synthesized choir and brass beds, and long instrumental swells. Where pagan metal reaches for actual folk instruments and regional modality, viking metal builds its atmosphere almost entirely from guitars, keyboards and layered chant, and it is far more anthemic and less blast-driven than the Norwegian black metal it grew out of.

items.name: Neoclassical Metal
items.lineage: Shred-guitar idiom codified by Yngwie Malmsteen's Rising Force (1984) after Ritchie Blackmore and Uli Jon Roth, and carried on by Tony MacAlpine, Jason Becker and Symphony X — harmonic-minor and Phrygian-dominant scalar runs, diminished-seventh sequences and pedal-point arpeggio sweeps modeled on Paganini and Bach, fast 4/4 or 6/8 double-kick backing, prominent Hammond or string-synth continuo, and a high operatic clean tenor over baroque chord cycles.
items.description: Neoclassical metal is the instrumental-virtuoso branch of 1980s metal, in which European art-music figuration — harmonic minor, diminished sequences, sweep-picked arpeggios, pedal-point cadenzas — is transferred wholesale to distorted electric guitar. Arrangements pair the guitar with organ or string synth in continuo-like counterpoint and use double-kick drumming as a motoric baroque pulse. Compared with power metal it is more soloist-centered and more strictly tonal-sequential, and compared with progressive metal it keeps conventional meters while spending its complexity on melodic line rather than form.

items.name: Kawaii Metal
items.lineage: Japanese idol-metal hybrid created in Tokyo in 2010 by producer Kobametal for BABYMETAL and extended by Ladybaby and Band-Maid — Amuse-trained teenage idol vocalists singing bright, major-key J-pop toplines in unison and thirds over a session band playing thrash and melodic-death riffing at 160-200 BPM with double-kick and blast passages, plus symphonic-metal keyboard beds, dubstep and chiptune interpolations, and abrupt genre-splice arrangements built for choreography.
items.description: Kawaii metal was assembled in Tokyo from 2010 onward by grafting the idol-pop vocal front — young female singers, tuned bright and doubled, delivering hook-dense major-mode melodies — onto genuinely technical metal backing tracks played by session musicians. Productions are maximalist and heavily edited: quantized double-kick, layered seven-string rhythm guitar, orchestral and chiptune synth interjections, and sudden splices into ska, dubstep or power ballad within one song. It differs from symphonic metal by keeping the untrained, deliberately cute idol timbre rather than an operatic voice, and from J-pop by the actual metal rhythm-section vocabulary.

items.name: Pirate Metal
items.lineage: Folk-metal novelty branch established by Running Wild's Under Jolly Roger (1987) and codified as a distinct style by Alestorm from 2008 — mid-to-fast 4/4 and 6/8 power-metal riffing with galloping double-kick, accordion, tin whistle and fiddle carrying diatonic major-key sea-shanty and jig melodies doubled by keyboard, singalong gang choruses on the refrain, and a hoarse shouted lead over nautical narrative lyrics.
items.description: Pirate metal is the maritime-themed strand of folk metal, prefigured by Running Wild in the late 1980s and given its modern shape by Alestorm's albums from 2008 on. Musically it is power metal with the folk layer doing the melodic work: accordion, whistle and fiddle lines, usually reinforced or replaced by keyboard patches, sit on top of galloping guitars, and every chorus is written for a crowd to shout. Against pagan metal's solemn, long-form modal music it is major-key, fast, humorous and tightly verse-chorus, and against straight power metal it substitutes shanty and jig tunes for neoclassical figuration.

items.name: Math Metal
items.lineage: Technical extreme-metal idiom formed in the 1990s United States through Meshuggah, Dillinger Escape Plan and Candiria out of death metal and metalcore — riffs written as long polymetric groupings of sevens, elevens and seventeens cycling against a steady 4/4 backbeat, extended-range seven- and eight-string guitars in drop tunings doubled note-for-note by bass, abrupt stop-start rests and metric modulations, jazz-derived chromatic passing harmony, and a barked or screamed vocal placed rhythmically rather than melodically.
items.description: Math metal is the rhythm-first branch of technical metal, worked out in the 1990s by bands who wrote riffs as odd-length cells looping across an unmoving common-time pulse until they realign. The recorded sound is dry, tightly gridded and low-tuned: extended-range guitars muted and doubled by bass in exact unison, triggered kick drums articulating every subdivision, and silence used as a structural device. It is distinguished from progressive metal by its refusal of long melodic development and from mathcore, its punk sibling, by slower tempos and mechanical precision rather than chaotic velocity.

items.name: Environmental (Kankyō Ongaku)
items.lineage: Japanese kankyō ongaku, formulated in Tokyo between 1979 and the early 1990s by Satoshi Ashikawa, Hiroshi Yoshimura, Midori Takada and Yoshio Ojima for galleries, showrooms and architectural commissions after Erik Satie and Brian Eno — slow, unmetered or very loosely pulsed textures at low dynamic level, FM and analog synth pads with long release, sparse diatonic or pentatonic piano and marimba figures, prepared field and water sounds, and no vocal or rhythmic focal point.
items.description: Environmental music is the Japanese ambient practice of the 1980s, made explicitly to occupy architectural and commercial spaces rather than to be listened to frontally. Its materials are digital FM and analog synthesizer tones with slow attack and long decay, isolated piano or tuned-percussion notes, occasional water and bird recordings, and very wide silences, mixed quietly and cleanly with minimal low end. It is closer to Satie's furniture music than to Western drone ambient in its use of clear diatonic pitch and discrete events, and distinct from new age in its refusal of climax, melody-forward writing and overt spirituality.

items.name: Austropop
items.lineage: Austrian dialect-language pop-rock codified in Vienna from about 1971 onward through Wolfgang Ambros's 'Da Hofa', Georg Danzer, Rainhard Fendrich, the STS trio and later Falco — mid-tempo 4/4 guitar-and-piano song forms at 90-130 BPM with Anglo-American rock and singer-songwriter chord vocabulary, Viennese-dialect lyrics carrying satire, Schmäh and social commentary, conversational half-sung baritone delivery, and Heurigen-derived accordion or Schrammel colour dropped into an otherwise standard band arrangement.
items.description: Austropop formed in Vienna in the early 1970s when Austrian musicians began setting rock and singer-songwriter forms to Viennese dialect rather than English, and remained the dominant domestic commercial idiom through the 1990s. Its sonic signature is a conventional analogue rock-band chain — clean-to-crunch electric guitar, piano, restrained kit — carrying an unusually forward, dry, conversational baritone vocal whose dialect diction and ironic phrasing are the point of the music; accordion or Schrammel string colour appears as local seasoning rather than structural folk material. Distinguished from German Neue Deutsche Welle by its rock-band rather than synth-and-new-wave foundation and by its melancholic satirical register, and from Alpine Volksmusik by its Anglo-American harmonic and rhythmic frame.

items.name: Balkan Pop
items.lineage: Southeast European commercial popular song that consolidated in Belgrade, Zagreb, Sofia and Skopje from the 1960s Jugoton/PGP-RTB era and mutated after 1990 into the pop-folk mainstream — 4/4 dance-pop tempos of 100-140 BPM with occasional 7/8 and 9/8 quotation, melodic lines built on augmented-second Balkan and Ottoman-derived modes, heavily ornamented melismatic female lead vocals, and arrangements pairing synthesizers and drum machines with amplified accordion, clarinet and tapan.
items.description: Balkan pop is the commercial popular-song mainstream of the former Yugoslavia and Bulgaria, built first inside the state labels of the 1960s-80s and then, after the socialist collapse, in the private cassette-and-television economy that produced turbo-folk and chalga. Its defining sound is a Western pop rhythm section — programmed or played four-on-the-floor, synth pads, electric bass — supporting a folk-derived melodic surface: augmented-second modes, dense vocal melisma and slides, and lead lines doubled by amplified accordion or clarinet playing in the fast ornamented style of village wedding bands. It differs from Balkan brass fanfara in being song-led and studio-produced rather than processional and acoustic, and from Western Europop in the modal and ornamental vocabulary of its melodies.

items.name: Laïkó (modern Greek popular song)
items.lineage: The post-1975 mainstream continuation of Greek laïkó, centred on the Athens pista nightclub circuit and the Minos-EMI and Sony Greece catalogues — codified through Yannis Parios, Antonis Remos, Notis Sfakianakis, Despina Vandi and the songwriters Fivos and Nikos Karvelas, with amplified four-course electric bouzouki riffs over 4/4 tsifteteli and zeibekiko frames at 80-125 BPM, dromos-based melodic writing, string-synth and drum-machine backing, and declamatory ornamented lead vocals sustained across ten-minute live medleys.
items.description: Modern laïkó is the Greek popular mainstream as it developed after the fall of the junta, when the classic 1950s-60s laïkó of Kazantzidis and Chiotis was absorbed into a fully electrified nightclub industry. The sound centres on the amplified tetrachordo bouzouki playing tremolo lead lines and riff hooks over programmed or played tsifteteli and zeibekiko rhythms, with synthesizer strings, close-miked dry lead vocals and heavy melodic ornamentation drawn from the dromoi. It is distinguished from classic laïkó by its digital-era production, faster dance orientation and pop songwriting economy, and from éntekhno by its lack of literary art-song ambition and its nightclub rather than concert-hall context.

items.name: Nederpop
items.lineage: Dutch pop-rock that emerged in The Hague and Amsterdam from the mid-1960s beat scene — Shocking Blue, Golden Earring, Focus, later Doe Maar and De Dijk — combining British-beat and blues-rock guitar with unusually strong hook-writing, 4/4 tempos of 110-140 BPM, close two- and three-part harmony, Hammond and Farfisa organ, and a shift after 1980 to Dutch-language lyrics over ska- and reggae-inflected backbeats.
items.description: Nederpop names the Dutch popular-music mainstream from the mid-1960s onward, first as an English-singing export scene (Shocking Blue's 'Venus', Golden Earring's 'Radar Love', Focus's instrumental prog) and after 1980 as a Dutch-language idiom led by Doe Maar and De Dijk. Its production is compact British-beat-derived guitar-bass-drums with prominent combo organ, generous tape compression and a distinctly hook-first arrangement discipline; the later wave adds skanking offbeat guitar and dub-inflected bass under conversational Dutch vocals. It differs from British beat by its slightly harder, drier rhythm-section sound and export-oriented songwriting, and from Austropop and Neue Deutsche Welle by its blues-rock rather than cabaret or synth lineage.

items.name: Latin Ballad (balada romántica)
items.lineage: Pan-Hispanic romantic ballad codified in Mexico City, Madrid and Rio between roughly 1965 and 1975 through Roberto Carlos, Camilo Sesto, José José, Juan Gabriel and the arranger-producers of RCA Mexico and Ariola — slow 4/4 and 12/8 forms at 60-80 BPM, bolero-derived harmonic motion with descending bass lines and dramatic key-change final choruses, nylon-string guitar and piano foundation, lush string and horn charts, and a declamatory, vibrato-heavy lead vocal that builds from near-whisper to full belt.
items.description: The balada romántica consolidated in the late 1960s as the bolero's commercial successor, built simultaneously in Mexico, Spain and Brazil and circulated across the whole Spanish-speaking market by RCA, Ariola and CBS. Its defining sound is a slow, rubato-tolerant ballad carried by nylon-string guitar and piano, orchestral strings that swell against the vocal rather than under it, and a lead voice recorded very close through a tube chain so that breath and vibrato are audible at the quiet openings before the arrangement lifts into an amplified final chorus. It differs from the bolero proper in abandoning the clave-linked rhythm section for a straight pop-ballad backbeat, and from nueva canción in being unpolitical, professionally arranged and industry-produced.

items.name: Louisiana Swamp Pop
items.lineage: South Louisiana and southeast Texas hybrid created by young Cajun and Creole musicians circa 1955-1965 — recorded by Jay Miller in Crowley and Floyd Soileau in Ville Platte — pairing New Orleans triplet R&B piano and honking tenor saxophone with Cajun-French melodic phrasing, slow 12/8 ballad shuffles at 60-75 BPM alongside up-tempo two-beat dance numbers, plaintive high-tenor lead vocals with audible French-accented diction, and a thick, slapback-drenched small-studio mix.
items.description: Swamp pop was made between roughly 1955 and 1965 by French-speaking Cajun and Black Creole teenagers in the Acadiana parishes who took up New Orleans rhythm and blues instead of their parents' accordion dance music. The core sound is the rolling triplet piano and honking tenor sax of the Crescent City tradition slowed into a 12/8 ballad, with a strained, emotionally exposed high tenor lead, tape slapback on everything, and a boxy mono small-studio ambience from Miller's and Soileau's rooms. It is distinguished from Cajun music by having no fiddle-and-accordion dance-hall foundation and singing largely in English, and from mainstream New Orleans R&B by its Cajun melodic contour, French-accented phrasing and unhurried, mournful delivery.

items.name: Motorpop
items.lineage: Pop songcraft built on the krautrock motorik pulse, emerging from Düsseldorf and Cologne in the mid-1970s around Neu!, Michael Rother and La Düsseldorf and carried forward by Stereolab, Broadcast and their descendants — a strict 4/4 eighth-note hi-hat and equal-stress kick-snare pattern at 130-150 BPM held without variation, single-chord or two-chord harmonic fields, chorused arpeggiated guitar, analogue synth and organ drones, and detached, often wordless or repeated-phrase vocal melodies floating above the pulse.
items.description: Motorpop describes the strand of German experimental rock, and its later international revival, that applied conventional pop melody and song length to the motorik rhythm invented by Klaus Dinger — an unvarying forward-driving 4/4 that behaves more like a drone than a groove. Recordings favour a dry, tightly compressed kit high in the mix, layered chorused guitar and analogue synth textures, minimal harmonic movement, and vocals treated as another repeating timbral layer rather than a narrative foreground. It differs from cosmic or kosmische krautrock by keeping to concise song forms and hooks, and from later indie revivalism by its 1970s German studio-DIY sound rather than digital reconstruction.

items.name: New Romanticism (New Romantic)
items.lineage: British club-born movement of 1979-1983, incubated at the Blitz in Covent Garden and codified by Visage, Duran Duran, Spandau Ballet, Ultravox and Japan — 110-130 BPM four-on-the-floor or LinnDrum-driven pop with sequenced analogue synth bass and arpeggios, chorused fretless or slap electric bass, gated reverb on the snare, sweeping polysynth pads, fretless-toned lead lines and a theatrical crooning baritone delivered with deliberate glamour.
items.description: New Romanticism began as a London club-dress movement in 1979 and became, within three years, the dominant sound of British chart pop and early MTV. Musically it welded the sequenced analogue synthesizer vocabulary of Kraftwerk and Bowie's Berlin records to funk-derived bass playing and glossy major-studio production: LinnDrum or gated-reverb live snare, layered Jupiter and Prophet pads, chorus on everything, and an unabashedly romantic, theatrical lead vocal. It differs from earlier British synthpop by keeping a real rhythm section and dance-funk bass rather than being all-electronic, and from post-punk by its embrace of luxury, melody and studio gloss.

items.name: Orchestral Pop
items.lineage: Popular song arranged for full studio orchestra, established in the American and British major-label studios of the late 1950s and 1960s through arrangers such as Nelson Riddle, Burt Bacharach, Jack Nitzsche and Paul Buckmaster and revived by Scott Walker, the Left Banke and Divine Comedy — song-length forms at 60-120 BPM in which strings, French horns, harp and timpani are compositional voices rather than sweetening, with written countermelodies, modulating bridges, and a lead vocal cut live against the orchestra in a large hall.
items.description: Orchestral pop is the branch of popular song in which a written orchestral score carries structural weight — countermelody, harmonic reharmonization, dramatic modulation — rather than merely padding a rhythm section, and it was made possible by the large live rooms of the major labels between the late 1950s and early 1970s. Its sound is defined by real strings and horns captured with distant tube pairs in a hall, a close vocal balanced against that bloom, and arrangements whose formal ambition exceeds the three-minute pop norm. It differs from easy listening in that the song, not the mood, is the object, and from film scoring in that everything serves a sung verse-chorus form.

items.name: Psychedelic Pop
items.lineage: Studio-centred pop written under the influence of 1966-1969 psychedelia in London and Los Angeles — the Beatles of Revolver, the Beach Boys of Smile, the Zombies, the Left Banke, the Small Faces and Curt Boettcher's productions — retaining two-to-three-minute verse-chorus forms and close vocal harmony while adding modal and chromatic mediant harmony, Mellotron, harpsichord and sitar colour, backwards and varispeed tape, and heavy artificial double-tracking and chamber reverb on the voice.
items.description: Psychedelic pop is the melodic, song-form wing of the 1966-69 psychedelic moment: bands who kept the three-minute single and its harmony vocals but used the multitrack studio as a colouring instrument. The identifying features are unusual keyboard and world-instrument timbres (Mellotron flutes, harpsichord, sitar, tack piano), tape manipulation — reversed guitar, varispeed, flanging — chamber and plate reverb used to place sounds at different depths, and vocals doubled or ADT-treated into a glowing composite. It differs from psychedelic rock in avoiding extended jamming and volume as an end in itself, and from baroque pop in that its ornament is electro-acoustic and tape-based rather than orchestrally scored.

items.name: Space Age Pop
items.lineage: American instrumental mood music of roughly 1955-1965 written for the new stereo hi-fi market — Les Baxter, Martin Denny, Esquivel, Juan García Esquivel's RCA ping-pong stereo sessions and the Enoch Light Command Records catalogue — light Latin and lounge tempos of 80-130 BPM, exotic orchestration built on vibraphone, celesta, marimba, muted brass and theremin or Ondes Martenot, wordless cooing vocal choirs, abrupt stereo channel-to-channel effects and bird calls or percussion novelties used as arrangement punctuation.
items.description: Space age pop is the bachelor-pad instrumental mood music produced by American major labels through the stereo-demonstration boom of the late 1950s and early 1960s, closely overlapping exotica. Its identity is entirely orchestrational and technological: vibraphone, celesta, marimba and muted brass in place of a rhythm-section foreground, theremin or Ondes Martenot for the 'space' signifier, wordless choral oohs, and arrangements deliberately written so that motifs leap between the two stereo channels — Esquivel's hallmark — captured with wide tube-mic pairs at Capitol and Webster Hall. It differs from easy listening by its novelty-forward, futurist orchestration and from lounge jazz by being fully arranged with almost no improvisation.

items.name: Surf Pop (vocal surf)
items.lineage: Southern Californian vocal branch of the surf craze, 1962-1965, codified by Brian Wilson with the Beach Boys and by Jan Berry with Jan & Dean — mid-tempo 4/4 rock-and-roll at 130-165 BPM with a shuffling or straight backbeat, doo-wop and Four Freshmen-derived four- and five-part block harmony, falsetto lead, reverb-drenched single-coil guitar figures, honking sax, and Los Angeles session-player backing tracked live in small chamber-equipped rooms.
items.description: Surf pop is the sung counterpart to instrumental surf rock, made in Los Angeles between 1962 and 1965 for a teenage market built around beaches, cars and school. Its signature is dense, wide-voiced vocal harmony — jazz-choral block writing inherited from the Four Freshmen laid over a rock-and-roll rhythm section — with falsetto lead lines, spring- and chamber-reverbed guitar, and mono session tracking in small rooms fed to live echo chambers. It differs from instrumental surf, whose subject is the wet reverb guitar itself, by putting the voices in front, and from contemporaneous East Coast girl-group pop by its harmony-group rather than lead-and-answer construction and its Californian subject matter.

items.name: Traditional Pop Music
items.lineage: American and British mainstream popular song from roughly 1930 to 1955, built on Tin Pan Alley and Broadway 32-bar AABA writing by Berlin, Porter, Kern and Van Heusen, arranged for big band or lush string orchestra by Nelson Riddle, Gordon Jenkins and Axel Stordahl, and delivered by microphone-intimate crooners and torch singers at slow-to-medium swung or ballad tempos with legato phrasing, wide vibrato and conversational rubato.
items.description: Traditional pop is the pre-rock mainstream of the American and British record industry, roughly 1930 to 1955, in which professionally written 32-bar songs were sung over staff-notated big-band or string-orchestra charts. Its sound is defined by close-microphone crooning, legato phrasing with rubato, muted brass and sectional strings, and brushed drums kept low in the balance. Unlike the jazz vocal tradition it borrows repertoire from, the singer stays close to the written melody and the arrangement, not improvisation, carries the interest.

items.name: Vispop
items.lineage: Cebuano-language pop songwriting movement launched in Cebu City in 2013 by the Vispop compilation and competition series, codified by Kurt Fick, Jewel Villaflores and Kyle Wong, characterized by mid-tempo 80-110 BPM acoustic-guitar and piano ballads with unaffected conversational Bisaya vocals, simple diatonic loops and lightly programmed drums built entirely in home DAWs.
items.description: Vispop emerged in Cebu in 2013 as a deliberate campaign to make Cebuano a viable language for contemporary Philippine pop, organized around an annual songwriting competition and compilation album. The sound is deliberately plain: strummed acoustic guitar or piano, soft programmed or lightly played kit, minimal reverb, and a close, untrained-sounding lead vocal foregrounding the Bisaya lyric. It differs from Manila's Tagalog OPM mainstream chiefly in language, regional identity and its smaller, home-studio production scale.

items.name: Wonky Pop
items.lineage: British press-coined pop tendency of 2007-2010 centred on London club nights of the same name, associated with Mika, Alphabeat, Frankmusik and Little Boots, characterized by 110-130 BPM major-key synth and piano hooks, theatrical wide-interval falsetto vocals, glockenspiel and handclap ornament, abrupt key and tempo lurches, and knowingly camp arrangement borrowed from 70s glam and 80s synthpop.
items.description: Wonky pop was a short-lived UK label of the late 2000s for chart pop that used deliberately eccentric, off-kilter hooks and theatrical vocal delivery instead of the smooth R&B-derived idiom then dominant. Its markers are bright stacked synths, cabaret piano, falsetto leaps, handclaps and glockenspiel, and arrangements that change direction mid-song. Against straight synthpop revival it is more song-cycle theatrical and more harmonically restless, and against indie pop it is fully studio-constructed.

items.name: Space House
items.lineage: French and Belgian house variant of the mid-to-late 1990s associated with Alan Braxe, Stardust, I:Cube and the Roule and Versatile labels, characterized by 118-126 BPM disco-derived kicks, cosmic analogue synth arpeggios and phaser-swept pads over filtered loops, sustained vocoder or heavily processed vocal fragments, and slow-evolving one-chord builds owing more to 70s space disco than to Chicago tracks.
items.description: Space house is the cosmic wing of 1990s French touch, taking the filtered disco loop of the Paris scene and pushing it toward the wide analogue synth textures and vocoded voices of 1970s space disco. Tracks are long, largely instrumental, built on a single loop with slow filter and phaser motion rather than song sections. It is distinguished from mainstream filter house by its synthetic, non-sample-led pads and from Italo house by its cooler, more static harmonic language.

items.name: Scouse House
items.lineage: Liverpool and North West England hard-house offshoot of roughly 1997-2010, propagated through the 3 Beat and Clubland circuit and DJs such as Ultrabeat and Flip & Fill, characterized by 140-150 BPM four-on-the-floor kicks with the distinctive detuned 'donk' offbeat percussion hit, pitched-up female vocal hooks or reworked pop toplines, simple major-key sawtooth stabs and short breakdowns.
items.description: Scouse house, later known as bounce or donk, formed around Liverpool and the North West English club circuit from the late 1990s, spreading through cheap CD compilations and bedroom production software. Its defining element is the donk, a hard detuned offbeat percussive stab, set against a fast pounding kick and pitched-up vocal hooks lifted from pop or trance records. It is faster, more repetitive and far less harmonically ambitious than mainstream UK hard house, and openly proudly populist in its use of familiar melodies.

items.name: Progressive Breaks
items.lineage: UK and US crossover style of roughly 1996-2005 developed by Hybrid, BT, Way Out West and the Distinctive and Bedrock labels, characterized by 128-134 BPM chopped syncopated breakbeats replacing the four-on-the-floor kick, long filtered progressive-house pads, orchestral or cinematic string layers, sub-bass ostinati and eight-to-ten-minute arrangements built on extremely gradual DJ-friendly transitions.
items.description: Progressive breaks grafted the chopped breakbeat of UK big beat and nu-skool breaks onto the long-arc harmonic structures of progressive house, peaking commercially around 1999-2003. Tracks run long, layer sub-bass and evolving filtered pads over a shuffling non-four-to-the-floor drum edit, and often add cinematic string and choir samples. It is distinguished from nu-skool breaks by its slower emotional build and melodic content, and from progressive house purely by the drum programming.

items.name: Beach Music (Carolina)
items.lineage: Coastal Carolina dance-club repertoire that crystallized between the late 1940s and the mid 1960s along the Grand Strand and Myrtle Beach pavilions, built around jukebox R&B and vocal-group sides selected for the mid-tempo shag dance at roughly 110-130 BPM in a 12/8 or shuffled 4/4 with walking bass, honking tenor saxophone breaks, triplet piano and warm four-part male harmony behind a gritty lead.
items.description: Carolina beach music is defined less by a production style than by a dance and a listening community: mid-tempo rhythm and blues and vocal-group records adopted by white and Black beach crowds along the Carolina coast for the shag. Musically it favours shuffled 12/8 or relaxed 4/4 grooves, tenor sax solos, triplet piano and group harmony, and it later produced its own studio bands writing to that template. It is slower and more harmony-focused than northern soul, and warmer and less driving than Motown.
exemplars: General Johnson and the Chairmen of the Board

items.name: Modern Soul
items.lineage: British collector-scene term for the uptempo soul of roughly 1973-1982 that displaced 1960s stompers on the northern circuit, centred on Philadelphia, Detroit and independent West Coast productions, characterized by 105-120 BPM four-on-the-floor grooves with sixteenth hi-hats, sweetened string and flute arrangements, electric piano and clavinet, melodic bass lines and smooth multi-tracked lead and backing vocals.
items.description: Modern soul is a scene classification rather than a production centre: it names the smoother, faster 1970s soul records that UK northern soul DJs turned to once the supply of unheard 1960s sides ran thin. Sonically it means Philadelphia-style sweetening, Rhodes and clavinet comping, sixteenth-note hi-hat drive and layered vocal arrangements over a danceable four-on-the-floor. Against northern soul it is later, glossier and less percussively hard; against boogie it retains full live string and horn arrangements rather than synth substitution.

items.name: Northern Soul
items.lineage: English club movement of 1968-1981 centred on the Twisted Wheel, Wigan Casino and Blackpool Mecca and named by journalist Dave Godin, built on rare mid-1960s American soul 45s played at 120-135 BPM with insistent four-on-the-floor kick, driving eighth-note tambourine, punchy horn stabs, walking or pumping bass and urgently belted lead vocals over Motown-derived changes.
items.description: Northern soul is an English dancefloor canon assembled from obscure mid-1960s American soul singles, not a style produced by its own scene. The records selected share a hard four-on-the-floor kick, constant tambourine, brass punctuation and a high-energy vocal, generally cut fast and mono for jukebox impact. It is separated from Motown proper by rarity and tempo rather than technique, and from later modern soul by its rawer, harder-hitting rhythm sections.
exemplars: Frank Wilson - Do I Love You (Indeed I Do)
Dobie Gray - Out on the Floor
R. Dean Taylor - There's a Ghost in My House

items.name: Psychedelic Soul
items.lineage: American soul mutation of 1967-1973 codified by Norman Whitfield at Motown, Sly Stone in San Francisco and George Clinton's Funkadelic, characterized by extended one-chord vamps at 95-115 BPM, fuzz and wah electric guitar, phased and heavily reverberated mixes, layered congas and hand percussion, group-passed lead vocals trading lines, and socially pointed lyrics stretched across multi-part arrangements of six minutes or more.
items.description: Psychedelic soul emerged in the late 1960s when Black American producers absorbed the studio effects and long-form structures of psychedelic rock into soul and early funk. Its markers are fuzz and wah guitar, phasing and heavy plate reverb, dense conga-layered percussion, static modal vamps in place of chord-driven song form, and lead vocals passed around a group. It sits between the tight three-minute Motown single and full-blown funk, keeping soul harmony and vocal groups while adopting rock's textural experiment.
exemplars: The Temptations - Papa Was a Rollin' Stone

items.name: Reggae Bultrón
items.lineage: Puerto Rican underground style of the mid-to-late 1990s San Juan marquesina and caserío scene, codified by DJ Nelson (Reggae Bultrón, 1997), DJ Playero and DJ Negro out of the earlier Playero mixtape series — Jamaican dancehall riddims (Dem Bow, Bam Bam) re-sequenced on hardware samplers at 90-100 BPM under Spanish-language duo toasting, with heavily gated kick-and-tresillo snare, sirens, gunshot stabs and cassette-generation hiss.
items.description: Reggae Bultrón is the mid-to-late-1990s Puerto Rican underground stage between Jamaican dancehall and fully formed reggaetón, named for DJ Nelson's 1997 compilation and grown out of the Playero and Noise mixtape culture of San Juan housing projects. Its sound is a looped Dem Bow tresillo pattern under aggressive Spanish-language dual-MC toasting, with sampler-chopped dancehall riddims, sirens and effect stabs, and the compressed, cassette-dubbed low end of underground distribution. It differs from Jamaican ragga by language and by the fixed Dem Bow loop replacing changing riddim beds, and from post-2004 reggaetón by its rawer mix, longer freestyle passages, and absence of pop songform.

items.name: Ragga
items.lineage: Jamaican digital dancehall style dating from the 1985 Sleng Teng riddim, codified by Wayne Smith, King Jammy, Steely & Clevie, Shabba Ranks and Buju Banton — Casio and drum-machine riddims at roughly 90-105 BPM with all-electronic kick, rimshot and bassline, no live band, and a hoarse, rapid-fire chatted DJ delivery in Jamaican Patois riding a single recycled riddim.
items.description: Ragga is the fully digital branch of Jamaican dancehall that opened with King Jammy's 1985 Sleng Teng riddim, the first reggae backing built entirely on a preset Casio rhythm rather than a studio band. Its markers are skeletal electronic drums, a synthesized bassline carrying almost all the harmony, one riddim voiced by dozens of DJs across competing labels, and a chatted, percussive vocal that sits between singing and speech. Compared to roots reggae it discards the one-drop live rhythm section and the mystical lyric register; compared to later 1990s dancehall it is thinner and drier, with less pop melody and less studio layering.
exemplars: Wayne Smith - Under Mi Sleng Teng

items.name: Raggamuffin
items.lineage: Late-1980s to early-1990s transatlantic development of digital dancehall between Kingston and Black British studios in Brent, Hackney and Birmingham, carried by Rebel MC, Asher D & Daddy Freddy, Tippa Irie, Papa San and Super Cat — 90-105 BPM computer riddims thickened with sampled breakbeats, sound-system sub-bass, and a fast, syllable-dense ragga chat cut to dubplate for clash use.
items.description: Raggamuffin is the late-1980s and early-1990s sound-system culture built on digital dancehall riddims, developed as much in Black British studios and pirate-radio circles as in Kingston. It keeps ragga's electronic riddim and chatted Patois vocal but adds sampled funk breaks, denser sub-bass mixed for large speaker stacks, and a dubplate-special economy of exclusive cuts made for clashes. It is distinguished from Jamaican ragga proper by its diaspora production values and breakbeat borrowing, and from the jungle that grew directly out of it by remaining at dancehall tempo rather than accelerating the break to 160 BPM.
exemplars: Asher D & Daddy Freddy - Ragamuffin Hip-Hop

items.name: Rocksteady
items.lineage: Jamaican style of roughly 1966-1968, formed at Studio One and Treasure Isle when ska's fast shuffle slowed to about 80 BPM in the hot summer of 1966 — codified by Alton Ellis (Get Ready Rock Steady), Hopeton Lewis, the Techniques and Duke Reid's productions, with the horn section receding, Jackie Jackson and Leroy Sibbles' melodic walking basslines moving to the front, guitar and piano on the offbeat skank, and close soul-harmony vocal trios.
items.description: Rocksteady is the short-lived Jamaican style that bridged ska and reggae between 1966 and 1968, made at Studio One and Duke Reid's Treasure Isle. Slowing the tempo to a loping mid-80s BPM freed the bass to play composed melodic figures rather than walking quarters, cut the horn arrangements back to occasional punctuation, and put American soul vocal-harmony writing at the centre. Against ska it is slower, sparser and bass-led; against the reggae that followed it lacks the one-drop kick displacement and the organ bubble, and its lyrics remain romantic rather than Rastafarian.

items.name: Afro-Punk
items.lineage: Black American hardcore and alternative-rock current running from Washington DC's Bad Brains (1977 onward) and Los Angeles' Fishbone and Living Colour through the 2003 Afro-Punk documentary and the Brooklyn festival scene it created — fast downstroked power chords and hardcore backbeats interleaved with reggae dub breaks, funk syncopation and gospel-shouted vocal delivery.
items.description: Afro-Punk names the Black presence in American hardcore and alternative rock, running from Bad Brains' 1977 DC beginnings through Fishbone and Living Colour and formalized as a scene by James Spooner's 2003 documentary and the Brooklyn festival that followed. Sonically it is hardcore's speed and downstroke attack repeatedly broken open by dub reggae passages, funk basslines and church-derived vocal power, so records swing between blast-tempo thrash and half-time skank inside a single song. It differs from straight hardcore punk in its rhythmic range and vocal virtuosity, and from funk-metal in that its roots are in the DIY punk circuit rather than the arena.

items.name: British Invasion
items.lineage: British beat-group wave that broke in the United States in 1964 following The Beatles' Ed Sullivan appearance, produced largely at EMI Abbey Road, Decca and IBC on four-track — Liverpool and London bands recasting American R&B, Chuck Berry and Brill Building songwriting as compact two-to-three-minute guitar-bass-drums records at 120-150 BPM with tight two- and three-part harmony, tambourine backbeat and heavily limited mono mixes.
items.description: The British Invasion is the 1964-1967 wave of UK beat and R&B groups that took over the American charts after The Beatles' Ed Sullivan broadcast. Its records are short, mono, four-track productions built on jangling single-coil guitar, driving eighth-note bass, tambourine-reinforced backbeat and close vocal harmony, with American rhythm-and-blues repertoire filtered through English vocal accent and Tin Pan Alley songcraft. Set against the American rock and roll it borrowed from, it is tighter, more harmonically adventurous and more producer-shaped; set against the psychedelia that followed it, it is still constrained to dance-single length and form.
exemplars: The Beatles - A Hard Day's Night
The Rolling Stones - The Rolling Stones (1964)
The Kinks - You Really Got Me
The Animals - The House of the Rising Sun

items.name: Roots Rock
items.lineage: Late-1960s American reaction against psychedelia, formed around Woodstock and the Bay Area with The Band's Music from Big Pink (1968), Creedence Clearwater Revival and Bob Dylan's John Wesley Harding — moderate 90-120 BPM backbeats, unaffected guitar tones, piano and Hammond organ, gospel-derived group harmony and country, blues and R&B forms recorded with minimal overdubbing.
items.description: Roots rock is the late-1960s turn away from studio psychedelia toward older American forms, announced by The Band's Music from Big Pink and Dylan's John Wesley Harding and carried commercially by Creedence Clearwater Revival. Its markers are dry unprocessed guitar and drums, prominent acoustic piano and Hammond, rotating lead vocals with rough gospel-style harmony, and songwriting drawn from country, hymnody, blues and rockabilly rather than blues-rock virtuosity. It differs from country rock by leaning on rhythm-and-blues and gospel as much as on Nashville, and from the Americana that later descends from it by belonging to a mainstream rock market rather than an alt-country one.
exemplars: Creedence Clearwater Revival - Willy and the Poor Boys

items.name: Spazzcore
items.lineage: Mid-1990s chaotic-hardcore offshoot of American and Japanese powerviolence, named for the band Spazz and carried by Charles Bronson, Melt-Banana, The Locust and Arab on Radar — songs of ten to sixty seconds built on abrupt blast-beat to stop-time cuts, atonal dissonant guitar stabs, treble-heavy bass and shrieked or yelped vocals, recorded fast and cheap on DIY budgets.
items.description: Spazzcore is the mid-1990s chaotic wing of hardcore punk, taking its name from the California band Spazz and overlapping with powerviolence and noisecore. Tracks last seconds rather than minutes and are assembled from violent tempo cuts between blast beats and lurching half-time, atonal or chromatic guitar stabs instead of riffs, and vocals delivered as shrieks, yelps and barks; releases arrive as split seven-inches on tiny labels. It is distinguished from grindcore by its punk rather than metal lineage and its refusal of steady groove, and from noise rock by extreme brevity and hardcore tempo.

items.name: Time Lord Rock
items.lineage: Doctor Who fan-music genre (Trock) begun in 2008 when Charlie McDonnell and Alex Day formed Chameleon Circuit and released through YouTube and DFTBA Records — bedroom-recorded pop-punk and acoustic power-pop at 120-160 BPM, close-miked doubled lead vocals over strummed acoustic and clean electric guitar, programmed or lightly played drums, and lyrics narrating specific episodes and characters.
items.description: Time Lord Rock, or Trock, is a small British-led fan genre of songs about Doctor Who, launched in 2008 by Chameleon Circuit and distributed through YouTube channels and DFTBA Records rather than conventional labels. Musically it is bedroom-produced acoustic power-pop and pop-punk with doubled untrained lead vocals well forward, simple diatonic progressions, programmed or minimally tracked drums, and dense narrative lyrics that assume episode knowledge. It differs from wizard rock, its nearest neighbour, only in source text; it differs from general indie bedroom pop in that the subject matter, not a sound, defines membership.
exemplars: Alex Carpenter / The Ministry of Magic

items.name: New Acoustic
items.lineage: US late-1970s acoustic-string idiom formed around David Grisman's San Francisco quintet and Tony Rice's Bay Area circle, codified on Grisman's 1977 'Dawg Music' sessions — bluegrass instrumentation (mandolin lead, flatpicked dreadnought, fiddle, five-string banjo, upright bass) played over jazz-derived changes, minor and modal keys, hemiola-laced 6/8 and odd-metre heads, extended solo choruses at 100-200 BPM with no vocals and no backbeat.
items.description: New Acoustic emerged in the San Francisco Bay Area in the late 1970s when David Grisman, Tony Rice, Darol Anger and Mike Marshall began playing bluegrass instruments over jazz harmony, gypsy-swing phrasing and Balkan-derived meters. The sound is entirely acoustic and almost entirely instrumental: close-miked mandolin and flatpicked guitar trading long improvised choruses over a walking upright bass, with wide dynamic shading and no drum kit. It differs from bluegrass proper in its absence of high-lonesome vocals and its use of extended chords and modulation, and from jazz in retaining flatpicked string attack and fiddle-tune formal structure.
exemplars: Strength in Numbers - The Telluride Sessions

items.name: Original Score (Film & Media)
items.lineage: Purpose-composed narrative underscore for film and television, codified in 1930s-40s Hollywood by Max Steiner, Erich Korngold and Bernard Herrmann and extended by Ennio Morricone, John Williams and Hans Zimmer — through-composed orchestral cues timed to picture at fixed frame-rates with click tracks, leitmotif recurrence, tempo and metre subordinated to onscreen action, and recording on a scoring stage against projected image.
items.description: Original score is music composed specifically for a moving image, established as a craft in Hollywood during the 1930s and continuously reinvented from Herrmann's astringent chamber writing through Morricone's timbral collage to Zimmer's hybrid orchestral-electronic textures. Its defining constraints are external: cues begin and end on picture cues, tempo is governed by click and streamer rather than musical shape, and orchestration serves dramatic function, so through-composed development and abrupt textural change are normal. It is distinguished from concert orchestral music by its dependence on synchronization and from the compiled soundtrack by being written rather than licensed.
exemplars: Ennio Morricone - Once Upon a Time in the West
Jonny Greenwood - There Will Be Blood

items.name: Chicano Rock
items.lineage: East Los Angeles Mexican-American rock and R&B scene of the late 1950s-60s, codified by Ritchie Valens, Thee Midniters, Cannibal & the Headhunters and the Whittier Boulevard dance-hall circuit — 12/8 shuffle ballads and mid-tempo 4/4 stompers built on doo-wop changes, honking tenor saxophone, Farfisa or Hammond organ, tremolo-heavy single-coil guitar, tight harmony vocals and Spanish-language interpolations of ranchera and huapango material.
items.description: Chicano rock formed in the barrios of East Los Angeles between the late 1950s and the late 1960s, where Mexican-American teenagers absorbed R&B, doo-wop and Latin dance rhythms and fed back ranchera melodies and Spanish lyrics. The characteristic record is a small-studio recording with plate-and-chamber reverb, a saxophone-and-organ front line, group harmony and either a rolling 12/8 ballad feel or a driving Latin-inflected backbeat. It differs from mainstream 1960s garage rock in its R&B horn vocabulary and Spanish-language repertoire, and from Tejano conjunto in using electric band instrumentation rather than accordion and bajo sexto.

items.name: New Mexico Music
items.lineage: Hispano regional popular style of the upper Rio Grande valley, consolidated in Albuquerque and Espanola from the 1940s onward around Al Hurricane, Tiny Morrie and Baca Records — Spanish-language rancheras, valses, corridos and polkas fused with mid-century rock and roll rhythm section, twin-fiddle or violin lead inherited from the Hispano baile tradition, accordion or organ, and a shuffling 'Nuevo Mexicano' backbeat under lyric Spanish vocals.
