items.description: New Mexico music is the Hispano popular tradition of the Rio Grande corridor north of El Paso, distinct from both Tejano and Mexican norteno because it descends from a colonial Spanish-speaking community that was never part of the twentieth-century border migration. Its records, largely cut for family-run Albuquerque labels from the 1950s on, pair the old baile fiddle repertoire and 3/4 vals with a rock-and-roll drum kit, electric guitar and organ under Spanish vocals. The fiddle rather than the accordion is the identifying lead voice, and the rhythmic feel leans toward a loping shuffle rather than the conjunto two-beat.

items.name: A Cappella (Contemporary Vocal)
items.lineage: Unaccompanied multi-voice arrangement of popular repertoire, established on US and UK college campuses from the mid-twentieth century and codified commercially by the Bobs, Take 6, the King's Singers' pop sets and post-2000 groups such as Pentatonix — four to sixteen voices covering bass line, chordal pads and lead, with vocal percussion supplying kick, snare and hi-hat, close-miked and multitracked, in strophic pop forms at 70-130 BPM.
items.description: Contemporary a cappella is the practice of rendering popular songs entirely with voices, grown from the collegiate glee and jazz-vocal-group traditions and standardized after the 1980s by groups that assigned voices to instrumental roles. Records are heavily produced: each part is close-miked and multitracked, vocal bass is often octave-shifted, and a beatboxer supplies the drum kit, so the finished sound is dense and studio-constructed rather than choral. It differs from barbershop in repertoire and equal-tempered pop harmony, and from choral music in its instrument-imitating arrangement and per-voice studio processing.

items.name: Cantique
items.lineage: French-language devotional hymn tradition of France, Quebec, Brittany and Francophone Africa and the Caribbean, formalized in seventeenth- and eighteenth-century parish collections and diffused through nineteenth-century cantique books — strophic verse-and-refrain settings in duple or triple metre, sung in unison or simple parts by congregation and choir over harmonium or pipe organ, with syllabic text-setting in vernacular French rather than Latin.
items.description: The cantique is the vernacular French devotional song of Catholic worship, distinct from Latin liturgical chant and used for popular piety, processions, Christmas and Marian devotions from the seventeenth century onward. Musically it is plain and strophic: a memorable refrain alternating with narrative verses, sung syllabically by the whole assembly in unison or easy harmony, supported by harmonium or organ in a reverberant stone church. Its Breton and Quebecois branches preserve older modal melodies, and its African and Haitian branches add local percussion, but the defining marker across all of them is French-language congregational strophic singing rather than trained choral polyphony.
exemplars: Les Petits Chanteurs a la Croix de Bois

items.name: Gregorian Chant
items.lineage: Latin liturgical monophony of the Western church, synthesized from Roman and Frankish practice in the Carolingian empire during the eighth and ninth centuries and notated in neumes from circa 900, restored by the Solesmes monks in the nineteenth century — unaccompanied male or female unison voices, free unmeasured prose rhythm following the Latin text, eight-mode system, syllabic psalm tones through melismatic graduals and alleluias, sung antiphonally in resonant stone spaces.
items.description: Gregorian chant is the unaccompanied Latin monophony of the Roman rite, assembled under Frankish rule in the eighth and ninth centuries and preserved through neumatic and later square notation. Its defining traits are total absence of harmony and instruments, free prose rhythm governed by the accents of the Latin text, an eight-mode tonal framework, and long reverberation from the stone churches it was written for. It differs from Byzantine and Ambrosian chant in repertoire and modal theory, and from later polyphony in remaining strictly single-line even when sung by a large schola.
exemplars: Monks of Santo Domingo de Silos

items.name: African Heavy Metal
items.lineage: Continental African metal scenes formed from the late 1980s onward in Botswana, Angola, Kenya, Madagascar and South Africa, codified by Wrust, Skinflint, Overthrust and the Gaborone leather-cowboy subculture — NWOBHM and thrash templates at 120-190 BPM with downtuned humbucker guitars and double-kick drumming, but with Setswana, Swahili or Portuguese lyrics, local praise-song melodic contours and occasional talking drum or call-and-response chant layered over the riff.
items.description: African heavy metal names the metal scenes that took root across the continent from the late 1980s, most visibly the Botswana scene around Gaborone with its distinctive leather-and-stetson visual code, alongside Angolan, Kenyan, Malagasy and South African bands. Musically it is built on classic heavy metal and thrash riffing and double-kick drumming recorded on modest digital budgets, but repertoire and delivery draw on indigenous language, praise-singing phrase shapes and sometimes local percussion, giving vocal lines a chanted, communal contour uncommon in European metal. It differs from South African rock more broadly in its metal instrumentation and tempo, and from Western thrash in its lyrical language and its polyrhythmic and call-and-response inflections.

items.name: Kwela
items.lineage: South African township street music of the early 1950s, born on Johannesburg and Pretoria pavements and commercialized through Gallo by Spokes Mashiyane and the Lerole brothers, built on a bright pennywhistle lead improvising over a bouncing 4/4 marabi-derived I–IV–I(6/4)–V cycle at 130–160 BPM with strummed guitar, tea-chest or double bass, and a chugging offbeat.
items.description: Kwela arose in the early 1950s among township youth in Johannesburg and Pretoria who adopted the cheap German pennywhistle as a street instrument, and became South Africa's first international pop export with Spokes Mashiyane's records and the Lerole brothers' 'Tom Hark'. The sound is a single piercing six-hole whistle blown breathily and rhythmically over a four-chord marabi cycle carried by guitar and tea-chest bass, with the whistle player bending and overblowing in place of a singer. It differs from the mbaqanga and sax-jive that succeeded it in being almost entirely instrumental, whistle-led, and acoustic rather than electric and vocal-group based.
exemplars: Elias Lerole & His Zig Zag Jive Flutes

items.name: Maloya
items.lineage: Créole ancestor-worship and protest music of Réunion, descended from Malagasy and East African slave servis kabaré rites and revived from 1970 by Firmin Viry, Granmoun Lélé and Danyèl Waro, driven by the low roulèr bass drum, rattling kayamb tray-shaker and triangle in a slow-building 6/8-into-4 pulse under a hoarse solo call and unison Creole chorus response that accelerates across a single trance-length cycle.
items.description: Maloya is the ritual and protest music of Réunion's Créole descendants of enslaved Malagasy and African labourers, suppressed by French authorities into the 1970s and revived as an explicitly political idiom by Firmin Viry, Granmoun Lélé and Danyèl Waro before UNESCO listing in 2009. Its texture is entirely percussive and vocal: the seated roulèr laying a deep two-stroke bass figure, the kayamb hissing a continuous shuffle, hand clapping and a strained solo voice trading short Kreol phrases with a shouted chorus over a single cell that tightens and speeds toward trance. Séga, its island neighbour, is fast, sweet, secular and later took on guitars and horns, while maloya stays slow-starting, drum-only and tied to servis kabaré ancestor ceremony.

items.name: Séga (Mauritian creole dance song)
items.lineage: Continuing Mauritian creole dance-song and recorded séga practice, 1950-present. Creole dance song of Mauritius, Rodrigues and Réunion with slave-era roots, professionalized on record from the late 1950s by Ti Frère and Serge Lebrasse, built on the goatskin ravanne frame drum's driving triplet-inflected 6/8, the kayamb or maravanne rattle and triangle, a fast accelerando toward the closing 'séga tipik' break, and light strophic Kreol verses with call-and-response chorus.
items.description: Séga is the national dance music of Mauritius, descended from the music of enslaved Mozambican and Malagasy people and moved from beach and yard gatherings onto commercial records from the late 1950s. The core is the fire-tuned ravanne frame drum playing a rolling triplet pattern, the maravanne or kayamb shaker filling the offbeats, and short strophic Kreol verses about work, love and gossip, with the tempo pushed steadily upward until the closing frenzy. It is faster, lighter and more secular than Réunionnais maloya, and unlike maloya it readily absorbed guitar, bass and later horn sections into its 'séga moderne' recorded form.

items.name: Seggae
items.lineage: Mauritian fusion of séga and Jamaican roots reggae created in the mid-1980s by Kaya (Joseph Reginald Topize) and developed by Ras Natty Baby, laying the ravanne's triplet séga pulse across a reggae one-drop at 70–90 BPM with skanking offbeat guitar, dubwise bass, organ bubble and Kreol lyrics of Rastafari and Creole social grievance.
items.description: Seggae was invented in Mauritius around 1985 by Kaya, who set ravanne-driven séga rhythm over reggae's one-drop and Rastafari-inflected Kreol lyrics, and it became the island's protest idiom after his death in police custody in 1999 triggered nationwide riots. The records combine a reggae rhythm section — bubbling organ, chopped offbeat guitar, melodic bass — with the ravanne and maravanne still audible under the kit, and a rough, plain-spoken vocal delivery. It differs from Jamaican roots reggae in its Creole language, its triplet-leaning percussion layer, and from séga proper in its halved tempo and bass-forward mix.

items.name: Museve
items.lineage: Zimbabwean guitar-band dance style named by Simon Chimbetu in the late 1980s from his dendera branch of sungura, running a fast 4/4 at roughly 130–150 BPM with a rapid rolling snare-and-hi-hat kit pattern, two interlocking clean electric guitars trading cyclic mbira-derived riffs, walking bass and Shona narrative vocals in warm two- and three-part harmony.
items.description: Museve is the Zimbabwean dance-band idiom that split from sungura in the late 1980s, the label Simon Chimbetu applied to his Dendera Kings sound and which spread across Harare's studios through the 1990s. It is guitar-band music in which two clean electrics weave short repeating figures modelled on mbira interlocking patterns, over a fast kit groove with the snare rolling in near-continuous sixteenths, hosho shaker on top, and Shona lyrics of migrancy, morality and love sung in close harmony. Against Congolese soukous it is faster and drier with no horn section, and against chimurenga it uses the guitar-band frame rather than direct mbira transcription and political allegory.

items.name: Anison (Japanese anime theme song)
items.lineage: Japanese commercial song written for anime opening and closing titles, established as a distinct trade in the 1960s–70s by Columbia and Nippon Columbia sessions for Ichirou Mizuki and Isao Sasaki, characterized by a 90-second broadcast edit, declamatory belted male or bright female lead, marching or driving 4/4 at 130–170 BPM, brass-and-string sweetened rock backing, shouted title hooks and abrupt key-lifting final choruses.
items.description: Anison is the Japanese industry category for songs commissioned as anime title music, professionalized in the 1960s and 70s around specialist singers such as Ichirou Mizuki and Isao Sasaki and later around JAM Project and tie-in J-pop acts. Its constraints are formal: a tightly compressed 90-second broadcast cut, an immediate hook, a heroic full-throated belt often shouting the show's title, brisk march-derived 4/4 with brass stabs and string counterlines, and a modulation into the last chorus. It is distinguished from general J-pop less by harmony than by function and delivery — declamatory rather than intimate, structurally truncated, and built to survive a weekly title sequence.

items.name: Fann at-Tanbura
items.lineage: Afro-Gulf ritual and entertainment music of Bahrain, Kuwait and the Saudi Eastern Province, carried by communities descended from East African and Sudanese people from the nineteenth century, centred on the six-string tanbura lyre played over a slow-building 6/8 or compound cycle, the mangūr goat-hoof rattle belt shaken by a dancer, tār frame drums, hand clapping and a leader's call answered by a heavy unison male chorus.
items.description: Fann at-tanbura is the lyre-and-rattle music kept by Afro-Arab communities of the Arabian Gulf littoral, performed in dedicated dūr houses in Muharraq, Kuwait City and Qatif for healing, celebration and, historically, alongside the pearling economy. The tanbura, a large bowl lyre of East African descent, is strummed in a continuous ostinato while the mangūr — a belt of stitched goat hooves worn by a standing dancer — supplies a dry sizzling counter-rhythm, over which frame drums, clapping and antiphonal male chorus intensify across a long single cycle. It sits apart from other Gulf repertoires such as sawt or fijiri in retaining an explicitly African instrument and trance-oriented, spirit-related function.
exemplars: Dār tanbura troupes of Muharraq, Bahrain
Gulf recordings by Poul Rovsing Olsen

items.name: Khalījī (Gulf dance song)
items.lineage: Popular song of the Arabian Gulf states shaped from the 1950s onward by Kuwaiti and Bahraini radio and by Saudi singers such as Talal Maddah and Mohammed Abdu, setting Gulf dialect lyrics over the distinctive limping khalījī 2/4 and 6/8 patterns played on mirwās and ṭabl with hand claps, an oud-led maqām melody doubled by massed violins and qānūn, and an ornamented but relatively unforced solo vocal.
items.description: Khalījī is the shared popular idiom of Kuwait, Bahrain, Saudi Arabia, Qatar and the Emirates, consolidated through Gulf state radio orchestras from the 1950s and 60s and carried into pan-Arab stardom by Talal Maddah, Mohammed Abdu and later Abdallah Al Rowaished and Nawal. Its identifying feature is rhythmic: the syncopated Gulf patterns hit on paired mirwās hand drums and ṭabl with clapping, which pull against an otherwise Egyptian-style ensemble of oud, qānūn and unison violin section playing quarter-tone maqām lines. Against Egyptian ṭarab it is shorter-formed, faster and drum-forward; against the older sawt tradition it is orchestrated, notated in part, and built for broadcast rather than for the intimate ṣawt majlis.

items.name: Liwa (Swahili-Omani coastal dance)
items.lineage: Coastal Swahili dance-music of Zanzibar, Mombasa and the Omani-Gulf diaspora, carried by Hadhrami and Baluchi communities from the 19th century and maintained by neighbourhood liwa associations — a loud outdoor style built on a paired double-headed drum battery and shaker ostinato at brisk 4/4 processional tempo under the piercing continuous circular-breathed zumari (conical shawm), with call-and-response Swahili and Arabic chorus shouting over the drums.
items.description: Liwa is an outdoor drum-and-shawm dance tradition of the Swahili coast and the Omani Gulf, sustained by community associations in Zanzibar, Mombasa and Muscat since the 19th-century Indian Ocean trade era. Its sound is a dense, unbroken drum ostinato topped by the nasal, circular-breathed zumari and shouted responsorial refrains, with no melodic instruments in the European sense. Unlike taarab, the coast's other Arab-influenced idiom, liwa is loud, non-strophic, entirely percussion-led and played standing in the street rather than seated in a hall.

items.name: Onkyokei (Japanese onkyo improvisation)
items.lineage: Tokyo improvised-music movement crystallized around the Off Site venue circa 1998-2004 and codified by Otomo Yoshihide, Sachiko M, Toshimaru Nakamura and Taku Sugimoto — extremely quiet, near-static music of sine tones, no-input mixing-board feedback, contact-mic scrapes and long silences, with no pulse, no harmony and structure emerging from the acoustics of the room itself.
items.description: Onkyokei emerged in Tokyo's small improvisation venues around 1998, most associated with the Off Site space in Yoyogi. It works at the threshold of audibility: unmodulated sine tones, feedback held at the edge of self-oscillation in a mixing desk with nothing plugged in, tiny physical noises, and silences long enough to expose the room and the audience. It differs from European free improvisation in its refusal of gesture and virtuosity, and from ambient music in that it is performed live, unlooped and without harmonic bed.

items.name: Chutney Soca
items.lineage: Trinidadian hybrid launched by Drupatee Ramgoonai's 1987 recordings and formalized by the Chutney Soca Monarch competition from 1996 — chutney's dholak and dhantal layered onto a 4/4 soca rhythm section of programmed kick, electric bass, brass stabs and synth, at carnival tempo around 130-150 BPM with English-Bhojpuri call-and-response hooks.
items.description: Chutney soca is the carnival-stage fusion of Indo-Trinidadian chutney with soca, dating from Drupatee Ramgoonai's late-1980s crossover records and institutionalized by the annual Chutney Soca Monarch. It keeps the dholak, dhantal and tassa but sets them over a soca kick pattern, synth brass and a big compressed mix built for outdoor fete sound systems. Against acoustic chutney it is louder, English-dominant and hook-driven; against mainstream soca it is marked by the Indian percussion layer and harmonium-derived melodic turns.

items.name: Méringue (Haitian salon and carnival)
items.lineage: Haiti's 19th-century national dance, formed in Port-au-Prince salons from contredanse and Afro-Haitian rhythm and elevated by Occide Jeanty, Ludovic Lamothe and later Issa el Saieh's big bands — a moderate 2/4 with a distinctive quintolet-inflected bass-drum figure, played by piano or wind band in its lente salon form and by carnival brass in the street.
items.description: Méringue is the older Haitian dance from which konpa was drawn, current from the mid-19th century in both a refined salon form for piano or chamber wind band and a rowdier carnival form for brass and tanbou. It is built on a lilting 2/4 with a syncopated bass-drum figure and European harmonic phrasing coloured by Afro-Haitian percussion. It is separated from Dominican merengue by tempo and drum roster, and from konpa by its notated, composer-led repertoire and lack of an electric rhythm section.

items.name: Carnatic kacheri (South Indian concert practice)
items.lineage: South Indian art-music concert format consolidated in Madras in the 1920s-30s around the Music Academy sabha, drawing on the Trinity's 18th-19th century kriti repertoire and Ariyakudi Ramanuja Iyengar's programme template — raga alapana and kalpanaswara improvisation framing composed kritis, sung to tanpani drone with violin accompaniment, mridangam laying the tala and ghatam or kanjira joining for the tani avartanam percussion solo.
items.description: The Carnatic kacheri is the concert form of South Indian classical music as standardized in early-20th-century Madras: a graded sequence of composed kritis interleaved with alapana, niraval and kalpanaswara, resting on a constant tanpura drone and a 72-melakarta raga system. The violin shadows and answers the singer heterophonically while mridangam articulates the tala cycle, culminating in the tani avartanam. Against Hindustani practice it is far more composition-centred, faster in gamaka ornamentation, and organized around fixed tala cycles rather than extended unmetered alap.

items.name: Celtic Folk (pan-Celtic revival)
items.lineage: Pan-Celtic revival repertoire consolidated in Ireland, Scotland and Brittany from the mid-1960s by Planxty, The Bothy Band, Alan Stivell and Silly Wizard — dance tunes in Dorian and Mixolydian modes played in unison by fiddle, flute and pipes over bouzouki or guitar in modal open voicings, with bodhran driving reels and jigs and unaccompanied or lightly backed ballad singing between sets.
items.description: Celtic folk is the arranged, ensemble-based revival music that grew out of Irish, Scottish and Breton session traditions from the 1960s onward. It keeps the modal dance tunes and their cranned, rolled ornamentation but adds bouzouki and guitar backing, arranged tune sets, and studio recording, alternating instrumental sets with ballads. It is distinguished from unaccompanied sean-nós or a pub session by its fixed arrangements and harmonic accompaniment, and from Celtic rock by its acoustic roster and absence of a drum kit.
exemplars: Alan Stivell — Renaissance de la Harpe Celtique

items.name: Ode (ancient Greek sung ode)
items.lineage: Sung strophic poetry of archaic and classical Greece — Sappho's monodic lyric on Lesbos in the 7th century BC and Pindar's choral victory odes in the 5th — reconstructed from the Delphic hymns and Mesomedes fragments as syllabic melody in Pythagorean-tuned diatonic and enharmonic genera, voice doubled heterophonically by kithara or lyre with aulos, phrase shape governed by quantitative poetic metre rather than a drum pulse.
items.description: The ode was the sung lyric of ancient Greece, either monodic self-accompanied song or choral hymn performed at festivals and victory celebrations. Modern realizations rest on surviving notated fragments — the Delphic paeans, Seikilos, Mesomedes — and give a mostly syllabic, narrow-ambitus melody in Pythagorean intervals, sung with lyre or kithara doubling and aulos drone, its rhythm dictated by long and short syllables. It is separated from later Byzantine chant by its instrumental accompaniment and quantitative metre, and from any surviving folk lineage by being a scholarly reconstruction rather than a continuous practice.
exemplars: Atrium Musicae de Madrid — Musique de la Grèce Antique

items.name: Polka (Central European dance)
items.lineage: Bohemian couple dance from the 1830s that swept European ballrooms within a decade and was carried by Czech, German and Polish emigrants to the American Midwest and Texas — a fast duple with the half-step hop figure, oom-pah bass from tuba or bass on beats one and three, off-beat chords, and a lead of clarinet, trumpet or accordion in bright parallel thirds.
items.description: The polka originated in Bohemia around 1830 and became a mass ballroom dance across Europe before emigrant communities replanted it in Wisconsin, Minnesota, Chicago and central Texas. Its constant marker is the fast 2/4 with a tuba or bass oom-pah and off-beat chording under paired clarinets, trumpets or accordion, harmonized in thirds over simple tonic-dominant progressions. Regional variants diverge sharply: Czech-style keeps brass and clarinet, Slovenian-style features button accordion and banjo, and the Texas-Czech line fed directly into conjunto and Tejano.

items.name: Worldbeat
items.lineage: Anglo-American pop hybrid of the mid-1980s built in flagship multitrack studios by Peter Gabriel, Paul Simon, David Byrne and Talking Heads — African and Latin percussion batteries and mbaqanga or soukous guitar figures set against gated drum sounds, Fairlight and sampled loops, fretless or high-life bass and layered guest vocalists, at mid-tempo 4/4 with tightly compressed studio polish.
items.description: Worldbeat names the mid-1980s wave of Western pop records that folded African, Caribbean and Latin rhythm sections and guest vocalists into high-budget studio production, from Graceland and So through Remain in Light's precedents. Sonically it is defined by dense layered percussion and interlocking guitar lines placed inside a gated, heavily compressed 1980s mix with samplers and synth pads. It is distinguished from the source traditions themselves by that studio construction and Anglophone songwriting, and from later world-music reissue culture by being new hybrid composition rather than curation.

items.name: Baila (Sri Lankan)
items.lineage: Sri Lankan Portuguese-Burgher dance song codified commercially in Colombo from the 1960s-70s by Wally Bastian and above all Maxwell Mendis and M.S. Fernando, then arena-scaled by Desmond de Silva and Anton Jones — built on a fast 6/8 kaffringha lilt over rabana frame-drum and conga, strummed acoustic and clean single-coil guitar, walking electric bass, accordion or organ fills, and a shouted-communal call-and-response chorus in Sinhala with the singer improvising rhyming verses.
items.description: Baila is Sri Lanka's Portuguese-creole party music, descended from the kaffringha and chikothi dances of the island's Afro-Portuguese Kaffir communities and turned into a national commercial idiom in Colombo between the 1960s and 1980s. Its signature is a headlong 6/8 shuffle carried by rabana frame drum and hand percussion, chordal guitar and bass, and a lead voice trading shouted rhyming couplets with a crowd chorus, often with topical or comic Sinhala lyrics. It is distinguished from Sri Lankan sarala gee and film-derived pop by its dance function, its Iberian rather than Indian rhythmic root, and its improvised verse-capping tradition.

items.name: Bhojpuri Lok Geet (village folk song)
items.lineage: Village song repertoire of the Bhojpuri-speaking belt of eastern Uttar Pradesh and western Bihar, documented from the nineteenth century and carried into print and recording by Bhikhari Thakur's Launda Nach theatre from the 1920s — seasonal and life-cycle cycles (kajri, chaita, sohar, vivah geet, birha, purbi) sung mostly by women in unison or by a male birha soloist, over dholak and naal with harmonium drone and manjira, in short strophic cycles at moderate walking tempo with nasal, high-tessitura, heavily portamento-laden delivery.
items.description: Bhojpuri lok geet is the pre-commercial folk song tradition of the Bhojpuri region of eastern India, organised around agricultural seasons (kajri for the monsoon, chaita for spring) and household ritual (sohar for birth, vivah geet for weddings), plus the male narrative form birha. Texture is thin and drone-anchored: dholak or naal keeping a tight kaharwa or dadra cycle, harmonium sustaining a tonic, and unison female voices in a narrow, ornamented, strongly portamento range. It differs from Bhojpuri pop, its commercial descendant, in having no fixed authorship, no electronic backing and no double-entendre hook economy, and from Hindustani classical in its short strophic cycles and absence of raga elaboration.

items.name: Pop Sunda
items.lineage: West Javanese popular song formalised in Bandung from the late 1970s by Nano Suratno and the Detty Kurnia and Nining Meida recordings, and mass-marketed on cassette through the 1980s-90s — Sundanese-language verse over kacapi zither and suling flute lines in pelog degung, kendang drumming articulating the phrase endings, with electric bass, drum machine or kit and sheet synth pads, sung in a high, fluid, sliding female register carried straight over from tembang Sunda.
items.description: Pop Sunda is the West Javanese regional pop that grafts Sundanese classical material — kacapi-suling texture, degung pelog tuning, and the ornamented tembang Sunda vocal line — onto a cassette-era pop arrangement of bass, drums and synthesizer. It flourished from the late 1970s through the 1990s in Bandung, sold overwhelmingly on regional cassette rather than national release, and kept Sundanese as its language of performance. Against Indonesian dangdut it is slower and less percussive with no tabla-derived gendang hook, and against gamelan degung proper it accepts equal-tempered synth harmony behind the pelog melody.

items.name: Ragini (Hindustani feminine-mode repertoire)
items.lineage: The feminine-consort modes of the North Indian ragamala system, systematised in the medieval raga-ragini classifications and painted in the Rajput and Pahari ragamala albums from the sixteenth century, and surviving in performance through gharana khayal and dhrupad treatments of Todi, Asavari, Bhairavi, Gauri and Malkauns's consorts — slow unmetered alap over tanpura drone, then a bandish in vilambit and drut laya on tabla, with sarangi or sitar shadowing a heavily meend- and gamak-inflected vocal line.
items.description: Ragini names the feminine modes paired with the male ragas in the medieval North Indian raga-ragini iconographic system, each carrying a fixed pictorial and emotional program alongside its scale, phrase set and prescribed hour. In performance the raginis are realised in ordinary Hindustani fashion — free-time alap unfolding the mode over a tanpura drone, then a composed bandish cycled through slow and fast tala with tabla and sarangi accompaniment — but the repertoire is bound to the ragamala painting tradition and to characteristically plaintive modes such as Asavari, Todi and Bhairavi. It differs from mainstream khayal practice in being a classificatory and iconographic frame rather than a performance format, and from Carnatic melakarta theory in resting on affective pairing and imagery rather than combinatorial scale derivation.

items.name: Arrocha
items.lineage: Bahian romantic dance song that emerged in Itabuna and Salvador around 1999-2003 through Zé Maria, Silvano Sales and the Pagode/brega circuit — slow to mid-tempo 4/4 at roughly 75-100 BPM with a lurching offbeat keyboard-and-bass push, cheap romantic synth strings and organ, clean guitar arpeggios, programmed drums, and an unadorned, sob-inflected male lead voice singing plain-spoken heartbreak lyrics for close partner dancing.
items.description: Arrocha formed in southern Bahia around 2000 as a slow, sentimental offshoot of brega and pagode baiano, named for the tight 'squeeze' of the couple dance it accompanies. Its arrangements are deliberately cheap and keyboard-forward — preset string and organ patches, a dragging offbeat bass-and-chord push, programmed drums, sparse clean guitar — under a frank, tearful male vocal that avoids melisma. It is slower and more balladic than the later arrochadeira and batidão, and unlike sertanejo universitário it keeps a Northeastern working-class circuit, low-budget production and an explicit dance function rather than an FM-radio sheen.

items.name: Batidão Romântico
items.lineage: Bahian and Northeastern romantic dance pop consolidated around 2014-2018 by Léo Santana, Tayrone and Unha Pintada out of arrocha and pisadinha — mid-tempo 4/4 at about 100-115 BPM built on a programmed, heavily quantised kick-and-clap 'batidão' with a bouncing synth-bass, accordion or accordion-sampled hooks, glossy pad and pluck patches, and a smooth belted male lead with layered gang-vocal responses on the chorus.
items.description: Batidão romântico is the streaming-era, high-gloss descendant of arrocha and pisadinha that broke nationally in Brazil in the mid-2010s. It keeps arrocha's romantic lyric register and couple-dance function but replaces the lurching keyboard shuffle with a hard-quantised programmed 'batidão' — punchy kick, layered claps, a springy synth bass and sampled accordion motifs — mastered loud for phone playback and released as short singles and live-DVD cuts. Against pisadinha it is slower and more sung than danced, and against sertanejo universitário it is Northeastern in accent, accordion-led rather than guitar-led, and fully programmed rather than band-tracked.

items.name: Brega Funk
items.lineage: Recife hybrid formed around 2015-2018 by Shevchenko e Elloco, MC Troia and Japãozin, fusing Pernambucan brega with Rio funk — 128-135 BPM tamborzão-derived programmed beat with a swung, off-grid snare, cheap sampled brass and synth stabs, deep 808 sub, and rapid-fire half-sung MC delivery over two- or four-bar loops, choreographed for viral passinho dance videos.
items.description: Brega funk is the Recife strain of Brazilian funk that surfaced in the mid-2010s and went national around 2019, welding the melodic sentimentality and sampled-brass gestures of Pernambucan brega onto the tamborzão beat grid of Rio funk. The beat sits at roughly 130 BPM with a distinctly swung, dragging snare, huge sub-bass and short looping synth or brass hooks, over MCs who alternate sung hooks with fast spoken verses. It is slower and more melodic than funk mandelão, more brass- and chord-driven than funk 150, and unlike Bahian arrocha it is beat-first dance music built for social-media choreography.
exemplars: MC Loma e As Gêmeas Lacração

items.name: Funk Mandelão
items.lineage: São Paulo periphery funk subgenre codified around 2020-2022 by DJ Arana, DJ Ws da Igrejinha and DJ Guh Mix — 130-140 BPM tracks built from a hard-clipped, deliberately distorted kick, dry gunshot-like snare and rapid triplet hat rolls, sirens, pitched vocal chops and cut-up MC ad-libs, arranged as long unresolved loops with abrupt drops and no harmonic movement, mixed to overload on phone speakers.
items.description: Funk mandelão is the São Paulo periphery style that took over Brazilian funk around 2020, named after the Mandela favela complex and defined by extreme, intentional distortion. Producers overdrive the kick and bass into clipping, strip away melody almost entirely, and build long hypnotic loops from siren stabs, pitched vocal fragments and repeated MC shouts, with drops that arrive without harmonic preparation. Compared with funk carioca's tamborzão and brega funk's melodic hooks, mandelão is harsher, more minimal and more percussion-only, and it circulates natively through short vertical video rather than DJ sets.

items.name: Funk Capixaba
items.lineage: Espírito Santo regional funk from Vitória and Serra, taking shape from about 2018 through DJ Deivinho ES and local Vila Velha producers — mid-130s BPM tracks over a dry, heavily gated kick-clap pattern with rimshot-driven off-beats, low-passed sub, sparse pitched sirens and looped erotic or provocative MC hooks, often released as long DJ-mixed 'set' files rather than discrete singles.
items.description: Funk capixaba is the Espírito Santo regional dialect of Brazilian funk, developed in the Vitória metropolitan area from the late 2010s and spread through DJ set files and social video rather than label singles. Its beats are drier and more spacious than São Paulo mandelão — gated kicks and claps with rimshot accents, minimal melodic content and a strong low-passed sub — while MC hooks are short, repeated and often deliberately transgressive. It sits between funk carioca's syncopation and mandelão's distortion, sharing the loop economy of both but keeping a cleaner, less clipped mix.

items.name: Funk MTG (Montagem)
items.lineage: Producer-driven Brazilian funk edit form crystallised online from 2019 onward through Zetaphunk, DJ Miller and the Brazilian phonk-adjacent SoundCloud scene — 130-160 BPM 'montagem' collages that rapid-cut a single sampled vocal or melodic fragment into stuttered rhythmic patterns over the tamborzão or mandelão kick, using heavy pitch-shifting, reverse hits, sudden filter sweeps and abrupt tempo or key jumps within one track.
items.description: Funk MTG, short for montagem, is the editing-centred wing of Brazilian funk that grew out of bedroom producers on SoundCloud and YouTube from around 2019 and became a global internet style through its overlap with Brazilian phonk. The music is defined by its cut technique rather than its beat: one sampled voice or riff is chopped into machine-gun stutters, pitched up and down, reversed and filtered, over a mandelão or tamborzão kick pattern, with structural jump-cuts replacing arrangement. Unlike brega funk or funk melody there is often no MC performance at all, and unlike mandelão the interest lies in sample manipulation rather than distortion pressure.

items.name: Mega Funk
items.lineage: Southern Brazilian car-sound-system style developed in Santa Catarina and Rio Grande do Sul from the early 2010s by DJ Cleber Mix, DJ Bilb and DJ Cassula — 130-135 BPM tracks that lay a four-on-the-floor electro-house kick and sidechained bass under funk carioca vocal samples and Eurodance or pop melodic hooks, arranged as long continuous mixes with build-and-drop structure tuned for loud automotive subwoofers.
items.description: Mega funk is the southern Brazilian variant of funk built for car audio competitions and long mixed sets, established in Santa Catarina and Rio Grande do Sul in the early 2010s. It abandons the syncopated tamborzão for a straight electro-house four-on-the-floor kick with pumping sidechained bass, then drops funk carioca vocal samples and bright Eurodance-style lead hooks on top, mastered for extreme low-end output. That four-on-the-floor foundation and its EDM build-and-drop arrangement are exactly what separate it from Rio funk, mandelão and brega funk, all of which keep a broken, syncopated beat.

items.name: Funk Melody
items.lineage: Rio de Janeiro melodic funk of the early-to-mid 1990s, codified by Latino, Copacabana Beat, Claudinho e Buchecha and the Furacão 2000 sound system — 100-115 BPM Miami-bass-derived programmed beats with long 808 sub decay, sweet major-key synth pads and bell leads, and sung romantic Portuguese hooks in duet or falsetto rather than shouted chants, arranged in verse-chorus pop form for radio.
items.description: Funk melody is the romantic, sung branch of Rio funk that dominated Brazilian radio in the first half of the 1990s, built directly on imported Miami bass records and freestyle production. Its beats are slower and softer than later funk carioca, with long sub-bass tails, warm major-key pad and bell synthesis, and full verse-chorus songs about love rather than favela reportage, frequently delivered as male duets. It is the direct ancestor of funk ostentação and brega funk's melodic side, and it is distinguished from tamborzão-era funk carioca by its slower tempo, harmonic content and complete absence of the aggressive chanted MC style.

items.name: Roda de Samba
items.lineage: The informal urban circle-session format of Rio de Janeiro samba, running from the 1920s Estácio and Praça Onze quintal gatherings through the 1980s Cacique de Ramos and Fundo de Quintal revival, in which players sit around a table at 90-110 BPM with cavaquinho and violão de sete cordas trading harmony, pandeiro, tantã and repique de mão supplying the groove, and singers cycling repertoire in shared chorus.
items.description: The roda de samba is a participatory table-circle session rather than a repertoire, the social form in which Rio samba is transmitted and from which pagode emerged in the 1980s. Its sound is mid-tempo and conversational: hand-drum percussion (pandeiro, tantã, repique de mão) instead of a bateria, seventh-string violão walking basslines under cavaquinho comping, and everyone present joining the refrain. It is quieter, more harmonically detailed and more improvisatory than samba-enredo, and urban and instrumentally richer than Bahian samba de roda.

items.name: Partido-Alto
items.lineage: Rio de Janeiro samba subgenre of Afro-Bahian descent that crystallized in the morro communities in the 1930s-70s, built on a fixed responsorial refrain answered by improvised sung verses (partido-alto improvisation duels), a syncopated pandeiro-and-hand-percussion clave, and cavaquinho/violão accompaniment at around 100 BPM, codified in recordings by Candeia, Martinho da Vila and Wilson Moreira.
items.description: Partido-alto is the improvised-verse branch of Rio samba, in which a short collective refrain alternates with extemporized solo couplets, often competitive and satirical. Musically it is marked by its distinctive syncopated pandeiro pattern and a lean, hand-percussion-plus-cavaquinho texture at relaxed tempo. What separates it from the roda de samba generally is the formal improvisation contest at its center, and from samba-enredo its complete refusal of a fixed composed narrative.

items.name: Jovem Guarda
items.lineage: Brazilian rock-and-roll-derived pop movement launched by the São Paulo TV Record program Jovem Guarda (1965-1968) and led by Roberto Carlos, Erasmo Carlos and Wanderléa, translating Anglo-American beat and rockabilly into Portuguese with clean single-coil electric guitar, simple electric bass and drum-kit backbeat at 110-140 BPM, ié-ié teen-romance lyrics and light reverbed baritone-tenor lead vocals.
items.description: Jovem Guarda was Brazil's mid-1960s teen-pop wave, built around a weekly São Paulo television show and the songwriting partnership of Roberto and Erasmo Carlos. Its records use a small beat-group lineup — twangy clean electric guitar, electric bass, kit with tambourine, occasional combo organ — behind smooth Portuguese-language romantic vocals cut to valve-console tape. It is distinguished from contemporaneous Tropicália by its deliberate simplicity and apolitical romance, and from later Brazilian rock by its rockabilly and Italian-ballad ancestry rather than blues or punk.

items.name: Forró de Favela (forró eletrônico das periferias)
items.lineage: Peripheral-urban electronic forró that took shape in Rio and Northeastern favelas and periferias from the 2000s onward, built in home DAW setups on programmed baião and arrasta-pé patterns at 130-150 BPM with sampled zabumba and triangle, sub-heavy synthesized bass, keyboard-emulated sanfona lines and autotuned melodic-romantic or piseiro-style vocals distributed via WhatsApp and streaming rather than label release.
items.description: Forró de favela is the bedroom-produced, periphery-circulated electronic branch of forró that overlaps with piseiro and forró eletrônico. Zabumba and triangle survive as samples or keyboard patches over 808-derived sub bass, accordion is usually a synthesized emulation, and vocals carry heavy pitch correction and slapback. Against forró tradicional it is fully studio-constructed and loudness-maximized for phone playback; against baile funk it keeps the baião bass-on-the-downbeat feel and accordion melodic identity.

items.name: Forró Gospel
items.lineage: Evangelical adaptation of Northeastern forró that spread through Brazilian Assembleia de Deus and neo-Pentecostal congregations from the 1990s onward, keeping the sanfona-zabumba-triângulo baião and xote rhythms and their tempos while replacing romantic and drinking lyrics with louvor texts, adding electric bass, kit and congregational chorus, and recording in church-affiliated studios for cassette and later digital distribution.
items.description: Forró gospel carries the baião and xote of Northeastern Brazil into Pentecostal worship, retaining accordion, zabumba and triangle while adding a modern rhythm section and a responsorial congregational chorus. Recordings are made in church-attached rooms with dynamic vocal mics and direct-injected bass, mixed for loud PA playback. It is separated from forró tradicional by lyric function and the presence of drum kit and electric guitar, and from mainstream Brazilian louvor by its explicitly regional Northeastern rhythmic base.

items.name: Carimbó (Pará Amazonian carimbó)
items.lineage: Afro-indigenous round dance of coastal Pará in Brazilian Amazonia, named for the curimbó log drum straddled and hand-struck by the player, documented in Marapanim and Salvaterra and professionalized on record in the 1960s-70s by Pinduca and Verequete — fast duple pulse around 120-140 BPM with two curimbós, maracas, banjo or guitar, transverse flute or clarinet and short responsorial verses.
items.description: Carimbó is the round dance of coastal Pará, built on paired curimbó log drums played by seated hand-strikers, with maraca, plucked string accompaniment and a wind lead over short call-and-response verses. Recorded commercially from the late 1960s in Belém, it acquired guitar, sax and kit and fed directly into lambada in the 1980s. It differs from Northeastern coco in its Amazonian log-drum timbre and melodic wind lines, and from samba in its flat duple pulse rather than teleco-teco syncopation.

items.name: Aboio de Vaqueiro (Brazilian cattle-herder call-song)
items.lineage: Unaccompanied cattle-driving vocal genre of the Brazilian sertão — Ceará, Pernambuco, Bahia and Piauí — sung by vaqueiros to move and calm herds, documented from the colonial period and recorded ethnographically from the mid-20th century: free-meter melismatic aboio on open vowels and long descending glissandi, mixolydian and neutral-third inflections, and rhymed toada verses about drought, cattle and the leather-clad rider, sometimes answered by the herd's bells.
items.description: The aboio de vaqueiro is the herding call of the Brazilian sertão: a solo, unmetered, largely wordless vocal line sung on open vowels with long falling portamento and microtonally shaded thirds, functionally addressed to cattle rather than an audience. When it moves toward song it becomes the toada de vaqueiro, occasionally accompanied by viola. Unlike coco or forró it has no fixed pulse and no percussion, and unlike the cantoria repente duel it is not competitive or metrically bound.

items.name: Viola Caipira (música caipira, moda de viola)
items.lineage: Rural song tradition of the São Paulo, Minas Gerais, Goiás and Paraná interior, carried on the ten-string viola caipira in cebolão and rio-abaixo tunings and first commercially recorded in 1929 by Cornélio Pires, built on parallel-third duet singing (dupla caipira) in slow moda de viola and mid-tempo cateretê and cururu, with fingerpicked ponteado lines and unadorned nasal chest vocals.
items.description: Música caipira is the rural interior tradition of southeastern Brazil, centered on the ten-string viola caipira and on paired voices singing in near-constant parallel thirds. Its core forms are the long narrative moda de viola, sung almost without percussion, and the danced cateretê and cururu. It is the direct ancestor of commercial sertanejo but keeps open viola tunings, ponteado fingerpicking and rough unpolished dupla harmony where sertanejo substitutes guitars, kit and studio gloss.

items.name: Rock Caipira
items.lineage: Brazilian interior fusion emerging in the 1980s-90s in São Paulo, Minas and the Center-West, setting viola caipira tunings, moda de viola melodies and dupla third-singing against a distorted electric-guitar rock rhythm section, popularized by Almir Sater's crossover work and by bands blending cateretê and pagode-de-viola rhythms with 4/4 rock backbeat at 110-140 BPM.
items.description: Rock caipira grafts the ten-string viola caipira and the rural moda repertoire of interior Brazil onto an amplified rock band. Records keep the open viola tunings and parallel-third dupla singing but add distorted electric guitar, electric bass and kit backbeat, sometimes with slide or pedal steel. It is louder and more harmonically conventional than música caipira, and distinguished from mainstream sertanejo universitário by keeping the viola audible as a lead voice rather than as decoration.

items.name: Lambadão (Cuiabá)
items.lineage: Mato Grosso dance music consolidated in Cuiabá in the 1990s-2000s from lambada and the local siriri/cururu tradition — 120-140 BPM in 4/4, built on a tremolo- and delay-drenched electric lead guitar answering the vocal, programmed drum-machine kit with hard timbale fills, keyboard brass stabs, and shouted call-and-response over a bass-heavy sound-system mix.
items.description: Lambadão is the dance music of Cuiabá and the Mato Grosso interior, an inland offshoot of Pará lambada that hardened in the 1990s around cheap home studios and neighbourhood sound systems. The lead electric guitar, soaked in tremolo and slapback delay, carries the melodic identity while the rhythm section is entirely programmed and mixed for sub-bass reinforcement outdoors. It is faster and more guitar-fronted than Belém's tecnobrega and less percussion-layered than carimbó.

items.name: Paracaná (batidão paraense)
items.lineage: Belém do Pará sound-system dance style of the 2000s named for the group Paracanã, fusing carimbó and lambada figures with tecnobrega production — 140-160 BPM in 4/4, a hammered programmed tom-and-kick batidão, sampled cuíca and whistle hits, chanted unison refrains, and MC exhortations tracked straight to DAW for aparelhagem playback.
items.description: Paracaná names both a Belém band and the hyper-fast batidão dance style it popularised in the Amazonian Pará capital during the 2000s. Production is entirely in-the-box and deliberately loud and clipped, with a relentless tom-driven pattern, sampled Afro-Brazilian percussion timbres and chanted crowd refrains designed to carry over the towering aparelhagem rigs. It runs markedly faster and more percussive than romantic tecnobrega, which shares its studios but favours sustained synth pads and sung melody.

items.name: Bloco afro (Salvador carnival)
items.lineage: Salvador da Bahia carnival percussion movement launched by Ilê Aiyê in 1974 and reshaped by Olodum's samba-reggae in the mid-1980s under Neguinho do Samba — massed surdos in three tuned voices playing a displaced reggae-derived bass pattern under repique lead calls, snapping caixas and tamborim breaks at roughly 100 BPM, with unison black-consciousness refrains sung over the top while marching.
items.description: The blocos afro arose in 1970s Salvador as explicitly Afro-Brazilian carnival organisations barred from and rejecting the white-dominated clubs. Their sonic invention was samba-reggae: surdos tuned in registers and struck in a syncopated interlock that suggests a one-drop, cut by repique calls and tamborim viradas, all far heavier and slower than a Rio bateria. Where Rio's escolas foreground a sung enredo with cavaquinho harmony, the bloco afro is almost purely percussion plus chanted refrain.

items.name: Violão brasileiro (solo Brazilian guitar)
items.lineage: Brazilian art-of-the-guitar tradition running from turn-of-the-century Rio choro accompanists through Villa-Lobos's 1920s-40s Chôros and Études, Dilermando Reis's romantic valsas, Garoto's harmonically advanced 1940s pieces and Baden Powell's Afro-Bahian 1960s writing — nylon strings played fingerstyle with an independent bass thumb, the seven-string violão adding a low B for contrapuntal baixaria lines under syncopated 2/4 choro and waltz forms.
items.description: The Brazilian solo guitar tradition sits between concert repertoire and popular practice: its players read and compose but derive their language from choro accompaniment and its running baixaria bass lines. Characteristic sound is warm nylon fingerstyle with a strongly independent thumb, dense chromatically voiced chords and rubato phrasing, often on a seven-string instrument whose added low B extends the counterpoint. It is distinguished from Spanish classical guitar by its syncopated Brazilian rhythmic vocabulary and from bossa nova by being instrumental and contrapuntal rather than sung over a strummed batida.

items.name: Sanfona nordestina (Brazilian accordion tradition)
items.lineage: Accordion tradition of the Brazilian Northeast, moving from the eight-bass pé-de-bode to the 120-bass sanfona and codified nationally by Luiz Gonzaga from 1946 — right-hand melody in bellows-articulated thirds and sixths over left-hand bass-chord alternation, locked to the zabumba's low-and-muffled beat one and the triangle's continuous sixteenths at 100-140 BPM across baião, xote, xaxado and arrasta-pé.
items.description: The sanfona is the defining melodic instrument of northeastern Brazil, carried from rural forró dances into national popular music by Luiz Gonzaga's postwar recordings. Its idiom is bellows-punched parallel thirds over a rocking left-hand bass, sitting in the classic trio with zabumba — struck with a mallet on the beat and a thin bacalhau stick underneath — and steel triangle. Compared with Argentine chamamé accordion it is duple-metered and far more percussion-locked, and unlike the Colombian vallenato accordion it favours modal, raised-fourth northeastern scales.

items.name: Tecnobrega (Belém aparelhagem style)
items.lineage: Belém do Pará electronic style formed around 2002 in bedroom studios and the aparelhagem sound-system circuit, codified by producers such as DJ Waldo Squash and Beto Metralha — 130-150 BPM 4/4 built from cracked-software drum machines, cheap FM keyboard leads, melodic hooks lifted from calypso and 1980s brega ballads, heavily sidechained bass, and pitched or filtered vocal chants distributed free on CD-R and pen drive.
items.description: Tecnobrega is the fully digital 2000s reworking of Pará's romantic brega, made on pirated software and circulated outside the record industry through sound-system parties and street CD vendors. Its palette is unashamedly cheap: preset FM leads, canned drum machines, sidechain pumping and sung or MC'd Portuguese hooks recycled from older brega and Caribbean calypso melodies. It is more melodic and mid-tempo than the paracaná batidão and far more synthetic than the guitar-led brega paraense it descends from.

items.name: Brega romântico (1970s-80s Brazilian romantic brega)
items.lineage: Working-class Brazilian romantic popular song of the 1970s and 80s, dismissed as brega ('tacky') by the MPB press and carried by Odair José, Reginaldo Rossi and Amado Batista on regional labels such as Rozenblit and Continental — slow 4/4 boleros and rock-tinged ballads at 60-80 BPM with sustained string or organ pads, clean arpeggiated electric guitar, and an unironically declamatory tenor delivering plainspoken lyrics of infidelity and poverty.
items.description: Brega romântico is the sentimental mass-market Brazilian song of the 1970s and 80s, made for jukeboxes, AM radio and provincial dance halls rather than the critic-approved MPB market. Arrangements are ballad-tempo with bolero or slow-rock feel, organ or string pads, restrained clean guitar and a foregrounded, emotionally unguarded lead vocal singing frankly about sex, drink and being poor. It differs from the contemporaneous jovem guarda in its explicitly lower-class address, and from later Pará brega in its national studio production and lack of a lead-guitar signature.

items.name: Brega saudade (slow nostalgic Belém brega)
items.lineage: Slow, nostalgic subgenre of Pará brega that consolidated in Belém in the 2000s-2010s at aparelhagem 'melody' hours and on brega-saudade radio programmes — 90-110 BPM 4/4 with a swaying tecnobrega kick, soft sustained synth pads and reverb-washed FM bell leads, sampled 1980s Caribbean and brega melodies, and a plaintive lead vocal drenched in long-tail digital reverb and delay.
items.description: Brega saudade is the slow, wistful wing of Belém's brega ecosystem, played late in aparelhagem sets and on dedicated nostalgia radio blocks. Production keeps tecnobrega's digital means but drops the tempo, foregrounding wide reverberant pads, glassy FM bell leads and a lonely reverb-soaked vocal, often quoting melodies from 1980s Caribbean and older brega records. It is distinguished from mainstream tecnobrega by tempo and mood and from 1970s brega romântico by being wholly synthetic and produced on laptops rather than by a studio band.

items.name: Brega paraense (guitar-led Pará brega)
items.lineage: Guitar-driven brega of Belém and the Pará interior, formed in the 1970s-90s around Vieira, Teddy Max and Pinduca and the region's Caribbean radio reception — 100-130 BPM 4/4 lambada-and-merengue-inflected beats with a bright, tremolo- and chorus-treated single-coil lead guitar that answers every vocal phrase, cavaquinho or keyboard comping, congas and shaker, and a high, clipped tenor lead.
items.description: Brega paraense is the Amazonian branch of Brazilian brega, shaped as much by Guyanese, Antillean and Caribbean signals reaching Belém radio as by southern Brazilian pop. Its signature is the lead electric guitar — bright single-coil tone with tremolo and chorus, phrased in fast answering runs between vocal lines — riding lambada and merengue-derived beats with congas and shaker. It is livelier and more dance-oriented than the ballad-centred brega romântico of the Northeast and Southeast, and it supplies the melodic vocabulary that tecnobrega later sampled wholesale.

items.name: Nova Música Pernambucana
items.lineage: Recife/Olinda scene of the late 1990s–2000s that followed manguebeat, codified by Mestre Ambrósio, Cordel do Fogo Encantado, Silvério Pessoa and Otto — rabeca-and-zabumba-led maracatu, coco and forró rhythms (2/4 baião and 4/4 maracatu de baque virado at 100–130 BPM) recombined with electric guitar, sampler loops and declamatory or chanted northeastern vocals.
items.description: A Pernambuco scene that emerged in Recife and Olinda in the wake of manguebeat during the late 1990s, taking rural rhythms — maracatu de baque virado, coco, ciranda, cavalo-marinho — into rock and studio production. Rabeca, zabumba and alfaia carry the groove under electric guitar and loops, with vocals delivered as chant, repente-style recitation or shouted refrain. It differs from manguebeat proper in leaning less on funk/hip-hop breakbeats and more on unmediated sertão and coastal folk repertoire.

items.name: Cumbia amazónica
items.lineage: Peruvian jungle cumbia from Pucallpa, Iquitos and Moyobamba in the late 1960s–1970s, codified by Juaneco y su Combo, Los Mirlos and Los Wemblers de Iquitos — 95–105 BPM cumbia paseo with surf-toned tremolo electric guitar carrying pentatonic-inflected Amazonian melodies over Farfisa organ, timbales, güiro and congas.
items.description: The Amazonian branch of Peruvian cumbia, made in oil-boom river towns from the late 1960s onward. Its signature is a heavily reverbed, tremolo- and wah-treated guitar playing modal riffs drawn from Shipibo and Quechua melodic contours, riding a straight cumbia bass and güiro pulse with Farfisa organ counterlines. It is warmer and more melodically pastoral than coastal Lima chicha, and slower and more guitar-dominated than Colombian cumbia orquestal.

items.name: Cumbia andina mexicana
items.lineage: Mexican reinterpretation of Peruvian and Bolivian cumbia that consolidated in Mexico City and Puebla in the 1980s–1990s through Grupo Kual?, Chico Che sound-system circuits and Los Askis — mid-tempo 90–100 BPM cumbia with quena and zampoña-imitating synth leads, sustained Andean-flavored minor-key melodies and dense electronic percussion.
items.description: A Mexican urban style that absorbed Andean melodic material — panpipe and quena lines, minor-pentatonic tunes — into the cumbia dance format, spreading through Mexico City barrio dances and sonidero circuits from the 1980s. Synthesizers usually stand in for the pipes, and the arrangements are wistful and minor-key over an unvarying cumbia bass-and-güiro pattern. It differs from cumbia sonidera in being a played repertoire rather than a DJ practice, and from Bolivian cumbia in its Mexican vocal phrasing and heavier keyboard sound.

items.name: Cumbia ranchera
items.lineage: Mexican hybrid consolidated in the 1970s–1990s in Monterrey, Guadalajara and the Bajío, codified by Los Bukis, Los Tigres del Norte's cumbia sides and Grupo Bryndis — ranchera and norteño melodic and lyrical style set on a 92–100 BPM cumbia bass-and-güiro groove with accordion or bajo sexto doubling and emotive solo tenor lead.
items.description: Mexican cumbia sung with the vocal manner and sentimental lyric content of ranchera, popular in northern and central Mexico from the 1970s and central to grupero radio. The rhythm section holds a plain cumbia pulse while accordion, bajo sexto or synth brass fill in ranchera-style, and a single male lead sings with the wide-open, aching delivery of the ranchera tradition. It is distinguished from norteño by the cumbia rather than polka/redova rhythm, and from cumbia sonidera by its songwriting-first, radio-oriented shape.

items.name: Cumbia editada
items.lineage: Argentine and Mexican DJ-edit practice of the 2010s, developed by producers such as Douster, Sonido Berzerk and the Buenos Aires digital-cumbia circuit — existing cumbia and sonidera records re-cut in the DAW with time-stretching, beat-quantized loops, added 808 sub-kick, stutter edits and delay throws for club and sound-system play.
items.description: A DJ-producer practice rather than a band style: catalogue cumbia tracks are edited in software into extended, loop-locked club tools with reinforced sub-bass, tightened percussion and dramatic delay and reverb throws. It grew out of sonidero DJ effects culture as those DJs moved from cassette manipulation to laptops in the 2000s and 2010s. Unlike nu-cumbia, which composes new material from samples, cumbia editada keeps the source record intact and audible, restructuring it for the floor.

items.name: Cumbia paraguaya
items.lineage: Paraguayan cumbia developed in Asunción from the 1970s onward, codified by Grupo Generación, Los Ojos Negros and Juan Carlos Oviedo's tropical bands — 95–105 BPM cumbia with Paraguayan harp or synth arpeggios, Guaraní- and Spanish-language lyrics, guarania-derived melodic phrasing and a bright electric-bass-and-güiro core.
items.description: Paraguay's national variant of cumbia, shaped by the country's harp tradition and by guarania melodic sensibility. Rippling arpa paraguaya or keyboard arpeggios sit above a standard cumbia bass pattern, and lyrics move freely between Spanish and Guaraní. It is more melodically ornate and lighter in percussion than Colombian or Argentine cumbia, and unlike cumbia villera carries no marginal-urban lyric stance.

items.name: Cumbia boliviana
items.lineage: Bolivian cumbia of Cochabamba, Santa Cruz and La Paz from the late 1970s, codified by Maroyu, Grupo Néctar's Bolivian antecedents and Los Ronisch — minor-key 90–100 BPM cumbia with charango and zampoña or synth-panpipe leads, huayno-derived melodic cells and a plaintive high male vocal.
items.description: Bolivian cumbia fuses the coastal cumbia dance pattern with Andean highland melody — charango strumming, panpipe or synth leads, and huayno's minor-mode melodic turns. It emerged in Cochabamba and Santa Cruz from the late 1970s and circulated widely on cassette across the altiplano. Compared with Peruvian chicha it foregrounds keyboards and charango rather than surf guitar, and its melancholy vocal register sets it apart from the brighter Colombian tropical sound.

items.name: Cumbia sureña
items.lineage: Southern-cone cumbia of southern Chile and Argentine Patagonia consolidated in the 1990s–2000s around Chiloé, Osorno and Neuquén dance circuits — brisk 100–110 BPM cumbia with brass or synth-brass hooks, accordion, snare-heavy kit and shouted call-and-response choruses for large open-air bailes.
items.description: The cumbia played for mass outdoor dances across southern Chile and Argentine Patagonia, faster and more brass-forward than the northern varieties. Arrangements are built for volume and crowd participation: unison horn or synth-brass riffs, a hard backbeat on the kit, and choruses shouted back by the audience. It is less sentimental than cumbia ranchera and more band-oriented than the DJ-driven sonidera and villera scenes.

items.name: Salsa choke
items.lineage: Afro-Colombian Pacific style from Buenaventura and Cali around 2010, codified by Cali Flow Latino, Míster Black and Kevin Flórez — salsa clave and montuno chopped down to a 95–100 BPM half-time groove with reggaeton dembow underpinning, programmed timbales and hi-hats, shouted hooks and a dance-step call structure.
items.description: A Colombian Pacific-coast hybrid that appeared around 2010 in Buenaventura and Cali, mixing salsa piano montunos and clave with reggaeton and urban-beat programming. Tracks are built in the DAW, run at a heavier, half-time feel than dance salsa, and are organized around chanted dance instructions rather than sung verses. Its clave and horn stabs distinguish it from straight reggaeton, while its programmed rhythm section and lack of a live band separate it from salsa dura and Cali's classic orchestral salsa.

items.name: Salsa urbana
items.lineage: Late-1990s–2010s Puerto Rican and New York studio hybrid, codified by Víctor Manuelle's crossovers, N'Klabe and Marc Anthony's urban collaborations — salsa montuno and mambo sections at 95–105 BPM cut against reggaeton dembow, rap verses, sampled loops and heavily compressed programmed percussion alongside a live rhythm section.
items.description: Salsa reworked for urbano-era radio, in which full horn arrangements, piano montunos and a live percussion section are combined with reggaeton programming, rap features and modern pop mixing. It took shape in San Juan and New York studios from the late 1990s as salsa artists sought crossover with the reggaeton audience. It keeps far more of salsa's harmonic and arranging apparatus than salsa choke, and is glossier and more vocal-led than salsa dura.

items.name: Rumba catalana
items.lineage: Barcelona Gypsy style of the Gràcia and Hostafrancs barrios formed in the late 1950s, codified by Peret and Antonio González 'El Pescaílla' — Cuban guaracha rhythm reworked on flamenco guitar with the ventilador percussive strum, palmas and bongos at 110–130 BPM, plus rasping copla-inflected vocals and short cyclic refrains.
items.description: Rumba catalana was created by Catalan Gitano musicians in Barcelona around 1960, adapting Cuban dance rhythms returning from the Americas to flamenco technique. Its identifying device is the ventilador — a fanning right-hand strum that percusses the guitar top while chording — supported by palmas, bongos and bass, with hoarse, rhythmically clipped singing. It is lighter and more danceable than cante flamenco proper and, unlike Cuban rumba, is guitar-and-song music with a harmonic scheme rather than a drum-battery tradition.

items.name: Boogaloo (Latin boogaloo)
items.lineage: Nuyorican dance style crystallized in East Harlem and the South Bronx between 1965 and 1969 when second-generation Puerto Rican bandleaders fused Afro-Cuban son montuno with black American R&B and soul: mid-tempo 4/4 with a heavy backbeat handclap over a 2-3 clave feel, English and Spanglish shout-chorus vocals, hammered piano montunos, blaring two- or three-horn frontline, and a rhythm section of congas, timbales and electric bass punctuated by party shouts and cowbell.
items.description: A short-lived but decisive New York style of roughly 1965-69 in which young Puerto Rican musicians grafted R&B backbeat, handclaps and English lyrics onto the Cuban son montuno their parents' bands played. The records are deliberately raw — crowd noise, party shouts, unison chorus lines, a percussive piano montuno and a small, loud horn section over congas and timbales — and were aimed at teenage dancers rather than the palladium mambo audience. It differs from the salsa that displaced it in its simpler harmony, its slower tempo, its Anglophone hooks, and its refusal of the arranged sophistication of the charanga and mambo bands.
exemplars: Pete Rodríguez, "I Like It Like That"

items.name: Bolero cubano
items.lineage: Born in Santiago de Cuba in the 1880s with Pepe Sánchez's "Tristezas" and reshaped for radio and the LP in 1940s-50s Havana by Isolina Carrillo, Beny Moré and the filin generation: slow 2/4 with the cinquillo figure in bongó and güiro, arpeggiated guitar or lush piano-and-strings accompaniment, a soloist singing long legato phrases with heavy rubato and portamento, and lyrics of romantic reproach organized in two contrasting sixteen-bar sections.
items.description: The Cuban romantic song form that emerged in eastern Cuba in the 1880s from trova guitar practice and became, through Havana radio and the pre-1959 record industry, the template for slow love song across Latin America. Its rhythmic signature is the cinquillo — a five-stroke 2/4 cell carried by bongó, güiro and the guitar's thumb — under a singer who stretches phrases well behind the beat with wide portamento and open chest tone. Compared with the Mexican bolero it kept the Afro-Cuban percussion audible and the tempo more elastic, and compared with son it abandons the montuno call-and-response for through-sung couplets.

items.name: Nueva canción (pan-Latin American)
items.lineage: Continental movement of politically committed song consolidated between the late 1950s and the early 1970s from Violeta Parra's Chilean folklore collecting, Atahualpa Yupanqui's Argentine criollo guitar, and Uruguayan and Cuban parallels: acoustic guitar or charango with quena, siku and bombo, modal Andean melody in 6/8 or 2/4 huayno feel, unamplified group singing, plain declamatory vocal delivery and long strophic texts of land, labour and repression.
items.description: The Latin American song movement of the 1960s and early 1970s that treated rural and Andean folk material as the vehicle for anti-imperialist and social-justice lyrics, running from Chile and Argentina through Uruguay, Bolivia and Cuba. Recordings favour acoustic textures — nylon guitar, charango, quena and siku, bombo legüero on the strong beats — with clear diction and modest, unmannered singing so that the text stays foremost. It differs from commercial folklórico in its authored, topical lyrics and from urban protest folk in its insistence on indigenous instruments and Andean modal melody.

items.name: Nueva trova chilena
items.lineage: Post-1973 exile and internal-resistance continuation of the Chilean nueva canción, sustained abroad by Quilapayún and Inti-Illimani on European labels and at home by the canto nuevo circuit of the late 1970s: charango, quena, tiple and bombo behind massed male chorus singing in fourths and fifths, cueca-derived 6/8 hemiola alternating with slow tonada, and coded metaphorical lyrics replacing the direct slogans of the Unidad Popular years.
items.description: The strand of Chilean committed song that survived the 1973 coup, split between exiled ensembles recording in Paris, Rome and East Berlin and the domestic canto nuevo scene of peñas and university halls. Musically it is denser and more arranged than the early nueva canción: full Andean wind-and-string batteries, tightly rehearsed male choral writing in open fourths and fifths, and cueca hemiola alternating with slow declamatory tonada. Its lyrics turn allegorical and elegiac where the earlier movement had been declarative, and its recordings are studio-polished European productions rather than local label sessions.

items.name: Canto popular uruguayo
items.lineage: Montevideo song movement of the late 1960s through the 1985 return to democracy, built by Alfredo Zitarrosa, Daniel Viglietti and Los Olimareños on milonga and candombe rather than Andean sources: guitar-led 2/4 milonga ostinato or candombe tamboril patterns behind a grave low-register baritone, spoken-sung recitation, and censorship-evading allusive lyrics carried on long strophic forms.
items.description: Uruguay's own committed-song movement, running from the late 1960s through the 1973-85 dictatorship, when many of its singers worked from exile and its records circulated clandestinely. Its rhythmic identity is Rioplatense rather than Andean: the guitar's driving 2/4 milonga ostinato, and increasingly the chico-repique-piano tamboril pattern of candombe, under a dark, unornamented baritone that often drops into spoken recitation. That candombe underpinning and its milonga guitar figures separate it plainly from the charango-and-quena sound of Chilean and Argentine nueva canción.

items.name: Murga porteña (Buenos Aires carnival murga)
items.lineage: Buenos Aires neighbourhood carnival practice descended from late-nineteenth-century Spanish and Uruguayan murga and revived after the 1983 return of the corsos: dozens of costumed dancers over a percussion line of bombo con platillo, redoblante and cymbals playing the 2/4 marcha camión at roughly 90-110 BPM, with shouted unison canciones de crítica, glosas and retiradas sung by an untrained mass chorus.
items.description: The street-carnival murga of Buenos Aires, performed at neighbourhood corsos by large costumed troupes whose musical engine is the bombo con platillo — a bass drum with a cymbal mounted on top, struck simultaneously — driving the 2/4 marcha camión that the dancers kick to. Vocals are shouted in unison by a whole troupe rather than sung by a trained chorus, with satirical lyrics set to borrowed popular melodies. It is louder, cruder and more dance-driven than the Uruguayan murga across the river, which centres on elaborate arranged choral harmony and a comparatively restrained percussion trio.
exemplars: Los Reyes del Movimiento de Saavedra

items.name: Techengue (Uruguayan cumbia plena)
items.lineage: Montevideo cumbia dialect of the 2000s-2010s grown out of Uruguayan plena and cumbia villera in the barrios and marginal-neighbourhood sound systems: 4/4 cumbia at roughly 95-105 BPM built on a hard synthetic kick-and-güira pattern, cheap sampled brass and organ stabs, MIDI accordion and timbale fills, and gang-chanted refrains delivered in raspy street register over minimal two-chord loops.
items.description: A Uruguayan variant of cumbia developed in Montevideo's working-class barrios in the 2000s, sitting between the local plena tradition and Argentine cumbia villera. Productions are made almost entirely in the box: hard programmed kick, scraped güira sixteenths, cheap sampled brass and organ hits, and an accordion patch over a two-chord loop, with shouted collective refrains and rough solo vocals recorded on modest home rigs. It is faster and drier than Colombian cumbia and less rock-inflected than cumbia villera, and its identifying feature is the plena-derived percussive kick-and-scrape pulse that gives the style its name.

items.name: RKT (Argentine reggaetón-cumbia)
items.lineage: Buenos Aires conurbano style named for the "rikitiki" pattern, produced from roughly 2016 by DJ Alex, DJ Tao and Perreo Circuit and popularised by L-Gante's Cumbia 420 crossover: 95-105 BPM fusion of the reggaetón dembow snare with cumbia güira and organ, hard 808 sub, minor two- or three-chord synth loops, DJ tag drops, and half-sung half-rapped local slang vocals heavy with autotune, released to YouTube and streaming rather than to labels.
items.description: An Argentine bedroom-producer style of the late 2010s that welds the reggaetón dembow to cumbia's güira scrape and cheap organ stabs, named onomatopoeically after its rikitiki rhythmic cell. Tracks are short, loop-based and sub-heavy, tagged with the producer's shouted DJ drop, and carry heavily autotuned vocals in conurbano slang trading between singing and rapping. It is distinguished from Puerto Rican reggaetón by the cumbia keyboard and güira layer and from cumbia villera by its 808 low end, its rapped delivery, and its native-to-streaming production and distribution.

items.name: Folklore surero (Argentine pampa)
items.lineage: Song tradition of the Buenos Aires and La Pampa plains, consolidated in the late nineteenth century among gauchos and given literary form by payadores such as Gabino Ezeiza and later by José Larralde and Argentino Luna, centred on the slow milonga campera in duple 3-3-2 ostinato, the estilo with its free-tempo opening and measured cifra middle section, and the improvised payada de contrapunto — all sung in a low declamatory baritone over a single guitar picking bass-and-chord punteo.
items.description: Folklore surero is the guitar-and-voice tradition of the flat southern pampas, dominated by milonga campera, estilo and the improvised payada rather than by the dance forms of the northwest. Texture is austere: one voice, one guitar, no percussion, the milonga's habanera-derived 3-3-2 bass carrying the pulse while long narrative texts about rural labour and dispossession unfold in near-speech. It differs from the northwestern folklores in its absence of bombo, its lower tessitura and its literary, sometimes overtly political payador lineage.

items.name: Folclore salteño
items.lineage: Regional folklore of Salta province in Argentina's northwest, professionalised from the 1940s-50s by Los Chalchaleros, Eduardo Falú and the poet Manuel J. Castilla, whose repertoire centres on the slow 6/8 zamba with its rubato pañuelo phrasing, the fast chacarera and the bagualas of the valleys sung with caja over a major-triad three-note scale, scored for close male four-part vocal harmony with two or three guitars, bombo legüero and occasional erke or quena colour.
items.description: The Salta variant of Argentine folklore is the most vocally polished of the northwestern regional styles, defined by tight male quartet harmony singing zambas over guitars and bombo. Its signature is the zamba's suspended 6/8, where the melody floats behind the guitar's rasguido and the singers hold long unison lines before splitting into thirds and sixths. Compared with the harder, faster Santiago del Estero repertoire it favours lyricism, sustained cadences and the high-valley baguala's caja-and-shout timbre as a contrasting colour.

items.name: Folclore santiagueño
items.lineage: Folklore of Santiago del Estero, the bilingual Quechua-Spanish province of northern Argentina, carried from rural patios into national repertoire by Andrés Chazarreta from 1906, Los Hermanos Ábalos from 1932 and the Carabajal family thereafter, built on chacarera, escondido and gato in fast 6/8 hemiola with bombo legüero, guitar rasguido, violin doubling and — uniquely — the santiagueño violin and Quichua-language coplas of Sixto Palavecino.
items.description: Santiago del Estero is the acknowledged hearth of chacarera, and its folklore is the most percussive and least urbanised of Argentina's regional traditions, played at rural gatherings where the bombo legüero, clapping and zapateo dominate. Melodies are simple and syllabic, harmony rarely exceeds tonic-dominant, and the persistent 6/8 versus 3/4 ambiguity is treated as the point of the music rather than an ornament. The province's Quichua substrate produces bilingual coplas found nowhere else in the country.

items.name: Folclore jujeño
items.lineage: Andean-facing folklore of Jujuy province on the Argentine puna and Quebrada de Humahuaca, documented from the early twentieth century and popularised by Ricardo Vilca and Tomás Lipán, centred on the fast duple carnavalito danced in a chain with siku, quena and charango, the copla sung solo to the square caja frame drum on a narrow three-note tritonic scale, and the reed erke and erkencho sounding at carnival in February.
items.description: Jujuy's folklore belongs musically to the Andean highlands rather than to the guitar-and-bombo world of the Argentine lowlands, sharing repertoire and instruments with Bolivia across the border. Carnavalito supplies bright pentatonic panpipe-and-quena melodies over a trotting 2/4 bombo, while the coplera tradition sets solitary women's voices against the caja in an open-throated, high, non-vibrato cry. What separates it from neighbouring Salta is the near-absence of zamba and the presence of seasonal ritual instruments tied to carnival and the Pachamama cycle.

items.name: Folclore tucumano
items.lineage: Folklore of Tucumán in Argentina's sugar-growing northwest, given national form by Atahualpa Yupanqui from the 1930s and by Mercedes Sosa and the Nuevo Cancionero manifesto issued in nearby Mendoza in 1963, dominated by the zamba in slow 6/8 with rubato guitar rasguido and a lyric-tenor or contralto lead, alongside chacarera and the vidala sung in unison to caja over a minor-inflected melody at the pace of a walking step.
