The 1980s Yaoundé version transposes the balafon figure onto a thin, wiry, tremolo-picked guitar and drives it with floor-tom-heavy kit at very high tempo. Compared to Cameroon's other export, makossa, bikutsi is faster, in compound meter, harmonically static and rougher-edged rather than smooth and 4/4.

items.name: Semba
items.lineage: Luanda's urban Angolan dance music codified in the musseques between the late 1950s and 1975 by Bonga, Ngola Ritmos, Os Kiezos and David Zé — 100-120 BPM in a two-feel with a snapping snare-and-rim accent, dikanza scraper and interlocking nylon-and-electric guitar counterpoint under raspy Kimbundu lead vocals whose lyrics carried nationalist and street commentary.
items.description: Semba is the parent urban style of Luanda, consolidated in the shanty districts during the late colonial period and inseparable from Angolan independence-era song. Its signature is a lilting two-feel with the dikanza scraper marking every subdivision, twinned guitars trading arpeggiated lines, and a hoarse, conversational Kimbundu vocal. It is drier and more guitar-conversational than Congolese rumba next door, and far more percussive and up-tempo than the kizomba that descended from it.

items.name: Funaná
items.lineage: Santiago island Cape Verdean dance music, long rural and suppressed under Portuguese rule, brought into the electrified national repertoire after 1975 by Bulimundo, Finaçon and Ferro Gaita — built on a diatonic gaita accordion riff over a relentless ferrinho iron-scraper pulse at 120-160 BPM, with a two-beat bass and shouted Kriolu verses alternating strophic narrative and refrain.
items.description: Funaná is the accordion-and-scraper dance music of Santiago, Cape Verde, a rural badiu tradition that colonial authorities marginalised and that became a symbol of post-independence national identity in the late 1970s and 1980s. Two instruments define it: the gaita accordion pumping a short cyclic riff and the ferrinho scraped with a knife on every eighth, producing a rasping, breathless drive. It is the hot counterweight to Cape Verde's slow morna and coladeira, sharing their Kriolu language but almost none of their melancholy or harmonic subtlety.

items.name: Urban Kiz
items.lineage: Lisbon and Paris Angolan-diaspora dance and production style that split from kizomba around 2012-2014 through DJs and producers such as Nelson Freitas' circle, Dj Ricardo Ribeiro and Ateliê da Kizomba — 80-95 BPM with a stiffened, near-halftime kick-and-snare grid, long sustained pad chords, filtered sub bass and semi-tone-shifted vocal samples that strip out semba's swing to suit the style's linear, staccato dance footwork.
items.description: Urban kiz is the European diaspora offshoot of kizomba, consolidated in Lisbon and Paris in the mid-2010s as a partner dance with straight, gliding footwork and a matching production aesthetic. The beat is deliberately rigid and uncrowded — a heavy dry kick, a snare on the backbeat, minimal percussion — under wide reverbed pads and cool, often remixed R&B vocal lines. It differs from traditional kizomba and its parent semba by removing the tresillo lilt and the live percussion entirely, and from zouk by its slower tempo and colder, sparser mix.

items.name: Batida (Lisbon Angolan Electronic)
items.lineage: Electronic dance style built in Lisbon's Angolan, Cape Verdean and São Toméan suburbs from the late 2000s and codified by the Príncipe Discos roster — DJ Marfox, Nídia, DJ Nigga Fox, Niagara — running kuduro and tarraxinha rhythms at 130-145 BPM through cheap DAW and FruityLoops workflows into hard, dry, clipped percussion loops, distorted stab synths and abrupt structural cuts with little or no sung vocal.
items.description: Batida is the Lisbon periphery's own electronic music, made on pirated laptop software by producers from Angolan and Cape Verdean families and released internationally from 2011 onward through Príncipe Discos. It keeps kuduro's forward-leaning triplet-against-four percussion but strips melody to a few abrasive synth stabs, favouring raw untreated mixes, sudden silences and sharply gated drums. Where Angolan kuduro is vocal-fronted and shout-driven, batida is largely instrumental, harder and more structurally jagged.

items.name: Sgija
items.lineage: South African township dance strain that surfaced around 2019-2021 in Gauteng out of amapiano and Pretoria's Bacardi house, driven by Felo Le Tee, Mellow & Sleazy, Kabza-adjacent producers and dance crews — 112-118 BPM, dominated by a long pitched log-drum bass figure, dry shaker-and-clap grid, siren-like synth stabs and repeated shouted isiZulu/Sepitori chants rather than sung verses.
items.description: Sgija is the harder, chant-led wing of the amapiano complex, named after a Gauteng dance and consolidated between 2019 and 2021. It leans on the log drum's rolling bass melody and a sparse percussion grid, drops the jazz chords and soulful sung hooks of mainstream amapiano, and puts crowd chants and producer tags in their place. Against gqom it is slower, groovier and log-drum-based rather than built on a hammering minimal 4/4 kick.

items.name: Bolobedu House
items.lineage: Limpopo dance style from the Bolobedu region around Tzaneen, popularised nationally from about 2016 by Makhadzi, Master KG, DJ Call Me and Prince Benza — roughly 110-118 BPM, marrying khelobedu-language call-and-response vocals and traditional Balobedu dance rhythms to a four-on-the-floor house kick, bright marimba-like synth riffs, hand claps and shouted group refrains.
items.description: Bolobedu house comes from the Balobedu areas of Limpopo and reached national scale in the late 2010s through Makhadzi and Master KG. It fuses village dance rhythms and Khelobedu-language chanted call-and-response with a straightforward house kick, plus bright plucked or marimba-timbre synth loops and layered group vocals. Compared to amapiano it is faster, harder on the downbeat and far more vocal-led, and compared to gqom it is major-key, celebratory and melodic rather than dark and minimal.

items.name: Zilizopendwa
items.lineage: Swahili term ('the beloved ones') for the classic East African dance-band repertoire of Kenya and Tanzania recorded roughly 1965-1985 by Orchestra Maquis Original, Simba Wanyika, Mlimani Park and Les Wanyika — Congolese rumba's guitar-and-horn template slowed to 100-120 BPM, with two or three chiming guitars, a cadenced snare-and-conga groove and smooth paired Swahili harmony vocals opening onto an extended instrumental chorus.
items.description: Zilizopendwa is the retrospective Swahili name for the golden-age East African dance-band records of the 1960s through 1980s, kept alive by Kenyan and Tanzanian radio programmes devoted to the repertoire. Musically it is the Nairobi-and-Dar reworking of Congolese rumba: interlocking clean-toned guitars, restrained horn punctuation, gentle two-part Swahili vocals and a long instrumental section that never reaches soukous' frantic seben. It is softer and slower than Kinshasa rumba and more band-oriented and lyrical than Kenya's Luo benga.

items.name: Benga
items.lineage: Luo guitar-band style of western Kenya and Nairobi codified in the 1960s and 1970s by Daniel Owino Misiani, George Ramogi and the Kabaselleh and Victoria Kings circles — nyatiti lyre plucking patterns transferred to electric guitar in a fast running quaver line at 130-150 BPM over a driving bass, snare-and-hi-hat shuffle and pentatonic paired vocals that give way to a shouted-name instrumental cadenza.
items.description: Benga developed among Luo musicians in western Kenya and Nairobi in the 1960s, translating the nyatiti lyre's fast repeating figures and the orutu fiddle's lines onto electric guitar and bass. Records typically open with tight two-voice pentatonic singing in Dholuo before breaking into a long, galloping guitar-and-bass chase with shouted dedications to patrons. It is markedly faster, brighter and more relentlessly rhythmic than the rumba-derived zilizopendwa bands of Nairobi and Dar es Salaam, and it dispenses almost entirely with horns.

items.name: Ohangla
items.lineage: Luo dance music of Nyanza and Nairobi, Kenya, grown from village ohangla drum ensembles into an electrified nightclub form during the 1990s-2000s and codified by Tony Nyadundo, Osogo Winyo and Prince Indah — 130-160 BPM eight-beat hand-drum battery under fast benga-derived interlocking electric guitar arpeggios, walking bass, thin synth pads and hoarse call-and-response Dholuo praise vocals that name patrons mid-song.
items.description: Ohangla is the Luo dance style of western Kenya that moved from ceremonial drum troupes into amplified club and funeral-night bands from the 1990s onward. Its signature is a bank of hand-struck ohangla drums driving a relentless fast eight-beat while one or two electric guitars trade high interlocking figures and a shouting lead singer improvises praise-naming over cyclic Dholuo choruses. It is faster, more percussion-forward and more vocally abrasive than benga, its immediate parent, and unlike taarab it carries no Arabic modal inflection.

items.name: Kadongo Kamu
items.lineage: Ugandan Luganda-language narrative song style whose name means 'one little guitar', formed in Kampala in the 1960s with Elly Wamala and Fred Masagazi and codified by Christopher Sebaduka, Herman Basudde and Paulo Kafeero — moderate 90-110 BPM rolling guitar arpeggios in a repeated two- or three-chord loop, a light kick-and-shaker groove, and long strophic verses of proverb-laden storytelling delivered in a conversational near-spoken tenor.
items.description: Kadongo kamu emerged in 1960s Kampala as a guitar-and-voice storytelling music sung in Luganda, its name referring to the single guitar that originally carried the whole accompaniment. The texture stays deliberately thin — a looping fingerpicked guitar figure, understated bass and shaker — so that the words, dense with Ganda proverb, social commentary and often bawdy humour, dominate across verses that can run many minutes. It differs from Ugandan kidandali and band-driven Afropop by its slow tempo, narrative length and refusal of dance-floor arrangement, and from West African griot song by having no hereditary caste basis.

items.name: Sungura
items.lineage: Zimbabwean guitar-band dance music formed in Harare in the early 1980s from Congolese rumba-soukous imported by migrant musicians and codified by Ephraim Joe, the Khiama Boys, Nicholas Zakaria, System Tazvida and Alick Macheso — roughly 120-140 BPM with a snare-and-hi-hat kanindo shuffle, three-guitar stratification of lead, rhythm and bass playing rapid triplet-feel runs, and paired Shona vocals over a long instrumental seben break.
items.description: Sungura is Zimbabwe's dominant working-class guitar-band music, built in Harare studios of the 1980s on the chassis of Congolese rumba and Kenyan kanindo but sung in Shona and pitched at a faster, busier tempo. The defining sound is a stack of clean single-coil guitars — a lead playing near-continuous sixteenth-note runs, a rhythm guitar answering, and an unusually melodic bass — over a shuffling hi-hat and shared close-harmony vocals, with the second half of a track given over to an extended dance break. It is faster and denser than soukous, and unlike chimurenga it takes no material from mbira patterns.

items.name: Jit
items.lineage: Zimbabwean fast dance-band style of the late 1970s-1980s associated with the Bhundu Boys, the Four Brothers and Jonah Moyo's Devera Ngwena — 140-170 BPM built on a rapid three-drum village jiti pattern transposed to kit, bright chiming lead guitar lines that transcribe mbira interlocking figures onto strings, walking bass, and high unison Shona vocals in short cyclic refrains.
items.description: Jit, sometimes marketed abroad as jit-jive, is the fast Zimbabwean guitar-band music that took the rural jiti drumming pattern into township dance halls and, via the Bhundu Boys, onto 1980s European stages. Its markers are a sprinting tempo, a treble-bright lead guitar whose repeating figures imitate the interlocking left- and right-hand lines of the mbira, and short high-register vocal refrains rather than long narrative verses. Against sungura it is faster, sparser and more mbira-derived than rumba-derived; against Thomas Mapfumo's chimurenga it is dance-oriented rather than ceremonial and political.

items.name: Zimbabwean Urban Grooves
items.lineage: Zimbabwean youth pop that exploded in Harare after the 2001 broadcasting policy mandating 75 percent local content, made almost entirely on home PCs by producers such as Delani Makhalima and Fortune Muparutsa — 90-105 BPM programmed R&B and dancehall drums, cheap sampled strings and rounded synth bass, Auto-Tuned melisma and rapped bridges, with lyrics code-switching between Shona and English.
items.description: Urban Grooves is the Zimbabwean pop wave of roughly 2001-2010, created by a generation of Harare bedroom producers whose records suddenly had guaranteed radio airtime under the local-content quota. Sonically it is imported American R&B and Jamaican dancehall templates — programmed kits, sampled string stabs, glossy synth pads and heavily processed lead vocals — carried by young singers alternating Shona and English. It is distinguished from sungura and jit by having no live band, no interlocking guitars and no seben, and from South African kwaito by its slower R&B ballad orientation rather than house-derived pulse.

items.name: Kora Jaliya (Mandinka Harp-Lute Music)
items.lineage: Repertoire of the Mandinka jali harp-lute of the Gambia, Casamance, Guinea-Bissau and Mali, traced to seventeenth-century Kaabu and codified through the Diabaté, Suso and Konte lineages — 21 strings on a calabash-and-cowhide body tuned to one of four modes (sauta, tomora, hardino, silaba), a repeating bass-and-thumb kumbengo ostinato under improvised treble birimintingo runs, and pieces such as Kelefaba, Alalake and Kaira played solo or in duo at flexible tempo.
items.description: Kora jaliya is the instrumental art of the Mandinka 21-string bridge-harp, played by hereditary jali families across the Senegambia and Mali. Every piece rests on a kumbengo — a fixed interlocking bass-and-accompaniment cycle assigned to a named historical patron — over which the player spins birimintingo, fast improvised treble filigree, occasionally breaking into spoken or sung praise. Its tuning is a non-tempered heptatonic set with four standard modes, and the counterpoint of two independent thumb and index lines separates it from the plucked ngoni and from the struck balafon, both of which share the same repertoire.

items.name: Ngoni Music (Mande Lute)
items.lineage: Music of the Mande skin-faced spike lute of Mali and Guinea, the jeli ngoni of the Kouyaté and Sissoko lineages and the hunters' donso ngoni of Wassoulou, documented since the fourteenth-century Mali empire and brought to modern prominence by Banzoumana Sissoko, Moriba Koïta and Bassekou Kouyaté — four to seven strings plucked with a dry percussive attack, cyclic pentatonic ostinati at 90-130 BPM, buzzing metal jangler resonance, and interlocking with a second ngoni and calabash percussion under praise or hunters' song.
items.description: The ngoni is the small skin-topped lute at the centre of Mande music, existing in a courtly jeli form used for praise narrative and a larger hunters' donso ngoni and youth kamele ngoni used in Wassoulou. Its sound is dry, staccato and buzzing, with short sustain that pushes players toward dense repeated pentatonic figures rather than sustained melody, and ensembles typically stack two or three ngoni parts over struck calabash. Compared with the kora it is more rhythmically percussive and less harmonically open; compared with balafon ensembles it carries the vocal narrative more directly.

items.name: Balafon Music (Mande and Voltaic)
items.lineage: Gourd-resonated wooden xylophone tradition of the Mande, Sambla, Senufo and Bwa peoples of Mali, Guinea and Burkina Faso, whose Sosso-Bala at Niagassola is tied by oral history to the thirteenth-century Sunjata epic and whose modern voices include Kélétigui Diabaté, Neba Solo and Balla Kouyaté — heptatonic or pentatonic keys over calabash resonators fitted with buzzing spider-egg membranes, played with rubber-headed mallets in fast interlocking two- and three-player parts at 120-160 BPM against djembe and dunun.
items.description: The balafon is the gourd-resonated xylophone of the West African savanna, played both as a jeli praise instrument in the Mande heartland and as a large ensemble tradition among the Sambla and Senufo of Burkina Faso and Côte d'Ivoire. Its timbre is defined by the mirliton membranes stretched over holes in each calabash, which add a nasal buzz to every stroke, and its texture by two or three players sharing one or several instruments in tightly interlocked ostinati over dunun and djembe. Where the kora is lyrical and harmonic, balafon playing is percussive and metrically driven, and unlike orchestral marimba music its scales are locally tuned near-equidistant sets rather than twelve-tone.

items.name: Musique Mandingue
items.lineage: The pan-Mande national-orchestra idiom formalised in Guinea and Mali after independence, above all through Sékou Touré's state Syliphone label and its Bembeya Jazz National, Balla et ses Balladins and Rail Band de Bamako from 1960 to the mid-1970s — jeli kumbengo cycles rescored for horn section, twin electric guitars and Latin-derived rhythm section at 110-140 BPM, with epic praise texts on Sunjata and Almamy Samory sung over long modal guitar solos.
items.description: Musique mandingue names the orchestral electrification of Mande repertoire carried out by state-sponsored dance bands in Conakry and Bamako in the 1960s and 1970s. Arrangers took the fixed kumbengo ostinati and pentatonic modes of jeliya and voiced them for horns and two electric guitars over a Cuban-derived rhythm section, keeping the epic praise texts and the strained high griot voice intact while adding extended modal guitar improvisation. It sits between unaccompanied jeliya and later Mande pop: more brass-heavy and Latin-inflected than either, and distinguished from Congolese rumba by its pentatonic modality and epic subject matter rather than seben-driven romantic song.

items.name: Musique Peule
items.lineage: Music of the Fulɓe (Peul, Fulani) herding and fishing communities spread from the Senegal River valley through Mali, Niger and northern Cameroon, transmitted by gawlo praise singers and pastoral flute players and brought to record by Baaba Maal and Mansour Seck from the 1980s — slow to moderate free or loosely metered song built on the hoddu lute's short pentatonic cycles, bowed nyanyeru fiddle, overblown serdu flute doubled by the player's own hummed drone, and clear high melismatic solo singing in Pulaar over struck calabash.
items.description: Musique peule is the music of the Fulɓe pastoralists strung across the Sahel from Senegal to Cameroon, carried by hereditary gawlo praise singers and by herders playing solo flute in the bush. Its core sounds are the hoddu, a small three- or four-string lute plucked in tight pentatonic loops, the single-string bowed nyanyeru, and the serdu flute played with a simultaneous vocal drone that produces a rasping two-part texture; over these a soloist sings long, ornamented, largely unmetred Pulaar lines. It is sparser and more voice-dominated than Mande jeliya, uses no kora or balafon, and its melodic ornament and drone practice place it closer to Saharan and Songhai music than to the Mande south.

items.name: Musique soninke (Soninke griot song)
items.lineage: Repertoire of the Soninke people of the upper Senegal River valley (Mali–Mauritania–Senegal border, heirs of the Wagadu/Ghana empire), carried by hereditary geseru griot lineages on the gambare lute and kora and codified commercially from the 1970s by Mauritanian and Malian cassette artists — long strophic praise texts declaimed in Soninke over a repeating pentatonic donkilo ostinato at moderate 12/8 or slow 4/4, with calabash and hand-clap accompaniment, ululation, and a hard nasal female lead over a men's responsorial ground.
items.description: Soninke griot music comes from the Senegal River valley communities of Mali, Mauritania and eastern Senegal, and reached wide audiences through migrant-community cassettes from the 1970s onward. The texture is a short pentatonic lute or kora ostinato with calabash and clapping under a declamatory, heavily ornamented lead voice that alternates sung praise with spoken genealogy. Compared with Mandinka jeliya it uses tighter, more speech-driven phrasing and a heavier reliance on female lead singers and diaspora audiences.

items.name: Musique touareg (Tuareg traditional repertoire)
items.lineage: Pre-electric music of the Kel Tamasheq across Mali, Niger, Algeria and Libya, documented ethnographically from the 1950s onward — the noble imzad one-string fiddle accompanying men's sung poetry in free rubato, the women's tinde mortar-drum ensembles driving fast handclapped 6/8 possession and camel-race songs, and the tehardent lute repertoire of the inhaden artisan caste, all in narrow pentatonic modes with heavy portamento and ululation.
items.description: The traditional Tuareg repertoire of the central Sahara divides between the imzad fiddle, played only by women to accompany men's praise poetry in flexible unmetered lines, and the tinde drum circle, where a mortar covered with skin drives handclapped 6/8 song with dense female choral response. Melodies stay inside a narrow pentatonic with sliding, breathy delivery and no harmony. It is the acoustic parent of Tuareg electric guitar, and differs from it in being unmetered or clap-metered rather than riff-cycled.

items.name: Malian blues (Niger Bend guitar song)
items.lineage: Guitar-and-voice style of the Niger Bend around Niafunké and Timbuktu, brought to record by Ali Farka Touré from the mid-1970s and extended by Afel Bocoum, Boubacar Traoré and Vieux Farka Touré — Songhai, Peul and Bambara song forms transferred to fingerpicked acoustic or clean electric guitar over a droning open-string bass, moderate 4/4 or lilting 6/8 marked by calabash and njarka fiddle, and a low conversational vocal on modal pentatonic melodies that resemble Mississippi blues without its twelve-bar harmony.
items.description: Malian blues formed along the Niger river in northern Mali, where Songhai and Peul vocal repertoire was adapted to guitar by Ali Farka Toure from the 1970s. Its texture is a repeating fingerpicked figure over a drone bass string, calabash or njarka fiddle answering the voice, and a relaxed spoken-to-sung baritone lead. It is warmer and more song-shaped than Tuareg guitar and, unlike American blues, keeps a single modal center with no cadential harmony.
exemplars: Ali Farka Toure & Toumani Diabate - In the Heart of the Moon

items.name: Tamazight (Amazigh-language song, Middle Atlas)
items.lineage: Tamazight-language song of Morocco's Middle Atlas, carried by the izlan and ahidus repertoires of Khenifra and Azrou and professionalized from the 1970s by cassette artists such as Rouicha Mohamed, Hadda Ouakki and the amdyaz poet-singers — lotar three-string lute ostinato and bendir line-drumming in an even 6/8 or 4/4, antiphonal male-female verse exchange in a narrow pentatonic range, and long strophic poems on love, drought and migration sung in a high tense open-throated voice.
items.description: Tamazight song of Morocco's Middle Atlas is built from izlan couplets exchanged antiphonally between men and women over a lotar lute figure and a bank of bendir frame drums. Melodies sit in a narrow pentatonic band with a high, pressed vocal placement and very little harmonic movement, and the poetry rather than the tune carries the interest. It is more rural, more percussive and less guitar-based than Kabyle chanson, and unlike Moroccan chaabi it stays inside a single tempo rather than accelerating.

items.name: Mezwed (Tunisian)
items.lineage: Tunisian urban working-class dance genre named for the mezwed bagpipe, formed in the shanty neighbourhoods of Tunis in the 1960s-70s and popularized on cassette by Hedi Habbouba, Salah Farzit and Samir Loussif — the double-reed bagpipe carrying a continuous ornamented drone-melody over bendir and darbuka playing the fast 6/8 fezzani and 4/4 saidi patterns at 120-150 BPM, with rough colloquial-Tunisian vocals about poverty, prison and exile and dense audience handclapping.
items.description: Mezwed is the dance music of Tunisia's urban poor, built around the mezwed bagpipe whose continuous reedy drone and rapid ornamentation dominate the mix. Bendir and darbuka lock into fast six- and four-beat patterns while a rasping voice trades verses with mass handclapping, usually at wedding and cabaret volume with distorted PA-style sound. It is louder, coarser and more relentlessly cyclic than Tunisian malouf, and unlike rai it has stayed largely acoustic and reed-led.

items.name: Maghreb (Maghrebi popular music, pan-regional)
items.lineage: The shared popular-music field of Morocco, Algeria and Tunisia as it consolidated through state radio, cassette kiosks and the Paris migrant market from the 1950s onward — Andalusi modal inheritance and Arabic-Amazigh bilingual verse set to mandole, oud, violin, qanun and bendir, later synthesizer and drum machine, over 6/8 and shuffled 4/4 cycles with dense ornamentation, mawwal-style free vocal preludes, and choral refrains shared by chaabi, rai, malhun and Amazigh song.
items.description: Maghrebi popular music is the common repertoire and studio idiom of Morocco, Algeria and Tunisia, formed through national radio orchestras and the cassette trade from the 1950s. It is recognizable by mandole and violin unisons over bendir and darbuka, quarter-tone-inflected Andalusi modes, free mawwal openings, and bilingual Arabic-Amazigh strophic texts. Rather than a single genre it is the shared frame from which chaabi, rai, malhun and Amazigh song each specialize.

items.name: Dabke (Levantine line-dance music)
items.lineage: Line-dance music of Lebanon, Syria, Palestine and Jordan, played at village weddings for centuries and turned into an amplified cassette genre from the 1980s by Syrian and Palestinian wedding singers such as Omar Souleyman, Ali El Deek and Samir Shukri — mijwiz or arghul double-clarinet riffs, later Korg keyboards imitating them, over tabl and derbouka driving a stamping 4/4 or 6/8 at 100-160 BPM, with maqam-based sung couplets and shouted ataba and mijana vocal preludes.
items.description: Dabke is the music that accompanies the Levantine stamping line dance, historically played on mijwiz and tabl at village weddings across Lebanon, Syria, Palestine and Jordan. In its modern wedding-cassette form a Korg keyboard replaces the reeds, holding a fast repeated riff over a hammering four-beat drum pattern while the singer improvises ataba couplets before the danceable refrain. Compared with Egyptian shaabi it is reed-derived and driven by a dance floor of interlocked dancers rather than solo hip movement.

items.name: Sefardi Song (Judeo-Spanish Romancero)
items.lineage: Judeo-Spanish repertoire carried out of Iberia after 1492 and preserved in the Ottoman Balkans, Salonica, Izmir, Istanbul and Morocco, documented by Manuel Manrique de Lara and later Samuel Armistead — strophic ballads (romansas), lifecycle songs and koplas sung in Ladino, unaccompanied or with oud and frame drum, in Ottoman makam or Moroccan Andalusi modes with free-ish declamation and heavy melodic ornament.
items.description: Sefardi song is the Ladino-language repertoire of the Iberian Jewish diaspora, sustained largely by women in domestic and lifecycle settings across the eastern Mediterranean and Morocco for four centuries after the expulsion. Melodies are modal and heavily ornamented, absorbing Ottoman makam in the Balkan branch and Andalusi nuba color in the Moroccan branch, typically strophic over a repeating melodic frame with oud or frame drum. It is distinguished from Ashkenazi Jewish song by language, mode and the absence of klezmer instrumental idiom, and from liturgical piyyut by its secular narrative subject matter.

items.name: Khaleeji-Iraqi Song
items.lineage: Gulf-Iraqi urban style crystallized in mid-twentieth-century Basra, Kuwait and Baghdad where the Iraqi maqam tradition of Mohammed al-Qubbanchi met the Gulf sawt of Abdullah Fadhala and Awad al-Doukhi — sung in Iraqi and Gulf dialect over the limping 6/8 khaleeji sawt rhythm and the 10/8 jurjina, with oud lead, mirwas and darbuka hand drums, choral handclaps and violin sections added in the radio era.
items.description: This is the shared Basra-Kuwait-Baghdad repertoire in which Iraqi maqam melodic practice fused with Gulf sawt song forms during the pearl-trade and early-radio decades. It is recognizable by the loping 6/8 sawt rhythm with off-beat handclaps, oud taqsim introductions, and long ornamented vocal lines that dwell on maqam degrees foreign to equal temperament. It differs from Egyptian tarab in its rhythmic asymmetry and smaller ensemble, and from pure Iraqi maqam recital in its lighter, dance-adjacent song forms.

items.name: Shailat
items.lineage: Saudi and wider Gulf tribal chant genre that exploded on YouTube and WhatsApp after roughly 2010, descended from the Najdi 'ardah war chant and nabati poetry recitation — sung in Najdi dialect by a lead voice answered by a massed male chorus in unison, largely without melodic instruments, driven by handclaps and frame drums with heavy studio reverb, doubling and pitch correction applied to the chorus.
items.description: Shailat is a contemporary Gulf Arab genre of tribal praise chant that took its modern form on Saudi social media in the 2010s, extending the Najdi 'ardah and nabati poetry recitation into a laptop-produced format. The sound is deliberately austere: a solo caller and a thick unison male chorus, handclaps or frame drum, no chordal harmony, and conspicuous digital reverb, delay and vocal stacking that give it a cavernous processed sheen. Unlike khaleeji pop it avoids melodic instruments almost entirely, and unlike traditional 'ardah it is a studio construction rather than a live processional.

items.name: Latmiya
items.lineage: Shia mourning chant of Iraq, Iran, Lebanon, Bahrain and the Gulf performed in Muharram husseiniya gatherings for the commemoration of Ashura, formalized in Iraqi and Bahraini radud practice through the twentieth century — a solo radud declaims elegiac Arabic verse and a massed male congregation answers while beating their chests, the latm strokes supplying the meter, unaccompanied by melodic instruments and rising in tempo and register across a strophe.
items.description: Latmiya is the chest-beating elegy of Shia Muharram observance, sung in husseiniyat across Iraq, Iran, Lebanon and the Gulf to commemorate the martyrdom of Husayn at Karbala. A lead radud sings maqam-based elegiac verse and the congregation responds in unison while the collective latm — the flat-handed chest stroke — furnishes the only percussion, tightening and accelerating as the lament peaks. It differs from Sunni nasheed in its explicitly mourning function and from instrumental devotional genres in its strict avoidance of melodic instruments in the ritual context.

items.name: Oyun Havası
items.lineage: Turkish instrumental dance-tune repertoire performed at weddings, henna nights and circumcision feasts across Anatolia and Thrace, professionalized by Roman (Çingene) musician families in Istanbul and Edirne — brisk 9/8 karşılama and roman havası, 4/4 çiftetelli and 7/8 patterns led by clarinet, zurna or cümbüş over davul and darbuka, with heavily ornamented improvised gazino breaks between fixed dance strains.
items.description: Oyun havası is the Turkish dance-tune repertoire that drives weddings and street celebrations, largely the professional domain of Roman musician lineages in Istanbul, Edirne and the Aegean. It runs on limping aksak meters — 9/8 karşılama and roman havası above all — with clarinet or zurna carrying fiercely ornamented lines over davul and darbuka, and short improvised taksim-like flourishes inserted between the fixed strains. Unlike arabesk it is instrumental and functional rather than song-based, and unlike Balkan brass it keeps the reed-and-hand-drum ensemble rather than a brass band.

items.name: Karadeniz Türküleri
items.lineage: Folk-song and dance repertoire of Turkey's eastern Black Sea provinces — Trabzon, Rize, Artvin, Giresun — collected from the 1930s by Ankara Radio ekipleri and popularized nationally from the 1970s by Volkan Konak, Kâzım Koyuncu and Birol Topaloğlu, built on the three-string kemençe's fast bowed double-stops and the tulum bagpipe's drone over rapid 7/16 and 2/4 horon rhythms, with tight nasal shouted vocals and short repeated melodic cells.
items.description: Karadeniz türküleri are the songs and horon dance tunes of Turkey's eastern Black Sea coast, a repertoire distinct from central Anatolian folk in scale, meter and instrument. The three-string kemençe saws rapid narrow-interval double-stops and the tulum bagpipe supplies an unbroken drone, both driving 7/16 and fast 2/4 horon patterns, while singers deliver short repeated couplets in a hard nasal shout, often in Laz or Hemşin alongside Turkish. Compared with bozlak or Ege zeybek it is faster, narrower in melodic compass, and drone-based rather than long-lined.

items.name: Rumeli Türküleri
items.lineage: Turkish-language folk repertoire of the Balkan Ottoman lands — Thrace, Macedonia, Kosovo, Bulgaria — carried into Turkey by muhacir populations after 1878 and 1923 and codified in the TRT repertoire by collectors such as Muzaffer Sarısözen, marked by 9/8 karşılama and 7/8 meters, clarinet and accordion lead over davul and darbuka, major-leaning makams like hicaz and rast, and lyrical march-tempo strophic songs.
items.description: Rumeli türküleri are the Turkish-language songs of the European Ottoman provinces, preserved by muhacir communities resettled in Thrace and western Anatolia and standardized through TRT radio collection from the 1940s. They favor buoyant 9/8 karşılama and 7/8 dance meters, brighter hicaz and rast melodies, and a clarinet-plus-accordion sound closer to Balkan practice than to central Anatolian saz music. Against Karadeniz repertoire they are more harmonically shaded and melodically expansive; against arabesk they retain a village strophic frame rather than an orchestral pop arrangement.

items.name: Bozlak
items.lineage: Long-form lament genre of the central Anatolian Türkmen and Abdal communities of Kırşehir, Kırıkkale and Yozgat, codified in the twentieth century by Muharrem Ertaş, Çekiç Ali and Neşet Ertaş — an unmetered high-tessitura vocal outcry descending stepwise over a sustained bağlama drone, punctuated by cries of 'aman' and free-rhythm instrumental responses before resolving into a metered kırık hava.
items.description: Bozlak is the free-rhythm lament of central Anatolia's Abdal and Türkmen musicians, a uzun hava form built on a single towering vocal arc rather than a repeating strophe. The singer enters at the top of the range with a sustained cry and descends by degrees over a droning bağlama, filling the line with grace notes and glottal breaks before the piece often settles into a metered kırık hava tail. It is distinguished from other uzun hava types such as maya or hoyrat by its higher opening register, its Kırşehir Abdal lineage, and the bağlama's role as sole accompanist.

items.name: Bağlama (Aşık Saz Tradition)
items.lineage: Anatolian long-necked lute practice at the center of Turkish and Alevi folk music, transmitted through the aşık bards from Pir Sultan Abdal and Karacaoğlan to Âşık Veysel and Neşet Ertaş — fretted with microtonal ties for makam-derived ayak modes, played with plectrum or bare-fingered şelpe, sustaining an open-string drone beneath a melody in 2/4 or aksak 5/8, 7/8 and 9/8, most often self-accompanying a solo declaimed verse.
items.description: The bağlama is the long-necked lute that anchors Turkish folk music, built in sizes from the small cura to the large divan saz and fretted with movable ties that place microtonal degrees between the equal-tempered ones. Its idiom is drone-based: open middle and low courses ring continuously while the top course carries a modal ayak melody, played with a plectrum or with the bare-fingered şelpe technique, usually as self-accompaniment to a sung or half-declaimed verse. In Alevi cem practice the instrument is treated as sacred, which distinguishes this lineage from the purely secular saz playing of dance and wedding contexts.

items.name: Mevlevi Ayin
items.lineage: Sufi ceremonial music of the Mevlevi order founded at Konya in the thirteenth century around Jalal al-Din Rumi, its ayin-i şerif suites composed from the fifteenth century onward by dervish composers including Köçek Mustafa Dede, Itri and Dede Efendi — a fixed liturgy of naat, taksim, peşrev and four selam sections in one makam, ney and kudüm-led over shifting usul cycles, accompanying the whirling sema turn with sung Persian and Turkish Rumi verse.
items.description: The Mevlevi ayin is the composed suite that accompanies the whirling sema ceremony of the Konya dervish order, and it is the most extended through-composed form in Ottoman music. Each ayin unfolds in a single makam through a sung naat, a solo ney taksim, an instrumental peşrev and four selam movements whose usul cycles change to mark the dervishes' stages of turning, with the breathy ney and the paired kudüm kettledrums as the defining timbres. It differs from Türk sanat müziği concert repertoire by being liturgy rather than entertainment, and from other Sufi zikr musics by its notated, large-scale architecture rather than accelerating repetitive chant.

items.name: Sufi zikr chant (dhikr recitation)
items.lineage: Congregational dhikr/zikr chanting practised across Sufi tariqas from the medieval Islamic world into modern Turkey, Egypt, Syria, the Maghreb and South Asia, codified in orders such as the Naqshbandiyya, Qadiriyya, Rifa'iyya and Mevleviyya — unison or responsorial repetition of divine names (Allah hu, la ilaha illa'llah) over a breath-locked pulse that accelerates from slow free declamation to a fast 2- or 4-beat panting ostinato, led by a solo munshid singing melismatic maqam phrases above the group, with frame drums (daf, bendir) and occasionally ney entering only in the faster stages.
items.description: Zikr is the breath-and-body chanting rite of Sufi orders, performed in lodges, shrines and homes from Cairo and Konya to Lahore. Its sound is cumulative rather than melodic: a short formula repeated hundreds of times, accelerating and rising in register while a soloist improvises maqam melisma over the top, frame drums reinforcing the collective exhalation. Unlike qawwali or inshad, which are composed songs with poetic verses and metric cycles, zikr is a trance technology built on repetition of a single divine name and has no fixed song form.
exemplars: Al-Kindi Ensemble with Sheikh Hamza Shakkur

items.name: Hindustani vocal (gayaki tradition)
items.lineage: North Indian classical singing lineage running from 15th-century dhrupad at the Gwalior and Darbhanga courts through 18th-century khayal codified by Sadarang and Adarang and the gharana system documented by V.N. Bhatkhande — unmetered alap opening on tanpura drone, then bandish in vilambit and drut laya over teental, jhaptal or ektaal with tabla, harmonium or sarangi shadowing the line, and vocal technique built on meend glides, gamak oscillation, taan runs and sargam improvisation within a single raga.
items.description: The vocal branch of North Indian classical music, treated by its own practitioners as the primary art from which instrumental styles derive their phrasing. A recital unfolds as a long arc: unmeasured alap over tanpura, a slow bandish where each phrase tests one raga interval, then accelerating taan work against tabla. It is distinguished from instrumental Hindustani music by text and by the gayaki emphasis on meend and voiced gamak, and from Carnatic vocal music by its slower expositional pacing and absence of pre-composed kriti-plus-kalpanaswara architecture.

items.name: Bhangra (Punjabi harvest dhol dance)
items.lineage: Harvest dance of the Majha and Doaba districts of Punjab, restaged as a national folk form in post-1947 Indian Punjab through Patiala's Punjabi University troupes and Manohar Deepak's choreography — built on the dhol's chaal pattern struck with dagga and tilli sticks at roughly 130–150 BPM, tumbi's single-string ostinato, algoza double-flute drone and chimta jingles, with shouted boliyan couplets answered by the dancing circle in a high open-throated Punjabi register.
items.description: The village and akhara form of bhangra, danced outdoors in a circle around a standing dhol player, is a percussion-first music: everything else in the ensemble exists to decorate the chaal. Tumbi and algoza supply a repeating pentatonic hook while boliyan verses are shouted rather than sung, ending in a collective 'balle balle' response. It is the acoustic ancestor of, and sonically distinct from, the sampled UK-diaspora bhangra of the 1980s onward, which replaced the dhol with drum machines and added Western harmony.

items.name: Punjabi folk (boliyan and tappe village song)
items.lineage: Village song repertoire of undivided Punjab — tappe, boliyan, mahiya, dholi and jugni forms sung at weddings, harvests and giddha circles, carried through the 20th century by Yamla Jatt, Asa Singh Mastana and Surinder Kaur and archived by the Punjabi Academy — mostly free or loosely metric couplets over tumbi, algoza and dholak, with handclaps for giddha, sung in a strained high tessitura with long held vowels and abrupt terminal drops, harmonium entering only in recorded/broadcast settings.
items.description: The domestic and occupational song stock of Punjab, distinct from the dance-floor bhangra it feeds: short rhyming couplets sung by women in giddha circles or by a solo male voice with tumbi, often unmetered until a dholak enters at the refrain. The vocal style is deliberately loud and pinched, projecting across open courtyards, with melodies confined to a narrow pentatonic band. Where bhangra is built around the dhol's chaal, this repertoire is text-led and percussion-optional.

items.name: Bengali folk (lokgeeti of Bengal and Bangladesh)
items.lineage: Regional song stock of Bengal and Bangladesh — bhawaiya of Rangpur and Cooch Behar, bhatiali of the river delta, jhumur of the Rarh plateau and gambhira of Chapainawabganj — collected by Abbasuddin Ahmed, Nirmalendu Chowdhury and the Kolkata Folk and Tribal Cultural Centre from the 1930s onward; dotara and ektara supply a bright metallic ostinato under khol or dholak in dadra and keherwa cycles, with long free-breath opening calls and a lightly nasal upper-register male delivery carrying wave-like meend.
items.description: Lokgeeti covers the secular regional songs of Bengal on both sides of the 1947 border: boatmen's bhatiali, cattle-herders' bhawaiya, harvest jhumur. Texture is thin and voice-forward, with the dotara's four wire strings giving a chiming, slightly detuned halo and the khol's clay-shelled bass-treble contrast replacing tabla. Unlike the Baul repertoire, which is mystic and mendicant, lokgeeti is occupational and romantic in subject, and unlike Rabindrasangeet it is unauthored and transmitted orally.

items.name: Indian folk (pan-regional lok geet)
items.lineage: Umbrella category of India's non-classical regional song traditions — Bhojpuri kajri and chaiti, Garhwali and Kumaoni jhoda, Gujarati garba, Chhattisgarhi pandavani, Malwi and Haryanvi ragini — surveyed institutionally from the 1950s by All India Radio's folk units and the Sangeet Natak Akademi; typically a solo or call-and-response voice over dholak or nagara in keherwa and dadra, with harmonium and manjira added in broadcast and cassette contexts, melodies in narrow pentatonic or raga-derived bands and text carrying seasonal, ritual or agricultural function.
items.description: Lok geet is the collective term for India's village and regional song outside the classical and film systems, tied to calendar, caste occupation and life-cycle ritual rather than to concert performance. The common sonic denominator across regions is a dholak-and-handclap pulse, a leader-and-chorus structure, and a hard unamplified vocal placed high in the range. It is distinguished from filmi 'folk' numbers by having no fixed arrangement or authorship, and from bhajan by its secular seasonal subject matter.
exemplars: Sangeet Natak Akademi folk archive recordings

items.name: Keroncong asli (Indonesian kroncong classic form)
items.lineage: Urban Indonesian song style descended from 16th-century Portuguese-Eurasian moresco fado brought by Mardijker communities to Batavia, standardised in the early 20th century as the 28-bar keroncong asli form by Jakarta and Solo ensembles and popularised on radio by Gesang and Waldjinah — a slow to moderate 4/4 at 60–90 BPM in which cak (high ukulele) plays offbeat strums, cuk answers on the beat, cello is plucked pizzicato as a kendang substitute, double bass walks sparse roots and violin and flute weave heterophonic countermelody under a light, straight-toned vocal with slow terminal vibrato.
items.description: Keroncong asli is the strict-form core of Indonesia's oldest urban popular music, a Portuguese-descended string ensemble idiom refined in Solo and Jakarta and canonised by songs like Gesang's Bengawan Solo. The characteristic sound is the interlocking cak-and-cuk rhythm — an offbeat/onbeat pair that replaces drums entirely — with pizzicato cello mimicking kendang fills and no percussion in the ensemble at all. It is more harmonically Western and rhythmically restrained than campursari or langgam Jawa, which graft gamelan scales and instruments onto the same frame.

items.name: Campursari (Javanese gamelan-keyboard crossover)
items.lineage: Central Javanese hybrid popularised from the early 1990s by Manthous and his Orkes Campursari Gunung Kidul, building on 1960s experiments by RM Samsi — literally 'mixed essence', it sets langgam Jawa and keroncong melodies over a pelog/slendro-tuned electronic keyboard doubling saron and gender parts, with kendang leading the tempo, siter and suling ornamenting, bass guitar walking under, at a relaxed 90–110 BPM behind a sinden-derived Javanese vocal using narrow ornamented cengkok phrasing.
items.description: Campursari is the cassette-era fusion that reconciled Javanese gamelan tuning with Western-tuned popular instruments, most audibly through keyboards custom-programmed to pelog and slendro so that saron and synth can play the same line. Manthous's ensembles set this against kendang-driven keroncong and dangdut rhythms, producing a mid-tempo, warmly diatonic-yet-not-quite-tempered sound heard at Central Javanese weddings. It differs from keroncong in admitting gamelan instruments and tunings outright, and from dangdut in its slower gait and Javanese-language lyric register.

items.name: Dangdut koplo (East Javanese kendang koplo)
items.lineage: East Javanese regional mutation of dangdut emerging around Surabaya, Pasuruan and Kediri in the late 1990s and dominating Indonesian live music through Monata, New Pallapa and singers Inul Daratista and Via Vallen — the classic dangdut 'ndut' kendang pattern is doubled and syncopated into the koplo groove at 130–160 BPM with a busy filling tabla-and-kendang dialogue, chorus-drenched single-coil guitar and suling flute answering the line, synth brass stabs, and a bright cengkok-ornamented female lead vocal cued live to a dancing crowd.
items.description: Koplo is the fast, kendang-obsessed East Javanese strain of dangdut that overtook the slower Melayu-Indian original from the 2000s onward, spread first by VCD recordings of open-air orkes shows and later by YouTube. Its defining feature is the kendang player as lead soloist, filling almost continuously against a doubled-time backbeat, with the melodic instruments reduced to short answering hooks. Compared with classic Rhoma Irama dangdut it is roughly twice as busy rhythmically and far more locally Javanese in vocal ornament and language.

items.name: Sundanese Traditional
items.lineage: West Javanese Sundanese repertoire complex — tembang Sunda cianjuran vocal poetry codified in mid-19th-century Cianjur under Bupati R.A.A. Kusumahningrat, gamelan degung, and kacapi-suling chamber music — marked by free-rhythm mamaos vocal lines over zither ostinato, breathy end-blown suling ornament, and pentatonic laras pelog/degung and salendro tunings, with kendang-driven jaipongan and bamboo angklung as its rural and popular offshoots.
items.description: The traditional music of the Sundanese of West Java, centred on tembang Sunda cianjuran and kacapi-suling chamber playing rather than on a large bronze orchestra. Texture is sparse and voice-led: a plucked kacapi zither lays a rippling ostinato, the suling flute answers with sliding microtonal ornament, and the singer moves in unmetered rubato before settling into pentatonic pelog degung phrases. Compared with Central Javanese gamelan it is quieter, thinner-textured, far more melismatic, and it prizes soloistic freedom over colotomic cycle.

items.name: Lagu Bali (Pop Bali)
items.lineage: Balinese-language popular song that emerged from Denpasar radio and the 1980s-90s cassette trade through Yan Bero, Widi Widiana, Ayu Laksmi and later Nanoe Biroe, pairing colloquial Balinese lyrics with pop and light rock backing at mid-tempo 4/4 while quoting gamelan colour — gender or suling lines, kendang fills and kebyar-derived melodic turns — over guitar, bass, kit and synth.
items.description: Balinese-language popular song, a cassette-era and later local-TV genre centred on Denpasar. Arrangements are conventional pop-rock, but singers carry Balinese vocal inflection and producers routinely drop in gender, suling or kendang figures as identity markers. It is looser and more guitar-driven than pop Sunda, and completely distinct from gong kebyar in metre, harmony and tuning, borrowing only surface gamelan colour.

items.name: Lagu Melayu (Malay Asli)
items.lineage: Malay traditional song repertoire of the Riau-Johor-Malacca littoral, formalized on record from the 1930s-60s through bangsawan theatre and Singapore-Malaya EMI sessions with singers such as P. Ramlee and Saloma, comprising the slow rubato-ornamented asli, the brisk duple joget and inang, and the Arab-derived zapin, accompanied by violin, accordion, gendang or rebana frame drums and punctuating gong, with heavily ornamented patah lagu vocal turns.
items.description: The classical-popular song tradition of the Malay world, spanning the languid asli, the quick joget and inang dances, and zapin. Its identity lies in the vocal line: dense, sliding patah lagu ornament over a slow gendang cycle marked by a single gong, with violin and accordion shadowing the singer heterophonically. Unlike later Malay pop it retains free-flowing rubato phrasing and drum-cycle form rather than verse-chorus pop structure.

items.name: Dikir Barat
items.lineage: Kelantanese Malay competitive group-singing form consolidated in the mid-20th century on the Malaysia-Thailand border and popularized nationally from the 1980s, in which a tukang karut improvises rhyming pantun verse and a juara leads while a seated awok-awok chorus of twenty or more answers in unison with synchronized hand-clapping and body movement, driven by rebana and kompang frame drums, canang kettle gongs and a gong, accelerating from a slow declamatory opening to a fast interlocked chant.
items.description: A Kelantan-based Malay choral and percussion form built for competition between village troupes. A solo tukang karut improvises satirical or topical rhymed verse and the massed seated chorus answers in loud unison with clapping and coordinated gesture, over frame drums and small kettle gongs that tighten and accelerate through each piece. It differs from other Malay vocal traditions in being antiphonal, unaccompanied by melody instruments, and dependent on live improvised text rather than fixed song.
exemplars: Dikir Barat Kelantan (Malaysian national competition troupes)

items.name: Rondalla
items.lineage: Philippine plucked-string ensemble descended from the Spanish rondalla and standardized in the late 19th and early 20th centuries under Colegio and municipal band teachers, scored for tremolo-picked bandurria carrying the melody, laud and octavina in inner voices, guitar for chords and bajo de uñas or double bass on the bottom, playing danzas, kundiman, polkas and folk airs in equal temperament with a signature sustained plectrum tremolo.
items.description: The Philippine plucked-string orchestra, adapted from Iberian models and institutionalized through schools and town ensembles. Its defining sound is the shimmering bandurria tremolo carrying a lyric melody while laud and octavina fill mid-range counterpoint and guitar plus bass supply a plain harmonic floor. Unlike the Mexican or Spanish string groups it descends from, the rondalla uses a fixed four-part instrumentation, plays largely from notation or arrangement rather than improvising, and serves as accompaniment to kundiman and folk-song repertoire.

items.name: Manila Sound
items.lineage: Mid-1970s Metro Manila pop movement launched by Hotdog's Ikaw Ang Miss Universe Ng Buhay Ko and Manila and carried by VST & Company, Cinderella, Rico J. Puno and Hagibis, blending soft-rock and disco-funk rhythm sections at 100-120 BPM with Taglish lyrics, sweet close-harmony backing vocals, clean single-coil guitar, Rhodes or clavinet comping, congas and occasional horn stabs, recorded on multitrack in Manila studios for the local label boom.
items.description: The commercial Manila pop style of roughly 1973-1980, the first mass-market Filipino-language pop wave. It runs on light soft-rock and disco grooves with clean electric guitar, electric piano, congas and glossy group backing vocals, and its lyrics mix Tagalog and English in a conversational, often comic register. It is distinguished from the concurrent Pinoy rock scene by its polish and dance orientation, and from kundiman by its urban vernacular text and full rhythm-section production.

items.name: Bisrock
items.lineage: Cebuano-language rock movement launched in Cebu City in the late 1990s and named around 2002 by Missing Filemon and the Bisrock compilations, applying alternative-rock and ska-punk arrangements — distorted humbucker guitar, driving 4/4 kit and electric bass at 130-170 BPM, shouted-to-sung Visayan vocals — to lyrics of local humour, protest and provincial identity, produced cheaply in Cebu and Davao project studios.
items.description: Cebuano-language rock centred on Cebu City from the late 1990s, a deliberate regional counterweight to Tagalog-dominated Manila pop-rock. Musically it is standard guitar-band alternative rock with ska and pop-punk inflections, cut in modest DAW-era studios, but the Visayan text and colloquial, often satirical delivery define it. It is rougher and cheaper-sounding than mainstream Pinoy rock and explicitly language-political in a way Manila Sound never was.

items.name: Phleng Phuea Chiwit
items.lineage: Thai "songs for life" protest rock formed among Bangkok student activists around the 1973-76 uprisings and codified by Caravan and later Carabao, welding mid-tempo 4/4 folk-rock strumming and country-rock backbeats to Isan reed timbres (khaen, phin), plainspoken baritone lead vocals in unison group choruses, and lyrics on rural poverty, labor and dictatorship.
items.description: Phleng phuea chiwit emerged in Thailand in the mid-1970s as the soundtrack of the student left, initially acoustic and semi-clandestine, then arena-scaled in the 1980s under Carabao. Its signature is a Western folk-rock band chassis colored by Isan instruments — the free-reed khaen drone and the buzzing phin lute — under declamatory, grainy male vocals delivered close to speech. Unlike luk thung, which stays inside melismatic Thai popular-song phrasing and sentimental themes, songs-for-life keeps melody plain and subordinates it to text.

items.name: Thai Folk (Village Traditions)
items.lineage: Village song traditions of Thailand's Central, Northern and Isan regions — repartee genres such as lam klon, phleng choi and so phrae — carried by itinerant singers into the twentieth century and documented by mid-century field collectors, built on free-reed khaen drone-and-ostinato, plucked phin or sueng, hand-drum and ching cymbal timekeeping, and rapid syllabic call-and-response verse improvised over a single mode.
items.description: Thai rural song is regional and functional — courtship duels, harvest songs, ordination processions — rather than a single repertoire, and outside the court it uses roughly equidistant seven-tone tuning without fixed Western pitch. Texture is thin and cyclic: a khaen or fiddle sustains a modal drone while a solo voice spins improvised verse in fast syllabic patter, answered by a partner or the crowd. It differs from Thai classical piphat in having no fixed composition, no gong-circle ensemble, and no fixed instrumental hierarchy.

items.name: Cambodian Rock (Phnom Penh Psych)
items.lineage: Phnom Penh popular music of roughly 1963-1975, made by Sinn Sisamouth, Ros Serey Sothea, Pen Ran and Yol Aularong for radio and nightclub, grafting surf-reverb and fuzz guitar, combo organ, Farfisa-and-saxophone bandstand arrangements and a-go-go or slow-rock backbeats onto Khmer ramvong and romvong dance rhythms, with high, nasal, heavily ornamented Khmer vocal delivery on top.
items.description: Cambodian rock formed when American Forces radio and French yé-yé records reached Phnom Penh nightclubs, and it kept Khmer melodic ornament and vocal placement intact while borrowing wholesale from surf, garage and soul instrumentation. Recordings are dry-to-slapback, often small-room and lightly overdubbed, with organ and reverbed guitar sharing the top and horns arranged in unison stabs. What separates it from Thai string and Vietnamese kích động nhạc of the same years is the vocal line: intensely melismatic, high-set, and phrased against the beat rather than with it. The scene ended abruptly in 1975, and most of its principals were killed.

items.name: Cambodian Traditional (Village and Wedding)
items.lineage: Rural Khmer repertoires outside the court — the phleng kar wedding cycle, arak spirit-possession music, ayai sung repartee and the solo chapei dang veng bardic tradition — carried orally through village ceremony and codified in the late twentieth century largely through Kong Nay and post-genocide revival projects, built on chapei long-necked lute, tro fiddles, khim dulcimer, skor daey hand drum and chhing cymbals under speech-rhythm vocal narration.
items.description: Village Khmer music is small-ensemble and event-bound: the multi-movement phleng kar suite paces a three-day wedding, arak music summons healing spirits, and chapei dang veng is one man with a two-string lute improvising rhymed social commentary between instrumental refrains. Textures are sparse and heterophonic, fiddles and dulcimer trailing the singer, with cymbals rather than a drum kit holding time. Against pinpeat it is quiet, indoor, non-bronze, and improvisatory — the singer's text, not a fixed dance cue, drives the form.

items.name: Vietnamese Bolero (Nhạc Vàng)
items.lineage: Slow sentimental Vietnamese popular song crystallized in Saigon from the late 1950s through 1975 by writers such as Trúc Phương, Lam Phương and Trần Thiện Thanh, using the Latin bolero's slow duple pulse and dotted bongo-and-guitar rhythm under minor-mode, pentatonically inflected melodies, guitar phím lõm scalloped-fret bends, and a high, nasal, heavy-vibrato solo vocal; banned in the North after 1975 and sustained on cassette by the overseas diaspora.
items.description: Vietnamese bolero borrows the Cuban-by-way-of-Mexico bolero tempo and accompaniment pattern but sets it to Vietnamese-language melodies that lean on pentatonic contour and the vọng cổ tradition's ornamental sighs, most audibly in the scalloped-fret guitar's deep between-note bends. Arrangements stayed modest — nylon guitar, bass, brushed or light kit, later home-organ and synth pads on diaspora cassettes and Paris By Night video productions. Its nearest neighbour, tân cổ, folds the same songs into cải lương recitative; bolero proper keeps strophic verse-chorus form throughout.

items.name: Tân Cổ Giao Duyên
items.lineage: Southern Vietnamese hybrid form invented in Saigon in the early 1960s, credited to lyricist Viễn Châu, that alternates strophic modern popular song (tân nhạc) with the six-phrase vọng cổ recitative of cải lương theatre, accompanied by đàn tranh zither, đàn bầu monochord, đàn nguyệt moon lute and scalloped-fret guitar over free-breathing phrases that cadence together on the song bar with trống chầu punctuation.
items.description: Tân cổ is deliberately bilingual in musical idiom: a verse of Western-harmonized Vietnamese pop hands off, mid-track, to unmeasured vọng cổ, where the singer drifts ahead of and behind the accompanists until the whole ensemble lands together on the phrase-ending song beat. The instrumental writing is heterophonic and highly ornamented, with the đàn bầu's whole-tone pitch bends and the guitar's scalloped-fret vibrato imitating vocal inflection. It is distinguished from straight bolero by that recitative section and from full cải lương by having no staged drama around it.

items.name: Nhạc Thiếu Nhi
items.lineage: Vietnamese children's song repertoire built from the 1950s onward for schools, Young Pioneer organizations and state radio and television, composed by figures such as Phạm Tuyên and Hoàng Long, in bright major keys and simple duple or 6/8 meters, sung by unison children's choir over piano, accordion, glockenspiel and later home-keyboard backing, with short strophic forms and didactic, patriotic or animal-themed texts.
items.description: Unlike inherited nursery rhymes, nhạc thiếu nhi is largely a composed and institutionally distributed body of songs, taught in classrooms and broadcast, with named authors and printed sheet music. Its sound is deliberately clean and legible: unison or simple two-part children's voices, tonal Western harmony, tempos steady enough to march or clap to, and thin accompaniment that never obscures the words. Later commercial recordings replace the accordion-and-piano radio texture with preset keyboard and drum-machine backing, but the melodic and formal simplicity is unchanged.

items.name: Kayōkyoku
items.lineage: Mainstream Japanese popular song of roughly 1950-1990, produced by label-and-agency systems (Nippon Columbia, Victor, Watanabe Productions) with composers such as Hachidai Nakamura and Kyōhei Tsutsumi, joining Western pop and jazz-orchestra arranging — full string sections, brass, drum kit, electric bass — to yonanuki pentatonic melody, sentimental strophic AABA forms and a controlled, vibrato-forward solo vocal at mid-tempo.
items.description: Kayōkyoku is the broad postwar Japanese hit-song category from which enka and later J-pop separated, and its defining sound is a lush arranged backing — strings, horn section, electric rhythm section, occasionally shamisen for period color — supporting a single foregrounded vocalist recorded close and compressed. Melodies favor the yonanuki pentatonic scales, giving even fully tonal arrangements a distinctly Japanese contour. Against enka, kayōkyoku is lighter, more jazz- and Western-pop-derived, and less committed to the heavy kobushi vocal ornament; against city pop it is more orchestral and less funk-inflected.

items.name: Ryūkōka
items.lineage: Japanese popular song of the Taishō and early Shōwa eras, roughly 1914-1945, spread by Nippon Victor and Columbia shellac discs and composers such as Masao Koga and Shinpei Nakayama, mixing Western salon-orchestra scoring — violin, mandolin, accordion, Hawaiian steel guitar, light brass — with yonanuki minor melodies and a restrained, throat-forward vocal delivery over slow waltz, foxtrot and duple march tempos.
items.description: Ryūkōka is the first mass-mediated Japanese popular song, born with electrical recording, radio and the record industry, and audible today through the bandwidth-limited midrange of 78rpm shellac. Arrangements are chamber-scale — a handful of strings, reeds and plucked instruments, often with no drum kit at all — behind a single vocalist whose delivery sits between shinnai narration and Western light-opera singing. It is the direct ancestor of both kayōkyoku and enka, differing from them in its thinner, pre-amplified ensemble and its unmistakably prewar salon-orchestra harmony.

items.name: Oshare kei
items.lineage: Bright, candy-colored offshoot of Japanese visual kei that crystallized in Osaka and Tokyo indies venues circa 2001-2003 around bands on the Peace & Smile Committee and Indie PSC circuit, trading gothic black for pastel layered hair, plastic accessories and polka dots while musically leaning on 170-200 BPM pop-punk and emo eighth-note downstrokes, bubblegum major-key choruses, gang-vocal 'oi' backings and high nasal boyish lead vocals over chorus-drenched clean guitar verses and octave-riff bridges.
items.description: Oshare kei emerged in the early 2000s Japanese indies scene as the deliberately cheerful inverse of visual kei's gothic wing, keeping the elaborate costuming and makeup but discarding the minor-key theatricality. The sound is fast pop-punk and emo with major-key hooks, clipped downstroke guitars, brief synth stabs and a thin bright mix that favors vocal and cymbal top end. It differs from mainstream visual kei in tempo and mode, and from Western pop-punk in its high boyish vocal placement, key-change final choruses and heavy use of unison gang shouts.
exemplars: Ando Yuko / Antic Cafe circle releases

items.name: Shakuhachi (sankyoku ensemble repertoire)
items.lineage: Chamber practice in which the shakuhachi joined the koto-and-shamisen jiuta-sokyoku trio, displacing the bowed kokyu across the late Edo and Meiji periods (roughly 1830-1900) as Kinko-ryu and then Tozan-ryu players entered secular concert life, playing heterophonic lines that shadow and decorate the koto melody in the in-scale with meri-kari microtonal shading, at slow to moderate free-breathing tempi articulated by the koto's plectrum attacks rather than a drum.
items.description: Sankyoku is the three-part Japanese chamber ensemble of koto, shamisen and shakuhachi that became standard in the nineteenth century when the flute took over the kokyu's role. Texture is heterophonic rather than harmonic: all parts trace one melody, the koto supplying the metrical spine while the shakuhachi bends around it with meri-kari pitch inflection and breath noise, and a singer often carries the jiuta text. It is distinct from solo honkyoku in being metered, ensemble-bound, notated and secular rather than a Zen breathing discipline.

items.name: Tsugaru-jamisen
items.lineage: Percussive virtuoso shamisen style of the Tsugaru plain in Aomori, northern Honshu, developed from the 1870s by itinerant blind bosama beggar-musicians — Nitabo (Akimoto Nitaro) is the traditional founder — using the heavy futozao thick-necked instrument with a thick-skinned body struck rather than plucked by a large bachi, built on the fast triplet-driven Jongara-bushi, Yosare-bushi and Aiya-bushi tune families with extended improvised maebiki preludes and rough, forced min'yo vocal delivery.
items.description: Tsugaru-jamisen turned an accompanying instrument into a solo attack vehicle: the bachi strikes the skin as well as the strings, producing an audible drum thud under every note, and players compete in speed, dynamic contrast and improvised preludes. Repertoire centers on a handful of Tsugaru folk-song frameworks that function like blues heads, over which the soloist elaborates before the singer enters with a strained, high, heavily ornamented delivery. Compared with nagauta or jiuta shamisen it is louder, thicker-necked, rhythmically aggressive and improvisatory rather than notated.

items.name: Taiko (North American kumi-daiko)
items.lineage: Diasporic drum-ensemble tradition founded in California — San Francisco Taiko Dojo under Tanaka Seiichi in 1968, Kinnara Taiko at Senshin Buddhist Temple in Los Angeles in 1969, San Jose Taiko in 1973 — adapting Japanese kumi-daiko to Japanese-American identity work with wine-barrel-built nagado drums, choreographed full-body stances, shime-daiko keeping the ji base pulse under odaiko solos, unison kiai shouts and pieces built as sectional grooves at 100-160 BPM rather than festival-cycle accompaniment.
items.description: North American taiko began in 1960s California as a Japanese-American community practice rather than an import, with groups building their own drums from wine barrels because instruments were unavailable. Musically it foregrounds composed multi-section ensemble pieces, visible choreography, and a layered rhythmic texture in which shime-daiko holds a fast ji ostinato while nagado and odaiko players trade phrases and kiai shouts. It differs from Japanese matsuri-bayashi in being concert-framed, composed and detached from shrine calendar function, and from Japanese kumi-daiko groups in its explicit civil-rights-era identity politics.

items.name: Ryukyu koten ongaku (Okinawan classical court music)
items.lineage: Court repertoire of the Ryukyu Kingdom at Shuri, systematized in the eighteenth century when Yakabi Choki (1716-1775) devised the kunkunshi tablature and the music was formalized for reception of Chinese sappushi envoys and for kumiodori dance-drama created by Tamagusuku Chokun in 1719 — very slow, sung in courtly Okinawan to the ryukyu scale on sanshin with kutu koto, kucho spike fiddle, fue flute and sparse taiko punctuation, in ryuka thirty-syllable verse form.
items.description: Ryukyu koten ongaku is the aristocratic sanshin song repertoire of the former Ryukyu Kingdom, notated in Yakabi Choki's kunkunshi tablature and preserved through the Nomura and Afuso schools. Tempos are extremely slow, the singing is restrained and nasally focused with long sustained syllables, and the heterophonic ensemble of sanshin, koto, kucho and fue moves in near-unison with wide spaces between events. It is sharply distinct from Okinawan min'yo in tempo, diction and social setting, and from mainland Japanese sokyoku in its ryukyu scale with its raised fourth and seventh.

items.name: Okinawan min'yo
items.lineage: Village folk-song tradition of the Ryukyu islands, transmitted orally through work, festival and awamori-party settings and commercially codified from the 1950s by singers such as Kadekaru Rinsho and Fukuhara Tsuneo, based on the ryukyu pentatonic with its raised fourth and seventh, sanshin accompaniment with the singer playing his own part, interjected hayashi shout-calls of hiyamiaachi and iyasasa, and the fast open-ended kachashi finale in a driving duple pulse with paranku frame drums and hand claps.
items.description: Okinawan min'yo is the everyday song repertoire of the Ryukyus, sung in the Okinawan language over self-accompanied sanshin, covering work songs, love songs, laments for the 1945 battle and celebration numbers. Its identifying marks are the ryukyu scale, the bright snakeskin-bodied sanshin timbre, shouted hayashi interjections from the room, and the kachashi ending in which tempo doubles and everyone dances with raised hands. It differs from mainland Japanese min'yo in scale and instrument, and from Ryukyu court music in its fast tempi, colloquial diction and communal participation.

items.name: Uchina pop (Okinawan pop)
items.lineage: Okinawan popular-music hybrid launched by Kina Shoukichi and Champloose's 1977 'Haisai Ojisan' and consolidated through the 1990s by Rinken Band, Nenes and BEGIN, setting the ryukyu scale and sanshin against electric guitar, bass, drum kit and synthesizers at mid-tempo rock and reggae pulses, retaining hayashi calls, kachashi double-time codas and Okinawan-language refrains inside verse-chorus pop structures.
items.description: Uchina pop is the electrified Okinawan popular style that carried island melody and language into the Japanese national market from the late 1970s onward. The sanshin stays audible as a lead colour over a full rock rhythm section, choruses lean on the ryukyu scale's raised fourth and seventh, and many tracks accelerate into a kachashi coda with paranku and clapping. It differs from mainland J-pop in modal vocabulary and instrumentation, and from Okinawan min'yo in its studio production, drum kit and fixed song forms.

items.name: Ainu upopo and rimse (song and dance)
items.lineage: Communal song-and-dance repertoire of the Ainu of Hokkaido and formerly Sakhalin, performed seated in a circle around a lidded shintoko container beaten as a drum for upopo round-songs sung in short overlapping canon, and standing for rimse circle dances such as the crane dance sarorun rimse and the sword dance emush rimse, with tonkori zither and mukkuri bamboo jaw harp providing instrumental colour; documented in Pilsudski's 1902-1905 cylinders and revived from the 1960s through preservation societies at Shiraoi and Akan.
items.description: Upopo are short strophic Ainu songs sung by seated women in staggered entries so that the phrases overlap in a rough canon, while rimse are the accompanying circle dances performed standing. Textures are narrow in range, strongly cyclic and driven by a lid-beaten container or handclaps rather than a membrane drum, with the tonkori five-string zither and the buzzing mukkuri adding timbral rather than melodic weight. It differs from Ainu yukar epic recitation, which is solo, narrative and stick-marked, and from Sami yoik in its group canonic overlap.
exemplars: Ainu Museum Shiraoi Poroto Kotan ensembles

items.name: Trot (contemporary revival)
items.lineage: Twenty-first-century Korean revival of trot triggered by Hong Jin-young and Jang Yoon-jeong's crossover hits and detonated commercially by TV Chosun's Miss Trot (2019) and Mr. Trot (2020), keeping the genre's duple ppongjjak backbeat, minor pentatonic melodies and heavily inflected kkeokk-neun vocal breaks while replacing the analog band with programmed drums, synth bass, EDM-adjacent risers and semi-trot arrangements that borrow K-pop production gloss at 110-135 BPM.
items.description: The trot revival of the late 2010s brought a genre associated with older listeners back to the top of the Korean charts through audition television, producing arena-scale stars in Lim Young-woong and Song Ga-in. The music keeps trot's characteristic two-beat ppongjjak feel and the ornamented, sob-inflected vocal delivery, but sits on modern programmed drums, sub bass and bright mastered mixes, with semi-trot tracks folding in dance-pop and even brass-band figures. It differs from mid-century trot in production and tempo, and from K-pop in its minor pentatonic melody, vocal ornamentation and solo-singer format.

items.name: Korean minyo (regional folk song)
items.lineage: Korean folk-song repertoire transmitted orally by village and professional singers and codified into regional tori dialects during the twentieth century — Gyeonggi minyo with its light, clear sesetgarum triple-shake, Namdo minyo of Jeolla with the heavy yukjabaegi wide vibrato and downward slides, Seodo minyo of the northwest with nasal tremulous delivery, and Dongbu minyo of the east — typically in 6/8 or 12/8 jangdan cycles played on the janggu hourglass drum, with call-and-response between a lead singer and chorus.
items.description: Korean minyo is the country's folk-song body, sorted by regional tori — melodic dialects defined less by scale than by which notes are shaken, bent or approached from above. Gyeonggi songs like Arirang and Doraji are bright and evenly ornamented; Namdo songs such as Yukjabaegi use a broad slow vibrato and a heavy descending slide that carries into pansori. Accompaniment is usually a janggu marking a compound-metre jangdan with optional melodic instruments doubling the voice heterophonically; unlike pansori it is strophic, communal and short-form rather than epic narrative.

items.name: Korean jeongak (court and literati music)
items.lineage: Aristocratic Korean repertoire of the Joseon court and yangban literati, notated in jeongganbo mensural tablature devised under King Sejong in the fifteenth century and preserved through the Jangagwon court music bureau and its successor the National Gugak Center, comprising ritual aak, banquet suites such as Sujecheon and Yeongsan hoesang, and the vocal jeongga forms gagok, gasa and sijo — extremely slow, in long 20-beat and 10-beat cycles marked by janggu and buk, with geomungo, gayageum, daegeum, piri, haegeum and ajaeng in heterophony.
items.description: Jeongak is the 'correct music' of the Korean court and scholar class, standing opposite the folk minsogak repertoire in nearly every parameter. Tempos are among the slowest in world practice, individual tones swell and are shaped by nonghyeon left-hand pressure vibrato, and the ensemble proceeds heterophonically with the piri's reedy double-reed cutting above the string body while the janggu marks very long cycles. Against sanjo or minyo it is notated, restrained in dynamics and emotionally cool rather than virtuosic; against Japanese gagaku it is more linear and less chordal, lacking the sho's cluster harmony.
exemplars: National Gugak Center Court Music Orchestra

items.name: Gayageum byeongchang (self-accompanied gayageum song)
items.lineage: Korean solo form in which a performer sings pansori excerpts and short folk-derived songs while simultaneously accompanying herself on the twelve-string gayageum, developed in the late nineteenth century out of the sanjo circle around Kim Chang-jo and carried into the twentieth by Oh Tae-seok, Park Gwi-hui and Kang Jeong-suk — the zither punctuating rather than doubling the vocal line, both parts riding a janggu jangdan cycle in jinyang, jungmori or jajinmori, with the gruff pansori chest voice and wide yukjabaegi vibrato intact.
items.description: Byeongchang is the practice of singing and playing the gayageum at once, drawing texts from pansori episodes such as the Chunhyangga and from short danga and folk numbers. The zither does not simply shadow the voice: it fills the gaps between vocal phrases and reinforces cadences, while the left hand's nonghyeon pressure vibrato mirrors the singer's ornamentation. It differs from sanjo, which is purely instrumental and improvisatory, and from full pansori, which is a solo voice with only a barrel-drum accompanist and runs to several hours.

items.name: Joseon pop
items.lineage: Korean fusion style named around LEENALCHI's 2020 album Sugungga and its single 'Tiger Is Coming', in which pansori-trained singers deliver Sugungga narrative text over a rhythm section of two electric basses, drum kit and no harmony instrument, at steady mid-tempo post-punk and disco pulses, so that the sori vocal's yukjabaegi bends and jangdan phrasing sit against a Western groove; developed in Seoul indie circles alongside Ssing Ssing's earlier shaman-song glam-rock experiments from 2017.
items.description: Joseon pop is the label attached to the pansori-meets-post-punk sound that LEENALCHI made internationally visible in 2020.
