items.lineage: Named for the drum pattern Discharge codified on 'Why?' and 'Hear Nothing See Nothing Say Nothing' (Stoke-on-Trent, 1980-82) — kick on 1 and the 'and' of 2 against a snare backbeat with open ride or hats, at 170-200 BPM, under one- and two-chord distorted riffs, a bass mirroring the guitar, and shouted anti-war lyrics in short repeated slogans.
items.description: D-beat is less a scene than a transmissible rhythmic template: the specific Discharge kick-snare cadence that hundreds of bands worldwide adopted wholesale from the early 1980s onward, often signalling allegiance in their names (Disclose, Disfear, Dischange). The music is minimal in pitch content — one or two chords held for whole sections — and maximal in distortion and repetition, with the drum figure functioning as the genre's identity. Distinct from generic hardcore in that the beat itself, not tempo or attitude, is the defining criterion.

items.name: Crack Rock Steady
items.lineage: New York Lower East Side hybrid coined by Choking Victim and carried forward by Leftover Crack and INDK in the mid-1990s to 2000s — offbeat ska upstrokes and horn lines abruptly cut against thrash-tempo hardcore blasts and metal tremolo, with a nasal snarled lead vocal delivering squatter, anarchist and anti-police lyrics over organ stabs and a walking-to-galloping bass.
items.description: Crack Rock Steady names the ska-punk-metal fusion built by the Choking Victim / Leftover Crack circuit around New York squats and C-Squat from about 1994. Songs whiplash between skanking rocksteady verses with cheap organ and a small horn section and full-speed crust or thrash choruses, with heavily political, deliberately confrontational lyrics. It is far darker and more metallic than the contemporaneous third-wave ska-punk it superficially resembles, and more melodically structured than the crust punk it borrows its tempos from.

items.name: Queercore
items.lineage: North American queer punk movement launched by the Toronto zine J.D.s (G.B. Jones and Bruce LaBruce, 1985) and realized musically by Fifth Column, Team Dresch, Pansy Division and Limp Wrist from the late 1980s through the 1990s — standard punk instrumentation at 150-200 BPM with explicitly gay, lesbian and trans lyrics, ranging from Pansy Division's melodic pop-punk to Limp Wrist's thrash-speed hardcore.
items.description: Queercore began as a zine culture in mid-1980s Toronto and became a recorded scene in the 1990s United States, overlapping heavily with riot grrrl and the Pacific Northwest and Bay Area indie networks. Musically it does not carry a fixed sound — the shared markers are lyric content, self-released or small-label production, and a raw, unglossed band recording — spanning Team Dresch's angular post-hardcore, Pansy Division's Ramones-derived pop-punk and Limp Wrist's twenty-second hardcore blasts. It is distinguished from surrounding punk not by a rhythm or riff vocabulary but by an explicit, first-person queer subject.

items.name: Egg Punk
items.lineage: Internet-named strand of 2010s DIY punk crystallizing around Chicago's Erik Nervous, Coneheads, Big Zit and the Lumpy Records / Neck Chop orbit circa 2015-2020 — trebly, thin, deliberately cheap-sounding guitar, cheap monosynth or Casio bleeps, drum-machine or brittle live drums, hiccupping yelped vocals and short 120-170 BPM songs mixed midrange-forward in home recordings.
items.description: Egg punk is a late-2010s label — originally a message-board joke opposing it to the burlier 'chain punk' — for lo-fi, synth-tinged, Devo-descended DIY punk recorded at home and issued on small-run vinyl and Bandcamp. The sound is defined by absence: almost no low end, no reverb, brittle nasal vocals, and cheap keyboard tones sitting where a second guitar would be. It separates from ordinary garage punk by its deliberate cartoonishness and its heavier debt to first-wave synth-punk and Devo than to the Ramones.

items.name: Gypsy Punk
items.lineage: New York City style codified by Gogol Bordello (Eugene Hutz, from 1999) and paralleled by Balkan Beat Box and Golem — Romani and Balkan wedding-band material with accordion and violin leads over aksak and fast duple frameworks, accelerating from 120 to 200 BPM within a song, fused with punk distorted guitar, driving eighth-note bass and shouted, heavily accented vocals.
items.description: Gypsy punk formed in the New York immigrant club circuit at the turn of the 2000s, welding Eastern European Romani dance repertoire to punk-rock energy and stagecraft. The defining texture is a melodic front line of accordion and violin playing ornamented minor-mode and freygish lines over a distorted rock rhythm section, with tempos ratcheting upward through a song toward a frenzied coda. It differs from Balkan brass revival acts in centring rock instrumentation and English-language punk delivery rather than a horn ensemble.

items.name: Celtic Punk
items.lineage: Style established by The Pogues in London from 1982 and expanded by the Dropkick Murphys and Flogging Molly in 1990s Boston and Los Angeles — Irish session repertoire and jig/reel phrasing carried by tin whistle, tenor banjo, mandolin, accordion and bodhran over distorted guitar and punk backbeat at 140-180 BPM, with hoarse, slurred emigration-and-drink balladry sung in a shouted brogue.
items.description: Celtic punk began with The Pogues playing Irish traditional material at punk tempo and volume in early-1980s London, then took a heavier, more anthemic American form through the Dropkick Murphys and Flogging Molly a decade later. Its signature is the collision of a genuine trad melodic front line — whistle, tenor banjo, mandolin, accordion — with electric guitar, a rock kit and gang choruses, usually built on Dorian and Mixolydian modes rather than punk's blues pentatonic. Unlike folk-rock, the traditional tunes keep punk speed and attack instead of being smoothed into rock arrangements.

items.name: Horror Punk
items.lineage: Invented by the Misfits in Lodi, New Jersey between 1977 and 1983 and continued by Samhain, Blitzkid and the Italian scene of the 2000s — 1950s doo-wop and Buddy Holly turnarounds with 'whoa-oh' backing vocals played at 160-200 BPM punk tempo under B-movie and gore lyrics, topped by a baritone crooned-then-barked lead vocal doused in tape slapback.
items.description: Horror punk is the Misfits' particular formula: pre-Beatles American pop songcraft — I-vi-IV-V progressions, major-key melodies, layered 'whoa' choruses — rendered with distorted guitar, hardcore tempos and horror-film imagery, plus a visual identity of devilocks and skull makeup. Glenn Danzig's Elvis-derived baritone, wet with slapback echo, is as diagnostic as any riff. It differs from deathrock, its goth-side contemporary, by being fast, major-key and campy rather than slow, minor and atmospheric.

items.name: Gothabilly
items.lineage: Term circulating from The Cramps' orbit and made a scene label in the 1990s by Ghoultown, The Quakes and Zombie Ghost Train — 1950s rockabilly form (slapback-echoed hollowbody twang, slapped upright bass, minimal kit, walking 4/4 at 130-170 BPM) recast in minor and harmonic-minor keys with reverb-drenched tremolo guitar and theatrical, sepulchral crooned vocals.
items.description: Gothabilly is rockabilly played in the dark: the psychobilly-adjacent 1990s and 2000s scene that keeps the slapped upright bass, tape slapback and twanging hollowbody of Sun-era rock and roll but shifts to minor tonalities with horror and Western-gothic imagery. Production consciously imitates 1950s mono tracking — ribbon mics, tube front ends, heavy tape echo — rather than modern punk clarity. Against psychobilly it is slower and moodier, and against horror punk it retains the acoustic rockabilly rhythm section instead of distorted electric bass and hardcore tempos.

items.name: Deathrock
items.lineage: Los Angeles offshoot of punk formed 1979-1983 around Christian Death, 45 Grave, Kommunity FK and Super Heroines — mid-tempo 100-140 BPM tom-heavy tribal drumming, high melodic bass carrying the riff, thin chorused and heavily reverbed guitar playing single-note minor figures, cheap string synth or organ pads and declamatory, theatrical vocals over horror and decadence imagery.
items.description: Deathrock is the American, punk-descended branch of gothic rock, born in Los Angeles clubs like the Vex and the Cathay de Grande around 1980. The rhythm section inverts rock convention — bass takes the melodic lead while guitar supplies scraping chorus-and-delay atmospherics and the drums lean on floor toms and open snare rather than backbeat — and the vocals are spoken, shouted and wailed rather than sung. It is rawer, faster and more punk-rooted than English goth rock, and unlike horror punk it stays in minor tonality and plays the horror straight.

items.name: Minimal Wave
items.lineage: Retroactive category defined by Veronica Vasicka's Minimal Wave label (New York, 2005) for European and North American DIY synth records of roughly 1979-1985 — monophonic and cheap polyphonic synths, primitive drum machines at 100-130 BPM, single-take four-track cassette production, cold detached vocals often in French, German or Dutch, and short repetitive minor-key sequences with almost no arrangement development.
items.description: Minimal wave names the private-press and cassette-label synth music made across Belgium, France, Germany, the Netherlands and the United States in the early 1980s, rediscovered and canonized by reissue labels from about 2005. The records are austere by circumstance as much as intent: one or two synths, a drum machine, a home four-track, and vocals delivered flat and close, yielding cold, hissy, hypnotically repetitive songs. It sits between synthpop and coldwave — more song-shaped and vocal-led than pure minimal synth, but far bleaker and less produced than the chart electropop of the same years.

items.name: Sovietwave
items.lineage: Russian- and Ukrainian-language internet synth genre that coalesced on VKontakte and Bandcamp circa 2013-2016 around Хмурый (Khmury), Маяк, and СOSMORTUS, built from slow 90-110 BPM analog-poly-synth arpeggios, string-machine pads, LinnDrum-style gated snares, and sampled Soviet television, cosmonaut-broadcast and newsreel speech, with sparse Russian vocals or none at all, expressing nostalgia for a Soviet space-age future that never arrived.
items.description: Sovietwave formed in the Russian-speaking internet around 2013 as a post-Soviet counterpart to synthwave, though it trades synthwave's neon-noir Americana for Gagarin-era optimism. The sound is slow, major-key and deliberately unhurried: layered analog-style pads, simple diatonic arpeggios, brushed gated drums low in the mix, and archival Soviet radio and film speech used as the main vocal element. Unlike synthwave it is rarely dance-functional and rarely uses driving basslines; unlike vaporwave it is sincere rather than ironic, and composes original material instead of chopping existing records.

items.name: Neoclassical darkwave
items.lineage: European darkwave offshoot codified 1988-1998 by Dead Can Dance, Ataraxia, Stoa, Elend and the Projekt and Cold Meat Industry rosters, marrying gothic-rock pacing to bowed strings, cathedral-reverb piano, sampled or real choir and timpani, in slow duple or free-pulse settings, with operatic soprano or breathy contralto lead over minor-modal and Phrygian harmony and near-total absence of drum kit.
items.description: Neoclassical darkwave emerged in Western and Southern Europe in the late 1980s and peaked through 1990s labels such as Projekt, Prikosnovenie and Cold Meat Industry. Its texture is orchestral rather than rhythmic: sustained string writing, sampled or recorded choir, cavernous artificial reverb, and a lead voice trained toward early-music or operatic delivery, often singing in Latin, Italian or invented language. What separates it from ordinary darkwave is the near-elimination of the backbeat and the guitar, and from martial industrial the absence of percussive militarism and distortion.

items.name: Hardvapour
items.lineage: Online micro-genre launched in late 2015 by Dream Catalogue affiliates Sandtimer and Wanderer, explicitly framed as an aggressive rebuttal to vaporwave's mall-lounge softness: 150-180 BPM distorted 909 and gabber kicks, detuned hoover and rave-stab leads, blown-out mastering, Eastern-European and post-Soviet imagery, and screamed, pitched-down or entirely absent vocals.
items.description: Hardvapour was invented in November 2015 as a deliberate stylistic reaction inside the vaporwave network, and its releases circulated almost entirely as Bandcamp and YouTube uploads. Sonically it is closer to gabber and hard trance than to anything vaporwave: clipped distorted kick drums, rave hoovers, industrial noise beds and intentionally crushed loudness-war mastering. It keeps vaporwave's conceptual framing and album-art conventions while inverting the tempo, the aggression and the emotional register.

items.name: Slushwave
items.lineage: Vaporwave subgenre named around 2016-2018 and codified by 猫 シ Corp., t e l e p a t h テレパシー能力者, Hantasi and Vaperror, built by pitching sampled easy-listening or new-age loops down 30-60 percent, drowning them in cascaded reverb and delay, and stretching two- to four-bar cycles across ten- to thirty-minute beatless tracks with no discernible pulse.
items.description: Slushwave appeared in the late 2010s as the most ambient branch of vaporwave, taking the loop-and-slow method to its limit. Source material — lounge, smooth jazz, new age, corporate library music — is slowed until timbres smear, then buried under long convolution reverb tails so that individual events lose their attack entirely. Compared with classic vaporwave it discards the danceable pulse and the ironic sample-recognition game; compared with drone ambient it retains audible chord loops and the tape-hiss surface of its found sources.
exemplars: t e l e p a t h テレパシー能力者

items.name: Utopian virtual
items.lineage: Vaporwave-adjacent aesthetic named after James Ferraro's Far Side Virtual (2011) and extended by Vektroid, Dan Mason and INTERNET CLUB, using unaltered General MIDI patches, FM bells, Windows startup jingles and corporate-demo sound design at moderate tempos with clipped rhythmic phrases, ad-copy spoken text and no analog warmth at all.
items.description: Utopian virtual crystallised in 2011 around Far Side Virtual and the surrounding hypnagogic-pop network, and it is the branch of vaporwave that composes rather than samples. Its palette is aggressively synthetic and unsentimental: stock GM soundfonts, ringtone bells, sampled interface chimes, ad-voiceover fragments, and an unnaturally clean digital mix with no tape saturation or vinyl noise. That clarity is its signature — where classic vaporwave signals decay and nostalgia through hiss and pitch-shift, utopian virtual signals the airless optimism of a product demo.

items.name: Wonky
items.lineage: Term applied by UK critics around 2008 to a transatlantic beat current — Flying Lotus, Hudson Mohawke, Rustie, Zomby, Joker and Dorian Concept — defined by unquantised, deliberately lurching drum programming, heavy pitch-bend and LFO detune on mid-range synth leads, 808 sub-bass, and 70-160 BPM tracks that shift metric feel mid-phrase rather than holding a grid.
items.description: Wonky named a cluster of producers active roughly 2007-2011 who shared a method rather than a tempo: drums nudged off the grid so the pulse feels drunk, and mid-range synths bent continuously so no note sits at fixed pitch. The Glasgow LuckyMe and Los Angeles Brainfeeder camps supplied the two poles, one maximal and neon, the other jazz-inflected and smeared. Against dubstep it abandons the half-step bass drop as an organising event, and against instrumental hip-hop it foregrounds detuned synthesis over sample flips.

items.name: Bounce (New Orleans)
items.lineage: New Orleans street-rap style dated to MC T. Tucker and DJ Irv's 'Where Dey At' (1991) and carried by DJ Jubilee, Magnolia Shorty, Partners-N-Crime and Big Freedia, running roughly 95-105 BPM over the near-mandatory Triggerman ('Drag Rap') and Brown Beat loops, with call-and-response ward and project shout-outs, chanted repetitive hooks and relentless triplet-inflected snare rolls.
items.description: Bounce is New Orleans' own rap dialect, in continuous local circulation since 1991 and organised around two sampled loops — the Showboys' 'Drag Rap' (Triggerman) and Cameron Paul's 'Brown Beat' — that recur across hundreds of records almost unchanged. Performance is closer to a party MC's call-and-response than to written verse: ward roll-calls, chanted couplets, and long stretches of repeated commands to the dancers. The sissy bounce wing led by Big Freedia and Katey Red brought queer performers to the front without altering the underlying beat, and the style stands apart from Southern rap generally by its fixed loop, its faster pulse and its dance-floor call format.

items.name: Gym Phonk
items.lineage: Post-2021 offshoot of drift phonk shaped by TikTok and Instagram workout edits, associated with Ghostface Playa, DVRST, Freddie Dredd remixers and the Phonk Killer catalogue, built on a wide-tuned aggressive cowbell riff, four-on-floor or half-time 808 at 145-160 BPM, brickwalled loudness with almost no dynamic range, and short 60-to-120-second run times engineered for clip loops.
items.description: Gym phonk is the platform-optimised branch of phonk that surfaced from 2021 onward, written explicitly to survive phone speakers and short-form video compression. Tracks are extremely short, front-load the hook within a few seconds, and use a single distorted cowbell motif plus a maximised 808 with almost every other element removed. Against drift phonk it is even more compressed and more melodically simple, and against mainstream EDM it retains the Memphis-derived cowbell timbre rather than a synth supersaw lead.

items.name: Drain (post-cloud rap)
items.lineage: Stockholm-based cloud-rap aesthetic formed 2012-2016 around the Drain Gang collective — Bladee, Ecco2k, Thaiboy Digital and producer Whitearmor, in the Sad Boys orbit of Yung Lean — characterised by heavily Auto-Tuned thin high vocals, reverb-drowned bell and pad textures, sparse trap hi-hat programming at 130-150 BPM half-time, and fragmentary aphoristic lyrics about dissociation and luxury.
items.description: Drain is the internet-native Swedish rap sound built by Drain Gang and producer Whitearmor from roughly 2012 onward, extending American cloud rap into a colder, more ethereal register. The vocals are pitched high and processed with hard Auto-Tune until they read as an instrument, set against glassy bell patches, long reverb tails and skeletal 808 programming that often abandons the trap hi-hat roll entirely. It differs from US cloud rap in its emphasis on sung, almost hymnal melody over rapped cadence, and from hyperpop in retaining a trap rhythmic frame rather than a maximalist pop chorus.

items.name: Dungeon Rap
items.lineage: Underground internet rap style of the 2010s-2020s associated with Ghost, Kill Bill: The Rapper, Vio the Villain and the Dungeon Family Records/SoundCloud circuit, using tape-degraded loops of horror soundtracks and medieval or dungeon-synth textures under muffled murky 808s at 60-80 BPM half-time, with a low, half-mumbled and heavily reverbed rap delivery.
items.description: Dungeon rap is a lo-fi underground style that spread through SoundCloud and Bandcamp in the mid-2010s, welding the atmosphere of dungeon synth and horror-film scoring to slow, murk-mixed trap drums. Loops are deliberately buried under hiss and tape wobble, the 808 is filtered dark rather than clipping, and vocals sit low in the mix with long reverb so words dissolve into the pad. It is slower and more atmospheric than phonk, which foregrounds cowbell and Memphis samples, and unlike horrorcore it usually foregoes explicit gore narrative in favour of pure ambience.

items.name: Proto-Rap
items.lineage: Pre-1979 spoken-rhythmic Black American forms that fed directly into hip hop — the Jamaican-derived toasting of Kool Herc's Bronx block parties from 1973, the jazz-poetry declamation of the Last Poets and Gil Scott-Heron from 1968-1971, and the rhymed radio patter of DJs like Jocko Henderson — delivered over funk breakbeats, congas or bare percussion in loose 4/4 with a chanted call-and-response hook rather than a written verse-chorus form.
items.description: Proto-rap covers the immediately pre-commercial layer of rhythmic speech over groove that existed in New York and the Caribbean diaspora before Rapper's Delight in 1979. Its sources are Jamaican toasting brought north by Kool Herc, the militant jazz-poetry of the Last Poets and Gil Scott-Heron, and the rhyming showmanship of Black radio announcers, all set against extended funk breaks looped between two turntables. It is distinguished from later hip hop by the near-total absence of fixed sixteen-bar verse structure and studio recording, surviving mostly on party cassettes rather than commercial masters.
exemplars: Grandmaster Flash & the Furious Five (live tapes)

items.name: Battle Rap
items.lineage: Competitive rhymed-insult performance descending from Bronx park-jam MC clashes of the late 1970s, formalised through Scribble Jam and Blaze Battle in the 1990s, BET 106 & Park's Freestyle Friday, and after 2008 the a cappella league format of Smack/URL, King of the Dot and Don't Flop — three timed rounds, no instrumental backing, written multi-bar schemes packed with rebuttals, delivered at conversational tempo to a crowd whose reaction is part of the performance.
items.description: Battle rap is the competitive branch of hip hop in which two MCs trade prepared and improvised rhymed attacks before a judging crowd. Since the late 2000s the dominant league format is a cappella: no beat, no hook, just breath, cadence and crowd noise captured on a handheld mic and a camera rig, distributed on YouTube. That absence of instrumental is what separates it sonically from all other rap traditions, and its emphasis on rebuttal and scheme construction separates it from open freestyle cyphers, where improvisation rather than writing is the point.

items.name: Horrorcore
items.lineage: Violent-narrative rap subgenre formed 1988-1995 through the Geto Boys' Houston records, Esham's Detroit acid rap, the Memphis tape scene of Three 6 Mafia and Tommy Wright III, and New York's Gravediggaz — minor-key horror-soundtrack samples, detuned organ and bell figures, boom-bap or Memphis 808 drums at 85-100 BPM, and first-person psychotic-narrator verses often layered with screams and film dialogue.
items.description: Horrorcore crystallised at the turn of the 1990s in Houston, Detroit and Memphis as rap that borrowed the imagery, samples and pacing of slasher and occult cinema. Productions favour minor-mode organ, detuned bells, reversed cymbals and sampled screams over hard boom-bap or early Memphis 808 patterns, with vocals doubled and pitched down to sound inhuman. It differs from gangsta rap by treating violence as supernatural narrative rather than street reportage, and it is the direct historical source of the Memphis tapes that phonk later resampled.
exemplars: Geto Boys — We Can't Be Stopped

items.name: Grime
items.lineage: East London MC-and-producer genre formed 2000-2003 out of UK garage and jungle by Wiley, Dizzee Rascal, More Fire Crew and the Roll Deep and Ruff Sqwad crews on pirate radio — 140 BPM instrumentals with a syncopated 8-bar or 16-bar skeletal structure, square-wave and sine sublows, sparse Playstation-era FruityLoops synth stabs, and rapid-fire aggressive MCing in London slang delivered over a spare, mostly beatless-in-the-middle arrangement.
items.description: Grime emerged in East London around 2001-2003 when garage MCs and producers stripped the genre's soulful vocals and swung shuffle down to a hard, angular 140 BPM instrumental built in FruityLoops on cheap PCs. The instrumentals are deliberately empty — a bass sine, a couple of dissonant square stabs, and a skeletal kick-snare figure that leaves space for the MC, who delivers rapid, clipped bars over pirate-radio transmission. It differs from UK garage by discarding the four-to-the-floor R&B pull for a jagged eskibeat pattern, and from US rap by its faster tempo, its clash culture and its bass-weight sound-system heritage.
exemplars: Dizzee Rascal — Boy in da Corner

items.name: UK Funky
items.lineage: London dance genre of 2008-2010 built by Crazy Cousinz, Roska, Marcus Nasty, Geeneus and Lil Silva after grime's chart decline — 128-132 BPM four-to-the-floor or broken kick patterns overlaid with soca, kuduro and Afro-Latin percussion (congas, timbales, shaker), sparse synth pads, and sung or MC'd hooks drawn from UK garage's vocal tradition.
items.description: UK funky formed in London around 2008 as the city's Black dance producers turned from grime and dubstep toward house tempos infused with African and Caribbean percussion. The template is a house-weight kick under layered conga, timbale and shaker patterns lifted from soca and kuduro, with a warm pad or organ vamp and a vocal hook that recalls the garage era. It is distinguished from house by its tribal percussion foreground and broken kick variants, and from grime by tempo, four-to-the-floor pulse and sung rather than rapped delivery.

items.name: UK Garage
items.lineage: London club genre of 1994-2001 grown from sped-up US garage-house dubs by Todd Edwards, Tuff Jam, Grant Nelson, MJ Cole and Artful Dodger — 130-135 BPM shuffled swing, chopped and pitched R&B vocal fragments, filtered organ and piano stabs, ducking sub-bass, and dubplate-driven pirate-radio circulation with MCs riding the mix.
items.description: UK garage began in mid-1990s London as DJs pitched up the dub sides of New Jersey garage-house records for a faster, more swung dancefloor, then developed its own production language of sliced vocal microedits, gospel-house organ stabs and a rounded, sidechained sub. By 1999 it had a chart-pop wing built on sung R&B hooks and an MC culture inherited from jungle. It differs from US garage house in its shuffle and its bass weight, and from jungle in dropping the breakbeat chop for a swung four-four or two-step frame.

items.name: 2-Step
items.lineage: The dominant UK garage variant of 1997-2001, codified by Steve Gurley, Zed Bias, El-B, Sunship and Groove Chronicles, defined by a syncopated kick pattern that omits beats two and four, skipping shuffled hi-hats and shakers at 130-135 BPM, a swung sub-bass locked to the gaps, and soulful female R&B vocals cut into stuttering fragments.
items.description: 2-step is the broken-beat strain of UK garage that took over London clubs from about 1997, replacing the four-to-the-floor kick with a lurching two-kick-per-bar pattern that leaves the backbeat open. The resulting swing is carried by ghost-note hats, shakers and a bass that answers the missing kicks, while chopped soulful vocals float above with heavy reverb and pitch-shifted stutters. It is the immediate parent of both 2000s UK R&B-pop crossovers and, once the vocals and swing were stripped away, of dubstep and grime.
exemplars: Craig David — Born to Do It

items.name: Halftime Drum & Bass
items.lineage: Emerged circa 2012-2015 across London, Prague and Vienna out of the neurofunk and autonomic wings of drum & bass, codified by Ivy Lab, Alix Perez's 1985 Music, Sam Binga and Fracture — retaining the 170-175 BPM drum-and-bass grid and 32-bar arrangement while programming the kick-snare backbone at half that rate so the snare lands on beat three, leaving space for swung trap-derived hi-hat triplets, heavily resampled and time-stretched breaks, and a foregrounded distorted sub-bass or Reese line with no vocal lead beyond chopped fragments.
items.description: Halftime drum & bass formed in the early 2010s London and Central European bass scenes as producers kept the 170 BPM drum & bass tempo grid but halved the felt backbeat, so the music reads as roughly 85 BPM hip-hop while still mixing with standard D&B. Its signature is the snare on beat three, swung triplet hi-hat filigree borrowed from trap, deeply sound-designed Reese and sub-bass movement, and long unresolved atmospheric pads instead of a drop-and-release structure. It differs from neurofunk in refusing the fast two-step rollout, from trap in its 170 BPM host tempo and breakbeat sample sourcing, and from jungle in its near-total absence of chopped Amen density.

items.name: Digital Hardcore
items.lineage: Coined in Berlin in 1993 by Alec Empire, who founded the Digital Hardcore Recordings label and Atari Teenage Riot to fuse hardcore punk's shouted political sloganeering with 180-220 BPM breakbeat programming — Amen and Funky Drummer breaks pushed into clipping distortion, downtuned electric guitar riffs cut into sampler-triggered stabs, screamed dual male-female vocals in German and English, and an anti-fascist agitprop lyric stance shaped by the post-reunification squat scene.
items.description: Digital hardcore was invented in Berlin in 1993 as an explicit collision of punk ideology and rave technology, most visibly through Alec Empire's Digital Hardcore Recordings roster and Atari Teenage Riot. The sound is defined by breakbeats sampled to the point of clipping and red-lined through cheap gear, downtuned guitar stabs treated as percussion, tempos between 180 and 220 BPM, and shouted or screamed political vocals traded between two singers rather than sung hooks. It is distinguished from gabber by its punk band roster and guitar content, from breakcore by its song-shaped verse-chorus scaffolding, and from industrial rock by using samplers rather than a live rhythm section.

items.name: Speedcore
items.lineage: Split off from Rotterdam and Frankfurt gabber around 1993-1995 via Moby's 'Thousand', Delta 9 in Washington DC and Noizecreator in Germany — defined by tempos from 300 BPM upward, a distorted TR-909 kick clipped into a pitched tonal thud that carries the entire bassline, horror-film and pornographic vocal samples, no harmonic development, and short violent tracks built for endurance rather than dancefloor pacing.
items.description: Speedcore emerged in the mid-1990s from the fastest edge of Dutch and German gabber, defined purely by tempo: 300 BPM and above, where the distorted kick drum fires so rapidly it fuses into a pitched tone. Tracks are short, deliberately abrasive, and structured around a single overdriven 909 kick, screaming sirens, and shock-value spoken samples with almost no melodic or harmonic content. It differs from mainstream gabber by roughly doubling the tempo, from extratone by remaining below the point where individual kicks stop being audible as beats, and from industrial hardcore by rejecting atmosphere in favour of speed alone.

items.name: Extratone
items.lineage: An internet-native extreme of speedcore consolidated in the mid-2000s through European netlabels and the Extratone forum scene, with producers such as m1dy, Nasenbluten-adjacent circles and later Mocha and DJ Kurara — defined by tempos above roughly 1000 BPM where kick repetitions exceed 16 Hz and fuse into a continuous buzzing pitched drone, so rhythm is perceived as timbre and 'melody' is written by modulating the kick's repetition rate.
items.description: Extratone is the terminal case of speedcore, circulated almost entirely through netlabels, forums and file-sharing from the mid-2000s onward. Above roughly 1000 BPM the individual kick drum hits cross the threshold of pitch perception and become a continuous tone, so producers compose by sweeping the repetition rate itself, layering noise beds and heavily clipped samples over the resulting drone. It is distinguished from speedcore by that perceptual threshold, from harsh noise wall by retaining a nominal BPM and kick source, and from power electronics by its rave lineage and DAW-native distribution.

items.name: Frenchcore
items.lineage: Formed in the mid-1990s French free-party and teknival circuit around Micropoint, Radium and the Audiogenic label, and revived commercially in the 2010s by Dr Peacock and Sefa — running 190-220 BPM with a long, pitch-bent, heavily overdriven kick whose tail supplies the bassline, offbeat hoover stabs, acid-derived 303 lines, and cinematic breakdown-to-drop arrangements adapted from Dutch hardcore.
items.description: Frenchcore grew out of the French free-party sound systems of the mid-1990s and became a festival-scale genre in the 2010s. Its identity rests on a long, downward-pitch-bent distorted kick that doubles as the bass instrument at 190-220 BPM, offbeat hoover and acid stabs, and a rolling forward momentum rather than the stop-start punch of Rotterdam gabber. It differs from uptempo hardcore by staying below 230 BPM and keeping melodic content, from terrorcore by its danceable groove, and from hardstyle by its far higher tempo and rawer distortion.

items.name: Uptempo Hardcore
items.lineage: Consolidated in the Netherlands and Belgium circa 2014-2018 out of the raw hardcore scene via producers such as N-Vitral, Dr Donk, Lunatic and Killshot on labels like Barbaric Records and Triumph — running 200-260 BPM with a short, brutally clipped and pitched kick programmed in rolling triplet and gabber-roll patterns, screamed or pitch-shifted vocal shouts, and drops built from kick-pattern variation rather than melody.
items.description: Uptempo hardcore crystallised in the Low Countries in the mid-2010s as the fastest mainstream branch of Dutch hardcore, sitting between 200 and 260 BPM. The kick is short, screamingly distorted and explicitly tuned, arranged in rolls and triplets so that kick programming carries the hook, with shouted or formant-shifted vocal one-liners and minimal melodic material. It is separated from mainstream and raw hardcore by tempo and kick-roll density, from frenchcore by its punchier short kick and absence of long pitch bends, and from speedcore by remaining structured for large festival stages.

items.name: Xtra Raw
items.lineage: A late-2010s Dutch offshoot of raw hardstyle, driven by producers such as Rebelion, Sub Sonik, Vertile and Sickmode on Gearbox and Dirty Workz — running 150-165 BPM with an extremely overdriven, screech-tailed reverse-bass kick, minor-key detuned lead screeches, heavy sidechained pumping, and drops whose energy comes from kick timbre and pitch bending rather than the euphoric melodies of classic hardstyle.
items.description: Xtra raw is the most distorted wing of Dutch raw hardstyle, named and popularised around 2017-2019 through Rebelion, Sub Sonik and Sickmode. It runs at 150-165 BPM with a screeching, heavily saturated kick whose tail is pitch-bent into an audible melodic line, paired with detuned minor-key screech leads and aggressive sidechain pumping. It is distinguished from euphoric hardstyle by discarding uplifting melody and vocals, from mainstream raw by an even more extreme kick distortion profile, and from uptempo hardcore by its markedly lower tempo and reverse-bass grid.

items.name: Hands Up
items.lineage: A German and Dutch commercial rave style codified 2003-2010 through labels like Zoo Digital, Aqualoop and Andorfine and acts such as Cascada, Manian, Rocco and Italobrothers — 140-160 BPM four-on-the-floor with an offbeat detuned supersaw bass, sugary major-key trance-derived leads, pitch-shifted or heavily processed female vocal hooks, and euphoric build-breakdown-drop structures descended from happy hardcore and eurodance.
items.description: Hands up is a German-Dutch commercial rave genre of the 2000s, named for the crowd gesture it was engineered to trigger. It runs at 140-160 BPM with a clean four-on-the-floor kick, offbeat detuned supersaw bass, bright major-key trance leads and prominent sped-up or processed female vocal hooks, always resolving to an anthemic drop. It differs from happy hardcore in using a house-style kick rather than a distorted one, from eurodance in tempo and the absence of a rap verse, and from uplifting trance in its shorter, hook-first pop song structure.

items.name: Tekk (German Hard Dance)
items.lineage: Developed in eastern Germany, especially Saxony and Leipzig, from the mid-2000s as a hard-dance descendant of Dutch jumpstyle and hardtekk, spread through Talstrasse 3-5, Frank Nitzsche and countless MySpace and YouTube producers — 150-170 BPM with a punchy compressed kick, an offbeat detuned bass, simple minor-key synth leads and short repeating vocal hooks, arranged for jumpstyle dancing in car parks and village discos.
items.description: Tekk is an East German hard-dance style that grew out of jumpstyle in the late 2000s and circulated largely through amateur producers on MySpace, YouTube and free download portals. It sits at 150-170 BPM with a hard compressed kick, offbeat detuned bass stab, minimal minor-key lead riff and looped vocal fragments, built for jump-dance rather than club mixing. It is distinguished from hands up by its darker, sparser palette and lack of vocal anthems, from hardstyle by its lighter kick and lower production budget, and from hardtekk by predating that scene's rave-nostalgic sound design.

items.name: Hardtekk
items.lineage: A Leipzig- and Chemnitz-centred German revival of tekk that broke widely between 2019 and 2023 through Rakete, Sonikku-adjacent producers, Nakkarin and Aria (Aria Grande), plus TikTok circulation — 150-170 BPM built on a short punchy distorted kick with an offbeat rumble bass, 1990s rave hoover and piano stabs, sped-up pop and hip-hop vocal samples, and abrupt drop-heavy edits made almost entirely in FL Studio.
items.description: Hardtekk is the 2019-2023 German revival of tekk, centred on Leipzig and Chemnitz and propelled by TikTok and free-download culture. It runs 150-170 BPM over a short distorted kick and offbeat rumble bass, layered with 1990s rave hoovers, piano stabs and sped-up vocal samples lifted from contemporary pop and rap. It differs from its 2000s tekk parent by its rave-nostalgic sample palette and far more polished bass design, from hardstyle by its lighter, rolling kick, and from schranz by its melodic hook orientation.

items.name: Raggatek
items.lineage: Formed in the French and Spanish free-party teknival circuit in the early 2000s around Sirius, Da Mongoloids and the Rotule and Jah Gunz collectives — 170-200 BPM tribe-and-hardtek kick patterns overlaid with pitched-up Jamaican ragga and dancehall vocal samples, siren melodica lines, chopped Amen fills and dub-style delay throws, played from mobile sound systems at outdoor teknivals.
items.description: Raggatek arose in the European free-party teknival scene of the early 2000s, mainly in France and Spain, by grafting Jamaican ragga and dancehall vocal samples onto the fast hardtek and tribe kick grid. It runs 170-200 BPM with a driving distorted kick, offbeat bass, chopped breaks, dub delay throws and pitched-up MC samples that carry the melody. It differs from ragga jungle by its four-on-the-floor teknival kick rather than breakbeat foundation, from frenchcore by its lighter kick and vocal-sample focus, and from mainstream hardcore by its illegal-party sound-system context.

items.name: Acidcore
items.lineage: Emerged in the mid-1990s across the UK Spiral Tribe diaspora and the French and Czech teknival networks — 160-200 BPM hard techno kick patterns driven by one or several overdriven Roland TB-303 lines whose resonant filter sweeps and accent patterns constitute the entire melodic content, with metallic 909 percussion, no vocals, and hypnotic long-form arrangements built for all-night outdoor sound systems.
items.description: Acidcore developed in the mid-1990s free-party circuit that Spiral Tribe carried from Britain into France, Italy and the Czech Republic. It couples a hard 160-200 BPM techno kick with stacked, overdriven TB-303 lines whose live filter and accent manipulation supply all melody and development across long hypnotic tracks. It is set apart from acid techno by its faster, harder kick and teknival context, from hardcore techno by keeping the 303 rather than the distorted kick as the lead voice, and from frenchcore by its unbroken hypnotic arrangement without drop structures.

items.name: Industrial Hardcore
items.lineage: Codified in the Netherlands and Germany around 1997-2005 on the Enzyme, PRSPCT and Meta4 labels through Ophidian, Tymon, Sei2ure and Hellfish — 170-200 BPM with a heavily distorted but slowly evolving kick, sampled factory and machine noise, chopped Amen and industrial breakbeats, dissonant atonal drones, and dark cinematic arrangements that favour tension and texture over drop-and-release.
items.description: Industrial hardcore took shape in Dutch and German hardcore circles around the turn of the millennium, above all on Enzyme and PRSPCT. It combines a distorted 170-200 BPM kick with sampled machinery, chopped breakbeats, dissonant drones and dub-influenced space, favouring slow-building atmosphere and textural detail over the drop-driven arc of mainstream hardcore. It is distinguished from gabber by its slower tempo and sound-design ambition, from breakcore by keeping a steady kick spine, and from industrial techno by its hardcore-scene kick distortion and breakbeat sourcing.

items.name: Mincecore
items.lineage: Coined by Belgian band Agathocles in Deinze around 1987 as a deliberate rejection of the term grindcore, mincecore fuses 200-plus-BPM blastbeat bursts with mid-tempo d-beat crust punk stomps, downtuned buzzsaw guitar, and alternating low guttural growls and hoarse shouted political sloganeering across songs often under ninety seconds, released almost exclusively on split 7-inches and tape trades.
items.description: Mincecore emerged in late-1980s Flanders as Agathocles' own name for their raw, anarcho-political variant of grindcore, and the label was adopted by a wider DIY tape-trading network across Europe, Brazil and Southeast Asia. The sound alternates violently between blastbeat sprints and lurching mid-paced crust riffs, with bass distorted into a rumble and vocals split between a low growl and a shouted upper register. Unlike death-metal-influenced grindcore it stays deliberately unpolished and punk in allegiance, refusing studio clarity, technical soloing and long song forms.

items.name: Flashcore
items.lineage: Formalized in Paris around 1998-2003 by La Peste and the Hangars Liquides label alongside Australia's Xanopticon and Japan's DJ Technorch, flashcore pushes hardcore techno past 300 BPM into rapid-fire clusters of resynthesized distorted kicks, granular micro-edits and abrupt silences, abandoning the steady four-on-the-floor pulse for arrhythmic, compositionally-structured bursts closer to musique concrete than dancefloor gabber.
items.description: Flashcore crystallized in the French hardcore underground at the turn of the 2000s as an explicitly avant-garde exit from gabber, driven by Laurent Mialon's La Peste project and the Hangars Liquides catalogue. Kicks are synthesized and pitch-swept rather than sampled, tempos sit between 250 and 1000 BPM, and structure proceeds by dense event clusters and hard cuts rather than sixteen-bar loops. Where speedcore simply accelerates the gabber template, flashcore dissolves the pulse entirely and treats the distorted kick as a spectral compositional object.

items.name: Deconstructed Club
items.lineage: Formed circa 2012-2016 around Berlin's Janus parties, Mexico City's NAAFI, Lisbon's Principe and London's Night Slugs/Fade to Mind axis, deconstructed club strips ballroom, grime, reggaeton and trance to skeletal negative-space arrangements — arrhythmic kick placement, metallic percussion and orchestra-hit stabs, sirens, weaponized foley, pitched-down vocal fragments — at 130-150 BPM with dramatic drop-outs replacing conventional build-and-release.
items.description: Deconstructed club is a mid-2010s international network style in which producers dismantle regional dance idioms into unstable, collage-like tracks built for club systems but resistant to sustained mixing. Its markers are sudden silence, unquantized percussive hits, industrial and foley textures, hyperreal digital sheen, and vocals treated as processed shards rather than hooks. It differs from its Jersey club and ballroom sources in refusing a continuous danceable pulse, and from noise or industrial music in retaining club-functional tempos and sound-design gloss.

items.name: Ballroom (House Ballroom Scene)
items.lineage: Grown out of Harlem and downtown New York drag balls from the late 1980s and codified on record by MikeQ, Vjuan Allure and the Qween Beat and Vogue Knights circles from the mid-2000s, ballroom is 128-135 BPM 4/4 house built on a chopped 'Ha' crash sample from Masters at Work's 'The Ha Dance', clattering triplet snare rolls, whistle and chant vocals, and commentator ad-libs cued to runway categories.
items.description: Ballroom is the functional dance music of the Black and Latine LGBTQ house-ball community, tied to competitive categories and the live MC's chant. Its signature is the 'Ha' crash — a sampled brass-and-cymbal hit from The Ha Dance placed on the fifth beat of the pattern — over hard house drums, plus stuttered snare fills that cue the dancer's dip. Distinct from Chicago house and garage in that its arrangement serves floor performance cues rather than DJ-mix continuity, and from its vogue-fem derivative in retaining fuller house instrumentation.
exemplars: Masters at Work – The Ha Dance

items.name: Wave (Hardwave)
items.lineage: Emerging around 2014-2016 out of London and continental European Soundcloud circles via Klimeks, Skit, Plastician's Terrorhythm label and the Liquid Ritual crew, wave sets 140-150 BPM halftime trap drums under cavernous reverbed detuned supersaw and bell leads, sub-bass swells and pitched vocal chops, with hardwave sharpening the same template into distorted, aggressive drops.
items.description: Wave formed in the mid-2010s online underground as a melancholic successor to witch house and trap-influenced bass music, characterized by huge reverb tails, detuned saw and bell pads, halftime 808 patterns and a deliberately cinematic emotional register. Hardwave, from around 2018, keeps the harmonic language but adds heavily distorted drops and faster, more aggressive percussion. Compared with future garage it is slower-feeling and more melodically foregrounded, and unlike vaporwave it is composed rather than sample-derived.

items.name: Dreampunk
items.lineage: Named around 2016 by the Dream Catalogue label under HKE in the wake of the 2 8 1 4 records, dreampunk slows vaporwave's sample logic into 60-80 BPM or beatless long-form ambient — heavily reverbed and time-stretched synth pads, dial-tone and rain field recordings, distant Mandarin or Japanese speech samples, tape hiss and cassette wow — arranged as continuous album-length dystopian-city atmospheres.
items.description: Dreampunk grew directly out of the vaporwave network around Dream Catalogue in 2015-2016, trading mall-muzak nostalgia for a cyberpunk-city ambient palette of vast reverb, degraded tape texture and spoken-word fragments. Rhythm is usually absent or reduced to a slow pulse, and tracks run long, unfolding through timbral drift rather than harmonic movement. It differs from mallsoft in its dystopian rather than consumerist imagery, and from classic ambient in its sample-based, deliberately lo-fi digital-decay surface.
exemplars: t e l e p a t h テレパシー能力者

items.name: Glitchcore
items.lineage: Crystallized on TikTok and SoundCloud in 2019-2021 out of the hyperpop and nightcore edit scenes, glitchcore takes 160-180 BPM pitched-up vocals and applies stutter-repeat, bitcrush, timestretch and beat-repeat edits at sub-beat resolution over clipped 808s and blown-out drums, matched to strobing hyper-cut video and produced almost entirely in-the-box by teenage bedroom producers.
items.description: Glitchcore is a platform-native style that appeared around 2019 as hyperpop's most editing-intensive offshoot, defined by rapid stutter and bitcrush processing applied to sped-up pop vocals over distorted, clipped drums. Tracks are typically short, extremely dense, and structured around abrupt digital-artifact transitions rather than conventional builds. It is distinguished from IDM glitch by its pop-vocal source material and social-video context, and from nightcore by its aggressive destructive editing rather than simple pitch and tempo acceleration.

items.name: Dariacore
items.lineage: Invented by New Jersey producer Leroy (Kaitlyn 'dltzk' Bee) with the 2021 album Dariacore, the style is maximalist mashup music at roughly 150-170 BPM that stacks dozens of instantly recognizable pop, rap and meme samples into rapid Jersey-club-derived triplet kick patterns, air-horns, crowd noise and abrupt key-shifting cuts, sequenced so that no idea lasts more than a few bars.
items.description: Dariacore is a 2021 internet microgenre named after the album that launched it, built from hyper-fast collage of familiar samples over Jersey club and breakbeat rhythms, with deliberate sensory overload as the aesthetic goal. Its sources are drawn from mainstream pop, rap ad-libs, video game audio and memes, cut so densely that recognition becomes a rhythmic device. Unlike mashup culture it does not aim for seamless blends, and unlike plunderphonics it is functionally danceable and rooted in club-tempo drum programming.

items.name: HexD
items.lineage: Coalescing on SoundCloud around 2020-2022 out of Memphis phonk, hyperpop and Brazilian funk edits, HexD is defined by extreme bitcrushing and sample-rate reduction applied to the entire mix — clipped 808s, pitched-up chipmunk vocals, cowbell phonk patterns at 130-160 BPM — plus deliberate MP3 artifacting and mono, distorted phone-speaker mastering.
items.description: HexD is an early-2020s SoundCloud style whose defining move is treating digital degradation as the primary instrument: bit-depth and sample-rate reduction, hard clipping and lossy-codec artifacts are applied to whole tracks until the sound resembles an overdriven phone speaker. Musically it inherits phonk's cowbell-and-808 patterns and hyperpop's sped-up vocals. Where lo-fi hip hop uses tape warmth for comfort, HexD uses digital destruction for abrasion, and unlike glitchcore its damage is applied globally rather than as sub-beat editing.

items.name: Bubblegum Bass
items.lineage: Codified in London from 2013 by A. G. Cook's PC Music label together with SOPHIE and QT, bubblegum bass sets 130-150 BPM hard-clipped square and rubbery FM bass leads under extremely pitch-shifted, formant-raised and heavily retuned female vocals, borrowing eurodance and J-pop chord loops while treating hyper-glossy commercial sheen and synthetic textures as an explicit conceptual stance.
items.description: Bubblegum bass is the mid-2010s London studio style around PC Music and SOPHIE that recombines eurodance, trance and J-pop hooks with synthetic bass design and radically processed vocals. Its sonic markers are formant-shifted saccharine voices, latex-like plastic bass timbres, hyper-compressed transients and an absence of any acoustic reference. It is the direct precursor of hyperpop, from which it differs in its cooler, conceptual and less emo-rap-inflected orientation, and it separates from mainstream EDM by rejecting the drop-driven festival template.

items.name: Nightcore
items.lineage: Begun in 2002 by Norwegian students Thomas S. Nilsen and Steffen Ojala Soderholm as a school project, nightcore is a transformation rather than a composition: existing eurodance, trance and later pop tracks are sped up roughly 10-35 percent with pitch raised in tandem, producing 160-180 BPM four-on-the-floor tracks with distinctively childlike, formant-raised vocals, distributed as YouTube uploads over anime stills.
items.description: Nightcore originated as a Norwegian duo's 2002 remix project and became a self-propagating YouTube practice in which any track is accelerated and pitch-raised together, producing the scene's signature chipmunk vocal. The underlying material is usually eurodance or hands-up trance, so the results keep four-on-the-floor kicks, supersaw hooks and simple diatonic loops at extreme tempo. Unlike a conventional remix nothing is re-arranged, and unlike chipmunk soul the speed change affects the whole mix rather than a chopped sample, which is exactly why it became the tempo and vocal baseline for later hyperpop and glitchcore.
exemplars: Nightcore (Thomas S. Nilsen & Steffen Ojala Soderholm)

items.name: Denpa Song
items.lineage: Formed in Japan through late-1990s and 2000s bishoujo-game and doujin circles around Momoi Halko, MOSAIC.WAV and the Under17 duo, denpa pairs deliberately shrill high-register anime-style vocals and nonsense onomatopoeic hooks with 150-190 BPM chiptune-flavoured eurobeat and akiba-pop backing, abrupt key changes, and call-and-response otagei chant sections built for audience participation.
items.description: Denpa is a Japanese otaku-culture pop idiom that emerged from eroge theme songs and Akihabara doujin releases around the turn of the 2000s, named after the slang for someone receiving strange radio waves. It is defined by intentionally piercing, cute vocal delivery, meaningless syllabic hooks, hyperactive tempos and chiptune, eurobeat and moe-pop arrangement borrowings, with structures engineered around otagei chant responses. Against mainstream J-pop it courts irritation rather than polish, and against Vocaloid music it centres a human voice performing an exaggerated anime persona.

items.name: Touhou doujin arrange music
items.lineage: Japanese fan-arrangement circuit built on ZUN's Touhou Project shooting-game themes (1996 onward, PC-98 FM then Windows-era PCM), codified from the early 2000s at Comiket by circles such as IOSYS, Alstroemeria Records, SOUND HOLIC, COOL&CREATE and Demetori — 150-190 BPM covers of a fixed melodic canon rebuilt as eurobeat, hardcore, power metal, jazz-fusion or trance, keeping the originals' harmonic-minor and Phrygian-dominant tunes, rapid 16th-note arpeggiated backing and abrupt key-shifting B-sections, with a high anime-inflected female lead or an all-instrumental shred arrangement.
items.description: Touhou arrange music is the doujin (self-published) arrangement scene that grew around ZUN's Touhou Project game soundtracks, consolidating in Japan in the early-to-mid 2000s through Comiket sales and Niconico uploads. Its material is a closed melodic canon — a few hundred game themes in harmonic minor and Phrygian dominant, densely arpeggiated at 150-190 BPM — rearranged wholesale into whatever host genre the circle works in, so a single tune may exist as eurobeat, melodic death metal and piano trio. Unlike Vocaloid production, the melodies are borrowed rather than original and the vocals are human; unlike ordinary game-music covers, arrangement is the point and the circles operate as a self-sustaining commercial ecosystem.

items.name: Demoscene tracker module music
items.lineage: European computer-demo subculture music, formed on the Commodore Amiga after Karsten Obarski's Ultimate Soundtracker (1987) and carried onto PC by ProTracker, Scream Tracker, FastTracker II and Impulse Tracker — composed by Purple Motion, Skaven, Jesper Kyd, Lizardking and Necros for Future Crew, Triton and Renaissance demos and shown at Assembly and The Party — 120-165 BPM four-to-thirty-two-channel patterns of short looped samples entered as hexadecimal note tables, with heavy use of volume/pitch effect columns, sample offset tricks and slot-sharing to fake extra voices inside a few hundred kilobytes.
items.description: Demoscene music is the tracker-module repertoire written from 1987 onward to soundtrack real-time computer demos, first on the Amiga's four-channel Paula chip and then on PC soundcards. The idiom is shaped by file-size ceilings: a handful of one-shot samples reused across bass, lead and pads, aggressive per-row effect commands standing in for envelopes and filters, and multi-part structures that develop over five or six minutes rather than looping. Unlike chipmusic proper it is sample-based rather than chip-synthesised, and unlike game soundtracks it is through-composed for a fixed non-interactive visual sequence, which is why its arrangements build and modulate like concert pieces.
exemplars: Jesper Kyd — The Silents / Amiga demos

items.name: Commodore 64 SID music
items.lineage: British and Northern European game-music practice of 1983-1992 written for the MOS 6581/8580 SID chip in the Commodore 64, codified by Rob Hubbard, Martin Galway, Ben Daglish, Jeroen Tel and Chris Huelsbeck via hand-written 6502 assembly players — three voices only, so chords are rendered as 50Hz arpeggio cycling, bass and lead share a channel through rapid note interleaving, and colour comes from pulse-width modulation, hard sync, ring modulation and the chip's resonant analog filter, over driving 130-160 BPM patterns whose drums are the noise oscillator with a fast pitch envelope.
items.description: SID music is the body of Commodore 64 game and demo soundtracks written between roughly 1983 and 1992, when a handful of composers turned a three-voice chip with one shared analog filter into a recognisable compositional style. Its hallmarks are the chirping fast arpeggio used as a chord substitute, channel-stealing that makes three voices sound like five, filter sweeps and ring-modulated metallic timbres, and long loopable cues that develop through variation rather than a chorus. Compared to Famicom/NES writing it is far more timbrally varied because of the filter and pulse-width control, and compared to later chipmusic it was produced commercially under deadline for cassette- and disk-loaded games rather than for live performance.
exemplars: Rob Hubbard — Monty on the Run

items.name: Algorave (live-coded algorithmic dance music)
items.lineage: UK-originated live-coding dance practice named by Alex McLean and Nick Collins in 2011-2012 out of Sheffield, Nottingham and the TOPLAP live-coding movement — performers write and rewrite code on stage in TidalCycles, SuperCollider, Sonic Pi or Hydra with the editor projected behind them, generating 120-180 BPM sample-and-synthesis patterns whose Euclidean rhythms, polymetric cycle-lengths and probabilistic substitutions mutate audibly with each evaluated line, over techno-derived kick foundations and glitch-heavy percussive grain.
items.description: Algorave is dance music generated by code written live in front of the audience, named in 2012 by Alex McLean and Nick Collins and spreading from UK warehouse nights into an international network of events. Musically it sits on a techno chassis but the material is pattern algebra: Euclidean and polymetric cycles of differing lengths drifting in and out of phase, randomised sample substitution, and abrupt structural jumps that happen when a line of code is re-evaluated rather than at bar 16. It is distinguished from DJ sets and hardware-jam techno by the absence of pre-made tracks and by the projected source code, which makes the compositional decision-making part of the performance.

items.name: Psydub (psychedelic dub)
items.lineage: Mid-2000s downtempo offshoot of the psytrance chillout room, codified by Ott (Hallucinogen in Dub, 2002; Blumenkraft, 2003), Kaya Project, Bluetech and Kalya Scintilla on Twisted and Interchill — 70-110 BPM half-time dub drum patterns with heavy siren-tail delay and spring-style reverb on every hit, deep sine sub-bass, phased and filter-swept psytrance lead patches slowed to a crawl, and sampled tabla, hand percussion and South Asian or Middle Eastern vocal fragments layered as texture.
items.description: Psydub is the dub-processing branch of psychedelic chillout, consolidated in the UK and North America in the mid-2000s when Ott's remix work applied Jamaican mixing-desk technique to psytrance sound design. The result runs at 70-110 BPM with skanking half-time drums drenched in feedback delay, a clean sine sub, and slow-modulating resonant synth lines that are recognisably psytrance patches stretched out, threaded with sampled tabla, frame drums and world-vocal fragments. Against classic dub it is entirely constructed in-the-box with no live band, and against psychill it keeps a hard rhythmic backbone and dub's echo-throw performance gestures rather than dissolving into ambient pads.

items.name: Psychill (psychedelic chillout)
items.lineage: Chillout-tent music of the 1990s-2000s psytrance festival circuit, codified by Shpongle (Simon Posford and Raja Ram, from 1996), Entheogenic, Carbon Based Lifeforms and the Twisted, Ultimae and Interchill catalogues — 80-120 BPM loose downtempo or beatless passages, long evolving pad beds and reverse-reverb swells, phrase-length arrangements that move by texture rather than chorus, sampled bansuri, didgeridoo, throat singing and spoken-word fragments, and pitch-shifted wordless vocals used as timbre.
items.description: Psychill is the ambient wing of psytrance culture, formalised in the late 1990s by Shpongle and the chillout rooms of Goa-descended festivals across Europe and Australia. It runs at 80-120 BPM or drifts beatless, favouring wide stereo pad beds, slow filter and phaser movement, sampled acoustic ethnic instruments and treated vocal fragments arranged as a continuous psychedelic narrative rather than verse-chorus. It is separated from generic downtempo by the psytrance sound-design lineage — the same resonant, heavily modulated synth voices in slow motion — and from psydub by its lack of dub's delay-throw discipline and skank rhythm.

items.name: Zenonesque
items.lineage: Mid-tempo psychedelic style named for Melbourne's Zenon Records (founded 2007 by Sensient), codified through the 2010s by Grouch, Kliment, Zen Mechanics and Way Out West festival culture — 125-140 BPM with a rolling but non-relentless kick-bass relationship, offbeat and swung hi-hat and shaker layers borrowed from techno and tribal house, granular and field-recording textures placed as percussion, dark modal or near-atonal micro-motifs instead of trance melody, and long eight-to-sixteen-bar morphs as the main structural device.
items.description: Zenonesque is the mid-tempo, groove-led branch of psytrance that grew around Australia's Zenon Records after 2007 and became the default sound of daytime and sunrise floors at European and Australian outdoor festivals. It sits at 125-140 BPM, replacing full-tilt psytrance drive with a swung, percussion-rich groove closer to tribal techno, and puts sound design — granular textures, resonant blips, field recordings used rhythmically — where trance would put melody. Against progressive psytrance it is darker, drier and less harmonically resolved; against techno it retains psytrance's continuously morphing modulation and its dedicated outdoor-festival audience.

items.name: Forest psy
items.lineage: Night-forest offshoot of psytrance formed in Finland, Russia and Denmark from the late 1990s around Parvati Records, Insomnia and the Fungus Funk / Psykovsky / Ka-Sol axis — 145-165 BPM with a tight short kick and continuous rolling 16th-note offbeat bass, FM and ring-modulated squelch leads that gurgle and pitch-bend organically rather than sing, no chord movement and only fragmentary minor motifs, dense stacking of ten or more short modulated layers, and outdoor woodland night-floor mixing that keeps the low mids scooped for open-air rigs.
items.description: Forest psy is the woodland night variant of psytrance, consolidated from the late 1990s in Finland, Denmark and Russia and given its canonical catalogue by Parvati Records. It runs at roughly 145-165 BPM over a relentless rolling bassline and a short punchy kick, with lead material made of organic-sounding FM and ring-modulated squelches, insect chirps and voice-like formant sweeps rather than melody, layered so densely that the texture reads as a continuous chattering organism. Compared to darkpsy it is generally slower, more organic and less atonally violent; compared to full-on psytrance it discards uplifting melodic hooks and the big-room build-and-drop entirely.

items.name: Nitzhonot
items.lineage: Israeli late-1990s Goa-trance variant (from nitzachon, 'victory'), built on the Phonokol and Krembo Records compilation series and the post-army Sinai and Negev party circuit — 145-155 BPM with a hard four-on-floor kick and continuous 16th-note offbeat bass, extended uplifting lead melodies in harmonic minor and Hijaz with Middle Eastern ornament and rapid trills, stacked supersaw and PPG-style digital lead layers, and long two-to-four-minute breakdowns that strip to pad and melody before an anthemic full return.
items.description: Nitzhonot is the Israeli 'victory trance' style of roughly 1996-2001, a faster and more overtly melodic reading of Goa trance carried by domestic compilation series and the Sinai desert party scene. It is identified by 145-155 BPM tempos, an unbroken rolling offbeat bass under a hard kick, and long singable lead melodies in harmonic-minor and Hijaz modes decorated with Middle Eastern trills and grace notes, arranged around euphoric extended breakdowns. Against classic Goa trance it is faster, brighter and more harmonically direct with less acid squelch; against later full-on psytrance it is melody-first rather than bassline-and-sound-design-first.

items.name: Hi-tech psytrance
items.lineage: Fastest branch of psytrance, formed in Russia, Israel and Japan from the mid-2000s around labels such as Anomalistic, Hi-Tech Doctor and the Indian and Israeli underground circuits — 190-230 BPM with a very short clicky kick and a sixteenth-note bass so fast it fuses into a drone, granular and FM-generated micro-leads chopped and re-triggered every sixteenth, glitch edits and pitch-jumped speech samples used as rhythm, near-total absence of harmony or sustained melody, and bright treble-forward mastering built for high-powered outdoor rigs.
items.description: Hi-tech psytrance is the extreme-tempo wing of the psytrance family, emerging in the mid-2000s in Russia, Israel and Japan and pushing 190-230 BPM. Its material is almost purely rhythmic sound design: a short dry kick, a sixteenth-note bass that reads as a continuous tone at speed, and constantly retriggered granular and FM fragments, glitch stutters and mangled speech placed with sample-level precision, with harmony reduced to a single implied root. It is distinguished from darkpsy by speed and by a cleaner, brighter, more digitally surgical texture, and from forest psy by discarding organic squelch and forest ambience in favour of machine-like precision.

items.name: Acid Techno
items.lineage: Formed in London and Chicago between 1988 and 1993 and codified by Liberator DJs, Chris Liberator, Lochi and the Stay Up Forever label out of the UK squat-party circuit, built on a 135-150 BPM four-on-the-floor TR-909 kick with open-hat offbeats and one or more overdriven Roland TB-303 lines whose cutoff, resonance and accent are performed live over long single-chord loops with little or no vocal.
items.description: Acid techno emerged around 1990 when UK free-party producers pushed the Chicago acid house 303 sound to faster tempos and harder distortion. The music is almost entirely instrumental: a relentless 909 kick and hats under stacked, screaming resonant basslines whose filter sweeps carry all the drama. It is faster and more abrasive than Chicago acid house and more monotimbral and loop-locked than Detroit techno.

items.name: Italo Disco
items.lineage: Italian and West German studio-producer dance music of 1979-1988, codified by Giancarlo Meo, Claudio Simonetti and the ZYX and Discomagic labels, using a 118-128 BPM electronic four-on-the-floor with LinnDrum or TR-808 claps, arpeggiated Juno/Prophet basslines, glossy string-machine pads and lightly accented English vocals often doubled by vocoder.
items.description: Italo disco formed in Italian and German studios as American disco collapsed, replacing live orchestras with drum machines and polysynths on small budgets. Its signature is a bright arpeggiated synth bass, spacious reverbed claps and earnest, melodically simple vocals in heavily accented English. Compared with post-disco boogie it is whiter in rhythm and more melodic, and unlike Hi-NRG it sits slower and leans on song hooks rather than pure propulsion.

items.name: New Italo Disco
items.lineage: A 2007-2015 revivalist scene centred on Dutch, Italian and Scandinavian net-labels such as Bordello a Parigi and Slow Motion, reconstructing early-1980s Italo templates at 115-125 BPM using vintage Juno-106 and TR-808 hardware or emulations, long instrumental intros, deep-reverb claps and deliberately cold, deadpan vocals.
items.description: New Italo disco is the reconstructed, DJ-oriented descendant of 1980s Italo, produced almost entirely in home studios from roughly 2007 onward. It keeps the Juno arpeggios, gated claps and analogue sequencer basslines but strips the pop-song scaffolding in favour of long, mixable instrumental structures and drier, more melancholic vocals. It is slower and more nostalgic than nu-disco proper and far less song-driven than the original Italo it imitates.

items.name: Euro Hi-NRG
items.lineage: European gay-club dance music of 1982-1990 built on the San Francisco Hi-NRG template and codified in London by Stock Aitken Waterman and in Italy by producers for ZYX, running 128-140 BPM with a hammering octave-jumping synth bass, four-on-the-floor kick with sixteenth open hats, orchestra-hit stabs and belted, heavily double-tracked female lead vocals.
items.description: Euro Hi-NRG carried Patrick Cowley's San Francisco disco formula into British and continental European chart pop through the mid-1980s. Its defining features are a driving octave synth bass, unrelenting sixteenth-note hats and an emotionally maximal, gospel-adjacent female vocal delivery. It runs faster and harder than Italo disco and, unlike Eurobeat's later Japanese variant, was made for domestic European clubs and singles charts.
exemplars: Divine - You Think You're a Man
Dead or Alive - You Spin Me Round
Miquel Brown - So Many Men, So Little Time

items.name: Disco Polo
items.lineage: Polish provincial dance-pop that formed at rural wedding halls and roadside markets in the late 1980s and was codified on cassette by Blue Star and Green Star labels around 1992-1996, using 125-140 BPM preset drum-machine beats, cheap keyboard brass and accordion patches, simple I-V-vi-IV loops and plain-toned male vocals singing sentimental or bawdy Polish lyrics.
items.description: Disco polo grew out of Polish wedding-band repertoire in the last years of the communist period and boomed on cheap cassettes after 1989. It pairs generic Euro-dance drum machine patterns with keyboard imitations of accordion and brass, and its centre of gravity is the unadorned, folk-inflected Polish vocal rather than the groove. Unlike Eurodance it is sung entirely in Polish, keeps village dance-band harmony, and never adopted rap verses or club production values.

items.name: Melodipop
items.lineage: A late-1980s-to-1990s melodic electronic pop current documented across Eastern Europe and the post-Soviet space, descended from Italo disco via ZYX-style imports, built on 110-125 BPM drum-machine four-on-the-floor, minor-key diatonic melodies carried by monophonic synth leads, sparse arpeggiated bass and untrained, plaintive lead vocals in the local language.
items.description: Melodipop names the melody-first strain of synthesizer dance-pop that spread through Eastern and Southeastern Europe as Italo records reached the region in the 1980s. Its productions are thin by Western standards, foregrounding a single memorable minor-key synth hook and an emotionally direct vocal over rudimentary machine rhythm. It differs from Italo disco in its minor-mode local-language songwriting and from Eurodance in having no rap breaks and far less low-end weight.

items.name: Space Disco
items.lineage: French, Italian and German disco of 1977-1981 codified by Jean-Marc Cerrone, Didier Marouani's Space and Giorgio Moroder's Munich productions, using a 115-125 BPM sequenced Moog bass pulse under four-on-the-floor kick and open hats, vocoder and synthesized choir textures, phased string washes and long instrumental suites with sci-fi sound effects in place of verses.
items.description: Space disco is the European branch of late-1970s disco that traded orchestral soul for synthesizer futurism, most visibly on French and Munich twelve-inches built around sequencer pulses and vocoded voices. Tracks are long, instrumental and sectional, with elaborate synth arrangements and cosmic effects rather than sung choruses. Against Philadelphia disco it is machine-locked and largely wordless, and against Italo it retains live drums and full-scale studio orchestration.
exemplars: Giorgio Moroder - From Here to Eternity
Droids - Do You Have the Force

items.name: Post-Disco
items.lineage: New York and Chicago black dance music of 1980-1985 made after the disco backlash, codified by producers such as Kashif, Leon Sylvers III and the Prelude and West End labels, running 100-118 BPM with a slapped or synth-doubled electric bassline, LinnDrum and TR-808 programming, brittle syncopated electric-piano and clavinet comping and conversational soul lead vocals with group answer parts.
items.description: Post-disco, later called boogie, is what New York dance-floor R&B became once orchestras and strings were cut from budgets in 1980. Drum machines and synth bass replaced the rhythm section, tempos dropped below disco's, and space opened around a funk-derived syncopated groove and a foregrounded soul vocal. It is slower and more song-oriented than the electro that grew beside it and warmer and more R&B-rooted than Italo disco.
exemplars: D Train - You're the One for Me
Peech Boys - Don't Make Me Wait

items.name: Electro
items.lineage: New York electro-funk of 1982-1986 codified by Afrika Bambaataa and Arthur Baker on 'Planet Rock' and by Tommy Boy, Streetwise and Sunnyview, built on a syncopated TR-808 breakbeat at 110-130 BPM with tuned 808 kick bass, Kraftwerk-derived synth melodies, vocoder and talkbox vocals and turntable scratching in place of live drums.
items.description: Electro crystallised in 1982 when New York hip-hop producers replaced live funk bands with the Roland TR-808 and Kraftwerk's synthetic melodic vocabulary. Its rhythmic signature is the broken, non-four-on-the-floor 808 pattern with a long tuned kick doing bass duty, topped by robotic vocoded or talkbox voices and scratched samples. Unlike post-disco boogie it abandons the human rhythm section and sung chorus, and unlike techno it stays breakbeat-based rather than four-to-the-floor.
exemplars: Afrika Bambaataa & Soulsonic Force - Planet Rock
Man Parrish - Hip Hop, Be Bop

items.name: Techno Bass
items.lineage: Detroit hybrid of electro and techno codified 1991-1998 by Underground Resistance, Aux 88, Will Web and DJ Assault on Direct Beat and 430 West, running 125-140 BPM with a syncopated 808/909 electro breakbeat carrying a deep detuned sub-bass line, cold sequenced synth motifs, vocoded vocals and militant sci-fi track titles.
items.description: Techno bass is the Detroit answer to Miami bass, formed in the early 1990s when Underground Resistance and Aux 88 fused 808 electro syncopation with techno's sequencer discipline and sub-heavy mixing. Tracks keep the broken electro drum pattern rather than a straight four-four, but their synth writing, tempo and austerity are Detroit techno's. It is colder and more machine-abstract than Miami bass and rhythmically broken where Detroit techno proper is four-on-the-floor.

items.name: Bleep Techno
items.lineage: Yorkshire dance music of 1989-1992 codified by Unique 3, LFO, Nightmares on Wax and Warp Records in Sheffield and Leeds, running 118-130 BPM with sparse sine-wave 'bleep' melodies, enormous sound-system sub-bass drops derived from local reggae culture, dry 808/909 drums and occasional ragga or house vocal samples.
items.description: Bleep techno, sometimes called bleep and bass, was Britain's first indigenous techno idiom, made in northern English cities where Jamaican sound-system bass culture met imported Detroit records. Its arrangements are extremely spare: a few pure-tone bleeps, hard dry drums and a sub-bass so low it registers as pressure rather than pitch. It is emptier and more bass-defined than Detroit techno and far more restrained than the breakbeat hardcore that grew out of it a year or two later.

items.name: Minimal Techno
items.lineage: Detroit and Berlin from the mid-1990s, codified by Robert Hood's Minimal Nation (1994), Daniel Bell, Basic Channel and later the Berlin Hardwax/Perlon axis — 125-135 BPM four-on-the-floor with a stripped kit, a single evolving loop, heavy use of subtractive filtering and sends, near-total absence of melody or vocal, arranged as long slow-mutating DJ tools inside a DAW or hardware sequencer.
items.description: Minimal techno emerged in the mid-1990s from Robert Hood's Detroit reduction of techno to kick, hat and one figure, and was consolidated in Berlin studios through the 2000s. Its defining features are extreme subtraction — a handful of elements looped for eight or more minutes, changes made through filter and send automation rather than new parts — plus sidechain-pumped kick relationships and very controlled sub-bass. It differs from Detroit techno by discarding chordal and string-pad melody, from microhouse by lacking that style's clicky swing and vocal fragments, and from industrial techno by its clean, low-distortion mixdown.

items.name: Outsider House
items.lineage: New York, Glasgow and London circa 2011-2015 around L.I.E.S., Mister Saturday Night and Trilogy Tapes, with Ron Morelli, Legowelt, DJ Slugo-influenced raw-hardware producers and Huerco S. — 118-126 BPM house tracked live from drum machines and cheap samplers to cassette or one-take stereo, deliberately overdriven and detuned, with hiss, clipping and mis-timed loops kept in the mix.
items.description: Outsider house is the raw hardware-house current that formed around Ron Morelli's L.I.E.S. label in New York from 2011 and spread through Glasgow and London tape labels. Tracks are jammed live on cheap drum machines and monosynths, printed with saturation, tape hiss and audible clipping, and structured as one long unquantized take rather than an arranged record. It is distinguished from lo-fi house proper by its harsher, more industrial and less nostalgic palette, and from deep house by its refusal of clean mixdowns and jazz chords.

items.name: Gospel House
items.lineage: Chicago and New York 1988-1996, codified by Marshall Jefferson and Curtis McClain, Frankie Knuckles with Robert Owens and Jamie Principle, and by Kerri Chandler and Tony Humphries at Club Zanzibar — 118-124 BPM four-on-the-floor with piano vamps, organ pads, hand claps and tambourine, topped by full-throated Black church belting, testifying ad-libs and choir-response stacks tracked in New York and Chicago commercial rooms.
items.description: Gospel house is the strain of late-1980s and 1990s American house that carried Black church vocal practice intact onto the dance floor — sustained organ, gospel piano vamps over the 909, and lead singing full of melisma, testimony and call-and-response with a stacked choir. It grew from the Chicago house scene and the New York/New Jersey garage clubs, and stayed a working-church-singer idiom rather than a sampled one.
