It differs from garage house generally by making the vocal, not the groove, the centre of the record, and from deep house by its major-key uplift and explicitly devotional lyrics.
exemplars: Marshall Jefferson & Curtis McClain – Move Your Body

items.name: Hard House
items.lineage: London and the UK club circuit 1994-2003 (Trade, Tidy Trax, Nukleuz), codified by Tony De Vit, Ian M and the Tidy Boys out of NRG and Belgian hoover techno — 145-155 BPM with a hard offbeat bassline, gated hoover stabs, filtered white-noise risers, drum-roll breakdowns and pitched-up diva vocal snatches, produced on hardware and early DAWs and mastered loud for large club rigs.
items.description: Hard house is the UK club style of the mid-1990s and early 2000s built on a hammering offbeat bass, the Belgian hoover stab, and long noise-sweep breakdowns resolving into drum rolls. Tempos of 145-155 BPM and heavy limiting made it a large-room and after-hours music, championed by Tony De Vit at Trade and released in volume by Tidy Trax and Nukleuz. It is distinguished from hard trance by its offbeat bass drive and absence of long melodic arpeggios, and from hardstyle by its earlier date, cleaner kick and house rather than gabber ancestry.

items.name: Funky Breaks
items.lineage: UK and US clubs circa 1994-2003 (Bomb the Bass and Freestylers in London, Rennie Pilgrem's TCR, Florida breaks in Orlando) — 130-140 BPM chopped funk and hip-hop breakbeats over a heavy syncopated synth or sampled bassline, with turntable scratching, ragga and old-school rap samples and filtered disco stabs, assembled from vinyl samples in hardware samplers and early DAWs.
items.description: Funky breaks — also called nu-skool breaks or big beat's dancefloor cousin — is the mid-1990s breakbeat style built on chopped funk drums at 130-140 BPM rather than a four-on-the-floor kick, with a fat syncopated bassline and scratched vocal samples on top. It ran through London labels like TCR and Freskanova and through Florida's club-oriented breaks scene. It differs from drum and bass by running roughly half the drum tempo without a time-stretched Amen, from big beat by its DJ-tool functionality over rock-sample bombast, and from house by the broken rather than straight kick pattern.

items.name: Harsh Noise Wall
items.lineage: Emerging from Japanese and European harsh noise around 2003-2008 and named through Vomir, The Rita and the Hospital Productions/Turgid Animal cassette networks — a single static, unvarying mass of amplified distortion and crushed low-mid frequency held for twenty to sixty minutes with no rhythm, event, dynamic change or vocal, generated by chained pedals, contact mics and feedback loops recorded direct to cassette or CD-R.
items.description: Harsh noise wall is the reductionist extreme of noise music, consolidated in the mid-2000s cassette underground around Romain Perrot's Vomir and Sam McKinlay's The Rita. A piece is one continuous unmodulated block of distortion — no gestures, no build, no silence — held at fixed amplitude for the whole running time, so that all musical incident is displaced into micro-texture. It is distinguished from Japanoise and power electronics, which are violently dynamic and often vocal, precisely by its stasis and its ideological refusal of change or performance.

items.name: Martial Industrial
items.lineage: Central and Northern Europe from the early 1990s (Cold Meat Industry in Sweden, Der Blutharsch in Austria, Les Joyaux de la Princesse in France) — slow processional 60-80 BPM marching-snare and timpani patterns, synthesized brass and orchestral samples, tolling bells, male choir pads and archival wartime speech samples, mixed dark and reverberant in DIY studios onto CD.
items.description: Martial industrial developed in the 1990s European post-industrial scene, chiefly on Sweden's Cold Meat Industry, as a slow, ceremonial style built from marching snare rolls, timpani, synthetic brass fanfares, bells and choral pads, frequently over sampled interwar speech and film dialogue. The mood is funereal-triumphal and the arrangements are through-composed rather than looped for a dancefloor. It differs from EBM by its slow processional tempo and absence of sequenced bass, and from neofolk by using orchestral and electronic sources rather than acoustic guitar and voice.

items.name: Drone Folk
items.lineage: North America and Britain from the late 1990s, associated with Charalambides, Pelt, Six Organs of Admittance and the Jewelled Antler circle — open-tuned acoustic and 12-string guitar, bowed dulcimer, shruti box and harmonium sustaining a fixed tonic under free-tempo modal melody and wordless voice, recorded in rooms and cabins with minimal miking and long natural decay.
items.description: Drone folk takes the modal fingerstyle vocabulary of American primitive guitar and Appalachian song and stretches it over a continuous sustained tonic supplied by shruti box, harmonium, bowed dulcimer or open bass strings. Formed in the late 1990s underground around Texas duo Charalambides, Virginia's Pelt and Ben Chasny's Six Organs of Admittance, it favours slow free tempo, wordless or barely articulated voice and unedited long takes in resonant rooms. It differs from free folk by keeping a fixed tonal centre and a legible melody rather than collective improvisation, and from drone metal by acoustic sources and folk melodic material.
exemplars: Six Organs of Admittance – Dark Noontide

items.name: Free Folk
items.lineage: New England and the American Northeast circa 1998-2008 around Sunburned Hand of the Man, No-Neck Blues Band and the Brattleboro/Ecstatic Peace and Time-Lag circles — collectively improvised, largely unmetered sessions on acoustic guitar, hand percussion, harmonium, flute and untrained group voice, captured in one take on cassette or portable recorder in houses and lofts and issued in tiny CD-R editions.
items.description: Free folk names the loose American collective-improvisation scene of the early 2000s, centred on Massachusetts and Vermont communes and lofts, in which folk instruments were played with the ethos of free jazz and the Japanese psychedelic underground. Sessions are group jams without fixed song, meter or key, drifting between hand-drum ritual, acoustic guitar clusters and chanted group vocals, and were released almost entirely on self-dubbed cassettes and CD-Rs. It differs from freak folk, which retains written songs and studio arrangement, and from drone folk, which holds a single tonic rather than roaming freely.

items.name: New Weird America
items.lineage: US underground folk current named by David Keenan in a 2003 Wire feature and centered on the Brattleboro/Providence axis (Sunburned Hand of the Man, Six Organs of Admittance, Josephine Foster, the Jewelled Antler collective), fusing Appalachian modal ballad and open-tuned fingerpicking with free-improvised drone, unmetered group ritual jams, tape-hiss home recording, and untrained keening or whispered vocal delivery over droning harmonium and bowed banjo.
items.description: A loose American underground folk movement that crystallized around 2000-2006 in New England and the Pacific Northwest, taking its name from a 2003 Wire magazine piece. It couples Appalachian and British-revival ballad materials with free-improv drone, communal untracked jams, and deliberately lo-fi home tape recording. Unlike the songwriter-centered indie folk it overlaps with, it privileges texture, ritual duration and collective noise over verse-chorus form.

items.name: Psychedelic Folk
items.lineage: Late-1960s British and American acid-folk, codified 1967-1971 by the Incredible String Band, Vashti Bunyan, Comus and Pearls Before Swine, applying modal fingerstyle guitar in altered tunings to raga-derived drone (sitar, tanpura, hand percussion), free-floating tempo, chamber-string and recorder overdubs, and high, unforced close-miked vocals treated with tape flange and reverse tape.
items.description: Emerging in Britain and California between 1966 and 1971, psychedelic folk grafted Indian drone instruments, medieval and Middle Eastern timbres, and studio tape manipulation onto acoustic ballad forms. Its signature is a suspended, tempo-free floating feel with layered exotic overdubs and childlike or declamatory vocal delivery. It differs from electric folk-rock in refusing drum-kit propulsion, and from straight revival folk in its studio artifice.
exemplars: The Incredible String Band - The Hangman's Beautiful Daughter
Vashti Bunyan - Just Another Diamond Day

items.name: Chamber Folk
items.lineage: Anglo-American acoustic songwriting recorded with classical chamber forces, traceable to Robert Kirby's string arrangements for Nick Drake (1969-70) and revived from the late 1990s by Sufjan Stevens, Andrew Bird and Ólöf Arnalds — slow-to-moderate tempo, aeolian and phrygian modal harmony, fingerpicked or nylon guitar doubled by cello, violin, clarinet and harmonium, brushed or absent drums, and close, breathy, low-vibrato vocal delivery.
items.description: Chamber folk sets singer-songwriter material in a written classical chamber setting rather than a rock band, with strings, winds and reed organ arranged rather than jammed. It descends from Nick Drake's late-sixties Robert Kirby charts and re-emerged as an indie idiom around 2000. Against psychedelic folk's tape haze and drone, it is precisely notated, dry, and dynamically restrained.

items.name: Exotica
items.lineage: American instrumental mood music of 1957-1963 codified by Martin Denny at the Hawaiian Village and by Les Baxter and Arthur Lyman on Capitol and HiFi Records — languid rumba and bolero tempos, pentatonic and whole-tone melodies carried on vibraphone, marimba and celesta over congas and bongos, with bird calls, gongs, wordless soprano vocalise, and extravagant stereo reverb evoking an imagined Polynesia.
items.description: Exotica was a Hollywood and Honolulu studio genre of the stereo-hi-fi boom, roughly 1957 to 1963, built for domestic listening rather than dance. Vibraphone and mallet lead lines float over Afro-Cuban percussion, punctuated by animal calls, gongs and wordless vocalise, all bathed in the Capitol Tower echo chambers. It is distinguished from lounge and easy listening by its percussion-forward, quasi-ethnographic sound design, and from genuine Pacific traditions by being wholly a studio invention.
exemplars: Les Baxter - Ritual of the Savage
Yma Sumac - Voice of the Xtabay

items.name: Library Music (Production Music)
items.lineage: European production-music industry of 1959-1980 centred on KPM, De Wolfe, Bruton and Italy's Cometa, where staff composers (Keith Mansfield, Alan Hawkshaw, Brian Bennett, Piero Umiliani, Janko Nilović) cut short cue-length instrumentals to brief — brisk funk drum-kit breaks, fuzz and wah guitar, Hammond and early synthesizer leads, flute and string sweeteners — recorded fast in London and Rome sessions and pressed to catalogue LPs for broadcast licensing.
items.description: Library music is instrumental production music written on spec for film, television and radio licensing, at its creative peak in London and Rome between the mid-1960s and late 1970s. Cues are short, tightly arranged, mood-labelled, and recorded by top session players in single fast dates, spanning funk breaks, bossa, jazz-rock, easy listening and early electronics. It differs from soundtrack composition in that no picture exists: the music is written to abstract categories, which is exactly why its drum breaks became prime hip-hop sampling stock.

items.name: Music Hall
items.lineage: British urban variety song of roughly 1850-1920, born in London public-house saloon theatres and codified by Marie Lloyd, Gus Elen, Harry Champion and Vesta Tilley — brisk 2/4 and 6/8 comic patter and waltz choruses, cockney or regional dialect delivery pitched between speech and song, chorus lines written for mass audience singalong, backed by pit piano with cornet, trombone and tuba, and preserved on acoustic-horn 78s.
items.description: Music hall was the dominant popular song form of Victorian and Edwardian Britain, performed in licensed variety theatres between 1850 and the First World War. Its songs are comic or sentimental character pieces in working-class dialect, with simple diatonic tunes and hook choruses built for the audience to bellow back. It differs from American vaudeville and Tin Pan Alley in its class-specific dialect comedy and from operetta in its unaccompanied-chorus, pit-piano economy.

items.name: Song-Poem
items.lineage: American vanity-record industry from the 1950s to the early 1980s, in which mail-order firms (Preview, Halmark, Film City, MSR) set amateurs' submitted lyrics to music for a fee — house bands and singers such as Rodd Keith, Gene Marshall and Bobbi Blake cutting one- or two-take tracks in Hollywood, Nashville and Los Angeles rooms, over generic three-chord country, twist or Chamberlin-organ backing, with awkward scansion and unedited lyric text as the defining marker.
items.description: Song-poems are commercial vanity recordings made from lyrics mailed in by amateurs who answered magazine adverts, produced in bulk by small US firms from the 1950s into the 1980s. Sessions were cut in a single pass with a hired band, so the tracks pair slick professional playing with unsingable, uncut amateur text and hasty melodic fitting. What distinguishes the form from ordinary demo pop is that the customer, not the label, was the market, and no revision was ever possible.
exemplars: The American Song-Poem Anthology: Do You Know the Difference Between Big Wood and Brush

items.name: Salon Music
items.lineage: European domestic art music of roughly 1820-1900, cultivated in bourgeois and aristocratic drawing rooms of Paris, Vienna and Leipzig and codified by Field, Chopin, Fanny Hensel, Gottschalk and Cécile Chaminade — short character pieces, nocturnes, waltzes, romances without words and parlour songs for piano alone or piano with violin, cello or voice, written for amateur hands with rubato-rich cantabile melody over broken-chord accompaniment.
items.description: Salon music is the nineteenth-century repertoire of the private drawing room: short, self-contained character pieces and romances published for amateur performers rather than the concert stage. Its idiom is singing right-hand melody, arpeggiated left-hand support, expressive rubato, and modest technical demands with maximum sentimental effect. It is separated from the concert-hall Romantic repertoire by scale and intent, and from popular parlour song by its notated, conservatory-derived harmonic language.

items.name: Minnesang
items.lineage: German-language courtly love-song tradition of circa 1150-1350 at the Hohenstaufen courts, codified by Walther von der Vogelweide, Neidhart and Heinrich von Morungen and preserved in the Manesse and Jena codices — monophonic strophic song in Pythagorean-tuned church modes, Bar form (Stollen-Stollen-Abgesang), largely unmeasured declamatory delivery by a solo male voice, sometimes doubled by vielle, psaltery or portative organ in modern reconstruction.
items.description: Minnesang is the German courtly song tradition of the high Middle Ages, roughly 1150 to 1350, transmitting texts of idealized love, political satire and pastoral parody. Surviving sources give text far more often than notation, and the melodies that do survive are monophonic, modal and in Bar form, so performance rests on strophic repetition and speech-shaped delivery. It parallels the troubadour and trouvère repertoires but in Middle High German, with a stronger later strain of rustic dance-song (Neidhart) absent from the Occitan corpus.

items.name: Trouvère Song
items.lineage: Northern French langue d'oïl courtly song of circa 1180-1300, centred on Arras, Champagne and the royal court and codified by Thibaut de Champagne, Adam de la Halle, Blondel de Nesle and Gace Brulé — monophonic strophic chansons courtoises alongside rondeaux, motets and pastourelles, notated in largely unmeasured neumes in the chansonniers, sung by solo voice in Pythagorean modal tuning with optional vielle or harp doubling.
items.description: The trouvère repertoire is the northern French counterpart to the Occitan troubadours, flourishing between about 1180 and 1300 and far better preserved musically, with over two thousand melodies in the chansonniers. Its songs are modal, monophonic and strophic, though Arras figures such as Adam de la Halle extended the tradition into polyphonic rondeaux and the sung play Le Jeu de Robin et Marion. Compared with troubadour song it is later, more urban and bourgeois in patronage, and it hands the repertoire directly into thirteenth-century motet practice.
exemplars: Adam de la Halle - Le Jeu de Robin et Marion

items.name: Troubadour Song (Occitan)
items.lineage: Occitan courtly lyric of circa 1100-1290 in Aquitaine, Provence and Toulouse, begun by Guilhem IX of Aquitaine and codified by Bernart de Ventadorn, Raimbaut de Vaqueiras, Guiraut Riquier and the trobairitz Comtessa de Dia — monophonic strophic cansos, sirventes and albas in church modes, only about 250 melodies surviving in unmeasured notation, delivered by solo voice with vielle, harp or Mediterranean plucked-lute accompaniment.
items.description: Troubadour song is the earliest documented European vernacular art-song tradition, composed in Occitan at southern French and Catalan courts between about 1100 and the Albigensian collapse of the thirteenth century. The surviving melodies are monophonic, modal and strophic, notated without rhythm, so realization depends on text declamation and on debated Andalusi-influenced instrumental accompaniment. It precedes and models the trouvère and Minnesang traditions, but with far fewer surviving tunes and a stronger Mediterranean-Arab performance hypothesis.
exemplars: Bernart de Ventadorn - Can vei la lauzeta mover
Comtessa de Dia - A chantar m'er

items.name: Ars Subtilior
items.lineage: Late-fourteenth-century Franco-Cypriot courtly polyphony of circa 1370-1420 around Avignon, Foix and the Aragonese court, written by Baude Cordier, Solage, Jacob de Senleches and Matteo da Perugia and preserved in the Chantilly and Modena codices — extreme rhythmic notation with simultaneous mensurations, syncopation across the tactus, chromatic inflection, eye-music heart- and circle-shaped scores, and three- or four-voice ballades and rondeaux for solo voices with vielle, harp and lute.
items.description: Ars subtilior is the hyper-refined secular polyphony written for a handful of southern French, Cypriot and Aragonese courts between about 1370 and 1420, in the wake of the papal schism. It pushes Ars Nova mensural notation to its limit, layering conflicting mensurations, proportional shifts and cross-rhythms so dense that the surface sounds nearly free, and it delights in visually elaborate manuscript notation. Against the contemporaneous Italian trecento it is far more rhythmically complex and less melodically cantabile, and it marks the end of the mannerist medieval line before Dufay's smoothing.
exemplars: Jacob de Senleches - La harpe de melodie

items.name: Italian Trecento Polyphony
items.lineage: Fourteenth-century Italian secular polyphony centred on Florence, Bologna and Padua and codified by Jacopo da Bologna, Francesco Landini, Gherardello and Niccolò da Perugia in the Squarcialupi Codex — two- and three-voice madrigals, cacce and ballate in Italian mensural notation with divisiones, long florid melismatic upper-voice openings and closes, cantabile stepwise motion, canonic hunting cacce, and the under-third Landini cadence.
items.description: The Italian trecento is the fourteenth-century secular polyphonic tradition of northern and central Italy, its main forms the madrigal, the canonic caccia and the ballata, with Francesco Landini as its central figure and the illuminated Squarcialupi Codex as its great source. Its idiom is lyrical and vocal: long melismas at phrase beginnings and endings, mostly consonant two-voice writing, and the distinctive Landini cadence. It contrasts with the contemporaneous French Ars Nova and Ars Subtilior in favouring melodic sweetness and clear text-setting over rhythmic complexity.
exemplars: Jacopo da Bologna - Non al suo amante
Gherardello da Firenze - Tosto che l'alba

items.name: Franco-Flemish School
items.lineage: Sacred and secular polyphony of the Low Countries and northern France c.1450-1560, carried across Europe by Ockeghem, Josquin, Willaert and Lassus — four to six equal voices in continuous pervading imitation over cantus firmus or paraphrase tenors, mensural notation with proportional canons, long-breathed overlapping phrases avoiding cadential coincidence, and Latin mass and motet texts sung one or two per part in resonant chapel acoustics.
items.description: The dominant European compositional style from roughly 1450 to 1560, exported by singers trained in Cambrai, Bruges and Antwerp to courts and chapels from Rome to Vienna. Its sound is a seamless woven texture of independent equal voices in pervading imitation, with cadences deliberately elided so the flow rarely stops, and a preference for smooth Pythagorean-leaning intervals and long modal spans. Against the Italian madrigal it is text-neutral and structural rather than pictorial; against earlier Burgundian song it is denser, longer-breathed and technically canonic.

items.name: English Renaissance (Tudor Polyphony)
items.lineage: Tudor and early Stuart music c.1500-1620 — Taverner, Tallis, Byrd, Gibbons and Weelkes — built on a distinctly English taste for full sonority: broad florid melismatic Latin votive antiphons, then post-Reformation vernacular anthems and services in clear syllabic declamation, alongside consort songs, viol fantasias and lute ayres, using false relations, a rich thirds-and-sixths harmony and mean-tone keyboard temperament.
items.description: English composition between the Eton Choirbook generation and the death of Gibbons, spanning Latin votive polyphony, Anglican anthems and services, viol consort fantasias and lute ayres. It is recognisable by full-textured harmony rich in thirds, the characteristic false relation between simultaneous major and minor thirds, and long melismatic upper lines over slow-moving lower voices. Compared with contemporary Franco-Flemish writing it is less canonic and more vertically sonorous; compared with the Italian madrigal it is more restrained in chromaticism even in its secular repertoire.

items.name: Italian Baroque
items.lineage: Italy c.1600-1750 — Monteverdi's seconda pratica, then Corelli in Rome codifying the trio sonata and concerto grosso, Vivaldi in Venice fixing the ritornello concerto and Scarlatti-era opera seria — driven basso continuo of cello plus harpsichord or theorbo, sequential tonal harmony, terraced dynamics, motoric semiquaver figuration at brisk steady tempo, and violin-idiomatic solo writing with improvised cadential ornamentation.
items.description: The Italian strand of Baroque practice, running from the Florentine and Venetian monodists through Corelli's Roman string school to Vivaldi's Venetian concertos and Neapolitan opera. Its markers are a functional bass line realised in continuo, ritornello form alternating tutti refrain with solo episodes, propulsive unbroken rhythmic drive and violin writing that treats sequence and arpeggio as primary material. It is separated from French Baroque by its speed, sequential harmony and vocal bel canto, and from later Galante music by continuo texture and unbroken motoric surface.

items.name: French Baroque
items.lineage: Music of the French court from Lully at Versailles in the 1670s through Couperin and Rameau to c.1760 — the ouverture with dotted grand rhythm and fugal fast section, tragedie lyrique with recitative bent to French prosody, dance suites of allemande, courante, sarabande and gigue, notes inegales performance of even quavers, a dense codified agrement ornament table, and a wind-rich orchestra of transverse flutes, oboes and bassoons over string band.
items.description: The court-centred French style consolidated by Lully under Louis XIV and extended by Couperin, Marais and Rameau. It is identified by the French overture's double-dotted opening, the dance suite as primary architecture, notes inegales swing applied to written-even quavers, and an exhaustively notated ornament vocabulary of ports de voix, tremblements and coules. Where Italian Baroque prizes sequence and virtuoso momentum, French Baroque prizes dance metre, ornament and instrumental colour, with the viol and harpsichord repertoire especially deliberate and rhetorically slow.

items.name: Spanish Baroque
items.lineage: Iberian and colonial Hispanic music c.1600-1750 — Juan Hidalgo and Sebastian Duron at the Madrid court, Correa de Arauxo and Cabanilles at the organ, Jose de Nebra and the New World chapelmasters — vernacular Castilian villancicos in refrain-and-copla form, hemiola-heavy 6/8 against 3/4 dance metres, guitar and cross-strung harp continuo instead of harpsichord, tiento organ writing on split-keyboard horizontal reeds, and zarzuela's mix of sung and spoken theatre.
items.description: The Baroque as practised in Spain, Portugal and the Spanish Americas, notable for keeping vernacular and dance idioms inside sacred institutions long after Italy had Latinised its repertoire. Its hallmarks are the villancico with estribillo refrain, persistent 6/8 against 3/4 hemiola inherited from the folia and jacara, plucked guitar and harp as continuo, and Iberian organs with horizontal trumpet stops used in tiento partido. It differs from Italian Baroque in its lighter, more percussive continuo and dance-derived metre, and from French Baroque in its comparatively plain ornamentation.

items.name: Galante Era
items.lineage: European transitional style c.1720-1770 centred on Naples, Dresden, Mannheim and Berlin — Pergolesi, Johann Christian Bach, Sammartini and the Mannheim school under Stamitz — short periodic phrases in balanced two- and four-bar antecedent-consequent units, thin melody-and-accompaniment texture with Alberti bass replacing contrapuntal continuo, slow harmonic rhythm, graceful appoggiatura ornamentation, and the fortepiano and clarinet entering the orchestra alongside crescendo effects.
items.description: The galant and empfindsam style that displaced late Baroque counterpoint between roughly 1720 and 1770, cultivated in Neapolitan opera buffa, the Mannheim orchestra and the Berlin circle around C.P.E. Bach. Its defining sound is deliberate lightness: symmetrical periodic phrasing, a single singing melody over Alberti or repeated-note accompaniment, sparse harmony that changes slowly, and expressive sighing appoggiaturas. It is thinner and more sectional than Italian Baroque, and less developmentally ambitious than the Viennese Classical style that grew directly out of it.

items.name: Post-Romantic Era
items.lineage: c.1890-1930 in Vienna, Munich, Paris and Helsinki — Mahler, Richard Strauss, Scriabin, Szymanowski, Zemlinsky and late Sibelius — tonality stretched to breaking with mystic and quartal chords, polytonal superimposition and floating unresolved suspensions, gigantic orchestras deployed chamber-like for isolated soloistic colour, ironic collage of marches and folk tunes, extreme registral extremes, and vast multi-movement symphonies and tone poems with vocal and choral finales.
items.description: The generation that pushed Romantic tonality to its structural limit between about 1890 and 1930, centred on Mahler, Strauss and Scriabin. Its hallmarks are harmony hovering at the edge of atonality through quartal and mystic sonorities, orchestras of enormous size treated as a reservoir of soloistic chamber colours rather than blended mass, and an ironic, quotation-laden expressive register that admits banality alongside the sublime. It is separated from the late Romantic era by that irony and by harmony that frequently fails to resolve at all, and from serialism by retaining tonal reference points.

items.name: Serialism
items.lineage: Devised by Arnold Schoenberg in Vienna around 1921-23 and extended to rhythm, dynamics and attack by Boulez, Stockhausen and Babbitt at Darmstadt after 1949 — a fixed ordering of all twelve chromatic pitches deployed in prime, inversion, retrograde and retrograde-inversion forms with no pitch privileged, pointillistic Webernian textures of isolated attacks across extreme registers, irregular non-repeating rhythm, and precisely notated dynamics changing note by note.
items.description: Twelve-tone composition, invented by Schoenberg in the early 1920s and generalised into total serialism at Darmstadt after 1949. All twelve pitch classes circulate in a fixed row order and its transformations so no key can assert itself, and in the postwar integral variant duration, dynamic and articulation are governed by analogous series. The audible result is athematic, metrically unpredictable and often pointillistic, with wide leaps and constantly shifting timbre. It differs from post-Romantic free atonality by its systematic ordering, and from aleatoric or minimalist modernism by leaving nothing to chance or repetition.

items.name: Totalism
items.lineage: New York downtown movement of the late 1980s and 1990s — Michael Gordon, Julia Wolfe and David Lang with Bang on a Can, plus Mikel Rouse, Rhys Chatham and critic Kyle Gann — steady fast pulse with conflicting tempo layers stacked as 3:4 or 5:7 rhythmic dissonance over it, harmony richer and more dissonant than minimalism, amplified mixed ensembles of electric guitar, bass, drums, piano and winds played at rock volume but with through-composed formal scale.
items.description: Totalism named the second-generation downtown New York style of the late 1980s and 1990s, associated with Bang on a Can and theorised by Kyle Gann. It keeps minimalism's constant pulse and audible process but layers mutually dissonant tempos over it and admits far more chromatic and sometimes just-intoned harmony, performed by amplified mixed ensembles at rock dynamic levels. Against classic minimalism it is harmonically restless and rhythmically conflicted rather than gradually phasing; against serialism it is pulse-driven, consonance-tolerant and physically loud.

items.name: Post-Minimalism
items.lineage: Emerging in New York and Britain circa 1975-1990 as composers including John Adams, Michael Nyman, Louis Andriessen, Arvo Pärt and the Bang on a Can circle absorbed Reich-Glass pulse technique back into functional harmony, expressive phrase-shape and long-form architecture — steady eighth-note motor pulse, additive but audibly directional harmonic rhythm, mixed amplified chamber forces (piano, mallets, electric guitar, saxophones, strings), fully notated with no improvisation and dynamic arcs the earlier minimalists refused.
items.description: Post-minimalism formed in the late 1970s and 1980s when composers who had absorbed Reich and Glass reintroduced goal-directed harmony, contrast and dramatic climax into pulse-based music. The sound is a driving amplified chamber ensemble — piano and mallet percussion locked to a constant subdivision, electric guitar and saxophones cutting through strings — with harmonic changes that arrive as events rather than as slow process. It is distinguished from classic minimalism by audible cadence and phrase-shape, and from mainstream orchestral modernism by its rock-derived rhythmic literalism and amplification.

items.name: Xenharmonic Music
items.lineage: Named by Ivor Darreg in the 1970s out of the Harry Partch and Erv Wilson lineage in California and consolidated online from the 1990s through the Alternate Tuning List and Xenharmonic Wiki, it is composition built explicitly on non-12-TET lattices — 19-, 22- and 31-note equal divisions, Bohlen-Pierce, and rank-2 temperaments — realized on refretted guitars, retuned synthesizers and purpose-built instruments, with harmony judged by comma-pump and consonance behaviour rather than by common-practice function.
items.description: Xenharmonic music is a post-1970s composer-theorist practice defined by deliberate use of tuning systems outside 12-tone equal temperament — equal divisions such as 19-, 22- and 31-EDO, the Bohlen-Pierce scale, and just-intonation-derived temperaments. Its sonic signature is chords that sound consonant yet unplaceable, beating-free thirds or intervals with no 12-TET analogue, usually realized on refretted guitars, retuned software synths and custom keyboards. It differs from historical microtonal composition in being tuning-system-first — the temperament is the compositional premise, and the community is a distributed online theory culture rather than a concert-hall lineage.

items.name: Microtonal Music (interval-scale practice)
items.lineage: Twentieth-century concert practice codified by Alois Hába in Prague from 1923 with quarter-tone piano and clarinet, Ivan Wyschnegradsky in Paris, Julián Carrillo in Mexico and later Ligeti, Haas and the spectral school, using intervals smaller than the semitone — quarter- and sixth-tones, beating dyads and slow glissando drift — on retuned pianos, specially fingered winds and unfretted strings, fully notated with accidental systems invented for the purpose.
items.description: Microtonal music as a notated concert tradition runs from Hába's Prague quarter-tone school of the 1920s through Wyschnegradsky and Carrillo to Ligeti, Georg Friedrich Haas and the spectralists. Its hallmark is intervals smaller than a semitone used structurally — beating dyads, gradual pitch drift, harmonies tuned toward or away from the overtone series — on paired detuned pianos, quarter-tone clarinets and unfretted strings. It is more score-bound and orchestral than xenharmonic practice, which starts from a chosen temperament, and unlike just-intonation drone music it retains through-composed form and rapid textural change.

items.name: Wandelweiser
items.lineage: Founded in Germany in 1992 by Antoine Beuger and Burkhard Schlothauer as a composers' collective and publishing house, extending Cage's 4'33" into a full practice — long durations built mostly of measured silence, single quiet sustained tones on flute, clarinet, strings, piano or sine tone placed at notated intervals, near-static dynamics at the edge of audibility, and performance rooms where ambient sound is treated as part of the score.
items.description: The Wandelweiser group formed in Germany in 1992 around Antoine Beuger and Burkhard Schlothauer and has since spread through Jürg Frey, Michael Pisaro and Radu Malfatti. Pieces are mostly silence: isolated quiet tones — a bowed string, a breath-thin clarinet note, a sine tone — are placed at notated time points across durations that can run an hour, so room tone and incidental noise become audible content. Unlike free improvisation's quiet end, everything here is scored and counted, and unlike ambient electronics the material is acoustic, unprocessed and deliberately sparse rather than continuous.

items.name: Sound Collage
items.lineage: Running from Cage's Imaginary Landscape No. 5 (1952) and the Buchanan-Goodman break-in records through the Residents, Negativland, John Oswald's Plunderphonics (1985) and the tape-trading underground, it assembles finished music into new work by splice, turntable, sampler and radio capture — abrupt cuts between unrelated sources, recognizable fragments left legible, speech and broadcast material foregrounded, and no continuous metre unless a host loop imposes one.
items.description: Sound collage is the practice of building music out of other recordings left audibly intact — radio broadcasts, advertisements, commercial records, found speech — spliced or sampled into abrupt juxtaposition. It runs from Cage's radio pieces and 1950s break-in novelty singles through Negativland, John Oswald and the Bomb Squad's densest work, and is bound up with copyright confrontation. Unlike acousmatic music it keeps its sources recognizable and often satirical, and unlike sample-based hip hop it usually refuses a steady beat, treating the cut itself as the rhythmic event.
exemplars: The Avalanches — Since I Left You

items.name: Avant-Garde Jazz
items.lineage: Formed in New York and Chicago from 1959 onward through Ornette Coleman, Cecil Taylor, late Coltrane, Albert Ayler and the AACM, it abandons fixed chord changes and often steady tempo — collective simultaneous improvisation, saxophone in the altissimo and overblown register, arco and pizzicato bass freed from walking, drums playing pulse-free wash, and pieces framed by short unison heads or open notated cells.
items.description: Avant-garde jazz emerged around 1959-1965 as Ornette Coleman, Cecil Taylor, Albert Ayler and the late Coltrane quartet dropped functional chord progressions, then broadened through Chicago's AACM and the New York loft scene. The texture is dense collective improvisation at high intensity: multiphonics and screaming altissimo saxophone, piano played in tone clusters, bass and drums generating turbulence rather than time. It differs from modal jazz in discarding the underlying scale-frame entirely, and from European free improvisation in retaining blues cry, gospel shout and often a stated theme.

items.name: Jazz-Funk
items.lineage: Consolidated 1969-1977 in New York and Los Angeles around Creed Taylor's CTI, Blue Note's later roster and Herbie Hancock's Headhunters, it fuses jazz soloing with a sixteenth-note funk rhythm section — electric bass playing composed slap or fingered ostinatos, drums locked to a syncopated one-drop backbeat around 95-110 BPM, Fender Rhodes and clavinet comping, and horn or saxophone leads over static two-chord vamps with congas layered on top.
items.description: Jazz-funk crystallized between 1969 and 1977 as soul-jazz organ grooves gave way to electric bass, Rhodes and clavinet and to James Brown's sixteenth-note rhythmic vocabulary. Tracks sit on one or two chords for minutes at a time while a written bassline and tight syncopated drums hold the floor and horns or saxophone improvise above; production is close, compressed and punchy rather than airy. Against jazz-rock fusion it is groove-first and rarely uses odd metres or distorted guitar, and against instrumental funk it keeps extended improvised solos and jazz harmony in the comping.

items.name: Afro-Cuban Jazz
items.lineage: Created in New York in 1947-1949 when Dizzy Gillespie hired Chano Pozo and Mario Bauzá and Machito's Afro-Cubans commissioned Cubop charts, it welds bebop horn writing and improvisation onto Cuban clave — son and rumba clave underpinning a full percussion section of congas, timbales, bongos and bell, piano montuno and tumbao bass, with mambo and moña shout sections behind the solos.
items.description: Afro-Cuban jazz was made in New York in the late 1940s by Mario Bauzá, Machito, Chano Pozo and Dizzy Gillespie, and continued through Tito Puente, Cal Tjader and Chucho Valdés. Everything is organized by clave: piano montuno and bass tumbao interlock against congas, timbales and bongo bell while bebop-voiced brass plays riff-based mambo sections and soloists improvise across the two-bar cell. It is distinct from Brazilian-derived Latin jazz in its percussion battery and clave discipline, and from commercial salsa in foregrounding extended instrumental improvisation over sung coro-pregón.

items.name: West African Jazz
items.lineage: Developed in Lagos, Accra, Bamako and Dakar from the late 1950s through the 1970s in the dance-band highlife orbit — Fela Kuti's pre-Afrobeat Koola Lobitos, Guy Warren, Manu Dibango, the Bembeya and Rail Band circles — setting bebop and hard-bop horn language over highlife and Mande grooves: 4/4 or 12/8 clave-adjacent patterns, tenor and trumpet lead lines, clean single-coil guitar arpeggios, kora or balafon lines, and long vamp-based solo sections.
items.description: West African jazz grew out of the Ghanaian and Nigerian dance-band highlife scene and the Malian and Senegalese state orchestras between roughly 1957 and 1978, when musicians who had absorbed Parker, Coltrane and Blakey applied that vocabulary to local rhythm. Horn sections play riff heads over cyclic highlife or Mande vamps while clean electric guitar, kora or balafon supplies the interlocking ostinato and hand drums carry the pulse. It differs from Afrobeat in keeping jazz solo form and shorter arrangements rather than Fela's twenty-minute two-chord structures, and from American hard bop in its cyclic, non-modulating harmonic ground.
exemplars: Guy Warren — Africa Speaks, America Answers

items.name: South African Jazz
items.lineage: Formed in Sophiatown and Cape Town from the 1940s marabi and kwela lineage and codified by the Jazz Epistles, Abdullah Ibrahim, Chris McGregor's Blue Notes and the exile generation after 1964 — a rolling I-IV-V or three-chord marabi cycle at mid tempo, hymn-derived voicings, sung-tone alto and tenor saxophone, muted or open trumpet and trombone, and township-jive backbeat under long collective vamps.
items.description: South African jazz took shape in Johannesburg's Sophiatown and Cape Town's District Six, joining the marabi shebeen cycle and kwela penny-whistle music to American swing and bebop; the Jazz Epistles' 1959 record is its founding statement and the Blue Notes carried it into London exile. Its identity is the repeating three-chord marabi ground, hymn-like church harmony under the horns, and a broad singing saxophone tone rather than bebop's rapid articulation. Against American hard bop it is more cyclic and less harmonically mobile, and against township jive it foregrounds extended improvisation and jazz instrumentation over pop song form.

items.name: Swing Revival
items.lineage: A mid-1990s Californian and American club movement led by Royal Crown Revue, Big Bad Voodoo Daddy, the Brian Setzer Orchestra and Squirrel Nut Zippers, reviving 1930s-40s jump blues and big-band swing for Lindy Hop dancers — shuffle and jump grooves near 180 BPM, riffing brass sections, honking tenor solos, slap upright bass, hollow-body archtop rhythm guitar and shouted crooner vocals, cut with modern rock-level drum recording.
items.description: Swing revival was a 1993-2000 American club phenomenon tied to the Lindy Hop dance resurgence, centred on Los Angeles and popularized by Zoot Suit-styled bands on film soundtracks and beer commercials. Musically it is jump blues and small big-band swing at fast dance tempos: riffing horn sections, honking tenor breaks, slapped upright bass and archtop rhythm guitar, topped by a shouting crooner. It differs from the original swing era in production — close-miked modern drums, compressed rock-loud mixes — and from trad-jazz revivalism in taking Louis Jordan and Louis Prima rather than New Orleans polyphony as its model.
exemplars: Brian Setzer Orchestra — The Dirty Boogie
Cherry Poppin' Daddies — Zoot Suit Riot

items.name: Contemporary post-bop
items.lineage: Post-1995 New York small-group idiom codified at Smalls and the Village Vanguard by Brad Mehldau, Mark Turner, Kurt Rosenwinkel and Chris Potter — extended-form originals with slow-moving upper-structure harmony, long asymmetric phrase groupings over 4/4 or shifting 5/4 and 7/4, elastic ride-cymbal time and conversational drum interaction, and a soft-attack tenor and nylon-clean guitar timbre far from hard bop's blues declamation.
items.description: Contemporary post-bop is the acoustic small-group mainstream that consolidated in New York from the mid-1990s onward, descending from the Miles Davis mid-1960s quintet and Wayne Shorter's compositional model rather than from Blue Note hard bop. It is marked by originals with irregular phrase lengths, harmony built from slash voicings and pedal-anchored upper structures, drummers who imply rather than state the pulse, and a deliberately unforced, high-resolution recorded tone. It differs from hard bop by rejecting blues-and-gospel vocabulary as the default rhetoric, and from ECM-school jazz by keeping American swing feel and bebop line-construction at the centre rather than open Nordic space.

items.name: Chicago bop
items.lineage: South Side Chicago tenor-and-rhythm bop lineage of the 1950s-70s carried by Von Freeman, Johnny Griffin, Clifford Jordan, Ira Sullivan and drummer Wilbur Campbell in clubs such as the Sutherland Lounge and the New Apartment — hard-driving medium-up 4/4 swing, blues-saturated changes, an intentionally wide-pitched and vocalized tenor tone with slurred altissimo, and long cutting-contest solo forms over organ or piano trio.
items.description: Chicago bop names the distinct South Side strain of bebop and hard bop that developed largely outside the New York recording economy, sustained in neighbourhood lounges through the 1950s to the 1970s. Its hallmarks are an aggressively vocalized tenor saxophone sound with deliberately unstable intonation and altissimo cries, blues form treated as an endlessly reharmonizable vehicle, propulsive brush-and-ride swing, and marathon jam-session structures shaped by cutting contests rather than album programming. It is rougher and more blues-anchored than East Coast hard bop of the same years, and unrelated to the earlier 1920s Chicago jazz of the Austin High Gang.

items.name: Jazz metal
items.lineage: Late-1980s onward fusion of extreme metal with post-bop harmony, crystallized by Florida's Atheist and Cynic and continued in Europe by Ephel Duath, Shining (Norway) and Panzerballett — palm-muted downtuned riffing recast in 7/8 and 5/4, chromatic altered-dominant and diminished harmony under blast-beat and jazz-ride alternation, fretless-inflected bass counterlines, and saxophone or clean vocal passages interleaved with death-metal growls.
items.description: Jazz metal is the technically maximalist meeting of extreme metal instrumentation with jazz harmony and metre, first realized on Atheist's Unquestionable Presence (1991) and Cynic's Focus (1993) and later pursued by European bands adding actual horn sections. The music keeps metal's distorted rhythm guitar, double-kick drumming and growled vocals while replacing power-chord modality with altered-dominant, diminished and quartal voicings, and replacing steady 4/4 with constantly shifting odd metres. Unlike progressive metal it derives its harmonic language specifically from bebop and fusion rather than classical or symphonic sources, and unlike jazzcore it remains composed and precision-tracked rather than improvised and abrasive.

items.name: Jazzcore
items.lineage: Mid-1980s downtown New York and Chicago collision of hardcore punk speed with free-jazz improvisation, codified by John Zorn's Naked City, Last Exit and later The Flying Luttenbachers and Zu — sub-minute compositions of jump-cut blocks, blast-tempo drumming under squealing alto saxophone, detuned or noise-processed guitar, and screamed vocal bursts used as percussive punctuation rather than lyric line.
items.description: Jazzcore grew out of the Lower East Side improvised-music scene of the mid-1980s, where players moved freely between hardcore bands and free-jazz sessions, and was consolidated by Naked City's file-card compositions and the Zorn/Laswell orbit. It is defined by extreme dynamic and stylistic jump-cutting, hardcore tempos and distortion carrying saxophone-led free improvisation, and structures measured in seconds rather than choruses. It sits closer to noise rock and grindcore than to jazz metal, which is comparatively composed and harmonically systematic, and it foregrounds abrupt discontinuity where no-wave jazz favoured sustained atonal texture.

items.name: Jazztronica
items.lineage: Late-1990s Scandinavian and British hybrid of live jazz improvisation with programmed electronics, codified by Nils Petter Molvær's Khmer (1997), Bugge Wesseltoft's New Conception of Jazz and Jaga Jazzist — 90-140 BPM broken-beat and drum-and-bass programming under long modal trumpet or saxophone lines, dub-scale delay and granular processing on horns, Rhodes and analogue synth pads, and post-production editing treated as a compositional stage equal to the take.
items.description: Jazztronica names the studio-constructed strand of jazz-electronic hybrid that emerged around Oslo and London from about 1996, where improvising horn players worked over programmed beats and effect chains rather than a rhythm section alone. Its sonic identity comes from static modal harmony, heavily processed and spatialized lead instruments, dub-derived delay and filtering, and loop-based cyclic form assembled in the DAW. It differs from 1970s fusion by placing the producer and editing desk at the centre instead of live band virtuosity, and from acid jazz by favouring ambient and drum-and-bass textures over dancefloor funk and rare-groove sampling.

items.name: Musique acadienne (Maritime Acadian tradition)
items.lineage: French-language traditional music of the Acadian Maritimes — southeast New Brunswick, southwest Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island and the Îles-de-la-Madeleine — carried orally since the eighteenth century and revived from the 1970s by Édith Butler, 1755 and later Barachois and Vishtèn: crooked-metre fiddle reels with irregular bar counts, seated podorythmie foot percussion, diatonic accordion and spoons, and unaccompanied complainte and chanson à répondre call-and-response singing in Acadian French.
items.description: Musique acadienne is the surviving French-language folk tradition of the Maritime provinces, distinct from the Louisiana Cajun music that descends from the same 1755 deportation. Its markers are fiddle tunes with 'crooked' asymmetrical phrase lengths preserved from oral transmission, foot-tapped podorythmie supplying the percussion, button accordion and spoons, and a large ballad repertoire of complaintes and answer-back drinking songs sung in Acadian French with sparse or no accompaniment. Compared with Cajun it lacks the accordion-and-triangle two-step dance-hall format and blues inflection, and compared with Québécois trad it is more song-driven and less reel-band oriented.

items.name: Musique traditionnelle québécoise
items.lineage: Québec's French-Canadian dance and song tradition of the Saint Lawrence valley, documented from the nineteenth century, professionalized by La Bolduc and fiddler Jean Carignan and revived from the 1970s by La Bottine Souriante and Le Vent du Nord — crooked reels and gigues at 110-130 BPM driven by seated podorythmie foot percussion, diatonic accordion and fiddle in unison, ragtime-inflected piano backing, and chansons à répondre with turlutte mouth-music refrains.
items.description: Traditional Québécois music is the kitchen-party and veillée repertoire of French Canada, built on fiddle-and-accordion dance tunes and responsorial song, and continuously performed rather than reconstructed. Its unmistakable features are podorythmie — the fiddler's own seated foot-tapping as the rhythm section — irregular 'crooked' tune structures with added or dropped beats, a piano accompaniment style borrowed from ragtime and vaudeville, and turlutte vocal mouth-music standing in for instruments. It shares Celtic modal tune shapes with Irish and Cape Breton traditions but is distinguished by the foot-percussion drive, the French song layer, and the tolerance for asymmetrical bar counts that Scottish and Irish repertoires largely regularized away.

items.name: Métis fiddle
items.lineage: Red River Valley fiddle tradition of the Manitoba, Saskatchewan and North Dakota Métis, formed in the early nineteenth-century fur trade from Scottish, French-Canadian and Orcadian tunes crossed with Cree and Anishinaabe rhythmic sensibility, and codified on record by Andy De Jarlis and Reg Bouvette — crooked jigs and Red River jigs with beats added or dropped mid-phrase, bow-driven melodic-rhythmic accent instead of vibrato, clogging or foot-tap percussion, and guitar or piano vamp accompaniment for the changing-steps dance.
items.description: Métis fiddling is the distinctive dance-fiddle style of the Red River Métis, developed in fur-trade communities where European settler tunes were reshaped by Indigenous rhythmic practice and transmitted entirely by ear. Its defining traits are the crooked tune — phrases of irregular length that the dancers know and follow — heavy rhythmic bowing with double-stop drones, foot percussion or clogging, and the Red River Jig's alternation between high and low parts governing the changing steps. Against Cape Breton or Québécois fiddling it is sparser, less ornamented with grace-note filigree, and far freer with bar counts, and its accompaniment stays a simple vamp rather than a driving piano tradition.

items.name: Cape Breton fiddle and piano tradition
items.lineage: Gaelic Scottish fiddle repertoire carried to Cape Breton Island, Nova Scotia by Highland Clearance emigrants after 1800 and preserved there in older form than in Scotland, codified on record by Winston 'Scotty' Fitzgerald and Buddy MacMaster — strathspey-reel medleys driven at square-dance tempo with pronounced Scotch-snap dotting, cuts and grace notes bowed rather than fingered, foot-tapping, and a percussive chordal piano accompaniment unique to the island.
items.description: The Cape Breton tradition is the Scottish Gaelic fiddle and dance music of northeastern Nova Scotia, retained through nineteenth-century isolation and now regarded as preserving eighteenth-century Highland bowing and repertoire more faithfully than mainland Scotland. Its signatures are the strathspey-to-reel medley built for square sets, dotted Scotch-snap rhythm and bow-driven ornament, insistent foot-tapping, and an off-beat, chordally dense piano backing developed locally rather than imported. Compared with Irish session music it is squarer and less legato-ornamented, and compared with the island's own Gaelic milling-frolic songs it is instrumental and dance-functional rather than work-song vocal.

items.name: Newfoundland traditional song and dance music
items.lineage: Anglo-Irish and French-Newfoundland repertoire of the island's outports, transmitted orally since eighteenth-century West Country and Waterford settlement, collected by Maud Karpeles and Kenneth Peacock and revived from the 1970s by Figgy Duff and Ryan's Fancy — unaccompanied ballad singing in a high nasal outport delivery, single and double jigs for the kitchen set dance played on accordion and crooked-tuned fiddle, and accordion-led 'lancers' with bodhrán or ugly-stick percussion.
items.description: Newfoundland traditional music is the outport repertoire of ballads, dance tunes and recitations that survived on the island through isolation from mainland Canada until 1949, drawing on English West Country, Irish and French-Newfoundland sources. It is characterized by long unaccompanied narrative ballads sung in a tight, high, ornamented outport voice, button-accordion-led single jigs for kitchen sets and lancers, fiddle playing full of crooked bars and idiosyncratic tunings, and improvised percussion on spoons and ugly stick. It is broader than the island's sea-shanty and work-song layer, which is occupational and shipboard, and differs from Irish session music by its accordion-first instrumentation and the persistence of English-language broadside ballads as core repertoire.

items.name: Contra dance band music
items.lineage: New England grange-hall dance music descended from English country dance and French contredanse, sustained in Vermont, New Hampshire and Massachusetts and reshaped from the 1970s by Rodney Miller, Bob McQuillen and Wild Asparagus — 112-124 BPM reels and jigs played in 64-bar tune medleys matched exactly to the caller's figures, fiddle lead with piano and guitar supplying a swung, syncopated chordal drive, and modulating tune sets escalating in energy across the dance.
items.description: Contra dance music is the living New England dance-band idiom that accompanies called longways set dances in grange halls and town halls, continuous since colonial times and substantially revitalized during the 1970s folk revival. Musically it is defined by strict 64-bar AABB tune structure locked to the caller's 32-count figures, a driving syncopated piano-and-guitar rhythm section that swings the beat rather than marching it, and medleys that shift key and tune mid-dance to lift the room. It draws on Irish, Scottish, Québécois and old-time repertoire but is distinguished from all of them by the caller's architecture, the fixed phrase length, and a harmonically adventurous backup style that would be foreign to an Irish session.

items.name: Shanty (Shipboard Work Song)
items.lineage: The functional labour song of Atlantic deep-water merchant sail, consolidated roughly 1815-1875 on packet and clipper crews out of Liverpool, London, Mobile and New York and first systematically transcribed by Richard Runciman Terry, Cecil Sharp, W.B. Whall and later Stan Hugill, whose Shanties from the Seven Seas remains the codifying text; a shantyman improvised solo lines against a fixed crew refrain, with the pull or push of the work fixing the metre - short-drag shanties with two hauls per verse, halyard shanties with a longer chorus, capstan shanties in continuous rolling 6/8 or 4/4 for windlass work - sung unaccompanied at moderate tempo in open chest voice.
items.description: The working shanty is not a song genre so much as a labour tool of Atlantic square-rig merchant sail between roughly 1815 and the 1870s, sung to coordinate hauling, heaving and pumping. Its sound is unaccompanied and strictly functional: a shantyman leading with improvised, often bawdy or topical couplets drawn from a floating stock of verses, and the whole crew answering on a short fixed refrain timed to the pull, with the ship's own gear - chain, capstan pawls, stamping feet - supplying the percussion. It is distinguished from the later revival repertoire by having no instruments, no fixed text and no audience, and from forecastle songs and ballads by its metre being dictated by work rather than by narrative.

items.name: Sea Shanty (Revival Repertoire)
items.lineage: The post-1950s folk-club and festival performance form of maritime song, shaped in Britain by A.L. Lloyd and Ewan MacColl's 1956 Blow Boys Blow, by Stan Hugill's residencies at the Falmouth and Mystic Seaport shanty festivals from the 1970s, and by the Fisherman's Friends and Sea Shanty TikTok waves of 2010 and 2021; performed at fixed brisk tempos in strophic verse-and-chorus form with strong unison male chorus on the refrain, frequently with concertina, melodeon, fiddle or guitar accompaniment that the working original never had.
items.description: The revival sea shanty is the concert-hall and folk-club descendant of shipboard work song, established through the British folk revival of the 1950s-60s and sustained by Cornish and New England maritime festivals into the twenty-first century. Texts are fixed rather than improvised, tempos are steady and singable rather than governed by a hauling rhythm, and instrumental accompaniment - anglo concertina, melodeon, fiddle, occasionally guitar - is standard, with the mass chorus refrain as the emotional centre. It differs from the working shanty in being audience-facing, text-stable and accompanied, and from the broadside ballad tradition in its call-and-response chorus architecture and maritime subject matter.
exemplars: Ewan MacColl and A.L. Lloyd, Blow Boys Blow

items.name: Szanty
items.lineage: The Polish sailor-song movement that emerged from Baltic yacht clubs and student sailing culture in the 1970s-80s, institutionalised by the Shanties festival in Krakow (from 1981) and by groups such as Stare Dzwony, Mechanicy Shanty, Perły i Łotry and Ryczące Dwudziestki; sung in Polish - part translated Anglo-American repertoire, part newly composed - at driving 4/4 or 6/8 tempos with strummed acoustic guitars, accordion, fiddle and a shouted unison male chorus, closer to campfire student song (piosenka turystyczna) than to shipboard labour practice.
items.description: Szanty is the Polish maritime song scene that grew out of Baltic and inland sailing clubs in the late 1970s and became a mass festival culture centred on Krakow, Gdynia and Wrocław. Its sound is guitar-driven and rousing: fast strummed chord cycles, accordion and fiddle counterlines, an upright bass or bass guitar underneath, and a loud shouted male chorus on every refrain, with Polish-language lyrics that are frequently original compositions rather than translations. Unlike Anglo revival shanty it is fully instrumental-accompanied and songwriter-driven, and unlike the German Seemannslieder tradition it is amateur, participatory and festival-based rather than orchestrated commercial schlager.

items.name: Seemannslieder
items.lineage: German-language sailor song as a commercial and choral genre, rooted in nineteenth-century Hamburg and Bremen harbour repertoire and in the 1930s-40s Hans Albers film songs (La Paloma, Auf der Reeperbahn nachts um halb eins), then dominated by Freddy Quinn's Polydor recordings from 1956 onward; typically moderate 3/4 or 4/4, orchestrated with strings, accordion and light rhythm section, sung in a warm baritone with a nostalgic Fernweh lyric and an anthemic male-chorus refrain, alongside an amateur Shanty-Chor branch singing the same material a cappella in four parts.
items.description: Seemannslieder is the German maritime song repertoire as it crystallised commercially in the mid-twentieth century, moving from Hamburg harbour and Reeperbahn cabaret into film song and postwar schlager. The archetypal record is a tube-warm baritone lead over strings, accordion and discreet rhythm section, resolving into a broad male-chorus refrain, with texts of longing for distant ports and home. It differs from Anglo shanty in being through-composed popular song with fixed harmony and orchestration rather than call-and-response labour music, and from Dutch shantykoren in being a soloist-and-studio tradition rather than an amateur choral one.

items.name: Shantykoren
items.lineage: The Dutch and Flemish amateur shanty-choir movement, launched by Rotterdam's Rotterdam Shantykoor and Urk's Crescendo in the late 1970s-80s and now numbering several hundred choirs across the Low Countries; forty to eighty older male singers in unison and simple two- or three-part harmony, accompanied by a front line of accordions with occasional banjo-family strings and bass, performing Dutch, English and German maritime songs at steady march-like 4/4 or lilting 6/8 tempos in harbour-festival and community-hall settings.
items.description: Shantykoren are the amateur male shanty choirs of the Netherlands and Flanders, a community-music phenomenon that expanded rapidly from the 1980s around harbour towns such as Urk, Volendam, Rotterdam and Antwerp. The sound is a large, unforced massed male unison thickened by simple harmony, carried by a bank of accordions rather than a rhythm section, with tempo held steady by a conductor and repertoire mixing Dutch-language originals with translated Anglo shanties. It is distinguished from Anglo revival shanty by choir scale and accordion-front accompaniment, and from German Seemannslieder by its participatory amateur basis rather than a commercial soloist tradition.

items.name: Military Cadence (Jody Call)
items.lineage: The chanted running and marching call of the United States armed forces, conventionally traced to Private Willie Duckworth at Fort Slocum in 1944 whose Sound Off became the model, thereafter standardised across Army, Marine Corps and Navy basic training; a drill instructor calls a two- or four-bar line on a narrow two- or three-note contour and the formation answers in unison on the left-foot strike, locked to a 4/4 march at roughly 110-120 steps per minute or a faster double-time run cadence, with boot-fall and hand-clap as the only percussion.
items.description: The military cadence, or jody call, is a functional American armed-forces chant developed during and after the Second World War to synchronise marching and running formations. Its music is minimal by design: a leader's improvised or stock rhymed line on a narrow declamatory contour, answered by mass unison response, with the downbeat pinned to the left foot and the ambient percussion of boots on pavement or dirt. It is distinguished from work song by its ambulatory rather than task-cycle metre, and from drum-and-bugle traditions by having no melodic instruments at all - the formation itself is the instrument.
exemplars: US Marine Corps recruit depot cadence recordings
Yo Left! Marine Corps cadence collections

items.name: Marching Band
items.lineage: The American outdoor wind-and-percussion ensemble that fused European military band instrumentation with post-Civil-War town-band culture, professionalised by Patrick Gilmore and John Philip Sousa in the 1880s-90s and reinvented in the twentieth century by university and HBCU programs - Florida A&M's Marching 100 under William P. Foster from 1946 - which added dance-derived body movement, R&B and funk arrangements and a heavily amplified sousaphone bass line; standard scoring is trumpets and mellophones over trombones, baritones and sousaphones with a battery of snares, tenors and bass drums plus a front pit, playing at 120-180 beats per minute in strict cut time.
items.description: The marching band is the American stadium and parade ensemble of brass, woodwinds and marching percussion, descended from nineteenth-century military and town bands and codified through Sousa's touring band and, in the twentieth century, through school, university and HBCU programs. Its sonic signature is high-register trumpet and mellophone scoring over a sousaphone bass, a battery drumline whose snare rudiments carry the groove, and enormous outdoor dynamic range with almost no reverberant support. It differs from the concert band in being memorised, mobile and visually choreographed, and from drum corps in retaining woodwinds and a full brass complement rather than a bugle-derived brass line.
exemplars: Jackson State Sonic Boom of the South

items.name: Fife and Drum Corps
items.lineage: The martial signalling ensemble of eighteenth-century European and colonial American armies, preserved after its battlefield obsolescence by New England ancient corps from the 1880s onward and by the Company of Fifers and Drummers founded in Ivoryton, Connecticut in 1965; a section of six-hole keyless B-flat fifes plays two-part duty tunes and quicksteps in D and G over rope-tension snare drums beating rudimental long rolls, flams and drags with a bass drum on the march beat, all outdoors, unamplified and at roughly 110-120 steps per minute.
items.description: Fife and drum is the martial field music of eighteenth- and nineteenth-century armies, kept alive as a living tradition by the ancient corps of Connecticut, Massachusetts and the Hudson Valley. The sound is deliberately piercing and narrow-band: keyless fifes doubling a two-part tune in the top octave with no harmonic filling, over rope-tension snares whose gut snare-beds and rudimental sticking supply all the rhythmic detail, plus a march-beat bass drum. It is distinguished from the marching band by its tiny instrumentation and lack of brass, and from drum corps by its pre-industrial fife rather than valved bugle melody line.
exemplars: The Company of Fifers and Drummers
Ancient Mariners Fife and Drum Corps

items.name: Concert Band
items.lineage: The seated indoor wind-and-percussion ensemble that grew from nineteenth-century military and municipal bands, professionalised by Patrick Gilmore, John Philip Sousa and the Goldman Band, and given a serious concert repertoire by Holst's Suites in E-flat and F (1909, 1911), Vaughan Williams's Folk Song Suite (1923) and the American school-band literature of Persichetti, Grainger and Frank Ticheli; large doubled sections of flutes, clarinets, saxophones, cornets, horns, trombones, euphoniums and tubas with full percussion, reading fully notated scores at conventional concert tempos.
items.description: The concert band is the seated symphonic wind ensemble in its large, section-doubled form, established as a civic and school institution across the United States and Britain from the late nineteenth century onward. Its texture is dense and blended: multiple clarinets carrying the string-substitute middle voice, saxophones filling the tenor register, cornets and trumpets on top, and a tuba-euphonium foundation, all notated and conducted with no improvisation. It differs from the marching band in being stationary, seated and score-read rather than memorised and choreographed, and from the wind ensemble in doubling parts heavily rather than assigning one player per line.
exemplars: Royal Northern College of Music Wind Orchestra
Gustav Holst, First Suite in E-flat

items.name: Wind Ensemble
items.lineage: The one-player-per-part symphonic wind medium founded by Frederick Fennell with the Eastman Wind Ensemble in 1952 as a deliberate reform of the doubled concert band, giving composers a transparent chamber-scaled wind palette exploited by Schoenberg, Stravinsky's Symphonies of Wind Instruments as ancestor, and by Husa, Karel Husa's Music for Prague 1968, Dahl, Maslanka and Joan Tower; variable instrumentation drawn from the full woodwind, brass and percussion families, fully notated, often in extended tonality or serial and aleatoric idioms with mixed and shifting metres.
items.description: The wind ensemble is the transparent, one-per-part symphonic wind medium created by Frederick Fennell at Eastman in 1952 and adopted worldwide as the vehicle for serious contemporary wind writing. Because parts are single rather than doubled, individual timbres stay audible, allowing composers to write chamber-textured counterpoint, extended techniques, complex metric shifts and dissonant harmonic language impossible in a massed band. It differs from the concert band chiefly in scoring philosophy and repertoire - modernist and commissioned rather than march-and-transcription - while sharing the same instrument families and notation-bound practice.
exemplars: Eastman Wind Ensemble under Frederick Fennell

items.name: Drum and Bugle Corps
items.lineage: The American competitive field ensemble that grew out of post-First-World-War American Legion and VFW veterans' units using surplus valveless bugles, reorganised under Drum Corps International from 1972 and progressively liberalised to three-valve brass in 2000 and any-key brass in 2014; a brass line of trumpets, mellophones, baritones, euphoniums and contrabass bugles plus a marching battery of snares, tenors and basses and an amplified front-ensemble pit of mallet keyboards and synthesisers, performing eleven-minute memorised competitive programs with extreme dynamic contrast and metric complexity.
items.description: Drum and bugle corps is the competitive American field-show idiom that evolved from veterans' bugle units into the Drum Corps International circuit after 1972. Its sound is an all-brass line with no woodwinds - trumpets, mellophones, baritones and contrabasses - paired with a virtuosic marching battery and an amplified front pit of mallet percussion and electronics, performing memorised through-composed programs with wide dynamic swings and frequent metric modulation. It differs from the marching band in excluding woodwinds and in its competitive, through-composed show format, and from the concert band in being memorised, mobile and heavily arranged from orchestral and contemporary sources.

items.name: Afro drill
items.lineage: Formed in London and Lagos circa 2019-2021 when UK drill producers and Nigerian-Ghanaian diaspora artists fused the 138-142 BPM sliding 808 drill pattern with Afrobeats' 3-2 log-drum and shaker feel, codified by Kwengface, Tion Wayne, Odumodublvck and producers like Ghosty and Gotcha, marked by triplet hats, a melodic Afro guitar or log-drum loop over the drill bass slide, and pidgin/Yoruba-inflected melodic hooks alternating with flat-affect road rap verses.
items.description: Afro drill emerged around 2019 in London's Nigerian and Ghanaian diaspora scenes and quickly reflected back into Lagos and Accra. It keeps UK drill's sliding, portamento 808 bass and skittering triplet hi-hats at roughly 140 BPM but replaces the grey minor-key piano and glide-bass menace with warm Afrobeats material: log-drum and talking-drum figures, plucked nylon guitar loops, and sung pidgin hooks. Against straight UK drill it is brighter and more melodic; against Afrobeats proper it is far darker, sparser and rhythmically stiffer.

items.name: Detroit trap
items.lineage: Emerged on Detroit's east and west sides circa 2015-2019 through Sada Baby, Tee Grizzley, 42 Dugg, Babyface Ray and producers Helluva and Antt Beatz, using 95-110 BPM double-time-feel beats with a swung shuffled hi-hat, dry punchy kick and clap rather than long 808 slides, chopped soul or eerie synth loops, and a conversational, off-kilter, punchline-dense flow that lands deliberately behind and around the grid.
items.description: Detroit trap is a late-2010s regional rewrite of Atlanta's template that swaps the sliding 808 for dry, shuffling drums and a nervous swung hi-hat pattern, often built by producers like Helluva around a looped soul or synth fragment and a signature bell or vocal tag. Rappers ride the beat conversationally, crowding syllables and landing behind the grid in a way that reads as almost comic-aggressive. Compared with Atlanta trap it is faster-feeling, less bass-dominated and much rougher in mix; compared with Michigan's older hip-hop it is far more melodically minimal.

items.name: Bay Area hip-hop (mobb music lineage)
items.lineage: Developed in Oakland, Vallejo and Richmond from the mid-1980s through the 1990s by Too $hort, E-40, Spice 1, Mac Dre, Digital Underground and producers Khayree and Ant Banks, built on 85-100 BPM funk-derived grooves with live-feel slap electric bass, P-funk synth leads and talkbox, sparse gated drums, and pimp-narrative or rapid-fire regional-slang vocal delivery cut for independent trunk-oriented mixes.
items.description: Bay Area hip-hop, often called mobb music, grew out of Oakland and Vallejo's independent tape-and-trunk economy from the mid-1980s onward, largely outside major-label systems. Its beats favour slapping live or sampled electric bass, greasy P-funk synth leads and talkbox over hard breakbeats, with vocals ranging from Too $hort's laconic drawl to E-40's elastic, slang-inventing cadences. It is looser and more bass-forward than Los Angeles G-funk, which it partly prefigured, and its later hyphy phase pushed the same funk lineage into faster, more manic territory.

items.name: Jazz rap
items.lineage: Formed in New York and London between 1988 and 1994 through the Native Tongues collective — A Tribe Called Quest, De La Soul, Gang Starr, Digable Planets and Guru's Jazzmatazz — built on 88-96 BPM boom-bap breakbeats layered with sampled or live upright bass, muted trumpet, Rhodes and vibraphone from Blue Note and CTI records, swung MPC-quantised drums, and a relaxed, conversational, often abstract or Afrocentric lyric.
items.description: Jazz rap took shape at the turn of the 1990s when New York producers began building boom-bap tracks from hard-bop and soul-jazz records rather than funk breaks alone, sometimes replaying the material with live players. The result pairs warm walking upright bass, Rhodes chords and muted horn fragments with swung, deliberately un-quantised MPC drums and low-key conversational rapping. Against gangsta rap of the same years it is harmonically far richer and dynamically softer; against the later lo-fi hip-hop it descends from, it retains full-length verses and a real MC-centred structure.
exemplars: A Tribe Called Quest — The Low End Theory
De La Soul — 3 Feet High and Rising

items.name: Narco rap
items.lineage: Emerged circa 2010 in Reynosa, Matamoros and the Tamaulipas border corridor of northeastern Mexico, spread by Cartel de Santa's precedent and artists such as Rowsty, Dan Sanchez and El Komander-adjacent rap crews, built on 70-90 BPM half-time trap and boom-bap beats with dark minor synth pads, heavy 808s, occasional sampled accordion or bajo sexto quotes, and blunt first-person cartel narrative delivered in a hard Norteño Spanish over YouTube-distributed, home-mixed audio.
items.description: Narco rap is the Spanish-language border-corridor rap that grew up around Reynosa and Matamoros from about 2010, functioning as a hip-hop parallel to the narcocorrido: commissioned or self-authored chronicles of cartel figures, operations and rivalries. Musically it is stripped-down Mexican trap — dark synth pads, heavy 808s, half-time drums — produced on home DAW rigs and distributed almost entirely through YouTube and social channels rather than labels. What separates it from other Mexican trap is documentary lyrical function and its acoustic-corrido citations; what separates it from the corrido tumbado is that the instrumentation stays electronic.

items.name: Trap Brasileiro
items.lineage: Formed in São Paulo and Rio between 2016 and 2019 out of the rap-battle and YouTube-cypher circuit, codified by Matuê, Teto, Derek, WIU and producers Papatinho and Sidoka's circle, applying 130-150 BPM half-time 808 trap production with dark plucked-synth and piano loops to Brazilian Portuguese flows, plus periodic funk-carioca tamborzão or samba percussion inserts and sung Auto-Tuned refrains.
items.description: Trap Brasileiro is the late-2010s Brazilian assimilation of Atlanta trap, driven less by radio than by YouTube cyphers, battle-rap alumni and independent collectives like 30PRAUM. Production keeps the tuned 808, triplet hats and sparse minor loop, but the Portuguese cadences sit differently on the grid and tracks frequently splice in tamborzão or samba-derived percussion breaks. It is distinct from funk carioca, which stays on a fast continuous dembow-derived pulse, and from Brazilian boom-bap rap nacional, which is verse-heavy and sample-based rather than melodic and 808-driven.

items.name: Phonk Brasileiro
items.lineage: Emerged online around 2020-2022 as Brazilian producers on SoundCloud and TikTok fused drift-phonk's cowbell-driven 130-150 BPM template with funk carioca's tamborzão and beat-mandela rhythms, codified by producers such as MXZI, Yzomandias-adjacent Brazilian circles, Kordhell imitators and the 'funk phonk' / 'brazilian phonk' YouTube channel economy, marked by distorted 808 cowbell melodies, sidechained subs, chopped Memphis-style vocal samples and Portuguese shouted or pitched vocal chops.
items.description: Phonk Brasileiro is a fully platform-native genre that appeared around 2020 when Brazilian bedroom producers grafted drift phonk's distorted cowbell riffs and heavy sidechain onto funk carioca's tamborzão and 'beat bruxaria' rhythmic vocabulary. Tracks are short, loud, mono-dense and mixed to survive phone speakers, built from clipped 808 cowbells, sub-bass pumping against the kick, and chopped Memphis or Portuguese vocal fragments. It is faster, more percussive and less nostalgic than US drift phonk, and unlike mainstream funk carioca it foregrounds melodic cowbell riffing over vocal MCs.

items.name: Dark plugg
