exemplars: Phyu Phyu Kyaw Thein — A Girl is Broken-hearted (2012)
Phyu Phyu Kyaw Thein — A Shone Htet Po Thaw (2019)

items.name: Ambient IDM
items.lineage: The atmospheric, lower-intensity branch of listening-oriented IDM, represented here by Arovane’s Tides (2000): intricate sample-built rhythm, environmental recordings and edited guitar fragments arranged around quiet melodic space. Later Arovane/Porya Hatami collaborations extend the electronics/environmental-sound intersection. This is a selected calm, broken-beat branch rather than all IDM or all Arovane releases.
items.description: Ambient IDM retains carefully edited rhythmic events while giving atmospheric harmony and negative space more weight than percussion. Arovane’s Tides supplies a concrete sample-based branch: small jazz-record fragments, field recordings and edited improvised guitar coexist with downbeat grooves. The default uses one sampler for detailed beat/texture editing, a gently moving pad and clean guitar fragments; this is a reusable reduction rather than the album’s complete instrument inventory. Compared with IDM, percussion and intensity recede; compared with ambient techno, broken-beat detail replaces a regular techno machine pulse. Unlike beatless space ambient, discrete rhythmic edits remain audible. Synth construction and recording equipment are authored choices.

items.name: Ambient psychill
items.lineage: The spacious, predominantly instrumental synthesizer branch of psychedelic chillout represented by Carbon Based Lifeforms’ Hydroponic Garden (2003) and World of Sleepers (2006), on Ultimae. Slow electronic rhythms, resonant bass, environmental samples and layered harmony sustain an ambient listening space. This narrower branch does not stand for the entire psychill festival repertoire or presume its acoustic-instrument and vocal collage.
items.description: Ambient psychill selects the unhurried, spacious electronic end of psychedelic chillout: slowly developing pads and melodic bass carry the track while programmed percussion stays recessed and environmental samples add depth. Carbon Based Lifeforms’ credited Ultimae albums and firsthand account of melody/bass relationships, added drums and field-recording practice anchor this model. The roster deliberately omits generic flute, didgeridoo and sung-vocal defaults from the broader psychill entry. Compared with ambient IDM, its underlying loop is more stable and its bass/filter motion less chopped; compared with space ambient, it retains a quiet beat and resonant bass sequence. It is a narrower ambient branch of existing psychill, with an authored synth/sampler configuration.
exemplars: Carbon Based Lifeforms — World of Sleepers (2006)

items.name: Ambient synth
items.lineage: Synthesizer-led ambient in which articulated patterns and changing electronic timbres remain recognizable, represented by Steve Hauschildt’s solo work around Strands (2016). A harmonic bed can give rise to arpeggios and aleatoric sequences, then be shaped through processing and editing. This selected pattern-oriented branch differs from beatless, steady-state space ambient and from the historically specific Berlin School.
items.description: Ambient synth centers the synthesizer as a played or programmed sound source: slowly changing harmony, gently articulated figures and interacting electronic voices create the space without requiring drums or acoustic instruments. The selected Hauschildt branch combines arpeggiated motion with flexible timing and detailed processing, rather than treating every synth part as an undifferentiated drone. The default pairs a soft short-envelope triangle figure with harmonic FM tones; these are authored ways to achieve the sourced practice, not claims about Strands’ instruments. Unlike space ambient, repeated note attacks remain a compositional foreground; unlike Berlin School, neither a 1970s tape ensemble nor a fixed ostinato defines the scope.
exemplars: Steve Hauschildt — Where All Is Fled (2015)

items.name: Space ambient
items.lineage: Beatless spatial electronic ambient, represented here by Steve Roach’s long-form steady-state Immersion work. Sustained polyphonic tones, slow timbral change and deep artificial space make duration and immersion more prominent than melody or sequence. This entry models the non-pulsed branch; space-oriented music also includes more rhythmic or dramatic forms that are not its default.
items.description: Space ambient is represented by a beatless, sustained-tone branch of space music, with slow changes in register and spectral color creating an enveloping field rather than a foreground beat or a repeating note sequence. Projekt’s Immersion: One release describes a continuous, minimal steady-state zone designed for extended low-volume listening; Roach’s firsthand synthesis account supports held chords and electronic sound construction. The default uses a stable sine tone and slowly morphing polyphonic wavetable layer with deep stereo reverberation. Unlike ambient synth’s articulated pattern branch, note attacks recede; unlike new age, a melodic tune or acoustic ensemble is not required. The modern two-synth chain is an authored reusable model.

items.name: Detroit house
items.lineage: Detroit producer-led house associated with Theo Parrish, Moodymann and Sound Signature: disco and soul sampling, jazz-informed keyboard movement, elastic groove and independent record culture. This selection follows the sample-and-keyboard strand rather than equating all Detroit electronic music with techno.
items.description: Selected Detroit sample-and-keyboard house: a swung programmed pulse supports soul/disco fragments, rounded synth bass and repeating jazz-informed electric-piano figures. Theo Parrish discusses sampling as musicianship and the relation between jazz, Chicago house and Detroit techno; his label records provide the concrete repertoire anchor. This does not prescribe a single sound for Detroit or classify his entire work as house. Unlike the Chicago-house seed, keyboard movement and elastic sample texture lead rather than an acid-bass template; unlike Detroit techno, soul/disco material and harmonic pocket outweigh mechanical synthesis. The small ensemble, equipment, bit depths and 13 axes are authored operational models, not inventories of Parallel Dimensions sessions.

items.name: Piano house
items.lineage: Transatlantic piano-led house vocabulary carried from 1990s club records into contemporary productions by Mark Knight, ATFC and Gene Farris: a recurring piano riff supplies the principal harmonic hook above kick, clap, offbeat hats and bass. This is an arrangement practice rather than the historical Italian Italo-house scene.
items.description: Piano house names a piano-riff-led arrangement practice spanning early house, 1990s anthems and current club production. Toolroom documents Mark Knight’s reworking of a 1995 Mr Roy record with piano, chopped vocals, clap snares and offbeat hats; ATFC describes played piano arpeggios and chords in The Spirit of House. This selected contemporary instrumental-led model foregrounds a ringing piano figure against tightly programmed percussion, bass and sampled hook texture. The catalog’s Italo-house record specifically represents the late-1980s/early-1990s Italian production scene and diva-vocal lineage, whereas this entry covers a broader transatlantic technique and its later revival. The grand piano is an editable timbral equivalent for acoustic, sampled or keyboard piano sounds; its brand, tracking setup and numeric axes are authored choices.
exemplars: Mark Knight vs Mr Roy — Something About U
ATFC and Gene Farris — The Spirit of House

items.name: Organic house
items.lineage: International emotive house network represented by All Day I Dream, Lee Burridge, Lost Desert and Pippi Ciez. Understated pulse, detailed melodic textures and hand-played or hand-like percussion support gradual development; organic here describes an aesthetic that can use substantial synthesis.
items.description: Selected All Day I Dream organic-house strand: detailed melodic sequences and layered textures develop over an understated groove, with percussion that feels played rather than merely rigid. Burridge identifies emotion as the label’s core and describes the organic-house name as a later category for music initially spread across genres. Lost Desert describes hybrid analog/software production; Pippi Ciez documents synth sequences and hand-played electronic percussion. Organic therefore does not require an acoustic-only ensemble or an invented ethnic-instrument palette. The three chairs model synthesis, hand-like sampled rhythm and looped textures; they are catalog equivalents, not the exact equipment on Melt. Compared with tropical house, extended instrumental development replaces a radio-pop vocal/drop template; compared with melodic house, the selected seed gives softer rhythmic weight and more intimate texture. Gear, room and axes remain authored.
exemplars: Lee Burridge and Lost Desert — Melt (2019)

items.name: Speed house
items.lineage: Late-2010s and 2020s international rave-house strand developed around Haus of Panda, Speed House Movement and CHYL, joining bass-house sound design with speed-garage and hard-house energy. Rapid club pulse and compact, forceful bass-led sections define this selected recipe.
items.description: Speed house combines rapid house pulse with bass-house timbral movement and speed-garage/hard-house rave energy. Monstercat’s Haus of Panda biography identifies that hybrid explicitly, and CHYL’s biography documents fast, bass-heavy production; Ignite provides a credited collaborative release. This selected instrumental drop model uses a rigid layered drum grid, animated speech-like synthesized bass and short sampled cuts, commonly in the roughly 140–160 BPM zone. Tempo is a descriptive target rather than a parameter encoded by the 13-axis schema. Distinct from bass house through the rapid rave context, and from UK hard house through bass-music sound design rather than making Hoover stabs compulsory; speed garage retains its own swung garage rhythmic identity. Wavetable architecture, limiter and exact sample settings are authored defaults, not documented Ignite gear.
exemplars: CHYL and Haus of Panda feat. MYLK — Ignite (2023)

items.name: Deep disco house
items.lineage: Disco-informed deep-house intersection represented by COEO and the Toy Tonics network: sample-based funk, soul and disco material joins a rounded bass pocket and chordal accompaniment. This selected strand uses the deeper harmonic groove rather than requiring the heavy filter-sweep arrangement of the broad disco-house record.
items.description: Selected disco-flavoured deep house within the COEO/Toy Tonics network: disco and funk sampling meets soulful chord movement, rounded bass and an elastic house pocket. The label describes COEO’s sample-based funk and its connection to deep-house charts, French touch and early Masters at Work; the artist’s Back In The Days release supplies repertoire and Munich practice context. This is an overlapping stylistic intersection rather than a separate birthplace claim. The broad disco-house record models filter sweeps, audible disco loops and strong pumping as the arrangement engine; this seed instead foregrounds bass pocket, chordal accompaniment and less forceful parallel dynamics. Unlike soulful deep house it need not put a sung gospel/soul lead at the front. Editable bass and Rhodes chairs reconstruct supported timbral roles without asserting live players on the exemplar; exact drum circuitry, parts and axes are authored.

items.name: Experimental hip hop
items.lineage: Hip-hop organized around experimentation with sound, form and performance rather than one compulsory lyric style. The Seattle Shabazz Palaces strand, represented by Black Up and Lese Majesty, anchors this selected electronic studio model: fragmented sample layers, changing electronic textures and a foreground MC. It is a broad practice designation, not a synonym for associative lyric writing or a requirement for industrial abrasion.
items.description: Experimental hip hop tests the genre’s production and formal assumptions, encompassing many incompatible sounds. Shabazz Palaces supplies this selected Seattle electronic strand: independent MC phrasing within a fragmented, layered production and suite-oriented repertoire. The sampler and sustained polysynth are an authored compact realization, not a complete personnel list for Black Up or Lese Majesty. Unlike abstract_hip_hop, associative lyrics are not the defining requirement; unlike alternative_hip_hop, the emphasis is active sonic and formal experiment rather than the entire alternative category. Unlike glitch_hop this retains a foreground MC and does not prescribe a fixed bass-music groove, while industrial_hip_hop makes abrasive noise a central requirement. Sample workflow, polyphonic hardware, octave doubling and effects are authored choices.

items.name: Industrial hip hop
items.lineage: Hip-hop intersecting industrial and noise practice through abrasive sound construction, processed found sound and beat-centered MC performance. clipping.’s Los Angeles CLPPNG strand anchors this model, particularly Work Work, whose musicians explain using field recordings of metal objects and broken cinder blocks in place of conventional drum samples. Industrial describes the sonic construction rather than a lyrical obligation or one mandatory rock backline.
items.description: Industrial hip hop gives abrasive noise, distorted processing and machine-like or found-sound percussion structural weight within rap. This selected clipping. model uses a foreground rapid MC with a sampler carrying metallic field-recording percussion and textural noise. Song Exploder’s Work Work breakdown documents the conversion of thermos taps, cinder blocks and a beer can into playable rhythmic material; the compact sampler chair represents this constructed accompaniment rather than an ordinary drum kit. It differs from abstract_hip_hop by its production criterion, from the broader experimental_hip_hop by requiring an abrasive industrial/noise emphasis, and from rap metal by not requiring guitar riffs or a rock drummer. Distortion, projection and multitrack response settings are creative approximations, not claims that every exemplar uses those exact effects.
exemplars: clipping. / Cocc Pistol Cree — Work Work (2014)

items.name: Trap soul
items.lineage: Mid-2010s intersection of trap-influenced programmed production and R&B song delivery. Bryson Tiller’s Louisville-linked T R A P S O U L (2015) anchors this selected model, alternating melodic singing and speech-derived rhythmic phrasing over spare bass-heavy accompaniment. The genre is a musical intersection rather than every rapper’s use of a melodic hook.
items.description: Trap soul combines R&B lead-song sensibility and hip-hop phrasing with trap-derived bass and programmed rhythm. RCA explicitly frames Bryson Tiller’s T R A P S O U L as hip-hop/R&B, and his early interview emphasizes a stripped-down solo debut. This selected sung passage uses a restrained, close crooning lead above a long 808-derived bass pulse and sustained electronic accompaniment, with the melodic lead carrying more weight than ornamental backing. It differs from dark_trap’s ominous baritone spoken-rap default and from the broader rnb default by the sparse trap-derived bass/rhythm emphasis. Neither soul in the label nor Tiller’s vocal training implies a choir or live soul rhythm section. Subtle correction, unison doubling, sine oscillator and plate reverb are authored options rather than a transcript of the original sessions.
exemplars: Bryson Tiller — T R A P S O U L (2015)

items.name: UK alternative hip hop
items.lineage: British alternative rap encompassing individual departures from dominant beat and persona conventions. Little Simz and Inflo’s GREY Area (2019) anchors this selected London strand, emphasizing a live-played rhythm section and a direct personal MC rather than requiring grime or drill programming. Other UK alternative hip-hop recordings can be sample-based or electronic.
items.description: UK alternative hip hop situates broad alternative rap within British artist networks, without treating national identity as an instrument or vocal timbre. This selected London model follows Little Simz’s GREY Area collaboration with Inflo: her firsthand interviews describe experimentation, session musicians and mostly live-played accompaniment, with her own engagement in guitar, bass and drums. A direct narrative MC over locked bass, clipped clean guitar and live kit is an authored small-band reduction of that practice, not a complete track credit list. It differs from the catalog’s alternative_hip_hop sample-collage default and from UK drill or grime by choosing live-band groove rather than making either beat grammar compulsory. It is not synonymous with all British hip-hop. Guitar, wood, strings, microphone and compression settings are authored studio choices.

items.name: Avant-garde black metal
items.lineage: Experimental black-metal practice represented by Norwegian Dødheimsgard, whose turn from raw black metal toward eclectic composition is documented by Peaceville. Black Medium Current (2023) extends the amplified core with reflective piano passages and contrasting atmospheres. This seed selects tremolo guitar and sustained piano against a rough solo vocal, modeling sectional contrast rather than the whole record’s changing ensemble.
items.description: Avant-garde black metal retains a black-metal lineage while treating arrangement, texture and form as open compositional problems. Dødheimsgard’s Black Medium Current supplies the selected reference for a heavy guitar-band frame interrupted by reflective piano and contrasting passages. Tremolo guitar, picked bass, sticks, sustained piano and a rough voice form a compact authored reduction. Unlike the broad avant_metal_classic record, this entry starts specifically from black-metal practice; unlike atmospheric_black_metal, discontinuity and sectional contrast take priority over a continuous immersive wash. Piano is supported by the release description; no additional chamber or folk ensemble is inferred. The digital recording model and material selections are authored choices.

items.name: Dissonant death metal
items.lineage: Death-metal strand prioritizing abrasive harmonic friction and fractured rhythmic composition, represented by Gorguts’ Obscura (1998) and Colored Sands (2013). Season of Mist’s release accounts document dissonant guitar writing and unconventional rhythm/harmony, plus the guitar-vocal, second-guitar, bass and drum roster. The available palm-muted technique pin is an authored riff-attack reduction, not a transcription of the extended guitar vocabulary.
items.description: Dissonant death metal makes unstable harmonic relationships and fractured riff organization central rather than treating complexity as an instrumental athletic display. Gorguts’ Obscura and Colored Sands anchor this selection. The default reduces the documented guitar, bass, drums and vocal personnel to one editable guitar chair with palm-muted attack, a defined bass pulse and close rough voice. Unlike technical_death_metal, this model gives harmonic friction and through-built structure priority over ornamented fretboard display or jazz-fusion virtuosity. Unlike cavernous_death_metal, close articulation and shifting structures lead rather than reverberant decay. The catalog cannot encode each dissonant chord shape; the technique, tuning and modern chain are authored approximations.

items.name: Cavernous death metal
items.lineage: Spatially dense death-metal production and composition aesthetic represented here by Finnish Krypts’ Cadaver Circulation (2019). Dark Descent describes reverberant atmosphere, unsettling chords and deep harsh vocals, and gives guitar, drums, bass/vocal and in-house recording credits. The selected down-tuned chordal model pairs heavy decay with slow weight while retaining the death-metal band frame.
items.description: Cavernous death metal foregrounds obscured depth, reverberant guitar mass and low harsh vocal weight within death-metal writing. Krypts’ Cadaver Circulation is the concrete reference: its label account explicitly combines reverb with unsettling chords and deep vocal sound, while Remnants of Expansion places blasting passages beside doom-weighted material. The authored band reduction selects low chordal guitar, saturated picked bass, stick percussion and a reverberant rough vocal. Unlike dissonant_death_metal, the priority is spatial decay and low-register mass rather than fractured attack; unlike generic doom, the source practice retains death-metal intensity and blast-capable passages. Neither throat-chanting technique nor precise studio hardware is inferred for the default.

items.name: Cosmic black metal
items.lineage: Cosmos-themed black-metal and electronic practice represented by anonymous Australian duo Mesarthim. Avantgarde explicitly tags the label cosmic black metal and describes their atmospheric-black-metal/trance fusion. Anthropic Bias / Departure supplies a concrete guitar, blast-beat and synthesizer account. The recipe models a synth-melodic black-metal passage rather than claiming astronomy itself specifies a musical technique.
items.description: Cosmic black metal combines a black-metal frame with expansive electronic space and cosmic conceptual imagery. This selected Mesarthim model follows the label’s documented atmospheric-black-metal and trance intersection: tremolo guitar and a driven kit support arpeggiated synthesis and a distant rough vocal. The synth chair is a reusable equivalent, and the drum chair does not assert live drumming by this studio duo. Unlike atmospheric_black_metal’s stock guitar/bass/drums model, electronically voiced melodic motion is central; unlike ambient_black_metal’s drone-and-sampler passage, this selection retains prominent pulse and moving synth figures. Cosmic imagery alone is not treated as evidence of instruments, tuning or a unique birthplace.

items.name: Folk black metal
items.lineage: Folk-inflected black-metal practice represented by Windir’s Sogn-centered repertoire. Season of Mist describes their black/heavy-metal music with old Norwegian folk elements and documents the four 1997-2003 albums and the shift to a full band on 1184. The compact authored seed carries folk-facing melodic continuity through guitar and voice rather than inferring a compulsory folk-instrument ensemble.
items.description: Folk black metal applies folk-derived melodic and narrative orientation inside a black-metal ensemble. Windir is the selected anchor: the label documents old Norwegian folk elements, regional Sogn identity and the full-band 1184 milestone. The default authors ringing tremolo melody, steady bass, sticks and a rough sung voice. It does not claim a collected traditional tune, ethnic vocal technique or compulsory accordion, pipes or bowed lyres. Unlike pagan_metal’s expansive folk-instrument and chorus roster, this is a compact black-metal band model; unlike atmospheric_black_metal, melodic and regional repertoire identity leads rather than a long diffuse soundfield. The Sogn marker describes this exemplar network, not the location of every folk-black-metal scene.

items.name: Georgian pop
items.lineage: Selected late-2000s Georgian television and international disco-pop crossover represented by Stephane & 3G and We Don't Wanna Put In (2009). This English-language commercial branch belongs to Georgia's pop scene alongside Georgian-language singles and ballads; it does not describe the country's polyphonic church, supra or regional folk repertoires.
items.description: Selected Georgian commercial disco-pop, anchored by the 2009 national-selection recording of Stephane & 3G. The seed authors clipped lead-and-answer singing, dance-stab keyboard, scratch guitar, slapped bass and a four-beat drum-kit pulse as a compact disco arrangement. These chairs and studio settings are reusable design choices rather than original-session credits. Distinct from Georgian polyphony and supra singing through tempered commercial song backing, an amplified rhythm section and studio vocal arrangement. The selected English-language crossover is one pop practice, not a summary of all Georgian-language music.
exemplars: Stephane & 3G — We Don't Wanna Put In (2009)

items.name: Kazakh pop
items.lineage: Selected 2015-onward Kazakh-language Q-pop associated with Ninety One and JUZ Entertainment, combining commercial vocal hooks and dance performance with rap and R&B influences. This youth-oriented branch is part of wider Kazakh popular music and is distinct from dombyra-led steppe song, aqyn recitation and other traditional repertoires.
items.description: Selected Kazakh-language Q-pop in the Ninety One/JUZ production lineage, documented as danceable commercial song combining catchy melody with rap, R&B and other popular idioms. The authored seed represents the sung group-hook side: nimble syllables, stacked thirds/fifths, short synth plucks, layered sample hits and sub-supported bass. Rap verses can be configured separately; a single voice card does not encode all members' roles. This is distinct from kazakh_traditional through commercial sectional songwriting and programmed production rather than a dombyra or qobyz ensemble. The studio, synth model and pitch-processing settings are authored designs, not band session credits.

items.name: Mongolian pop
items.lineage: Selected late-2010s Mongolian producer-led commercial singles associated with Uka and Ocean Grey, anchored by Do It (2018) and the contemporaneous Don't Stop release. This modern digital-pop branch is distinct from socialist-era zohioliin duu, urtyn duu and throat-singing repertoires; Mongolian language alone does not prescribe a vocal technique or instrumental ensemble.
items.description: Selected Mongolian digital single practice around Uka's Do It (2018), with Ocean Grey's production association documented through its concert announcement and artist press briefing. The seed is a deliberately compact dance-pop design: emphatic doubled lead, sub-register subtractive synth and rigid sampled kick/hits. These musical settings are authored rather than a transcription or exact credit list. Unlike zohioliin_duu, this record models contemporary producer-led singles instead of notated socialist-era authored song with long-song-derived pentatonic contour and folk/orchestral chairs. No urtyn-duu, epic, khoomei or overtone technique is inferred from nationality.

items.name: Uzbek pop
items.lineage: Selected 1990s Uzbek folk-and-commercial-pop crossover associated with Yulduz Usmanova's Blue Flame albums Jannona (1995) and Binafscha (1996). The label describes village-song material modernized through Western rock, pop and dance production with traditional instruments and electronics. This branch does not replace shashmaqam, regional oral repertoires or all contemporary Uzbek dance singles.
items.description: Selected Uzbek crossover pop around Yulduz Usmanova's mid-1990s Blue Flame albums. The label explicitly describes traditional song material combined with Western rock/pop/dance and electronic backing, with doira and a strong emotional lead. The seed keeps a doira layer against keyboard hooks, bass and kit as an authored band reduction; it omits the label's tambur because the registered Persian/Kurdish tanbur does not establish an Uzbek instrument model. Distinct from uzbek_traditional by commercial song sections and electronic/rhythm-section backing, without importing shashmaqam usul, awj or a named maqam vocal system. Contemporary digital tracking models a new production of this practice, not the original 1995 session.

items.name: Kyrgyz pop
items.lineage: Selected Kyrgyz-language urban commercial song represented by Mirbek Atabekov's Kechki Bishkek (2022), released through Infinity Music, and his contemporary digital-release/concert practice. This melodic popular-song branch is separate from Manas recitation, komuz kuu and mountain-nomad traditional ensembles; it does not summarize every Kyrgyz pop or dance recording.
items.description: Selected Kyrgyz urban melodic pop anchored by Mirbek Atabekov's Kechki Bishkek (2022), with the artist's official site and Infinity Music release metadata documenting a contemporary commercial song circuit. The authored default is a restrained pop-ballad reduction: smooth single lead, chordal piano, clean arpeggiated guitar, muted bass and a flexible sampled pulse. Sources establish artist, song and distribution context, not those exact instrumental or vocal settings. Distinct from kyrgyz_traditional through concise studio-song form and tempered chordal backing; no manaschy recitation, komuz gesture or throat technique is inherited. Bishkek anchors the artist/song circuit rather than all Kyrgyz musical life.

items.name: Belgian techno
items.lineage: Belgium-based techno production and club networks represented by Charlotte de Witte, Amelie Lens, Joyhauser and Marco Bailey. The selected branch follows de Witte’s documented stripped, slowly evolving construction from kick, bass, background texture and treated samples.
items.description: A regional techno discovery cluster spanning several generations of Belgian producers. The default emphasizes repetitive electronic percussion, a restrained low-frequency figure and slowly changing sampled textures rather than a melodic house chorus. Ghent and Brussels club activity documents one local network; this is broader than one producer or label and is not a claim that all Belgian techno uses the same tempo or gear.

items.name: Greek house
items.lineage: Greece’s house music scene spans deep, tech and vocal house through local clubs, producers and independent labels. Athens-centered networks connect dance-floor production with international DJ circulation.
items.description: Programmed percussion and repeating bass patterns support sampled hooks, spacious synth textures and occasional newly recorded vocals. Deep-house harmony and leaner tech-house grooves form overlapping strands of the regional repertoire.
exemplars: CJ Jeff featuring Georges Perin — Around

items.name: Classic house
items.lineage: A heritage-oriented house music field encompassing foundational producers and enduring club repertoires. Chicago and New York traditions connect drum-machine rhythms, disco-derived samples, soulful keyboard harmony and vocal hooks.
items.description: Programmed kicks and swinging percussion underpin sampled breaks, keyboard bass and electric-piano chords. Repeated hooks and extended rhythmic passages support dancing, with sampled fragments or full vocal performances entering the arrangement.

items.name: Ambient lo-fi
items.lineage: An online ambient scene combining quiet piano, sustained electronic textures and intimate, softened recording surfaces. Its contemporary repertoire ranges from repeating keyboard miniatures to slowly evolving soundscapes and environmental recordings.
items.description: Restrained piano figures and long synthesizer tones unfold in spacious, low-intensity arrangements. Gentle repetition and subtle timbral change take priority over a foreground beat; recorded environmental sounds and lo-fi coloration provide additional textures.

items.name: Ambient trance
items.lineage: The atmospheric listening side of trance, associated with the late-1990s onward psychill and ambient-electronic scene. Hypnotic sequences, resonant bass and extended melodic layers connect dance-music repetition with ambient space.
items.description: Lingering synthesizer pads and repeating bass figures support a subdued programmed pulse. Arrangements develop gradually, with less emphasis on peak-time builds and climaxes; the repertoire also includes passages with little or no percussion.
exemplars: Solar Fields — Until We Meet the Sky

items.name: Ambient worship
items.lineage: Contemporary Christian devotional music combining ambient soundscapes with reflective songs, hymns and instrumental meditation. Developed in independent worship and listening contexts, it supports private prayer as well as quieter moments within communal worship.
items.description: Intimate singing, gently resonant piano and sustained electronic layers alternate with spacious instrumental passages. Soft dynamics, restrained ornament and long reverberation emphasize contemplation rather than a driving congregational-band crescendo.
exemplars: Salt of the Sound — Beyond Here
Salt of the Sound — Lent, Vol. 3
Salt of the Sound & Khamir Music — words unspoken

items.name: Argentine ambient
items.lineage: Argentina’s contemporary ambient and electroacoustic scene connects home recording and local sound environments with international independent labels. Its varied practices include synthesizer composition, guitar textures, tape collage and field-recording loops.
items.description: Slowly evolving electronic tones, sparse guitar fragments and layered recorded sounds form intimate, loosely pulsed textures. Repetition, small imperfections and subtle changes in timbre are central; individual musicians draw on different combinations of acoustic and electronic material.

items.name: Australian ambient
items.lineage: Australia’s ambient and experimental sound scene includes electronic composition, environmental listening and electroacoustic work. Independent networks such as Brisbane’s ROOM40 connect local sound practices with international collaborations and releases.
items.description: Sustained electronic layers and transformed environmental recordings create slowly changing spatial textures. Irregular recorded events, subtle spectral motion and extended tones often replace an insistent beat, with approaches ranging from quiet detail to dense immersive sound.
exemplars: David Toop & Lawrence English — The Shell That Speaks the Sea (2023)

items.name: Deep ambient
items.lineage: An immersive ambient practice built around extended drones, slow harmonic movement and barely perceptible changes in texture. Electronic synthesis and sustained electroacoustic layers connect it closely with space ambient and other long-form listening music.
items.description: Broad synthesizer tones and looped guitar sustain merge into a continuous sound field. Sparse attacks, subdued dynamics and gradual timbral change foreground duration and depth rather than a regular beat or rapid melodic development.
exemplars: Steve Roach & Dirk Serries — Low Volume Music
Steve Roach — Nostalgia for the Future

items.name: Drone
items.lineage: Sustained-tone music organizes long durations through held pitches, overtones and slowly changing relationships between tones. It became central to experimental minimalism in the 1960s and extends across bowed strings, amplified instruments and electronic sound.
items.description: Continuous tones and subtle beating between pitches carry the musical form. Sustained bowing offers an acoustic realization, with just intonation bringing overtone relationships into focus; electronic and other instrumental traditions develop the same durational approach in different ways.

items.name: Drone psych
items.lineage: Psychedelic rock extends guitar sustain and noisy texture into long ensemble improvisation. Bardo Pond’s Philadelphia recordings support a twin-guitar, bass, drums, voice and flute practice; electronics are also documented. The catalog represents the guitar role with one guitar chair, not a claim that the documented band has only one guitarist.
items.description: A psychedelic ensemble practice in which sustained amplified guitar and dense noise coexist with open-ended collective playing. The chosen Bardo Pond model adds flute and voice to bass and drums, letting instrumental texture lead the vocal song. Specific pickup, drumhead, flute construction and effects settings are author choices, not documented band equipment.

items.name: Drone rock
items.lineage: A rock practice that builds extended passages from repetitive accompaniment and sustained guitar feedback. Spacemen 3’s live Geneva album is explicitly described as drone rock by its label; Sonic Boom’s firsthand notes describe sustained keys and feedback guitars. The modern recording chain and instrument build choices are representative, not a reconstruction of the 1989 stage rig.
items.description: Repeated bass/drum accompaniment and long amplified guitar tones support extended rock passages. The selected Spacemen 3 model foregrounds feedback and repetition while retaining a vocal chair. The default describes one reusable studio arrangement, not every track or the exact historical live equipment.
exemplars: Spacemen 3 — Live at the New Morning, Geneva, Switzerland, 18.05.1989

items.name: Experimental ambient
items.lineage: An exploratory branch of ambient music that treats acoustic resonance, recorded sound, noise and electronic transformation as compositional material. It connects atmospheric listening with electroacoustic montage and experimental studio practice.
items.description: Layered samples, granular textures and processed tones form shifting spaces without a compulsory beat. Dissonance, distortion and abrupt spectral changes can coexist with quiet or melodic passages, extending ambient music beyond uniformly smooth backgrounds.

items.name: Indian ambient
items.lineage: Ambient work combining Indian classical melodic instruments and contemporary electronic production also operates across the diaspora. The selected sitar-led branch follows Al Gromer Khan’s documented Vilayat Khani training and sitar/synth recordings. This grouping does not imply a single religion, an exclusively Indian production location or one compulsory raga. Performer-relative tuning avoids asserting measured interval ratios; construction and recording settings remain authored choices.
items.description: The selected palette places ornamented sitar melody against sustained synthesizer accompaniment. Sitar Secrets documents both straight raga pieces and electronic combinations, with tabla appearing on some tracks. This default represents a spacious, percussion-free branch, rather than prescribing the complete alap–jod–jhala–gat sequence or treating all Indian ambient music as traditional concert performance.
exemplars: Prem Joshua & Manish Vyas — Water Down the Ganges (2002)

items.name: J-ambient
items.lineage: Japanese ambient music spans the environmental music of the 1980s and later electronic and electroacoustic experimentation. Home-studio synthesis, restrained melodic patterns and attention to listening space connect its varied generations.
items.description: Soft electronic tones, repeating figures and carefully spaced recorded fragments form an understated soundscape. Harmonic FM synthesis supplies clear, bell-like colors; acoustic material and environmental sounds also enter the wider scene through sampling and collage.

items.name: Nordic ambient
items.lineage: Ambient music from the Nordic countries combines electronic composition, sampled environments and electroacoustic listening practices. Its regional networks include Norwegian artists such as Biosphere, whose work helped establish a widely heard synthesis-and-sampling approach.
items.description: Sustained synthesizer layers and repeating recorded fragments create immersive, slowly shifting spaces. Sparse events and restrained dynamics bring texture into focus, with acoustic contributions varying across artists and releases.

items.name: Organic ambient
items.lineage: An ambient approach in which interwoven sounds evolve through subtle variation, recording and electronic processing. Contemporary independent labels apply the term to both sample-and-synth work and music integrating acoustic instruments or environmental recordings.
items.description: Layered samples and sustained tones develop gradual changes in color and spatial depth. Uneven repetitions and small details lend the texture a living, shifting quality; acoustic sources may remain recognizable or dissolve into the surrounding electronic sound.

items.name: Polish ambient
items.lineage: Poland’s contemporary ambient scene encompasses electronic composition, field recording and processed acoustic ensembles. Independent musicians connect chamber-instrument timbres with experimental studio methods, alongside more purely electronic approaches.
items.description: Quiet electronic layers and transformed recordings surround sustained strings, plucked keyboard tones and wind lines. Sparse activity, resonance and gradual timbral change organize the texture, with instrumentation varying across the regional scene.

items.name: Pop ambient (Kompakt beat-free electronics)
items.lineage: The largely beat-free electronic idiom associated with Wolfgang Voigt’s Kompakt Pop Ambient compilations, launched in 2001. It develops pop’s harmonic immediacy into extended instrumental atmospheres rather than conventional vocal song arrangements.
items.description: Sampled harmonic material, soft synthesizer layers and piano tones unfold in slow, overlapping phrases. Loops and resolving drones provide continuity without a driving dance beat, emphasizing melody, warmth and spaciousness.

items.name: Ritual ambient
items.lineage: An experimental ambient field linking ceremonial imagery, incantatory voices and sustained sound. It encompasses electronic studio composition and ritual-centered performance, drawing on varied practices rather than one shared religious institution.
items.description: Unmetered vocal phrases and low, sustained electronic layers build an immersive ceremonial atmosphere. Repetition, reverberation and transformed recordings extend the voice; some branches also use percussion or other ritual instruments.

items.name: Warm drone
items.lineage: A texture-oriented branch of ambient drone emphasizing soft, enveloping sustained harmony. Guitar-based and electronic practices overlap, using long resonance and gradual change to create an intimate, slowly moving sound field.
items.description: Sustained guitar, quiet bass and synthesizer layers blend into continuous harmony. Soft attacks, overlapping decay and restrained intensity place resonance ahead of riffs or a driving beat, while small changes in tone provide movement.
exemplars: Leandro Fresco & Rafael Anton Irisarri — Una Presencia En La Brisa

items.name: World meditation
items.lineage: Cross-cultural instrumental music for meditative listening, developed through contemporary studio production and international acoustic influences. Flutes, bowed strings, drones and resonant percussion appear in varied combinations with electronic atmosphere.
items.description: Slow melodic gestures float above sustained tones and widely spaced resonances. Breath-rich flute, bowed string, plucked drone and singing-bowl colors blend with soft synthesis, emphasizing quiet dynamics and an unhurried flow.

items.name: Afro house angolano
items.lineage: Angolan house music developed through Luanda’s club and production networks, connecting electronic house rhythms with local semba and kuduro influences. Producers and independent labels helped circulate this regional dance sound internationally.
items.description: Programmed percussion and repeating bass figures support syncopated loops, sampled hooks and occasional sung contributions. Layered rhythmic accents and tightly cycling phrases give the tracks their dance-floor momentum.

items.name: Australian house
items.lineage: Australia’s house music scene connects local clubs, producers and touring DJ networks, including a prominent bass-driven Melbourne strand. Contemporary studio production joins programmed rhythms with synthesized hooks and edited vocals.
items.description: Chugging bass motifs, crisp electronic percussion and short vocal hooks drive tightly cycling arrangements. Sidechain movement, rhythmic variation and carefully spaced breaks keep the groove active across instrumental and vocal sections.
exemplars: Dom Dolla & Sonny Fodera — Moving Blind

items.name: Brazilian house
items.lineage: Brazilian house music encompasses melodic, vocal and groove-centered electronic production within the country’s club and independent-label networks. Synthesizers and programmed rhythms frequently meet influences from musicians working across dance music and pop.
items.description: Repeating house percussion supports melodic synth phrases, bass movement and clean guitar textures. Layered harmony and gradual filtering provide motion, with acoustic contributions and vocal material varying across the scene.

items.name: Brazilian tech house
items.lineage: Brazil’s tech-house scene joins local producers and DJs with international club and label circuits. Its groove-centered productions combine house rhythm with concise bass hooks and electronically shaped percussion.
items.description: Short programmed drums, repeating bass figures and sampled vocal hooks leave space within lean club arrangements. Offbeat accents, swing and changes in filtering or saturation provide momentum without crowding the central groove.
exemplars: Vivi Seixas & Keskem — Smoke and Sweat

items.name: Deep groove house
items.lineage: An international bass-and-hook house discovery cluster including Dom Dolla, James Hype, Tchami, Endor and Ferreck Dawn. The selected contemporary branch is grounded in Dom Dolla’s documented in-the-box production, tightly programmed drums and repitched self-recorded vocal hooks.
items.description: The label’s verified roster is oriented toward contemporary groove-driven club producers, so it is not interpreted literally as an extra-deep soul-jazz house category. This default centers a chugging synthetic bass motif and crisp drum programming, with a short manipulated vocal hook leaving room for rhythmic repetition. Longer instrumental passages can open into hook returns. It overlaps tech and bass-house practice without being equated with either whole umbrella.
exemplars: Dom Dolla & Sonny Fodera — Moving Blind

items.name: Progressive electro house
items.lineage: A melodic electronic dance field linking progressive festival house with electro-oriented production. Layered synthesizer hooks, forceful programmed rhythms and edited vocal material connect its diverse club and festival repertoire.
items.description: Clear repeating lead phrases and compact drum patterns establish the hook. Filter movement, arrangement breaks and returning bass or vocal motifs build contrast, balancing melodic development with the impact of electronic timbre.

items.name: Austrian drum and bass
items.lineage: Austria’s drum-and-bass scene grew through producers, promoters and clubs, with Vienna an important center. Its varied repertoire spans liquid, deep and dance-floor styles alongside detailed bass sound design.
items.description: Fast broken drum patterns, sharply shaped snares and evolving synthesized bass anchor layered arrangements. Modulation, filtering and contrasting textures create movement, while melodic passages and quieter breaks vary the intensity.

items.name: Dutch drum and bass
items.lineage: Dutch drum and bass developed through interconnected producer, label and club networks, including influential studios in Groningen. Detailed rhythm and bass production coexist with melodic, experimental and more restrained strands.
items.description: Edited drum hits and broken rhythms interact with changing synthetic bass textures. Layering, resampling and selective distortion give individual sounds definition; contrasting sections balance dense rhythmic activity with space.

items.name: Japanese techno
items.lineage: Japan-centered techno networks encompassing Ken Ishii, Takkyu Ishino, Wata Igarashi and DJ Nobu. This default selects the early-1990s Ishii branch, where compact FM and PCM keyboards and sampled percussion support melodic machine music influenced by Detroit techno.
items.description: Regional techno cluster spanning melodic, minimal, industrial and experimental artists. The selected arrangement uses articulate FM lead, piano-like PCM keyboard and layered sampled drum hits. It is a reduced reconstruction informed by Ishii’s account of Fading Sky; no acoustic Japanese folk instrument or compulsory 303/909 setup is inferred from nationality.

items.name: French techno
items.lineage: French techno developed through electronic producers and club networks working across sequenced dance music, electro and more forceful contemporary styles. Hands-on synthesis, sampling and studio editing connect its varied approaches.
items.description: Changing subtractive sequences and bright FM figures interlock with programmed drum samples. Repeated patterns develop through timbral manipulation, edited performances and shifts in density, with a strong electronic pulse supporting the arrangement.

items.name: Swedish techno
items.lineage: Swedish techno connects Stockholm production networks with international club and label circuits. Successive generations combine forceful grooves, hands-on synthesis and exploratory electronic textures.
items.description: Programmed drums and repeating synth sequences create a firm rhythmic center. Filter movement, sample manipulation and changes in density build sustained momentum across stripped passages and more intense sections.

items.name: Pop house
items.lineage: Pop house brings song-centered writing and prominent vocal hooks into house production. Collaborations between singers, songwriters and electronic producers connect club releases with mainstream pop circulation.
items.description: Sung verses and refrains sit over repeating house percussion and synthesized bass. Accessible melodies, concise hooks and changes in arrangement create contrast while retaining a steady dance pulse.
exemplars: MEDUZA featuring Goodboys — Piece of Your Heart

items.name: German tech house
items.lineage: A Germany-based tech-house production network represented in the discovery roster by Format:B, Marek Hemmann, Kaiserdisco, Daniel Steinberg and Monika Kruse. Format:B’s first-person description grounds the selected model in a house/techno mixture with funky percussion and rolling sub-bass.
items.description: The regional roster links multiple German club-production scenes rather than one national sound. This default favors a rolling low-frequency pattern, interlocking electronic percussion and short synthesizer punctuation, making rhythmic movement more prominent than an extended sung chorus. It represents the Format:B branch while leaving the roster’s more melodic or minimal approaches available as deliberate alternatives.

items.name: Turkish deep house
items.lineage: Turkish deep house connects producers and singers working across deep house, indie dance and electronic pop. Networks around Bursa and Istanbul link melodic club production with local and international vocal collaborations.
items.description: Sung hooks and edited vocal material meet steady programmed percussion, synthetic bass and spacious electronic textures. Melodic phrases and restrained harmonic movement provide warmth while breaks and returning grooves shape the arrangement.
exemplars: Mahmut Orhan featuring Sena Şener — Feel

items.name: Swedish tropical house
items.lineage: Swedish tropical house joins electronic producers and pop collaborators in a melodic dance-music field. Home-studio production, memorable sung hooks and international release networks connect its overlapping pop and club strands.
items.description: Light programmed percussion, rounded bass and bright, short synth phrases support clear vocal melodies. Open spacing and simple repeating hooks give the arrangement an easy, buoyant pulse.
exemplars: Mike Perry featuring Shy Martin — The Ocean

items.name: Swiss house
items.lineage: Swiss house encompasses a regional network of producers, DJs and collaborators working across melodic and vocal club music. Compilation releases and shared production projects connect its varied local scenes with international dance floors.
items.description: Programmed house percussion supports repeating electronic hooks, bass figures and melodic keyboard textures. Tracks range from instrumental grooves to vocal songs, using breaks and timbral changes to renew the rhythmic momentum.

items.name: Japanese house
items.lineage: Japanese house developed through local producer and club networks, including Tokyo’s Far East Recording circle. Sampling, digital keyboards and influences from house and hip-hop helped shape an enduring strand of the scene.
items.description: Reworked drum breaks and repeating sample fragments interlock with digital keyboard chords, stabs and pads. Warm harmonic layers and small rhythmic variations give loop-based arrangements an inviting, flowing groove.
exemplars: Soichi Terada — Sounds From The Far East

items.name: Russian witch house
items.lineage: A Russian witch-house discovery cluster whose roster includes IC3PEAK, CHVRN, Summer Of Haze and Fraunhofer Diffraction. The selected 2010s–2020 electronic branch is represented by IC3PEAK’s contrast between floating synthesizers, heavy 808-type beats and a lead voice moving between high singing and harsher delivery.
items.description: A dark electronic song-and-texture model centered on processed lead voice, sustained synthetic atmosphere and heavy drum-machine low end. The recipe selects the abrasive electronic branch documented around IC3PEAK’s TRRST era. It does not treat every later IC3PEAK recording as witch house: the duo’s later Coming Home explicitly moved toward guitar and live instruments. National scope does not imply one folk melody, religion or language requirement for all members.

items.name: Canadian house
items.lineage: Canadian house production with a selected Montréal deep-house branch represented by Fred Everything. His first-person accounts connect Québec City beginnings and Montréal record-shop/club networks to a hardware-rich workflow using sampled drums, analog synthesizers and keyboard harmony.
items.description: A geographically scoped house entry, with this default selecting Fred Everything’s warm, melodic studio branch. Sample-programmed percussion supports polyphonic synthesizer chords and short sampled figures; repetition and arrangement changes develop the groove. This does not prescribe a single Canadian national style or equate all Canadian house with festival electro-house. The selected instruments represent documented practices, while individual patch settings and material variants remain authored.

items.name: House argentino
items.lineage: Argentine house connects DJs, producers and labels across progressive, deep and other club-oriented styles. Buenos Aires networks and international collaborations helped establish a prominent melodic progressive strand.
items.description: Repeating percussion and bass support slowly evolving synth layers and sampled textures. Harmonic space, filtering and gradual changes in density develop long rhythmic passages and melodic transitions.

items.name: German house
items.lineage: German house spans interconnected clubs, labels and producers working across deep, soulful and more minimal dance music. Sampling and electronic rhythm coexist with sung songs and live keyboard or rhythm-section contributions.
items.description: Steady programmed percussion supports repeated bass figures and warm keyboard harmony. Vocal hooks, short instrumental phrases and shifts in arrangement renew the groove, with restrained passages opening into fuller textures.

items.name: Latin tech house
items.lineage: Latin tech house links producers and dance-floor networks across Spain, Latin America and international club circuits. Tech-house repetition meets expressive vocal material, rolling bass and varied approaches to percussion.
items.description: A close kick-and-bass connection anchors short drum accents and repeating sample hooks. Syncopation, timbral changes and breaks create movement within lean arrangements, ranging from synth-led grooves to denser percussion textures.

items.name: Nordic house
items.lineage: Nordic house connects northern European producers, songwriters and singers through melodic electronic dance-pop and house collaborations. Software-based production and cross-border partnerships link club releases with accessible vocal songs.
items.description: Clear synth figures and programmed percussion frame sung verses and refrains. Layered electronic harmony, memorable hooks and contrasting breaks support a bright, steady dance pulse.

items.name: UK house
items.lineage: UK house developed through British clubs, producers and labels, drawing on house, soul and overlapping garage traditions. Electronic experimentation and collaborations with singers connect club repetition with fully developed songs.
items.description: Swinging drum programming and short synth figures support rhythmic bass and foreground vocal hooks. Harmonic loops and changing percussion patterns sustain movement, while song sections and instrumental breaks provide contrast.

items.name: Romanian house
items.lineage: Romanian house connects producers and singers working across melodic club music and electronic pop. Internationally circulating releases brought distinctive instrumental hooks and accessible vocal songs into the regional dance-music scene.
items.description: Repeating electronic drums and synthetic bass support clear sung melodies and short answering instrumental phrases. Accordion-led hooks form one recognizable strand alongside synth-centered arrangements, with breaks and refrain returns shaping the pulse.
exemplars: Edward Maya featuring Vika Jigulina — Stereo Love

items.name: Dutch tech house
items.lineage: A Dutch groove-led house/tech-house discovery network including Chris Stussy, ANOTR, Joris Voorn and Franky Rizardo. Stussy’s first-person production account grounds the selected model in software drum-machine voices, pitched drum samples, analog-style synth emulations, filtered pads and bass sketches.
items.description: The regional entry joins minimal and classic-house influences with contemporary club production. Its chosen Stussy-informed model uses a compact kick-and-percussion loop, a short repeating bass pattern and a gently modulated synth layer. Filter/LFO movement and drum-sample treatment provide variation. Hardware names in his interview describe software sounds and emulations: he explicitly identifies his workflow as in-the-box, so no physical vintage-synth ownership is inferred.

items.name: British post-rock
items.lineage: A British post-rock network spanning Mogwai, Maybeshewill, Bark Psychosis and related groups. The selected Mogwai branch layers mostly instrumental guitar, bass, drums and synthesizer parts in arrangements developed from individual sketches.
items.description: This regional entry selects an electronic-textural guitar-band branch. Sustained guitar phrases open into reverberant washes while a live rhythm section and synthesizer retain melodic shape. The default is instrumental; vocals occur elsewhere in the roster. Compared with the global extended post-rock entry, it foregrounds the documented guitar/synth interaction rather than making bowed strings mandatory.

items.name: Canadian post-rock
items.lineage: Canadian post-rock connects experimental bands and independent recording networks, with Montréal an important center. Extended ensemble compositions combine amplified rock instruments, bowed strings and manipulated recorded sound.
items.description: Sustained guitar and violin layers open into forceful full-band passages. Bass and drums support changing rhythmic patterns, while drones, feedback and environmental recordings provide transitions and contrasting textures.
exemplars: Godspeed You! Black Emperor — Asunder, Sweet and Other Distress
Godspeed You! Black Emperor — Lift Your Skinny Fists Like Antennas to Heaven

items.name: Belgian stoner rock
items.lineage: Belgian stoner rock draws together heavy-riff bands working across blues rock, grunge and psychedelic influences. Local scenes and touring networks connect compact vocal songs with more extended and experimental approaches.
items.description: Fuzzed guitar riffs, weighty bass and live drums create a rough, grounded pulse. Strong vocal phrases and changes in riff density give shape to energetic songs and longer instrumental passages.

items.name: Canadian psychedelic rock
items.lineage: A Canadian psychedelic-rock network including Black Mountain, Elephant Stone, Pink Mountaintops and Tess Parks. The selected Black Mountain IV-era branch combines amplified riffs and live rhythm-section interaction with keyboard orchestration and vocal interplay.
items.description: The default keeps guitar and Mellotron as separate voices instead of treating psychedelic as a synonym for fuzz alone. A sustained keyboard layer changes the weight of the arrangement around bass/drums, guitar phrases and paired singing. This is a contemporary Canadian branch drawing on older sounds, not a claim that the whole national scene reproduces one 1960s studio or requires sitar.

items.name: Boston rock
items.lineage: Boston rock encompasses guitar bands shaped by the city’s venues, independent recordings and regional music networks. Its alternative-rock strand combines direct song forms with contrasting guitar colors and abrupt shifts in energy.
items.description: Interlocking rhythm and lead guitars surround a firm bass-and-drum foundation. Compact sung phrases, rough-edged overdrive and quieter passages create contrast, with instrumental hooks and dynamic changes carrying the songs.

items.name: British indie rock
items.lineage: A British-centered indie-rock discovery network including Bombay Bicycle Club, The Vaccines, Blossoms, Editors and The Cribs. This default selects Bombay Bicycle Club’s song-based combination of played guitars, bass and drums with chopped sample textures.
items.description: A hybrid guitar-band model puts a lead vocal above a live rhythm section and edited loops. It follows documented sampling and slice-editing practice rather than assuming indie means exclusively analog or low fidelity. The broader roster includes more stripped-back guitar bands and international associates. A sampled film-song texture does not justify adding unsourced Indian instruments to every arrangement.
exemplars: Bombay Bicycle Club — So Long, See You Tomorrow
Bombay Bicycle Club — My Big Day

items.name: British alternative rock
items.lineage: British alternative rock connects bands exploring varied approaches to amplified song, from direct guitar music to electronic-rock hybrids. Independent scenes and touring networks support contrasting vocal styles, rhythmic approaches and production methods.
items.description: Processed guitar riffs, bass and acoustic drums frame sung phrases and forceful changes in arrangement. Synth layers and expressive filtering extend the palette in electronic-facing branches, alternating dense unison figures with more open passages.
exemplars: Enter Shikari — A Kiss for the Whole World
Enter Shikari — (Pls) Set Me on Fire

items.name: Classic Canadian rock
items.lineage: A retrospective Canadian rock discovery label, represented here by Rush’s early-1980s guitar/bass/drums and synthesizer integration. The selected model draws on the band’s account of developing Tom Sawyer and the producer’s description of Moving Pictures sessions.
items.description: This heritage branch combines a compact amplified trio texture with a distinct synthesizer figure and lead singing. Instrumental sections can change rhythmic emphasis while retaining a recognizable song framework. It is a representative progressive-leaning branch of Canadian rock history, not a claim that all classic Canadian records use complex meters or keyboards.

items.name: Classic rock
items.lineage: A retrospective rock-repertoire label with a selected mid-1970s Boston studio-rock branch. Tom Scholz’s own recording account documents layered electric guitar, acoustic twelve-string contrast, bass, drums and Brad Delp’s vocal overdubs.
items.description: The default emphasizes the contrast between chiming octave-paired acoustic strings and sustained amplified guitar, with a full rhythm section and layered singing. This is one documented album-rock branch within the broader classic-rock umbrella; neither this instrumentation nor a particular decade is imposed on every record associated with the label.

items.name: Dance rock
items.lineage: Dance rock combines rock-band performance with dance-floor rhythm, connecting post-punk, funk, disco and electronic influences. Bands translate repeating rhythmic patterns into interlocking instrumental parts and direct vocal songs.
items.description: Short guitar figures and active bass lines interlock around a firm kick and crisp hi-hat pulse. Repeated hooks, lead-and-backing vocal exchanges and changing instrumental density sustain momentum without requiring rigid machine timing.

items.name: Comedy rock
items.lineage: Comedy rock brings humorous writing and theatrical performance into rock songcraft. Original comic songs, parody and exaggerated rock gestures appear in formats ranging from acoustic duos to amplified full bands.
items.description: Guitar-driven rhythms support sung exchanges, emphatic refrains and sharply timed pauses. Changes in delivery and arrangement heighten the humor, while riffs and melodic hooks retain the energy and familiarity of rock songs.

items.name: Brazilian indie rock
items.lineage: Brazilian indie rock connects independent bands across several cities, labels and touring networks. Guitar-centered songwriting meets psychedelic experimentation, collective improvisation and studio electronics within this varied scene.
items.description: Intertwined guitar figures and sung melodies develop over bass and drums. Fuzz, moving delays and occasional synth layers transform repeated phrases, while editing and changing ensemble density shape the finished songs.

items.name: Canadian rock
items.lineage: Canadian rock encompasses regional scenes and successive generations of guitar bands, from melodic songwriting to forceful hard rock. Studio production and live performance connect direct vocal hooks with a broad range of amplified sounds.
items.description: Prominent sung melodies ride over electric guitar riffs, bass and live drums. Heavy guitar tones and doubled vocals give weight to harder branches, with quieter passages and melodic instrumental figures providing contrast.

items.name: Czech pop rock
items.lineage: Czech pop rock connects song-oriented bands through local recording, touring and broadcast networks. Guitar-based arrangements and accessible vocal melodies coexist with horn-led and keyboard-rich approaches.
items.description: Clear sung phrases and repeated guitar patterns anchor a live bass-and-drum foundation. Acoustic strumming and separate saxophone, trumpet and trombone lines can add warmth and rhythmic emphasis around the refrain.

items.name: Danish alternative rock
items.lineage: Danish alternative rock connects bands working across melodic guitar music, heavier riffs and experimental or progressive arrangements. Keyboard textures and varied studio production extend the traditional amplified rhythm section.
items.description: Guitar riffs, bass and live drums support sung melodies and instrumental passages. Sustained Mellotron colors, fuzz, phasing and reverberation broaden the arrangement, while changes in density and form create contrast.
exemplars: Dizzy Mizz Lizzy — Forward in Reverse

items.name: Cinematic post-rock
items.lineage: Cinematic post-rock emphasizes evocative instrumental development within the wider post-rock field. Guitar ensembles, piano and electronic textures connect intimate melodic passages with expansive changes in scale and intensity.
items.description: Piano attacks and articulated guitar figures share the foreground above bass and drums. Sustained synth layers, delay and reverberation expand the sound, while contrasts in density and dynamics shape extended wordless arrangements.
exemplars: Explosions in the Sky — The Earth Is Not a Cold Dead Place

items.name: Colombian rock
items.lineage: A broad Colombian rock network containing Aterciopelados, Don Tetto, Diamante Eléctrico and many other projects. This default selects Aterciopelados’ Oye-era return to an arranged live-band approach, with singing, electric guitar, bass, acoustic drums and a separate rattle-percussion layer.
items.description: A melodic vocal line sits over guitar and bass figures while played drums and maracas give the rhythm two distinct attack textures. The selected percussion color comes from the album’s credited instrumental practice, not an assumption that Colombian rock always carries a folk instrument. Other tracks and eras use wind instruments, electronics or additional percussion; this is a compact arrangement model rather than an exhaustive album inventory.

items.name: Brazilian techno
items.lineage: Brazilian techno production network, represented here by the darker machine-driven strand of São Paulo producer Gui Boratto. His wider catalog also crosses house and song forms; this selected arrangement emphasizes repeating synthesizer figures and programmed percussion.
items.description: A regional techno category, broader than any one producer. The default foregrounds a repeating saturated synth figure, short gated articulation and straight programmed kick. These are authored choices for a darker instrumental branch, without prescribing Brazilian acoustic percussion or the clean-guitar house arrangement used by the neighboring Brazilian-house record.

items.name: Bubble trance
items.lineage: Bubble trance is a discovery label for buoyant melodic European rave and trance-adjacent repertoire. Repeating electronic hooks, simple low-note patterns and sampled drum sounds connect the field with dance records of the 1990s.
items.description: Bright, detuned synthesizer phrases repeat over offbeat bass and electronic percussion. Filtered loops, clear rhythmic spacing and returning hooks give the arrangement a springy, direct dance-floor character.
exemplars: Da Hool — Meet Her at the Loveparade

items.name: Italian techno
items.lineage: Italy-centered techno networks spanning several club generations. Enrico Sangiuliano’s Milan production practice supplies this compact synth-and-drum default; Marco Carola, another documented member of the scene, illustrates the photographic record.
items.description: The authored model sets a focused repeating lead against firm synthesized percussion. Timbre changes and short articulations supply movement while the arrangement leaves room around its hook. This selected contemporary studio branch is not a universal Italian gear list; melodic duos, harder acid acts and older club styles occupy the same geographic network.

items.name: Polish techno
items.lineage: Polish techno developed through local producers and independent electronic-music networks, linking club tracks with experimental studio practice. Synthesis, sampling and changing rhythmic textures form an important strand of this history.
items.description: Short synth figures and manipulated percussion samples create a pulsing foundation. Small shifts in timbre, sequencing and placement animate repeating patterns, with exploratory textures entering and receding around the beat.

items.name: Swiss techno
items.lineage: Swiss techno connects local and expatriate producers through international electronic-music networks. Club rhythm, experimental synthesis and dub-influenced production coexist with harder and more direct dance-floor styles.
items.description: Shifting synth layers and rearranged samples sustain a repeating pulse. Electric-piano figures, delay and reverberation add harmonic color and depth in spacious, groove-centered arrangements.

items.name: Norwegian techno
items.lineage: Norwegian techno developed through producer and label networks including an influential early Tromsø scene. Electronic dance rhythms, sampling and atmospheric synthesis connect this history with later harder and more varied club production.
items.description: Machine percussion and repeating sample layers support sustained synth tones. Gradual shifts in texture and rhythmic emphasis create spacious grooves, balancing melodic atmosphere with a clear electronic pulse.

items.name: Dutch trance
items.lineage: Dutch trance grew through producers, clubs, labels and international DJ networks associated with the Netherlands. Theme-led electronic composition and carefully shaped builds connect instrumental tracks with vocal collaborations.
items.description: Recurring synth melodies and arpeggios develop over bass and steady programmed percussion. Harmonic changes, phrase variation and contrasting breaks guide long builds and returning rhythmic peaks.

items.name: Destroy techno
items.lineage: Destroy techno is a discovery label connecting electro, techno and fidget-adjacent club repertoire. Its varied artists combine rhythmic experimentation, synthesis and sample-based production with playful melodic ideas.
items.description: Short synth figures, chopped rhythmic samples and driven electric-piano patterns create an animated groove. Irregular fills and changes in timbre interrupt repeated phrases while preserving a danceable pulse.

items.name: Spanish techno
items.lineage: Spanish techno connects producers, clubs and labels working across lean grooves, harder electronic rhythm and atmospheric sound design. Hardware and computer-based studio practice support the scene’s varied approaches.
items.description: Short low synth figures and dry kick-led percussion establish a compact rhythmic center. Small changes in phrasing, filtering and drum texture provide movement within extended repeating passages.

items.name: Danish techno
items.lineage: Danish techno spans melodic studio production and the harder Copenhagen underground. Modular synthesis, drum-machine rhythm and international label networks connect contrasting approaches within the scene.
items.description: Evolving synth phrases and articulated electronic percussion sustain a repeating pulse. Arpeggios, live timbral adjustment and spacious effects shape melodic passages, while changes in density create contrast.

items.name: Chilean techno
items.lineage: Chilean techno connects local and expatriate producers through transnational club and recording networks. Minimal rhythmic production, sampling and electronic experimentation form an influential strand alongside more expansive approaches.
items.description: Understated synth bass and small sample fragments interlock with finely articulated machine percussion. Repetition, space and evolving microdetail sustain the groove, with subtle changes in placement and texture replacing large melodic refrains.

items.name: Russian techno
items.lineage: Russian techno encompasses producers and label networks working across lean club grooves, noisier electronics and faster rhythmic styles. Hardware synthesis, computer sequencing and sampled percussion connect its varied production approaches.
items.description: Repeated low synth figures and sharply shaped drum hits create a hypnotic foundation. Spacious arrangement, small rhythmic variations and effects provide movement, while vocal or noisier layers enter in different branches of the scene.

items.name: Finnish techno
items.lineage: Finnish techno developed through electronic producers and independent networks, including the Turku and Sähkö milieu. Sparse machine rhythms and stark synthesized tones form a notable strand alongside melodic and more expansive club music.
items.description: Short electronic tones and sharply delimited percussion leave substantial space between gestures. Repetition, silence and small changes in timbre give the groove tension, with restrained layering making each sound distinct.

items.name: Experimental techno
items.lineage: Experimental techno reworks machine rhythm, electronic sound sources and the formal expectations of dance music. Hardware experimentation, sampling and noise-oriented production connect club structures with exploratory listening practices.
items.description: Fragmented sample patterns and synthetic transients alternate with gaps and changing textures. Irregular articulation, unexpected timbral shifts and manipulated repetition probe the boundary between a recognizable pulse and abstraction.

items.name: Arabic jazz
items.lineage: Arabic jazz brings Arab musical traditions into dialogue with jazz composition and improvisation. Transnational ensembles explore modal melody, ornament and responsive accompaniment through varied combinations of traditional and modern instruments.
items.description: Ornamented oud phrases converse with low reed lines and a flexible plucked-bass pulse. Space between gestures and changing phrase lengths support attentive ensemble interplay, with melody and improvisation guiding the flow.

items.name: Austrian jazz
items.lineage: Austria-connected jazz musicians working in international ensembles. Wolfgang Muthspiel’s Rising Grace quintet supplies this selected branch: electric guitar, trumpet and piano converse above acoustic bass and drums.
items.description: An authored lightly amplified quintet balances sustained guitar phrases, lyrical unmuted trumpet and responsive piano voicings. Bass and brushed/stick percussion support overlapping exchanges rather than a rigid sequence of solos. The acoustic-guitar side of the reference album remains optional; exact guitar construction, piano model and drum materials are authored choices.

items.name: Indie jazz
items.lineage: Indie jazz links jazz improvisation with independent rock, electronic rhythm and contemporary composition. Small ensembles often translate loop-like patterns and production ideas into acoustic instrumental interplay.
items.description: Repeated piano cells, plucked bass figures and sharply articulated drum patterns build propulsive grooves. Cyclic motifs develop through accent shifts, layering and dynamic contrast, combining the precision of electronic patterns with responsive ensemble playing.
exemplars: GoGo Penguin — A Humdrum Star (2018), acoustic core

items.name: Italian contemporary jazz
items.lineage: Italian contemporary jazz encompasses composition and improvisation across small ensembles, solo performance and larger projects. Modern jazz harmony interacts with diverse song traditions and exploratory approaches to form and instrumental colour.
items.description: Melodic ideas become material for variation, reharmonization and shifts of register. In the solo-piano strand, changing density and contrasting articulations connect reflective passages with more animated improvisation.
exemplars: Stefano Bollani — Piano Solo (2006), selected Impro miniatures

items.name: Italian jazz fusion
items.lineage: Italian jazz fusion brings jazz improvisation into contact with electric rock textures, progressive composition and groove-based rhythm. Guitar-led groups and other amplified ensembles combine instrumental interplay with rhythmically assertive arrangements.
items.description: Clean electric-guitar lines and tightly linked bass and drums move between composed figures and improvised exchanges. Syncopated accents, changes of meter and contrasting dynamics balance melodic clarity with rhythmic drive.
exemplars: Trio Bobo — core concert trio: Alessio Menconi, Faso and Christian Meyer

items.name: German jazz
