items.description: Evolving modular tones and sequenced gestures can unfold without a sung foreground. Changes in timbre, patch relationships and density give sparse electronic passages their internal movement.

items.name: Italian electronica
items.lineage: Italian electronica is represented by Clap! Clap! — selected Desert Stone field-recording and programmed core. One documented branch receives an authored present-day studio realization.
items.description: Clap! Clap!’s Liquid Portraits develops field-recording and sound-design composition. The selected Desert Stone core represents Crisci’s electronic assemblage, with no invented live instrumentalist. His label specifies Martha Da’ro’s vocal contribution on Moving On, which is excluded here. The numeric axes, exact gear, tuning and recording settings are authored choices.
exemplars: Clap! Clap! — selected Desert Stone field-recording and programmed core

items.name: Japanese edm
items.lineage: Japanese EDM encompasses producers and performers working across a range of electronic dance styles. Studio experimentation and local club experience contribute to both instrumental tracks and vocal collaborations.
items.description: Wavetable synthesis and manipulated samples can supply pads, plucked lines, rhythmic material and transformed vocal fragments. Layering and changes in sound design shape a dance-oriented arrangement.

items.name: Japanese electronic
items.lineage: Japanese electronic music encompasses production and performance practices connecting sampling, synthesis and instrumental ideas.
items.description: A sampler and electronic keyboard can build repeating rhythmic and melodic phrases into a live instrumental texture. Changes in layers and harmonic support allow compact electronic material to develop over time.
exemplars: Anchorsong — solo MPC and keyboard performance core

items.name: Japanese idm
items.lineage: Japanese IDM connects exploratory electronic composition with detailed rhythmic programming and sound design.
items.description: Everyday recordings can become melodic and percussive material through sampling, editing and layering. Small changes in texture and timing give instrumental patterns movement beyond a fixed dance groove.

items.name: Korean electronic
items.lineage: Korean electronic music includes independent producers, club communities and live electronic performance, with Seoul an important meeting point.
items.description: Hands-on sampling and beatmaking form one instrumental strand. Chopped phrases and layered percussion can create compact rhythmic pieces within a wider field of synthesis and dance music.

items.name: Dusseldorf electronic
items.lineage: Düsseldorf electronic music draws on a long history of electronic experimentation and independent production. Contemporary musicians continue to connect instrumental performance with new ways of generating and processing sound.
items.description: Piano and live sampling form one electro-acoustic strand: repeated notes and struck resonances can become layered rhythms and textures. The interaction between acoustic gestures and electronic reshaping gives instrumental passages their movement.

items.name: Finnish electro
items.lineage: Finnish electro includes playful keyboard-led instrumental groups alongside electronic production and club traditions.
items.description: Bright electronic keyboard lines and a live drum kit can produce a propulsive ensemble sound. Repeated melodies, syncopation and contrasting keyboard colours connect electronic timbres with band performance.

items.name: Finnish electronic
items.lineage: Finnish electronic is represented here by Fanu / FatGyver — Adventures In Imperfection instrumental sampling branch. This is one documented branch with an authored present-day studio realization.
items.description: Finnish electronic is represented by Janne Hatula’s FatGyver alias, explicitly linked by the artist’s label to Fanu. The Adventures In Imperfection release documents instrumental sample-based hip-hop built from records, breaks and film material; Helsinki is supported by the release and Ableton’s trainer profile. Exact model equipment, techniques, tuning, numeric axes and production chain are authored choices unless explicitly sourced.
exemplars: Fanu / FatGyver — Adventures In Imperfection instrumental sampling branch

items.name: German dance
items.lineage: German dance music encompasses club production and performance traditions shaped by house, techno and other electronic styles. Some contemporary ensembles reinterpret this repertoire with acoustic instruments.
items.description: A brass-and-percussion approach can place bright trumpet figures over low sousaphone support, bass-drum pulse and mallet patterns. Repeated phrases preserve the music’s dance structure while acoustic attack gives it a different texture.

items.name: Finnish edm
items.lineage: Finnish EDM includes producers working across trance, house and other electronic dance styles. Studio production and live performance connect local musicians with an international club and festival field.
items.description: An instrumental trance-oriented branch layers synthesizer arpeggios, sampled lead sounds and workstation textures over programmed percussion. Repetition and changes in density give extended phrases their momentum.

items.name: Experimental synth
items.lineage: Experimental synth music treats synthesis as a medium for exploring timbre, movement and musical form. Modular instruments have been important in live electronic improvisation and composition.
items.description: Sequences, evolving patches and interacting control signals can develop without a conventional song structure. Changes in tone, density and spatial impression provide continuity through an instrumental electronic performance.

items.name: Jordanian pop
items.lineage: Jordanian pop connects Arabic-language songwriting with contemporary band music and other popular styles. Independent groups have helped develop an urban pop-rock strand alongside more traditional vocal approaches.
items.description: Sung melodies and shared refrains can ride over electric guitar, bass and drums, with keyboards adding harmonic colour. Clean chordal playing and a steady band pulse support clear song structures.

items.name: K-pop girl group
items.lineage: K-pop girl groups developed within South Korea’s recording, training and performance industries, combining coordinated group identities with varied pop production.
items.description: Multiple singers share melodic hooks and contrasting vocal passages. A gentler band-oriented arrangement can use guitar, bass and keyboard, while other songs emphasize programmed dance rhythms, rap and layered studio vocals.

items.name: Karadeniz pop
items.lineage: Karadeniz pop connects Black Sea song traditions with contemporary popular-band arrangements. Regional languages, melodies and instrumental colours remain important within a changing performance culture.
items.description: A singing voice can combine with kemençe and tulum alongside electric guitar, bass and drums. Bowed melodic lines and bagpipe sonorities interact with rhythmic band accompaniment; accordion and other colours can broaden the texture.

items.name: Khasi pop
items.lineage: Khasi pop joins Khasi-language songwriting and regional musical identity with contemporary popular-music arrangements. Shillong’s independent musicians have developed both band-oriented and folk-fusion approaches.
items.description: A sung melody can sit over interlocking electric guitar and bass in a spare popular-song arrangement. Repeated hooks and local-language storytelling provide continuity as accompaniment moves between intimate and fuller textures.

items.name: Konkani pop
items.lineage: Konkani pop brings Konkani-language song into contemporary recording, film and live popular-music settings. Goan musicians have combined regional expression with rock and other international styles.
items.description: Direct vocal hooks and repeating guitar-and-bass figures can give songs a compact rock-oriented shape. Rhythmic riffs and accessible refrains support language, storytelling and crossover appeal.

items.name: Kosovan pop
items.lineage: Kosovan pop includes Albanian-language popular songwriting and a range of band, electronic and soul-influenced approaches. Local performers connect regional audiences with wider popular-music styles.
items.description: A lead singer can draw on clean electric guitar, bass, piano and drums for a warm band arrangement. Chordal support, recurring refrains and dynamic changes keep attention on melody and vocal expression.

items.name: Electro trash
items.lineage: Electro trash combines electronic dance energy with rough-edged synthesizer textures and confrontational pop performance.
items.description: A forceful sung lead and prominent synthesizer line create a compact, abrasive sound. Repetition and sudden changes in intensity can give electronic phrases the urgency of a live band.

items.name: Dutch experimental electronic
items.lineage: Dutch experimental electronic music includes exploratory synthesis, live electronic improvisation and approaches that connect sound design with club rhythm.
items.description: A modular system can generate rhythmic patterns, bass figures and evolving textures within one performance. Sequenced control signals and changing patch relationships let music develop through timbre and density.

items.name: Frankfurt electronic
items.lineage: Frankfurt electronic music connects the city’s dance-music history with independent electronic production, including quieter ambient and experimental strands.
items.description: A modular-synthesis approach can combine repeated figures with slowly changing tones. Sparse rhythmic movement and evolving layers give instrumental pieces continuity without requiring a vocal foreground.

items.name: Estonian electronic
items.lineage: Estonian electronic music includes independent production, experimental synthesis and electro-acoustic sound work. Musicians connect local practice with wider electronic-music institutions and communities.
items.description: Modular tones can interact with field recordings and sounds drawn from everyday objects. A textural approach reshapes recorded fragments and synthesized gestures into evolving instrumental patterns.

items.name: Electronica argentina
items.lineage: Electrónica argentina encompasses local and diaspora musicians working with electronic composition and performance. Song, dance rhythms and experimental production meet in varied instrumental and vocal settings.
items.description: A duo-oriented branch combines singing and electric bass with synthesizers, samples and machine percussion. Repeated patterns and layered electronic textures support the interaction between voices and low-register movement.

items.name: Electro dub
items.lineage: Electro dub brings synthesizer-led production and electronic performance into the echo-rich mixing practices of dub. It connects roots-derived rhythm with steppers and other bass-oriented styles.
items.description: A vocal lead can enter and leave a field of synthesizer figures, low-register phrases and repeated echoes. Delay and changes in mix density become part of the arrangement rather than merely a final recording effect.

items.name: Dutch edm
items.lineage: Dutch EDM connects producers and performers across house, progressive, big-room and other electronic dance styles. Instrumental club tracks and collaborations with singers are both important parts of the field.
items.description: Synthesizer lines and manipulated samples can form an instrumental production. Repeating hooks, layered textures and changes in energy shape the arrangement without requiring a live singer.

items.name: Electronica cristiana
items.lineage: Electrónica cristiana connects Christian songwriting and worship communities with electronic dance production. Its performers use contemporary club-derived sounds for faith-centered expression.
items.description: A sung lead moves over synthesizer chords, programmed kicks and changes in rhythmic intensity. Repeating hooks and dance-oriented drops can give devotional songs an energetic electronic shape.

items.name: Electronica chilena
items.lineage: Electrónica chilena includes Chilean electronic songwriting, independent production and dance-oriented performance. Musicians draw together sung pop and varied forms of synthesis.
items.description: A lead voice can move over digital synthesizer lines, monophonic electronic figures and programmed percussion. Layers and repeating hooks connect intimate vocal expression with a stronger dance pulse.

items.name: Georgian electronic
items.lineage: Georgian electronic music develops through local and international networks of producers, performers and collaborators. Acoustic and amplified instruments can meet synthesis, sampling and experimental studio techniques.
items.description: A vocal branch can combine guitar and bass with contrasting synthesizers, sample loops and electronic percussion. Layers may develop independently, allowing melodic detail and changing rhythmic density to share the foreground.

items.name: Electronica peruana
items.lineage: Electrónica peruana brings electronic production into contact with Peru’s varied musical practices. Afro-Peruvian percussion and singing form one important fusion branch within a broader contemporary field.
items.description: Voices, guitar, bass and organ can interact with samples and a varied percussion ensemble. Cajón, cajita and quijada contribute distinct attacks alongside congas, bongos and timbales, with loop production shaping the combined texture.

items.name: Electronica venezuela
items.lineage: Electrónica Venezuela connects Venezuelan and diaspora artists working with electronic composition, performance and song. Experimental collaborations extend the field across countries and artistic communities.
items.description: A vocal production can combine monophonic synthesis, machine percussion and manipulated recorded sound. Contrasts between the human voice, electronic tones and environmental textures shape a flexible arrangement.

items.name: EDM
items.lineage: Electronic dance music encompasses a broad family of club, festival and studio practices built around electronically produced rhythm and sound. Instrumental tracks coexist with song-oriented collaborations and crossover popular music.
items.description: One song-focused branch combines a lead voice with synthesis, workstation keyboard sounds and programmed sample-based drums. Repeating rhythmic foundations support melodic hooks and changes in texture and intensity.

items.name: German electronica
items.lineage: German electronica is represented by Schneider TM — Guitar Sounds electric-guitar improvisations. One documented branch receives an authored present-day studio realization.
items.description: Schneider TM explores processed electric guitar through spontaneous improvisation on Guitar Sounds, recorded in Berlin. This selects its instrumental guitar branch within German electronica. The numeric axes, exact gear, tuning and recording settings are authored choices.
exemplars: Schneider TM — Guitar Sounds electric-guitar improvisations

items.name: Indian edm
items.lineage: Indian EDM connects local producers and live electronic performers with international dance-music styles. Its independent scenes draw on house, acid, breakbeat and other programmed forms.
items.description: Repeating synthesizer phrases can provide melody, bass movement and rhythmic momentum in a compact live electronic approach. Layering and timbral changes shape the build and release of a dance-oriented performance.

items.name: Irish electronic
items.lineage: Irish electronic music includes independent production that connects instrumental composition with sampling, tape treatment and electronic sound design.
items.description: Piano motifs can interact with recorded fragments and environmental sounds in a quieter electronic arrangement. Repetition and changes in texture allow acoustic attacks to blend with processed layers.

items.name: Leipzig electronic
items.lineage: Leipzig electronic music includes independent producers who connect club rhythms with varied recorded and acoustic source material.
items.description: A sampler can reshape recorded sounds into contrasting rhythmic layers. Repetition, editing and changes in density transform small fragments into instrumental electronic arrangements.

items.name: Lithuanian electronic
items.lineage: Lithuanian electronic music includes independent production that moves between electronic rhythm, instrumental recording and experimental texture.
items.description: Electric guitar and bass can interact with sampled drums in an electronically reshaped arrangement. Sustained guitar resonance, grounded bass and edited percussion let acoustic attacks and processed sound coexist.

items.name: Hungarian edm
items.lineage: Hungarian EDM includes electronic producers and live acts that connect dance production with rock-band performance.
items.description: Lead singing, electric guitar and bass can meet live drums and sampled percussion. Strong riffs, contrasting drops and changes in rhythmic density join band energy with bass-music and dance influences.

items.name: Indonesian edm
items.lineage: Indonesian EDM connects local electronic producers with international club and festival networks, including contemporary house and bass-oriented styles.
items.description: Sampled phrases and programmed rhythmic material can anchor a dance arrangement. Repetition, pitch treatment and changes in layers turn compact hooks into larger builds and releases.

items.name: Indonesian electronic
items.lineage: Indonesian electronic music includes experimental producers and performers working between recorded sound, live instruments and digital manipulation.
items.description: Piano phrases can be overlaid on sampled sequences and altered in real time. The contrast between played notes and repeating recorded material gives instrumental pieces their changing density and momentum.

items.name: Keller synth
items.lineage: Keller synth connects underground synthesizer music with dark fantasy atmosphere, home recording and an intentionally intimate sound.
items.description: Sustained keyboard colours and simple melodic figures can frame whispered vocal fragments. Sparse layers and subdued changes in texture help create a closed, uncanny listening space.

items.name: Horror synth
items.lineage: Horror synth draws on the synthesizer language of suspense and horror soundtracks, often crossing into progressive and rock-influenced instrumental music.
items.description: Repeating synth melodies and sequences can combine with electric bass and live drums. Tension develops through recurring motifs, rising density and the contrast between electronic patterns and played rhythm.

items.name: Latvian electronic
items.lineage: Latvian electronic music includes independent producers who build compositions from their own recordings and everyday sonic surroundings.
items.description: Piano notes and sampled household or environmental sounds can become rhythmic and melodic building blocks. Editing, layering and repetition connect familiar acoustic material with a constructed electronic texture.

items.name: Lithuanian edm
items.lineage: Lithuanian EDM includes internationally circulating dance productions and local approaches to popular electronic music.
items.description: Reworked vocal recordings can become pitched hooks within sample-built dance arrangements. Repeating phrases and changes in rhythmic and textural weight give these tracks their club-oriented momentum.

items.name: Hamburg electronic
items.lineage: Hamburg electronic includes producers and live performers connected with the city’s electronic-music communities. House-derived rhythm and detailed sound design meet in varied studio and stage practices.
items.description: A compact hardware-oriented setup can combine sample sequencing, synthesized percussion and a pitched synthesizer. Small changes in pattern, timbre and layering create movement within a recurring groove.

items.name: Modular synth
items.lineage: Modular synthesizer music grows from electronic instruments whose components are connected into flexible signal and control networks. Concert improvisation and studio composition both use this open-ended approach.
items.description: Sequencers, modulation and changing patch connections generate evolving rhythms and timbres. Layers can build, interact and dissolve within a single instrumental performance, with the patch itself shaping musical form.

items.name: Organic electronic
items.lineage: Organic electronic music emphasizes the interaction of played instruments and electronic production rather than a strict separation between acoustic and synthetic sound.
items.description: Live drums and repeating synthesizer patterns can shape a fluid dance-oriented arrangement. Small variations in timing and touch work alongside sequenced repetition and changes in timbre.

items.name: Macedonian electronic
items.lineage: Macedonian electronic music connects independent local producers with wider experimental and dance-music networks. Ambient and exploratory synthesis form one strand.
items.description: A sparse modular patch can develop slowly through changing control signals and timbral detail. Instrumental textures suggest space and movement without requiring a conventional sung foreground.

items.name: Luxembourgian electronic
items.lineage: Luxembourgian electronic music includes collaborations that link electronic production with songwriting and played instruments. Folk-facing and experimental approaches sit alongside more dance-oriented work.
items.description: A lead singer and acoustic guitar can meet live drums and electronic keyboard colour. The contrast between strummed attacks, sustained accompaniment and rhythmic pulse allows an intimate song to open into a fuller electronic-band texture.

items.name: NZ electronic
items.lineage: New Zealand electronic music includes studio producers and live acts working across dance-oriented and exploratory styles. Local scenes connect with international performance and production networks.
items.description: A sample-based live branch combines layered playback with keyboard-workstation sequencing and pitched sounds. Repetition, timbral changes and live mixing allow a small electronic setup to sustain a developing arrangement.

items.name: Polish electronica
items.lineage: Polish electronica includes independent producers who connect electronic composition with local recorded traditions and international production techniques.
items.description: Samples from jazz and other recordings can be reorganized into rhythmic and harmonic layers. Editing and repetition create instrumental pieces whose acoustic colours remain audible inside an electronic construction.

items.name: Neo-synthpop
items.lineage: Neo-synthpop revisits synthesizer-led popular songwriting through newer independent bands and production approaches. Electronic patterns can coexist with the physical presence of a live rhythm section.
items.description: A sung lead and electric bass interact with repeating synthesizer figures. Strong hooks and changes in density give an electronic arrangement the directness of a compact pop band.

items.name: Munich electronic
items.lineage: Munich electronic music includes experimental producers and performers alongside the city’s wider dance-music culture. Modular synthesis offers one route into ambient and exploratory composition.
items.description: Layered electronic tones and sequenced gestures can evolve within a compact modular system. Changes in patch relationships and texture create movement without requiring a conventional sung foreground.

items.name: Russian synthpop
items.lineage: Russian synthpop connects synthesizer-led songwriting with independent electronic production and earlier popular-music influences.
items.description: A lead voice moves over sustained keyboard colours and repeating electronic figures. Clear melodic phrases and contrasting layers give songs an intimate or more expansive electronic setting.

items.name: Polish experimental electronic
items.lineage: Polish experimental electronic music explores sound design, sampling and performance beyond a single dance style. Producers and live acts develop personal relationships between rhythm, texture and electronic composition.
items.description: Samples and synthesized sounds can form an instrumental arrangement with shifting density and low-register emphasis. Live control of repetition and timbre allows composed material to remain responsive in performance.

items.name: Persian electronic
items.lineage: Persian electronic music includes Iranian and diaspora artists who work with synthesis, recorded sound and experimental production.
items.description: Field recordings and found sounds can be reshaped into glitched or detailed electronic textures. Editing and spatial arrangement turn recognizable fragments into new instrumental relationships.

items.name: Romanian electronic
items.lineage: Romanian electronic music includes club production and exploratory live projects that combine electronic and amplified instruments. Audiovisual performance provides one setting for these hybrid approaches.
items.description: Synthesizers and machine rhythms can interact with distorted guitar, with instruments such as theremin extending the palette in some groups. Repeated electronic patterns contrast with the attack and sustain of amplified strings.

items.name: Pakistani electronic
items.lineage: Pakistani electronic music includes DIY producers and collaborative communities, with Karachi’s independent networks supporting experimental approaches.
items.description: Small recorded fragments, beats and chord layers can be assembled into playful electronic pieces. Sampling and live manipulation create movement through repetition, interruption and shifts in texture.
exemplars: Rudoh — Tales of Scrap sampling core

items.name: Mexican electronic
items.lineage: Mexican electronic music includes independent producers working across club styles, electronica and ambient sound.
items.description: A sustained polyphonic-synthesizer approach can develop through slow changes in tone and harmony. Layers and repeated gestures create instrumental continuity without needing a sung foreground.

items.name: Scottish electronic
items.lineage: Scottish electronic music connects club traditions with independent ambient and experimental production.
items.description: An evolving modular patch can combine granular textures, changing tones and irregular rhythmic movement. Random and sequenced controls introduce variation within an instrumental electronic soundscape.

items.name: Russian electronic
items.lineage: Russian electronic music includes independent synthesis, club production and electronic songwriting, with artists moving between instrumental and vocal approaches.
items.description: A sung lead can meet repeating analog-synthesizer figures and changing keyboard layers. Melodic hooks and sequenced repetition connect personal vocal expression with electronic texture.

items.name: Polish synthpop
items.lineage: Polish synthpop combines electronic songwriting with the energy of independent pop and live performance.
items.description: A lead voice and synthesizer sequences can ride a played drum groove. Repeated hooks, contrasting keyboard colours and shifts between spare and fuller passages organize the songs.

items.name: Russian experimental electronic
items.lineage: Russian experimental electronic music connects artists working across sound design, composition and live electronic performance. Local and diaspora practice includes interdisciplinary work and varied approaches to rhythm and texture.
items.description: Monophonic synthesizers, samplers and electronic percussion can form a compact performance system. Routing, pattern changes and timbral development let the musician reshape a composition in real time.

items.name: Nu electro
items.lineage: Nu electro renewed electro’s machine rhythms and synthesizer vocabulary through late-twentieth-century and newer electronic production.
items.description: Keyboard layers and synthesized drum patterns form a compact instrumental arrangement. Repeating motifs, electronic bass movement and changes in texture give a programmed groove its shape.

items.name: Pinoy EDM
items.lineage: Pinoy EDM connects Filipino producers and performers with contemporary electronic dance styles and international club networks.
items.description: Arpeggiated digital-synthesizer figures can supply a melodic dance-oriented texture. Repeated hooks and changes in density build momentum within a wider field that also includes vocal and percussion-focused production.

items.name: Russian dance
items.lineage: Russian dance music combines electronic club production with popular-song influences and recurring references to earlier dance styles.
items.description: Digital synthesizer figures can repeat and develop through changes in tone and layering. Modern production gives familiar melodic ideas a stronger club pulse, alongside other vocal and instrumental approaches.

items.name: Russian EDM
items.lineage: Russian EDM includes internationally circulating producers working with layered electronic dance arrangements and popular vocal hooks.
items.description: Digital-synthesizer lines and workstation sounds can support a lead vocal in a melodic dance arrangement. Repeated motifs, changing density and contrasting sections connect the hook with larger builds and releases.

items.name: Magyar retro dance
items.lineage: Magyar retro dance revisits established Hungarian electronic-pop and dance repertoire through recordings, nostalgic programming and newer live interpretations.
items.description: Shared singing can meet synthesizer figures, electric guitar and played drums. Familiar hooks and a regular dance pulse retain the songs’ identity while live instrumental colour gives them a fresh setting.

items.name: Mexican EDM
items.lineage: Mexican EDM includes producers and live electronic performers working across club and festival styles.
items.description: Sample-triggered percussion and live finger-drumming can add an immediate rhythmic layer to electronic dance music. One-shot sounds and repeated patterns give this performance strand its momentum within a broader range of melodic and vocal productions.

items.name: Serbian electronic
items.lineage: Serbian electronic music includes synthesizer-led songwriting as well as instrumental and club-oriented production. Independent projects connect local voices with a wider electronic-pop vocabulary.
items.description: Sung melodies can ride repeating synthesizer patterns and drum-machine rhythms. Guitar and other played textures may join the electronic foundation, alongside more purely instrumental approaches.

items.name: Singaporean electronic
items.lineage: Singaporean electronic music connects local and diaspora producers with live electronic performance and international dance production. Solo performers can combine instrumental control with their own singing.
items.description: Synthesizer patterns, programmed drums and processed vocals build flexible live or studio arrangements. Repeated figures and changes in vocal treatment move between song-focused and dance-oriented textures.

items.name: Slovak electronic
items.lineage: Slovak electronic music includes a synth-pop strand established by local groups in the late twentieth century, alongside newer production approaches. Bratislava bands such as Monte Rosa developed songs around synthesizers and rhythm machines.
items.description: Voices interact with repeating keyboard figures and programmed percussion. Shared singing and contrasting electronic layers can give compact arrangements the presence of a band.

items.name: Slovenian electronic
items.lineage: Slovenian electronic music includes local and cross-border collaborations working with synthesis, machine rhythms and electronic songwriting. Slovene-language synthwave forms one part of this wider field.
items.description: Vocoder-treated singing can combine with repeating subtractive-synthesizer figures and drum-machine patterns. The contrast between recognizable song phrasing and transformed vocal colour gives this branch its character.

items.name: South african electronic
items.lineage: South African electronic music encompasses dance production and electronic songwriting shaped by local artists and collaborative networks. Vocal house is one strand within a much broader national electronic field.
items.description: Lead and supporting voices can unfold over sustained synthesizer chords and programmed percussion. Cyclic grooves support melodic exchange, with changes in density and texture developing the arrangement.

items.name: Spanish electronic
items.lineage: Spanish electronic music includes independent songwriters and producers working between electronic texture, ambient sound and popular-song forms.
items.description: A melodic voice can emerge from sustained synthesizer layers and slowly changing harmonic colour. Sparse electronic arrangements coexist with more rhythmic and band-oriented production across the scene.

items.name: Spanish synthpop
items.lineage: Spanish synthpop places electronic keyboards at the centre of popular songwriting, connecting independent production with the broader history of synthesizer-based pop.
items.description: Vocal hooks and layered keyboard colours shape the songs. Sustained chords, recurring figures and changes between spare and fuller textures allow electronic sound to carry both rhythm and atmosphere.

items.name: Swedish electronic
items.lineage: Swedish electronic music includes producers and bands that connect electronic rhythm with distinctive vocal songwriting and played instruments.
items.description: A lead voice can interact with synthesizer lines and programmed drum patterns. Live rhythm-section and keyboard colours also enter the field, giving electronic arrangements different degrees of band-like touch.

items.name: Swedish synthpop
items.lineage: Swedish synthpop connects electronic songwriting with local independent bands and a wider synthesizer-pop tradition.
items.description: Layered synthesizer chords and repeating figures support melodic singing. Lead and supporting voices can broaden the arrangement, while changes in electronic texture carry the songs between spare and fuller passages.

items.name: Synth funk
items.lineage: Synth funk places electronic keyboards and drum-machine grooves at the centre of funk, extending the sound of boogie and electronic soul.
items.description: Played synthesizer lines and sustained chords move against a repeating electronic beat. Syncopated phrasing and small changes in keyboard touch keep the groove flexible; instrumental tracks and vocal songs both belong to the style.

items.name: Synth prog
items.lineage: Synth prog combines prominent synthesizer writing with progressive rock’s instrumental development and ensemble interplay.
items.description: Recurring keyboard patterns interact with electric guitar, bass and drums. Layered tones, changing sections and contrasts in rhythmic weight allow electronic repetition and played rock energy to develop together.

items.name: Synthwave brasileiro
items.lineage: Brazilian synthwave connects local electronic-pop and band scenes with the retro keyboard colours of synthwave and retrowave.
items.description: Singing and sustained synthesizer layers can unfold over guitar, bass and drums. The live-band strand joins melodic hooks and electronic atmosphere, alongside more fully programmed approaches.

items.name: Taiwan electronic
items.lineage: Taiwanese electronic music includes club production, experimental performance and sound practices that draw on local environments and voices.
items.description: Sampled noise, improvised electronic textures and whispered speech form one experimental branch. Fragmented sounds and changing layers can carry an arrangement without a conventional sung melody or fixed harmonic progression.

items.name: Tijuana electronic
items.lineage: Tijuana electronic music connects border-city experimentation with synthesizers, machine rhythms and collaborative electronic songwriting.
items.description: Sustained keyboard layers and programmed percussion can frame a vocal melody. Repetition and changing electronic colour give compact arrangements room for both song and more exploratory textures.

items.name: Turkish edm
items.lineage: Turkish EDM connects producers and vocal collaborators with house, indie-dance and the wider international club circuit.
items.description: Melodic synthesizer figures, electronic drum patterns and vocal hooks build dance-oriented arrangements. Repeated rhythmic foundations leave space for expressive melodic phrasing and changes in texture.

items.name: Turkish electronic
items.lineage: Turkish electronic music includes synthesizer-based songs, independent bands and instrumental production. Local synth-pop groups connect electronic colour with popular songwriting.
items.description: A sung lead can interact with repeating synthesizer figures and shifting harmonic layers. Guitar and rhythm-section playing also enter the scene, alongside compact voice-and-synthesizer arrangements.

items.name: Uk experimental electronic
items.lineage: UK experimental electronic music includes artists exploring synthesis, sampling and unconventional composition or performance systems. Individual projects develop different relationships between sound design, rhythm and musical form.
items.description: A monophonic synthesizer and sample-based tracker can form a compact production setup. Sequencing, editing and changes in timbre allow a small set of tools to generate varied instrumental textures.

items.name: Ukrainian electronic
items.lineage: Ukrainian electronic music encompasses dance production and experimental composition, including encounters between electronic synthesis and vocal traditions.
items.description: Modular patterns and evolving electronic textures can interact with a solo voice. This exploratory branch lets the singer and electronic layers shape an unfolding listening space rather than requiring a fixed dance beat.

items.name: Vintage french electronic
items.lineage: Vintage French electronic music brings together early synthesizer composition, studio experimentation and electronic popular music from the later twentieth century.
items.description: Melodic synthesizer lines and repeating electronic figures shape compact instrumental pieces. Layering and tape-loop practices can extend the keyboard palette, from exploratory listening music to more rhythm-oriented approaches.

items.name: Argentine jazz
items.lineage: Argentine jazz connects jazz improvisation with local musical life and regional rhythmic traditions, including milonga, chacarera and candombe.
items.description: Piano, plucked double bass and drums offer a flexible small-group foundation. Harmonic interplay and improvised melodic development can meet Argentine and wider Latin American rhythmic inflections.

items.name: Chinese jazz
items.lineage: Chinese jazz includes instrumental and vocal musicians working across local and international jazz communities. Contemporary approaches connect personal composition and cultural references with jazz ensemble playing.
items.description: A singing voice can interact with guitar, piano, double bass and drums. Instrumental solos, flexible accompaniment and contrasting ensemble colours support the melodic foreground; horns and strings can expand the palette.

items.lineage: Appenzeller folk music connects instrumental and vocal traditions of the Appenzell region. Dance melodies, local ensemble playing and solo instrumental performances sustain a varied repertoire.
items.description: The hackbrett can carry a melody through struck string courses and resonant accompaniment. Solo playing offers one branch alongside ensembles and regional singing practices.

items.name: Synthetic classical
items.lineage: Synthetic classical music realizes composed concert repertoire through electronic sound generation. Keyboard performance, synthesis and layered production can reinterpret instrumental lines and musical forms.
items.description: A modular synthesizer can give separate melodic and harmonic parts contrasting timbres. Controlled keyboard phrasing and layered recording bring composed textures together without requiring an acoustic orchestra.

items.name: Arab folk
items.lineage: Arab folk encompasses regional song, instrumental and dance traditions across diverse communities. Contemporary collaborations can connect these practices with other acoustic and popular musical approaches.
items.description: An oud and acoustic guitar can exchange melodic phrases and plucked accompaniment in one cross-cultural instrumental branch. Singing, percussion and other regional instruments offer additional settings across the wider field.

items.name: Austin americana

items.description: Stevens’s own account documents his Austin base and solo touring with acoustic guitars and harmonicas; his release page explicitly identifies him as an Austin Americana artist. Exact studio and performance settings are authored modern choices.

items.name: Austin singer-songwriter
items.lineage: Austin singer-songwriters place individual songwriting within a varied local performance community. Personal stories and close attention to language meet folk, country and other popular influences.
items.description: Singing and acoustic guitar provide an intimate foundation, with a second voice adding harmony in one representative branch. Fuller arrangements offer other ways to develop the songs.

items.name: Algerian folk
items.lineage: Algerian folk encompasses diverse regional song and instrumental traditions alongside contemporary acoustic songwriting. Musicians connect local languages and melodic references with changing performance contexts.
items.description: A singing voice and guitar offer one intimate contemporary branch. Melodic phrasing and text lead the arrangement, while other traditions use broader vocal and instrumental ensembles.

items.name: Bahamian folk
items.lineage: Bahamian folk includes varied song, instrumental and community music traditions. Guitar-centred performances form one distinctive strand alongside other vocal and ensemble practices.
items.description: Fingerpicked guitar can combine bass figures, chords and an independent melody, with sung phrases entering around the instrumental lines. The interaction between voice and guitar gives this branch its conversational character.

items.name: Alternative metalcore
items.lineage: Alternative metalcore connects heavy guitar-band music with alternative and nu-metal approaches. Rhythmic riffs and contrasting vocal textures shape a field that overlaps broader modern heavy music.
items.description: Distorted guitars, bass and drums build a dense rhythmic foundation beneath a vocal lead. Muted guitar attacks and emphatic band accents can contrast with more open melodic passages.

items.name: Classical saxophone quartet
items.lineage: Classical saxophone quartets develop chamber repertoire through original works and arrangements. Soprano, alto, tenor and baritone saxophones provide four contrasting but closely related registers.
items.description: The four voices can blend into sustained harmony or exchange independent melodic lines. Shared phrasing, articulation and dynamic balance shape the relationship between solo detail and ensemble sound.

items.name: Kosovan folk
items.lineage: Kosovan folk music includes regional vocal, instrumental and dance practices. Traditional melodies continue through community performance and contemporary collaborations.
items.description: A solo kaval offers an intimate wind-instrument branch, shaping a melody through breath and ornament. Other settings bring singing, additional instruments and different ensemble textures.

items.name: Swiss country
items.lineage: Swiss country connects local performers and audiences with country songwriting and performance traditions. Traditional and newer approaches appear in concerts, recordings and festival settings.
items.description: Lead and harmony singing can combine with acoustic and electric guitars, bass, drums and fiddle. Rhythmic accompaniment and melodic fills give a full band room to balance direct songs with instrumental colour.

items.name: Swiss folk
items.lineage: Swiss folk includes varied regional instrumental and vocal traditions maintained through community performance, teaching and festivals. Contemporary musicians also develop new arrangements and solo approaches.
items.description: Solo hackbrett can carry melody and accompaniment through struck string courses and ringing resonance. Ensembles and regional singing practices offer other textures within the wider folk field.

items.name: Afrikaans gospel
items.lineage: Afrikaans gospel centres Christian devotional music in the Afrikaans language. Song ministry, worship and recorded repertoire connect personal expression with shared religious practice.
items.description: A singing voice and acoustic guitar offer an intimate setting for melody and devotional text. Choral, keyboard-led and fuller band arrangements provide other branches of the broader repertoire.

items.name: Australian blues
items.lineage: Australian blues develops through local performers and touring communities interpreting acoustic and amplified blues traditions. Songwriting and instrumental personality connect the field with wider blues practice.
items.description: Singing and fingerpicked acoustic guitar offer an intimate branch, with alternating bass figures and melodic responses around the vocal line. Electric bands and other guitar approaches broaden the palette.

items.name: Argentine reggae
items.lineage: Argentine reggae connects local songwriting and performance communities with Jamaican roots and subsequent reggae traditions. Spanish-language songs and band arrangements sustain a varied national scene.
items.description: Voice, clean guitar, keyboards, bass and drums build an offbeat rhythmic foundation. Saxophone and trumpet can add melodic responses and coordinated accents, while dub versions open space around the rhythm section.

items.name: Australian reggae fusion
items.lineage: Australian reggae fusion brings reggae rhythms into contact with roots, rock and other popular styles. Local bands develop varied combinations of singing, groove and instrumental colour.
items.description: Lead and supporting voices can sit above clean guitar, bass, keyboards and drums, with saxophone adding melodic detail. The band can shift between relaxed offbeat accompaniment and more emphatic rock-derived passages.

items.name: Australian ska
items.lineage: Australian ska includes bands drawing on Jamaican ska and later revival traditions. Local club and festival communities combine dance rhythms, song and prominent brass and reed sections.
items.description: Offbeat guitar and keyboard chords meet mobile bass lines and drums. Lead and supporting voices alternate with saxophone, trumpet and trombone figures, giving the ensemble a lively call-and-response character.

items.name: Brazilian ska
items.lineage: Brazilian ska connects local musicians with ska and reggae traditions through vocal bands and instrumental ensembles. Horn arrangements and rhythmic interplay are important parts of its varied sound.
items.description: An instrumental band can combine guitar, bass, keyboards and drums with saxophone, trumpet, trombone and flute. Offbeat accompaniment supports contrasting melodic lines and coordinated horn accents.

items.name: Chinese reggae
items.lineage: Chinese reggae brings reggae rhythms into contact with local languages, songwriting and regional musical references. Contemporary bands connect community performance with a wider international reggae network.
items.description: Singing, guitar, keyboards, bass and drums provide a flexible rhythmic core. Wind instruments, guest voices and other local colours can extend the ensemble without defining a single fixed arrangement.

items.name: Czsk reggae
items.lineage: Czech and Slovak reggae connects local song and performance communities with roots reggae, dub and related styles. Live ensembles and studio production contribute to this shared regional field.
items.description: Singing and backing voices can combine with guitar, bass, keyboards and drums, with saxophone and trumpet supplying melodic accents. Loops and sampled material can add a further production layer alongside the live band.

items.name: East coast reggae
items.lineage: East Coast reggae connects performers along the eastern United States with roots reggae, dub and other reggae-derived approaches. Local songwriting and live-band communities give the field varied regional voices.
items.description: Singing sits above clean guitar, keyboards, bass and drums. Offbeat chordal accompaniment and a prominent bass line support the song, while guest instruments and production effects can broaden an arrangement.

items.name: Euskal reggae
items.lineage: Euskal reggae connects Basque language and cultural life with Jamaican reggae traditions. Local bands develop songs through the interaction of regional identity and an international rhythmic vocabulary.
items.description: Singing, clean guitar and a prominent bass line meet drums, piano and organ. Trumpet and trombone can answer the vocal melody, with additional percussion and other colours appearing in wider arrangements.

items.name: Experimental dub
items.lineage: Experimental dub extends dub mixing and rhythmic space into exploratory electronic composition. Synthesized sound, repetition and effects can become as important as a conventional song structure.
items.description: Subtractive and FM synthesis can combine with electronically generated percussion. Short tonal gestures, layered timbres and echo create changing depth around a recurring rhythmic foundation.

items.name: Finnish reggae
items.lineage: Finnish reggae develops through local bands and communities engaging with roots reggae, early reggae and ska. These connected approaches support both original songs and reinterpretations of earlier styles.
items.description: Lead and supporting voices can sit above guitar, keyboards, bass and drums, with trombone adding contrasting phrases. Offbeat accompaniment and an active bass line keep the arrangement grounded.

items.name: French dub
items.lineage: French dub connects live-band reggae foundations with electronic and studio experimentation. Collaborations and soundsystem performance sustain a field in which mixing and instrumental interplay share the foreground.
items.description: Bass, drums and guitar can combine with organ, electric piano and synthesizer. Voice, saxophone and flute introduce contrasting melodic colours, while echo and changes in density reshape the ensemble.

items.name: French reggae
items.lineage: French reggae brings local song and performance communities into dialogue with Jamaican reggae traditions. Roots-oriented bands, vocal collaborations and studio versions form overlapping branches.
items.description: Lead and backing singing ride a guitar, keyboard, bass and drum foundation. Saxophone and brass can add melodic answers and warm ensemble chords; hand percussion may broaden the rhythmic texture.

items.name: German reggae
items.lineage: German reggae develops through local live bands, studios and soundsystem communities. Roots reggae and dub influence a varied repertoire of songs and instrumental versions.
items.description: Lead and supporting voices can combine with clean guitar, keyboards, bass and drums. Offbeat chords and a weighty bass line carry the song, while alternate mixes open space for production effects.

items.name: German ska
items.lineage: German ska includes revival bands, ska-punk and acoustic ska-jazz ensembles. Local musicians adapt offbeat dance rhythms to a wide range of instrumental and vocal settings.
items.description: An acoustic branch uses piano, plucked double bass and drums beneath saxophone and trombone lines. Interlocking accents and improvised melodic exchanges give the compact ensemble its buoyant movement.

items.name: Indonesian reggae
items.lineage: Indonesian reggae connects local songs and musical communities with roots reggae, dub and newer experimental approaches. Bands develop their own combinations of rhythm, melodic phrasing and production.
items.description: Voice, guitar, bass and drums can interact with synthesizer textures. A recurring groove supports the song while electronic colour and echo offer room for more exploratory arrangements.

items.name: Indonesian ska
items.lineage: Indonesian ska includes local scenes drawing on ska, rocksteady and punk-related styles. Guitar-led bands coexist with larger ensembles and horn-led arrangements.
items.description: A compact ska-punk branch uses singing, electric guitar, bass and drums. Offbeat chords contrast with firmer rock accents, allowing the same small ensemble to move between danceable lightness and amplified intensity.

items.name: Italian reggae
items.lineage: Italian reggae connects local singers, bands and listeners with Jamaican roots and later reggae traditions. Early-reggae influences, vocal harmony and contemporary recording approaches coexist within the field.
items.description: Lead and supporting voices can combine with guitar, bass, drums, piano and electronic keyboards. Short chordal accents and bass movement support melodic songs, while guest instruments and dub mixes provide other textures.

items.name: Italian ska
items.lineage: Italian ska develops through local bands connecting Jamaican-derived offbeat rhythms with revival and punk approaches. Live performance and independent releases sustain a varied national scene.
items.description: Singing, guitar, bass and drums can combine with trumpet and trombone. Short rhythmic chords and bright horn responses alternate with more forceful amplified passages.

items.name: Dancehall chileno
items.lineage: Chilean dancehall connects local electronic production with dancehall, dembow and reggaeton-derived rhythms. Producers reshape these influences through synthesizers, samples and club-oriented arrangements.
items.description: Layered synth patterns and programmed percussion can support chopped vocal material. Repetition, rhythmic displacement and changes in timbral density give an instrumental production its movement.

items.name: Dancehall colombiano
items.lineage: Colombian dancehall develops through local vocal and production communities in dialogue with reggae, hip-hop and other Caribbean-derived styles. Live-band and electronically programmed approaches coexist.
items.description: Lead and supporting voices can interact with guitar, synthesizers and programmed percussion. Melodic hooks and rhythmically delivered lines share a recurring dance-oriented foundation.

items.name: Dancehall guyanaise
items.lineage: French Guianese dancehall connects local and diaspora expression with dancehall and ragga traditions. Musicians combine rhythmic vocal delivery with varied live and electronic arrangements.
items.description: A live-band branch brings voice and flute together with guitar, bass and drums. Melodic instrumental responses can contrast with the vocal rhythm, while wider arrangements include electronics and additional percussion.

items.name: Dancehall mauricien
items.lineage: Mauritian dancehall connects local singers and audiences with reggae-dancehall traditions and wider Indian Ocean performance networks. Both live bands and recorded rhythmic backing support the songs.
items.description: A lead voice can interact with guitar, keyboards, bass and drums. Repeated rhythmic patterns support direct vocal phrases, with accompaniment moving between clipped accents and more sustained melodic colour.

items.name: J-reggae
items.lineage: J-reggae encompasses Japanese musicians working with reggae rhythms, song and production traditions. Local bands connect roots influences with contemporary popular styles and varied vocal approaches.
items.description: Lead and supporting voices can ride a guitar, keyboard, bass and drum foundation. Short offbeat chords, a prominent bass line and rim-click accents give one band arrangement its rhythmic shape.

items.name: Japanese dub
items.lineage: Japanese dub draws on reggae and rocksteady while developing distinctive studio and live-band approaches. Song, repetition and spatial production can coexist within the same musical setting.
items.description: Voice, guitar, bass, drums and synthesizer form a flexible band palette. Echo and reverberation let phrases recede into space while the rhythm section maintains continuity.

items.name: NZ reggae
items.lineage: New Zealand reggae connects local and South Pacific musical communities with roots reggae and related styles. Songwriting, vocal interplay and live-band grooves are central to many performances.
items.description: Lead and harmony voices can combine with guitar, bass, drums and synthesizer. Baritone saxophone and trumpet add contrasting melodic responses and fuller ensemble accents in one representative band setting.

items.name: Reggae català
items.lineage: Reggae català brings Catalan-language expression into reggae and rub-a-dub practice. Local singers, producers and bands connect songs with the rhythmic and studio vocabulary of Jamaican music.
items.description: A lead voice can sit above guitar, organ, bass and drums. Offbeat chord accents and a steady low end support the vocal line, with versions and mixes giving the accompaniment different spatial shapes.

items.name: Reggae peruano
items.lineage: Peruvian reggae develops through local musicians and communities engaging with roots reggae and wider Latin American reggae networks. Songwriting and live-band performance coexist with studio and dub approaches.
items.description: Lead and supporting voices can interact with guitar, bass and drums, while piano, organ and synthesizer provide contrasting keyboard colours. Short chords and melodic responses move around the bass-led groove.

items.name: Reggae tuga
items.lineage: Reggae tuga connects Portuguese musicians with roots reggae and related song traditions. Local concerts, recordings and collaborations sustain a varied vocal and instrumental field.
items.description: Lead and backing voices ride guitar, keyboard, bass and drum accompaniment. Saxophone can add melodic replies or longer phrases above the repeating rhythmic foundation.

items.name: Reggae uruguayo
items.lineage: Uruguayan reggae develops within local scenes where reggae, ska and rock often meet. Bands combine songwriting with danceable rhythms and varied instrumental arrangements.
items.description: Voices, electric guitars, bass and drums provide a core ensemble. Saxophone, trumpet and trombone can strengthen the melodic response, linking reggae accompaniment with brighter ska-derived accents.

items.name: Russian reggae
items.lineage: Russian reggae includes local roots-oriented bands and crossovers with dancehall, ragga and electronic styles. Musicians connect song and rhythmic vocal expression with both live and studio-based arrangements.
items.description: Multiple voices can interact with guitar, bass, drums and synthesizer. Offbeat accents provide a reggae foundation, while changing electronic textures and rhythmic emphasis allow more hybrid approaches.

items.name: Latin ska
items.lineage: Latin ska connects ska rhythms with Latin American songwriting and local musical influences. Bands range from compact guitar-and-keyboard groups to larger ensembles with brass and percussion.
items.description: A compact setting brings voice, guitar, keyboards and drums into an interlocking rhythmic arrangement. Offbeat chords and syncopated accents support the song; larger groups can add independent bass, horns and additional percussion.

items.name: Modern reggae
items.lineage: Modern reggae brings established reggae foundations into contemporary songwriting and production. Live-band instrumentation, electronic keyboards and varied vocal approaches coexist within a broad, overlapping field.
items.description: Singing can ride clean guitar, bass, drums and synthesizer accompaniment. Saxophone and trumpet add melodic responses, while production choices shape the space between the recurring instrumental figures.

items.name: Polish reggae
items.lineage: Polish reggae develops through local bands and audiences engaged with roots reggae and later related styles. Song, vocal harmony and instrumental interplay form central parts of the scene.
items.description: Lead and supporting voices can combine with guitar, bass, drums, synthesizer and electric piano. Saxophone adds melodic colour above short chordal accents and a prominent bass line.

items.name: Reggae cristão
items.lineage: Reggae cristão joins Christian devotional messages with reggae song and band traditions. Brazilian gospel-reggae performers use the style for worship, testimony and shared religious expression.
items.description: Singing and supporting voices can combine with acoustic and electric guitars, bass and drums. Offbeat accompaniment supports the devotional text, balancing a steady groove with melodic vocal phrases.

items.name: Reggae do Maranhão
items.lineage: Reggae do Maranhão connects the state’s reggae communities with roots-reggae performance and local musical life. São Luís is an important centre for bands, audiences and reggae circulation.
items.description: Lead and supporting voices can sit above guitar, keyboards, bass and drums. Repeated offbeat chords, melodic bass movement and measured drum accents give a roots-oriented band its foundation.

items.name: Reggae gaúcho
items.lineage: Reggae gaúcho connects Rio Grande do Sul musicians and audiences with reggae song and band traditions. Porto Alegre is one centre of a regional field that includes roots influences and wider popular connections.
items.description: Lead and supporting voices can combine with electric guitar, bass and drums. Offbeat chord accents and melodic bass movement support the songs, while fuller arrangements add other instrumental colours.

items.name: Anthem emo
items.lineage: Anthem emo brings emotionally direct songwriting together with prominent hooks and expansive alternative-rock dynamics. Intimate melodic passages can build toward a forceful communal chorus.
items.description: Voice, guitar, bass and drums provide a compact band foundation. Clean arpeggios, firm rhythmic accompaniment and changes in intensity create contrast; keyboards and strings can broaden more layered arrangements.

items.name: Pinoy reggae
items.lineage: Pinoy reggae connects Filipino singers and musical communities with reggae traditions. Live bands and digital rub-a-dub productions offer different ways to combine local vocal expression with recurring reggae rhythms.
items.description: A voice over programmed sample-based percussion provides one compact digital branch. Repeated rhythmic figures support melodic or rhythmically delivered phrases, while live ensembles offer a broader instrumental palette.

items.name: Reggae boliviano
items.lineage: Bolivian reggae develops through local performers connecting roots reggae with rock and other popular approaches. Vocal collaboration and live-band energy contribute to its varied sound.
items.description: Lead and backing voices can interact with guitar, bass, drums and synthesizer. Trumpet and trombone add melodic responses, with the ensemble balancing repeated grooves and stronger rock-derived accents.

items.name: Reggae cover
items.lineage: Reggae covers reinterpret existing songs through reggae rhythm, phrasing and arrangement. The approach can transform material from other styles or revisit songs already connected with reggae.
items.description: Singing can ride clean guitar, keyboards, bass and drums, with brass adding responses and accents. Offbeat accompaniment and a reworked bass line give familiar melodies a different rhythmic setting.

items.name: Reggae en español
items.lineage: Reggae en español connects Spanish-language song and vocal expression with reggae traditions across multiple countries. Local scenes develop roots, contemporary and hybrid approaches within this shared language field.
items.description: Lead and supporting voices can sit above guitar, keyboards, bass and drums. A prominent low end and short offbeat chords frame melodic lines and rhythmically delivered phrases.

items.name: Reggae maghreb
items.lineage: Reggae Maghreb connects reggae and dub with North African musical references, including gnawa, chaâbi and raï. Local and diaspora musicians develop these relationships through song, instrumental exchange and production.
items.description: Singing, guembri and mandole can interact with electric guitar, bass, drums and synthesizer. Plucked melodic and bass textures meet offbeat band rhythms, with different traditions contributing distinct phrases and timbres.

items.name: Reggae tico
items.lineage: Reggae tico develops through Costa Rican musicians and communities engaging with roots reggae and related styles. Local songwriting and band performance connect the field with wider regional reggae networks.
items.description: A lead voice can combine with guitar, synthesizer, bass and drums. Offbeat chordal accompaniment and recurring bass figures support the song, leaving room for melodic fills and production detail.

items.name: Reggaetón cristiano
items.lineage: Reggaeton cristiano brings Christian messages into reggaeton and wider urbano practice. Performers connect testimony and devotional themes with rhythmic vocal delivery and contemporary beat production.
items.description: Lead vocals move over programmed sample-based percussion. Recurring dance rhythms and melodic hooks support the text, with electronic sounds and vocal arrangement providing further contrast.

items.name: Romanian folk
items.lineage: Romanian folk music encompasses regional song, pastoral instrumental repertories and music for communal dancing. Oral transmission links village practice to professional folk musicians and revival performance, while local traditions preserve different melodic, rhythmic and ensemble conventions.
items.description: The field includes lyrical doina and regional dance repertories rather than a single national instrumental configuration. Fiddle-led music is prominent in many local traditions; Maramureş also preserves shepherd-associated instrumental melodies and accompanying string instruments. Flexible solo expression and regular dance rhythms coexist. A particular fiddle-and-guitar example illustrates one local practice but does not define the whole Romanian field.

items.name: Serbian folk
items.lineage: Serbian folk music joins regional singing, instrumental melodies and social dance traditions. Village practice and later ensemble performance preserve local styles, with the communal kolo dance an important part of celebrations and cultural transmission.
items.description: Melodic instruments support dance tunes and regional repertories, while singing has its own varied practices. The frula is one characteristic solo voice, but Serbian folk music is not restricted to an unaccompanied flute: modern kolo ensembles can include keyboards and drums or a rhythm section with bass and guitar. Instrumentation and arrangement depend on locality and occasion; communal dance function is more fundamental than any single recorded lineup.
exemplars: Unspecified frula player — Serbia: Dance Tunes, Folk Music of Yugoslavia (1952)

items.name: Slovak folk
items.lineage: Slovak folk music encompasses regional singing, dance and pastoral instrumental traditions. Central Slovakia’s shepherd culture is closely associated with the fujara, while other local traditions use different ensembles and vocal styles.
items.description: The fujara is a long three-hole flute whose low tones and upper overtones shape a distinctive pastoral repertoire. Its music is an important Central Slovak tradition and has moved from shepherd settings to folk festivals and concert presentation. It should be understood within the wider Slovak folk field rather than as its sole instrument or repertoire; a national profile must also acknowledge regional singing and dance practices.
exemplars: Folkart Slovakia — Idem, idem, real-fujara MP3 demonstration in A

items.name: Slovenian folk
items.lineage: Slovenian folk music includes regional song and dance traditions and the accordion-led polka and waltz music that became widely associated with the country. During the twentieth century, popular folk ensembles such as the Avsenik Ensemble extended these sounds into a distinct and influential folk-pop tradition.
items.description: Accordion-led accompaniment, clear dance rhythms and singing are characteristic of the popular polka branch. Small voice-and-accordion performances coexist with fuller ensembles using clarinet, trumpet, guitar and bass, and with vocal duets or trios. Yodelling belongs to some Alpine repertories but does not define all Slovenian singing. The wider folk field should not be reduced to either a single archival polka or the later Oberkrainer ensemble format.
exemplars: Unspecified yodeler and accordionist — Polka (Slovenia), Songs and Dances of Yugoslavia (1951)

items.name: Rez country
items.lineage: Rez country is country music rooted in Native American reservation communities, including a strong country-rock circuit on the Navajo Nation. Bands connect local community identity with the wider language of country songwriting and amplified dance-band performance.

Lead vocals ride steady bass and drum patterns, with electric rhythm guitar supporting the harmony and lead guitar adding fills. The Navajo Nation’s country-rock circuit includes bands such as Stateline, whose energetic performances connect local community identity with the broader language of country music.

items.name: Rune folk
items.lineage: Rune folk is a contemporary discovery label connecting Nordic-inspired folk and dark acoustic song. Its repertories engage with regional poetry, landscape and historical imagination; these modern recordings should not be mistaken for direct documentation of ancient ritual music.
items.description: One acoustic branch centres on an exposed singing voice and fingerpicked guitar, using sparse textures to foreground poetry and atmosphere. Other artists associated with the wider field use different ensembles and production approaches. Norwegian dark-folk duo Havnatt illustrates the intimate song-oriented branch, but its repertoire and recording personnel do not define the whole category. The label describes a modern musical grouping rather than an authenticated historical performance system.
exemplars: Havnatt — Myrulla, Havdøgn EP (2012 remaster of the early recording)

items.name: South African country
items.lineage: South African country encompasses local approaches to country song and acoustic roots music. Alongside its broader popular-country audience, an alternative-country strand combines close vocal harmonies and guitar-led songwriting with instruments associated with country and folk ensembles.
items.description: The acoustic country-alt branch favours clear song melodies, strummed guitar, harmony singing and supportive bass, with pedal steel or accordion adding sustained responses and colour. These instruments need not appear in every performance. Artists such as the Hinds Brothers connect this vocabulary with South African songwriting and performance; local identity and scene context distinguish the field without requiring an exclusive national guitar sound.
exemplars: Hinds Brothers — Like a Stone, Ocean of Milk (2013)

items.name: Telugu folk
items.lineage: Telugu folk music comprises orally transmitted songs and regional performance traditions associated with Telugu-speaking communities. Contemporary musicians also bring folk melodies and vernacular expression into amplified popular music, including reggae-influenced and band-based arrangements.
items.description: Singing and local-language expression remain central while rhythm, instrumentation and function vary across regional traditions. Contemporary folk-pop bands may combine electric guitar, bass, drums and programmed sound, placing folk-derived song material over an amplified groove. This modern branch does not replace the wider traditional field, and its electronic accompaniment need not imply a particular synthesizer architecture. Ram Miriyala and Chowraasta are examples of this exchange between folk, reggae and pop.

items.name: Australian R&B
items.lineage: Australian R&B draws on soul and rhythm-and-blues songwriting within Australia’s contemporary music scenes. Neo-soul musicians such as Nai Palm connect expressive singing and harmonically rich guitar writing with wider band and studio production practices.
items.description: Vocal phrasing and groove provide the musical centre, with harmony ranging from direct song accompaniment to jazz-influenced chord movement. Guitar-led solo performances offer an intimate version of this language, while other arrangements use fuller rhythm sections and electronic production. A sparse voice-and-guitar setting is a valid representative branch, not the universal instrumentation of Australian R&B or a reconstruction of one artist’s recording.
exemplars: Nai Palm — solo voice-and-guitar performance branch

items.name: African gospel
items.lineage: African gospel brings Christian devotional song into dialogue with African vocal, rhythmic and community traditions. Local church practices, professional choirs and contemporary popular styles sustain a diverse field across regions and languages.
items.description: African gospel joins Christian devotional song with diverse local vocal and rhythmic traditions. Choral harmony, solo-and-group exchange and repeated phrases support congregational participation and concert performance. Unaccompanied groups create harmonic weight and rhythmic momentum through voices, while instrumental settings add further rhythmic and melodic layers. Soweto Gospel Choir is a prominent exponent of the South African choral strand.
exemplars: Soweto Gospel Choir — unaccompanied gospel repertoire

items.name: Ska català
items.lineage: Ska català develops ska through Catalan music scenes, local songs and regional performance networks. Guitar-led bands combine Jamaican-derived offbeat rhythms with lead vocals, group responses and horn melodies.

Lead and backing voices alternate or join in refrains. Ensembles such as La Banddarra illustrate the energetic guitar-and-saxophone band texture heard within this regional scene.

items.name: Ska chileno
items.lineage: Ska chileno develops Jamaican-derived offbeat music within Chile’s local songwriting and band scenes. Amplified rhythm sections, singing and horn melodies support an energetic, dance-oriented performance style.

Trumpet and saxophone lines provide memorable hooks, short riffs and responses between vocal phrases. The interaction of offbeat accompaniment, moving bass and ensemble accents gives Chilean ska bands their rhythmic lift.

Keyboard chords may reinforce or alternate with the guitar offbeats, while trumpet, trombone and saxophone can provide a compact melodic section.
