exemplars: China Record Corporation recordings of Liu Hai Kan Qiao (Liu Hai Cuts Firewood)

items.name: Ganju (Jiangxi opera)
items.lineage: Opera of northeastern Jiangxi, from the Raohe (Poyang) and Guangxin troupe traditions, joined under the name Ganju in the 1950s; it keeps the old Yiyang high-tune style, in which one singer leads and others take up the line over gongs and drums without strings, alongside tanqiang tunes accompanied by a huqin fiddle (the erhu card stands in) and other strings. It entered China's national intangible heritage list in 2006.
items.description: Archaic high-tune singing in which a lead voice is answered by a group over loud gongs and drums with no strings, alternating with string-accompanied arias led by a bright fiddle.

items.name: Hakka caichaxi (Taiwanese Hakka tea-picking opera)
items.lineage: Hakka-language opera of the Taoyuan, Hsinchu and Miaoli hill country of Taiwan, which grew from the 'three-role tea-picking' play (sanjiao caicha) of one clown and two female roles brought by Hakka settlers from the mainland, and in the early twentieth century expanded into full-length stage drama borrowing from beiguan and Beijing-opera practice; tea-picking plays were issued on 78 rpm discs in the 1930s. Its arias draw on Hakka mountain-song and tea-picking tunes such as laoshange, shangezi and pingban. In the three-role plays the civil section is two fiddles, the panghu (the kezaixian card stands in) and the erxian (the erhu card stands in), and a single percussionist plays drum, small cymbals and gongs.
items.description: Hakka-dialect singing in mountain-song and tea-picking tunes, light and teasing in comic scenes and plaintive in slow laments, over a pair of bowed fiddles, with drum, small cymbals and gongs marking the stage action.
exemplars: 1930s Hakka-language 78 rpm recordings of tea-picking plays

items.name: Qiongju (Hainan opera)
items.lineage: Opera of Hainan Island sung in Hainanese, a Min dialect, which developed into a mainly banqiang (beat-type) opera with a smaller body of qupai tunes; it entered China's national intangible heritage list in 2006 and is also performed in Hainanese communities in Southeast Asia. A lead huqin fiddle (the erhu card stands in) carries the melody, with drum, gong and cymbals for the stage action.
items.description: Hainanese-dialect arias in beat-type tunes, sung with a bright, carrying tone over a lead fiddle, with gong, drum and cymbal patterns driving the stage action.

items.name: Guiju (Guilin opera)
items.lineage: Opera of northeastern Guangxi centred on Guilin, sung in Guilin dialect, a Southwestern Mandarin; its main music is tanqiang (nanlu and beilu, kin to erhuang and xipi), with some gaoqiang and kunqiang. It entered China's national intangible heritage list in 2006. A huqin fiddle leads (the erhu card stands in), with moon lute and sanxian, over drum and gong.
items.description: Guilin-dialect arias in nanlu and beilu modes, delicate and lyrical in the dan roles, led by a bowed fiddle over plucked moon lute and sanxian, with drum and gong cueing the stage action.

items.name: Dianju (Yunnan opera)
items.lineage: Opera of Yunnan centred on Kunming, sung in Yunnan dialect, whose three main tune systems are sixian (from Qinqiang bangzi), huqin (from the shipai tune of Hui opera, akin to erhuang) and xiangyang (from the Xianghe school of Han opera, akin to xipi); it entered China's national intangible heritage list in 2008. Sixian tunes are led by the juqin, a wood-faced fiddle close to the Qinqiang erguxian (the banhu card stands in), and huqin and xiangyang tunes by a huqin (the erhu card stands in), with drum, gong and cymbals.
items.description: Yunnan-dialect arias moving between bangzi-style tunes over a shrill, wood-topped fiddle and lighter, nimble tunes over a softer fiddle, with drum, gong and cymbals cueing the stage action.

items.name: Huayin laoqiang (Shaanxi old-tune shadow-theatre song)
items.lineage: Shadow-puppet theatre singing of Shuangquan village in Huayin, eastern Shaanxi, long kept within the Zhang family lineage and listed as national intangible cultural heritage in 2006. The lead singer plays the yueqin, with erhu, large and small gongs, bangzi and a wooden block (jingmu) pounded on a long bench, and the whole troupe joins in on the refrains (the muyu card stands in for the bangzi and the bench-struck block).
items.description: Rough, full-throated singing over plucked yueqin and erhu, with gongs, woodblock and a block pounded on a bench driving the beat; the whole troupe bursts in together on the long refrain tails.
exemplars: Zhang Ximin and the Huayin laoqiang troupe
Tan Weiwei with Huayin laoqiang singers, 'Huayin Laoqiang Yisheng Han' (CCTV Spring Festival Gala, 2016)

items.name: Wanwanqiang (Huaxian shadow-puppet theatre song)
items.lineage: Shadow-puppet theatre singing of Huaxian (now Huazhou, Weinan) and Huayin at the northern foot of Mount Hua in eastern Shaanxi, also called dengwanqiang or ruanerqiang, named for the small brass bowl (wanwan) struck to mark the beat; it was on the first national intangible cultural heritage list in 2006, and Shaanxi shadow puppetry is part of the Chinese shadow puppetry inscribed by UNESCO in 2011. The lead singer voices every role, the yueqin and the brass bowl lead the accompaniment and banhu and other fiddles support it (the chazi card stands in for the struck brass bowl).
items.description: Delicate, lyrical singing in a soft, restrained voice over a bright plucked yueqin and fiddle, with the small struck brass bowl ringing out the beat.

items.name: Yangbanxi (revolutionary model opera)
items.lineage: The model works promoted during the Cultural Revolution (1966-1976), led by revolutionary modern Peking operas such as The Red Lantern, Shajiabang and Taking Tiger Mountain by Strategy, alongside the ballets The Red Detachment of Women and The White-Haired Girl. Jingju singing and gong-and-drum percussion were set against a combined orchestra in which the jinghu, jing erhu and yueqin played beside Western strings, horns and timpani.
items.description: Heroic, high-projected Peking-opera arias and declamation punctuated by gong-and-drum patterns, carried by a jinghu-led ensemble blended with Western strings, horns and timpani in martial, triumphant arrangements.
exemplars: China Record Corp. cast recordings of 'The Red Lantern' (Hongdeng ji)
China Record Corp. cast recordings of 'Taking Tiger Mountain by Strategy' (Zhiqu Weihushan)

items.name: Jingyun dagu (Beijing-style drum song)
items.lineage: Sung narrative (quyi) shaped in Tianjin and Beijing in the late Qing and early Republican years from the Hebei wooden-clapper drum song, adopting Beijing pronunciation; listed as national intangible cultural heritage in 2006. A standing singer beats a small flat drum on a stand with a single stick and holds a pair of clappers in the other hand, accompanied by the large sanxian and the four-string sihu, sometimes with pipa (the acoustic_membrane_drum card stands in for the shugu drum and the paiban card for the clappers).
items.description: A single standing singer alternates lyrical, ornamented melody with half-spoken narration, marking the beat with crisp drum strokes and clappers over a close-knit accompaniment of sanxian and four-string fiddle.
exemplars: Luo Yusheng, 'Jian'ge wen ling' and 'Chongzheng heshan dai housheng'
China Record Corp. jingyun dagu recordings

items.name: Shandong kuaishu (Shandong fast-tale clapper recitation)
items.lineage: Rhythmic storytelling of Shandong in rhymed Shandong-dialect verse, performed by a solo standing teller who accompanies himself with a pair of crescent-shaped copper clappers (yuanyang ban) held in one hand; its core repertoire is the cycle of tales of the hero Wu Song. Listed as national intangible cultural heritage in 2006 (the paiban card stands in for the copper clappers).
items.description: Brisk, rhymed recitation half-spoken in strong dialect rhythm, propelled and punctuated by the rapid clatter of hand-held clappers, with the teller acting out voices, fights and sound effects.
exemplars: Gao Yuanjun recordings of Wu Song tales
China Record Corp. Shandong kuaishu recordings

items.name: Henan zhuizi (zhuiqin-accompanied ballad singing)
items.lineage: Sung narrative of Henan named for its accompanying instrument, the zhuizi or zhuiqin, a fretless bowed fiddle with a long board-like neck; centred on Kaifeng and Zhengzhou, it spread across northern China and is on the national intangible cultural heritage list. The singer beats time on a pair of wooden clappers (jianban) while the fiddler follows the voice line by line (the zhuihu card is the zhuiqin and the paiban card, set to its two-piece form, stands in for the two-slat jianban).
items.description: A strong, earthy solo voice tells the story in sung verse with spoken asides, shadowed phrase by phrase by the gliding, speech-like slides of the fiddle, with dry clapper strokes keeping time.
exemplars: China Record Corp. Henan zhuizi recordings

items.name: Sichuan qingyin (Sichuan pure-tone song)
items.lineage: Sung quyi of Chengdu and Chongqing that grew from Ming and Qing popular little tunes, usually performed by a woman singer who keeps time on a small drum (zhugu) and sandalwood clappers (tanban), accompanied by pipa, yueqin and erhu; listed as national intangible cultural heritage in 2006 (the acoustic_membrane_drum card stands in for the zhugu and the paiban card for the tanban).
items.description: A bright, high female voice sings lilting little-tune melodies and narrative pieces studded with rapid, laughing staccato 'haha' ornaments, over plucked pipa and yueqin, a light fiddle line and the singer's own drum and clapper strokes.
exemplars: China Record Corp. Sichuan qingyin recordings

items.name: Danxian paiziqu (Beijing sanxian tune-suite song)
items.lineage: Beijing sung narrative that grew out of the Manchu bannermen's octagonal-drum (bajiaogu) entertainment in the Guangxu years of the late Qing, when the amateur Sui Yuanle sang his own texts to bajiaogu tunes while playing the sanxian; it strings named tunes (paizi) into suites and was added to the national intangible cultural heritage list in 2008. The singer holds the small octagonal jingle drum and is accompanied on the sanxian (the credited_frame_drums card stands in for the bajiaogu).
items.description: Clear, well-enunciated Beijing-dialect singing that moves through a chain of named tunes, each with its own melody and meter, over the dry, nimble plucking of the large sanxian, with the octagonal drum's jingles adding light accents.

items.name: Shaanbei shuoshu (northern Shaanxi storytellers' song)
items.lineage: Storytelling of the northern Shaanxi Loess Plateau around Yan'an and Yulin, traditionally performed by blind itinerant singers who accompany themselves on a three-string lute (sanxian, or the local pipa) with clappers tied on to beat time; it is on the national intangible cultural heritage list. In the 1940s Yan'an storytellers set new revolutionary tales to its tunes.
items.description: A rough, carrying solo voice alternates rapid recited verse with sung refrains in the high, open northern Shaanxi manner, driven by a strummed and plucked three-string lute and the steady knock of strapped-on clappers.
exemplars: Field recordings of blind Shaanbei shuoshu singers

items.name: Fengyang huagu (Anhui flower-drum song)
items.lineage: Song-and-drum performance of Fengyang in northern Anhui, carried for centuries by itinerant performers, often women, who sang while beating a small two-headed drum with a pair of thin sticks, partnered by a small-gong player; its best-known song, the 'Fengyang ge', laments the district's famine years. It is on the national intangible cultural heritage list (the acoustic_membrane_drum card stands in for the flower drum and the gong_tamtam card for the small gong).
items.description: Bright, folk-voiced strophic singing over the crisp, rolling patter of a small two-headed drum struck with two thin sticks, answered by the clang of a small hand gong between verses.
exemplars: China Record Corp. Fengyang huagu recordings

items.name: Yangzhou qingqu (Yangzhou seated chamber song)
items.lineage: Seated sung quyi of Yangzhou, also called Guangling or Weiyang qingqu and popularly 'xiaochang', developed from the popular tunes and little songs of the Ming and Qing periods and sung in Yangzhou dialect through named tunes (qupai); it is popular in Yangzhou, Zhenjiang and Shanghai and is on the national intangible cultural heritage list. Traditionally from one or two up to eight or nine performers accompanied their own seated singing on pipa, sanxian, yueqin, sihu, erhu and yangqin, with sandalwood clappers, saucers and wine cups for percussion (the paiban card stands in for the clappers).
items.description: Soft, refined dialect singing with gentle melisma, moving through a chain of tunes over a heterophonic bed of plucked pipa and sanxian, hammered dulcimer and fiddles, with light tapping of clappers, saucers and cups.

items.name: Naamyam (Cantonese southern-tone narrative song)
items.lineage: Cantonese narrative song of the Pearl River Delta and Hong Kong, not to be confused with the Minnan nanyin of Fujian. Its deishui branch was sung by blind professional musicians in teahouses and at private gatherings; the singer accompanies himself or herself on the zheng and beats time on a wooden clapper, sometimes joined by the coconut-shell yehu fiddle.
items.description: A lone voice unfolds long, slow strophic verses in Cantonese, self-accompanied on the plucked zheng, with steady wooden clapper strokes marking the beat and short instrumental interludes between lines.
exemplars: Dou Wun, recorded by Bell Yung at the Fu Lung teahouse, Hong Kong, 1975

items.name: Muk-yu (Cantonese wooden-fish song)
items.lineage: Long Cantonese narrative songs chanted from printed wooden-fish songbooks (mukyu shu) in mostly seven-syllable rhymed lines, sung across the Pearl River Delta and above all in Dongguan, much of it by women at home; Dongguan muk-yu is on China's national intangible cultural heritage list. It is normally sung without instrumental accompaniment, to a flexible recitative melody shaped by the tones of the words.
items.description: A single unaccompanied voice chants long rhymed stanzas in Cantonese to a repeating, speech-shaped melody, the tune bending with the tones of the words.
exemplars: Dongguan muk-yu singer recordings (national intangible cultural heritage documentation)
Hong Kong intangible cultural heritage inventory recordings of muk-yu

items.name: Liam-koa (Taiwanese Hokkien recitative ballad)
items.lineage: Taiwanese Hokkien narrative song in which a singer half-chants long rhymed tales from kua-a songbooks to a small stock of tunes, self-accompanied on the long-necked Taiwanese moon lute (gueh-khim), often with a partner on the daguangxian fiddle; liam-koa was already on Taiwanese 78 rpm records in the 1930s (the yueqin card stands in for the gueh-khim).
items.description: Half-sung, half-chanted Hokkien verse in a plain, speech-close voice, with the twang of the singer's own moon lute and a buzzing fiddle answering between lines.

items.name: Gesar epic singing (Tibetan bardic recitation)
items.lineage: Bardic tradition of the epic of King Gesar of Ling, performed across the Tibetan plateau and also in Mongol and Tu versions, by singers who include 'inspired' bards (babdrung) said to receive the episodes in dreams; inscribed by UNESCO in 2009 as the Gesar epic tradition. Episodes alternate spoken narration with sung verse, each character having its own melody, and bards usually perform without instruments.
items.description: A solo bard moves between rapid spoken narration and strophic sung verse, switching to a distinct melody for each character, in a strong, open-throated voice without accompaniment.
exemplars: Samdrup (Sangzhub) recordings, Tibet Academy of Social Sciences

items.name: Jangar (Oirat Mongol heroic epic singing)
items.lineage: Heroic epic of the Oirat Mongols about the khan Jangar and his warriors of the land of Bumba, sung by specialist jangarchi among the Oirat of Xinjiang (Hoboksar, Bortala, Ili) and the Kalmyks of Russia, and listed as Chinese national intangible cultural heritage in 2006. Singers chant long alliterative verse to a recurring melody, sometimes accompanied by the two-string tovshuur lute.
items.description: Long heroic verse chanted in a steady, declamatory voice to a recurring short melody, with the two-string lute repeating a plucked figure beneath the words.

items.name: Khuuriin ülger (Khorchin Mongol fiddle storytelling)
items.lineage: Mongolian sung storytelling of the Khorchin region of eastern Inner Mongolia, centred on Tongliao, in which a huurchi narrates and sings long tales, many adapted from Chinese historical novels, accompanying himself on the low-pitched four-string fiddle (dörvön chikhtei khuur, the sihu card); listed as national intangible cultural heritage in 2006.
items.description: A single narrator-singer alternates spoken and sung passages of a long tale, the four-string fiddle bowing a constant repeating figure under the voice and filling the gaps between lines.

items.name: Yimakan (Hezhen sung-and-spoken storytelling)
items.lineage: Narrative tradition of the Hezhen (Nanai) of north-east Heilongjiang along the Songhua, Heilong and Wusuli rivers, performed in the Hezhen language by a solo storyteller who alternates sung verse with spoken prose, without instrumental accompaniment. Episodes recount tribal alliances and battles, the deeds of mergen heroes, shamanic ritual, fishing and hunting; the tradition is inscribed on UNESCO's List of Intangible Cultural Heritage in Need of Urgent Safeguarding.
items.description: A single unaccompanied voice moves between plain spoken narration and sung passages, each storyteller shaping the melody freely to fit the episode and its characters.
exemplars: Heilongjiang field recordings of Hezhen yimakan (UNESCO urgent-safeguarding documentation)

items.name: Zhangha (Xishuangbanna Dai narrative singing)
items.lineage: Sung verse of the Dai of Xishuangbanna in southern Yunnan; zhangha names both the singer and the genre. Singers perform solo or in duet, accompanied either by the ding, a Dai stringed instrument, or by the bi, a Dai reed pipe (the hulusi card stands in), with repertoire ranging from improvised songs and set blessings and prayers to long narrative songs from fixed texts. Zhangha is sung at Dai New Year, the Buddhist lent-closing and lent-opening festivals, house-raisings and weddings, and is listed on China's national intangible-heritage register.
items.description: A gentle, speech-inflected vocal line, part recited and part sung, closely follows the tones of the words over a soft reed-pipe accompaniment.
exemplars: Xishuangbanna field recordings of Dai zhangha (national intangible-heritage documentation)

items.name: Dabenqu (Bai sanxian narrative song of Dali)
items.lineage: Narrative singing of the Bai of the Dali basin around Erhai Lake, sung in the Bai language by one singer accompanied by a sanxian player, from long 'big book' scripts of historical tales, legends and local stories. Southern, northern and Haidong schools of tune are distinguished, and dabenqu is listed on China's national intangible-heritage register.
items.description: One singer tells long stories in measured verse, moving between speech-like recitation and tuneful passages, while a plucked three-string lute keeps a steady supporting line and fills the gaps between phrases.
exemplars: Dali Bai quyi recordings of dabenqu (national intangible-heritage documentation)

items.name: Hua'er (Gansu-Qinghai-Ningxia 'flower' songs)
items.lineage: Folk song of Gansu, Qinghai and Ningxia sung in local Chinese dialects by Hui, Han, Tu, Dongxiang, Bao'an, Salar and Tibetan communities, among others; tunes are known as ling (such as the Hezhou ling) and verses on love and daily life are improvised to them. Singers gather in great numbers at seasonal hua'er festivals such as those at Lianhuashan in Kangle and Songmingyan in Hezheng, and hua'er is inscribed on UNESCO's Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.
items.description: High, ringing solo voices, men often in falsetto, hold long tones at phrase ends and leap across wide intervals in free, open-air delivery; at festivals singers answer one another in improvised exchanges.

items.name: Xintianyou (northern Shaanxi Loess Plateau mountain song)
items.lineage: Mountain song of northern Shaanxi and the neighbouring Loess Plateau, sung by drovers, carters and farm workers out on the hills. Each song is built from rhyming couplets of an upper and a lower line, often opening with an image from nature, repeated with new words; it is the best-known genre of Shaanbei folk song, which is listed on China's national intangible-heritage register.
items.description: A solo unaccompanied voice launches high, long-held opening tones and falls through wide leaps in free rhythm, each pair of lines answering the last in an open-air, far-carrying sound.

items.name: Hakka shan'ge (Meizhou and Taiwan Hakka mountain songs)
items.lineage: Hakka-dialect song of Meizhou in north-east Guangdong and of the Hakka districts of Taiwan such as Miaoli, sung in rhyming four-line verses of seven syllables that are often improvised and traded between a man and a woman in sung contests. Meizhou Hakka shan'ge is listed on China's national intangible-heritage register; in Taiwan the core tunes are laoshan'ge, shan'gezi and pingban.
items.description: Solo voices, often a man and a woman in turn, sing ornamented lines with long cadential tones, each answering the other's improvised verse.
exemplars: Taiwan Hakka TV archive recordings of Hakka shan'ge

items.name: Wuge (Wu-dialect songs of the Taihu region)
items.lineage: Folk song of the Wu-speaking Taihu Lake region around Suzhou, Wuxi and Changshu, comprising short field and love songs and long narrative songs; the long ballad Wu guniang (Five Girls) was collected from singers at Lusi in Wujiang. Wuge is listed on China's national intangible-heritage register.
items.description: Soft, lilting solo singing closely follows the speech tones of the Wu dialect, from short strophic songs to long sung narratives delivered verse after verse.
exemplars: Lusi village field recordings of Wuge

items.name: Chuanjiang haozi (Upper Yangtze boatmen's work chants)
items.lineage: Work chants of the boatmen and trackers of the Upper Yangtze (Chuanjiang) and its tributaries through Sichuan and Chongqing. A lead chanter, the haozi tou, sets the rhythm of the work and the crew answers, with different chant types for rowing on calm water, hauling against the current and driving through rapids; Chuanjiang haozi is listed on China's national intangible-heritage register.
items.description: A leader's high, melodic call is answered by the crew's short, forceful unison response, the tempo slowing or racing to match the effort of the work.
exemplars: Chongqing field recordings of Chuanjiang haozi leaders and crews (national intangible-heritage documentation)

items.name: Hengchun minyao (Hengchun peninsula moon-lute folk song)
items.lineage: Taiwanese Hokkien folk song of the Hengchun peninsula in southern Pingtung, sung to a small set of named tunes such as Sixiangqi and Pingpudiao, with the singer accompanying himself on the long-necked two-string moon lute (the yueqin card stands in). The tradition reached national attention through the 1967 folk-song collecting campaign of Hsu Tsang-houei and Shih Wei-liang.
items.description: A solo voice sings long, ornamented lines over sparse plucked figures on a two-string moon lute, the singer improvising new verses to the same tune.
exemplars: 1967 Hsu Tsang-houei and Shih Wei-liang folk-song collection recordings

items.name: Haam seui go (Tanka salt-water songs of the Pearl River Delta)
items.lineage: Songs of the Tanka boat-dwelling fishing communities of the Pearl River Delta and the Hong Kong coast, sung in Cantonese without accompaniment, solo or traded between two or more singers, for courtship, at weddings and funerals, and in daily life afloat; passed on orally, they were seldom written down. The Zhongshan form (xianshui ge) is listed on China's national intangible-heritage register, and salt-water songs are on Hong Kong's intangible cultural heritage inventory under the performing arts.
items.description: Unaccompanied voices sing simple, gently swaying melodies shaped by Cantonese speech tones, alone or trading verses between singers.
exemplars: Hong Kong intangible cultural heritage inventory recordings of Tanka salt-water songs

items.name: Layi and lu (Amdo Tibetan love songs and folk songs)
items.lineage: Song of the Amdo Tibetan herding and farming communities of Qinghai and southern Gansu. Layi (la gzhas) are love songs sung only out in the hills, away from the village and from relatives, while lu (glu) are songs for weddings, drinking and community gatherings; both circulate through field recordings and through the Tibetan-language VCD and CD industry of Xining.
items.description: Solo voices sing long, high, free-rhythm lines with melismatic turns and held notes that carry across open pasture; the lu songs are more regular and strophic and are often sung in company.
exemplars: Amdo Tibetan field recordings of layi
Xining Tibetan-language VCD and CD releases of Amdo folk song

items.name: Gorshey (Kham Tibetan guozhuang circle-dance song)
items.lineage: Circle-dance song of the Kham Tibetans of Chamdo and Garze, sung and danced by villagers at festivals, weddings and gatherings: men and women form the two arcs of a circle and answer each other verse by verse, stamping and turning as the tempo builds from a slow opening to a fast close. Chamdo guozhuang and other local guozhuang forms are listed on China's national intangible-heritage register.
items.description: Two groups of unaccompanied voices, men and women, trade strophes back and forth around a moving circle, the singing quickening as the dancers' stamping steps speed up.
exemplars: Chamdo and Garze field recordings of guozhuang (national intangible-heritage documentation)

items.name: Batang xianzi (Garze Tibetan fiddle dance-song)
items.lineage: Dance-song of the Tibetans of Batang county in western Garze, Sichuan, in which men playing the two-string bowed fiddle (piwang; xianzi, 'strings', in Chinese) lead a circle of singing dancers, the women swinging long sleeves, through slow and lively songs at festivals and gatherings. Batang xianzi is listed on China's national intangible-heritage register.
items.description: Bowed two-string fiddles play a lilting melody in unison with the dancers' group singing over the steady, swaying pulse of the circling steps.
exemplars: Garze field recordings of Batang xianzi (national intangible-heritage documentation)

items.name: Dolan muqam (Dolan Uyghur muqam of the Yarkand River)
items.lineage: Muqam suites of the Dolan Uyghurs of Merkit, Maralbeshi and Awat along the Yarkand River on the edge of the Taklamakan, performed by a group of male singers with the Dolan rawap and Dolan ghijek (both with sympathetic strings), the qalun zither and several dap frame drums; the rawap_kashgar, ghijek_uyghur and kalun_uyghur_zither cards stand in for the Dolan instruments. Each muqam opens with an unmetred section sung at full voice and moves through faster metred sections that draw dancers into the gathering; Dolan muqam is part of UNESCO's inscription of the Uyghur Muqam of Xinjiang and is distinct in repertoire and style from the Twelve Muqam.
items.description: A loud, high, strained unison of men's voices rides over buzzing plucked and bowed strings with sympathetic resonance, a sliding zither and pounding frame drums, rising from an unmetred opening into accelerating dance sections.
exemplars: Field recordings of Dolan muqamchi of Merkit and Awat

items.name: Kgal laox (Kam / Dong grand song)
items.lineage: Polyphonic choral song of the Kam (Dong) of south-east Guizhou and neighbouring Guangxi and Hunan, sung without conductor or instruments by village choirs of the same sex, often in the drum tower, to pass on history, moral teaching and courtship. A large group sustains a low part while one or two lead singers carry the upper melody, and some songs imitate cicadas and birdsong; the Grand Song of the Dong is inscribed on UNESCO's Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.
items.description: A massed choir holds long, sustained low tones and slowly moving harmony while one or two high voices weave the melody above, with imitative songs filling the texture with trilled, insect-like figures.
exemplars: Field recordings of Dong grand-song choirs of Liping and Congjiang

items.name: Lusheng yue (Qiandongnan Miao mouth-organ ensembles)
items.lineage: Mouth-organ music of the Hmub (Miao) of Qiandongnan in south-east Guizhou, played by ensembles of lusheng in graded sizes, from small high instruments to bass lusheng with long pipes, while the players dance in circles at lusheng festivals, sacrifices and courting gatherings; tunes are tied to spoken texts that listeners recognise. Miao lusheng dance and the mangtong lusheng music of Danzhai are listed on China's national intangible-heritage register.
items.description: Chords from many mouth organs of different sizes sound together in a sustained, buzzing reed mass that pulses with the players' dance steps, the largest instruments adding deep bass tones.
exemplars: Qiandongnan lusheng festival field recordings (national intangible-heritage documentation)

items.name: Guge and feige (Qiandongnan Miao ancient songs and flying songs)
items.lineage: Vocal traditions of the Hmub (Miao) of Qiandongnan in south-east Guizhou. The ancient songs are long epic cycles on the creation of heaven and earth, the origins of humankind and the migrations of the Miao, sung in question and answer between paired singers at festivals, weddings and sacrifices; the flying songs (feige) are loud, high outdoor songs called across the hills. Miao ancient songs are listed on China's national intangible-heritage register.
items.description: Ancient songs unfold as long sung exchanges of question and answer between pairs of singers in a steady recitational style, while flying songs launch high, full-voiced held tones that carry across valleys.
exemplars: Taijiang field recordings of Miao ancient songs

items.name: Zhuang shan'ge (Guangxi antiphonal song-fair singing)
items.lineage: Sung-verse culture of the Zhuang of Guangxi, in which young men and women trade memorised and improvised verses in antiphonal exchange at seasonal song fairs (gexu), the largest around the third day of the third lunar month; the legendary singer Liu Sanjie personifies the tradition. In Mashan and neighbouring counties the Zhuang also sing two- and three-part songs, listed with other multipart folk songs on China's national intangible-heritage register.
items.description: Unaccompanied voices trade sung verses back and forth between groups of men and women, each answer taking up the challenge of the last; in the multipart styles two or three voices sing at once.
exemplars: Mashan Zhuang multipart song (national intangible-heritage documentation)

items.name: Hani multipart song (Honghe duoshengbu minge)
items.lineage: Multipart folk song of the Hani of Honghe prefecture in southern Yunnan, whose villages farm the Honghe rice terraces; groups of singers perform songs in several simultaneous parts, including songs for transplanting rice, and Hani multipart folk song is listed on China's national intangible-heritage register.
items.description: Several voice parts enter one after another and overlap on sustained tones, building a dense multipart texture sung outdoors without accompaniment.
exemplars: Honghe Hani multipart song field recordings (national intangible-heritage documentation)

items.name: Haicaiqiang (Shiping Yi sea-vegetable tune)
items.lineage: Song form of the Nisu Yi villages around Yilong Lake in Shiping county, Honghe, also called daobanjiang ('rowing back the oar'), named after the lake's 'sea vegetable' water plant. A complete performance is a large multi-section vocal suite (juqiang, kongqiang, zhengqiqiang and baihuaqiang sections) combining solo, antiphonal, leader-and-chorus, unison and choral singing; tied to a courting custom of young men and women, it was listed in the first batch of China's national intangible-heritage register.
items.description: Long, drawn-out melismatic phrases that demand sustained breath pass between soloists, paired male and female singers and a responding group, in a sectional suite sung without instruments.
exemplars: China Record Corporation recordings of Shiping Yi haicaiqiang
Shiping Yi haicaiqiang field recordings (national intangible-heritage documentation)

items.name: Qiang multipart song (Songpan two-part singing)
items.lineage: Two-part folk song of the Qiang that survives only in a few mountain villages of Xiaoxing and Zhenping townships in Songpan county, Aba prefecture, northern Sichuan; its repertoire spans mountain songs, work songs, drinking songs, custom songs and dance songs, and it was listed with other multipart folk songs on China's national intangible-heritage register.
items.description: One singer leads and a second part follows, rising above the lead line; the two parts meet in fourths, fifths and major seconds, sung with a wide, slow vibrato rarely heard elsewhere in China.
exemplars: Songpan Qiang multipart song field recordings (Aba prefecture)

items.name: Sayeerhe (Tujia funeral song-dance)
items.lineage: Funeral song-dance of the Tujia of the middle Qingjiang valley in western Hubei (Changyang, Wufeng and Badong), performed through the night at the wake of an elder: a drummer beating a large drum beside the coffin leads the high-pitched songs, and the men who dance answer him; it is listed on China's national intangible-heritage register as a traditional dance. The acoustic membrane drum card stands in for the funeral drum.
items.description: Steady drum strokes drive call-and-response singing between the drummer-leader and the dancers, with vocable refrains repeated through a long night-time sequence of dances.
exemplars: Changyang Tujia sayeerhe field recordings (national intangible-heritage documentation)

items.name: Pasibutbut (Bunun millet-prayer polyphony)
items.lineage: Pasibutbut is the Bunun prayer for a good millet harvest, sung by a circle of men in the millet-planting season; voices in four parts start low and rise gradually, each singer adjusting to the others, and the overtones of the ascending chord led to its Taiwanese description as 'eight-part harmony'. Kurosawa Takatomo recorded it in 1943.
items.description: Wordless male voices in a close circle hold a slowly rising, sustained chord in four parts, sliding upward in small steps while overtones ring above the blend.
exemplars: Kurosawa Takatomo 1943 recordings of Bunun pasibutbut
Wind Records Taiwan aboriginal music series (Bunun)

items.name: Amis polyphonic song (Pangcah leader-and-chorus singing)
items.lineage: Vocal polyphony of the Amis (Pangcah) of Taiwan's eastern coast, sung at the harvest festival (ilisin) and at work and drinking gatherings: a lead singer's phrase is answered and overlapped by the group, whose voices move in freely combined parts on vocable syllables. Recordings by Difang and Igay Duana, including their 1988 Paris concert, carried it abroad.
items.description: A leader's call is answered by a group that overlaps and weaves its own lines around the melody on vocable syllables, producing loose, ringing polyphony over a steady dance pulse.
exemplars: Wind Records Taiwan aboriginal music series (Amis)

items.name: Paiwan nose flute and drone song (Pingtung)
items.lineage: The Paiwan of the Pingtung and Taitung hills sing songs in which a leader's melody runs over a drone held by the group, and play the double nose flute (lalingedan), usually with one pipe fingered for the melody over a second pipe that sounds mainly a drone; the nose flute, a man's instrument associated with courtship and mourning, and the double mouth flute are registered in Taiwan as an Important Traditional Performing Art. The tongali card stands in for the Paiwan nose flute.
items.description: A soft, breathy double flute plays a narrow melody over its own drone pipe, and in the songs a leader's line rides over a sustained group drone.
exemplars: Wind Records Taiwan aboriginal music series (Paiwan)
Taiwan Music Institute archive recordings of Paiwan nose flute

items.name: Tao (Yami) song (Lanyu vocal tradition)
items.lineage: Vocal music of the Tao (Yami) of Lanyu (Orchid Island) off Taiwan's southeast coast, a tradition without musical instruments: men and women sing solo and group songs at the inauguration of new houses and plank boats, at work and in the women's hair-swinging dance.
items.description: Slow, narrow-range songs with long-held tones are sung solo or by groups in near-unison, where small differences of pitch and timing between singers thicken the line.
exemplars: Wind Records Taiwan aboriginal music series (Tao/Yami)
Lu Ping-chuan field recordings of Yami song

items.name: Pas-taai songs (Saisiyat ritual of the little people)
items.lineage: Pas-taai, the ritual of the little people (ta'ay), is held by the Saisiyat of the Nanzhuang and Wufeng hills every two years, with a larger celebration every ten; through its nights a fixed cycle of ritual songs, sung only in the ritual season, accompanies a circle dance in which dancers wear jingling hip bells. The shaker card stands in for the hip bells.
items.description: A slow, repetitive song cycle is sung by the circling dancers, led by elders, over the steady shimmer of hip bells swinging with each step.
exemplars: Taiwan Music Institute archive recordings of Saisiyat pas-taai songs

items.name: Lmuhuw (Atayal genealogy chant)
items.lineage: Lmuhuw is the Atayal chanted oral tradition through which elders recite genealogy, migration history and customary law in a special poetic language, sometimes as an exchange between two chanters; it is registered in Taiwan as an Important Traditional Performing Art.
items.description: Free-rhythm recitative chant on a few pitches, delivered solo or in dialogue, in which the text sets the pacing and phrases close on held tones.
exemplars: Wind Records Taiwan aboriginal music series (Atayal)
Taiwan Important Traditional Performing Arts documentation of Atayal lmuhuw

items.name: Mayasvi songs (Tsou war-and-triumph ritual)
items.lineage: Mayasvi is the war and triumph ritual of the Tsou communities of Tfuya and Tapangu in the Alishan hills, centred on the kuba men's house; after the rites of offering, men and women dance in a linked circle in front of the kuba while singing ritual songs.
items.description: Solemn group songs led by men's voices and taken up by the circle, carried at a slow, heavy pace by the stepping of the linked dancers.
exemplars: Taiwan Music Institute archive recordings of Tsou mayasvi

items.name: Geming gequ (Chinese revolutionary mass song)
items.lineage: Mass song (qunzhong gequ) for unison or choral singing that grew out of the anti-Japanese national-salvation movement of the 1930s, with composers such as Nie Er and Xian Xinghai, developed in wartime Yan'an and became the official song repertoire of the People's Republic; it was revived from the 1990s as 'red songs' (hongge).
items.description: Strophic, march-like songs in square duple metre with fanfare-shaped and stepwise melodies, sung in unison or plain choral harmony by declamatory voices over brass and snare drum.
exemplars: Nie Er — March of the Volunteers (1935)

items.name: Yishu gequ (Chinese art song)
items.lineage: Chinese art song for solo voice and piano, setting classical and modern Chinese poetry, emerged from the 1920s New Culture movement with composers such as Zhao Yuanren, Huang Zi and Qing Zhu, and continues in conservatory recital and recording practice.
items.description: A classically trained solo voice with vibrato and careful diction sings composed melodies, often pentatonic in contour, over a through-composed piano part in Western functional harmony.
exemplars: Zhao Yuanren — Jiao wo ruhe bu xiang ta (How Can I Not Miss Her, 1926)
Huang Zi — Meigui san yuan (Three Wishes of the Rose, 1932)

items.name: Xibeifeng (Northwest Wind pop)
items.lineage: Mainland Chinese popular-song wave of roughly 1987-1989 that set melodies modelled on folk songs of the northwestern loess plateau, especially Shaanbei xintianyou, to loud rock and disco backing, sung in a forceful, rough, open-throated voice; the song from the film Red Sorghum (1987) was among its emblems.
items.description: A big, rough, shouted chest voice rides heavy backbeat drums, electric bass, guitar and synthesizer, with wide-leaping folk-derived melodies sung at full force.
exemplars: 'Meimei ni dadan de wang qian zou' (song from the film Red Sorghum)

items.name: Hanmai (shouted-MC livestream music)
items.lineage: Internet song genre that emerged in northeastern China in the 2000s and spread through the YY live-streaming platform in the 2010s, in which an MC shouts rhymed, slogan-like verses in a northeastern accent over fast, high-energy club dance tracks; its leading figure, MC Tianyou, was banned from streaming platforms in 2018.
items.description: A loud, declaimed voice shouts rhymed lines in even rhythm over fast, pounding electronic dance tracks with heavy bass.

items.name: Gandrung Banyuwangi (Osing night song-dance)
items.lineage: All-night song-dance of the Osing people of Banyuwangi at the eastern tip of Java, in which a professional female singer-dancer, the gandrung, sings and dances with male guests from evening until dawn. She is accompanied by one or two violins, kendang drumming, the small kethuk kettle gong, kempul and gong, and the kluncing triangle (here the concert-triangle card).
items.description: A high, penetrating female voice sings long strophic songs over a lilting violin line, with interlocking kendang strokes, a ringing triangle and gong punctuation keeping a steady dance cycle.
exemplars: Smithsonian Folkways: Music of Indonesia, Vol. 1 — Songs Before Dawn: Gandrung Banyuwangi (SFW 40055)

items.name: Kendang kempul (Banyuwangi Osing-language pop)
items.lineage: Regional popular song of Banyuwangi that took shape in the 1980s as an attempt to give the region its own modern sound, sung in the Osing language. It keeps the kendang drums and kempul gongs of gandrung, which give the genre its name, and adds electronic organ or keyboard, violin and guitar; later songs absorbed dangdut, pop and dangdut koplo rhythms.
items.description: A bright solo vocal in a regional language over a syncopated kendang groove that sounds unlike standard dangdut drumming, with kempul gong strokes, violin fills, guitar and keyboard chords on a steady dance pulse.
exemplars: Banyuwangi Osing-language kendang kempul cassette and VCD releases

items.name: Gambang kromong (Betawi and Chinese-Indonesian ensemble)
items.lineage: Ensemble of the Betawi and Chinese-Indonesian (peranakan, Cina Benteng) communities of Jakarta and Tangerang, named for the gambang wooden xylophone (here the xylophone card) and the kromong row of small kettle gongs (here the bonang card). Chinese two-string fiddles (tehyan, kongahyan, sukong), suling (here the generic bamboo-flute card), kendang (here the generic hand-drum card), kecrek and gong complete it, playing an older Chinese-derived lagu dalem repertoire and the later lagu sayur songs for weddings and lenong theatre.
items.description: Wooden xylophone runs and the chiming kettle-gong row lay a pentatonic heterophony under the nasal, sliding lead of two-string fiddles and a bamboo flute, with kendang patterns and gong strokes closing each cycle.
exemplars: Smithsonian Folkways: Music of Indonesia, Vol. 3 — Music from the Outskirts of Jakarta: Gambang Kromong (SFW 40057)

items.name: Tanjidor (Betawi brass band)
items.lineage: Brass-band tradition of the Betawi villages on the outskirts of Jakarta, traced to the bands of enslaved musicians kept by colonial-era estate owners. Clarinet, trumpet or cornet, trombone and a tuba-type bass horn (here the sousaphone card) over a large bass drum and snare drum play marches and Betawi songs, often by ear, for weddings and street processions.
items.description: A loose, open-air band sound: clarinet and trumpet carry the tune in rough unison while the trombone and tuba thump out the bass line over a booming bass drum and a rattling snare on a steady march pulse.
exemplars: Smithsonian Folkways: Music of Indonesia, Vol. 5 — Betawi and Sundanese Music of the North Coast of Java (SFW 40421)

items.name: Topeng Betawi (Betawi masked-theatre music)
items.lineage: Music for the topeng masked dance-theatre of the Betawi villages around Jakarta, an evening of dances, comic sketches and songs by female singer-dancers. A small ensemble of rebab, kendang (here the generic hand-drum card), a small set of kettle gongs (here the kenong card), kempul, gong and kecrek cymbals accompanies it.
items.description: A bowed rebab leads a sinuous melody that the singer shadows in a high, ornamented voice, while kendang strokes cue the dancers and comic turns and small gongs mark a short repeating cycle.
exemplars: Smithsonian Folkways: Music of Indonesia, Vol. 5 — Betawi and Sundanese Music of the North Coast of Java (SFW 40421)

items.name: Gamelan degung (Sundanese bronze chamber ensemble)
items.lineage: Sundanese bronze ensemble associated with the courts of the Priangan regents and tuned to the pentatonic degung scale, a pelog-type tuning. A bonang degung kettle-gong row leads, with saron and peking metallophones, jengglong hanging gongs (here the kempul card), goong, kendang and the four-holed suling degung; degung kawih adds a female singer to the instrumental degung klasik.
items.description: Soft, mellow bronze: the kettle-gong row spins the melody in even strokes over metallophones and deep hanging gongs, while a breathy end-blown flute floats ornamented lines above a gently pulsing drum.

items.name: Angklung (Sundanese bamboo rattle ensemble)
items.lineage: Sundanese ensemble of tuned bamboo rattles, each frame sounding one pitch so that players interlock to build melodies. Older rice-ritual forms such as angklung buhun and angklung dogdog lojor, played with long dogdog drums (here the generic membrane-drum card), stand beside the diatonic angklung Padaeng devised by Daeng Soetigna and taught at Saung Angklung Udjo in Bandung; Indonesian angklung is on the UNESCO Representative List.
items.description: Clattering, hollow bamboo tones: each shaken frame gives a single pitch with a soft rattling tremolo, and many players interlock their notes into melodies and chords over a light drum pulse.

items.name: Calung (Sundanese struck bamboo tubes)
items.lineage: Sundanese music for calung, tuned bamboo tubes struck with a mallet (here the bamboo tube-xylophone card), either strung on a cord (calung rantay) or fixed on a hand-held frame (calung jinjing). From 1960 arts activists at Universitas Padjadjaran in Bandung developed calung jinjing, each player carrying one, into a stage entertainment of songs and comic banter that the singer Darso later carried onto pop Sunda cassettes.
items.description: Dry, woody bamboo tones in interlocking pentatonic patterns, with singers trading verses and spoken banter over a light drum pulse.

items.name: Tarawangsa (Sundanese rice-ritual fiddle and zither)
items.lineage: Ritual music of Rancakalong in Sumedang and other upland West Javanese communities, played at rice-harvest ceremonies such as ngalaksa that honour the rice goddess Dewi Sri. A two-string bowed tarawangsa (here the rebab card) carries the melody over the jentreng, a small seven-string plucked zither (here the kacapi card), while participants dance, some into trance.
items.description: A bowed two-string fiddle repeats short melodic figures over a soft, ringing plucked-zither ostinato, the two cycling for long stretches with no drums and no voice.

items.name: Pantun Sunda (Sundanese epic with kacapi)
items.lineage: Sundanese oral epic in which a specialist juru pantun narrates, voices dialogue and sings tales of the Pajajaran kingdom, such as Lutung Kasarung and Mundinglaya, through the night while accompanying himself on the boat-shaped kacapi zither. Performances also carry a ritual protective role.
items.description: A single male voice moves between half-spoken narration, stylised character dialogue and sung passages, over his own rippling, repetitive kacapi figures.
exemplars: Ki Atjeng Tamadipura (juru pantun documented by Ajip Rosidi's Pantun and Sundanese Folklore Research Project)

items.name: Ketuk tilu (Sundanese three-kettle dance music)
items.lineage: Sundanese village dance-party music in which a ronggeng singer-dancer performs with men who come forward to dance, accompanied by rebab, kendang, the three small kettle gongs (ketuk, here the kethuk card) that name the genre, kecrek and goong. It was a principal source for jaipongan, which Gugum Gumbira built from it in Bandung.
items.description: A high, ornamented female voice and a bowed rebab weave over a short cycle of three small kettle-gong pitches, while the kendang drives and answers the dancers with sharp, flexible strokes.
exemplars: Sundanese ketuk tilu commercial cassettes (West Java)

items.name: Wayang golek and kliningan (Sundanese salendro gamelan)
items.lineage: Sundanese rod-puppet theatre and its concert counterpart kliningan, both carried by gamelan salendro: rebab, kendang, saron, bonang, kenong, jengglong, goong, gambang and kecrek, with a pesinden singer. In wayang golek the dalang narrates, voices every character and cues the ensemble; through cassettes and broadcasts the Giri Harja dalang family of Jelekong, Bandung, dominated the form from the 1980s.
items.description: A florid female voice and the rebab float over a dense salendro gamelan whose kendang leaps between calm cycles and sudden fight-scene bursts, with the puppeteer's narration and character voices cutting in between pieces.
exemplars: Asep Sunandar Sunarya (Giri Harja III) wayang golek cassettes
Andrew Weintraub, Power Plays: Wayang Golek Puppet Theater of West Java (2004)

items.name: Kendang pencak (Sundanese pencak silat drumming)
items.lineage: Music for Sundanese pencak silat demonstrations: large and small kendang drums, a tarompet double-reed shawm (here the serunai card) and a small gong play fixed drum patterns to which the fighters shape their moves. Pencak silat traditions are on the UNESCO Representative List.
items.description: Loud, driving drums trade dense interlocking patterns while a piercing, nasal shawm spins long ornamented phrases above them, with a small gong stroke closing each cycle.
exemplars: Sundanese kendang penca cassettes (terompet and kendang)

items.name: Tembang macapat (Javanese sung verse)
items.lineage: Javanese sung poetry in fixed verse forms such as dhandhanggula, sinom, asmaradana, pangkur and kinanthi, each with a set number of lines, syllables per line and line-final vowels. It is sung solo and unaccompanied in slendro or pelog at macapatan reading gatherings and on radio, and gamelan vocal music draws on it.
items.description: A single unaccompanied voice sings each line in free rhythm, mostly syllabic but with long ornamented melismas on the line endings, in a calm, inward delivery.
exemplars: Lokananta and RRI recordings of macapatan (Surakarta)

items.name: Tayuban (Javanese tayub dance-party gamelan)
items.lineage: Javanese social dance event in which female singer-dancers (ledhek or waranggana) sing with a gamelan and invite men to dance with them in turn. It is held at village cleansing ceremonies, harvest feasts and weddings in regions such as Blora and Nganjuk.
items.description: A bright, ornamented female voice over a lively gamelan in which the kendang drives the dance, with metallophones and gongs locking into short, repeating cycles that speed up for the dancers.
exemplars: Regional tayub cassette recordings from Blora and Nganjuk

items.name: Reog Ponorogo (East Javanese masked-dance ensemble)
items.lineage: Masked dance-drama of Ponorogo in East Java, centred on the huge tiger-head and peacock-feather mask of Singa Barong. A gamelan reyog of kendang and ketipung drums, kenong, kethuk, kempul, angklung rattles and the slompret shawm (here the serunai card) accompanies it; it is on the UNESCO Urgent Safeguarding List.
items.description: A shrill shawm melody rides over pounding, interlocking drums, rattling bamboo and rapid gong strokes in a loud, hypnotic outdoor cycle.
exemplars: UNESCO Urgent Safeguarding List 2024: Reog Ponorogo performing art

items.name: Jaranan (Javanese hobby-horse trance music)
items.lineage: Hobby-horse trance dance of East and Central Java, called jaranan around Kediri, jathilan near Yogyakarta, ebeg in Banyumas and kuda lumping in general use, in which dancers riding woven bamboo horses are brought into trance. The music uses kendang, kempul and gong, kenong or bonang, and a slompret shawm (here the serunai card) in a fast repeating cycle.
items.description: Insistent kendang patterns and gong strokes lock into a short, fast cycle under a shrill shawm, building in intensity as the dancers fall into trance.
exemplars: Kediri jaranan trance-dance cassette and VCD recordings

items.name: Calung Banyumasan (Banyumas bamboo gamelan with lengger)
items.lineage: Bamboo ensemble of the Banyumas region of Central Java that takes over gamelan roles on bamboo: struck bamboo xylophones (here the bamboo tube-xylophone card) as gambang and slenthem, bamboo kenong, a blown bamboo gong and kendang. It accompanies lengger female singer-dancers and sung songs in Banyumas dialect.
items.description: Bright, dry bamboo xylophones interlock in fast gamelan-style patterns over a booming blown-bamboo bass, with lively kendang and a high female voice singing in regional dialect.
exemplars: Smithsonian Folkways: Music of Indonesia, Vol. 14 — Lombok, Kalimantan, Banyumas: Little-known Forms of Gamelan and Wayang (SFW 40441)

items.name: Gamelan Cirebon (Cirebonese court gamelan)
items.lineage: Gamelan tradition of the Cirebon courts (Kasepuhan and Kanoman) on the north coast of West Java, played on paired sets in prawa, a five-tone tuning, and pelog. It serves court ceremonies, topeng Cirebon masked dance and wayang, and the region also keeps antique ensembles such as gamelan sekaten (gong sekati), gong renteng and denggung.
items.description: Bright, brisk bronze: kettle-gong rows and metallophones drive the melody in tight cycles marked by gongs, with an agile kendang and a flute line weaving above.
exemplars: Gamelan Sinar Surya (dir. Richard North): Gamelan of Java, Vol. 5 — Cirebon Tradition in America (Lyrichord, 2010)

items.name: Saronen (Madurese shawm band)
items.lineage: Outdoor shawm band of Madura, said to have originated in Sumenep and named after its lead instrument, the saronen, a conical wooden shawm (here the serunai card). The documented nine-piece band sets the saronen over a large gendang and a small gendang dik-gudik (here the generic membrane-drum card), three kenong, a kempul, a large gong and a korca, and it accompanies the kerapan sapi bull races and sapi sonok cattle contests as well as ritual ceremonies and processions.
items.description: A piercing, ornamented shawm melody rides over loud interlocking drums and gong strokes in a fast, driving festive cycle made to carry outdoors.
exemplars: Aural Archipelago field recordings of saronen (Sumenep)
Field recordings of kerapan sapi bull-race music

items.name: Gamelan gong gede (Balinese temple orchestra)
items.lineage: Large ceremonial bronze orchestra of Balinese temple festivals and the former courts, and the ensemble from which gong kebyar developed; only a few villages, such as Batur and Sulahan, still keep one. Its stately lelambatan pieces are led by trompong kettle-gong rows (here the reyong card in trompong form) over jublag and jegogan metallophones, paired kendang, large ceng-ceng kopyak cymbals, a kajar and a cycle of hanging gongs.
items.description: Slow, majestic bronze music: a singing kettle-gong lead unfolds over a heavy, steady core melody on deep metallophones, punctuated by great gong strokes and crashing cymbal choruses.
exemplars: CREM-CNRS sound archive: Balinese gong gede recordings ('Kapi Raja')
Field recordings of temple gong gede ensembles (Batur, Sulahan)

items.name: Gamelan semar pagulingan (Balinese court chamber gamelan)
items.lineage: Refined bronze gamelan of the old Balinese courts, named for Semara, god of love, and traditionally played near the royal sleeping chambers. The seven-tone form is led by a trompong kettle-gong row (here the reyong card in trompong form) with suling flutes over gangsa, jublag and jegogan metallophones, small kendang and ceng-ceng; ensembles in Teges and Kamasan are noted for it.
items.description: Sweet, lyrical bronze chamber music: a singing kettle-gong line and breathy flutes over gently interlocking metallophones with a shimmering paired-tuning beat, softer and more flowing than kebyar.
exemplars: Nonesuch Explorer: Gamelan Semar Pegulingan — Gamelan of the Love God (Teges Kanyinan)

items.name: Gambuh (Balinese court dance-drama ensemble)
items.lineage: Oldest surviving Balinese dance-drama, enacting Panji tales in Kawi dialogue and song, and a source of much later Balinese dance and gamelan repertoire. Its ensemble is led by several very long suling gambuh flutes and a rebab, with paired kendang, kajar and small gongs and cymbals; Batuan and Pedungan are among the villages that keep it.
items.description: A deep, breathy unison of long bamboo flutes and a reedy fiddle line drifts over soft drum patterns and light gong and cymbal punctuation, with declaimed and sung dialogue from the dancers.
exemplars: King Record World Music Library Bali series: gambuh
UNESCO 2015 inscription, Three genres of traditional dance in Bali (gambuh)

items.name: Gender wayang (Balinese shadow-play metallophone quartet)
items.lineage: Quartet of ten-keyed bronze gender metallophones in slendro, two larger pemade and two smaller kantilan an octave higher (here the gender card and the kantilan card for the smaller pair), each player striking with a mallet in each hand and damping with the same hands. It accompanies wayang kulit shadow-puppet plays and also plays for tooth-filing and cremation rites; Sukawati and Kayumas are noted centres.
items.description: Four bronze metallophones weave fast two-handed interlocking figuration over a slower bass melody, the paired tuning producing a constant shimmering beat; dense, bright and intimate.
exemplars: Nonesuch Explorer: Music for the Balinese Shadow Play — Gender Wayang from Teges Kanyinan, Pliatan, Bali

items.name: Gamelan angklung (Balinese four-tone temple gamelan)
items.lineage: Small four-tone bronze gamelan played for temple festivals and above all for cremations and other death rites, named after the bamboo angklung rattles that older ensembles included. Light gangsa metallophones play interlocking figuration over jublag and jegogan, with a four-kettle reyong, small kendang, ceng-ceng and a ringing kajar, and the set is light enough to be carried in procession.
items.description: Bright, light bronze ensemble music in a narrow four-note scale: quick interlocking figuration chimes over a plain core melody and a steady ringing pulse, sweet rather than loud.
exemplars: Colin McPhee, Music in Bali (1966): documentation of gamelan angklung
Field recordings of gamelan angklung at Balinese cremation rites

items.name: Gamelan selonding (Bali Aga sacred iron gamelan)
items.lineage: Sacred iron-keyed gamelan of the Bali Aga villages of eastern Bali, above all Tenganan Pegringsingan, where the instruments are kept as sacred heirlooms and played for village rites. Its instruments carry heavy iron keys over trough resonators and play in a seven-tone pelog system, and it is regarded as one of the oldest Balinese ensembles.
items.description: Dark, heavy iron tones with a dull clang and slow bloom, played in measured interlocking patterns; austere and archaic beside bronze gamelan.
exemplars: King Record World Music Library Bali series: gamelan selonding

items.name: Jegog (West Balinese bamboo gamelan)
items.lineage: Bamboo gamelan of Jembrana regency in western Bali, built from large bamboo tubes struck with rubber-tipped mallets, the biggest so long that the players sit on the frame. Its four-tone ensembles play interlocking figuration over a booming bass and meet in mebarung contests where two groups play at once; the t'rung card stands in for the jegog tube instruments.
items.description: Thunderous, woody bamboo resonance: rapid interlocking patterns on the upper tubes ride a deep, booming bass felt as much as heard, building to loud, competitive climaxes.
exemplars: Commercial and field recordings of jegog from Jembrana

items.name: Joged bumbung (Balinese bamboo social dance)
items.lineage: Flirtatious Balinese social dance in which a female joged dancer invites men from the audience to dance with her, accompanied by a bamboo gamelan of grantang tube xylophones (here the t'rung card), suling flutes (here the generic bamboo-flute card), kendang and ceng-ceng. It is especially popular in Buleleng and Jembrana, and UNESCO's inscription of traditional Balinese dance includes it among the entertainment dances.
items.description: Bright, clattering bamboo xylophones play fast interlocking patterns with a flute melody on top and lively drum cues that push the dance along.
exemplars: UNESCO 2015 inscription, Three genres of traditional dance in Bali (joged bumbung)
Balinese cassette and field recordings of joged bumbung

items.name: Gamelan beleganjur (Balinese processional gamelan)
items.lineage: Processional gamelan of Bali, carried in temple processions and cremation parades. Paired kendang lead a large section of crashing ceng-ceng kopyak cymbals, a reyong whose kettles are carried by four players, a small timekeeping gong and hanging gongs; it has also become a competition form, lomba beleganjur, for youth groups.
items.description: Loud, clangorous marching music: interlocking cymbal crashes and drum patterns surge over a steady gong pulse and repeating kettle-gong figures, built on abrupt contrasts of tempo and dynamics.
exemplars: Michael Bakan, Music of Death and New Creation: Experiences in the World of Balinese Gamelan Beleganjur (1999), with CD

items.name: Gamelan gambang (Balinese cremation xylophone ensemble)
items.lineage: Archaic sacred ensemble of Bali played chiefly at cremations and other death rites, and in some villages at temple festivals. Four gambang xylophones with bamboo keys, struck with forked two-headed mallets, play rapid interlocking patterns in seven-tone pelog against one or two bronze saron that carry the slower melody.
items.description: Dry, clattering bamboo-key xylophones in fast, irregular interlocking rhythms over a slow ringing bronze melody; hypnotic and austere.
exemplars: Field recordings of gamelan gambang at Balinese cremation rites

items.name: Genggong (Balinese jaw-harp ensemble)
items.lineage: Balinese ensemble of genggong, string-pulled jaw harps made from sugar palm (here the angkuoch card), played together with suling (here the generic bamboo-flute card), kendang and small gongs and cymbals. It is played for entertainment and dance and is closely associated with the village of Batuan.
items.description: Twanging, buzzing jaw harps interlock in nasal, vowel-shaped rhythms under a light flute melody, with soft drums and small gongs keeping a playful dance cycle.
exemplars: King Record World Music Library Bali series: genggong

items.name: Arja (Balinese sung dance-opera)
items.lineage: Balinese dance-opera in which the characters sing their roles, developed from gambuh and sung tembang poetry and performed in Balinese with Kawi passages, dramatising Panji and other romances. Its light gamelan geguntangan is built around suling flutes (here the generic bamboo-flute card), small kendang, ceng-ceng, a small timekeeping gong (the kempli card) and guntang bamboo tube zithers that mark the gong cycle (no card).
items.description: Long, highly ornamented solo songs, high and melismatic, float over a soft bed of flutes, light drumming and hollow plucked pulses, alternating with spoken comic dialogue.

items.name: Sanghyang (Balinese trance-dance chorus)
items.lineage: Exorcistic trance rites of Bali, among them sanghyang dedari, in which two young girls dance in trance, and sanghyang jaran, in which a man riding a hobby horse dances through burning coconut husks. The music is chiefly vocal: a women's chorus sings the songs that call and release the deities, often with a men's chorus of interlocking cak syllables, the source of kecak; UNESCO lists sanghyang dedari among the sacred dances in its inscription of traditional Balinese dance.
items.description: Repetitive, hypnotic choral songs in unison swell and quicken as the dancers enter trance, sometimes over a rapid interlocking chant of men's voices.
exemplars: Field recordings of sanghyang dedari choruses

items.name: Kakawin and kidung (Balinese sung poetry)
items.lineage: Balinese vocal art in which Old Javanese kakawin and Middle Javanese kidung poetry are sung unaccompanied by members of pesantian groups; in mabebasan sessions a singer intones each kakawin line and a partner paraphrases it in Balinese. Kidung are sung during temple and life-cycle ceremonies, and pesantian singing also circulates on Balinese radio and in recordings.
items.description: A single unaccompanied voice draws out each line of poetry in long, ornamented melismas at a slow, free pace, answered by a plainer half-spoken paraphrase.
exemplars: Raechelle Rubinstein, Beyond the Realm of the Senses: The Balinese Ritual of Kekawin Composition (2000)

items.name: Gendang beleq (Sasak big-drum ensemble)
items.lineage: Sasak drum-and-gong ensemble of Lombok named after its pair, occasionally two pairs, of large male and female drums (beleq, 'big'; here the generic membrane-drum card), struck with a mallet in the right hand by drummers who carry the drums on straps and dance as they march. They are followed by a large gong carried by several men, a suling (here the generic bamboo-flute card), hand-held kettle gongs (here the canang card) and many ceng-ceng cymbals, and the ensemble leads wedding processions and festivals.
items.description: Big, booming drums lock into a driving interlocking groove under crashing cymbals and steady gong strokes, loud enough to carry a procession through the street.
exemplars: Lombok cassettes and VCDs of gendang beleq

items.name: Saluang jo dendang (Minangkabau flute-and-song)
items.lineage: Night-time Minangkabau entertainment of West Sumatra in which singers trade dendang, sung pantun verses often melancholy in tone, accompanied by the saluang, an end-blown bamboo flute open at both ends and played with circular breathing (here the credited bamboo-flute card). Performances run through the night at weddings and village gatherings; the related dendang Pauah comes from Pauh in Padang.
items.description: A breathy, unbroken bamboo flute line spins continuous ornamented melody around a plaintive, melismatic voice singing quatrain verses, with no percussion.
exemplars: Smithsonian Folkways: Music of Indonesia, Vol. 6 — Night Music of West Sumatra: Saluang, Rabab Pariaman, Dendang Pauah (SFW 40422)

items.name: Rabab Pariaman (Minangkabau fiddle storytelling)
items.lineage: Coastal Minangkabau tradition of West Sumatra in which a singer accompanies himself on the rabab Pariaman, a three-string spike fiddle with a coconut-shell body (here the generic fiddle card), to sing kaba, long narrative tales, through the night, interspersed with lighter songs. The related rabab pasisia of Pesisir Selatan uses a violin instead.
items.description: A nasal, ornamented voice sings long strophic narrative verse in alternation with a raspy fiddle that doubles and answers the melody.
exemplars: Smithsonian Folkways: Music of Indonesia, Vol. 6 — Night Music of West Sumatra: Saluang, Rabab Pariaman, Dendang Pauah (SFW 40422)

items.name: Talempong (Minangkabau gong-chime music)
items.lineage: Minangkabau gong-chime music of West Sumatra played on small bronze kettle gongs (here the canang card). In talempong pacik several players each hold gongs in the hand and interlock their parts into a melody, while in talempong duduak the gongs lie in a row on a frame; both are usually joined by gandang drums and often a sarunai shawm, for weddings, processions and randai theatre.
items.description: Bright, ringing kettle gongs interlock into quick repeating melodic cycles over drumming, with a reedy shawm line on top; festive outdoor music.
exemplars: Smithsonian Folkways: Music of Indonesia, Vol. 12 — Gongs and Vocal Music from Sumatra (SFW 40428)

items.name: Randai (Minangkabau circle theatre)
items.lineage: Minangkabau folk theatre of West Sumatra, documented in detail by Kirstin Pauka, in which a troupe moving in a circle (galombang) alternates silek martial-arts movement with acted scenes and sung episodes (dendang) that tell a kaba story. Between scenes the circle players slap their stretched trousers in interlocking patterns (tapuak galembong; the hand-clap card stands in), and the songs and interludes are accompanied by talempong kettle gongs (the canang card stands in), the saluang end-blown bamboo flute (the generic bamboo-flute card stands in), the sarunai shawm and the gandang drum (the Malay gendang card stands in).
items.description: Sung verses in a high, ornamented melodic line alternate with spoken dialogue and with sharp, interlocking slaps on the players' trousers as the circle moves through martial-arts steps. Kettle-gong, flute and shawm interludes mark entrances and scene changes.
exemplars: Kirstin Pauka, Theater and Martial Arts in West Sumatra: Randai and Silek of the Minangkabau (1998)
Minangkabau cassette and VCD recordings of randai troupes

items.name: Gandang tasa (Pariaman tabuik drumming)
items.lineage: Drum ensemble of the tabuik festival of Pariaman on the West Sumatran coast, the local form of the Muharram commemoration of the martyrdom of Husain at Karbala, rooted in South Asian Shia practice brought to the coast in the colonial era; Bengkulu's related tabot festival keeps its own dol-and-tasa drumming. A single tasa, a small kettle-shaped drum of the South Asian tasha family with a thin head beaten with rattan sticks (the tasha card), leads a group of large double-headed gandang tambua drums carried by their players (the generic membrane-drum card stands in).
items.description: Loud outdoor processional drumming in which the dry, cutting rolls and signal patterns of the tasa drive massed, booming strokes from the large drums, rising in tempo and density as the tabuik towers are paraded. The music is purely percussive and tightly cyclic.
exemplars: Field and festival recordings of the Pariaman tabuik gandang tasa

items.name: Gamad (Padang coastal song)
items.lineage: Song genre of the Minangkabau west coast, centred on Padang, that grew from the acculturation of Minang pantun singing with Western music, a history local writers trace to the Portuguese presence on the coast from the sixteenth century; the name is often derived from gamit, to touch someone to draw their attention. Pantun verses sung in Minang are accompanied by violin, accordion, guitar, bass, a gendang drum and a tambourine-like frame drum (the generic frame-drum card stands in).
items.description: Lilting couple-dance songs in which a singer delivers Minang pantun quatrains in an ornamented, sentimental line over violin and accordion melody, strummed guitar and a light frame-drum and drum pulse.
exemplars: Padang cassette and Minang Record releases of gamad songs

items.name: Gondang sabangunan (Toba Batak ceremonial ensemble)
items.lineage: Outdoor ceremonial ensemble of the Toba Batak of North Sumatra, played for adat feasts, funerals and tortor dancing and formerly for offerings to the ancestors. The sarune bolon double-reed shawm leads over the taganing, a set of five tuned drums played melodically with sticks, and the large gordang drum (the generic membrane-drum card stands in for both), with four hanging ogung gongs and the hesek, a struck metal timekeeper (the auxiliary-percussion card stands in).
items.description: A piercing, unbroken shawm melody is doubled and answered by the melodic tuned-drum set over an interlocking cycle of four gongs and a steady metallic timekeeper; pieces are requested in turn by the hosts and danced to in slow tortor steps.
exemplars: Smithsonian Folkways, Music of Indonesia vol. 4: Music of Nias and North Sumatra (SFW 40420)
Artur Simon field recordings of Toba Batak gondang (Museum für Völkerkunde Berlin)

items.name: Gondang hasapi (Toba Batak lute ensemble)
items.lineage: Indoor chamber ensemble of the Toba Batak, also called uning-uningan, the softer counterpart of the outdoor gondang sabangunan. It is built around the hasapi, a two-string boat lute played in pairs (the sundatang two-string boat-lute card stands in), with the sulim transverse bamboo flute (the generic bamboo-flute card stands in), the garantung wooden xylophone (the xylophone card stands in) and the hesek metal timekeeper (the auxiliary-percussion card stands in).
items.description: Light, bright instrumental music in which two plucked lutes interlock a busy, repeating melody with the flute and wooden xylophone, held together by a metallic timekeeper; softer and more intimate than the outdoor drum-and-shawm gondang.
exemplars: Artur Simon field recordings of Toba Batak music (Museum für Völkerkunde Berlin)

items.name: Gendang lima sendalanen (Karo Batak ensemble)
items.lineage: Principal ensemble of the Karo Batak of the North Sumatran highlands, whose name means 'five instruments in one ensemble': the sarune double-reed shawm, two small double-headed drums beaten with sticks, the gendang singanaki and singindungi (the generic membrane-drum card stands in), and two gongs, the small penganak and the larger gung. It accompanies dancing at guro-guro aron youth festivities, weddings, funerals and spirit rites; a smaller ensemble built around the keteng-keteng bamboo tube zither is a related form.
items.description: A shrill, continuously ornamented shawm melody rides over fast, tightly interlocking patterns from the two small stick-beaten drums, while the small and large gongs mark a steady alternating cycle.
exemplars: Smithsonian Folkways, Music of Indonesia vol. 4: Music of Nias and North Sumatra (SFW 40420)

items.name: Gordang sambilan (Mandailing nine-drum ensemble)
items.lineage: Ceremonial ensemble of the Mandailing of southern North Sumatra, once reserved for the great feasts (horja) of the ruling families and now also played at weddings and festivals; its name means 'nine drums'. Nine long drums of graduated size (the generic membrane-drum card stands in), shared among several players beating with sticks, sound with two large ogung gongs and a smaller doal, small mongmongan gongs (the canang card stands in), a pair of small tali sasayak cymbals and a sarune shawm.
items.description: Thunderous interlocking patterns across the graduated drums, from deep bass strokes to higher rolling figures, build over a slow cycle of large and small gongs, with cymbal accents and a piercing shawm line above.
exemplars: Field recordings and Mandailing ceremonial VCDs of gordang sambilan

items.name: Hoho (Nias choral song)
items.lineage: Choral singing of southern Nias, the island off the west coast of North Sumatra, used to recite origin stories, genealogies and customary law at feasts and other village occasions. A leader sings each line of text and groups of singers answer in dense, sustained multipart chords; the maena of Nias, a lighter circle-dance song with a choral refrain, is a related form.
items.description: A solo leader's declaimed line is taken up by groups of singers who enter in turn on long, overlapping, close-pitched chords, producing a dense, wavering choral sound without instruments.
exemplars: Smithsonian Folkways, Music of Indonesia vol. 4: Music of Nias and North Sumatra (SFW 40420)

items.name: Rapa'i (Acehnese frame-drum ensembles)
items.lineage: Acehnese ensembles of rapa'i frame drums, an instrument whose name local tradition links to the Sufi Rifa'iyah order; Margaret Kartomi documented their many regional forms. In rapa'i geleng a row of seated men beat hand-held rapa'i in interlocking patterns while swaying and singing Islamic-themed verses led by a solo singer, while rapa'i pasee of North Aceh uses very large suspended frame drums in competitive outdoor playing (the generic frame-drum card stands in for both).
items.description: Tight, rapid interlocking strokes from a row of frame drums accelerate in waves beneath a solo singer's verses and the players' choral responses; the large suspended drums of the pasee form give a booming, outdoor sound.
exemplars: Margaret Kartomi field recordings of Acehnese rapa'i (Monash University)
Acehnese cassette recordings of rapa'i geleng

items.name: Seudati (Acehnese body-percussion dance-song)
items.lineage: Acehnese dance-song, strongest in Pidie and along the north coast, performed by eight male dancers led by a syeh, with two singers (aneuk syahi) who sing the verses. No instruments are used: the rhythm comes from finger snaps, slaps to the chest and sides (the hand-clap card stands in) and stamping, and the verses range over religious, historical and topical themes.
items.description: The singers' strident, ornamented verses are answered by the dancers' unison responses, while sharp finger snaps, chest slaps and stamps lock into fast, accelerating unison rhythms.
exemplars: Margaret Kartomi field recordings of seudati (Monash University)

items.name: Didong (Gayo sung poetry duel)
items.lineage: Sung poetry contest of the Gayo highlands of central Aceh, studied by John Bowen, in which two clubs face each other through the night, each led by a ceh poet-singer who sings newly composed verses on history, religion, morality and current affairs while the club members respond in chorus. The members keep time with hand claps and by striking small cushions held in their hands.
items.description: A lead poet's solo verses in a high, ornamented line are answered by full-throated choral refrains from his club over interlocking claps and the muffled thud of struck cushions; the two sides take turns, trading sung arguments.
exemplars: John R. Bowen, 'Poetic Duels and Political Change in the Gayo Highlands of Sumatra' (American Anthropologist, 1989)

items.name: Mak yong (Malay dance-drama)
items.lineage: Malay dance-drama of Kelantan, the Patani region and the Riau Islands, proclaimed by UNESCO a Masterpiece of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity and later inscribed on its Representative List; it combines acting, dance, song and improvised dialogue, and the leading prince role (Pak Yong) is played by a woman.
