Performances open by saluting the rebab, the three-string spike fiddle that leads the ensemble of a pair of gendang barrel drums, a pair of hanging tetawak gongs and, in some pieces, serunai shawm, canang kettle gongs and kesi cymbals.
items.description: Sung episodes in a high, ornamented vocal line, with a chorus answering the lead, alternate with spoken comic dialogue over the rebab's sinuous melody, interlocking drum patterns and a slow cycle of deep gong strokes.
exemplars: Smithsonian Folkways, Music of Indonesia vol. 11: Melayu Music of Sumatra and the Riau Islands (SFW 40427)

items.name: Batanghari sembilan (South Sumatran guitar song)
items.lineage: Solo guitar-and-voice song of South Sumatra, named after the nine rivers (batanghari sembilan) that drain the Palembang hinterland, a region extending into northern Lampung, and sung in local languages with rhymed verses of longing and love. Smithsonian Folkways' Music of Indonesia vol. 20, Indonesian Guitars, presents it as lagu Batang Hari Sembilan.
items.description: A single singer delivers long, melancholy rhymed verses in a free, ornamented line over a repeating fingerpicked guitar figure that fills the gaps between phrases.
exemplars: Smithsonian Folkways, Music of Indonesia vol. 20: Indonesian Guitars (SFW 40447)

items.name: Urai (Mentawai shamans' and dance songs)
items.lineage: Vocal music of the Mentawai people of Siberut, where singing is the principal kind of music-making: urai sikerei sung by the shaman-healers (sikerei) in curing and other rites, urai turuk dance songs that often depict animals, and songs about daily life and love. Ceremonies and the turuk laggai healing dances are accompanied by gajeuma drums (the generic membrane-drum card stands in).
items.description: Repetitive, chant-like song lines sung solo or together by groups of sikerei alternate with dance episodes in which gajeuma drums keep steady, driving patterns.
exemplars: Smithsonian Folkways, Music of Indonesia vol. 7: Music from the Forests of Riau and Mentawai (SFW 40423)

items.name: Musik panting (Banjar lute ensemble)
items.lineage: Banjar folk ensemble of South Kalimantan named after the panting, a small plucked lute related to the gambus (the oud card stands in); it first accompanied a singer alone and grew into an ensemble with babun drum (the generic membrane-drum card stands in), gong and violin, playing Banjar-language songs for weddings and celebrations. It is represented on Smithsonian Folkways' Music of Indonesia vol. 13, Kalimantan Strings.
items.description: Brisk, bright songs in which the lute's rapid plucked figures and the violin share the melody over a light drum pulse and gong punctuation, with a singer delivering Banjar verses.
exemplars: Smithsonian Folkways, Music of Indonesia vol. 13: Kalimantan Strings (SFW 40429)

items.name: Tingkilan (Kutai Malay pantun song)
items.lineage: Malay song of the Kutai of Tenggarong, East Kalimantan, whose name refers to taunting or answering through pantun; it developed with the coming of Islam to Kutai and is heard at the Erau festival, weddings and other customary occasions. Its original ensemble was a gambus lute (the oud card stands in) and two small ketipung drums (the generic membrane-drum card stands in), later joined by kendang and violin, while singers trade pantun verses in Kutai Malay with each other and with the audience.
items.description: Singers trade witty pantun quatrains over a lively, repeating plucked-lute melody and crisp patterns from the small drums, with the violin doubling the tune.
exemplars: Smithsonian Folkways, Music of Indonesia vol. 13: Kalimantan Strings (SFW 40429)
Tingkilan performances at the Erau festival, Tenggarong

items.name: Madihin (Banjar rhymed verse with terbang)
items.lineage: Banjar oral poetry of South Kalimantan in which one or two performers (pamadihinan) improvise rhymed quatrains, humorous, advisory or topical, while beating a terbang frame drum themselves (the generic frame-drum card stands in); when two perform they answer and tease each other in turn. It is performed at weddings and celebrations and circulates widely on cassette and VCD.
items.description: Fast, rhythmic rhymed verse delivered half-sung on a few repeated pitches, punctuated by the performer's own frame-drum strokes between lines and at each punch line.
exemplars: Banjar cassette and VCD recordings of madihin

items.name: Gamelan Banjar (South Kalimantan gamelan)
items.lineage: Gamelan of the Banjar people of South Kalimantan, tied in local histories to Javanese influence and to the former Banjar court, which accompanies the wayang kulit Banjar shadow play and topeng Banjar masked dance. Tuned in salindro, the Banjar form of slendro, its instruments include sarun metallophones (the saron card stands in), kanung kettle gongs (the kenong card stands in), hanging gongs and the babun drum (the generic membrane-drum card stands in); Smithsonian Folkways' Music of Indonesia vol. 14 includes Banjar wayang music.
items.description: Bright metallophone melody and kettle-gong figures move over a slower cycle of hanging gongs, with the drum leading tempo changes for the shadow-play narration and the masked-dance entrances.
exemplars: Smithsonian Folkways, Music of Indonesia vol. 14: Lombok, Kalimantan, Banyumas (SFW 40441)

items.name: Dayak ritual gong music (Kalimantan tiwah and belian rites)
items.lineage: Gong-and-drum music of the Dayak peoples of Central and East Kalimantan that accompanies the chants and dances of ritual specialists in two major rites: the tiwah, the Ngaju secondary funeral that sends the souls of the dead to the upper world, and the belian healing ceremonies of the Benuaq, led by a shaman. Ensembles combine large hanging bossed gongs (the tawak card stands in), a row of small kettle gongs such as the Benuaq kelentangan (the canang card stands in) and drums (the generic membrane-drum card stands in).
items.description: Repeating patterns on a row of small kettle gongs ring over the deep, pulsing strokes of large hanging gongs and drums, continuing at length while a ritual specialist chants and dances. The texture is loud, metallic and cyclic, with the chanted invocations heard above it.
exemplars: Smithsonian Folkways, Music of Indonesia vol. 17: Kalimantan: Dayak Ritual and Festival Music (SFW 40444)

items.name: Ma'badong (Toraja funeral circle chant)
items.lineage: Funeral song-dance of the Toraja of the South Sulawesi highlands, performed during the rambu solo' funeral feast. Mourners link arms or little fingers in a large circle and step and sway slowly while chanting badong verses that recount the life of the deceased and accompany the soul's departure; the chant is unaccompanied.
items.description: A large circle of voices chants slow, drawn-out phrases together, the melody repeated verse after verse as the dancers sway and step as one. There are no instruments; the sound is sombre, collective and hypnotic.
exemplars: Smithsonian Folkways, Music of Indonesia vol. 18: Sulawesi: Festivals, Funerals, and Work (SFW 40445)

items.name: Pa'pompang (Toraja bamboo band)
items.lineage: Bamboo band of Tana Toraja in South Sulawesi that took shape in the mid-twentieth century as a local adaptation of European wind instruments, introduced through schools and the church, with gospel teachers playing a large part; it has since gained sacred standing as a marker of Torajan identity. Large sets of pompang, blown bamboo tubes of graded sizes made from petung and tallang bamboo (the generic horn card stands in), sound chords under the melody of a few suling bamboo flutes (the generic bamboo-flute card stands in), with a drum (the generic membrane-drum card stands in). Bands play at rambu solo' funerals, rambu tuka' thanksgiving rites and church services.
items.description: Massed bamboo tubes sound sustained chords in a hollow, breathy low and middle register beneath bright bamboo flutes that carry the tune, with a drum keeping steady time as the band plays strophic hymn and song melodies.
exemplars: CREM-CNRS archives: (Toraja) Orchestre de trompes (musik bambu)

items.name: Sinrilik (Makassar sung epic)
items.lineage: Sung narrative of the Makassar people of South Sulawesi, performed by a pasinrilik who sings long verse stories of local heroes and history while accompanying the singing on the keso-keso, a small two-string bowed fiddle (the fiddle card stands in).
items.description: A single narrator sings long, ornamented verse lines, shadowed and answered by short, nasal figures on a small bowed fiddle played by the singer. Delivery moves between declaimed storytelling and sustained melodic cadences.
exemplars: Smithsonian Folkways, Music of Indonesia vol. 15: South Sulawesi Strings (SFW 40442)

items.name: Kacaping (South Sulawesi boat-lute song)
items.lineage: Song accompanied by the kacaping, a two-string plucked boat lute of the Bugis, Makassar and Mandar peoples of South and West Sulawesi, played by the singer or alongside singers for entertainment. A two-string boat-lute card stands in for the kacaping.
items.description: Short, repeated plucked figures on a two-string lute set up a bright, drone-anchored ostinato under a voice singing verse in a freer, ornamented line.
exemplars: Smithsonian Folkways, Music of Indonesia vol. 15: South Sulawesi Strings (SFW 40442)

items.name: Gandrang pakarena (Gowa court dance drumming)
items.lineage: Music of the pakarena, the women's dance of the former Gowa court of the Makassar in South Sulawesi. Two drummers on the gandrang, a double-headed barrel drum struck with a stick and the hand (the Malay gendang card and the generic membrane-drum card stand in), play fast, forceful patterns with the puik-puik shawm (the serunai card stands in) and a gong, while the dancers move with slow, restrained grace; that contrast is the form's hallmark.
items.description: Two drums hammer out loud, rapid interlocking rolls and accents under the piercing, continuous line of a shawm, punctuated by gong strokes, while the dance it accompanies stays slow and composed.
exemplars: Field and festival recordings of gandrang pakarena ensembles from Gowa

items.name: Kolintang (Minahasa wooden xylophone ensemble)
items.lineage: Ensemble of the Minahasa of North Sulawesi built from wooden-keyed xylophones over box resonators, each instrument covering its own register from melody down to bass. Developed in the twentieth century from an older wooden xylophone into a full diatonic band, it plays popular, church and regional songs and accompanies singing. The orchestral xylophone and marimba cards stand in for the higher and lower kolintang instruments.
items.description: Several wooden xylophones in different registers play chords, tremolo melodies and a moving bass line together, giving a bright, woody, quickly decaying sound that rolls through popular and church tunes in strict time.
exemplars: Regional cassette and festival recordings of Minahasa kolintang ensembles

items.name: Musik bambu (Minahasa bamboo band)
items.lineage: Village wind bands of the Minahasa of North Sulawesi, modelled on European brass and wind bands and built from local bamboo. Types include musik bambu melulu, played on bamboo flutes alone; musik bambu klarinet, led by bamboo clarinets (the clarinet card stands in); and musik bambu seng, whose horns are shaped from sheet zinc in imitation of brass (the generic horn card stands in). Large bamboo bass horns underpin the bands, which play marches, hymns and popular songs at festivals and community events.
items.description: A bamboo wind band plays marches and hymn-like tunes in block harmony: flutes or reedy bamboo clarinets carry the melody over the thick, hollow pulse of large bamboo bass horns, with a breathy, woody band sound.
exemplars: Field and festival recordings of Minahasa musik bambu bands

items.name: Maengket (Minahasa harvest dance-song)
items.lineage: Group dance-song of the Minahasa of North Sulawesi in which lines of men and women sing and dance under a leader, accompanied by a tambur drum (the generic membrane-drum card stands in). It is performed in three parts: maowey kamberu, thanksgiving for the rice harvest; marambak, the consecration of a new house; and lalayaan, a dance of young people's courtship.
items.description: A leader's sung phrases are answered by the full group of dancers in unison or simple parts, over a steady drum beat that marks the dance steps.
exemplars: Regional cassette and festival recordings of Minahasa maengket groups

items.name: Masamper (Sangihe choral song)
items.lineage: Group singing tradition of the Sangihe and Talaud islands of North Sulawesi whose name derives from the Dutch zangvereniging (singing society); it grew from older local song and the diatonic hymn singing brought by Christian missions. Groups led by a conductor sing in parts and answer one another in turn (mebawalase), with movement, at community gatherings and in formal competitions.
items.description: Unaccompanied voices sing strophic songs in chordal parts, with groups trading verses back and forth in reply; performances add movement and a competitive, projected delivery.
exemplars: Regional cassette and VCD recordings of Sangihe masamper groups

items.name: Sasando (Rote tube-zither music)
items.lineage: Music of the sasando, a tube zither of Rote island in East Nusa Tenggara: strings stretched around a bamboo tube are plucked with both hands inside a fan-shaped resonator of folded lontar palm leaf (the valiha tube-zither card stands in). The older sasando gong, with fewer strings in a pentatonic tuning, accompanies traditional songs and dances, while the sasando biola, with many more strings, plays diatonic melodies with chords.
items.description: Plucked metal strings ring inside a palm-leaf resonator with a bright, harp-like shimmer, the player's two hands interleaving melody, bass notes and arpeggiated chords.
exemplars: Kupang cassette recordings of sasando music

items.name: Gong waning (Sikka gong-and-drum ensemble)
items.lineage: Struck percussion ensemble of the Sikka region around Maumere in eastern Flores, made up of waning drums (the generic membrane-drum card stands in), a set of gongs (the gong card stands in) and the peli anak, also called saur (the auxiliary-percussion card stands in). It accompanies dance in customary sacred rites and at festive entertainment.
items.description: Interlocking gong patterns ring over driving drum rhythms in a tight, repeating cycle that carries the dancers, with a smaller struck part adding a crisp pulse.
exemplars: Smithsonian Folkways, Music of Indonesia vol. 8: Vocal and Instrumental Music from East and Central Flores (SFW 40424)

items.name: Jungga songs (Sumba lute song)
items.lineage: Song of the island of Sumba in East Nusa Tenggara accompanied by the jungga, a small plucked lute with few strings, played by the singer or by a partner (a two-string boat-lute card stands in).
items.description: A solo voice sings verse over short repeated figures on a small, twangy plucked lute, in an intimate, sparse texture.
exemplars: Smithsonian Folkways, Music of Indonesia vol. 16: Music from the Southeast: Sumbawa, Sumba, Timor (SFW 40443)

items.name: Tifa totobuang (Ambon gong-chime and drum ensemble)
items.lineage: Ensemble of Ambon and the central Moluccas that pairs the totobuang, a set of small kettle gongs laid in a wooden frame (the bonang card stands in), with tifa drums of several sizes (the generic membrane-drum card stands in) and a large hanging gong. It accompanies dances, welcomes and other customary and festive occasions.
items.description: Bright, ringing kettle-gong patterns repeat over interlocking drum parts in several registers, with deep gong strokes marking the cycle; the music is fast, loud and dance-driven.
exemplars: Field and festival recordings of Ambonese tifa totobuang ensembles

items.name: Wor (Biak ceremonial song)
items.lineage: Ceremonial song of the Biak people of Biak and the neighbouring islands of Papua, sung at life-cycle rites and feasts. Songs pass between a lead singer and a responding group and are often accompanied by single-headed hourglass drums (the kundu card, a related New Guinea drum, stands in).
items.description: A soloist's sung lines are taken up and answered by a group, over the steady beat of hand-held hourglass drums.
exemplars: Smithsonian Folkways, Music of Indonesia vol. 10: Music of Biak, Irian Jaya: Wor, Church Songs, Yospan (SFW 40426)

items.name: Yospan (Papuan string-band dance music)
items.lineage: Popular social dance music of Papua whose name joins two dances, yosim and pancar. Bands of guitars and ukuleles with a bass and tifa hourglass drums (the kundu card stands in) accompany singers and lines of dancers at celebrations and festivals.
items.description: Bright strummed guitars and ukuleles drive a fast, bouncing dance rhythm over a plucked bass and hand drums, with group vocals singing short, repeated verses and refrains.
exemplars: Smithsonian Folkways, Music of Indonesia vol. 10: Music of Biak, Irian Jaya: Wor, Church Songs, Yospan (SFW 40426)

items.name: Qasidah modern (Indonesian Islamic pop bands)
items.lineage: Indonesian popular form of Islamic song that grew out of rebana frame-drum qasidah singing into amplified bands from the 1970s, with Indonesian-language lyrics of moral and religious message. The all-woman group Nasida Ria, founded in Semarang in 1975, became its best-known cassette act. Bands keep the rebana frame drums (the credited frame-drum card stands in) beside electric guitar, bass and keyboards.
items.description: Women's voices sing catchy, lightly ornamented melodies in unison and in leader-and-chorus exchanges over rebana frame-drum patterns, with electric guitar, bass and keyboard filling out a bright, danceable band arrangement.

items.name: Orkes gambus (Hadhrami-Malay gambus song)
items.lineage: Song tradition of the Arab-descended, largely Hadhrami communities of Indonesia and the Malay peninsula, named for the gambus, a short-necked lute of the oud family (the oud card stands in). Orkes gambus bands set Arabic and Malay lyrics for voice with gambus, violin and small marwas hand drums (the generic hand-drum card stands in), and play for weddings, community celebrations and the zapin dance; mid-twentieth-century bands recorded widely.
items.description: A solo singer delivers ornamented, Arabic-inflected melodies, doubled and answered by plucked lute and violin, over lively interlocking hand-drum rhythms suited to dancing.

items.name: Funkot (Jakarta funky kota house)
items.lineage: Fast club dance music from the discotheques of the Kota district of old Jakarta, its name a contraction of funky kota, which took shape around the turn of the 2000s. DJs and producers rework dangdut, Indonesian pop and dance hits over a hard four-on-the-floor house beat at very high tempos; the style spread through DJ mixes and VCD and MP3 compilations and later fed bedroom remix idioms.
items.description: A pounding four-on-the-floor kick at breakneck tempo drives a rapid off-beat bass, fast hi-hats and shrill synth leads, while chopped vocal hooks from familiar songs loop over the top.
exemplars: Jakarta discotheque funkot DJ mixes and VCD/MP3 compilations (2000s)

items.name: Wayang kulit Kelantan (Malay shadow-play music)
items.lineage: Music of the Kelantanese shadow play (wayang kulit Kelantan, formerly called wayang Siam), in which a single tok dalang voices every puppet and narrates the Hikayat Maharaja Wana (Ramayana) repertoire while directing the ensemble. The troupe plays serunai shawm, a pair of gedombak goblet drums (the generic membrane-drum card stands in), paired gendang and geduk barrel drums, a pair of canang kettle gongs, kesi cymbals and a pair of hanging tetawak gongs.
items.description: A nasal, ornamented serunai line rides over interlocking goblet and barrel drums and a cycle punctuated by kettle gongs and deep hanging gongs, while the dalang alternates declaimed narration, puppet voices and short sung passages. Tempo and density shift abruptly on the dalang's cues for fights and processions.
exemplars: Patricia Matusky's documentation of Kelantan wayang kulit music (Malaysian Shadow Play and Music, 1993)
Recordings of the troupe of dalang Dollah Baju Merah, Kelantan

items.name: Nobat (Malay royal court ensemble)
items.lineage: Royal ceremonial ensemble of the Malay sultanates, held as regalia and played only for coronations, installations and other court rites; it survives in Kedah, Terengganu, Perak and Selangor and in Brunei. The core ensemble is the nehara kettledrum (a Persian-Indian naqareh card stands in), a pair of gendang nobat barrel drums, the serunai shawm and the long silver nafiri trumpet, with a gong in the Kedah ensemble.
items.description: Slow, solemn ceremonial pieces in which a wailing, heavily ornamented serunai melody and long held calls of the nafiri sit over a steady pattern of kettledrum and barrel-drum strokes and widely spaced gong beats. The texture is sparse, loud and outdoor-projecting rather than dance-driven.
exemplars: Kedah royal nobat ensemble, Balai Nobat, Alor Setar
Archival recordings of the Kedah and Terengganu royal nobat ensembles

items.name: Gamelan Melayu (Terengganu court gamelan)
items.lineage: Malay court gamelan that reached the Pahang court from Riau-Lingga in the nineteenth century and was later kept at the Terengganu palace to accompany joget gamelan dance. Revived for public and university ensembles from the late 1960s with Mubin Sheppard's documentation, it is tuned to a five-tone slendro-type scale and uses a keromong kettle-gong row (the bonang card stands in), saron metallophones, kenong, hanging gongs and a two-headed gendang.
items.description: Bronze metallophones carry the melody in a steady pulse while the kettle-gong row elaborates it and large hanging gongs mark the end of each cycle. A hand-played gendang leads tempo changes, giving a light, dance-oriented texture.
exemplars: Gamelan Melayu ensemble recordings of Akademi Seni (ASWARA) and UiTM
Mubin Sheppard documentation of the Terengganu palace gamelan

items.name: Ghazal Melayu (Johor Malay ghazal)
items.lineage: Malay ghazal as it took shape in Johor, where it has flourished since the late nineteenth century. Sung Malay verse is accompanied by harmonium, tabla, gambus lute (the oud card stands in), violin and maracas, often with guitar and tambourine, the gambus and harmonium reflecting Arab and Indian links.
items.description: A lyrical, ornamented solo voice sings Malay quatrains over a gently swaying tabla pattern and maracas, with harmonium chords and violin and gambus lines doubling and answering the melody. Moods are tender and nostalgic rather than virtuosic.
exemplars: Kumpulan Ghazal Pak Lomak LP and cassette recordings, Johor

items.name: Dondang sayang (Malacca pantun love song)
items.lineage: Malay love-song tradition of Malacca, shared by Malay and Baba-Nyonya (Peranakan Chinese) communities, in which singers trade improvised pantun quatrains in a slow, ornamented melody. It is accompanied by violin, rebana frame drums (the kompang card stands in) and a gong, and was inscribed on UNESCO's Representative List in 2018.
items.description: Two singers answer each other with witty or tender rhymed quatrains in a slow, melismatic line, while violin shadows the voice heterophonically over a soft frame-drum pattern and a recurring gong stroke. Applause and laughter follow well-turned verses.
exemplars: Baba-Nyonya and Malay dondang sayang recordings from Malacca (UNESCO RL 2018 documentation)

items.name: Boria (Penang sketch-and-chorus song)
items.lineage: Penang popular theatre-song form rooted in nineteenth-century Muharram street performance, now staged as a comic sketch followed by songs. A tukang karang (lead singer and lyricist) sings topical verses answered by a dancing chorus, accompanied by violins, gambus lute (the oud card stands in), tabla and marwas hand drums (the membrane-drum card stands in), often with accordion, cymbals and harmonica as well.
items.description: A lead singer delivers topical, often humorous verses and a uniformed chorus answers in unison while dancing, over a brisk, regular drum groove with violin and gambus carrying the tune. Songs are short, strophic and catchy.
exemplars: Tan Sooi Beng documentation of Penang boria

items.name: Pop yeh-yeh (1960s Malay kugiran beat)
items.lineage: Malay-language guitar-band music of Singapore and Malaysia in the mid to late 1960s, when kugiran (guitar groups) inspired by British beat and instrumental guitar bands backed singers such as A. Ramlie, Jeffrydin and M. Osman. It was issued mainly on EP records and declined by the early 1970s.
items.description: Bright, twangy lead guitar riffs and clean strummed rhythm guitar over a busy beat drummer and bass, with an earnest Malay vocal and group backing vocals on the choruses. Songs are short, upbeat and dance-oriented.
exemplars: Sublime Frequencies compilation of 1960s Singapore and Malaysian pop yeh-yeh

items.name: Main puteri (Malay healing séance music)
items.lineage: Malay shamanic healing performance of Kelantan and Terengganu in which a bomoh or tok puteri enters trance to identify and placate the spirits troubling a patient. The tok minduk, playing the rebab, sings and converses with the shaman and the spirits, accompanied by a pair of gendang drums and a pair of tetawak hanging gongs.
items.description: A rasping rebab plays repeated melodic phrases while the rebab player and the entranced shaman exchange sung and half-spoken lines, over insistent drum patterns and gong strokes that intensify as the trance deepens. Long sessions alternate calm dialogue with driving, accelerating passages.
exemplars: Carol Laderman's documentation of main peteri seances in Terengganu (Taming the Wind of Desire, 1991)

items.name: Mek mulung (Kedah folk theatre)
items.lineage: Malay folk dance-drama of northwest Kedah, kept chiefly by the troupe of Kampung Wang Tepus near Jitra. Its largely percussive orchestra of rebana frame drums (the kompang card stands in), gong and kecerek concussion sticks is led melodically by a small serunai, and performances open with the bertabuh ritual in which all instruments sound together. Mek mulung was inscribed on UNESCO's Urgent Safeguarding List in 2023.
items.description: Sung and spoken story scenes alternate with dance episodes over layered frame-drum patterns, gong punctuation and dry clicking sticks, while a thin, piercing serunai carries the only melody. The sound is rustic and close, with performers answering the lead singer in chorus.
exemplars: Mek mulung troupe of Kampung Wang Tepus, Jitra (UNESCO Urgent Safeguarding List 2023)

items.name: Kertok (Kelantan coconut xylophone ensemble)
items.lineage: Kelantanese ensemble of kertok kelapa, each a single wooden bar laid across a hollowed coconut shell resonator and struck with a padded beater, played by groups at festivals, receptions and competitions. The gabbang bamboo-xylophone card stands in for the coconut-resonated kertok.
items.description: Massed wooden strokes with a hollow, resonant clack ring out in fast, repeating rhythmic patterns that build in speed and volume. The texture is percussive and bright rather than melodic.
exemplars: Kelantanese kertok ensemble recordings documented in Matusky and Tan, The Music of Malaysia (2004)

items.name: Rebana ubi (Kelantan giant-drum ensemble)
items.lineage: Kelantanese ensemble of rebana ubi, very large single-headed drums with hide heads laced and wedged to the body, once used for signalling and now played by village teams at harvest celebrations, official welcomes and inter-village competitions. Teams of drummers combine distinct rhythmic parts into interlocking patterns.
items.description: Deep, booming open strokes and sharp slaps from a row of giant drums lock into dense interlocking patterns that accelerate and swell toward a thunderous climax. Played outdoors, the sound carries over long distances.
exemplars: Kelantan rebana ubi festival and competition recordings

items.name: Gendang silat (Malay martial-arts drum ensemble)
items.lineage: Ensemble that accompanies displays of Malay silat, especially at weddings and ceremonies on the Malay Peninsula: a pair of gendang barrel drums (gendang ibu and gendang anak) interlock under a serunai shawm, with a hanging gong marking the cycle. Silat was inscribed on UNESCO's Representative List for Malaysia in 2019.
items.description: Two hand-played barrel drums lock into a driving interlocking pattern under a nasal, continuously ornamented serunai melody, with a gong stroke closing each short cycle. Tempo follows the fighters, from slow stalking movements to fast exchanges.
exemplars: Silat performance recordings documented in UNESCO's 2019 Silat nomination (Malaysia)

items.name: Temiar dream songs (Orang Asli healing ceremonies)
items.lineage: Songs of the Temiar, an Orang Asli people of the Kelantan and Perak interior, received in dreams from spirit guides and sung by mediums at night-long healing ceremonies. The medium sings each line and a chorus of women answers it while beating pairs of bamboo tube stampers (the tagunggak card stands in) against a log.
items.description: A soft, steady two-tone pulse of bamboo tubes underlies a medium's short melodic phrases, each echoed by a chorus of women's voices in overlapping response. The repetition is hypnotic and unhurried, set against the sounds of the surrounding forest night.
exemplars: Smithsonian Folkways SFW 40417, Dream Songs and Healing Sounds in the Rainforests of Malaysia (Marina Roseman)

items.name: Magagung (Kadazandusun gong ensemble)
items.lineage: Gong ensembles of the Kadazandusun of Sabah's west coast and interior, played for the sumazau dance, the Kaamatan harvest festival and weddings. Several large and medium hanging bossed gongs (the tawak and gong cards stand in), each with its own pattern, interlock over a large drum (the generic membrane-drum card stands in).
items.description: Interlocking strokes on deep and mid-pitched bossed gongs build a repeating, ringing rhythmic texture over a steady drum beat, with long overlapping decays. The pattern is stable and dance-paced, swelling when dancers join.
exemplars: Jacqueline Pugh-Kitingan field recordings of Kadazandusun gong music, Sabah

items.name: Sompoton (Kadazandusun gourd mouth organ)
items.lineage: Music of the sompoton, the Kadazandusun gourd mouth organ of Sabah, made of bamboo pipes with free reeds set into a dried gourd wind chest and associated especially with Tambunan. It is played solo or to accompany dancing; the Iban engkerurai card, a closely related gourd mouth organ, stands in.
items.description: A soft, reedy chord cluster sounds continuously as the player breathes in and out, with a short melody moving above sustained chord tones in repeating dance-length phrases. The tone is hushed, buzzing and intimate.
exemplars: Sabah field recordings of sompoton players (Pugh-Kitingan)

items.name: Taboh (Iban gong-and-drum music)
items.lineage: Taboh, the gong-and-drum music of the Iban of Sarawak, also referred to as gendang (as in gendang rayah), played for the ngajat dance and at Gawai Dayak and other festivals and rites. The ensemble combines the engkerumong, a rack of small bossed gongs (the canang kettle-gong card stands in), the large tawak and the smaller bebendai hanging gongs (the gong card stands in for bebendai) and the ketebung or dumba drum (the generic membrane-drum card stands in).
items.description: A row of small gongs rings out a quick repeating figure against interlocking strokes on large and small hanging gongs and a driving drum pattern. The sound is bright, metallic and festive, built for dancing in the longhouse gallery.
exemplars: Sarawak Museum and Radio Sarawak archival recordings of Iban gong music

items.name: Ngiup suling and ngiup bas (Lun Bawang bamboo band)
items.lineage: Bamboo band of the Lun Bawang of Lawas and Ba Kelalan in northern Sarawak, made up of bamboo flutes (ngiup suling) and large bamboo bass horns (ngiup bas) modelled on brass-band instruments, and played at church occasions and festivals such as Irau Aco Lun Bawang. The source-unspecified bamboo-flute card stands in for the flutes and the source-unspecified horns card for the bamboo bass horns.
items.description: Massed breathy bamboo flutes carry the melody over the buzzing, hollow tones of large bamboo bass horns marking the beat. The sound is airy and festive, carried outdoors in procession.
exemplars: The Lun Bawang Bamboo Band Ensemble (UNIMAS institutional repository study)
Bamboo band performances at Irau Aco Lun Bawang, Lawas

items.name: Branyo (Kristang Portuguese-Eurasian dance song)
items.lineage: Social dance song of the Kristang, the Portuguese-Eurasian community of the Portuguese Settlement in Malacca, sung in the Kristang creole with verses traded between singers, as in the well-known Jinkli Nona. It is accompanied by violin, guitar and a rabana frame drum (the source-unspecified pandero card stands in), and is closely related to the Malay joget.
items.description: A lively violin tune and strummed guitar ride a bouncing frame-drum rhythm while singers exchange playful verses and the gathering joins the refrain. The feel is informal, quick and made for couple dancing.
exemplars: Kristang community recordings of Jinkli Nona
Margaret Sarkissian, D'Albuquerque's Children: Performing Tradition in Malaysia's Portuguese Settlement (2000)

items.name: 24 Festive Drums (Malaysian Chinese drum troupe)
items.lineage: Malaysian Chinese drum genre (ershisi jieling gu) created in Johor Bahru in 1988 by Tan Hooi Song and Tan Chai Puan, in which troupes beat twenty-four large drums named for the twenty-four solar terms of the Chinese calendar with choreographed movement. It spread through Chinese schools and associations across Malaysia; the generic membrane-drum card stands in for the large barrel drums.
items.description: Massed large drums struck with sticks in tightly synchronised unison patterns, with sudden accents and dynamic swells shaped by the choreography. The sound is loud, booming and precise.
exemplars: Johor Bahru 24 Festive Drums troupe performance recordings

items.name: Darangen (Maranao epic chant)
items.lineage: Epic of the Maranao of Lake Lanao in Mindanao, some 72,000 lines in seventeen cycles centred on the hero Bantugan, chanted in Maranao by specialist singers over several nights at weddings and celebrations. It was proclaimed a UNESCO Masterpiece in 2005 and inscribed on the Representative List in 2008.
items.description: A solo unaccompanied voice chants long narrative lines in free rhythm, phrase by phrase, with held tones at phrase ends. The delivery is unhurried and declamatory, sustained over hours.
exemplars: Maranao chanter field recordings (UNESCO Representative List 2008 documentation)

items.name: Gangsa (Cordillera flat-gong ensemble)
items.lineage: Ensemble music of handheld flat bronze gongs (gangsa) played by men among the Kalinga, Bontoc, Ifugao, Kankanaey and Ibaloi of the Cordillera in northern Luzon, for weddings, peace pacts, harvest feasts and other community rites. Two playing styles are documented: topayya, in which seated players strike gongs resting on their laps with the palms, and pattong or palook, in which players strike gongs with sticks while dancing in a line. The gong_tamtam card stands in for the gangsa; the drum card stands in for the drums some Benguet ensembles add.
items.description: Several flat gongs, each sounding its own short ostinato, interlock into a bright, ringing composite rhythm that repeats for long stretches under dancing, with palm-damped or stick-struck strokes.
exemplars: José Maceda / UP Center for Ethnomusicology field recordings of Cordillera gangsa ensembles

items.name: Ullalim (Kalinga epic chant)
items.lineage: Sung epic of the Kalinga of the Cordillera in northern Luzon, chanted by a solo singer at peace-pact (bodong) gatherings, weddings and other social occasions. Its episodes recount the deeds and courtships of figures such as Banna and Laggunawa. It is distinct from the hudhud of the neighbouring Ifugao.
items.description: A single unaccompanied voice chants long narrative verses to a narrow, repeating melodic formula, with no instrumental support.
exemplars: UP Center for Ethnomusicology field recordings of Kalinga ullalim

items.name: Salidummay (Cordillera communal song)
items.lineage: Communal song of the Kalinga and neighbouring Cordillera peoples of northern Luzon, named for its vocable refrains (salidummay, dong-dong-ay), sung by groups at gatherings, celebrations and work, with new verses set to familiar tunes. Cordillera activist and popular singers have since adopted the form for new songs, often with guitar.
items.description: Groups sing a simple, repeating strophic tune whose verses alternate with a familiar vocable refrain, in an easy, steady pulse and plain unison.
exemplars: Cordillera activist and popular recordings of salidummay songs

items.name: Pala'wan basal and kusyapi (southern Palawan highlands)
items.lineage: Music of the Pala'wan of the southern Palawan highlands: the basal ensemble of hanging bossed gongs with a drum, played at rice-wine feasts and rituals; the two-string kusyapi boat lute, played solo; and the tultul epic, chanted through the night by a bard. The kutiyapi card stands in for the kusyapi, and the gong card (bossed) for the basal gongs.
items.description: Hanging bossed gongs and a drum lock into repeating interlocking patterns for feasting, while the boat lute plays a buzzing drone-and-melody line and the epic singer chants long narrative phrases.
exemplars: Nicole Revel and José Maceda field recordings of Pala'wan highland music

items.name: T'boli hegelong and s'ludoy (Lake Sebu)
items.lineage: Instrumental and sung music of the T'boli of Lake Sebu in South Cotabato, Mindanao, centred on the hegelong, a two-string boat lute with one melody and one drone string, and the s'ludoy, a bamboo tube zither whose strings are cut from the bamboo skin, alongside the kumbing jaw harp and the t'nonggong drum. The kutiyapi card stands in for the hegelong, valiha for the s'ludoy and the drum card for the t'nonggong.
items.description: A two-string boat lute plays a repeated, ornamented melody over a drone string, answered by the soft plucked chime of a bamboo tube zither, with an occasional drum and voice.
exemplars: Field recordings of T'boli hegelong and s'ludoy music, Lake Sebu

items.name: Buklog (Subanen thanksgiving ritual)
items.lineage: Thanksgiving ritual system of the Subanen of the Zamboanga Peninsula, Mindanao, inscribed by UNESCO in 2019 on the List of Intangible Cultural Heritage in Need of Urgent Safeguarding. The community builds a springy, trampoline-like platform (buklogan) of dulugan wood bound with rattan; as it sags under the dancers, a pole beneath it (phetaw) strikes a half-buried hollowed log with a booming sound, while agong and kulintang gong music is played. The foot_stomp card (hollow platform) stands in for the platform and log resonator, and the gong card (bossed) for the agong and kulintang gongs.
items.description: Deep booms from a pole striking a hollow log, as dancers bounce the platform, pulse under repeating agong and kulintang gong patterns, amid the noise of a community dancing outdoors.
exemplars: UNESCO Urgent Safeguarding List documentation of the Subanen buklog (2019)

items.name: Tausug gabbang and sindil (Sulu sung repertoire)
items.lineage: Sung repertoire of the Tausug of Jolo and the Sulu Archipelago in which the gabbang bamboo xylophone, often joined by the biola (violin), accompanies songs such as the sindil, a bantering sung exchange between a man and a woman. The religious and moral chants lugu and tarasul are sung unaccompanied. The fiddle card stands in for the biola.
items.description: A bamboo xylophone keeps up a running, ornamented accompaniment with a violin doubling the tune, while two singers trade witty, melismatic verses back and forth.
exemplars: Ricardo Trimillos field recordings of Tausug music, Jolo

items.name: Kutiyapi (Maguindanao and Maranao boat-lute music)
items.lineage: Solo repertoire of the kutiyapi, the two-string fretted boat lute of the Maguindanao and Maranao of Mindanao, in which one string carries the melody while the other drones; it is played outside the kulintang gong ensemble, alongside other solo instruments such as the kubing jaw harp and the palendag bamboo flute. The bamboo flute card stands in for the palendag.
items.description: A twangy two-string boat lute spins fast, ornamented melodies over a steady drone, sometimes answered by a buzzing bamboo jaw harp or a breathy bamboo flute.
exemplars: Folkways FE 4536 Music of the Magindanao in the Philippines (José Maceda)
Samaon Sulaiman, Maguindanao kutiyapi master (GAMABA awardee)

items.name: Kwintangan kayu (Yakan hanging-log xylophone)
items.lineage: Music of the kwintangan kayu of the Yakan of Basilan: five wooden beams hung horizontally one above another in order of pitch and struck at the edge with beaters. It is played only during the rice-growing season and is said to make the rice happy. The gabbang card (Yakan form, small five-to-nine-key size) stands in for the hanging logs.
items.description: Five hanging logs, struck at their edges, ring out hollow, woody pitches in short repeating patterns in the open air of the fields.
exemplars: UP Center for Ethnomusicology field recordings of Yakan music, Basilan

items.name: Agung ensembles (Lumad hanging-gong music of Mindanao)
items.lineage: Ensembles of large suspended bossed gongs (agung) among non-Muslim Mindanao peoples such as the Bagobo, Manobo and Tiruray (Teduray), in which several players each sound one or two gongs in interlocking patterns, sometimes with a drum, for rituals, festivities and dances. They differ from the kulintang tradition, which leads with a row of small gongs. The gong card (bossed) stands in for the agung.
items.description: Deep, booming hanging gongs, each repeating its own short figure, interlock into a dense rolling pulse over a drum, with long resonant decays.
exemplars: José Maceda field recordings of Mindanao agung ensembles

items.name: Laji (Ivatan lyric song)
items.lineage: Lyric song of the Ivatan of the Batanes islands, the northernmost Philippines: short poetic songs about love, the sea, hardship and island life, sung unaccompanied, often by elders, at work and at social gatherings.
items.description: An unaccompanied voice sings slow, intimate lyric verses with lengthened phrase endings and gentle ornaments.
exemplars: NCCA documentation and field recordings of Ivatan laji, Batanes

items.name: Pabasa ng Pasyon (Tagalog Holy Week chanted Passion)
items.lineage: Lenten tradition of Tagalog and other lowland Catholic communities in which the pasyon, a verse narrative of the life and Passion of Christ in five-line stanzas of eight-syllable lines, is chanted continuously by relays of singers, day and night, during Holy Week before a home altar or chapel. Singers set the stanzas to many inherited tunes, and some groups add guitar accompaniment.
items.description: Pairs or small groups of untrained voices take turns chanting stanza after stanza of narrative verse to a repeating strophic tune, nasal and full-voiced, for hours on end.
exemplars: Tagalog cassette recordings of pabasa ng pasyon
Field recordings of Holy Week pabasa

items.name: Sarswela (Filipino zarzuela)
items.lineage: Filipino vernacular musical theatre adapted from the Spanish zarzuela in the late 19th century and flourishing in Tagalog, Ilocano, Cebuano and other languages in the early 20th century, alternating spoken dialogue with songs, duets and choruses accompanied by a small orchestra, often on domestic, social and patriotic themes. The fiddle card stands in for the orchestra's violins.
items.description: Lyrical solo songs, duets and choruses in the vernacular over a small theatre orchestra led by violins, with clarinet and piano, framed by spoken scenes.
exemplars: Walang Sugat (Severino Reyes and Fulgencio Tolentino) revival productions

items.name: Balitaw (Visayan sung courtship debate)
items.lineage: Courtship song-and-dance of the Visayas, especially Cebu and Bohol, in which a man and a woman trade improvised sung verses, the man wooing and the woman parrying, accompanied by guitar and sometimes bandurria or other string instruments.
items.description: A man and a woman alternate playful improvised verses over a lilting strummed guitar, with a bandurria filling between stanzas.

items.name: Dung-aw (Ilocano funeral lament)
items.lineage: Improvised chanted lament of the Ilocano of northern Luzon, sung over the body of the dead during the wake, usually by women of the family, who address the deceased, recall their life and voice the grief of the bereaved.
items.description: A lone, weeping voice chants free-rhythm phrases of address to the dead, falling at each line end, between sobs and spoken asides.
exemplars: UP Center for Ethnomusicology field recordings of Ilocano dung-aw

items.name: Subli (Batangas Holy Cross devotional dance)
items.lineage: Catholic devotional dance of Bauan and Alitagtag, Batangas, performed as a prayer to the Holy Cross at the feast of the Mahal na Poon in May by paired men and women dancers (manunubli). It has no melodic instruments: drums beat throughout, punctuated by wooden castanets (kalaste) clacked by the men, and women may open with a chant narrating the finding of the cross in archaic metaphorical Tagalog. The castanets card stands in for the kalaste.
items.description: A steady, unpitched drum beat with sharp wooden clacks drives the dance, opened by a plain chant sung by women.
exemplars: Ramon Obusan documentation of the Batangas subli

items.name: Banda (Philippine town brass band)
items.lineage: Civic brass bands of Philippine towns, rooted in Spanish-era and American-period military and parish bands, that play at fiestas, processions, funerals and band contests, with marches, pasodobles and arrangements of kundiman and popular songs; Bulacan, Malabon and Batangas towns keep long-standing bands. Bamboo bands (musikong bumbong), whose bamboo instruments imitate the brass band's, belong to the same town tradition.
items.description: A full-voiced street band of cornets, clarinets, saxophones, trombones and sousaphone plays bright marches and song arrangements over snare and bass drum, heard in the open air of a town fiesta or procession.

items.name: Budots (Davao street dance music)
items.lineage: Electronic dance music and dance craze from Davao City, named from Bisaya slang for a slacker or idle youth, built on house music and the tangonggo rhythms of the Sama-Bajau. Sherwin Tuna (DJ Love), a choreographer working in an internet cafe, turned the street dance into a musical genre in the late 2000s, producing tracks and remixes on home computer software for neighbourhood dance crews. The DAW source cards stand in for that software production.
items.description: A fast, hypnotic dance beat (around 140 bpm) built on heavy looped percussion and a hypnotic bass, with high-pitched whistle hooks and samples of everyday city noises.

items.name: Likurai (Timorese women's drum dance)
items.lineage: Drum dance of Covalima (Suai) and neighbouring areas of southern Timor-Leste, originally performed by women to welcome warriors returning from battle and now danced at ceremonies and celebrations, in which women dancers beat small babadok drums held under the arm while dancing. It is distinct from the linked-arm tebe song-dance.
items.description: Many small hand drums beaten together lock into a fast, insistent dance rhythm, crisp and dry, with accents shifting as the dancers move.
exemplars: Field recordings of likurai drum dance, Covalima
UNESCO ichLinks video documentation of likurai, Timor-Leste

items.name: Heer gayaki (Punjabi qissa singing)
items.lineage: Sung recitation of the Punjabi qissa verse romances, above all Waris Shah's 18th-century Heer, alongside Mirza-Sahiban and Sassi-Punnu, in which a solo singer delivers the couplets to traditional melodies associated with each poem. After 1947 EMI Pakistan records and Radio Pakistan carried the style to mass audiences, and the Lok Virsa archive holds recordings. The chimta card stands in for the jingled fire-tongs some singers play while singing.
items.description: A single high, carrying voice draws out the long, ornamented phrases of each couplet over a sustained reed-organ line, often in free rhythm, with jingled tongs adding a metallic pulse in some performances.
exemplars: Lok Virsa archive recordings of Heer singing

items.name: Dhamal (Sufi shrine drumming of Pakistan)
items.lineage: Ecstatic devotional drumming and dance at Sufi shrines of Pakistan, above all the evening dhamal at the shrine of Lal Shahbaz Qalandar in Sehwan Sharif, Sindh, and the Thursday-night gatherings at the shrine of Shah Jamal in Lahore. Dhol and naqqara drums drive devotees into whirling, head-tossing dance, with chanted invocations of the saint. The naqareh card, in its large naqqar-khana size, stands in for the shrine naqqara kettledrums.
items.description: Thunderous double-headed drums pound a driving, cyclic rhythm over the boom of kettledrums, while a crowd shouts devotional invocations and dances toward trance.
exemplars: Gunga Sain — dhol at the shrine of Shah Jamal, Lahore
Lok Virsa field recordings of dhamal

items.name: Lollywood film song (Pakistani film playback)
items.lineage: Playback song of the Urdu and Punjabi film industry centred on the studios of Lahore after 1947, composed by music directors such as Khurshid Anwar and Nisar Bazmi, sung by playback singers including Noor Jehan, Ahmed Rushdi, Mehdi Hassan and Mala, and issued on EMI Pakistan records. It developed separately from the Bombay film-song industry.
items.description: A bright, ornamented lead playback voice sings strophic film songs over a studio orchestra of bowed strings, plucked lute, flute, reed organ and hand drums, with instrumental interludes between verses.
exemplars: Noor Jehan — Lollywood film songs (EMI Pakistan)
Film scores of music director Khurshid Anwar

items.name: Ginan (Nizari Ismaili devotional hymns)
items.lineage: Devotional hymns of the Nizari Ismaili Satpanth tradition attributed to pirs such as Pir Shams, Pir Sadr al-Din and Pir Hasan Kabir al-Din, composed in Sindhi, Gujarati, Punjabi, Hindi and related languages and sung in jamatkhanas of Sindh, Gujarat and the diaspora. Ginans are sung by individual reciters, with the congregation often joining in; a jamatkhana cassette tradition preserves the repertoire in recordings, and Ali Asani has studied it.
items.description: A lead voice sings strophic devotional verses to a steady, lyrical melody, without instruments, and the gathered congregation often joins the refrains in unison.

items.name: Sheedi goma (Afro-Pakistani drum song of Karachi)
items.lineage: Music of the Sheedi, Pakistanis of East African descent concentrated in Karachi's Lyari and in coastal Sindh and Makran, heard above all at the annual Sheedi Mela at the shrine of Pir Mangho in Manghopir. Songs are sung over drums of African lineage such as the mugarman and musindo; lewa is a related Afro-Baloch dance of the Makran coast. The drum cards stand in for the mugarman and musindo.
items.description: Large and small drums lock into a heavy, repeating dance rhythm while a group of singers chants short refrains over them.
exemplars: Lok Virsa documentation of Sheedi Mela music, Manghopir

items.name: Kalasha festival song and drum dance (Chitral valleys)
items.lineage: Songs and drum dances of the Kalasha of the Bumburet, Rumbur and Birir valleys of Chitral, central to their religion and performed at festivals such as Chilam Joshi in spring and Chaumos at the winter solstice, and at funerals. Women dance in linked semicircles and lines around the drummers in dances such as dushak, cha and drazhailak, while men and women sing. The drum card stands in for the Kalasha drums.
items.description: Groups of voices sing short repeating song phrases while drummers at the centre of the dancers keep a steady beat, the tempo changing with each dance from slow lines to fast circling.
exemplars: Kalasha Audio-Visual Archive (Elizabeth Mela-Athanasopoulou, Aristotle University of Thessaloniki)
Third Danish Expedition to Central Asia field recordings (Moesgaard Museum)

items.name: Harip (Hunza shawm and drum ensemble)
items.lineage: Loud celebratory instrumental music of Hunza in Gilgit-Baltistan, played by ensembles of the surnai shawm of apricot wood, the dadang double-headed juniper drum and the dhamal pair of small metal kettledrums, the drums struck with sticks. It was played mostly by the Bericho (Domaki-speaking) musician community of Mominabad for the court of the Mirs of Hunza, at polo matches, seasonal festivals and shamanic trance ceremonies, and declined after the princely state was abolished; revival efforts have since brought it back to festivals and stages. The surnai card stands in for the Hunza surnai, the drum card for the dadang and the naqareh card for the dhamal.
items.description: A piercing shawm plays ornamented melodies over a loud, stick-beaten double-headed drum and a pair of small kettledrums, in upbeat, driving dance rhythms.
exemplars: Lok Virsa Gilgit-Baltistan field recordings of harip
Bericho harip ensembles of Mominabad, Hunza

items.name: Khowar song (Chitrali sitar music)
items.lineage: Song of the Khowar-speaking people of Chitral in northern Pakistan, sung by a soloist to the Chitrali sitar, a long-necked lute unrelated to the Hindustani sitar whose name relates to the setar: its body is carved from mulberry wood with a thin wooden table, and its five very thin metal strings, in three courses, are plucked with the index finger. It accompanies Khowar poetry in love songs and other lyric genres, and Radio Pakistan Peshawar and Lok Virsa have recorded Chitrali sitar singers. The sanavr card, a mulberry-bodied long-necked lute of neighbouring Badakhshan, stands in for the Chitrali sitar.
items.description: A solo voice sings lyrical strophic songs over the bright, buzzing plucked figures of a thin-strung long-necked lute that also plays the interludes.
exemplars: Radio Pakistan Peshawar recordings of Chitrali sitar singers
Lok Virsa recordings of Khowar song

items.name: Jari gan (Bengali Karbala narrative song)
items.lineage: Bengali Muslim narrative song recounting the martyrdom of Husayn at Karbala and related episodes, performed especially around Muharram in Manikganj, Mymensingh, Dhaka and other districts of Bangladesh. A lead singer (bayati) narrates and sings while a chorus (dohar) answers and dances in a circle wearing ankle bells; commercial jari pala cassettes and the Bangla Academy folklore archive document it. The shaker card stands in for the ankle bells.
items.description: A lead singer declaims and sings the story while a dancing chorus answers with refrains, over drum, small cymbals and the jingle of ankle bells.
exemplars: Bangla Academy folklore archive recordings of jari gan
Commercial jari pala cassettes from Bangladesh

items.name: Sari gan (Bengali boat-race and work song)
items.lineage: Collective work song of Bangladesh sung by rowers in the long boats of the nouka baich boat races and by people working together in rows, notably in Sylhet and Barisal. A leader sings a line and the crew answers in chorus, the pulse following the strokes of the oars; Bangladesh Betar and the Bangla Academy have recorded it. The drum and cymbal cards stand in for the dhol and cymbals that keep the stroke.
items.description: A leader calls out short sung lines and a large crew roars back the refrain in unison, locked to a strong, regular stroke beaten on drum and cymbals.
exemplars: Bangladesh Betar recordings of sari gan
Bangla Academy folklore recordings of boat-race songs

items.name: Murshidi and marfati gan (Bengali Sufi song)
items.lineage: Bengali Sufi song of Bangladesh: murshidi songs address the spiritual guide (murshid) and marfati songs the inner, mystical knowledge (marifat) of the divine, closely related to the dehatattva songs of the body. Sung by fakirs and folk singers, the repertoire reached HMV 78s and radio through Abbasuddin Ahmed and Abdul Alim, and Bangladesh Betar has broadcast it since.
items.description: A solo voice with a plaintive, carrying tone sings devotional verses in slow, flowing melodies over a chiming plucked lute, a sustained reed organ and soft hand drums.
exemplars: Abdul Alim — murshidi and marfati recordings
Bangladesh Betar broadcasts of murshidi songs

items.name: Bichar gan (Bengali sung philosophical debate)
items.lineage: Bengali sung debate, also called pala gan, in which two singers argue opposing sides of a philosophical or religious question, such as guru and disciple, man and woman, or shariat and marifat, in alternating rounds of song before an audience, each backed by a chorus and instrumentalists. It flourishes in Manikganj, Dhaka and neighbouring districts, has a large commercial cassette and VCD output, and has been documented by the Bangla Academy. The cymbals card stands in for the small hand cymbals.
items.description: Two lead singers take turns in long sung arguments, partly declaimed and partly melodic, each round closing on a refrain taken up by a chorus over reed organ, drum and plucked lute.
exemplars: Bangla Academy recordings of bichar gan

items.name: Maijbhandari gan (Chittagong Sufi shrine song)
items.lineage: Devotional song of the Maijbhandari Sufi order founded by Syed Ahmadullah Maijbhandari at Maijbhandar in Fatikchhari, Chittagong, sung at the shrine's gatherings and annual urs, with a large body of songs by Ramesh Shil and other poets. A cassette industry spread it across Bangladesh, and Hans Harder's study documents the order and its songs. The cymbals card stands in for the small hand cymbals.
items.description: A lead singer and a responding group sing devotional songs in a lilting, repeating dance rhythm over reed organ, drum and small cymbals, building as listeners join in.

items.name: Dhamail (Sylheti women's dance-song)
items.lineage: Women's circle dance-song of Sylhet and Sunamganj in Bangladesh and of the neighbouring Barak Valley, performed at weddings and other domestic and devotional occasions, with a large repertoire composed by Radharaman Dutta. Dancers move in a circle and clap while a lead singer starts each song and the group takes it up; Bangladesh Betar Sylhet has broadcast it.
items.description: A circle of women's voices takes up each song after a leader, over steady massed hand-clapping that drives the circling dance.
exemplars: Bangladesh Betar Sylhet broadcasts of dhamail

items.name: Chatgaiya gan (Chittagonian regional song)
items.lineage: Regional song of Chittagong sung in the Chittagonian language, with romantic and humorous themes, made widely known across Bangladesh by the male-female duets of Shefali Ghosh and Shyam Sundar Baishnab broadcast and recorded by Bangladesh Betar Chittagong.
items.description: Male and female voices trade and join verses of lilting strophic songs in a lively dance rhythm, over reed organ, hand drum and bamboo flute.
exemplars: Shefali Ghosh and Shyam Sundar Baishnab — Bangladesh Betar Chittagong recordings

items.name: Dhallywood film song (Bangladeshi film playback)
items.lineage: Playback song of the Bengali-language film industry of Dhaka, centred on the studios of the Bangladesh Film Development Corporation, founded in 1957 as the East Pakistan Film Development Corporation. Playback singers such as Runa Laila, Sabina Yasmin and Andrew Kishore recorded songs by film music directors, issued by EMI and later by local labels such as Sargam.
items.description: A bright lead playback voice carries strophic film songs over a studio orchestra of bowed strings, flute, reed organ and hand drums, with melodic instrumental interludes between verses.

items.name: Panche baja (Nepali Damai wedding band)
items.lineage: Auspicious outdoor ensemble of the Damai tailor-musician caste of Nepal, played at weddings and wedding processions (janti), temple rites and other life-cycle and calendrical occasions; the name means 'five instruments', and the larger naumati baja has nine. It combines the sahanai shawm (or the narsinga curved horn and karnal straight trumpet), the jhyali cymbals, the large damaha kettledrum, the small tyamko kettledrum and the dholaki barrel drum. The karna card stands in for the karnal, the horns card for the narsinga, the dhamsa card for the damaha and the tasha card for the tyamko.
items.description: Nasal shawms carry the melody over blasts of long trumpets and horns, clashing cymbals, the deep thud of a large kettledrum and crisp small-drum patterns, played outdoors in procession.
exemplars: Carol Tingey, Auspicious Music in a Changing Society: The Damai Musicians of Nepal (SOAS), with recordings
Music Nepal recordings of panche baja

items.name: Dapha (Newar devotional choral song)
items.lineage: Devotional hymn singing of Newar men's groups in Bhaktapur and other Kathmandu Valley towns, performed at shrines and public rest-houses on a calendar of festivals and seasons. Songs in Newari, Maithili and Sanskrit are set to named ragas and talas, and the group divides into two halves that sing alternately, accompanied by drum and cymbals. Richard Widdess's study with audio recordings documents the Bhaktapur tradition. The drum and cymbal cards stand in for the Newar drums and cymbals.
items.description: Two halves of a male group sing alternate lines of slow, modal hymns in unison, with drum and cymbals keeping a cyclic metre beneath them.
exemplars: Richard Widdess, Dapha: Sacred Singing in a South Asian City (2013), audio recordings

items.name: Dhimay baja (Newar dhimay drum ensemble)
items.lineage: Processional drumming of the Newar Jyapu farming community of the Kathmandu Valley, played on the large double-headed dhimay drum with bhusyah cymbals at festivals, jatras and processions to shrines. Gert-Matthias Wegner's study The Dhimaybaja of Bhaktapur documents its repertoire. The cymbals card stands in for the bhusyah.
items.description: Groups of large double-headed drums, struck with a stick on one head and the hand on the other, roar out loud, fast processional patterns locked to heavy cymbals.
exemplars: Jyapu dhimay baja groups of Bhaktapur

items.name: Gunla bajan (Newar Buddhist processional music)
items.lineage: Processional music of Newar Buddhist music groups of Kathmandu and Patan, played during the holy month of Gunla on daily pilgrimages to Swayambhu and other stupas and monasteries. The two-headed dhaa drum leads, with the small taa and large bhusya cymbals, while trumpets and clarinets now play the tune once carried by the local mwahali shawm and basuri flute. The drum card stands in for the dhaa, the cymbals card for the taa and bhusya, and the horns card for the wind players.
items.description: A two-headed drum and cymbals keep steady, repeating processional patterns under a wind melody as the group walks through the streets to the shrines.
exemplars: Newar Buddhist gunla bajan groups of Kathmandu and Patan

items.name: Charya giti (Newar Vajrayana ritual song)
items.lineage: Esoteric Buddhist ritual songs of the Newar Vajracharya priests of the Kathmandu Valley, descending from the medieval carya songs of the Buddhist siddhas, sung in ritual and to accompany the charya nritya dances that embody deities. The songs are set to ragas and talas and sung to small cymbals; Ratna Kazi Vajracharya taught the repertoire, and Richard Widdess has written on it. The cymbals card stands in for the small Newar cymbals.
items.description: A solo voice sings slow, melismatic ritual verses over the quiet ringing strokes of small cymbals marking the metre.
exemplars: Ratna Kazi Vajracharya (charya song and dance teacher)

items.name: Gaine git (Nepali Gandharva sarangi song)
items.lineage: Song of the Gandharva (Gaine) caste of hereditary itinerant musicians of Nepal, who sing to their own four-string bowed sarangi, carrying news and praise songs and karkha ballads that recount the deeds of heroes. Batulechaur near Pokhara is a noted Gandharva settlement; Mireille Helffer's Musee de l'Homme LP documents the tradition.
items.description: A solo singer delivers strophic narrative verses while a small bowed fiddle doubles the voice and answers with short, repeating melodic figures between lines.
exemplars: Mireille Helffer, Castes de musiciens au Népal (Musée de l'Homme LP)
Field recordings of Gandharba sarangi singers of Batulechaur

items.name: Tamang selo (damphu dance-song)
items.lineage: Song and dance genre of the Tamang people of the hills around the Kathmandu Valley, especially Makwanpur, Nuwakot and Rasuwa, accompanied by the damphu frame drum and the tungna lute, with singers exchanging verses. Radio Nepal and Music Nepal releases carried it to national audiences.
items.description: Voices trade short verses over the rolling, lilting beat of a frame drum and the light strummed pattern of a small lute, in a swinging dance rhythm.
exemplars: Radio Nepal recordings of Tamang selo

items.name: Deuda (far-western Nepal circle song-dance)
items.lineage: Song-dance of far-western Nepal (Sudurpashchim and parts of Karnali), sung in Doteli and neighbouring dialects at festivals such as Gaura and at village fairs. Participants hold hands in a circle and step together while two sides trade improvised couplets, often as courtship or teasing dialogue. The circle is often sung without instruments, carried by the dancers' steps; Radio Nepal broadcasts and commercial deuda albums add madal and other accompaniment.
items.description: Group singing in a ring: a short repeating melody carries improvised couplets exchanged between two sides, over the shuffle and stamp of linked dancers, with a light madal pulse in recordings.

items.name: Ghatu (Gurung ritual song-dance)
items.lineage: Ritual song-dance of the Gurung of Lamjung, Gorkha and neighbouring hill districts of western Nepal, held in a festival season that closes at Baisakh Purnima. Young girls dance in a trance state while male gurus sing the long narrative cycle of the dance and keep time on the madal; named forms include sati ghatu.
items.description: Slow, repetitive group singing by male elders over a steady madal pattern, the narrative unfolding verse by verse in a hypnotic cycle.
exemplars: Radio Nepal recordings of Gurung ghatu

items.name: Sorathi (Magar and Gurung dance-drama song)
items.lineage: Dance-drama song of the Magar of Nepal's western hills, among them Syangja, taken up also by the Gurung and neighbouring peoples. Village troupes perform it for about two weeks from Laxmi Puja in the Tihar festival to Thuli Ekadashi: sung episodes tell the story of King Jayasinge and his daughter Sorathi while a male dancer as the king dances in turn with dancers representing his queens, accompanied by madal drums.
items.description: Strophic narrative songs sung by a group of singers over a steady madal rhythm, each verse advancing the story as the dancers act it out.

items.name: Tharu song-dance (sakhiya, maghauta, jhumra)
items.lineage: Song-dance repertoire of the Tharu of Nepal's western and central Terai, among them Dang, Bardiya, Kailali and Chitwan. Sakhiya is danced by women in a circle from Krishna Janmashtami through Dashain and Tihar while men play the madal; maghauta is danced at Maghi, the Tharu new year; and jhumra is a western Tharu song-dance sung at Dashain and other festive occasions. Radio Nepal and Music Nepal have carried Tharu-language songs.
items.description: Circles of dancers sing short repeated phrases in groups over a driving two-headed drum rhythm, the steps of the dance marking each turn of the cycle.

items.name: Palam (Limbu sung courtship dialogue)
items.lineage: Sung dialogue of the Limbu (Yakthung) of Taplejung, Panchthar and the eastern hills of Nepal, performed during ya·lang, the paddy dance, in which young men and women link arms in a slow circle and trade improvised verses of courtship, wit and riddle. Palam has been issued on commercial recordings in Nepal, and Limbu cultural organisations document the form.
items.description: Unaccompanied, slow-moving melodic dialogue in which male and female singers answer each other with improvised verses on a recurring tune, paced by the slow steps of the circle dance.
exemplars: Commercial Limbu palam recordings issued in Nepal
Limbu cultural archive recordings of palam

items.name: Sakela (Kirat Rai ritual dance music)
items.lineage: Ritual dance music of the Kirat Rai of the eastern hills of Nepal, among them Bhojpur and Khotang, performed at the Ubhauli and Udhauli festivals of the agricultural year. A silimangpa leads the dance circle through sili, figures that imitate farming work, animals and birds, to the beat of the large dhol drum and jhyamta cymbals; a generic membrane-drum card stands in for the dhol and the cymbals card for the jhyamta.
items.description: A steady, heavy two-headed drum pattern locked with clashing cymbals, repeated in long cycles as the dance circle moves through its figures.
exemplars: Community recordings of Ubhauli and Udhauli sakela gatherings

items.name: Hudke (Karnali hudko-drum ballads)
items.lineage: Ballad song-dance of the Karnali region of western Nepal, once widely popular in Jumla and in parts of Kalikot and Mugu. Male singer-dancers play the hudko, a hand-held hourglass drum headed with dried goat skin, while they sing ballads and narrative songs, and they perform with the panche baja band at weddings, bratabandha and other social and cultural celebrations; the form is now described as on the verge of disappearance. The Uttarakhand hudka card stands in for the related hudko.
items.description: Narrative singing over the singer's own hourglass drum, its pressure-bent tones punctuating each line as the performer dances.
exemplars: Radio Nepal far-west recordings of hudke

items.name: Jhankri (Nepali shamanic drumming and chant)
items.lineage: Healing and divination rites of the jhankri shamans (with the related dhami) of Nepal's hill peoples, among them the Tamang, Magar, Gurung, Rai and Limbu. In night-long seances the shaman beats the dhyangro, a two-sided frame drum with a carved wooden handle, while chanting invocations, origin stories and dialogues with spirits on the way into trance. The frame-drum card stands in for the dhyangro. Larry Peters and Michael Oppitz are among the anthropologists who documented the practice.
items.description: Rapid, insistent frame-drum beating under rhythmic chanted invocation, the drumming rising in speed and intensity as the trance deepens.
exemplars: Michael Oppitz, Shamans of the Blind Country (documentary film on Northern Magar shamans)
Larry Peters' ethnographic documentation of Tamang shamans

items.name: Tovil (Sri Lankan low-country exorcism rite)
items.lineage: Exorcism and healing rites of the Sinhala low country around Galle and Matara, among them the sanni yakuma, performed through the night by ritual specialists for a patient's household. Drummers on the double-headed yak bera drive chanted and sung verses, masked and costumed dance and comic dialogue with the demons, with talampata hand cymbals. A generic membrane-drum card stands in for the yak bera and the manjira card for the talampata. Bruce Kapferer's A Celebration of Demons is the classic study.
items.description: Fast, intricate hand-drumming on double-headed drums propels chanted verse and cymbal ostinatos, with sudden accelerations marking the dancers' spins and the demons' entrances.
exemplars: Ethnographic field recordings of low-country tovil and sanni yakuma

items.name: Sabaragamuwa natum (Sri Lankan davula dance drumming)
items.lineage: Dance and drumming school of Sabaragamuwa province, centred on Ratnapura, counted with the up-country Kandyan and the low-country styles as one of the three Sinhala dance traditions and associated with the cult of the deity Saman. It is driven by the davula, a cylindrical double-headed drum struck with a stick on one head and the hand on the other; a generic membrane-drum card stands in for the davula.
items.description: Dense rhythmic patterns on stick-and-hand barrel drums, sharp stick strokes on one head answered by open hand tones on the other, punctuating the dancers' footwork.
exemplars: SLBC recordings of Sabaragamuwa dance drumming
Ministry of Culture recordings of Sabaragamuwa dance

items.name: Hewisi (Sri Lankan Buddhist temple drum offering)
items.lineage: Ceremonial drum offering (hewisi pooja) of Sinhala Buddhist temples, best known from the daily services at the Temple of the Tooth (Dalada Maligawa) in Kandy and from perahera processions. The ensemble joins the davula barrel drum, the tammattama pair of stick-struck drums and the horanewa double-reed oboe; a generic membrane-drum card stands in for the davula, the nagara card for the tammattama and the Nepali sahnai card for the horanewa.
items.description: A penetrating double-reed melody over interlocking barrel-drum and paired stick-drum patterns, played in set sequences that mark the stages of the temple offering.
exemplars: Daily hewisi offerings at the Temple of the Tooth, Kandy

items.name: Nurthi (Sinhala stage-musical song)
items.lineage: Song of the Sinhala musical stage drama that grew up in Colombo from the late nineteenth century under the influence of touring Parsi theatre companies from Bombay, setting Sinhala lyrics to North Indian raga-based stage melodies. The productions of John de Silva, staged at the Tower Hall theatre, and the plays of Charles Dias made it the leading popular entertainment of the early twentieth century, and nurthi songs were issued on gramophone 78s with harmonium and tabla accompaniment.
items.description: Declamatory, raga-flavoured solo songs projected over harmonium and tabla, with the full-voiced, ornamented delivery of the open stage.
exemplars: Gramophone 78s of nurthi songs from John de Silva and Charles Dias stage productions

items.name: Nadagam (Sinhala folk-drama song)
items.lineage: Sung folk drama of Sri Lanka's western coastal belt, adapted in the nineteenth century from South Indian Tamil nadagam and associated with the Catholic communities around Negombo and Moratuwa; Philippu Sinno is remembered as its pioneer. A narrator-singer, the pothe gura, introduces the action and the actors sing their roles to drum and cymbal accompaniment. Ediriweera Sarachchandra drew on it for his stage play Maname. A generic membrane-drum card stands in for the drum and the manjira card for the talampata cymbals.
items.description: Narrated and sung dramatic verse on South Indian-derived melodies, a narrator's lines alternating with sung dialogue over a steady drum and small cymbals.
exemplars: SLBC archive recordings of nadagam songs

items.name: Sarala gee (Sinhala light-classical song)
items.lineage: Sinhala light song of the Radio Ceylon era, from the mid-twentieth century, which set Sinhala poetry to melodies joining North Indian raga with Sinhala folk tunes. W. D. Amaradeva, trained at the Bhatkhande music institute in Lucknow, became its central composer-singer; Sunil Santha, who sought a Sinhala style independent of Hindustani models, and Nanda Malini are among its other major voices. Violin, sitar and tabla were usual accompaniment in radio and studio recordings; the fiddle card stands in for the violin.
items.description: Lyrical, raga-inflected solo song with gentle glides, sung over violin obbligato and a light tabla cycle.
exemplars: W. D. Amaradeva Radio Ceylon recordings

items.name: Virindu (Sinhala extempore verse with rabana)
items.lineage: Sinhala sung verse in which a singer improvises or recites four-line stanzas on topical, moral or humorous subjects to the hand-held rabana frame drum, sometimes as a contest between singers; it became a recognised broadcast genre on Sri Lankan radio. The frame-drum card stands in for the rabana.
items.description: Rapid, syllabic sung verse in four-line stanzas over a crisp frame-drum pattern, the melody recurring as the singer extemporises new lines.

items.name: Jana kavi (Sinhala folk verse song)
items.lineage: Village folk verse of the Sinhala countryside, sung in four-line kavi stanzas tied to work and the seasons: goyam kavi at the paddy harvest and threshing floor, pal kavi sung by watchers guarding crops from night-time huts, and others for further occasions. The verses are usually sung unaccompanied by individuals or small groups and have been collected in the folk-song archive of Sri Lankan radio.
items.description: Unaccompanied, free-flowing solo singing of four-line stanzas on a small set of recurring melodic formulas, with long held line-endings.
exemplars: SLBC folk-song archive recordings of jana kavi

items.name: Bakthi gee (Sinhala Buddhist devotional song)
items.lineage: Sinhala devotional songs sung by lay Buddhist groups during the Vesak and Poson full-moon festivals, when bakthi gee singing parties perform at roadside pandals and temples and national radio broadcasts special programmes; commercial bakthi gee albums followed. The songs praise the Buddha and his teaching and are sung in unison or by a leader and chorus, typically with harmonium and tabla.
items.description: Groups of singers in unison and leader-chorus alternation deliver gentle strophic devotional melodies over sustained harmonium and a light tabla pulse.

items.name: Batticaloa koothu (eastern Sri Lankan Tamil dance-drama)
items.lineage: Tamil dance-drama of the Batticaloa region on Sri Lanka's east coast, performed by village troupes in an open-air arena in two main styles, vadamodi (northern style) and thenmodi (southern style). An annavi, the troupe master, leads the singing to the maddalam drum and cymbals, and a chorus repeats the actors' sung lines. Research by S. Maunaguru and the Swami Vipulananda Institute of Aesthetic Studies has documented and revived it. A generic membrane-drum card stands in for the maddalam and the manjira card for the cymbals.
items.description: Sung dramatic verse repeated by a chorus, driven by a two-headed drum and ringing cymbals, with vigorous drum passages for the dancers' stepping.
exemplars: Swami Vipulananda Institute of Aesthetic Studies recordings of Batticaloa koothu
S. Maunaguru's documentation of vadamodi and thenmodi koothu

items.name: Eelam Tamil songs (Tamil national-movement song)
items.lineage: Songs of the Sri Lankan Tamil national movement, produced in Jaffna and the Vanni and circulated on cassette from the 1980s until the end of the civil war in 2009, with further releases in the diaspora. They set Tamil poetry on homeland, sacrifice and struggle for solo voices and chorus over keyboard and percussion arrangements.
items.description: Stirring solo and choral songs over keyboard-led arrangements with a steady march-like or dance pulse, recorded with the bright, compressed sound of the cassette era.
exemplars: Cassette releases of the Eelam Tamil national-movement song industry (1980s to 2000s)

items.name: Manha (Afro-Sri Lankan Kaffir song)
items.lineage: Song and dance of the Afro-Sri Lankan (Kaffir) community of Sirambiyadiya near Puttalam, descendants of Africans brought to the island in the colonial period.
