Their manha (manja) songs are sung in Sri Lanka Portuguese Creole as polyrhythmic music for voices and percussion; a documented ensemble used two dholak drums, a tambourine, metal spoons, coconut shells on a wooden box and an empty bottle with coins. The related kaffringha dance-song passed into Sinhala popular music and baila. Shihan de Silva Jayasuriya has documented the community's songs.
items.description: Lively group singing over layered two-headed drum, tambourine and clattering metal-spoon rhythms in a fast dance pulse.
exemplars: Shihan de Silva Jayasuriya's documentation of Sirambiyadiya manha songs

items.name: Vedda songs (Wanniyala-aetto song)
items.lineage: Songs of the Vedda (Wanniyala-aetto), the Indigenous forest people of eastern and central Sri Lanka, whose best-known community today lives at Dambana in Badulla district. Charles and Brenda Seligmann recorded Vedda songs on phonograph cylinders in 1907-08, and C. S. Myers' analysis in their monograph The Veddas (1911) described melodies built on two or three notes. The repertoire includes lullabies, hunting songs and invocations sung in the kirikoraha ceremony for the spirits of the dead.
items.description: Unaccompanied singing on two or three closely spaced pitches, short melodic cells repeated many times with small changes of text.
exemplars: Seligmann phonograph cylinders of Vedda song (1907 to 1908), Berlin Phonogramm-Archiv

items.name: Drametse ngacham (Bhutanese mask dance of the drums)
items.lineage: Sacred masked dance of Drametse village in Mongar district, eastern Bhutan, performed twice a year at the festival of the Ogyen Tegchok Namdroel Choeling monastery in honour of Padmasambhava; UNESCO proclaimed it a Masterpiece of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity and later inscribed it on the Representative List. Sixteen masked male dancers in monastic robes, wearing masks of real and mythical animals, move from a calm, contemplative part to a rapid, athletic one, accompanied by ten musicians on cymbals, trumpets and drums including the cylindrical bang nga, the hand-held lag nga and the nga chen beaten with a bent stick. Generic membrane-drum, frame-drum, cymbal and long-trumpet cards stand in for the bang nga, lag nga, cymbals and trumpets.
items.description: Deep, measured drum strokes and clashing cymbals pace the slow opening, then quicken into rapid drumming for the leaping wrathful section, with trumpet calls above.
exemplars: UNESCO Representative List documentation of the Drametse ngacham (2008)

items.name: Assiko (Bassa guitar-and-bottle dance music)
items.lineage: Dance music of the Bassa of the Littoral and Centre regions of Cameroon, in which a singer is accompanied by a guitar and by a percussionist striking an empty bottle with metal knives and forks. Jean Bikoko 'Aladin', whose singles of the 1960s and 1970s made the style widely known, is regarded as its leading exponent. The bottle-percussion card stands in for the struck bottle.
items.description: A singer over a briskly repeating guitar figure, with the bright metallic tick of cutlery on a bottle keeping a fast, even dance pulse.

items.name: Ambasse bey (Douala guitar song)
items.lineage: Guitar song of the Duala and the Cameroonian coast around Douala, the folk-urban style from which makossa later grew. Eboa Lotin, singing to his own guitar and harmonica, made it widely known on records from the 1960s.
items.description: Light, lilting song over acoustic guitar, with harmonica phrases answering the vocal lines.

items.name: Bend-skin (Douala drums-and-maracas street song)
items.lineage: Urban popular music of Douala that emerged in the 1990s and shares its name with the city's motorcycle taxis. It grew out of tchamassi, the Bamileke dance rhythm that André-Marie Tala had popularised, and is played on drums and maracas under a vocalist who both sings and raps; Kouchouam Mbada is its best-known group. A generic shaker card stands in for the maracas.
items.description: Fast, stripped-down dance music: a half-sung, half-rapped lead and answering voices over pounding drums and shakers, with no melodic instruments.

items.name: Mangambeu (Bangangté dance rhythm)
items.lineage: Dance rhythm of Bangangté in the Bamileke country of western Cameroon, carried into recorded popular music by Pierre Didy Tchakounté, whose 1980s LPs made it known nationally.
items.description: The recorded form puts the Bangangté dance rhythm on electric guitar, bass and drums, with a lead singer answered by backing voices.

items.name: Mbolé (Yaoundé funeral-vigil rhythm)
items.lineage: Urban rhythm born in the early 2000s in the Nkoldongo quarter of Yaoundé at ceremonies, above all funeral vigils, first sung without instruments and close to bikutsi in rhythm. It spread through the city's popular quarters and reached the studio in 2016, when Petit Malo's 'Dans mon Kwatta' became the first studio mbolé recording; djembe is its principal instrument, with maracas and keyboard.
items.description: Driving, percussion-heavy party music: a chanted lead and crowd-style responses over hard djembe patterns and maracas, with simple keyboard lines on top.

items.name: Mvet oyeng (Fang-Beti epic recitation)
items.lineage: Epic recitation of the Fang, Beti and Bulu of southern Cameroon, northern Gabon and Equatorial Guinea, in which the bard (mbom-mvet) sings and declaims the cycles of the immortal people of Engong while playing the mvet stick-zither, with a chorus and audience answering; a performance can last through the night. Herbert Pepper recorded the bard Zwè Nguéma in Gabon in 1960.
items.description: A single bard alternating sung lines and rapid declamation over plucked, buzzing stick-zither ostinatos, punctuated by chorus responses.
exemplars: Herbert Pepper: Un mvet de Zwè Nguéma (CREM, Gabon, 1960)
Wergo, Museum Collection Berlin: Mvet ai Mendzang: Die Musik der Beti in Kamerun (rec. 1984 and 1989)

items.name: Mendzang (Beti xylophone ensemble)
items.lineage: Xylophone ensemble music of the Beti of the Centre region around Yaoundé, in which several gourd-resonated mendzang xylophones of different registers interlock for dances and celebrations. Wergo's Museum Collection Berlin series issued mendzang ensembles recorded in Cameroon in 1984. It is the acoustic source of bikutsi, whose electric guitarists later imitated the xylophone patterns; the balafon card stands in for the mendzang.
items.description: Dense interlocking xylophone parts in several registers, buzzing resonators and drum under a leader and responding voices.
exemplars: Wergo, Museum Collection Berlin: Mvet ai Mendzang: Die Musik der Beti in Kamerun (rec. 1984 and 1989)

items.name: Liquindi (Baka water drumming)
items.lineage: Water drumming of Baka women of the rainforests of south-eastern Cameroon, who stand waist-deep in a stream and strike and scoop the surface with their hands to make interlocking drum-like sounds, often while singing. The water-percussion card stands in for liquindi.
items.description: Deep plops, slaps and splashes from several players' cupped hands on water, locking into a cycling pattern under women's group voices.
exemplars: Heart of the Forest (Baka forest people field recordings, Martin Cradick and Su Hart)

items.name: Bamum palace music (Foumban)
items.lineage: Court and ritual music of the Bamum kingdom, centred on the sultan's palace at Foumban, where Michel Houdry recorded palace dances and songs for Ocora in 1957. It is performed at palace ceremonies and in the Nguon, the kingdom's ritual of governance, which UNESCO inscribed on its Representative List. Generic drum, double-bell and shaker cards stand in for the palace percussion.
items.description: Ceremonial song with a leader and responding voices over drums, iron bells and rattles.
exemplars: Ocora SOR-3: Danses et chants Bamoun (rec. at the Foumban palace, 1957)
Sonafric SAF-50057: Musique traditionnelle du Cameroun, vol. 1: chants des Bamum

items.name: Bamileke palace and funeral music (Grassfields)
items.lineage: Music of the Bamileke chiefdoms of the western Grassfields, played at the chief's compound and above all at funerals, when the chiefdom's societies perform song and dance with drums, bells and rattles. Bernard Surugue recorded the funeral of a Bamileke queen in 1974 for a SELAF/ORSTOM LP. Generic drum, double-bell and shaker cards stand in for the instruments.
items.description: Outdoor ceremonial music: a leader and group voices over layered drums, iron bells and rattles.
exemplars: SELAF/ORSTOM CETO-746: Funérailles d'une reine Bamiléké (Bernard Surugue, 1974)

items.name: Gurna (Tupuri song-dance society)
items.lineage: Song-dance society of the Tupuri of the Mayo-Danay in Cameroon and the Mayo-Kebbi in Chad. Men gather in dry-season camps, where composers create new songs that the group then performs in large circle dances; the songs praise, criticise and comment on village life, as James Ignatowski's ethnography Journey of Song describes. Charles Duvelle recorded Tupuri songs in 1966. The voice card, set to a live group, carries the massed singing.
items.description: Massed men's voices singing newly composed topical songs together while dancing in a large circle.
exemplars: Charles Duvelle's 1966 Toupouri field recordings (CREM archive; Philips, Collection Prophet)

items.name: Mbum song and percussion (Adamawa)
items.lineage: Music of the Mbum (Mboum) of the Adamawa plateau around Ngaoundéré, known on record chiefly through Charles Duvelle's 1966 field recordings, issued by Philips in the Collection Prophet in 2001. The generic auxiliary-percussion card stands in for the Mbum percussion.
items.description: Village song, solo and group, over struck percussion, as captured on mid-1960s field tape.
exemplars: Charles Duvelle: Mbum du Cameroun (rec. 1966; Philips, Collection Prophet, 2001)

items.name: Katanga guitar (Copperbelt fingerstyle song)
items.lineage: Acoustic guitar song of the Katanga mining towns of Élisabethville (Lubumbashi) and Jadotville (Likasi) in the 1950s, picked with thumb and index finger in interlocking bass and melody lines. Hugh Tracey's recordings of Jean Bosco Mwenda, notably 'Masanga' (1952), issued on Gallotone 78s, spread the style across East and Central Africa; Losta Abelo and Edouard Masengo also recorded.
items.description: Intricate two-finger guitar picking, with a thumb-driven bass under a bright treble melody and relaxed singing.
exemplars: Jean Bosco Mwenda — Masanga (Gallotone 78, Hugh Tracey recording, 1952)
Hugh Tracey/ILAM recordings of Losta Abelo and Edouard Masengo

items.name: Mutuashi (Luba-Kasai hip dance rhythm)
items.lineage: Traditional dance rhythm of the Luba of Kasai, danced with rolling hip movements, which Tshala Muana carried into Congolese popular music from the 1980s, earning the title 'queen of mutuashi'; her albums set it for guitars, bass, drums and percussion.
items.description: Fast, rolling dance groove: a female lead answered by backing voices over bright electric guitars, bass and heavy drum and hand-drum patterns.

items.name: Tradi-moderne (Kinshasa amplified likembe music)
items.lineage: Music of Kinshasa ensembles formed by migrants from Kasai and by the Bazombo of the Angolan border, who play their home regions' trance and dance repertoires on electrically amplified likembe lamellophones, homemade percussion and voices, through improvised pickups and amplifiers that distort the sound. Konono No. 1, founded by Mingiedi Mawangu, and the Kasai Allstars reached international audiences through Crammed Discs' Congotronics series from 2004. The Congolese lukembi card stands in for the likembe.
items.description: Hypnotic, repeating likembe riffs pushed through overdriven homemade amplification into a buzzing, distorted roar, over relentless pots-and-pans percussion and chanted vocals.

items.name: Missa Luba and Zairean-rite Mass music
items.lineage: Congolese inculturated Catholic Mass music. The Missa Luba, a Latin Mass set in Congolese song and drumming styles, was arranged by the Belgian Franciscan Guido Haazen and recorded in 1958 for Philips by his choir Les Troubadours du Roi Baudouin of Kamina; the Zairean Use of the Roman Rite, approved in 1988, brought choirs, drums and dance into the liturgy across the country.
items.description: A solo voice calling and a full choir answering in close parallel harmony over steady hand-drum patterns, in Latin Mass texts.
exemplars: Les Troubadours du Roi Baudouin — Missa Luba (Philips, 1958)

items.name: Mangbetu harp song (Haut-Uele)
items.lineage: Song of the Mangbetu of the Uele region of north-eastern Congo, accompanied on the arched harp, an instrument often carved with a human head at the top of its neck. Didier Demolin recorded it for his CD Mangbetu: Haut-Uele (1992); the ngoma arched-harp card stands in for the Mangbetu harp.
items.description: A singer over a cycling, softly plucked harp ostinato, the voice weaving short phrases around the harp pattern.

items.name: Lokele slit-drum language (Upper Congo)
items.lineage: Drum language of the Lokele of the Congo River around Yakusu and Kisangani, in which the lokole, a wooden slit drum with two lips of different pitch, reproduces the tones of spoken Lokele to send announcements, names and messages between riverside villages. The missionary John F. Carrington described it in The Talking Drums of Africa (1949), and Hugh Tracey recorded it; the lenga slit-drum card stands in for the lokole.
items.description: A single slit drum beaten in two pitches, its phrases following the rise and fall and rhythm of speech rather than a dance meter.
exemplars: Hugh Tracey/ILAM: Talking drums of the Upper Congo

items.name: Kasàlà (Luba praise and funeral chant)
items.lineage: Declaimed praise poetry of the Luba of Kasai and Katanga, chanted at funerals and celebrations by a soloist who piles up names, epithets and the deeds of the dead or the honoured. Patrice Mufuta documented it in his study Le chant kasàlà des Lubà (1969).
items.description: A single voice in rapid, heightened declamation, poised between speech and song, building long chains of praise names.
exemplars: Hugh Tracey's 1957 recordings of Luba music (ILAM)
Royal Museum for Central Africa (Tervuren) sound archive: Luba vocal music

items.name: Bobongo (Ekonda dance-theatre)
items.lineage: Ceremonial dance-theatre of the Ekonda, a Mongo people of the Lake Mai-Ndombe region, staged by organised troupes of singers, dancers and drummers. Alan Merriam recorded it in 1952 for the Riverside LP Ekonda: Tribal Music of the Belgian Congo.
items.description: Leader and chorus song over drums, paced for staged dance sequences.
exemplars: Riverside: Ekonda: Tribal Music of the Belgian Congo (Alan Merriam, rec. 1952)

items.name: Salampasu ritual and lamellophone music (Kasai)
items.lineage: Music of the Salampasu of western Kasai around Luiza, recorded by Jos Gansemans in 1973 and issued by Ocora: songs with lamellophones and drums for rituals and dances. The Congolese lukembi card stands in for the Salampasu lamellophones.
items.description: Voices over cycling, buzzing lamellophone patterns and drums.
exemplars: Ocora: Zaïre: musique des Salampasu (Jos Gansemans, rec. 1973)

items.name: Bwami songs (Lega initiation association)
items.lineage: Songs of bwami, the graded initiation association of the Lega of South Kivu and Maniema, sung during the rites through which members rise in grade, where sung aphorisms accompany the display of carved ivory and wooden figures. Daniel Biebuyck documented and recorded the rites during his fieldwork among the Lega in the early 1950s. Generic drum and shaker cards stand in for the rites' percussion.
items.description: Leader-and-chorus initiation song: sung aphorisms answered by group voices over drum and rattle percussion.
exemplars: Daniel Biebuyck's field recordings of Lega bwami rites (early 1950s)

items.name: Gbaya chants à penser (sanza thinking songs)
items.lineage: Solo song of the Gbaya of western Central African Republic that Vincent Dehoux studied as 'thinking songs' (chants à penser): a singer accompanies reflective verses on a sanza lamellophone, often sung alone, for the singer himself. The Congolese lukembi card stands in for the Gbaya sanza.
items.description: A single voice in reflective, speech-near phrases over cycling plucked sanza figures, quiet and inward rather than performed for a crowd.
exemplars: Ocora C 580008 'Centrafrique: Musique Gbáyá, chants à penser' (Vincent Dehoux)

items.name: Nzakara and Zande harp poetry (Bangassou)
items.lineage: Sung poetry of the Nzakara and Zande of south-eastern Central African Republic, carried by a five-string arched harp (kundi) whose short repeating formulas underlie the singer's verses; harpists were attached to the courts of the Bandia rulers. Recordings by Eric de Dampierre and Marc Chemillier span 1965 to 1993, and Chemillier analysed the canonic structure of the harp formulas. The adungu arched-harp card stands in for the Nzakara-Zande harp.
items.description: A solo singer declaims and sings poetic verses over short, endlessly repeating five-string harp ostinatos built from interlocking canonic patterns.
exemplars: Le Chant du Monde CNR 2741009, 'Musiques des anciennes cours Bandia / Music of the former Bandia courts' (Marc Chemillier and Eric de Dampierre, rec. 1965-93)

items.name: Ngbaka-Ma'bo chantefables and sanza song (Lobaye)
items.lineage: Music of the Ngbaka-Ma'bo of the Lobaye forest region of Central African Republic, documented in Simha Arom and Geneviève Dournon's 1964-67 recordings and on Arom's 1970 SELAF disc of tales and chantefables: spoken tales are broken by sung refrains that the narrator leads and listeners answer, and a separate song strand is accompanied by the sanza lamellophone. The Congolese lukembi card stands in for the sanza.
items.description: A narrated tale broken by short sung refrains, the leader's line answered by a responding group; sanza songs add cycling plucked metal-key patterns.
exemplars: CREM recordings of Simha Arom and Geneviève Dournon, Lobaye (1964-67)

items.name: Manza xylophone song (central Centrafrique)
items.lineage: Song of the Manza (Mandja) of the Kémo and Nana-Grébizi regions of Central African Republic accompanied by xylophone, documented in Vincent Dehoux's 1986 CREM recordings of music for voice and xylophone. The gourd-resonated mbila mutondo card stands in for the Manza xylophone.
items.description: A sung line set against repeating, interlocking struck-wood xylophone figures with a resonant, buzzing attack.
exemplars: Vincent Dehoux, CREM 'Manza: musique pour chant et xylophone' (1986)

items.name: Sara harp, xylophone and initiation song (southern Chad)
items.lineage: Music of the Sara peoples of southern Chad (Madjingaye, Ngambaye, Sara Kaba and others), recorded by Charles Duvelle and Michel Vuylsteke in 1966 for the Sara volume of Ocora's anthology of Chadian music: arched-harp song, xylophone ensembles with drums, and the songs of yondo initiation. The adungu and mbila mutondo cards stand in for the Sara arched harp and xylophone.
items.description: Arched-harp songs for solo voice alternate with xylophone-and-drum ensembles and leader-and-chorus initiation singing, all built on short repeating cycles.
exemplars: Ocora OCR 36, Anthologie de la musique du Tchad: Les Sara (Charles Duvelle and Michel Vuylsteke, rec. 1966)

items.name: Moundang drum and horn music (Léré)
items.lineage: Music of the Moundang of Mayo-Kebbi in south-western Chad, whose kingdom is centred on Léré. Charles Duvelle and Michel Vuylsteke recorded it in 1966 for the Mayo-Kebbi volume of Ocora's Chad anthology, documenting drum-accompanied dances and ceremonies with horns, trumpets and bells, among them funeral music for trumpet and drums. Generic drum and horn cards stand in for the drums, horns and trumpets.
items.description: Drum-driven dance and ceremonial music punctuated by horn and trumpet calls, including funeral pieces for trumpet and drums.
exemplars: Ocora OCR 37, Anthologie de la musique du Tchad: Le Mayo-Kebbi occidental (Massa, Moundang, Toupouri; Charles Duvelle and Michel Vuylsteke, rec. 1966)

items.name: Kanem sultan's orchestra (Kanembu court music, Mao)
items.lineage: Ceremonial music of the court of the sultan (alifa) of Kanem at Mao, in the Sahelian court tradition of Kanem-Bornu, whose royal ensembles combine long metal trumpets, shawms and drums; Monique Brandily's recordings of the sultan's orchestra are held in the CREM archive. The kakaki, the Kanuri-form algaita and a generic drum card represent the ensemble.
items.description: Sustained long-trumpet blasts and a nasal, ornamented shawm line over drum patterns in an open-air ceremonial ensemble.
exemplars: Monique Brandily, CREM recordings 'Kanem: Orchestre du sultan' (Mao)

items.name: Teke ngwomi and sanza song (Batéké plateaux)
items.lineage: Song of the Teke (Batéké) of the plateaux straddling south-eastern Gabon and the Republic of Congo, accompanied by the ngwomi (ngomi), a many-stringed plucked instrument, and by sanza lamellophones; Pierre Sallée recorded the ngwomi among the Gabonese Teke in 1966-68, and his Ocora LP of Gabonese music gives a side to the Batéké. The adungu arched-harp and Congolese lukembi cards stand in for the ngwomi and sanza.
items.description: A solo voice over repeating plucked-string patterns from the ngwomi, alternating with songs carried by cycling sanza figures.
exemplars: Pierre Sallée, CREM recordings of the Teke ngwomi (1966-68)
Pierre Sallée, Ocora LP of Gabonese music (Batéké side)

items.name: Kongo village music (Bembe, Lari and Kongo)
items.lineage: Village music of the Kongo-group peoples of the southern Republic of Congo - Bembe, Lari and Kongo of the Pool and Bouenza regions - including dance songs and matanga wake songs, documented in Charles Duvelle's 1966 recordings for Ocora's 'Musique Kongo'. Generic drum and shaker cards stand in for the drums and rattles.
items.description: Leader-and-chorus dance and wake songs over drums and rattles, with overlapping responses and repeating rhythmic cycles.
exemplars: Ocora OCR 35 'Musique Kongo: Ba-Bembé, Ba-Congo, Ba-Lari' (Charles Duvelle, rec. 1966)

items.name: Puíta (São Tomé plantation dance)
items.lineage: Dance brought to São Tomé and Príncipe by Angolan contract workers, which became one of the most popular dances on the plantations (roças) in the colonial period and a national genre after independence; the conjunto Os Úntués later carried its rhythm into electric dance-band music. Generic drum and shaker cards stand in for its percussion.
items.description: Drum-led dance rhythm with rattles and sung refrains, steady and cyclic, played outdoors for dancing.
exemplars: Os Úntués - puíta-based conjunto recordings (Bongo Joe 'Léve Léve: São Tomé & Príncipe Sounds 70s-80s')

items.name: Socopé (São Tomé dance rhythm)
items.lineage: Dance rhythm of São Tomé that arose, like puíta and danço-congo, among the islands' slave-descended population; in the 1970s Os Úntués and other conjuntos set it for electric guitars and dance band, mixing in European pop and soukous elements. This entry models that recorded conjunto form as a live-room tape capture.
items.description: Electric dance-band setting of the socopé rhythm: bright guitar lines over bass and drum kit with shaker, a lead singer and answering chorus.
exemplars: Os Úntués - recordings on Bongo Joe 'Léve Léve: São Tomé & Príncipe Sounds 70s-80s'

items.name: Danço-congo (São Tomé masked dance-drama)
items.lineage: Masked music, dance and theatre of São Tomé, also called the Captain's Dance, in which costumed characters enact a drama to drumming and rattles; it is a separate form from tchiloli. Its rhythms were among those that conjuntos such as Os Úntués carried into electric dance-band music. Generic drum and sucalo rattle cards carry the ensemble.
items.description: Dense outdoor drumming with seed-basket rattles, driving masked dancers through a staged drama.
exemplars: Os Úntués - conjunto adaptations of danço-congo rhythms (Bongo Joe 'Léve Léve: São Tomé & Príncipe Sounds 70s-80s')

items.name: Puxa (São Tomé electric dance music)
items.lineage: Electric dance-band music of São Tomé and Príncipe in the 1970s-80s, associated above all with the band África Negra, whose long dance tracks set a lead singer and answering chorus over interlocking guitars, bass, drum kit and hand percussion. A generic hand-drum card carries the hand percussion.
items.description: Interlocking clean electric guitars over a rolling bass and drum-kit groove with hand percussion, a lead singer and answering chorus stretched over long dance tracks.
exemplars: Bongo Joe 'Léve Léve: São Tomé & Príncipe Sounds 70s-80s'

items.name: Rebita (Luanda accordion ballroom dance)
items.lineage: Couple dance and music of Luanda, with the Ilha do Cabo as a stronghold, formed in the colonial period from European ballroom dances; couples move in a circle under a master of ceremonies, accompanied by accordion and harmonica with a dikanza scraper and drums. The reco-reco card in bamboo stands in for the dikanza.
items.description: Lilting couple-dance music led by accordion and harmonica over a scraped bamboo dikanza and drum, with sung verses and choruses.
exemplars: Luanda rebita groups of the Ilha do Cabo and the Luanda Carnival

items.name: Kazukuta (Luanda carnival dance)
items.lineage: Carnival dance of Luanda's musseques, performed with umbrellas and canes by the city's carnival groups to drums, the dikanza scraper and sung refrains, and one of the signature dances of the Luanda Carnival parade alongside semba. The reco-reco card in bamboo stands in for the dikanza.
items.description: Carnival drumming with a scraped dikanza and sung group refrains for a processional dance performed with umbrellas and canes.

items.name: Kilapanga (Angolan conjunto dance rhythm)
items.lineage: Angolan dance rhythm played, alongside semba, by Luanda's electric conjuntos of the 1960s-70s and still presented as one of the country's signature rhythms. The reco-reco card in bamboo stands in for the dikanza, and a generic hand-drum card carries the hand percussion.
items.description: Electric dance-band groove of interlocking guitar lines, bass, drum kit, hand drums and a scraped dikanza under a lead singer and chorus.
exemplars: Analog Africa 'Angola Soundtrack' compilations of 1960s-70s Luanda conjunto recordings

items.name: Tarraxinha (slow Angolan kizomba offshoot)
items.lineage: Slow, bass-heavy electronic offshoot of kizomba that took shape in Angola in the 2000s for a close, slow-grinding couple dance; producers such as DJ Znobia and DJ Madabaya made it a club form in Luanda and the Lusophone diaspora.
items.description: Slow, minimal electronic groove of heavy sub-bass, sparse programmed drums and synth pads, largely instrumental and built for a slow couple dance.

items.name: Ovimbundu song and bow music (Angolan Central Highlands)
items.lineage: Music of the Umbundu-speaking Ovimbundu of Angola's Central Highlands around Huambo and Bié, documented in Ulrich Martini's 1971-72 recordings: songs with lamellophone and pieces on the ground bow and the scraped bow. The Congolese lukembi card stands in for the Ovimbundu lamellophone and the chizambi card for the scraped bow.
items.description: Songs over cycling lamellophone patterns alternate with buzzy, percussive musical-bow pieces built on a single string's few pitches.
exemplars: Ulrich Martini's 1971-72 field recordings of Ovimbundu music (Acoustic Music Records)

items.name: Chokwe mukanda and lamellophone music (Lunda, Angola)
items.lineage: Music of the Chokwe (Tshokwe) of north-eastern Angola, recorded by the Diamang company's Museu do Dundo in the 1950s and 1960s: songs and drumming of the mukanda boys' circumcision and initiation camp and its masked makishi dancers, and personal song with the cisanji lamellophone. The Congolese lukembi card stands in for the cisanji.
items.description: Leader-and-chorus initiation songs over driving drums for masked dancers, alongside intimate songs with cycling lamellophone patterns.
exemplars: Museu do Dundo (Diamang) recordings of Chokwe music, Lunda

items.name: Nhã nhạc (Huế royal court music)
items.lineage: Ceremonial court music of the Nguyễn dynasty (1802-1945) at Huế, played at state sacrifices such as the Nam Giao rite, at coronations, royal audiences and palace banquets, and proclaimed a UNESCO Masterpiece of the Oral and Intangible Heritage in 2003. It used two orchestras: the loud đại nhạc of kèn shawms and drums, and the softer tiểu nhạc of bamboo flute, đàn nhị fiddle and plucked lutes. After near-disappearance in the twentieth century it has been revived since the 1990s by Huế court-music troupes. A generic membrane-drum card stands in for the court drums.
items.description: Stately ceremonial pieces in which the nasal, penetrating kèn shawm leads over measured court drum strokes, alternating with a quieter heterophonic chamber texture of bamboo flute, two-string fiddle and plucked pear-shaped lute.
exemplars: Hue Royal Court Music Ensemble recordings
UNESCO Masterpiece of the Oral and Intangible Heritage documentation (2003)

items.name: Cồng chiêng (Central Highlands gong ensembles)
items.lineage: Gong music of the Central Highlands peoples, among them the Ê Đê, Jarai, Bahnar, M'nông and Xơ Đăng of Gia Lai, Đắk Lắk, Kon Tum, Đắk Nông and Lâm Đồng, proclaimed by UNESCO in 2005 as the Space of Gong Culture. Ensembles of bossed gongs (cồng) and flat gongs (chiêng), each player sounding a single gong, accompany rites of the agricultural and life cycle, buffalo sacrifices, funerals and village festivals, often together with a drum. The gong card stands in for both cồng and chiêng, and a generic membrane-drum card for the ensemble drum.
items.description: Interlocking gong patterns in which each gong contributes one pitch to a cyclic, layered texture of ringing bossed tones and shorter flat-gong strokes, repeated in long cycles over a steady drum pulse.
exemplars: Vietnam Institute for Musicology field recordings of Central Highlands gong ensembles
UNESCO Space of Gong Culture documentation (2005)

items.name: Chầu văn (Mother Goddess spirit-possession song)
items.lineage: Ritual song of the Đạo Mẫu Mother Goddess religion of northern Vietnam, sung for lên đồng ceremonies in which a medium embodies a succession of spirits; the practices were inscribed by UNESCO in 2016, and the Phủ Dầy temples of Nam Định are a principal centre. The band of cung văn musicians is led by a singer playing the đàn nguyệt moon lute, with phách clappers, drum and small bronze percussion, and each spirit is greeted with its own melodies and tempos. Generic drum, cymbal and gong cards stand in for the drum and the small bronze percussion (cảnh, thanh la).
items.description: Strophic songs over a driving moon-lute ostinato and bright clattering percussion, changing melody and tempo for each incarnated spirit, from slow invocations to fast songs for the medium's dances.
exemplars: Barley Norton — Songs for the Spirits: Music and Mediums in Modern Vietnam (University of Illinois Press, 2009), with audio-visual field recordings

items.name: Ca Huế (Huế chamber song)
items.lineage: Chamber song of Huế that grew among the aristocratic and literati circles of the Nguyễn capital and is still performed by Huế singers and instrumentalists, including on boats on the Perfume River. Its repertoire divides into điệu Bắc pieces of bright character and điệu Nam pieces of sorrowful character such as Nam ai and Nam bình, sung by a solo singer with đàn tranh zither, đàn tỳ bà, đàn nguyệt, đàn bầu and bamboo flute.
items.description: Delicate, heavily ornamented solo singing shaped by the tones of the words over a soft heterophonic ensemble of plucked zither and lutes, monochord harmonics and flute, moving between bright pieces and slow, grieving ones.
exemplars: Institute for Musicology archival recordings of ca Huế

items.name: Bài chòi (Central Vietnamese card-game singing)
items.lineage: Folk art of Central Vietnam, practised in the central provinces from Quảng Bình to Khánh Hòa and inscribed by UNESCO in 2017. At Lunar New Year players sit in bamboo huts (chòi) holding cards while a male or female caller (Hiệu) draws cards and sings verses hinting at each card's name, accompanied by musicians in the central hut; the singing also grew into a staged bài chòi folk theatre. The đàn nhị card stands in for the đàn cò fiddle and a generic membrane-drum card for the troupe drum.
items.description: A caller's half-sung, half-declaimed folk verses in central dialect, set to a small stock of traditional tunes and punctuated by two-string fiddle and drum.
exemplars: Central Vietnamese bài chòi troupes (UNESCO 2017 nomination audio-visual documentation)

items.name: Ví and giặm (Nghệ Tĩnh folk song)
items.lineage: Folk songs of Nghệ An and Hà Tĩnh provinces, inscribed by UNESCO in 2014, sung while working — weaving, rowing, farming — and at leisure, often as exchanges of improvised verses between men and women. Ví is free in rhythm and lyrical; giặm is metred and narrative or didactic, in lines of five syllables; both are normally sung without accompaniment.
items.description: Unaccompanied solo voices in local dialect: ví floats freely over long-held syllables and tonal inflections, while giặm moves in an even, syllabic pulse that carries a story or an argument.
exemplars: Voice of Vietnam archive recordings of ví and giặm
Nghệ An folk-song clubs (UNESCO 2014 nomination documentation)

items.name: Then (Tày, Nùng and Thái ritual song)
items.lineage: Ritual practice of the Tày, Nùng and Thái peoples of northern Vietnam, inscribed by UNESCO in 2019, in which a then master sings long song cycles narrating a journey to the heavenly realm to pray for peace, healing and good harvests. The master accompanies the singing on the đàn tính, a long-necked lute with a gourd body, and shakes a cluster of small bells (chùm xóc nhạc). The đàn tam card stands in for the đàn tính and the shaker card for the bell cluster.
items.description: A solo voice carrying a long sung narrative over the light, repeating plucked figures of the gourd lute, with the jingle of shaken bells marking the pulse.
exemplars: Then masters' ritual recordings (UNESCO 2019 nomination documentation)

items.name: Hát xẩm (northern Vietnamese street-singers' song)
items.lineage: Song of blind and itinerant street singers of the northern Red River Delta, performed at markets, wharves and, in early twentieth-century Hanoi, on the trams, with narrative, moralising and topical texts. The singer is accompanied by đàn nhị fiddle, đàn bầu monochord, sênh tiền coin clappers and a small drum. Hà Thị Cầu of Ninh Bình was its best-known late traditional exponent, and Hanoi revival groups have performed it since the 2000s. A generic hand-drum card stands in for the small drum.
items.description: Plaintive narrative street song in which the voice is shadowed by a nasal two-string fiddle and monochord and punctuated by the jingle of coin clappers and a small drum.
exemplars: Hà Thị Cầu (xẩm singer, Ninh Bình)

items.name: Nhạc tiền chiến (pre-1954 Vietnamese romantic song)
items.lineage: The first generation of Vietnamese tân nhạc (new music), composed from the late 1930s to the early 1950s by writers such as Đặng Thế Phong, Văn Cao and Đoàn Chuẩn, setting Vietnamese lyric poetry to Western-style melody and harmony in verse-and-refrain forms. After 1954 the repertoire was kept alive chiefly in Saigon, where singers recorded it for radio and records with guitar, piano and small studio orchestras.
items.description: Lyrical, slow-to-moderate romantic songs with long-breathed melodies, sung legato with clear diction and gentle vibrato over guitar and piano, often with strings.

items.name: Nhạc đỏ (Vietnamese revolutionary song)
items.lineage: Revolutionary and patriotic song repertoire composed from the 1940s in the Việt Minh resistance and in North Vietnam, and nationwide after 1975, by composers such as Văn Cao, Đỗ Nhuận, Hoàng Hiệp and Phạm Tuyên. Marches and lyrical mass songs for soloists, choirs and group singing were broadcast by the Voice of Vietnam and performed by army and state song-and-dance troupes with Western orchestral and band instruments. Generic string and horn cards stand in for the orchestral and band instruments.
items.description: Rousing marches and broad lyrical anthems sung by massed voices in unison or by soloists, in Western major and minor keys with strong downbeats over strings and open brass.
exemplars: Vietnam National Song and Dance Ensemble recordings

items.name: Nhạc trẻ (1960s-70s Saigon rock and soul)
items.lineage: Youth music of Saigon in roughly 1966-1975, played by local bands and singers in clubs, at dance parties and on radio for young Vietnamese audiences and American servicemen, mixing covers of Anglo-American rock, soul and go-go hits with Vietnamese-language songs in the same styles. The recordings were rediscovered through reissue compilations from 2010 onward.
items.description: Fuzz- and reverb-toned electric guitars, bass and a hard backbeat behind Vietnamese and English vocals, sometimes with combo organ, ranging from garage-rock stompers to soul ballads.
exemplars: Sublime Frequencies — Saigon Rock & Soul: Vietnamese Classic Tracks 1968-1974 (2010)

items.name: Hát trống quân (Red River Delta antiphonal song)
items.lineage: Antiphonal folk singing of the northern Red River Delta, notably Hưng Yên and the Hanoi region, in which young men and women exchange improvised courting and riddling verses, traditionally in the season of the Mid-Autumn festival. It takes its name from the trống quân, an earth drum made from a cord stretched over a board laid across a pit and struck with sticks to keep the beat. A generic hand-drum card stands in for the earth drum.
items.description: Two sides trade sung verses in lục bát meter on a short recurring tune, framed by the dull, thudding beat of the earth drum.
exemplars: Institute for Musicology field recordings of trống quân

items.name: Hát ru (Vietnamese lullaby)
items.lineage: Vietnamese cradle songs sung by mothers and grandmothers while rocking a hammock or cradle, setting lục bát folk poems (ca dao) to slow regional tunes, with vocables such as à ơi in the north and ầu ơ in the south. The genre has been collected in the field by the Institute for Musicology and is widely recorded on commercial albums.
items.description: Soft, unaccompanied solo singing in free rhythm, drawing out the opening vocables and following the tones of the words, rising and falling with the sway of the hammock.
exemplars: Institute for Musicology lullaby field collections

items.name: Lý (Central and Southern Vietnamese folk song)
items.lineage: Lý is a genre of short strophic folk songs of central and southern Vietnam, sung for leisure and courtship rather than to accompany work, with hundreds of named songs such as lý con sáo, lý ngựa ô and, in Huế, lý mười thương. In the south lý songs belong to the dân ca Nam Bộ repertoire and were absorbed into đờn ca tài tử and cải lương; they are widely recorded by folk singers with đàn tranh, đàn bầu and bamboo flute.
items.description: Compact, tuneful strophic songs with refrains of vocables, sung with gentle ornament and tonal inflection over plucked zither, monochord and flute.

items.name: Ngâm thơ (Vietnamese chanted poetry)
items.lineage: Melodic recitation of Vietnamese verse, chiefly in lục bát and song thất lục bát meters, using named tunes such as ngâm sa mạc and ngâm sổng; chanting the Tale of Kiều (ngâm Kiều) is a classic form. From the 1950s it was a staple of radio, on the Voice of Vietnam in Hanoi and on Radio Saigon's poetry programmes, where reciters were accompanied by bamboo flute, đàn tranh and đàn bầu improvising around the voice.
items.description: Free-rhythm, tone-led chanting of poetry that lingers on vowels and ends lines with long melismatic falls, while flute, zither and monochord weave fills between the phrases.

items.name: Nhạc lễ Nam Bộ (southern Vietnamese ritual ensemble music)
items.lineage: Ceremonial instrumental music of southern Vietnam, brought south by settlers from central Vietnam and related to Huế court ritual music, played at communal-house (đình) and temple rites, ancestor worship, weddings and above all funerals; revival classes have been held in Cần Thơ. Bands combine a loud section (phe võ) of kèn shawms, drums, small gong and cymbals with a softer section (phe văn) led by đàn cò and đàn gáo fiddles. The kèn bầu card stands in for the southern kèn, the đàn nhị card for the đàn cò, and a generic membrane-drum card for the ritual drums.
items.description: Loud, nasal shawm melodies over pounding ritual drums alternating with quieter heterophonic passages for two-string fiddles, in long suites of named ceremonial pieces.
exemplars: Vietnam Institute for Musicology field recordings of nhạc lễ
Cần Thơ nhạc lễ revival ensembles

items.name: Tụng kinh (Vietnamese Buddhist liturgical chant)
items.lineage: Liturgical chanting of Vietnamese Mahayana Buddhism, in Sino-Vietnamese and vernacular Vietnamese, performed by monastics and lay congregations at pagodas for daily services, repentance rites, funerals and festivals. Recitation (tụng) is paced by the mõ wooden fish and punctuated by the bowl bell, while hymns (tán) are more melodic; Huế is known for its Buddhist ritual-music tradition, and the Plum Village communities have carried recorded Vietnamese chant abroad. The temple-bell card stands in for the chuông bowl bell.
items.description: Steady unison recitation driven by the even knock of the wooden fish, with sustained, resonant bell strokes marking the sections and slower, more ornamented hymn passages.

items.name: Cham music of Ninh Thuận (Katê festival and ritual music)
items.lineage: Music of the Cham of Ninh Thuận and Bình Thuận on Vietnam's south-central coast, heard at the Katê festival at the Po Klong Garai and Po Rome towers and at life-cycle rites. Its core ensemble pairs the saranai shawm with the double-headed ginăng drum and the single-headed baranưng frame drum, accompanying ritual dance. The serunai card stands in for the saranai, and generic membrane-drum and frame-drum cards for the ginăng and baranưng.
items.description: A piercing, ornamented shawm line over interlocking hand-and-stick drum patterns on barrel and frame drums, driving festival processions and ritual dance.
exemplars: Vietnam Institute for Musicology field recordings of Cham music

items.name: Khan and hơmon (Central Highlands epic recitation)
items.lineage: Long heroic epics of the Central Highlands, among them the Ê Đê khan, such as the epic of Đam San, and the Bahnar hơmon, recited by a single narrator through one or several nights in the communal longhouse, alternating speech-like narration with sung passages. Between 2001 and 2007 a Vietnam Academy of Social Sciences project recorded and transcribed a large body of epics from living narrators.
items.description: A lone voice moving between rhythmic, speech-like declamation and sustained sung lines, with the heroes' speeches and battle scenes given heightened, dramatic delivery.
exemplars: Vietnam Academy of Social Sciences Central Highlands epic project recordings (2001-2007)

items.name: Mo Mường (Mường funeral epic chant)
items.lineage: Funeral chant of the Mường people of Hòa Bình and neighbouring provinces, sung by a mo priest (thầy mo) over the nights of a funeral to guide the soul of the dead. Its central narrative, Đẻ đất đẻ nước (Birth of the Earth and the Water), recounts the creation of the world and the origins of the Mường; Mo Mường is recognised as national intangible cultural heritage in Vietnam.
items.description: Long solo chanting in the Mường language, half sung and half recited, carrying a vast narrative in verse through the night.
exemplars: Hòa Bình cultural-heritage recordings of mo masters

items.name: Xòe and khắp (Thái dance-song of northwest Vietnam)
items.lineage: Song and dance of the Thái (Tai Dam and Tai Don) people of the northwestern uplands of Vietnam, in Sơn La, Điện Biên, Lai Châu and the Mường Lò valley of Yên Bái. Xòe, inscribed on UNESCO's Representative List as the Art of Xòe dance of the Tai people, is danced in ritual, circle and presentational forms at rituals, weddings and village festivals, the circle form with joined hands around a fire or a jar of rice wine; khắp is Thái sung poetry performed at festivals, weddings and courtship. The music is played on the tính tẩu gourd lute, the khèn bè mouth organ, reed pipes, drums, gongs and cymbals in a steady duple beat; the khaen card stands in for the khèn bè and generic drum, gong and cymbal cards for the percussion, and the gourd lute has no card.
items.description: A steady, cyclic dance pulse of drum, bossed gong and cymbals under the reedy drone and melody of the mouth organ, with sung verses in a speech-tone-bound melodic style.
exemplars: UNESCO Representative List documentation of the Art of Xòe dance of the Tai people (2021)
Vietnamese regional radio recordings of Thái khắp singing

items.name: Salo-so-sueng (Lanna northern Thai string band and so song)
items.lineage: Traditional music of the Lanna region of northern Thailand, centred on Chiang Mai, the former capital of the Lanna kingdom. Its best-known village band pairs the salo, a spike fiddle with a coconut resonator, with the sueng, a plucked lute, and accompanies so, a repartee song in which male and female singers improvise verses in the northern Thai dialect; so may also be accompanied by the pi chum free-reed pipes. The phin card stands in for the sueng.
items.description: Light, gentle heterophony of a thin, sweet spike fiddle and a plucked lute repeating a short melodic cycle, under alternating male and female voices that answer each other verse by verse.
exemplars: Chiang Mai field and radio recordings of so repartee singing with salo and sueng accompaniment

items.name: Nora (southern Thai dance-drama music)
items.lineage: Dance-drama of southern Thailand, strongest in Phatthalung, Nakhon Si Thammarat and Songkhla, inscribed on UNESCO's Representative List. The lead nora performer, in a beaded costume and crown, sings improvised verses and dances, and troupes also perform the rong khru ritual that honours nora ancestors. The ensemble consists of the pi oboe, the thap pair of goblet drums that follows the dancer, a klong drum, the mong pair of gongs, ching cymbals and the trae wooden clappers. The pi nai card stands in for the nora pi, a hand-drum card for the thap, generic drum and gong cards for the klong and mong, a generic cymbal card for the ching and an auxiliary-percussion card for the trae.
items.description: Fast, insistent drumming on paired goblet drums, driven by clapper and cymbal strokes and the alternating pitches of two gongs, under a piercing oboe line and a rapid, syllabic sung verse.
exemplars: UNESCO Representative List documentation of Nora, dance drama in southern Thailand (2021)

items.name: Nang talung (southern Thai shadow-puppet theatre music)
items.lineage: Shadow-puppet theatre of southern Thailand, centred on Nakhon Si Thammarat, Phatthalung and Songkhla, in which a single puppeteer (nai nang) moves cut-leather puppets behind a lit screen and voices every character, alternating sung verse with comic spoken dialogue in the southern dialect. Its small ensemble shares instruments with nora: pi oboe, thap goblet drums, klong drum, mong gongs and ching, and some modern troupes add Western drum kit and keyboard. The pi nai card stands in for the pi, a hand-drum card for the thap, generic drum and gong cards for the klong and mong, and a generic cymbal card for the ching.
items.description: One narrating voice shifting between chanted verse and rapid spoken comedy, punctuated by bursts of goblet-drum rhythm, gong strokes and a shrill oboe at each scene change.
exemplars: Southern Thai nang talung troupe cassette recordings
Nakhon Si Thammarat nang talung field recordings

items.name: Likay (Thai popular folk opera)
items.lineage: Popular musical theatre of central Thailand that took shape in Bangkok in the late nineteenth century, growing out of Muslim religious chanting (dikay) into a costumed commercial drama played at temple fairs and on travelling stages. Actors improvise sung and spoken dialogue around stock plots, much of the sung text is carried by the signature ranikloeng melody, and a piphat ensemble of ranat xylophone, gong circle, pi oboe, drums and ching accompanies the songs and stage action. Likay troupes reached a large audience through cassette, VCD and television recordings.
items.description: Florid sung dialogue in long ornamented phrases, answered by bright xylophone and gong-circle heterophony, a reedy oboe and drum-and-cymbal cues for entrances and fights.
exemplars: Commercial likay cassette and VCD releases

items.name: Kantrum (Northern Khmer song of Surin)
items.lineage: Music of the Northern Khmer communities of lower Isan in Thailand, chiefly Surin, Buriram and Sisaket provinces, sung in the Northern Khmer language for festivals, weddings and dancing. The traditional band accompanies singers with the tro fiddle, drums and ching cymbals; later singers made electrified kantrum, with keyboards and drum kit, a commercial genre on cassette. The tro u card represents the tro and a generic drum card the drums.
items.description: A bright, insistent dance pulse of drum and cymbal under a wiry fiddle that shadows a high, ornamented vocal line in short repeating strophes.
exemplars: Isan regional compilations of Surin kantrum

items.name: Thet mahachat (Thai Vessantara sermon chanting)
items.lineage: Thai Buddhist recitation of the Vessantara Jataka (Mahachat), the story of the Buddha's penultimate life, preached by monks in Thai verse in thirteen chapters (kan) at temple festivals. Celebrated preachers deliver it in the melodic lae style, an ornamented, heightened intonation of the text, and lae passages have also been borrowed into lûk thûng songs. It differs from Pali chant in being a Thai-language sermon meant to move and entertain the lay audience.
items.description: A single male voice moving between speech-like delivery and long, melismatic sung phrases in free rhythm, rising and falling with the tones of the Thai text.
exemplars: Thai temple recordings of thet mahachat
Lae passages on lûk thûng records

items.name: Lam phi fa (Isan spirit-healing song)
items.lineage: Healing ritual of the Lao-speaking Isan region of northeastern Thailand, in which a troupe of mediums, mostly older women, sing lam verses and dance to the khaen to call the phi fa, a sky spirit, to diagnose and cure a sick patient. Terry Miller documented it as the ritual branch of the Isan lam tradition, distinct from its entertainment genres.
items.description: Women's voices taking turns in long, speech-tone-shaped sung invocations over a continuous drone-and-melody on the mouth organ, building intensity as the dancing begins.
exemplars: Terry E. Miller field recordings of Isan lam phi fa

items.name: Pong lang (Kalasin log-xylophone band)
items.lineage: Ensemble music of Kalasin province in Isan, northeastern Thailand, built around the pong lang, a xylophone of hardwood logs strung together and hung at an angle from a post, played by two players. It was developed into a stage band in the later twentieth century, notably by Plueang Chairatsami, and became the emblem of Kalasin and a staple of school ensembles. The band adds khaen, phin, the wot circular panpipe, drums and cymbals. The ranat ek card stands in for the pong lang.
items.description: Hard, dry wooden-bar patterns in quick repeated figures over a bouncing drum groove, with mouth-organ drone and plucked lute riffs in bright, festive dance tunes.

items.name: Khrueang sai (Thai classical string ensemble)
items.lineage: One of the three principal ensembles of Thai classical music, alongside piphat and mahori, played indoors for entertainment and refined listening. The standard ensemble combines the saw duang and saw u fiddles, the jakhe floor zither, the khlui duct flute, the thon-rammana drums and ching; the khrueang sai pi chawa variant adds the pi chawa oboe and replaces the thon-rammana with klong khaek drums. The krapeu card stands in for the jakhe and a hand-drum card for the thon-rammana.
items.description: A soft, intimate heterophony in which high and low fiddles, a buzzing plucked zither and a breathy flute each ornament the same melody, over light hand-drum patterns and the ching marking the cycle.
exemplars: Thai Fine Arts Department khrueang sai recordings

items.name: Sepha (Thai narrative recitation with krap)
items.lineage: Thai narrative recitation in which a solo reciter delivers verse from the epic Khun Chang Khun Phaen, keeping time with krap sepha, two pairs of hardwood bars clicked together in each hand. In the early Bangkok period a piphat sepha ensemble was added to play pieces between passages of recitation, and its repertoire became part of the Thai classical canon. An auxiliary-percussion card stands in for the krap sepha and a generic drum card for the ensemble drum.
items.description: A single reciting voice declaiming rhymed verse to the crisp clicking of hardwood clappers, alternating with full ensemble pieces of xylophone, gong circle and oboe.
exemplars: Thai Fine Arts Department sepha recordings

items.name: Mohori (Khmer entertainment ensemble)
items.lineage: Khmer entertainment ensemble, played at the royal court for banquets and dance and in towns and villages for festivities, with sung texts on love and nature. It combines the roneat xylophone, the tro sau and tro u fiddles, the krapeu crocodile zither, flute, small drums and chhing cymbals with a singer. After the Khmer Rouge period the repertoire was rebuilt and taught by the Royal University of Fine Arts.
items.description: A light, lilting heterophony of soft-mallet xylophone, high and low fiddles and a plucked zither tremolo around a sung melody, over small hand drums and a gentle cymbal cycle.
exemplars: Royal University of Fine Arts mohori ensemble recordings

items.name: Smot (Khmer Buddhist chanted poetry)
items.lineage: Unaccompanied chanted poetry of Cambodian Theravada Buddhism, sung in Khmer mainly at funerals and memorial ceremonies and at other temple rites, by monks and by lay singers. Smot verses retell Buddhist teachings and jataka stories in a slow, heavily ornamented vocal line. The art was nearly lost under the Khmer Rouge and has been passed on through master-apprentice teaching such as that of Cambodian Living Arts.
items.description: A single voice in free rhythm, stretching each line into long melismatic arcs with wavering ornaments and held tones, mournful and meditative.
exemplars: Cambodian Living Arts smot master-apprentice recordings

items.name: Lakhon bassac (Khmer popular opera)
items.lineage: Popular theatre created by Khmer people near the Bassac river in the Mekong Delta of southern Vietnam at the beginning of the twentieth century, and taken up by troupes in Phnom Penh and across Cambodia. Drawing on Chinese opera, it combines costume, face painting, acrobatics and fight scenes with sung dialogue, and its orchestra joins the tro fiddle and other melodic instruments with drums, gongs, chimes and wood blocks. Generic drum, gong and auxiliary-percussion cards stand in for the percussion section.
items.description: Sung dialogue shadowed by a fiddle, broken up by loud, clattering drum, gong, cymbal and wood-block cues that drive the fight and entrance scenes.
exemplars: Cambodian Living Arts lakhon bassac recordings

items.name: Yike (Khmer folk opera)
items.lineage: Khmer sung theatre (lakhon yike) that enacts folk tales and legends through singing, dance and spoken passages, performed by village troupes and by the Royal University of Fine Arts. Its sound is led by the skor yike, a set of frame drums of graded sizes of which the largest is the skor mei, with traditional and modern melodic instruments completing the ensemble. The frame-drum card stands in for the skor yike and the tro sau card for the melodic instruments.
items.description: Booming, layered frame-drum rhythms from large and small drums framing sung verses and choral refrains, with a fiddle tracing the vocal melody.
exemplars: Royal University of Fine Arts yike troupe recordings

items.name: Chhayam (Khmer festival procession drumming)
items.lineage: Comic processional dance-music of Cambodia that leads ceremonial processions at the Khmer New Year in April and at Kathin, when gifts are carried to the monks at the end of the rainy season. Drummers on brightly decorated long drums (skor chhayam), with wooden krab clappers and hand cymbals, drive exaggerated clowning dances and raucous call-and-response singing that bystanders may join. A generic drum card stands in for the skor chhayam and an auxiliary-percussion card for the krab.
items.description: Loud, bouncing long-drum grooves, clacking clappers and crashing hand cymbals under shouted calls and group responses, festive and rowdy.
exemplars: Khmer New Year festival field recordings

items.name: Kantaoming (Khmer funeral gong ensemble of Siem Reap)
items.lineage: Funeral ensemble (kantoam ming) of Siem Reap province and its surroundings, also commonly called trai leak, played for cremations and other funeral rites. It joins the sralai oboe in its toam ming form with a gong chime of eight or nine bossed gongs set on a frame and struck with mallets, and percussion; its repertoire is of post-Angkorian origin, and the gong chime, long kept alive in Khmer funeral rites, is now taught in Siem Reap classes run by Cambodian Living Arts. A generic gong card stands in for the gong chime and a generic drum card for the percussion.
items.description: A plaintive, sustained oboe line over the ringing, melodic strokes of a bossed-gong chime, paced by steady drumming.
exemplars: Sounds of Angkor documentation of the kantoam ming funeral ensemble

items.name: Khap thum (Luang Prabang repartee song)
items.lineage: Vocal genre of Luang Prabang, the former royal capital of northern Laos, in which male and female singers alternate verses of courtship and wit. Unlike the khaen-accompanied lam and khap of other regions, khap thum is accompanied by a classical ensemble of the Luang Prabang type, with xylophone, gong circle, fiddle, flute, drum and cymbals, which plays between the sung verses. It is documented in Lao National Radio recordings and in Terry Miller's research.
items.description: Male and female voices trading ornamented verses, each answered by a gentle ensemble refrain of soft-mallet xylophone, gong circle, fiddle and flute over light drum and cymbal.
exemplars: Lao National Radio archive recordings of khap thum
Recordings of khap thum with Luang Prabang classical orchestras

items.name: Khap ngeum (Vientiane repartee song)
items.lineage: Repartee song of the Vientiane area of central Laos, one of the Lao khap genres, in which a man and a woman alternate improvised poetic verses to khaen accompaniment. It is distinguished from neighbouring khap and lam genres by its own melodic formulas, and it was recorded for the Lao National Radio archive and described by Terry Miller.
items.description: Alternating male and female voices in speech-tone-led melodic phrases over a continuous drone-and-melody from the mouth organ.
exemplars: Lao National Radio archive recordings of khap ngeum

items.name: Khap sam neua (Houaphan song)
items.lineage: Sung poetry of Houaphan province in northeastern Laos, named after the provincial capital Xam Neua and one of the northern Lao khap genres. Male and female singers alternate verses to khaen accompaniment, using the melodic formulas particular to the province, and it has been recorded for the Lao National Radio archive.
items.description: Male and female voices answering one another in long sung lines shaped by the tones of the words, carried on the sustained harmony of the mouth organ.
exemplars: Lao National Radio archive recordings of khap sam neua

items.name: Lam siphandone (Si Phan Don khaen song)
items.lineage: Regional lam style of the Si Phan Don ('four thousand islands') reach of the Mekong in Champasak province, one of the locally named lam genres of southern Laos, also written lam sithandone. It is an alternating song, which may be exchanged between a male and a female singer, delivered in Lao verse to the accompaniment of a single khaen mouth organ.
items.description: Lao-language vocal phrases shaped by the tones of the words, set over the continuous drone and melodic figures of a solo khaen, with two voices taking turns.
exemplars: Laos: Traditional Music of the South (UNESCO Collection, Smithsonian Folkways), track 'Lam Sithandone'

items.name: Lam khon savan (Savannakhet singer-and-khaen duet)
items.lineage: Lam style of Savannakhet province in Laos, one of four lam styles sung there alongside lam ban sok, lam phu thai and lam tang vay. It is performed as a duet between a singer and a khaen player. Lam mahaxay, the regional style named for Mahaxay in neighbouring Khammouane province, is a related singer-and-khaen lam and is included in this entry.
items.description: One voice in dialogue with one khaen: the mouth organ sustains a reedy drone under the singer's tone-shaped Lao phrases and takes up the melody between them.
exemplars: Molam Lao — Music from Southern Laos (Nimbus Records), southern regional lam including lam mahaxay

items.name: Lam phu thai (Phu Thai khaen song)
items.lineage: Lam of the Phu Thai, a Tai-speaking people of Savannakhet province in Laos, where it is one of the four local lam styles, and of the Isan provinces of Kalasin, Sakon Nakhon, Nakhon Phanom and Mukdahan across the Mekong in Thailand. Singers perform it in its own melodic style to khaen accompaniment, and it circulates on Lao and Isan cassette recordings.
items.description: Tone-shaped vocal phrases over the reedy drone and repeating melodic figures of a khaen, in the melodic style identified with the Phu Thai.
exemplars: Lao and Isan cassette recordings of lam phu thai

items.name: Qeej (Hmong funeral reed-pipe music)
items.lineage: Music of the qeej, the Hmong free-reed mouth organ of six bamboo pipes, played in the Hmong communities of Laos, Thailand and Vietnam and in the diaspora of the United States, France and Australia. Its melodies encode Hmong words through the tones of the language, so the player speaks ritual texts through the instrument; at funerals the qeej addresses the dead and guides the soul on its journey to the ancestors, played with the funeral drum, and it is also heard at New Year. The lusheng card in its qeej form stands in for the qeej, and a generic membrane-drum card for the funeral drum.
items.description: A buzzing, chordal reed sound with several pipes sounding together, phrased like speech as the player moves in dance steps, with the funeral drum beaten alongside.
exemplars: Amy Catlin's documentation of Hmong qeej players (Hmong Musicians in America)

items.name: Kwv txhiaj (Hmong sung poetry)
items.lineage: Sung poetry of the Hmong of Laos and the neighbouring highlands and of the Hmong diaspora, composed from formulaic and newly made verse. Kwv txhiaj are sung for courtship, above all at the New Year festival, and to voice longing, grief, orphanhood and the experience of war and exile.
items.description: A single unaccompanied voice whose melody follows the tones of the Hmong words, unfolding long lines of formulaic verse.
exemplars: Victoria Vorreiter — Songs of Memory: Traditional Music of the Golden Triangle (2009), field recordings

items.name: Tøøm (Kammu sung poetry)
items.lineage: A principal song genre of the Kammu (Khmu), an Austroasiatic-speaking people of northern Laos, notably in Luang Namtha, Oudomxay and Luang Prabang provinces, with communities in Thailand, Vietnam and China. Tøøm is sung poetry in formal verse; it and the other Kammu vocal genres are documented in Håkan Lundström's study of the repertoire of one traditional singer, published with recordings.
items.description: A single unaccompanied voice delivering lines of formal poetry, the melody bending to the words.
exemplars: Håkan Lundström — I Will Send My Song: Kammu Vocal Genres in the Singing of Kam Raw (NIAS Press, 2010), with recordings

items.name: Nat pwe (Burmese spirit-festival music)
items.lineage: Music for nat pwe, the Burmese ceremonies in which nat kadaw spirit mediums dance to invite and embody the nats, the spirits of the pantheon of thirty-seven and of local cults. A hsaing waing ensemble led by the pat waing drum circle and the hne shawm plays while a singer performs the songs belonging to each spirit; the largest gatherings are the annual festivals at Taungbyone near Mandalay and at Mount Popa.
items.description: Loud outdoor ensemble music in which the tuned drum circle, gongs and a piercing shawm drive fast, insistent dance pieces for the possessed medium, alternating with songs addressed to the spirit.
exemplars: Field recordings of Taungbyone nat festival hsaing troupes

items.name: Sandaya (Burmese piano)
items.lineage: Burmese style of piano playing, the instrument known as sandaya, through which the classical mahagita song repertoire was adapted to the keyboard. Pianists carry the idioms of the saung harp, the pattala xylophone and the hsaing waing ensemble over to the piano, playing the melody in both hands in octaves and interlocking figures rather than with Western chords, decorated with quick ornamental notes.
items.description: Solo piano playing Burmese classical melodies in octaves and quick interlocking figures between the hands, heavily ornamented, without chordal accompaniment.
exemplars: U Ko Ko sandaya piano recordings

items.name: Thangyat (Thingyan satirical chant)
items.lineage: Burmese performance genre of rhymed satirical verse chanted by a lead performer and answered by a chorus, to the beat of traditional drums or a hsaing waing ensemble and interspersed with song and dance routines. Troupes perform during Thingyan, the water festival before the Burmese New Year in April, voicing social and political criticism. Thangyat was permitted again in 2013, after a ban imposed by the military government in 1989, on condition that troupes submit their verses in advance, and in 2019 members of the Peacock Generation troupe were sentenced to prison for a performance satirising the army. A generic membrane-drum card stands in for the drums.
items.description: Rhymed verses chanted by a leader in a driving metre, each answered by a massed chorus over steady drumming.

items.name: Manau (Kachin festival dance music)
items.lineage: Music of the manau, the great dance festival of the Kachin (Jinghpaw) peoples of northern Myanmar, held most prominently at Myitkyina and also celebrated by the Jingpo of Yunnan. Long lines of dancers follow their dance leaders along winding paths around the painted manau posts to the beating of large drums and gongs. Generic drum and gong cards stand in for the manau drums and gongs.
items.description: A steady, repeated pulse of large drums and bossed gongs carrying a long procession of dancers around the festival ground, outdoors and resonant.

items.name: Shan (Tai Yai) long-drum and gong music
items.lineage: Festival and dance music of the Shan (Tai Yai), the Tai-speaking people of Shan State in Myanmar and of Mae Hong Son and other districts of northern Thailand. The kong kon yao long drum leads an ensemble of cymbals of several sizes and a set of small gongs for processions, the Poi Sang Long novice ordinations and the bird and toh dances, and the related mong seng ensemble pairs its drum with large cymbals and small gongs. The Burmese ozi card stands in for the Shan long drum, with generic gong and cymbal cards.
items.description: A deep long drum plays driving patterns over the steady ring of gongs and the clash of cymbals, music for festival processions and dances.
exemplars: Tai Yai long-drum ensembles of the Poi Sang Long processions, Mae Hong Son

items.name: Karen harp song and hta poetry
items.lineage: Traditional music of the Karen (Sgaw and Pwo) peoples of Kayin State and the Myanmar-Thailand borderlands. Its best-known instrument is the Karen arched harp, which accompanies song, and its oral literature lives in hta, sung poetry that carries history, moral teaching and courtship. The Burmese saung gauk card stands in for the smaller Karen harp.
items.description: A voice singing verses of poetry to the plucked, gently ringing accompaniment of an arched harp, intimate and unhurried.
exemplars: Victoria Vorreiter — Songs of Memory: Traditional Music of the Golden Triangle (2009), field recordings

items.name: Mon traditional music (piphat mon ensemble)
items.lineage: Music of the Mon of Lower Myanmar, around Mawlamyine in Mon State, and of the Mon communities of central Thailand such as those of Pathum Thani and Phra Pradaeng. Its emblem is the piphat mon ensemble, led by the large pi mon oboe with a flared metal bell, with khong mon gong circles set in upright crescent-shaped frames, ranat xylophones, the poeng mang khok frame of tuned drums and a barrel drum; in Thai custom it is the ensemble played at funerals. Mon chamber music also uses the kyam crocodile zither. The Thai khong wong yai card stands in for the khong mon, a generic membrane-drum card for the poeng mang khok and the taphon card for the Mon barrel drum.
items.description: A plaintive, nasal oboe leads a slow heterophonic texture of gong circles and xylophone over tuned drums, solemn music for funeral rites.
exemplars: Mon piphat recordings of the Mon community of Pathum Thani

items.name: Akha song and ritual chant
items.lineage: Vocal traditions of the Akha, a Tibeto-Burman-speaking highland people of Yunnan, Shan State, northern Laos and the Chiang Rai hills of Thailand, closely related to the Hani. Akha custom is carried orally: reciters chant long ritual texts and genealogies at funerals and ancestral rites, and songs accompany courtship and village festivals.
items.description: Unaccompanied voices: a reciter's long, steady recitation of ritual verse, and sung verses for courtship and festivals.
exemplars: Victoria Vorreiter — Songs of Memory: Traditional Music of the Golden Triangle (2009), field recordings

items.name: Lahu gourd-pipe dance music
items.lineage: Music of the Lahu, a Tibeto-Burman-speaking highland people of Yunnan, Shan State, northern Laos and the Chiang Mai and Chiang Rai hills of Thailand. Its emblem is the naw, a gourd mouth organ with bamboo pipes set in a gourd wind chest, which men play while leading the circle dances of the New Year festival on the village dance ground. The lusheng card stands in for the naw.
items.description: A buzzing gourd mouth organ repeats short dance phrases in steady metre, several pipes sounding together, for dancers circling the village dance ground.
exemplars: Victoria Vorreiter — Songs of Memory: Traditional Music of the Golden Triangle (2009), field recordings

items.name: Lisu gourd-pipe and lute dance music
items.lineage: Music of the Lisu, a Tibeto-Burman-speaking people of the Nujiang valley of Yunnan, of Kachin and Shan States in Myanmar and of the hills of northern Thailand. At the New Year festival villagers dance in circles on the village dance ground to the gourd mouth organ and a long-necked plucked lute. The lusheng card stands in for the Lisu gourd pipe and the sanxian card for the Lisu lute.
items.description: A reedy gourd mouth organ and a plucked long-necked lute repeat short, lilting dance figures in steady metre for a circling line of dancers.
exemplars: Victoria Vorreiter — Songs of Memory: Traditional Music of the Golden Triangle (2009), field recordings

items.name: Iu Mien Taoist ritual music
items.lineage: Ritual music of the Iu Mien (Yao), whose religion is a form of Taoism carried from southern China to Laos, Thailand and Vietnam and on to the diaspora in the United States. Priests conduct ordinations, funerals and other rites by chanting from ritual manuscripts written in Chinese characters, in a liturgical language distinct from everyday Mien, accompanied by drum, gong and cymbals. Generic drum, gong and cymbal cards stand in for the ritual instruments.
items.description: Priests' chanted recitation of ritual texts, punctuated and driven by drum strokes, gong and clashing cymbals.
exemplars: Victoria Vorreiter — Songs of Memory: Traditional Music of the Golden Triangle (2009), field recordings

items.name: Tia-Piah (Kiowa Gourd Dance songs)
items.lineage: Song repertoire of the Kiowa Gourd Clan (Tia-Piah society), a Kiowa warrior-society dance revived at Carnegie, Oklahoma, in the mid-twentieth century and since taken up by Comanche, Cheyenne and many other nations, where a gourd dance is often held in the afternoon before a powwow. Singers seated at a large shared drum sing the society's songs while the men dance in place, shaking rattles in time with the drum and stepping toward it as the song builds. The powwow drum card stands in for the gourd-dance drum and a generic shaker card for the dancers' rattles.
items.description: A steady, moderate drumbeat under a Southern Plains male chorus singing in open-throated unison after the lead's opening phrase, each song repeated several times while dozens of hand rattles shimmer in tight synchrony with the drum.
exemplars: Indian House 'Kiowa Gourd Dance' Vols. 1 and 2
Kiowa Gourd Clan annual ceremonial at Carnegie

items.name: Forty-nine songs (Southern Plains late-night social songs)
items.lineage: Social songs of the Kiowa and other Southern Plains peoples, sung late at night after powwows and spread through intertribal gatherings across the United States and Canada during the twentieth century. Kiowa tradition traces them to songs sung by war parties setting out on expeditions; today most are love and teasing songs, many with English verses set between vocables, sung by a group around a drum while the dancers, arms linked, circle around the singers. A generic hand-drum card stands in for the drum.
items.description: Relaxed group singing over a steady drumbeat, the lead's phrase taken up by the others, with English lines of love and teasing set among vocables and the whole song repeated round and round as the circle of dancers moves.

items.name: Stomp dance (Southeastern leader-and-response dance songs)
items.lineage: Night-long dance of the Muscogee (Creek), Cherokee, Seminole, Yuchi, Shawnee and related Southeastern peoples, held at ceremonial grounds around a sacred fire, including at the Green Corn ceremony, and maintained chiefly in eastern Oklahoma since Removal. A male leader sings short calls and the men following him in line answer in chorus as the line winds counterclockwise around the fire, while women shell shakers set the rhythm with turtle-shell or can rattles tied to their legs; there is no drum. A generic shaker card stands in for the shell shakers.
items.description: Short calls from a leader answered at once by a male chorus in quick alternation, over the steady chug of leg rattles stamped in time with the dancers' steps, the exchange building in energy through each dance episode.
exemplars: Indian House 'Stomp Dance' album series (eastern Oklahoma ceremonial-ground singers)

items.name: Mvskoke hymn singing (Muscogee and Seminole church hymnody)
items.lineage: Christian hymns sung in the Mvskoke language in Muscogee (Creek) and Seminole Baptist and Methodist churches of eastern Oklahoma, a congregational practice that grew from nineteenth-century missions and is still sung at church services, camp meetings and funerals. The melodies are carried orally (the texts are printed in Mvskoke hymnals) and the hymns are sung unaccompanied, a song leader starting each hymn and the congregation joining in.
items.description: Unhurried, unaccompanied congregational singing in the Mvskoke language: a song leader begins and the church joins in a full, slightly heterophonic unison, phrases ending on long held tones.
exemplars: Muskogee (Seminole/Creek) Documentation Project hymn recordings (College of William & Mary)
Frank Speck recordings of Muscogee (Creek) hymns, American Philosophical Society

items.name: Kiowa hymns (Kiowa-language Christian song)
items.lineage: Christian hymns composed and sung in the Kiowa language by Kiowa Baptist and Methodist congregations of southwestern Oklahoma since the late nineteenth century, carried orally and sung unaccompanied at church services, funerals and community gatherings. Their melodies are Kiowa songs in Kiowa musical style rather than tunes borrowed from Euro-American hymnals, and the tradition is the subject of the collaborative study The Jesus Road by Luke Eric Lassiter, Clyde Ellis and Ralph Kotay.
items.description: Unaccompanied group singing of Kiowa-language hymns, a leader starting each song and the others joining in unison on long, repeated melodic phrases, unhurried and solemn.
exemplars: Ralph Kotay, Kiowa Hymns (University of Nebraska Press CD, 2004)

items.name: Haudenosaunee Longhouse ceremonial songs (Iroquois Midwinter and Feather Dance)
items.lineage: Ceremonial songs of the Longhouse religion of the Seneca, Cayuga, Onondaga, Mohawk, Oneida and Tuscarora, shaped by the Gaiwiio teachings of the Seneca prophet Handsome Lake from the end of the eighteenth century and sung through the cycle of thanksgiving ceremonies, above all the Midwinter ceremony with its Great Feather Dance and Drum Dance, and the Green Corn and Strawberry festivals. In the Great Feather Dance two singers seated astride a bench beat snapping-turtle rattles on it while the dancers circle the longhouse; other dances use the water drum and cow-horn rattles. A hand-drum card stands in for the water drum and a generic shaker card for the rattles.
items.description: Short, strongly metrical songs sung in unison by a pair or small group of male singers, the rapid, even strokes of turtle rattle or water drum driving each repeated section as the dancers' steps sound on the floor.
exemplars: Library of Congress AFS L6 'Songs from the Iroquois Longhouse' (William N. Fenton, 1942)

items.name: Haudenosaunee social dance songs (Eskanye, Smoke Dance and water-drum songs)
items.lineage: Social dance repertoire of the Six Nations, sung at socials in longhouses and community halls at Six Nations of the Grand River, Allegany, Cattaraugus, Akwesasne and other communities: the women's shuffle dance (Eskanye), Standing Quiver, Rabbit, Alligator, Fish and Smoke dances among many others. A lead singer plays the small wooden water drum and the other singers accompany him on cow-horn rattles, singing in unison or answering his phrases. A hand-drum card stands in for the water drum and a generic shaker card for the horn rattles.
items.description: Brisk, buoyant songs over the bright, ringing tap of the water drum and the crisp chatter of horn rattles, the lead singer's phrases answered or joined by the group at a steady, danceable tempo.

items.name: Midewiwin songs (Grand Medicine Society)
items.lineage: Ritual songs of the Midewiwin, the Grand Medicine Society of the Ojibwe, Menominee, Potawatomi and other Great Lakes peoples, sung in the society's initiation and healing ceremonies and recorded on wax cylinder from Mide singers in Minnesota in the early twentieth century. Mide songs were remembered with the help of pictographs incised on birchbark scrolls, and are accompanied by the Mide water drum and rattles.
