A hand-drum card stands in for the water drum and a generic shaker card for the rattles.
items.description: Solemn solo and small-group male ritual singing over an even, resonant water-drum or rattle pulse, the melodies descending to a low final tone.
exemplars: Frances Densmore, Chippewa Music (Bureau of American Ethnology Bulletins 45 and 53, 1910 and 1913), Library of Congress cylinders

items.name: Big Drum songs (Ojibwe and Menominee Drum Dance)
items.lineage: Songs of the Big Drum religion (Drum Dance or Dream Dance), which spread from the Dakota to the Ojibwe, Menominee and Potawatomi of Wisconsin and Minnesota from the late nineteenth century, after the vision in which a Dakota woman was given the drum. Each consecrated drum, a large drum suspended from four curved, decorated legs, has its own members, offices and songs, sung by the drummers seated around it during seasonal ceremonies. The powwow drum card stands in for the dance drum.
items.description: Male drummers seated around one large suspended drum sing in unison after the lead opens each song in a high register, over a steady, even drumbeat with accented strokes at fixed points in the song.
exemplars: Thomas Vennum, The Ojibwa Dance Drum (Smithsonian Folklife Studies, 1982)
Frances Densmore, Menominee Music (Bureau of American Ethnology, 1932)

items.name: Round dance songs (Cree and Northern Plains hand-drum songs)
items.lineage: Round dance songs of the Plains Cree, Saulteaux, Nakoda, Dakota and neighbouring peoples of the Canadian prairies and the northern United States, sung at winter round dances held to honour and remember the dead and at social gatherings, where the dancers join hands in a large circle that moves sideways around the singers. The singers stand together in the centre, each beating a hand-held frame drum, and the repertoire runs from vocable songs to newer songs with English love-song verses; it has become a large recorded genre on Canadian and American Indigenous labels.
items.description: High, Northern-style unison singing over hand drums beating a lilting strong-weak pulse, the lead's opening phrase answered by the group and the whole song repeated several times, sometimes with English verses between the vocables.
exemplars: Northern Cree round dance albums (Canyon Records)
Sweet Grass Records round dance releases

items.name: Sun Dance songs (Lakota and Plains Sun Dance)
items.lineage: Songs of the Sun Dance (Wiwanyang Wacipi), the summer renewal ceremony of the Lakota and of the Cheyenne, Arapaho, Shoshone, Blackfoot, Crow and other Plains nations, held over several days in a circular arbor around a central tree. Singers at a large drum carry the dancers through each round while the dancers blow eagle-bone whistles; Teton Sioux Sun Dance songs were among those Frances Densmore recorded on cylinder for Teton Sioux Music. The powwow drum card stands in for the Sun Dance drum.
items.description: Intense, high-pitched male group singing at a large drum with a steady, driving beat, the songs repeated through long dance rounds and pierced by the shrill, continuous peeping of the dancers' bone whistles.
exemplars: Frances Densmore, Teton Sioux Music (Bureau of American Ethnology Bulletin 61, 1918), Library of Congress cylinders

items.name: Ghost Dance songs (1889-90 movement and its survivals)
items.lineage: Songs of the Ghost Dance, the religious movement begun by the Northern Paiute prophet Wovoka in western Nevada in 1889 and taken up by the Arapaho, Cheyenne, Lakota, Caddo, Kiowa, Pawnee and other nations, whose followers danced in a circle with joined hands, singing without drums. Arapaho and Caddo Ghost Dance songs were recorded on cylinder in 1894 and their texts printed in The Ghost-Dance Religion (1896), and some songs are still sung among the Caddo of Oklahoma.
items.description: Unaccompanied songs sung in unison by men and women dancing in a circle with joined hands, built from short melodic phrases each sung twice in succession, within a narrow range and at an even, walking pace.
exemplars: James Mooney cylinder recordings of Arapaho and Caddo Ghost Dance songs (1894), Library of Congress

items.name: Hethuska (Omaha and Ponca war-dance society songs)
items.lineage: Songs of the Hethuska, the warrior society of the Omaha, whose dance passed to the Ponca, Kaw, Osage and others and, as the Omaha dance of the Lakota, became a principal source of the Plains war dance, the Northern grass dance and the Southern straight dance. The society's songs honour warriors' deeds and are sung by men seated around a large drum; Omaha Hethuska songs were recorded on cylinder by Alice Fletcher and Francis La Flesche in the late nineteenth century, and the dance continues in the Ponca Hethuska society of Oklahoma. The powwow drum card stands in for the society drum.
items.description: Powerful unison male singing around a large drum, the lead pitching the opening phrase high and the group taking it up over a fast, even drumbeat that carries the dancers, with words naming warriors' deeds set among vocables.
exemplars: Library of Congress 'Omaha Indian Music: Historical Recordings from the Fletcher/La Flesche Collection' (1985)

items.name: Hako (Pawnee calumet ceremony songs)
items.lineage: Song cycle of the Hako, the Pawnee calumet ceremony in which a party carrying a pair of feathered pipe-stems travelled to another band or nation to establish a bond of ritual kinship, its songs sung in fixed order over several days by the ceremonial leader (kurahus) and his assistants. It is known chiefly from the songs and explanations the kurahus Tahirussawichi gave to Alice C. Fletcher, recorded and published with James R. Murie as The Hako: A Pawnee Ceremony (Bureau of American Ethnology, 1904).
items.description: Solemn male ritual chant in a long fixed sequence of songs, short text lines repeated many times to simple melodic phrases, as heard on early phonograph recordings of a single ceremonial singer.
exemplars: Alice C. Fletcher cylinders and transcriptions, The Hako: A Pawnee Ceremony (BAE 22nd Annual Report, 1904)

items.name: Hopi katsina songs (Hopi masked-dance songs)
items.lineage: Songs of the katsina dances held in the village plazas of the Hopi mesas of northern Arizona between the winter solstice and July, in which lines of masked katsina dancers sing in unison as they dance, many songs composed anew for each occasion by men of the village; the Hopi also sing social dances such as the Butterfly Dance. The dancers carry gourd rattles and wear turtle-shell rattles at the knee. A generic shaker card stands in for the rattles.
items.description: A line of masked men singing in unison in a low, rough-edged, powerful chest register, long songs moving through contrasting sections with shifting phrase lengths over the shake of gourd rattles and the clatter of turtle-shell knee rattles.
exemplars: Folkways FE 4394 'Hopi Katcina Songs and Six Other Songs by Hopi Chanters'

items.name: Zuni songs (Shiwi ceremonial and social dance songs)
items.lineage: Ceremonial and social song of Zuni Pueblo in western New Mexico, sung by kachina dance groups, medicine societies and social dancers through a yearly cycle that culminates in the Shalako ceremony in early winter, together with social dances such as the Comanche dance. In 1890 Zuni songs were recorded on wax cylinder for the Hemenway Expedition, among the earliest ethnographic field recordings, and further Zuni songs were published from recordings in 1957. A generic membrane-drum card stands in for the large double-headed dance drum and a generic shaker card for the rattles.
items.description: A unison male chorus in a low, full-bodied register over a deep double-headed drum and gourd rattles, long songs in several sections with shifting phrase lengths.
exemplars: Jesse Walter Fewkes, Hemenway Expedition Zuni cylinders (1890)
Frances Densmore, Music of Acoma, Isleta, Cochiti and Zuni Pueblos (Bureau of American Ethnology, 1957)

items.name: Rio Grande Pueblo dance songs (Tewa, Tiwa and Keres feast-day dances)
items.lineage: Dance songs of the Tewa, Tiwa, Towa and Keres pueblos of the Rio Grande valley in New Mexico, sung for the corn, buffalo, deer, eagle and Comanche dances of saints' feast days and the seasonal calendar, and for the round dances of Taos. A male chorus stands beside the dance lines while a drummer plays a large double-headed drum, and the dancers carry gourd rattles and wear tortoise-shell rattles and bells. A generic membrane-drum card stands in for the pueblo drum and a generic shaker card for the rattles.
items.description: A large male chorus sings in low, strong unison over a deep, booming double-headed drum, the long songs changing pattern between sections as the drum cues the dancers' turns, with the rattles of the dance lines shimmering beneath.
exemplars: Smithsonian Folkways SFW 40408 'Music of New Mexico: Native American Traditions'
Indian House Taos Pueblo and San Juan Pueblo albums

items.name: Waila (Tohono O'odham chicken scratch)
items.lineage: Social dance music of the Tohono O'odham and Akimel O'odham of southern Arizona, played for all-night dances at village feasts, weddings and birthdays. It grew from the fiddle-and-guitar bands of the late nineteenth century, and from the mid-twentieth century bands added button accordion and saxophones, playing polkas, two-steps, chotes (schottisches) and mazurkas, later also cumbias, usually without vocals; Canyon Records has issued a long series of chicken-scratch albums.
items.description: Instrumental dance music in which button accordion and alto saxophone play the tune together in unison or parallel harmony over bajo sexto or guitar chords, electric bass and a light drum kit, at brisk polka and two-step tempos.
exemplars: Gu-Achi Fiddlers (old-time O'odham fiddle band, Canyon Records)

items.name: O'odham traditional song (Tohono O'odham ceremonial and social song)
items.lineage: Song of the Tohono O'odham (formerly called Papago) and Akimel O'odham (Pima) of the Sonoran Desert, sung in cycles for the summer saguaro-wine rain ceremony, for curing, for the Wi:gita ceremony, and for social round and skipping dances. Singers accompany themselves with gourd rattles and by striking or scraping an overturned basket used as a drum, and a large Papago repertoire was recorded on cylinder in the early 1920s for Papago Music (1929). A hand-drum card stands in for the basket drum and a generic shaker card for the gourd rattles.
items.description: Unison group singing of short songs repeated in long cycles, over the dry swish of gourd rattles and the hollow thud or rasp of an overturned basket.
exemplars: Frances Densmore, Papago Music (Bureau of American Ethnology Bulletin 90, 1929), Library of Congress cylinders

items.name: Bird songs (Cahuilla, Kumeyaay and Colorado River song cycles)
items.lineage: Song cycles of the Cahuilla, Serrano, Kumeyaay (Kumiai), Quechan, Mojave, Cocopah and neighbouring peoples of southern California, the lower Colorado River and northern Baja California, recounting in cycles of hundreds of songs the journeys of the first people and the birds, sung through the night at memorials, gatherings and celebrations. A line of men sings in unison, each shaking a gourd rattle filled with seeds, while women dance in a line before them; the Cahuilla belong to a different language family from the Yuman peoples but share the genre.
items.description: Male voices in close unison over the steady, crisp shake of seed-filled gourd rattles, each short song repeated several times before the next in a long night-time sequence.
exemplars: Alvino Siva and Robert Levi (Cahuilla bird singers)
Richard Lando recordings of Cahuilla bird songs at the Malki Fiesta, Morongo Reservation (1968), UC Riverside Special Collections

items.name: Salt Songs (Southern Paiute and Chemehuevi mourning cycle)
items.lineage: A long cycle of songs of the Southern Paiute and Chemehuevi that traces a journey, the Salt Song Trail, through sacred places of their homelands in present-day Nevada, Utah, Arizona and California, sung through the night at funerals and memorial gatherings to accompany the spirit of the dead. Singers accompany themselves with gourd rattles. The Salt Song Project brought singers from many bands together to revive the cycle, as documented in the film The Salt Song Trail: Bringing Creation Back Together (2005). The shaker card stands in for the gourd rattle.
items.description: Group singing of short strophic songs in a steady pulse kept by shaken gourd rattles, one song following another through the night in a long, unhurried sequence.
exemplars: The Salt Song Trail: Bringing Creation Back Together (documentary film, 2005)

items.name: Mamakwanhkap (Ute Bear Dance songs)
items.lineage: Songs of the Bear Dance, the spring dance of the Ute held by the Southern Ute at Ignacio, the Ute Mountain Ute and the Northern Ute of Utah, whose Ute name, mama-kwa-nhká-pú, means 'woman-return dance' because women choose their partners, and in which facing lines of dancers step toward and away from each other. The singers accompany it on moraches, notched sticks rasped with a bone or smaller stick over a resonator to make a growling sound associated with the bear. Frances Densmore published Northern Ute bear dance songs from her cylinder recordings in Northern Ute Music (BAE Bulletin 75, 1922). The reco-reco card, set to ribbed wood, stands in for the morache.
items.description: A group of singers repeats short songs over the loud, rasping growl of many scraped notched sticks amplified by a resonator, a steady scraping pulse that carries the back-and-forth dance lines.
exemplars: Frances Densmore cylinder recordings published in Northern Ute Music (BAE Bulletin 75, 1922)

items.name: Brush Dance and Jump Dance songs (Hupa, Yurok and Karuk)
items.lineage: Ceremonial songs of the Hupa, Yurok and Karuk of the Klamath and Trinity river valleys in northwestern California: the Brush Dance, a healing ceremony held for a sick child, and the world-renewal Jump Dance and White Deerskin Dance, held to keep the world in balance. A lead singer stands among a line of dancers who sustain a low, rhythmic vocal accompaniment. Pliny Earle Goddard and A. L. Kroeber made cylinder recordings of these songs in the early twentieth century, held at the Phoebe A. Hearst Museum of Anthropology.
items.description: A solo song line carried over a low, pulsing vocal accompaniment from a line of dancers, with the dancers' stamping marking the pulse.
exemplars: P. E. Goddard and A. L. Kroeber cylinder recordings, Phoebe A. Hearst Museum of Anthropology

items.name: Washat (Seven Drums longhouse songs)
items.lineage: Song worship of the Washat, also called the Seven Drums or Longhouse religion, of Columbia Plateau peoples including the Yakama, Umatilla, Nez Perce, Wanapum and Warm Springs, which took its present form in the nineteenth century under prophets such as the Wanapum leader Smohalla. Services and first-foods feasts in the longhouse are led by seven drummers beating hide hand drums in unison, a leader rings a hand bell to mark the songs, and the congregation sings and dances. The University of Washington Ethnomusicology Archives hold Plateau longhouse recordings. The hand-drum card stands in for the rawhide hand drums.
items.description: A steady unison beat from a row of hand drums under congregational singing, each song set off by the ring of a small hand bell while worshippers dance.
exemplars: University of Washington Ethnomusicology Archives Plateau longhouse recordings

items.name: Kwakwaka'wakw potlatch songs (Hamatsa and Tseka winter ceremonial)
items.lineage: Ceremonial songs of the Kwakwaka'wakw of northern Vancouver Island and the adjacent mainland, sung in the big house at potlatches and in the winter ceremonial (Tseka), whose dances include the Hamatsa. Song leaders beat time with batons on a long wooden log drum, joined by hide frame drums, as masked and blanketed dancers enter; songs are hereditary property of chiefs and families, and the ceremonies were kept up through the decades of the Canadian potlatch ban. Ida Halpern's 1967 Folkways album Indian Music of the Pacific Northwest Coast (FE 4523) documents Kwakwaka'wakw singers. The slit-gong card, set to cedar and ceremonial use, stands in for the log drum and the hand-drum card for the frame drums.
items.description: A massed chorus of singers in strong unison over heavy, resonant wooden strokes beaten on a cedar log in unison patterns, with frame drums thickening the beat in a resonant wooden hall.
exemplars: Ida Halpern, Indian Music of the Pacific Northwest Coast (Folkways FE 4523, 1967)

items.name: Nuu-chah-nulth songs (west coast of Vancouver Island)
items.lineage: Songs of the Nuu-chah-nulth nations of the west coast of Vancouver Island, formerly called Nootka, including potlatch songs, songs of the Tlukwana wolf ritual, whaling songs and songs for the bone (lahal) game, held as hereditary rights by chiefs and families. Singers accompany themselves on hide frame drums. Ida Halpern's 1974 Folkways album Nootka Indian Music of the Pacific North West Coast (FE 4524) documented the repertoire with Nuu-chah-nulth singers. The hand-drum card stands in for the frame drums.
items.description: Solo and group singing over steady frame-drum beats, with vocable passages alternating with texted phrases.
exemplars: Ida Halpern, Nootka Indian Music of the Pacific North West Coast (Folkways FE 4524, 1974)

items.name: Tsimshianic feast songs and limx'ooy laments (Nisga'a, Gitxsan, Tsimshian)
items.lineage: Songs of the Nisga'a, Gitxsan and Tsimshian of the Nass and Skeena river valleys, sung at the feasts (potlatches) where house groups validate names, crests and territories, including the limx'ooy, dirges owned by a house and sung for its dead. Hide frame drums and chiefs' carved rattles accompany the dance songs, while the laments are slow and solemn. Marius Barbeau, working with the Tsimshian ethnographer William Beynon, recorded these songs on wax cylinders between 1915 and 1929 for what is now the Canadian Museum of History.
items.description: Slow, solemn group laments with long melodic phrases sung in unison, contrasting with dance songs driven by frame drum and rattle.
exemplars: Marius Barbeau wax-cylinder recordings (1915-1929), Canadian Museum of History

items.name: Coast Salish smokehouse and canoe-journey songs
items.lineage: Songs of the Coast Salish peoples of the Salish Sea, among them the Stó:lō, Musqueam and Lummi. In the winter spirit dancing (syowen) of the smokehouse, each initiated dancer's personal spirit song is taken up by the assembled drummers and singers, and on the summer Tribal Canoe Journeys, revived with the 1989 Paddle to Seattle, arriving canoes ask permission to land and nations share protocol songs. Pamela Amoss described the winter ceremonial in Coast Salish Spirit Dancing (1978), and the University of Washington Ethnomusicology Archives hold recordings. The hand-drum card stands in for the hide frame drums.
items.description: Many hide frame drums beaten together in a loud, driving pulse under a leader's song that the whole house takes up.
exemplars: University of Washington Ethnomusicology Archives Coast Salish recordings
Pamela Amoss, Coast Salish Spirit Dancing (1978)

items.name: Innu nikamu (teueikan drum songs)
items.lineage: Drum songs of the Innu of Nitassinan in Quebec and Labrador, sung by a man accompanying himself on the teueikan, a large hide frame drum with snares strung across its heads that add a buzzing rattle. The songs are received in dreams and tied to the caribou hunt, and are sung in thanks and at the makushan, the feast of caribou bone marrow, where people dance. The Canadian Museum of History and Labrador Innu community projects hold field recordings. The hand-drum card stands in for the teueikan.
items.description: A solo voice sings short repeated phrases over a steady, even drumbeat whose snares give every stroke a buzzing rattle.
exemplars: Canadian Museum of History field recordings of Innu drum songs

items.name: Wabanaki and Mi'kmaq songs (Passamaquoddy, Penobscot, Wolastoqiyik, Mi'kmaq)
items.lineage: Songs of the Wabanaki peoples of Maine and the Canadian Maritimes, the Passamaquoddy, Penobscot, Wolastoqiyik (Maliseet), Abenaki and Mi'kmaq, including social and ceremonial dance songs such as the Mi'kmaq ko'jua, honour and welcome songs, and trading songs. Singers accompany themselves on hand drums and on the Mi'kmaq ji'kmaqn, a split-ash rattle struck against the palm. In March 1890 Jesse Walter Fewkes recorded Passamaquoddy songs and tales on wax cylinders at Calais, Maine, the first ethnographic field recordings, now at the Library of Congress. The hand-drum and shaker cards stand in for the hand drum and the ji'kmaqn.
items.description: Songs with vocable refrains sung over a steady hand-drum beat and the dry clatter of a split-wood rattle, solo or with a group joining the refrains.
exemplars: Jesse Walter Fewkes Passamaquoddy wax-cylinder recordings (1890), Library of Congress

items.name: Dene drum dance (tea dance) songs
items.lineage: Drum dance songs of the Dene of the Northwest Territories and neighbouring regions, among them the Tłı̨chǫ, Dene Tha' and Gwich'in, sung at gatherings, feasts and assemblies, where a row of drummers sings while beating hide hand drums and dancers move in a circle. The occasion is also called a tea dance, and its repertoire includes prayer songs; it is a community dance distinct from the competitive hand game. Dene communities and CBC North have recorded drum dances.
items.description: A line of drummer-singers beats hide hand drums in close unison under a repeated vocable melody while dancers shuffle round in a circle.
exemplars: CBC North recordings of Tłı̨chǫ drum dances

items.name: Electric powwow (powwow-step)
items.lineage: Club music from Ottawa, where the DJ collective A Tribe Called Red, formed in 2007 and later renamed The Halluci Nation, ran Electric Pow Wow nights that mixed recordings of powwow drum groups with hip hop, moombahton and dubstep beats. This powwow-step sound set drum-group songs over bass-heavy electronic production; the group's records appeared on Tribal Spirit and Radicalized Records, and it won the 2014 Juno Award for Breakthrough Group of the Year. The powwow-drum and voice cards stand for the sampled drum-group recordings.
items.description: Looped powwow drum-group chants and big-drum hits laid over heavy sub-bass, half-time and dembow-style club grooves and hard programmed drums, cut and dropped like a DJ set.
exemplars: A Tribe Called Red — Nation II Nation (2013)
A Tribe Called Red — We Are the Halluci Nation (2016)

items.name: Comcaac icoos (Seri song)
items.lineage: Songs of the Comcaac (Seri) of the Gulf of California coast of Sonora, centred on Punta Chueca and El Desemboque, sung in the Cmiique Iitom language at the girls' puberty fiesta, for healing and in a large repertoire about animals, places, the sea and the desert. Songs are often sung by a single unaccompanied singer. Seri field recordings appear in the INAH Testimonio Musical de México series and in the Archive of the Indigenous Languages of Latin America (AILLA).
items.description: Short songs for a single unaccompanied voice built from repeated melodic phrases.
exemplars: INAH Testimonio Musical de México, Música indígena del Noroeste (Seri field recordings)
Seri song recordings, Archive of the Indigenous Languages of Latin America (AILLA)

items.name: Rarámuri (Tarahumara) ritual and fiesta music
items.lineage: Music of the Rarámuri of the Sierra Tarahumara in Chihuahua. In the yúmari and tutuguri ceremonies a chanter sings while shaking a gourd rattle as people dance for rain, crops and the dead; at Holy Week, groups of fariseos and soldados process to the steady beat of large double-headed drums with cane flutes; and at fiestas such as the matachín dances, locally made violins and guitars play repeated dance tunes. The INAH Testimonio Musical de México series documents the music. Generic drum, flute and shaker cards stand in for the Rarámuri drum, cane flute and gourd rattle.
items.description: Bright, repetitive violin dance tunes over strummed guitar alternate with the relentless thud of double-headed drums under thin cane-flute melodies, and with a lone chanter's song over a gourd rattle.
exemplars: INAH Testimonio Musical de México, Música indígena del Noroeste (Rarámuri recordings)

items.name: Náayeri mitote and Judea (Cora ceremonial music)
items.lineage: Ceremonial music of the Náayeri (Cora) of the Sierra del Nayar in Nayarit. At the mitote, the night dance of the agricultural cycle held around a fire, a singer chants while striking a large musical bow that rests on a gourd resonator; at Holy Week in Jesús María the Judea, with its painted dancers, is accompanied by cane flute and drum. Konrad Theodor Preuss recorded Cora songs on phonograph cylinders in 1905-1907 for the Berlin Phonogramm-Archiv. The ugubhu card, a gourd-resonated struck bow, stands in for the mitote bow, and generic flute and drum cards for the Judea flute and drum.
items.description: A chanted song line over the dry, low twang of a struck musical bow beaten in a steady pulse, alternating at Holy Week with shrill cane flute over a pounding drum.
exemplars: Konrad Theodor Preuss phonograph cylinders (1905-1907), Berlin Phonogramm-Archiv
INAH field recordings of Cora ceremonial music

items.name: Danza de los Voladores (Totonac flyers' pipe and drum)
items.lineage: Music of the ritual of the flyers of the Totonac of Papantla, Veracruz, inscribed by UNESCO on its Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage. The caporal, standing on the small platform at the top of a tall pole, plays a small cane flute and a small double-headed drum at the same time, saluting the four directions, while four flyers tied by ropes descend head-down in widening circles. Generic flute and drum cards stand in for the flute and drum.
items.description: A thin, high cane-flute melody of short repeated phrases over light, steady taps of a small drum played by the same musician, heard in the open air.
exemplars: INAH field recordings of the caporal's flute and drum
UNESCO Representative List documentation of the Ritual ceremony of the Voladores (2009)

items.name: Son de costumbre (Huasteca Nahua and Teenek ritual sones)
items.lineage: Instrumental sones played on violin and jarana by Nahua and Teenek musicians of the Huasteca in Veracruz, Hidalgo and San Luis Potosí for the costumbre, the community and household rituals of the agricultural cycle such as the offerings to Chicomexóchitl, the spirit of the maize, and for Xantolo, the Days of the Dead. Sones are played at set moments of the offering, and the repertoire is distinct from the sung secular son of the Huasteca trio. INAH and CDI field recordings document the repertoire.
items.description: A violin plays short, repeated melodies over the jarana's strummed rhythmic chords, an instrumental duo without singing, played at length during offerings.
exemplars: INAH field recordings of sones de costumbre
CDI field recordings of Huasteca ritual music

items.name: Mazatec velada chant (Huautla de Jiménez)
items.lineage: Night-long healing chants of the Mazatec curers (chjota chjine) of Huautla de Jiménez in the Sierra Mazateca of Oaxaca, sung in Mazatec during the velada, a vigil in which participants take psilocybin mushrooms. The best-known chanter, María Sabina, was recorded by R. Gordon Wasson and Valentina Pavlovna Wasson in 1956, and the tape was issued by Folkways in 1957. The chant repeats formulaic lines naming the curer and sacred beings, broken by clapping, humming and whistling.
items.description: A solo voice in the dark, chanting long chains of repeated formulaic lines in a narrow melodic range, punctuated by sharp hand claps, hums and whistles.
exemplars: R. Gordon Wasson and Valentina Pavlovna Wasson recordings, Mushroom Ceremony of the Mazatec Indians of Mexico (Folkways FW 8975, 1957)

items.name: Tzotzil and Tzeltal fiesta music (Highland Chiapas)
items.lineage: Ceremonial music of the Tzotzil and Tzeltal Maya of the Chiapas highlands around San Cristóbal de las Casas, notably San Juan Chamula and Zinacantán. Ensembles of harp, violin and guitar, often with singing in Tzotzil, accompany the religious officials (cargo holders) at saints' fiestas and household rites, while cane flutes and drums lead processions and carnival. The 1975 Folkways albums Modern Mayan: The Indian Music of Chiapas, Mexico (FE 4377 and FE 4379) document the repertoire. The harpa card, a diatonic folk harp, stands in for the Chamula harp, and generic flute and drum cards for the procession flute and drum.
items.description: A violin and voice in unison over plucked harp bass and chords and strummed guitar, a short tune repeated many times, with cane flute and drum for processions.
exemplars: Modern Mayan: The Indian Music of Chiapas, Mexico (Folkways FE 4377 and FE 4379, 1975)

items.name: Maya Pax (Quintana Roo Maya ceremonial music)
items.lineage: Ceremonial music of the Maya of the Cruzo'ob shrine centres of central Quintana Roo, in the municipalities of Felipe Carrillo Puerto and Tulum, played as an offering to the Holy Cross at fiestas and rituals; the term maya pax covers the music, its instruments, the dance and its performers. The ensemble joins the Maya violin with the tarola snare drum, the bombo bass drum and a cane flute. The Quintana Roo state legislature has declared it intangible cultural heritage of the state. The generic drum card stands in for the bombo and the generic flute card for the cane flute.
items.description: Violin dance melodies played slowly and solemnly over snare and bass-drum beats, with a cane flute joining the tune.
exemplars: INAH Testimonio Musical de México recordings
Yucatec Maya community recordings of maya pax ensembles

items.name: Chastushka (Russian topical quatrain song)
items.lineage: A short rhymed song form, usually a four-line stanza, that spread through Russian villages and factory settlements from the later 19th century, sung to a small stock of repeating tunes with topical, humorous, satirical or love texts that singers adapt or improvise on the spot. Singers trade verses in turn, commonly over the garmon (button accordion) or balalaika, and the genre was widely issued on Melodiya village LPs and sung by state folk choirs such as the Pyatnitsky Choir.
items.description: Quick, syllabic quatrains delivered in a bright, forthright chest voice, singers alternating stanzas over a looping two- or four-bar accordion or balalaika figure that fills the gaps between verses.

items.name: Khorovod (Russian round-dance song)
items.lineage: Songs sung by the dancers themselves in the khorovod, the circle and chain dance of Russian village youth held outdoors from spring through the summer festivals; in southern Russia the form is called karagod. Many khorovod songs are game songs whose texts direct the figures of the dance. Folklorists documented them from the 19th century, Melodiya issued village recordings, and staged versions entered the repertoire of state ensembles such as Beryozka.
items.description: Unaccompanied group singing, mostly women's voices, in strophic songs at a walking pace, a leading line taken up by the group and loosely branched in heterophony, the steady pulse set by the circling steps.
exemplars: Melodiya ethnographic LPs of Russian village song

items.name: Svadebnye pesni (Russian wedding song cycle)
items.lineage: The songs that accompany the Russian village wedding as a ritual lasting several days, from the matchmaking and the bride's farewell to her family through to the feast: the bride's laments (prichitaniya), lyrical songs of her girlfriends, velichaniya praising the couple and guests, and teasing korilnye songs that mock the matchmaker and guests. Regional cycles are held in the Pushkin House (IRLI) phonogram archive, and the Dmitri Pokrovsky Ensemble set village wedding songs beside Stravinsky's Les Noces.
items.description: Unaccompanied women's group singing that alternates slow, mournful songs and solo laments with brisk praise and teasing songs, the voices branching from a leading line into open fifths and octaves.
exemplars: Pushkin House (IRLI) phonogram archive wedding recordings
Dmitri Pokrovsky Ensemble, Les Noces with village wedding songs (Nonesuch)

items.name: Kalendarnye pesni (Russian calendar-ritual songs)
items.lineage: Songs tied to the peasant agricultural year: kolyadki sung by groups going from house to house at the midwinter holidays, vesnyanki that call in the spring, songs of the Maslenitsa carnival before Lent, and Kupala songs of midsummer. Western and southern regions such as Bryansk, Belgorod and Smolensk kept many of these cycles into the 20th century; they were recorded on ethnographic expeditions issued by Melodiya and form part of the repertoire of the Dmitri Pokrovsky Ensemble.
items.description: Short melodic formulas sung by groups of women and girls in a loud, open chest voice and repeated many times to carry long ritual texts, spring songs ending phrases in high calls and winter carols built on recurring refrains.
exemplars: Melodiya ethnographic series of Russian village song

items.name: Kuvikly (Kursk women's panpipe playing)
items.lineage: Women's playing of kuvikly (also kugikly), sets of two to five cane or reed pipes of graded length, in the villages of Kursk and Bryansk oblasts in southern Russia. Several players each hold a set and divide the tune between them, alternating blown notes with short sung whoops so that pipes and voices interlock; the practice was captured in Melodiya field recordings from Kursk villages and taken up by the Dmitri Pokrovsky Ensemble.
items.description: Breathy pipe notes and high sung whoops interlock between two or three players in fast, repeating dance figures, a hocketed texture with little sustained melody.
exemplars: Melodiya field recordings of Kursk village musicians

items.name: Vladimirskiy rozhok (Vladimir shepherd-horn ensemble)
items.lineage: The rozhok, a wooden lip-blown horn with fingerholes traditionally made from two carved halves bound with birch bark, was the shepherds' instrument of the Vladimir region, used for herding signals and for dance and song tunes (naigryshi). In the late 19th century Nikolai Kondratyev formed a choir of horn players from village shepherds that toured Russian cities, and ensembles of horns in several sizes continued in the region through the Soviet period, when they were recorded for Melodiya.
items.description: A small group of horns in several sizes plays song and dance tunes in loose heterophony, the bright, nasal horn tone flecked with quick grace notes.
exemplars: N. V. Kondratyev's choir of Vladimir horn players
Melodiya recordings of Vladimir horn ensembles

items.name: Garmon naigryshi (Russian accordion dance tunes)
items.lineage: Instrumental dance and song tunes (naigryshi) played on the garmon, the Russian diatonic button accordion that spread through the villages from the mid-19th century in regional models such as the Saratov garmonika with its small bells and the Livenka. Standard tunes such as the barynya and tsyganochka and local plyaska and stradaniya tunes accompany dancing and the singing of chastushki, and the tradition reached a national audience through Gennady Zavolokin's television programme Igray, garmon!
items.description: A single button accordion repeats short dance figures over a pumping alternation of bass and chord buttons, varying them across many repetitions, sometimes joined by strummed balalaika and wooden spoons marking the dance pulse.
exemplars: Melodiya recordings of village garmon players

items.name: Pskov gusli (Russian wing-shaped psaltery playing)
items.lineage: Village playing of the krylovidnye (wing-shaped) gusli, a plucked psaltery held on the knees, which survived into the 20th century in the Pskov and Novgorod regions of north-western Russia, where players strummed across the strings while the fingers of the other hand damped those not wanted, to accompany dances and chastushki. Soviet folklorists recorded the last village players in the Pskov region, and their style became a basis of the modern gusli revival.
items.description: Bright, ringing strummed chords on metal strings repeat a short dance pattern, the chords changed by damping strings rather than stopping them, sometimes with a singer's verses over the top.
exemplars: Archival field recordings of Pskov village gusli players

items.name: Don Cossack song (village polyphony of the Don)
items.lineage: The song tradition of the Cossack stanitsas along the Don, whose old capital was Starocherkassk, with historical, military and drawn-out lyrical songs sung by groups of men and women. Its polyphony sets a high solo upper voice, the dishkant, above the leading line and a body of lower voices. Aleksandr Listopadov collected the repertoire with the phonograph and in the field for his Pesni donskikh kazakov, and the emigre Don Cossack Choir of Serge Jaroff carried an arranged choral form abroad.
items.description: Full-voiced group singing in a broad, open chest tone, one high voice soaring over the leading line while the lower voices fill out the harmony, with long-held phrase ends in the slow songs and a firm marching pulse in the military ones.
exemplars: A. M. Listopadov, Pesni donskikh kazakov (song collection)
Don Cossack Choir Serge Jaroff (Deutsche Grammophon)

items.name: Kuban Cossack song (Black Sea Cossack song of the Kuban)
items.lineage: Songs of the Cossacks of the Kuban, where Black Sea Cossacks from the Zaporozhian lands of Ukraine settled at the end of the 18th century and kept a Ukrainian-based dialect (balachka) alongside the songs of the Russian line Cossacks. Historical, military, wedding and lyrical songs are sung by mixed village groups, and the Kuban Cossack Choir, directed from 1974 by Viktor Zakharchenko, staged and recorded the repertoire for Melodiya with bayan, balalaika and percussion.
items.description: A large mixed choir in bright, open voices sings lyrical melodies and dance songs with a lead singer's line answered by the full group, over bayan and balalaika with a driving duple pulse in the faster songs.

items.name: Semeiskie song (Transbaikal Old Believer polyphony)
items.lineage: The Semeiskie are Old Believers deported to Transbaikalia in the second half of the 18th century from the western frontier lands where they had taken refuge; they settled in villages such as Tarbagatay in present-day Buryatia and kept their dress, rites and songs. Their drawn-out lyrical and ritual songs are sung in dense multi-voiced polyphony, and UNESCO proclaimed the cultural space and oral culture of the Semeiskie a Masterpiece of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity.
items.description: Slow, drawn-out songs in which a lead voice is answered by the full group branching into several independent lines, with long melismas on single syllables in wide-open chest voices and cadences closing on the unison or octave.
exemplars: Semeiskie village ensemble recordings from Tarbagatay

items.name: Dukhovny stikh (Russian spiritual verse)
items.lineage: Para-liturgical sung verses on biblical subjects, the lives of saints, the Last Judgement and death, sung outside the church service. They were the repertoire of the itinerant blind singers known as kaliki perekhozhie and were kept above all by Old Believer communities of northern Russia, who sang them at home and at gatherings. The Pushkin House phonogram archive holds field recordings, and the Moscow ensemble Sirin has recorded spiritual verses alongside chant.
items.description: Strophic verses sung solo or by a small unison group in a plain, unhurried voice, the text carried syllabically on a narrow-range modal tune repeated through many stanzas with little vibrato or ornament.
exemplars: Pushkin House (IRLI) phonogram archive recordings of spiritual verse

items.name: Kolokolny zvon (Russian Orthodox bell-ringing)
items.lineage: The ringing of church bells in the Russian Orthodox tradition, in which the bells hang fixed and a single ringer, the zvonar, sounds them by ropes tied to their clappers, working the heaviest bell by rope or pedal while playing the smaller ones with the hands. Named types of ringing include the blagovest on one large bell and the full trezvon on all the bells. The bells of the Rostov Kremlin at Rostov Veliky, with their own historic named ringings, were recorded for Melodiya LPs. The carillon card stands in for a set of fixed church bells.
items.description: Freely overlapping strikes of bells in several sizes: a slow, deep bell marking the pulse, middle bells in a repeating figure and rapid patterns on the small bells, their long decays merging into a dense ringing wash.
exemplars: Melodiya LPs of the Rostov Kremlin bells

items.name: Early Soviet avant-garde (1920s futurist and constructivist music)
items.lineage: The modernist music of the first Soviet decade, from Nikolai Roslavets's system of synthetic chords and Arthur Lourie's futurist pieces to Alexander Mosolov's Zavod (Iron Foundry), an orchestral episode from the ballet Steel that imitates factory machinery, and Arseny Avraamov's Symphony of Factory Sirens, performed in Baku in 1922 with ship and factory sirens, steam whistles and artillery. The Association for Contemporary Music in Moscow promoted this repertoire until official policy turned against it around 1930.
items.description: Orchestral writing built on ostinato machine rhythms, clangorous brass and struck metal, dissonant chord blocks and abrupt surges of volume, set beside spare, atonal piano and chamber textures.
exemplars: Arseny Avraamov, Symphony of Factory Sirens
ReR Megacorp CD Baku: Symphony of Sirens (2008)

items.name: Rogovaya muzyka (Russian one-note horn orchestra)
items.lineage: Music for an ensemble of valveless horns in which each horn sounds a single note, devised in 1751 by the Bohemian horn player J. A. Maresch for the Russian aristocracy in St Petersburg. Horns graded from a few centimetres to several metres long combine like the pipes of an organ, each player entering only on his own note, to play chords, melodies and arrangements. The practice faded in the 19th century and was revived in St Petersburg by Sergei Polianichko's Russian Horn Orchestra on reconstructed instruments. The natural-horn card stands in for the straight one-note horns.
items.description: Sustained horn tones, each pitch from a different player, assemble in hocket into slow chords and hymn-like melodies with an organ-like blend and soft, round attacks.
exemplars: Russian Horn Orchestra of St Petersburg (Sergei Polianichko)

items.name: Massovaya pesnya (Soviet mass song and Red Army choir)
items.lineage: The Soviet mass song (massovaya pesnya), a strophic song with a singable refrain written for collective singing at work, on the march and at public celebrations, was promoted from the 1930s by composers such as Isaak Dunayevsky, Alexander Alexandrov and Matvey Blanter and spread by radio, film and records. Its emblematic performer is the Alexandrov Red Army Song and Dance Ensemble, founded in 1928, whose male choir and soloists sing with an orchestra that joins folk instruments such as bayan, balalaika and domra to brass and winds.
items.description: A large male choir in full, ringing unison and block harmony carries march-tempo and broad lyrical refrains, a tenor or bass soloist leading the verses over an orchestra of bayan, balalaikas, domras and brass.
exemplars: Soviet 78 rpm records of mass songs (1930s to 1950s)

items.name: Tea-jazz (1930s-50s Soviet jazz)
items.lineage: Soviet popular jazz of the 1930s to the 1950s, typified by Leonid Utyosov's Tea-Jazz (teatralny jazz, theatrical jazz) orchestra, founded in Leningrad in 1929, which mixed dance-band arrangements with song, comedy and staged numbers and reached a mass audience through the film Jolly Fellows (1934). Alexander Tsfasman's orchestra in Moscow and Eddie Rosner's State Jazz Orchestra of Belarus played swing-based dance music in the same years, before jazz was suppressed in the late 1940s.
items.description: A dance orchestra of trumpets, trombone and saxophones plays bright, punchy arrangements of foxtrots and songs over piano, double bass and drums, a crooning or theatrical vocalist up front and short hot solos between choruses.
exemplars: Leonid Utyosov's Tea-Jazz orchestra, 78 rpm records

items.name: Sibirsky pank (Siberian punk)
items.lineage: A punk scene of Omsk, Novosibirsk and Tyumen from the mid-1980s, led by Yegor Letov's Grazhdanskaya Oborona, Yanka Dyagileva and Kommunizm, which recorded at home on reel-to-reel and cassette at Letov's GrOb Records studio in Omsk and circulated by magnitizdat tape copying. Its songs pair abrasive distorted guitar and crude drums with existential and political lyrics, and the albums were later reissued on CD.
items.description: Fuzz-saturated guitar, thin bass and primitive drums recorded straight to tape in a small room under a shouted or plaintive vocal, with hiss, noise and overload left in and folk-like melodies buried inside the din.

items.name: Munajat (Volga-Tatar devotional song)
items.lineage: Unaccompanied religious song of the Volga Tatars, sung in Tatar to poetic texts of prayer, repentance and praise of God outside the mosque liturgy. Its melodies share the pentatonic scales of Tatar folk song and are sung in free rhythm with melismatic ornament; recordings are held in the archive of Tatarstan state radio.
items.description: A solo voice, unaccompanied, unfolds long free-rhythm lines on a pentatonic scale, with melismas and gentle grace notes on held syllables and a calm, inward tone.
exemplars: Tatarstan state radio archive recordings of munajat

items.name: Kryashen song (baptized Tatar song)
items.lineage: Songs of the Kryashens, Volga Tatars who have been Orthodox Christians since conversions of the 16th to 18th centuries, living in Tatarstan districts such as Mamadysh and in neighbouring regions. Their repertoire of calendar, wedding, lyrical and dance songs in Tatar is regarded by folklorists as keeping older melodic layers, and it has been recorded on field expeditions of the Kazan Conservatory and performed by village folk ensembles.
items.description: Group singing of strophic songs in Tatar on tunes close to the pentatonic scales of Tatar song, the voices in unison or loose heterophony, slow lyrical songs alternating with brisk dance songs.
exemplars: Kazan Conservatory field recordings of Kryashen song

items.name: Bashkir kurai and uzun-kyuy (Bashkir long song)
items.lineage: The kurai, an end-blown flute traditionally cut from the stem of an umbellifer plant, is the national instrument of the Bashkirs of the southern Urals and is played with a drone hummed in the throat beneath the melody. Its core repertoire is the uzun-kyuy, slow, free-rhythm and heavily ornamented long songs on historical and lyrical subjects, alongside quicker dance tunes, and its 20th-century masters included Ishmulla Dilmukhametov and Gata Suleymanov. The sybyzgy card stands in for the kurai.
items.description: A breathy, husky flute line over a continuous throat drone unfolds slow, free-rhythm melody with heavy trills and grace notes, the pentatonic tune rising in wide arches, sometimes alternating with a singer's long-held phrases.
exemplars: Melodiya recordings of Bashkir kurai music

items.name: Kubair (Bashkir sesen epic recitation)
items.lineage: Epic tradition of the Bashkirs of the southern Urals, in which sesen, improvising poet-singers, recited kubair, the Bashkir epic verse form, to tell epics such as Ural-batyr, the tale of a hero who defeats the divs and pours out the water of eternal life over the land instead of drinking it. Sesen delivered the verse in a chanted recitative and could accompany themselves on the dumbyra, a long-necked plucked lute represented here by the dombyra card; Ural-batyr was written down from sesen performance in the early twentieth century.
items.description: A single narrator delivers long runs of regular, alliterating verse in a chanted recitative built on a few repeated melodic formulas, with a plucked lute marking the lines.
exemplars: Ufa Institute of History, Language and Literature folklore archive (Bashkir epic recordings)

items.name: Chuvash song and instrumental music (Chuvashia)
items.lineage: Song and village instrumental music of the Chuvash, a Turkic people of the middle Volga centred on Cheboksary, whose songs are built largely on anhemitonic pentatonic scales. Songs are sung solo and in groups, and village instruments include the kesle board zither, represented here by the gusli card, the shapar bladder bagpipe, represented by the card of the neighbouring Mari bagpipe, and the parappan drum, represented by a generic membrane drum. The repertoire has been recorded on Melodiya and staged by the Chuvash State Song and Dance Ensemble.
items.description: Short strophic songs on gapped five-note scales, sung solo or by groups, alternate with dance tunes in which a droning bladder bagpipe and a plucked zither play over a steady drum.
exemplars: Chuvash State Song and Dance Ensemble

items.name: Erzya and Moksha song (Mordvin multipart singing)
items.lineage: Village song of the Erzya and Moksha, the two Mordvin peoples of the middle Volga, centred on the Republic of Mordovia around Saransk. Songs are typically sung by groups, often of women, in two or more independent voice parts rather than in unison; village instruments included the fam bagpipe and the nudey reed pipe, but this default is the unaccompanied multipart song. The repertoire is documented on Melodiya Mordovian folk LPs and by the Torama ensemble.
items.description: Groups of voices, often women's, sing broad strophic songs in several independent parts that branch away from and rejoin a shared melody, in a strong, open-throated delivery without accompaniment.

items.name: Komi song (Komi-Zyrian, Izhma and Komi-Permyak)
items.lineage: Song tradition of the Komi, a Permic Finno-Ugric people of north-eastern European Russia: the Komi-Zyrians of the Komi Republic around Syktyvkar, the reindeer-herding Izhma Komi of the lower Pechora and the Komi-Permyaks of the upper Kama. Lyrical songs, wedding songs and laments are sung solo or by groups of women, and village instruments included the sigudok bowed lute; this default is unaccompanied song. The Izhma repertoire is documented in Pushkin House field recordings and the wider tradition on Melodiya Komi folk LPs.
items.description: Unaccompanied voices sing long, drawn-out lyrical and wedding songs, solo or in a small women's group, with free, speech-shaped phrasing and lament-like falling lines.
exemplars: Pushkin House (IRLI) field recordings of Izhma Komi song

items.name: Southern Udmurt village song (Kiyasovo)
items.lineage: Non-ritual village song of the southern Udmurts, documented in the Kiyasovo district of the Udmurt Republic by the ethnomusicologist Irina Pchelovodova and the folklorist Nikolai Anisimov and published online by the Estonian Literary Museum as Songs of the Southern Udmurt. The repertoire spans lyrical songs, chastushki, dancing and game songs, teasing songs and songs borrowed from neighbours, and is a separate regional repertoire from the improvised krez singing of the northern Udmurts; the Besermyan of north-western Udmurtia keep yet another local tradition not modelled here.
items.description: Village singers, mostly in small groups, move between lyrical strophic songs and brisk, short dance and teasing songs, sung unaccompanied in an open, unprocessed field-recording sound.
exemplars: Songs of the Southern Udmurt (Pchelovodova and Anisimov), Estonian Literary Museum edition of Kiyasovo field material
Udmurt Institute for Research in History, Language and Literature (Izhevsk) field recordings of southern Udmurt song

items.name: Illi (Chechen and Ingush heroic song)
items.lineage: Heroic and historical song of the Chechens and Ingush, the Vainakh peoples of the north-eastern Caucasus, recounting the deeds of mountain heroes and past battles, and distinct from the lyrical esharsh songs. An illi is sung by a solo male singer who often accompanies himself on the dechig-pondar three-string plucked lute (the phandyr card) or the bowed adkhoku-pondar; recordings are held in the Chechen-Ingush State Radio archive.
items.description: A solo male voice declaims long heroic verses in a wide-ranging, strongly projected line, over a plucked three-string lute that repeats short figures between phrases.
exemplars: Chechen-Ingush State Radio archive recordings of illi

items.name: Avar song (Dagestan highland song)
items.lineage: Song tradition of the Avars, the largest people of Dagestan, centred on the highland Khunzakh plateau. Lyrical and heroic songs are sung by a solo voice to the bowed chagana spike fiddle, represented here by the neighbouring Ossetian kissyn-fandyr card, and the plucked pandur and tamur lutes, represented by the Nakh phandyr card; outdoor wedding and dance music on zurna and double-headed drum is part of the wider tradition but is left out of this song default. It is documented in Melodiya's Dagestan folk series and the Makhachkala Radio archive.
items.description: A solo voice sings ornamented lyrical and heroic songs, shadowed by a rasping bowed spike fiddle and carried by the steady figures of a plucked long-necked lute.

items.name: Ossetian song and Nart kadaeg (North Ossetia)
items.lineage: Song tradition of the Ossetians, an Iranian-speaking people of the central Caucasus centred on Vladikavkaz. Men's songs set a solo voice against a male chorus that holds a lower supporting part, and the heroic kadaeg, including songs of the Nart sagas, were traditionally sung to the bowed kissyn-fandyr; the accordion accompanies song and dance, as does the plucked dala-fandyr, which this default leaves out. The repertoire is documented on Melodiya Ossetian folk LPs.
items.description: A leading male voice sings heroic and table songs over a sustained lower chorus, with a horsehair-strung bowed fiddle shadowing the melody and a button accordion for dance tunes.

items.name: Karachay-Balkar song (north-central Caucasus)
items.lineage: Song tradition of the Turkic-speaking Karachay and Balkar peoples of Karachay-Cherkessia and Kabardino-Balkaria. Many songs set a soloist against a male chorus singing a sustained lower part, with the refrain word orayda giving its name to a class of songs, and instruments include the bowed kyl-kobuz, represented here by the neighbouring Circassian bowed-fiddle card, and the diatonic accordion. The repertoire is documented in Melodiya's North Caucasus folk series.
items.description: A solo singer leads over a steady male choral drone with a recurring refrain, joined by a bowed horsehair fiddle and, in dance songs, a button accordion.
exemplars: Melodiya North Caucasus folk music series

items.name: Kai (Altai throat-sung epic)
items.lineage: Epic singing of the Altai people of the Altai Republic, in which a kaichi performs heroic epics such as Maadai-Kara in kai, a low, guttural throat-singing voice, accompanying himself on the two-string topshur plucked lute, represented here by the two-string dombyra card. Epic performances could last through the night, and the tradition was recorded from leading kaichi in the twentieth century and continues among younger performers.
items.description: A deep, growling throat voice chants long verse lines to a steady, galloping two-string lute ostinato, with occasional passages in a plainer narrating voice.

items.name: Khai and chatkhan (Khakas throat-sung epic and zither)
items.lineage: Khakas tradition of Khakassia in southern Siberia, in which the khaiji sings heroic epics (alyptyg nymakh) in khai, a guttural throat-singing voice, to the chatkhan long box zither or the two-string khomys lute; this default pairs the voice with the chatkhan. The chatkhan is also played solo and to accompany song, and the tradition has been recorded on Melodiya Khakas LPs and by the Sabjilar ensemble.
items.description: A low, guttural throat voice chants epic verse over the rippling, repeated figures of a plucked box zither, the strings ringing under the voice.

items.name: Yokhor (Buryat circle-dance song)
items.lineage: Communal round dance of the Buryats of the Baikal region, in which dancers link arms or shoulders and move sunwise in a ring, often at night around a fire, while singing; a leader starts each verse and the circle takes it up, and the tempo quickens as the dance goes on. It is danced at summer festivals and gatherings in Aga, Khori and other Buryat districts and is staged by the Baikal State Ensemble.
items.description: A lead voice calls out each verse and a large ring of voices repeats it over the shuffle of stepping feet, starting slow and steadily accelerating.

items.name: Abai Geser uliger (Buryat epic recitation)
items.lineage: Western Buryat heroic epic of Abai Geser, a celestial hero sent down to earth to rid it of evil, performed by uligershin storytellers in long sung and recited verse among the Ekhirit and Bulagat Buryats of the Ust-Orda district west of Lake Baikal. It is the Buryat branch of the Inner Asian Gesar epic, and versions taken down from uligershin performance are kept with recordings in the Ulan-Ude archives.
items.description: A single storyteller moves between chanted narration and sung passages on short recurring melodies, the verse unfolding at length in a plain, unaccompanied voice.
exemplars: Peokhon Petrov's version of Abai Geser
Ulan-Ude archive recordings of uligershin performance

items.name: Toyuk (Sakha improvised solo song)
items.lineage: Solo improvised song of the Sakha (Yakuts) of north-eastern Siberia, in which the singer extemporises long, unmetered lines on nature, feeling and praise in the drawn-out dieretii yrya style, decorated throughout with kylyhakh, a characteristic throat-produced break and flutter in the voice. Toyuk is the old core of Sakha vocal art, related to the sung passages of olonkho, and is still sung at Ysyakh festivals and by Sakha concert singers.
items.description: A single unaccompanied voice draws out long, free-rhythm phrases, each held tone broken by rapid throat-produced flips and flutters that give the line a shimmering, ornamented edge.

items.name: Osuokhai (Sakha circle-dance song)
items.lineage: Sakha round dance in which men and women link arms in a ring and step sunwise while a lead singer improvises verses line by line and the circle repeats them. It is the central communal dance of the Ysyakh summer festival, where rings can grow very large, and its verses praise the sun, nature and the gathered community.
items.description: A lead voice sings each improvised line and a large ring of voices answers with it in unison, over the soft, even rhythm of stepping feet.

items.name: Algys (Sakha ritual blessing chant)
items.lineage: Sung blessing of the Sakha, performed by the algyschyt, a ritual specialist who addresses the aiyy sky deities and the spirits of the land. At the opening of the Ysyakh summer festival the algyschyt chants the algys before the gathered people while offering kumys to the fire and the earth, and blessings are also sung at other rites.
items.description: A single solemn voice chants long blessing lines in an elevated, unmetered recitative, rising and falling on a few tones in the open air.

items.name: Evenki song and shamanic chant
items.lineage: Music of the Evenki, a Tungusic reindeer-herding and hunting people spread across central and eastern Siberia, with a historic centre at Tura in Evenkia. Personal and improvised songs are sung solo, and the shaman's seance sets chanted invocations against a large single-headed frame drum, represented here by a generic frame-drum card, and the iron pendants of the costume; the repertoire is preserved in the Pushkin House phonogram archive and on Melodiya LPs of the musical folklore of the peoples of the North and Siberia.
items.description: A solo voice chants short, repeated invocation phrases over the dry, booming strokes of a large frame drum and the clatter of metal pendants, alternating with quiet personal songs.
exemplars: Pushkin House (IRLI) phonogram archive recordings of Evenki song
Melodiya LPs of the musical folklore of the peoples of the North and Siberia

items.name: Even song and hede circle dance
items.lineage: Music of the Evens, a Tungusic reindeer-herding people of north-eastern Siberia from Yakutia to Magadan and Kamchatka. The hede is a communal circle dance in which a leader sings and the dancers answer with refrains as the ring moves, and personal songs and sung tales (nimkan) are performed solo; the repertoire is preserved in the Pushkin House phonogram archive and by Even folk ensembles.
items.description: A leader's voice sings out over a moving ring of dancers who answer each phrase with short refrain calls, the steady stepping keeping the pulse.
exemplars: Pushkin House (IRLI) phonogram archive recordings of Even song

items.name: Nivkh music (bear-festival tree drum, tyngryng and jaw harp)
items.lineage: Music of the Nivkh, a fishing people of the lower Amur and northern Sakhalin. At the bear festival women beat a suspended dry log, the musical tree, with sticks, represented here by a generic auxiliary-percussion card; the one-string tyngryng fiddle and the jaw harp, represented by the khomus card, are played solo and with song. The repertoire is preserved in the Pushkin House phonogram archive and Sakhalin field recordings.
items.description: Dry, knocking stick strokes on a hollow log set a repeating rhythm, while a thin one-string fiddle and a twanging jaw harp trace short melodies around voices.
exemplars: Pushkin House (IRLI) phonogram archive recordings of Nivkh music
Sakhalin field recordings of Nivkh music

items.name: Nanai and Ulch song and shamanic music (Lower Amur)
items.lineage: Music of the Nanai and Ulch, Tungusic fishing peoples of the lower Amur in Khabarovsk Krai. Shamanic rites are led by a shaman chanting invocations to a single-headed frame drum, represented here by a generic frame-drum card, and the clanging iron cones of the shaman's belt, while secular songs are sung solo and the one-string ducheke fiddle is played. The repertoire is preserved in the Pushkin House phonogram archive and Amur field recordings.
items.description: A shaman's chanted invocations ride over steady frame-drum beats and jangling metal, alternating with solo songs and the thin, reedy line of a one-string fiddle.
exemplars: Pushkin House (IRLI) phonogram archive recordings of Nanai and Ulch music

items.name: Yukaghir song (Kolyma Odul solo song)
items.lineage: Song of the Yukaghir (Odul), a small Paleo-Siberian people of the Kolyma basin whose upper-Kolyma community lives at Nelemnoye in Yakutia. Waldemar Jochelson recorded Yukaghir singing on wax cylinders for the Jesup North Pacific Expedition in 1901-02, and the documented repertoire is mostly solo song sung without accompaniment.
items.description: A single unaccompanied voice sings short, freely paced melodic phrases within a narrow range, repeating and varying them as the words unfold.
exemplars: Waldemar Jochelson, Jesup North Pacific Expedition wax cylinders of Yukaghir song (1901-02)

items.name: Chukchi drum-dance (yarar ensemble song)
items.lineage: Ensemble drum-dance of the Chukchi of Chukotka, performed at seasonal gatherings such as Kilvei, the reindeer herders' spring antler festival, and staged since the Soviet period by the Ergyron ensemble of Anadyr. Seated drummers sing while beating the yarar, a large handled frame drum with a thin membrane struck with a slender stick, represented here by the generic frame-drum card; the ensemble repertoire is distinct from the personal songs each Chukchi owns.
items.description: A row of singer-drummers beats a steady pulse on thin-skinned frame drums under short, repeated melodic phrases with vocables, while the dancers add calls over the drums.
exemplars: Waldemar Bogoras, Jesup North Pacific Expedition cylinders (1900-01)

items.name: Siberian Yupik drum song (Chaplino and St. Lawrence Island)
items.lineage: Drum-dance song of the Central Siberian Yupik, whose language and dance repertoire are shared by the Chukotka coast villages around Novoe Chaplino and the St. Lawrence Island communities of Gambell and Savoonga in Alaska. Singers beat large handled frame drums with thin membranes, represented here by the qilaat card of the related Inuit handled drum, to accompany dances at village festivities; Waldemar Bogoras recorded Asiatic Eskimo song during the Jesup North Pacific Expedition.
items.description: Several singers strike thin frame drums in unison while singing short strophes of vocables and text, the song repeated with the drumming growing louder and faster.
exemplars: Miriam C. Stryker, Eskimo Songs from Alaska (Folkways FE 4069, 1966), recorded at Savoonga and Gambell, St. Lawrence Island
Waldemar Bogoras, Jesup North Pacific Expedition cylinders of Asiatic Eskimo song

items.name: Kham algysh (Tuvan shamanic invocation)
items.lineage: Ritual singing of the Tuvan kham (shaman), whose algysh, sung invocations and blessings addressed to spirits, are performed in healing and purification rites to the beat of the dungur, a handled frame drum struck with a beater, represented here by the generic frame-drum card. Shamanic practice re-emerged publicly in Kyzyl after the Soviet period through shaman societies such as Dungur, founded under the ethnographer Mongush Kenin-Lopsan.
items.description: A solo voice chants long lines of invocation in an insistent, half-sung declamation over a continuous frame-drum beat, with the jangle of metal pendants on the costume colouring the drum.

items.name: Nganasan shaman séance (Taymyr)
items.lineage: Séance singing of the Nganasan, the northernmost Samoyedic people of the Taymyr Peninsula, in which the shaman's songs call on helping spirits while he beats a large frame drum, represented here by the generic frame-drum card. The séances of Tubyaku Kosterkin of Ust-Avam, among the last Nganasan shamans, were recorded by visiting fieldworkers in the 1970s and 1980s.
items.description: One voice carries long, repeated melodic formulas that change in register and colour from section to section, driven by a steady frame-drum beat that quickens and swells toward the climax.
exemplars: Tubyaku Kosterkin séance recordings, Ust-Avam (1970s-80s fieldwork)

items.name: Biyelgee (Western Mongolian ger dance)
items.lineage: Dance of the Oirat and other ethnic groups of Khovd and Uvs aimags in western Mongolia, performed in the confined space of the ger with movements mainly of the upper body, hands and shoulders, and inscribed on UNESCO's List of Intangible Cultural Heritage in Need of Urgent Safeguarding. It is accompanied by the tovshuur, the two-string plucked lute of the western Mongols, and the morin khuur horse-head fiddle.
items.description: Short, tightly looping dance tunes in a steady lilting pulse are strummed on a two-string lute and doubled by a bowed horse-head fiddle, the phrases repeating for as long as the dance continues.
exemplars: UNESCO Urgent Safeguarding List file: Mongol Biyelgee (2009)
Western-aimag biyelgee ensemble recordings, Khovd and Uvs

items.name: Tuuli (Mongolian heroic epic)
items.lineage: Oral heroic epic of Mongolia, recited by the tuulch, an epic singer, in performances of hundreds to thousands of lines that combine praise, benedictions and tales of heroes, and inscribed on UNESCO's List of Intangible Cultural Heritage in Need of Urgent Safeguarding. The tradition survives chiefly among the Oirat groups of western Mongolia, where the tuulch accompanies the recitation on the tovshuur, often in a deep, guttural voice; the repertoire comprises many epics besides the Jangar cycle.
items.description: One singer chants long runs of alliterative verse in a low, guttural voice to a few recurring melodic formulas, strumming a two-string lute between and under the lines.
exemplars: UNESCO Urgent Safeguarding List file: Mongol Tuuli (2009)
Oirat tuulch recordings from Uvs and Khovd aimags

items.name: Tsuur (Altai Uriankhai end-blown flute)
items.lineage: Music of the tsuur, a three-hole vertical end-blown pipe played by the Altai Uriankhai of Khovd aimag in western Mongolia, inscribed on UNESCO's List of Intangible Cultural Heritage in Need of Urgent Safeguarding. The player hums a low guttural drone in the throat while blowing, so that pipe tone and voice sound together, and the repertoire, including praises of the Altai mountains, imitates the sounds of water, birds and animals.
items.description: A breathy, wind-like pipe melody floats over a continuous throat drone from the same player, in free, unhurried phrases with sliding pitches and bird-like figures.
exemplars: UNESCO Urgent Safeguarding List file: Traditional music of the Tsuur (2009)

items.name: Hunnu rock (Mongolian folk-metal)
items.lineage: Heavy rock from Ulaanbaatar that sets Mongolian throat singing, the morin khuur horse-head fiddle, the tovshuur lute and the jaw harp over electric guitar, bass and drums; the name is the one The HU, a band formed in 2016, gave its style, after the Hunnu (Xiongnu), the ancient steppe empire. The Mongolian tömör khuur jaw harp is represented by the khomus card in its Altai temir-komus form, and the earlier Ulaanbaatar band Altan Urag had already combined the morin khuur and throat singing with rock.
items.description: Stomping mid-tempo riffs on distorted guitar and bass lock with heavy drums while gravelly subharmonic throat singing carries chant-like melodies, with horse-head fiddle lines and a twanging jaw harp cutting through the mix.

items.name: Kalattuut (Greenlandic accordion dance music)
items.lineage: Social dance music of Greenland, where the kalattuut, a polka-like dance, developed from European dances introduced by whalers and traders and is played on the accordion, often with fiddle. It accompanies community festivities and has been recorded for the ULO label and KNR, the Greenlandic national broadcaster.
items.description: Bright, bouncing duple-time dance tunes on accordion, doubled or answered by fiddle, repeat in short sections over a steady oom-pah bass.
exemplars: ULO label recordings of kalattuut dance music

items.name: Greenlandic hymn and choir singing (Kalaallit church choirs)
items.lineage: Hymn and choral singing in the Greenlandic language, rooted in the eighteenth-century Lutheran mission of Hans Egede and the Moravian mission near Nuuk, whose hymns became the basis of a strong tradition of part-singing. Choirs remain central to church and civic life across Greenland and have been recorded by the ULO label and KNR.
items.description: Mixed choirs sing hymns and anthems in full, warm four-part chordal harmony at an unhurried, even pace in resonant wooden churches.

items.name: Iñupiaq drum dance (North Slope Eskimo dance)
items.lineage: Drum-dance of the Iñupiat of Alaska's North Slope, performed by community dance groups in which a row of seated men beat large handled frame drums, the qilaun, while men and women sing behind the dancers; the qilaat card of the closely related Greenlandic Inuit drum stands in for the qilaun. The Kivgiq messenger feast, revived at Utqiaġvik by the North Slope Borough in the late twentieth century, gathers dance groups from across the region.
items.description: A line of frame drums struck on the rim from below drives a hard unison beat under a short song sung through once quietly and then repeated louder and faster, with sharp accented strokes cueing the dancers' gestures.

items.name: Koo.éex' song (Tlingit memorial-party song)
items.lineage: Ceremonial song of the Tlingit of southeast Alaska, sung at the koo.éex', the memorial party or potlatch at which clans display their crests and sing clan-owned mourning songs and dance songs to frame drums, represented here by the generic frame-drum card. Louis Shotridge recorded Tlingit songs on wax cylinders for the University of Pennsylvania Museum, and the biennial Celebration organised by Sealaska Heritage Institute in Juneau now gathers Tlingit, Haida and Tsimshian dance groups.
items.description: A group sings slow, weighty mourning songs and steadier dance songs in unison, on vocables and Tlingit text, over a firm frame-drum beat set off by a song leader.

items.name: Gwich'in fiddle music (Athabascan old-time fiddling)
items.lineage: Fiddle dance music of the Gwich'in (Kutchin) of the Yukon River around Fort Yukon, where the fiddle arrived with Hudson's Bay Company traders in the mid-nineteenth century and Scottish and French-Canadian jigs, reels and square-dance tunes were taken up by local players. Craig Mishler documented it for Folkways in 1974, and the Athabascan Old-Time Fiddling Festival in Fairbanks continues the tradition.
items.description: A lively fiddle plays jigs, reels and square-dance tunes with driving, rhythmically flexible bowing over strummed guitar chords.
exemplars: Craig Mishler, Music of the Alaskan Kutchin Indians (Folkways FE 4253, 1974)

items.name: Alaskan Athabascan potlatch song (Interior Alaska)
items.lineage: Ceremonial and dance song of the Athabascan peoples of Interior Alaska, including the Koyukon, Tanana, Tanacross and Ahtna, sung above all at potlatches, the memorial feasts at which mourning songs composed for the dead are followed by dance songs. The Alaska Native Language Center at the University of Alaska Fairbanks holds recordings of these repertoires.
items.description: Groups of men and women sing short, repeated strophes of vocables and words in unison, slow and plaintive in the mourning songs and brisk and rhythmic in the dance songs.
exemplars: Alaska Native Language Center (University of Alaska Fairbanks) song recordings

items.name: Nunatsiavut Moravian choir and brass (Labrador Inuit church music)
items.lineage: Church music of the Labrador Inuit of Nunatsiavut, where Moravian missionaries founded Nain in the late eighteenth century and later Hopedale and other stations, and Inuit choirs came to sing chorales and anthems in Inuktitut in four-part harmony. Brass players, represented here by the generic horns card, perform chorales for church festivals, and the repertoire has been documented by Tom Gordon through Memorial University of Newfoundland's Research Centre for Music, Media and Place (MMaP).
items.description: Mixed choirs sing chorales and anthems in full four-part harmony, and a brass group plays the same chorale tunes in broad, sustained block chords.
exemplars: Tom Gordon / Memorial University MMaP recordings of Nain and Hopedale church music

items.name: Doukhobor psalm singing (Kootenay psalmy)
items.lineage: Sacred singing of the Doukhobors, Russian dissenting Christians who rejected the Orthodox liturgy and priesthood, about 7,500 of whom emigrated to Canada at the end of the nineteenth century and later settled in the Kootenay valleys of British Columbia around Castlegar and Grand Forks. Their psalms, transmitted orally as the 'Living Book', are sung unaccompanied at prayer meetings alongside later hymns and folk songs; the folklorist Kenneth Peacock published a study of them, 'Songs of the Doukhobors', through the National Museum of Canada.
items.description: A congregation sings slow, drawn-out psalm melodies in dense multipart heterophony, each syllable stretched over long melismas with no regular beat, swelling into full sustained chords.
exemplars: Kenneth Peacock, Songs of the Doukhobors (National Museum of Canada, 1970)

items.name: Palessie village song (Belarusian Polesian polyphony)
items.lineage: Village song of Palessie, the marshy Pripyat basin of southern Belarus around Pinsk and Turaŭ, where groups of women sing calendar, wedding and lyrical songs in heterophonic two- and three-part textures. The repertoire is held in the folklore archive of the Belarusian Academy of Sciences and was collected and published by the ethnomusicologist Zinaida Mazheika.
items.description: A small group of women sings in loud, open chest voices, the parts splitting from unison into two or three lines and closing again at cadences on long held final notes.
exemplars: Belarusian Academy of Sciences folklore archive recordings

items.name: Belarusian calendar-ritual song (vyasnyanki, Kupalle, Dazhynki)
items.lineage: Ritual songs of the Belarusian village year, each season with its own melodic type: winter kalyadki carols, vyasnyanki sung outdoors to call in the spring, Kupalle songs for the midsummer bonfire night, and reaping and dazhynki songs that close the harvest. Sung mainly by groups of women, the cycle is documented in the recordings of Belarusian State Radio and the folklore archive of the Belarusian Academy of Sciences.
items.description: Groups of women sing short, formulaic tunes repeated many times over, often outdoors with ringing shouted calls at phrase ends, moving between unison and simple two-part heterophony.
exemplars: Belarusian Academy of Sciences folklore archive recordings

items.name: Tsymbaly folk orchestra (Belarusian State Folk Orchestra)
items.lineage: Orchestral folk music of Belarus led by the tsymbaly, the Belarusian trapezoidal hammered dulcimer, represented here by the generic hammered-dulcimer card, together with bayans and string bass, in the manner of the State Folk Orchestra of Belarus, the oldest musical collective in the country. The tsymbaly virtuoso Iosif Zhinovich, founder of the Belarusian professional tsymbaly school, was among its founding musicians and later led it as artistic director and conductor; the orchestra now bears his name, and its recordings were issued by Melodiya.
items.description: Massed hammered dulcimers ring in rapid tremolos and running figures over bayan chords and a plucked bass, playing arranged folk dances and songs with bright, sparkling attacks.
exemplars: Belarusian State Folk Orchestra under Iosif Zhinovich (Melodiya recordings)

items.name: Begena song (Ethiopian Orthodox box-lyre devotion)
items.lineage: Paraliturgical devotional song of Ethiopian Orthodox Christians, sung by a solo performer to the begena, a large ten-string box lyre associated with King David whose strings are made to buzz by small leather pieces set between them and the bridge. It belongs to private and domestic devotion rather than the church service and is heard above all in the Lenten fasting season, with texts on God, mortality and the vanity of worldly life.
items.description: A single unhurried voice sings meditative strophes in a low register, moving closely with the deep, buzzing ostinato figures of a ten-string box lyre.
exemplars: Alemu Aga, Ethiopiques 11 'The Harp of King David' (Buda Musique)

items.name: Beta Israel liturgy (Ethiopian Jewish Ge'ez prayer chant)
items.lineage: Liturgical chant of the Beta Israel, the Jews of Ethiopia, historically centred in villages of the Gondar region such as Ambober, whose prayers are sung mainly in Ge'ez. Services were led by priests in the prayer house, with a drum and a small gong sounding in some of them; the drum and gong cards stand in for these. Wolf Leslau's recordings from the 1940s were issued by Folkways, and Kay Kaufman Shelemay later studied and transcribed the liturgy, before most of the community emigrated to Israel.
