items.description: Groups of priests chant prayers in a syllabic, formulaic style, with slow drumbeats and the strokes of a small gong punctuating some services.
exemplars: Religious Music of the Falashas (Jews of Ethiopia), Folkways, recorded by Wolf Leslau
Kay Kaufman Shelemay, Music, Ritual, and Falasha History (study and transcriptions of the liturgy)

items.name: Menzuma (Ethiopian Muslim devotional song)
items.lineage: Islamic devotional song of Ethiopian Muslims, composed and sung in Amharic, Oromo and other Ethiopian languages rather than in Arabic, with poems praising the Prophet and saints and conveying religious teaching. It is closely tied to the Sufi scholarship of Wollo, is performed at religious gatherings, and since the late twentieth century has circulated widely on commercial cassettes and video discs.
items.description: A lead singer delivers rhymed devotional verse to a steady, chant-like melody, answered by a chorus and carried by group hand-clapping.
exemplars: Ethiopian commercial menzuma cassette and VCD recordings

items.name: Dorze polyphony (Gamo highlands multipart song)
items.lineage: Multipart singing of the Dorze, an Omotic-speaking people of the Gamo highlands around Chencha in southern Ethiopia, also known for their weaving. Groups of singers combine several distinct, overlapping voice parts in feast songs, work songs and spinning songs. Bernard Lortat-Jacob recorded the repertoire in 1974 and 1975; the recordings were issued by Le Chant du Monde and are held in the CREM-CNRS archives.
items.description: Several voices enter with short, repeating melodic parts that overlap and interlock into a dense, cyclic polyphonic texture.
exemplars: Ethiopie: polyphonies des Dorze, Bernard Lortat-Jacob recordings (Le Chant du Monde)

items.name: Hamar music (South Omo song, lyre and mouth-bow)
items.lineage: Music of the Hamar, agro-pastoralists of the South Omo region of southern Ethiopia around Turmi. Ivo Strecker's field recordings document mouth-bow playing, flute and lyre music, songs for voice and lyre, running songs, leaping dances and war songs. The mongongo card stands in for the Hamar mouth-bow, the generic flute card for the Hamar flute and the krar for the Hamar lyre.
items.description: Quiet solo pieces for mouth-bow, flute and lyre sit beside songs in which the voice interweaves with the lyre, and beside group running, leaping-dance and war songs sung by many voices.
exemplars: Ivo Strecker, Nyabole: Music of the Hamar (1970s field recordings, southern Ethiopia)

items.name: Guragigna (Gurage dance-song)
items.lineage: Song and dance music of the Gurage, a Semitic-speaking people of the Gurage Zone south-west of Addis Ababa, around towns such as Wolkite and Butajira. Its fast group dances are driven by sung verses and intense hand-clapping, and the style reached a national audience through Guragigna songs recorded by Addis Ababa singers such as Mahmoud Ahmed.
items.description: Short sung lines traded between a leader and the dancers ride over fast, crisp hand-clapping patterns that drive the jumping footwork of the dance.
exemplars: Mahmoud Ahmed, Guragigna recordings (Mainz African cassettes archive)

items.name: Fukera and shellela (Amhara war-boast and war chant)
items.lineage: Martial vocal genres of the Amhara highlands of Gondar, Gojjam and Shewa. In fukera a man declaims a boast of his own bravery and deeds, and in shellela a singer chants heroic verses that once roused warriors before battle; both are still performed at weddings, holidays and public ceremonies, and the saxophonist Getatchew Mekurya adapted the shellela style to his instrument.
items.description: A lone male voice declaims rapid, rhythmically charged boasting verse in a loud, projected delivery, shading into sustained chanted lines of heroic exhortation.
exemplars: Ethiopian field recordings of shellela war chant from the Gondar region

items.name: Lalibalocc (Amhara dawn blessing songs)
items.lineage: Songs of the Lalibalocc, a hereditary group of itinerant singers in the Amhara region around Gondar who go from house to house before dawn, singing blessings and praise outside each door until the household gives food or money. The practice is popularly linked with leprosy, which the singing is said to ward off, and Itsushi Kawase has documented it in field recordings and films.
items.description: Two voices, often a man and a woman, alternate and overlap short blessing and praise phrases in the open air, unaccompanied and projected to carry into the house.
exemplars: Itsushi Kawase, Lalibalocc field recordings and films (Kyoto University ASAFAS)

items.name: Ashenda (Tigray and Amhara girls' festival songs)
items.lineage: Seasonal song festival of girls and young women in Tigray and northern Amhara, held in late August at the close of the Filseta fast for the Virgin Mary, and known also as Ashendye, Shadey, Solel and Mariya in different localities. Groups of girls in festive dress go from house to house and through the streets singing and dancing in circles, beating drums and receiving gifts.
items.description: Bands of girls sing short, bright call-and-response refrains while one of them beats a double-headed drum, with clapping and circling dance steps keeping a steady, cyclic beat.
exemplars: Ethiopian radio and television broadcast recordings of Ashenda songs

items.name: Tigre song (Eritrean lowland Tigre music)
items.lineage: Song and dance music of the Tigre, a Semitic-speaking, largely Muslim people of Eritrea's northern and western lowlands and Red Sea coast around Keren, Massawa and the Barka. Songs are commonly accompanied by the krar lyre, with drum and hand-clapping for dancing, and Tigre-language songs by singers such as Ibrahim Goret circulate on Eritrean recordings.
items.description: A lead voice sings strophic verses over the repeating figures of a plucked lyre, with drum and hand-clapping marking the dance pulse and a chorus answering the refrains.
exemplars: Ibrahim Goret, Tigre-language songs (including 'Safir Hilet' on the Asmara All Stars album Eritrea's Got Soul)

items.name: Kunama song and dance (Gash-Barka)
items.lineage: Music of the Kunama, a Nilo-Saharan-speaking people of the Gash-Barka region of south-western Eritrea around Barentu. Its dance-songs for weddings and community celebrations are documented in a Barentu wedding-dance recording in the CREM-CNRS archives, and the singer Faytinga has carried Kunama-language song into modern recordings. Generic drum and clap cards stand in for the dance accompaniment.
items.description: Dance-songs led by a singer and answered by a group move over a drummed and clapped pulse.

items.name: Dhaanto (Somali camel-step dance-song)
items.lineage: Somali folk dance-song associated especially with the pastoralist Somali Region of Ethiopia around Jigjiga, whose dance steps are said to imitate the gait of camels. Performed with sung verse, clapping and foot-stamping at gatherings and celebrations, it was recorded at Radio Mogadishu and Radio Hargeisa and remains a staple of Somali dance troupes at home and in the diaspora.
items.description: A lead singer's verses and a group refrain move in a rocking, swaying rhythm marked by clapping and stamped steps.
exemplars: Radio Mogadishu and Radio Hargeisa dhaanto recordings

items.name: Buraanbur (Somali women's song-poetry and dance)
items.lineage: The principal Somali genre of poetry composed and performed by women, sung at weddings, celebrations and other gatherings with drumming, clapping and dance; its verse can praise, celebrate, advise or comment on public events. Buraanbur performances are preserved in the Somali radio archives catalogued by Francesco Giannattasio.
items.description: Women's voices sing poetic verses in leader-and-chorus alternation over hand-beaten drums and clapping, punctuated by ululation.
exemplars: Somali radio archive recordings of women's buraanbur (Giannattasio catalogue, Roma Tre)

items.name: Mingis (Somali saar possession ceremony music)
items.lineage: Music of mingis, a Somali spirit-possession cult related to saar and practised in Mogadishu and other Somali towns, in which songs and drumming call the possessing spirits and bring participants into trance during healing ceremonies. Francesco Giannattasio recorded mingis ceremonies in 1982 for the Centro Studi Somali.
items.description: Insistent drumming and clapping underpin repeated sung invocations led by a ceremony leader and answered by participants, building in intensity toward trance.
exemplars: Francesco Giannattasio 1982 mingis ceremony recordings (Centro Studi Somali, Roma Tre)

items.name: Haqiba (Omdurman vocal song, 1920s-1940s)
items.lineage: Urban vocal song of Omdurman that took shape in the 1920s, when singers carried the style of Sufi madih praise-singing over to secular love poetry in colloquial Sudanese Arabic, accompanied only by a responding chorus, the tambourine and hand-clapping. Pioneers included Mohamed Ahmed Sorour, Abdel Karim Karouma and the poet-singer Khalil Farah, many of whose songs were issued on 78 rpm discs; the name comes from the later radio programme Haqibat al-Fann ('the bag of art') that rebroadcast them.
items.description: A lead singer delivers ornamented pentatonic melodies over a jingling frame drum and clapped rhythm, while a small chorus echoes each line.

items.name: Madih and dhikr (Sudanese Sufi praise song)
items.lineage: Sufi devotional singing of central and northern Sudan, where madih nabawi, sung poetry in praise of the Prophet, and the dhikr of the Sufi orders are performed at mosques, saints' tombs and religious festivals. The madih repertoire draws on Sudanese poets such as the nineteenth-century Hajj al-Mahi of Kassinger and is sung by a lead singer answered by a chorus over tar frame drums; at the Friday dhikr held at the tomb of Hamad al-Nil in Omdurman, Qadiriyya dervishes chant and dance to large drums. The frame-drum card stands in for the tar and the nuggara card for the large drums.
items.description: A lead singer delivers strophic praise poetry to pentatonic melodies, answered by a unison chorus over steady frame-drum patterns; in the dhikr, repeated chanted formulas over heavy drumming build gradually in tempo and intensity.
exemplars: Museum Collection Berlin: Dikr und Madih (Sudan)

items.name: Zar (Sudanese bori and tambura spirit ceremonies)
items.lineage: Spirit-possession healing ceremonies of Sudan, in which participants, most of them women, are brought into trance by songs addressed to particular spirits. Zar bori ceremonies are led by a female shaykha with a chorus of women over drums and percussion, while the tambura (tumbura) branch, kept by communities in Omdurman and Khartoum, centres on a male leader playing the large six-string tanbura lyre and a dancer wearing the mangur hoof-rattle belt. The membrane-drum card stands in for the dalluka and other drums.
items.description: Cyclic spirit songs, each tied to its own rhythm, are sung by a leader and answered by a chorus over insistent drumming and clapping; in tambura ceremonies a deep, buzzing lyre ostinato and the dry swish of the hoof-rattle belt drive the dancing toward trance.

items.name: Shaigiya tambour song (Nile-bend lyre song)
items.lineage: Song tradition of the Shaigiya of the Nile bend in Sudan's Northern State, around Karima and Merowe, in which a singer accompanies himself on the tambour, the local bowl lyre, for which the kissar card stands in. Abu Obaida Hassan's tambour recordings have been compiled by Ostinato Records.
items.description: A strong solo voice sings strophic songs over a repeating strummed lyre figure in a pentatonic mode, with handclaps marking the dance rhythm.
exemplars: Abu Obaida Hassan & His Tambour, 'The Shaigiya Sound of Sudan' (Ostinato Records)

items.name: Beja music (eastern Sudan lyre song and electric bands)
items.lineage: Music of the Beja peoples of eastern Sudan's Red Sea Hills and coast, around Port Sudan and Kassala, sung in Bedawiyet and Tigre. Its core is song accompanied by the basankob bowl lyre, for which the kissar card stands in; in Port Sudan, bands such as Noori & His Dorpa Band carry the lyre riffs onto an electrified lyre-guitar hybrid, for which the electric guitar card stands in, and add saxophone, bass and drums.
items.description: Hypnotic, repeating pentatonic riffs drive the songs; in the electric band form the riff passes to a twangy lyre-guitar doubled by saxophone over bass and drums.
exemplars: Noori & His Dorpa Band, 'Beja Power!' (Ostinato Records)

items.name: Waza (Berta gourd-trumpet ensemble)
items.lineage: Ensemble music of the Berta people of the Blue Nile borderlands of Sudan and Ethiopia, played on waza, end-blown trumpets built from joined gourd segments. Sets of many differently sized and tuned trumpets are each blown by one player sounding a single tone, so that melodies are assembled in hocket at communal celebrations; the bigwala card, another single-tone gourd-trumpet set, stands in for the waza.
items.description: Each trumpet contributes one buzzing, breath-driven tone at its place in a repeating cycle, so that the interlocking blasts of the whole group combine into a single circling melody with a broad, hollow sound.
exemplars: UNESCO/Folkways: Sudan, Music of the Blue Nile Province: The Ingessana and Berta Tribes (Robert Gottlieb)

items.name: Gaam music (Ingessana of the Tabi Hills)
items.lineage: Music of the Gaam-speaking people known as the Ingessana, of the Tabi Hills in Sudan's Blue Nile State, documented in Robert Gottlieb's recordings for the UNESCO collection, which present flute ensembles and songs accompanied by the lyre. The kissar card stands in for the Ingessana lyre and the flute card for their flutes.
items.description: Flute-ensemble pieces alternate with songs over a strummed lyre, in a sparse acoustic village sound.
exemplars: UNESCO/Folkways: Sudan, Music of the Blue Nile Province: The Ingessana and Berta Tribes (Robert Gottlieb)

items.name: Mardoum and hakkamat song (Baggara of Kordofan and Darfur)
items.lineage: Song and dance of the Baggara cattle-herding Arabs of Kordofan and Darfur in western Sudan. The mardoum (merdoum) is their communal dance rhythm, and the hakkamat are women singer-poets whose songs praise courage and generosity and comment on the community's affairs. The mardoum rhythm was carried into Sudanese urban popular music above all by the Kordofan-born singer Abdel Gadir Salim; the membrane-drum card stands in for the local drums.
items.description: A woman lead singer declaims praise verses in a strong, carrying voice, answered by a chorus and clapping over a steady drum in the mardoum dance rhythm.
exemplars: Abdel Gadir Salim All-Stars, 'The Merdoum Kings Play Songs of Love' (World Circuit)

items.name: Nuer song (Naath ox-songs and personal songs)
items.lineage: Song tradition of the Nuer (Naath) of South Sudan's Upper Nile and the Gambella region of Ethiopia, in which men compose personal songs about their display oxen, their kin and themselves, alongside songs for communal dances. Songs are sung unaccompanied or with the thom, a plucked string instrument that also accompanies contemporary Nuer singers.
items.description: A solo singer delivers personal songs of praise and self-description, over a plucked string accompaniment repeating short figures beneath the voice.

items.name: Isukuti (Isukha and Idakho drum-dance)
items.lineage: Drum-dance of the Isukha and Idakho, Luhya communities of Kakamega in western Kenya, performed at births, weddings, funerals and other community occasions, and inscribed on UNESCO's List of Intangible Cultural Heritage in Need of Urgent Safeguarding. Drummers play a set of isukuti drums of different sizes for fast, energetic dancing, with singing; the membrane-drum card stands in for the isukuti set.
items.description: Fast, interlocking patterns on drums of several sizes drive an energetic dance, with sung calls and choral responses riding over the drumming.
exemplars: UNESCO Urgent Safeguarding List dossier, Isukuti dance of Isukha and Idakho communities (2014)

items.name: Nyatiti song (Luo bowl-lyre tradition)
items.lineage: Song tradition of the Luo of the Lake Victoria region of western Kenya, around Siaya and Kisumu, in which a male singer accompanies himself on the eight-string nyatiti bowl lyre, marking the beat with an iron ring on his toe struck against the instrument and with ankle bells. Its repertoire includes praise songs and songs for funerals, and its interlocking lyre patterns shaped the guitar style of benga.
items.description: Rapid interlocking ostinatos on the lyre, played with both hands, underpin a narrative or praise vocal line, while the metallic clink of the toe ring and the shimmer of ankle bells keep the pulse.
exemplars: Ayub Ogada, 'En Mana Kuoyo' (Real World Records)
Singing Wells, Kenya: music of the Luo

items.name: Obokano song (Gusii bass-lyre tradition)
items.lineage: Lyre song of the Abagusii of the Kisii highlands in south-western Kenya, accompanied by the obokano, a very large bowl lyre with a deep bass register, played by the singer. Grandmaster Masese is a prominent contemporary player.
items.description: A deep, resonant bass ostinato from the huge lyre carries a declaimed or sung vocal line in a heavy, hypnotic groove.

items.name: Litungu song (Bukusu lyre tradition)
items.lineage: Lyre song of the Bukusu, a Luhya people of Bungoma in western Kenya, accompanied by the seven-string litungu lyre. Hugh Tracey recorded litungu songs for the International Library of African Music, and Singing Wells has made new recordings.
items.description: Repeating plucked lyre patterns with selectively damped strings support a solo singer's verses over a steady pulse.
exemplars: ILAM 1950 Hugh Tracey recordings of Bukusu litungu songs

items.name: Mugithi (Kikuyu one-man-guitar bar music)
items.lineage: Popular dance music of Kikuyu-speaking central Kenya, played in the bars and clubs of Nairobi, Nakuru and the central highlands by a singer-guitarist, typically a one-man-guitar performer backed by a programmed rhythm, who strings Kikuyu songs together into long medleys while dancers form a train, from which the genre takes its name (mugithi, 'train').
items.description: A lead vocal over bright, clean electric guitar and a steady programmed beat runs through long medleys without breaks, holding a constant mid-tempo dance pulse.

items.name: Mwomboko (Kikuyu accordion dance-song)
items.lineage: Couple dance-song of the Kikuyu of central Kenya, associated especially with Murang'a, that emerged in the 1940s around the accordion. Hugh Tracey recorded mwomboko for the International Library of African Music in 1952, and Singing Wells has recorded the Kangema Mwomboko Dancers.
items.description: Accordion melodies and chordal bass patterns set a steady dance tempo, with group singing over the accordion as couples dance.
exemplars: ILAM 1952 Hugh Tracey Kenya recordings of mwomboko

items.name: Omutibo (Luhya fingerpicked guitar song)
items.lineage: Acoustic guitar song style of the Luhya of western Kenya, associated with George Mukabi, one of the guitarists of the acoustic-guitar recording boom of the late 1950s and early 1960s in Kenya, who played fast fingerpicked guitar patterns accompanied by a rhythm tapped on a glass soda bottle. Mississippi Records issued a compilation of his recordings, Furaha Wenye Gita, in 2017.
items.description: Rapid, rolling fingerpicked guitar patterns over an alternating bass sit under a relaxed vocal, while a bottle struck in a steady pattern keeps time.

items.name: Mijikenda ngoma (Giriama and Digo drum-song, sengenya)
items.lineage: Drum-song and dance music of the Mijikenda peoples of the Kenyan coast and its hinterland, among them the Giriama of Kilifi and the Digo of Kwale, performed at weddings, funerals and community celebrations; named dances include sengenya. Ensembles combine several drums with kayamba raft rattles and, in some dances, the chivoti transverse flute, under a leader's songs answered by a chorus. The membrane-drum card stands in for the drum set.
items.description: Layered drum patterns and the dry swish of raft rattles build a dense, driving groove, over which a shrill flute line and call-and-response singing circle.
exemplars: Mukunguni: New Recordings from Coast Province, Kenya (Honest Jon's Records)

items.name: Chakacha (Swahili women's wedding dance-music)
items.lineage: Women's dance-music of the Swahili coast of Kenya, from Lamu to Mombasa, performed by women's groups with drums and singing at wedding celebrations to accompany a hip-centred dance. Its rhythm was later taken up by coastal popular bands, distinct from the orchestral taarab of the same towns.
items.description: A rolling, insistent drum rhythm and clapping carry women's call-and-response songs, with ululation punctuating the dancing.
exemplars: Folkways: Music of the Waswahili of Lamu, Kenya
Mombasa Roots (coastal band adaptation of the chakacha rhythm)

items.name: Maulidi (Swahili sung praise of the Prophet, Lamu)
items.lineage: Devotional poetry in Swahili and Arabic honouring the birth of the Prophet Muhammad, sung along the Kenyan coast and above all during the annual Maulidi festival of Lamu, which centres on the town's Riyadha mosque. Some forms, such as maulidi ya homu, set lead singers against a responding male chorus over frame drums, and kasida hymns belong to the same repertoire; the frame-drum card stands in for the local frame drums.
items.description: Lead voices intone Arabic and Swahili verses and a male chorus answers in unison, carried in the homu style by a steady pulse of hand-struck frame drums.
exemplars: Alan Boyd, 'Music of the Waswahili of Lamu, Kenya, Vol. 1: Maulidi' (Folkways)

items.name: Arbantone (Nairobi sample-based street rap)
items.lineage: Nairobi youth rap-and-dance style that broke through around 2023, associated with the Buruburu estate and widely described as an offshoot or successor of gengetone. Producers re-cut beats and melodies from older Kenyan and Jamaican throwback hits into fast, bass-heavy dance beats, and artists rap and chant in Sheng about the lives of young Kenyans.
items.description: Fast, pulsating dance beats with heavy basslines carry chopped, re-looped fragments of familiar older songs, while rappers deliver quick Sheng verses and chanted hooks.

items.name: Kidumbak (Zanzibar small-ensemble taarab)
items.lineage: Small-ensemble wedding and dance music of the Ng'ambo neighbourhoods of Zanzibar Town, long described as the popular, participatory counterpart of orchestral taarab and sharing much of its song repertoire. A singer and chorus are backed by one or two violins, the sanduku (a one-string tea-chest bass), a pair of small clay drums that give the genre its name, and rattles; the hand-drum card stands in for the kidumbak drums and the shaker card for the rattles.
items.description: A lead voice and answering chorus sing Swahili verses over a busy, danceable pulse of two small hand drums and rattles and a thudding one-string bass, with a violin winding the melody around the voice.
exemplars: Makame Faki and the Sina Chuki kidumbak group (Zanzibar)

items.name: Mchiriku (Dar es Salaam Zaramo drum-and-keyboard street music)
items.lineage: Neighbourhood party music of Dar es Salaam rooted in the drumming of the Zaramo people of the surrounding coast, played at weddings and all-night street dances. Groups combine several hand-beaten drums with a cheap electronic keyboard and a singer, amplified through overdriven loudspeakers, and their rhythms later fed the sampled beats of singeli; the keyboard card stands for the small Casio-type keyboards the groups use.
items.description: Fast interlocking hand-drum patterns drive a raw, overdriven sound in which a keyboard repeats short melodic riffs and a singer chants and shouts over the groove.

items.name: Beni ngoma (Swahili-coast brass-band dance societies)
items.lineage: Competitive dance associations that arose in the Swahili coastal towns of Kenya in the 1890s, led by rival societies in Mombasa, and spread through Tanganyika and much of eastern Africa in the early 20th century, adapting the uniforms, drill and military-band music of the colonial forces. Bands of bugles or brass with side and bass drums accompanied processions and marching dances, and Hugh Tracey recorded beni bands for the International Library of African Music in the early 1950s; the credited-horns card stands in for the bugles and brass, the snare-drum card for the side drums and the membrane-drum card for the bass drum.
items.description: Bugles and brass play bright, march-like tunes in unison and rough harmony over steady side- and bass-drum cadences that keep the dancers moving in formation.
exemplars: Hugh Tracey, International Library of African Music recordings of beni brass bands (early 1950s)

items.name: Modern taarab (Dar es Salaam mipasho keyboard taarab)
items.lineage: Dance-oriented taarab that took shape in Dar es Salaam in the 1990s, when troupes such as TOT Taarab and Muungano Cultural Troupe replaced much of the orchestral ensemble with electronic keyboards, electric guitar, bass and drums. Its songs, often called mipasho or rusha roho, trade pointed, teasing lyrics between rival singers and groups, and later bands such as Jahazi Modern Taarab carried the style through the 2000s.
items.description: A lead singer delivers ornamented Swahili verses, answered by a chorus, over layered electronic keyboard lines, a clean picked guitar, a busy electric bass and a steady dance beat.

items.name: Sukuma dance-society music (bugobogobo and rival ngoma guilds)
items.lineage: Song and drum music of the dance societies of the Sukuma of northwestern Tanzania, rival guilds led by celebrated dance-masters whose competitions are a central entertainment of the region. Bugobogobo, the dance of the farmers' societies, sets work-song texts to drumming and hoe-wielding choreography, and the Bujora Cultural Centre near Mwanza keeps the snake dance and other society repertoires; Frank Gunderson studied and recorded the farming societies' songs. The membrane-drum card stands in for the Sukuma drums.
items.description: A dance-leader's solo lines are answered by a large chorus over steady, heavy drumming, with work-song verses repeated in long cycles as the dancers move together.
exemplars: Frank Gunderson's field recordings of Sukuma farmers' society songs

items.name: Hadza song (Lake Eyasi forager singing and epeme dance)
items.lineage: Vocal music of the Hadza, hunter-gatherers of the Lake Eyasi basin in northern Tanzania whose language, Hadzane, is unrelated to those of their neighbours. Women and men sing together in camp, and on moonless nights the sacred epeme dance joins the women's singing to the stamping of male dancers who come forward one at a time.
items.description: Overlapping voices repeat short melodic phrases in a loose group texture, and in the night dance the singing is punctuated by the heavy, rhythmic stamping of a single dancer on bare earth.
exemplars: Kink Gong (Laurent Jeanneau), 'Hadza Bushmen of Tanzania', Musée du quai Branly audio collection

items.name: Kiganda royal court music (Buganda palace xylophone and drum-chime ensembles)
items.lineage: Instrumental music of the court of the Kabaka of Buganda at Mengo in Kampala, played by hereditary court musicians until the kingdoms were abolished in 1967. Palace ensembles included the twelve-key amadinda and larger akadinda log xylophones played by several interlocking players, the entenga tuned drum chime, ennanga bow-harp songs and flute and trumpet bands; Hugh Tracey recorded them for the International Library of African Music in the early 1950s. The membrane-drum card stands in for the entenga drums.
items.description: Two or three players on one log xylophone interlock fast, evenly spaced strokes into dense composite melodies on a five-note scale, and in the drum chime tuned drums interlock melodies in the same way.
exemplars: Hugh Tracey, 'Royal Court Music from Uganda' (SWP Records / ILAM)

items.name: Baakisimba (Kiganda dance-drumming)
items.lineage: Central dance-music of the Baganda of central Uganda, said to have begun at the royal court and now performed at ceremonies, celebrations and by cultural troupes. A large baakisimba drum, a small nankasa drum beaten with sticks and the long engalabi lead the ensemble, often joined by the endingidi tube fiddle and singing, while dancers move the waist and hips to the drums. The stick-beaten drum card stands in for the nankasa and the membrane-drum card for the baakisimba and empuunyi drums.
items.description: Layered drums lock into a rolling, swaying groove led by a deep main drum and crisp stick strokes on a small drum, with a tube fiddle and voices adding short repeating melodies.

items.name: Kadodi (Bagisu imbalu circumcision drumming)
items.lineage: Processional drum-and-song music of the Bagisu (Bamasaaba) of the Mount Elgon region around Mbale in eastern Uganda, played for imbalu, the male circumcision ceremonies held in even-numbered years. Kadodi groups of drummers and singers escort the young candidates from home to home in the days before the cut while crowds dance alongside; the membrane-drum card stands in for the kadodi drums.
items.description: Driving, fast patterns on several drums keep a relentless dance pulse while crowds of singers chant short responsorial phrases on the move.

items.name: Larakaraka and bwola (Acholi courtship and royal dances)
items.lineage: Two of the principal dances of the Acholi of northern Uganda. Larakaraka is the courtship and wedding dance, in which young men and women dance in lines to singing and percussion, and bwola is the royal dance of the chiefdoms, in which men beat small drums as they dance in a wide circle around a leader while women dance within it. The membrane-drum card stands in for the Acholi drums.
items.description: Many small drums beaten by the dancers themselves lock into steady unison patterns under a leader's direction, while groups of singers trade short call-and-response lines.
exemplars: Vanderbilt University East African Recordings (Acholi dances, 2004-05)

items.name: Acholi electronic wedding music (Gulu)
items.lineage: Electronic dance music of Gulu, northern Uganda, made in small studios for weddings and parties. From the early 2000s the singer Otim Alpha and the producer Leo Palayeng reworked larakaraka and other Acholi wedding songs on computer software, setting them to drum-machine beats and keyboards at high tempos, and later Gulu producers followed; from 2017 Nyege Nyege Tapes releases brought the style to international audiences.
items.description: Rapid, relentless programmed drum patterns and bright looping keyboard riffs carry call-and-response wedding songs, sung at full tilt over the electronic beat.
exemplars: Otim Alpha, 'Gulu City Anthems' (Nyege Nyege Tapes, 2017)
'Electro Acholi Kaboom from Northern Uganda' (Nyege Nyege Tapes compilation)

items.name: Orunyege-Ntogoro (Banyoro and Batooro courtship dance)
items.lineage: Courtship dance-music of the Banyoro and Batooro of western Uganda, centred on Hoima, Masindi and Fort Portal and performed at weddings and celebrations. It takes part of its name from the ebinyege, rattles strapped to the male dancers' legs, which sound against drumming and singing; the shaker card stands in for the leg rattles.
items.description: Brisk drumming and the rhythmic swish of rattles on the dancers' legs drive a fast, bouncing pulse, while a lead singer and chorus exchange short courtship verses.
exemplars: Vanderbilt University East African Recordings (Banyoro and Batooro dances)

items.name: Ekitaguriro (Ankole cattle dance)
items.lineage: Dance-song of the Banyankole of southwestern Uganda, centred on Mbarara, whose stamping, arm-raising movements imitate the gait and horns of the long-horned cattle at the heart of Ankole herding life. Songs in praise of cattle alternate with okwevuga, rapid recited praise-poetry declaimed by the performers, and the dance is often accompanied by the endingidi tube fiddle.
items.description: A rasping one-string tube fiddle repeats short melodic figures under group singing and the dancers' heavy stamping, broken by bursts of fast, declaimed praise-poetry.
exemplars: Royal Museum for Central Africa (Tervuren), folk music from Ankole recordings

items.name: Embaire (Busoga log-xylophone music)
items.lineage: Xylophone music of the Basoga of eastern Uganda, around Kamuli and Iganga, played on the embaire, a large log xylophone whose keys are laid across banana stems and struck by several players at once in interlocking parts, with drums and singing for dances and celebrations. Village embaire groups reached international release through Nyege Nyege Tapes in 2023.
items.description: Several players hammer a single huge wooden xylophone in fast interlocking patterns that build a dense, propulsive wall of tone, with drums and voices riding on top.

items.name: Akazehe (Burundian women's greeting song)
items.lineage: Vocal greeting genre of Burundian women and girls, in which two or more singers exchange greetings and good wishes in short, overlapping, interlocking phrases. Michel Vuylsteke recorded examples in 1967, and they are held in the CREM-CNRS sound archive in Paris.
items.description: Two women's voices overlap in quick, interlocking phrases, each answering the other before the line is finished, producing a continuous rhythmic duet without instruments.
exemplars: Michel Vuylsteke, akazehe recordings (1967), CREM-CNRS archive

items.name: Danza de tijeras (Andean scissors dance music)
items.lineage: Danza de tijeras is the competitive ritual dance of the danzaq of Huancavelica, Ayacucho and Apurímac, inscribed on UNESCO's Representative List in 2010, in which each dancer clashes two loose metal blades held in one hand while performing feats of strength and agility in contests called atipanakuy. Every dancer is accompanied by his own harpist and violinist, and the rival harp-and-violin pairs answer one another tune for tune through the contest. The metal-spoons card stands in for the scissor blades.
items.description: A plucked harp bass and a bright, ornamented violin line spin short repeated tunes while the dancer's metal blades ring out a bright clatter over them, the pace rising with each challenge.
exemplars: Máximo Damián Huamaní (Ayacucho violinist of the scissors dance)
Archivo de Música Tradicional Andina (PUCP) field recordings of danza de tijeras

items.name: Huaylas (Mantaro Valley carnival dance-song)
items.lineage: Huaylas, or huaylarsh, is the carnival courtship dance of the Mantaro Valley around Huancayo in Junín, rooted in the valley's agrarian festivities and now played in two broad styles: the older huaylas antiguo and the faster, competition-driven huaylas moderno. Its modern sound is the Junín orquesta típica of saxophones, clarinets, violins and Andean harp, often with a sung verse before the instrumental sections.
items.description: A massed saxophone and clarinet section in wide-vibrato unison drives a fast, stamping duple tune over harp bass and violins, the lines repeating in short cycles for the dancers' zapateo.
exemplars: Smithsonian Folkways, Traditional Music of Peru Vol. 2: The Mantaro Valley
Junín orquesta típica recordings of huaylas

items.name: Santiago (Mantaro Valley cattle-marking songs)
items.lineage: The Santiago, or herranza, is the cattle-marking fiesta of the Mantaro Valley in Junín, held around the feast of St James on 25 July, at which families mark and adorn their animals with ribbons to songs that call for the herd's increase. Women singers lead in a high, piercing voice while beating the tinya, a small hand drum, answered by the wakrapuku, a spiral trumpet built from joined cattle horns, and by violin. The membrane-drum card stands in for the tinya and the horns card for the wakrapuku.
items.description: High, strident women's voices sing short repeated verses over the dry tap of small hand drums, while blaring horn trumpets and a scraping violin answer between phrases.
exemplars: Smithsonian Folkways, Traditional Music of Peru Vol. 2: The Mantaro Valley

items.name: Muliza (Pasco and Tarma carnival song)
items.lineage: The muliza is a carnival song-dance of Peru's central highlands, strongest in Cerro de Pasco and Tarma, whose name and lore tie it to the muleteers who drove mule trains through the region. It is sung to estudiantina string bands of mandolins, guitars and violins or to orquestas típicas with saxophones, clarinets, violin and harp, and it accompanies the carnival comparsas.
items.description: A sung strophic melody rides over strummed mandolins and guitars or a reed-and-violin band with harp, the verses giving way to instrumental interludes for the dancing comparsas.
exemplars: Central-highland orquesta típica and estudiantina recordings of mulizas

items.name: Harawi (Quechua women's ritual song)
items.lineage: Harawi is an old Quechua song genre of the southern Peruvian highlands, sung chiefly by older women at agricultural rites such as sowing and harvest, at weddings, roof-raisings and farewells, in a very high voice with long held tones that fall away at phrase ends. It is usually sung without instruments, and its name gave rise to the colonial mestizo yaraví.
items.description: Unaccompanied women's voices hold piercing high tones on a few pitches, each long phrase sliding downward at its close, in free rhythm.
exemplars: Archivo de Música Tradicional Andina (PUCP) field recordings of harawi

items.name: Q'ero song and pinkuyllu (Paucartambo high puna)
items.lineage: The Q'ero communities of the high puna of Paucartambo in Cusco keep a repertoire of songs addressed to their llamas and alpacas and to the mountain beings, sung chiefly by women in a high voice, while men play the pinkuyllu, a long duct flute, at Carnival. John Cohen's Folkways recordings and Holly Wissler's later fieldwork document this repertoire. The flute card stands in for the pinkuyllu.
items.description: High women's voices sing short, repeated phrases in the open air while the low, breathy hoot of long duct flutes sounds alongside, each line kept close to a few pitches.
exemplars: John Cohen, Mountain Music of Peru (Smithsonian Folkways)
Holly Wissler, From Grief and Joy We Sing (Q'eros study)

items.name: Qoyllur Rit'i (Sinakara pilgrimage music)
items.lineage: Qoyllur Rit'i is the pilgrimage to the Sinakara valley below the Qullqipunku glacier in Cusco, held in the days before Corpus Christi and inscribed by UNESCO in 2011, to which dance troupes of ch'unchu, qhapaq qolla and other nations climb with their own musicians. Each troupe's small band, of cane flutes and drum or of violin and harp, plays its own dance tunes, so the sanctuary resounds with many ensembles at once, cut by the falsetto calls and whistles of the ukuku guardians. The quena card stands in for the troupes' cane flutes and the membrane-drum card for their drums.
items.description: Many small flute-and-drum and violin-and-harp bands play different dance tunes at once in a vast mountain amphitheatre, the overlapping layers pierced by squeaking falsetto calls.
exemplars: Smithsonian Folkways, Traditional Music of Peru Vol. 1: Festivals of Cusco

items.name: Wititi (Colca Valley courtship dance music)
items.lineage: Wititi is the courtship dance of the young people of the Colca Valley in Arequipa, performed during the religious feasts of the rainy season and inscribed by UNESCO in 2015, in which troupes of couples dance in rows to the beat of a band, the men wearing layered women's skirts. Villages compete to field the best troupes, renewing the dance while keeping its traditional character. The horns, bass-drum, snare and cymbal cards stand in for the accompanying band.
items.description: A street band's horns repeat a short, lilting dance tune over a steady bass-drum and snare beat with cymbal crashes, cycling for rows of couples in procession.
exemplars: Smithsonian Folkways, Traditional Music of Peru Vol. 3: Cajamarca and the Colca Valley

items.name: Huaconada (Mito New Year ritual dance music)
items.lineage: The huaconada is the ritual dance of Mito in Concepción province, Junín, performed in the first days of January and inscribed by UNESCO in 2010, in which masked men called huacones, carrying whips, dance through the plaza as guardians of communal order. Their stately, swaggering steps are played by the Mantaro orquesta típica of clarinets, saxophones, violin and harp.
items.description: Clarinets and saxophones carry a slow, heavily ornamented melody with wide vibrato over violin and harp, its measured gait repeating for the masked dancers' procession.
exemplars: UNESCO 2010 inscription file: Huaconada, ritual dance of Mito
Junín orquesta típica recordings of the huaconada

items.name: Hatajo de negritos (south-central coast Christmas troupes)
items.lineage: The hatajos de negritos and de pallitas are Afro-Peruvian Christmas devotional troupes of Peru's south-central coast, centred on El Carmen in Chincha and inscribed by UNESCO in 2019, who sing and dance before the Christ Child from late December to the Epiphany. A violinist leads the negritos, who ring handbells and stamp zapateo footwork between their sung verses, while the pallitas are troupes of girls and young women who sing in chorus. The Ballumbrosio family of El Carmen are the tradition's best-known keepers.
items.description: A lone violin leads short devotional verses sung by a troupe in unison, the ringing of hand-held bells and the stamp of footwork marking the pulse between the lines.
exemplars: Hatajo de negritos of El Carmen, Chincha

items.name: Tondero (northern Peruvian coastal dance-song)
items.lineage: Tondero is the mestizo couple dance-song of Peru's northern coast, centred on Piura and Lambayeque and related to the marinera and zamacueca family, whose pieces run in three sections: the glosa, the dulce and the fuga. It is played on guitars with cajón and handclaps and sung by a soloist or a pair of voices.
items.description: Strummed and picked guitars set a lilting couple-dance rhythm, with cajón and handclaps pushing the accents as the song moves from verse to a slower section and a quick closing fuga.
exemplars: Smithsonian Folkways, Traditional Music of Peru Vol. 4: Lambayeque

items.name: Son de los diablos (Afro-Peruvian carnival devils' dance)
items.lineage: The son de los diablos is the Afro-Peruvian carnival dance of Lima in which a troupe of masked devils led by a caporal parades through the streets with acrobatic zapateo footwork; a colonial-era festival custom painted by Pancho Fierro in the nineteenth century, it faded in the early twentieth and was revived on stage by Afro-Peruvian folklore companies from the mid-century. Its music is carried by guitar, cajón and the quijada, the rattled jawbone of a donkey.
items.description: Guitar strums a repeating dance pattern while cajón slaps and the buzzing rattle of the jawbone drive a quick, accented street-parade rhythm.

items.name: Eshuva (Harakmbut sung prayers)
items.lineage: Eshuva are the sung prayers of the Harakmbut-speaking Huachipaire (Wachiperi) people of Madre de Dios in the Peruvian Amazon, inscribed on UNESCO's Urgent Safeguarding List in 2011, sung only in Harakmbut to call on the spirits of the natural world to heal illness and ease hardship. They are learned orally by listening to elders and are sung by the voice alone.
items.description: A single unaccompanied voice chants soft, repetitive invocations on a narrow range of pitches, close and intimate, without any instrument.
exemplars: UNESCO 2011 Urgent Safeguarding List file: Eshuva, Harakmbut sung prayers of Peru's Huachipaire people
Peruvian Ministry of Culture documentation of eshuva

items.name: Ayarachi (Paratía panpipe-and-drum music)
items.lineage: Ayarachi is a Quechua panpipe-and-drum music and dance of Puno, kept in its older form chiefly in Paratía in Lampa province and in Cuyocuyo in Sandia, played by large troupes of men who sound big panpipes in interlocking paired halves with drums. Its slow, solemn tunes are linked in local tradition to mourning and the dead. The siku card stands in for the ayarachi panpipes and the membrane-drum card for the drums.
items.description: A troupe of breathy, low panpipes trade notes between paired players to build slow, solemn melodies, each phrase pressed out over a steady, heavy drumbeat.
exemplars: Archivo de Música Tradicional Andina (PUCP) field recordings of ayarachi

items.name: Indigenismo (Peruvian Andean-nationalist art music)
items.lineage: Peruvian indigenist art music is the early-twentieth-century concert school that built piano pieces, art songs, zarzuelas and orchestral works on Andean pentatonic melody and huayno and yaraví rhythms. Daniel Alomía Robles, whose zarzuela El cóndor pasa dates from 1913, and Teodoro Valcárcel of Puno led it, and the immigrant composers André Sas and Rodolfo Holzmann extended it in Lima from the 1920s and 1930s.
items.description: Concert piano sets pentatonic Andean melodies in tonal and modal harmony, with art songs sung in a trained voice over chordal piano accompaniment.

items.name: Morenada (Bolivian brass-band fraternity dance)
items.lineage: Morenada is the dance of the morenos of the Bolivian altiplano and Puno, a central fraternity dance of the Carnaval de Oruro and La Paz's Gran Poder, whose dancers in heavy, ornate costumes whirl wooden matracas, ratchets that rattle over the music. It is played by bandas de bronce of trumpets, trombones, baritone horns and tubas over bass drum, snare and cymbals at a slow, heavy, swaying duple gait. The sousaphone card stands in for the bands' tubas.
items.description: A massed brass band of trumpets, trombones, baritones and tubas plays a slow, heavy, swaying duple march, bass drum and cymbals landing hard on the beat.

items.name: Caporales (Bolivian saya-caporal dance)
items.lineage: Caporales is a Bolivian fraternity dance created in La Paz in 1969 by the Estrada Pacheco brothers, who drew its central figure, the whip-carrying overseer, from the Afro-Bolivian saya, and it now fills the Gran Poder and Oruro carnival parades. Its bright, fast duple music is played by bandas de bronce while bells on the male dancers' boots ring with each leap, and sung caporales became a staple of Bolivian folk-pop groups such as Los Kjarkas. The sousaphone card stands in for the bands' tubas.
items.description: A brass band punches out a bright, brisk duple tune in stabbing unison, snare and cymbals driving the leaps, the trumpets riding high above heavy tubas.

items.name: Saya afroboliviana (Yungas Afro-Bolivian drum-song)
items.lineage: The saya is the drum-song of the Afro-Bolivian communities of the Yungas valleys of La Paz, around Coroico and Tocaña, in which women sing coplas, traditional and improvised verses answered by the group, over the men's drums and a scraped cuancha. Kept alive in community fiestas and, from the late 1980s, by the Movimiento Cultural Saya Afroboliviana, it is the source of the caporal figure of Bolivian festival dance. The membrane-drum card stands in for the saya drums and the güiro card for the cuancha.
items.description: Women's voices trade sung verses and group answers over a steady pounding of drums and the rasp of a scraper, the pulse cycling unchanged for the circling dancers.

items.name: Tarkeada (altiplano tarka carnival troupes)
items.lineage: Tarkeada is the carnival and rainy-season (anata) music of the Bolivian and southern Peruvian altiplano, played by large troupes of tarkas, hexagonal wooden duct flutes made in three sizes that sound in parallel octaves and fifths, over bombos and snare drums. The players blow hard for the tarka's deliberately hoarse, buzzing tone, and the troupe dances through fields and streets.
items.description: Dozens of hoarse, reedy wooden duct flutes play one tune in thick parallel octaves and fifths over pounding bass drums and snares, rough and buzzing in the open air.
exemplars: Ocora and Le Chant du Monde Bolivian altiplano anthologies (tarka troupes)

items.name: K'antu (Charazani panpipe-and-drum troupes)
items.lineage: Panpipe-and-drum troupe music of the Kallawaya region around Charazani in Bautista Saavedra province, in the highlands of La Paz department, Bolivia, part of the Andean cosmovision of the Kallawaya that UNESCO recognises as Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity. Men play k'antu panpipes split into two complementary rows, ira and arka, in several sizes doubling the melody at parallel intervals, many of them beating a large drum (wankara) as they play, while a triangle rings above. The siku card stands in for the k'antu panpipes and the membrane-drum card for the wankara.
items.description: Dozens of breathy cane panpipes in several registers alternate the notes of a slow, insistent melody between paired players, doubled at parallel intervals that beat against one another, over a steady unison drum pulse struck by the pipers themselves and a bright metallic ring.
exemplars: UNESCO Masterpiece documentation 'Andean Cosmovision of the Kallawaya' (2003)
Field and commercial recordings of the k'antu troupes of Charazani

items.name: Pinkillu (Norte Potosí rainy-season flutes and wayñu)
items.lineage: Rainy-season music of the Quechua-speaking ayllus around Macha in Norte Potosí, Bolivia, documented by the ethnomusicologist Henry Stobart in Music and the Poetics of Production in the Bolivian Andes. Through the growing season leading up to Carnival, men play consorts of pinkillu cane duct flutes in several sizes and young women sing wayñu songs to their tunes, music bound up with the growth of the crops; in the dry season other instruments, among them the julajula panpipes, take their place. The bamboo-flute card stands in for the pinkillu.
items.description: Consorts of buzzing duct flutes in several sizes play a repeating dance tune in parallel, the dense, slightly mistuned blend thickening each note, while a group of young women sings the same melody in a piercing high register.
exemplars: Henry Stobart, Music and the Poetics of Production in the Bolivian Andes (Ashgate, 2006), with field recordings from the Macha region

items.name: Pujllay and Ayarichi (Yampara music of Tarabuco)
items.lineage: Music and dance of the Yampara culture around Tarabuco in Chuquisaca, Bolivia, on UNESCO's Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity. Pujllay belongs to the rainy season and Carnival and celebrates the renewal of life brought by the rains: men dance in sandals fitted with large metal spurs while musicians play flutes and a horn clarinet. Ayarichi belongs to the dry season and the saints' feasts: four male dancer-musicians play panpipes and drums at once, with two to four young women who dance and sing. The flute card stands in for the Pujllay flutes and the horns card for the horn clarinet.
items.description: In the rainy season flutes and a horn clarinet repeat short dance phrases over the clink of the dancers' metal spurs; in the dry season panpipes and drums, played by the dancers themselves, carry the plaintive songs of young women over a steady drum pulse.
exemplars: UNESCO Representative List file 'Pujllay and Ayarichi, music and dances of the Yampara culture' (2014)
Field recordings of Pujllay and Ayarichi at Tarabuco

items.name: Taquirari (eastern Bolivian lowland song-dance)
items.lineage: Song-dance of the eastern Bolivian lowlands of Santa Cruz and Beni, the camba repertoire that also takes in the chovena of the Moxos plains, popularised on record from the mid-twentieth century by the singer Gladys Moreno and by lowland groups and trios. It is carried by voices with strummed guitars, and in festival settings by drums and bands.
items.description: A bright, lilting duple dance in which strummed guitars set a skipping, syncopated pattern under a clear lead voice, with a drum marking the steps.
exemplars: Commercial recordings of Santa Cruz lowland trios and groups

items.name: Cueca boliviana (and bailecito de tierra)
items.lineage: The Bolivian form of the cueca, the handkerchief couple-dance in 6/8 shared with Chile and Argentina, cultivated in regional styles such as the chuquisaqueña of Sucre, the potosina, the paceña and the tarijeña, together with the related bailecito de tierra. It was written for piano by the Sucre composer Simeón Roncal and recorded by estudiantinas of mandolins, guitars and charangos and by guitar-and-voice duos.
items.description: Strummed guitars, charango and tremolo mandolins drive a lilting 6/8 that slips into 3/4 cross-accents, under two voices singing in parallel thirds, with hand-claps and shouts marking the sections of the dance.
exemplars: Estudiantina recordings of cuecas chuquisaqueñas and potosinas

items.name: Música chapaca (Tarija valley seasonal music)
items.lineage: Music of the chapacos, the country people of the Tarija valley in southern Bolivia, whose instruments follow the festive calendar: the erke, a cow horn sounded through a thin cane tube with a reed, played with the caja at Carnival; the caña, a long cane trumpet heard at the Fiesta de San Roque with its chunchos dancers; the violín chapaco; and the camacheña cane flute. The caja, a shallow double-headed drum struck with a single beater, also accompanies women's sung coplas. The horns card stands in for the erke and caña and the bamboo-flute card for the camacheña.
items.description: A horn pipe or long cane trumpet blows raw, sustained overtone pitches over the dry thud of a beater-struck double-headed drum; in other seasons a scratchy violin or a shrill cane flute carries short dance tunes, and women sing couplets over the drum alone.
exemplars: Field and commercial recordings of the Fiesta de San Roque in Tarija
Recordings of chapaco coplas with caja

items.name: Bomba del Chota (Afro-Ecuadorian Chota Valley)
items.lineage: Afro-Ecuadorian song-dance of the Chota-Mira valley on the border of Imbabura and Carchi provinces, kept by the descendants of Africans enslaved on the valley's colonial sugar haciendas. The bomba, a double-headed hand drum that gives the genre its name, plays with guitars, requinto, güiro and maracas under sung verses, while the related banda mocha imitates a brass band with orange leaves, gourds, horns and bass drum. Groups such as Marabú took it onto record. The hand-drum card stands in for the bomba.
items.description: Strummed guitars and a picked requinto lead line ride a swaying, syncopated hand-drum groove filled out by scraper and shakers, under a lead voice singing short verses.
exemplars: Garland Encyclopedia of World Music vol. 2, 'Ecuador' (Afro-Ecuadorian music of the Chota valley)

items.name: Música rocolera (Ecuadorian rockola cantina song)
items.lineage: Working-class popular song of Ecuador, named after the rockolas (jukeboxes) of the bars and cantinas where it was heard, which grew out of the pasillo and the bolero in the 1970s and 1980s with singers such as Segundo Rosero, Jaime Enrique Aymara and Mélida Jara. Its songs of heartbreak, betrayal and drink are sung over guitars and requinto, later with electric bass; the ethnomusicologist Ketty Wong analysed it in Whose National Music? Identity, Mestizaje, and Migration in Ecuador (2012).
items.description: A plaintive, vibrato-laden lead voice sings slow, first-person laments of lost love over strummed guitar, a weeping picked requinto line answering each phrase and a plain bass underneath.
exemplars: Ketty Wong, Whose National Music? (Temple University Press, 2012)

items.name: Amorfino (Montubio coastal sung couplets)
items.lineage: Improvised sung couplets of the Montubio people, the mestizo farmers and horsemen of Ecuador's coastal lowlands in Manabí, Los Ríos and Guayas. Amorfinos are short rhymed verses of love, wit and rural life, often traded as a challenge between a man and a woman or between rival singers, sung to a simple recurring tune with or without guitar, and they are held up as a core expression of Montubio identity.
items.description: Two singers trade short rhymed verses on a simple repeating tune, half sung and half declaimed, over sparse strummed guitar chords or none at all, each answer pointed at the last.
exemplars: Montubio field recordings and festival albums of amorfinos (Manabí and Los Ríos)

items.name: Canelos Kichwa song (Ecuadorian Amazonian Runa)
items.lineage: Song of the Canelos Kichwa (Canelos Quichua) of Pastaza province in the Ecuadorian Amazon, studied by the anthropologist Norman E. Whitten Jr.; the Soul Vine Shaman recordings made with him document the songs shamans sing during ayahuasca sessions to the rustle of a leaf-bundle rattle, and the songs women sing to spirits and kin. At community festivals men beat drums for the dancing. The shaker card stands in for the leaf-bundle rattle.
items.description: A single voice sings soft, repeating melodic phrases close to speech, over the steady dry rustle of a shaken leaf rattle, in an intimate night-time setting.
exemplars: Soul Vine Shaman (Sacha Runa Research Foundation), recordings of Canelos Quichua shamans' and women's songs made with Norman E. Whitten Jr.

items.name: Kamba Kua (Afro-Paraguayan San Baltazar drumming)
items.lineage: Drumming, song and dance of Kamba Kua, the Afro-Paraguayan community of Fernando de la Mora on the edge of Asunción, descended from the Black lancers who followed the Uruguayan leader José Gervasio Artigas into exile in Paraguay in the early nineteenth century. Its music centres on the feast of San Baltazar on 6 January, when drummers play for the dancers, and is carried on by the community's Ballet Kamba Kua.
items.description: Several hand-beaten drums lock into a driving, interlocking dance rhythm, with group singing over the drums as dancers circle in festival procession.
exemplars: Ballet Kamba Kua, the community's drum and dance troupe
Documentation of the San Baltazar festival of Kamba Kua

items.name: Mbyá-Guaraní prayer-house song (opy)
items.lineage: Sacred song and dance of the Mbyá-Guaraní of eastern Paraguay, held in evening gatherings in the opy prayer house under a religious leader; their sacred texts were recorded by León Cadogan in Ayvu Rapyta. Men accompany the singing on the mbaraka, a five-string guitar strummed in a steady pattern, and the rave, a small fiddle, while women beat the earth with takuapu bamboo stamping tubes. The guitar, fiddle and bamboo stamping-tube cards stand in for the mbaraka, rave and takuapu.
items.description: A circle of voices sings short repeated phrases over a steady strummed guitar pattern and a thin fiddle line, while bamboo tubes thump the ground in an even pulse.
exemplars: León Cadogan, Ayvu Rapyta: textos míticos de los Mbyá-Guaraní del Guairá (1959)
Field recordings of Mbyá opy ritual song (Caaguazú and Guairá)

items.name: Rabinal Achí (Xajooj Tun dance-drama music)
items.lineage: Music of the Rabinal Achí, or Xajooj Tun ('dance of the tun'), a masked Maya Achi dance-drama of Rabinal in Baja Verapaz, Guatemala, that tells of the capture, trial and sacrifice of a K'iche' warrior; it is performed for the feast of Saint Paul in January and UNESCO recognises it as Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity. Its text was first written down in the mid-nineteenth century. The speeches and dances are accompanied by the tun, a wooden slit drum, and long trumpets. The maguaré card stands in for the tun and the horns card for the long trumpets.
items.description: Long trumpets sound slow, sustained, wavering calls over the hollow, two-toned knock of a wooden slit drum repeating a short pattern for the slow steps of masked dancers.
exemplars: UNESCO Masterpiece documentation 'Rabinal Achí dance drama tradition' (2005)
Field recordings of the tun-and-trumpet music of the Rabinal Achí

items.name: Chirimía y tun (Guatemalan highland Maya shawm and drum)
items.lineage: Shawm-and-drum music of the K'iche' and other highland Maya of Guatemala, played for cofradía processions, saints' feasts and masked dance-dramas, notably at Chichicastenango. The chirimía, a double-reed shawm brought in the colonial period, plays long modal melodies over a large drum and the tun slit drum. The dulzaina card stands in for the chirimía and the maguaré card for the tun.
items.description: A piercing, nasal double-reed shawm winds through long ornamented modal phrases over the deep beat of a large drum and the hollow knock of a slit drum, outdoors in procession.
exemplars: Field recordings of chirimía and tun at Chichicastenango cofradía festivals
Garland Encyclopedia of World Music vol. 2, 'Guatemala'

items.name: Son q'eqchi' (Maya harp, violin and guitar)
items.lineage: String-band music of the Q'eqchi' Maya of Alta Verapaz, Guatemala, and of the Maya communities of Toledo District in southern Belize, where a diatonic harp, a violin and often a guitar play short repeated sones for saints' feasts, ceremonies and dances. The Belizean harpist Florencio Mess recorded the repertoire for Stonetree Records. The floor-harp card stands in for the Maya harp.
items.description: A diatonic harp plays a repeating bass-and-melody figure while a violin doubles the tune in a thin, slightly rough tone over a strummed guitar, short sections cycling over and over.
exemplars: Florencio Mess, Q'eqchi' harp, violin and guitar recordings (Stonetree Records)
Field recordings of Q'eqchi' harp ensembles in Alta Verapaz and Toledo District

items.name: Brukdown (Belizean Kriol boom-and-chime)
items.lineage: Kriol dance music of Belize, which grew from the music of the nineteenth-century logging camps and is played at house parties and Christmas festivities with accordion, banjo, guitar, drum and a donkey jawbone scraped with a stick, under teasing topical songs in Kriol. Its best-known exponent, the accordionist Wilfred Peters, led Mr. Peters' Boom and Chime, recorded by Stonetree Records.
items.description: A pumping button accordion and plucked banjo play bouncy, repeating dance tunes over strummed guitar, a thumping drum and the rattling rasp of a scraped jawbone, with a lead voice singing playful verses.
exemplars: Mr. Peters' Boom and Chime (Wilfred Peters), Stonetree Records

items.name: Chanchona (eastern Salvadoran string band)
items.lineage: String-band dance music of eastern El Salvador, around San Miguel and La Unión, named after the double bass (the chanchona, 'big sow') at its core, which joins one or two violins, guitar and percussion to play cumbias, rancheras and other dances for village fiestas. Los Hermanos Lovo carried the style to Salvadoran communities in the United States. The upright-bass card stands in for the plucked chanchona.
items.description: Two violins play the tune in sweet, slightly rough thirds over a thumping plucked double bass, strummed guitar, conga and scraper in a bouncing cumbia beat, with a lead voice.
exemplars: Los Hermanos Lovo recordings and performances

items.name: Xuc (Salvadoran dance-band genre)
items.lineage: Salvadoran dance genre created in the 1940s by the bandleader and composer Francisco 'Paquito' Palaviccini, whose Orquesta Internacional Polío recorded it with a dance-band line-up of trumpets, saxophones, trombones, piano, bass and drums. His 'El carnaval de San Miguel' tied the xuc to the carnival of San Miguel, and it is often described as El Salvador's national dance.
items.description: A brass-and-reed dance band punches out bright unison riffs and answering sax lines over a light, bouncing duple beat from piano, bass and drums, in festive, march-like dance pieces.
exemplars: Paquito Palaviccini y su Orquesta Internacional Polío recordings

items.name: El Güegüense (Diriamba dance-drama sones)
items.lineage: Music of El Güegüense, also called Macho Ratón, a satirical colonial-era dance-drama in a mixture of Spanish and Nahuatl performed in Diriamba, Carazo, Nicaragua, during the January fiestas of San Sebastián, and recognised by UNESCO as Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity. Its masked dancers move to a cycle of short sones played on violin, a small flute (pito) and a drum. The flute card stands in for the pito.
items.description: A scratchy violin and a shrill little flute play short, repeating dance tunes in unison over a steady drum, each son cycling while masked dancers parade and banter.
exemplars: Field recordings of the Güegüense sones at the San Sebastián fiestas of Diriamba

items.name: Palo de Mayo (Bluefields Creole maypole music)
items.lineage: Palo de Mayo is the maypole dance music of the Afro-Caribbean Creole communities of Nicaragua's southern Caribbean coast, centred on Bluefields, where the month-long Mayo Ya! festival in May celebrates the decorated maypole tree with dancing and street parades; it grew from British May Day maypole customs taken up and transformed by Creole song and dance. Its songs, sung largely in Creole English by a leader with an answering chorus, were carried to national popularity by Caribbean-coast bands such as Dimensión Costeña with electric guitar, bass, keyboards and drum kit.
items.description: A fast, hip-swinging duple groove on drum kit and bass carries bright electric guitar and keyboard riffs, while short sung calls are answered by a chorus and repeated until the dancers tire.
exemplars: Dimensión Costeña recordings of Palo de Mayo songs
Recordings of Bluefields Palo de Mayo bands and the Mayo Ya! festival

items.name: Son nica (Nicaraguan son)
items.lineage: Son nica is the Nicaraguan popular song genre created by the composer Camilo Zapata, regarded as its father, and developed by composers such as Víctor M. Leiva, drawing on the rural sones and marimba dances of the Pacific region in a lilting triple metre. Its songs portray country life, local places and national pride and are sung with guitars and marimba; Carlos Mejía Godoy's recordings later carried its rhythms into Nicaraguan national song.
items.description: A warm voice sings strophic verses over strummed nylon-string guitars and a rippling wooden marimba, the lilting triple pulse shifting its accents between groups of two and three.
exemplars: Camilo Zapata son nica compositions and their recordings

items.name: Marimba de arco (Masaya marimba-and-guitar trio)
items.lineage: The marimba de arco is the small diatonic marimba of Nicaragua's Pacific region, named for the wooden arc fixed to its frame and centred on the Indigenous barrio of Monimbó in Masaya. It is played in a trio with a guitar and a guitarrilla, a small guitar, for festive dances such as the baile de la marimba, also called the baile de las inditas. The Central American marimba card stands in for the marimba de arco and the requinto card for the guitarrilla.
items.description: A small wooden marimba plays a bright, rolling diatonic melody with quick repeated-note figures over the chopped strum of a guitar and a higher small guitar, in a lilting dance pulse.
exemplars: Monimbó (Masaya) marimba de arco trio recordings, commercial and field

items.name: Música segoviana (northern Nicaraguan mazurka and polka)
items.lineage: Música segoviana is the rural dance music of Las Segovias, the northern highlands of Nicaragua around Estelí, Nueva Segovia, Madriz and Jinotega, where the European mazurka and polka, arriving in the nineteenth century, became campesino dance music. A violin leads the tunes over guitar accompaniment in long instrumental sets for village dances, and string groups of the region have recorded the repertoire.
items.description: A bright, slightly rough violin plays lilting three-beat mazurkas and brisk two-beat polkas over strummed guitar chords with a thumbed bass line, each tune repeated in sections for dancing.
exemplars: Los Soñadores de Saraguasca (Jinotega) recordings of mazurcas and polkas
Recordings of northern Nicaraguan violin-and-guitar música campesina groups

items.name: Calipso limonense (Costa Rican Caribbean calypso)
items.lineage: Calipso limonense is the calypso of the Afro-Caribbean community of Costa Rica's Limón province, descendants of Jamaican and other West Indian workers who came from the late nineteenth century to build the railway and work the banana plantations. Its songs, in Limón Creole English, comment with wit on local life and are sung to guitar with light percussion; Walter 'Gavitt' Ferguson of Cahuita is its best-known singer-composer, and the genre has been declared part of Costa Rica's cultural heritage.
items.description: A relaxed, conversational voice tells witty stories over a strummed acoustic guitar in a swinging two-beat rhythm, with a light shaker keeping the pulse.

items.name: Música guanacasteca (Guanacaste marimba dance music)
items.lineage: The folk dance music of Guanacaste, Costa Rica's northwestern province around Liberia, Santa Cruz and Nicoya, which shares much with neighbouring Nicaragua: the punto guanacasteco, honoured as Costa Rica's national dance, and the tambito and parrandera dance tunes, played on the diatonic marimba with guitars. Dances pause for bombas, humorous rhymed verses called out by a dancer when the music stops. The Central American marimba card stands in for the Guanacaste marimba.
items.description: A wooden marimba drives a bright, lilting tune in quick triple time over strummed guitars, stopping short for a shouted rhymed verse before the dance resumes.
exemplars: Guanacaste marimba recordings on Costa Rican folkloric LPs

items.name: Congo (Afro-Panamanian Costa Arriba drum-song)
items.lineage: Congo is the drum-song and dance-drama tradition of the Afro-Panamanian communities of the Costa Arriba of Colón, centred on Portobelo, whose people descend from enslaved and maroon Africans. In the Carnival season Congo groups re-enact the struggle against slavery in plays with devil figures (diablos), while women lead the songs in call-and-response with a chorus over drums and hand-clapping. UNESCO has inscribed the ritual and festive expressions of the Congo culture on its Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage. The membrane-drum and hand-drum cards stand in for the Congo drums.
items.description: Hard-struck hand drums lock into a fast, insistent pattern while a strong lead voice throws out short calls answered by a clapping chorus, the cycle repeating as the dancers spin.
exemplars: Field recordings of Congo drumming and song from Portobelo

items.name: Gammu burwi (Guna panpipes and chant)
items.lineage: Music of the Guna (Kuna) people of Guna Yala, Panama's Caribbean coast and island territory. Men play gammu burwi, panpipes whose notes are divided between paired players who interlock them, while dancing in a line with women who shake rattles; alongside the pipes stand the long ritual chants (ikar) of curing specialists and the chanting of chiefs in the gathering house. Folkways issued Cuna recordings on 'Music of the Indians of Panama', and Joel Sherzer and Sandra Smith have studied the chanting and the panpipes. The bamboo-flute card stands in for the gammu burwi.
items.description: Breathy cane panpipes split between paired players weave one interlocking line of short repeating phrases over the dry swish of rattles, beside long solo chants delivered in a steady recitative.
exemplars: Folkways FE 4326, Music of the Indians of Panama: The Cuna (Tule) and Choco (Embera) Tribes

items.name: Queh-queh (Afro-Guyanese wedding ring-play)
items.lineage: Queh-queh is the Afro-Guyanese pre-wedding celebration held on the night before a marriage, in which family and neighbours form a ring to sing and dance play songs, many of them bawdy and meant to prepare the couple, in call-and-response over drumming and hand-clapping. Of African origin, it is documented by Vibert C. Cambridge in 'Musical Life in Guyana'. The hand-drum card stands in for the drums.
items.description: A lead singer lines out short teasing verses that the ring answers in full-throated chorus, over a hand drum and brisk hand-clapping that quicken as dancers step into the centre.
exemplars: Field and commercial recordings of Guyanese queh-queh songs
Queh-queh documented in Vibert C. Cambridge, Musical Life in Guyana (University Press of Mississippi, 2015)

items.name: Masquerade (Guyanese Christmas fife-and-drum bands)
items.lineage: Masquerade bands are the Christmas street bands of Georgetown and other Guyanese towns and villages, in which a flute or fife leads over the kettle drum, a snare-type side drum, and the big bass drum, while dancers called flouncers spin and costumed characters, among them the stilt-walking Mother Sally, perform for coins. Rooted in the Christmas festivities of the enslaved, it is documented by Vibert C. Cambridge in 'Musical Life in Guyana'.
items.description: A shrill fife skirls a short repeating tune over the crisp rattle of a snare and the heavy thump of a bass drum, in a fast swaying two-beat that drives the spinning street dancers.
exemplars: Field recordings of Georgetown Christmas masquerade bands

items.name: Comfa (Afro-Guyanese spirit-manifestation drumming)
items.lineage: Comfa, also spelled cumfa or komfa, is an Afro-Guyanese religious practice in which drumming, singing and dancing bring on the manifestation of spirits of the dead, including spirits associated with Guyana's different peoples, who then counsel and heal those present. Ceremonies combine hymn-like songs with drum-driven spirit songs; Kean Gibson's 'Comfa Religion and Creole Language in a Caribbean Community' is its main study. The membrane-drum card stands in for the Comfa drums.
items.description: A steady, insistent drum pattern builds under a leader's sung lines and the gathering's answering chorus, intensifying until dancers are seized by the spirit.
exemplars: Comfa ceremonies documented in Kean Gibson, Comfa Religion and Creole Language in a Caribbean Community (SUNY Press, 2001)

items.name: Shanto (Guyanese topical song)
items.lineage: Shanto is a Guyanese topical song form related to calypso, popularised by Bill Rogers (Augustus Hinds), known as the King of Shanto, whose humorous songs in Guyanese Creole commented on Georgetown life, politics and customs. Vibert C. Cambridge's 'Musical Life in Guyana' traces the genre.
items.description: A wry, half-spoken voice delivers verse after verse of topical storytelling over a steadily strummed guitar in a jaunty two-beat, each stanza landing on its punchline.

items.name: Chowtal (Indo-Caribbean Phagwah group song)
items.lineage: Chowtal is the springtime group song of the Phagwah (Holi) festival among Hindus of Guyana, Trinidad and Suriname, brought by Bhojpuri-speaking indentured labourers from north India in the nineteenth century. Two rows of men sit facing each other and alternate the verses of devotional and seasonal songs, many about Krishna and Rama, over the dholak and large jhanjh cymbals, the tempo and volume rising to a climax. Peter Manuel documents it in 'East Indian Music in the West Indies'. The manjira card, set to its jhanj form, stands for the jhanjh.
items.description: Two groups of male voices hurl alternating lines at each other over a pounding barrel drum and crashing brass cymbals, the tempo and volume surging to a frenzied peak before dropping back for the next song.
exemplars: Field recordings of Phagwah chowtal groups discussed in Peter Manuel, East Indian Music in the West Indies (2000)

items.name: Winti prei (Afro-Surinamese spirit-dance ceremony)
items.lineage: Winti prei ('winti play') is the ceremonial music of Winti, the Afro-Surinamese Creole religion, in which drumming and song call the winti spirits to possess dancers, each class of spirit having its own rhythms and songs. The apinti talking drum leads a set of hand drums under a song leader and responding chorus; Charles Wooding's study of Winti documents the practice. The membrane-drum card stands in for the other winti drums.
items.description: A high, speaking lead drum talks over interlocking hand drums while a song leader's calls are answered by a chorus, the rhythms shifting as each spirit is called.
exemplars: Field recordings of winti prei ceremonies from Paramaribo
Winti ceremonies documented in Charles Wooding's study of Afro-Surinamese Winti religion

items.name: Saramaka Maroon song and drumming
items.lineage: Music of the Saramaka, a Maroon people of the upper Suriname River descended from Africans who escaped plantation slavery and won their freedom by treaty in the eighteenth century. Its genres include sêkêti, topical dance songs sung in call-and-response with hand-clapping, and the drumming and papá songs of funeral and ancestral rites, with the apinti talking drum among other hand drums. Richard and Sally Price recorded it for the Folkways album 'Music from Saramaka: A Dynamic Afro-American Tradition'. The membrane-drum card stands in for the other Saramaka drums.
items.description: Light, swinging songs traded between a leader and a clapping chorus alternate with drum pieces in which a high talking drum plays against deeper hand drums.
exemplars: Folkways FE 4225, Music from Saramaka: A Dynamic Afro-American Tradition (Richard and Sally Price, 1977)

items.name: Pop Jawa (Surinamese Javanese pop)
items.lineage: Pop Jawa is the popular song of the Javanese community of Suriname, descendants of contract labourers brought from Java under Dutch colonial rule from 1890, who also brought gamelan. Sung in Javanese over Western band instruments, it is popular among Javanese-Surinamese audiences in Suriname and the Netherlands.
items.description: A smooth, lightly ornamented voice sings sentimental melodies over clean electric guitar, keyboard pads, bass and a gently swaying drum-kit groove.
exemplars: Javanese-Surinamese pop Jawa recordings from Paramaribo
Pop Jawa recordings of the Javanese-Surinamese community in the Netherlands

items.name: Kasékò (French Guianese Creole drum-dance)
items.lineage: Kasékò is the principal Creole drum-dance genre of French Guiana, centred on Cayenne. A long drum laid on the ground is played with the hands while sticks (tibwa) beat on wood and shakers (chacha) keep the pulse, under a lead singer answered by a chorus of dancers. It shares its name, usually glossed from French 'casser le corps', with the Surinamese kaseko band genre but is a distinct drum-and-song form. The membrane-drum card stands in for the kasékò drum and the palitos card for the tibwa.
items.description: A deep hand-played drum pounds a fast, syncopated cycle against dry sticks clacking on wood and shaken rattles, while a lead singer's calls draw the dancers' chorus into reply.
exemplars: Guianese Creole kasékò drum-group recordings from Cayenne

items.name: Ìyẹ̀rẹ̀ Ifá (Yoruba Ifá divination chant)
items.lineage: Chanted poetry of the Yoruba Ifá divination system, in which babaláwo priests memorise the ẹsẹ verses attached to the 256 odù signs and recite them at consultations, initiations and festivals. Verses are delivered both in speech-like recitation and in ìyẹ̀rẹ̀, a sung chant mode in which other priests join in chorus. UNESCO proclaimed the Ifá divination system a Masterpiece of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity and later inscribed it on the Representative List.
items.description: A lead priest moves between rapid recitation and an elevated, sustained chant whose melody follows the rise and fall of the tonal language, with a unison chorus of voices taking up his lines, largely without instruments.
exemplars: UNESCO documentation of the Ifá divination system (proclaimed 2005, inscribed 2008)
Field recordings of babaláwo ìyẹ̀rẹ̀ Ifá chant
