items.name: Ìlù bàtá (Yoruba bàtá drumming for Ṣàngó)
items.lineage: Drumming and song of the Yoruba bàtá ensemble, the drum family sacred to Ṣàngó, the orìṣà of thunder and deified king of Ọ̀yọ́, and also played for Egúngún masquerades. A set of conical double-headed bàtá drums led by the ìyá ìlù mother drum renders praise texts in drum speech alongside sung praise for the orìṣà. William Bascom's field recordings of Yoruba drumming, made around 1951, were issued on the Folkways LP Drums of the Yoruba of Nigeria. The bata card stands in for the Nigerian bàtá set.
items.description: Sharp, dry slaps and muffled strokes from conical double-headed drums of graded sizes interlock in dense patterns, the lead drum breaking into speech-like phrases while voices answer one another in praise song.
exemplars: Drums of the Yoruba of Nigeria (Folkways FE 4441, recorded by William Bascom)

items.name: Ìjálá (Yoruba hunters' chant)
items.lineage: Chanted poetry of Yoruba hunters, devotees of Ògún the deity of iron, performed at hunters' gatherings, Ògún festivals and social ceremonies, and studied by S. A. Babalola in The Content and Form of Yoruba Ijala. Chanters such as Ogundare Foyanmu and Alabi Ogundepo later issued ìjálá on commercial LPs and cassettes, often with talking-drum accompaniment. The dùndún card stands in for the accompanying talking drums.
items.description: A solo chanter declaims long breath-phrases, the melody shaped by speech tones and broken by quick asides, while talking drums answer and fill between lines.

items.name: Ewì (Yoruba recorded poetry)
items.lineage: Modern Yoruba poetic genre in which an akéwì poet declaims moral, topical and praise verse for radio, television and records, usually over percussion accompaniment. A leading exponent, Olanrewaju Adepoju, released about a hundred LP, cassette and CD albums. The dùndún card stands in for the accompanying talking drums.
items.description: A single poet's voice declaims in measured, rhythmic speech that lifts into half-sung phrases, set against a light bed of talking drum that punctuates the ends of lines.

items.name: Wákà (Yoruba Muslim women's song)
items.lineage: Yoruba song genre that grew from the songs of Muslim women at religious and social occasions and became a commercial popular music on record. Alhaja Batile Alake was among its first recording stars, and Salawa Abeni's 1976 debut LP became the first million-selling record by a Yoruba woman singer. The dùndún card stands in for the talking drums of wákà bands.
items.description: An ornamented female lead voice trades lines with a women's chorus over talking drums and gourd rattle, the percussion settling into a steady, rolling dance pulse.

items.name: Dadakúàdà (Ilorin oral-poetry music)
items.lineage: Oral-poetry music of the Yoruba of Ilorin in Kwara State, in which a lead chanter delivers praise, history and social commentary answered by a chorus and talking drums. Its best-known exponent, Odolaye Aremu, recorded more than two dozen albums between 1977 and 1990. The dùndún card stands in for the Ilorin talking-drum group.
items.description: A strong, slightly rough lead voice chants long praise and commentary lines in speech rhythm, answered by a short choral refrain and by talking drums that echo and comment on the words.

items.name: Aṣíkò (Lagos frame-drum dance music)
items.lineage: Dance music associated with Christian Yoruba communities in early twentieth-century Lagos, played on frame drums with group singing, which Christopher Waterman identifies in Jùjú: A Social History and Ethnography of an African Popular Music (1990) as one of the precursors of jùjú. It was recorded on 78 rpm discs from the 1930s to the 1950s. The frame-drums card stands in for the aṣíkò drums.
items.description: Hand-struck frame drums of several sizes lock into a brisk, cycling dance rhythm under group singing, heard through the narrow band and surface noise of early shellac discs.
exemplars: Lagos 78 rpm recordings of aṣíkò groups (1930s to 1950s)

items.name: Bòòríí (Hausa spirit-possession music)
items.lineage: Music of the bòòríí spirit-possession cult of the Hausa of northern Nigeria and Niger, in which each spirit has its own praise epithets and instrumental motifs that call it to mount a devotee, its "horse". Musicians play either the two-string garaya lute with gourd rattles or the one-string gòge fiddle with calabash idiophones. Fremont Besmer documented the cult in Kano in his book Horses, Musicians, and Gods: The Hausa Cult of Possession-Trance. The inverted-calabash card stands in for the calabash idiophones.
items.description: A buzzing plucked lute or a rasping one-string fiddle repeats short, insistent motifs over pounded calabash and rattles, while praise singers call out epithets and the cycle intensifies toward trance.
exemplars: Kano bòòríí music documented by Fremont Besmer in Horses, Musicians, and Gods (1983)

items.name: Gòge (Hausa fiddle dance music)
items.lineage: Hausa dance and praise music led by the gòge one-string bowed fiddle with a calabash body and skin face, played for social dancing and entertainment as well as in bòòríí possession rites. Garba Liyo and Audu Yaron Goge were among its best-known recording artists, and Smithsonian Folkways issued Alhaji Garbo Leao and His Goge Music. The goje card stands in for the gòge and the inverted-calabash card for the calabash idiophones.
items.description: A nasal, rasping fiddle line weaves ornamented melody around a singer's praise verses and a chorus refrain, over a dry, driving beat struck on calabashes.
exemplars: Alhaji Garbo Leao and His Goge Music (Smithsonian Folkways)

items.name: Bandiri (Hausa Sufi drum-chant)
items.lineage: Devotional drum-chant of Qadiriyya Sufi adherents in Kano, in which male singers praise the Prophet Muhammad and Sufi saints in Hausa over bandiri frame drums. Brian Larkin showed that many bandiri songs set new devotional texts to melodies borrowed from Hindi film songs, circulated on cassettes and video CDs in the Kano market. The frame-drums card stands in for the bandiri.
items.description: A lead singer's tuneful devotional melody is answered by a massed male chorus over the steady, booming pulse of several hand-struck frame drums.
exemplars: Kano cassette and video CD recordings of Qadiriyya bandiri groups

items.name: Egwu ekpili (Igbo story-song)
items.lineage: Igbo story-song tradition of Anambra, also called akụkọ na egwu ("story and song"), named after the ekpili rattles, in which a lead singer narrates folktales, moral lessons and the praise of patrons. Morocco Maduka recorded more than 120 albums and Akunwafor Ezeagu was another leading exponent. The shaker card stands in for the ekpili rattles.
items.description: A lead singer half-speaks, half-sings a long narrative over shaken rattles and the bright, clanging timeline of an iron gong, with a chorus coming in on short refrains.

items.name: Swange (Tiv dance music)
items.lineage: Urban recreational dance music of the Tiv of Benue State, central Nigeria, in which men and women dance together in the circle formation of village dances, and traditional musical themes are adapted to highlife rhythms played on a combination of Tiv and Hausa instruments. A traditional horn is often sounded continuously over the drumming, singing and dancing, and swange spread on commercial cassettes. The membrane-drum card stands in for the drums and the horns card for the horn.
items.description: Drums play highlife-inflected dance rhythms in a steady cycle while a horn sounds over them almost without a break and singers carry the dance song above.
exemplars: Commercial cassette recordings of Tiv swange bands

items.name: Owigiri (Ijaw highlife dance music)
items.lineage: Popular dance music of the Ijaw (Izon) of the Niger Delta, a sub-genre of highlife sung in Izon. A study in the NISC journal examines how owigiri artists such as Robert Ebizimor and Barrister Smooth express Ijo identity through language, local occupations, wrestling, myth, dance styles and dress.
items.description: Bright, interlocking electric guitar lines ride a busy hand-drum groove, while a lead singer and chorus trade lines in a steady, danceable cycle.

items.name: African pianism (Nigerian art-music piano school)
items.lineage: Piano music by Nigerian composers in the idiom Akin Euba named African pianism, which treats the piano percussively and draws on the repeated patterns and themes of African traditional music, especially drumming, within the Nigerian art-music tradition pioneered by Fela Sowande. Its Nigerian exponents include Akin Euba and Ayo Bankole, and SOMM Recordings' African Pianism series collects such works.
items.description: A solo concert piano sets percussive, repeating figures against crossing rhythmic patterns and melodies drawn from traditional song, cleanly recorded in a concert acoustic.

items.name: Street-pop (Lagos street-hop)
items.lineage: Nigerian popular style that grew in Lagos in the 2010s, rapped and sung in Yoruba, Pidgin and street slang over Afrobeats-derived programmed beats. It is associated with Olamide and his YBNL label, Naira Marley's Marlian Music and Zlatan, and fed the shaku shaku and zanku dance crazes of the late 2010s.
items.description: Raw, chanted rap hooks and shouted ad-libs ride a hard, looping programmed groove of crisp percussion and deep sub-bass, built for dance-floor call-and-response.

items.name: Gẹ̀lẹ̀dẹ́ (Yoruba masquerade song and drumming)
items.lineage: Song and drumming of the Gẹ̀lẹ̀dẹ́ masquerade of the western Yoruba around Kétou and neighbouring communities in Benin, Nigeria and Togo, staged to honour the mothers, female elders and ancestral powers, with masked dancers moving to drum patterns and to songs of praise and satire. UNESCO proclaimed the Oral Heritage of Gelede a Masterpiece of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity and later inscribed it on the Representative List. The membrane-drum card stands in for the Gẹ̀lẹ̀dẹ́ drums and the agogo card for the iron bell.
items.description: A drum ensemble of graded sizes drives layered dance patterns under a ringing iron-bell timeline, while a lead singer and chorus exchange praise and mocking song lines.
exemplars: Field recordings of Gẹ̀lẹ̀dẹ́ songs from the Kétou area
UNESCO documentation of the Oral Heritage of Gelede

items.name: Vodun ceremonial music (Fon of southern Benin)
items.lineage: Ceremonial drumming and song of vodun worship among the Fon and neighbouring Gbe-speaking peoples of southern Benin, centred on the former Dahomey capital Abomey and the coastal town of Ouidah, where each vodun deity has its own rhythms, songs and dances performed by initiates. Ensembles of drums with an iron double bell and gourd rattles accompany call-and-response singing. The membrane-drum card stands in for the vodun drums and the agogo card for the iron bell.
items.description: Drums of graded sizes interlock over a ringing iron double-bell pattern and shaken rattles, the lead drum improvising against the cycle while a lead singer and chorus of initiates call and answer.
exemplars: Ocora field recordings of vodun ceremonial music from Benin

items.name: Zinli (Fon funeral music of Abomey)
items.lineage: Funeral music of the Fon of Abomey in southern Benin, also written zilin, associated in tradition with the court of the Danxomè kings and still played at funerals. Its characteristic percussion is the kpezin, played with iron gongs, rattles and handclaps beneath songs and dance; Alèkpéhanhou of Abomey, called the king of zinli, has recorded more than thirty albums of it. A generic percussion card stands in for the kpezin and a generic bell card for the gongs.
items.description: A lead voice and answering chorus sing long, grave lines over a steady bed of deep percussion strokes, ringing iron-gong patterns, rattles and handclaps.

items.name: Tchinkoumé (Stan Tohon's tchink system, Savalou)
items.lineage: A traditional rhythm of Savalou, in the Mahi country of central Benin, modernised by Stan Tohon as the "tchink système", which set the rhythm and its hand percussion beneath an electric dance band of guitar, bass and drum kit. Tohon recorded it on many albums.
items.description: Electric guitar and bass lock with drum kit and hand drums in an insistent dance groove, under a lead singer answered by chorus.
exemplars: Stan Tohon recordings with his Tchink System band

items.name: Kabiyè soo orchestras and lithophones (Kara)
items.lineage: Music of the Kabiyè of the Kara region of northern Togo: soo orchestras of drums and other percussion with flutes, whistles and trumpets, and the rare pichanchalassi lithophones of struck stones, played for entertainment and at the initiation rites of young men, including the evala wrestling contests held each July. A generic percussion card stands in for the stones, a generic membrane-drum card for the drums and a generic flute card for the flutes and whistles.
items.description: Ringing strokes on struck stones, drums and percussion repeat short, locked patterns, cut through by flutes and whistles, beneath group singing and shouts.
exemplars: 'Togo: Kabiyè Orchestras and Lithophones' (Ocora / Radio France, 2013)
'Togo: musique kabiyè' (Ocora; field recordings by Raymond Verdier and Anne-Marie de Lavilléon)

items.name: Adowa (Akan funeral dance music)
items.lineage: Funeral and celebratory dance music of the Akan, most associated with Asante around Kumasi and documented by J. H. Kwabena Nketia. A lead singer and women's chorus alternate with an ensemble of atumpan talking drums, petia and apentemma hand drums, a donno hourglass drum and the dawuro iron bell, the dancers' gestures answering the drum language; a generic bell card stands in for the dawuro.
items.description: A lead singer and women's chorus trade lines over a lilting ensemble of paired talking drums, hand drums, a pitch-bending hourglass drum and a ringing iron-bell timeline.
exemplars: J. H. Kwabena Nketia, 'Drumming in Akan Communities of Ghana' (1963)
Royal Museum for Central Africa (Tervuren) documentation of the Asante adowa ensemble

items.name: Fontomfrom (Asante state drum orchestra)
items.lineage: Court drum orchestra of the Asante and other Akan states, played for the Asantehene and paramount chiefs at durbars, festivals and royal funerals. A pair of tall fontomfrom drums leads atumpan talking drums, petia and other supporting drums and the dawuro bell in dance pieces and drummed praises; a generic card stands in for the bell.
items.description: Massive, booming strokes from a pair of tall drums lead talking drums and supporting drums in powerful, speech-shaped phrases over a ringing bell, building to thunderous ceremonial climaxes.
exemplars: J. H. Kwabena Nketia, 'Drumming in Akan Communities of Ghana' (1963), which documents the fontomfrom ensemble

items.name: Nnwonkoro (Akan women's song)
items.lineage: Recreational song genre of Akan women, studied by Kwasi Ampene in the book 'Female Song Tradition and the Akan of Ghana: The Creative Process in Nnwonkoro', which comes with a CD. A lead singer and a women's chorus sing in call and response, accompanied by handclaps and small idiophones; generic bell and rattle cards stand in for them.
items.description: A woman cantor leads and a women's chorus answers in close harmony, over crisp handclaps and the light tapping of a bell and rattle.
exemplars: CD accompanying Kwasi Ampene, 'Female Song Tradition and the Akan of Ghana' (Ashgate, 2005)

items.name: Seperewa song (Akan harp-lute song)
items.lineage: Song accompanied on the seperewa, the Akan harp-lute of Ghana, an older court and social instrument whose role was largely taken over by the guitar in the 20th century. Osei Korankye is its best-known modern player and recording artist.
items.description: A solo voice sings over bright, interlocking plucked ostinatos on a harp-lute, its strings ringing in short repeating cycles between the sung lines.

items.name: Asafo (Fante warrior-company music)
items.lineage: Music of the asafo, the patrilineal warrior companies of Fante coastal towns such as Anomabu, Cape Coast and Elmina, which once served as town militias and now turn out for festivals, funerals and installations. Company members sing asafo songs in call and response over drums and iron bells; generic cards stand in for the company drums and bells.
items.description: Massed voices shout and sing defiant call-and-response songs over pounding drums and sharp iron-bell patterns, rising to a forceful processional intensity.
exemplars: Field recordings of Fante asafo company songs and drumming (Cape Coast, Anomabu)

items.name: Agbadza (Ewe social dance-drumming)
items.lineage: Recreational dance-drumming of the Ewe of south-eastern Ghana and Togo, a slower social form of the old war dance atrikpui, played at funerals and community occasions. The gankogui double bell and axatse rattles carry the timeline, kagan and kidi answer, the sogo leads in drum language, and the group sings call-and-response songs. David Locke and Gideon Foli Alorwoyie published its songs and drum language with recordings.
items.description: A twelve-pulse iron-bell timeline and shaken rattles anchor interlocking response drums while a lead barrel drum calls phrases and a chorus answers the song leader.
exemplars: Gideon Foli Alorwoyie and David Locke, 'Agbadza: Songs, Drum Language of the Ewes' (with companion recordings)

items.name: Atsiagbekor (Ewe war-dance drumming)
items.lineage: War dance of the Anlo-Ewe of south-eastern Ghana, also called agbekor, now performed at festivals, funerals and by cultural troupes. The atsimevu master drum cues the dancers' formations over sogo, kidi and kagan, the gankogui bell and axatse rattles, with songs of war and history. David Locke's study 'The Music of Atsiagbekor' transcribed its drumming.
items.description: A tall master drum calls sharp, speech-like commands over dense interlocking support drums, a twelve-pulse double-bell timeline and rattles, with a vigorous sung chorus.
exemplars: David Locke's recordings and transcriptions of Atsiagbekor

items.name: Gahu (Ewe recreational dance-drumming)
items.lineage: Recreational dance music that reached the Anlo-Ewe of Ghana from the Gun (Egun) people of the Benin–Nigeria coast in the mid-20th century, danced by clubs and cultural groups. The gankogui bell and axatse lay a four-beat timeline under the large boba (gboba) lead drum with sogo, kidi and kagan, and call-and-response songs. David Locke's 'Drum Gahu' documents it with recordings.
items.description: A buoyant four-beat bell pattern and rattles drive a deep lead drum and interlocking supporting drums under cheerful call-and-response singing.

items.name: Borborbor (northern Ewe neo-traditional dance music, Kpando)
items.lineage: Neo-traditional recreational music of the northern Ewe that emerged around Kpando in the Volta Region in the mid-20th century, its creation credited to the bandleader F. C. Nuatro, and spread through Ewe towns as music for social occasions. Groups sing call-and-response songs over a set of drums, iron bells and rattles; generic drum cards stand in for the borborbor drums.
items.description: Lilting, mid-tempo group songs in call and response ride over a rolling drum ensemble, ringing double bells and rattles in a steady dance groove.
exemplars: Tufts University Digital Library recordings of borborbor bands

items.name: Adzogbo (Ewe dance-drumming of Fon origin)
items.lineage: Dance-drumming of Fon origin in present-day Benin, taken up by the Ewe of Ghana and Togo; once a spiritual dance, it is now performed with a men's warrior section and a women's section, led by a master drum whose phrases cue the dancers. The Ewe atsimevu, sogo, kidi, kagan, gankogui and axatse cards stand in for its ensemble.
items.description: Fast, intricate exchanges between a master drum and interlocking support drums, over iron-bell and rattle timelines, punctuate energetic dancing and group song.
exemplars: C. K. Ladzekpo's documentation of Adzogbo (Adzohu) dance-drumming

items.name: Yeve (Ewe thunder-cult ritual music)
items.lineage: Ritual music of Yeve, the Ewe vodu society devoted to the thunder deity Xebieso (So), centred in Anlo and other Ewe areas of Ghana and Togo. Its ceremonies run through a sequence of distinct dance-drumming pieces, among them sovu, sogba and husago, sung by initiates over drums, iron bells and rattles; the Ewe drum, bell and rattle cards stand in for the society's own set.
items.description: Initiates' call-and-response songs ride over a suite of contrasting drum rhythms, each set over its own iron-bell timeline and rattles, with a master drum leading the dancers.
exemplars: Yeve ritual music as documented in a University of Ghana thesis (UGSpace)

items.name: Kpanlogo (Ga recreational drum-dance, Accra)
items.lineage: Recreational music and dance created by Ga youth in the Bukom area of central Accra in the early 1960s and credited to Otoo Lincoln, drawing on older Ga rhythms and on highlife and rock and roll dancing. Groups of peg-tuned kpanlogo drums play under call-and-response songs with a bell, rattles and handclaps; generic cards stand in for the bell and rattle.
items.description: Bright, conversational hand-drum patterns interlock over a bell and shaker timeline while a song leader and chorus trade short lines in a buoyant dance groove.
exemplars: Recordings of Accra kpanlogo groups in the Bukom tradition of Otoo Lincoln

items.name: Gome (Ga box-drum dance music, Accra)
items.lineage: Ga music and dance of Accra built around the gome, a large wooden box-frame drum that the player sits on and re-pitches by pressing the head with his heels; it is traced to Ga workers returning from Fernando Po (Bioko). Call-and-response songs are accompanied by gome, bells, rattles and handclaps; generic cards stand in for the bell and rattle.
items.description: A deep, pitch-bending box drum thumps a rolling bass pattern under bells, rattles and handclaps, with a song leader answered by a chorus.
exemplars: Wulomei recordings featuring the gome drum

items.name: Dagara gyil funeral music (Lawra, Upper West)
items.lineage: Funeral music of the Dagara (Dagaaba) and neighbouring Lobi of Ghana's Upper West Region and adjoining Burkina Faso, played on the gyil, a pentatonic xylophone with gourd resonators whose membranes add a buzzing timbre. At funerals a pair of gyils plays with the kuor calabash drum alongside sung laments; the gyil also serves recreational dances such as bewaa. A generic membrane-drum card stands in for the kuor.
items.description: Two buzzing gourd-resonated xylophones interlock fast, rippling pentatonic patterns over a calabash drum, while singers raise wailing laments above them.
exemplars: 'Dagara – Gyil Music of Ghana's Upper West Region' (2021)

items.name: Gondze (Dagbamba one-string fiddle music)
items.lineage: Fiddle music of the Dagbamba (Dagomba) of northern Ghana, centred on Yendi and Tamale, played on the gondze (gonje), a one-string bowed spike fiddle of the Sahelian goje family. Groups of fiddlers perform for chiefs and at social occasions, singing over the fiddles with gourd-rattle accompaniment; a generic shaker card stands in for the rattles.
items.description: A rasping, nasal one-string fiddle line circles through short repeating melodic phrases, answered by further fiddles and by sung and responding voices, over a steady pulse of shaken gourd rattles.
exemplars: Master Fiddlers of Dagbon (Rounder; recorded and annotated by John Miller Chernoff)

items.name: Simpa (Dagbamba dance music, Tamale)
items.lineage: Simpa is a recreational drum-and-dance genre of Dagbamba youth in Tamale and the towns of Dagbon in northern Ghana, sung in Dagbani. Its digital form, made by small Tamale producers who sequence sampled drums in software to recreate the dance rhythms, circulated on locally released VCDs and radio; generic synthesis-sequencing and drum-machine cards stand in for the software set-up.
items.description: Programmed, sample-based recreations of the dance-drum patterns loop under bright synthesized lines and a lead singer, with short repeated phrases and answering vocal lines.
exemplars: Studio Simpa: Digital Dance Music on VCD from Dagbon, Northern Ghana (Autotune the World / Sahel Sounds; producer Mohamed 'Ebony' Fuseini)

items.name: Kasena music (jongo flute-and-drum dance)
items.lineage: Music of the Kasena (Kassena) people of the Ghana-Burkina Faso border around Navrongo, Paga and Po. The jongo (djongo) dance is accompanied by ensembles of flutes and drums with singing, a repertoire documented in field recordings of Kasena flute-and-drum ensembles; generic flute and drum cards stand in for the local instruments.
items.description: Several small flutes interlock in short hocketed figures over drum patterns, with call-and-response singing joining the cycle for the dance.
exemplars: James Koetting field recordings of Kasena flute-and-drum ensembles (Brown University Library)

items.name: Guitar-band highlife and concert party (Akan)
items.lineage: Akan branch of highlife from the Ashanti and Fante hinterland of Ghana, grown from palm-wine guitar playing and led by small guitar bands rather than brass dance orchestras. From the 1950s guitar bands were joined to the concert party, a travelling comic popular theatre in Akan languages whose shows are framed by band music; acoustic and later electric guitars, the box bass lamellophone and hand percussion make up the band, with a generic hand drum standing in for its drums.
items.description: Interlocking picked guitar lines over a plucked box-bass figure and light hand percussion carry relaxed Twi singing, with short repeated guitar cycles between verses.
exemplars: African Brothers International Band (Nana Kwame Ampadu)

items.name: Burger highlife (Ghanaian-German synth highlife)
items.lineage: Highlife made in the 1980s by Ghanaian migrant musicians in West Germany, above all in Hamburg, and carried back to Kumasi and Accra; the name, taken from Hamburg, became the Ghanaian slang borga for migrants returned from abroad. Synthesizers, drum machines and electric bass replaced the horn and guitar-band line-ups while Twi singing and highlife guitar figures stayed; generic synthesizer and drum-machine cards stand in for the varied gear.
items.description: Glossy synthesizer chords and a programmed drum-machine beat drive a mid-tempo highlife groove, with clean picked guitar figures, a busy electric bass and smooth Twi lead vocals.

items.name: Ghanaian choral art music (Amu school)
items.lineage: Choral art music founded by the composer Ephraim Amu, who set Twi and Ewe texts with rhythms and melodic contours shaped by speech tone and local song, and brought the atenteben bamboo flute into concert use; later Ghanaian composers carried the tradition on in church, school and choral-society singing. A generic bamboo-flute card stands in for the atenteben.
items.description: Mixed choir in clear four-part writing, with vowels and rhythms following the spoken tones of the texts; some pieces add a bamboo flute line.

items.name: Zaouli (Guro masked dance music)
items.lineage: Music and dance of the Guro communities of the Bouaflé and Zuénoula departments of central Côte d'Ivoire, inscribed on the UNESCO Representative List in 2017 and inspired by the Blou and Djela masks. A single masked dancer performs rapid footwork locked to an orchestra of drums and flutes, with songs; generic flute and drum cards stand in for the local instruments.
items.description: Fast, driving drum patterns and shrill flute calls lock to the masked dancer's rapid footwork, with singers adding short sung phrases over the cycle.
exemplars: UNESCO audiovisual documentation of zaouli (Representative List, 2017)
Zaouli de Manfla (village troupe, filmed performances)

items.name: Gbofe of Afounkaha (Tagbana transverse-horn music)
items.lineage: Music, song and dance of the Tagbana community of Afounkaha in central Côte d'Ivoire, proclaimed a UNESCO Masterpiece of the Oral and Intangible Heritage in 2001 and inscribed on the Representative List in 2008. Transverse horns of different sizes, covered with cowhide, sound phrases that a women's chorus translates into words, while drummers beat time; a generic horn card stands in for the gbofe horns and a generic drum for the drums.
items.description: Hoarse, speech-like horn phrases pass between horns of different sizes, answered by a women's chorus singing the words, over steady time-keeping drums.
exemplars: UNESCO audiovisual documentation of the Gbofe of Afounkaha (Masterpiece proclamation, 2001)

items.name: Dan mask music (Yacouba, western Côte d'Ivoire)
items.lineage: Music of the Dan (Yacouba) of the Man region of western Côte d'Ivoire and the neighbouring Liberian and Guinean borderlands, where masks appear at festivals, funerals and village events with their own songs, drumming and horn playing. The repertoire was documented in Hugo Zemp's 1960s field recordings held in the CNRS-Musée de l'Homme sound archive; generic drum and horn cards stand in for the local instruments.
items.description: Leader-and-chorus songs answer one another over layered drum patterns, with horn calls marking the appearance and dance of the masks.
exemplars: Hugo Zemp — The Music of the Dan (UNESCO Collection, Anthology of African Music)
Hugo Zemp's Dan field recordings in the CNRS-Musée de l'Homme sound archive (CREM)

items.name: Ziglibithy (Ivorian Bété dance pop)
items.lineage: Ivorian popular dance music created in the 1970s by the singer Ernesto Djédjé, who set rhythms of Bété dance music from the Daloa region on an electric band of guitars, bass, drum kit and hand percussion. Djédjé died in 1983; a generic hand drum stands in for the percussion.
items.description: Bright interlocking electric guitar lines and a pumping bass sit over a fast, syncopated dance rhythm on kit and hand drums, with a lead singer answered by a chorus.

items.name: Zoblazo (Ivorian Nzima dance pop)
items.lineage: Ivorian popular dance music launched by the singer Meiway with his 1989 album, drawing on the traditional music of the Appolo (Nzima) of the south-eastern coast around Grand-Bassam and played by an electric dance band with keyboards and percussion; dancers wave white handkerchiefs. A generic keyboard card stands in for the band's keyboards and a generic hand drum for its percussion.
items.description: Up-tempo festive dance groove of kit, hand drums and electric bass under bright keyboards and guitar, with a lead singer and answering chorus.

items.name: Senegalese Afro-Cuban dance-band music (Dakar salsa)
items.lineage: Dakar nightclub dance-band music of the 1960s to 1980s in which Senegalese and Gambian bands played Cuban son, pachanga and later salsa learned from imported GV-series 78s, singing in Spanish, Wolof and Mandinka. The bands brought griot vocal styles and Senegalese rhythms into the Cuban forms, preparing the ground for mbalax.
items.description: Clave-based son and salsa grooves on congas and timbales under looping electric guitar figures and saxophone lines, with ornamented lead vocals answered by a chorus.

items.name: Xassida (Mouride sung poetry, Touba)
items.lineage: Group chanting of the xassida (qasida), the Arabic devotional poems of Cheikh Ahmadou Bamba, founder of the Mouride Sufi order, by kurel groups of singers in Touba, at the Grand Magal pilgrimage and at religious gatherings across Senegal; the related zikr of the Baye Fall is folded into this entry. Performances circulate widely on cassette, radio and online.
items.description: Unaccompanied voices chant long Arabic verses in measured rhythm, a lead singer setting each phrase and the group answering in strong unison, with melismatic turns at line ends.
exemplars: Kurel xassida cassette and radio recordings from Touba

items.name: Taasu (Wolof declaimed poetry)
items.lineage: Wolof genre of rapid, rhythmically declaimed poetry performed chiefly by women at sabar dances, naming ceremonies and weddings in Dakar and across Senegal, delivered over sabar drumming and often cited as a forerunner of Senegalese rap.
items.description: A solo voice fires off rhymed lines in fast, tightly rhythmic speech over crackling sabar drum patterns and hand claps, with drummers and dancers answering its breaks.
exemplars: Aby Ngana Diop — 'Liital' (Awesome Tapes From Africa reissue)

items.name: Ekonting songs (Jola folk lute, Casamance)
items.lineage: Song tradition of the Jola of Casamance in southern Senegal and of the Gambia, accompanied by the ekonting (akonting), a three-string folk lute with a gourd body and skin top played with a downstroking technique and regarded as a relative of the banjo.
items.description: A repeating plucked lute pattern with a ringing drone string supports a singer, the short cyclic figure turning beneath each sung phrase.
exemplars: Ears of the People: Ekonting Songs from Senegal and the Gambia (Smithsonian Folkways, 2023)

items.name: Njuup (Serer song, Sine-Saloum)
items.lineage: Song tradition of the Serer of the Sine and Saloum regions of west-central Senegal, often led by women singers with a responding chorus, drumming and hand claps at wrestling matches, ceremonies and community gatherings; Senegalese musicians cite its rhythms as a source of mbalax. A generic drum card stands in for the Serer drums.
items.description: A strong female lead voice calls out ornamented lines answered by a chorus, over driving drum patterns and hand claps.
exemplars: Youssou N'Dour & Yandé Codou Sène — 'Gainde: Voices from the Heart of Africa' (1995)

items.name: Ndëpp (Lebu possession-healing ceremony)
items.lineage: Healing and possession ceremony of the Lebu and Wolof of the Cap-Vert peninsula around Rufisque and Dakar, led by officiants, most often women, to reconcile a patient with the rab ancestral spirits through drumming, sung invocations and dancing over several days. The mbung mbung card stands for the sabar-family drums used in the rite.
items.description: Insistent sabar-family drum patterns build in intensity under a lead singer and answering group, with hand claps driving the dance toward trance.
exemplars: Ethnographic recordings of ndëpp ceremonies of the Lebu of Rufisque and Dakar

items.name: Kankurang (Mandinka initiation masquerade)
items.lineage: Masquerade rite of the Mandinka of Casamance and the Gambia, also kept in Mbour and other Senegalese towns, proclaimed a UNESCO Masterpiece in 2005 and inscribed on the Representative List in 2008 as the Kankurang, Manding initiatory rite (Senegal and Gambia). The kankurang, a masked figure covered in tree-bark fibre, appears during the circumcision and initiation of boys and is escorted through the streets by drummers and a chanting crowd. Generic membrane-drum cards stand in for the Mandinka drums.
items.description: Driving processional drumming under call-and-response chanting by the escorting crowd of initiates and followers, loud and outdoors.
exemplars: UNESCO documentation of the Kankurang, Manding initiatory rite (Senegal and Gambia)

items.name: Takamba (Gao lute-and-calabash dance music)
items.lineage: Music and dance of the Songhai and Tuareg communities of the Gao region of eastern Mali, played at weddings and celebrations, in which a singer is accompanied by the small tehardent lute, often amplified, and calabash percussion while dancers move with slow, stylised arm and shoulder gestures. Recordings by Gao groups such as Super Onze and reissued Gao cassettes have carried it beyond the region.
items.description: Repeating plucked lute figures with a swaying lilt ride over a steady pulse of hand-struck calabash, under a lead singer's praise and love verses.
exemplars: Sahel Sounds reissues of Gao takamba cassettes

items.name: Dogon funeral and mask music (Bandiagara)
items.lineage: Ritual song and drumming of the Dogon of the Bandiagara Escarpment, performed at funerals and at the dama, the collective end-of-mourning rite in which masked dancers escort the souls of the dead away from the village. Mourning songs (baja ni) are sung for the deceased, and drum ensembles accompany the mask dances. Generic membrane-drum cards stand in for the Dogon drums.
items.description: Massed drumming in insistent, repeating patterns carries the mask dances, alternating with mourning songs sung by groups of villagers in a lamenting, declaimed style.
exemplars: Ocora field recordings of Dogon music
CREM (CNRS-Musée de l'Homme) archive recordings of Dogon ritual music

items.name: Holey (Songhay-Zarma spirit-possession music)
items.lineage: Music of the holey spirit-possession ceremonies of the Songhay and Zarma of western Niger and the Gao region of Mali, in which mediums are possessed by spirits, among them the hauka, each family called by its own melodies and praise mottoes. The godji, a one-string bowed fiddle, carries the spirit melodies over gourd drums beaten with sticks, while sorko praise-singers address the spirits. Bernard Surugue documented its music and Jean Rouch filmed its ceremonies. The goje card stands in for the godji and the inverted-calabash card for the gourd drums.
items.description: A rasping one-string fiddle spins insistent repeating melodies over the dry clatter of stick-beaten gourd drums, building in intensity as dancers enter trance, with chanted praise lines laid over the top.
exemplars: Bernard Surugue's documentation of Zarma-Songhay sacred music (1972)
Jean Rouch's ethnographic films of Songhay possession dances

items.name: Balani show (Bamako amplified balafon street party)
items.lineage: Neighbourhood street-party music of Bamako built around the balani, a small high-pitched balafon, played through pickups and loud public-address systems with drums and singers who address the dancing crowd. Sahel Sounds documented the scene on the compilation Balani Show Super Hits (2014).
items.description: Rapid interlocking balafon runs, amplified until they distort, over pounding drum patterns, with shouted vocals urging on the dancers.
exemplars: Sahel Sounds compilation Balani Show Super Hits (2014)

items.name: Mossi court music (Moogo Naaba palace drumming)
items.lineage: Court music of the Mossi kingdoms of Burkina Faso, centred on the palace of the Moogo Naaba in Ouagadougou. Hereditary court drummers led by the bendr-naaba recite royal genealogies and histories on the bendré, a large calabash drum with a skin head, alongside lunga hourglass talking drums and praise singing at palace ceremonies. The bara card stands in for the bendré and the talking-drum card for the lunga.
items.description: Deep, resonant strokes on large calabash drums articulate speech-like genealogical recitation, answered by pitch-bending hourglass drums and declaimed praise lines at a stately ceremonial pace.
exemplars: CREM (Musée de l'Homme) archival recordings of Mossi court music

items.name: Warba (Mossi dance of Ganzourgou)
items.lineage: Mossi dance and song form of the Ganzourgou province around Zorgho in Burkina Faso, danced at celebrations to an ensemble of drums and voices. Its rhythms have been taken up by Burkinabè popular musicians, among them the electronic band Burkina Electric. Generic drum cards stand in for the warba drums.
items.description: Fast, insistent drum patterns with layered hand-drum interplay drive vigorous dancing, under group singing in call and response.
exemplars: Burkina Electric recordings drawing on warba rhythm

items.name: Yaake and geerewol (Wodaabe dance-songs)
items.lineage: Dance-songs of the Wodaabe, nomadic Fulɓe cattle herders of Niger, performed at the worso gatherings that close the rainy season, when lines of young men with painted faces sing and dance the yaake and the geerewol to be judged by women; the ruume circle dance belongs to the same repertoire. Sandrine Loncke's recordings and study document its multipart singing.
items.description: Unaccompanied men's chorus in interwoven multipart singing, carried by steady hand claps and stamping feet as the dancers sway in line.
exemplars: CREM collection of Sandrine Loncke's Wodaabe geerewol recordings

items.name: Milo jazz (Freetown street percussion band)
items.lineage: Freetown street-band music popularised by Dr. Oloh and His Milo Jazz Band, a percussion-and-voice street band whose music was issued on LP. Its name comes from the Milo tin filled with stones and shaken as a rattle; the shaker card stands in for it, a bass-drum card for the large drum and a hand-drum card for the smaller drums.
items.description: Busy, propulsive hand percussion and a booming bass drum under a lead singer answered by a chorus, with the gritty rattle of a stone-filled tin cutting through.
exemplars: Dr. Oloh & His Milo Jazz Band LPs

items.name: Bubu (Temne pipe music, Sierra Leone)
items.lineage: Processional music of the Temne of northern Sierra Leone, associated with the Ramadan period, played on bubu pipes of bamboo or metal tubing whose short figures interlock in hocket over percussion and call-and-response singing. Janka Nabay carried the bubu patterns into an electric band, recorded by Luaka Bop as Janka Nabay & the Bubu Gang. The vaksin card stands in for the bubu pipes.
items.description: Hooting pipe tones interlock in fast hocketed patterns over a driving percussion groove, with a lead singer and chorus trading lines.
exemplars: Janka Nabay & the Bubu Gang 'En Yay Sah' (Luaka Bop, 2012)

items.name: Sande/Bondo (women's society songs, Sierra Leone)
items.lineage: Songs of the Sande, called Bondo among the Temne, the women's initiation society of the Mende, Temne, Vai and neighbouring peoples of Sierra Leone and Liberia, which prepares girls for womanhood. Society women and initiates sing in leader-and-chorus form, above all at the public coming-out celebrations where the sowei helmet masks, danced by senior women, appear. The shekere card stands in for the segbure, the bead-netted gourd rattle that accompanies the singing.
items.description: Women's voices in leader-and-chorus singing over the crisp swish of bead-netted gourd rattles and hand claps, rising at the dances of the masked figures.
exemplars: Folkways FE 4322 'Music of the Mende of Sierra Leone' (1965), Mende solo-and-refrain songs with segbure rattle

items.name: Woi epic (Kpelle sung narrative, Liberia)
items.lineage: Epic performance of the Kpelle, a Mande-speaking people of central Liberia and Guinea, in which a narrator-singer recounts episodes of the hero Woi, answered by a chorus and supported by instrumentalists. Ruth M. Stone recorded Kpelle music in Bong County, issued on Folkways as Music of the Kpelle of Liberia, and analysed the epic in Dried Millet Breaking (1988). A source-unspecified percussion card stands in for the accompaniment.
items.description: A solo narrator moves between spoken and sung lines, answered by a responding chorus over light, steady percussion, the performance alternating storytelling, song and dramatised dialogue.
exemplars: Folkways FE 4385 'Music of the Kpelle of Liberia' (Ruth M. Stone)

items.name: Tina (Guinea-Bissau women's water-drum song)
items.lineage: Women's song genre of Bissau and Bolama, sung in Guinea-Bissau Kriol at community gatherings and celebrations and named after its central instrument, the tina, a calabash floated upside down in a tub of water and struck. Hand claps and call-and-response singing complete the texture; singer Karyna Gomes has recorded tina repertoire and a 2023 AMI manual documents the genre. The inverted-calabash card stands in for the water drum.
items.description: Deep, rounded thumps of a floating calabash water drum drive a lilting groove under women's lead-and-chorus singing and dense hand clapping.

items.name: Kola San Jon (Cape Verdean St John drumming)
items.lineage: Drum-and-dance tradition of the São João (St John) festivities of São Vicente and Santo Antão in Cabo Verde, centred on Ribeira de Julião and Porto Novo around 24 June. Drummers lead processions in which model ships are carried and dancers bump hips and bellies in pairs (the kola), with whistles adding signals; it was presented at the 1995 Smithsonian Festival of American Folklife Cape Verde programme. A generic membrane-drum card stands in for the tambor drums.
items.description: Loud, insistent drum patterns drive the procession and the paired dancing, punctuated by shrill whistle blasts.
exemplars: Smithsonian Festival of American Folklife 1995 Cape Verde program recordings

items.name: Medh (Haratin praise songs of the Prophet)
items.lineage: Devotional song of the Haratin of Mauritania, a men's practice in which a lead singer and a responding chorus sing praise of the Prophet Muhammad, giving voice to the community's spiritual life. Together with the women's bondja it forms a Haratin repertoire distinct from the music of the iggawin griots; both were recorded by a heritage-preservation project and studied by Elhadj Ould Brahim.
items.description: A lead voice intones praise verses answered by a male chorus in repeated, rhythmically measured refrains.
exemplars: Haratin bondja and medh preservation project recordings (Heritage Management Organization)

items.name: Bondja (Haratin women's song and dance)
items.lineage: Song and dance practice of Haratin women in Mauritania, also written bonja or bemdjé, in which a lead singer is answered by a chorus of drummers, singing about relations between women and men, social relationships and daily life, and recalling oasis and caravan life. It was recorded together with the men's medh by a heritage-preservation project. A source-unspecified hand-drum card stands in for the drums.
items.description: A lead singer's verses are answered by a chorus of women who also play the drums, in a steady, danceable groove.
exemplars: Haratin bondja and medh preservation project recordings (Heritage Management Organization)

items.name: Aïta (cheikhat song of the Atlantic plains)
items.lineage: Rural sung poetry of the Arabic-speaking Atlantic plains of Morocco (Abda, Doukkala, Chaouia), performed by women singers called cheikhat with male musicians, in regional styles such as the hasbawi aita of Safi and Abda and the marsawi aita of the Chaouia. Its texts and melodies became a main source of Moroccan wedding chaabi. The violin card stands in for the upright-held kamanja.
items.description: Strophic sung poetry traded between a lead woman singer and a chorus, with high open-throated calls over a violin line and taarija and bendir rhythms that speed up into a fast dance close.
exemplars: Fatna Bent El Houcine with the Ouled Ben Aguida troupe (LP and cassette recordings)

items.name: Rrways (Souss Amazigh troubadour song)
items.lineage: Professional song of Tashelhit-speaking Amazigh troupes of the Souss in southern Morocco, each led by a rais (poet-singer) who composes and sings with musicians and dancers at festivals, weddings and markets. Hadj Belaid recorded rrways songs for 78 rpm labels in the 1930s, and later raises and raissas made it a large cassette repertoire. The rabab_maghribi card stands in for the single-string Amazigh ribab, and the anvil card in its brake-drum form for the naqus, a piece of metal struck with iron rods; the troupe's lotar lutes have no card.
items.description: A nasal, high single-string fiddle line circles around the lead singer's verses, answered by a chorus over a steady, repeating metallic beat.

items.name: Aïssawa (ʿIsawiyya brotherhood hadra)
items.lineage: Ritual music of the ʿIsawiyya Sufi order founded in Meknes by the sixteenth-century saint Sidi Muhammad ibn ʿIsa, whose shrine in Meknes hosts the order's annual moussem and whose lodges across Moroccan cities hold hadra ceremonies. Chanted dhikr and praise poetry lead into trance dancing, with ghaita shawms and tbel drums outdoors and bendir and taarija frame and clay drums indoors. Paul Bowles recorded the order in 1959 for the Library of Congress.
items.description: Collective chant and repeated invocations over interlocking frame and clay drums, building in tempo and volume until piercing shawms and pounding drums carry the trance dance.
exemplars: Paul Bowles 1959 Library of Congress field recordings of the Aissawa
Institut du Monde Arabe CD recordings of the Aïssawa brotherhood

items.name: Hamadsha (Zerhoun brotherhood trance music)
items.lineage: Trance music of the Hamadsha, a Moroccan brotherhood whose two branches follow the saints Sidi Ali ben Hamdouch and Sidi Ahmed Dghoughi, buried in villages of the Zerhoun massif near Meknes. Its hadra drives adepts into trance with ghaita shawms and clay hand drums (gwal) and invokes the jinniya Aisha Qandisha; it was recorded by Paul Bowles in 1959 and studied by the anthropologist Vincent Crapanzano in his monograph The Hamadsha. The taarija card in its large size stands in for the gwal.
items.description: Pairs of shrill shawms play insistent repeating phrases over driving clay-drum patterns that accelerate in waves, with shouted invocations from the dancers.
exemplars: Paul Bowles 1959 Library of Congress recordings of the Hamadsha

items.name: Jilala (Moroccan Qadiri brotherhood music)
items.lineage: Ritual music of the Jilala, Moroccan devotees of the saint ʿAbd al-Qadir al-Jilani of Baghdad, whose night ceremonies bring adepts into trance with an end-blown cane flute (gasba) over bendir frame drums and sung praise. Brion Gysin and Paul Bowles recorded a Jilala group for the 1965 Trance Records LP Jilala, and the Moroccan band Jil Jilala later took its name from the brotherhood.
items.description: A breathy cane flute spins long, ornamented phrases above massed buzzing frame drums whose ostinato tightens and speeds up, with chanted praise between instrumental passages.
exemplars: Jilala LP (Trance Records, 1965; recorded by Brion Gysin and Paul Bowles)
Paul Bowles Moroccan Music collection, Library of Congress

items.name: Samaʿ wa madih (Moroccan Sufi a cappella song)
items.lineage: Moroccan Sufi vocal art in which brotherhood choirs and their munshid leaders sing mystical poetry (samaʿ) and praise of the Prophet (madih), including al-Busiri's Burda and Hamziyya, on the melodic modes of the Andalusi tradition and without instruments, in Fez, Tetouan, Salé, Marrakech and other cities.
items.description: Unaccompanied men's chorus singing in unison and octaves, alternating with a soloist's melismatic modal improvisations, in slow free sections that move into measured hymns.
exemplars: Fes Festival of World Sacred Music broadcasts of samaʿ wa madih

items.name: Dakka marrakchia (Marrakech Ashura percussion-song)
items.lineage: Percussion-and-chant genre of Marrakech, with a related form in Taroudant (dakka roudania), performed by men's troupes during the Ashura festivities of the tenth of Muharram. Massed taarija clay drums and a struck iron (naqqus) accompany sung verses in sections that move from slow to very fast. The anvil card in its brake-drum form stands in for the naqqus.
items.description: Dozens of small clay drums lock into dense interlocking patterns with a ringing struck-metal beat, under unison chant and clapping, the tempo rising section by section to a roaring climax.
exemplars: Marrakech National Festival of Popular Arts recordings of dakka troupes

items.name: Taqtuqa jabaliya (Jbala mountain song)
items.lineage: Song of the Arabic-speaking Jbala highlands of north-western Morocco around Chefchaouen, Ouazzane and the hinterland of Tetouan, sung at weddings and seasonal festivities and sold on a regional cassette market; Chama Zaz became its best-known recorded voice. The violin card stands in for the kamanja.
items.description: A bright lead voice sings short, lilting strophes answered by a chorus, with violin doubling and decorating the tune over light hand-drum rhythms.
exemplars: RTM (Moroccan radio-television) folklore broadcasts of Jbala song

items.name: Reggada (north-eastern Moroccan warrior dance)
items.lineage: Dance music of the Beni Snassen and neighbouring communities of north-eastern Morocco around Berkane, Oujda and Nador, historically a warriors' dance in which lines of men holding rifles move their shoulders and stamp to the gasba cane flute and bendir frame drums. It remains a staple of weddings and regional festivals and circulates on cassettes and wedding videos.
items.description: A reedy cane flute plays short, repeating phrases over hard, bouncing bendir rhythms with shouted interjections, built for stamping, shoulder-driven group dancing.
exemplars: Oujda and Berkane reggada cassettes and wedding videos

items.name: Guedra (Saharan kneeling trance dance-song)
items.lineage: Dance-song of Saharan communities of southern Morocco around Guelmim and Tan-Tan, named for the guedra, a cooking pot covered with skin and beaten as a drum. A woman dances on her knees with veiled head and expressive hand movements while a circle of men and women clap and chant around her; it is performed at the Moussem of Tan-Tan, a UNESCO-listed cultural space. The acoustic membrane drum card stands in for the guedra pot drum.
items.description: A single deep pot drum beats a steady heartbeat pulse that gradually quickens, under massed clapping and repeated chanted phrases from the surrounding circle.

items.name: Matrouz and piyyut (Moroccan Jewish song)
items.lineage: Paraliturgical song of Moroccan Jews: Hebrew piyyutim and the bakkashot sung on winter Sabbath nights, and the matrouz, in which Hebrew and Judeo-Arabic lines alternate within one song, set to the modes of Moroccan Andalusi music. Cantors and singers such as Samy Elmaghribi, Haim Louk and Emile Zrihan carried it into recordings in Morocco, France, Canada and Israel. The fiddle card stands in for the upright-held kamanja and the hand-drum card for the derbouka goblet drum.
items.description: A melismatic cantor's voice alternates with congregational refrains, accompanied by oud and violin in heterophony over a light goblet-drum pulse.
exemplars: Jewish Music Research Centre (Jerusalem) recordings of Moroccan Jewish song

items.name: ʿAbidat rma (Chaouia hunters' troupe song)
items.lineage: Sung and danced art of the hunters' guilds of central Morocco (the Chaouia, Ourdigha and Tadla plains around Khouribga, Oued Zem and Beni Mellal), historically performed to serve and entertain hunting parties. A troupe led by a mqaddem sings poetry in chorus to bendir frame drums and taarija clay drums, with the beat marked by a large pair of shears (mqass) struck with an iron rod, which has no card; dancers add broad cadenced movements, stamping and synchronised clapping. Troupes appear at the national Abidat Rma festival in Khouribga and on Moroccan radio-television.
items.description: Massed men's voices answer a leader in short repeated phrases over brisk bendir and clay-drum rhythms, a clanging struck-metal beat and synchronised clapping, loud and outdoors.
exemplars: National Abidat Rma Festival (Khouribga) troupe performances
Marrakech Festival of Popular Arts and RTM recordings of ʿabidat rma troupes

items.name: Gharnati (Tlemcen school of Andalusi music)
items.lineage: The school of Andalusi music centred on Tlemcen in western Algeria, which traces its repertoire to Granada (gharnati, 'of Granada') and is organised in nuba suites; it is also cultivated in Oran and, across the border, in Oujda and Rabat. Cheikh Larbi Bensari of Tlemcen was among its first masters on 78 rpm records. The fiddle card stands in for the upright-held kamanja, the tar_frame_drum card for the small jingled tar and the hand-drum card for the derbouka goblet drum.
items.description: Voices and plucked and bowed instruments move together in ornamented heterophonic unison through suites of linked songs, from measured slow movements to faster closing sections over frame drum and goblet drum.
exemplars: Recordings of the Ahbab Cheikh Larbi Bensari association of Tlemcen

items.name: Hawzi (Tlemcen urban sung poetry)
items.lineage: Urban sung-poetry genre of Tlemcen, set to dialectal Arabic poems by Tlemcen poets such as Ibn Msayeb and Bensahla and sung with the instruments and modes of the gharnati Andalusi school, but as freer single songs rather than full nuba suites. Cheikha Tetma, Abdelkrim Dali and Nouri Koufi are among its recorded singers. The fiddle card stands in for the upright-held kamanja, the tar_frame_drum card for the small jingled tar and the hand-drum card for the derbouka goblet drum.
items.description: A solo singer delivers long strophic love and praise poems with melismatic ornament, the oud, kwitra and violin doubling and answering the line over frame drum and goblet drum.

items.name: Ahellil (Gourara Zenati choral poetry)
items.lineage: Poetic and musical genre of the Zenati Amazigh communities of the Gourara oases around Timimoun in the Algerian Sahara, sung at religious festivities, pilgrimages, weddings and community gatherings. A solo singer and a flute player are surrounded by a chorus of up to a hundred people standing shoulder to shoulder in a circle, who move slowly around them while clapping. It was proclaimed a UNESCO Masterpiece of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity and later inscribed on the Representative List, and was documented by Mouloud Mammeri. The credited flute card stands in for the end-blown bengri flute.
items.description: A soloist's long lines are taken up by a large circling chorus in slow, layered responses, with a breathy flute weaving between them and soft massed clapping, unfolding through the night.
exemplars: UNESCO Collection album Algeria: Sahara - Music of Gourara
UNESCO documentation of the Ahellil of Gourara

items.name: Chaoui song (Aurès Amazigh)
items.lineage: Song of the Chaoui (Shawiya) Amazigh people of the Aurès mountains of eastern Algeria around Batna and Khenchela, traditionally sung to the gasba cane flute and bendir frame drums and danced as rahaba at celebrations. Aïssa Djermouni recorded Chaoui songs on 78s in the 1930s; later artists such as Houria Aïchi and Katchou brought it to concert and popular recordings.
items.description: A powerful, high, open-voiced singer delivers long-breathed melodic lines, with a breathy cane flute answering and bendir rhythms carrying the dance sections.

items.name: Staïfi (Sétif popular song)
items.lineage: Popular dance song of Sétif and the eastern High Plateaus of Algeria, sung at weddings and parties and sold on cassette and CD by singers such as Samir Staïfi and Bekakchi El Kheir. The electronic keyboard card stands for the keyboard that carries the melody in commercial recordings, and the hand-drum card for the derbouka goblet drum.
items.description: A lead singer rides fast, bouncing goblet-drum and frame-drum rhythms, with keyboard riffs answering each line in short repeating dance phrases.
exemplars: Bekakchi El Kheir cassettes and CDs

items.name: Bédoui (Algerian gasba-and-guellal Bedouin song)
items.lineage: Bedouin sung poetry of Algeria's High Plateaus and the Oran hinterland, in which a singer delivers long strophic poems in dialectal Arabic over one or two gasba end-blown cane flutes, often with the guellal clay drum marking the pulse. Cheikh Hamada of Mostaganem and Khelifi Ahmed made its best-known recordings for record labels and Algerian radio, and the bédoui of the Oran region is cited as a direct source of raï.
items.description: A full-throated, melismatic solo voice declaims long stanzas while breathy, hoarse cane flutes drone and answer between lines over a sparse, dry clay-drum pulse.

items.name: Wahrani (Oran modern song)
items.lineage: Urban popular song of Oran whose modern orchestral form flourished in the 1950s and 1960s, when singers such as Blaoui Houari and Ahmed Wahby set Oranian dialect poetry to an ensemble led by oud, violins and darbuka, drawing on the local bédoui and Andalusi repertoires. It was carried by Algerian radio and records and fed later Oran popular music.
items.description: A warm, ornamented lead voice sings strophic dialect songs over unison violin melodies and plucked oud, carried by a lilting darbuka dance rhythm.

items.name: Stambeli (Tunisian healing-trance music)
items.lineage: Ritual music of Tunisia's communities of sub-Saharan descent, played in possession and healing ceremonies addressed to a pantheon of Muslim saints and black spirits, kept in houses such as Dar Barnu in the Tunis medina. A master musician (yinna) plays the three-string gumbri bass lute while a chorus sings and beats large iron shqashiq castanets; the guembri and qraqeb cards stand in for the Tunisian gumbri and shqashiq.
items.description: Deep, buzzing bass-lute ostinatos lock with the metallic clatter of iron castanets in accelerating cycles, under a leader's call and a group's chanted response that build toward trance.
exemplars: Richard Jankowsky, Stambeli: Music, Trance, and Alterity in Tunisia (2010)

items.name: Zār (Egyptian spirit-possession ritual music)
items.lineage: Women-led ritual of spirit possession and healing practised in Cairo and across Egypt, in which leaders called kodia sing to the spirits over large jingled frame drums and the goblet-shaped tabla. Egyptian practice combines several strands, including a Sudanese-derived tanbura style with the bowl lyre and the manjur rattle belt of goat hooves; the Mazaher ensemble, based at Makan (Egyptian Center for Culture and Art) in Cairo, has brought it to the concert stage.
items.description: Pounding frame drums and goblet drum drive repeating rhythmic cycles under a woman leader's raw call and a chorus response, joined in the tanbura songs by a ringing bowl lyre and the dry clatter of a hoof-rattle belt.
exemplars: Makan (Egyptian Center for Culture and Art) zar concerts and recordings

items.name: Simsimiyya (Suez Canal lyre song)
items.lineage: Song of the Canal Zone cities of Port Said, Ismailia and Suez, accompanied by the simsimiyya lyre at weddings and neighbourhood gatherings, where a lead singer and a male chorus trade verses of love, the sea and the Canal cities' wartime resistance. The El Tanbura band, founded in Port Said at the end of the 1980s by Zakaria Ibrahim, revived the older Port Said repertoire and recorded it for international labels.
items.description: Bright, ringing lyre riffs repeat over clapped and drummed dance rhythms while a lead singer's verses are answered by a full-throated male chorus.

items.name: Al-Sīra al-Hilāliyya (Egyptian Hilali epic singing)
items.lineage: Oral epic of the Bani Hilal tribe's migration from Arabia to North Africa, sung by professional poet-singers (sha'ir) of Upper Egypt and the Nile Delta who accompany themselves on the two-string rababa spike fiddle or a frame drum, in performances that can run over many nights. UNESCO proclaimed it a Masterpiece in 2003 and inscribed it in 2008; the rebaba card stands in for the Egyptian two-string rababa.
items.description: A single poet-singer narrates rhymed verse in a strong declamatory voice, each line framed by short, scratchy spike-fiddle refrains that also shadow the melody.
exemplars: Dwight Reynolds, Sirat Bani Hilal digital archive

items.name: Ibtihālāt (Egyptian devotional supplication)
items.lineage: Solo devotional supplications in classical Arabic sung by Egyptian munshids trained in Qur'an recitation, usually unaccompanied and improvised through the maqamat, and broadcast before the dawn prayer and during Ramadan on Egyptian Radio, above all in the 1960s and 1970s. Sayed Naqshabandi and Nasr el-Din Tobar are its most celebrated radio voices.
items.description: A single, powerful voice unfolds long free-rhythm melismatic phrases through shifting modes, with soaring high climaxes and pauses, entirely unaccompanied.

items.name: Ṭaqṭūqa (early Egyptian light song)
items.lineage: Short strophic light song of Cairo's early recording era, flourishing from the 1910s to the 1930s, built on a recurring refrain with verses in Egyptian colloquial Arabic, often witty or risqué, and accompanied by a small takht. Women stars such as Munira al-Mahdiyya and Na'ima al-Masriyya recorded it extensively on 78 rpm discs for labels including Odeon, Gramophone and Baidaphon.
items.description: A bright, playful lead voice alternates short verses with a catchy recurring refrain over a small ensemble of plucked lute, zither, violin and jingled frame drum, heard through the narrow band and hiss of early discs.
exemplars: AMAR (Foundation for Arab Music Archiving and Research) 78 rpm transfers

items.name: Zajal (Lebanese improvised sung-poetry duel)
items.lineage: Strophic poetry in Lebanese colloquial Arabic, improvised and sung by teams of poets who answer one another in verbal jousts before an audience, with a chorus repeating the refrains to frame drum and darbuka. It is on the UNESCO Representative List and is associated with poets such as Zaghloul el-Damour and Moussa Zgheib, whose duels were widely recorded; the riq card stands in for the Lebanese def frame drum.
items.description: Solo poets declaim rhymed verses in a projected, half-sung chant, each stanza capped by the chorus singing back its refrain over a steady frame-drum and goblet-drum pulse, with audience cheers between rounds.
exemplars: UNESCO documentation of Al-Zajal, recited or sung poetry

items.name: ʿAtāba and mījana (Levantine sung improvisation)
items.lineage: Free-rhythm vocal genre of the rural Levant, across Lebanon, Syria, Palestine and Jordan, in which a singer improvises quatrains of colloquial poetry whose first three lines end on the same punning word and the last on a rhyme in -ab, often followed by the measured refrain 'ya mijana'. It opens wedding songs and dabke sets, answered by oud, buzuq or mijwiz, and became a showpiece of Lebanese radio and festival singers such as Wadih El Safi, Nasri Shamseddine and Sabah.
items.description: A full, ringing voice stretches each poetic line into long free-rhythm melismas, echoed by short plucked-lute or reed-pipe fills, then breaks into a lilting measured refrain.

items.name: Al-Qudūd al-Ḥalabiyya (Aleppine measured song)
items.lineage: Repertoire of measured songs associated with Aleppo, many setting secular words to older religious melodies, sung in maqam by a soloist and chorus with a takht of oud, qanun, nay, violin and riq, and performed in suites alongside muwashshahat at weddings, gatherings and concerts. It is on the UNESCO Representative List and was carried to wide audiences on radio, records and the concert stage from the 1950s onward by singers such as Sabah Fakhri and Sabri Moudallal.
items.description: A powerful lead voice and an answering chorus sing tuneful metered songs over a heterophonic ensemble of lute, zither, reed flute and violin, with jingled frame-drum cycles and vocal improvisations that rouse the listeners.

items.name: As-Sāmer (Jordanian Bedouin clap-chant dance-song)
items.lineage: Evening wedding and celebration performance of Jordan's Bedouin and rural communities, in which rows of men facing each other clap and sway while chanting alternating verses led by a poet, sometimes with a dancer moving between them; the related sahja is sung in northern Palestine. UNESCO inscribed As-Samer in Jordan on the Representative List in 2018.
items.description: Two rows of male voices chant short verses back and forth in a low, rhythmic drone, driven by unison hand claps and swaying, with a poet's lead lines cutting through.
exemplars: UNESCO documentation of As-Samer in Jordan (2018)
Jordanian radio and wedding recordings of samer

items.name: Shiʿr al-rabāba (Bedouin rababa sung poetry)
items.lineage: Sung Bedouin poetry of the deserts of Jordan, northern Arabia and Syria, in which a poet-singer accompanies himself on the rababa, a one-string spike fiddle with a skin-covered frame, framing and doubling his recitation at tent and guest-house gatherings. It belongs to the oral culture recognised in UNESCO's 2008 inscription of the Cultural Space of the Bedu in Petra and Wadi Rum.
items.description: A single voice recites rhymed verse to a narrow, repeating melody shadowed by the reedy, buzzing tone of a one-string fiddle, intimate and unhurried.
exemplars: UNESCO documentation of the Cultural Space of the Bedu in Petra and Wadi Rum
Jordanian and Saudi radio archive recordings of rababa poets

items.name: Samaritan liturgical chant (Mount Gerizim)
items.lineage: Liturgy of the Samaritan community of Kiryat Luza on Mount Gerizim and of Holon, chanted by men in Samaritan Hebrew and Aramaic in unaccompanied group heterophony led by priests, including the Torah readings and the prayers of the Passover sacrifice held on the mountain. It has been recorded for the National Sound Archive and the Jewish Music Research Centre in Jerusalem.
items.description: A body of male voices chants the texts together in loose, overlapping heterophony, forceful and ornamented, with drone-like held tones rising from the group.
exemplars: National Sound Archive (Jerusalem) recordings of Samaritan prayers and Passover
Jewish Music Research Centre recordings of Samaritan liturgy

items.name: Choubi (Iraqi dance song)
items.lineage: Iraqi wedding and party dance music, the country's counterpart to the Levantine dabke, built on a driving signature beat topped by crisp, rapid-fire figures on the khishba hand drum. Fiddles, double-reed shawms, oud, bass and keyboards can carry the melody, and the style is heard on Iraqi wedding and party recordings from the 1980s onward; the darbuka card stands in for the khishba.
items.description: A hard-driving dance beat with rapid-fire hand-drum figures on top propels a strong lead vocal, while fiddle or keyboard riffs repeat the hooks and oud lines weave through.
exemplars: Choubi Choubi! Folk and Pop Sounds from Iraq (Sublime Frequencies compilations)

items.name: Ghināʾ rīfī (southern Iraqi rural song)
items.lineage: Rural song of southern Iraq around Nasiriyah, Amarah and the Mesopotamian marshes, sung in the southern dialect and centred on the abudhiya, a four-line poem whose first three lines end in a punning homonym and whose last ends in -iyya, delivered in a long free-rhythm melismatic style before a measured song. Singers such as Hudhairi Abu Aziz and Dakhil Hassan brought it to Iraqi Radio in the mid-20th century.
items.description: A high, plaintive voice draws out each poetic line in long, sobbing melismas and microtonal bends, lingering on the final rhyme before settling into a simpler metered song.
exemplars: Iraqi Radio recordings of rural song

items.name: Hoyrat (Kirkuk Turkmen free-rhythm song)
items.lineage: Short sung verse form of the Turkmen of Kirkuk, Tal Afar and other northern Iraqi towns, in which seven-syllable lines built on homonym rhymes (cinas) are delivered in long, unmetred melismatic phrases on a set of local melody types. A hoyrat is often sung alone or as the free prelude to a metred song with lute and drum; the oud and hand drum cards stand for that accompaniment.
items.description: A single high, ornamented voice stretches each short verse into long unmetred melismas with held cries and falling phrases, sometimes over a quiet lute before a metred song with drum begins.
exemplars: Iraqi radio Turkmen-language broadcast recordings of Kirkuk hoyrat

items.name: Qewl (Yazidi sacred hymnody)
items.lineage: Sacred hymns of the Yazidi religion, sung in Kurmanji by the qewwals, a hereditary class of religious musicians based mainly in Bashiqa and Bahzani, at religious ceremonies and at festivals at Lalish such as the autumn Feast of the Assembly. The qewwals accompany the hymns on the def, a large frame drum, and the shibab, a long end-blown flute; the frame drums card stands for the def and the shabbaba card for the shibab.
items.description: Solemn group chanting of long hymn texts over the steady boom of large frame drums and the breathy, wavering line of a long end-blown flute.
exemplars: Christine Allison field recordings of Yazidi oral tradition in Iraqi Kurdistan

items.name: ʿArḍa najdiyya (Najdi sword-and-drum war dance)
items.lineage: Ceremonial war dance of Najd in central Arabia, once performed before battle and now at national celebrations and festivals such as Janadriyah, in which rows of men holding swords chant lines of nabati poetry given out by a poet while drummers in their midst beat large and small drums. It is inscribed on UNESCO's Representative List; the acoustic membrane drum card stands for the large stick-beaten drums and the frame drums card for the hand-held frame drums.
items.description: Massed male voices chant poetry in slow, heavy unison lines after a leader, over pounding large and small drums that set a measured, martial step.
exemplars: Saudi state television broadcasts of the ardah at the Janadriyah festival

items.name: Mizmār ḥijāzī (Hijazi stick dance with drums)
items.lineage: Group stick dance of the Hijaz, performed in Jeddah, Mecca, Taif and Medina at weddings, holidays and national celebrations, in which men spin and wield long sticks, often in pairs, while the group chants to the beat of large and small drums. Almezmar is inscribed on UNESCO's Representative List; the acoustic membrane drum and hand drum cards stand for its drums.
items.description: Driving, layered drumming with sharp high accents over a deep pulse carries a call-and-response chant of male voices that rises as the dancers take the floor.
exemplars: UNESCO documentation of Almezmar, drumming and dancing with sticks (2016)
Hijazi mizmar troupe recordings from Jeddah

items.name: Majass and sahba (Hijazi urban song)
items.lineage: Urban vocal art of Mecca, Medina, Jeddah and Taif built on the Arabic maqam, centred on the majass, an unmetred sung improvisation on lines of poetry, together with the dana and the sahba, a group song sung at weddings and gatherings. Singers such as Mohammed Ali Sindi carried the repertoire into the record and radio era, and later Hijazi singers drew on it; the fiddle card stands for the violin of its oud-led ensembles.
items.description: A solo voice unfolds long, unmetred melismatic phrases through the maqam, answered by lute and violin, before metred songs settle over a light frame-drum rhythm.

items.name: Sāmrī (Najdi seated drum-song)
items.lineage: Evening song-dance of Najd, especially of the Qassim towns, also performed in Kuwait, in which two facing rows of men kneel or sit, beating frame drums and swaying from side to side as they sing alternating lines of nabati poetry.
items.description: Two rows of male voices trade sung lines of poetry over a dense, rolling pulse of many frame drums, the bodies' sway locking the rhythm.
exemplars: Najdi samri troupe recordings from Qassim

items.name: Al-Taghrooda (Bedouin camel-riders' chanted poetry)
items.lineage: Chanted Bedouin poetry of the deserts of the United Arab Emirates and Oman, composed and sung by men riding camels, a lead rider chanting a line and a second group answering, to pass the time on long desert journeys; it is also sung around campfires, at weddings and at camel races. UNESCO inscribed it as an element shared by the two countries.
items.description: Unaccompanied open-air chant in which a single voice calls a line of poetry in a narrow, swaying melody and a group of voices answers it, unhurried and spacious.
exemplars: UNESCO documentation of Al-Taghrooda (UAE and Oman, 2012)
Abu Dhabi heritage-authority recordings of taghrooda

items.name: Al-ʿĀzī (Emirati chanted praise poetry)
items.lineage: Chanted performance of poetry of praise, pride and fortitude in the United Arab Emirates, in which a lead poet declaims the verses of a poem while a chorus answers with a fixed refrain; no instruments are used. It is inscribed on UNESCO's List of Intangible Cultural Heritage in Need of Urgent Safeguarding.
items.description: A single declaiming voice delivers rhymed verses in strong, measured phrases, each answered by a unison male chorus repeating the same refrain, with no instruments.
exemplars: UNESCO documentation of Al Azi (Urgent Safeguarding List, 2017)
Emirati heritage festival recordings of al-azi troupes

items.name: Al-Barʿah (Dhofari dagger-dance music)
items.lineage: Bedouin music and dance of the valleys of Dhofar in southern Oman, performed by a semicircle of men who chant poetry while two dancers at a time step forward brandishing khanjar daggers to the rhythm of the kasir and rahmani drums; each tribe keeps its own variant. It is inscribed on UNESCO's Representative List; the acoustic membrane drum and hand drum cards stand for the two drums.
items.description: A semicircle of male voices chants poetry in steady unison phrases over two interlocking drum patterns that drive the dancers' movements.
exemplars: Oman Centre for Traditional Music archive recordings

items.name: Dān and ṣawt ḥaḍramī (Hadrami song)
items.lineage: Song tradition of the Hadramawt in eastern Yemen, spanning the dan, in which poets and singers develop verses over set melodies at evening gatherings, and the urban Hadrami sawt sung to the lute with drums. Singers such as Mohammed Jum'a Khan and Abu Bakr Salem Balfaqih, born in Tarim, carried it onto records and Gulf radio with ensembles of oud, violins and hand drums; the fiddle card stands for the violins and the hand drum card for the mirwas.
items.description: A warm, ornamented lead voice sings long strophic poems over plucked oud and unison violins, carried by a light, lilting hand-drum rhythm.

items.name: Ghināʾ laḥjī (Lahji song)
items.lineage: Song school of Lahij, north of Aden, shaped in the early twentieth century by the poet-composer Ahmed Fadl al-Qumandan of the Lahij sultanate, who set colloquial poetry to the melodies and rhythms of the surrounding countryside. Later Lahji singers such as Faisal Alawi carried it through radio, records and cassettes, singing to the oud with violins and hand drums; the fiddle card stands for the violins.
items.description: A bright lead voice sings short strophic songs over plucked oud and violin unisons, driven by lilting, dance-like hand-drum rhythms.

items.name: Al-ughniya al-ʿadaniyya (Adeni modern song)
items.lineage: Modern song of Aden that took shape in the 1950s and 1960s, when singer-composers such as Mohammed Murshid Naji and Ahmed Qasim, working with the city's radio and record companies, set new lyric poetry for oud, violins and percussion, drawing on Lahji, Sanaani and Hadrami song and on Egyptian song; the fiddle card stands for the violins.
items.description: A smooth lead voice sings strophic love songs over oud and violins playing unison melodies and answering phrases, set on a steady hand-drum rhythm.

items.name: Zāmil (Yemeni tribal chanted poetry)
items.lineage: Short two-line poem of the tribes of the northern Yemeni highlands, composed by a poet for an occasion such as a wedding, the arrival of guests or the settling of a dispute, and chanted in unison by a group of men, often as they move in procession. The anthropologist Steven Caton documented its composition and performance in his study Peaks of Yemen I Summon.
items.description: A massed male chorus chants a two-line poem in loud, rhythmic unison, repeating it over and over on a narrow, insistent melody, with no instruments.
exemplars: Steven C. Caton field documentation in Peaks of Yemen I Summon (1990)
Yemeni cassette and online zamil recordings

items.name: Barāʿ (Yemeni highland dagger dance)
items.lineage: Men's dagger dance of the tribes of the Yemeni highlands, danced in lines or a circle with the jambiya drawn, to drumming on the small tasa kettle drum and the larger marfa'; a performance moves through sections that grow faster and more intricate, and each region and tribe keeps its own steps and rhythms.
