The hand drum card stands for the tasa and the acoustic membrane drum card for the marfa'.
items.description: Two drums lock a sharp, high patter against a deep beat in repeating cycles that speed up and grow more intricate from section to section, with no singing.
exemplars: Yemeni television folklore broadcasts of bara'

items.name: Diwan (Yemenite Jewish Shabazi song)
items.lineage: Paraliturgical song of the Jews of Yemen, drawn from the diwan, a collection of Hebrew, Aramaic and Judeo-Arabic poems led by those of the seventeenth-century poet Shalom Shabazi, and sung by men at weddings, circumcisions and Sabbath gatherings. A lead singer and his partner alternate with the company through an unmetred nashid, a metred shira that brings dancing and a closing hallel, with rhythm beaten on a tin can or copper tray in place of instruments; the credited auxiliary percussion card stands for that tin. The repertoire continues among Yemenite Jews in Israel.
items.description: Male voices trade ornamented lines of poetry, opening in free rhythm and then breaking into metred, dance-driven singing over the bright clatter of a beaten tin.
exemplars: Jewish Music Research Centre (Hebrew University) recordings of Yemenite diwan singing
Folkways field recordings of Yemenite Jewish song

items.name: Zeybek (Aegean dance-song)
items.lineage: Dance and dance-song repertoire of the Aegean hinterland of western Anatolia around Aydın, Muğla, Denizli and İzmir, named after the zeybek and efe irregulars of the late Ottoman countryside. Its signature is the slow, heavy ağır zeybek in a long nine-beat aksak metre (often written 9/4, the quicker kıvrak zeybek in 9/8), danced solo or in small groups with arms raised, beside quicker kıvrak zeybeks; outdoors it is played by davul and zurna, indoors on bağlama or with sung verses, and state radio collectors recorded it widely for the TRT folk-music archive.
items.description: A slow, weighty nine-beat pulse lands its long final beat on the bass drum while the shawm's piercing, ornamented line stretches over it; in the lute-and-voice form the same limping meter carries a measured, proud sung melody.
exemplars: TRT Türk Halk Müziği archive zeybek recordings

items.name: Halay (Anatolian davul-zurna line dance)
items.lineage: Line and circle dance music of central, eastern and southeastern Anatolia, called govend in Kurdish, in which dancers link arms, shoulders or little fingers behind a leader who waves a handkerchief at the head of the line. Davul and zurna play it outdoors at weddings and festivals, and many halays are sung folk songs that open at a moderate tempo and accelerate into a fast closing section; Sivas, Erzincan, Elazığ, Diyarbakır and Gaziantep keep distinct regional halay repertoires.
items.description: Thunderous bass-drum strokes and a screaming, circular-breathed shawm drive a repetitive line-dance groove that starts steady and speeds toward a frenzied finish, the shawm spinning ornamented variations over the fixed pattern.
exemplars: TRT Türk Halk Müziği archive halay recordings

items.name: Cem (Alevi-Bektaşi ritual song and semah)
items.lineage: Ritual music of the Alevi and Bektaşi cem ceremony of Anatolia, in which a zâkir accompanies himself on the bağlama, treated as sacred in the rite, singing deyiş and nefes hymns by poets such as Pir Sultan Abdal and Hatayi, düvaz-imam hymns naming the Twelve Imams, and the music of the semah, a turning ritual dance performed by men and women together that moves from slow to fast sections. Semah, Alevi-Bektaşi ritual is inscribed on UNESCO's Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage.
items.description: A single voice sings strophic devotional verse over a strummed, drone-ringing long-necked lute; in the semah sections the strumming quickens in stages from a stately pulse to a rapid, whirling one.
exemplars: Kalan Müzik cem and nefes recordings

items.name: Mehter (Ottoman Janissary military band)
items.lineage: Military band of the Ottoman state attached to the Janissary corps, whose mehterhane of zurnas, boru trumpets, kös and nakkare kettledrums, davul and zil cymbals played on campaign, in battle and at state ceremonies, and whose sound inspired the alla turca style of eighteenth-century European composers. Abolished together with the Janissary corps under Mahmud II, it was revived in the twentieth century, and the Mehter Takımı of the Istanbul Military Museum performs and records the repertoire today, with the verses of many marches sung in unison by the band. The karna card (a long natural trumpet of the related Persian naqqareh-khaneh) stands in for the boru and the cymbal card for the zil.
items.description: A massed wall of shrill shawms and blaring trumpets plays a unison modal melody over booming kettledrums, bass drums and crashing cymbals in a stately, heavy marching meter, with the band chanting the verses in unison.

items.name: Kanto (late-Ottoman Istanbul stage song)
items.lineage: Popular stage song of late-Ottoman Istanbul, sung in the tuluat improvised theatres and music halls of Pera and Direklerarası from the late nineteenth century into the 1920s, often by Armenian and Greek women singers, between acts or as featured numbers. Its light, often comic or flirtatious songs blended makam melody with Western-influenced light-music rhythms and were accompanied by small theatre orchestras in which violin and clarinet were prominent; a large corpus of 78rpm records from the 1900s to the 1920s has been reissued by Kalan Müzik.
items.description: A bright, flirtatious lead voice delivers strophic stage songs over a jaunty violin-and-clarinet theatre band with plucked zither and light goblet-drum accents, heard through the narrow, surface-noise-laden sound of early disc records.
exemplars: Kalan Müzik reissues of 1900s–1920s kanto 78rpm records

items.name: Mevlid (Turkish chanted nativity-poem ceremony)
items.lineage: Ceremonial chanting of the Vesîletü'n-Necât, the Turkish verse poem on the birth of the Prophet Muhammad completed by Süleyman Çelebi in Bursa in the early fifteenth century, performed in mosques and homes on the Prophet's birthday and holy nights, at births, and at memorials for the dead. Trained mevlidhan reciters take up its sections in turn, unaccompanied, moving through a succession of makams, with Qur'an recitation, prayers and ilahi hymns between the sections.
items.description: Solo male voices chant rhymed couplets unaccompanied in free rhythm, unfolding long melismatic phrases through a succession of modes, each reciter taking up the poem in turn.

items.name: Teke zortlatması (Western Taurus Yörük dance music)
items.lineage: Music of the Teke region of southwestern Anatolia around Burdur, Antalya and Isparta, rooted in its Yörük pastoralist communities. Its best-known form is the zortlatma, fast and vigorous men's dance tunes in aksak 9/8 played on the sipsi, a small single-reed cane pipe, together with the bağlama, alongside sung türkü; TRT recordings and Kalan Müzik regional anthologies document the repertoire.
items.description: A buzzing, reedy cane pipe races through tightly ornamented, repeating dance phrases in a quick limping 9/8, doubled by a brightly plucked long-necked lute, with sung verses dropping in between instrumental passages.
exemplars: Kalan Müzik Teke and Yörük anthologies

items.name: Özgün müzik (Turkish political song-poetry)
items.lineage: Politically engaged Turkish song movement of the late 1970s to the 1990s that set poetry by writers such as Nâzım Hikmet and Ahmed Arif, alongside the singers' own lyrics, to arrangements joining the bağlama and Anatolian folk melody with guitar, bass and Western harmony, building on the earlier political folk singing of Ruhi Su. It circulated widely on cassette and LP, and its leading voices included Zülfü Livaneli, Ahmet Kaya and the collective Grup Yorum.
items.description: An earnest, grainy lead voice declaims poetic verses over strummed long-necked lute and acoustic guitar with a supporting bass line, mixing folk-modal melody with simple Western chord progressions in a sober, intimate studio sound.

items.name: Türk Beşleri (Turkish Five national-school art music)
items.lineage: Art music of the Turkish Five, Ahmed Adnan Saygun, Ulvi Cemal Erkin, Cemal Reşit Rey, Necil Kazım Akses and Hasan Ferit Alnar, composers born in the first decade of the twentieth century who answered the early Republic's call for a national art music by setting Anatolian folk modes and aksak rhythms in Western orchestral, chamber, choral and operatic forms. Most trained in Paris, Vienna or Prague, and Saygun accompanied Béla Bartók on his folk-song collecting trip in Anatolia. The string-orchestra card stands in for the orchestra's violin sections.
items.description: Full orchestral textures carry modal, folk-derived melodies and additive limping rhythms through developed symphonic and choral forms, with pungent modal harmony and woodwind colours that evoke rural instruments.
exemplars: Ahmed Adnan Saygun — Yunus Emre Oratorio

items.name: Sıra gecesi (Şanlıurfa gathering music)
items.lineage: Music of the sıra gecesi, evening gatherings of men held in rotation in the homes of Şanlıurfa in southeastern Turkey, where friends share food and conversation and take turns singing the city's türkü, hoyrat and gazel in its own makam-based style with a small ensemble of local musicians. The gatherings are among the Traditional Sohbet meetings inscribed on UNESCO's Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage.
items.description: A powerful, high and ornate male voice launches into free-rhythm improvised laments before plucked lute and zither join with goblet drum for metred songs, in the close, convivial sound of a crowded room.

items.name: Türk tangosu (Turkish tango-song)
items.lineage: Turkish-language tango song that flourished in Istanbul from the 1930s into the 1950s, after Argentine and European tango reached the city's dance halls and gramophone market. Necip Celal Andel is credited with composing the first Turkish tangos, singers such as Seyyan Hanım and İbrahim Özgür recorded the repertoire on 78rpm discs, and the songs set Turkish lyrics of longing to the four-beat tango rhythm, accompanied by small Western-style dance orchestras of violin, piano and bass.
items.description: A crooning, wistful voice sings over a marcato four-beat tango pulse laid down by piano and bass, with the violin weaving sighing countermelodies, heard through the warm, narrow band of 78rpm discs.

items.name: Ta'zieh (Iranian Shi'a passion-play music)
items.lineage: Musical passion play of Iranian Shi'a Islam re-enacting the martyrdom of Imam Hossein and his companions at Karbala, staged above all during Muharram in tekyeh arenas and village squares and developed into a great court spectacle under the Qajars. Actors playing the protagonists sing their lines in the modes of Persian classical music while the antagonists declaim theirs, and a small band of long karna trumpets, drums and cymbals signals entrances, battles and turns of the drama; UNESCO has inscribed the Ritual dramatic art of Ta'zīye on its Representative List.
items.description: Solo singers deliver lamenting, highly ornamented modal lines in free rhythm, answered by loud, unsung declamation, while blaring trumpets, pounding drums and clashing cymbals punctuate the action in an open-air arena.
exemplars: Iranian national radio and festival recordings of ta'zieh

items.name: Zurkhaneh (morshed chant for varzesh-e pahlavani)
items.lineage: Music of the Iranian zurkhaneh, the traditional gymnasium where athletes perform the ritual exercises of varzesh-e pahlavani in a sunken pit. From a raised seat the morshed beats a large goblet drum, the zarb, and rings a bell to honour arriving champions and mark transitions, chanting verses from Ferdowsi's Shahnameh, mystical poetry and praises of the Prophet and Imam Ali in rhythms matched to each exercise; UNESCO has inscribed the Pahlevani and Zoorkhanei rituals on its Representative List. The tombak card stands in for the zarb.
items.description: A single chanting voice declaims rhymed epic and devotional verse over a deep, insistent goblet-drum rhythm that shifts tempo with each exercise, punctuated by a bright bell stroke.
exemplars: Field and broadcast recordings of zurkhaneh morsheds

items.name: Bakhshi (Khorasani dotar bards)
items.lineage: Bardic music of the bakhshis of Khorasan in northeastern Iran, who sing epic and romance narratives, mystical poetry and lyric songs in Kurmanji Kurdish, Khorasani Turkic, Turkmen and Persian while accompanying themselves on the dotar, a long-necked two-string lute. The Persian-speaking school of Torbat-e Jam and the northern schools around Quchan and Bojnurd form distinct regional styles, and the Music of the Bakhshis of Khorasan is inscribed on UNESCO's Representative List. The dutar card, in its Turkmen bagshy setting (Turkmen-language bakhshis are one of Khorasan's own schools), stands in for the Khorasani dotar.
items.description: A tense, full-throated voice declaims narrative and lyric verse over rapid strummed patterns on a two-string long-necked lute, alternating sung episodes with brilliant instrumental passages.
exemplars: UNESCO-documented music of the bakhshis of Khorasan

items.name: Bakhtiari music (Zagros tribal song and dance)
items.lineage: Music of the Bakhtiari, a Luri-speaking tribal confederation of the central Zagros whose seasonal pastures span Chaharmahal and Bakhtiari and Khuzestan. Its repertoire includes lyrical and heroic songs, women's mourning laments (gagriveh), and outdoor dance music for weddings and celebrations played on sorna and dohol, with the kamancheh accompanying songs; the Mahoor Institute has issued regional anthologies.
items.description: A ringing, open-throated voice sings long-breathed songs and laments over a bowed spike fiddle, while dance pieces switch to a piercing shawm and pounding double-headed drum in a bright outdoor acoustic.

items.name: Lori music (Lorestan song, chamar and dance)
items.lineage: Music of the Lurs of Lorestan in the western Zagros, centred on Khorramabad and sung in Luri dialects. It ranges from lyrical and heroic songs accompanied by the kamancheh to the sorna-and-dohol dance music of weddings and the chamar, a mourning music played on sorna and dohol at funerals; the Mahoor Institute has issued a Lorestan anthology.
items.description: A piercing, wailing shawm and a heavy double-headed drum drive circling dance tunes and slow funeral laments outdoors, while sung pieces pair a plaintive voice with a bowed spike fiddle.

items.name: Kalam (Yarsan sacred tanbur song)
items.lineage: Sacred music of the Yarsan (Ahl-e Haqq) of the Guran region and Kermanshah province in western Iran, whose kalam hymns, Gurani verses attributed to the faith's founding figures, are sung in the communal jam assembly to the tanbur, a long-necked fretted lute treated as sacred. The repertoire is transmitted orally through lineages of tanbur players and singers.
items.description: A long-necked lute plays insistent, drone-ringing modal figures with rapid strummed flourishes under a solemn, fervent voice singing strophic sacred verse, building in intensity across a sequence of melodic modes.

items.name: Siyah-chamaneh and hore (Gurani free-rhythm song)
items.lineage: Free-rhythm solo vocal genres of the Gurani-speaking Hawraman highlands on the Iran–Iraq border and of the neighbouring southern Kurdish Kermanshah region. Siyah-chamaneh is sung unaccompanied by a single voice in long, high, melismatic lines on Gurani verse, and hore is an unmetred, deeply ornamented song of lament, longing and devotion sung by singers of the Kermanshah region; both are documented on Kurdish radio and Mahoor field recordings.
items.description: A single unaccompanied voice sustains long, high, free-rhythm phrases dense with melismatic turns and throat ornaments, rising to piercing climaxes and falling away in lamenting cadences.
exemplars: Kurdish radio recordings of Hawrami siyah-chamaneh singers

items.name: Bandari (Hormozgan Persian Gulf dance-song)
items.lineage: Dance-song music of Iran's Persian Gulf coast and islands around Bandar Abbas, Qeshm and Minab in Hormozgan, shaped by long maritime contact with Arabia, East Africa and South Asia. Traditional bandari is played on sorna, the neyanban bagpipe and drums for weddings and for ceremonies including the leiva and zar rites, while the modern form that spread across Iran and its diaspora sets its bouncing 6/8 dance rhythm on electronic keyboard; the Mahoor Institute has issued a Hormozgan anthology.
items.description: A buoyant, bouncing six-beat dance groove of drums and handclaps underpins a nasal shawm or bright keyboard melody that repeats short, catchy modal phrases beneath a lead voice.

items.name: Gilaki music (Gilan Caspian folk song)
items.lineage: Folk song of the Gilaks of Gilan on Iran's Caspian coast, sung in the Gilaki language and tied to the region's rice-farming and village life, including work songs and lyrical love songs, and related to the music of neighbouring Mazandaran. Songs are sung solo or with the end-blown shepherd's flute, for which a generic end-blown flute card stands in, and singers recorded the repertoire for Iranian radio and records.
items.description: A clear, lilting voice sings short strophic melodies in a narrow modal range, answered by the breathy, airy tone of an end-blown flute, in an unhurried, intimate delivery.

items.name: Qashqai music (Fars tribal wedding and bardic song)
items.lineage: Music of the Qashqai, a Turkic-speaking nomadic tribal confederation that migrates between summer and winter pastures in Fars province in southern Iran. Wedding and festival music is played on shawm and naqqareh drum (sāz o naqqāreh), with tunes for the women's handkerchief dance (dastmal bazi) and the men's stick dance, while ashiq bards sing lyric and epic songs in Qashqai Turkic. The sorna card stands in for the Qashqai shawm and the generic drum card for the naqqāreh drum that partners it.
items.description: A piercing, circular-breathed shawm spins out repeating dance melodies over the crisp, driving strokes of a stick-beaten drum, shifting between a lilting handkerchief-dance tune and a hard-hitting rhythm for the stick dance.
exemplars: Sāz o naghāreh Qashqāi recordings (University of Cambridge repository)
Mahoor Institute and Iranian radio field recordings of Qashqai musicians

items.name: Motrebi and ruhowzi (Tehran entertainers' song)
items.lineage: Light popular music of the motrebs, professional entertainers who played at weddings, feasts and private parties in Qajar and Pahlavi Tehran, and of ruhowzi, the improvised comic theatre staged on boards laid over a courtyard pool, in which songs, dances and comic routines alternated. Its witty, often bawdy songs in Tehrani dialect use the lighter modes of Persian music, with tombak and dayereh rhythms under voice, tar or violin.
items.description: A cheeky, speech-inflected voice rattles off comic strophic verses over brisk goblet-drum and jingling frame-drum patterns, with plucked lute and violin doubling the catchy modal tunes and filling dance breaks.

items.name: Herati music (Herat dutar and chaharbeiti song)
items.lineage: Regional music of Herat in western Afghanistan, documented by John Baily in his study of the city's professional musicians and by Veronica Doubleday among Herati women. Men's local music centres on the long-necked dutar, which Herati players enlarged in the twentieth century from two strings to three and later fourteen, with a goblet or frame drum; women sing chaharbeiti quatrains and wedding songs to the daireh frame drum, for which the doira card stands; the dutar card, set to its Turkmen two-string folk form (the nearest setting it offers), stands for the Herati dutar.
items.description: A bright plucked long-necked lute, ringing with sympathetic strings, carries a solo voice through strophic quatrain songs, while a jingling frame drum or goblet drum keeps a light dance pulse.
exemplars: John Baily recordings of Herati professional musicians (with Music of Afghanistan, Cambridge 1988)
Veronica Doubleday recordings of Herati women's daireh songs

items.name: Tappa and landay (Pashto folk couplet song)
items.lineage: Folk song of the Pashtuns of southern and eastern Afghanistan and the Pakistani frontier, built on the landay or tappa, an anonymous couplet of nine and thirteen syllables sung in long strings of verses, alongside longer stanzaic forms such as the charbeta. Widely broadcast by Radio Afghanistan and Peshawar radio, it is sung by soloists or alternating singers with rubab, harmonium and drum, and by women among themselves at home and at weddings.
items.description: A high, ornamented solo voice delivers short couplets one after another, each stretched over a recurring melodic formula, while a plucked lute answers between verses over a reed-organ drone and a hand-drum pulse.
exemplars: Radio Afghanistan Pashto folk broadcast recordings

items.name: Attan (Pashtun dhol-and-surnai circle dance)
items.lineage: Circle dance of the Pashtuns of Afghanistan and the Pakistani frontier, regarded as Afghanistan's national dance and danced at weddings, festivals and gatherings, with distinct regional and tribal variants. Dancers circle a dhol drummer, often joined by the surnai shawm, turning and swinging their heads as the tempo rises from a slow opening to a fast close; the dohol card stands for the Afghan dhol.
items.description: A heavy stick-beaten barrel drum drives a cyclic dance rhythm that starts stately and accelerates to a frenzy, while a piercing shawm spins ornamented melody over it in the open air.
exemplars: Radio Afghanistan dhol-surnai attan broadcast recordings
Afghan wedding field recordings of attan

items.name: Qataghani (northern Afghan dambura song)
items.lineage: Regional song style of the former Qataghan province of north-eastern Afghanistan, around Kunduz, Baghlan and Takhar, sung to the two-string dambura lute. Mark Slobin documented the dambura and its song repertoire in his monograph Music in the Culture of Northern Afghanistan; the dombyra card stands for the dambura, and a goblet drum may join for dance songs.
items.description: A brisk strummed two-string lute pattern fuses drone and melody under a strong, high solo voice singing short strophic verses, often over a dance rhythm.
exemplars: Mark Slobin field recordings of northern Afghanistan

items.name: Waj (Nuristani arched-harp song)
items.lineage: Music of the Nuristani peoples of the Hindu Kush valleys of eastern Afghanistan, the region formerly called Kafiristan, whose emblematic instrument is the waj, a small arched harp and a rare survival of the arched harp in Asia, played to accompany songs and dances. It was recorded in the field by the Danish ethnographer Lennart Edelberg and the anthropologist Schuyler Jones; the aiumaa card, a Caucasian arched harp, stands for the waj.
items.description: A small plucked arched harp repeats short, bright ostinato figures under a solo or group vocal line.
exemplars: Lennart Edelberg and Schuyler Jones field recordings of Nuristan

items.name: Kabul golden-age pop (1960s-70s Radio Afghanistan song)
items.lineage: Popular song of Kabul in the 1960s and 1970s, when Radio Afghanistan and its studio musicians broadcast new Dari and Pashto songs that joined Afghan and Indian-derived melody to Western instruments. The leading singers of the period recorded with harmonium and tabla alongside electric guitar, organ and drum kit, and their LPs and radio tapes later circulated widely in the diaspora.
items.description: A warm, crooning lead voice with light melismatic turns sings strophic love songs over tabla and harmonium, with electric organ and guitar fills and a drum kit underneath.

items.name: Galoba (Georgian Orthodox polyphonic chant)
items.lineage: Liturgical chant of the Georgian Orthodox Church, sung in an indigenous three-part polyphony and handed down orally through regional schools such as those of Gelati in Imereti, Shemokmedi in Guria and the Kartli-Kakhetian tradition associated with the Karbelashvili family. Chanters including the Karbelashvili brothers transcribed large parts of the repertoire into staff notation, and after Soviet-era suppression church choirs revived the chant from these transcriptions.
items.description: Three male voice parts move together through text-bound phrases in a harmony built on fourths and fifths, settling onto open fifths and octaves at cadences, sung unaccompanied with calm, even declamation in a resonant stone church.

items.name: Kalakuri simghera (Tbilisi city song)
items.lineage: The European-oriented strand of Tbilisi's urban song, which took shape in the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries as Georgian singers combined their own part-singing with the harmony of Russian and European romance. Sung by small ensembles in three-part harmony or by soloists with guitar, it was widely recorded by Melodiya and stands beside the Eastern-oriented sazandari repertoire as one of the two strands of Georgian city music.
items.description: Sweet, close three-part vocal harmony in major and minor keys floats over fingerpicked or strummed guitar chords in lyrical, sentimental songs.
exemplars: Melodiya LPs of Tbilisi city songs

items.name: Sazandari (Tbilisi tar, kamancha and daira ensemble)
items.lineage: The Eastern-oriented strand of Tbilisi's urban music, played by sazandari trios of tar, kamancha and daira frame drum at feasts and in the taverns of the old city, sharing modes and repertoire with Persian, Armenian and Azerbaijani urban traditions; the doira card stands for the daira, and the kamancha card keeps its Garabagh-school setting, the nearest Caucasian one it offers. Songs attributed to the eighteenth-century Tbilisi bard Sayat-Nova belong to its repertoire, and the ensembles were recorded by Melodiya and the Tbilisi Conservatoire.
items.description: A bright plucked lute and a singing spike fiddle wind ornamented modal melodies around a melismatic voice, over the jingling strokes of a frame drum.
exemplars: Melodiya and Tbilisi Conservatoire recordings of sazandari ensembles

items.name: Apsua song (Abkhaz polyphonic singing)
items.lineage: Vocal music of the Abkhaz of the north-western Caucasus, in which a lead singer's melody is carried over a sustained or slowly moving bass drone sung by the group, mostly in two parts and sometimes three. Work, hero, ritual and dance songs are sung unaccompanied or with the two-string bowed aphyartsa and plucked achamgur, and were recorded by Melodiya from state and village ensembles.
items.description: A solo melody voice rises over a sustained bass drone held by the group in rough-edged two-part harmony, sometimes framed by a scratchy bowed two-string fiddle or a plucked two-string lute.
exemplars: Melodiya recordings of Abkhaz state and village song ensembles

items.name: Mestvireoba (Georgian gudastviri bagpipe bards)
items.lineage: Tradition of the mestvire, itinerant Georgian bard-musicians who sang humorous, satirical and topical verses to the gudastviri, a bagpipe with a skin bag and a double chanter, notably in Racha and Kartli; in Adjara the related bagpipe is the chiboni, and the chiboni card, set to its gudastviri form, stands for the gudastviri.
items.description: A reedy, buzzing bagpipe with two chanter pipes plays a drone-and-melody figure while the piper breaks off to declaim or sing short, witty verses, alternating voice and pipe.
exemplars: Tbilisi State Conservatoire archive field recordings of mestvire gudastviri players

items.name: Rabiz (Yerevan urban popular song)
items.lineage: Urban popular music of Yerevan that grew in the 1970s and 1980s among singers performing at weddings, restaurants and celebrations, setting Armenian songs in the ornamented vocal style and dance rhythms shared with the wider Middle Eastern and Caucasian city tradition. The name is usually traced to rabis, the Soviet abbreviation for art workers; the style spread on cassette, at concerts and later on video.
items.description: A heavily ornamented, emotional lead voice sings over a keyboard arranger's synthesized strings and dance beat, with a clarinet answering in fast melismatic runs.

items.name: Sasna Tsrer (Armenian Sasun epic recitation)
items.lineage: Oral performance of the Armenian heroic epic of the Daredevils of Sasun, whose four cycles follow generations of heroes down to David of Sasun and his son Pokr Mher. Folk tellers, many from the Mush and Sasun districts and their descendants in Armenia, deliver it in alternating prose narration and sung verse; it was first written down from a teller in the nineteenth century and is inscribed on the UNESCO Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.
items.description: A single unaccompanied teller alternates spoken narration with short chanted verse passages on a narrow recurring melody, moving between storytelling voice and song.
exemplars: Institute of Archaeology and Ethnography (Yerevan) recordings of Sasun epic tellers

items.name: Caz-muğam (Azerbaijani jazz-mugham)
items.lineage: Fusion of jazz with the modes and improvisational design of Azerbaijani mugham, developed in Baku from the 1960s by the pianist Vagif Mustafazadeh in piano-led small groups recorded by Melodiya, and carried on from the 1990s by his daughter and by later Baku pianists and ensembles.
items.description: An acoustic piano trio in which the piano unfolds modal melodies with rapid ornamental runs and trills modelled on the lute and voice of mugham, moving between free rubato passages and driving jazz time.

items.name: Zhyr and terme (Kazakh zhyrau epic recitation)
items.lineage: Kazakh tradition of sung epic (zhyr) and terme, a fast recitative of moral and reflective verse, performed by zhyrau and zhyrshy who accompany themselves on the dombyra. The Syr Darya school around Kyzylorda is its best-known living centre, where singers deliver long heroic and historical epics in a forceful, throaty voice over steady dombyra strumming.
items.description: A forceful, throaty voice rapidly declaims long verse lines on a few repeated pitches, opening phrases with sustained cries, over a driving, repetitive two-string lute strum.
exemplars: Kazakh radio archive recordings of Syr Darya zhyrshy

items.name: Lazgi (Khorezm dance music)
items.lineage: Dance and dance music of the Khorezm oasis in north-western Uzbekistan, inscribed on the UNESCO Representative List as Khorazm dance, Lazgi. A lazgi opens slowly and accelerates to a fast, exuberant close, played by surnay and doira in the open air, by garmon accordion and doira, and in estrada arrangements; the surnai card stands for the surnay.
items.description: A loud shawm or accordion repeats a lilting dance tune over jingling frame-drum patterns, starting slow and accelerating steadily to a breathless finish.
exemplars: Surnay-doira and estrada lazgi recordings from Khorezm

items.name: Khalfa (Khorezm women's ritual and wedding singers)
items.lineage: Professional women singers of Khorezm who lead songs at weddings, women's gatherings and other life-cycle rituals, singing to their own garmon accordion with a doira player, in a repertoire running from lyric songs to religious and epic narratives. Razia Sultanova traced the khalfa's role between older shamanic healing practice and Sufi devotion in her study From Shamanism to Sufism.
items.description: A strong female voice sings strophic songs and narrative verses over pumping accordion chords and melody, with a jingling frame drum keeping the rhythm.
exemplars: Khorezm khalfa field recordings documented by Razia Sultanova

items.name: Zhyraw and baqsy (Karakalpak epic and lyric singers)
items.lineage: Two singer traditions of the Karakalpaks of the lower Amu Darya: the zhyraw, who chants heroic epics such as Qyrq Qyz to the bowed qobyz in a strained, guttural voice, and the baqsy, who sings lyric and epic songs to the dutar, often joined by the ghirjek spike fiddle, for which the gijjak card stands; the dutar card is set to its Khorezm and Turkmen forms, the neighbouring schools nearest to the Karakalpak dutar. Both were recorded by Melodiya and in field collections from Karakalpakstan.
items.description: A rough, throaty voice chants epic verse over the hoarse, drone-heavy bowing of a horsehair fiddle, or sings brighter lyric strophes over a plucked two-string lute doubled by a spike fiddle.
exemplars: Melodiya and field recordings of Karakalpak zhyraws and baqsys

items.name: Doston (southern Uzbek baxshi epic singing)
items.lineage: Epic singing of the Uzbek baxshis of Surkhandarya and Kashkadarya in southern Uzbekistan, who perform dostons such as Alpamysh in alternating prose and verse, accompanying themselves on the two-string dombra, for which the dombyra card stands. The southern school is known for bo'g'iq ovoz, a deep, muffled throat voice; UNESCO has proclaimed the cultural space of Boysun District and inscribed the bakhshi art of Uzbekistan.
items.description: A deep, muffled throat voice growls long recitative verse lines over a repetitive strummed two-string lute, alternating sung passages with spoken narration.
exemplars: Baxshi festival recordings of Surkhandarya and Kashkadarya doston singers

items.name: Sozanda (Bukharan women's wedding song ensemble)
items.lineage: Ensembles of professional women singer-dancers of Bukhara, many of them Bukharan Jewish, who performed at women's wedding and celebration gatherings, singing songs in Tajik and Uzbek to the doira frame drum. Songs from the sozanda repertory appear on the Smithsonian Folkways album Bukhara: Musical Crossroads of Asia.
items.description: Bright women's voices sing strophic songs in lead-and-refrain over several jingling frame drums beating interlocking dance rhythms.
exemplars: Smithsonian Folkways, Bukhara: Musical Crossroads of Asia (SFW40050)

items.name: Karnay-surnay (Central Asian ceremonial trumpet and shawm band)
items.lineage: Outdoor ceremonial band of the Uzbek and Tajik oasis cities, in which long straight brass karnay trumpets sound sustained blasts while the surnay shawm plays the melody over naqqora kettledrums and doira, heralding weddings, festivals such as Navruz and public celebrations; the karna card stands for the karnay, the surnai card for the surnay and the nagora card for the naqqora.
items.description: Deep, braying blasts from long brass trumpets punctuate a shrill, ornamented shawm melody over pounding kettledrums and frame drum, all played at full volume in the open air.
exemplars: Wedding and festival field recordings of karnay-surnay ensembles in Uzbekistan

items.name: Küşt depdi (Turkmen ritual song-dance)
items.lineage: Rite of singing and dancing of the Turkmen, inscribed on the UNESCO Representative List, performed at weddings, festivals and other celebrations: a lead singer sings verses while a group of dancers moves in a circle, answering with stamping steps, clapping and shouted refrains. It is kept up by village performers and by folklore ensembles.
items.description: A lead voice sings short verses while a circle of dancers answers with rhythmic shouts, accelerating foot stamps and clapping, building to an ecstatic close.
exemplars: Turkmen folklore-ensemble recordings of küşt depdi

items.name: Marabi (Johannesburg slumyard keyboard and dance-band music)
items.lineage: Working-class urban music of the Johannesburg slumyards of the 1920s and 1930s, such as Doornfontein and Prospect Township, played at shebeen parties on a pedal organ or piano, often with a pebble-filled tin rattle, over a short, endlessly repeated cycle of tonic, subdominant and dominant chords. In the 1930s and 1940s African dance bands such as the Jazz Maniacs and the Merry Blackbirds carried the marabi cycle onto 78 rpm records, and it became a root of kwela, mbaqanga and South African jazz. The shaker card stands in for the tin rattle.
items.description: A keyboard pounds out a short repeating cycle of tonic, subdominant and dominant chords at a steady dance tempo while a shaken rattle keeps time; in the dance-band form saxophones riff on the same cycle over drums, heard through the narrow, surface-noisy band of a 78 rpm disc.

items.name: Malombo (Mamelodi guitar, flute and drum jazz)
items.lineage: Style created in the 1960s in Mamelodi, Pretoria, by guitarist Philip Tabane, who formed the Malombo Jazzmen with flautist Abbey Cindi and drummer Julian Bahula and later worked with percussionist Gabriel Thobejane. It is named after malombo, the drum-led spirit-possession and healing music of the Venda, whose drum patterns and melodies Tabane joined to improvised jazz guitar. The 1969 album The Indigenous Afro-Jazz Sounds of Philip Tabane and His Malombo Jazzmen was reissued by Matsuli Music in 2021. The membrane-drum card stands in for the malombo drums.
items.description: Electric guitar spins long improvised lines and repeated figures over interlocking hand-drum patterns, with flute weaving around the guitar and occasional chanted or hummed vocals, in a sparse small-group texture closer to ritual drumming than to swing.
exemplars: Philip Tabane & His Malombo Jazzmen, The Indigenous Afro-Jazz Sounds of (1969; Matsuli Music reissue 2021)

items.name: Kiba (Pedi reed-pipe and drum dance)
items.lineage: Pedi (Northern Sotho) dance of Sekhukhuneland in which each man in a team blows a single-note end-blown pipe (dinaka) from a graded set, the pipes combining in hocket into one repeating melody over drums; women's kiba, mmapadi, is a sung dance in which a leading singer is answered by a chorus over the same drums. Migrant workers carried kiba to hostels and competitions on the Witwatersrand. Hugh Tracey recorded it for ILAM and it has been studied in the journal African Music. The flute card stands in for the dinaka pipes and the membrane-drum card for the meropa drums.
items.description: Many single-note pipes sounding in rapid hocket interlock into one breathy, hooting melody that cycles over pounding drums; in the women's form a solo voice leads a responding chorus over the drums.
exemplars: Hugh Tracey ILAM field recordings of Pedi kiba

items.name: Tshikona (Venda reed-pipe national dance)
items.lineage: The national dance of the Venda of the Soutpansberg, performed at chiefs' courts for installations, rituals and other important occasions. Men each blow a single-note end-blown pipe from a graded set, the pipes interlocking in hocket into a single repeating melody, while women play the large ngoma, medium murumba and small thungwa drums. John Blacking's 1950s field recordings, held at the University of Washington Ethnomusicology Archives, and the CNRS-CREM archive document it. The flute card stands in for the pipes and the membrane-drum card for the drums.
items.description: A large circle of pipers, each sounding one breathy note, interlocks in rapid hocket so that a single repeating melody seems to rotate around the group, over a deep, steady drum pulse with faster patterns on the smaller drums.
exemplars: John Blacking Venda field recordings (University of Washington Ethnomusicology Archives)
CNRS-CREM archive recordings of Venda tshikona

items.name: Domba (Venda girls' initiation python dance)
items.lineage: Final stage of Venda girls' initiation, organised at a chief's court, in which the initiates dance in a tight, linked line likened to a python while a large drum is played and domba songs are sung in call and response; the teachings of the school are passed on through its songs and formulas. John Blacking recorded and studied domba in the 1950s, and his recordings are held at the University of Washington Ethnomusicology Archives. The membrane-drum card stands in for the ngoma drum.
items.description: A leader's call and a large chorus of young women's voices answer one another in short, repeated phrases over the steady beat of a large drum, the song cycling for as long as the line of dancers keeps moving.
exemplars: John Blacking Venda field recordings of domba (University of Washington Ethnomusicology Archives)

items.name: Cape Malay choirs (nederlandslied and moppie)
items.lineage: Competition choirs of Cape Town's Muslim community, the Malay choirs or nagtroepe, which compete each year under bodies such as the Cape Malay Choir Board in categories including the nederlandslied and the moppie. The nederlandslied, a song in Dutch or Afrikaans descended from old Dutch repertoire, sets a solo voice with dense melismatic ornament against the choir, while the moppie is a fast comic song. The choirs are accompanied by a string band of guitars, banjos and bass, with the ghoema drum in the comic songs. The banjo card stands in for the banjos and the hand-drum card for the ghoema.
items.description: In the nederlandslied a high solo voice draws out each phrase in long, ornamented melismas while a men's choir answers in sustained harmony over strummed guitars, banjos and bass; the moppie switches to brisk, comic choral verses driven by the drum.
exemplars: Cape Malay Choir Board competition recordings (Cape Town)

items.name: Kaapse Klopse (Cape Town minstrel-carnival troupes)
items.lineage: New Year carnival of Cape Town's working-class Coloured communities, in which costumed troupes (klopse) march through the city on Tweede Nuwe Jaar, 2 January, and then compete in stadium contests. It grew from New Year street celebrations after the emancipation of slaves at the Cape and absorbed the blackface minstrel shows that toured Cape Town in the later nineteenth century. Troupes sing ghoemaliedjies, street songs over the ghoema drum, with banjos, guitars and brass; Denis-Constant Martin has documented the carnival. The hand-drum card stands in for the ghoema drum.
items.description: Massed voices bellow singalong street songs over the syncopated, swaying two-beat pattern of the ghoema drum, with strummed banjos and guitars and blaring brass, the sound loud, festive and moving with the marching crowd.
exemplars: Kaapse Klopse troupe and carnival compilation recordings (Cape Town)

items.name: Langarm (Cape ballroom dance-band music)
items.lineage: Ballroom dance music of the Coloured communities of the Western Cape, named after the extended long-arm hold of its couple dances, played by dance bands at community dances through much of the twentieth century. Saxophone-led bands play waltzes and other ballroom rhythms for couples, and Denis-Constant Martin discusses the music in his study Sounding the Cape. The acoustic-bass card stands in for the band's bass.
items.description: A saxophone carries the dance melodies over a steady rhythm section of piano, bass and drums, moving between gliding waltzes and brisker ballroom rhythms for the couples on the floor.
exemplars: Cape langarm dance-band records discussed in Denis-Constant Martin, Sounding the Cape (2013)

items.name: Izihlabelelo zamaNazaretha (Shembe hymns and sacred dance)
items.lineage: Hymnody and sacred dance of the Nazareth Baptist Church (amaNazaretha), the African independent church founded by the prophet Isaiah Shembe, whose early centre was Ekuphakameni at Inanda, near Durban. Its hymnal, Izihlabelelo zamaNazaretha, holds isiZulu hymns by Isaiah Shembe and his son and successor Johannes Galilee Shembe, sung by the congregation and in the sacred dances of the church's festivals, where drums and long imbomu trumpets accompany the dancers. Carol Ann Muller studied the women's performance and edited the hymns with an accompanying CD. The membrane-drum card stands in for the drums and the horns card for the imbomu.
items.description: A song leader starts each hymn and a large barefoot congregation answers in slow, full-voiced harmony; in the sacred dances the singing turns rhythmic over heavy drumbeats and stamping feet, with long trumpets sounding sustained calls above.
exemplars: Shembe Hymns (ed. Carol Ann Muller, UKZN Press 2010, with CD)

items.name: Ingoma (Zulu competitive dance-song)
items.lineage: Zulu dance-song genre, also called indlamu, performed by teams of young men, rooted in rural KwaZulu-Natal and developed by migrant workers in Durban and Witwatersrand hostels into weekend competitions, with regional styles such as isishameni and isizingili. Dancers sing in call and response and end phrases with high kicks and forceful stamps that land together, often with drums and clapping. Hugh Tracey recorded ingoma for ILAM, and Louise Meintjes studied ngoma teams in Dust of the Zulu. The membrane-drum card stands in for the drum.
items.description: A leader's call and a chorus of young men's voices trade short, repeated phrases, punctuated by unison stamps that hit the ground like a bass drum, with drumming and clapping driving each routine to its climax.
exemplars: Hugh Tracey ILAM recordings of Zulu ingoma

items.name: Umakhweyana and ugubhu (Zulu musical-bow song)
items.lineage: Zulu song accompanied by gourd-resonated musical bows, played mainly by women: the ugubhu, a long unbraced bow whose struck string is stopped by the fingers, and the umakhweyana, a braced bow whose divided string gives two fundamentals. Princess Constance Magogo kaDinuzulu was its outstanding performer and was recorded by the ethnomusicologist David Rycroft. The braced makhoyane card, its Swazi counterpart, stands in for the umakhweyana.
items.description: A single singer sets a melody against the soft, buzzing pulse of a struck bow string, whose gourd, opened and closed against the body, lifts out shifting overtones above two alternating fundamental tones.
exemplars: Princess Constance Magogo kaDinuzulu (recorded by David Rycroft)

items.name: Amahubo (Zulu royal and regimental anthems)
items.lineage: Solemn collective anthems (singular ihubo) of the Zulu kingdom and its clans, sung by assembled regiments and people at royal ceremonies such as the umkhosi first-fruits festival and by clans at weddings and funerals; each clan and regiment has its own ihubo. They are sung by massed voices in call and response, without instruments. ILAM and SABC archival recordings document them.
items.description: Massed voices sing slow, weighty phrases in overlapping call and response, the leader's line and the deep group answer interlocking in a solemn, repetitive cycle with no instruments.
exemplars: ILAM archival recordings of Zulu amahubo

items.name: Ingoma yezangoma (Nguni diviners' healing song and dance)
items.lineage: Song and dance of Nguni diviner-healers, the izangoma of the Zulu and the amagqirha of the Xhosa, performed at intlombe gatherings, initiations and healing sessions, where diviners and initiates dance to call on the ancestors. A leader raises a song that the gathering answers in layered call and response, over drumming and hard rhythmic clapping. ILAM field recordings and Dave Dargie's recordings of Xhosa amagqirha songs document the practice. The membrane-drum card stands in for the drums.
items.description: A leader raises a song and the gathering answers in overlapping, multi-part call and response over insistent drumming and sharp, massed clapping, the repetition building in intensity as the diviners dance.
exemplars: Dave Dargie recordings of Xhosa amagqirha songs
ILAM field recordings of Nguni diviners' songs

items.name: Xitsonga traditional dance-song (xigubu, muchongolo, xibelani)
items.lineage: Traditional song and dance of the Tsonga (Shangaan) of Limpopo, Mpumalanga and southern Mozambique, including xigubu drum dances, the men's muchongolo dance and the women's xibelani dance, named after the layered skirt that the dancers' rapid hip movements set swirling. Songs are led by a singer and answered by the group over drums and clapping. ILAM recorded Tsonga music, and Thomas F. Johnston published studies of Shangana-Tsonga music. The membrane-drum card stands in for the drums.
items.description: A lead singer's call is answered by a bright group chorus over fast, interlocking drum patterns and clapping, the tempo pushing the dancers' quick, shaking hip and foot movements.
exemplars: ILAM recordings of Tsonga traditional music

items.name: Lekompo (Limpopo Sepedi dance music)
items.lineage: Electronic party and dance music from Limpopo, sung and chanted mainly in Sepedi, that rose to national prominence through local parties and streaming in the early 2020s. Producers build tracks from programmed drums and repeating keyboard riffs under chanted and shouted vocals, and performers such as Shebeshxt brought it national attention. Press accounts treat it as distinct from neighbouring Bolobedu house.
items.description: Chanted and shouted Sepedi vocals ride a fast, bouncing programmed beat and short repeating keyboard riffs, built for dancing at parties.

items.name: Voëlvry (1989 Afrikaans alternative rock movement)
items.lineage: Afrikaans-language protest-rock movement launched by Shifty Records, whose 1989 Voëlvry tour of university campuses brought Johannes Kerkorrel en die Gereformeerde Blues Band, Koos Kombuis and Bernoldus Niemand (James Phillips) to young Afrikaner audiences. Its songs mocked apartheid and the conservative Afrikaner establishment in blues- and punk-inflected rock and are regarded as a turning point in Afrikaans popular music. The name means both 'free as a bird' and 'outlawed'.
items.description: Sardonic vocals, half-sung and half-declaimed, ride raw electric guitar, bass, drums and keyboards in short, punchy rock songs that lean on blues riffs and punk directness.
exemplars: Johannes Kerkorrel en die Gereformeerde Blues Band

items.name: Riel (Khoi- and San-descended rieldans music)
items.lineage: Fast social dance of Khoi- and San-descended communities of the Western and Northern Cape, regarded as one of South Africa's oldest indigenous dance forms and known to the Nama as ikhapara, in which dancers in pairs or groups perform rapid, low footwork that raises dust. It is danced to riel songs played on guitar and fiddle, sometimes with banjo, accordion or drums, amid clapping and shouts. The ATKV runs a national rieldans competition, and groups such as the Nuwe Graskoue Trappers of Wupperthal in the Cederberg carry it on.
items.description: A strummed guitar and a fiddle drive a fast, repeating dance tune while singers and onlookers clap and shout encouragement over the scuffing footwork of the dancers.

items.name: Lifela (Basotho migrants' sung poetry)
items.lineage: Sefela (plural lifela), the sung poetry of Basotho men who travelled to work in the gold mines of the Witwatersrand, known as lifela tsa litsamaea-naha, 'songs of the inveterate travellers'. Each poet composes and performs his own long autobiographical text of journeys, mine labour, love and home in a rapid chanted delivery, sometimes in contests between poets; David Coplan's study In the Time of Cannibals documents its texts, performers and links with famo accordion song.
items.description: A single male voice pours out long chanted verse in rapid, speech-shaped phrases, with no accompaniment.
exemplars: Lifela texts and performances documented in David Coplan, In the Time of Cannibals (University of Chicago Press, 1994)

items.name: Mokorotlo (Basotho men's war song)
items.lineage: Mokorotlo is a group song of Basotho men, described as a war or riding song and sung on ceremonial and national occasions, with individual men stepping out to declaim lithoko praise poetry over the song while the singers stamp in a slow, stately dance. Hugh Tracey recorded unaccompanied mokorotlo with lithoko by groups of Sotho men for the International Library of African Music.
items.description: A deep massed men's chorus repeats a heavy unaccompanied song phrase over stamped steps while solo voices break out in rapid declaimed praise poetry above it.
exemplars: ILAM (Hugh Tracey) field tapes, 'Mokorotlo with Lithoko', Sotho men's group, 1957

items.name: Mbende Jerusarema (Zezuru dance-drumming)
items.lineage: Dance of the Zezuru Shona of Murewa and Uzumba-Maramba-Pfungwe in Mashonaland East, originally called mbende ('mole') and renamed Jerusarema in the colonial period to make it acceptable to missionaries. Men and women dance to drumming, singing and hand-clapping, the men in crouching, acrobatic movements; UNESCO has proclaimed it a Masterpiece of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity. The generic membrane-drum card stands in for the Shona ngoma drums.
items.description: Fast, insistent drum patterns drive leader-and-chorus singing and sharp hand-claps in a tight, energetic dance cycle.
exemplars: UNESCO intangible-heritage documentation of Mbende Jerusarema dance, Murewa

items.name: Muchongoyo (Ndau men's dance-drumming)
items.lineage: Dance of the Ndau of Chipinge and Chimanimani in south-eastern Zimbabwe, in which lines of men stamp and leap to drumming while women sing and clap. It is performed at community celebrations and festivals. The generic membrane-drum card stands in for the Ndau drums.
items.description: Pounding drums and the thud of stamped steps carry women's leader-and-chorus singing and hand-claps in a vigorous, martial dance cycle.
exemplars: Field recordings of Ndau muchongoyo dance, Chipinge district

items.name: Isitshikitsha (Ndebele dance-song of Matabeleland)
items.lineage: Dance-song of the Ndebele of Matabeleland in south-western Zimbabwe, performed by community and festival troupes and in the repertoire of the National Ballet of Zimbabwe. A song leader and chorus sing while dancers stamp and clap in unison.
items.description: A leader's call and the chorus's full answer ride on unison stamped steps and hand-claps in a steady, stately dance pulse.
exemplars: Festival and National Ballet of Zimbabwe performances of isitshikitsha

items.name: Mhande (Karanga ceremonial dance-song)
items.lineage: Ceremonial dance-song of the Karanga Shona of Masvingo province, performed in mukwerera rain-petitioning rites and in kurova guva, the ceremony that brings home the spirit of a deceased elder, where song and dance address the ancestors. It is sung in call and response to drumming, hosho rattles and hand-clapping, and has been documented in studies by the ethnomusicologist Jerry Rutsate. The generic membrane-drum card stands in for the ngoma drum.
items.description: Leader-and-chorus song over a rolling drum pattern, shaken gourd rattles and hand-claps, building in a long repeating ceremonial cycle.
exemplars: Mhande in kurova guva and mukwerera rites as documented in Jerry Rutsate's studies, Masvingo

items.name: Kwanongoma marimba (Zimbabwean marimba ensemble)
items.lineage: Ensemble music for the marimbas developed at the Kwanongoma College of African Music in Bulawayo from the early 1960s, built in soprano, tenor, baritone and bass sizes and played in interlocking parts with hosho rattles, often arranging mbira and other Zimbabwean songs. Dumisani Maraire, who studied at Kwanongoma, took the style to the University of Washington in Seattle in the late 1960s, seeding many North American Zimbabwean-style marimba bands. The orchestral marimba card, with padauk (Pterocarpus) bars, stands in for the Kwanongoma instruments, whose keys are cut from local mukwa (Pterocarpus) hardwood.
items.description: Several wooden-keyed marimbas from bright treble to booming bass interlock in repeating cycles under steady shaken rattles, with occasional sung refrains.
exemplars: Kwanongoma College of African Music marimba ensembles, Bulawayo
Dumisani Maraire's marimba ensembles at the University of Washington, Seattle

items.name: Vapostori hymnody (Zimbabwean Apostolic church song)
items.lineage: Congregational song of Zimbabwe's African Apostolic churches, chiefly the Johane Marange church of Manicaland and the Johane Masowe churches, whose white-robed members worship in the open air. Hymns in Shona are raised by a song leader and taken up by the whole congregation in close multi-part harmony, and singing runs through the long services and the large annual gatherings.
items.description: A song leader raises a hymn line and a large open-air congregation answers in full, overlapping multi-part harmony, repeating the cycle with growing intensity.
exemplars: Field and commercial recordings of Vapostori (Johane Marange and Masowe) congregational song

items.name: Kalindula (Zambian popular band music)
items.lineage: Zambian popular band music that grew in the 1970s and 1980s from the string-band dance music of Luapula and Northern Province, named after the kalindula, a homemade bass instrument of those bands. Sung mainly in Bemba, it became the leading Zambian band sound on radio and record through groups and singers such as Amayenge, PK Chishala and Mashombe Blue Jeans; the electric bass card stands in for the kalindula bass in band line-ups.
items.description: Bright interlocking electric guitar lines and a busy, bouncing bass run over brisk drums beneath a lead vocal.

items.name: Makishi masquerade music (Luvale mukanda, Zambia)
items.lineage: Music of the makishi masked dancers who appear during and at the close of mukanda, the boys' initiation of the Luvale, Chokwe, Luchazi and Mbunda peoples of North-Western and Western Zambia; the Makishi masquerade is on UNESCO's intangible heritage list. Women and initiates sing in call and response to a drum ensemble as the masks dance, and the masquerade is a centrepiece of the Luvale Likumbi lya Mize festival at Zambezi. The Zambian Luvale practice is entered separately from the Angolan Chokwe mukanda recordings. The generic membrane-drum card stands in for the Luvale drums.
items.description: Several drums lock into a driving pattern for the masked dancers while women's and boys' voices trade leader-and-chorus lines over clapping.
exemplars: UNESCO intangible-heritage documentation of the Makishi masquerade, Zambia
Makishi performances at the Likumbi lya Mize festival, Zambezi

items.name: Mooba (Lenje spirit dance of Central Zambia)
items.lineage: The main dance of the Lenje of Zambia's Central Province, also practised in parts of the Copperbelt and Lusaka provinces by both men and women, at funerals, harvest, healing sessions and the installation of traditional leaders. At its peak lead dancers may be possessed by ancestral spirits called BaChooba, said to take over the flow of the dancing, drumming and singing; dancers wear rattles around the calves. It is inscribed on UNESCO's Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage. The generic shaker card stands in for the calf rattles.
items.description: Insistent drumming and the shake of dancers' leg rattles drive communal singing that intensifies in long cycles toward trance.
exemplars: UNESCO intangible-heritage video documentation of the Mooba dance of the Lenje

items.name: Kalela (Copperbelt mine-town team dance)
items.lineage: Team dance-song of the Northern Rhodesian Copperbelt mine towns in the 1950s, performed by troupes of Bisa migrants from the Luapula region, smartly dressed in European clothes and led by a 'king', singing about town life and their home district to drums. J. Clyde Mitchell analysed it in The Kalela Dance (Rhodes-Livingstone Papers 27, 1956), and Hugh Tracey recorded kalela on the Copperbelt for ILAM. The generic membrane-drum card stands in for the kalela drums.
items.description: A song leader and a chorus of dancers sing topical verses in call and response over steady, interlocking drum patterns.
exemplars: ILAM (Hugh Tracey) Copperbelt recordings of kalela
J. Clyde Mitchell, The Kalela Dance (1956)

items.name: Lozi royal music (Kuomboka drums and silimba)
items.lineage: Music of the Lozi kingdom of Barotseland in Zambia's Western Province, centred on the court of the Litunga at Lealui. Its emblems are the royal maoma drums, beaten aboard the royal barge Nalikwanda as paddlers carry the Litunga from Lealui to Limulunga in the annual Kuomboka flood ceremony, and the silimba, the Lozi gourd-resonated xylophone heard at court and in dance. The generic membrane-drum card stands in for the maoma and the orchestral marimba card, with padauk (Pterocarpus) bars, for the silimba.
items.description: Massive royal drums boom a steady processional beat while a buzzing gourd-resonated xylophone spins repeating patterns and voices answer in chorus.
exemplars: ILAM (Hugh Tracey) recordings of Lozi silimba xylophone music, Barotseland

items.name: Ingoma (Ngoni war dance of Malawi and Zambia)
items.lineage: War dance-song of the Ngoni, descendants of Nguni groups, among them the followers of Zwangendaba, who migrated north across the Zambezi in the nineteenth century and settled in northern and central Malawi and eastern Zambia. Men in skins with shields and sticks dance in lines with high kicks and heavy stamping while singing war and praise songs; it is performed at the Umthetho festival of the M'mbelwa Ngoni at Mzimba and at the Ncwala ceremony of the Mpezeni Ngoni near Chipata.
items.description: A deep massed men's chorus answers its leader in heavy, martial phrases punctuated by unison stamping and claps.
exemplars: ILAM (Hugh Tracey) field recordings of Ngoni music, Mzimba district
Umthetho festival performances of ingoma, Mzimba

items.name: Mapiko (Makonde masked dance-drumming)
items.lineage: Masked dance of the Makonde of the Mueda plateau in Cabo Delgado, northern Mozambique, in which a dancer wearing a carved helmet mask (lipiko) and cloth costume performs to an ensemble of drums and the songs of a chorus. Paolo Israel's study In Step with the Times traces how mapiko troupes changed through the colonial, liberation-war and socialist periods. The generic membrane-drum card stands in for the mapiko drum ensemble.
items.description: A dense drum ensemble lays down fast, layered patterns and sharp breaks matched to the masked dancer's moves, while a chorus sings leader-and-response songs.
exemplars: Mapiko performance documentation in Paolo Israel, In Step with the Times (Ohio University Press, 2014)

items.name: Tufo (Makua women's frame-drum dance-song)
items.lineage: Dance-song of Muslim Makua women of Ilha de Moçambique and the Nampula coast, whose name derives from the Arabic ad-duff, the frame drum. Groups of women in matching capulana cloths and headscarves sing in Makua and dance with upper-body and arm movements to large round frame drums; once linked to Islamic celebrations, tufo is now also danced at secular festivities, and groups such as Tufo da Mafalala carry it in Maputo. The generic membrane-drum card stands in for the tufo frame drums.
items.description: Women's leader-and-chorus song floats over the deep thump and slap of several large frame drums in a swaying, repeating dance cycle.

items.name: Pandza (Maputo electronic dance-pop)
items.lineage: Mozambican popular dance music from Maputo that emerged in the 2000s, blending marrabenta rhythms with ragga and dancehall over programmed electronic beats, sung mostly in Portuguese and Changana. N'Star, Ziqo and Dj Ardiles popularised it, and singers such as Lizha James took it into the mainstream.
items.description: Bouncing programmed drums and synth riffs carry a quick marrabenta-style groove under chanted, dancehall-inflected vocals and catchy sung hooks.

items.name: Makwayela (southern Mozambican choral dance)
items.lineage: Makwayela is a choral song-and-dance form of southern Mozambique that grew up among the men who migrated to work in the South African mines; its name comes from makwaya, the local word for a choir. A line of singers performs songs in multi-part harmony while executing tightly synchronised steps and stamps, and after independence the form was widely performed by workers' groups in and around Maputo.
items.description: A chorus sings strophic songs in full multi-part harmony over the firm, even pulse of unison steps and foot stamps.

items.name: Nyanga (Nyungwe panpipe dance)
items.lineage: Nyanga is the panpipe dance of the Nyungwe people of Tete province in the Zambezi valley of Mozambique: a large group of men, each playing a set of a few reed pipes, dance in a circle while their notes interlock in hocket and their voices join the pipes. Andrew Tracey recorded it for the International Library of African Music and analysed it in the journal African Music; the ngororombe panpipe dance of north-eastern Zimbabwe is a closely related practice. The generic flute card stands in for the nyanga reed pipes.
items.description: Many short pipe parts, each only a few notes, interlock in a dense hocketed cycle, with breathy blown tones and voices weaving through the circling dance.
exemplars: Andrew Tracey field recordings of Nyungwe nyanga (International Library of African Music)

items.name: Tromba (Sakalava spirit-possession music)
items.lineage: Tromba is the spirit-possession practice of western and northern Madagascar, centred on the Sakalava, in which the spirits of deceased royalty are called to enter mediums during ceremonies driven by music. Ron Emoff's study Recollecting from the Past documents tromba music on the east coast, where accordion and valiha accompany singing, hand-clapping and rattles; the kayamba card stands in for the Malagasy raft rattle.
items.description: Insistent, cyclic accordion and zither figures repeat over shaken rattles and massed hand-claps while a leader and the gathered participants sing, the music building in intensity through the ceremony.
exemplars: Ron Emoff, Recollecting from the Past: Musical Practice and Spirit Possession on the East Coast of Madagascar (Wesleyan University Press, 2002)

items.name: Kalon'ny fahiny (Malagasy 'songs of olden times')
items.lineage: Kalon'ny fahiny ('songs of the past') is a song genre of the Merina highlands that derives from Malagasy-language theatre and operetta. It flourished in 1920–1940 at the Théâtre d'Isotry in Antananarivo, where pieces were written for piano with solo, duet or choral singing in Malagasy, and the pianist-composer Andrianary Ratianarivo founded Troupe Jeannette, which still performs there.
items.description: Sentimental strophic songs in Western major and minor harmony, sung by a solo voice, a duet or a small chorus over a gently lilting piano accompaniment.
exemplars: Andrianary Ratianarivo (pianist-composer; Troupe Jeannette, Théâtre d'Isotry)

items.name: Kilalaky (Menabe dance music)
items.lineage: Kilalaky is a dance-music genre from the Menabe region around Morondava on the west coast of Madagascar, built on a fast, driving groove. Modern kilalaky bands play it on electric guitar, bass, keyboards and drums, and the singer Tsiliva carried it to national popularity from the mid-2000s.
items.description: A fast, rolling dance groove of bright electric guitar, bass and drums carries a lead singer and answering backing vocals, built for nonstop dancing.

items.name: Basesa (east-coast Malagasy dance music)
items.lineage: Basesa is a fast, accordion-led dance music of the Betsimisaraka east coast of Madagascar around Toamasina. Bands play it with accordion over electric guitar, bass and drums, and the duo Mika sy Davis made it popular across the island.
items.description: A driving accordion line and quick electric guitar figures ride a fast dance beat under a lead singer and group refrains.

items.name: Beko (southern Malagasy vocal polyphony)
items.lineage: Beko is the funeral song of the Antandroy (Tandroy) of the dry far south of Madagascar: an a cappella polyphony, usually of two or three voices, in which a lead singer improvises verses recounting the deceased's genealogy, character and passions while the others sustain an accompanying part. Its specialist singers, the mpibeko, sing in a high register with a deliberately nasal, trembling timbre, partly stopping an ear with a finger to monitor the voice.
items.description: Two or three unaccompanied voices sing at once in a high, nasal, trembling register, a lead improvising long lines of text over a sustained accompanying voice, solemn and full-throated.
exemplars: CREM-CNRS (Musée de l'Homme) archive recordings of Antandroy beko

items.name: Kanmtole (Seychellois contredanse)
items.lineage: Kanmtole is a Seychellois figure dance for couples in the contredanse family, taken over from European country dancing and played by a small string-and-accordion band. It belongs to the islands' older European-derived dance repertoire and is distinct from the moutya drum dance.
items.description: Fiddle and accordion play bright, square-cut dance tunes in sections, over strummed banjo, a ringing triangle and a steady drum beat that marks the figures.
exemplars: Seychelles traditional-music recordings of kanmtole dance tunes

items.name: M'godro (Mayotte dance music)
items.lineage: M'godro is a Mahorais dance-song form, performed both at village festivities and by modern bands with electric guitar, bass, keyboards and drums, and it is the most widespread popular style of Mayotte. M'Toro Chamou is among its best-known performers.
items.description: A lilting, repetitive dance groove of electric guitar, bass, keyboards and drums supports a lead singer answered by group refrains.

items.name: Debaa (Mahorais women's Sufi chant)
items.lineage: Debaa is a devotional practice of women in Mayotte, in which groups in matching dress sing religious poems in praise of the Prophet, led by a soloist, accompanied by frame drums and performed with synchronised movements of the hands, arms and upper body.
items.description: A lead singer's devotional lines are answered by a chorus of women in unison over steady frame-drum patterns, in long, swaying repetitive cycles.
exemplars: Debaa groups documented by the DAC Mayotte (Musiques de Mayotte)

items.name: Shigoma (Comorian men's wedding dance)
items.lineage: Shigoma (chigoma) is a men's dance of the Comoros and Mayotte, performed above all during the festivities of the grand wedding, in which men in festive dress dance in formation to large drums and sung refrains. The generic membrane-drum card stands in for the Comorian drums.
items.description: Heavy, steady drumming drives a men's chorus answering a leader in short, repeated refrains for a dance in formation.
exemplars: CREM (Centre de recherche en ethnomusicologie) archive recordings of chigoma

items.name: Seperu (Basubiya folk dance)
items.lineage: Seperu is the folk dance of the Basubiya people of the Chobe District of northern Botswana, danced by men and women at weddings, celebrations and other social occasions to drumming, singing and hand-clapping. UNESCO inscribed Seperu folkdance and associated practices on its List of Intangible Cultural Heritage in Need of Urgent Safeguarding. The generic membrane-drum card stands in for the Basubiya drums.
items.description: Drums lay down a lively repeating beat under leader-and-chorus singing and massed hand-claps for a couple and group dance.
exemplars: UNESCO Urgent Safeguarding List documentation of Seperu folkdance and associated practices (2019)

items.name: Aixan/Gana/Ob#ANS TSI //Khasigu (Nama ancestral music)
items.lineage: The ancestral music of the Nama people of southern Namibia, inscribed by UNESCO on its List of Intangible Cultural Heritage in Need of Urgent Safeguarding. A leading melody and rhythm on the khab musical bow, the !guitsib guitar or the accordion is supported by harmony from other instruments, including the vlies (harmonica) usually played by women, with singing, humming and ululating, and it accompanies the Nama dance steps. The mouth-bow card stands in for the khab.
items.description: A bow, guitar or accordion leads a lilting dance melody while harmonica and other instruments fill in harmony beneath singing, humming and ululation.
exemplars: UNESCO Urgent Safeguarding List file for Aixan/Gana/Ob#ANS TSI //Khasigu, ancestral musical sound knowledge and skills (2020)

items.name: Shambo (Oshiwambo dance music)
items.lineage: Shambo is a popular dance music sung in Oshiwambo and centred in the north-central regions of Namibia, played by bands on electric guitar, keyboards, bass and drums. The Namibian Annual Music Awards recognise it as a genre category of its own.
items.description: Quick, chiming electric guitar riffs and keyboards ride a fast dance beat under a lead singer and group refrains.
exemplars: Releases in the Namibian Annual Music Awards shambo category

items.name: Oviritje (Otjiherero popular music)
items.lineage: Oviritje is a popular music of the Ovaherero of Namibia, sung in Otjiherero and drawing on Herero song, typically performed by singers over keyboard synthesiser and programmed beats. The Namibian Annual Music Awards recognise it as a genre category of its own.
items.description: Keyboard synthesiser melodies and chords and a programmed beat support a lead singer and answering voices in steady, repeating dance songs.
exemplars: Releases in the Namibian Annual Music Awards oviritje category

items.name: Damara punch (Khoekhoegowab dance music)
items.lineage: Damara punch is a popular dance music of the Damara people of Namibia, sung in Khoekhoegowab over keyboards and programmed or played drums. The Namibian Annual Music Awards recognise it as a genre category of its own.
items.description: Bouncy keyboard riffs and a quick, punchy beat drive a lead singer and group refrains in upbeat party songs.
exemplars: Releases in the Namibian Annual Music Awards Damara punch category

items.name: Kathakali sangeetham (Kerala dance-drama music)
items.lineage: Kathakali, the dance-drama of Kerala that took shape in the seventeenth century out of Ramanattam, is sung entirely by two singers standing behind the actors: the lead singer (ponnani) keeps time on the chengila, a bell-metal gong, and the second singer (singidi) answers him on ilathalam cymbals. They sing the Manipravalam padams of the play text in ragas and talas, while chenda and suddha maddalam drummers accompany the actors' gestures. Kerala Kalamandalam, founded by the poet Vallathol Narayana Menon, became its main training school.
items.description: Two male voices trade lines of raga-based song in a high, projected register over the clang of a small gong and cymbals, while a stick-beaten cylinder drum and a hand-played barrel drum surge and punctuate beneath them.
exemplars: Maison des Cultures du Monde (Inédit) 'Drames dansés de l'Inde du Sud' (Kathakali excerpts)
Le Chant du Monde 'South India: ritual music and theatre of Kerala' (Kathakali excerpts)

items.name: Sopana sangeetham (Kerala temple-step song)
items.lineage: Sopana sangeetham is the devotional singing of Kerala temples, performed by the Marar and Pothuval temple-servant communities on the steps (sopanam) that lead to the inner sanctum during worship, its central repertoire being the ashtapadi songs of Jayadeva's Gita Govinda. The singer accompanies himself on the idakka, the hourglass drum whose pitch is bent by squeezing its lacing. Njeralathu Rama Poduval carried the style from the temple to the concert platform.
items.description: A single voice sings slow, unhurried devotional verse in a plain, open tone, shadowed by the hourglass drum's gliding, pitch-bent strokes that follow the melody.
exemplars: Kerala temple field recordings of sopanam singing

items.name: Panchavadyam (Kerala temple five-instrument orchestra)
items.lineage: Panchavadyam ('five instruments') is a Kerala temple orchestra of four percussion instruments, the timila hourglass drum, the suddha maddalam barrel drum, the idakka and the ilathalam cymbals, with one wind instrument, the kombu horn, and a conch blown at the outset. Played at temple festivals and processions in central Kerala, a performance builds by stages from a slow, long rhythmic cycle to a fast climax; the Madathil Varavu at Thrissur Pooram is its best-known setting.
items.description: Rows of hand-struck hourglass drums lead a dense, interlocking percussion mass over barrel drums and pulsing bell-metal cymbals, with brass horns blaring at the ends of phrases as the tempo tightens to a climax.
exemplars: Thrissur Pooram Madathil Varavu field recordings

items.name: Chenda melam (Kerala temple drum orchestra)
items.lineage: Chenda melam is the massed drumming of Kerala temple festivals, in which ranks of chenda players, divided between the uruttu chenda that carries the rhythmic elaboration and the deeper veekku chenda that keeps the beat, play with ilathalam cymbals, kuzhal shawms and kombu horns. Its main forms include panchari melam, in a six-beat cycle played in stages of increasing tempo, and pandi melam, the form played in the Ilanjithara melam at Thrissur Pooram.
items.description: A wall of stick-beaten cylinder drums, rolling lead patterns over a pounding unison bass beat, locked to clashing bell-metal cymbals and pierced by shrill reeds and blaring horns, accelerating in stages to a thunderous peak.
exemplars: Thrissur Pooram Ilanjithara melam broadcasts (All India Radio Thrissur)

items.name: Thayambaka (Kerala solo chenda improvisation)
items.lineage: Thayambaka is a virtuoso chenda genre of Kerala temples in which a lead drummer improvises on the uruttu chenda against a group of accompanists who keep a steady beat on the veekku chenda and ilathalam cymbals. Usually performed in the evening at temple festivals, it moves through set stages of increasing tempo from a slow opening to fast improvised passages, and double and triple thayambaka share the lead between two or three drummers.
items.description: A single lead cylinder drum spins out fast, virtuosic stick patterns and rolls over a steady pulse of bass drums and cymbals, accelerating through stages to a dense, cracking climax.

items.name: Theyyam thottam (north Malabar ritual invocation song)
items.lineage: Theyyam is the ritual worship of north Malabar in Kerala, in which a performer from a hereditary community such as the Vannan, Malayan or Velan is costumed and embodies a deity at village shrines (kavu) during the festival season. The thottam, the invocatory song narrating the deity's story, is sung by the performer and his assistants before the deity appears, accompanied by chenda drums, ilathalam cymbals and the kuzhal shawm.
items.description: Chanted narrative verse in a hoarse, insistent voice over fast, stick-beaten cylinder drums and clashing cymbals, with a shrill reed joining as the drumming swells toward the deity's appearance.
exemplars: Field recordings of thottam songs at north Malabar kavu shrines

items.name: Mudiyettu (Kerala Kali ritual-drama music)
items.lineage: Mudiyettu is a ritual dance-drama of central Kerala enacting the battle of the goddess Kali with the demon Darika, performed by the Marar and Kuruppu communities in the Bhagavati temples (kavu) of villages along the Chalakudy, Periyar and Moovattupuzha rivers after the summer harvest. It begins with a drawing of Kali (kalam) in coloured powders and is carried by chenda drumming, ilathalam cymbals and songs. It is inscribed on UNESCO's Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage.
items.description: Loud stick-beaten cylinder drumming and clashing cymbals drive a night-long ritual drama, with sung invocations and declaimed exchanges between the masked characters riding above the percussion.
exemplars: UNESCO Representative List documentation of Mudiyettu (2010)
Sangeet Natak Akademi documentation of Mudiyettu

items.name: Judeo-Malayalam women's song (Cochin Jewish)
items.lineage: The Jews of Kerala, centred on Kochi (Cochin) and nearby towns such as Mala, Chendamangalam and Paravur, kept a repertoire of Malayalam-language songs sung by women at weddings and other life-cycle and festival occasions, alongside the Hebrew liturgy of the synagogue.
