After most of the community emigrated to Israel in the mid-twentieth century, the songs were documented by researchers in Israel and Kerala.
items.description: Women sing strophic Malayalam verse together, unaccompanied, in a plain and even tone over simple repeating melodies.
exemplars: Jewish Music Research Centre anthology 'Oh, Lovely Parrot! Jewish Women's Songs from Kerala'

items.name: Kathaprasangam (Malayalam musical storytelling)
items.lineage: Kathaprasangam is a Malayalam storytelling form in which a single narrator tells a story, often adapted from literature, alternating spoken narration with songs, accompanied by a small group on harmonium, tabla and other instruments. It emerged in early twentieth-century Kerala and reached mass popularity through V. Sambasivan, who adapted Malayalam and world literature and whose performances circulated widely on LP and cassette.
items.description: A single narrator moves between dramatic spoken storytelling and full-voiced songs, with harmonium and tabla stepping in under the sung passages and punctuating the climaxes.
exemplars: V. Sambasivan kathaprasangam LP and cassette recordings

items.name: Bharatanatyam music (nattuvangam margam ensemble)
items.lineage: Bharatanatyam, the classical dance of Tamil Nadu that grew out of sadir, the dance of temple and court dancers, is accompanied by a Carnatic ensemble led by the nattuvanar, who recites rhythmic syllables (sollukattu) and keeps time on small cymbals (nattuvangam; the manjira card stands in for them), with a vocalist, mridangam, violin and flute. The margam, the concert order running from alarippu and jatiswaram through varnam and padam to tillana, was codified by the Tanjore Quartet, four brothers at the Thanjavur court in the early nineteenth century.
items.description: A Carnatic voice, violin and flute carry the melody of each dance item while the mridangam and the crisp, ringing strokes of the conductor's cymbals mark the footwork, interleaved with rapid spoken rhythm syllables.
exemplars: HMV / Saregama Bharatanatyam margam accompaniment albums

items.name: Odissi sangita (Odia classical music)
items.lineage: Odissi music is the classical music of Odisha, rooted in the temple song of the Jagannath temple at Puri and in Jayadeva's twelfth-century Gita Govinda, with its own treatises, ragas and talas, and enlarged by Odia poet-composers such as Upendra Bhanja and Kavisurya Baladeva Rath. Sung with the mardala barrel drum and gini cymbals (the manjira card stands in for them), often joined by harmonium, it accompanies Odissi dance and is also performed as concert music.
items.description: A lyrical solo voice sings ornate, raga-based devotional and love poetry over the deep, rounded strokes of a barrel drum and the light tinkle of small cymbals, with harmonium shadowing the line.

items.name: Nata sankirtana (Manipuri ritual singing and drumming)
items.lineage: Sankirtana is the ritual singing, drumming and dancing of the Vaishnava Meitei of the Manipur valley, performed in temples and domestic courtyards for religious festivals and life-cycle ceremonies. Typically two drummers playing the pung barrel drum (the khol card, in its Manipuri pung form with a wooden shell, stands in for it) and about ten singer-dancers with large cymbals (kartal) perform in a circle of seated devotees, a leader opening each song and the group responding. It is inscribed on UNESCO's Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage.
items.description: A circle of male voices answers a leader in long devotional songs, ringing large cymbals together while two barrel drums weave fast, intricate patterns that swell toward ecstatic climaxes.
exemplars: UNESCO Representative List documentation of Manipuri sankirtana (2013)
Jawaharlal Nehru Manipur Dance Academy recordings

items.name: Lai Haraoba (Meitei pena and maibi ritual song)
items.lineage: Lai Haraoba ('merrymaking of the gods') is the ritual festival of the indigenous Meitei religion of Manipur, held at the shrines of the umang lai (local deities), in which maibi priestesses invoke the deities and lead ritual dances that enact creation and origin myths. Its music centres on the pena, a single-string bowed spike fiddle whose bow carries small bells, played by a male pena player to accompany the maibi's songs and the dances.
items.description: A priestess's chant-like song unfolds over the reedy, nasal melody of a single-string bowed fiddle, its bow jingling with small bells, in slow ritual dance time.
exemplars: Field recordings of maibi songs with pena at Lai Haraoba festivals

items.name: Khongjom Parba (Meitei war ballad with dholak)
items.lineage: Khongjom Parba is a Meitei ballad-singing genre of Manipur that began with Samjetsabam Leinou (Dhobi Leinou), who sang eyewitness accounts of the Anglo-Manipur War against the British, above all the stand of the Manipuri forces at Khongjom, first beating time on his knees or a tin can and later on the dholak. A lead singer narrates and sings the story to the dholak, the repertoire has widened to other historical and legendary episodes, and the genre has been performed on stage and broadcast by All India Radio Imphal.
items.description: A single storyteller-singer declaims and sings a heroic war narrative in long, ornamented phrases, driven by the crisp strokes of a two-headed hand drum.
exemplars: All India Radio Imphal recordings of Khongjom Parba

items.name: Meitei modern song (Manipuri popular and film song)
items.lineage: Modern Meitei-language song, composed lyric song as distinct from Manipur's ritual and traditional genres, spread through stage, radio and records and was broadcast by All India Radio Imphal; Manipuri cinema, beginning with Matamgi Manipur, the first Manipuri feature film, added film songs to the repertoire. Contemporary productions set the voice over guitar, keyboard, bass and drum kit.
items.description: A clear solo voice sings melodic, sentimental verse over strummed guitar, keyboard pads, bass and a light drum-kit groove, in a polished studio balance.
exemplars: All India Radio Imphal light-music archive

items.name: Yakshagana (coastal Karnataka theatre music)
items.lineage: Yakshagana is the night-long dance-theatre of coastal Karnataka, enacting episodes from the epics and Puranas. Its music ensemble (himmela) is led by the bhagavata, the singer-narrator who sings the verses of the play text and directs the performance while keeping time on small cymbals (the manjira card stands in for them), with the chande drum (the chenda card in its chande form) and the maddale barrel drum (the generic membrane-drum card stands in for it); the actors improvise spoken dialogue between the songs.
items.description: A high, piercing lead voice sings narrative verse while a stick-played cylinder drum and a hand-played barrel drum crash in behind the actors' entrances and battle scenes, the singer's cymbals marking the cycle.

items.name: Gamaka (Kannada epic recitation-singing)
items.lineage: Gamaka is the Kannada art of reciting classical poetry, above all old Kannada epics such as Kumaravyasa's Karnata Bharata Kathamanjari, in which a singer (gamaki) sings each verse to a raga chosen to suit its mood and a commentator (vyakhyanakara) then explains it in prose. It has been fostered by the Karnataka Gamaka Kala Parishat and broadcast by All India Radio.
items.description: A single voice sings old Kannada verse in slow, ornamented raga phrases, each stanza followed by a spoken prose explanation.
exemplars: All India Radio Bengaluru gamaka archive

items.name: Dollu kunitha (Karnataka barrel-drum dance)
items.lineage: Dollu kunitha is a drum dance of Karnataka performed by men of the Kuruba (shepherd) community, associated with the worship of Beereshwara. A troupe of dancers, each wearing a large barrel drum (dollu; the generic membrane-drum card stands in for it) slung from the shoulders, beats it with sticks while dancing in formations, slow and fast rhythms alternating under the direction of a leader with cymbals at the centre, and the performance is accompanied by singing.
items.description: A massed troupe of large barrel drums beaten with sticks booms in unison and interlocking patterns, alternating slow and fast sections at a cymbal player's signal, with sung passages between.
exemplars: Karnataka Janapada Academy field recordings of dollu kunitha

items.name: Bhuta kola paddana (Tulu spirit-worship epic song)
items.lineage: Bhuta kola (daiva kola) is the night-long spirit-worship ritual of the Tulu-speaking coast of Karnataka, in which a performer from the Pambada, Nalike or Parava communities embodies the daiva. Paddanas, the Tulu oral epics of the spirits and culture heroes, are sung at the rituals and in the paddy fields; Lauri Honko's Folklore Fellows team recorded singer Gopala Naika's Siri epic. The drum card stands in for the tembare, the drum that accompanies paddana singing.
items.description: A voice sings long epic verses on a steady, repeating melodic line over a drum's insistent beat, the drumming quickening and growing louder as the ritual intensifies.
exemplars: Lauri Honko's Folklore Fellows recordings of Gopala Naika's Siri epic
Regional Resources Centre for Folk Performing Arts, Udupi, archive

items.name: Harikatha kalakshepam (Tamil sung religious discourse)
items.lineage: Harikatha, or kathakalakshepam, is a solo religious discourse in which the performer (bhagavatar) tells a story from the epics or the lives of saints, moving between spoken exposition and songs in Carnatic ragas while keeping time on a pair of wooden clappers (chipla). It took shape in Thanjavur in the nineteenth century out of the Marathi Naradiya kirtan brought south under the Maratha rulers, with Thanjavur Krishna Bhagavatar as its founding exponent, and is accompanied by harmonium or violin and mridangam. The jingled chapri card stands in for the chipla.
items.description: A single storyteller-singer moves between spoken narration and raga-based song, the clack of hand-held wooden clappers marking time, with harmonium shadowing the melody and a barrel drum filling the rhythm beneath.
exemplars: C. Saraswathi Bai (early woman harikatha exponent)
All India Radio archive recordings of harikatha

items.name: Villu paattu (Tamil bow-song narrative)
items.lineage: Villu paattu ('bow song') is a narrative song form of southern Tamil Nadu, above all Tirunelveli and Kanyakumari, performed at temple festivals: the lead singer beats the string of a large bow hung with bells with a pair of sticks while telling the story, and a small troupe answers him in chorus and accompanies on the kudam (a clay pot), the udukkai hourglass drum and cymbals. Subbu Arumugam carried it to radio and the concert stage in the twentieth century, extending it from temple stories to social themes. The ghatam card stands in for the kudam.
items.description: A lead singer tells a story in song while striking a long bow string with sticks, its bells jangling on every stroke, and a small chorus answers his lines over the deep thump of a clay pot, an hourglass drum and small cymbals.
exemplars: Stuart Blackburn, documentation of Tamil bow-song performance in Kanyakumari district

items.name: Terukkuttu / Kattaikkuttu (Tamil Mahabharata street theatre)
items.lineage: Terukkuttu ('street theatre'), called Kattaikkuttu by its performers, is the all-night village theatre of northern Tamil Nadu that enacts episodes of the Mahabharata, above all during Draupadi temple festivals. Actors sing their own verses, which a chorus standing behind them repeats, over an ensemble of harmonium, mukhavina (a small double-reed pipe), mridangam and cymbals. The Kattaikkuttu Sangam, based near Kanchipuram, trains young performers, and Richard Frasca's study documented its performances.
items.description: Actors sing in loud, projected voices that a chorus behind them takes up and repeats, over the reedy whine of a small shawm, a sustaining harmonium, barrel-drum strokes and ringing cymbals that drive entrances and battle scenes through the night.
exemplars: Richard Frasca, The Theater of the Mahabharata: Terukkuttu Performances in South India (documentation)

items.name: Gaana (North Chennai street song)
items.lineage: Gaana is the street song of the working-class, largely Dalit neighbourhoods of North Chennai, sung at funerals, festivals and neighbourhood gatherings in colloquial Madras Tamil, its verses often improvised and full of wordplay. Singers perform over driving hand percussion; from the 1990s gaana songs entered Tamil film soundtracks, and Gaana Bala and The Casteless Collective, a band brought together by the Neelam Cultural Centre, carried it to wider audiences. The hand-drum card stands in for the assorted street percussion.
items.description: A raw, full-throated lead voice rattles off quick, rhyming verses over hard, fast hand-drum and barrel-drum rhythms that push toward dance.
exemplars: The Casteless Collective (Madras Records / Neelam Cultural Centre)

items.name: Parai attam (Tamil frame-drum ensemble and dance)
items.lineage: The parai is the Tamil frame drum, its head tightened over a fire and beaten with two sticks, a thin one and a heavier one, played in groups at funerals, temple festivals and processions; parai attam is the dance the drummers perform while playing. Long the hereditary duty of Dalit drummers, in recent decades it has been taken up as an art of pride and protest by troupes such as Buddhar Kalai Kuzhu.
items.description: A row of drummers beats wide frame drums with one thin and one heavier stick, producing loud, cracking interlocking patterns that speed up and shift together as the players dance.
exemplars: Parai drummers of The Casteless Collective

items.name: Burrakatha (Telugu ballad narrative)
items.lineage: Burrakatha is a Telugu narrative performance in which a lead storyteller, wearing ankle bells and strumming a tambura, sings and acts out the story while two companions beside him beat small dakki drums, interject comic and topical commentary and take up the refrains. It grew out of the narratives of the Jangam devotees of Shiva, and in the 1940s Sheikh Nazar and the Praja Natya Mandali troupes used it for political mobilisation in Andhra. The hand-drum card stands in for the dakki.
items.description: A lead storyteller sings and declaims over the rhythmic strum of a drone lute, while two companions beat small hand drums, throw in spoken asides and shout back the refrains.
exemplars: All India Radio Vijayawada archive recordings of burrakatha

items.name: Oggu katha (Telangana shepherd-caste ritual narrative)
items.lineage: Oggu katha is the ritual storytelling of the Kuruma and Golla shepherd castes of Telangana, sung by hereditary narrators who tell the legends of their deities Mallanna, Beerappa and Yellamma at the gods' weddings and community festivals. The lead narrator plays the oggu, an hourglass drum of the damaru type associated with Shiva, while his companions clash cymbals, act out roles and sing the refrains; Chukka Sattaiah became its best-known exponent. The hourglass-drum card stands in for the oggu.
items.description: Narrators sing and act out long devotional legends in strong, open voices, the leader beating an hourglass drum while his companions clash small cymbals and join the refrains.
exemplars: Telangana folk archive recordings of oggu katha

items.name: Bathukamma paatalu (Telangana women's festival songs)
items.lineage: Bathukamma is the autumn flower festival of Telangana, held over the nine days of Navaratri leading up to Dussehra, in which women stack seasonal flowers into a conical bathukamma, circle it each evening singing and clapping, and finally immerse it in a lake or tank. The songs are sung in call and response, a leader's line answered by the circle with a refrain such as 'uyyalo', and are issued in great numbers on commercial festival albums.
items.description: A circle of women sings strophic songs in call and response, each line of the leader answered by the group's repeated refrain, over steady unison clapping that marks the steps around the circle.
exemplars: Commercial Telangana Bathukamma festival song albums

items.name: Marfa (Hyderabadi Afro-Arab drum band)
items.lineage: Marfa is the fast celebratory drum music and dance of Hyderabad's Muslim communities, adapted from the Afro-Arab music of Hadhramawt in Yemen; it was brought to Hyderabad State by Siddis of East African descent, who served as cavalry guards in the Asaf Jahi Nizams' irregular army, and by the Hadhrami diaspora, and the Nizams patronised it at official ceremonies. Kept by the Chaush community, above all in Barkas, it is played at weddings and processions on marfa drums with daff, dhol, sticks, steel pots and wooden strips (thapi). The drum cards stand in for the marfa and the daff.
items.description: Stick-beaten drums, frame drums and a barrel drum lock into a loud, fast, syncopated groove, with clacking wooden strips and struck steel pots sharpening the attack as dancers move before the band.
exemplars: Barkas marfa band recordings of Hyderabad weddings and processions

items.name: Natya sangeet (Marathi stage song)
items.lineage: Natya sangeet is the song of Marathi musical theatre (sangeet natak), which began with Annasaheb Kirloskar's Sangeet Shakuntal in 1880 and drew its tunes increasingly from Hindustani classical and light-classical forms. In the 1910s and 1920s Bal Gandharva, who sang the heroines' roles for his Gandharva Natak Mandali, and Deenanath Mangeshkar made it a star repertoire, carried on 78 rpm discs, sung to harmonium or the stage organ and tabla.
items.description: A full, ornamented solo voice delivers raga-based stage songs with quick melodic runs, shadowed closely by harmonium and reed organ while tabla keeps a light-classical cycle beneath.

items.name: Bhavgeet (Marathi light poetic song)
items.lineage: Bhavgeet is Marathi light song that sets modern lyric poetry, by poets such as Mangesh Padgaonkar and Shanta Shelke, to simple, raga-tinged melodies. It took shape on gramophone records in the 1930s and spread through All India Radio, shaped by composer-singers such as Sudhir Phadke, composer of the radio song-cycle Geet Ramayan, and Shrinivas Khale, and by singers such as Arun Date.
items.description: A clear, gentle solo voice carries a lyric poem on a simple, raga-tinged tune, with harmonium, flute and tabla in a light, uncluttered accompaniment.

items.name: Gondhal (Marathi goddess ritual song)
items.lineage: Gondhal is a Marathi ritual performance in which Gondhali singers invoke the goddess, above all Tulja Bhavani of Tuljapur and Renuka of Mahur, through the night at family ceremonies such as weddings, singing invocations and narrative songs. The lead singer plays the tuntuna, a one-string plucked drone, while a companion beats the sambal, a pair of drums played with sticks, and others answer on cymbals and in chorus. The gopichand card, a one-string plucked drum, stands in for the tuntuna.
items.description: A lead singer calls on the goddess in strong, open-throated verses over the twang of a one-string drone and the dry, cracking strokes of a stick-beaten paired drum, with companions answering on cymbals and in chorus.
exemplars: Marathi devotional cassette releases of gondhal songs

items.name: Bharud (Marathi allegorical devotional song-drama)
items.lineage: Bharud is a Marathi devotional song-drama in which the performer takes on a stock character from village life and, through comic song, dialogue and mime, teaches a spiritual lesson. The saint Eknath of Paithan composed some three hundred bharuds in the sixteenth century, and Varkari performers still sing them in kirtans and on the pilgrimage to Pandharpur, with cymbals, mridang (pakhawaj) and harmonium.
items.description: A lead performer sings short, catchy verses and breaks into comic spoken dialogue, with a chorus repeating the refrain over a cymbal ostinato, a barrel drum and harmonium.
exemplars: Niranjan Bhakre bharud performances and recordings

items.name: Bhavai (Gujarati folk-theatre music)
items.lineage: Bhavai is the folk theatre of northern Gujarat, performed by hereditary troupes of the Targala (Nayak) community, who trace it to the fourteenth-century Asait Thakar. A troupe plays a sequence of short plays (vesh) in the village square through the night, mixing song, dance and comic dialogue. Its signature sound is the bhungal, a long copper trumpet, heard with pakhawaj, tabla and manjira cymbals; the karna card stands in for the bhungal.
items.description: Blasts from long metal trumpets announce each scene, and actors sing projected, ornamented songs over barrel drum, tabla and cymbals between bursts of dialogue and dance.
exemplars: Sangeet Natak Akademi documentation of Bhavai
All India Radio Gujarati recordings of Bhavai

items.name: Lok dayro (Saurashtra song-and-story session)
items.lineage: Dayro (lok dayro) is an evening gathering of Saurashtra in which folk singers and storytellers sit before an audience and alternate bhajans, folk songs, sung couplets (duha) and humorous or heroic stories, often until dawn; a santvani is a dayro given over to the bhajans of saint-poets. Sung to harmonium, tabla and cymbals, it circulates widely on commercial cassettes and recordings, with performers such as Hemant Chauhan and Praful Dave.
items.description: Singers and a storyteller take turns before an audience, moving from free, declaimed couplets to devotional and folk songs in full voice over harmonium, tabla and cymbals, with talk and laughter between items.
exemplars: Hemant Chauhan santvani and dayro recordings (Studio Saraswati)

items.name: Sidi goma (Afro-Indian Sufi drum dance of Gujarat)
items.lineage: Goma, also called dhamal, is the drum song and dance of the Sidi, Gujaratis of East African descent, performed in honour of their Sufi saints, above all Bava Gor, whose shrine stands on a hill near Ratanpur, and at urs festivals and weddings; dancers spin and leap as the music builds toward ecstatic states. Songs are sung over large and small drums and the mai misra rattle. Helene Basu's ethnography describes its ritual setting, and the Sidi Goma ensemble has toured internationally. The drum cards stand in for the goma drums.
items.description: Several drums lock into a fast, repeating dance rhythm under a shaken rattle, while a leader sings short devotional refrains that the group answers, the pace rising as the dancers whirl.
exemplars: Sidi Goma ensemble of Bharuch district (touring recordings and performances)
Helene Basu ethnographic documentation of Sidi music
Apsara Media documentation of Sidi music of Gujarat (Amy Catlin-Jairazbhoy)

items.name: Kalbelia (Rajasthani snake-charmer community song and dance)
items.lineage: The Kalbelia, a once-nomadic Rajasthani community of former snake catchers and charmers, perform songs and a dance in which women in swirling black skirts move with serpentine twists, while men play the been (the snake charmer's gourd pipe), the khanjari, dholak, dufli and the morchang jaw harp. Lyrics drawn from folklore and mythology are often composed and improvised during performance. The songs and dances were inscribed on UNESCO's Representative List in 2010, and Gulabo Sapera brought the dance to international stages. The hand-drum card stands in for the khanjari and dufli.
items.description: Voices sing bright folk melodies over the nasal drone and melody of the snake-charmer's gourd pipe, with frame drum, barrel drum and the buzz of a jaw harp driving a whirling dance.
exemplars: UNESCO documentation of Kalbelia folk songs and dances of Rajasthan

items.name: Pabuji ki phad (Bhopa epic of Rajasthan)
items.lineage: The epic of Pabuji, a medieval Rathore hero worshipped as a god in western Rajasthan, is performed through the night by a bhopa, a priest-singer, in front of the phad, a long painted cloth that serves as a portable shrine. The bhopa sings and dances while playing the ravanahatta spike fiddle, and his wife, the bhopi, lights episodes of the painting with an oil lamp and sings lines in turn with him. Performances are commissioned by devotees, many of them Rebari camel herders, to end illness or misfortune.
items.description: A man's voice sings long strophic narrative lines at full voice, doubled by a rasping bowed spike fiddle, and a woman's voice takes up alternate lines, with spoken passages explaining the story between sung sections.
exemplars: John D. Smith's recordings and edition of a bhopa's performance (The Epic of Pabuji, 1991)

items.name: Maand (Rajasthani courtly song)
items.lineage: Maand is the refined song style of the Rajput courts of Rajasthan, sung by hereditary professional singers in praise of rulers and in songs of love and longing; it sits between Rajasthani folk song and Hindustani classical music, and the raga Mand shares its name. Allah Jilai Bai, a court singer of Bikaner, became its best-known voice.
items.description: A solo voice spins slow, ornamented melody with long glides and held notes, shadowed by a bowed sarangi, over a light tabla cycle and harmonium.

items.name: Dhadi (Punjabi heroic ballad singing)
items.lineage: Dhadis are Punjabi ballad singers named after the dhadd, a small hourglass drum struck with the fingers whose pitch is bent by squeezing its lacing; here the hudka card stands in for the dhadd, and the sarangi card for the Punjabi folk sarangi. A dhadi jatha of two dhadd players and a sarangi player sings vars, heroic ballads of Sikh history, at gurdwaras and religious fairs, alternating sung verses with spoken narration, a practice the community traces to the patronage of Guru Hargobind. Sohan Singh Seetal was among its most celebrated twentieth-century singers.
items.description: Two voices sing stirring ballad verses in a high, declamatory style over the pitch-bending patter of small hourglass drums and a sawing folk fiddle, breaking off for spoken narration.

items.name: Sufiana kalam (Kashmiri Sufi art music)
items.lineage: Sufiana kalam, also called sufiana mausiqi, is the classical music of the Kashmir Valley, which grew out of the Persian music brought by Sufis from the fifteenth century; it sets Persian and Kashmiri mystic poetry in a system of its own modes (maqam) and rhythmic cycles. A group of singers who also play the santoor, the Kashmiri sehtar, the bowed saz-e-kashmir and the dukra pair of drums performs it at gatherings (mehfil); here the tanbur card (a long-necked fretted lute) stands in for the sehtar, and the ghichak and tabla cards for the saz-e-kashmir and dukra. The santoor of Hindustani concert music came from this tradition.
items.description: A small chorus sings mystic verse in unison over the shimmer of a hammered dulcimer, the plucked line of a long-necked lute and a bowed spike fiddle, with a pair of hand drums keeping a steady cycle.

items.name: Chakri (Kashmiri folk ensemble song)
items.lineage: Chakri is one of the most popular folk song forms of the Kashmir Valley, a responsorial song heard at weddings and festive gatherings and also used to tell love stories and tales. A lead singer and a chorus that repeats the refrain are accompanied by harmonium, rabab, sarangi, the clay pot noot, the goblet drum tumbaknari and the chimta tongs. Here the rubab card stands in for the Kashmiri rabab, the ghatam for the noot and the zerbaghali, a clay goblet drum, for the tumbaknari.
items.description: A lead voice sings verses that a chorus answers with a repeated refrain, over a reedy harmonium, a plucked short-necked lute and a bowed fiddle, driven by the slap of a clay pot and a goblet drum.

items.name: Rouf (Kashmiri women's line-dance song)
items.lineage: Rouf is sung and danced by Kashmiri women at Eid, during Ramadan nights and at weddings: two rows of women stand facing each other with linked arms and step forward and back in time, one row singing a verse and the other answering it. It is sung without instruments.
items.description: Two groups of women's voices trade short sung phrases back and forth in a steady, swaying rhythm, unaccompanied.
exemplars: Radio Kashmir Srinagar broadcasts of rouf songs

items.name: Jagar (Garhwal and Kumaon possession ritual song)
items.lineage: Jagar ('awakening') is the night ritual of Garhwal and Kumaon in which a lead singer (jagariya) sings the stories of local gods and ancestral spirits to call them into the bodies of mediums, who begin to dance as the drumming intensifies. The songs are accompanied by the hudka hourglass drum or by the dhol and the small kettledrum damau played by hereditary drummers; the dhol card stands in for the Garhwali dhol and the nagara card for the damau.
items.description: A lead singer chants invocations that helpers answer, over insistent hourglass-drum and barrel-drum patterns with a kettledrum, the rhythm tightening and quickening toward trance.
exemplars: Andrew Alter, Dancing with Devtas (2008), study of Garhwali drumming and possession

items.name: Alha (Bundelkhand heroic epic singing)
items.lineage: Alha singers of Bundelkhand and the wider Hindi-speaking region sing the Alha-Khand, the epic of the twelfth-century warrior brothers Alha and Udal of Mahoba and their battles in the service of the Chandela king Parmal, traditionally in the rainy season. The singer delivers the verses at full voice over the dholak, often with harmonium and cymbals added. Lallu Bajpai is among its best-known recorded singers.
items.description: A full, ringing male voice drives through rapid heroic verses over a pounding barrel drum, with harmonium and clashing cymbals swelling in the battle passages.
exemplars: Karine Schomer, field research on Alha performance

items.name: Nautanki (North Indian folk-operatic theatre)
items.lineage: Nautanki is the open-air musical theatre of Uttar Pradesh and neighbouring regions, which grew in the nineteenth century out of the older swang, with Hathras and Kanpur as its two main schools. Its dialogue is sung in verse metres such as doha and chaubola to the thunder of the nakkara kettledrums, with harmonium and dholak. Gulab Bai of the Kanpur school, among the first women to act in Nautanki, became its biggest star.
items.description: Singers trade sung verse dialogue at the top of their voices, punctuated by rolling cracks of a pair of kettledrums, with harmonium doubling the tune and a barrel drum keeping time.
exemplars: Gulab Bai (Kanpur-school Nautanki singer and actress)
Kathryn Hansen, Grounds for Play: The Nautanki Theatre of North India (1992)

items.name: Nagpuri jhumair (Chotanagpur folk song-dance)
items.lineage: Nagpuri song, sung in the Sadri language, is the shared folk music of the Chotanagpur plateau around Ranchi, with forms that follow the farming and festival year, among them jhumair, the domkach wedding dance and the songs of the karam festival. Men and women dance jhumair in linked lines to the mandar barrel drum, the nagara kettledrum and the bamboo flute; here a generic membrane drum card stands in for the mandar. Mukund Nayak carried the style to the stage and to recordings.
items.description: A lead voice and answering group sing short, repeating dance-song phrases over the round, bouncing strokes of a hand-played barrel drum, booming kettledrum accents and a bamboo flute.

items.name: Santal dance music (tamak' and tumdak')
items.lineage: The Santals of Jharkhand, West Bengal and Odisha sing and dance through a yearly cycle of festivals such as sohrai and baha, and sing dong songs at weddings and lagre songs for dancing. Women dance in long lines with linked arms while men play the tumdak' barrel drum, the tamak' kettledrum, bamboo flutes and the banam fiddle; here the dhamsa card stands in for the tamak' and a generic membrane drum for the tumdak'.
items.description: Women's voices sing short, cycling melodies in a group over interlocking barrel-drum strokes and deep kettledrum booms, with a bamboo flute and a bowed fiddle weaving around the tune.
exemplars: Field recordings of Santal dance songs (dong and lagre)

items.name: Tusu gaan (Manbhum winter-festival songs)
items.lineage: Tusu songs are sung by girls and young women of the Manbhum region, around Purulia, Bankura and neighbouring Jharkhand, through the month of Poush in gatherings before an image of Tusu, a folk goddess of the harvest; the festival ends at Makar Sankranti, when the image is carried to a river and immersed. Many songs are newly made each year and comment on everyday life.
items.description: Girls' and women's voices sing simple repeating strophic tunes together in a plain, open village style.

items.name: Chhau (eastern Indian martial dance music)
items.lineage: Chhau is the martial dance of eastern India in three styles, Purulia in West Bengal, Seraikela in Jharkhand and Mayurbhanj in Odisha, the first two masked; it is danced at night in open spaces, above all at the spring Chaitra Parva festival, and is inscribed on the UNESCO Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity. Its music comes from the mohuri and shehnai reed pipes over a battery of drums led by the dhol and the large dhamsa kettledrum; here the mukhavina card, a small double-reed pipe, stands in for the mohuri.
items.description: A piercing double-reed pipe plays wailing melody over thunderous barrel-drum and kettledrum rhythms that surge and break with the dancers' leaps.
exemplars: Field recordings of Purulia chhau dhol-dhamsa-mohuri ensembles

items.name: Pandavani (Chhattisgarhi Mahabharata ballad)
items.lineage: Pandavani is the sung and acted telling of the Mahabharata story of the Pandava brothers, with Bhima as its hero, in Chhattisgarh. The lead performer holds a tambura, used as a prop as well as a drone, and sings, speaks and acts out the episodes, while a seated group of harmonium, tabla, dholak and manjira players answers, one of them as the ragi who responds to the narrator. It has two styles, the seated vedamati and the theatrical kapalik, the style of Teejan Bai.
items.description: A powerful lead voice sings and declaims a heroic tale with dramatic shifts between song and speech, answered by a small chorus over a drone lute, harmonium, hand drums and small cymbals.

items.name: Panthi (Satnami devotional song-dance)
items.lineage: Panthi is the devotional song-dance of the Satnami community of Chhattisgarh, performed in praise of Guru Ghasidas, the founder of the Satnami sect, especially around his birth anniversary. Male dancers sing his teachings in a circle to the mandar barrel drum and the jhanjh cymbals as the tempo builds to a fast climax; here a generic membrane drum card stands in for the mandar. Devdas Banjare took Panthi to stages across India and abroad.
items.description: A lead voice sings devotional lines that a group answers, over a hand-played barrel drum and clashing cymbals that speed up steadily to an ecstatic climax.

items.name: Ganda baja and dalkhai (western Odisha folk ensemble)
items.lineage: Ganda baja, also called dulduli baja, is the folk band of western Odisha, played at weddings, festivals and dances by musicians of the Ganda community on the dhol, the large nisan kettledrum, the tasa and the double-reed mahuri. It accompanies dalkhai, the song-dance young women perform around Dussehra in honour of the goddess Dalkhai. Here the nagara card stands in for the nisan and the mukhavina card, a small double-reed pipe, for the mahuri.
items.description: A nasal double-reed pipe and women's voices carry the tune over a dense, fast drum band of barrel drum, booming kettledrum and crackling shallow drums.

items.name: Pala (Odia sung narrative)
items.lineage: Pala is a sung narrative performance of Odisha whose troupes worship Satya Pir, a figure revered by both Hindus and Muslims. A troupe of five or six performs it: the lead singer (gayaka), who holds a fly-whisk (chamara) and a pair of cymbals, sings and expounds stories from the Puranas and Odia poetry, answered by the chorus (palia), while the drummer (bayaka) plays the mrudanga; here the mardala card stands in for the mrudanga. It is performed seated (baithaki) or standing.
items.description: A lead singer moves between song and spoken exposition, answered by a small chorus over a two-headed barrel drum and ringing hand cymbals.

items.name: Daskathia (Odia ballad with kathi clappers)
items.lineage: Daskathia is a two-man ballad form of Odisha, strongest in Ganjam, in which the lead singer (gayaka) plays the kathi, a pair of wooden clappers, and his partner (palia) answers him and joins the refrains as they tell mythological stories in song and speech. The name joins das, a devotee, with the kathi he plays. Here the kartal card stands in for the kathi.
items.description: Two male voices alternate sung and spoken story lines, the lead keeping a crisp, clicking rhythm on handheld wooden clappers.
exemplars: Field recordings of daskathia from Ganjam

items.name: Jatra (Bengali open-air theatre song)
items.lineage: Jatra, the travelling open-air folk theatre of Bengal and Odisha, grew out of Vaishnava devotional processions and by the late nineteenth century was run by professional companies, many with offices on Chitpur Road in Kolkata. Mythological, historical and social plays are staged in the round and interspersed with songs, and a performance opens with an instrumental prelude (the 'concert') in which harmonium and tabla are joined by clarinet, cornet and violin.
items.description: Projected theatre song for an audience on all sides: a singing actor over harmonium and tabla, framed by a brassy instrumental prelude of clarinet, cornet and violin.

items.name: Shyama sangeet (Bengali Kali devotional song)
items.lineage: Shyama sangeet are Bengali Shakta devotional songs addressed to the goddess Kali (Shyama), a genre shaped in the eighteenth century by Ramprasad Sen, whose plain 'Ramprasadi' tunes became a model, and continued by Kamalakanta Bhattacharya and later by Kazi Nazrul Islam. In the gramophone era it became a staple of Calcutta recording, sung solo with harmonium and tabla.
items.description: Solo devotional song of yearning and surrender to the goddess, sung with gentle ornament over a harmonium and a light tabla cycle.
exemplars: Pannalal Bhattacharya, HMV recordings of Shyama sangeet

items.name: Kabigan (Bengali poets' sung debate)
items.lineage: Kabigan is the Bengali sung contest in which two kabiyals, each backed by a dohar chorus, answer one another in improvised verse on mythological, social and topical themes before a village or festival audience. It flourished in nineteenth-century Calcutta, with kabiyals such as Bhola Moira and Anthony Firingee, and survives in rural West Bengal and Bangladesh. The generic drum card stands in for the Bengali dhol and the chengila card for the kansi bell-metal plate.
items.description: Two poet-singers trade improvised sung arguments, each verse picked up by a chorus over driving drum and a struck bell-metal plate.
exemplars: Field and commercial recordings of kabiyals

items.name: Dhak drumming (Bengali Durga Puja)
items.lineage: The dhak, a large barrel drum slung from the shoulder and beaten with two thin sticks, is played by hereditary dhakis, many of whom travel from rural districts to Kolkata each autumn to be hired by puja committees. Its patterns mark the stages of Durga Puja worship, including the evening arati and the dhunuchi incense dance, usually with a kansi bell-metal plate keeping time; Durga Puja in Kolkata is inscribed on UNESCO's Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity. The chengila card stands in for the kansi.
items.description: Loud, booming stick-beaten barrel-drum patterns that accelerate through the puja rites, over a bright, clanging metal time-keeper.
exemplars: Field recordings of dhakis at Durga Puja in Kolkata

items.name: Bihu geet (Assamese spring-festival song)
items.lineage: Bihu geet are the songs of Rongali (Bohag) Bihu, the Assamese spring new-year festival, sung at open-air bihu dances and by husori groups who go from house to house. The ensemble centres on the double-headed dhol with the pepa buffalo-horn pipe, the gogona bamboo jaw harp, taal cymbals and bamboo flute; the kubing card, a bamboo jaw harp, stands in for the bamboo gogona, the manjira card for the taal and the flute card for the baanhi; the pepa is not given a card here.
items.description: High, ringing love and spring songs answered by a group, over fast, accented dhol rhythms with twanging jaw harp, cymbals and flute for dancing.

items.name: Zikir and zari (Assamese Sufi devotional song)
items.lineage: Zikir and zari are Assamese-language Islamic devotional songs attributed to Azan Fakir (Shah Miran), a seventeenth-century Sufi preacher who settled near Sivasagar. Zikir carry Sufi teaching in the idiom of Assamese folk melody, and zari are elegies on the martyrdom at Karbala; both are sung by a lead singer with a responding group.
items.description: Unaccompanied devotional song in folk-melody style, a leader's lines taken up by a group in plain, repeating refrains.
exemplars: AIR Dibrugarh and Guwahati recordings of zikir and zari

items.name: Ojapali (Assamese chorus narrative)
items.lineage: Ojapali is an Assamese chorus-narrative form, strongest in Darrang district, in which a lead singer (oja) sings and narrates episodes while a principal assistant (daina pali) comments and banters and the other palis sing refrains, clash small khuti taal cymbals and dance. Suknanni ojapali sings the Manasa (snake goddess) cycle of Sukavi Narayandev, and byah-gowa ojapali draws on the Ramayana and Mahabharata. The manjira card stands in for the khuti taal.
items.description: A lead singer-narrator alternates song and speech with an assistant's asides, while the chorus answers in refrains over clashing small cymbals.
exemplars: Sangeet Natak Akademi documentation of ojapali

items.name: Bodo kherai and bagurumba music
items.lineage: Traditional music of the Bodo (Boro) of lower Assam accompanies the kherai worship of the Bathou religion, in which the deodhani medium dances, and dances such as the bagurumba of the Bwisagu spring festival. The core ensemble is the long sifung bamboo flute, the kham drum, the bowed serja and jotha cymbals; the flute card stands in for the sifung, the generic drum for the kham and the sarinda card for the serja.
items.description: Breathy long-flute melody and a scratchy bowed fiddle over steady, cyclic drum and cymbal patterns for circling ritual and festival dances.
exemplars: AIR Kokrajhar recordings of Bodo kherai and bagurumba music

items.name: Li (Chokri Naga multipart folk song)
items.lineage: Li are the folk songs of the Chokri (Chakhesang Naga) of Phek district in Nagaland, sung in parts by groups of men or women at work in the fields, at festivals and for courtship, alongside related multipart singing among other Naga communities. The Tetseo Sisters, Chokri singers from Nagaland, have recorded and staged Chokri li, at times with the tati, a single-string instrument not given a card here.
items.description: Unaccompanied group song in interlocking parts, voices holding close against one another in a resonant, open-air blend.
exemplars: Tetseo Sisters recordings of Chokri li

items.name: Khasi traditional music (tangmuri, ksing, duitara)
items.lineage: Traditional music of the Khasi of the Meghalaya hills is led at dance festivals such as Shad Suk Mynsiem and Shad Nongkrem by the tangmuri shawm over ksing drums, while songs are accompanied by the duitara plucked lute and the besli flute; men chant phawar couplets during the dances. The kuzhal card stands in for the tangmuri, the generic drum for the ksing, the dotara card for the duitara and the flute card for the besli.
items.description: A piercing shawm melody over insistent drums for festival dance, with plucked-lute and flute songs and chanted couplets.
exemplars: AIR Shillong archive recordings of Khasi traditional music

items.name: Wangala (Garo harvest-festival drum music)
items.lineage: Wangala is the Garo post-harvest thanksgiving festival offered to Saljong, the sun deity, danced in long lines of men beating the long dama drums with women dancers, and accompanied by the adil buffalo-horn trumpet, brass gongs and bamboo flutes; it is staged each year as the Hundred Drums Festival at Asanang near Tura. The generic drum card stands in for the dama and the gong card for the brass gongs.
items.description: Massed long drums in a steady, rolling dance pulse, struck gongs and flute calls, with sung lines for the harvest offering.
exemplars: AIR Tura recordings of wangala songs

items.name: Lengkhawm zai (Mizo congregational singing)
items.lineage: Lengkhawm zai is the Mizo congregational singing style that grew out of the Christian revivals of the early twentieth century, setting hymns to Mizo melodies and rhythms sung by a seated gathering to the beat of the khuang, a large cylindrical drum, especially at funeral wakes and church fellowship. The generic drum card stands in for the khuang.
items.description: A gathered congregation singing slow, swelling hymn melodies together over the steady beat of a single large drum.
exemplars: Commercial lengkhawm zai albums from Mizoram

items.name: Mando and dulpod (Goan Konkani song)
items.lineage: Mando is the slow, sentimental Konkani song-and-dance of Goan Catholic society, shaped in the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries from Portuguese-era salon music and local melody on themes of love, separation and social events; dulpod are the quick, light songs of everyday life that follow it. They are sung, often by mixed groups, to violin, guitar and the ghumot clay-pot drum, and are showcased at the Goa Mando Festival.
items.description: Gentle, harmonised love song over strummed guitar, a singing violin line and the soft thump of a clay-pot drum; the dulpod that follow are brisk and playful.

items.name: Tiatr kantaram (Konkani theatre song)
items.lineage: Tiatr is Konkani-language popular musical theatre, first staged in Bombay at the end of the nineteenth century with Lucasinho Ribeiro's Italian Bhurgo and carried to Goa, where it remains a mass entertainment. Its kantaram are songs performed between the scenes, often comic or topical, satirical or political commentary independent of the plot, accompanied by a live band of keyboard, trumpet, saxophone, bass guitar and drums.
items.description: Clear, topical solo or duet song with comic and satirical bite, backed by a live theatre band of keyboard, trumpet, saxophone, bass guitar and drums.

items.name: Bombay jazz (Goan-led dance-band jazz)
items.lineage: From the 1930s to the 1960s Bombay's hotel ballrooms and nightclubs, led by the Taj Mahal Hotel, employed dance bands playing swing and foxtrots; American bandleaders such as Leon Abbey led early bands there, and Goan musicians trained in parish music schools soon became the core players and bandleaders. Many of them also arranged and played for Hindi film music.
items.description: Swinging hotel dance-band jazz: brass and reed section riffs and solos over walking bass, piano and brushed drums, with occasional crooned vocals.
exemplars: Chic Chocolate and his Music Makers
Micky Correa and his orchestra (Taj Mahal Hotel, Bombay)

items.name: Kota instrumental music (Nilgiri hills)
items.lineage: The Kota of the Nilgiri hills play instrumental music led by the kol, a double-reed shawm, with drums including the tabatk frame drum and the dobar, and kob horns, at funerals, the annual god ceremony and other festivals; a repertoire of god tunes is tied to particular ritual moments. Richard K. Wolf's fieldwork documents it in detail. The kuzhal card stands in for the kol, the frame-drum card for the tabatk and the generic drum for the dobar.
items.description: A nasal, reedy shawm melody, ornamented and insistent, over beaten frame and barrel drums for ritual processions and dances.
exemplars: Richard K. Wolf field recordings of Kota music

items.name: Banjara songs (Gor Lambadi song)
items.lineage: Songs of the Gor Banjara (Lambadi, Lambani), a formerly itinerant community whose settlements (tandas) are spread across Telangana, Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka and Maharashtra, sung in the Gor boli language. The repertoire includes women's songs for the Teej festival and weddings, among them the bride's farewell laments, and songs for the women's circle dances. The generic hand-drum card stands in for the drums used with the dance songs.
items.description: Women's group songs for festivals, weddings and circle dances, a leader's lines answered by the group, with hand claps and a drum.
exemplars: Commercial Banjara song cassettes from Telangana

items.name: Ailan Dans (Torres Strait Islander dance-song)
items.lineage: Song-and-dance tradition of the Torres Strait Islands, in which songs in Meriam Mir, Kala Lagaw Ya and Torres Strait Creole are sung by a group of singers to the warup, a long hourglass drum, while dancers in lines perform with handheld props. Jeremy Beckett and Trevor Jones's recordings were issued by the Australian Institute of Aboriginal Studies as Traditional Music of Torres Strait (1972), and the dances are now carried at festivals across the Strait and on the mainland. The kundu card stands in for the warup.
items.description: Strong group singing in steady, repeated verses driven by the deep, dry strokes of a long hourglass drum, with accents and breaks in the drumming that set the dancers' movements.
exemplars: Jeremy Beckett and Trevor Jones, Traditional Music of Torres Strait (AIAS LP, 1972)

items.name: Torres Strait island style (Thursday Island string-band song)
items.lineage: Secular popular song of Thursday Island and the Torres Strait that grew out of the pearling era, when Islander, Malay, Filipino, Japanese and Pacific Islander crews shared sea songs, Hawaiian and Pacific string-band tunes, blues and popular ballads; it is sung to acoustic guitar and ukulele at parties and social gatherings. The former pearl diver Seaman Dan (Henry Gibson Dan) recorded the style late in life, and his albums won ARIA awards for world music.
items.description: Relaxed, swaying songs in which a warm, easy lead voice rides strummed acoustic guitar and ukulele in a lilting two-beat feel, with bluesy turns and Pacific string-band melodies.

items.name: Yawulyu (Warlpiri women's ceremonial song)
items.lineage: Women's ceremonial song and dance of the Warlpiri of the Tanami Desert, held by senior women at Yuendumu, Lajamanu and neighbouring communities, in which song series follow the Jukurrpa (Dreaming) tracks of particular country and are performed with body painting and dance. Senior Yuendumu women documented their repertoire with linguists and musicologists in the book-and-audio publication Yurntumu-wardingki juju-ngaliya-kurlangu yawulyu (Batchelor Press, 2017).
items.description: Women's voices in close unison sing short verses over and over, each phrase stepping down from a high start to a low resting tone before the next begins, the rhythm set by the words.
exemplars: Yurntumu-wardingki juju-ngaliya-kurlangu yawulyu (Batchelor Press, 2017, book with audio)

items.name: Kun-borrk (western Arnhem Land public song-dance)
items.lineage: Public song-dance genre of western Arnhem Land, sung in Kunwinjku and neighbouring languages around Gunbalanya (Oenpelli), in which a songman keeping time on clapsticks is joined by a didjeridu player to accompany dancing at funerals, ceremonies and festivals, each songman holding his own song sets. Kun-borrk was recorded at Oenpelli by the 1948 American-Australian Scientific Expedition to Arnhem Land and is the subject of continuing community recording projects.
items.description: A songman's strong voice descends through short, repeated song items over a rhythmic didjeridu drone and an even clapstick beat, with the clapstick patterns changing to mark sections for the dancers.
exemplars: 1948 American-Australian Scientific Expedition to Arnhem Land recordings (Oenpelli)

items.name: Tiwi song (kulama and yoi of Bathurst and Melville Islands)
items.lineage: Song tradition of the Tiwi people of Bathurst and Melville Islands, north of Darwin, whose singers fit new texts to inherited melodic forms for the kulama yam ceremony, for yoi dancing at pukumani mortuary ceremonies and for everyday events. The Tiwi Strong Women's Group, working with researcher Genevieve Campbell on returning archival recordings to the community, released Ngarukuruwala: We Sing Songs (Skinnyfish, 2010).
items.description: Solo and group singing on a few recurring melodic formulas, the words fitted afresh to each occasion, over a firm hand-clapped beat that drives the dancers.
exemplars: Tiwi Strong Women's Group — Ngarukuruwala: We Sing Songs (Skinnyfish, 2010)

items.name: Central Australian Aboriginal hymn singing (Ntaria and Ernabella choirs)
items.lineage: Choral hymn singing of Central Australian Aboriginal communities, rooted in the Lutheran mission at Hermannsburg (Ntaria), founded in the late nineteenth century, where German chorales were translated into Western Arrernte, and in the Presbyterian mission at Ernabella (Pukatja), where hymns were sung in Pitjantjatjara. Women's choirs from these and other communities came together as the Central Australian Aboriginal Women's Choir, whose tour of Germany is followed in the documentary The Song Keepers (2017).
items.description: Strophic chorale-style hymns harmonised in parts and sung by a women's choir in Arrernte and Pitjantjatjara, in broad, steady phrases with a full, unforced tone and the tune firmly in the top voice.

items.name: Aboriginal country music (Koori and Murri country)
items.lineage: Country and gospel-country song made by Aboriginal singers on missions and reserves and in country towns from the mid-twentieth century, drawing on hillbilly records and radio and on a strong local voice-and-guitar tradition. Recorded artists include Jimmy Little, born at Cummeragunja, whose Royal Telephone was a 1963 hit, Dougie Young, Vic Simms, Harry Williams and the Country Outcasts and Roger Knox; Clinton Walker's book, CD compilation and film Buried Country (2000) documented the tradition.
items.description: Plain, heartfelt country singing over strummed acoustic guitar, twangy electric lead fills, a walking bass and a light two-beat or shuffle on drums, with occasional gospel-style harmony choruses.

items.name: Aboriginal rock and desert reggae (Indigenous band music)
items.lineage: Band music of Aboriginal communities in Central and northern Australia and in the cities, in which electric rock, country-rock and reggae carry songs in Aboriginal languages and English. The Warumpi Band's Jailanguru Pakarnu (1983), sung in Luritja, is often cited as the first rock song recorded in an Aboriginal language; the Central Australian Aboriginal Media Association (CAAMA) in Alice Springs became a leading label for desert bands, and Coloured Stone, No Fixed Address, Yothu Yindi, Saltwater Band and many community bands followed, some adding didjeridu and clapsticks to the line-up.
items.description: Driving electric-guitar band songs, from pub-rock chug and country-rock strum to offbeat reggae skank, with a declamatory lead voice, chanted group refrains and, in many bands, a didjeridu drone and clapstick beat woven into the rhythm section.

items.name: Gumleaf playing (Aboriginal gumleaf bands)
items.lineage: Leaf-blowing tradition of Aboriginal communities in south-eastern Australia, in which a eucalyptus leaf held against the lips is blown to play hymns, popular songs, marches and dance tunes. From the early twentieth century gumleaf bands from missions and reserves such as Wallaga Lake played at dances, sports carnivals and public events, and the Wallaga Lake Gumleaf Band walked to Sydney to play at the opening of the Harbour Bridge in 1932; the Australian Gumleaf Playing Championships at Maryborough, Victoria, continue the practice. The kazoo card stands in for the blown gum leaf.
items.description: Thin, piercing melody lines blown on leaves, sliding between notes with a wavering vibrato and played together by several players over march-time bass and snare drum.

items.name: Djatpangarri (Yolngu youth song-dance of Yirrkala)
items.lineage: Popular song-dance of young Yolngu men at Yirrkala in north-east Arnhem Land, sung for entertainment rather than ceremony, with light-hearted texts on everyday subjects set to the didjeridu and clapstick accompaniment of public song. Richard Waterman recorded djatpangarri at Yirrkala in the early 1950s, and recordings are held in the community archive of the Mulka Project.
items.description: Brisk, upbeat song items with group singing over a pulsing didjeridu drone and fast, even clapstick beats, kept short and repeated for dancing.

items.name: Nurlu (West Kimberley public song-dance)
items.lineage: Public song-dance genre of the West Kimberley around Broome and the Dampier Peninsula, sung by Yawuru, Nyikina and neighbouring peoples, in which songs said to be received by songmen in dreams are performed with clapstick accompaniment for dancers. Ray Keogh's doctoral research and recordings, held at AIATSIS, documented the genre's song structure.
items.description: A lead singer and supporting voices sing short, repeated song verses on descending melodic lines over a steady clapstick beat for the dancers.
exemplars: Ray Keogh West Kimberley nurlu recordings (AIATSIS)

items.name: Bush band (Australian colonial folk-song revival)
items.lineage: Australian folk-revival band style that took up colonial bush songs, convict ballads and dance tunes collected by John Meredith and others. The Sydney group the Bushwhackers, formed in the early 1950s, set the line-up of button accordion, lagerphone (a stick nailed with bottle tops), bush bass and voices, and from the 1970s the Bushwackers of Melbourne and many bush bands played the bush dance circuit with fiddle, banjo and guitar added. The accordion card stands for the button accordion, the tambourine card stands in for the lagerphone and the tea-chest bass card for the bush bass.
items.description: Rollicking dance tunes and ballads in which button accordion and fiddle carry the melody over a thumping bush bass and the jangling, stamped beat of the lagerphone, with rousing unison choruses.
exemplars: John Meredith folk collection (National Library of Australia)

items.name: Māori showbands (concert-party pop)
items.lineage: Popular entertainment bands of Māori musicians that grew from the concert-party tradition and toured New Zealand, Australia, Asia and the United States from the late 1950s into the 1970s, combining close-harmony singing, electric band backing and comedy with Māori songs and action songs and current pop and show tunes. The Howard Morrison Quartet recorded hits for La Gloria, and the Maori Volcanics, Quin Tikis and Maori Hi-Five were leading touring showbands.
items.description: Polished close-harmony vocal groups fronting clean electric guitar, bass and drums, moving between ballads, novelty numbers, rock'n'roll covers and action songs in bright, showy arrangements.
exemplars: Howard Morrison Quartet — My Old Man's an All Black (La Gloria, 1960)

items.name: Ura pa'u (Cook Islands drum dance)
items.lineage: Drum-dance tradition of the Cook Islands, centred on Rarotonga and Aitutaki, in which an ensemble of tōkere slit drums, the larger ka'ara and the skin-headed pa'u drum drives fast dances, alongside chanted pe'e and the ukulele-and-guitar kaparima action songs. Island and village teams compete at the Te Maeva Nui festival, and the Cook Islands National Arts Theatre has toured the repertoire. The Pacific slit-gong card stands in for the tōkere and ka'ara, and a generic membrane-drum card for the pa'u.
items.description: Fast interlocking patterns on high wooden slit drums over the deep thud of a skin drum, with sudden ensemble stops and accelerations cueing the dancers, framed by chanted calls and gentler ukulele-accompanied action songs.
exemplars: Te Maeva Nui festival drum-dance recordings

items.name: Fakaseasea and fakanau (older Tuvaluan song and dance)
items.lineage: Older song genres of Tuvalu that preceded the fatele: fakaseasea, slow and measured songs, and fakanau, men's dance-songs performed with rhythmic movements of the arms and body. Gerd Koch recorded both across the islands in 1960-61 and published texts, translations and a CD in Songs of Tuvalu (Institute of Pacific Studies, University of the South Pacific, 2000).
items.description: Group singing on repeated verses, slow and measured in the fakaseasea and firmer and more rhythmic in the men's fakanau.
exemplars: Gerd Koch, Songs of Tuvalu (Institute of Pacific Studies, USP, 2000, with CD of 1960-61 recordings)

items.name: Roro and jebwa (Marshallese chant and stick dance)
items.lineage: Traditional chant and dance of the Marshall Islands. Roro are chants recounting ancient legends, performed to give guidance during navigation and strength to mothers in labour; the jebwa (jobwa) is a stick dance, now kept for special occasions, in which men strike their staffs together as part of the choreography. Marshallese aje hourglass drums were formerly played almost exclusively by women, in ensembles of singer-drummers that accompanied men's dances. Recordings are held at the Alele Museum in Majuro, and Jessica Schwartz's Radiation Sounds (Duke University Press) documents Marshallese song. A generic membrane-drum card stands in for the aje.
items.description: Forceful, rhythmic group chanting, with the sharp clack of struck staffs and the dry beat of an hourglass drum marking the dancers' movements.
exemplars: Jessica Schwartz, Radiation Sounds (Duke University Press, 2021)

items.name: Kantan Chamorrita (Chamorro improvised verse song)
items.lineage: Improvised sung verse of the Chamorro people of Guam and the Northern Mariana Islands, in which singers trade four-line verses on a traditional melody, teasing, courting or debating one another in turn; it was sung during shared work such as husking corn and at social gatherings. Recordings of elder singers are held at the Micronesian Area Research Center of the University of Guam.
items.description: Unaccompanied singers answer one another with improvised quatrains on a simple, repeating melody, the words delivered clearly so the wit of each reply carries.
exemplars: University of Guam Micronesian Area Research Center recordings of kantan chamorrita

items.name: Leo kiʻekiʻe (Hawaiian falsetto and hula kuʻi song)
items.lineage: Hawaiian-language song style for hula kuʻi and later hula ʻauana, developed from the late nineteenth century when Hawaiian poetry was set to Western-influenced melodies with guitar and ukulele, and marked by leo kiʻekiʻe, a falsetto that leaps across the haʻi, the break between chest and head voice. Genoa Keawe and Bill Aliʻiloa Lincoln were celebrated falsetto singers, and the Aloha Festivals falsetto contest continues the style.
items.description: A high, ringing falsetto that flips audibly between registers on held notes and leaps, carried over strummed ukulele and guitar, a sliding steel guitar and a bouncing bass in an easy two-beat hula rhythm.

items.name: Himeni (Hawaiian hymn and choral song)
items.lineage: Hawaiian-language hymn singing introduced by the American Protestant mission of the early nineteenth century and taken into Hawaiian choral practice, sung in churches such as Kawaiahaʻo in Honolulu and shaping later Hawaiian part-singing. The Kamehameha Schools Song Contest, held since 1921, has student classes compete in choral arrangements of Hawaiian songs.
items.description: Hymns and Hawaiian songs in full, blended choral harmony, sung with open, clear vowels, smooth legato lines and gentle, sustained cadences.

items.name: Contemporary Hawaiian music (1970s Hawaiian Renaissance)
items.lineage: Hawaiian popular music of the 1970s Hawaiian Renaissance, when young musicians revived Hawaiian-language songs, slack-key guitar and falsetto and joined them to folk-rock and acoustic-band arrangements. Sunday Mānoa's Guava Jam (1969) is often treated as its starting point, followed by the Sons of Hawaii, Olomana, the Gabby Pahinui Hawaiian Band and releases on Panini Records.
items.description: Acoustic band songs with ringing ukulele, twelve-string and open-tuned guitar textures over upright bass, sung in Hawaiian and English in close vocal harmony with occasional falsetto breaks.

items.name: Meʻetuʻupaki (Tongan paddle dance-song)
items.lineage: Standing dance-song of Tonga performed by a large group of men holding carved paddles (paki), whose poetry and movements are counted among the oldest surviving in Tongan dance and were already reported by Captain Cook's voyages. The dancers sing the song themselves, often joined by other singers, while the dance master keeps the beat on a small lali slit drum; Adrienne Kaeppler's research on Tongan dance documents the form and its texts. The Pacific slit-gong card stands in for the small lali.
items.description: Measured group singing by the dancing men in steady, repeated phrases, kept in time by the dry, even strokes of a small wooden slit drum that coordinate the paddle movements.
exemplars: Adrienne Kaeppler field recordings and documentation of Tongan dance

items.name: Hiva kakala (Tongan string-band love song)
items.lineage: Tongan popular love-song genre, the 'fragrant' songs named for kakala flowers, sung in close harmony to string-band accompaniment of guitars and ukulele at kava-drinking gatherings (faikava), village dances and for the tauʻolunga solo dance. The repertoire was widely issued on Viking Records LPs and is played by kava-club string bands in Tonga and the diaspora.
items.description: Sweet, multi-part harmony singing over gently strummed guitars and ukulele, in a relaxed, swaying rhythm suited to the gliding tauʻolunga dance.

items.name: Hiva usu (Tongan old-style hymn polyphony)
items.lineage: Old style of unaccompanied Tongan congregational hymn singing, kept chiefly in smaller churches and minority Methodist bodies rather than in the choir-and-brass-band practice of the Free Wesleyan Church. A strong singer opens each hymn alone (the hua) and the congregation then joins, singing the Tongan text in several voice parts.
items.description: A single strong voice sets the opening of each hymn, then the whole congregation enters in full, broad multi-part harmony, moving through slow strophic verses without accompaniment.
exemplars: Recordings of Tongan hiva usu congregational singing

items.name: Maʻuluʻulu (Tongan seated group dance-song)
items.lineage: Tongan group dance-song performed by rows of seated performers who sing poetry while executing arm movements, distinct from the standing lakalaka. It is accompanied by wooden slit drums and is performed especially by school and church groups; Adrienne Kaeppler documented the form in her studies of Tongan dance.
items.description: A large seated chorus sings sung poetry in parts, the voices locked to the steady, insistent beat of wooden slit drums that drive the synchronized arm movements.
exemplars: Adrienne Kaeppler's documentation of Tongan maʻuluʻulu
Tongan school and church maʻuluʻulu performances

items.name: Kailao (Tongan war-club dance)
items.lineage: Men's war dance of Tonga, introduced from ʻUvea (Wallis), in which ranks of dancers brandish clubs in mock combat to shouted calls from a leader, accompanied by drumming. The Sipi Tau performed by the Tongan national rugby team is a form of kailao. The slit-gong card stands in for the accompanying drum.
items.description: Hard, rapid drumming drives men's shouted calls and answering group cries, with sudden stops and accents marking the strikes of the mock fight.
exemplars: Adrienne Kaeppler's documentation of Tongan kailao

items.name: Sere ni cumu (Fijian kava-party string-band song)
items.lineage: Fijian string-band songs sung at yaqona (kava) drinking gatherings, in close vocal harmony to guitars and ukulele; the same music accompanies the taralala, a side-by-side shuffling couple dance. The repertoire circulates on Suva-based labels and in village and town kava sessions.
items.description: Relaxed close-harmony singing over steadily strummed guitars and ukulele, with a lilting, even dance pulse suited to long social evenings.
exemplars: Fijian string-band recordings issued by South Pacific Recordings and Procera Music (Suva)

items.name: Indo-Fijian bhajan and chowtal (Fiji Hindi devotional and Holi song)
items.lineage: Song traditions of the descendants of Indian indentured labourers (girmitiya) brought to Fiji under the indenture system, sung in Fiji Hindi and Hindi. Bhajan, the most popular Indo-Fijian form, is sung at devotional gatherings to harmonium and dholak; chowtal, a Bhojpuri Holi song carried to Fiji by the indentured workers, is sung antiphonally by two facing rows of singers with a dholak drummer.
items.description: A leading voice and answering group trade devotional verses over pumped, sustained harmonium chords, driven by the brisk strokes of a double-headed drum.

items.name: Tautoga (Rotuman group dance-song)
items.lineage: The principal group dance of Rotuma, the Polynesian island dependency of Fiji, performed in lines by men and women at celebrations, with the dancers and accompanying singers performing songs in Rotuman. Alan Howard and Jan Rensel's Rotuma archive holds documentation and recordings.
items.description: Full-voiced group singing in parts, rhythmically tied to the movements of long lines of dancers and building in energy through repeated verses.
exemplars: Alan Howard and Jan Rensel Rotuma archive recordings

items.name: Haka of Te Henua ʻEnana (Marquesan chant and dance)
items.lineage: Chant and dance of the Marquesas Islands, revived in recent decades and showcased at the Matavaʻa o Te Henua ʻEnana arts festival: men's haka such as the haka manu (bird dance) and haka puaʻa (pig dance), together with older chant forms, accompanied by large skin drums (pahu) and body percussion. Jane Freeman Moulin has documented Marquesan music. The membrane-drum card stands in for the Marquesan pahu.
items.description: Deep, booming drums under guttural chorus chant, grunts and shouts, with slapped bodies and massed claps punctuating heavy, earthbound dance rhythms.
exemplars: Matavaʻa o Te Henua ʻEnana festival recordings
Jane Freeman Moulin's documentation of Marquesan music

items.name: ʻŪtē (Tahitian satirical song)
items.lineage: Secular Tahitian song genre with quick, witty and often teasing or satirical lyrics, sung by a lead singer answered by a chorus to guitars and ukulele at celebrations; ʻūtē is a competition category of the Heiva i Tahiti.
items.description: Playful, quick-witted lead verses over brisk strumming, answered by a lively chorus in short cyclic refrains.
exemplars: Heiva i Tahiti ʻūtē competition recordings

items.name: Riu (Rapa Nui traditional chant)
items.lineage: Inherited sung genres of Rapa Nui (Easter Island), including the riu, sung narratives and laments, the ute, and the kaikai chants recited while forming string figures, sung in the Rapa Nui language by groups. The Chilean musicologist Ramón Campbell recorded and studied the repertoire, and it is performed at the annual Tapati Rapa Nui festival.
items.description: Group chant in a narrow melodic range, the words carried in even, repeated phrases with a grave, recitational character.
exemplars: Ramón Campbell field recordings of Rapa Nui music

items.name: Ae-ae and pilou (Kanak customary dance-song)
items.lineage: Customary dance music of the Kanak of New Caledonia's Grande Terre, documented by Raymond Ammann in Kanak Dance and Music (1997, with CD): men's dance songs such as the ae-ae, sung by small groups for the pilou and other collective dances, accompanied by bark clappers (bwanjep) and bamboo stamping tubes struck on the ground. The cupped hand-clap card stands in for the bark clappers and the stamping-tube card for the Kanak bamboo tubes.
items.description: Small groups of men sing repeated phrases over dull, muffled clapper beats and the hollow thud of bamboo tubes pounded on earth.
exemplars: Raymond Ammann, Kanak Dance and Music (1997, with CD)
ADCK / Centre Culturel Tjibaou archive recordings

items.name: Tapéra (Loyalty Islands church choral song)
items.lineage: Choral church singing of the Protestant congregations of Lifou (Drehu) and Maré (Nengone) in New Caledonia's Loyalty Islands, whose churches grew from the London Missionary Society missions of the nineteenth century. Tapéra are sung unaccompanied in several parts in the local languages; Raymond Ammann has documented the style.
items.description: Unaccompanied congregational choir singing in several parts, bright and full, with sustained chords and strophic verses resonating in the church.
exemplars: ADCK / Centre Culturel Tjibaou recordings of tapéra
Raymond Ammann's documentation of Loyalty Islands church singing

items.name: Stringben (Papua New Guinea string band)
items.lineage: Acoustic guitar-and-ukulele band music that spread across Papua New Guinea after the Second World War and became a national popular idiom, sung in Tok Pisin, Motu and other local languages in close group harmony. Michael Webb's Lokal Musik (1993) documents the genre; bands such as the Paramana Strangers of Port Moresby recorded widely, and studios such as Pacific Gold in Rabaul issued stringben cassettes.
items.description: Bright, ringing strummed guitars and ukulele under high, close group harmonies, with a steady, swaying pulse and repeated verse-chorus cycles.

items.name: Bamboo band (Bougainville and Solomon Islands struck-tube band)
items.lineage: Bands of bamboo tubes of graded lengths, held in frames or bundles, whose open ends are struck with flat paddles or rubber sandals to sound pitched bass and melody lines; the style is played on Bougainville and Buka and in the Solomon Islands, often with guitars, ukulele and singing. The struck bamboo-tube card stands in for the Bougainville tube sets.
items.description: Deep, popping pitched thuds from struck bamboo tubes form a bouncing bass and melody under strummed strings and group singing, in tight repeating dance patterns.

items.name: Sepik sacred flutes and garamut (Iatmul and Abelam men's ritual music)
items.lineage: Ritual music of the Sepik region: among the Iatmul and Abelam, long side-blown bamboo flutes are played in pairs by initiated men, the two players interlocking to build melodies on the flutes' overtones, and ensembles of large carved wooden slit drums (garamut) beaten with heavy pounders sound signals, rhythms and ceremonial pieces. The credited bamboo-flute card stands in for the sacred flutes.
items.description: Paired breathy bamboo flutes leap between overtones in interlocking calls, set against the deep, resonant booms of massive slit drums.
exemplars: Institute of Papua New Guinea Studies recordings of Sepik music

items.name: Baining night dance (East New Britain fire-dance song)
items.lineage: Night dance of the Baining peoples of the Gazelle Peninsula, East New Britain, in which masked men dance into and through a large bonfire. The dancers are accompanied by a male chorus and by bamboo stamping tubes beaten in a steady rhythm. The stamping-tube card stands in for the Baining bamboo tubes.
items.description: A men's chorus sings repeated phrases over the relentless hollow pounding of bamboo tubes, building a hypnotic, driving pulse through the night.
exemplars: Institute of Papua New Guinea Studies recordings of Baining dance

items.name: Wosi milamala (Trobriand harvest-festival songs)
items.lineage: Songs (wosi) sung on Kiriwina in the Trobriand Islands during the milamala, the festival after the yam harvest when the spirits of the dead are held to return, and accompanying its dancing. The linguist Gunter Senft recorded and transcribed them, publishing them in The Tuma Underworld of Love. The kundu card stands in for the Trobriand hourglass drums that accompany the dancing.
items.description: Group singing of short repeated verses in a narrow range, set to the dry, light beat of hourglass drums that circle with the dancers.
exemplars: Gunter Senft, The Tuma Underworld of Love (2011)

items.name: Takū song and dance (Polynesian outlier atoll)
items.lineage: Song and dance repertoire of Takū (Takuu), a Polynesian outlier atoll north-east of Bougainville in Papua New Guinea, where sung poetry accompanies ceremonies and communal dances in the Takū language. Richard Moyle's Songs from the Second Float: A Musical Ethnography of Takū Atoll documents the repertoire.
items.description: Strong communal choruses sing sung poetry in unison and parts, phrased to dance movement and repeated in cycles.
exemplars: Richard Moyle, Songs from the Second Float: A Musical Ethnography of Takū Atoll (2007)

items.name: Tikopia songs (Polynesian outlier dance-songs and laments)
items.lineage: Song repertoire of Tikopia, a Polynesian outlier in the Temotu province of the Solomon Islands, including dance songs, laments and other sung genres. Raymond Firth recorded songs in 1952, building on texts gathered during his first fieldwork of 1928-29; with Mervyn McLean's transcriptions they were published as Tikopia Songs (Cambridge University Press, 1990).
items.description: Group singing in a narrow melodic range, ranging from rhythmic dance songs to slow, sorrowful laments, with repeated verses.
exemplars: Raymond Firth and Mervyn McLean, Tikopia Songs (Cambridge University Press, 1990)

items.name: Mungiki songs (Bellona and Rennell Polynesian song)
items.lineage: Song repertoire of the Polynesian outlier islands of Bellona (Mungiki) and Rennell (Mugaba) in the Solomon Islands, including old ritual songs addressed to the gods, dance songs and laments, sung in the Rennellese-Bellonese language. Jane Mink Rossen recorded and published the Bellona repertoire in Songs of Bellona Island.
items.description: Unaccompanied group song in a narrow range, solemn and recitational in the ritual songs and more rhythmic in the dance songs.
exemplars: Jane Mink Rossen, Songs of Bellona Island (1987)

items.name: Stringben (Ni-Vanuatu string band)
items.lineage: Acoustic string bands of Vanuatu, playing guitars, ukulele and a home-made one-string box bass (bush bass) behind harmonised singing in Bislama and local languages; a leading village and town popular music, showcased at the Fest'Napuan festival in Port Vila. The tea-chest bass card stands in for the bush bass.
items.description: Bright strummed guitars and ukulele over a thumping single-string box bass, carrying close group harmonies in a steady, bouncing dance groove.

items.name: Atingting (Ambrym and Malakula slit-drum ensembles)
items.lineage: Ensembles of large upright carved slit drums (atingting in Ambrym; tamtam in Bislama) on Ambrym and Malakula, beaten with wooden sticks in interlocking rhythms for dances such as the Rom masked dance and for grade-taking ceremonies, with men's singing. The Vanuatu Kaljoral Senta holds recordings, and the Back to My Roots festival on Ambrym presents the music. The slit-gong card stands in for the upright atingting.
items.description: Several upright slit drums of different sizes interlock in dense, rolling cross-rhythms, deep booms and sharp wooden strokes, under men's chanted singing.
exemplars: Back to My Roots festival recordings (Ambrym)

items.name: Changüí (Guantánamo proto-son)
items.lineage: Rural song-dance of the Guantánamo region of eastern Cuba, played at country parties and regarded as a direct forerunner of son.
