Its ensemble is the tres, the bongó de monte (a larger, lower-pitched bongó that improvises throughout), the marímbula as bass, the guayo metal scraper and maracas, with a lead singer answered by a chorus. The bongos card stands in for the bongó de monte.
items.description: The tres repeats short syncopated figures over a plucked marímbula bass and a rasping metal scraper, while the deep bongó cuts in with loud improvised strokes and the lead singer trades refrains with the chorus.
exemplars: Elio Revé — changüí-son recordings with Orquesta Revé

items.name: Nengón and kiribá (Baracoa proto-son)
items.lineage: Two related rural song-dance forms of the Baracoa area at the eastern tip of Cuba, kept by campesino groups and regarded, with the changüí of nearby Guantánamo, as early forms from which son developed. Sung verses alternate with choral refrains over the repeated figures of the tres and small rural percussion such as güiro and maracas.
items.description: A bright, steel-strung tres plays short repeating figures under a scraped güiro and shaken maracas, while a lead voice sings verses that a small chorus answers with a fixed refrain.
exemplars: EGREM field recordings of Baracoa campesino groups

items.name: Punto guajiro (Cuban improvised décima song)
items.lineage: Sung poetry of the Cuban countryside, in which singers, often improvising, set ten-line décimas to traditional melodies (tonadas) accompanied by laúd, tres, guitar and light percussion such as güiro and claves; UNESCO inscribed Punto on its Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity. Punto libre, where the accompaniment drops out under the free-rhythm vocal line, is tied to the west of the island and punto fijo, in strict time, to the centre; the controversia is a sung duel of improvised décimas between two poets.
items.description: A solo voice declaims ten-line stanzas in a high, ornamented line, the bright tremolo and runs of the laúd and the strummed guitar and tres filling the pauses between lines over a light scraper and clave pulse.
exemplars: Justo Vega and Adolfo Alfonso controversias (EGREM)

items.name: Tumba francesa (eastern Cuban Franco-Haitian drum-dance)
items.lineage: Drum, song and dance societies founded in eastern Cuba in the 19th century by Haitian-born and Franco-Haitian people who arrived with French planters after the Haitian Revolution; the surviving societies are La Caridad de Oriente in Santiago de Cuba, Pompadour Santa Catalina de Riccis in Guantánamo and Bejuco in Sagua de Tánamo, and UNESCO proclaimed the tradition a Masterpiece of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity. A lead singer (composé) sings in Creole and Spanish, answered by a chorus, over large hand-played drums (tumbas), the catá, a hollow log beaten with sticks, and the chachá, a metal rattle; masón, yubá and frenté are its main dances. A generic membrane-drum card stands in for the tumbas, the palitos card for the sticks on the catá and a generic shaker card for the chachá.
items.description: Large hand drums lock into a heavy rolling pattern under the dry knock of sticks on a hollow log and a shaken metal rattle, the lead drum improvising against the dancers' steps while the lead singer's lines are answered by the chorus.
exemplars: Tumba Francesa La Caridad de Oriente
EGREM Antología de la Música Afrocubana, tumba francesa volume

items.name: Conga santiaguera (Santiago de Cuba carnival conga)
items.lineage: Street carnival music of Santiago de Cuba, played by neighbourhood congas such as Los Hoyos, Paso Franco and San Agustín as they parade through the city in July, with the crowd singing short refrains, alongside the more choreographed comparsas of the carnival. Its sound centres on the corneta china, a Chinese-derived shawm adopted in the early 20th century, over bocúes (long drums slung from the shoulder and played by hand), larger stick-beaten drums, bells and car brake drums struck with metal beaters. A generic membrane-drum card stands in for the drums and the agogo card for the bells and brake drums.
items.description: A piercing, nasal shawm melody soars over a dense wall of hand and stick drums, clanging bells and ringing brake drums, the crowd shouting short refrains as the procession surges forward.
exemplars: Santiago de Cuba carnival field recordings

items.name: Abakuá (ñáñigo society drumming and chant)
items.lineage: Music of the Abakuá, a men's initiation and mutual-aid society established in the Havana port town of Regla in the first half of the nineteenth century by Africans from the Cross River region (Efik and Ejagham peoples of present-day Nigeria and Cameroon), whose lodges exist only in Havana, Matanzas and Cárdenas. Its public ceremonial ensemble (biankomé) sets the chants of a lead singer, answered by a chorus in the society's ritual language, over three small single-headed drums (enkomo), the lead drum bonkó enchemiyá, the ekón iron bell, itón sticks beaten on the bonkó's shell and erikundi basket rattles. A generic membrane-drum card stands in for the drums, the agogo card for the ekón, the palitos card for the itón and a generic shaker card for the erikundi.
items.description: A lead singer's chant is answered by a male chorus over a tight lattice of small high-pitched drums, a deep improvising lead drum, a piercing iron-bell pattern, sticks cracking on a drum shell and the swish of basket rattles.
exemplars: Conjunto Folklórico Nacional de Cuba (Abakuá repertoire)

items.name: Arará (Dahomeyan-Cuban ritual drumming)
items.lineage: Ritual music of the Cuban Arará, descendants of Ewe-Fon Africans from the former kingdom of Dahomey, whose cabildos and houses of worship for the vodún deities survive chiefly in Matanzas province, among them the Sabalú line of Jovellanos and the Magino line of Perico. Songs in a Fon-derived ritual language are led by a singer and answered by a chorus over a set of drums played with sticks and hands, an iron bell and a gourd rattle. A generic membrane-drum card stands in for the Arará drums and the agogo card for the bell.
items.description: A leader's songs are answered by the chorus over interlocking stick- and hand-played drums, a ringing iron-bell timeline and a beaded gourd rattle, the lead drum varying its phrases against the steady supporting parts.
exemplars: EGREM Antología de la Música Afrocubana, Música Arará volume

items.name: Iyesá (Matanzas cabildo drumming and song)
items.lineage: Music of the Iyesá, Cubans descended from the Ijesha subgroup of the Yoruba, whose Cabildo Iyesá Moddú San Juan Bautista in Matanzas, founded in the 19th century, keeps its own drums and songs for the orishas, separate from the batá repertoire of Lukumí worship. Call-and-response songs are accompanied by a set of double-headed cylindrical drums with iron bells. A generic membrane-drum card stands in for the Iyesá drums and the agogo card for the bells.
items.description: Double-headed drums lay down a driving interlocking pattern under ringing iron bells while a lead singer's praise songs are answered by the cabildo chorus.
exemplars: EGREM Antología de la Música Afrocubana, Música Iyesá volume
Cabildo Iyesá Moddú San Juan Bautista (Matanzas)

items.name: Yuka and makuta (Congo-Cuban secular drum-dance)
items.lineage: Secular drum-dances of Cubans of Congo (Central African, Bantu-speaking) descent, documented by Fernando Ortiz and counted among the forerunners of rumba. Yuka is played on three single-headed drums cut from hollowed tree trunks, the large caja, the middle mula and the small cachimbo, with a hoe blade or piece of iron struck as a bell and rattles; its couple dance includes the pelvic gesture (vacunao) later taken into guaguancó. Makuta, danced in the Congo cabildos, uses its own drums. A generic membrane-drum card stands in for the drums, the agogo card for the struck hoe blade and a generic shaker card for the rattles.
items.description: Three deep trunk drums interlock, the largest improvising over the steady middle and high drums, under a clanging iron pattern and rattles while a lead singer's short songs are answered by the dancers' chorus.
exemplars: EGREM Antología de la Música Afrocubana, vol. 5: Tambor Yuka (recorded at El Guayabo, Pinar del Río)
Conjunto Folklórico Nacional de Cuba yuka repertoire

items.name: Afrocubanismo (Cuban concert music)
items.lineage: Cuban art-music movement of the 1920s and 1930s, led by Amadeo Roldán and Alejandro García Caturla, that brought Afro-Cuban rhythms, instruments and song forms into orchestral, chamber and piano writing; Roldán's Rítmicas V and VI (1930), scored for Cuban percussion, are among the earliest concert works for percussion ensemble. Roldán's Rítmicas I to IV, for piano and wind quintet, are the model for the piano and woodwind cards; the orchestral works of the movement add strings and brass. Ernesto Lecuona's piano danzas and suites carried Cuban dance rhythms into the salon and concert repertoire of the same years.
items.description: Piano, woodwind and Cuban percussion textures built on Cuban dance rhythms, with clave, scraper and drum patterns layered against modernist harmony, angular woodwind lines and percussive piano figures.
exemplars: Alejandro García Caturla — Tres danzas cubanas

items.name: Zarzuela cubana (Havana lyric theatre)
items.lineage: Cuban branch of Spanish lyric theatre whose golden age came in Havana in the 1930s, with works staged from the late twenties into the forties, many of them first at the Teatro Martí, setting stories of colonial Cuba to scores that mix operatic arias and choruses with habanera, danza, guajira, son and Afro-Cuban numbers. Its best-known works are Gonzalo Roig's Cecilia Valdés (1932), Ernesto Lecuona's María la O (1930) and El cafetal, and Rodrigo Prats's Amalia Batista (1936). The voice card carries the soloists and chorus, and the string-quartet card stands in for the theatre orchestra's string section.
items.description: Full-voiced operatic soloists and a mixed chorus sing lyrical arias and ensembles over a theatre orchestra whose strings and winds shift between romantic melody and Cuban dance rhythms.
exemplars: Ernesto Lecuona — María la O (cast recordings)

items.name: Mozambique (1960s Havana percussion dance)
items.lineage: Dance rhythm created in Havana in 1963 by the percussionist Pedro Izquierdo, known as Pello el Afrokán, who drew on the conga and comparsa drumming of carnival and led a large band of congas, bass drums and cowbells with trumpets and trombones, a lead singer and an answering chorus. Hits such as María Caracoles made it a national dance craze in the mid-1960s. A generic membrane-drum card stands in for the bass drums.
items.description: A massed battery of congas, bass drums and cowbells drives a heavy carnival groove under punchy trumpet and trombone riffs, with a lead singer calling and the chorus answering.
exemplars: Pello el Afrokán — mozambique recordings of the mid-1960s

items.name: Órgano oriental (Manzanillo dance-organ music)
items.lineage: Dance music of Manzanillo and Holguín in eastern Cuba played on large crank-operated organs that read perforated cardboard music, first imported from France and later built locally, notably by the Borbolla family workshop in Manzanillo. The organ is joined by timbales, güiro and tumbadora to play danzones, sones and boleros for public dances.
items.description: A loud, reedy mechanical organ plays melody, chords and bass in steady dance time while timbales, a scraped güiro and a conga drum add a crisp percussion groove.

items.name: Kumina (St Thomas Bongo-nation ritual drumming)
items.lineage: Ancestral-spirit religion and ceremony of the parish of St Thomas in eastern Jamaica, kept by descendants of Central African (Kongo) indentured labourers who arrived after emancipation, known as the Bongo nation. At wakes, memorials and thanksgivings a Kumina queen or captain leads songs in a Kikongo-derived 'country' language and in Jamaican creole ('bailo'), answered by the gathering, over two drums, the deep kbandu and the lead playing cyas, whose seated player varies its pitch with a heel on the head, while catta sticks are beaten on a drum's body and shakas are shaken. A generic membrane-drum card stands in for the drums, the palitos card for the catta sticks and a generic shaker card for the shakas.
items.description: A lead voice's short refrains are taken up by the crowd over a deep, steady bass drum and a higher lead drum whose pitch bends under the player's heel, with sticks clicking on a drum shell and rattles shaken on the beat.
exemplars: Folkways FE 4461 Jamaican Cult Music (George Eaton Simpson, 1954)
Kenneth Bilby field recordings of Kumina

items.name: Revival Zion and Pukkumina (Jamaican Revivalist worship)
items.lineage: Afro-Christian Revival religion of Jamaica, grown from the Great Revival that swept the island in the mid-nineteenth century, with two branches: Zion, closer to Protestant worship, and Pukkumina (Pocomania), with stronger African retentions. Services set Sankey hymns, sung slow and drawn-out, and fast rhythmic choruses over a bass drum and a rattling side drum with hand clapping, while 'trumping' or 'labouring', a rhythmic over-breathing as worshippers circle, brings on possession by the spirit.
items.description: A congregation sings hymns and short choruses in full, heterophonic unison over a booming bass drum and a rattling side drum, hand claps and loud rhythmic breathing building the tempo toward trance.
exemplars: Folkways FE 4461 Jamaican Cult Music (George Eaton Simpson, 1954)
Olive Lewin / ACIJ Jamaica Memory Bank recordings

items.name: Kromanti play (Jamaican Maroon ceremonial music)
items.lineage: Ceremonial music of the Jamaican Maroons, descendants of Africans who escaped slavery and formed free mountain communities recognised by peace treaties with the British colonial government in the eighteenth century; it is kept by the Windward Maroons of Moore Town, whose heritage UNESCO proclaimed a Masterpiece of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity, and by the Leeward Maroons of Accompong. In Kromanti play, songs in Kromanti, a ritual language rich in Akan (Twi) words, are led and answered over drumming to call the ancestral spirits, who possess the dancers; the abeng, a side-blown cow horn, carries signals between communities. A generic membrane-drum card stands in for the Maroon drums.
items.description: Hand drums play driving interlocking rhythms while a lead singer's short phrases are answered by the group, the songs repeating and intensifying as the ceremony moves toward possession.
exemplars: Smithsonian Folkways SF 40412 Drums of Defiance: Maroon Music from the Earliest Free Black Communities of Jamaica (Kenneth Bilby)

items.name: Jonkonnu (Jamaican fife-and-drum masquerade)
items.lineage: Christmas masquerade of Jamaica, described since the 18th century, in which costumed characters such as Pitchy-Patchy, Horse Head, Cow Head, Belly Woman, the Devil and the King and Queen dance through villages and towns to a small band of fife, bass drum and rattling side drum. Unlike the large brass-and-cowbell parades of Bahamian Junkanoo, Jamaican Jonkonnu keeps this rural fife-and-drum band.
items.description: A shrill, ornamented fife melody rides over a pounding bass drum and a rattling side drum as the masqueraders dance along the road.
exemplars: Olive Lewin field recordings of Jonkonnu bands (ACIJ)
Jamaica Cultural Development Commission festival recordings

items.name: Etu (Hanover Yoruba-Jamaican feast dance)
items.lineage: Dance and song kept by a small community in the parish of Hanover in western Jamaica who trace their ancestry to Yoruba Africans brought to Jamaica after emancipation. Etu forms part of a 'play' performed at wedding feasts, nine-nights and other memorial feasts, with songs containing Yoruba-derived words led by a singer and answered by the group to drumming. A generic membrane-drum card stands in for the Etu drums.
items.description: A lead singer's short songs are answered by the group over steady hand drumming that carries the dancers through the feast.
exemplars: Olive Lewin field recordings of Ettu groups (Jamaica Memory Bank)

items.name: Dinki mini and gerreh (Jamaican nine-night wake music)
items.lineage: Music of Jamaican wakes, set-ups and nine-nights, the gatherings held on the nights after a death. Dinki mini, centred on St Mary and other eastern parishes, is a lively wake dance-song accompanied by drum, shakas, grater, katta sticks and the benta (a bamboo stick zither); gerreh is the related wake tradition of western parishes such as Hanover and Westmoreland. The membrane-drum card stands in for the drum, the shaker card for the shakas and the guayo (grater) card for the grater.
items.description: A leader raises short songs that the gathering answers over a steady drum, rattling shakers and a scraped grater, the singing and dancing meant to cheer the bereaved rather than mourn.
exemplars: Jamaica Memory Bank (ACIJ) recordings of dinki mini and gerreh
Olive Lewin, Rock It Come Over: The Folk Music of Jamaica (transcriptions)

items.name: Digging songs and ring-play songs (rural Jamaica)
items.lineage: Rural Jamaican work songs sung by digging and planting gangs, a leader raising a line and the group answering in time with the strokes of their tools, together with the ring-play (ring-game) songs sung and clapped in circle games. Louise Bennett recorded a selection of Jamaican folk songs for Folkways in the 1950s, and the African-Caribbean Institute of Jamaica holds field recordings.
items.description: Plain, full-voiced call-and-response singing in short repeating phrases, locked to the thud of tools in the field or to hand-claps and stepping in the ring games.
exemplars: Louise Bennett — Jamaican Folk Songs (Folkways FW 6846)
African-Caribbean Institute of Jamaica field recordings

items.name: Jamaican shuffle (pre-ska Kingston R&B)
items.lineage: Kingston recordings of the late 1950s cut for sound-system operators such as Clement 'Coxsone' Dodd and Duke Reid, first as exclusive sound-system records and then as local singles, modelled on US rhythm and blues. Jamaican players stressed the afterbeat of the shuffle rhythm, the step that led directly to ska around 1960.
items.description: Boogie-style piano and a swung shuffle beat with the off-beat pushed forward, honking tenor saxophone breaks, walking upright bass and plain, shouted R&B vocals.

items.name: Konbit songs (Haitian collective work songs)
items.lineage: Songs of the konbit (coumbite), the collective work party in which Haitian farmers clear or hoe a neighbour's field together. A song leader (simidor) improvises lines, often teasing or topical, that the work gang answers while a drummer keeps the hoes moving in time; Harold Courlander described and recorded the practice, and Alan Lomax recorded work songs in Haiti in 1936-37.
items.description: A solo singer's improvised lines answered by a chorus of workers over a steady drum beat, the song and the hoe strokes falling together in a strong, repeating work rhythm.
exemplars: Harold Courlander — Songs and Dances of Haiti (Folkways FE 4432)

items.name: Palos / atabales (Afro-Dominican sacred drumming)
items.lineage: Afro-Dominican sacred drumming on palos (atabales), long log drums played with sung responsorial verses at saints' festivals, velaciones and funerary rites of religious brotherhoods (cofradías). The Cofradía del Espíritu Santo de los Congos de Villa Mella, which plays its own congo drums with the canoíta and maracas, was proclaimed a UNESCO Masterpiece of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity; the membrane-drum card stands in for the palos and congo drums.
items.description: Several long hand drums interlock beneath a lead drum's improvised strokes, with maracas and a chorus answering a solo singer in steady, hypnotic cycles.
exemplars: Music from the Dominican Republic (Folkways, recorded by Verna Gillis)
Cofradía del Espíritu Santo de los Congos de Villa Mella

items.name: Salve dominicana (Dominican Marian devotional song)
items.lineage: The salve is a Dominican devotional song to the Virgin Mary and the saints, sung at velaciones and saints' festivals. Its sacred form (salve de la Virgen) is sung unaccompanied in a responsorial style derived from the Spanish Salve Regina, while the salve de pandero interpolates secular verses over a polyrhythmic accompaniment of panderos (frame drums), with the güira and other percussion in some communities; Martha Ellen Davis documented both.
items.description: A lead singer's devotional verses answered by a chorus, either bare and hymn-like or driven by layered frame-drum patterns and the rasp of a metal scraper.
exemplars: Music from the Dominican Republic (Folkways, recorded by Verna Gillis)
Martha Ellen Davis field recordings of salves

items.name: Mangulina and carabiné (Dominican campesino dances)
items.lineage: Rural Dominican dances of the south and the Cibao that are distinct from merengue: the mangulina, the carabiné of the south and the zapateo, a stamping dance. They are played by accordion, tambora and güira groups, with sung verses in some pieces; Verna Gillis recorded examples for Folkways. The membrane-drum card stands in for the two-headed tambora.
items.description: A bright accordion plays short repeated dance tunes over the hand-and-stick pattern of a two-headed drum and the scrape of the metal güira, carrying lively couple and group dances.
exemplars: Music from the Dominican Republic (Folkways, recorded by Verna Gillis)

items.name: Guloyas (Cocolo dance-drama of San Pedro de Macorís)
items.lineage: Masked dance-drama of the Cocolos, descendants of English-speaking migrants from the Eastern Caribbean who came to work in the sugar mills of San Pedro de Macorís from the late 19th century. The guloyas parade at Christmas and on the feast of St Peter, performing mummers' plays and dances to fife, kettle (snare) drum and bass drum; UNESCO proclaimed the Cocolo dance drama tradition a Masterpiece of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity.
items.description: A shrill fife melody over the crisp patterns of a snare drum and the beat of a bass drum, accompanying costumed dancers through the streets in marching and dance tunes.
exemplars: Cocolo dance drama tradition of San Pedro de Macorís (UNESCO, 2005)
Los Guloyas of San Pedro de Macorís

items.name: Danza puertorriqueña (Puerto Rican salon danza)
items.lineage: Puerto Rican salon dance that grew from the contradanza in the mid-19th century and was raised to a concert art by Manuel Gregorio Tavárez and his pupil Juan Morel Campos in Ponce. Danzas were written for piano and for dance orchestras in which the bombardino (euphonium) carries a characteristic countermelody, and the anthem 'La Borinqueña' is itself a danza.
items.description: A short paseo introduction gives way to a lyrical, gently ornamented melody over a syncopated left-hand dance figure, romantic and unhurried, with a contrasting answering phrase in the tenor register.
exemplars: Jesús María Sanromá — Puerto Rican danzas by Juan Morel Campos (Victor Red Seal album M-849, 1941)

items.name: Nueva trova puertorriqueña (Puerto Rican protest song)
items.lineage: Puerto Rican politically committed song movement of the late 1960s and 1970s, tied to the independence movement and university circles in San Juan. Singers such as Roy Brown and Andrés Jiménez and the group Haciendo Punto en Otro Son set topical texts to guitar and the cuatro, drawing on jíbaro forms such as the seis and aguinaldo, and early albums of the movement appeared on the independent Disco Libre label.
items.description: Clear, text-forward singing over strummed guitar and the bright double courses of the cuatro, with güiro and bass lifting the songs that borrow seis and aguinaldo rhythms.

items.name: Kalinda (Trinidad stick-fighting chant)
items.lineage: Trinidadian stick-fighting song, in which a chantwell leads call-and-response chants while drummers play skin drums for paired fighters in the ring (gayelle). Kalinda was central to the 19th-century canboulay and street carnival and is named among the roots of calypso; Alan Lomax recorded kalinda chants in Trinidad in 1962. The membrane-drum card stands in for the goatskin drums.
items.description: A hoarse lead chanter hurls short phrases that the crowd shouts back over fast, hard-hit hand drums, the rhythm rising with the fighting in the ring.
exemplars: Caribbean Voyage: Trinidad — Carnival Roots (Rounder, Alan Lomax 1962 recordings)

items.name: Tamboo bamboo (Trinidad bamboo-tube band)
items.lineage: Trinidadian carnival bands that took the place of skin drums after the colonial authorities restricted drumming in the late nineteenth century, using lengths of bamboo of different sizes (boom, foulé and cutter) stamped on the ground or struck with sticks, often joined by bottle-and-spoon. The steel band grew out of them and displaced them, but tamboo bamboo bands are still revived at carnival; the bamboo stamping-tube card stands in for the Trinidadian bamboos.
items.description: Deep hollow thumps of stamped bamboo interlock with the higher cracks of struck tubes, building a dense, driving processional rhythm.
exemplars: Tamboo bamboo bands at Trinidad Carnival

items.name: Orisha (Shango) drumming and song (Trinidad)
items.lineage: Trinidad Orisha worship, formerly called Shango, is an African-derived religion of Yoruba origin whose annual feasts at shrines feature songs to the orishas in a Yoruba-derived liturgical language, raised by a lead singer and answered by the congregation. A battery of three drums with shac-shac rattles accompanies the songs and the spirit possession they invite; George Eaton Simpson recorded the music for Folkways. The membrane-drum card stands in for the three drums.
items.description: Three drums lock into dense, accelerating patterns under rattles while a lead singer's invocations are answered by a full-throated chorus, cycling toward ecstatic peaks.
exemplars: Cult Music of Trinidad (Folkways FE 4478, George Eaton Simpson)

items.name: Spiritual Baptist (Shouter) hymn singing
items.lineage: Hymn singing of the Afro-Christian Spiritual Baptist (Shouter) churches of Trinidad and Tobago, whose worship was outlawed under the Shouters Prohibition Ordinance for more than three decades until its repeal at mid-century. Services centre on Sankey and other Protestant hymns sung slowly and elaborated by the congregation, rung in by a handbell, and on doption or trumping, rhythmic overbreathing and groaning that builds as worshippers enter the spirit.
items.description: Slow, swelling congregational hymns stretched and ornamented by many voices, giving way to rhythmic groaning, breathing and hand-clapping as the service intensifies.
exemplars: Cult Music of Trinidad (Folkways FE 4478, George Eaton Simpson)

items.name: Tassa drumming (Indo-Trinidadian drum ensemble)
items.lineage: Indo-Trinidadian drum ensemble brought by indentured labourers from North India, played for Hindu weddings and the Muslim Hosay (Muharram) processions. A lead cutter tassa improvises over one or more fuller tassas, a large bass drum and brass hand cymbals, all following named rhythmic patterns called hands; the bass-drum and cymbal cards stand in for the tassa band's bass and cymbals.
items.description: Cracking stick-beaten tassa drums trade fast, virtuosic rolls over a booming bass drum and clashing cymbals, the cutter's improvisations driving the ensemble to thunderous peaks.
exemplars: Caribbean Voyage: East Indian Music in the West Indies (Rounder)

items.name: Tan singing (Indo-Caribbean local classical song)
items.lineage: Indo-Caribbean local classical song of Trinidad and Guyana, developed by descendants of indentured labourers from North Indian light-classical and devotional song genres and sung at weddings and in competitions. A solo singer is accompanied by harmonium, dholak and dhantal (a struck steel rod), and the name comes from the tan, the virtuosic melismatic runs the singer improvises; Peter Manuel's study documents it.
items.description: A solo voice spins rapid, ornate melismatic runs over harmonium chords and a lilting dholak pattern, alternating sung verses with bursts of improvised virtuosity.
exemplars: Peter Manuel — East Indian Music in the West Indies: Tan-Singing, Chutney, and the Making of Indo-Caribbean Culture (2000)

items.name: Tambrin band music (Tobago reel and jig)
items.lineage: The tambrin band of Tobago, goatskin tambrin frame drums with a fiddle and a steel triangle, plays for the Tobago reel, a dance associated with the ancestral spirits, and for the jig and other social dances descended from British dances. It is a staple of the Tobago Heritage Festival; the frame-drum card stands in for the tambrins.
items.description: A sawing fiddle repeats short dance tunes over interlocking frame drums and a ringing triangle, a brisk, buoyant pulse for reels and jigs.

items.name: Tuk band (Barbados)
items.lineage: Barbadian band of double-headed bass drum, kettle (snare) drum, triangle and a penny whistle, which has largely replaced the earlier fiddle or flute; it is modelled on the regimental bands of the British military, played with African-derived rhythms. It accompanies the Barbados Landship, a friendly society whose members parade in naval uniform, and street masquerade characters at Crop Over and other festivals, moving from slow, stately tunes to fast, driving sections.
items.description: A shrill penny-whistle tune rides over a booming bass drum and rattling snare patterns, swinging from a stately march into fast, driving dance rhythm.

items.name: Spouge (Barbadian ska-calypso)
items.lineage: Barbadian popular dance music created by the singer Jackie Opel in the mid-1960s after he had recorded ska in Jamaica, fusing Jamaican ska with Trinidadian calypso and drawing on hymns, spirituals and sea shanties. The original band sound rested on cowbell, bass guitar and trap set with other electric and percussion instruments, later augmented by saxophone, trombone and trumpets (the saxophone card carries the horn section); two styles emerged, raw spouge (the Draytons Two style) and dragon spouge (the Cassius Clay style), and spouge bands stayed popular through the 1970s.
items.description: A bright, bouncing dance groove: a clanking cowbell pattern locked to bass guitar and trap set, with prominent guitar and punchy horn riffs under the lead vocal.

items.name: Rake-and-scrape (Bahamian saw-and-accordion dance music)
items.lineage: Out Island dance music of the Bahamas, strongest on Cat Island and Long Island, played on a carpenter's handsaw bent and scraped with a screwdriver or knife, a goatskin goombay drum and a button accordion, sometimes with guitar. It accompanied quadrilles and other social dances and is celebrated at an annual festival on Cat Island; the scraper card stands in for the saw and the hand-drum card for the goatskin drum.
items.description: The raspy scrape of saw teeth and a thumping goatskin drum drive a pumping accordion melody, loud and rough-edged, for brisk social dancing.

items.name: Rhyming spirituals (Bahamian anthems)
items.lineage: Unaccompanied sacred part-singing of the Bahamian Out Islands, especially Andros, in which a lead singer, the rhymer, chants long rhymed verses, often retelling Bible stories, against a chorus that sings a repeated refrain in harmony. Rhyming spirituals were recorded on tape for 1960s field LPs, and earlier by Alan Lomax, who recorded them alongside anthems in 1935.
items.description: A lead voice races through rhymed verses in a half-sung patter while the group answers with a rolling harmonized refrain, unaccompanied and building in fervour.
exemplars: Nonesuch Explorer — The Real Bahamas in Music and Song (1966)
Alan Lomax 1935 Bahamas recordings (Library of Congress)

items.name: Goombay (Nassau nightclub calypso)
items.lineage: Bahamian popular song of the mid-20th century, played for visitors in Nassau hotels and nightclubs, sharing calypso's humorous topical lyrics while keeping Bahamian folk songs and the beat of the goatskin goombay drum, played by small acoustic groups. Its best-known performers included the banjo player and singer Blind Blake (Alphonso Higgs), resident at the Royal Victoria Hotel and heard on 1950s LPs, and the singer George Symonette; the hand-drum card stands in for the goombay drum.
items.description: A relaxed, lilting acoustic groove of strummed banjo and guitar, shaken rattles and a goatskin hand drum behind a genial storytelling lead vocal with sing-along refrains.
exemplars: Blind Blake and the Royal Victoria Hotel Calypsos (Art Records, 1950s)

items.name: Big Drum (Carriacou Nation Dance)
items.lineage: Ancestral drum-dance of Carriacou in the Grenadines, whose dances are grouped by the African nations from which islanders trace descent (Cromanti, Igbo, Manding, Chamba, Moko, Temne, Arada, Kongo and others) alongside Creole dances such as juba and kalenda. It is held at tombstone feasts, boat launchings, weddings and community maroon feasts and opens with the Beg Pardon; three drums traditionally made from rum kegs, two boula and a lead cutter, accompany a woman chantwell and chorus with shak-shak rattles. The boula card stands for the two boula drums, the membrane-drum card for the cutter and the shaker card for the shak-shak.
items.description: Two keg drums hold steady interlocking patterns while a lead drum cuts in with sharp, shifting accents, under a woman's strong lead song answered by a chorus and rattles.
exemplars: Andrew Pearse 1956 Carriacou recordings — The Big Drum Dance of Carriacou (Folkways)
Alan Lomax 1962 recordings — Caribbean Voyage: Carriacou Calaloo (Rounder)

items.name: Carriacou string band (quadrille and parang serenade)
items.lineage: String bands of Carriacou, built around violin, cuatro and guitar, play for dances, among them the island's European-derived quadrille, and go serenading house to house in the Christmas parang season, now showcased at the Carriacou Parang Festival. Alan Lomax recorded Carriacou string-band music on his Caribbean field trip, and the ethnomusicologist Rebecca Miller has documented the tradition; the cuatro card stands in for the local four-string cuatro.
items.description: A sawing violin leads dance tunes and serenade melodies over brightly strummed cuatro and guitar chords, with group-sung choruses on the Christmas songs.
exemplars: Alan Lomax 1962 recordings — Caribbean Voyage: Carriacou Calaloo (Rounder)

items.name: Kwadril (Saint Lucian quadrille)
items.lineage: Saint Lucian Kwéyòl form of the European quadrille, a suite of figured set dances for couples, played by a band of violon (fiddle), banjo, cuatro and guitar with the chak-chak rattle. Long a mainstay of village dances, it is kept up by rural community groups and was documented on Smithsonian Folkways' Musical Traditions of St. Lucia; the shaker card stands in for the chak-chak.
items.description: A lilting fiddle lead over strummed banjo, cuatro and guitar and a steady rattle, moving through a suite of contrasting dance figures.
exemplars: Smithsonian Folkways — Musical Traditions of St. Lucia, West Indies (SF 40416)

items.name: La Rose and La Marguerite (Saint Lucian flower-society songs)
items.lineage: Songs of Saint Lucia's two rival flower societies, La Woz (La Rose) and La Magwit (La Marguerite), each organised as a mock royal court of kings, queens and other officers. Members meet in weekly séances to sing their society's Kwéyòl songs, led by a chantwèl, and celebrate their patron saints' feasts, 30 August for La Rose and 17 October for La Marguerite, with mass, a costumed procession and a feast; the shaker card stands in for the chak-chak rattle.
items.description: A woman lead singer lines out strophic songs that the society chorus answers in full-voiced harmony over a soft shaker pulse, by turns stately and teasing.
exemplars: Smithsonian Folkways — Musical Traditions of St. Lucia, West Indies (SF 40416)

items.name: Jwé (Saint Lucian wake and play songs)
items.lineage: Kwéyòl game songs (jwé, 'games') of Saint Lucia sung at wakes and other night gatherings: a chantwèl raises short, often bawdy or satirical songs answered by the group, alongside ring games and storytelling. They are among the genres documented on Smithsonian Folkways' Musical Traditions of St. Lucia.
items.description: Brisk call-and-response singing in short repeating phrases, a lead voice teasing and improvising lines while the group answers and claps.
exemplars: Smithsonian Folkways — Musical Traditions of St. Lucia, West Indies (SF 40416)

items.name: Jing ping (Dominica accordion band music)
items.lineage: Village dance-band music of Dominica played on accordion, a tambal (frame drum), a gwaj (metal scraper) and the boumboum, a length of bamboo blown as a bass. Jing ping bands play the island's European-derived Creole dances, among them the quadrille, mazouk, polka, waltz and heel-and-toe, and the style later fed into bouyon; the vaksin card (a blown bamboo trumpet) stands in for the boumboum, the hand-drum card for the tambal and the scraper card for the gwaj.
items.description: A wheezing accordion melody bounces over a buzzing blown-bass pulse, a thumping frame drum and the rasp of a metal scraper, brisk and danceable.
exemplars: Alan Lomax 1962 recordings — Caribbean Voyage: Dominica, Creole Crossroads (Rounder)

items.name: Bélé (Dominica drum-dance)
items.lineage: Drum-dance of Dominica in which a chantwèl (lead singer) raises Kwéyòl songs answered by a chorus while a drummer plays the tanbou bélé and dancers come forward in turn to answer the drum. It is performed at village gatherings and at Creole festivals such as Jounen Kwéyòl, and is related to the bèlè of Martinique; the membrane-drum card stands in for the tanbou bélé.
items.description: A single drum carries a rolling, accented rhythm beneath a strong lead voice and answering chorus, the drummer punctuating each dancer's steps.
exemplars: Alan Lomax 1962 recordings — Caribbean Voyage: Dominica, Creole Crossroads (Rounder)

items.name: Big drum and fife (St Kitts and Nevis Christmas Sports masquerade)
items.lineage: Music of the Christmas Sports of St Kitts and Nevis, the street plays and dances of the Christmas and New Year season. Masquerade troupes in ribboned costumes and masks dance to a big-drum band of fife, big (bass) drum and kettle (snare) drum, while other Sports such as the Mummies and the Bull have their own plays, and moko jumbie stilt dancers join the street festivities. Tea meetings, mock-formal contests of speeches and songs, and string bands belong to the same body of island folk performance.
items.description: A shrill, darting fife tune rides over a pounding big drum and a crackling kettle drum in fast, driving rhythms for leaping masquerade dancers.
exemplars: Alan Lomax 1962 recordings — Caribbean Voyage: Nevis & St. Kitts, Tea Meetings, Christmas Sports & the Moonlight Night (Rounder)

items.name: Quelbe (Virgin Islands scratch band)
items.lineage: Folk music of the U.S. Virgin Islands, rooted on St Croix, played by scratch bands of flute, banjo, ukulele, guitar, a squash (gourd scraper), a steel triangle and a blown bass pipe, and sung in Virgin Islands Creole English with topical, satirical and often bawdy lyrics. It accompanies quadrilles and other social dances and was later named the official music of the U.S. Virgin Islands by law; the fungi bands of the British Virgin Islands are a closely related scratch-band music. The vaksin card (a blown single-note pipe) stands in for the bass pipe and the scraper card for the squash.
items.description: A piping flute melody over chattering banjo, ukulele and guitar, a scraped gourd, a ringing triangle and a buzzing blown-pipe bass, bright and rhythmic under a sly topical vocal.
exemplars: Stanley and the Ten Sleepless Knights
New World Records — Zoop Zoop Zoop: Traditional Music and Folklore of St. Croix, St. Thomas and St. John (NW 262)

items.name: Cariso (St Croix women's song)
items.lineage: Women's song tradition of St Croix in the U.S. Virgin Islands, of West African descent, sung by women in call-and-response to barrel drums played by men; through it women spread news and scandal, commented on events, voiced praise and protest and competed in wit from the plantation era onward, especially at holiday celebrations. It is documented on the New World Records anthology Zoop Zoop Zoop; the membrane-drum card stands in for the barrel drums.
items.description: A woman lead singer delivers topical verses in a strong, declamatory line and a chorus of women answers with a short refrain over driving barrel-drum rhythms.
exemplars: New World Records — Zoop Zoop Zoop: Traditional Music and Folklore of St. Croix, St. Thomas and St. John (NW 262)

items.name: Tambú (Curaçao drum-song)
items.lineage: Afro-Curaçaoan song and dance in which a lead singer improvises topical, often critical verses answered by a chorus, over a single tambú drum, the chapi (a hoe blade struck with a metal rod) and hand-clapping. Long restricted by colonial law and condemned by the Catholic church, it is especially sung in the weeks before the New Year and is now a pillar of Curaçaoan heritage; the bell card stands in for the chapi.
items.description: A single deep drum and the hard metallic ring of a struck hoe blade lock into a rolling pulse with hand-claps, under a lead singer's pointed improvised verses and the chorus's reply.
exemplars: Zikinzá oral-history collection of Paul Brenneker and Elis Juliana (Nationaal Archief Curaçao)

items.name: Seú (Curaçao harvest procession)
items.lineage: Harvest-festival music of Curaçao, from the plantation custom of carrying the sorghum harvest to the storehouse in procession with singing and dancing. Now a yearly Easter Monday parade, costumed groups dance to work songs led by a singer and chorus, accompanied by the kachu (cow-horn trumpet), the chapi (struck hoe blade), the wiri (metal scraper) and drum; Bonaire's simadan is a related harvest celebration. The bell card stands in for the chapi and the scraper card for the wiri.
items.description: The clank and rasp of struck and scraped metal drive a steady processional beat with a drum, while a lead singer and chorus trade short work-song refrains.

items.name: Dande (Aruban New Year serenade)
items.lineage: New Year's serenade of Aruba: around New Year's Eve and New Year's Day small groups go from house to house, the lead singer improvising verses that wish each household good fortune by name while the group joins the refrain, accompanied by cuatro, guitar, the wiri (metal scraper) and drum. The tradition is documented by Aruba's Instituto di Cultura; the scraper card stands in for the wiri.
items.description: Strummed cuatro and guitar, a rasping metal scraper and a drum keep a bright, lilting beat while the lead singer improvises good wishes and the group joins each refrain.
exemplars: Instituto di Cultura (Aruba) documentation of dande groups

items.name: Bèlè (Martinique drum-dance)
items.lineage: Afro-Martinican drum-dance centred on the north Atlantic coast around Sainte-Marie, in which a lead singer and the lavwa chorus answer each other over the tanbou bèlè, played by a drummer seated astride it, while the tibwa player beats two sticks on the drum's body; dancers perform in quadrille-like sets of couples. Its family of dances includes bèlè, gran bèlè, bèlè linò and kalennda, and a late-twentieth-century revival brought it back into community swaré bèlè; the palitos card stands in for the tibwa.
items.description: A deep hand drum rolls under the dry clatter of sticks on its shell while a lead voice and answering chorus trade short phrases for the dancers.
exemplars: Alan Lomax 1962 recordings — Caribbean Voyage: Martinique, Cane Fields and City Streets (Rounder)

items.name: Danmyé (Martinican ladja combat-dance music)
items.lineage: Danmyé, also called ladja, is the Martinican combat dance in which two fighters spar inside a ring of onlookers, driven by the drum-and-song of the bèlè complex: the tanbou bèlè, a single-headed barrel drum played astride with the heel shifting its pitch, and the ti-bwa, a pair of sticks beaten on the drum's body, under a lead singer answered by the ring. Alan Lomax's 1962 Martinique field recordings include it, and the AM4 association has since worked to document and teach it. The membrane-drum card stands in for the tanbou bèlè and the palitos card for the ti-bwa.
items.description: A hard-hit barrel drum with heel-bent pitch and dry sticks clacking on its shell drive short sung calls and the ring's answers, the rhythm surging as the two fighters close.
exemplars: Alan Lomax 1962 Martinique field recordings of ladja
AM4 association documentation of danmyé and bèlè

items.name: Mas a po (Guadeloupean carnival skin-drum bands)
items.lineage: The groupes à peau, or mas a po, are Guadeloupean carnival bands that parade on foot behind massed goatskin drums, conch-shell horns, shakers and cracking whips, chanting Creole refrains in call and response. Akiyo of Pointe-à-Pitre and Voukoum of Basse-Terre made the form a vehicle of cultural and political assertion, and both groups have released recordings. The membrane-drum card stands in for the bands' skin drums and the shaker card for their chacha rattles.
items.description: Dozens of goatskin drums pound a heavy marching pulse under chanted call-and-response refrains, with shaker rattle and conch blasts cutting through the street noise.

items.name: Son palenquero (San Basilio de Palenque sexteto)
items.lineage: Son palenquero is the sexteto music of San Basilio de Palenque, the maroon village near Cartagena, which reworked the Cuban son heard on mid-20th-century radio and records into a local form sung in Spanish and Palenquero creole. Its best-known group, the Sexteto Tabalá, plays marímbula (a large plucked lamellophone box bass), drums, maracas and claves under a lead singer and a small answering coro. The acoustic-bass card stands in for the marímbula and the hand-drum card for the sexteto's drum.
items.description: A booming plucked box bass and dry hand drums carry a lilting son groove under claves and maracas, as a weathered lead voice trades lines with a small unison coro.
exemplars: Sexteto Tabalá, 'Colombie: Sexteto Tabalá - Le son de Palenque' (Ocora, 1998)

items.name: Alabaos and gualíes (Colombian Pacific wake songs)
items.lineage: Alabaos are the unaccompanied sacred songs that cantadoras and cantadores of Colombia's Pacific coast sing at wakes and novenas for adults, a leader raising verses that the gathering answers; gualíes, also called chigualos, are the songs and rounds of the wake for a dead child, sung with bombo, cununo and guasá. Both are documented by Colombia's Ministry of Culture among the Afro-Pacific traditions of Chocó, Cauca and Nariño. The membrane-drum card stands in for the bombo, the hand-drum card for the cununo and the shaker card for the guasá.
items.description: Women's voices raise slow, keening verses in free rhythm that the wake answers in unison; for a child's wake the singing turns brisk over a deep bass drum, hand drum and rattling shaker.
exemplars: Field recordings of alabaos sung by cantadoras of the Colombian Pacific
Colombian Ministry of Culture documentation of Pacific alabaos and gualíes

items.name: Chirimía chocoana (Quibdó street band)
items.lineage: The chirimía of Chocó is the Afro-Colombian wind-and-drum band of the Atrato river towns, above all Quibdó, where it leads the processions and street dancing of the Fiestas de San Pacho for Saint Francis of Assisi, inscribed by UNESCO in 2012. A typical band has clarinets, a bombardino (euphonium), redoblante (snare drum), tambora (bass drum) and platillos (cymbals), playing abozao, jota chocoana, porro and polka. The baritone-horn card stands in for the bombardino, the snare-drum card for the redoblante and the bass-drum card for the tambora.
items.description: Reedy clarinet lines and a blaring baritone-horn counter-melody ride a crashing snare, bass drum and cymbals in a loose, hot street-band swing.
exemplars: Fiestas de San Pacho (Quibdó) chirimía recordings
UNESCO 2012 Representative List documentation of the Festival of Saint Francis of Assisi, Quibdó

items.name: Carranga (Boyacá campesino string music)
items.lineage: Carranga is the rural string-band song of the Boyacá and Cundinamarca highlands, shaped from 1977 by Jorge Velosa and Los Carrangueros de Ráquira out of the region's campesino merengue, rumba and paseo dance tunes. It is played on tiple, requinto (a small high-pitched tiple), guitar and guacharaca scraper, with humorous, plain-spoken verses about peasant life. The requinto card stands in for the Colombian requinto and the guayo card for the guacharaca.
items.description: Bright strummed tiple and a chattering requinto lead over guitar bass runs and a rasping scraper, while a plain, conversational voice tells comic stories in a bouncy two-step.
exemplars: Jorge Velosa y Los Carrangueros de Ráquira (recordings from 1977 onward)

items.name: Torbellino and guabina (Santander-Boyacá highland song)
items.lineage: Torbellino and guabina are old rural song-dances of the eastern Andes of Santander and Boyacá. Torbellino, a circling couple dance and processional music in triple time, is played on tiple and requinto with the chucho cane rattle, sometimes adding guitar and the esterilla scraper; guabina is a slower sung form whose long, high, plaintive verses are celebrated at the Festival Nacional de la Guabina y el Tiple in Vélez. The shaker card stands in for the chucho and the requinto card for the Colombian requinto.
items.description: Tiple and requinto circle a short strummed triple-time figure over a soft cane rattle, while a high, plaintive voice stretches long phrases above it.
exemplars: Festival Nacional de la Guabina y el Tiple (Vélez) recordings

items.name: Música parrandera (Antioquian December party song)
items.lineage: Música parrandera is the festive party song of Antioquia, sung at the December holiday parrandas of Medellín and the paisa towns; it took shape in the 1950s and 1960s and was recorded on Medellín labels such as Codiscos. A guitar-and-requinto string combo with bass and guacharaca scraper backs a singer in quick, bouncy parranda and merengue rhythms, the lyrics full of double meanings and picaresque stories. The requinto card stands in for the requinto guitar and the guayo card for the guacharaca.
items.description: Twanging requinto runs and chopped guitar chords bounce over a plain bass and scraping guacharaca while a cheeky, half-shouted voice delivers double-meaning verses.

items.name: Jayeechi (Wayuu sung narratives)
items.lineage: Jayeechi are the sung narratives of the Wayuu of the Guajira peninsula, solo songs that recount lineage history, journeys, love and the herding of cattle and goats; the related yonna dance is driven by the kasha drum. Wayuu song is documented in ethnographic field recordings. The membrane-drum card stands in for the kasha.
items.description: A single voice unfolds long, free-flowing melodic lines and held tones, telling a story at its own pace; for the yonna a lone drum keeps a steady, dry beat.
exemplars: Ethnographic field recordings of Wayuu jayeechi and yonna

items.name: Guaracha colombiana (aleteo electronic dance)
items.lineage: Colombian guaracha, also called aleteo or zapateo, is an electronic dance style that grew in the 2010s in the party scenes of Medellín and other Colombian cities out of tribal and Latin house. Made by DJ-producers for the dance floor, it stacks dense, fast percussion loops, chanted vocal shouts and synth or horn stabs over a four-on-the-floor kick; aleteo names the flapping-arm dance that goes with it.
items.description: A pounding four-on-the-floor kick drives tightly layered percussion loops, chopped vocal chants and brassy synth stabs that build and drop in long DJ-mix arcs.
exemplars: Medellín aleteo DJ releases on streaming platforms (2015 onward)

items.name: Chimbangueles (San Benito drumming of Sur del Lago)
items.lineage: Chimbangueles are the Afro-Venezuelan drum ensembles of the southern shore of Lake Maracaibo, in Bobures, Gibraltar and neighbouring towns, that play for San Benito, the Black Franciscan saint, in the processions of his feast from late December into January. A set of drums, traditionally seven, each with its own name and role, is carried in procession and struck with sticks, while a lead singer raises the verses answered by drummers and devotees. The membrane-drum card stands in for the chimbángueles.
items.description: Several long drums hammer interlocking stick patterns in a relentless processional groove while a lead voice calls verses and the crowd shouts back.
exemplars: FUNDEF field recordings of the chimbangueles of Bobures
San Benito festival recordings (Sur del Lago, Zulia)

items.name: Calipso de El Callao (Venezuelan Guayana carnival calypso)
items.lineage: Calipso de El Callao is the carnival song of the gold-mining town of El Callao in Venezuela's Bolívar state, brought by English- and French-Creole-speaking migrants from Trinidad and the Antilles who came for the 19th-century gold rush. Sung in English Creole and Spanish, it is played on the bumbac (a large hand drum), cuatro, a rallo scraper and maracas, later with bass and electric instruments, and accompanies the carnival's madamas, mediopintos and diablos; UNESCO inscribed the carnival in 2016. The membrane-drum card stands in for the bumbac and the guayo card for the rallo.
items.description: A big hand drum thumps a bouncy two-beat under strummed cuatro, a scraping grater and maracas while a lead singer swaps English and Spanish lines with a carnival chorus.
exemplars: Carnival of El Callao recordings (UNESCO Representative List 2016)

items.name: Parranda de San Pedro (Guarenas and Guatire)
items.lineage: The Parranda de San Pedro is the 29 June devotion to Saint Peter in Guarenas and Guatire, Miranda state, which re-enacts the story of the enslaved woman María Ignacia, whose daughter the saint healed. Parranderos in frock coats and top hats sing to the saint with cuatro and maracas while the dancers strike the ground with cotizas, pieces of hard leather strapped to their feet; UNESCO inscribed it in 2013. The foot-stomp card stands in for the cotizas.
items.description: A strummed cuatro and maracas keep a lilting beat under sung verses to the saint, punctuated by the rhythmic slap of leather on the ground as the dancers turn.
exemplars: UNESCO Representative List 2013 documentation of La Parranda de San Pedro de Guarenas y Guatire
Local recordings of the Guatire and Guarenas parrandas

items.name: Diablos danzantes (Venezuelan Corpus Christi devil-dance music)
items.lineage: On Corpus Christi, cofradías of masked devils in San Francisco de Yare, Naiguatá, Chuao, Cuyagua, Ocumare de la Costa and other Venezuelan towns dance in procession to the church to submit before the Eucharist, a rite inscribed by UNESCO in 2012. In Yare the devils dance to a caja drum and the maracas they shake themselves, and the accompaniment varies from town to town. The membrane-drum card stands in for the caja.
items.description: A single drum rattles out a dry, insistent march-dance rhythm while dozens of maracas shaken by the dancers hiss in loose unison as the procession advances.
exemplars: UNESCO Representative List 2012 documentation of Venezuela's Dancing Devils of Corpus Christi
FUNDEF field recordings of the Diablos Danzantes de Yare

items.name: Aguinaldo venezolano (Venezuelan Christmas parranda)
items.lineage: Venezuelan aguinaldos are the Christmas songs carried from house to house by parrandas around Christmas, the religious aguinaldo telling of the Nativity and the secular parranda asking for food, drink and good cheer. The parranda plays cuatro, maracas, the furruco friction drum, a charrasca scraper and a small tambora drum, sometimes with guitar and mandolin, under a soloist answered by the group. The guayo card stands in for the charrasca and the membrane-drum card for the tambora.
items.description: Strummed cuatro and maracas bounce over the deep growl of a friction drum and a scraped charrasca while a lead singer trades festive verses with a full chorus.

items.name: Tamunangue (Lara sones de negro for San Antonio)
items.lineage: The tamunangue, or sones de negro, is the danced devotion to Saint Anthony of Padua held around 13 June in Lara state, centred on El Tocuyo and Curarigua. After a salve sung to the saint it runs through a fixed suite of sones, opening with La Batalla, a mock fight between two men with sticks, and continuing with pieces such as La Bella, La Juruminga, El Poco a Poco, El Galerón and El Seis Figuriao, played on cuatro, the five-string cinco, maracas and the tamunango drum under a lead singer and chorus. The cuatro card covers the cuatro and cinco and the membrane-drum card stands in for the tamunango.
items.description: Strummed strings and maracas lock into a driving, lilting groove with a booming drum, while a high lead voice calls each son's verses and the chorus answers between bursts of stick-clashing dance.
exemplars: FUNDEF recordings of the tamunangue of El Tocuyo
Recordings of the San Antonio de Padua festival, El Tocuyo

items.name: Golpe larense (golpe tocuyano)
items.lineage: The golpe is the secular festive dance-song of Lara state, especially El Tocuyo and Barquisimeto, played by golpero groups on cuatro, the five-string cinco, maracas and a stick-beaten tambora drum, with high lead singing answered by the group, and danced by couples at parties and festivals. Pío Alvarado and Los Golperos de Don Pío are its best-known recorded exponents. The cuatro card covers the cuatro and cinco and the membrane-drum card stands in for the tambora.
items.description: Rapid strummed cuatro and maracas churn a fast triple-time hemiola over a stick-beaten drum, with a piercing high lead voice and shouted group refrains.
exemplars: Pío Alvarado and Los Golperos de Don Pío

items.name: Merengue caraqueño (Venezuelan 5/8 merengue)
items.lineage: Merengue caraqueño, also called merengue venezolano, is the urban dance music of Caracas that took shape in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, notated in a lopsided 5/8 and danced as the merengue rucaneao. Small dance groups and later the city's dance orchestras played it for parties and on record, and from the 1980s the Ensamble Gurrufío recast it as chamber music for flute, mandolin, cuatro and double bass. The mandolin card stands in for the Venezuelan bandolín, and a generic flute card is used for the concert flute.
items.description: A limping five-beat pulse from the strummed cuatro chop and plucked bass carries flute and mandolin as they trade quick, syncopated melodic lines full of sudden accents and turns.

items.name: Vals venezolano (Venezuelan waltz)
items.lineage: The vals venezolano is the Venezuelan waltz, a 19th-century salon dance that became a national concert form, written for piano by composers such as Ramón Delgado Palacios and Heraclio Fernández and played by string groups of guitar, mandolin and cuatro. In the 20th century Antonio Lauro composed valses venezolanos for solo guitar that Alirio Díaz recorded and carried into the international guitar repertoire; its accompaniment habitually displaces the 3/4 with hemiola accents.
items.description: A lilting three-beat waltz whose accompaniment keeps tipping into two-against-three cross-accents, with a singing, fingerpicked guitar or piano melody rubato at the phrase ends over light strummed cuatro chords.
exemplars: Alirio Díaz recordings of Antonio Lauro's valses venezolanos

items.name: Onda nueva (Venezuelan jazz-joropo)
items.lineage: Onda nueva is the style that the Caracas composer, pianist and arranger Aldemaro Romero launched around 1970, resetting the 3/4 joropo in a soft, jazz-harmonised idiom for piano, bass, drum kit and cuatro with sung melodies. Its drum-kit adaptation of the joropo's accents was worked out with the drummer Frank 'Pavo' Hernández, and Romero promoted the style through his Onda Nueva LPs and the Festival de la Onda Nueva in the early 1970s.
items.description: A gliding 3/4 groove in which the drum kit plays the joropo's cross-accents lightly under extended jazz piano chords, round bass and strummed cuatro, with smooth voices floating relaxed melodies on top.
exemplars: Aldemaro Romero y su Onda Nueva LPs (1970s)

items.name: Música oriental (eastern Venezuelan galerón and polo)
items.lineage: The música oriental of eastern Venezuela, from Margarita Island and the coasts of Sucre and Anzoátegui, groups the galerón, in which singers improvise décimas in turn over a repeating harmonic cycle, with the slow polo margariteño, the malagueña and the jota. All are accompanied by cuatro, guitar, the eastern bandola or bandolín and maracas, and FUNDEF has documented them in the field. The mandolin card stands in for the eastern bandola.
items.description: A high, open voice spins long rhymed verses over strummed cuatro, guitar and a tremolo-plucked bandola cycling one chord pattern, maracas hissing in triple time; the polo slows the same strings into a wistful, lilting song.
exemplars: FUNDEF field recordings of galerón and polo

items.name: Joropo central (Tuy valleys harp joropo)
items.lineage: Joropo central, or joropo tuyero, is the harp joropo of the Tuy valleys of Miranda and of Aragua in north-central Venezuela, distinct from the plains joropo llanero. Its arpa central (arpa tuyera or mirandina) has metal strings in the treble, and the usual group is only harp and maracas, the maraquero often being the singer, in pasajes and in the revuelta, a linked suite of sections. The arpa llanera card stands in for the arpa central.
items.description: A bright, metallic-trebled harp runs fast arpeggiated figures over its own bass in a 3/4 that keeps tipping into 6/8, one pair of maracas drives the subdivision, and the maraca player sings long, high, ornamented phrases over it.
exemplars: FUNDEF field recordings of arpa central from the Tuy valleys

items.name: Fulía (Venezuelan Cruz de Mayo wake song)
items.lineage: The fulía is the Afro-Venezuelan devotional song of the velorio de Cruz de Mayo, the all-night May wake held before a decorated cross, sung above all in Barlovento and the coastal towns of Miranda and also in Sucre and on Margarita. A solo singer gives out a copla or décima and the gathering answers with a refrain, over cuatro, maracas and a small drum, and groups such as Un Solo Pueblo brought fulías to records from the late 1970s. The membrane-drum card stands in for the fulía drum.
items.description: A lone voice lines out a devotional verse and the whole wake answers in a swaying unison refrain, over a gently strummed cuatro, hissing maracas and a small drum tapping a lilting pulse through the night.
exemplars: FUNDEF field recordings of fulías and velorios de cruz

items.name: Changa tuki (Caracas barrio electronic dance)
items.lineage: Changa tuki, also called raptor house, is the electronic dance music of the barrios of Caracas, which grew from the 1990s in the minitecas, the mobile sound systems that played neighbourhood parties, as DJs reworked imported techno and house into a faster, percussion-heavy style for its own competitive street dance; its young followers are known as tukis, and the scene peaked in the 2000s. DJ Baba (DJ Babatr) is usually credited among its founders, alongside DJs such as DJ Yirvin.
items.description: A very fast four-on-the-floor kick drives clattering layered percussion loops, stabbing synth riffs and chopped vocal shouts, edited into short, relentless builds for dancers to battle over.

items.name: Warao song (Orinoco delta shamanic song)
items.lineage: The Warao of the Orinoco delta sing for curing, ritual and daily life, and their shamans, the wisiratu, hoarotu and bahanarotu, sing long healing and invocation songs, the wisiratu shaking a large sacred gourd rattle. Other repertories use the isimoi clarinet of the nahanamu festival, bone and cane flutes and the sekeseke violin. Dale A. Olsen recorded Warao music in the 1970s for the Folkways album Music of the Warao of Venezuela. The shaker card stands in for the shaman's gourd rattle.
items.description: A single voice chants long, repetitive incantatory phrases in a narrow range, over the steady swish of a large shaken gourd rattle.
exemplars: Music of the Warao of Venezuela: Song People of the Rain Forest (Folkways FE 4104, recorded by Dale A. Olsen)

items.name: Son de artesa (Costa Chica platform-dance son)
items.lineage: The son de artesa is the Afro-Mexican fandango of the Costa Chica of Guerrero and Oaxaca, kept above all in San Nicolás Tolentino and El Ciruelo, in which couples dance zapateado on the artesa, a long platform hollowed from a single tree trunk and carved with an animal's head, so that the dancers' feet sound as the ensemble's drum. A violin carries the melody over a guitar and a struck wooden box, under sung coplas, and INAH's Testimonio Musical de México series documented it. A generic percussion card stands in for the cajón, the struck wooden box, and the stomp card for the artesa.
items.description: Dancers' heels drum a booming, hollow wooden platform in tight six-against-three rhythms under a scraping lead violin, strummed guitar and a struck box, while singers trade short rhymed coplas between dance passages.
exemplars: INAH Testimonio Musical de México, Costa Chica recordings
Field recordings of son de artesa in San Nicolás Tolentino

items.name: Danza de los diablos (Costa Chica Afro-Mexican devil dance)
items.lineage: The danza de los diablos is the Afro-Mexican masked dance of the Costa Chica of Guerrero and Oaxaca, performed through the streets of towns such as Cuajinicuilapa and Collantes around the Days of the Dead by a troupe of devils with their leader and a man dressed as his wife. Its music comes from a harmonica, a donkey-jawbone rattle (charrasca) and the bote, a stick-friction drum, set against the dancers' stamping and shouts. The quijada card stands in for the charrasca and the friction-drum card for the bote.
items.description: A reedy harmonica loops a short tune over the dry buzz of a struck jawbone and the low, growling roar of a friction drum, while masked dancers stamp, whoop and shout in a rough street procession.
exemplars: INAH Testimonio Musical de México series, Costa Chica recordings

items.name: Jarana yucateca (Yucatecan vaquería dance band)
items.lineage: The jarana is the couple dance of Yucatán, danced at the vaquerías of town and village fiestas in two meters, the 6/8 jarana and the 3/4 jarana, with pauses in which a dancer recites a bomba, a comic or amorous verse. It is played by the orquesta jaranera, a band of clarinets, saxophone, trumpets and trombone over timbales, güiro and double bass, and Mérida ensembles such as the Orquesta Jaranera del Mayab and the Orquesta Típica Yukalpetén have recorded it.
items.description: Bright clarinets and trumpets state a brisk tune over trombone counterlines, plucked bass and crisp timbales and güiro, alternating a leaping 6/8 with a swaying 3/4 and halting abruptly for a spoken verse.

items.name: Huapango arribeño (Sierra Gorda topada)
items.lineage: Huapango arribeño is the music of the Sierra Gorda and the Zona Media where Guanajuato, Querétaro and San Luis Potosí meet, played by a four-man group: a trovador who improvises décimas while playing the guitarra quinta huapanguera, a vihuela and two violins. Its central event is the topada, an all-night contest in which two groups face each other from opposite tarimas, trading improvised poetry and playing sones and valonas for zapateado dancers. The single violin card stands for the pair of violins.
items.description: A trovador declaims improvised ten-line verses in a strong, open voice over the deep strum of a large bass guitar and a bright vihuela, while two violins saw out fast interludes for the dancers between stanzas.
exemplars: Guillermo Velázquez y Los Leones de la Sierra de Xichú recordings

items.name: Colombia de Monterrey (regiomontano cumbia vallenata)
items.lineage: From the 1960s the working-class barrios of Monterrey, above all Colonia Independencia, adopted Colombian cumbia and vallenato records as their own, and local accordion groups recreated them for neighbourhood dances and sound-system parties. Celso Piña, known as el rebelde del acordeón, and his Ronda Bogotá became the scene's leading band from the 1980s, and the anthropologist Darío Blanco Arboleda documented the movement as La Colombia de Monterrey.
items.description: A button accordion leads a loping cumbia over the steady scrape of a palm-wood scraper, conga patterns and a round electric bass, with a plain, nasal lead voice riding on top.
exemplars: Celso Piña y su Ronda Bogotá, 'Barrio Bravo' (2001)
Darío Blanco Arboleda, 'La Colombia de Monterrey' (ethnography)

items.name: Parachicos (Chiapa de Corzo January fiesta music)
items.lineage: In the Fiesta Grande de Enero of Chiapa de Corzo, Chiapas, held each January for the Lord of Esquipulas, San Antonio Abad and San Sebastián, masked parachico dancers parade through the town led by the patrón, who carries a guitar and a whip and plays a cane flute with one or two drummers, while the dancers answer his calls with shouts and shake rattles called chinchines. UNESCO inscribed the parachicos of the January feast on its Representative List in 2010. A generic flute card stands in for the patrón's cane flute (pito) and the shaker card for the chinchines.
items.description: A shrill cane flute repeats a short processional tune over a steady drum, answered by the massed shouts of masked dancers and the dense shimmer of their shaken rattles.
exemplars: INAH recordings of the Fiesta Grande de Enero
UNESCO Representative List inscription of the parachicos (2010)

items.name: Heikyoku (Heike biwa recitation)
items.lineage: Heikyoku is the chanted recitation of the Heike monogatari, the medieval Japanese chronicle of the Genpei war, by blind biwa hōshi accompanying themselves on a small four-string biwa; the blind men's guild, the Tōdō-za, organised its transmission from the fourteenth century. Of the Edo-period Maeda and Hatano schools, the Maeda tradition survived into the twentieth century through a handful of performers in Nagoya and Sendai.
items.description: A solo voice recites in formulaic melodic patterns, from plain syllabic narration to slow, high melismatic passages, while the biwa sounds short plucked phrases between the sung lines rather than under them.
exemplars: Tokyo National Research Institute for Cultural Properties archival recordings of Heike recitation

items.name: Satsuma biwa (Kagoshima narrative lute song)
items.lineage: Satsuma biwa grew up among the samurai of the Satsuma domain in southern Kyushu as narrative song for moral and martial instruction, and after the Meiji Restoration it moved to Tokyo and became a nationally popular Japanese recorded genre. Twentieth-century schools include the Kinshin-ryū and the five-string Nishiki-biwa, from which Tsuruta Kinshi developed her own school.
items.description: A declamatory voice delivers battle tales and laments in long, sustained phrases, cut by the wide plectrum slapping across strings and body in explosive, buzzing attacks; the high frets let the player push pitch upward by pressing.
exemplars: Hogaku LP and CD catalogues of Satsuma biwa

items.name: Chikuzen biwa (Hakata narrative lute song)
items.lineage: Chikuzen biwa, a Japanese narrative biwa song, took shape in Hakata in the Meiji era, when the blind-priest biwa of the Chikuzen region was reworked with the melodic style of shamisen music, and it spread nationally through the Tachibana and Asahi schools as a genre performed largely by women. Its instrument is a lighter four- or five-string biwa played with a smaller plectrum than the Satsuma biwa.
items.description: A lyrical voice, often a woman's, sings narrative pieces in smooth, ornamented lines, with the biwa supplying lighter, rounder plucked phrases and interludes.
exemplars: Nippon Columbia and King hogaku recordings of Chikuzen biwa
NHK hogaku archive broadcasts of Chikuzen biwa

items.name: Higo biwa (Kumamoto blind-priest biwa narrative)
items.lineage: Higo biwa is the mōsō, or blind-priest, biwa tradition of Kumamoto in central Kyushu, whose performers both carried out household rites such as purifying the kitchen hearth and recited long danmono tales at village gatherings. Yamashika Yoshiyuki of Nankan, known as the last biwa hōshi, was recorded in field and commercial sessions from about 1970, and Hugh de Ferranti's research documents his repertory. The biwa card stands in for the slender mōsō biwa.
items.description: A weathered solo voice recites long tales in a half-sung delivery close to speech, with plucked and strummed biwa figures between and beneath the phrases.
exemplars: Yamashika Yoshiyuki field and commercial recordings of Higo biwa
Hugh de Ferranti collection of Yamashika Yoshiyuki recordings (PARADISEC)

items.name: Tokiwazu-bushi (kabuki narrative shamisen song)
items.lineage: Tokiwazu-bushi is a Japanese jōruri narrative style founded in Edo in the mid-eighteenth century by Tokiwazu Mojidayū, a pupil of Miyakoji Bungonojō, and one of the Bungo-kei schools that grew out of Bungo-bushi. It accompanies kabuki dance dramas, sung by a row of tayū narrators with chūzao shamisen players, and is also performed in concert.
items.description: Weighty, dignified narrative singing alternates sung melody with dramatic declamation over medium-necked shamisen, the narrators and players moving between solo passages and unison.
exemplars: Nippon Columbia and Victor kabuki-music recordings of Tokiwazu
National Theatre of Japan kabuki performances

items.name: Kiyomoto-bushi (high-voiced kabuki narrative song)
items.lineage: Kiyomoto-bushi was founded in Edo in the early nineteenth century by Kiyomoto Enjudayū, who broke away from Tomimoto-bushi, itself an offshoot of Tokiwazu. It became one of the principal narrative musics of Japanese kabuki dance, sung by tayū with chūzao shamisen, and is known for its high, ornate and sensuous vocal style.
items.description: A high, tight, ornate vocal line full of quick turns and upper-register flourishes floats over medium-necked shamisen in the light, sensuous manner of kabuki dance accompaniment.
exemplars: Nippon Columbia and Victor kabuki-music recordings of Kiyomoto

items.name: Shinnai-bushi (Edo street-ballad jōruri)
items.lineage: Shinnai-bushi is a Japanese Bungo-kei jōruri named after Tsuruga Shinnai, a singer of the Tsuruga school in later eighteenth-century Edo. It developed away from the kabuki stage, as nagashi music played by pairs of musicians walking the streets and as recital music of the pleasure quarters, with a repertoire of doomed love and double suicide; Tsuruga Wakasanojō was recognised as a Living National Treasure.
items.description: A plaintive, high-lying voice draws out tearful laments over two shamisen, one playing the main part and the other a high, capoed counter-line that rings above it.

items.name: Kokyoku (Itchū, Katō, Miyazono and Ogie-bushi)
items.lineage: Kokyoku, the 'old songs', groups four early Japanese shamisen narrative and lyric styles kept in small lineages: Itchū-bushi, founded in Kyoto at the turn of the eighteenth century by Miyako Itchū; Katō-bushi, from early eighteenth-century Edo; Miyazono-bushi, a Kyoto jōruri of love-suicide pieces; and Ogie-bushi, a parlour style derived from nagauta in late eighteenth-century Edo. The four are designated together as an Important Intangible Cultural Property.
items.description: Restrained, refined voices sing slow, intimate pieces in a quiet chamber manner over shamisen, with long, subtle inflections instead of dramatic declamation.
exemplars: NHK and Nippon Columbia hogaku archive recordings of Itchū-bushi, Katō-bushi, Miyazono-bushi and Ogie-bushi

items.name: Kouta (Edo short shamisen song)
items.lineage: Kouta are short Japanese songs that took shape in Edo in the mid-nineteenth century, close to hauta and kiyomoto, and became the light, witty repertoire of geisha parlours. The shamisen is plucked with the fingernail rather than struck with a plectrum, and geisha singers recorded the genre extensively on SP and LP.
items.description: A light, conversational voice sings brief, witty songs in an intimate parlour manner over a soft shamisen plucked with the fingernail, its attack muted and rounded.
exemplars: Victor and Columbia SP and LP recordings of geisha kouta singers, including Ichimaru

items.name: Gendai hōgaku (contemporary music for Japanese instruments)
items.lineage: Gendai hōgaku is newly composed concert music for Japanese instruments that grew after the Second World War, as composers wrote for shakuhachi, koto, shamisen, biwa and percussion in mixed ensembles. Nihon Ongaku Shūdan, known abroad as Pro Musica Nipponia and founded in Tokyo in 1964 with the composer Miki Minoru as artistic director, made it a touring and recording repertoire, often using the seventeen-string bass koto.
items.description: Composed ensemble textures set breathy shakuhachi, plucked koto and bass koto, shamisen and biwa against one another in contrasting layers, joining traditional timbres and techniques to concert forms and extended sounds.
exemplars: Nihon Ongaku Shudan (Pro Musica Nipponia) LP and CD recordings

items.name: Shigin (chanted Chinese-style poetry)
items.lineage: Shigin is the chanting of kanshi, poems in classical Chinese read in Japanese, and of Japanese verse, a practice that spread from late Edo-period academies and became a mass amateur art in the twentieth century through schools such as the Nihon Shigin Gakuin. It also accompanies kenshibu sword and fan dance, and Nippon Columbia and King issued many recordings.
items.description: A single voice chants each line of a poem in long, sustained tones with deep, slow undulating ornaments and strong breath support, often over a sparse shakuhachi accompaniment.
exemplars: Nippon Columbia and King shigin recordings

items.name: Nachi no Dengaku (Nachi shrine field-music ritual)
items.lineage: Nachi no Dengaku is a ritual performing art of the Kumano Nachi Taisha shrine in Nachikatsuura, presented each July at the Nachi fire festival; it descends from medieval dengaku, the field music of rice-planting rites, and is inscribed on UNESCO's Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity. Dancers play binzasara, a clapper of strung wooden slats, and small drums, led by a flute. The auxiliary-percussion card stands in for the binzasara and the membrane-drum card for the drums.
items.description: A thin flute line floats over the dry, rattling clack of slat clappers and light drum strokes in steady, measured patterns as the dancers move in formation.
exemplars: UNESCO documentation of Nachi no Dengaku (inscribed 2012)
Association for the Preservation of Nachi Dengaku

items.name: Hayachine kagura (Iwate yamabushi kagura)
items.lineage: Hayachine kagura is the yamabushi kagura of the Take and Ōtsugunai troupes of Ōhasama in Hanamaki, Iwate, performed at the Hayachine shrine festival in August and in village houses through the year; it is inscribed on UNESCO's Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity. Masked dances of gods, warriors and a sacred lion are accompanied by a drum, hand cymbals and a transverse flute, with chanted verses.
