The membrane-drum card stands in for the kagura drum, the cymbals card for the hand cymbals and the kagurabue card for the flute.
items.description: Driving drum patterns and crashing hand cymbals push the masked dances forward under a shrill, looping transverse flute, with chanted verses sung over the ensemble.
exemplars: Take and Ōtsugunai kagura preservation-society recordings

items.name: Iwami kagura (western Shimane kagura)
items.lineage: Iwami kagura is the kagura of the old Iwami province in western Shimane, played by local troupes (shachū) at autumn shrine festivals that run through the night, and it belongs to the Izumo type of kagura plays. Many troupes use the fast eight-beat hatchō-byōshi and stage spectacular myths such as the eight-headed serpent Orochi, to an ensemble of large drum, small drum, hand cymbals and transverse flute. The odaiko and shime-daiko cards stand in for the large and small drums and the kagurabue card for the flute.
items.description: A fast, relentless eight-beat pattern on large and small drums, with clashing hand cymbals and a piercing flute, drives the masked dancers, while sung and declaimed lines carry the myth play.
exemplars: Iwami kagura troupe (shachū) CD and DVD recordings

items.name: Hanamatsuri (Oku-Mikawa yudate kagura)
items.lineage: Hanamatsuri is the all-night shimotsuki kagura of the Oku-Mikawa mountains in north-eastern Aichi, held in the winter months in villages of Tōei, Toyone and Shitara around a cauldron of boiling water, the yudate rite of the Ise type of kagura. Dancers, among them masked demons and groups of boys, circle the cauldron to drum and flute while onlookers shout the refrain 'tehohe'. The membrane-drum card stands in for the taiko and the kagurabue card for the flute.
items.description: A steady drum beat and a looping flute melody repeat for hours as dancers stamp around the cauldron, with sung verses and the crowd's shouted refrains swelling through the night.
exemplars: Ethnographic field recordings of Oku-Mikawa Hanamatsuri

items.name: Kawachi ondo (Osaka narrative bon-dance song)
items.lineage: Kawachi ondo is the narrative bon-dance song of the Kawachi area east of Osaka, centred on Yao, in which a professional ondo-tori singer chants long epics of outlaws, lovers and local events for the dance circle. The accompaniment of shamisen and taiko was later joined by electric guitar, and Izutsuya Koishimaru's epics were issued in the UNESCO Collection. The membrane-drum card stands in for the taiko.
items.description: A solo singer chants a long story in rapid, rhythmic verse over a steady dance beat of taiko, shamisen and twangy electric guitar, with the dancers and helpers answering in shouted calls.
exemplars: UNESCO Collection (Smithsonian Folkways): Koishimaru Izutsuya, Master of the Kawachi Ondo Epics

items.name: Goze-uta (Echigo blind women's shamisen song)
items.lineage: Goze were blind women who travelled in small groups through the villages of Echigo, in present-day Niigata, singing to the shamisen at farmhouses in return for lodging and rice, with their main guilds based in Takada and Nagaoka. Their repertoire included the long narrative saimon matsuzaka, kudoki ballads and folk songs, and Kobayashi Haru, the last Nagaoka goze, and the Takada goze were recorded from the 1970s.
items.description: A strong, plain woman's voice sings long strophic ballads to a repeated shamisen pattern, the tale unfolding verse by verse in a steady, unhurried rhythm.
exemplars: Kobayashi Haru recordings of Nagaoka goze songs
Recordings of the Takada goze (Sugimoto Kikue's troupe)

items.name: Kiyari (Edo timber-hauling and firemen's chant)
items.lineage: Kiyari began as work chants for hauling timber and stone, setting the pull of a crew to a leader's call, and in Edo the tobi construction workers and town firemen made them ceremonial songs for festivals, building rites and the New Year fire-brigade parade. Edo kiyari is kept in Tokyo by the Edo Shōbō Kinenkai, the preservation society of the old fire brigades.
items.description: A leader lifts long, high, melismatic phrases and a group of men answers in unison, unaccompanied and in a free, breath-paced rhythm.
exemplars: Hogaku LP recordings of Edo kiyari

items.name: Amami shima-uta (Amami Islands song)
items.lineage: Shima-uta of the Amami Islands, between Kyushu and Okinawa, are sung at gatherings and in song exchanges to a sanshin played with a thin bamboo plectrum, with a chijin drum and the answering calls of listeners. Singers flip between chest voice and a high falsetto break called guin, and much of the repertoire uses a scale closer to mainland min'yō than to the Okinawan Ryūkyū scale. Local masters were recorded by the Central Gakki label in Naze. The membrane-drum card stands in for the chijin.
items.description: A high voice sings slow, mournful verses that flip suddenly into falsetto ornaments, over a bright, crisp sanshin picked with a bamboo sliver and the occasional answer of a second singer or a light drum.
exemplars: Central Gakki recordings of Amami shima-uta masters

items.name: Yaeyama min'yō (Yaeyama Islands song, yunta and jiraba)
items.lineage: The songs of the Yaeyama Islands, centred on Ishigaki, range from yunta and jiraba, work songs sung in call and response between groups of men and women in the fields, to fushi-uta set to the sanshin and kept as a classical repertoire by Yaeyama koten schools. Tubarāma is the subject of an annual singing contest in Ishigaki.
items.description: Unaccompanied work songs trade lines between groups of men and women in call and response, while the sanshin songs set a long-breathed, ornamented solo voice over spare plucked accompaniment.
exemplars: King Records and Victor anthologies of Yaeyama folk song

items.name: Umui and kwena (Ryukyuan priestess ritual song)
items.lineage: Umui and kwena are the ritual songs of the noro priestesses and other women officiants of the Ryukyu Islands, sung as prayers to the gods at village rites and sacred groves. On Kudaka Island off Okinawa they culminated in Izaiho, the initiation of the island's women into the priesthood held every twelve years in the year of the horse; it was documented on film in 1966 and 1978, the last time it was held.
items.description: Women's voices chant narrow-range, repetitive prayer melodies together without accompaniment, in long incantatory lines broken by ritual calls.
exemplars: Izaihō, documentary film of the 1966 Kudaka Island rite
Okinawa Kudakajima no Izaihō, synchronised-sound film record of the 1978 rite

items.name: Orasho (Kakure Kirishitan hidden-Christian prayer chant)
items.lineage: Orasho are the prayers of the Kakure Kirishitan, the hidden Christians of the Nagasaki islands who kept the faith in secret after Christianity was banned in the early seventeenth century, passing on Latin and Portuguese texts by mouth in forms worn down by centuries of oral transmission. On Ikitsuki Island the men still recite them at their rites, and the sung prayer Gururiyoza was traced by the musicologist Minagawa Tatsuo to O gloriosa Domina, a Latin hymn as sung in sixteenth-century Spain.
items.description: Men's voices recite long prayers in a fast, low murmur and break into slow, unaccompanied unison song for the sung prayers, with old chant melodies worn into local vocal style.
exemplars: Ikitsuki Island orasho field recordings (studied by Minagawa Tatsuo)
Orasho performances documented by the Ikitsuki Island Museum Shima no Yakata

items.name: Goeika (Japanese Buddhist pilgrim hymns)
items.lineage: Goeika are Japanese Buddhist hymns on waka verses, first sung by pilgrims on the temple circuits such as the Saigoku and Shikoku pilgrimages and now practised by lay singing groups organised by sect schools, among them the Shingon Kongō-ryū based at Kōyasan and the Sōtō school's Baika-ryū. Singers keep time on a handbell (rei) and a small struck bowl bell (shōkin); the rin card stands in for the bowl bell and the temple-bell card for the handbell.
items.description: A lay group sings slow, drawn-out melismatic hymn lines in unison, punctuated by the ring of a handbell and the struck chime of a small bowl bell.
exemplars: Baika-ryū goeika temple and commercial CD recordings

items.name: Sekkyō-bushi (Hachiōji sermon-ballad narrative)
items.lineage: Sekkyō-bushi, a Japanese narrative song, grew out of medieval Buddhist sermon-ballads telling tales such as Sanshō Dayū and Oguri Hangan, and in the early Edo period became a shamisen-accompanied puppet-theatre narrative (sekkyō jōruri) before being eclipsed by gidayū-bushi. Late in the Edo period Satsuma Wakatayū revived it as sekkyō saimon, which spread to Hachiōji by the Meiji era; there the Satsuma and Wakamatsu schools still narrate the kuruma ningyō cart-puppet theatre.
items.description: A single narrator half-sings, half-declaims a long, mournful tale over spare shamisen phrases, moving between plaintive sung passages and spoken dialogue.
exemplars: Wakamatsu Wakatayū III with the Hachiōji kuruma ningyō
Satsuma-school sekkyō-bushi narration of Hachiōji kuruma ningyō performances

items.name: Chindon-ya (Japanese street advertising band)
items.lineage: Chindon-ya are costumed street bands hired to advertise shop openings and sales, a trade that grew in Osaka and Tokyo from the Meiji era and drew on the jinta street brass bands of the Meiji and Taishō eras. The chindon player wears a rig of a small gong and two small drums, joined by a bass drum (gorosu) and a melody player on clarinet or saxophone; the kane card stands in for the gong and the shime-daiko card for the small drums.
items.description: A bright clarinet carries popular songs and marches over the clatter of small drums and a clanging gong worn on one player's chest, with a booming bass drum keeping a walking street pulse.
exemplars: Off Note label chindon and jinta reissues

items.name: Rōkyoku (naniwa-bushi shamisen narrative song)
items.lineage: Rōkyoku, also called naniwa-bushi, is a Japanese narrative song in which a solo singer alternates sung verse and spoken dialogue to tell tales of loyalty, chivalry and gamblers, accompanied by a player of the thick-necked futozao shamisen (kyokushi) who also calls out encouragement. It grew from Osaka street storytelling in the Meiji era, became a national craze through Tōchūken Kumoemon in the 1900s, and ruled SP records and radio until the 1950s, its stars including Hirosawa Torazō.
items.description: A strong, husky solo voice switches between dramatic spoken dialogue and long, quavering sung phrases bent with heavy ornament, over a shamisen that answers each line and shouted calls from the player.
exemplars: Nichibunken Rōkyoku SP record digital archive

items.name: Gunka (Japanese military song)
items.lineage: Gunka are Japanese military and patriotic songs, begun in the Meiji era with pieces such as Battōtai, set by the French bandmaster Charles Leroux, and Setoguchi Tōkichi's Gunkan kōshinkyoku. Record companies issued them as wartime popular songs through the 1930s and early 1940s, among them Koseki Yūji's Roei no uta (1937), sung by solo singers or male groups over brass-led studio bands; the generic horn card stands in for the band's trumpets and trombones.
items.description: Square, strophic marching songs sung in firm unison or by a projected solo voice over a brass band with snare and bass drum, in bright major and somber minor pentatonic melodies.
exemplars: Nippon Columbia and King Records gunka SP and LP compilations
Roei no uta (music by Koseki Yūji, Columbia, 1937)

items.name: Enka-shi street song (sōshi enka and violin enka)
items.lineage: The first enka were the speech-songs of young political activists (sōshi) of the Meiji-era Freedom and People's Rights movement, who sang topical verses in the streets and sold the song sheets. Professional street singers (enka-shi) such as Soeda Azembō, author of Rappa-bushi and Nonki-bushi, turned them into satirical songs of city life and from the late Meiji era accompanied themselves on violin, a style recorded on SP by Ishida Ichimatsu and revived in the folk era by Takada Wataru.
items.description: A lone singer delivers wry, many-versed topical songs in a plain, half-spoken street voice, doubled and answered by a scratchy violin playing the tune.
exemplars: Takada Wataru — URC recordings of Soeda Azembō songs (revival)

items.name: Kansai foku (Kansai underground folk song)
items.lineage: Kansai foku was the protest and topical folk song movement of Osaka and Kyoto in the late 1960s, when singer-songwriters modelled on the American folk revival wrote blunt Japanese songs about war, labour, discrimination and student life. The Underground Record Club (URC), founded in 1969 as a mail-order label, issued songs major labels would not release by Okabayashi Nobuyasu, Takada Wataru and Takaishi Tomoya, and the Nakatsugawa Folk Jamboree became the movement's festival.
items.description: Plain, conversational voices sing many-versed songs over fingerpicked or strummed acoustic guitar and racked harmonica, in close, dry, low-budget recordings.

items.name: Koza rock (Okinawan base-town hard rock)
items.lineage: Koza rock is the hard rock scene of Koza, now Okinawa City, beside Kadena Air Base, where bands played long sets of British and American hard rock in English for US servicemen in the bars of the Vietnam War years. Groups such as Condition Green and the organ-led Murasaki grew out of this circuit and recorded LPs in the 1970s.
items.description: Loud, overdriven guitar riffs and long solos, a growling organ and heavy drums drive shouted English-language vocals in a raw, club-hardened hard rock sound.

items.name: Daechwita (Korean royal military processional music)
items.lineage: Daechwita is the processional music of the Joseon-dynasty military band that marched before the king and his troops, known in the court repertoire as Muryeongjigok, and is performed today by the National Gugak Center and in royal procession reenactments. The taepyeongso carries the only melody over a long brass trumpet (nabal), conch (nagak), cymbals, gong and drum; the generic horn card stands in for the nabal, the buk card for the yonggo drum and the cymbal card for the jabara.
items.description: A piercing shawm melody unfolds slowly over long single-note trumpet and conch blasts, heavy gong and drum strokes and crashing cymbals in a stately, majestic march.
exemplars: Royal procession reenactment performances in Seoul

items.name: Changgeuk (Korean staged pansori opera)
items.lineage: Changgeuk is staged Korean opera that divides the roles of a pansori story among many singers in costume, first presented at the Wongaksa theatre in Seoul in the last years of the Korean Empire. The National Changgeuk Company of the National Theater of Korea performs the pansori classics and new works with a traditional (gugak) instrumental ensemble, drum and chorus.
items.description: Rough, powerful pansori voices trade sung dialogue and narration as characters, with choral numbers and a traditional ensemble of zither, flutes, oboe and fiddle colouring the scenes over barrel-drum rhythms.
exemplars: National Changgeuk Company productions and recordings

items.name: Gugak gwanhyeonak (Korean traditional-instrument orchestra)
items.lineage: Gugak gwanhyeonak is the large conducted orchestra of Korean traditional instruments, arranged in sections like a Western orchestra and playing newly composed works (changjak gugak) and arrangements. The Seoul Metropolitan Traditional Music Orchestra was the first, followed by the KBS Korean Traditional Music Orchestra and the National Orchestra of Korea, which use enlarged and reformed instruments such as the 25-string gayageum.
items.description: Massed sections of plucked zithers, bowed fiddles, flutes and double reeds play composed, harmonised scores with sweeping dynamic swells and drum-driven climaxes.
exemplars: Seoul Metropolitan Traditional Music Orchestra recordings
KBS Korean Traditional Music Orchestra recordings

items.name: Donghaean byeolsingut (Korean east-coast village shaman rite)
items.lineage: Donghaean byeolsingut is the village rite held every few years for the fishing villages of Korea's east coast, from Busan to Gangwon, by hereditary shaman families; the Gangneung danogut of the Dano festival belongs to the same practice. Female shamans sing and dance the narratives while male musicians of the same families play janggu, kkwaenggwari, jing, cymbals and taepyeongso in long, complex rhythmic cycles. The rite was designated Important Intangible Cultural Property No. 82-1, with the hereditary musician Kim Seok-chul among its holders.
items.description: A shaman's narrative singing rides over intricate, shifting hourglass-drum and gong cycles that accelerate into dense, clangorous climaxes, with a keening shawm weaving free melody above.

items.name: Jeju simbang gut (Jeju Island shaman ritual)
items.lineage: Simbang are the shamans of Jeju Island off the southern Korean coast, whose gut rituals recite the island's own creation myths and deity narratives to the sound of drum, hourglass drum, gong and a struck brass bowl (seolsoe). Chilmeoridang yeongdeunggut, held each second lunar month at the Chilmeoridang shrine in Jeju City to welcome and send off the wind goddess Yeongdeung for divers and fishermen, is inscribed on UNESCO's Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage; the kkwaenggwari card stands in for the seolsoe.
items.description: A shaman chants long myth narratives in a recitative voice over steady, repetitive drum, gong and clanging brass-bowl patterns that quicken for dances.

items.name: Talchum (Korean mask-dance drama music)
items.lineage: Talchum are the masked dance-dramas of Korea, satirising apostate monks, aristocrats and quarrelling couples in scenes of dance, song and dialogue, among them Bongsan talchum, Yangju byeolsandae and Hahoe byeolsingut talnori, and are inscribed together on UNESCO's Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage. Most are accompanied by the samhyeon yukgak ensemble of two piri, daegeum, haegeum, janggu and buk playing dance tunes, while the Hahoe play is accompanied by pungmul-style village percussion.
items.description: Nasal double reeds, flute and fiddle play lilting dance tunes over swinging triple-feel drum cycles, broken by masked actors' shouted lines, songs and the crowd's laughter.
exemplars: Bongsan talchum and Yangju byeolsandae preservation-society recordings

items.name: Hyeongmyeong gayo (North Korean revolutionary song)
items.lineage: North Korean revolutionary songs praise the leaders, the party and the army, from the Song of General Kim Il-sung (1946) onward, and are the core repertoire of state ensembles such as the Korean People's Army Song and Dance Ensemble and its Merited Chorus. They are set as strophic marches and lyrical anthems in Western keys for soloists and massed choirs over orchestras that mix Western and reformed Korean instruments; generic string and horn cards stand in for the orchestra.
items.description: Massed male voices and bright soloists sing rousing, square marches and broad anthems in unison and plain harmony, over strings and open brass.
exemplars: North Korean state-label releases of revolutionary songs
Korean People's Army Merited Chorus recordings

items.name: North Korean electronic light music (Pochonbo-style ensembles)
items.lineage: North Korean light music (gyeongeumak) is state popular song played by electronic bands: the Wangjaesan Light Music Band (1983) and the Pochonbo Electronic Ensemble (1985), which brought synthesizers, electric guitars and drum kit to songs for female and male soloists. The all-woman Moranbong Band, formed in 2012, updated the sound with electric strings and keyboards.
items.description: Bright, clean female and male voices sing tuneful strophic songs over glossy synthesizer leads, clean electric guitar, bass and steady drum kit in a polished, sweet ensemble sound.
exemplars: Pochonbo Electronic Ensemble albums (North Korean state releases)

items.name: Pibada-sik gageuk (North Korean Sea of Blood-style revolutionary opera)
items.lineage: Pibada-style opera is the North Korean form launched with Sea of Blood (1971) and The Flower Girl (1972), the first two of the Five Great Revolutionary Operas. It replaces aria and recitative with strophic songs (jeolga), adds an offstage chorus (pangchang) that comments on the action, and sets them for a mixed orchestra of Western and Korean instruments; generic string and horn cards stand in for the orchestra.
items.description: Clear, high-projected voices sing tuneful strophic songs while a large offstage chorus swells between scenes, over lush orchestral strings and horns in melodramatic, heroic climaxes.
exemplars: Sea of Blood Opera Troupe recordings of Sea of Blood
Sea of Blood Opera Troupe recordings of The Flower Girl

items.name: Minjok eumak (North Korean reformed national music)
items.lineage: North Korean national music rebuilt Korean instruments from the 1960s so they could play in equal temperament and in orchestral sections: the haegeum became the four-string sohaegeum and its larger sizes, the taepyeongso the keyed jangsaenap, and new instruments such as the okryugeum zither were devised. Folk-song singing likewise replaced the husky pansori voice with a clear, bright tone, heard in Mansudae Art Troupe recordings. The taepyeongso card stands in for the jangsaenap and the modern extended-range gayageum variant for the reformed North Korean gayageum.
items.description: A bright, clear soprano with quick vibrato sings folk tunes in smooth, tempered harmony over plucked zither, bowed fiddles, flute and a keyed shawm in polished orchestral arrangements.

items.name: Saeta (Andalusian Holy Week processional song)
items.lineage: The saeta is the song addressed from a balcony or the street to the images of Christ and the Virgin carried in Andalusian Holy Week processions, sung while the float halts and the band falls silent. Older saetas survive as local forms such as the saetas cuarteleras of Puente Genil and the saetas of Marchena and Arcos de la Frontera; in the early twentieth century flamenco singers recast the song on the seguiriya and martinete, producing the saeta flamenca, which was recorded on 78-rpm discs from its first decades.
items.description: A single unaccompanied voice launches long, high, pressed melismatic phrases in free rhythm into the hush of a stopped procession, each phrase stretched to the length of a breath and closed on a held, wavering cadence, with the street's own echo as the only support.
exemplars: La Niña de los Peines saetas (78-rpm discs)

items.name: Fandangos de Huelva (Huelva village fandangos)
items.lineage: Fandangos de Huelva are the large family of local fandangos of Huelva province, sung and danced at village fiestas in the Andévalo and the Sierra and named after their towns — Alosno, Calañas, Almonaster and others — along with the choqueros of the city of Huelva. Singers such as Paco Toronjo of Alosno and Paco Isidro carried them onto commercial records, where they became one of the most widely recorded fandango families in flamenco.
items.description: A solo voice sings each fandango verse in long, ornamented lines over a lilting ternary guitar strum and palmas, the guitar filling the gaps between sung lines with rasgueado; the village styles are brighter, quicker and closer to the dance, with a firm clapped pulse.

items.name: Cantes mineros (taranta, minera, cartagenera)
items.lineage: The cantes mineros, or cantes de Levante, are the free-rhythm, fandango-derived flamenco songs of the mining districts of eastern Andalusia and Murcia: the taranta of Almería and Linares, the minera and cartagenera of La Unión and Cartagena, and the levantica and murciana. Antonio Chacón shaped several of them for the professional stage, and since 1961 the Festival Internacional del Cante de las Minas in La Unión has made them a competition repertoire; the metred taranto is their danceable offshoot.
items.description: A solo voice sings long, high, strained melismatic lines out of time, ending on dark, dissonant cadences, while the guitar answers between lines with rubato falsetas built on ringing open-string chords, leaving the voice exposed for most of each verse.
exemplars: Antonio Chacón cantes de Levante (78-rpm discs)
Festival Internacional del Cante de las Minas (La Unión) competition recordings

items.name: Tangos and tientos (flamenco four-beat palos)
items.lineage: Tangos flamencos are the festive four-beat palo of flamenco, with local schools in Cádiz, Triana, Jerez, Granada and Málaga; La Niña de los Peines made influential 78-rpm recordings of them. Tientos are the slow, heavy form of the same compás, which tradition credits to the Cádiz singer Enrique el Mellizo, and are often sung as an opening that speeds up into tangos.
items.description: Guitar rasgueado and interlocking palmas drive a binary four-beat compás with a dragging, swung feel, and the singer phrases short festive verses across it; in tientos the same pattern slows to a heavy, deliberate tread carrying longer, darker melismas.
exemplars: La Niña de los Peines tangos (78-rpm discs)

items.name: Cantes de ida y vuelta (guajira, colombiana, milonga)
items.lineage: The cantes de ida y vuelta ('there-and-back songs') are the flamenco palos shaped from Latin American song that travelled back to Andalusian ports: the guajira from Cuba, the milonga and vidalita from the River Plate, and the colombiana, which Pepe Marchena composed on Latin American models. Marchena's 78-rpm records of colombianas and guajiras and Juanito Valderrama's milongas made them popular.
items.description: These are sweeter, more major-key songs than core flamenco: the guajira sways in a twelve-beat alternation of six and three with lilting, lightly ornamented verses, while the colombiana and milonga move in an even binary pulse, the guitar strumming open major chords under a relaxed, crooning voice.
exemplars: Pepe Marchena colombianas and guajiras (1930s 78-rpm discs)

items.name: Ópera flamenca (1920s-1950s staged flamenco)
items.lineage: Ópera flamenca was the name under which flamenco toured theatres and bullrings from the mid-1920s to the 1950s, reportedly adopted because opera performances paid less tax than variety shows. Its stars — Pepe Marchena, Manuel Vallejo, La Niña de la Puebla and later Juanito Valderrama — favoured the lighter, melodic cantes, above all personal fandangos, colombianas, guajiras, milongas and cuplés por bulerías, and recorded them prolifically on 78-rpm discs and EPs.
items.description: A clear, sweet, high voice spins long ornamental runs, falsetto turns and held climactic notes over a single guitar, favouring melodic fandangos and Latin-tinged songs over rough, heavy cante, in a close, intimate period studio sound.
exemplars: La Niña de la Puebla recordings

items.name: Zambra gitana (Sacromonte cave zambra)
items.lineage: The zambra of Sacromonte is the song-and-dance performance of the Gitano families of the cave houses on Granada's Sacromonte hill, staged in the caves for visitors from the nineteenth century onward. Its set of three dances — the alboreá, the cachucha and the mosca — is said to retrace a Gitano wedding, and family troupes, central to Granada flamenco, sing and dance it to guitar, castanets, palmas and footwork.
items.description: Strummed guitar and a clatter of castanets set a quick, insistent pulse in a small, low room, with heels, palmas and shouts of encouragement packed around short, bright sung verses and group refrains.
exemplars: María la Canastera cave zambra troupe

items.name: Verdiales (Málaga hill-country pandas)
items.lineage: Verdiales is the fandango music of the Montes de Málaga and the neighbouring hill country, played by pandas: bands of violin, guitars, laúd, a large pandero frame drum, small cymbals and castanets, led by an alcalde with a staff, while a singer delivers fandango verses and couples dance. Its three styles are named after Montes, Almogía and Comares; the pandas meet every 28 December at the Fiesta Mayor de Verdiales, the tradition is inscribed as a Bien de Interés Cultural, and verdiales are commonly described as a root of the malagueña. The bandurria card stands in for the laúd.
items.description: A violin saws a short repeated figure over fast strummed guitars, laúd tremolo and a relentless pulse of big frame drum, clashing small cymbals and castanets, and a singer cuts in with a high, strained fandango verse; the whole sound is loud, raw and endlessly cyclical.
exemplars: Fiesta Mayor de Verdiales festival recordings
Panda recordings in the Montes, Almogía and Comares styles

items.name: Zambomba jerezana (Jerez Christmas villancico gathering)
items.lineage: The zambomba is Jerez de la Frontera's Advent and Christmas gathering, held in the courtyards of neighbourhood houses and in the streets of quarters such as Santiago and San Miguel, where people sing traditional villancicos and romances around a fire to the friction drum it is named after, tambourines, palmas, guitar and scraped anise bottles, often turning the songs into bulerías. The Cátedra de Flamencología de Jerez documented it in the record series 'Así canta nuestra tierra en Navidad', and it is inscribed as a Bien de Interés Cultural.
items.description: A ring of voices sings strophic villancicos, a leader answered by the group refrain, over the low grunting pulse of the friction drum, tambourine jingles and dense palmas, the songs sliding into the swing and accents of bulería.
exemplars: 'Así canta nuestra tierra en Navidad' record series (Cátedra de Flamencología de Jerez)

items.name: Auroros (Murcian dawn-song brotherhoods)
items.lineage: The auroros are lay Catholic brotherhoods, called campanas de auroros, of the Huerta de Murcia and neighbouring districts, who go out before dawn on Sundays to sing salves and coplas to the Virgin of the Rosary through the lanes and at the church door, and who also sing for the dead. A leader gives out each verse and the group answers in orally transmitted polyphony, while a bell marks the start and close of each copla; the tradition is inscribed as a Bien de Interés Cultural. The handbells card stands in for the campana.
items.description: A leader sings out each line of a slow devotional copla and a group of voices answers in dense, raw, unaccompanied chords that swell and fade in the open air, while a single bell rings to mark the start and end of each verse.
exemplars: Campana de Auroros del Rincón de Seca
University of Murcia field documentation of the auroros

items.name: Cuadrillas de ánimas (Murcian aguilando bands)
items.lineage: Cuadrillas de ánimas are village string bands of the Murcia region and the adjoining north-east of Almería, tied to brotherhoods of the souls in purgatory, which in the Christmas season go from house to house singing aguilandos and collecting alms for masses for the dead, then play for dancing. A cuadrilla combines violins, guitars, laúdes and bandurrias with small cymbals, castanets and tambourines, and its repertoire mixes aguilandos and pascuas with malagueñas, jotas and parrandas; the Fiesta de las Cuadrillas of Barranda, near Caravaca, gathers them each year. The bandurria card stands for the laúdes and bandurrias.
items.description: Several violins play a bright, scraping unison tune over strummed guitars and tremolo laúdes, with clashing small cymbals, castanets and tambourine driving a fast dance pulse; between instrumental passages a singer, answered by the group, delivers aguilando verses.
exemplars: Fiesta de las Cuadrillas de Barranda performances
Murcia Etnográfica documentation of the cuadrillas

items.name: Trovo (Alpujarra improvised sung verse)
items.lineage: The trovo is improvised verse in quintillas delivered in turn by two or more troveros who answer and taunt one another. In the Alpujarra of Granada and Almería the verses are sung to a fandango-derived tune that violin, guitar and bandurria play between them; a related tradition flourished in Cartagena and its mining district, where José María Marín was its best-known trovero.
items.description: Each trovero sings an improvised five-line verse to a plain, declamatory melody and his rival answers in turn, while violin, guitar and bandurria play a lively fandango-like tune between the verses.
exemplars: Trovo performances at the Festival de Música Tradicional de la Alpujarra

items.name: Cant d'estil (Valencian sung style-song)
items.lineage: Cant d'estil is the virtuoso solo song of the Valencian Horta and the surrounding comarques, often performed as a sung joust between singers, in forms such as l'u, l'u i dos and l'u i dotze; the last two are exclusively Valencian, while l'u belongs to the fandango family. Its accompaniment combines strings (guitar and guitarró) with wind instruments such as clarinet, trumpet and trombone, and the related albaes are night serenades sung to dolçaina and tabalet. The classical-guitar card stands for the guitar and guitarró, and the credited-horns card for the trumpet and trombone.
items.description: A soloist sings long, high, florid Phrygian-tinged lines with great rhythmic freedom against a steady three-beat accompaniment of strummed guitars, the winds playing interludes between sung lines while the harmony rocks only between tonic and dominant.

items.name: Música festera (Moros y Cristianos marches)
items.lineage: Música festera is the wind-band repertoire composed for the Moros y Cristianos festivals of Alcoi and the towns of Alicante province and the Valencian interior, played by local music societies as the Moorish and Christian companies parade. Its core genres are the slow, heavily percussive marcha mora, whose first example is usually given as Antonio Pérez Verdú's 'A-Ben-Amet', the brighter, more martial marcha cristiana, and the pasodoble festero; new marches are composed for the festivals every year. The credited-horns card stands for the band's trumpets, trombones and other brass.
items.description: A large wind band plays at a slow processional tread over a heavy, insistent bass drum and cymbal pattern, dark minor-key melodies in the clarinets swelling into massive brass climaxes; marchas cristianas switch to brighter fanfares at a quicker, stately pace.
exemplars: Unió Musical d'Alcoi recordings of música festera

items.name: Misteri d'Elx (Elche Assumption mystery play)
items.lineage: The Misteri d'Elx is a sung medieval drama of the death, Assumption and Coronation of the Virgin, performed in Valencian with some Latin inside the Basílica de Santa Maria in Elche every 14 and 15 August, with aerial machinery lowering angels from the dome. It is sung throughout by men and boys, the boys taking the female and angel roles, and combines monodic chant with polyphony added in the sixteenth century; UNESCO proclaimed it a Masterpiece of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity.
items.description: Solo boys' and men's voices sing plain, archaic modal chant into a vast reverberant church, alternating with sonorous unaccompanied polyphony from the choir as the aerial scenes descend from the dome.
exemplars: Capella del Misteri d'Elx performances (14-15 August)
Commercial recordings of the Misteri d'Elx

items.name: Cant de la Sibil·la (Mallorcan Christmas Sibyl chant)
items.lineage: The Cant de la Sibil·la is a medieval chant of the Last Judgement, sung in Catalan at Christmas Eve Matins in Palma Cathedral and in parish churches across Mallorca. A boy or girl in a tunic, holding a sword, sings the verses alone and unaccompanied, with organ interludes between the stanzas; Mallorca kept the chant after the Council of Trent suppressed it in most places, and UNESCO has inscribed it as intangible heritage. The credited-organ card stands for the church organ.
items.description: A single high, clear voice, traditionally a child's, sings a slow, melismatic modal chant alone in a vast stone church, each stanza answered by a short organ interlude while the long reverberation carries the bare line.
exemplars: Montserrat Figueras and Jordi Savall, 'El Cant de la Sibil·la' (Alia Vox)
Christmas Eve Matins at Palma Cathedral

items.name: Ball de bot and xeremiers (Mallorcan dance music)
items.lineage: Ball de bot is the family of Mallorcan couple dances — mateixes, jotes, fandangos and boleros — played either by xeremiers, a pair of musicians on the xeremies bagpipe and the flabiol pipe with tamborí drum, or by groups of singers with guitars, bandurrias and castanets, while work songs were sung unaccompanied in the fields. Alan Lomax made field recordings of these strands across the island. The gaita asturiana card stands in for the xeremies and the credited-flute card for the flabiol.
items.description: A bagpipe with a steady drone and a shrill pipe play bright, tightly ornamented dance tunes in quick triple time over the dry beat of a small tabor; in the string-band form, strummed guitars, bandurria tremolo and castanets back a high, strong sung verse between dance figures.
exemplars: Alan Lomax, 'Mallorca: The Balearic Islands' (Rounder, 1952 field recordings)

items.name: Baile del tambor (La Gomera drum-and-chácaras ballads)
items.lineage: The baile del tambor of La Gomera, in the Canary Islands, is a sung and danced form in which a soloist intones the verses of a traditional romance and a chorus answers each couplet with a fixed refrain, over a large drum beaten with a stick and the chácaras, the island's large castanets, while dancers move in facing lines at patronal fiestas and processions. The Gomeran romance repertoire was documented by Maximiano Trapero. The membrane-drum card stands in for the tambor and the castanets card for the chácaras.
items.description: A single high voice chants a long ballad narrative to a narrow, repeating melodic formula, answered after each couplet by a group refrain, over a hypnotic, unvarying beat from a large stick-struck drum and the dry, fast clatter of big castanets.
exemplars: ULPGC folk archive documentation of the Gomeran romancero (Trapero)
La Gomera field recordings of the baile del tambor

items.name: Seguidillas manchegas (La Mancha sung dance)
items.lineage: Seguidillas manchegas are the sung couple-dance of La Mancha, across Ciudad Real, Toledo, Albacete and Cuenca provinces, played by rondallas of guitars, bandurrias and laúdes with household and small percussion such as the brass mortar (almirez), the scraped anís bottle, the triangle (hierrillos) and castanets. Alan Lomax recorded in Castilla-La Mancha on his Spanish field trip, and the regional government has declared the seguidilla manchega a Bien de Interés Cultural in the category of intangible heritage. The bandurria card also covers the laúd, the triangle card stands for the hierrillos and the credited-percussion card for the almirez and the anís bottle.
items.description: Strummed guitars and tremolo-picked bandurrias drive a quick triple metre while a solo voice, often high and tense, delivers short sung couplets between instrumental interludes, with castanet rolls, the tick of the triangle, the ring of the brass mortar and the rasp of the scraped bottle marking the dance steps.
exemplars: Alan Lomax 1952 La Mancha rondalla recordings

items.name: Regueifa (Galician sung verse duel)
items.lineage: The regueifa is the Galician improvised verse duel in which two regueifeiros answer one another in sung quatrains, traditionally at wedding feasts in Bergantiños and neighbouring districts of A Coruña province, where the contest took its name from the regueifa, the festive bread disputed at the wedding. After decades of decline it was revived from the late twentieth century through public contests, festivals and media appearances, and it has been studied in the Boletín da Real Academia Galega.
items.description: Two unaccompanied voices trade improvised quatrains on a short, repeated melodic formula, each turn half-sung and half-declaimed with strong syllabic stress, while audience laughter and applause break in after a sharp riposte.
exemplars: Contemporary regueifa contests and festival performances in Galicia

items.name: Tamboradas (Spanish Holy Week drum rituals)
items.lineage: Tamboradas are the Holy Week drum-playing rituals of towns in Aragon, Murcia, Castilla-La Mancha, Andalusia and the Valencian Community, in which crowds of townspeople beat drums and bass drums together for hours on end, inscribed on UNESCO's Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity. In Calanda and the other towns of the Bajo Aragón Ruta del Tambor y Bombo the playing opens with the Rompida de la Hora at noon on Good Friday, while towns such as Hellín, Moratalla and Baena keep their own toques. The tenor-drum card stands for the rope-tensioned tambor and the membrane-drum card for the bombo.
items.description: A massed wall of drums beats in unison and near-unison rolls, the dry crackle of the snared drums layered over the deep pulse of the bass drums, swelling from a single cue into a continuous, deafening roar that fills streets and squares for hours.
exemplars: Recordings of the Rompida de la Hora at Calanda
Ruta del Tambor y Bombo (Bajo Aragón) tamboradas

items.name: Romancero (Spanish oral ballad singing)
items.lineage: The romancero of modern oral tradition is the body of narrative ballads in octosyllabic assonant verse, many descended from late-medieval romances, that survived in rural Spain, above all in Castile, León, Asturias, Galicia and the Canary Islands, sung chiefly by women at work and at home and in Asturias to carry the danza prima. Ramón Menéndez Pidal and María Goyri began collecting it at the start of the twentieth century, and their archive's field tapes, Alan Lomax's 1952 Spanish recordings and the Pan-Hispanic Ballad Project document thousands of versions of ballads such as Gerineldo and La Condesita.
items.description: A single unaccompanied voice, most often a woman's, repeats a short strophic tune through long narrative sequences of verse, with plain syllabic delivery, light ornament at the line ends and a steady, unhurried pulse that serves the story.
exemplars: Alan Lomax 1952 Spain recordings of romances

items.name: Cantigas de Santa María (Alfonsine Marian songs)
items.lineage: The Cantigas de Santa María are some 420 Marian songs in Galician-Portuguese compiled at the court of Alfonso X of Castile in the 1270s and 1280s and preserved in four manuscripts now held at El Escorial, Madrid and Florence, three of them with musical notation; the miniatures of the Escorial códice de los músicos show players of fiddles, lutes, psalteries, hurdy-gurdies, shawms, bagpipes and drums. The notation gives a single melodic line, so modern early-music ensembles reconstruct rhythm, drones and instrumentation, and the corpus has become one of the most recorded bodies of medieval song. The oud card stands for the lute shown in the miniatures.
items.description: A solo voice alternates refrain and verse over a modal melody while bowed fiddle, plucked lute and psaltery double or decorate it, the fiddle's open bourdon string sustains a drone, and frame drums mark the dance-like refrains.
exemplars: Jordi Savall and Hespèrion XX Cantigas recordings

items.name: Tonadilla escénica (Madrid theatre song-interlude)
items.lineage: The tonadilla escénica was a short sung comic interlude performed between the acts of plays in Madrid's public theatres, the Príncipe and the Cruz, from about the 1750s into the early nineteenth century, built from songs, duets and closing seguidillas for one or several singer-actors with a small theatre orchestra of strings with oboes or flutes and horns. Luis Misón, Pablo Esteve and Blas de Laserna were among its principal composers, many scores survive in Madrid's Biblioteca Histórica Municipal, and early-music performers have revived the repertoire on modern recordings.
items.description: Bright, quick-witted vocal numbers in Spanish over a light classical-era band of strings and horns, mixing patter-like syllabic verses, lyrical airs and spirited closing dances in triple time, with every word projected clearly for comic effect.
exemplars: Biblioteca Histórica Municipal de Madrid tonadilla scores

items.name: Bakalao (Valencian Ruta club sound)
items.lineage: Bakalao, or the sonido de Valencia, grew from the clubs on the coast road south of Valencia, such as Barraca, Chocolate and Spook Factory, where through the 1980s resident DJs mixed new wave, synth-pop, EBM and Belgian new beat into marathon weekend sessions that the press called the Ruta del Bakalao. In the early 1990s local producers and labels turned the sound into hard, fast, riff-driven club records with sampled stabs and chanted hooks, a commercial wave that peaked and faded by the mid-1990s and fed into makina. The credited-samples card stands for the sampler.
items.description: Four-on-the-floor kicks at fast club tempos drive stabbing, hook-like synthesizer riffs and sampled stabs, with sparse shouted or spoken vocal catchphrases over long, repetitive builds made for marathon dancing.

items.name: Desgarrada minhota (Minho sung challenge)
items.lineage: Cantares ao desafio, also called desgarrada, are the sung verse challenges of the Minho and neighbouring northern Portugal, in which two or more cantadores, very often a man and a woman, improvise alternating quatrains of teasing, argument and flirtation at fairs, romarias and village festivals. A concertina, in Portugal a diatonic button accordion, usually carries the repeated tune and interludes, sometimes with a triangle (ferrinhos), and northern cantadores have issued desgarradas on commercial cassettes and CDs since the late twentieth century; the accordion card stands for the concertina.
items.description: A button accordion pumps a bright, repeating tune and fills between verses while two voices, often male and female, alternate improvised quatrains in a high, open, projected chest voice, the triangle ticking the beat and the crowd reacting to each retort.

items.name: Cante ao baldão (Alentejo sung challenge with viola campaniça)
items.lineage: Cante ao baldão, also called cante ao despique, is the improvised sung challenge of the Baixo Alentejo, especially around Odemira, Ourique and Castro Verde, in which several singers take turns improvising verses on a fixed melody over the repeated accompaniment of the viola campaniça, the region's wire-strung folk guitar. It is distinct from the slow choral cante alentejano of the same region; it was revived from the late twentieth century, together with the viola campaniça, through the recordings and research of José Francisco Colaço and later players, and has been studied by INET-md.
items.description: A single viola campaniça repeats a short strummed and picked pattern with ringing open courses while singers in turn deliver improvised verses in a strong chest voice on a fixed melody, each answer taking up the theme of the last.

items.name: Gaita mirandesa and pauliteiros (Terra de Miranda)
items.lineage: In the Terra de Miranda of north-eastern Trás-os-Montes, where the Mirandese language is spoken, the gaita de foles mirandesa bagpipe with snare drum (caixa) and bass drum (bombo) plays for the pauliteiros, teams of men who dance the lhaços while striking wooden sticks together, and for processions, feasts and songs. The repertoire has been documented by Mário Correia's Sons da Terra recordings and carried on by younger groups; the single-drone Asturian gaita card stands in for the Mirandese bagpipe, the tenor-drum and membrane-drum cards for the caixa and bombo, and the credited-percussion card for the dancers' sticks.
items.description: A reedy bagpipe chanter plays short, repeated dance tunes over its drone while a snare drum rattles and a bass drum thumps the beat, and the dancers' sticks crack together in sharp, synchronized accents.

items.name: Corridinho (Algarve accordion dance)
items.lineage: The corridinho is the fast couple dance of the Algarve in southern Portugal, in a lively duple metre, danced by couples in quick turns across the floor. It is played above all on the accordion, which the Algarve has cultivated through generations of local accordionists, and is accompanied in ranchos folclóricos by triangle and bass drum and sometimes sung.
items.description: A brilliant accordion runs fast, ornamented melodies in quick duple time with punchy bellows accents and chordal bass, while the triangle and bass drum push a light, bouncing beat for spinning couples.

items.name: Pimba (Portuguese arraial popular song)
items.lineage: Pimba is the Portuguese popular song of village arraiais, summer festivals and emigrant gatherings, a name popularised in the 1990s by the refrain of Emanuel's song 'Pimba, Pimba' and applied to singalong songs full of double meanings and dance rhythms drawn from the marcha, the vira and modern pop. Its records usually set a solo singer over keyboards, drums, electric bass, guitar and accordion, and it is studied as working-class popular music by researchers at INET-md.
items.description: A bright solo voice sings jaunty, singalong verses and shouted refrains over bouncy keyboard and accordion riffs, a busy electric bass and a steady programmed dance beat, all mixed loud and cheerful for open-air festivals.

items.name: Marchas populares (Lisbon Santo António parades)
items.lineage: The marchas populares are the neighbourhood marching songs and costumed parades of Lisbon's Santo António festivities, run as a competition between the bairros since the interwar years, in which bairros such as Alfama, Mouraria, Bica and Madragoa each present a new marcha with its own song and choreography before parading down the Avenida da Liberdade on the night of 12 June. Each marcha's song is sung by its marchantes to a band that parades with them, and the year's official Grande Marcha de Lisboa and many neighbourhood marchas are issued on record. The credited-horns card stands for the band's brass and saxophones.
items.description: A crowd of marchers sings a bright, catchy tune in unison over a marching band of brass and clarinets, with snare and bass drum keeping a jaunty two-step marching pulse through repeated verse and chorus.
exemplars: Festas de Lisboa neighbourhood marcha recordings

items.name: Revista à portuguesa (Lisbon Parque Mayer revue song)
items.lineage: The revista à portuguesa is Lisbon's satirical musical revue, staged since the mid-nineteenth century and centred in the twentieth on the theatres of the Parque Mayer, where sketches of political and social satire alternated with songs, fados, marchas and dance numbers written for each season's show. Its songs, launched by the revue's stars with a small theatre orchestra, reached a wide public through records, radio and film. The credited-horns card stands for the orchestra's trumpet and other brass.
items.description: A star singer delivers witty, clearly enunciated verses and a big singalong chorus over a small theatre orchestra of piano, trumpet, clarinet, bass and drums, alternating jaunty marches and comic patter with sentimental, fado-tinged numbers.

items.name: Encomendação das almas (Portuguese Lenten souls chant)
items.lineage: The encomendação das almas is a nocturnal Lenten ritual of rural Portugal, found in the Beira Baixa, the Alto Alentejo, Trás-os-Montes and other regions, in which a group of villagers goes out after dark to crossroads, hilltops or other high places to sing slow chants commending the souls in purgatory and asking the living to pray for them. Michel Giacometti recorded it for his RTP television series Povo que Canta in the early 1970s.
items.description: A small group of unaccompanied voices sings a slow, free-rhythm chant in loose heterophony, the long held phrase-ends projected into the night air and carrying across the village from an open, high place.
exemplars: Michel Giacometti, Povo que Canta (RTP) recordings

items.name: Ottava rima improvvisata (Tuscan and Lazio poeti a braccio)
items.lineage: Improvised singing in ottava rima, the eight-line hendecasyllabic stanza of Italian narrative poetry, is the art of the poeti a braccio of the Maremma and other rural parts of Tuscany, upper Lazio and the Sabina, who sing extempore stanzas to traditional melodic formulas, often in a contrasto in which two poets argue opposing characters or themes and each stanza picks up the closing rhyme of the opponent's. It has been recorded for the ethnomusicology archive of the Accademia di Santa Cecilia since that archive's early years and later by the Istituto Ernesto de Martino, and continues at festivals and contests.
items.description: Two unaccompanied voices take turns singing improvised eight-line stanzas on a slow, ornamented melodic formula, each line stretched over a long breath and closing on a held cadence, the duel building through answered rhymes and audience reactions.
exemplars: Archivi di Etnomusicologia, Accademia Nazionale di Santa Cecilia field recordings

items.name: Vjersh (Arbëreshë multipart song of Calabria and Basilicata)
items.lineage: The Arbëreshë, descendants of Albanian communities who settled in southern Italy from the fifteenth century, keep a repertoire of multipart songs called vjersh, sung by small groups of men or of women in which one or two soloists carry the text over a drone held by the rest, used at weddings, at Easter and in other community celebrations. Diego Carpitella recorded it in the Arbëreshë villages of Calabria in the mid-twentieth century, and later field recordings from the Arbëreshë villages of Basilicata have been published.
items.description: One or two lead voices trade and overlap melismatic lines above a sustained group drone, the close dissonant intervals ringing against the held pitch in an open-throated, unaccompanied texture.

items.name: Griko song (Grecìa Salentina)
items.lineage: Grecìa Salentina is the cluster of towns south of Lecce, among them Calimera, Martano, Sternatia, Zollino and Corigliano d'Otranto, where Griko, a Greek dialect, is still spoken. Its song repertoire includes love songs and serenades, funeral laments (moroloja), work songs and Holy Week Passion songs, documented in late-twentieth-century field recordings and carried on by local groups.
items.description: A plain, warm voice sings strophic songs in a lilting metre over strummed guitar and accordion chords, the melodies curling with small ornaments, and in the laments slowing into a heavier, unaccompanied cry.
exemplars: 'Canto d'amore: voci, suoni, ritmi della Grecìa Salentina' (field recordings 1975-1985)

items.name: Courenta and balet (Occitan valleys of Piedmont dance music)
items.lineage: The dance music of the Occitan-speaking valleys of south-western Piedmont, such as the Varaita, Maira and Vermenagna valleys in the province of Cuneo, built around the courenta, the balet and other dances played for village feasts on diatonic accordion, fiddle and hurdy-gurdy (ghironda), with songs in Occitan. A folk revival led by groups such as Lou Dalfin brought the ghironda back and carried the repertoire to festivals and records. The accordion card stands in for the valley diatonic button accordion.
items.description: Bright reedy accordion and fiddle lines move together in a steady, springing dance pulse, tunes repeated in short sections for the dancers, with occasional sung verses over the instruments.
exemplars: Silvio Peron & Gabriele Ferrero, 'Dance of Occitan valleys of Italy' (Robi Droli, 1998)

items.name: Citira and bunkula (Val Resia dance music)
items.lineage: The music of Val Resia in the Julian Prealps of Friuli, whose people speak a Slovene dialect: dance tunes played on the citira, a violin tuned higher than usual so that it carries over the dancers, and the bunkula, an adapted cello or small three-stringed bass, for the Resian dances of Carnival (Püst) and the feast of the Assumption, alongside a repertoire of songs. Slovene and Italian ethnomusicologists, among them Julijan Strajnar, documented it in the field. The fiddle card stands in for the citira and the cello card for the bunkula.
items.description: A high, sharp, insistent violin melody cycles through short repeated phrases while the small bass fiddle saws a rhythmic, drone-like accompaniment beneath it, the dancers' stamping feet marking the tight, unbroken pulse.
exemplars: 'Friuli: Rezija, canti e musiche della Val di Resia' (Nota, 1997)
Julijan Strajnar field recordings of Resian music

items.name: Maggio drammatico (Apennine sung folk drama)
items.lineage: The maggio is a sung popular drama of the northern Apennines, from the Garfagnana and Lunigiana in Tuscany to the mountains of Reggio Emilia and Modena, performed outdoors in spring and summer by village companies of maggiarini. The actors sing chivalric, biblical and historical stories in rhymed stanzas to a small stock of traditional melodies, with short instrumental ritornelli between stanzas, traditionally on violin and later also accordion or guitar. Researchers of the University of Bologna and others have documented and recorded the companies, which remain active in villages such as Costabona.
items.description: Solo voices take turns singing stanza after stanza of the story to the same plain, projected melody in the open air, each stanza closed by a brief fiddle ritornello that hands over to the next character.
exemplars: University of Bologna field recordings of maggio companies

items.name: Canti delle mondine (Po valley rice-weeders' songs)
items.lineage: Songs of the mondine, the seasonal women workers who weeded and transplanted the flooded rice fields of the Vercelli, Novara and Lomellina plains and parts of Emilia from the late nineteenth century until mechanisation and herbicides ended the work in the decades after the Second World War. Sung together in the paddies and dormitories, the repertoire mixes work, love and protest songs, including songs of the struggle for the eight-hour day; folk-revival researchers recorded it from former mondine such as Giovanna Daffini, and community choirs such as the Coro delle Mondine di Novi still sing it.
items.description: A group of women's voices sings strophic tunes together, unaccompanied, in full open chest voice, the verses carried at a steady walking pace and the refrains taken up by everyone.
exemplars: Silvia Tarozzi & Deborah Walker, 'Canti di guerra, di lavoro e d'amore' (Unseen Worlds)

items.name: Canti di questua (Pasquella and Cantamaggio door-to-door songs)
items.lineage: Calendar begging songs of central Italy, sung by groups of singers and players who go from house to house at turning points of the year: the Pasquella or Befanata on the eve of Epiphany, the Cantamaggio or maggiolata on the night of 30 April. The songs wish good fortune on the household and ask for eggs, wine, food or money in return, and the bands, found across the Marche, Umbria, Abruzzo, Romagna and Tuscany, accompany them with organetto or accordion, guitar and tambourine.
items.description: A small band of voices sings a strophic greeting song at the door over strummed guitar chords, pumping organetto and a shaken tambourine, verse after verse to the same tune, ending in a louder call of thanks or request.
exemplars: Giovanni Zaffagnini, 'Siamo qua con canti e suoni' (Romagna Epiphany and Calendimaggio ritual songs, 2010)

items.name: Lamenti della Settimana Santa (Sicilian Holy Week multipart laments)
items.lineage: Multipart Passion laments sung in Sicilian and in Latin by small groups of male singers, often linked to confraternities, during the processions and devotions of Holy Week, especially in the inland province of Caltanissetta. A leading voice carries the text while the others join on sustained chords, unaccompanied; Ignazio Macchiarella studied the practice and recorded the Montedoro singers for the Nota release 'Sicilia: La Settimana Santa a Montedoro' (1996).
items.description: A tense, high leading voice draws out each line of the lament in slow free rhythm while a few male voices lock onto held chords beneath it, the close, rough harmony swelling and breaking off at the ends of phrases.
exemplars: Ignazio Macchiarella field recordings of Sicilian Holy Week chant

items.name: Banda da giro (Apulian touring wind band)
items.lineage: The bande da giro are the large wind bands of Puglia hired from town to town through the summer season of patronal feasts, where from illuminated bandstands in the piazza they play operatic fantasias and transcribed arias, symphonic marches and processional marches. The repertoire took shape in the nineteenth century, with the flugelhorn family (flicorni) and clarinets taking the singers' parts, and bands from towns such as Squinzano, Conversano and Lecce became renowned for it. The tenor horn and baritone horn cards stand in for the flicorno contralto and flicorno baritono, and the sousaphone card for the band's tuba-type basses.
items.description: A full open-air wind band plays operatic melodies with solo flugelhorn and clarinet taking the vocal lines in broad, rubato phrasing, over sustained brass chords, a heavy bass line and the boom of bass drum and cymbals in the march sections.
exemplars: Gran Concerto Bandistico Città di Squinzano
Gran Concerto Bandistico Città di Conversano
University of Salento studies of the Apulian band archives

items.name: Sceneggiata (Neapolitan song melodrama)
items.lineage: The sceneggiata is a Neapolitan popular stage form in which a well-known song is expanded into a short melodrama of love, betrayal, honour and revenge, spoken scenes building up to the song itself and played out by the stock figures of hero, heroine and villain (isso, essa e 'o malamente). It arose in Naples around the end of the First World War and was revived in the 1970s by Mario Merola, whose stage shows, records and films made it popular again, followed by singers such as Mario Trevi and Nino D'Angelo.
items.description: A big, sobbing tenor-baritone voice delivers a dramatic dialect song with swelling high notes and broken, half-spoken outbursts, carried by tremolo mandolin, guitar and strings that rise to meet each climax.

items.name: Canzone romanesca (Roman dialect popular song)
items.lineage: Popular song in Romanesco, the dialect of Rome, which grew out of the stornelli and serenades of the city's working districts and found a public stage in the San Giovanni song festival of the late nineteenth century and in café-chantant and variety theatre, where Ettore Petrolini made his name. After the Second World War singers such as Gabriella Ferri, Lando Fiorini and Alvaro Amici recorded it and sang it in Trastevere nightspots and on television, and songs from the stage musical Rugantino joined the repertoire.
items.description: A warm, chesty voice half-sings and half-speaks dialect verses with wry or nostalgic expression over guitar chords and mandolin fills, with stornello-like refrains drawn out at the cadences.

items.name: Cantus romanus (Old Roman chant)
items.lineage: The chant of the city churches of Rome, preserved in a small group of eleventh- to thirteenth-century manuscripts from Roman basilicas, among them the gradual of Santa Cecilia in Trastevere dated 1071; it shares most of its texts with the Gregorian repertory but sets them to its own melodies. Those melodies are more ornate and formulaic than their Gregorian counterparts, turning on recurring stepwise ornamental figures within a narrow range, and the tradition gave way to Gregorian chant in Rome during the thirteenth century. Modern reconstructions often sing it with a held drone beneath a florid solo line.
items.description: A solo voice winds long melismas around a few neighbouring pitches, repeating its characteristic turning figures, over a held drone of male voices in a resonant stone acoustic.
exemplars: Ensemble Organum / Marcel Pérès, 'Chants de l'Église de Rome' (Harmonia Mundi)
Gradual of Santa Cecilia in Trastevere (1071)

items.name: Lauda spirituale (Italian vernacular devotional song)
items.lineage: Vernacular Italian devotional song of the lay confraternities of laudesi, which spread from Umbria and Tuscany in the thirteenth century, carried in part by the flagellant movement that set out from Perugia in 1260, and sang praises of the Virgin, Christ and the saints at their evening gatherings and processions. Its earliest musical sources are the monophonic Laudario di Cortona of the late thirteenth century and the more florid fourteenth-century Laudario Magliabechiano of Florence, mostly in ballata form with a refrain (ripresa) returning between stanzas; polyphonic laude followed in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries.
items.description: A single voice sings each stanza of a simple, tuneful devotional melody and a small group answers with the returning refrain in unison, the alternation unfolding at an even, unhurried pace in a church acoustic.
exemplars: Laudario di Cortona (Cortona, Biblioteca Comunale, MS 91)

items.name: Frottola (north Italian court song, c. 1500)
items.lineage: Italian courtly secular song of about 1470 to 1530, cultivated above all at the Mantuan court of Isabella d'Este by composers such as Marchetto Cara and Bartolomeo Tromboncino and printed by Ottaviano Petrucci in Venice in a series of frottola books from 1504 to 1514. Set to light poetic forms such as the barzelletta and strambotto, usually in four parts with the tune in the top voice, it was sung by a vocal ensemble or by a solo singer with the lower parts played on lute or viols, and gave way to the madrigal in the 1520s and 1530s.
items.description: A clear solo voice sings a tuneful, syllabic strophic melody in short balanced phrases over chordal lute and a bowed viol bass, the lively dance-like rhythm and repeated refrain giving it the lightness of court entertainment.
exemplars: Modena Consort, 'Frottole: Songs from the Courts of Renaissance Italy'

items.name: Villanella alla napoletana (Neapolitan villanesca)
items.lineage: Light three-voice part-song in Neapolitan dialect that appeared in print in Venice from 1537 as the canzone villanesca alla napolitana, with Giovan Domenico da Nola among its first named composers, and was soon taken up and refined by northern composers including Adrian Willaert and Orlande de Lassus. Its strophic, mostly homophonic settings of rustic and comic love poems deliberately keep the parallel fifths of popular singing and parody the refined madrigal.
items.description: Three voices declaim a dialect verse together in plain block chords and parallel fifths, with brisk, dance-like rhythms and a catchy repeated refrain, lightly doubled by a plucked lute.
exemplars: Giovan Domenico da Nola, Canzoni villanesche (Venice, 1541)
Adrian Willaert, Canzone villanesche alla napolitana (Venice, 1545)

items.name: Minhag italiani (Italian-rite synagogue chant)
items.lineage: The liturgical chant of the Italian Jewish rite (minhag italiani, or bené Romì), the old local rite of Rome and of communities in central and northern Italy, distinct from the Ashkenazi and Sephardi rites also followed in Italian synagogues. Its cantillation and prayer melodies are passed on orally by cantors and congregations and differ from city to city; the ethnomusicologist Leo Levi recorded them across Italian communities between 1954 and 1961, in a collection held by the Accademia di Santa Cecilia and the Hebrew University's sound archive.
items.description: A cantor chants Hebrew prayer and scripture in free, speech-shaped rhythm on a small set of melodic formulas, and the congregation answers in unison with responses and sung refrains.
exemplars: Leo Levi Collection of Italian Jewish music (1954-1961)
Accademia Nazionale di Santa Cecilia ethnomusicology archive

items.name: Marċ brijuż (Maltese band-club festa march)
items.lineage: The wind bands of Malta's band clubs (każini tal-banda), founded in parish after parish from the mid-nineteenth century, are the musical heart of the village festa: on the feast days they march through the streets playing lively marches (marċi brijużi) by local bandmasters, give open-air programmes and accompany the procession of the patron saint's statue, while funeral marches serve the Good Friday processions. Rival clubs within the same town regularly commission new marches, and the repertoire is widely recorded. The sousaphone card stands in for the bands' tuba-type basses.
items.description: A loud street band plays a bright, fast march in strict two-beat time, clarinets and trumpets carrying the tune over pumping brass afterbeats and a booming bass drum and snare, its contrasting strains and trio repeated as the crowd moves through the streets.
exemplars: University of Malta studies of the band clubs

items.name: Żaqq u tanbur (Maltese bagpipe and drum music)
items.lineage: The żaqq is the Maltese bagpipe: a whole animal skin fitted with a double chanter of two parallel cane pipes ending in a horn bell, without separate drones. It was played with the tanbur, a large frame drum with jingles, for dancing and festive occasions, but by the later twentieth century only a few elderly players remained, recorded by fieldworkers in their last years of playing; the revival group Etnika later brought the żaqq and tanbur back on record.
items.description: The bagpipe's two reedy chanters buzz in a continuous, slightly beating line, one playing the tune and the other answering or holding a note, over the thump and jingle of a large frame drum in a repeating dance pulse.
exemplars: 1971-73 field recordings of Maltese żaqq players

items.name: Bumba-meu-boi do Maranhão (São Luís ox drama)
items.lineage: Ox-drama festivity of Maranhão performed in the June festival cycle around the feasts of São João, São Pedro and São Marçal, enacting the death and resurrection of a prized ox; it is registered as Brazilian cultural heritage by IPHAN and inscribed on the UNESCO Representative List. Groups are classed by sotaque (matraca, zabumba, orquestra, baixada and costa-de-mão), each with its own percussion and toada style. The cards follow the matraca sotaque of São Luís island, whose hardwood matraca blocks, large fire-tuned pandeirões and tambor-onça friction drum carry the toadas: palitos stand in for the matracas, a source-unspecified pandero for the pandeirões and a source-unspecified shaker for the amo's maracá.
items.description: Toadas led by a solo singer and answered by the whole troupe ride over a dense clatter of hardwood blocks and booming large frame drums, in a steady, swaying festival pulse.
exemplars: Boi de Maracanã recordings (sotaque de matraca)
Missão de Pesquisas Folclóricas (1938) São Luís recordings

items.name: Tambor de crioula (Maranhão punga drum dance)
items.lineage: Afro-Maranhense drum dance of São Luís and the Maranhão interior, danced by women in a circle with the punga belly-bump and often offered in devotion to São Benedito; IPHAN has registered it as Brazilian cultural heritage. Men play three hollow-log drums tuned at the fire (tambor grande, meião and crivador) while matracas beat on the wooden body of the tambor grande, and a soloist improvises toadas answered by the group. A generic membrane-drum card stands in for the three drums and palitos for the matracas.
items.description: Three hand-beaten log drums lock into a rolling, insistent groove under the dry tick of sticks on the drum's wooden shell, while an improvised solo verse alternates with the group's sung reply.
exemplars: Tambor de Crioula de Mestre Felipe recordings
Missão de Pesquisas Folclóricas (1938) São Luís recordings

items.name: Tambor de Mina (Maranhão Jeje-Nagô liturgy)
items.lineage: Afro-Brazilian religion of São Luís, Maranhão, centred on the Casa das Minas, founded in the nineteenth century by Dahomean (Jeje) women and devoted to voduns, and on the Casa de Nagô, with many later houses across Maranhão and Pará. Initiated women sing and dance to songs in Jeje- and Nagô-derived liturgical languages, accompanied by drums, an iron bell (ferro or gã) and gourd rattles (cabaças). A generic membrane-drum card stands in for the drums, the source-unspecified agogô for the iron and xequerê for the cabaças.
items.description: Women's voices answer a lead singer in short, repeated liturgical phrases over interlocking drums, a ringing iron bell pattern and shaken gourd rattles, in long cyclic songs that carry the dance.
exemplars: Missão de Pesquisas Folclóricas (1938) Tambor de Mina recordings, São Luís (Terreiro Fé em Deus)
Sérgio Ferretti field documentation of the Casa das Minas

items.name: Xangô de Pernambuco (Recife Nagô orisha liturgy)
items.lineage: Afro-Brazilian orisha religion of Recife and neighbouring Northeastern states, called Xangô after the thunder orisha and centred on Nagô houses such as the Sítio de Pai Adão (Ilê Obá Ogunté). Songs for the orishas in a Yoruba-derived liturgical language are led by a soloist and answered by the initiates over a set of ilú drums with an iron bell and a beaded gourd rattle. A generic membrane-drum card stands in for the ilú drums and the source-unspecified agogô for the bell.
items.description: A lead voice raises short modal songs that the congregation answers in unison over a driving set of hand drums, a cutting iron bell timeline and beaded gourd rattles.
exemplars: Missão de Pesquisas Folclóricas (1938) Recife xangô recordings

items.name: Jurema sagrada (catimbó toantes)
items.lineage: Ritual complex of the Northeastern Brazilian coast, strongest in Paraíba and Pernambuco, that joins Indigenous use of the jurema plant drink with Catholic and Afro-Brazilian elements; spirits of mestres and caboclos are called down with sung toantes. In catimbó sessions the singer keeps the pulse on a maracá rattle, and in Recife terreiros the toantes are also drummed. Maracas stand in for the maracá and a generic membrane-drum card for the terreiro drums.
items.description: Short strophic toantes sung by a leader and taken up by the room, paced by the steady shake of a rattle and, in terreiro sessions, a light drum pulse.
exemplars: Missão de Pesquisas Folclóricas (1938) catimbó recordings, Paraíba
Terreiro field recordings of jurema toantes

items.name: Batuque (Rio Grande do Sul orisha religion)
items.lineage: Afro-Brazilian orisha religion of Porto Alegre and Rio Grande do Sul, organised in nations (nações) such as Oyó, Ijexá, Jeje, Cabinda and Nagô, and carried from there into Uruguay and Argentina. Songs to the orishas in a Yoruba-derived language are led by the drummer-singer (alabê) and answered by the initiates, accompanied by a drum (tambor) and the agê, a gourd rattle netted with beads. A generic membrane-drum card stands in for the tambor and xequerê for the agê.
items.description: A drummer-singer leads repeated liturgical songs answered by the initiates, over a single resonant hand drum and the swishing pulse of a beaded gourd.
exemplars: Norton F. Corrêa's ethnographic documentation of Porto Alegre batuque
Porto Alegre terreiro recordings of tambor-and-agê liturgy

items.name: Caboclinho (Pernambuco carnival caboclo groups)
items.lineage: Carnival tradition of Recife and the Pernambuco Zona da Mata in which groups costumed as Indigenous warriors dance in rows to a small terno; IPHAN has registered it as Brazilian cultural heritage. The terno combines a small cane pipe (gaita), a shaker (caracaxá) and a bass drum, while the dancers click wooden bow-and-arrow preacás in rhythm. The credited bamboo-flute card stands in for the gaita, the surdo for the bass drum, a source-unspecified shaker for the caracaxá and palitos for the preacás.
items.description: A shrill cane pipe spins short repeated melodic figures over a fast, driving bass drum and shaker, punctuated by the sharp wooden clicks of the dancers' bows.
exemplars: Missão de Pesquisas Folclóricas (1938) cabocolinhos recordings

items.name: Ciranda (Pernambuco coastal circle dance)
items.lineage: Circle song-dance of the Pernambuco coast and Zona da Mata Norte, especially Itamaracá island, in which dancers hold hands in a ring and step to the strong beat of the bass drum. A mestre cirandeiro sings the verses and the ring answers with the refrain, accompanied by bass drum (bombo or zabumba), snare drum (caixa), ganzá and maracá. A generic membrane-drum card stands in for the bass drum and a source-unspecified shaker for the ganzá.
items.description: An unhurried, swaying beat with the bass drum landing on each step carries a solo singer's verses and the ring's sung refrain, with snare and shakers filling the gaps.
exemplars: Lia de Itamaracá, A Rainha da Ciranda (1977)

items.name: Cavalo-marinho (Pernambuco Zona da Mata folk drama)
items.lineage: Night-long folk drama of the sugar-cane Zona da Mata Norte of Pernambuco and neighbouring Paraíba, performed in the Christmas-to-Epiphany cycle, in which dozens of costumed figures, among them the Capitão, Mateus, Bastião and Catirina, play scenes between dances and sung loas; IPHAN has registered it as Brazilian cultural heritage. The music comes from the banco, a bench of musicians playing rabeca, pandeiro, bage (scraped bamboo) and mineiro (metal shaker), who also sing the toadas. The fiddle card stands in for the rabeca, a source-unspecified pandero for the pandeiro, the reco-reco for the bage and a source-unspecified shaker for the mineiro.
items.description: A raw, nasal fiddle saws out short repeating dance tunes over tambourine, bamboo scraper and metal shaker, alternating with sung verses and spoken scenes through the night.
exemplars: Mestre Salustiano rabeca and cavalo-marinho recordings
Cavalo Marinho Estrela de Ouro (Condado) recordings

items.name: Banda de pífanos (Northeastern cane-fife band)
items.lineage: Instrumental band tradition of the Northeastern agreste and sertão, also called zabumba or terno de pífanos, playing for saints' novenas, processions and festas: two cane fifes (pífanos) carry the tune in parallel over zabumba, snare drum and cymbals. The best-known group, the Banda de Pífanos de Caruaru of the Biano family, has made a long series of commercial records. The credited bamboo-flute card stands in for the cane pífano and a generic membrane-drum card for the zabumba bass drum.
items.description: Two shrill, breathy cane fifes play the melody in parallel over a thumping bass drum, crisp snare and cymbal crashes, in marches, baiões and processional tunes.
exemplars: Banda de Pífanos de Caruaru LPs (1970s onward)

items.name: Música armorial (Pernambuco Armorial Movement chamber music)
items.lineage: Art-music current of the Armorial Movement launched by Ariano Suassuna in Recife in 1970, which sought an erudite Brazilian music built on the rabeca, viola, pífano and the modal melodies of Northeastern folk and cordel traditions. Its ensembles included the Orquestra Armorial de Câmara and the Quinteto Armorial; the quintet, formed in the early 1970s and recorded on Discos Marcus Pereira, joined rabeca or violin, viola sertaneja, violão and flute or pífano. The fiddle card stands in for the rabeca, the viola caipira for the viola sertaneja and the credited bamboo-flute card for the pífano.
items.description: Composed chamber pieces in which a nasal fiddle and cane fife trade modal melodies over the bright doubled courses of the viola and a classical guitar, with folk dance rhythms set in a concert texture.
exemplars: Quinteto Armorial, Do Romance ao Galope Nordestino (Discos Marcus Pereira, 1974)

items.name: Reisado and guerreiro (Northeastern Epiphany folguedo)
