items.lineage: Epiphany-cycle folk drama of the Brazilian Northeast in which a troupe led by a mestre and contramestre, with kings, a queen, Mateus clowns and sword-bearing figures, dances and sings embassies and short scenes from Christmas to the Dia de Reis; the reisados of the Cariri region of Ceará around Juazeiro do Norte are among the best known. The guerreiro of Alagoas grew out of the reisado in the twentieth century, its dancers wearing tall mirrored headdresses. The accompaniment is a small band of accordion or fifes with zabumba and other percussion; a generic membrane-drum card stands in for the zabumba.
items.description: A mestre's sung commands and verses are answered by the troupe over an accordion and a pounding bass drum, alternating march-like entrances, sword dances and sung scenes.
exemplars: Field recordings of Cariri reisado troupes, Juazeiro do Norte
Field recordings of Alagoas guerreiro troupes

items.name: Pastoril (Northeastern nativity folguedo)
items.lineage: Christmas folk play of Pernambuco and Alagoas descended from Iberian nativity pastorals, in which girls and young women (pastoras) in two rival cordões, the blue and the red, with the Diana between them, sing and dance jornadas before the Nativity scene while the audience cheers its side. The pastoril profano of Recife added a ribald old clown, the Velho, whose jokes and songs alternate with the jornadas. The pastoras keep time on small tambourines (pandeirinhos), for which a source-unspecified pandero card stands in.
items.description: Bright songs sung in chorus by young women, shaken tambourine jingles marking the beat, interrupted by a comic singer's spoken patter and bawdy verses.
exemplars: Field recordings of pastoril jornadas from Pernambuco and Alagoas

items.name: Chegança (Northeastern nautical folk drama)
items.lineage: Sailors' folk drama of the Northeastern coast, strongest in Sergipe around Laranjeiras and also found in Alagoas and Bahia, in which a troupe in naval uniforms (marujos) re-enacts a voyage and a sea battle between Christians and Moors in sung scenes while playing tambourines. Related nautical plays called barca, fandango or marujada stage the ballad of the Nau Catarineta, a ship adrift at sea. A source-unspecified pandero card stands in for the marujos' tambourines.
items.description: A men's chorus sings strophic narrative songs in a marching gait, the tambourines' jingles and skin strokes driving each scene of the voyage and battle.
exemplars: Missão de Pesquisas Folclóricas (1938) barca recordings
Field recordings of Sergipe chegança troupes

items.name: Benditos and incelências (Cariri penitent and wake songs)
items.lineage: Folk-Catholic devotional singing of the Northeastern sertão, especially the Cariri region of Ceará. Benditos are strophic hymns sung by pilgrims and by the penitent brotherhoods of Barbalha, who sing them at night during Lent, and incelências are counted wake songs that women sing over the dead, verse after verse until the burial. Both are unaccompanied, led by a principal singer with the group answering or joining in.
items.description: Slow, unaccompanied strophic hymns and counted wake verses in plain folk voices, a leader's line answered by the group in loose unison.
exemplars: Field recordings of the Barbalha penitent brotherhoods

items.name: Maculelê (Santo Amaro stick dance)
items.lineage: Afro-Brazilian stick-fighting dance of Santo Amaro da Purificação in the Bahian Recôncavo, revived in the mid-twentieth century by Paulino Aluísio de Andrade (Popó do Maculelê) and since spread across Brazil through capoeira groups. Dancers in a ring strike pairs of wooden sticks (grimas) against their own and their partners' on the accented beats, to songs led by a soloist and answered in chorus over atabaques and agogô. Palitos stand in for the grimas and the source-unspecified agogô for the bell.
items.description: Hard, accented clashes of wooden sticks land on the beat over pounding hand drums and a double-bell timeline, while a lead singer's verses are answered by the ring.
exemplars: Recordings of Santo Amaro maculelê groups in the Popó do Maculelê lineage

items.name: Toré (Northeastern Brazilian Indigenous ritual dance)
items.lineage: Circle dance-song of Indigenous peoples of the Brazilian Northeast, among them the Kariri-Xocó, Fulni-ô, Pankararu, Xukuru and Potiguara, performed as ritual and as a public affirmation of Indigenous identity. Dancers move in a ring stamping the beat while singing toantes led by a singer and paced by maracá rattles; the Pankararu add masked praiá dancers. Maracas stand in for the maracá.
items.description: Repeated chanted toantes from a leader and a circle of dancers over the steady shake of rattles and the dull thud of feet stamping on earth.

items.name: Boi-bumbá de Parintins (Amazonas toada de boi)
items.lineage: Amazonian ox-drama festival of Parintins, Amazonas, held each June in the Bumbódromo as a contest between the boi Garantido (red) and the boi Caprichoso (blue), grown from a local folguedo into a large staged spectacle with an annual album industry. Its song form, the toada de boi, is sung by a lead singer (levantador de toadas) over a massed percussion section of drums, snares and rattles, called the batucada for Garantido and the marujada for Caprichoso, with keyboards and bass added in recording; a source-unspecified shaker card stands in for the rattles.
items.description: Anthemic sung toadas over a thundering massed drum section and rolling snares, filled out with keyboard pads and electric bass and answered by huge crowd choruses.

items.name: Marabaixo (Amapá Afro-Brazilian drum dance)
items.lineage: Afro-Brazilian song-dance of Macapá and black communities of Amapá such as Curiaú, performed in the Marabaixo cycle of Catholic feasts after Easter for the Holy Spirit and the Holy Trinity; IPHAN has registered it as Brazilian cultural heritage. Drummers beat caixa drums with sticks while singers raise ladrões, verses that comment on local life, answered by a circle of women dancers in long skirts. A generic membrane-drum card stands in for the caixas.
items.description: Stick-beaten drums keep a slow, swaying pulse under ladrão verses from a lead singer, answered by a chorus of women as the circle turns.
exemplars: Community caixa recordings of Macapá marabaixo groups (Curiaú, Laguinho)

items.name: Cururu and siriri (Cuiabá viola-de-cocho song-dance)
items.lineage: Song-dance traditions of the riverside communities of the Baixada Cuiabana in Mato Grosso, both played on the viola de cocho, a short lute carved from a single log, whose craft IPHAN has registered as Brazilian intangible heritage. Cururu is a men's circle of sung verses for saints' feasts, accompanied by viola de cocho and ganzá, here a notched bamboo scraper; siriri is a festive couple and line dance that adds the mocho, a leather-covered wooden stool struck as a drum. The reco-reco card stands in for the ganzá scraper and a generic membrane-drum card for the mocho.
items.description: Strummed viola de cocho chords drive a steady, bouncing pulse while voices sing short verses in a group, the dry rasp of the bamboo scraper and the thud of the struck stool marking the dance steps.
exemplars: IPHAN documentation of the viola-de-cocho craft (registered 2005)

items.name: Folia de Reis (Brazilian Epiphany house-visiting devotion)
items.lineage: Catholic devotional practice of the Brazilian Southeast and Centre-West in which a company (terno or companhia) of foliões, led by a mestre and carrying a saint's banner, travels from house to house between Christmas and 6 January re-enacting the Magi's journey, singing verses that ask for and give thanks for offerings, with masked clowns dancing between songs. The mestre's verse is answered by the company in layered voices that close on a high, sustained voice. Ensembles combine viola caipira, violão, accordion and often rabeca, with caixa drum and pandeiro; the folias do Divino of Goiás and São Paulo follow a similar company form. The fiddle card stands in for the rabeca, a generic membrane-drum card for the caixa and a generic pandero card for the pandeiro.
items.description: A lead singer's verse is taken up by a group of voices entering one after another and stacking into close harmony that ends on a piercing high held note, over strummed viola and guitar, accordion, a scraping fiddle line and a steady drum and tambourine pulse.
exemplars: Museu de Folclore Edison Carneiro field recordings of folia de reis

items.name: Caixeiras do Divino (Maranhão Holy Spirit festival drum-song)
items.lineage: Music of the Festa do Divino Espírito Santo in Maranhão, especially São Luís and Alcântara, where groups of women drummer-singers called caixeiras, led by a caixeira-mor, play caixas and sing the devotional verses that accompany each stage of the festival, from the raising of the mast to the procession and crowning of the child emperor. Many of these festas are held in the terreiros of tambor de mina. Elsewhere in Brazil the same festival, registered by IPHAN as heritage at Pirenópolis in Goiás, is served instead by viola-led folias do Divino. A generic membrane-drum card stands in for the caixa.
items.description: Women's voices sing devotional verses led by one singer and answered by the group, over a dense, rolling pattern of stick-beaten double-headed drums that carries the procession forward.
exemplars: Field recordings of caixeiras do Divino in São Luís and Alcântara

items.name: Congado mineiro (Reinado do Rosário guards)
items.lineage: Afro-Brazilian Catholic devotion to Nossa Senhora do Rosário, São Benedito and Santa Efigênia, kept by brotherhoods and black communities across Minas Gerais, in which guards (guardas) of Congo, Moçambique, Catopé, Marujo and Candombe escort crowned kings and queens of Congo in the Reinado festival. Moçambique guards sing slow call-and-response cantos to caixas, ankle rattles (gungas) and the patangome shaker; Congo guards move faster with caixas, pandeiros and reco-reco; the Candombe, held to be the oldest, plays three sacred drums. A generic membrane-drum card stands in for the caixas, a generic shaker card for gungas and patangome, and a frame-drum card for the pandeiros.
items.description: A captain's sung line is answered by the whole guard over interlocking drum patterns and the metallic swish of ankle rattles and shakers, the pulse steady enough to walk or dance to in procession.
exemplars: Glaura Lucas — Os sons do Rosário (study of the congado of the Arturos and Jatobá)

items.name: Batuque de umbigada (tambu of the São Paulo Médio Tietê)
items.lineage: Afro-Brazilian dance of the Médio Tietê region of São Paulo state, kept by black communities of Tietê, Piracicaba and Capivari descended from the enslaved workers of the region's sugar and coffee plantations; it is danced at feasts such as 13 May in Piracicaba, Holy Saturday in Capivari and the feast of São Benedito in Tietê. Dancers form facing rows and meet in the umbigada, the touching of navels, to the tambu, a large hollowed-log drum played astride, the smaller quinjengue, the matraca (sticks beaten on the tambu's body) and guaiá rattles, under modas sung by a leader and answered by the circle. A generic membrane-drum card stands in for the tambu, a hand-drum card for the quinjengue and a shaker card for the guaiá.
items.description: A deep, booming log drum and a higher answering drum lock into a cyclic groove, with sticks clacking on the drum's wooden body and rattles shaking, while a leader's sung verses are answered by the dancers.
exemplars: Community field recordings of the tambu, quinjengue and matraca ensembles of Tietê, Capivari and Piracicaba

items.name: Samba de bumbo (rural samba of São Paulo)
items.lineage: Rural samba of the São Paulo interior described by Mário de Andrade in his study O samba rural paulista, closely tied to the August pilgrimage festival of Bom Jesus at Pirapora do Bom Jesus, where black sambadores from across the state gathered; groups continue in Pirapora and Santana de Parnaíba, and a related samba campineiro belongs to Campinas. A large bumbo bass drum leads the samba, joined by caixa and chocalhos, while a leader raises short sung verses that the group repeats as the dancers follow the drum. A generic membrane-drum card stands in for the bumbo and a generic shaker card for the chocalhos.
items.description: The heavy bass drum sets a lurching, syncopated pulse under crisp snare strokes and metal shakers, while a leader's short verse is echoed again and again by the chorus.
exemplars: Mário de Andrade — O samba rural paulista (1937)
Field recordings of the sambadores of Pirapora do Bom Jesus and Santana de Parnaíba

items.name: Fandango caiçara (Paraná and São Paulo coast)
items.lineage: Dance-music of the caiçara fishing and farming communities of the coast of Paraná and southern São Paulo, from Paranaguá and Guaraqueçaba to Cananéia and Iguape, traditionally played at night-long bailes after collective work and registered by IPHAN as Brazilian intangible heritage. Its dances divide into batidos, stamped by men in wooden clogs, and bailados, danced in couples. Two singers in thirds are accompanied by locally built violas and a rabeca, with the adufo frame drum. The viola caipira card stands in for the viola fandangueira, the fiddle card for the rabeca and a frame-drum card for the adufo.
items.description: Two voices sing in parallel thirds over strummed violas and a reedy fiddle line, with a frame drum and, in the stamped dances, the clatter of wooden clogs on floorboards driving the rhythm.

items.name: Vissungo (Minas Gerais mining work songs)
items.lineage: Work songs in a Bantu-derived language sung by enslaved Africans and their descendants in the diamond and gold diggings around Diamantina, also sung while carrying the dead to burial. The folklorist Aires da Mata Machado Filho collected them at São João da Chapada and published them in O negro e o garimpo em Minas Gerais (1943). A leader opens each song solo and the work gang answers; a few elders still knew them late in the twentieth century.
items.description: Unaccompanied, a leader's free-flowing solo line is answered by a group refrain of men's voices, the songs short and repeated, by turns grave and lamenting.
exemplars: O Canto dos Escravos LP (1982) — Clementina de Jesus, Doca da Portela, Geraldo Filme
Aires da Mata Machado Filho — O negro e o garimpo em Minas Gerais (1943)

items.name: Vanguarda Paulista (Lira Paulistana scene)
items.lineage: Independent São Paulo song movement of about 1979-1985 centred on the Lira Paulistana theatre in Pinheiros and its label, with artists such as Arrigo Barnabé, Itamar Assumpção, Grupo Rumo, Premeditando o Breque and Língua de Trapo. Arrigo Barnabé brought atonal and serial writing into comic-strip song narratives for a horn-and-keyboard rock band, Itamar Assumpção built songs on interlocking bass and guitar riffs with funk and reggae, and Rumo developed a speech-melody style of singing.
items.description: Angular, irregularly phrased songs in which a half-spoken lead voice and answering backing singers ride repeated electric bass and guitar riffs, with dissonant saxophone and piano lines cutting across the beat.

items.name: Marchinha (Rio carnival march-song)
items.lineage: Brisk carnival march-song of Rio de Janeiro, conventionally traced to Chiquinha Gonzaga's Ó Abre Alas (1899), that dominated the carnival hits issued on 78 rpm records through the 1930s, 1940s and 1950s, the decades when composers such as Lamartine Babo and Braguinha wrote new marchinhas for each season. Records paired a singer and chorus with a studio orchestra of trumpets, trombones and reeds over samba percussion, and the songs remain the repertoire of street carnival bands.
items.description: A quick two-beat march in which a solo singer and a unison chorus trade a short, catchy, often comic refrain over punchy trumpet and trombone figures, clarinet runs and a bouncing bass drum and tambourine pulse.
exemplars: Mamãe Eu Quero (Jararaca and Vicente Paiva, 1937)
Odeon and Victor carnival 78s of the 1930s

items.name: Maxixe (tango brasileiro)
items.lineage: Urban dance of Rio de Janeiro that took shape in the late nineteenth century from the polka, habanera and lundu, notorious for its close, swaying couple steps, and published by composers such as Ernesto Nazareth and Chiquinha Gonzaga under the respectable label tango brasileiro. From 1902 Casa Edison recorded maxixes by military and fire-brigade bands and by flute-led groups of cavaquinho and guitars, and the dance became an international ballroom craze in Paris and New York in the 1910s.
items.description: A lively 2/4 dance tune with a syncopated, habanera-like lilt: flute and clarinet trade ornamented melodies over chopped cavaquinho chords, guitar runs and a low ophicleide bass line.
exemplars: Ernesto Nazareth and Chiquinha Gonzaga tango brasileiro repertoire

items.name: Modinha (Luso-Brazilian sentimental song)
items.lineage: Lyrical, sentimental song in Portuguese that the Rio-born poet-singer Domingos Caldas Barbosa made fashionable in Lisbon in the late eighteenth century, singing to the viola. Through the nineteenth century it became a salon song with piano at the imperial court of Rio de Janeiro and then a street serenade song with violão, and in the early twentieth century singers such as Eduardo das Neves and Mário Pinheiro recorded modinhas for Casa Edison.
items.description: A slow, tender melody, often in a minor key, sung with expressive rubato and vibrato by a solo voice over arpeggiated guitar or gentle piano accompaniment.
exemplars: Casa Edison 78 rpm modinha recordings (Eduardo das Neves, Mário Pinheiro)

items.name: Lundu (Afro-Brazilian dance-song)
items.lineage: Afro-Brazilian couple dance of colonial Brazil, described from the eighteenth century with hand-clapping and the umbigada, that became in the nineteenth century a comic, syncopated song genre of salons and theatres, the lundu-canção, sung alongside the modinha. Xisto Bahia's Isto é bom, sung by Baiano for Casa Edison in 1902, is usually cited as the first Brazilian commercial record. The lundu dance survives on the island of Marajó in Pará.
items.description: A bouncy, syncopated two-beat song in which a solo voice delivers teasing, humorous verses in a half-spoken manner over a rhythmic strummed guitar.
exemplars: Isto é bom (Xisto Bahia), sung by Baiano, Casa Edison 1902

items.name: Música colonial mineira (Minas Gerais colonial sacred music)
items.lineage: Sacred music written for the churches and lay brotherhoods of the eighteenth-century gold-mining towns of Minas Gerais, among them Vila Rica (Ouro Preto), Arraial do Tejuco (Diamantina) and São João del-Rei, largely by mulatto professional musicians such as José Joaquim Emerico Lobo de Mesquita, organist at Arraial do Tejuco in the 1780s, and Marcos Coelho Neto, in a style close to the early Classical, for choir with strings, horns and basso continuo. The musicologist Francisco Curt Lange rediscovered the manuscripts in the mid-twentieth century, and the orchestras Lira Sanjoanense and Ribeiro Bastos of São João del-Rei, which trace their origins to the eighteenth century, still perform this repertoire in the liturgy.
items.description: Mostly homophonic four-part choral writing with short solo passages, carried by violins over a continuo bass line on cello and double bass, with sustained horn chords colouring the cadences in a resonant church acoustic.
exemplars: Recordings of works by Lobo de Mesquita and Marcos Coelho Neto
Liturgical performances of the Lira Sanjoanense and Ribeiro Bastos orchestras (São João del-Rei)

items.name: Filarmônica and dobrado (Brazilian civic wind band)
items.lineage: Amateur civic wind bands, the sociedades filarmônicas, liras and corporações musicais, founded across Brazil from the nineteenth century and especially dense in the Recôncavo Baiano and Minas Gerais, where they play for religious processions, civic holidays, bandstand concerts and funerals and have trained generations of professional musicians. Their emblematic repertoire is the dobrado, a Brazilian quick march, alongside hymns, waltzes and arrangements. The sousaphone card stands in for the tuba and the snare-drum card for the caixa.
items.description: Clarinets carry the melody over brass countermelodies and a full low-brass bass line in a brisk march, with snare rolls and bass-drum strokes keeping strict marching time in an open-air acoustic.
exemplars: Filarmônicas of Cachoeira in the Recôncavo Baiano, such as the Lira Ceciliana and the Minerva Cachoeirana

items.name: Nativismo gaúcho (Califórnia da Canção Nativa song)
items.lineage: Festival-born song movement of Rio Grande do Sul launched by the Califórnia da Canção Nativa festival at Uruguaiana and followed by many regional nativist festivals, which renewed gaúcho song with literary lyrics about the pampa, the Missões and rural life, apart from the CTG traditionalist movement. Singers such as Noel Guarany and Cenair Maicá set these songs mostly to violão and accordion in milonga and other border rhythms.
items.description: A declamatory, poetic lead voice over fingerpicked and strummed nylon-string guitar in a loping milonga rhythm, with the accordion answering phrases and filling the interludes.
exemplars: Califórnia da Canção Nativa festival LPs (from 1971)

items.name: Santo Daime hinários (Acre ayahuasca hymnody)
items.lineage: Hymn repertoire of the Santo Daime religion, founded in Rio Branco, Acre, by Raimundo Irineu Serra (Mestre Irineu), whose hinário O Cruzeiro is its foundational hymnal. In rituals called trabalhos participants drink the daime brew and sing whole hinários in unison for hours, standing in formation and dancing a simple bailado in march, waltz and mazurka rhythms while shaking maracás; guitars and other instruments often accompany. The hinários of Padrinho Sebastião spread the church across Brazil and abroad.
items.description: Simple strophic hymns sung in unison by a large congregation of men and women, repeated many times, with massed rattles marking every beat of a march, waltz or mazurka and a strummed guitar underneath.
exemplars: Recorded hinários issued by Daime churches (O Cruzeiro of Mestre Irineu, Padrinho Sebastião)

items.name: Upper Xingu ritual and sacred-flute music (Kamayurá, Kuikuro, Wauja)
items.lineage: Ceremonial music shared by the many peoples of the Upper Xingu in the Parque Indígena do Xingu, among them the Kamayurá, Kuikuro, Kalapalo, Wauja and Yawalapiti, whose intertribal rites include the Kuarup mourning feast for dead chiefs. Sets of large sacred flutes, jakuí among the Kamayurá and kagutu among the Kuikuro, are played by men and kept from women's sight, pairs of long uruá flutes accompany dancing, and men sing in groups with maracá rattles. Rafael José de Menezes Bastos described Kamayurá musical thought in his book A musicológica Kamayurá. A generic flute card stands in for these flutes.
items.description: Low, breathy flutes play short interlocking motifs in long cyclic sequences, alternating with men's group singing over gourd rattles and the stamp of dancing feet on bare earth.
exemplars: Rafael José de Menezes Bastos — A musicológica Kamayurá (1978)

items.name: Kisêdjê (Suyá) akia and ngere song
items.lineage: Vocal music of the Gê-speaking Kisêdjê (Suyá) of the Xingu basin in Mato Grosso, studied by the ethnomusicologist Anthony Seeger in his book Why Suyá Sing. In the akia, men each shout-sing their own individual high song at the same time, songs meant to be heard by their sisters, while the ngere are songs the men sing together in unison, often with rattles, in ceremonies such as the Mouse ceremony that Seeger documented. The maracas card stands in for the gourd rattles.
items.description: Many men's voices shout-sing different high, tense melodies at once in a dense overlapping texture, alternating with unison group songs over shaken gourd rattles.
exemplars: Anthony Seeger — Why Suyá Sing (1987, with recordings)

items.name: A'uwẽ (Xavante) da-ño're and ceremonial song
items.lineage: Collective ceremonial song of the Gê-speaking A'uwẽ (Xavante) of eastern Mato Grosso, sung above all by groups of men within the age-set system whose initiation cycle (danhono) moves boys into adulthood. The da-ño're are collective songs that the Xavante describe as coming to young men in dreams; the dreamer teaches the song to his age-set, who sing and dance it together, a practice the anthropologist Laura R. Graham analysed in her book Performing Dreams. The Pimentel Barbosa (Etenhiritipá) community released its own recordings as the CD Etenhiritipá: Cantos da Tradição Xavante.
items.description: A body of men's voices sings short, strongly pulsed phrases together, repeating them many times while the dancers' feet mark the beat on bare earth.
exemplars: Etenhiritipá: Cantos da Tradição Xavante (1994, Pimentel Barbosa community)

items.name: Mebêngôkre (Kayapó) ceremonial song
items.lineage: Ceremonial song of the Gê-speaking Mebêngôkre (Kayapó) of southern Pará and northern Mato Grosso, whose great naming ceremonies, among them the Bemp and Tàkàk festivals that confer ceremonial 'beautiful names' on children, are carried by days and nights of collective singing and dancing in the village plaza. Men sing together as they dance, keeping time with gourd rattles. Ethnographers have recorded these ceremonies, and Mebêngôkre communities also record their own.
items.description: A men's chorus sings strong, repeated unison phrases over the steady shake of gourd rattles and the tread of dancing feet, cycling through long ceremonial nights.
exemplars: Ethnographic field recordings of Mebêngôkre naming ceremonies
Mebêngôkre community recordings of naming ceremonies

items.name: Boe (Bororo) funeral and ritual song
items.lineage: Ritual song of the Boe (Bororo) of central Mato Grosso, whose funeral cycle runs for weeks or months after a death, with nightly singing in the village plaza and men's house led by ritual song specialists. Groups of men answer a leading singer while shaking large gourd rattles (bapo), and in the funeral rites whirled bull-roarers give voice to the aije spirits. The Salesian missionaries César Albisetti and Ângelo Jayme Venturelli documented songs and rites in the Enciclopédia Bororo, and ethnographers have since recorded the funeral song cycles.
items.description: A leading voice is answered by a group of men in long, chanted phrases over the dry swish of large gourd rattles, while the low roar of whirled bull-roarers rises and falls in the background.
exemplars: Enciclopédia Bororo (Albisetti and Venturelli, Salesian documentation)
Ethnographic recordings of Bororo funeral song cycles

items.name: Yaokwa (Enawenê-Nawê ritual cycle)
items.lineage: The Yaokwa is the longest ritual of the Arawak-speaking Enawenê-Nawê of north-western Mato Grosso, held through the dry season over about seven months, when the clans take turns fishing at collective weirs and offering food to the yakairiti spirits so that cosmic and social order is maintained. Through the cycle the men play flutes, sing and dance together, a repertoire bound to the community's knowledge of fishing, food and the forest. IPHAN registered the ritual as Brazilian cultural heritage and UNESCO inscribed it on the List of Intangible Cultural Heritage in Need of Urgent Safeguarding. A generic flute card stands in for the Enawenê-Nawê flutes.
items.description: Breathy flutes repeat short motifs in long cycles, alternating and overlapping with men's group singing and the steady stamp of a line of dancers.
exemplars: UNESCO Urgent Safeguarding List documentation of the Yaokwa ritual (2011)
IPHAN registration dossier and documentary recordings (2010)

items.name: Yanomami shamanic chant and reahu feast song
items.lineage: Vocal practices of the Yanomami of the Brazil–Venezuela borderlands in Roraima and Amazonas. Shamans inhale yãkoana snuff and chant to call down and voice the xapiri spirits, and at the reahu, the intercommunity funerary feast, hosts and guests sing at night in the village plaza and men exchange wayamou, a chanted ceremonial dialogue. Davi Kopenawa described the xapiri and their songs in The Falling Sky, written with Bruce Albert, and ethnographers have recorded shamanic and feast singing on both sides of the border.
items.description: A shaman's solo chant moves in repeated, swooping phrases between song and speech, and at feasts voices sing and trade rhythmic, half-chanted lines through the night.
exemplars: Ethnographic field recordings of Yanomami shamanic and reahu singing (Brazil and Venezuela)

items.name: Huni meka (Huni Kuin nixi pae chants)
items.lineage: Ceremonial songs of the Pano-speaking Huni Kuin (Kaxinawá) of the Jordão and Tarauacá rivers in Acre, sung through the night of the nixi pae (ayahuasca) ceremony to call, guide and close the visions. Song masters (txana) hold the repertoire; the txana Ibã Huni Kuin has researched and transcribed the huni meka with his community, publishing them with translations in the songbook Nixi Pae: O Espírito da Floresta, and the MAHKU artists' collective (Movimento dos Artistas Huni Kuin) he co-founded paints the songs.
items.description: Voices sing long strophic chants together in a soft, steady flow, each melody returning many times with gently ornamented phrase endings.
exemplars: Ibã Huni Kuin (txana) — huni meka transcribed in Nixi Pae: O Espírito da Floresta
MAHKU (Movimento dos Artistas Huni Kuin) huni meka singing

items.name: Upper Rio Negro ritual music (Tukano, Desana, Baniwa)
items.lineage: Ritual music of the Tukanoan peoples, among them the Tukano and Desana, and their Arawak-speaking Baniwa neighbours on the upper Rio Negro and Vaupés on the Brazil–Colombia border. Sacred Jurupari flutes, played in pairs by initiated men and kept from women's sight, sound in initiation rites, while the dabucuri exchange feasts between groups bring dances with cariçu panpipes, sung chants and rattles. Acácio Tadeu de Camargo Piedade studied Tukano (Ye'pâ-masa) music, and Brazilian and Colombian field recordings document the repertoire. A generic flute card stands in for both the sacred flutes and the cariçu panpipes.
items.description: Paired flutes answer each other in deep, breathy interlocking calls, and panpipe dancers repeat short, rocking figures over rattles and stamping feet, with sung chants between the dances.
exemplars: Acácio Tadeu de Camargo Piedade's study of Tukano (Ye'pâ-masa) music
Brazil–Colombia field recordings of Upper Rio Negro dabucuri and Jurupari rites

items.name: Malambo (Argentine gaucho zapateo)
items.lineage: Solo men's competitive foot-tapping dance of the Argentine pampas and north-west, descended from contests of skill between gauchos, in which dancers take turns improvising and answering figures (mudanzas) of zapateo, heel, toe and sole strikes, over an unchanging accompaniment. Malambo norteño is danced in hard boots with fast, showy footwork, malambo sureño in soft boots with more restrained figures; a guitar strums a repeated chord cycle in fast 6/8 and the bombo legüero drives the pulse. The Festival Nacional de Malambo in Laborde, Córdoba, is its main competition.
items.description: A guitar strums the same fast 6/8 chord cycle over and over while the bombo pounds the pulse, and the dancer's boots rattle off rapid, accelerating volleys of heel and toe strikes.
exemplars: Festival Nacional de Malambo (Laborde) competition recordings
Folkloric malambo LPs of Argentine guitar-and-bombo ensembles

items.name: Chamarrita (Entre Ríos litoral song-dance)
items.lineage: Song-dance of the Argentine litoral centred on Entre Ríos, descended from the chamarrita of Azorean settlers in southern Brazil, which passed through Uruguay into the province. It is played on accordion with guitar and sung verses. The Entre Ríos singer-songwriter Linares Cardozo collected, studied and wrote chamarritas and promoted them as the province's own rhythm, distinct from the chamamé of Corrientes.
items.description: A diatonic accordion and strummed guitar set an easy, swaying dance lilt under a plain, unhurried voice singing verses of river and country life.
exemplars: Linares Cardozo recordings of Entre Ríos chamarritas

items.name: Chaya riojana (La Rioja carnival vidala chayera)
items.lineage: Carnival song of La Rioja province in north-western Argentina, sung at the February chaya, when people throw flour, water and basil at one another and the Pujllay, the carnival figure, is buried or burned at its close. The vidala chayera is sung by groups beating the caja, a small double-headed drum struck with a stick, often with guitar, in coplas whose lines are taken up and repeated by all; Riojan composers such as Ramón Navarro carried it onto stage and record. A generic membrane-drum card stands in for the caja.
items.description: Voices sing coplas together over the even beat of hand-held drums struck with a stick, a strummed guitar filling in as the verses repeat round and round.
exemplars: Ramón Navarro (Riojan composer and chaya singer)

items.name: Qom (Toba) song and n'vike fiddle
items.lineage: Music of the Guaycuruan-speaking Qom (Toba) of the Argentine Chaco and Formosa. The n'vike, a one-string fiddle with a tin or gourd resonator bowed with horsehair, carries the community's instrumental tunes, and singing ranges from older ceremonial songs to the hymns of the Qom evangelical churches that spread from the mid-twentieth century. The Coro Toba Chelaalapí of Resistencia sings in the Qom language and has released albums, and the Instituto Nacional de Musicología 'Carlos Vega' holds field recordings.
items.description: A thin, scratchy one-string fiddle repeats a short, nasal melody, and voices sing together in plain unison or simple harmony in the Qom language.
exemplars: Instituto Nacional de Musicología 'Carlos Vega' field recordings of Qom music

items.name: Wichí song (Gran Chaco)
items.lineage: Vocal music of the Mataguayan-speaking Wichí, formerly called Mataco, of the Gran Chaco in Salta, Formosa and Chaco provinces and across the Bolivian border. Shamans sing to heal while shaking a gourd rattle, and community songs accompany social dances and festive gatherings; the Instituto Nacional de Musicología 'Carlos Vega' and other collectors hold field recordings of Wichí communities.
items.description: A solo voice chants short, repeated melodic phrases over the steady shake of a gourd rattle, and group songs set plain, cyclic melodies for dancing.
exemplars: Instituto Nacional de Musicología 'Carlos Vega' field recordings of Wichí communities

items.name: Nacionalismo musical argentino (Argentine nationalist art music)
items.lineage: School of Argentine concert composers, from the late nineteenth to the mid-twentieth century, who built art music on criollo and gaucho folk sources: Alberto Williams, founder of the Buenos Aires Conservatory, Julián Aguirre, Carlos López Buchardo and Luis Gianneo, then Alberto Ginastera, whose ballet Estancia ends in a malambo, with Carlos Guastavino continuing the idiom in songs and piano pieces. They set the rhythms and modal turns of the malambo, gato, zamba, huella and vidala in orchestral, piano and vocal writing.
items.description: Orchestral and piano writing drives folk dance rhythms, hammered 6/8 against 3/4, through bright brass and percussion, while the songs set lyrical, guitar-like piano figures under a clear concert voice.
exemplars: Carlos Guastavino — Se equivocó la paloma

items.name: Canto a lo poeta (Chilean sung décima, a lo divino and a lo humano)
items.lineage: Sung poetry of rural central Chile in ten-line décimas, divided into canto a lo divino, religious verse sung at vigils for saints and at wakes for dead infants (velorios de angelito), and canto a lo humano, secular verse on history, love and wisdom that includes the improvised paya contest. Cantores accompany themselves on the guitarrón chileno, a 25-string guitar with coursed metal strings and short drone strings (diablitos) beside the fingerboard, or on guitar, playing repeated melodic formulas (entonaciones). Pirque, near Santiago, is a centre of guitarrón playing; the twelve-string card stands in for the guitarrón.
items.description: A solo singer delivers long décima verses over the shimmering, ringing strums and plucked drones of a many-stringed guitar, each stanza closing on the same melodic turn.
exemplars: Archivo de Música Tradicional (Universidad de Chile) field recordings

items.name: Cueca brava (Santiago urban cueca chilenera)
items.lineage: Urban cueca of the markets, slaughterhouse district and taverns of Santiago and Valparaíso, also called cueca chilenera or centrina, sung by men in a harder, faster and more ornamented style than the rural huaso cueca, to piano, guitar, accordion and pandero (tambourine) with hand claps. Los Chileneros, founded by Hernán 'Nano' Núñez, recorded the style's first LP, La cueca centrina, and Roberto Parra wrote and sang in the style; young Santiago groups such as Los Trukeros revived it around the turn of the twenty-first century in bars and fondas.
items.description: Several men's voices trade and overlap high, strained lines at a hard driving tempo, over pounding piano chords, strummed guitar, accordion, tambourine and sharp hand claps.

items.name: Bailes chinos (Chilean devotional flute brotherhoods)
items.lineage: Devotional brotherhoods of central Chile, whose members are mostly fishermen, miners and peasants, who honour the Virgin and the saints at patronal feasts by dancing while they blow large cane or wooden flutes, set out in two facing rows and jumping and crouching as they play. Each flute sounds a single harsh, beating tone (sonido rajado), the rows answer each other over a drum, and between dances the alférez sings improvised verses of praise. UNESCO inscribed the bailes chinos on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity; a generic flute card stands in for the chino flute.
items.description: Rows of flutes blare one rough, buzzing, beating tone back and forth in relentless alternation over a pounding drum, broken by a solo singer chanting verses of praise.
exemplars: UNESCO Representative List documentation of the bailes chinos (2014)
Field recordings of chino flute brotherhoods of the Valparaíso coast and Aconcagua valley

items.name: Música chilota (Chiloé archipelago dance music)
items.lineage: Dance music of the Chiloé archipelago in southern Chile, played for the vals chilote, sirilla, pericona, chocolate, trastrasera and the local cueca at mingas (communal work parties) and island fiestas. Conjuntos combine accordion, guitar, violin and the bombo, with voices singing coplas, and folklorists including Margot Loyola collected the repertoire. The fiddle card stands in for the violin and a generic membrane-drum card for the bombo.
items.description: Accordion and fiddles play lilting waltz and brisk couple-dance tunes over strummed guitar and a thudding bass drum, with voices singing short coplas between the tunes.
exemplars: Margot Loyola field collections from Chiloé
Chiloé conjunto recordings of accordion, guitar and rabel

items.name: Bailes religiosos de La Tirana (Norte Grande devotional dance bands)
items.lineage: Devotional dance music of the Fiesta de La Tirana in the Tarapacá pampa, held each July for the Virgen del Carmen and attended by hundreds of dance societies (bailes religiosos) from Iquique and the towns of the Chilean north. Each baile has its own band: brass bands of trumpets, trombones and tubas with bass drum, snare and cymbals (the sousaphone card stands in for the bass horn) play for the diabladas, morenos, who swing wooden ratchets, and other costumed dances, while lakitas play large panpipes over bass drums, and the dancers sing hymns of greeting and farewell to the Virgin.
items.description: Massed brass bands blast short repeating marches and dance tunes over thundering bass drums and snares, while panpipe groups play rough, breathy unison figures and dancers' ratchets clatter in the crowd.
exemplars: Field recordings of the La Tirana religious dance bands

items.name: Neofolklore chileno (1960s Chilean folk-pop vocal groups)
items.lineage: Commercial folk movement of mid-1960s Santiago in which vocal groups such as Los Cuatro Cuartos, Las Cuatro Brujas and Los de Ramón sang cuecas, tonadas and new songs in folk rhythms in polished close-harmony arrangements for radio, television and LP. It ran alongside, and was soon overtaken by, the nueva canción chilena.
items.description: Four or more voices sing tight, bright block harmonies over crisply strummed guitars and a light bombo, folk dance rhythms smoothed into polished, radio-ready arrangements.

items.name: Këngë kreshnikësh (Albanian lahuta frontier-warrior epic)
items.lineage: Heroic epic of the Gheg-speaking highlands of northern Albania, Kosovo and the Rugova gorge, sung by a lahutar who accompanies himself on the lahuta, a single-string bowed lute of the gusle type. Its central cycle tells of the frontier warriors (kreshnikë), above all Muji and his brother Halili. Albanian-language epic singers were recorded for the Milman Parry Collection at Harvard before the Second World War, and the repertoire was later collected by the Albanian Institute of Folk Culture. The gusle card stands in for the lahuta.
items.description: A single male voice declaims long narrative lines in a tense, high chest register, each line framed by the rasping, nasal tone of the one-string bowed lute, which shadows the vocal melody and fills the pauses between verses.
exemplars: Milman Parry Collection of Oral Literature (Harvard), Albanian-language epic recordings
Albanian Institute of Folk Culture archive recordings of lahutarë

items.name: Këngë qytetare (Albanian urban song of Shkodër and Elbasan)
items.lineage: Urban song of the old Ottoman-era towns of Albania, above all Shkodër in the north and Elbasan and Berat in the centre, sung at domestic and festive gatherings (aheng) on themes of love and town life. A solo singer is accompanied by a small saze ensemble of violin, clarinet, accordion and def frame drum, in melismatic, makam-inflected melodies; Radio Tirana recorded and broadcast the repertoire from the mid-twentieth century. The dayereh card stands in for the def (dajre) jingled frame drum.
items.description: A solo voice spins ornate, melismatic lines over violin and clarinet heterophony, soft accordion chords and the light jingle of a frame drum, moving between free-rhythm openings and steady song meters.
exemplars: RTSH (Radio Tirana) archive recordings of Shkodër urban song

items.name: Cântitsi armãneashti (Aromanian song and Farsherot polyphony)
items.lineage: Song of the Aromanians, a Romance-speaking people also called Vlachs, dispersed across Albania, Greece, North Macedonia and Bulgaria and singing in Aromanian at weddings, feasts and seasonal gatherings. The Farsherot (Fărșeroți) communities of southern and central Albania, around Korçë and the Myzeqe plain, sing multipart songs in which one or two solo voices weave over a sustained group drone, close to the iso-polyphony of their Albanian neighbours.
items.description: Two solo voices trade and overlap long ornamented phrases above a group holding a drone on a vowel, the parts rubbing in close intervals before settling back onto the drone pitch.
exemplars: Albanian Institute of Folk Culture field recordings of Aromanian (Farsherot) song

items.name: Ganga (Herzegovinian shouted group song)
items.lineage: Rural group song of Herzegovina and the neighbouring Dalmatian hinterland around Imotski, sung by Croats, Bosniaks and Serbs alike, by separate groups of men or of women. A leader sings the opening of a short verse and the others enter with the ganga, a loud, throat-shaken accompanying part (groktanje) pitched in close dissonant intervals, so that the voices fuse into one dense, beating sound. Ethnomusicologist Ankica Petrović made it the subject of extended fieldwork and her doctoral study.
items.description: A single voice launches a short line and is swamped by others singing loud, shaking, throaty tones packed into narrow seconds, a buzzing, beating chord that is held and then cut off abruptly.
exemplars: Institute of Ethnology and Folklore Research (Zagreb) archive recordings of ganga
Ankica Petrović field recordings of ganga

items.name: Ilahije and kaside (Bosniak Islamic devotional song)
items.lineage: Devotional songs of the Muslims of Bosnia and Herzegovina, sung in Bosnian and in older layers in Turkish and Arabic: the ilahija, a hymn of praise derived from the Ottoman ilahi, and the kasida, a sung religious poem. They are performed at mevlud gatherings for the Prophet's birthday, in Sufi tekke ceremonies and at religious festivals, by a soloist, in unison or by a leader answered by a group, sometimes over a frame drum, and since the late twentieth century by choirs on commercial recordings.
items.description: Voices sing strophic devotional melodies in unison or in leader-and-group alternation, steady and gently ornamented, with choir arrangements adding simple harmony.
exemplars: Radio Sarajevo / BHRT archive recordings of ilahije
VDE-Gallo recordings of Sarajevo ilahije by Nesidu-l-Huda (CNRS CREM archive)
Ilahije recordings of the Zagreb Mosque choir Arabeske

items.name: Bećarac (Slavonian couplet song)
items.lineage: Humorous, teasing couplet song of Slavonia, Baranja and Srijem in eastern Croatia, improvised at weddings, harvest work and village feasts and inscribed by UNESCO on its Representative List as bećarac singing and playing from Eastern Croatia. A leading singer calls out a two-line decasyllabic verse and the group joins on the repeat, accompanied by a tamburica band of small lead and middle lutes, chord-strumming bugarija and berde bass.
items.description: A lead singer shouts out a cheeky two-line verse and a group roars it back, carried by bright tremolo melody, offbeat strummed chords and a plucked bass in a brisk, steady two-beat pulse.
exemplars: Croatia Records tamburica albums of bećarac
Institute of Ethnology and Folklore Research (Zagreb) recordings of bećarac

items.name: Međimurska popevka (Međimurje folk song)
items.lineage: Lyric folk song of Međimurje, the northernmost region of Croatia between the Mura and Drava rivers, inscribed on the UNESCO Representative List. Popevke are sung mostly solo, by women and men, on love, work and village life, in slow, free-flowing melodies, many of them in old modal scales; they are also sung in groups or with local instrumental accompaniment.
items.description: A single voice sings a slow, unhurried strophic melody with gentle ornaments and long held tones, its modal turns and free pulse following the words.
exemplars: Institute of Ethnology and Folklore Research (Zagreb) archive recordings of Međimurje song
Croatia Records releases of međimurske popevke

items.name: Glagoljaško pjevanje (Croatian Glagolitic chant)
items.lineage: Oral tradition of liturgical singing in Old Church Slavonic within the Roman Catholic rite, kept in parishes of Istria, the Kvarner islands such as Krk, and the Dalmatian coast and islands, where the Glagolitic liturgy was permitted from the Middle Ages. Melodies were passed on by ear among priests and congregations rather than from notation and differ from parish to parish, sung in folk-style unison and multipart textures; Jerko Bezić documented its development in the Zadar area.
items.description: A priest's intoned lines are answered by a congregation or a men's group singing robust, unpolished melodies in unison and in parallel parts, with a full chest sound and a slow, word-led delivery in a resonant church.
exemplars: Institute of Ethnology and Folklore Research (Zagreb) field recordings of Glagolitic chant

items.name: Lijerica and linđo (Dubrovnik bowed-lira dance music)
items.lineage: Dance music of the Dubrovnik coast, the Konavle valley and the Pelješac peninsula, played on the lijerica, a small pear-shaped three-string bowed lira held upright on the knee, whose player keeps time by stamping his foot. Its best-known dance is the linđo, a couple dance of the poskočica type whose figures are called out in rhymed commands by a dance leader (kolovođa).
items.description: A single bowed lira plays a quick, repeating dance tune over sounding open strings, its rasping double-stops driven by a stamping foot, while a leader shouts out the dance figures.
exemplars: Croatia Records recordings of lijerica and linđo
Institute of Ethnology and Folklore Research (Zagreb) archive recordings of lijerica

items.name: Vlach music of eastern Serbia (Timok and Homolje)
items.lineage: Music of the Romanian-speaking Vlachs of north-eastern Serbia, in the Timok Krajina around Negotin and Zaječar and in Homolje and Braničevo, sung in the Vlach dialect at weddings, village dances and the rites of the life cycle. Songs and dance tunes were carried by the gajde bagpipe and the frula shepherd's flute, later joined and largely replaced by violin and accordion, and are presented at festivals such as Homoljski motivi in Kučevo.
items.description: A singer's ornamented, slightly nasal lines alternate with fast dance tunes on fiddle and accordion, while bagpipe drone and the breathy shepherd's flute carry the older layer of the repertoire.
exemplars: Institute of Musicology SASA field recordings of Vlach music from eastern Serbia

items.name: Vranjanska pesma (Vranje urban song)
items.lineage: Urban song of Vranje in southern Serbia, formed in the late Ottoman town where Serbian, Turkish and Roma musical life met, and carried into Serbian culture by Bora Stanković's play Koštana, whose songs remain part of the repertoire. A solo singer delivers melismatic love songs of longing (sevdah) to Roma ensembles of violin, clarinet, accordion and tarabuka drum; PGP-RTB recorded the style in the second half of the twentieth century. The toubeleki card stands in for the tarabuka goblet drum.
items.description: A solo voice draws out long, sobbing melismas over violin and clarinet weaving heterophonic lines, accordion chords and a crisp goblet-drum pattern, alternating slow lyrical songs with brisk dance-songs.

items.name: Čalgija (Macedonian Ottoman-urban ensemble)
items.lineage: Urban ensemble music of Ottoman-era Macedonian towns such as Skopje, Ohrid, Bitola, Veles and Štip, played by professional Christian, Muslim and Roma musicians at weddings, coffeehouses and feasts from the nineteenth century. The čalgija band combined ut (oud), kanon (kanun), violin, clarinet, tarabuka goblet drum and def frame drum, accompanying urban love songs and instrumental dance pieces in makam-derived modes; Macedonian Radio recorded čalgija ensembles in the mid-twentieth century. The toubeleki card stands in for the tarabuka and the dayereh card for the def.
items.description: Fretless lute, plucked zither, violin and clarinet weave the same ornamented modal melody in heterophony over goblet-drum and jingling frame-drum patterns, with a solo singer for the songs and free instrumental preludes between them.
exemplars: Macedonian Radio-Television (MRT) archive recordings of čalgija ensembles

items.name: Zurli i tapan (Macedonian shawm-and-drum music)
items.lineage: Outdoor music for weddings, saints' feasts and village dances across North Macedonia, Kosovo and southern Serbia, played mostly by professional Roma musicians. Zurlas, loud conical double-reed shawms, are played in pairs, one leading the ornamented melody with circular breathing while the other holds a drone, over the tapan, a large double-headed drum beaten with a heavy stick on one head and a thin switch on the other; it is the classic accompaniment of dances such as teškoto.
items.description: Two piercing shawms, one weaving a fast, heavily ornamented melody without a breath and the other holding a steady drone, ride over the booming strokes and dry switch-clicks of a big double-headed drum in driving additive dance rhythms.
exemplars: Macedonian Radio-Television (MRT) archive recordings of zurla and tapan
Jugoton releases of Macedonian zurla music

items.name: Nestinarstvo and Anastenaria (Strandzha fire-dance ritual music)
items.lineage: Ritual music of the fire-dancing rite held for Saints Constantine and Helena in the Strandzha village of Bulgari in south-eastern Bulgaria, inscribed on the UNESCO Representative List, and of its Greek counterpart, the Anastenaria of Agia Eleni and Lagadas, kept by descendants of refugees from Kosti and other Strandzha villages and studied by anthropologist Loring Danforth. Nestinari carrying icons enter a trance and dance barefoot across glowing embers to the sacred drum and the gaida bagpipe; among the Anastenarides the three-string Thracian lyra leads with the drum. The gadulka card stands in for the Thracian lyra.
items.description: A bagpipe drone and a bowed fiddle repeat a hypnotic dance melody over the insistent beat of a large double-headed drum, the cycle building in intensity as the dance goes on.
exemplars: Kostadin Varimezov (gaida) and Ognyan Vassilev (drum), recording of an old nestinar melody (Bulgarian National Radio)
Bulgarian field recordings of nestinari drum-and-gaida music

items.name: Rizitika (western Cretan table and road songs)
items.lineage: Songs of the villages at the foot of the White Mountains in western Crete, around Chania, Sfakia and Apokoronas, the name meaning songs of the roots of the mountain. They are sung by men without instruments, a leader singing each line and the company repeating it, and fall into slow, melismatic songs of the table (tis tavlas) sung at feasts and steadier songs of the road (tis stratas) sung while walking to weddings and celebrations; their texts treat heroism, freedom and the Cretan uprisings.
items.description: A leading male voice sings a slow, ornate line and a group of men answers with the same line in unison, full-chested and unaccompanied, each phrase drawn out on long melismas.
exemplars: Aerakis (Cretan Musical Workshop) recordings of rizitika
Society for the Dissemination of National Music (SDNM) recordings

items.name: Kantada (Ionian Islands serenade)
items.lineage: Serenade song of the Ionian Islands (Heptanese), above all Zakynthos, Kefalonia and Corfu, which grew from the Italian canzonetta and serenade during the centuries of Venetian rule; the related arekia of Zakynthos belong to the same harmonised song culture. A small group of men sings in Western tonal harmony, typically in parallel thirds over a bass part, accompanied by guitars and mandolins, and kantades were widely recorded on early 78-rpm discs.
items.description: Three or four male voices sing a sweet, lilting melody in close parallel-third harmony over a bass line, accompanied by softly picked guitars and tremolo mandolin in an unhurried, lilting tempo.
exemplars: Columbia and HMV Greek 78-rpm recordings of kantades (1920s-30s)

items.name: Polyphonic song of Epirus (Pogoni multipart song)
items.lineage: Multipart singing of the villages of Pogoni and other districts of Epirus in north-western Greece, shared with Albanian- and Aromanian-speaking communities of the region and related to the polyphony across the Albanian border. A leading voice (partis) states the melody, a second (gyristis) answers and turns it, a third (klostis) weaves ornaments, and a group of drone singers (isokrates) holds the tonal centre, on anhemitonic pentatonic scales; the Polyphonic Caravan safeguarding programme is inscribed on UNESCO's Register of Good Safeguarding Practices.
items.description: A leading voice and its answering partner exchange slow pentatonic phrases, a third voice winds ornaments around them, and a group holds a steady drone beneath, the parts meeting in close, rubbing intervals.
exemplars: Society for the Dissemination of National Music (Simon Karas) recordings of Epirote polyphony

items.name: Elafró tragoúdi (Athenian light song)
items.lineage: Light urban popular song of Athens of the interwar and early postwar decades, rooted in the Athenian kantada and operetta and absorbing European dance forms such as the tango, waltz and foxtrot. Its songs were written by composers working for revue and recording and sung by star vocalists to salon and dance orchestras of piano, strings, accordion, guitar and bass, issued on Columbia and Odeon 78-rpm discs.
items.description: A polished solo voice sings a sentimental, singable melody over a small orchestra of piano, violin, accordion, guitar and double bass, in a smooth tango, waltz or foxtrot rhythm.
exemplars: Columbia and Odeon Greece 78-rpm recordings of elafro tragoudi

items.name: Eptanisiaki and Ethniki Scholi (Greek Ionian and National School art music)
items.lineage: Greek concert and operatic music of two successive movements. The Ionian (Heptanese) School grew on Corfu and the other Ionian Islands in the nineteenth century under Italian influence, with Nikolaos Mantzaros, composer of the Greek national anthem, and later Spyridon Samaras and Pavlos Carrer writing operas, choral works and songs in an Italianate idiom. The National School, led from the early twentieth century by Manolis Kalomiris, set out to build a Greek concert music on folk-song melody, modal colour and dance rhythm within late-Romantic orchestral, piano and vocal writing; Nikos Skalkottas's 36 Greek Dances share the same concern with folk material.
items.description: Lyrical, Italianate vocal melody in the earlier operatic and song repertoire gives way to orchestral, chamber and piano writing that sets folk-like modal tunes and dance rhythms in rich late-Romantic harmony, with full string sonority and concert-hall resonance.

items.name: Violi kai laouto (Cypriot fiddle-and-lute dance music)
items.lineage: Village music of Greek-speaking Cyprus played by a duo of violin (violi) and laouto lute for weddings, feasts and saints'-day fairs (panigyria). Its repertoire joins the island's dances, among them the syrtos, the kartsilamades couple dances and the tatsia, with the fones, regional melody-types to which singers set traditional or improvised couplets in the fifteen-syllable line. Older ensembles also used the pithkiavli shepherd's flute and the tamboutsia frame drum, and the Cyprus Broadcasting Corporation recorded the repertoire from the mid-twentieth century.
items.description: A bright, ornamented violin line carries the melody over the laouto's strummed chords and plucked bass notes, alternating steady dance rhythms with freer song melodies on which a solo voice declaims rhymed couplets.
exemplars: CyBC (Cyprus Broadcasting Corporation) archive recordings of violi-laouto music

items.name: Colindat (Romanian men's-group Christmas carolling)
items.lineage: Christmas-time house-to-house carolling of Romanian villages, performed by a ceată, an organised group of young unmarried men who rehearse beforehand under a chosen leader and on Christmas Eve sing colinde at each house, wishing the household health and plenty and receiving gifts in return. Inscribed by UNESCO in 2013 for Romania and Moldova, it is especially strong in Transylvania, including Hunedoara, where the group often divides in two to sing alternate verses. Béla Bartók and Constantin Brăiloiu documented its texts and its distinctive asymmetric syllabic rhythms.
items.description: A group of male voices sings short strophic verses in a strong, open chest register, the two halves of the group answering one another, each verse closed by a recurring refrain and driven by an insistent, often asymmetric syllabic rhythm.
exemplars: Constantin Brăiloiu collection, Archives Internationales de Musique Populaire (VDE-Gallo)

items.name: Căluș (Romanian Whitsun ritual dance)
items.lineage: Ritual men's dance of southern Romania, centred on Olt and Argeș counties, performed at Rusalii (Whitsuntide) by a sworn group of călușari under a leader (vătaf), with a masked mute (mutul) and a flag topped with garlic and wormwood; the dancers were believed to heal those struck by the Rusalii spirits. Its music is a cycle of dedicated căluș melodies played by lăutari on violin and lăută, to which the dancers stamp, leap and click their heels, wearing bells on their legs and shouting calls. UNESCO proclaimed the Căluș ritual a Masterpiece in 2005. The cobza card stands in for the lăută.
items.description: A violin plays insistent, repeated dance figures over the lute's driving off-beat chords in fast duple time, punctuated by the dancers' stamps, heel-clicks, jingling leg bells and sharp shouted calls.
exemplars: Constantin Brăiloiu collection, Archives Internationales de Musique Populaire (VDE-Gallo)

items.name: Csángó zene (Moldavian Csángó song and dance music)
items.lineage: Music of the Csángós, Roman Catholic Hungarian-speaking communities of Romanian Moldavia around Bacău and the Siret valley, whose village repertoire kept archaic layers of Hungarian song alongside dance tunes shared with their Romanian neighbours. Unaccompanied ballads, laments and religious songs sit beside dance music for furulya duct flute, koboz lute, violin and a small drum (dob); Zoltán Kallós and other collectors recorded it from the mid-twentieth century, and Hungarian dance-house (táncház) musicians later took up the repertoire. The membrane-drum card stands in for the dob.
items.description: Richly ornamented, narrow-range solo singing in an old modal style contrasts with fast dance tunes in which a breathy duct flute or violin spins repeating figures over the koboz's rhythmic strumming and a light drum.
exemplars: Kallós Zoltán field recordings of Moldavian Csángó song
Hungaroton releases of Moldavian Csángó music

items.name: Muzică bănățeană (Banat taragot and dance music)
items.lineage: Regional folk and dance music of the Romanian Banat around Timișoara, in which the taragot, a keyed single-reed woodwind brought from Hungary, where it is called tárogató, by Banat lăutari in the twentieth century, became a leading melody instrument alongside violin, clarinet, saxophone, accordion and double bass. It accompanies Banat dances such as the brâu, often in a limping seven-beat metre, and the swift de doi couple dance, as well as slow songs and doinas, and its taragot soloists and singers were recorded by Electrecord and Radio Timișoara. The tárogató card stands in for the taragot.
items.description: A reedy, dark-toned taragot leads fast, heavily ornamented dance melodies, often in limping asymmetric metre, in unison or thirds with violin and saxophone, over off-beat accordion chords and a bouncing double-bass line, while songs take a slower, swaying pace.
exemplars: Electrecord LPs of Banat taragot players

items.name: Romanță and cântec de mahala (Bucharest urban song)
items.lineage: Urban song of Bucharest. The romanță, a sentimental strophic love song in Romanian that grew from nineteenth-century salon song and the Russian romance, was sung to piano, violin or small orchestra; the cântec de mahala (suburb song) was its lăutar counterpart in the city's outer neighbourhoods, sung with Ottoman-tinged melisma over violin, accordion, cimbalom and double bass. Both reached gramophone records in the interwar years through singers such as Zavaidoc and Jean Moscopol and were recorded after the war by Electrecord with Ioana Radu, Gică Petrescu and Maria Tănase.
items.description: A sentimental solo voice, rich in vibrato and sighing melisma, unfolds slow strophic love songs over a sobbing violin, rippling cimbalom, soft accordion chords and piano, the mahala style taking freer, more ornamented and nasal lines.

items.name: Gajdošská kultúra (Slovak gajdy bagpipe music)
items.lineage: Bagpipe tradition of Slovakia, inscribed by UNESCO in 2015, built on the gajdy, a goatskin bagpipe with a double chanter that sounds both melody and an accompanying pitch and a separate long drone, its stock often carved as a goat's head. Strongest in central and northern regions such as Liptov, Orava and Horehronie, the gajdoš played alone for song and dance or with fiddles, and the instrument's making and repertoire are handed on from master to pupil and through festivals. The gajda card stands in for the gajdy.
items.description: A continuous buzzing drone underpins a nasal, tightly ornamented chanter melody with its own accompanying pitch, the piper breaking off to sing verses or joined by fiddles for dance tunes.
exemplars: OPUS label recordings of Slovak gajdoši

items.name: Dudácká muzika (Chodsko and South Bohemian bagpipe band)
items.lineage: Bagpipe music of western and southern Bohemia, above all the Chodsko region around Domažlice and the Strakonice area, played on the Czech dudy (German Bock), a bellows-blown bagpipe with a single chanter and one long bass drone ending in a curved horn bell, usually decorated with a carved goat's head. The classic dudácká muzika pairs the dudy with a small E-flat clarinet and one or two violins for songs and dances, and the International Bagpipe Festival at Strakonice regularly gathers its players. The gajda card stands in for the dudy.
items.description: The low, steady drone and bright, nasal chanter of the bagpipe carry major-key dance tunes and songs, doubled and decorated by a shrill high clarinet and answered by fiddles playing harmony and countermelody.
exemplars: Supraphon recordings of Chodsko bagpipe bands

items.name: Kapela podwórkowa (Warsaw courtyard street-song band)
items.lineage: Street and courtyard ballad of working-class Warsaw, from districts such as Czerniaków and Praga, sung for coins in tenement courtyards and at taverns by small bands of accordion, banjo or mandolin and violin in the city's own street dialect. Its humorous, sentimental and underworld songs passed into recording around 1960 through Stanisław Grzesiuk, who accompanied himself on banjo and mandolin for Polish Radio and Polskie Nagrania, and later through bands such as Kapela Czerniakowska.
items.description: A rough, conversational voice delivers wry strophic ballads in street dialect over pumping accordion chords, the bright plink of banjo, mandolin tremolo and a fiddle doubling the tune, in a steady singalong rhythm.
exemplars: Polskie Nagrania recordings of Warsaw street songs

items.name: Tango polskie (Warsaw interwar cabaret song and tango)
items.lineage: Popular song of interwar Warsaw, written for revue cabarets such as Qui Pro Quo and for gramophone and film, in which the Argentine-derived tango and the slow foxtrot became the main vehicles for Polish-language sentimental song. Composers such as Jerzy Petersburski and Henryk Wars wrote for salon dance orchestras of violins, saxophones, piano, bass and drums that accompanied crooning singers and cabaret stars, recorded on 78s by Syrena Rekord and other labels.
items.description: A smooth crooning baritone or cabaret soprano sings melancholy, tightly composed refrains over a salon dance orchestra, with sweet violin and saxophone counter-lines, staccato piano and the clipped tango pulse of bass and brushed drums, heard through the narrow, crackling band of an electrical 78.

items.name: Yass (1990s Polish alternative-jazz scene)
items.lineage: Polish alternative jazz movement of the 1990s centred on Gdańsk and the Tri-City and on the Bydgoszcz club Mózg, whose musicians adopted the deliberately skewed name yass to set themselves against the established jazz mainstream. Bands such as Miłość, with Tymon Tymański, Leszek Możdżer and Mikołaj Trzaska, as well as Kury and Łoskot, mixed free jazz with punk, rock, noise and ironic quotation of Polish popular music.
items.description: Raw, punk-edged energy meets free improvisation: squalling saxophone over distorted guitar and heavy electric bass, a drummer switching between rock backbeats and free pulse, and abrupt cuts between lyrical piano passages and noisy collective climaxes.

items.name: Hutsulska muzyka (Hutsul Carpathian highland music)
items.lineage: Music of the Hutsuls, Ukrainian highlanders of the eastern Carpathians around Verkhovyna, Kosiv and the Cheremosh valley. A band of fiddle, small tsymbaly dulcimer and drum (buben) plays kolomyiky and the hutsulka dance, while shepherding instruments, the long wooden trembita horn, sopilka and floiara flutes and the drymba jaw harp, serve signalling, funeral and pastoral music; kolomyika couplets and lyrical songs are sung in a strong, ornamented voice. The hammered-dulcimer card stands in for the tsymbaly and the frame-drum card for the buben.
items.description: A fiddle saws out fast, repeating kolomyika phrases with sharp grace notes and drone strings over the dulcimer's bright hammered tremolo and the frame drum's even beat, while the long wooden horn's open overtone calls and breathy shepherd flutes carry the outdoor, pastoral side of the tradition.
exemplars: Rylsky Institute (Kyiv) field recordings of Hutsul music

items.name: Qırımtatar musiqisi (Crimean Tatar song and dance music)
items.lineage: Music of the Crimean Tatars, the Turkic Muslim people of the Crimean peninsula, whose repertoire shares modal melody and asymmetric dance rhythms with its Turkish and Balkan neighbours. Clarinet, violin, accordion and the daire frame drum accompany dances such as the haytarma, in a seven-beat metre, alongside lyrical songs. After the Soviet deportation of the Crimean Tatars during the Second World War the music was kept alive in exile, chiefly in Uzbekistan, where the state song and dance ensemble Haytarma (Qaytarma) was re-formed, and it returned with the community to Crimea at the end of the Soviet period. The frame-drum card stands in for the daire.
items.description: Clarinet and violin trade ornate modal melodies in heterophony over accordion chords and the frame drum's beat, with brisk dance tunes in limping asymmetric metres alongside songs that open in free rhythm before settling into a steady pulse.
exemplars: Melodiya LPs of Crimean Tatar song and dance

items.name: Partesnyi spiv and dukhovnyi kontsert (Ukrainian Baroque choral concerto)
items.lineage: Polyphonic sacred choral style of Ukrainian Orthodox church music. Partes singing, multi-voice part-writing for unaccompanied choir codified in Mykola Dyletsky's seventeenth-century Grammar of music, spread from the Kyiv and Lviv church brotherhoods into Muscovy; in the later eighteenth century it culminated in the a cappella sacred concerto of Dmytro Bortniansky, Maksym Berezovsky and Artem Vedel, trained in Hlukhiv, Kyiv and in Bortniansky's and Berezovsky's case in Italy, who joined Italianate counterpoint and dramatic contrast to Church Slavonic texts, writing for single and double choir.
items.description: An unaccompanied mixed choir in four or eight parts moves between massive homophonic blocks and imitative counterpoint, contrasting full tutti with lighter groups of voices and slow lyrical sections with brisk fugal finales, in a resonant church acoustic.
exemplars: Maksym Berezovsky — Ne otverzhy mene vo vremia starosti

items.name: Prostopinije (Carpatho-Rusyn plainchant)
items.lineage: Congregational plainchant of the Byzantine Catholic (Greek Catholic) Ruthenians of the Carpathians, in the eparchies of Mukachevo and Prešov, sung in Church Slavonic by a cantor (diak) and the whole congregation in unison without instruments, on melodies grouped in the eight tones. Rooted in older East Slavic church chant and coloured by local folk song, it was codified in Ioann Bokšaj's Uzhhorod chant book Cerkovnoje prostopinije and carried by emigrants to the Ruthenian Byzantine Catholic parishes of the United States.
items.description: A cantor's lead voice and the congregation sing in plain, syllabic unison and octaves, reciting the text on repeated tones and rounding each phrase with short, folk-like cadences in the warm resonance of a small church.
exemplars: Metropolitan Cantor Institute (Byzantine Catholic Archeparchy of Pittsburgh) recordings of prostopinije

items.name: Troisti muzyky (Ukrainian fiddle, tsymbaly and drum trio)
items.lineage: Instrumental village dance band of Ukraine, named for its classic three players, fiddle, tsymbaly dulcimer and drum (buben or baraban), sometimes joined or replaced by sopilka, a bass fiddle (basolia) or, later, accordion. It played kolomyiky, the kozachok and hopak, polkas and wedding marches for weddings and village dances across Galicia, Podillia and central Ukraine, and was carried to North America by emigrants, where the fiddler Pawlo Humeniuk recorded it on 78 rpm discs between the world wars. The hammered-dulcimer card stands in for the tsymbaly and the frame-drum card for the buben.
items.description: A lead fiddle drives fast, ornamented dance tunes over the dulcimer's shimmering hammered chords and runs, with the drum marking a heavy, even dance beat.
exemplars: Rylsky Institute (Kyiv) field recordings of troisti muzyky

items.name: Kaale romanilaulu (Finnish Roma song)
items.lineage: Song tradition of the Finnish Kaale (Finnish Roma), whose ancestors reached Finland by way of Sweden in the sixteenth century. Songs in Finnish and in the Kaale variety of Romani sing of honour, the family, love, horse-trading, prison and the travelling life, and are often sung solo in a free, ornamented style. Kai Åberg and Risto Blomster made field recordings among the Kaale of North Karelia, and the singing tradition is listed in the Finnish National Inventory of Living Heritage.
items.description: A single voice, usually unaccompanied, unfolds slow, freely timed melodies with sliding ornaments and melismatic turns on held syllables, in a plaintive, sustained tone.
exemplars: The Songs of the Finnish Kaale (JJVCD-76; field recordings in North Karelia by Kai Åberg and Risto Blomster, 1995-2009)

items.name: Sions sånger / Siionin laulut (Laestadian hymn singing)
items.lineage: Congregational hymn singing of the Laestadian revival begun in the mid-nineteenth century by the Swedish pastor Lars Levi Laestadius in Karesuando and Pajala, which spread through Swedish and Finnish Tornedalen, northern Norway and Ostrobothnia. Its songbooks, Sions sånger in Swedish and Siionin laulut in Finnish, are sung at seurat prayer meetings in prayer houses, and Svenskt visarkiv has recorded the orally carried tunes of tradition-bearers in northern Sweden.
items.description: A whole congregation sings strophic hymns without instruments, in a slow, even unison in which individual voices drift slightly around the shared line and the sound fills a plain wooden room.
exemplars: Svenskt visarkiv field recordings of oral Sions sånger singing in northern Sweden

items.name: Tornedalian folk song (Meänkieli song of the Torne Valley)
items.lineage: Vocal folk tradition of the Tornedalians, the Finnic-speaking minority of the Torne Valley on the Swedish side of the Swedish-Finnish border, sung in Meänkieli and Finnish. Home recordings made between 1971 and 1977 and issued by Caprice Records as Songs of Tornedalen document singing games, lullabies, work songs and religious songs.
items.description: Unaccompanied voices sing short strophic tunes at close range, from rocking lullabies and rhythmic game songs to plain, slow religious songs, with the intimacy of singing at home.
exemplars: Songs of Tornedalen (Caprice Records; home recordings 1971-77)

items.name: Romani viser (Norwegian Romani traveller song)
items.lineage: Song tradition of the Romani people / Tater, the travelling minority of Norway (resande in Sweden), whose secular and religious songs are sung in Norwegian or Swedish, unaccompanied or to guitar and accordion. Field recordings made in 2002 were issued by Etnisk musikklubb as Viser på vandring Vol. 1 - Songs of the Romany People in Norway, and the singer Elias Akselsen has become the tradition's best-known representative.
items.description: A clear, direct solo voice carries strophic songs and slow religious pieces, either alone or over plain guitar chords and accordion, with ornamented phrase endings and an unhurried, storytelling delivery.
exemplars: Viser på vandring Vol. 1 - Songs of the Romany People in Norway (Etnisk musikklubb, field recordings 2002)

items.name: Menuett och polska (Finland-Swedish Ostrobothnian fiddle dance)
items.lineage: Fiddle dance music of the Swedish-speaking communities of Ostrobothnia in western Finland, where the minuet, long gone from most of Europe, survived as a living folk dance alongside the polska, notably in Jeppo near Nykarleby. Otto Andersson's folk-music collection at Åbo Akademi documents it from the early twentieth century, Svenskt visarkiv later recorded fiddlers in Swedish-speaking Finland and Åland, and the minuet tradition of the Swedish-speaking areas is listed in the Finnish National Inventory of Living Heritage.
items.description: One or more fiddles play stately triple-time minuets and springing polskas for dancing, with bowed ornaments, open-string resonance and a steady, repeating dance phrase.
exemplars: Otto Andersson's folk-music collection at Åbo Akademi
Svenskt visarkiv field recordings of fiddlers in Swedish-speaking Finland and Åland

items.name: Rekilaulu (Finnish rhymed-couplet folk song)
items.lineage: The Finnish "new folk song" that in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries displaced the older Kalevala-metre runo song with short rhymed stanzas in regular, accentual metre, sung to simple major and minor tunes by young people at village gatherings, especially in Ostrobothnia and western Finland. The Finnish Literature Society folklore archive and the Folk Music Institute hold field recordings of the genre.
items.description: A single unaccompanied voice sings brisk syllabic stanzas to a short, repeated major or minor tune, the rhymed couplets landing squarely on the beat.
exemplars: Finnish Literature Society (SKS) folklore archive field recordings of rekilaulu

items.name: Kupletti and rillumarei (Finnish comic couplet song)
items.lineage: Finnish comic and topical song in couplet form, made popular on stage and record by J. Alfred Tanner, who made many 78 rpm records in the early twentieth century. A rustic comic-song style flourished again in the rillumarei films and records of the lyricist-singer Reino Helismaa and the accordionist-singer Esa Pakarinen after the Second World War.
items.description: A comic singer delivers verse after verse of humorous, topical lyrics over a bouncing piano or accordion accompaniment, each stanza building to a punchline and a short refrain.
exemplars: Reino Helismaa and Esa Pakarinen rillumarei recordings (1950s)

items.name: Jouhikko (Finnish-Karelian bowed lyre music)
items.lineage: Playing tradition of the jouhikko, a bowed lyre with two or three horsehair strings whose melody string is stopped from the side by the backs of the fingers while the others sound as drones, used in Finland and Karelia mainly for dance tunes. A. O. Väisänen documented the instrument and its players in the field; the revival led by Rauno Nieminen and later players such as Pekko Käppi returned it to performance, and the tradition is listed in the Finnish National Inventory of Living Heritage.
items.description: A short, raspy bowed melody circles over one or two droning open strings, the horsehair giving a grainy, breathy tone and the bow stroke a dance pulse.
exemplars: A. O. Väisänen field documentation of jouhikko players

items.name: Siionin virret (Finnish Awakening körtti hymn singing)
items.lineage: Congregational singing of the Awakening movement (herännäisyys), the Pietist revival within the Finnish Lutheran church associated with the lay leader Paavo Ruotsalainen, whose followers are known as körttiläiset.
