At seurat gatherings and the annual Herättäjäjuhlat summer festival, hymns from the movement’s own book Siionin virret are sung in a markedly slow, drawn-out congregational style, separate from the Laestadian movement and its songbooks.
items.description: A large congregation sustains each hymn line at a very slow, even pace, every syllable drawn out into a long held tone, producing a heavy, solemn and inward sound.
exemplars: Yle archive recordings of seurat and Herättäjäjuhlat singing

items.name: Poliittinen laululiike (Finnish 1970s political song movement)
items.lineage: Left-wing song movement of 1970s Finland that revived and rearranged Finnish workers' songs alongside new topical songs, carried by vocal groups such as Agit-Prop, which recorded workers' songs for Love Records, and by the KOM-teatteri ensemble with the composer Kaj Chydenius.
items.description: A small vocal group sings workers’ anthems and topical songs in clear close harmony over piano, with marching strophic tunes, crisp diction and a direct, rallying delivery.
exemplars: Agit-Prop recordings of workers' songs for Love Records (1970s)

items.name: Religiøse folketoner (Norwegian sacred folk tunes)
items.lineage: Orally transmitted versions of hymn and spiritual-song melodies that rural Norwegian singers reshaped outside the church, sung solo at home and at work with free rhythm, rich ornamentation and intervals that fall between the tempered steps, in valleys such as Setesdal and Telemark. Norsk folkemusikksamling holds field recordings, and singers such as Sondre Bratland and Kirsten Bråten Berg have recorded the repertoire for Kirkelig Kulturverksted.
items.description: A single unaccompanied voice sings a slow hymn melody in free rhythm, bending notes between the scale steps and decorating each line with quick turns and grace notes.
exemplars: Norsk folkemusikksamling field recordings of religiøse folketoner
Sondre Bratland and Kirsten Bråten Berg recordings for Kirkelig Kulturverksted

items.name: Langeleik (Valdres drone-zither music)
items.lineage: Playing tradition of the langeleik, a long box zither with one fretted melody string and several drone strings, strummed with a plectrum while the left hand stops the melody string, kept alive above all in Valdres. The National Library of Norway issued Høyre du mann - langeleikopptak 1955-83, a compilation of 42 archival langeleik recordings.
items.description: A strummed rhythmic pulse rings across open drone strings while a fretted melody line steps above it, giving a soft, shimmering, harmonically static dance tune.
exemplars: Høyre du mann - langeleikopptak 1955-83 (National Library of Norway)

items.name: Medeltida ballader (Swedish medieval ballad singing)
items.lineage: Narrative ballads of the pan-Scandinavian medieval ballad tradition, sung in Swedish to strophic tunes with recurring refrains and handed down orally into the twentieth century in regions such as Dalarna, Småland and Swedish-speaking Finland. Svenskt visarkiv and Sveriges Radio field recordings were issued by Caprice as Den medeltida balladen / The Medieval Ballad.
items.description: A lone unaccompanied singer tells a long story verse by verse to a short strophic tune, returning after each stanza to the same refrain line.
exemplars: Den medeltida balladen / The Medieval Ballad (Caprice / Svenskt visarkiv / Sveriges Radio field recordings)

items.name: Folklig koralsång (Swedish folk chorale singing)
items.lineage: Oral variants of the Swedish Lutheran hymn tunes, sung by rural singers who ornamented and reshaped the chorale melodies at home and in church until each parish and singer had its own versions, documented especially in Dalarna. Svenskt visarkiv researchers Margareta Jersild and Ingvar Åkesson studied the tradition, and Sveriges Radio made field recordings of its singers.
items.description: A single voice sings a hymn melody slowly and freely, filling the space between the chorale notes with slides, turns and passing tones until the familiar tune becomes a personal, richly decorated line.
exemplars: Svenskt visarkiv field documentation of folklig koralsång
Sveriges Radio field recordings of folk chorale singers

items.name: Väckelsesång (Swedish free-church revival song)
items.lineage: Devotional song of the nineteenth-century Swedish revival and free-church movements, whose core repertoire was written by Lina Sandell and set by Oscar Ahnfelt, who sang the songs to his own guitar (the parlour-guitar card stands in for his ten-string guitar), and which spread through mission-house songbooks such as Pilgrimsharpan. Einar Ekberg's 78 rpm records are among its best-known recordings.
items.description: Simple, tuneful strophic songs of faith are sung by a soloist or a gathered congregation over gentle guitar chords, in a warm, intimate tone.

items.name: Säckpipa (Swedish bagpipe music of Dalarna)
items.lineage: Music of the Swedish bagpipe, a mouth-blown pipe with a cylindrical chanter and a single drone, which survived in western Dalarna into the twentieth century. Per Gudmundson's Caprice album Säckpipa, recorded in 1982-83, carried it into the folk-music revival, where polskas, marches and walking tunes are often played together with fiddle.
items.description: A reedy chanter plays dance tunes and marches over a steady single drone without a break in the sound, often doubled by a fiddle in unison.

items.name: Gammaldans (Nordic old-time couple-dance music)
items.lineage: Couple-dance music of Sweden and Norway built on the nineteenth-century dances that reached the countryside, such as the hambo, schottis, polka, mazurka, waltz and reinlender, played above all on accordion with fiddle and later guitar and double bass for dances in barns, outdoor dance floors and halls. Kalle Jularbo's accordion records, made over four decades of the twentieth century, shaped the Swedish style, while Norway keeps a gammeldans class at Landskappleiken and a strong two-row torader accordion tradition.
items.description: A bright accordion leads bouncy hambos, schottisches, polkas and waltzes over guitar off-beat chords and a walking bass, with fiddle doubling the tune at a steady, danceable tempo.

items.name: Højskolesang and fællessang (Danish communal songbook singing)
items.lineage: Communal singing from Højskolesangbogen, the songbook of the Danish folk high schools that grew out of N. F. S. Grundtvig’s ideas, in which a whole assembly sings hymns, national songs and popular songs to piano. The practice reaches a national audience through DR’s fællessang broadcasts with DR Pigekoret and DR Koncertkoret.
items.description: A large room of untrained voices sings strophic songs in hearty unison over a steady piano accompaniment, every verse at an even, singable tempo with the words clearly carried.
exemplars: DR fællessang broadcasts with DR Pigekoret and DR Koncertkoret

items.name: Revyvise (Danish revue song)
items.lineage: Comic and topical songs of the Danish revue theatre, which flourished in Copenhagen in the first half of the twentieth century and lives on in summer revues such as the Cirkusrevyen at Bakken, sung by actor-singers to piano or a small theatre band with clear diction and a punchline in each verse. Recordings by Liva Weel and Osvald Helmuth preserve the classic style.
items.description: An actor-singer delivers witty verses in a conversational, half-spoken style over a light piano accompaniment, timing each line for the laugh before a sung refrain.

items.name: Dansk visesang (Danish vise song)
items.lineage: Danish tradition of the vise, a strophic song in which the text leads, sung to guitar or piano in a clear, conversational voice. In the later twentieth century it was renewed in Copenhagen song clubs and on record by singers such as Povl Dissing and the poet-songwriter Benny Andersen, and it is cultivated by the Visens Venner societies.
items.description: A solo singer tells a story in plain, speech-like phrasing over fingerpicked or strummed acoustic guitar, keeping the melody simple so that every word of the verse comes through.
exemplars: Povl Dissing and Benny Andersen recordings

items.name: Passíusálmar gömlu lögin (Icelandic folk Passion-hymn singing)
items.lineage: Traditional singing of Hallgrímur Pétursson’s seventeenth-century Passíusálmar (Hymns of the Passion) to the old melodies (gömlu lögin), oral variants of hymn tunes sung slowly and with ornaments in Icelandic homes, especially during Lent. Twentieth-century archive recordings of traditional singers are held by the Árni Magnússon Institute, and the repertoire has been revived in programmes at Hallgrímskirkja.
items.description: A single unaccompanied voice sings long hymn stanzas to a slow, freely stretched melody, with small ornaments at the ends of lines and a grave, plain tone.
exemplars: Árni Magnússon Institute archive recordings of traditional Passíusálmar singers

items.name: Torviseitsikko (Finnish brass septet)
items.lineage: Finnish brass septet of E-flat cornet, two B-flat cornets, E-flat tenor horn, two baritones and tuba (the cornopean card stands in for the cornets and the credited-horns card for the tuba), first organised by Adolf Leander within the Guards' Band in Helsinki and from the late nineteenth century the common band of villages, societies and fire brigades across Finland, playing marches, dances and arrangements. Jean Sibelius wrote six pieces for brass septet, some for the Loviisa fire-brigade septet, and ensembles such as Sointu-Seitsikko, founded in Turku in 1971, keep the repertoire in concert and on record.
items.description: Seven mellow conical brasses play marches, waltzes and chorale-like pieces in close, warm harmony, the cornets carrying the melody over a soft, rounded bass.
exemplars: Sointu-Seitsikko recordings of traditional brass septet repertoire
Recordings of Jean Sibelius's brass septet pieces, such as the Overture in F minor and Andantino and Menuetto

items.name: Bagad (Breton pipe band)
items.lineage: Breton pipe band modelled on the Scottish pipe band, joining a section of bombardes to a section of biniou braz, the Great Highland bagpipe as adopted in Brittany (the biniou card set to its bras register), and a drum corps of snare, tenor and bass drums. The federation Bodadeg ar Sonerion, founded during the Second World War, organised the bands and their national championship of bagadoù, contested since 1949, and the Festival Interceltique de Lorient became a principal stage for the bands' arranged suites of Breton dance tunes, airs and marches.
items.description: Massed bombardes and bagpipes play Breton dance tunes and marches in unison and in harmonised sections over the pipes' constant drones, while a corps of snares, tenors and bass drum adds crisp rudimental rolls and a driving pulse; suites move between slow airs and fast dance sets at full outdoor volume.

items.name: Galoubet-tambourin (Provençal pipe and tabor)
items.lineage: Provençal pipe-and-tabor tradition in which a single musician, the tambourinaire, fingers the three-hole galoubet with one hand while beating the long, deep tambourin drum hung from the same arm with a stick held in the other. It accompanies the farandole and other processional dances, aubades and festivals of Provence, is kept up by tambourinaire associations and conservatoire classes in the region, and is documented in field recordings held by the CREM-CNRS sound archive.
items.description: A shrill, bright three-hole pipe, overblown into its upper harmonics, plays quick ornamented dance melodies while the same player keeps a steady booming pulse on a long, deep snared drum; several tambourinaires often play together in unison for processional dances.
exemplars: CREM-CNRS archive item France-Provence, Le galoubet-tambourin
Maurice Guis and the Musiciens de Provence recordings (Arion)

items.name: Cant pirenenc (Béarnais and Bigourdan polyphonic song)
items.lineage: Polyphonic singing in Gascon Occitan from Béarn and Bigorre in the western French Pyrenees, sung by groups of men, and today also by women and mixed groups, in cafés, at village fêtes such as the mid-August feast of Notre-Dame at Laruns in the Ossau valley, at church services and at the song festivals of Siros in Béarn and Ibos in Bigorre. A melody is doubled by a second voice moving mostly in parallel thirds, with further voices added in larger groups; the repertoire mixes pastoral and love songs, including songs attributed to the eighteenth-century Béarnais poet Cyprien Despourrins, with sacred chants, and the ethnomusicologist Jean-Jacques Casteret has documented the practice.
items.description: Unaccompanied men's voices sing strophic songs at a slow, broad tempo, the melody shadowed by a second voice in parallel thirds and supported by further voices in fuller groups, with long held notes at phrase ends and a full-throated, resonant chest tone.
exemplars: Song-festival recordings from Siros and Ibos
Jean-Jacques Casteret's field documentation of Gascon Pyrenean polyphony

items.name: Banda (southwest French festive brass band)
items.lineage: Festive brass-and-percussion bands of the Landes, Gers, Béarn and French Basque Country that play in the streets and arenas at férias, bullfights, rugby matches and village fêtes. Bands in matching costume play pasodobles, marches and popular tunes taken up by the crowd, a repertoire drawing heavily on the Spanish pasodoble, and many gather each year at the festival of bandas in Condom, documented in the INA regional archive.
items.description: Trumpets, saxophones and trombones blare pasodoble and march melodies in loud unison and simple harmony over sousaphone bass, snare, bass drum and cymbals, with crowd singing, shouts and hand claps joining the choruses as the band plays in the street or the arena stands.
exemplars: INA archive: Le festival de bandas de Condom

items.name: Carnaval de Dunkerque (Dunkirk carnival song)
items.lineage: Street carnival of the port of Dunkirk in French Flanders, traditionally traced to the feasts given to fishermen before they sailed for the Icelandic cod fishery. Each bande marches behind a band of fifes, drums and brass, the musique, led by a tambour-major (the piccolo card stands in for the fifes and the generic horns card for the brass), while masked and costumed carnavaleux sing carnival songs in French and Flemish dialect, press together in the chahut and end the day at the Place Jean-Bart singing the Cantate à Jean Bart on their knees; OPCI-Ethnodoc catalogues recordings of the songs.
items.description: Shrill fifes and brass play short, endlessly repeated march and song tunes over snare rolls and bass drum, while a dense crowd of costumed marchers roars the choruses in unison, shouting, stamping and surging together; the day ends with a slow, solemn hymn sung by the whole crowd.
exemplars: OPCI-Ethnodoc: Echos du carnaval de Dunkerque recordings

items.name: Chants de marins (French maritime work song)
items.lineage: Work and leisure songs of French sailors on the merchant, fishing and naval ships of the Breton and Atlantic coasts: chants à hisser for hauling halyards, chants à virer for the capstan and windlass, and gaillard d'avant forecastle songs for rest hours. Collected from former sailors along the coast, the repertoire was revived from the 1980s by the maritime heritage magazine Le Chasse-Marée, whose multi-volume anthology of sea-song field recordings documents it, and by festivals such as the chant de marin festival at Paimpol.
items.description: A solo shantyman sings each verse line and a crew of men answers with a short refrain, the rhythm of hauling or heaving marked by strong accented beats; forecastle songs are slower and more lyrical. Voices are plain, robust and unaccompanied.
exemplars: Le Chasse-Marée: Anthologie des chansons de mer (field-recording series)

items.name: Trobamuffin (Occitan raggamuffin)
items.lineage: Occitan-language ragga developed in Marseille from the mid-1980s by Massilia Sound System, whose members named it trobamuffin, joining Jamaican sound-system toasting to the troubadour heritage and to Provençal Occitan and Marseille street speech. Its songs on local identity, politics and fêtes were carried by self-organised sound-system parties and concerts, and in Toulouse the Fabulous Trobadors developed a related Occitan chatted-verse style.
items.description: Fast, rhythmic toasting in Occitan and French rides on reggae and ragga riddims of programmed drums, deep bass and offbeat chords, with chanted call-and-response choruses for the crowd and a festive sound-system energy.

items.name: Opéra bouffe (Offenbach-era Parisian operetta)
items.lineage: Comic operetta genre of Second Empire Paris, created by Hervé and above all by Jacques Offenbach, who opened the Théâtre des Bouffes-Parisiens in 1855. Works such as Orphée aux enfers (1858), La belle Hélène (1864) and La vie parisienne (1866) parodied classical myth and contemporary society through spoken dialogue, strophic couplets, patter songs, ensemble finales and galop dance numbers, and the genre became a model for Viennese and English operetta. The generic strings and flute cards stand in for the theatre orchestra's string section and flutes.
items.description: Bright, brisk theatre-orchestra numbers alternate with spoken dialogue: strophic couplets with chorus refrains, rapid patter, parodies of grand-opera style and ensemble finales that accelerate into galop and can-can rhythms, sung with clear comic diction.
exemplars: Marc Minkowski recordings of Orphée aux enfers and La belle Hélène
Michel Plasson and the Orchestre du Capitole de Toulouse, Offenbach recordings

items.name: Opéra-comique (French spoken-dialogue opera)
items.lineage: French opera genre in which spoken dialogue alternates with sung numbers, grown from the plays with songs of the eighteenth-century Paris fair theatres and identified with the Opéra-Comique company, housed at the Salle Favart from 1783. Grétry, Boieldieu, Hérold, Auber and Adam shaped its romances, couplets and ensembles, and by the later nineteenth century the term also covered serious works such as Bizet's Carmen, premiered there with spoken dialogue in 1875. The generic strings and flute cards stand in for the orchestra's string section and flutes.
items.description: Spoken scenes alternate with tuneful, clearly declaimed arias, romances, strophic couplets and choruses over a light, transparent orchestra of strings and solo woodwinds, favouring melodic grace and French diction over vocal display.

items.name: Mélodie (French art song)
items.lineage: French art song for solo voice and piano setting French lyric poetry, grown from the simpler romance in the mid-nineteenth century through Berlioz's Les nuits d'été and the songs of Gounod. Fauré, Duparc, Chausson, Debussy, Ravel and Poulenc made it a major genre on poems by Verlaine, Baudelaire, Leconte de Lisle, Hugo and Apollinaire, performed in salons and recitals.
items.description: A single trained voice declaims French verse with clear, nuanced diction and restrained legato phrasing over a richly coloured piano part of arpeggiated figures and shifting modal and chromatic harmony, favouring intimacy and subtle shading over operatic power.
exemplars: Pierre Bernac and Francis Poulenc recordings

items.name: Chants de Taizé (Taizé meditative chant)
items.lineage: Ecumenical meditative chant of the Taizé Community, the monastic community founded by Brother Roger, who settled in the Burgundian village of Taizé during the Second World War. From 1975 the composer Jacques Berthier, working with the brothers, wrote short ostinato refrains, canons, litanies and acclamations, first mostly in Latin and later in many languages, so that the international gatherings of young pilgrims could sing together; the community's Ateliers et Presses de Taizé has issued recordings.
items.description: A large congregation sings a short, simple refrain in four-part harmony over and over at a soft, steady tempo, while a solo voice sings verses above it and guitar, flute, oboe and cello add gentle accompaniment and countermelodies; the repetition builds a calm, meditative atmosphere in a resonant church.
exemplars: Ateliers et Presses de Taizé recordings
Music of Unity and Peace, Taizé (Deutsche Grammophon, 2015)

items.name: Afro trap (French)
items.lineage: French rap style named by the Paris rapper MHD, from the 19th arrondissement, whose Afro Trap series of videos from 2015 set rap and chanted hooks over beats mixing trap drum programming with the rhythms and guitar-like riffs of West and Central African popular dance music. The series and his 2016 debut album spread the style among French and Francophone African audiences, and other French rappers took up the formula.
items.description: Chanted, catchy rap hooks and short verses ride bright looping riffs and syncopated dance percussion layered over trap hi-hat rolls and long sliding 808 bass, at a danceable mid tempo built for group singalongs.

items.name: Lied (German art song)
items.lineage: German-language art song for solo voice and piano setting lyric poetry by Goethe, Heine, Müller, Eichendorff, Rückert and others, centred on Vienna through Franz Schubert, who wrote more than six hundred songs including the cycles Die schöne Müllerin (1823) and Winterreise (1827). Schumann, Brahms, Hugo Wolf, Mahler and Richard Strauss extended it, and it lives in the Liederabend recital of singer and pianist as equal partners.
items.description: A single trained voice sings German poetry with close attention to word and declamation, while the piano paints the text in figures that run through the whole song, from simple strophic tunes to through-composed ballads with dramatic modulations.
exemplars: Dietrich Fischer-Dieskau and Gerald Moore, Schubert Lieder (Deutsche Grammophon)

items.name: Singspiel (German spoken-dialogue opera)
items.lineage: German-language opera, mostly comic, in which spoken dialogue replaces recitative between songs, arias and ensembles. Johann Adam Hiller and the librettist Christian Felix Weisse established it in Leipzig in the 1760s and 1770s, and in Vienna Emperor Joseph II founded a National Singspiel in 1778, for which Mozart wrote Die Entführung aus dem Serail (1782); Dittersdorf's Doktor und Apotheker (1786) and Mozart's Die Zauberflöte (1791), written for Schikaneder's Theater auf der Wieden, carried the form to its height. The generic strings and flute cards stand in for the orchestra's string section and flutes.
items.description: Spoken German scenes alternate with simple strophic songs in a folk-like vein, florid arias and ensembles over a Classical orchestra of strings, paired woodwinds and horns, mixing comic patter, sentiment and moments of magical or exotic colour.
exemplars: Die Zauberflöte — Karl Böhm, Berlin Philharmonic (Deutsche Grammophon)
Die Entführung aus dem Serail — John Eliot Gardiner, English Baroque Soloists

items.name: Wiener Walzer (Viennese Strauss-era waltz)
items.lineage: Ballroom and concert dance music of nineteenth-century Vienna, developed from the 1820s by Joseph Lanner and Johann Strauss I with their dance orchestras and raised to its peak by Johann Strauss II, whose waltzes such as An der schönen blauen Donau (1867) and the Kaiser-Walzer (1889) were played alongside polkas and marches by the family orchestra with his brothers Josef and Eduard. The Vienna Philharmonic's New Year's Concert keeps the repertoire before a world audience. The generic strings and flute cards stand in for the dance orchestra's string section and flutes.
items.description: Sweeping string melodies float over an oom-pah-pah triple-time accompaniment whose second beat is played slightly early, with elastic rubato, a slow free introduction, a chain of contrasting waltz tunes and a brilliant coda.
exemplars: Vienna Philharmonic New Year's Concert recordings
Willi Boskovsky and the Vienna Philharmonic, Strauss recordings (Decca)
Marco Polo/Naxos Johann Strauss II Edition

items.name: Serbska ludowa hudźba (Sorbian folk music of Lusatia)
items.lineage: Song and dance music of the Sorbs (Wends), a West Slavic minority of Upper and Lower Lusatia whose cultural centre is Bautzen in eastern Saxony. Village dances were played on the kozoł, a large goatskin bagpipe with a single drone, together with the Sorbian fiddles (husle), while the song repertoire was gathered by Leopold Haupt and Jan Arnošt Smoler in their two-volume Volkslieder der Wenden (1841-43). The cimpoi card stands in for the kozoł, and the fiddle card for the Sorbian fiddles.
items.description: A reedy bagpipe chanter over a steady drone doubles the fiddle on brisk, strophic dance tunes, and strophic songs are sung plainly in Sorbian, solo or by village groups.
exemplars: Berlin Phonogramm-Archiv wax-cylinder recordings of Sorbian song
Sorbian National Ensemble (Serbski ludowy ansambl, Bautzen) recordings

items.name: Posaunenchor (German Protestant church brass choir)
items.lineage: Amateur brass choirs of German Protestant parishes, which go back to the trombone choirs of the Moravian Brethren at Herrnhut in the eighteenth century and grew into a mass movement during the nineteenth-century revival in Minden-Ravensberg, Westphalia. Johannes Kuhlo of Bethel near Bielefeld shaped its repertoire of four-part chorale settings and its non-transposing notation, and the choirs play in services, at open-air and tower music and at large church festivals.
items.description: A choir of brass plays chorale tunes in sustained, homophonic four-part harmony, soprano melody in trumpets and flugelhorns over baritone horns, trombones and tubas, with broad phrasing, gentle dynamics and a warm, rounded blend that blooms in a reverberant church.
exemplars: Deutscher Evangelischer Posaunentag massed brass-choir performances (Leipzig 2008, Dresden 2016)

items.name: Arbeiterlied and Kampflied (German workers' fighting song)
items.lineage: Political song of the German labour movement, carried by workers' choral societies from the late nineteenth century and sharpened in the Weimar years into the Kampflied, a short marching song for unison singing. Hanns Eisler's settings of Bertolt Brecht and other poets, among them the Solidaritätslied and the Einheitsfrontlied, became its core, and Ernst Busch's recordings of them from the 1930s and later on the East German labels Lied der Zeit and Aurora fixed the performance style.
items.description: A hard-edged baritone declaims short strophic verses with crisp, forceful diction over a marching beat, piano or small brass band pounding out bass and off-beat chords, and a male chorus comes in on the refrains in blunt unison.
exemplars: Ernst Busch recordings of Hanns Eisler songs (1930s)
Ernst Busch LPs on the East German labels Lied der Zeit and Aurora

items.name: Munich sound (1970s Eurodisco)
items.lineage: Disco made in West Germany from the mid-1970s, centred on Munich, where Giorgio Moroder and Pete Bellotte produced at Musicland Studios and Michael Kunze and Sylvester Levay created Silver Convention, whose 'Fly, Robin, Fly' topped the US chart in 1975. Producer-led studio teams built records from session rhythm sections, string and horn charts and stacked choruses, and Frank Farian's Boney M., on the Hansa label, carried West German Eurodisco across Europe.
items.description: A steady four-on-the-floor kick with off-beat open hi-hat locks with an octave-bouncing bass, while sweeping strings, brass stabs and chant-like, multitracked choruses in accented English ride long, loop-like grooves, with sequenced synthesizer pulses moving to the foreground by the late 1970s.
exemplars: Musicland Studios (Munich) productions of Giorgio Moroder and Pete Bellotte

items.name: Basler Trommeln und Pfeifen (Basel Fasnacht piccolo-and-drum music)
items.lineage: Street music of the Basel carnival, played by cliques of piccolo players and drummers from the Morgenstreich at four in the morning on the Monday after Ash Wednesday through three days of processions. Its marches combine piccolos in several parts with the Basel drum, a deep rope-tensioned side drum played in a distinctive local rudimental style, for which the tenor-drum card stands in; Basel Carnival is inscribed on the UNESCO Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.
items.description: Massed piccolos play shrill, bright march tunes in close two- and three-part harmony over rope-tension drums beating tightly unison patterns of rolls, flams and accented drags, the sound bouncing off the walls of narrow streets.
exemplars: Morgenstreich recordings of the Basel cliques

items.name: Chanzuns rumantschas (Romansh folk and choral song)
items.lineage: Song in Romansh, the Rhaeto-Romance language of Graubünden, from Engadine (Ladin) folk songs and the Chalandamarz songs that children sing on 1 March with cowbells to drive out the winter, to the village men's and mixed choirs that carry much of the repertoire today. As early as 1912-15 the Engadine poet Peider Lansel recorded Ladin folk songs on a phonograph, and the folklorist Alfons Maissen later collected Romansh folk song.
items.description: Strophic songs in Romansh are sung plainly by a solo voice or, more often, by a village choir in warm, homophonic four-part harmony, with simple major-key melodies, even phrasing and clear diction.
exemplars: Peider Lansel phonograph recordings of Ladin folk songs (1912-15)
Alfons Maissen collection of Romansh folk song

items.name: Psautier de Genève (Genevan Psalter metrical psalmody)
items.lineage: Metrical psalmody of the Reformed church of Geneva: the Genevan Psalter, completed in 1562, set the French verse psalms of Clément Marot and Théodore de Bèze to 125 melodies, many of them by Louis Bourgeois, for unaccompanied congregational singing in unison. Claude Goudimel's four-part settings of 1564 brought the tunes into domestic and choral use, and the melodies spread with the Huguenots in France and to Reformed churches in the Netherlands and beyond.
items.description: Syllabic psalm tunes move in a dignified, speech-like rhythm of long and short notes, each line closing on a held note, sung in unison by a congregation or in plain note-against-note four-part chords by a small unaccompanied choir.
exemplars: Ensemble Claude Goudimel (dir. Christine Morel), Psaumes de la Réforme

items.name: Psalmzingen op de oude wijze (Dutch Reformed slow psalm singing)
items.lineage: Congregational psalm singing of orthodox Reformed churches in the Dutch Bible Belt, from Zeeland to Staphorst, where the Genevan psalm melodies in the 1773 Dutch metrical psalter are sung 'op de oude wijze', the old way, with every note levelled to the same long value. The whole congregation sings in unison, led and sustained by the church organ, keeping the levelled rhythm that took hold in Dutch churches in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, which most other Dutch Protestant churches gave up for the original rhythmic tunes in the twentieth century.
items.description: Hundreds of voices sing psalm tunes in massive unison at a very slow, even pace, every syllable held for the same long note, while a full church organ underpins and leads them, the sound swelling and hanging in the reverberant nave.
exemplars: Congregational field recordings of psalm singing in Staphorst

items.name: Midwinterhoornblazen (Twente midwinter horn blowing)
items.lineage: Seasonal custom of the Twente and Achterhoek regions in the eastern Netherlands, in which players blow the midwinterhoorn, a curved, end-blown wooden horn about a metre long, from the start of Advent to Epiphany. Players often blow their calls over the opening of a farmyard well, which carries the sound across the fields, and local groups and competitions keep the custom, which is listed in the Dutch national inventory of intangible heritage; the tautari card stands in for the midwinterhoorn.
items.description: A single wooden horn sounds short, freely timed calls on the notes of its natural harmonic series, with a hoarse, mournful edge and long held tones that ring out over open, frozen fields.
exemplars: Field recordings of midwinterhoorn blowing in Twente

items.name: Palingsound (Volendam pop)
items.lineage: Melodic pop from the fishing town of Volendam, named after the smoked eel (paling) the town is known for, that grew out of local beat groups in the 1960s. The Cats set its template of soft, sentimental songs with close-harmony vocals, and BZN, later the 3JS and Jan Smit carried it on into the twenty-first century.
items.description: Gentle mid-tempo ballads and lilting songs put a warm lead voice in front of smooth close-harmony backing, strummed acoustic and chiming electric guitars and soft string pads, in a polished, sweet and sentimental production.

items.name: Bubbling (Dutch-Antillean sped-up dancehall)
items.lineage: Party music of Dutch-Antillean, mostly Curaçaoan, youth in The Hague and Rotterdam, begun in the late 1980s and early 1990s when DJ Moortje played Jamaican dancehall records at a faster speed, and MCs chatted over them in Papiamento. Producers later made original tracks at the raised tempo, and its fast, syncopated drum patterns fed into Dutch house in the 2000s.
items.description: Dancehall riddims pitched up to a hurried, high-energy tempo, with chipmunk-bright vocals, skittering syncopated drum-machine patterns and bouncing bass, while live MCs chat and hype the crowd over the top.
exemplars: Bubbling compilations documented by Wayne Marshall

items.name: Popcorn (Belgian slow-soul dance scene)
items.lineage: Belgian club and DJ scene that grew from 1969 around De Oude Hoeve in Vrasene, East Flanders, where DJs played slow and mid-tempo American records of the 1950s and 1960s, rhythm and blues, soul, girl-group, Latin-tinged and pop sides, for a distinctive slow dance. DJs and collectors prize obscure 45s with a lilting, unhurried swing, and the repertoire lives on in Flemish clubs and on compilation series such as Popcorn Oldies.
items.description: Slow-to-mid-tempo 45s with a lilting, swaying swing: a soulful lead voice over backing vocals, honking or crooning saxophone, piano triplets, light guitar and a relaxed brushed or stick backbeat, often with a minor-key or Latin-tinged lilt.

items.name: Airs de Gilles (Binche carnival music)
items.lineage: Music of the Carnival of Binche in Hainaut, where the Gilles, costumed dancers in wooden clogs with belts of bells, dance through the streets on Shrove Tuesday to short airs beaten out by drummers and played on the viole, a barrel organ, with brass bands joining the processions. UNESCO proclaimed the carnival a Masterpiece of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity, and it is now on the Representative List; the tenor-drum card stands in for the carnival drums and the shaker card for the belts of bells.
items.description: An insistent drum pulse drives short, endlessly repeated dance airs on barrel organ or brass, while hundreds of stamping clogs and jangling belt bells thicken the street into a dense, shimmering rhythmic mass.
exemplars: Recordings of the airs de Gilles of the Carnival of Binche

items.name: Cramignon and chanson wallonne (Walloon song of Liège)
items.lineage: Song in the Walloon language of the Liège region, whose best-known form is the cramignon, a chain dance in which a long line of dancers holding hands winds through the streets behind a leader while singing short strophic songs. Cramignon texts and tunes were collected and published under the Société liégeoise de littérature wallonne in the 1870s, and cramignons are still danced at summer village festivals in the Basse-Meuse.
items.description: A crowd of dancers sings short, strophic Walloon songs in lively duple time, simple major-key tunes repeated verse after verse as the line moves, with the voices loud, informal and slightly ragged in the open street.
exemplars: Cramignon collections of the Société liégeoise de littérature wallonne

items.name: Ring shout (McIntosh County coastal Georgia shout)
items.lineage: Counterclockwise sacred shuffle-dance and song of the Gullah-Geechee communities of the Georgia and South Carolina coast, described in accounts of the 1860s and regarded as the oldest African American performance tradition still practised in North America. In Bolden (Briar Patch), McIntosh County, the McIntosh County Shouters kept it alive and brought it to wider attention in the 1980s. A songster raises the song, a group of basers answers, and a stickman beats time with a broomstick on the wooden floor while the shouters move in a ring with shuffling feet that never cross, clapping; the auxiliary-percussion card stands in for the stick and the foot-stomp card for the shouters' feet.
items.description: A leader's call is answered by a low, driving chorus over the hard knock of a stick on floorboards, sharp handclaps and shuffling feet, the song repeating and building in tempo and intensity as the ring turns.
exemplars: McIntosh County Shouters - Slave Shout Songs from the Coast of Georgia (Folkways FE 4344, 1984)
Library of Congress field recordings of coastal Georgia shouts (1930s)

items.name: Shout band (United House of Prayer trombone choir)
items.lineage: Brass choirs of the United House of Prayer for All People, the church founded by Bishop Charles Manuel 'Sweet Daddy' Grace, which play for worship, baptisms, convocations and parades in its congregations from the Carolinas to Washington, DC and the Northeast. A shout band can field a dozen or more trombones led by a lead trombonist who phrases like a gospel singer, with baritone horns and sousaphone beneath and snare drum, bass drum and cymbals; hymn melodies stretch into long, accelerating riff vamps that drive the congregation's shouting.
items.description: A massed wall of trombones swells from a hymn tune into riffing, accelerating vamps, a lead trombone wailing and sliding over baritone horns, sousaphone and pounding marching drums.
exemplars: Saints' Paradise: Trombone Shout Bands from the United House of Prayer (Smithsonian Folkways, 1999)

items.name: Dr. Watts hymnody (African American lined-out hymns)
items.lineage: Congregational hymn practice of Black Baptist and other Protestant churches, above all in the devotional service that opens worship: a deacon or leader chants out a line or couplet of a hymn by Isaac Watts or another English hymn writer, and the congregation answers by singing it very slowly in long meter. It continues the lining out of 17th- and 18th-century British and colonial churches, transformed in African American worship into long, melismatic, heterophonic singing without instruments; Library of Congress field recordings and William T. Dargan's study Lining Out the Word document it.
items.description: A leader's half-chanted line gives way to the whole congregation drawing out the same words in an extremely slow, moaning unison that splinters into overlapping ornamental turns, with no instruments and no steady beat.
exemplars: Negro Religious Songs and Services (Library of Congress AFS L10)
William T. Dargan, Lining Out the Word (University of California Press, 2006)

items.name: Old Regular Baptist lined hymnody (southeastern Kentucky)
items.lineage: Unaccompanied congregational hymn singing of the Old Regular Baptists, a conservative Baptist association of the central Appalachian coalfields of eastern Kentucky, southwestern Virginia and southern West Virginia that uses no instruments in worship. A song leader chants each line of a hymn from a words-only hymnbook and the congregation follows in slow, free-flowing unison, each singer adding personal ornaments so that the voices overlap in a dense heterophony; Smithsonian Folkways issued recordings made among the Indian Bottom Association of Letcher County and neighbouring congregations in 1997.
items.description: Slow, keening congregational unison in which each chanted line is stretched and individually ornamented, so the voices drift around one another in a thick, plaintive heterophony with no instruments and no regular pulse.
exemplars: Songs of the Old Regular Baptists: Lined-Out Hymnody from Southeastern Kentucky (Smithsonian Folkways SFW40106, 1997)
Indian Bottom Association of Old Regular Baptists

items.name: American Moravian music (Salem and Bethlehem trombone choirs and anthems)
items.lineage: Sacred and instrumental music of the Moravian Church settlements founded in the 18th century at Bethlehem and Nazareth, Pennsylvania, and Salem (now Winston-Salem), North Carolina, whose collegia musica performed European concert music and whose own composers, among them Johann Friedrich Peter and Jeremiah Dencke, wrote German-texted anthems and arias for voices with strings, winds and organ. Trombone choirs spanning soprano to bass instruments announce deaths, play chorales for church festivals and lead the Easter sunrise service, a practice that continues; the Moravian Music Foundation in Winston-Salem holds the manuscript archives. The fiddle card stands for the violins.
items.description: Mellow chorales voiced across a family of trombones from soprano to bass alternate with Classical-style anthems in which choir and soloists sing over strings and organ, in clear, homophonic, gently ornamented textures.
exemplars: Boston Baroque - Lost Music of Early America: Music of the Moravians (Telarc, 1998)

items.name: Alabados (New Mexican Penitente hymns)
items.lineage: Spanish-language devotional hymns of the Hermanos Penitentes, the lay brotherhoods of Nuestro Padre Jesús Nazareno in the villages of northern New Mexico and southern Colorado, sung in their moradas, in Holy Week processions and at wakes. Long strophic texts on the Passion, the Virgin and the saints, descended from Spanish colonial religious song, are sung slowly and without fixed meter by the brothers or by a solo singer, and in procession a pitero answers the verses on the pito, a small homemade wooden flute, for which a source-unspecified flute card stands; Juan B. Rael recorded alabados for the Library of Congress in 1940.
items.description: Slow, unmetered strophic hymns sung by men's voices in rough unison, answered between verses by the piercing, wavering tones of a small wooden flute.
exemplars: Music of New Mexico: Hispanic Traditions (Smithsonian Folkways SF 40409, 1992)
Juan B. Rael 1940 Library of Congress recordings of northern New Mexico and southern Colorado

items.name: Molokan singing (Russian Spiritual Christian psalms, California)
items.lineage: Unaccompanied sacred singing of the Molokans, Russian Spiritual Christians who reject icons and instruments, brought to California by families who began emigrating from the Transcaucasus in about 1904 and settled on Potrero Hill in San Francisco and in the Boyle Heights 'Flats' of Los Angeles. Psalms and spiritual songs in Russian are begun by a song leader and taken up by the whole congregation in slow, richly ornamented heterophonic part-singing; Sidney Robertson Cowell recorded singing and preaching at the Russian Molokan Church on Potrero Hill in 1938 for the WPA California Folk Music Project.
items.description: A single voice sets the opening of a psalm and the congregation enters in slow, swelling part-singing, the lines weaving ornamental turns around one another without instruments.
exemplars: Sidney Robertson Cowell, WPA California Folk Music Project recordings at the Russian Molokan Church, Potrero Hill (1938, Library of Congress)

items.name: California mission music (Franciscan canto figurado)
items.lineage: Liturgical music of the Franciscan missions of Alta California from the 1770s to the 1830s, taught to choirs and instrumentalists drawn from the missions' Native converts by friars such as Narciso Durán at Mission San José and Juan Bautista Sancho at Mission San Antonio de Padua. The repertory joins plainchant with canto figurado, measured part-singing in two to four voices copied into large mission choirbooks, and concerted masses with violins, cellos, bass and winds; Craig H. Russell's research and editions underlie modern recordings. The fiddle card stands for the violins.
items.description: Unison chant alternates with sturdy measured part-singing and with festive mass movements in which the voices are framed by violins, cellos and bass, all resonating in a plastered adobe church.
exemplars: Craig H. Russell, From Serra to Sancho: Music and Pageantry in the California Missions (Oxford University Press, 2009)

items.name: Gospel hymn (Moody-Sankey revival song)
items.lineage: Popular evangelical song of the urban revival campaigns led by the preacher Dwight L. Moody with the singer Ira D. Sankey from the 1870s, collected in Gospel Hymns and Sacred Songs (1875) and its many successors and written by Fanny Crosby, Philip P. Bliss, William H. Doane and others. Verse-and-refrain songs with simple tonic-dominant harmony and personal, testimonial texts were sung by a soloist at a reed organ and taken up by mass congregations and choirs, and Homer Rodeheaver, song leader for the evangelist Billy Sunday, carried the style onto records in the 1910s and 1920s.
items.description: A clear, earnest solo voice sings each verse over sustained reed-organ chords, and the congregation or choir joins in a rousing, four-square refrain built on a few simple chords.
exemplars: Gospel Hymns and Sacred Songs (Bliss and Sankey, 1875)

items.name: North Mississippi fife-and-drum (cane fife picnic music)
items.lineage: African American fife-and-drum band music of the north Mississippi hill country around Como, Senatobia and Gravel Springs in Panola and Tate counties, played at summer picnics and dances. Alan Lomax recorded Sid Hemphill's band in 1942, and Napoleon Strickland and Othar Turner's Rising Star Fife and Drum Band carried it to the end of the 20th century, continued by Turner's granddaughter Sharde Thomas. A homemade cane fife plays short, blues-inflected riffs and hollered phrases over two snare drums and a bass drum locked in dense polyrhythmic patterns, while dancers press close around the drummers.
items.description: A breathy, piercing cane fife cries short bluesy riffs over a booming bass drum and two snares weaving tight interlocking patterns in a hypnotic, repeating dance groove.
exemplars: Othar Turner & the Rising Star Fife and Drum Band - Everybody Hollerin' Goat (Birdman, 1998)
Alan Lomax 1942 Library of Congress recordings of Sid Hemphill's band

items.name: Texas contest fiddling (long-bow Texas style)
items.lineage: Virtuosic fiddle style shaped by the fiddle contests of Texas and the Southwest, whose first landmark on record was Eck Robertson's 1922 Victor recording of 'Sallie Gooden', and which Benny Thomasson, Major Franklin and their contemporaries developed into an elaborated contest repertoire in the mid-20th century, kept up at contests such as the Hallettsville fiddlers' frolics. Breakdowns, hornpipes, waltzes and rags are played with long, smooth bow strokes and many varied passes through each strain, backed by a guitarist playing closed, swing-derived chord shapes and moving bass runs.
items.description: Smooth, long-bowed fiddle lines spin continuous variations through each strain of a breakdown or waltz, over a guitar that walks bass runs and swings closed chord shapes in a relaxed, driving two-beat.

items.name: Freedom songs (US civil-rights movement singing)
items.lineage: Congregational protest singing of the Southern civil-rights movement of the 1950s and 1960s, made by adapting spirituals, hymns, gospel and union songs with new words in mass meetings, marches and jail cells. It was especially strong in the 1961-62 Albany Movement in Georgia, out of which Cordell Reagon, Bernice Johnson (Reagon), Rutha Harris and Charles Neblett formed the SNCC Freedom Singers in 1962 to carry the songs on tour. A song leader raises or lines out a verse and the crowd answers in full-voiced unison and harmony, usually unaccompanied except for handclaps.
items.description: A strong lead voice raises each verse and a packed room answers in full-throated unison and harmony over steady handclaps, the refrains repeating and swelling as new verses are made up.
exemplars: Voices of the Civil Rights Movement: Black American Freedom Songs 1960-1966 (Smithsonian Folkways SFW40084, 1997)

items.name: Juré and la-la (Louisiana Creole pre-zydeco music)
items.lineage: Older layers of the Black Creole French music of the prairies of southwest Louisiana, before zydeco took its name. Juré was unaccompanied singing for dancing, a leader answered by a group over handclaps and stamping feet, recorded by John and Alan Lomax in 1934 around Jennings; la-la was the Creole house-dance music in which a single-row diatonic accordion and fiddle played two-steps, waltzes and bluesy reels over a scraped rubboard, kept up into the late 20th century by the accordionist Alphonse 'Bois Sec' Ardoin and the fiddler Canray Fontenot. The Cajun-accordion card stands for this single-row diatonic button accordion, an instrument Creole and Cajun musicians share.
items.description: Hoarse, high-pitched French singing answered by a group over clapping and stamping, beside a wheezing accordion and scratchy fiddle playing bluesy two-steps and waltzes over a ringing scraped rhythm.
exemplars: Jimmy Peters and ring dance singers, Lomax 1934 Library of Congress recordings (Louisiana Cajun and Creole Music 1934, Swallow)

items.name: Isleño décimas (St. Bernard Parish Canary Islander ballads)
items.lineage: Sung Spanish narrative poems of the Isleños, descendants of Canary Islanders settled by the Spanish colonial government in St. Bernard Parish, Louisiana, in the late 18th century, whose trapping and fishing communities centred on Delacroix Island. Décimas recount local events, storms, hunting and courtship alongside older Spanish romances, sung unaccompanied by a solo singer in a free, declamatory style; Irván Pérez, named an NEA National Heritage Fellow in 1991, was its best-known singer and composer, and Samuel G. Armistead documented the repertoire.
items.description: One unaccompanied voice sings long strophic stories, half-declaimed and half-sung, with free, speech-led phrasing and a plain, weathered tone.
exemplars: Samuel G. Armistead field recordings of Isleño folk literature

items.name: Música nuevomexicana (northern New Mexico Hispano folk)
items.lineage: Older Spanish-language folk music of the Hispano villages of the upper Rio Grande, from Taos and Rio Arriba County into southern Colorado, before the postwar electric New Mexico style. Fiddle and guitar play the baile repertoire of valses, polkas, chotises, the varsoviana, the cuna and the valse de la escoba for weddings and dances, and singers keep romances, corridos and inditas; Cleofes Vigil of San Cristóbal and the field collections of the John Donald Robb Archive at the University of New Mexico document it.
items.description: A sweet, slightly rough fiddle leads lilting waltzes, polkas and schottisches over strummed guitar chords, alternating with plain-voiced Spanish ballads sung to the guitar.
exemplars: Music of New Mexico: Hispanic Traditions (Smithsonian Folkways SF 40409, 1992)
John Donald Robb Archive of Southwestern Music, University of New Mexico

items.name: Polish-American polka (Chicago honky and Eastern styles)
items.lineage: Dance music of Polish-American communities in Chicago, Buffalo, Detroit, Connecticut and the Northeast. The Chicago 'honky' or 'push' style, launched in the postwar years by Li'l Wally Jagiello's records on his own Jay Jay label, slowed the tempo and centred a Chemnitzer concertina, one or two trumpets, bass and drums behind singing in Polish and English, and was later shaped by Eddie Blazonczyk's Versatones; the brassier, faster Eastern style favoured clarinets and trumpet sections in tight harmony. The concertina card stands in for the Chemnitzer.
items.description: A reedy concertina pumps melody and bellows-shaken chords beside bright trumpets and clarinet over a bouncing two-beat of bass and drums, with hearty bilingual singing at a relaxed, swinging dance tempo.
exemplars: Charles Keil et al., Polka Happiness (1992)

items.name: Cleveland-style polka (Slovenian-American)
items.lineage: Polka style of the Slovenian-American neighbourhoods of Cleveland, Ohio, which reworked Slovenian folk tunes and dance songs into a smooth, swinging American dance-band sound; Frankie Yankovic's 1948 Columbia hit 'Just Because' made it nationally popular, alongside the accordionists Johnny Pecon and Lou Trebar. The lead is a piano or button accordion, often doubled by a saxophone in close harmony, over a banjo chording on the offbeats, bass and drums, with vocals in English or Slovenian.
items.description: A bright accordion leads in smooth, swinging phrases doubled by a saxophone, over offbeat banjo chords, walking bass and light drums, in bouncy polkas and lilting waltzes.

items.name: Kef music (Armenian-American dance ensemble)
items.lineage: Party and dance music of Armenian-American communities in Fresno, Watertown, Detroit, New York and Providence, played at 'kef time' picnics, weddings and church dances by ensembles of oud, clarinet, violin, kanun and dumbek, later joined by electric bass and keyboards. Its repertoire grew from the Anatolian music the immigrants brought from their home towns in the Ottoman Empire, with improvised taksims, line dances in even and odd meters and songs in Armenian and Turkish; the Fresno oudist Richard Hagopian, an NEA National Heritage Fellow, is among its best-known players. The darbuka card stands in for the dumbek.
items.description: Oud and kanun trade ornate, freely improvised preludes before clarinet, violin and goblet drum lock into lively line-dance grooves in even and odd meters, with heterophonic melody and modal turns.
exemplars: Richard Hagopian - Armenian Music Through the Ages (Smithsonian Folkways)

items.name: Yiddish theatre song (Second Avenue operetta)
items.lineage: Song and operetta of the Yiddish theatre of New York's Lower East Side and Second Avenue from the 1880s to the 1950s, where composers such as Joseph Rumshinsky, Sholom Secunda, Abraham Ellstein and Alexander Olshanetsky wrote for stars including Boris Thomashefsky, Molly Picon and Aaron Lebedeff. Show tunes and comic patter songs mixed Eastern European Jewish modes and cantorial-style melisma with waltzes, marches, tangos and American popular-song forms, sung over a pit orchestra of strings, clarinet, brass and piano and widely issued on 78 rpm records.
items.description: A theatrical lead voice swings between comic patter and sobbing, melismatic laments in minor modes, riding a bright pit orchestra of violins, clarinet, trumpet and piano in waltz, march and foxtrot rhythms.
exemplars: 78 rpm recordings of Aaron Lebedeff, Molly Picon and Boris Thomashefsky
YIVO and Yiddish Book Center sound archives

items.name: Mummers string band (Philadelphia New Year's parade)
items.lineage: Costumed marching bands of the Philadelphia Mummers Parade held every New Year's Day, organised as clubs rooted in the South Philadelphia neighbourhoods around Two Street and judged in a String Band Division. Parade rules bar brass instruments, so dozens of banjos and saxophones with accordions, violins, string basses, glockenspiels and drums play arranged popular songs and marches while the members strut in elaborate costumes; the Ferko String Band's 'Alabama Jubilee' became a national hit in 1955.
items.description: A massed, jangling wall of banjos and saxophones carries brisk marches and old popular tunes in a strutting two-beat, sparkled by glockenspiel, accordion and violins over string bass and drums.
exemplars: Ferko String Band - Alabama Jubilee (Media Records, 1955)
Philadelphia Mummers Parade String Band Division recordings

items.name: Pachuco boogie (1940s Los Angeles caló jump)
items.lineage: Mexican-American jump and boogie-woogie of 1940s Los Angeles, sung in caló, the slang of the zoot-suited pachuco youth, over swing-band and jump-blues arrangements. The Don Tosti Band's 'Pachuco Boogie' of 1948, half-spoken in caló over a boogie piano and saxophone groove, became one of the biggest-selling Latin records of its day, and Lalo Guerrero, later called the father of Chicano music, recorded caló boogies and swing numbers in the same years.
items.description: A rolling boogie-woogie piano bass and honking tenor saxophone drive a swinging jump groove while the singer half-talks, half-sings streetwise slang lines with laid-back, conversational swagger.

items.name: West Side Sound (San Antonio Chicano R&B)
items.lineage: Rhythm-and-blues, soul and rock-and-roll scene of San Antonio from the late 1950s, in which Mexican-American groups such as Sunny & the Sunliners played alongside Anglo musicians such as Doug Sahm and Augie Meyers, mixing horn-driven R&B and doo-wop-style ballads with conjunto, polka and country. Sunny & the Sunliners' 'Talk to Me' reached the national charts in 1963, and Sahm and Meyers carried the scene's Vox-organ and horn-section sound into the Sir Douglas Quintet.
items.description: Tight horn riffs and a reedy combo organ punch over twangy guitar, bass and backbeat drums, alternating sweet, aching soul ballads with stomping dance numbers that borrow a polka bounce.
exemplars: Sunny & the Sunliners - Talk to Me (1963)

items.name: Minstrel-show music (19th-century blackface stage song)
items.lineage: Music of the blackface minstrel show, the racist stage entertainment in which mostly white performers caricatured African Americans, launched as a full evening by the Virginia Minstrels in New York in 1843 and dominant in American popular theatre through the later 19th century; Black troupes also worked within the form after the Civil War. The early minstrel band of fretless, gut-strung five-string banjo, fiddle, bones and tambourine played reels, jigs and walkarounds behind comic songs and dances, while later shows added sentimental ballads and brass bands, and minstrel songs were among the material on the first commercial cylinders.
items.description: A plunky, gut-strung banjo and scraping fiddle play bouncing reels and jigs while bones clatter and a tambourine jingles, framing comic songs and sentimental ballads in a brisk, theatrical stage style.
exemplars: Billy Golden minstrel cylinders and 78s (Library of Congress National Jukebox)

items.name: American parlor song (19th-century sentimental ballad)
items.lineage: Sentimental songs for voice and piano published as sheet music for middle-class American homes from the 1820s through the 1890s by composers including Henry Russell, Stephen Foster, George F. Root and Henry Clay Work, on themes of home, lost love, mothers, death and temperance. Strophic verses, often with a refrain for vocal quartet, sit over simple tonic-dominant accompaniment on the parlor piano or guitar; the songs passed into early commercial recordings and into later historically informed revivals.
items.description: A clear, earnest voice sings simple strophic melodies of home and loss over gentle broken-chord piano in an intimate domestic room, with plain harmony and an unhurried, sentimental lilt.
exemplars: Jan DeGaetani and Leslie Guinn - Songs by Stephen Foster (Nonesuch, 1972)
early Edison cylinders of parlor ballads

items.name: Cowboy poetry (ranch-country recitation)
items.lineage: Rhymed, metered verse about ranch work, horses, weather and the open range, composed and recited by working cowboys and ranch people of the American West since the late 19th century, with classics by poets such as Badger Clark and Bruce Kiskaddon circulating orally. The National Cowboy Poetry Gathering, first held in Elko, Nevada in 1985 and organised by the Western Folklife Center, revived it as a public performance form in which poets such as Waddie Mitchell and Baxter Black recite from memory, usually without accompaniment.
items.description: A single unaccompanied speaking voice delivers rhymed, steadily metered verse in a dry, conversational drawl, timing pauses and punchlines for a listening audience.
exemplars: National Cowboy Poetry Gathering recordings (Western Folklife Center archive, Elko)

items.name: Toasts (African American narrative recitation)
items.lineage: Long rhymed narrative poems of African American men's oral tradition, recited on street corners, in bars and barbershops and above all in prisons from at least the early 20th century, with stock heroes and tricksters such as the Signifying Monkey, Stagolee, Shine of the Titanic and Dolemite. Roger D. Abrahams collected them in South Philadelphia for Deep Down in the Jungle (1964) and Bruce Jackson recorded them in prisons and cities between 1964 and 1976; Rudy Ray Moore's party records brought the form to LP, and its boasting, rhymed delivery is often cited among the roots of rap.
items.description: One unaccompanied voice rolls through long rhymed couplets in a strong, swaggering spoken rhythm, shifting into character voices for dialogue and landing each comic or violent punchline for a live audience.
exemplars: Bruce Jackson field recordings, Get Your Ass in the Water and Swim Like Me (Rounder)
Roger D. Abrahams, Deep Down in the Jungle (1964)

items.name: Novelty piano (1920s keyboard novelty)
items.lineage: Virtuoso solo piano genre of the early 1920s that succeeded ragtime, written largely for the piano-roll and sheet-music trade; Zez Confrey's 'Kitten on the Keys' (1921) launched it, followed by his 'Dizzy Fingers' and pieces by Roy Bargy and others. Showy pieces at strict, bright tempos use syncopated three-note figures running across the bar, parallel fourths, whole-tone and chromatic runs and harmonic colours borrowed from impressionism, played with crisp, mechanical precision.
items.description: Glittering solo piano spins rapid syncopated cross-rhythms, chromatic runs and parallel-fourth flourishes over a steady striding left hand, with the brittle, precise attack of a piano roll.
exemplars: Zez Confrey - Kitten on the Keys (1921) piano rolls and 78s

items.name: West gallery music (English village church bands and quires)
items.lineage: Psalmody and anthems sung by village choirs (quires) and played by small church bands from galleries at the west end of English parish churches and chapels, roughly 1700 to 1850, until Victorian church reform replaced them with surpliced chancel choirs and organs or harmoniums. Provincial psalmodists wrote plain and fuging settings in three or four parts, usually with the tune in the tenor, and bands of fiddles, flutes, clarinets, bassoons, serpents and bass viols doubled the voices. Thomas Hardy portrayed the Mellstock quire in Under the Greenwood Tree, and the repertoire has been revived by West Gallery Music Association quires. The cello card stands in for the church bass viol.
items.description: Four-part psalm tunes and anthems are sung full-voiced by a mixed village choir with the tune in the tenor, while fiddle, clarinet, bassoon, serpent and bass viol double the vocal lines in a reverberant stone nave; plain chordal verses alternate with fuging passages in which the parts enter one after another.

items.name: Change ringing (English full-circle church bell ringing)
items.lineage: The ringing of a ring of tuned church bells, commonly six, eight, ten or twelve, hung to swing through a full circle, each bell rung by one ringer pulling a rope, so that the bells strike in constantly changing orders by mathematical methods rather than playing tunes. It developed in seventeenth-century England: the Ancient Society of College Youths was founded in London in 1637, and Tintinnalogia (1668) and Fabian Stedman's Campanalogia (1677) set out the first methods. A full peal of some 5,000 changes lasts around three hours. The carillon card stands in for the tower ring of bells.
items.description: Heavy bronze bells tuned to a descending major scale strike one after another in an even, unbroken stream, first in rounds and then in constantly permuting orders, with a slight gap at each handstroke lead; the long, beating hum of the larger bells overlaps the following strokes, heard from outside the tower as a continuous wash that finally returns to rounds.
exemplars: Central Council of Church Bell Ringers

items.name: Lambeg drumming (Ulster Lambeg drum and fife)
items.lineage: The Lambeg, named after a village near Lisburn, is a very large double-headed drum, roughly three feet across, carried on a harness and beaten on both goatskin heads with two curved canes, often with a fife playing the tune. It belongs to the Orange marching tradition of counties Antrim, Armagh, Down and Tyrone and to competitive drumming matches between drummers. Gary Hastings documented the drumming and its fife tunes in his book With Fife and Drum.
items.description: A thunderous, continuous roll of dense, rattling cane strokes on both heads of a huge, tightly braced drum, with a shrill fife carrying march and dance tunes above it; at matches several drums are beaten side by side in the open air and their roar carries a great distance.
exemplars: Gary Hastings, With Fife and Drum (Blackstaff Press, 2003)

items.name: Ulster flute bands (blood-and-thunder and melody marching bands)
items.lineage: Marching bands of flutes and drums that lead the parades of the Orange Order, the Royal Black Institution and the Apprentice Boys of Derry through the Northern Ireland marching season around the Twelfth of July. Blood-and-thunder bands play simple-system B-flat flutes in unison over loud side drums and a bass drum swung with exaggerated strokes, while melody and part-music flute bands play keyed flutes in arranged parts and compete in band contests. Gordon Ramsey's study of the bands documents their music and identity; the generic flute card stands in for the band flutes.
items.description: A massed line of shrill flutes plays march tunes in unison or in parts at a strict marching tempo over crisp, loud side drums, cymbal crashes and a pounding bass drum, recorded in the street as the band passes, with crowd noise and echo from terraced housing.
exemplars: Gordon Ramsey, Music, Emotion and Identity in Ulster Marching Bands (Peter Lang, 2011)
BBC Northern Ireland Twelfth of July parade broadcasts

items.name: Sliabh Luachra music (Cork-Kerry polkas and slides)
items.lineage: Dance music of the Sliabh Luachra uplands where counties Cork, Kerry and Limerick meet, around Ballydesmond, Knocknagree, Gneeveguilla and Scartaglen, associated above all with the fiddle master Pádraig O'Keeffe and his pupils Denis Murphy, Julia Clifford and Paddy Cronin. Its staple tunes are polkas and slides for the local set dances, alongside jigs, reels and hornpipes, played on fiddle and button accordion; the Topic LP Kerry Fiddles and the recordings of accordionists Johnny O'Leary and Jackie Daly documented it.
items.description: Bouncy, driving polkas in 2/4 and slides in 12/8 on fiddle and button accordion, often played in unison as a duet, with a strong rhythmic lift for set dancing, open-string drones and double stops, and a punchy, accented attack rather than dense ornament.

items.name: Donegal fiddle tradition (Ulster highlands and mazurkas)
items.lineage: The fiddle music of County Donegal in north-west Ulster, carried by travelling tinsmith fiddlers such as John Doherty and his family and by settled players in districts such as Glenties, Teelin and Gweedore. Beside reels, jigs and hornpipes it keeps highlands, barndances, germans and mazurkas, many tunes shared with Scotland through seasonal migration for farm work, and it is played at fast tempos with much single-note bowing; Tommy Peoples, James Byrne and Mairéad Ní Mhaonaigh of Altan carried it into the revival.
items.description: Fast, driving reels, highlands and mazurkas on solo or paired fiddles, with mostly single-note bowing, crisp bowed triplets in place of fingered rolls, and droning open strings and double stops that give a hard, ringing edge.

items.name: Showband (Irish ballroom dance bands)
items.lineage: Seven- or eight-piece touring dance bands that filled Irish ballrooms through the 1960s, a style begun in the 1950s by the Clipper Carlton of Strabane, who stood and put on a show instead of sitting behind music stands. A front line of trumpet, trombone and saxophone with electric guitar, bass, drums and keyboards backed a lead singer through covers of current pop, rock and roll and country hits; the Royal Showband's 'The Hucklebuck' (1965) and Dickie Rock and the Miami Showband's singles reached number one in Ireland.
items.description: Bright brass-and-saxophone riffs and a tight rhythm section of twangy electric guitar, bass and drums back a lead vocalist in danceable covers of pop, rock and roll and country songs, with horn stabs, saxophone breaks and a polished, cheerful ballroom energy.
exemplars: The Royal Showband with Brendan Bowyer, The Hucklebuck (1965)
Dickie Rock and the Miami Showband

items.name: Irish Traveller song (Mincéir ballad singing)
items.lineage: Singing of the Irish Travellers (Mincéirí or Pavees), a nomadic ethnic minority whose singers kept long narrative ballads, including rare Child ballads, alongside topical and street songs, mostly sung unaccompanied. The collector Tom Munnelly recorded John Reilly of Boyle in the 1960s, and Traveller street singers Margaret Barry and Pecker Dunne, who accompanied themselves on banjo, reached revival audiences; Musical Traditions' From Puck to Appleby gathers Jim Carroll and Pat Mackenzie's recordings of Irish Traveller singers living in and around London.
items.description: A single unaccompanied voice delivers long strophic ballads at a slow, flexible pace, in a strong, carrying tone with decorated melodic turns and long-held notes, stretching or hurrying lines to suit the words.
exemplars: From Puck to Appleby (Musical Traditions MTCD325-6)

items.name: Romanichal song (English Gypsy singing)
items.lineage: Singing of the Romanichal, the Romani Gypsies of England, who kept a large repertoire of narrative ballads, broadside and local songs, sung unaccompanied at family gatherings, horse fairs and pubs. Singers recorded from the 1950s onward include Phoebe Smith of Woodbridge in Suffolk and members of Gypsy families in Sussex and Kent, and their recordings were issued in Topic's Voice of the People series.
items.description: A single unaccompanied voice sings long strophic ballads with a forthright, carrying tone, small slides and grace notes, and a free, speech-shaped rhythm that lingers on held notes at the ends of lines.
exemplars: Topic Records, The Voice of the People series (tracks by English Gypsy singers)

items.name: Black British gospel (UK gospel choirs)
items.lineage: Gospel music of Black British churches, rooted in the Pentecostal and other Black-majority congregations founded by Caribbean migrants after the Second World War and later by West African communities, with choirs singing in a style drawn from African American gospel. The London Community Gospel Choir, founded in 1982, took it to concert and television audiences, and the Kingdom Choir's performance of 'Stand by Me' at a 2018 royal wedding led to a Sony album.
items.description: A large choir sings in close three-part harmony behind a soloist who improvises melismatic runs, over organ, piano, bass and drums, building from quiet verses through key changes to shouted, hand-clapping vamps.
exemplars: The Kingdom Choir, Stand By Me (Sony, 2018)

items.name: Ballad opera (Georgian English song-play)
items.lineage: An English stage form launched by John Gay's The Beggar's Opera (1728), in which spoken dialogue alternates with short songs set to well-known tunes, broadside airs and borrowed opera melodies, with an overture and basses arranged by Johann Christoph Pepusch. Its satire of Italian opera started a vogue for ballad operas in London and the provinces over the following decade, and modern productions and recordings use either period instruments or later arrangements.
items.description: Short strophic airs on simple, catchy popular tunes are sung by actors in plain, clearly enunciated English between stretches of spoken dialogue, accompanied by a small band of strings and oboe over a harpsichord continuo.
exemplars: The Beggar's Opera (John Gay and Johann Christoph Pepusch, 1728)
The Broadside Band, The Beggar's Opera (Hyperion)

items.name: Savoy opera (Gilbert and Sullivan comic opera)
items.lineage: The comic operas written by W. S. Gilbert and Arthur Sullivan between 1871 and 1896 and most of them produced by Richard D'Oyly Carte and named after the Savoy Theatre in London that Carte built for them in 1881, among them H.M.S. Pinafore, The Pirates of Penzance, The Mikado and The Gondoliers. The D'Oyly Carte Opera Company kept the performing tradition as a fixed house style and recorded the canon repeatedly, for HMV and from 1949 for Decca, until the company closed in 1982.
items.description: Crisply enunciated patter songs rattle off rapid comic verse over light orchestral accompaniment, alternating with lyrical ballads, madrigal-like ensembles and full choruses that echo the soloists, in a bright, tuneful theatre-orchestra sound that puts clear diction ahead of vocal display.
exemplars: D'Oyly Carte Opera Company recordings (HMV, Decca)

items.name: English pastoral school (folk-song-based concert music)
items.lineage: A strand of early twentieth-century English concert music led by Ralph Vaughan Williams, who began collecting folk songs in 1903, and George Butterworth, and continued by Ivor Gurney, Gerald Finzi and E. J. Moeran, which drew melody and modal harmony from English folk song and Tudor church music. Characteristic works include The Lark Ascending, Butterworth's A Shropshire Lad rhapsody and The Banks of Green Willow, and song cycles on Housman and Hardy; the composer Elisabeth Lutyens's jibe 'cowpat music' became its nickname.
items.description: Modal melodies shaped like folk songs float over slowly shifting string harmonies, with parallel chords, gentle woodwind and horn solos and a high, rhapsodic solo violin, unfolding in unhurried, freely paced phrases and soft, glowing orchestral colour.
exemplars: Ralph Vaughan Williams, The Lark Ascending
Lyrita and Chandos recordings of English pastoral repertoire

items.name: Trad (British traditional jazz boom)
items.lineage: The British revival of New Orleans and Dixieland jazz that grew in London clubs after the Second World War with Humphrey Lyttelton, Ken Colyer and Chris Barber, whose band also launched the skiffle craze through Lonnie Donegan, and that became a mass pop fad around 1959 to 1962. Chris Barber's 'Petite Fleur', Acker Bilk's 'Stranger on the Shore' and Kenny Ball's 'Midnight in Moscow' were international hits before beat groups displaced the bands after 1963. The generic banjo card stands in for the four-string banjos most bands used.
items.description: A front line of trumpet, clarinet and trombone weaves collective polyphony over a steady banjo-and-bass four-beat, the clarinet weaving around the lead with a warm, wide vibrato, as the band stomps through marches, rags and pop tunes at bright, danceable tempos.
exemplars: Acker Bilk, Stranger on the Shore (1961)
Kenny Ball and his Jazzmen, Midnight in Moscow
Chris Barber's Jazz Band, Petite Fleur

items.name: Drawing-room ballad (Victorian and Edwardian parlour song)
items.lineage: Sentimental strophic songs for voice and piano written for the Victorian and Edwardian middle-class drawing room and sold as sheet music, including the 'royalty ballads' that publishers such as Boosey promoted by paying star singers a royalty on sheet-music sales to perform them, notably at the London Ballad Concerts begun in 1867. Arthur Sullivan's 'The Lost Chord' and Frederic Weatherly's lyrics such as 'Danny Boy' typify it, and Clara Butt, John McCormack and Peter Dawson recorded the repertoire extensively in the acoustic era.
items.description: A trained solo voice, often a rich contralto or baritone, sings a slow, sentimental strophic melody with a soaring final refrain over simple arpeggiated piano chords, every word clearly enunciated, heard through the narrow band and surface hiss of an acoustic-horn 78.

items.name: Theatre organ (British cinema and ballroom organ)
items.lineage: Light music played on the theatre organs installed in British cinemas and dance halls from the 1920s, mainly Wurlitzer and Compton unit organs whose tibia and string ranks, heavy tremulants and built-in percussion let one player sound like an orchestra. Reginald Dixon, organist at the Blackpool Tower Ballroom from 1930 to 1970, made it a dance-band sound with strict-tempo medleys and his signature tune 'I Do Like to Be Beside the Seaside', and Sandy MacPherson broadcast on the BBC Theatre Organ. The pipe organ card is set to its theatre voicing.
items.description: A single organist plays strict-tempo dance medleys and popular tunes on a theatre organ, with throbbing tremulant on fluty and string ranks, bouncy staccato chords over the pedal bass, and splashes of built-in xylophone, glockenspiel and drum effects, filling a vast ballroom with a lush, swirling sound.
exemplars: Reginald Dixon at the Blackpool Tower Ballroom Wurlitzer

items.name: Glee and catch (Georgian English club part-song)
items.lineage: Unaccompanied part-songs for men's voices sung in London gentlemen's clubs and taverns. The catch, a comic and often bawdy round, flourished from the Restoration, when Henry Purcell wrote dozens, and the glee, a short harmonised song for three or more solo voices, flourished from the founding of the Noblemen and Gentlemen's Catch Club in 1761 into the nineteenth century, with Samuel Webbe among its leading composers; the Glee Club and many provincial glee clubs followed.
items.description: Three or four solo men's voices, often including a high male alto, sing unaccompanied in clean, blended harmony; glees move through contrasting chordal and imitative sections, while catches are rounds whose interlocking entries create hidden puns and comic double meanings.
exemplars: Noblemen and Gentlemen's Catch Club repertoire

items.name: Shirei Eretz Yisrael (Hebrew songs of the Land of Israel)
items.lineage: Hebrew-language song repertoire created from the 1920s through the 1950s in the Jewish settlements of Mandate Palestine and early Israel, much of it written by composers such as Mordechai Zeira, Nahum Nardi and Yedidya Admon for the pioneer (halutz) movement, kibbutz festivals, youth movements and shira b'tzibur community-singing evenings. Its melodies drew on Eastern European Jewish and Russian song, hora dance tunes and Yemenite and Arab modal inflections, and the songs spread through songbooks, radio and accordion-led group singing before Hed Arzi and Kol Israel recordings fixed many of them on disc.
items.description: Strophic Hebrew songs with clear syllabic melodies, often in minor or modal keys with a hora dance lilt, sung by a solo voice or a singing crowd over accordion, piano or guitar chords.
exemplars: Theodore Bikel, Folk Songs of Israel (Elektra, 1955)

items.name: Lehakot tzva'iyot (Israeli army entertainment troupes)
items.lineage: Entertainment troupes of the Israel Defense Forces, beginning with the Nahal troupe founded in 1950 and followed by the Central Command, Northern Command, Navy and other unit troupes, in which conscript singers performed songs, sketches and choreographed numbers for soldiers and civilian audiences. Songwriters including Naomi Shemer and Yair Rosenblum wrote for them, their LPs on Hed Arzi and CBS Israel carried the songs to radio from the 1950s to the 1970s, and many Israeli popular singers began their careers in them.
