items.description: Massed young voices sing bright, tightly arranged unison and harmony refrains and trade lines with soloists over accordion, guitar, piano, bass and light drums, in marching, ballad and comic-song numbers.
exemplars: Lehakat HaNahal (Nahal troupe) LPs on Hed Arzi
Central Command and Navy troupe recordings on Hed Arzi and CBS Israel

items.name: Shirat nashim (Yemenite Jewish women's song)
items.lineage: Judeo-Arabic songs of Yemenite Jewish women, who were not taught the Hebrew liturgy of the men and kept their own oral repertoire for the henna night before a wedding, the wedding itself, births and circumcisions and daily work. A woman singer or a pair of singers leads songs on love, the bride and groom, family and current events while beating a tin can or a copper tray, which the credited auxiliary percussion card stands for. The practice continued among Yemenite Jews in Israel after the 1949-50 migration.
items.description: Women's voices sing short, repeating modal phrases in alternation and answer one another, ornamenting the line over a steady, rattling beat struck on a tin can or metal tray.
exemplars: National Sound Archive (National Library of Israel) field recordings of Yemenite Jewish women's song
Jewish Music Research Centre (Hebrew University) documentation

items.name: Abayudaya music (Ugandan Jewish song)
items.lineage: Liturgical and communal song of the Abayudaya, the Jewish community founded around 1919 by Semei Kakungulu near Mbale in eastern Uganda. Hebrew prayers, psalms and Sabbath songs are sung to locally composed melodies and in Luganda translation, in call-and-response and choral harmony, often with acoustic guitar and drums; the acoustic membrane drum card stands for the local hand drums.
items.description: A leader's voice calls and the congregation answers in warm, close choral harmony over strummed guitar patterns and hand-drum rhythm, in steady, cyclic song forms.
exemplars: Smithsonian Folkways SFW 40504, Abayudaya: Music from the Jewish People of Uganda (2003)

items.name: Maftirim (Ottoman Sephardic hymnody in makam)
items.lineage: Paraliturgical Hebrew hymns sung by male choirs of the Sephardic congregations of Edirne, Istanbul, Izmir and other Ottoman cities, a practice traced to seventeenth-century Edirne, where the choirs sang suites of these poems before the Sabbath morning service. The hymns were set in the makam and usul of Ottoman court and Mevlevi music, often to existing compositions, and grouped into suites resembling the Ottoman fasıl; the repertoire was gathered in printed song collections, recordings of the last Edirne singers and the Sephardic Center of Istanbul's collection preserve it, and a maftirim choir still sings in Istanbul.
items.description: Male voices sing Hebrew hymns in unison through long, ornamented makam melodies, alternating free-rhythm solo passages with measured choral sections in the manner of an Ottoman vocal suite.
exemplars: Ottoman Hebrew Sacred Songs (Jewish Music Research Centre), sung by Samuel Benaroya of the Edirne maftirim choir
Sephardic Center of Istanbul maftirim recording collection
Edwin Seroussi documentation of the Edirne and Istanbul maftirim corpus

items.name: Francarabe (Judeo-Arabic popular song of the Maghreb)
items.lineage: North African urban popular song of Algeria and Tunisia recorded from the 1920s into the 1960s, first on Gramophone, Pathé and Baidaphon 78s and later for radio and LP, mixing Arabic and French lyrics and setting hawzi, chaabi and Andalusi-derived melodies to tango, paso doble, rumba and foxtrot rhythms. Many of its leading singers were Algerian and Tunisian Jews who carried the repertoire to Paris after independence; the fiddle card stands for the violin, the hand drum card for the derbouka goblet drum and the credited frame drums card for the jingled tar.
items.description: A crooning lead voice slides between Arabic and French over oud, violin and piano, ornamenting modal melodies while goblet drum and frame drum lay down tango, rumba and foxtrot rhythms.

items.name: Spanish and Portuguese synagogue music (Western Sephardic rite)
items.lineage: Liturgical music of the Western Sephardic congregations founded by former conversos in Amsterdam, London, Hamburg, Curaçao and New York from the seventeenth century, sung in Hebrew by a hazzan and congregation to a melodic tradition passed down within these communities. Amsterdam's Portuguese Synagogue (the Esnoga, 1675) and London's Bevis Marks (1701) maintain the chant alongside a male choir that sings composed hymns and settings unaccompanied, largely in major and minor keys.
items.description: A cantor's measured Hebrew chant alternates with congregational responses and a male choir singing stately, hymn-like melodies in major and minor keys, unaccompanied in a large resonant sanctuary.
exemplars: Portuguese Synagogue of Amsterdam choir recordings
Jewish Music Research Centre studies by Edwin Seroussi

items.name: Ashkenazi choral synagogue music (Sulzer-Lewandowski school)
items.lineage: Choral liturgy of the nineteenth-century Central European synagogue, shaped by Salomon Sulzer, cantor of the Vienna Stadttempel from 1826 and compiler of Schir Zion, and by Louis Lewandowski, music director of Berlin's synagogues, whose Kol Rinnah and Todah W'simrah set the service for cantor, four-part choir and, in Reform congregations, organ. Their harmonized settings of the traditional prayer modes spread through the choral synagogues of Germany, Austria and Eastern Europe and remain in use in Ashkenazi congregations worldwide.
items.description: A cantor's solo prayer lines lead and answer a four-part choir singing hymn-like harmonized settings of the old prayer modes in sustained, balanced chords that fill a large reverberant sanctuary.
exemplars: Milken Archive of Jewish Music recordings

items.name: Babylonian Jewish liturgy and pizmonim (Iraqi Jewish rite)
items.lineage: Synagogue chant and paraliturgical song of the Arabic-speaking Jews of Baghdad and other Iraqi cities, whose rite follows the Babylonian tradition and whose cantors set prayers and Hebrew pizmonim hymns in the maqamat of Iraqi art music, a repertoire many Jewish musicians also played in Baghdad's secular chalghi ensembles. A. Z. Idelsohn transcribed it in the second volume of his Thesaurus of Hebrew Oriental Melodies, and it continued in Israeli congregations after the community's emigration in 1950-51.
items.description: A cantor's ornamented Hebrew chant moves through maqam melodic paths with quarter-tone inflections, answered by the men of the congregation singing hymn refrains in unison.
exemplars: A. Z. Idelsohn, Thesaurus of Hebrew Oriental Melodies, vol. 2 (Babylonian Jews)
National Sound Archive (National Library of Israel) recordings of Iraqi Jewish liturgy

items.name: Ghetto and partisan songs (Yiddish songs of the Holocaust)
items.lineage: Songs written and sung by Eastern European Jews in the ghettos, camps and partisan units of the Nazi occupation, mostly in Yiddish and often set to existing folk, theatre or Soviet melodies, ranging from lullabies and laments to satirical street songs and resistance anthems such as Hirsh Glik's Zog nit keyn mol from the Vilna ghetto. Shmerke Kaczerginski, Moshe Beregovski and other collectors gathered the repertoire from survivors from 1944 onward, and it is still sung at memorial gatherings.
items.description: A single unaccompanied voice sings strophic Yiddish songs to minor-key folk and march melodies, ranging from hushed lullaby and lament to defiant marching refrains.
exemplars: ORT Music and the Holocaust archive

items.name: New Jewish School (Society for Jewish Folk Music art music)
items.lineage: Art-music movement launched by the Society for Jewish Folk Music, founded in St Petersburg in 1908, whose composers, among them Joel Engel, Joseph Achron, Mikhail Gnesin, Lazare Saminsky and Moshe Milner, arranged and transformed Ashkenazi folk song, cantorial modes and Hasidic melody into art songs, piano pieces and chamber works in a late-Romantic idiom. The touring Zimro chamber ensemble spread the repertoire abroad, and many of the composers emigrated to Palestine, Western Europe and the United States in the 1920s.
items.description: Lyrical violin, clarinet and voice lines spin augmented-second modes and cantorial-style ornaments over rich late-Romantic piano harmony, in concise art songs and chamber pieces.
exemplars: Milken Archive of Jewish Music recordings
Joseph Achron, Hebrew Melody (violin and piano)

items.name: Badkhones (Yiddish wedding-jester recitation)
items.lineage: The art of the badkhn, the Eastern European Ashkenazi wedding entertainer who improvised rhymed Yiddish verses at each stage of a traditional wedding, from the moralizing kale bazetsn that brought the bride to tears before the veiling to the jests and gift announcements at the feast, chanted over the sustained accompaniment of the klezmer band. Nineteenth-century badkhonim such as Elyokum Zunser of Vilna published their verses as songs, early Yiddish 78s preserved wedding routines, and the role continues at Hasidic weddings.
items.description: A half-sung, half-declaimed voice rhymes and chants in free rhythm, rising to sobbing cadences, while fiddle and clarinet hold sustained chords and answer each verse with mournful modal phrases.
exemplars: Early Yiddish 78 rpm recordings of badkhn wedding routines (kale bazetsn)

items.name: Ashkenazi Torah cantillation (leyning)
items.lineage: Chanted public reading of the Hebrew Bible in Ashkenazi synagogues, in which the reader (baal koreh) sings each word to the melodic motif of its ta'amei ha-mikra accent sign, with distinct motif sets for the Torah, the haftarah, the scrolls of Esther, Lamentations and the festival megillot, and the High Holy Days. The system is passed on orally and through trope charts in bar and bat mitzvah training, and its melodies differ from the Sephardi, Yemenite and other reading traditions.
items.description: One voice chants Hebrew scripture in free speech rhythm, each phrase built from short recurring melodic motifs whose rising and falling cadences mark the structure of the verse.
exemplars: A. Z. Idelsohn, Thesaurus of Hebrew Oriental Melodies
Jewish Music Research Centre comparative Torah-reading recordings

items.name: Vlach Roma song (loki and khelimaski djili)
items.lineage: Vocal music of the Vlach (Oláh) Roma of Hungary and neighbouring countries, Romani-speaking Lovari, Kalderash and related groups who, unlike the Romungro restaurant musicians, made music largely without instruments. Slow songs (loki djili) are sung solo or by a group in free rhythm, while dance songs (khelimaski djili) are carried by voices, an oral bass of rhythmic vocables (szájbőgő), finger snaps and the beating of a water can and spoons; the vocal percussion card stands for the oral bass and the credited auxiliary percussion card for the can. Rudolf Víg and Katalin Kovalcsik documented the repertoire, and Kalyi Jag and Ando Drom brought it to stage and studio from the late 1970s.
items.description: Free-rhythm slow songs pour out in ornamented, sobbing solo lines, while dance songs drive forward on group voices, a buzzing mouth-made bass, finger snaps and the clatter of a beaten can and spoons.
exemplars: Hungaroton LP Gypsy Folk Songs from Hungary (1976)

items.name: Servika Roma song (Slovak Romani song)
items.lineage: Song repertoire of the Servika Roma, the long-settled Romani communities of Slovakia and of the Czech lands to which many moved after the war, documented from the 1950s above all by Milena Hübschmannová. Slow songs (halgatone gila, from Hungarian hallgató, 'for listening') voice grief, poverty and longing in free, ornamented melody, while csardas dance songs are sung to clapping or to Romani string bands of violin, cimbalom and double bass; Ida Kelarová and Kmeťoband are among the artists who brought the songs to concert and studio. The fiddle card stands for the violin.
items.description: A grieving solo voice stretches slow, ornamented lines in free rhythm, then turns to brisk csardas dance songs over sobbing violin, rippling cimbalom and bowed bass.
exemplars: Museum of Romani Culture (Brno) sound archive

items.name: Ottawa Valley fiddling and step dance (Ontario old-time)
items.lineage: Old-time fiddle and step-dance music of the Ottawa Valley along the Ontario-Quebec border, formed in the lumbering communities of Renfrew County and neighbouring districts where Irish, Scottish and French-Canadian settler traditions mixed. Fiddlers play reels, jigs, clogs and waltzes for the Valley's own style of step dancing, usually backed by piano chording, and the Pembroke Old Time Fiddling and Stepdancing Championship has been its main contest stage since the 1970s. The foot-tap card stands for the step dancer's hard-shoe footwork.
items.description: A driving solo fiddle plays brisk reels, jigs and clogs in steady dance time over chorded piano and strummed guitar, while the dancer's hard-shoe taps add a bright, clattering rhythmic layer on a wooden board.
exemplars: Pembroke Old Time Fiddling and Stepdancing Championship recordings
Canadian Museum of History fiddle field recordings

items.name: Down East old-time fiddling (Canadian Maritime dance-band style)
items.lineage: Canadian old-time dance fiddling spread from the Maritimes by the New Brunswick-born fiddler Don Messer, whose band the Islanders broadcast from Charlottetown radio from 1939, recorded for the Apex label and reached a national audience on CBC radio and on the Halifax-produced CBC television show Don Messer's Jubilee until its cancellation in 1969. The style plays reels, jigs, hornpipes, breakdowns, waltzes and two-steps with a clean, lightly ornamented melody in strict dance tempo over a small band of piano, bass, guitar and drums, and it became a standard of Canadian old-time fiddling and its contests.
items.description: A clean, smooth-bowed fiddle states each tune plainly in strict, bouncy dance tempo, backed by on-the-beat piano chords, a walking upright bass, strummed guitar and light drums in a close, warm dance-band sound.
exemplars: Don Messer and His Islanders (Apex 78s and LPs)
CBC broadcasts of Don Messer's Jubilee

items.name: Prince Edward Island fiddling (Island Scottish and Acadian fiddle)
items.lineage: Community fiddle tradition of Prince Edward Island, played for house parties, square dances, ceilidhs and church picnics, with a Scottish-derived style strongest in the east of the Island, especially Kings County, and an Acadian French style in the Evangeline region of Prince County. Ken Perlman's fieldwork documented both strands and how they differ from neighbouring Cape Breton fiddling, and the Prince Edward Island Fiddlers Society keeps its repertoire of Scottish, Irish and local reels, jigs, strathspeys and marches in community play. Fiddlers commonly keep time with their feet and are accompanied by piano or guitar; the foot-tap card stands for that foot percussion.
items.description: A lilting, lightly ornamented fiddle drives reels, jigs and strathspeys in steady dance time, its bowing accented against chorded piano or guitar while the player's feet thump out the beat on a wooden floor.
exemplars: Ken Perlman's field recordings of Prince Edward Island fiddlers (Rounder)

items.name: Miramichi lumberwoods song (Maritime Anglo-Canadian balladry)
items.lineage: English-language ballad and song tradition of New Brunswick and Nova Scotia, sung in lumber camps, on river drives and at kitchen gatherings, mixing old British broadside and Child ballads with locally made songs about logging deaths, drownings and local events by woods poets such as Larry Gorman and Joe Scott. Louise Manny founded the Miramichi Folksong Festival in 1958, whose singers were recorded for Folkways, and Helen Creighton had collected the Nova Scotia repertoire since 1928.
items.description: A single unaccompanied voice sings long strophic narratives in a plain, speech-like delivery, stretching and shortening phrases freely around the words over modal tunes, with no instrument behind it.
exemplars: Folk Songs of the Miramichi: Lumber and River Songs (Folkways, 1962)
Helen Creighton field recordings, Folk Music from Nova Scotia (Folkways)

items.name: Lange Wies (Old Colony Mennonite long-tune hymn singing)
items.lineage: Slow unison congregational hymn singing of the Old Colony (Altkolonier) Mennonites, Russian-Mennonite settlers who took up the West Reserve of southern Manitoba in the 1870s and later carried the practice to Mexico and South America. Without instruments, part-singing or printed tunes, the congregation sings High German hymns from the Gesangbuch, each line started by Vorsaenger (song leaders), and stretches every syllable over long melodic formulas that have drifted far from the original chorale melodies through oral transmission. Wesley Berg's From Russia with Music (1985) set it beside the separate, notated strand of four-part Ziffern (numeral-notation) choirs in other Russian-Mennonite churches.
items.description: A whole congregation sings in slow unison and octaves, drawing each syllable out over long, slowly turning melodic figures so that a single hymn line spreads into a sustained, swelling wall of plain voices in a wooden meeting house.
exemplars: Mennonite Heritage Archives (Winnipeg) recordings of Old Colony Lange Wies singing

items.name: Zabava (Ukrainian-Canadian prairie dance-band music)
items.lineage: Dance-band music of the Ukrainian communities of the Canadian prairies, rooted in the block settlements of immigrants from Galicia and Bukovyna who arrived from the end of the nineteenth century, and played at weddings, community-hall dances (zabavy) and festivals. Bands mix kolomyika, polka, waltz and hutsulka dance tunes and Ukrainian songs with country and pop, using violin, accordion and tsymbaly (hammered dulcimer) over electric bass, guitar and drum kit, and Winnipeg's V Records was among the labels that issued it on LP. The hammered-dulcimer card stands in for the tsymbaly.
items.description: Fast two-beat kolomyika and polka tunes race along on violin and accordion with the shimmering tremolo of a hammered dulcimer, over a bouncing electric bass, guitar chop and an offbeat-heavy drum kit, alternating with swaying waltzes and sung choruses.
exemplars: V Records (Winnipeg) LPs of Ukrainian-Canadian dance bands

items.name: Musique actuelle (Montreal creative music)
items.lineage: Montreal-centred current of composed and improvised music that took the name musique actuelle in the early 1980s, when the Ambiances Magnetiques label, run by a collective of Montreal musicians, and the Festival International de Musique Actuelle de Victoriaville (FIMAV), both founded in 1983, gave it a label and a stage. Its musicians, among them guitarist Rene Lussier and saxophonist and flutist Jean Derome, combine free improvisation, rock, jazz, Quebec folk song, noise and contemporary composition, with a taste for collage, humour and the French language.
items.description: Jagged electric guitar, saxophone and flute cut between composed riffs, collage-like jump cuts and open free improvisation over shifting bass and drums, with spoken and sung French voices woven into the texture.
exemplars: Ambiances Magnetiques label (Rene Lussier, Jean Derome, Joane Hetu)
Rene Lussier — Le tresor de la langue

items.name: Toronto Jamaican-Canadian soul and reggae
items.lineage: Music of the Jamaican community that grew in Toronto after Canada opened its immigration to the Caribbean in the 1960s, when Kingston musicians including keyboardist Jackie Mittoo and singer Leroy Sibbles settled in the city and worked its clubs and sessions. Local bands mixed rocksteady and reggae rhythms with American soul and funk, a sound gathered on the Light in the Attic reissue Jamaica to Toronto (2006), and from the 1980s bands such as Messenjah made Canadian reggae a recording scene of its own.
items.description: Deep, melodic electric bass and offbeat guitar and organ skanks carry a soul singer over one-drop and funk drum grooves, with tight horn lines punctuating the choruses.
exemplars: Jamaica to Toronto: Soul Funk & Reggae 1967-1974 (Light in the Attic, 2006)
Wayne McGhie & the Sounds of Joy

items.name: Australian convict and colonial ballads (traditional bush song)
items.lineage: Traditional English-language songs of colonial Australia, from transportation and convict ballads such as Jim Jones at Botany Bay and Moreton Bay to bushranger, goldfields, shearing and droving songs, many set to Irish, Scottish and English tunes and handed on orally among bush workers. The goldfields entertainer Charles Thatcher published his songs of the 1850s and 1860s in songsters, and from the 1950s collectors led by John Meredith recorded surviving traditional singers, mostly unaccompanied, in recordings now held by the National Library of Australia; this entry is that sung tradition, not the later bush-band revival.
items.description: A plain, unaccompanied voice tells long strophic stories of transportation, outlawry and bush work over old modal and major tunes, in a direct, speech-inflected delivery with a free sense of time.
exemplars: John Meredith collection of traditional singers (National Library of Australia)
Wattle Records LPs of Australian bush songs (1950s)
A. L. Lloyd Australian song LPs for Topic

items.name: New Zealand colonial folk song (goldfields, whaling and shearing songs)
items.lineage: Songs of European settler life in nineteenth- and early twentieth-century New Zealand, from Otago and West Coast goldfields songs to whaling, shearing, swagging and station songs, often new local words set to British and Irish tunes. Rona Bailey and Herbert Roth's songbook Shanties by the Way (1967) and Neil Colquhoun's Song of a Young Country, a 1971 Kiwi Records double LP followed by a 1972 songbook, gathered the repertoire, and revival singers such as Phil Garland recorded it with acoustic folk accompaniment.
items.description: A plain storytelling voice sings strophic verses of gold-digging, whaling and shearing life over strummed guitar and the reedy chords of a concertina, with simple choruses meant for joining in.
exemplars: Song of a Young Country (Neil Colquhoun, Kiwi Records double LP, 1971)
Rona Bailey and Herbert Roth, Shanties by the Way (1967 songbook)

items.name: Xpressway noise underground (Dunedin lo-fi experimental rock)
items.lineage: Experimental rock underground of Dunedin and nearby Port Chalmers in the late 1980s and early 1990s, named after the Xpressway cassette label that Bruce Russell of The Dead C ran from 1988 to 1993. Its musicians, among them The Dead C, Alastair Galbraith, Peter Jefferies and Gate, recorded cheaply on cassette and four-track and pushed the local guitar-pop lineage toward improvised noise, drones and feedback, reaching listeners abroad through Flying Nun and the US label Siltbreeze.
items.description: Two electric guitars grind out droning, feedback-laden noise and slow-forming riffs over loose, shambling drums, with buried, murmured vocals, all smeared by the saturation and hiss of home cassette recording.

items.name: Asian American creative jazz (Asian Improv movement)
items.lineage: Movement of Asian American jazz musicians centred in the San Francisco Bay Area from the early 1980s, who joined post-bop and free jazz with Chinese and Japanese melodies and instruments and with themes of Asian American history and activism. The band United Front recorded for RPM in 1981, and pianist Jon Jang and saxophonist Francis Wong founded Asian Improv Records in 1987, whose catalogue includes pianist Glenn Horiuchi and bassist Mark Izu; drummer Anthony Brown led the Asian American Orchestra.
items.description: Saxophone and piano trade fiery post-bop and free solos over acoustic bass and drums, while an erhu sings pentatonic melodies and booming taiko drums break in, in long suite-like pieces that move from open improvisation to composed themes.
exemplars: Asian Improv Records (Jon Jang, Francis Wong, Glenn Horiuchi)

items.name: Kachi-kachi (Puerto Rican music of Hawaii)
items.lineage: Music of the Puerto Rican community of Hawaii, descended from the laborers recruited to the islands' sugar plantations who arrived at the start of the twentieth century. Derived from the jibaro music of rural Puerto Rico, it kept seis, aguinaldo and dance repertoire while developing its own local style, known in the islands as kachi-kachi (cachi-cachi), played on cuatro, six-string guitar and gueiro at house parties, dances and community celebrations; ethnomusicologist Ted Solis documented how it diverged from music on the home island.
items.description: A bright cuatro picks quick melodic runs over strummed guitar and a steady scraped gueiro, driving brisk, often very fast dance tunes under a singer's ringing verses.
exemplars: Ted Solis field recordings of Puerto Rican music in Hawaii

items.name: Rock beur (Franco-Maghrebi rock of the 1980s)
items.lineage: French rock of the 1980s made by the children of North African immigrants, above all around Lyon, where the band Carte de Sejour, fronted by Rachid Taha, formed at the start of the decade and sang in Arabic and French over punk and new-wave rock laced with North African melody. Its 1986 version of Charles Trenet's Douce France, released amid the anti-racist movement of the period, became an emblem of the beur generation.
items.description: Wiry electric guitar riffs bend through Arabic-sounding modal turns over a tight new-wave bass and drum backbeat, while a raw lead voice switches between Arabic and French, half sung and half shouted.

items.name: Rai'n'B (French rai-R&B crossover)
items.lineage: French crossover of the 2000s in which singers and producers of Maghrebi heritage set rai vocals, Arabic melisma and North African rhythms against contemporary R&B and hip-hop production, often pairing a rai singer with French R&B singers and rappers. The producers Kore and Skalp launched the Rai'n'B Fever compilation series in 2004, which gave the style its name and its place in the French charts.
items.description: A melismatic, ornamented lead voice in Arabic trades verses with smooth French R&B vocals and rap over programmed booming kick, crisp snares and synth pads, with looped North African percussion patterns under polished choruses.

items.name: Rodriguan accordion dances (kotis, laval, polka, mazok)
items.lineage: On the island of Rodrigues the European couple and set dances - the kotis (schottische), polka, waltz, mazok (mazurka), quadrille and the local laval - survive as a living repertoire played on the diatonic button accordion, which the island's music is almost entirely built on, over drum and triangle; it is kept distinct from the island's sega tambour. The general accordion card stands in for the two-row button accordion.
items.description: A bright accordion plays square-cut waltz, polka and schottische tunes over a steady drum beat, with a triangle marking the dance pulse.
exemplars: Île Rodrigues vol. 2: Accordéon (Takamba field recordings, 1996-1998; CREM-CNRS archive)
Sakili, with Rodriguan accordionist Ricardo Legentil - Creole Sounds from the Indian Ocean

items.name: Raizal music (San Andrés and Providencia)
items.lineage: The Raizal people, the English-Creole-speaking Protestant islanders of San Andrés, Providencia and Santa Catalina, keep a string-band dance music of polka, mazurka, waltz and schottische alongside mento and calypso, played by the conjunto típico of mandolin, guitar, fiddle, the one-string washtub bass (tub bass or tinajo), horse-jawbone rattle and maracas, next to the islands' Baptist hymn singing. The tea-chest-bass card stands in for the washtub bass.
items.description: Mandolin and fiddle trade bright dance tunes over strummed guitar, a thudding one-string tub bass and a rattling jawbone, moving between lilting waltzes, brisk polkas and swaying calypso.
exemplars: Elkin Robinson (Providencia) - Putumayo-released island folk with washtub bass and jawbone
